Part 1

Concept

What is Java?

Java is a strongly typed, object-oriented, platform-independent, general-purpose programming language designed to minimize implementation dependencies. It follows the principle of "Write Once, Run Anywhere" (WORA) — Java source code is compiled into an intermediate bytecode format that the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) executes on any platform.

Java is not merely a language — it is a complete ecosystem encompassing:

  • A language specification (syntax, semantics, type system)
  • A virtual machine (JVM) that executes bytecode
  • A standard library (Java SE API) covering I/O, networking, collections, concurrency, and more
  • A toolchain (javac, jar, jshell, javadoc, jlink, jpackage)
  • A community process (JCP/JEP) that governs evolution

Core Language Characteristics

Characteristic Description
Object-Oriented Everything (except primitives) is an object
Platform-Independent Bytecode runs on any JVM
Strongly Typed All variables must be declared with a type
Automatic Memory Management Garbage Collector reclaims unused memory
Multithreaded Built-in thread model and concurrency APIs
Distributed Designed with network computing in mind
Secure Bytecode verifier, SecurityManager, sandboxing
Robust Eliminates pointers, strong exception handling
Part 2

History

Java Timeline: 1991–2025

1991 ────── Sun Microsystems starts "Project Green" (James Gosling)
            Language named "Oak" — designed for set-top boxes

1995 ────── Java 1.0 released publicly
            "Write Once, Run Anywhere" coined
            Netscape Navigator adds Java applet support

1996 ────── JDK 1.0 — First stable release
            AWT, applets, basic I/O

1997 ────── JDK 1.1 — JDBC, RMI, Inner Classes, JavaBeans

1998 ────── J2SE 1.2 "Playground" — Collections Framework, Swing, JIT compiler

1999 ────── Java 2 Platform split: J2SE, J2EE, J2ME

2000 ────── J2SE 1.3 — HotSpot JVM default, JNDI, RMI over IIOP

2002 ────── J2SE 1.4 — assert, NIO, regex, XML parsing (JAXP)

2004 ────── J2SE 5.0 (1.5) — Generics, Annotations, Enums,
            Autoboxing, Varargs, Enhanced for-loop (MAJOR release)

2006 ────── Java SE 6 — Scripting API, JDBC 4.0, JAX-WS
            Sun open-sources Java under GPL (OpenJDK)

2009 ────── Oracle acquires Sun Microsystems ($7.4B)

2011 ────── Java SE 7 — try-with-resources, NIO.2, Fork/Join,
            Diamond operator, String in switch

2014 ────── Java SE 8 (LTS) — Lambda expressions, Streams API,
            Optional, default methods, new Date/Time API
            (Most impactful release since Java 5)

2017 ────── Java SE 9 — Module System (Project Jigsaw), JShell,
            reactive streams (Flow API)
            6-month release cadence begins

2018 ────── Java SE 10 — Local variable type inference (var)
            Java SE 11 (LTS) — HTTP Client, TLS 1.3,
            Oracle JDK no longer free for production

2019 ────── Java SE 12, 13 — Switch expressions (preview), text blocks

2020 ────── Java SE 14, 15 — Records (preview), sealed classes (preview),
            helpful NullPointerExceptions

2021 ────── Java SE 16, 17 (LTS) — Records, sealed classes, pattern
            matching for instanceof, strong encapsulation of JDK internals

2022 ────── Java SE 18, 19 — Virtual threads (preview, Project Loom),
            structured concurrency, pattern matching for switch

2023 ────── Java SE 20, 21 (LTS) — Virtual threads GA, sequenced
            collections, record patterns, string templates (preview)

2024 ────── Java SE 22, 23 — Unnamed patterns, stream gatherers,
            structured concurrency (2nd preview), class-file API

2025 ────── Java SE 24, 25 (LTS expected) — AOT compilation improvements,
            Project Valhalla value types (preview), Leyden milestones

Part 3

Problem Statement

Problems Java Was Designed to Solve

1. Platform Fragmentation (The Primary Problem)

Before Java, deploying software across platforms was a nightmare:

Pre-Java Reality:
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ C/C++ Application                                    │
│                                                      │
│  Source.c  ──[compile for Windows]──► Windows .exe  │
│  Source.c  ──[compile for Linux]────► Linux binary  │
│  Source.c  ──[compile for macOS]────► macOS binary  │
│  Source.c  ──[compile for Solaris]──► Solaris binary│
│                                                      │
│  Problem: Different OS APIs, different compilers,   │
│  different pointer sizes, different byte order,     │
│  different calling conventions, undefined behavior  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Java Solution (WORA):
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Java Application                                     │
│                                                      │
│  Source.java ──[javac]──► Bytecode (.class)         │
│                                  │                  │
│              ┌───────────────────┼───────────────┐  │
│              ▼                   ▼               ▼  │
│         JVM(Windows)      JVM(Linux)      JVM(macOS)│
│              │                   │               │  │
│         Windows App         Linux App       macOS App│
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

2. Memory Safety Problems (C/C++ Pain Points)

Problem C/C++ Java Solution
Buffer overflow Manual bounds checking required Array bounds checked at runtime
Dangling pointers Manual memory management No raw pointers; references only
Memory leaks malloc/free must be balanced Garbage Collector manages deallocation
Null dereference Segfault — hard to debug NullPointerException with stack trace
Double free Undefined behavior, security vuln GC tracks object lifecycle
Use after free Heap corruption GC prevents premature collection

3. Security Problems

Early networked applications (browser applets, downloaded code) required:

  • Code verification before execution (bytecode verifier)
  • Sandboxing of untrusted code (SecurityManager — now deprecated in favor of OS-level sandboxing)
  • No direct memory access — cannot read arbitrary memory addresses
  • Class loader isolation — different class loaders for different trust levels

4. Developer Productivity Problems

  • C++ had no standard library for common tasks (collections, networking, I/O)
  • Header files, makefiles, and linkers added build complexity
  • Object-oriented features in C++ were inconsistent and complex (multiple inheritance, templates)
  • Java provided a rich standard library from day one
Part 4

Why Java? Design Philosophy

James Gosling's Design Goals

Java was explicitly designed by removing complexity from C++. The core philosophy was:

> "Java is C++ without the guns, knives, and clubs." — James Gosling

Features Deliberately Removed from C++

C++ Feature Reason Removed in Java Java Alternative
Pointers/pointer arithmetic Memory safety, security Object references
Multiple inheritance of classes Diamond problem, complexity Single class inheritance + interfaces
Operator overloading Readability, predictability Well-named methods
Header files Separate compilation model Unified .java source files
Preprocessor/macros Hidden complexity, debugging Annotations, constants
Global functions OOP purity Static methods in classes
Unsigned integers Platform-dependent behavior All integers are signed
Destructor/RAII Requires manual memory model Garbage Collection + try-with-resources
Goto statement Spaghetti code Labeled break/continue
Stack-allocated objects Complex lifetime management All objects on heap
Templates (initially) Complexity Generics added in Java 5

Java's Design Principles

  1. Simplicity — Should be familiar to C/C++ developers with fewer sharp edges
  2. Object-Oriented — Everything is organized around objects and classes
  3. Distributed — Built-in support for TCP/IP networking, RMI
  4. Interpreted + Compiled — Bytecode interpreted by JVM, JIT-compiled to native
  5. Robust — Strong type checking, exception handling, no raw memory access
  6. Secure — Bytecode verification, class loader hierarchy, no pointer arithmetic
  7. Architecture-neutral — Bytecode works on any processor architecture
  8. Portable — Primitive type sizes are fixed (int is always 32 bits)
  9. High-performance — JIT compilation closes the gap with native code
  10. Multithreaded — First-class thread support built into the language
  11. Dynamic — Runtime class loading, reflection, late binding

Internal Working

The Java Compile-Load-Run Model

┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              JAVA EXECUTION PIPELINE                              │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

STEP 1: SOURCE CODE
┌─────────────────┐
│  HelloWorld.java│
│  (Human-readable│
│   source code)  │
└────────┬────────┘
         │
         ▼
STEP 2: COMPILATION (javac)
┌─────────────────┐
│  Java Compiler  │  Lexical Analysis → Parsing → Semantic Analysis
│  (javac)        │  → Bytecode Generation
└────────┬────────┘
         │  Produces platform-neutral bytecode
         ▼
STEP 3: BYTECODE
┌─────────────────┐
│ HelloWorld.class│  Stack-based instruction set (~200 opcodes)
│ (Bytecode)      │  e.g., iconst_5, iadd, invokevirtual, astore
└────────┬────────┘
         │
         ▼
STEP 4: CLASS LOADING (ClassLoader)
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Bootstrap ClassLoader  → loads rt.jar (core Java)  │
│  Platform ClassLoader   → loads JDK modules         │
│  Application ClassLoader→ loads your classpath      │
│                                                     │
│  Phases: Loading → Linking → Initialization         │
│    Linking = Verification + Preparation + Resolution│
└────────┬────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         │
         ▼
STEP 5: BYTECODE VERIFICATION
┌─────────────────┐
│  Bytecode       │  Ensures type safety, no stack overflow,
│  Verifier       │  valid control flow, correct method signatures
└────────┬────────┘
         │
         ▼
STEP 6: JVM EXECUTION
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                  JVM RUNTIME ENGINE                  │
│                                                      │
│  ┌───────────────┐     ┌────────────────────────┐    │
│  │  Interpreter  │────►│  JIT Compiler          │    │
│  │  (slow start) │     │  (C1: client compiler) │    │
│  └───────────────┘     │  (C2: server compiler) │    │
│                         │  (Graal: optional)     │    │
│                         └────────────────────────┘    │
│                                │                     │
│                         ┌──────▼──────┐              │
│                         │  Native     │              │
│                         │  Machine    │              │
│                         │  Code       │              │
│                         └─────────────┘              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         │
         ▼
STEP 7: OS EXECUTION
┌─────────────────┐
│  Operating      │  System calls, hardware I/O
│  System         │  Process/thread management
└─────────────────┘

Bytecode Example

// Source
int a = 5 + 3;

// Equivalent bytecode
iconst_5        // push 5 onto operand stack
iconst_3        // push 3 onto operand stack
iadd            // pop two ints, add, push result (8)
istore_1        // pop and store in local variable slot 1

Stack Frame Contents

Each method invocation creates a stack frame containing:

Component Description
Local Variable Array Method parameters + local variables (index 0 = this for instance methods)
Operand Stack Working area for bytecode instructions (push/pop)
Frame Data Reference to constant pool, return address, exception table
Part 8

Execution Flow

HelloWorld Execution Trace

public class HelloWorld {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Hello, World!");
    }
}

Step-by-step execution trace:

1. OS starts JVM process
   └─ java HelloWorld

2. Bootstrap ClassLoader loads core classes
   └─ java.lang.Object, java.lang.String, java.lang.System, ...

3. Application ClassLoader loads HelloWorld.class
   └─ Reads HelloWorld.class from filesystem/classpath
   └─ Bytecode verification passes
   └─ Class initialized (no static initializers here)

4. JVM finds main(String[]) entry point
   └─ Method signature: public static void main([Ljava/lang/String;)V

5. New Thread ("main" thread) starts
   └─ Stack frame created for main()
   └─ Local variable slot 0 = args (empty String[])

6. Bytecode execution of main():
   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ Bytecode (disassembled with javap -c HelloWorld):       │
   │                                                         │
   │  0: getstatic     #7  // System.out (PrintStream)       │
   │     → Pushes System.out reference onto operand stack    │
   │                                                         │
   │  3: ldc           #13 // String "Hello, World!"         │
   │     → Pushes String constant onto operand stack         │
   │                                                         │
   │  5: invokevirtual #15 // PrintStream.println(String)    │
   │     → Pops String + PrintStream, calls println()        │
   │     → New stack frame created for println()             │
   │     → Native call to OS write() system call             │
   │     → Output written to stdout file descriptor          │
   │     → Stack frame for println() popped                  │
   │                                                         │
   │  8: return                                              │
   │     → main() stack frame popped                         │
   │     → main thread exits                                 │
   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

7. JVM detects all non-daemon threads have terminated
   └─ Shutdown hooks run
   └─ Finalizers run (if any)
   └─ JVM process exits with code 0
Part 9

Performance

JIT Compilation and the Warmup Curve

Java's performance model is fundamentally different from ahead-of-time (AOT) compiled languages. The JVM starts by interpreting bytecode and progressively compiles hot code paths to native machine code.

JAVA APPLICATION THROUGHPUT OVER TIME

Requests/sec
     ▲
 High│                              ┌─────────────────────────
     │                           ╱─┘  Peak throughput
     │                        ╱─┘     (JIT-compiled + optimized)
     │                     ╱─┘
     │                  ╱─┘
     │              ╱──┘
 Med │          ╱──┘  C1 compiled (client compiler)
     │       ╱─┘      ~1000-10000 invocations
     │    ╱─┘
     │  ╱┘  Interpreted (very slow)
 Low │╱    first few thousand invocations
     └─────────────────────────────────────────────────► Time
       Start  1s    5s    30s   2min   5min+
              │      │     │
              │      │     └── C2 (server compiler) kicks in
              │      └──────── Profile-guided optimizations
              └─────────────── Interpreter phase

JIT Compilation Tiers (Tiered Compilation — Java 7+)

Tier Compiler Threshold Optimizations Use Case
0 Interpreter Always None — pure bytecode interpretation Cold code / startup
1 C1 (simple) ~100 invocations Basic inlining, no profiling Simple, short methods
2 C1 (profiled) ~1,500 invocations Profiling counters added Moderate frequency
3 C1 (full) ~5,000 invocations Full C1 with all profiling Methods awaiting C2
4 C2 (server) ~10,000-40,000 Aggressive opts: inlining, escape analysis, loop unrolling, dead code elimination Hot paths

Key JIT Optimizations

  • Method Inlining: Replaces method calls with the method body — removes call overhead, enables further optimization
  • Escape Analysis: If an object doesn't escape a method, it can be allocated on the stack (or scalar-replaced)
  • Loop Unrolling: Reduces branch overhead by repeating loop body
  • Dead Code Elimination: Removes code paths never executed
  • Lock Elision: Removes synchronization on objects that can't escape
  • Intrinsics: Replaces Java library methods with hand-optimized CPU-specific instructions (e.g., String.indexOf, Math.sqrt, Arrays.copyOf)

Java vs Native Performance Reality

Scenario Java Performance Notes
Long-running server apps 95-105% of C++ JIT catches up and can exceed C++ via profile-guided opts
Startup (cold) 5-50x slower than Go/Rust GraalVM native-image solves this
Memory overhead 2-5x more than C Object headers, GC metadata, JVM overhead
GC pauses 0ms–200ms (tunable) ZGC/Shenandoah deliver sub-millisecond pauses
Throughput (warm) Comparable to C++ JIT with profile info often beats static compilation

Time Complexity of Core Java Operations

Operation Data Structure Time Complexity Notes
ArrayList.get(i) ArrayList O(1) Direct array access
ArrayList.add(e) ArrayList O(1) amortized O(n) on resize
ArrayList.remove(i) ArrayList O(n) Shifts elements
LinkedList.get(i) LinkedList O(n) Traversal required

PriorityQueue.offer/poll PriorityQueue O(log n) Binary heap
Arrays.sort(int[]) Primitive array O(n log n) Dual-pivot quicksort
Collections.sort(List) Object List O(n log n) TimSort
String.charAt(i) String O(1) Backed by char[]
String.substring(i,j) String O(n) Creates new String
String.indexOf String O(n·m) Naive; JIT may use SIMD
StringBuilder.append StringBuilder O(1) amortized Like ArrayList
ConcurrentHashMap.get/put ConcurrentHashMap O(1) average Lock-striped segments

JVM Operation Costs (Approximate, Tuning Reference)

Operation Approximate Cost Notes
Method call (virtual) ~1-5 ns (JIT-inlined: ~0) Depends on inline cache state
Object allocation ~5-20 ns TLAB bump pointer; GC overhead separate
null check ~0.1-1 ns CPU branch prediction handles well
Synchronized block (uncontended) ~5-20 ns Biased locking (removed Java 17+)
Synchronized block (contended) ~500 ns–10 µs OS mutex + context switch
System.out.println ~100 µs–1 ms Synchronized I/O — never in hot paths
GC minor collection ~1-100 ms Stop-the-world for Young Gen
GC major collection (G1) ~10-500 ms Concurrent + STW phases

Space Complexity

Memory Overhead of Java Objects

Object Header (on 64-bit JVM, CompressedOops enabled):
┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Mark Word (8 bytes)                                  │
│  → hash code, GC age, lock state, monitor pointer    │
├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Class Pointer (4 bytes with CompressedOops)          │
│  → points to class metadata in Metaspace             │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Total minimum header: 12 bytes (+ 4 bytes padding = 16 bytes)

Java Collection Memory Comparison

Collection Empty Size Per-Element Overhead Notes
Object[] (array) 16 bytes + 4*n 4 bytes (reference) Most compact
ArrayList<T> ~88 bytes 4 bytes/element + header Backed by Object[]
LinkedList<T> ~48 bytes ~40 bytes/element Node = obj header + 3 refs
HashMap<K,V> ~384 bytes ~80 bytes/entry Entry = header + hash + key + value + next
TreeMap<K,V> ~48 bytes ~64 bytes/entry Entry = header + 5 fields
HashSet<T> ~384 bytes ~80 bytes/element Backed by HashMap
String (16 chars) ~56 bytes varies Header + char[] + coder field

Space Complexity of Common Algorithms in Java

Algorithm / Operation Space Complexity Notes
Recursive DFS (depth d) O(d) stack frames Risk of StackOverflowError
Iterative BFS O(w) where w = max width Queue holds frontier nodes
Merge Sort O(n) auxiliary Java's TimSort is O(n)
Quick Sort (in-place) O(log n) stack Dual-pivot quicksort used for primitives
Stream pipeline O(1) to O(n) Lazy evaluation; terminal ops may buffer
String.split(regex) O(n) Returns String[]
Collections.sort() O(n) TimSort uses temp array

Example 2: Greeting (Parameters, StringBuilder, Varargs)

/**
 * Demonstrates: method parameters, String handling, varargs,
 * conditional expressions, StringBuilder for efficient concatenation.
 */
public class Greeting {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(greet("Alice"));
        System.out.println(greet("Bob", "Good evening"));
        System.out.println(greetAll("Morning", "Alice", "Bob", "Carol"));
    }

    /**
     * Greets a person with a default "Hello" prefix.
     */
    public static String greet(String name) {
        return greet(name, "Hello");
    }

    /**
     * Greets a person with a custom prefix.
     * Uses String.format for readable concatenation.
     */
    public static String greet(String name, String prefix) {
        if (name == null || name.isBlank()) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Name must not be blank");
        }
        return String.format("%s, %s!", prefix, name);
    }

    /**
     * Greets multiple people using varargs.
     * Demonstrates StringBuilder efficiency over String concatenation in loops.
     */
    public static String greetAll(String prefix, String... names) {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        for (int i = 0; i < names.length; i++) {
            sb.append(prefix).append(", ").append(names[i]).append("!");
            if (i < names.length - 1) {
                sb.append("\n");
            }
        }
        return sb.toString();
    }
}

Output:

Hello, Alice!
Good evening, Bob!
Morning, Alice!
Morning, Bob!
Morning, Carol!

Example 3: ObjectCreationDemo

/**
 * Demonstrates: class definition, constructors, instance fields,
 * instance methods, toString, equals, hashCode, static factory methods.
 */
public class ObjectCreationDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Stack holds reference; object lives on heap
        Person person1 = new Person("Alice", 30);
        Person person2 = Person.of("Bob", 25);         // Static factory
        Person person3 = new Person("Alice", 30);

        System.out.println(person1);                    // toString()
        System.out.println(person2);

        // == compares references; equals() compares content
        System.out.println(person1 == person3);         // false (different refs)
        System.out.println(person1.equals(person3));    // true  (same content)
        System.out.println(person1.hashCode() == person3.hashCode()); // true

        // instanceof check
        System.out.println(person1 instanceof Person);  // true
        System.out.println(person1 instanceof Object);  // true — all objects extend Object
    }

    static class Person {
        private final String name;   // final = immutable after construction
        private final int age;

        public Person(String name, int age) {
            if (name == null || name.isBlank()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Name required");
            if (age < 0 || age > 150) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid age: " + age);
            this.name = name;
            this.age = age;
        }

        // Static factory method — more expressive than constructor
        public static Person of(String name, int age) {
            return new Person(name, age);
        }

        public String getName() { return name; }
        public int getAge()     { return age; }

        @Override
        public String toString() {
            return "Person{name='" + name + "', age=" + age + "}";
        }

        @Override
        public boolean equals(Object o) {
            if (this == o) return true;
            if (!(o instanceof Person other)) return false;
            return age == other.age && name.equals(other.name);
        }

        @Override
        public int hashCode() {
            int result = name.hashCode();
            result = 31 * result + age;
            return result;
        }
    }
}

Example 4: JavaVersionInfo

/**
 * Demonstrates: System properties, Runtime API, feature detection.
 * Useful for diagnostic logging at application startup.
 */
public class JavaVersionInfo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        printJavaInfo();
        printRuntimeInfo();
        printSystemInfo();
    }

    private static void printJavaInfo() {
        System.out.println("=== Java Version Information ===");
        System.out.println("Java Version   : " + System.getProperty("java.version"));
        System.out.println("Java Vendor    : " + System.getProperty("java.vendor"));
        System.out.println("Java Home      : " + System.getProperty("java.home"));
        System.out.println("Java Spec Ver  : " + System.getProperty("java.specification.version"));
        System.out.println("Class Version  : " + System.getProperty("java.class.version"));

        // Runtime.Version API (Java 9+)
        Runtime.Version version = Runtime.version();
        System.out.println("Feature        : " + version.feature());
        System.out.println("Interim        : " + version.interim());
        System.out.println("Update         : " + version.update());
        System.out.println("Patch          : " + version.patch());
    }

    private static void printRuntimeInfo() {
        Runtime runtime = Runtime.getRuntime();
        long mb = 1024 * 1024;
        System.out.println("\n=== JVM Runtime Information ===");
        System.out.println("Available CPUs : " + runtime.availableProcessors());
        System.out.println("Max Heap       : " + (runtime.maxMemory() / mb) + " MB");
        System.out.println("Total Heap     : " + (runtime.totalMemory() / mb) + " MB");
        System.out.println("Free Heap      : " + (runtime.freeMemory() / mb) + " MB");
        System.out.println("Used Heap      : " + ((runtime.totalMemory() - runtime.freeMemory()) / mb) + " MB");
    }

    private static void printSystemInfo() {
        System.out.println("\n=== System Information ===");
        System.out.println("OS Name        : " + System.getProperty("os.name"));
        System.out.println("OS Version     : " + System.getProperty("os.version"));
        System.out.println("OS Arch        : " + System.getProperty("os.arch"));
        System.out.println("JVM Name       : " + System.getProperty("java.vm.name"));
        System.out.println("JVM Vendor     : " + System.getProperty("java.vm.vendor"));
        System.out.println("JVM Version    : " + System.getProperty("java.vm.version"));
    }
}

Spring Boot Preview

Why Spring Boot Dominates Java Backend Development

Spring Boot is the de facto standard for building Java microservices and web applications. It eliminates boilerplate configuration through convention over configuration and auto-configuration.

// A complete REST API endpoint — just 15 lines with Spring Boot
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/v1/users")
public class UserController {

    private final UserService userService;

    public UserController(UserService userService) {
        this.userService = userService;
    }

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<User> getUser(@PathVariable Long id) {
        return userService.findById(id)
            .map(ResponseEntity::ok)
            .orElse(ResponseEntity.notFound().build());
    }
}

Part 16

Architect Perspective

When to Choose Java: An Architect's Decision Framework

As a Solution Architect, technology choices must balance technical merit, organizational constraints, and long-term maintainability. Java's position is unique:

Java's Structural Advantages for Large Organizations

  1. Talent Pool: Java is consistently in the top 1-3 languages globally. Hiring is predictable.
  2. Backward Compatibility: Oracle's commitment to backward compatibility means Java 8 code (2014) still compiles and runs on Java 21 (2023). Migration risk is low.
  3. Ecosystem Maturity: Every enterprise integration pattern has a library. Kafka, Elasticsearch, Redis, gRPC, OAuth2, SAML — all have first-class Java clients.
  4. Tooling Excellence: IntelliJ IDEA, Eclipse JDT, JFR (Java Flight Recorder), JMC (Mission Control), VisualVM, YourKit — unmatched developer tooling.
  5. APM Support: Every major APM (Datadog, Dynatrace, New Relic, AppDynamics) provides deep Java instrumentation.
  6. Regulatory Compliance: Banking, healthcare, and government sectors often mandate Java due to its audit trail capabilities and security track record.

Java's Structural Disadvantages

  1. Verbosity: Java requires more lines of code than Python, Kotlin, or Go for equivalent logic (mitigated by Records, Lambdas, var in modern Java)
  2. Startup time: Cold starts are expensive — container restarts, serverless invocations, and CLI tools suffer (mitigated by GraalVM native image)
  3. Memory baseline: JVM overhead (~50-200 MB minimum) makes it expensive for ultra-lightweight services
  4. Learning curve: Full understanding of GC, JIT, concurrency model, class loading takes years
  5. Null safety: Null reference exceptions remain common (Kotlin's type system is superior here)

Architectural Decision Record (ADR) Template: Java Selection

ADR-001: Backend Service Language Selection

Context:
  Building a payment processing microservice requiring:
  - High throughput (10K TPS)
  - Sub-100ms P99 latency
  - 5-year maintainability horizon
  - Team of 8 Java engineers

Options Considered:
  1. Java 21 + Spring Boot 3
  2. Go 1.22
  3. Kotlin + Spring Boot 3

Decision: Java 21 + Spring Boot 3

Rationale:
  - Existing team expertise (8 Java engineers, 0 Go engineers)
  - Spring Boot ecosystem for observability (Actuator, Micrometer)
  - Virtual threads (Java 21) addresses concurrency requirements
  - Strong JPA/Hibernate support for ACID transactions
  - ZGC for sub-1ms GC pauses
  - 5-year backward compatibility guarantee

Trade-offs:
  - 200MB container overhead vs ~20MB for Go
  - 2-3s startup vs ~100ms for Go
  - Mitigated by: container pre-warming, GraalVM native image POC for v2

Consequences:
  - Use -XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational for GC
  - Container: -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 -XX:+UseContainerSupport
  - Monitor: JFR for profiling, Micrometer for metrics

Common Mistakes

Beginner Mistakes

Mistake Wrong Code Correct Code Explanation
String comparison with == if (s1 == s2) if (s1.equals(s2)) == compares references, not content
Integer cache boundary Integer a=128; Integer b=128; a==b → false Use .equals() always Integer cache only covers -128 to 127
Modifying list during iteration for(T t : list) list.remove(t) Use Iterator.remove() or removeIf() ConcurrentModificationException
Ignoring exceptions catch (Exception e) {} At minimum: log.error("msg", e) Silent failures are impossible to debug
Using + in loops String s = ""; for(...) s += x; Use StringBuilder O(n²) memory allocation pattern
Float/double for money double price = 0.1 + 0.2; Use BigDecimal Floating point is not exact
Null return from collections return null; from List method return Collections.emptyList(); Forces null checks on callers
Checked vs unchecked confusion Catching RuntimeException in signature Understand the exception hierarchy Checked = must handle, unchecked = programming error

Production Mistakes (Senior/Architect Level)

Mistake Consequence Prevention
Unbounded thread creation Thread exhaustion, OOM, system crash Use ExecutorService with bounded thread pools; Java 21: virtual threads
Missing connection pool limits Database connection exhaustion Configure HikariCP maximumPoolSize; monitor pool metrics
Default heap sizing in containers OOM kill by container runtime Use -XX:+UseContainerSupport -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0
Synchronous calls in reactive pipelines Thread blocking, throughput collapse Never block in reactive streams; use async adapters
Long GC pauses in latency-sensitive apps SLA violations, cascading timeouts Switch to ZGC/Shenandoah; tune -Xmx and GC flags
Loading classes in hot paths Performance degradation, GC pressure Warm up application; pre-load critical classes
PermGen/Metaspace unbounded growth JVM crash after hours/days Set -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize; monitor for class loader leaks
Memory leaks via static collections Gradual heap exhaustion Avoid static mutable state; use WeakReference for caches
Improper equals/hashCode in HashMap keys Silent data corruption or O(n) HashMap Always implement both consistently
Overusing synchronized keyword Lock contention, performance bottleneck Use java.util.concurrent classes; ReentrantLock, CAS operations
Finalizer usage Non-deterministic cleanup, GC pressure Use try-with-resources and Cleaner API instead
Deserialization of untrusted data Remote code execution vulnerability Use ObjectInputFilter; prefer JSON/Protobuf for external data
Part 20

Interview Questions

Junior Developer Level

  1. Q: What is the difference between JDK, JRE, and JVM?
    - A: JVM is the runtime engine that executes bytecode. JRE = JVM + standard libraries. JDK = JRE + development tools (javac, javadoc, jshell, etc.). Since Java 9, JRE is no longer distributed separately.

  2. Q: What is the difference between == and .equals() in Java?
    - A: == compares object references (memory addresses). .equals() compares object content. For primitive types, == compares values directly. Always use .equals() for String and object comparison.

  3. Q: What is the difference between int and Integer?
    - A: int is a primitive — stored on the stack, no object overhead. Integer is a wrapper class — an object on the heap wrapping an int. Java autoboxes/unboxes between them automatically, but this has performance implications. Integer is required for generics: List<Integer> (not List<int>).

  4. Q: What does public static void main(String[] args) mean?
    - A: public = accessible from anywhere. static = belongs to class, no instance needed. void = returns nothing. main = JVM entry point by convention. String[] args = command-line arguments.

  5. Q: What is a NullPointerException and how do you prevent it?
    - A: NPE occurs when you call a method or access a field on a null reference. Prevention: null checks, Optional<T>, defensive programming, Kotlin-style null-safe operators, Objects.requireNonNull().

Mid-Level Developer

  1. Q: Explain the Java memory model — heap vs stack.
    - A: Stack stores method frames (local variables, parameters, return addresses) — per-thread, LIFO. Heap stores all objects — shared among threads, GC-managed. Primitives in local variables go to stack; objects always go to heap (their references may be on the stack).

  2. Q: What is the difference between ArrayList and LinkedList?
    - A: ArrayList is backed by an array — O(1) random access, O(n) insert/delete at arbitrary position, good cache locality. LinkedList is a doubly-linked list — O(n) access, O(1) insert/delete at known position, poor cache locality. In practice, ArrayList is preferred for most use cases due to cache performance.

  3. Q: How does HashMap work internally?
    - A: Uses array of buckets + linked list/tree (Java 8+ uses TreeMap for buckets with >8 entries). put(k,v): compute k.hashCode(), compress to bucket index, store entry. Collision = multiple entries in same bucket. Load factor (default 0.75) triggers resize at 75% capacity. hashCode() and equals() contract must be consistent.

  4. Q: What is the difference between Comparable and Comparator?
    - A: Comparable defines the natural ordering of a class (implemented by the class itself, compareTo()). Comparator is an external comparison function (passed to sort/collections). Comparators allow multiple orderings without modifying the class.

  5. Q: What is garbage collection and how does G1GC work?

    • A: GC automatically reclaims heap memory from unreachable objects. G1 (Garbage First) divides heap into equal-size regions (~1-32MB), classifies them as Eden/Survivor/Old. Minor GC collects Eden+Survivors. G1 prioritizes regions with most garbage (hence "Garbage First"). Aims for configurable pause targets (-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200).

Senior Developer

  1. Q: What is the Java Memory Model (JMM) and why does it matter for concurrent programming?

    • A: The JMM defines when writes by one thread are visible to other threads. Without proper synchronization, the JVM/CPU may reorder operations for performance. The volatile keyword ensures visibility (writes immediately visible to other threads) but not atomicity. synchronized ensures both. Understanding the happens-before relationship is critical for lock-free algorithms.

  2. Q: Explain virtual threads (Project Loom) and how they differ from platform threads.

    • A: Platform threads are OS threads — expensive (~1MB stack, ~2ms creation). Virtual threads are JVM-managed lightweight threads — millions can exist simultaneously, mounted/unmounted from carrier (platform) threads. Blocking I/O on a virtual thread unmounts it, allowing the carrier thread to run other virtual threads. Key benefit: enables simple blocking code to achieve I/O concurrency equivalent to reactive programming.

  3. Q: How does JIT compilation work and what is tiered compilation?

    • A: JIT profiles bytecode execution, identifies hot methods, compiles them to native machine code. Tiered compilation uses C1 (fast compile, some opts) for moderately hot code and C2 (slow compile, aggressive opts) for very hot code. Optimizations include inlining, escape analysis, loop unrolling, speculative deoptimization.

Solution Architect Level

  1. Q: How do you design Java services for containers/Kubernetes?

    • A: Use -XX:+UseContainerSupport so JVM reads cgroup limits. Set -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 (leave 25% for JVM overhead, buffers). Use ZGC for low-latency. Implement health endpoints (Spring Actuator /actuator/health). Use JFR for profiling without production overhead. Pre-warm instances before routing traffic. Consider GraalVM native-image for fast startup.

  2. Q: How would you diagnose a Java production memory leak?

    • A: 1) Monitor heap usage trend (rising, never drops after GC = leak). 2) Take heap dump: jmap -dump:format=b,file=heap.hprof <pid>. 3) Analyze with Eclipse MAT or JVisualVM — find dominator tree, leak suspects. 4) Check for: static collections growing, event listeners not removed, thread-local not cleaned, class loader leaks (Metaspace), session objects not expiring. 5) Use JFR allocation profiling in production for continuous monitoring.

  3. Q: Explain the trade-offs between Java monolith and microservices for a financial system.

    • A: Monolith: ACID transactions trivial (one DB), no network overhead, simpler deployment, easier debugging. Microservices: independent scaling, team autonomy, fault isolation, polyglot possible. For financial systems: start with modular monolith (single JVM, multiple modules), extract services only when team/scaling boundaries are clear. Distributed transactions (Saga pattern) add significant complexity. Java's strong typing and tooling make large monoliths maintainable longer than other languages.

Glossary

Term Definition
Bytecode Platform-neutral instruction set for the JVM; output of javac
JVM Java Virtual Machine — runtime engine that executes bytecode
JDK Java Development Kit — JVM + compiler + tools
JRE Java Runtime Environment — JVM + standard libraries (no compiler)
HotSpot Oracle's primary JVM implementation; named for the "hot spots" it JIT-compiles
JIT Just-In-Time compilation — translating bytecode to native machine code at runtime
AOT Ahead-Of-Time compilation — compiling to native code before runtime (GraalVM native-image)
GC Garbage Collector — JVM subsystem that automatically reclaims unused heap memory
Heap JVM memory region where all objects are allocated
Stack Per-thread JVM memory region holding method frames
Metaspace JVM memory (off-heap) holding class metadata; replaced PermGen in Java 8
ClassLoader JVM component that loads .class files into the runtime
WORA Write Once, Run Anywhere — Java's platform independence promise
OpenJDK Open-source reference implementation of Java SE; governs the spec
LTS Long-Term Support — Java versions with multi-year extended support (8, 11, 17, 21)
Virtual Thread Lightweight JVM-managed thread (Java 21+); millions can run concurrently
GraalVM Polyglot VM with superior JIT and AOT (native-image) capability
PermGen Permanent Generation — pre-Java 8 fixed-size class metadata space (now Metaspace)
TLAB Thread-Local Allocation Buffer — per-thread heap region for fast object allocation
Tiered Compilation JVM strategy using C1 then C2 JIT as methods get hotter
Escape Analysis JIT optimization determining if objects escape their creation scope
Safepoint Point in execution where JVM can pause threads for GC or deoptimization
Deoptimization Reverting JIT-compiled code to interpreter when speculative assumptions fail
Fat JAR JAR file containing application code + all dependencies (Spring Boot default)

Practice — Lesson 1

Easy Exercises

  1. Hello Name: Write a Java program that accepts a name as a command-line argument (args[0]) and prints "Hello, <name>!". Handle the case where no argument is provided by printing "Hello, World!".

  2. System Info Printer: Write a class that prints the Java version, OS name, available processors, and max heap memory using System.getProperty() and Runtime.getRuntime().

  3. Primitive Explorer: Write a program that declares one variable of each of Java's 8 primitive types, prints their values and the result of sizeof equivalent (use wrapper class .BYTES field: e.g., Integer.BYTES).

  4. String Operations: Write a program demonstrating: length(), charAt(), substring(), indexOf(), toUpperCase(), trim(), split(), and String.format().

  5. Calculator: Write a simple command-line calculator that takes three arguments: <number1> <operator> <number2> and prints the result. Support +, -, *, /. Handle division by zero with an appropriate message.

Medium Exercises

  1. FizzBuzz with Stream API: Implement FizzBuzz (1 to 100) using IntStream.rangeClosed() and a lambda expression. Then implement it again using a traditional for loop. Compare the code readability.

  2. Object Equality Lab: Create a Point class with x and y fields. Implement equals(), hashCode(), and toString(). Create a HashSet<Point> and verify that duplicate points are deduplicated. Then break it: remove one of equals()/hashCode() and observe what happens.

  3. Memory Measurement: Use Runtime.getRuntime() to measure heap before and after creating 1 million String objects vs. 1 million Integer objects. Report the heap usage difference. Draw conclusions about object overhead.

  4. Compile and Inspect: Write a class with 3 methods (arithmetic). Compile it with javac, then disassemble with javap -c. Identify the bytecode instructions for: loading a constant, performing addition, calling a method, and returning a value.

  5. JVM Version Compatibility: Take the JavaVersionInfo example from Part 12 and extend it to detect whether the current JVM supports virtual threads (Thread.ofVirtual()), pattern matching (instanceof with binding), and records. Use Runtime.version().feature() for version checks.

Advanced Exercises

  1. Bytecode Analysis: Write a Java method that sums integers 1 to N. Disassemble it with javap -c -verbose. Then rewrite it as a recursive version. Compare bytecodes. Observe the difference in stack frame usage and identify the loop-to-bytecode mapping.

  2. ClassLoader Exploration: Write a program that prints the full ClassLoader chain for a user-defined class, String.class, and int.class (hint: primitives return null). Explain why String.class.getClassLoader() returns null.

  3. GC Tuning Experiment: Write a program that allocates 100MB of objects in a loop. Run it three times with: (a) default GC, (b) -XX:+UseZGC, (c) -XX:+UseParallelGC. Add JVM flags -verbose:gc -Xms256m -Xmx512m. Compare GC pause times and frequency from the output.

  4. Performance Warmup Measurement: Write a microbenchmark (or use JMH) that measures the time to execute a method (e.g., string concatenation) for the first 1, 10, 100, 1000, 10,000, and 100,000 invocations. Plot the warmup curve and identify where JIT compilation kicks in.

  5. Native Image Comparison: Build the JavaVersionInfo example as a fat JAR and measure startup time (time java -jar app.jar). Then build it with GraalVM native-image and compare startup time and binary size. Document the trade-offs.

Production Scenarios

  1. Container Sizing Calculator: Given a Spring Boot application with default settings deployed in a 512MB container, calculate: expected Max Heap (-Xmx), Metaspace allowance, thread stack allowance (assume 200 threads × 512KB), Code Cache, and residual overhead. Derive recommended JVM flags using the formula: MaxHeap = ContainerRAM × 0.75 - OtherJVMOverhead.

  2. Memory Leak Hunt: You are given a service where heap usage grows 50MB/hour and never drops after GC. List the 5 most likely causes in order of probability. For each: describe how to confirm it using jmap, JFR, or heap dump analysis.

  3. GC Tuning for SLA: A payment service has a P99 latency SLA of 100ms. Current setup uses G1GC with -Xmx4g and experiences 200ms GC pauses at the 99th percentile. What GC changes would you recommend? Write the complete JVM flags with justification.

  4. Cold Start Optimization: A Lambda function using Java 21 takes 3.2 seconds to start (cold start). Enumerate 5 techniques to reduce cold start time, ordered by implementation effort. For each, provide the expected improvement and implementation approach.

  5. Kafka Consumer Sizing: A Kafka consumer written in Java processes 100K messages/second with each message being a 1KB JSON payload. Estimate: thread pool size, heap requirements, GC strategy, and JVM flags. Justify each decision.

Debugging Exercises

  1. NPE Archaeology: Given a stack trace from a production NPE, practice reading it: identify the class, method, line number, and call chain. Write 3 different versions of code that produce the same NPE, each from a different cause (null field, null return, null argument).

  2. OutOfMemoryError Scenarios: Write three distinct programs that each produce a different type of OOM: (a) java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space, (b) java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace, (c) java.lang.StackOverflowError. For each, explain the root cause and fix.

  3. Thread Dump Reading: Generate a thread dump of a running Java process with jstack <pid> or kill -3 <pid>. Identify: main thread, GC threads, JIT compiler threads, and any blocked threads. Explain the difference between RUNNABLE, WAITING, TIMED_WAITING, and BLOCKED thread states.

  4. ConcurrentModificationException: Write code that reproduces a ConcurrentModificationException in: (a) a for-each loop, (b) a ListIterator, (c) a parallel stream. Fix each case with the appropriate solution.

Interview Challenges

  1. Architecture Question: "Your team is building a new payment processing service that will handle 50,000 transactions per second. A colleague suggests Python because the team knows it better. How do you evaluate this decision? What Java-specific features would you highlight? When would you agree with the Python suggestion?"

    • Expected answer should cover: latency requirements, team ramp-up time, GC tuning for payment latency, JVM ecosystem (JFR, APMs), transaction throughput benchmarks, and the trade-off between team velocity and long-term performance.

  2. Deep Dive Question: "Explain what happens, at every level of abstraction, between when you type java HelloWorld and when Hello, World! appears on screen."

    • Expected answer should cover: OS process creation, JVM startup, bootstrap/platform/app classloading, bytecode verification, main() thread creation, stack frame creation, bytecode interpretation, getstatic/ldc/invokevirtual bytecodes, native method for println, OS write() syscall.

  3. Trade-off Question: "Java has automatic garbage collection. A colleague argues this makes Java unsuitable for ultra-low-latency trading systems requiring sub-microsecond response times. Is this true? How would you respond?"

    • Expected answer: Partially true for traditional GC. ZGC/Shenandoah achieve sub-1ms pauses. Azul Zing's C4 GC achieves near-zero pauses. Chronicle libraries bypass GC entirely. Off-heap memory (ByteBuffer.allocateDirect) avoids GC. The Java ecosystem (Aeron, Chronicle) is used in many low-latency trading systems today.

  4. Modern Java Question: "What are virtual threads (Project Loom) and how do they change the architecture of Java backend services? When would you NOT use virtual threads?"

    • Expected answer: Virtual threads are JVM-managed, lightweight threads (not OS threads). Millions can exist. Blocking I/O unmounts from carrier thread. Eliminates reactive programming complexity for I/O-heavy services. NOT suitable for: CPU-bound tasks (use platform threads), pinning operations (synchronized blocks, native code), where thread-local assumptions exist.

Part 1

Concept

What Are JDK, JRE, and JVM?

These three acronyms represent the three distinct layers of the Java platform. Confusing them leads to misdiagnosed bugs, wrong Docker base images, bloated containers, and licensing headaches. Every Solution Architect must have razor-sharp clarity on where each layer begins and ends.

JRE Java Runtime Environment JVM + standard class libraries needed to run Java programs
JDK Java Development Kit JRE + tools needed to develop, compile, and debug Java programs

- You compile with the JDK.
- You run with the JRE (which includes the JVM).
- The JVM alone is the execution engine that actually processes bytecode.

Part 2

History

Timeline of JDK Packaging Changes

Year Event Impact
1996 JDK 1.0 released by Sun Microsystems JDK and JRE bundled together
1997 JDK 1.1 — JRE introduced as separate package Users could install just JRE to run apps
2006 Java 6 (JDK 1.6) — JRE widely distributed separately Browsers used JRE plugin for applets
2011 Java 7 — Oracle acquires Sun, inherits JDK Oracle JDK becomes the de-facto standard
2014 Java 8 — Last version with separate JRE downloads JRE available standalone until Java 8 EOL
2017 Java 9 — JPMS (Java Platform Module System) JRE as a separate product deprecated internally
2018 Java 10, 11 — 6-month release cadence LTS every 3 years; JRE no longer separately published
2019 Oracle changes licensing Oracle JDK requires commercial license for production; OpenJDK becomes primary
2021 Java 17 LTS — GraalVM gains traction AOT compilation available; Temurin/Corretto rise as default distros
2023 Java 21 LTS — Virtual Threads (Project Loom) GA JVM execution model fundamentally extended
2024 Java 22/23 (non-LTS) Stream gatherers, unnamed patterns, string templates (preview)
2025 Java 25 LTS (upcoming) Next enterprise long-term support target

Key Takeaway for Architects

Java 8 was the last era where a user could install a "JRE-only" runtime. From Java 9 onwards, the JDK ships as a monolithic modular unit and you use jlink to carve out a custom minimal runtime. The separate JRE download is effectively dead.

Part 3

Problems Solved

Why Do These Three Layers Exist?

Before Java, deploying software meant compiling for each target OS and CPU architecture. Java's "Write Once, Run Anywhere" promise required a new architecture:

Problem 1: Platform Portability
- C/C++ programs compile to native machine code — tied to OS and CPU.
- Java compiles to bytecode, a platform-neutral intermediate form.
- The JVM, tailored for each OS/CPU, interprets/compiles bytecode at runtime.
- Result: one .jar file runs on Windows, Linux, macOS, AIX, embedded devices.

Problem 2: Compile-Time vs Runtime Separation
- Developers need a compiler (javac), debugger (jdb), documentation generator.
- End users only need a runtime — no compiler required.
- JDK = developer bundle, JRE = user/production bundle.

Problem 3: Standard Library Distribution
- Java programs rely heavily on the standard library (java.lang, java.util, etc.).
- Bundling the standard library with the runtime (JRE) eliminates dependency hell.
- All Java programs get the same String, ArrayList, HashMap implementations.

Problem 4: Security Sandbox
- The JVM provides a managed execution environment.
- Bytecode verifier rejects invalid or malicious code before execution.
- Security manager (now deprecated post-Java 17) allowed fine-grained permission control.

│  Hello.class  →  [JVM]  →  Output          │
│  Bytecode         ↕                        │
│                [JRE libs]                  │
│          java.lang, java.io, etc.          │
└────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Responsibilities by Layer

Layer        Responsibility                           Required In
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
JVM          Execute bytecode, manage memory (GC),    Runtime
             JIT compile hot methods, load classes

JRE          Provide standard library (APIs),         Runtime
             configuration files, native libs,
             wrap JVM into a usable runtime

JDK          Compile source, document code,           Build / Dev
             debug, profile, package apps,
             create custom runtime images (jlink)

Security Sandbox Concept

The JVM executes code in a controlled environment:
- Bytecode verifier — ensures class files conform to JVM spec before execution.
- Class loader hierarchy — prevents user classes from masquerading as system classes.
- Type safety — runtime type checks prevent memory corruption attacks common in C.

Part 5

Internal Working: javac Compilation Pipeline

Source to Bytecode: Step by Step

Hello.java (Source)
       │
       ▼
 ┌──────────────┐
 │  Lexer       │  Tokenizes source: keywords, identifiers, literals
 └──────┬───────┘
        │ Token Stream
        ▼
 ┌──────────────┐
 │  Parser      │  Builds Abstract Syntax Tree (AST)
 └──────┬───────┘
        │ AST
        ▼
 ┌──────────────┐
 │  Semantic    │  Type checking, symbol resolution,
 │  Analyzer    │  annotation processing
 └──────┬───────┘
        │ Annotated AST
        ▼
 ┌──────────────┐
 │  Code Gen    │  Emits JVM bytecode instructions
 └──────┬───────┘
        │
        ▼
 Hello.class (Bytecode)

Class File Format Overview

ClassFile {
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Magic Number: 0xCAFEBABE           │  — Java class file identifier
  │  Minor Version / Major Version      │  — JDK version compatibility
  │  Constant Pool                      │  — String literals, class refs
  │  Access Flags                       │  — public, abstract, final, etc.
  │  This Class / Super Class           │  — Inheritance chain
  │  Interfaces []                      │  — Implemented interfaces
  │  Fields []                          │  — Field declarations
  │  Methods []                         │  — Bytecode per method
  │  Attributes []                      │  — SourceFile, LineNumberTable, etc.
  └─────────────────────────────────────┘
}

The javap -c Hello.class command disassembles any .class file and shows the bytecode instructions — a critical skill for performance diagnosis.

Part 6

JVM Implementation Deep Dive

HotSpot JVM Architecture

HotSpot (the JVM bundled with OpenJDK/Oracle JDK) has three major subsystems:

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    HotSpot JVM                           │
│                                                          │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │         CLASS LOADER SUBSYSTEM                     │  │
│  │   Bootstrap CL → Extension/Platform CL → App CL   │  │
│  │   + Custom Class Loaders (OSGi, App Servers)       │  │
│  └────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────┘  │
│                           │ Loaded Classes               │
│  ┌────────────────────────▼───────────────────────────┐  │
│  │         RUNTIME DATA AREAS                         │  │
│  │  ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌───────────────────┐  │  │
│  │  │  Heap    │ │Metaspace │ │  JVM Stacks (per  │  │  │
│  │  │  (GC)    │ │ (class   │ │  thread) + PC Reg  │  │  │
│  │  │          │ │ metadata)│ │  + Native Stacks   │  │  │
│  │  └──────────┘ └──────────┘ └───────────────────┘  │  │
│  └────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────┘  │
│                           │ Bytecode / Native methods     │
│  ┌────────────────────────▼───────────────────────────┐  │
│  │         EXECUTION ENGINE                           │  │
│  │  ┌──────────────┐  ┌─────────────┐  ┌──────────┐  │  │
│  │  │ Interpreter  │→ │  C1 (Client │→ │ C2       │  │  │
│  │  │              │  │  Compiler)  │  │ (Server  │  │  │
│  │  │              │  │  Tier 3     │  │ Compiler)│  │  │
│  │  └──────────────┘  └─────────────┘  └──────────┘  │  │
│  │                       Profiling Data feeds C2       │  │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                                                          │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  Garbage Collectors: G1 (default) | ZGC | Shenandoah│ │
│  │  GraalVM Compiler (optional, polyglot)             │  │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Class Loader Hierarchy (Delegation Model)

Bootstrap ClassLoader  (loads rt.jar / java.base module)
        ↑  delegates up
Platform ClassLoader   (formerly Extension CL, loads java.se.* modules)
        ↑  delegates up
Application ClassLoader (loads classpath / module path)
        ↑  delegates up
Custom ClassLoader     (OSGi, Tomcat, Spring Boot fat-jar)

Delegation principle: A class loader always delegates to its parent first. Only if the parent cannot find the class does the child attempt to load it. This prevents user code from overriding java.lang.String.

JIT Tiered Compilation (Tiered Compilation — Java 7+)

Tier Mode Description
0 Interpreted Initial execution, no compilation
1 C1 compiled Fast compile, simple optimizations
2 C1 + limited profiling Profile counters for branch prediction
3 C1 + full profiling Full method and call profiling
4 C2 compiled Aggressive optimizations using profiling data

The JVM promotes methods up tiers based on invocation count and loop iteration count (hotness). Cold paths remain interpreted; hot paths get native-speed C2 compilation.

Part 7

Memory Layout

Complete JVM Memory Map

JVM Process Memory
│
├── HEAP (managed by GC — shared across all threads)
│   │
│   ├── Young Generation
│   │   ├── Eden Space          ← New objects allocated here
│   │   ├── Survivor Space S0   ← Objects that survived 1 GC
│   │   └── Survivor Space S1   ← Objects that survived 2+ GCs
│   │
│   └── Old Generation (Tenured)
│       └── Long-lived objects promoted from Young Gen
│
├── METASPACE (off-heap since Java 8)
│   ├── Class metadata (structure, method bytecode)
│   ├── Runtime constant pool
│   ├── Field/Method data
│   └── Static variables (moved from PermGen in Java 8)
│
├── JVM STACKS (one per thread)
│   └── Stack Frames (one per method call)
│       ├── Local Variable Array
│       ├── Operand Stack (evaluation stack)
│       └── Frame Data (return address, dynamic link)
│
├── PC REGISTER (one per thread)
│   └── Points to current bytecode instruction
│
├── NATIVE METHOD STACKS (one per thread)
│   └── Used for native (JNI) method calls
│
├── CODE CACHE (off-heap)
│   ├── JIT-compiled native code
│   └── Profiling stubs
│
└── DIRECT MEMORY (off-heap, NIO)
    └── ByteBuffer.allocateDirect() regions

GC Flag Quick Reference

# Heap sizing
-Xms512m          # Initial heap size
-Xmx2g            # Maximum heap size

# Metaspace
-XX:MetaspaceSize=256m
-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=512m

# GC selection
-XX:+UseG1GC      # G1 (default Java 9+)
-XX:+UseZGC       # ZGC (low-latency, Java 15+ production)
-XX:+UseShenandoahGC  # Shenandoah (Red Hat, Java 17+)

# Code Cache
-XX:ReservedCodeCacheSize=256m
Part 8

Execution Flow

From java Command to main()

$ java -cp . Hello
         │
         ▼
1. JVM STARTUP
   ├── Parse JVM flags from command line
   ├── Initialize JVM internal structures
   └── Select GC algorithm

         │
         ▼
2. BOOTSTRAP CLASS LOADING
   ├── Bootstrap ClassLoader loads java.lang.Object
   ├── Loads java.lang.String, java.lang.System, etc.
   └── Core platform classes available

         │
         ▼
3. APPLICATION CLASS LOADING
   ├── Application ClassLoader locates Hello.class
   ├── Reads .class bytes from filesystem/jar
   └── Passes to Bytecode Verifier

         │
         ▼
4. BYTECODE VERIFICATION
   ├── Structural checks (valid class file format)
   ├── Type safety checks (no illegal casts)
   └── Control flow checks (no dead code traps)

         │
         ▼
5. LINKING
   ├── Preparation: allocate memory for static fields
   ├── Resolution: resolve symbolic references to direct refs
   └── Initialization: run static initializers / static {}

         │
         ▼
6. LOCATE main() METHOD
   └── JVM finds public static void main(String[] args)

         │
         ▼
7. CREATE MAIN THREAD
   ├── Allocate Thread object
   ├── Allocate JVM Stack for main thread
   └── Push initial stack frame for main()

         │
         ▼
8. EXECUTE BYTECODE
   ├── Interpreter executes instructions (initial runs)
   ├── Profiler tracks method hotness
   ├── C1 compiles warm methods
   └── C2 aggressively optimizes hot methods

         │
         ▼
9. PROGRAM COMPLETION
   ├── main() returns, stack frame popped
   ├── JVM waits for non-daemon threads to finish
   ├── Runs shutdown hooks
   └── JVM process exits
Part 9

Performance

JVM Startup Cost

JVM startup is a known overhead — relevant when you need fast cold starts (serverless, CLI tools):

Startup Component Approximate Cost
JVM initialization 20–80 ms
Bootstrap class loading 50–200 ms
Application class loading 100 ms – 2 s (depends on classpath size)
JIT warm-up (to peak throughput) 10 s – 2 min (depends on app complexity)

Techniques to Reduce Startup Time

1. Class Data Sharing (CDS) — Java 5+, improved Java 10+

# Step 1: Create shared archive
java -Xshare:dump -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa

# Step 2: Use shared archive at startup
java -Xshare:on -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa -cp . Hello

CDS pre-processes class metadata into a memory-mapped file, eliminating repeated parsing. Spring Boot 3.3+ supports CDS natively via spring-boot:process-aot and CDS training runs.

2. Application Class Data Sharing (AppCDS) — Java 10+

# Step 1: Record loaded classes during trial run
java -XX:DumpLoadedClassList=classes.lst -cp . Hello

# Step 2: Create AppCDS archive including app classes
java -Xshare:dump -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa \
     -XX:SharedClassListFile=classes.lst -cp . Hello

# Step 3: Run with AppCDS
java -Xshare:on -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa -cp . Hello

3. GraalVM Native Image (AOT Compilation)

# Compile entire app to platform-native binary
native-image -cp app.jar com.example.Hello

# Result: ./hello binary starts in < 10ms, uses 5-10x less memory
# Trade-off: No dynamic class loading, no JIT warm-up benefits at runtime
Approach Startup Time Peak Throughput Dynamic Features
Standard JVM 500ms – 2s Excellent (JIT) Full
JVM + CDS 200ms – 1s Excellent (JIT) Full
GraalVM Native 5–50ms Good (no JIT) Limited
Leyden (future) TBD Excellent Full
Part 10

Complexity: Class Loading

Class Loading Complexity Analysis

Operation Time Complexity Notes
Class lookup (loaded) O(1) HashMap in ClassLoader
Class loading (first time) O(n) in file size Disk I/O + parsing
Bytecode verification O(m) in method count One pass per method
Class initialization O(s) in static block Runs static {} once
Class hierarchy walk O(d) in inheritance depth Rare; interface impl check
ClassLoader delegation O(h) in hierarchy depth Usually 3–4 levels

Class Loading States

State Machine per Class:
  [Not Loaded] → [Loading] → [Loaded/Verified] → [Prepared]
                                                       ↓
                                                  [Resolved]
                                                       ↓
                                                 [Initialized]
                                                       ↓
                                             [Unloaded] (GC only)

A class can only be unloaded when its ClassLoader becomes garbage — which means all classes loaded by that ClassLoader are simultaneously unloaded. This is why application server hot-redeploy can cause OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace (ClassLoader leaks).

Part 11

Complexity: JIT Compilation

JIT Decision Heuristics

Metric Default Threshold Flag
Method invocation count (C1) 1,500 -XX:Tier3InvocationThreshold
Method invocation count (C2) 10,000 -XX:CompileThreshold
Loop back-edge count (C2) 140,000 -XX:Tier4BackEdgeThreshold
Code cache full action Deoptimize to interpreted -XX:ReservedCodeCacheSize

Deoptimization

JIT-compiled code can be deoptimized (thrown away and reverted to interpretation) when:
- Class hierarchy changes invalidate an inlined method.
- An uncommon trap is hit (e.g., null seen where non-null was assumed).
- On-stack replacement (OSR) fails.

This is normal JVM behavior but can cause latency spikes — relevant in low-latency trading or real-time systems.

Production: JDK Distributions

Which JDK Do Banks and Enterprises Use?

In 2019, Oracle changed its licensing such that Oracle JDK required a paid subscription for production use. This drove a rapid shift to OpenJDK-based distributions:

Distribution Vendor License LTS Support Common Use Case
Eclipse Temurin Adoptium / Eclipse Foundation GPLv2+CE ✅ Yes Default for most enterprises, banks
Amazon Corretto Amazon GPLv2+CE ✅ Yes AWS workloads, preferred on EC2/ECS
Microsoft Build of OpenJDK Microsoft GPLv2+CE ✅ Yes Azure, GitHub Actions
Azul Zulu Azul Systems GPLv2+CE (CE) / Commercial ✅ Yes Compliance-focused orgs
Azul Zing / Platform Prime Azul Systems Commercial ✅ Yes Ultra-low latency (trading, fintech)
Red Hat OpenJDK Red Hat GPLv2+CE ✅ Yes RHEL, OpenShift environments
Oracle JDK Oracle Commercial (NFTC since Java 17) ✅ Yes Oracle-shop customers with support
GraalVM CE Oracle / Community GPLv2+CE ✅ Yes Native image, polyglot, ahead-of-time
GraalVM EE Oracle Commercial ✅ Yes Enterprise native image, G1 GC + NI

Recommendation for most architects: Eclipse Temurin (free, TCK-verified, backed by major vendors including Microsoft, Red Hat, Alibaba) is the default choice. Switch to Corretto for AWS-native workloads.

Container JDK Images

# Preferred: Eclipse Temurin official images
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine      # Minimal JRE for running apps
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk-alpine      # JDK for build stages
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-jammy       # Ubuntu 22.04 for broader compat

# Amazon Corretto
FROM amazoncorretto:21-alpine3.19       # AWS-preferred

# Multi-stage build (best practice)
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN ./mvnw package -DskipTests

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /app/target/myapp.jar .
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "myapp.jar"]

Never use eclipse-temurin:21-jdk in production containers unless you need runtime compilation (rare). Use -jre images — they are ~200MB smaller and have a smaller attack surface.

Part 14

Spring Boot and JVM

How Spring Boot Uses JRE/JVM

Spring Boot applications are typically packaged as executable fat JARs — a single .jar containing all dependencies and an embedded servlet container.

myapp.jar (Fat JAR structure)
├── BOOT-INF/
│   ├── classes/          ← Your compiled .class files
│   └── lib/              ← All Maven/Gradle dependencies
├── META-INF/
│   └── MANIFEST.MF       ← Main-Class: org.springframework.boot.loader.JarLauncher
└── org/springframework/boot/loader/
    └── JarLauncher.class  ← Spring's custom ClassLoader bootstrap

JVM starts
    ↓
Loads JarLauncher (Spring Boot's custom ClassLoader)
    ↓
JarLauncher sets up nested JAR ClassLoader
    ↓
Loads your @SpringBootApplication class
    ↓
Spring ApplicationContext initializes
    ↓
Embedded Tomcat (or Jetty/Undertow) starts on JVM
    ↓
HTTP port opens — app ready

Key insight: Embedded Tomcat runs inside the same JVM process as your application. There is no separate Tomcat JVM. This means:
- One JVM, one process, one heap.
- Tomcat thread pool + Spring thread pool + GC all share the same memory.
- JVM tuning flags apply to the entire application including the server.

JVM Flags for Spring Boot Production

java \
  -Xms512m -Xmx1g \
  -XX:+UseZGC \
  -XX:+ZGenerational \
  -XX:MetaspaceSize=256m \
  -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=512m \
  -XX:ReservedCodeCacheSize=256m \
  -Dspring.profiles.active=prod \
  -jar myapp.jar
Part 15

Microservices: JVM Per Container

Container-Aware JVM Configuration

Pre-Java 10, the JVM could not detect container memory limits — it would see the host machine's total RAM and over-allocate, causing OOMKilled pods in Kubernetes.

Java 10+ Container Awareness (default enabled):

# JVM reads cgroup memory limits automatically
# In a container with 1GB limit:
java -XX:+UseContainerSupport \   # default: true since Java 10
     -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 \  # use 75% of container memory for heap
     -jar myapp.jar

Container Memory: 1GB
    ├── JVM Heap:       750MB (75% via MaxRAMPercentage)
    ├── Metaspace:      ~100MB
    ├── Thread Stacks:  ~50MB (depends on thread count)
    ├── Code Cache:     ~64MB
    └── OS/JVM overhead: ~136MB

JVM Per Microservice Pattern

Kubernetes Pod                Kubernetes Pod
┌─────────────────────┐       ┌─────────────────────┐
│  JVM Process        │       │  JVM Process        │
│  ┌───────────────┐  │       │  ┌───────────────┐  │
│  │ order-service │  │       │  │payment-service│  │
│  │ Spring Boot   │  │       │  │ Spring Boot   │  │
│  └───────────────┘  │       │  └───────────────┘  │
│  Memory: 512MB-1GB  │       │  Memory: 256-512MB  │
└─────────────────────┘       └─────────────────────┘

Architect considerations:
- JVM startup time matters in autoscaling — consider CDS or GraalVM Native Image for services requiring sub-second cold starts.
- Each JVM has its own heap and GC — there is no shared heap across microservices.
- Virtual threads (Java 21 Loom) dramatically reduce memory per concurrent request — a single JVM can now handle 100,000+ concurrent requests with low memory.

Memory Sizing Rules of Thumb

Service Type Heap Total JVM Memory
Lightweight REST API 256–512MB 512MB–1GB
Spring Boot with DB 512MB–1GB 1–2GB
Batch processing 1–4GB 2–6GB
In-memory cache (Hazelcast) 4–16GB 6–20GB
Analytics / Spark executor 8–32GB 12–40GB

Part 19

Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: Using JRE-Only in Production (Pre-Java 9 Mistake)

❌ WRONG (production container with no diagnostic tools):
FROM java:8-jre-alpine
# Cannot: jstack, jmap, jcmd, javap — these are JDK tools

✅ CORRECT for production (use JRE image, add jcmd via JDK debug sidecar if needed):
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine
# For debugging, attach a separate container with JDK

Since Java 9, there is no separate JRE download — you use the JDK and optionally jlink to create a custom minimal runtime.

Mistake 2: Wrong JAVA_HOME

# WRONG — pointing to bin directory
export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-21/bin
# Results in: /usr/lib/jvm/java-21/bin/bin/java (double bin)

# CORRECT — point to JDK root
export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-21-openjdk-amd64
export PATH=$JAVA_HOME/bin:$PATH

# Verify
$JAVA_HOME/bin/java -version   # should work
which java                      # should resolve to $JAVA_HOME/bin/java

Mistake 3: Mixing JDK Versions in Build and Runtime

❌ WRONG:
Build:   Java 17 (javac --release 17 by default)
Runtime: Java 11 JRE
Error:   UnsupportedClassVersionError: class compiled with newer version

✅ CORRECT:
Build:   Java 21, compile with --release 11 for compatibility
         javac --release 11 Hello.java
Runtime: Java 11+

Always use --release N flag to target an older JVM if needed.

Mistake 4: Ignoring Container Memory Limits (Pre-Java 10)

# On Java 8u191+: UseContainerSupport is backported but verify:
java -XshowSettings:all -version 2>&1 | grep -i heap

# If JVM sees host RAM (e.g., 64GB) instead of container limit (1GB):
# → JVM allocates 16GB heap in a 1GB container → OOMKilled

# Fix: Always set explicit limits OR use Java 10+ with MaxRAMPercentage
java -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 -jar app.jar

Mistake 5: Installing JDK on Production Servers "Just in Case"

Security risk: JDK includes javac — a production server should not compile code.
Tools like jstack and jmap in JDK can expose sensitive heap data if server is compromised.

Best practice: Use JRE-equivalent (custom jlink image) in production.
Add JDK tools via out-of-band access (debug sidecar, ephemeral debug container).

Mistake 6: Not Setting -Xms and -Xmx Together

# WRONG: JVM can resize heap repeatedly causing GC pauses
java -Xmx2g -jar app.jar   # Xms defaults to 1/64 of RAM or 1MB

# CORRECT: Pre-allocate full heap to eliminate resize GCs
java -Xms2g -Xmx2g -jar app.jar
Part 20

Interview Questions

All Levels: JDK, JRE, JVM Differences

Level: Junior (L1–L2)

Q1: What is the difference between JDK, JRE, and JVM?
> JVM executes bytecode (the engine). JRE = JVM + standard libraries (needed to run Java programs). JDK = JRE + development tools like javac, jar, jdb (needed to build Java programs). JDK ⊃ JRE ⊃ JVM.

Q2: Do I need to install the JDK to run a Java application in production?
> No. You only need the JRE (or a JVM with standard libraries). The JDK includes development tools (compiler, debugger) that are unnecessary and potentially a security risk in production.

Q3: What does javac do?
> javac is the Java compiler. It translates .java source files into .class files containing JVM bytecode. It is part of the JDK and not present in the JRE.

Q4: What is bytecode?
> Bytecode is an intermediate binary format — not native machine code and not source code. It is platform-neutral and stored in .class files. The JVM interprets or JIT-compiles bytecode to native machine code at runtime.

Level: Mid (L3–L4)

Q5: What changed with JDK packaging in Java 9?
> Java 9 introduced the Java Platform Module System (JPMS). The JRE as a separate downloadable product was deprecated. Oracle no longer ships a standalone JRE download. Developers use the full JDK, and jlink can create custom minimal runtime images containing only required modules.

Q6: Explain the ClassLoader delegation model.
> When a ClassLoader is asked to load a class, it first delegates to its parent ClassLoader. Only if the parent cannot find the class does the child attempt to load it. The hierarchy is: Bootstrap → Platform → Application → Custom. This prevents user code from replacing core JDK classes like java.lang.String.

Q7: What is the difference between HotSpot C1 and C2 compilers?
> C1 (Client Compiler) performs fast, light optimizations and is used for methods that are warm (invoked ~1,500 times). C2 (Server Compiler) performs aggressive optimizations using profiling data collected during interpretation and C1 execution, applied to hot methods (invoked ~10,000 times). Tiered compilation uses both in sequence.

Q8: What is Metaspace and why did it replace PermGen?
> PermGen (Permanent Generation) was a fixed-size heap region in HotSpot for class metadata. It was prone to OutOfMemoryError: PermGen space because its size was capped. Java 8 replaced it with Metaspace, which is off-heap (native memory) and grows dynamically (up to MaxMetaspaceSize). Class metadata now does not compete with heap objects for GC.

Level: Senior (L5–L6)

Q9: A Java process in a Kubernetes pod is being OOMKilled despite the JVM heap being within limits. What do you check?
> Total JVM memory consumption is NOT just heap. Check: Metaspace (-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize), thread stacks (each thread ~512KB–1MB), Code Cache (-XX:ReservedCodeCacheSize), Direct Memory (-XX:MaxDirectMemorySize for NIO), and JVM internal overhead. Also verify UseContainerSupport is enabled and the JVM correctly reads cgroup memory limits. Use jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory for a full breakdown.

Q10: When would you choose GraalVM Native Image over standard JVM?
> Native Image is best for: CLI tools needing instant startup, serverless functions (Lambda, Cloud Run) where cold start is billed, Docker images where startup speed affects autoscaling response time. Avoid it when: the application uses heavy reflection, dynamic class loading (OSGi, certain Spring features without AOT config), or runtime bytecode generation (cglib without native hints).

Q11: What is CDS (Class Data Sharing) and how does it help production applications?
> CDS pre-serializes JVM class metadata into a shared memory-mapped archive. At startup, the JVM memory-maps this archive instead of parsing class files — reducing startup time by 20–50% and allowing multiple JVM processes to share read-only class metadata pages. AppCDS extends this to application classes. Spring Boot 3.3+ provides first-class CDS support via spring-boot:process-aot and training runs.

Key Flags to Remember

-Xms          # Initial heap size
-Xmx          # Maximum heap size
-XX:+UseZGC   # Enable ZGC collector
-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0   # Heap as % of container RAM
-XX:+UseContainerSupport    # Read cgroup limits (default true, Java 10+)
-XX:MetaspaceSize=256m      # Initial Metaspace
-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=512m   # Cap Metaspace
-Xshare:on                  # Enable CDS
-XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa  # CDS archive path
