Memory Layout

Call Stack During Recursive Call

processOrder() calls validate() calls checkInventory():

JVM Stack (grows downward):

┌────────────────────────────────────┐  ← Stack Top (newest frame)
│  Frame: checkInventory()           │
│    #0: this                        │
│    #1: skuId (String)              │
│    #2: quantity (int)              │
│  Return addr: validate() line 42   │
├────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Frame: validate()                 │
│    #0: this                        │
│    #1: order (Order ref)           │
│    #2: result (boolean)            │
│  Return addr: processOrder() line 18│
├────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Frame: processOrder()             │
│    #0: this                        │
│    #1: order (Order ref)           │
│    #2: paymentResult (ref)         │
│  Return addr: Controller line 55  │
├────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Frame: Controller.handleRequest() │
│    ...                             │
└────────────────────────────────────┘  ← Stack Bottom
         ↑
  Default JVM stack size: 512KB–1MB per thread
  Each frame uses space for local variables + operand stack
  StackOverflowError when stack is exhausted

Heap vs Stack for Method Data

Method call: createOrder(String customerId, List<Item> items)

STACK (fast, thread-local):           HEAP (shared, GC-managed):
┌────────────────────────┐            ┌──────────────────────────┐
│ customerId ref = 0xAA  │───────────▶│ String "CUST-001" @0xAA  │
│ items ref      = 0xBB  │───────────▶│ ArrayList @0xBB          │
│ orderId (int)  = 12345 │            │   → Item @0xCC           │
│ total (double) = 99.99 │            │   → Item @0xDD           │
└────────────────────────┘            └──────────────────────────┘
  Popped when method returns             Lives until GC collects
  O(1) allocation/deallocation           Managed by GC
Part 8

Execution Flow

Method Chaining Execution

// Each method returns 'this' — calls chain left-to-right
Order order = new OrderBuilder()
    .customerId("C001")    // returns OrderBuilder (this)
    .addItem("SKU-1", 2)   // returns OrderBuilder (this)
    .addItem("SKU-2", 1)   // returns OrderBuilder (this)
    .withDiscount(0.10)    // returns OrderBuilder (this)
    .build();              // returns Order (new object)

Execution order:

1. new OrderBuilder()         → creates builder on heap
2. .customerId("C001")        → sets field, returns same builder ref
3. .addItem("SKU-1", 2)       → adds to list, returns same builder ref
4. .addItem("SKU-2", 1)       → adds to list, returns same builder ref
5. .withDiscount(0.10)        → sets discount, returns same builder ref
6. .build()                   → creates and returns Order object

varargs Execution

public void log(String level, String message, Object... args) { ... }

// Call: log("INFO", "User {} logged in from {}", userId, ipAddress)
// Compiled as: log("INFO", "User {} logged in from {}", new Object[]{userId, ipAddress})

varargs is syntactic sugar — the compiler creates an array. If zero varargs are passed, an empty array is passed (not null).

Recursion Execution Trace

factorial(4):
  → factorial(3)
    → factorial(2)
      → factorial(1)
        → factorial(0) returns 1
      ← returns 1 * 1 = 1
    ← returns 2 * 1 = 2
  ← returns 3 * 2 = 6
← returns 4 * 6 = 24

Stack growth during factorial(4):
                              [factorial(0)] depth=4
                    [factorial(1)] depth=3
          [factorial(2)] depth=2
[factorial(3)] depth=1
[factorial(4)] depth=0  ← entry point

Each recursive call adds a stack frame. For factorial(10000), 10000 frames → StackOverflowError.

Part 9

Performance Analysis

Method Call Overhead

Invocation Type Overhead Notes
invokestatic ~1-3 ns No dispatch, directly resolved
invokevirtual (monomorphic) ~2-5 ns JIT inlines after profiling
invokevirtual (polymorphic) ~5-15 ns Multiple dispatch paths
invokeinterface ~5-20 ns Larger vtable scan
invokedynamic (lambda) ~2-5 ns after warmup JIT optimizes heavily

JIT method inlining: The JIT compiler inlines small methods (typically < 35 bytecodes) — the method body is copied to the call site, eliminating all call overhead. This is why getter methods in Java are effectively free in production.

Overloading — No Runtime Cost

Overload resolution happens at compile time. By runtime, the JVM already knows exactly which method to call — there is zero extra cost from overloading at runtime.

Recursion vs Iteration Performance

Recursive factorial(n):          Iterative factorial(n):
- n stack frames allocated       - 1 stack frame
- n frame allocations/pops       - 1 loop variable
- Risk of StackOverflowError     - No overflow risk
- Harder for JIT to optimize     - Loop optimized by JIT

For n > ~5000, recursion risks StackOverflowError.
JVM default stack: 512KB-1MB, each frame ~100-200 bytes.
Max safe recursion depth: ~5000-8000 levels.

Tail Recursion — JVM Does NOT Optimize

// Tail recursive — LAST action is the recursive call
public long factorial(int n, long acc) {
    if (n <= 1) return acc;
    return factorial(n - 1, n * acc);  // tail call
}

In Scala/Haskell/functional languages, the compiler optimizes this to iteration. The JVM does NOT do this automatically. The JIT may inline some cases, but there is no guaranteed TCO. Workaround: use explicit iteration.

Part 10

Time Complexity

Method Feature Time Complexity Notes
Method call overhead O(1) Constant per call
Overload resolution O(1) at runtime Resolved at compile time
Virtual dispatch O(1) vtable index lookup
Recursive method O(n) stack depth Space concern, not time per call
varargs array creation O(k) k = number of varargs
Method chaining O(n) total Each step is O(1)

Important: The complexity of a method is determined by its body, not its invocation mechanism. A method call itself is always O(1).

Part 11

Space Complexity

Feature Stack Space Heap Space
Method call frame O(p) — p = parameter count + locals O(0) frame itself
Recursion depth n O(n) — n frames on stack O(0) unless objects created
varargs (k args) O(1) — reference on stack O(k) — array on heap
Method chaining O(1) O(0) if returning this
Objects created in method O(1) reference O(size of object)

StackOverflowError: When the JVM stack is exhausted by too many nested/recursive calls. Default stack size is 256KB-1MB. Increase with: java -Xss2m MyApp

Part 12

Code Examples

Example 1: Method Signatures and Overloading

public class TaxCalculator {

    // Basic method
    public double calculate(double income) {
        return income * 0.30;
    }

    // Overload 1: different parameter type
    public double calculate(int income) {
        return income * 0.30;
    }

    // Overload 2: different parameter count
    public double calculate(double income, String bracket) {
        return switch (bracket) {
            case "LOW"    -> income * 0.10;
            case "MEDIUM" -> income * 0.20;
            case "HIGH"   -> income * 0.30;
            default       -> throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown bracket: " + bracket);
        };
    }

    // Overload 3: varargs
    public double calculateTotal(double... incomes) {
        double total = 0;
        for (double income : incomes) {
            total += calculate(income);
        }
        return total;
    }

    // Static utility method
    public static boolean isAboveThreshold(double income, double threshold) {
        return income > threshold;
    }

    // void method — side effect only
    public void printSummary(double income, double tax) {
        System.out.printf("Income: %.2f | Tax: %.2f | Rate: %.1f%%%n",
            income, tax, (tax / income) * 100);
    }
}

Example 2: Pass-by-Value Demonstration

public class PassByValueDemo {

    // PRIMITIVE — caller's variable NEVER changes
    public static void tryToModifyPrimitive(int n) {
        n = 999;  // Only modifies local copy
        System.out.println("Inside: " + n);  // 999
    }

    // OBJECT — can mutate object's state, cannot reassign caller's reference
    public static void modifyObject(StringBuilder sb) {
        sb.append(" World");  // Mutates the SHARED object — caller WILL see this
        sb = new StringBuilder("Completely new");  // Only changes local copy of reference
    }

    // ARRAY — same as object: can mutate contents, cannot reassign
    public static void modifyArray(int[] arr) {
        arr[0] = 999;        // Caller WILL see this (shared array)
        arr = new int[]{1, 2, 3};  // Caller WON'T see this (new local reference)
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Primitive test
        int x = 5;
        tryToModifyPrimitive(x);
        System.out.println("After: " + x);   // Still 5 ✓

        // Object test
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("Hello");
        modifyObject(sb);
        System.out.println(sb);  // "Hello World" — mutation visible, reassignment not ✓

        // Array test
        int[] arr = {10, 20, 30};
        modifyArray(arr);
        System.out.println(arr[0]);  // 999 — mutation visible ✓
    }
}

Example 3: Recursion and Conversion to Iteration

public class RecursionExamples {

    // Recursive — elegant but limited depth
    public long factorialRecursive(int n) {
        if (n <= 1) return 1;
        return n * factorialRecursive(n - 1);
    }

    // Iterative — production-safe, handles any n
    public long factorialIterative(int n) {
        long result = 1;
        for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++) {
            result *= i;
        }
        return result;
    }

    // Recursive tree traversal (appropriate use of recursion)
    public void printTreePreorder(TreeNode node) {
        if (node == null) return;
        System.out.println(node.value);
        printTreePreorder(node.left);
        printTreePreorder(node.right);
    }

    // Tail-recursive Fibonacci (JVM still creates frames!)
    public long fibTailRecursive(int n, long a, long b) {
        if (n == 0) return a;
        if (n == 1) return b;
        return fibTailRecursive(n - 1, b, a + b);  // Still O(n) stack!
    }

    // Iterative Fibonacci — O(1) space
    public long fibIterative(int n) {
        if (n <= 1) return n;
        long a = 0, b = 1;
        for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++) {
            long next = a + b;
            a = b;
            b = next;
        }
        return b;
    }
}

Example 4: Method Chaining (Builder Pattern)

public class QueryBuilder {
    private String table;
    private List<String> conditions = new ArrayList<>();
    private int limit = 100;
    private String orderBy;

    public QueryBuilder from(String table) {
        this.table = table;
        return this;  // Return this for chaining
    }

    public QueryBuilder where(String condition) {
        this.conditions.add(condition);
        return this;
    }

    public QueryBuilder limit(int n) {
        this.limit = n;
        return this;
    }

    public QueryBuilder orderBy(String column) {
        this.orderBy = column;
        return this;
    }

    public String build() {
        StringBuilder sql = new StringBuilder("SELECT * FROM ").append(table);
        if (!conditions.isEmpty()) {
            sql.append(" WHERE ").append(String.join(" AND ", conditions));
        }
        if (orderBy != null) sql.append(" ORDER BY ").append(orderBy);
        sql.append(" LIMIT ").append(limit);
        return sql.toString();
    }
}

// Usage:
String sql = new QueryBuilder()
    .from("orders")
    .where("status = 'ACTIVE'")
    .where("amount > 1000")
    .orderBy("created_at DESC")
    .limit(50)
    .build();

Example 5: varargs in Practice

public class Logger {

    // varargs enables: log("INFO", "msg"), log("INFO", "msg", arg1), log("INFO", "msg", a, b, c)
    public void log(String level, String template, Object... args) {
        String message = args.length > 0 ? String.format(template, args) : template;
        System.out.printf("[%s] %s%n", level, message);
    }

    // Varargs with other parameters
    public static <T> List<T> listOf(T first, T... rest) {
        List<T> list = new ArrayList<>();
        list.add(first);
        if (rest != null) Collections.addAll(list, rest);
        return list;
    }

    // Passing array as varargs
    public static void demo() {
        Logger log = new Logger();
        log.log("INFO", "Server started");
        log.log("DEBUG", "User %s logged in from %s", "alice", "192.168.1.1");

        // Array can be passed as varargs
        Object[] extraArgs = {"arg1", "arg2"};
        log.log("INFO", "Values: %s and %s", extraArgs);
    }
}
Part 13

Real Production Examples

1. Banking: Service Layer Method Design

@Service
public class AccountService {

    // Clear method signature: noun-verb, all params purposeful
    public TransferResult transferFunds(
            String sourceAccountId,
            String targetAccountId,
            BigDecimal amount,
            Currency currency,
            String initiatedBy) {

        // Guard clauses first
        Account source = accountRepository.findById(sourceAccountId)
            .orElseThrow(() -> new AccountNotFoundException(sourceAccountId));
        Account target = accountRepository.findById(targetAccountId)
            .orElseThrow(() -> new AccountNotFoundException(targetAccountId));

        validateTransfer(source, target, amount, currency);  // Extracted method
        BigDecimal convertedAmount = currencyService.convert(amount, currency, target.getCurrency());

        // Atomic operation
        return executeTransfer(source, target, convertedAmount, initiatedBy);
    }

    // Private method — decomposition keeps public API clean
    private void validateTransfer(Account source, Account target,
                                   BigDecimal amount, Currency currency) {
        if (amount.compareTo(BigDecimal.ZERO) <= 0) {
            throw new InvalidAmountException("Transfer amount must be positive");
        }
        if (source.getBalance().compareTo(amount) < 0) {
            throw new InsufficientFundsException(source.getId(), amount);
        }
        if (source.isBlocked() || target.isBlocked()) {
            throw new AccountBlockedException("One or both accounts are blocked");
        }
    }
}

2. Method Overloading for API Flexibility

public class NotificationService {

    // Overloaded for convenience — internal canonical form
    public void send(Notification notification) {
        sendInternal(notification);
    }

    public void send(String userId, String message) {
        send(Notification.builder()
            .userId(userId)
            .message(message)
            .type(NotificationType.INFO)
            .build());
    }

    public void send(String userId, String message, NotificationType type) {
        send(Notification.builder()
            .userId(userId)
            .message(message)
            .type(type)
            .build());
    }

    // Varargs overload for bulk sends
    public void sendBulk(String message, String... userIds) {
        for (String userId : userIds) {
            send(userId, message);
        }
    }

    private void sendInternal(Notification notification) {
        // Actual send logic
    }
}

3. Recursive Data Structure Processing

@Service
public class CategoryService {

    // Recursive: appropriate for tree structures of bounded depth
    public CategoryDto buildTree(Long categoryId) {
        Category category = categoryRepository.findById(categoryId)
            .orElseThrow(() -> new CategoryNotFoundException(categoryId));

        CategoryDto dto = CategoryMapper.toDto(category);

        // Recurse for children (typically 3-5 levels max in production)
        List<CategoryDto> children = category.getChildren().stream()
            .map(child -> buildTree(child.getId()))  // Recursive call
            .collect(Collectors.toList());

        dto.setChildren(children);
        return dto;
    }

    // Iterative alternative using explicit stack — safe for deep hierarchies
    public List<Long> getAllDescendantIds(Long rootId) {
        List<Long> result = new ArrayList<>();
        Deque<Long> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
        stack.push(rootId);

        while (!stack.isEmpty()) {
            Long id = stack.pop();
            result.add(id);
            categoryRepository.findChildIds(id).forEach(stack::push);
        }
        return result;
    }
}

@PostConstruct — Method Lifecycle Hooks

@Service
public class CacheWarmupService {

    private final ProductRepository productRepository;
    private Map<String, Product> productCache;

    // Constructor injection (preferred over @Autowired on field)
    public CacheWarmupService(ProductRepository productRepository) {
        this.productRepository = productRepository;
    }

    // @PostConstruct: called AFTER dependency injection, BEFORE first request
    @PostConstruct
    public void warmUpCache() {
        log.info("Warming up product cache...");
        productCache = productRepository.findAllActive()
            .stream()
            .collect(Collectors.toMap(Product::getSku, p -> p));
        log.info("Cache warm-up complete: {} products loaded", productCache.size());
    }

    // @PreDestroy: called before bean is destroyed
    @PreDestroy
    public void clearCache() {
        productCache.clear();
        log.info("Product cache cleared");
    }
}

REST API Method Design

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/v1/products")
public class ProductController {

    private final ProductService productService;

    // Constructor injection — no @Autowired needed (single constructor)
    public ProductController(ProductService productService) {
        this.productService = productService;
    }

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<ProductDto> getProduct(@PathVariable String id) {
        return productService.findById(id)
            .map(ResponseEntity::ok)
            .orElse(ResponseEntity.notFound().build());
    }

    @PostMapping
    public ResponseEntity<ProductDto> createProduct(
            @RequestBody @Valid CreateProductRequest request,
            UriComponentsBuilder uriBuilder) {

        ProductDto created = productService.create(request);
        URI location = uriBuilder.path("/api/v1/products/{id}")
            .buildAndExpand(created.getId())
            .toUri();
        return ResponseEntity.created(location).body(created);
    }
}

Part 16

Architect Perspective

Method Design Principles (Clean Code)

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│          ARCHITECT'S METHOD DESIGN CHECKLIST                │
│                                                             │
│  ✓ Single Responsibility — one method does ONE thing       │
│  ✓ Command-Query Separation — either mutate OR return      │
│  ✓ Max 3-4 parameters — more → introduce a parameter object│
│  ✓ Max ~20 lines — longer → extract methods               │
│  ✓ Verb-noun naming — processPayment(), getOrder()         │
│  ✓ Guard clauses first — fail fast on invalid state       │
│  ✓ No boolean flag parameters — extract two methods        │
│  ✓ Avoid output parameters — return value instead         │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Parameter Object Pattern (When You Have Too Many Parameters)

// BAD: 6+ parameters — hard to read, easy to pass in wrong order
public Order createOrder(String customerId, String addressId, 
                          String couponCode, boolean expressShipping,
                          String paymentMethod, boolean giftWrap) { ... }

// GOOD: Group into meaningful object
public record CreateOrderRequest(
    String customerId,
    String addressId,
    String couponCode,
    boolean expressShipping,
    String paymentMethod,
    boolean giftWrap
) {}

public Order createOrder(CreateOrderRequest request) { ... }

Command-Query Separation (CQS)

// VIOLATION: This both mutates AND returns — hard to reason about
public Order processAndReturn(String orderId) {
    Order order = repository.findById(orderId);
    order.setStatus(PROCESSED);
    repository.save(order);
    return order;  // Mixed command + query
}

// CQS COMPLIANT:
public void process(String orderId) {  // Command: mutates state
    Order order = repository.findById(orderId);
    order.setStatus(PROCESSED);
    repository.save(order);
}

public Order getOrder(String orderId) {  // Query: returns without mutation
    return repository.findById(orderId);
}

Part 19

Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: Misunderstanding Pass-by-Value

// BUG: Thinking this swaps the caller's variables
public static void swap(int a, int b) {
    int temp = a;
    a = b;
    b = temp;
    // Only the local copies are swapped — caller sees no change
}

int x = 1, y = 2;
swap(x, y);
System.out.println(x + " " + y);  // Still: 1 2 (not swapped!)

// Real swap requires array or AtomicInteger wrapper
public static void swap(int[] arr, int i, int j) {
    int temp = arr[i];
    arr[i] = arr[j];
    arr[j] = temp;
    // arr is shared — caller WILL see the swap
}

Mistake 2: varargs Ambiguity

void print(String s) { System.out.println("String: " + s); }
void print(String... ss) { System.out.println("varargs"); }

print("hello");  // COMPILE ERROR: ambiguous — both match!

// Fix: Don't create overloads where one is a single-arg version of varargs

Mistake 3: Overload Trap with Autoboxing

void process(int n)    { System.out.println("int"); }
void process(Integer n){ System.out.println("Integer"); }
void process(long n)   { System.out.println("long"); }

int x = 5;
process(x);   // "int" — exact match wins over autoboxing
              // If int overload removed: "long" (widening before boxing)
              // This precedence surprises many developers

Mistake 4: Returning Mutable Internal State

// BUG: Caller can mutate internal list directly!
public class OrderService {
    private List<Order> pendingOrders = new ArrayList<>();

    public List<Order> getPendingOrders() {
        return pendingOrders;  // Exposes internal state!
    }
}

// Fix: Return defensive copy or unmodifiable view
public List<Order> getPendingOrders() {
    return Collections.unmodifiableList(pendingOrders);
    // OR return new ArrayList<>(pendingOrders);
}

Mistake 5: Recursion Without Base Case

// BUG: No base case — infinite recursion → StackOverflowError
public int sum(int[] arr, int index) {
    return arr[index] + sum(arr, index + 1);  // Never stops!
}

// Fix: Always have a base case
public int sum(int[] arr, int index) {
    if (index >= arr.length) return 0;  // Base case
    return arr[index] + sum(arr, index + 1);
}

Mistake 6: Confusing Method Hiding with Overriding

class Parent {
    public static void staticMethod() { System.out.println("Parent"); }
    public void instanceMethod()     { System.out.println("Parent"); }
}

class Child extends Parent {
    public static void staticMethod() { System.out.println("Child"); }  // HIDING, not overriding
    @Override
    public void instanceMethod()     { System.out.println("Child"); }   // OVERRIDING
}

Parent p = new Child();
p.staticMethod();   // "Parent" — resolved at compile time (type is Parent)
p.instanceMethod(); // "Child"  — resolved at runtime (actual type is Child)
Part 20

Interview Questions

Beginner

Q1: What is the difference between a parameter and an argument?
> A parameter is the variable declared in the method definition: void process(Order order) — order is the parameter. An argument is the actual value passed at the call site: process(myOrder) — myOrder is the argument.

Q2: What does void mean as a return type?
> void means the method does not return any value. It performs a side effect (mutation, I/O, etc.) but callers cannot capture a return value. Such methods are "commands" in Command-Query Separation terminology.

Q3: What is method overloading?
> Multiple methods in the same class with the same name but different parameter lists (different number, types, or order of parameters). Return type alone cannot distinguish overloads. Resolution happens at compile time.

Intermediate

Q4: Is Java pass-by-value or pass-by-reference? Prove it.
> Java is strictly pass-by-value. For objects, the "value" passed is a copy of the reference. Proof: in a method, reassigning the parameter (obj = new Obj()) never affects the caller's variable — only the local copy of the reference changes. If Java were pass-by-reference, reassignment would affect the caller.

Q5: Why doesn't Java optimize tail recursion?
> The JVM specification does not mandate Tail Call Optimization (TCO). Additionally, accurate stack traces (for debugging and exception handling) require every active call to have a stack frame. JVM-based functional languages (Scala, Clojure) implement their own TCO at the compiler level, not relying on JVM guarantees.

Q6: How does varargs work internally? What is the performance concern?
> varargs is syntactic sugar — the compiler creates an array from the varargs arguments. The method receives an array. Performance concern: a new array is heap-allocated per call. For hot paths with zero or one arg, this can create GC pressure. Overloaded non-varargs versions are sometimes provided for common arities (e.g., List.of() has 10 specific overloads before List.of(E... elements)).

Advanced / Architect

Q7: ArrayList.get() vs LinkedList.get() — both have the same method signature. What decides which is called at runtime?
> Virtual dispatch via vtable. The JVM looks at the actual runtime type of the object (not the declared type). If declared as List<T> list, the JVM calls list's actual class's vtable entry for get(). For ArrayList, it jumps to O(1) index access; for LinkedList, it jumps to O(n) traversal. This is polymorphism at work.

Q8: A method has 8 parameters. As an architect, what do you do?
> Introduce a Parameter Object (encapsulate related parameters into a class or record). Check if the method violates Single Responsibility (too many params often means the method does too many things). Apply Builder pattern if the parameters are optional. Check if some params can be derived from others. Target: max 3-4 parameters per method.

Q9: How does invokedynamic relate to lambda expressions?
> Lambda expressions compile to invokedynamic instructions (JEP 292). The first time the lambda site is executed, the JVM calls a bootstrap method (in LambdaMetafactory) which generates the lambda class bytecode dynamically. Subsequent calls use the cached class. This approach was chosen over anonymous inner classes to allow JVM evolution without fixing the lambda representation in bytecode.

Part 21

Revision Sheet

Must-Know Facts

  1. Method signature = name + parameter types (return type NOT included)
  2. Java is always pass-by-value — objects pass copies of references
  3. Reassigning a parameter in a method never affects the caller
  4. Mutating an object through a parameter does affect the caller (shared object)
  5. Overloading is resolved at compile time; overriding at runtime
  6. invokevirtual for instance methods; invokestatic for static; invokedynamic for lambdas
  7. Each method call creates a stack frame — popped on return
  8. varargs compiles to an array — every call allocates an array on heap
  9. JVM does NOT guarantee tail call optimization
  10. Default stack is 512KB-1MB per thread; deep recursion causes StackOverflowError
  11. JIT inlines small methods (< ~35 bytecodes) — effectively zero call overhead
  12. @PostConstruct runs after injection; @PreDestroy runs before bean destruction

Quick Reference

METHOD MODIFIERS:
  public/protected/private  → access control
  static                    → no instance needed, invokestatic
  final                     → cannot override, JIT can inline
  abstract                  → no body, must be overridden
  synchronized              → acquires monitor lock on entry

OVERLOAD vs OVERRIDE:
  Overload: same class, same name, DIFFERENT params → compile-time
  Override: subclass, same name, SAME params        → runtime

PASS-BY-VALUE RULES:
  Primitive argument    → caller's variable NEVER changes
  Object mutation       → caller DOES see mutation (shared object)
  Object reassignment   → caller does NOT see reassignment (local copy)
  Array element change  → caller DOES see it (shared array)
  Array reassignment    → caller does NOT see it (local copy)

Practice — Lesson 7

Easy Exercises

  1. Write a class Calculator with overloaded add() methods accepting: (int, int), (double, double), (int, int, int).
  2. Demonstrate pass-by-value: write a method doubleValue(int n) that doubles n inside, and show the caller's variable is unchanged.
  3. Write a Logger class with a method log(String level, String message, Object... args) using varargs.
  4. Implement StringUtils.join(String separator, String... parts) using varargs.

Medium Exercises

  1. Write a BankAccount class with method chaining: deposit(double).withdraw(double).transfer(String, double) — each returns this.
  2. Write factorial(int n) both recursively and iteratively. Test with n=10, n=100, n=10000 — which throws StackOverflowError?
  3. Implement a swap method that actually works (hint: use array or int[] wrapper).
  4. Write processOrder(Order order) using guard clauses and extracted private helper methods (validateOrder, reserveInventory, chargePayment).

Advanced Exercises

  1. Implement retry(Supplier<T> operation, int maxAttempts, Class<? extends Exception> retryOn) as a generic method.
  2. Create a QueryBuilder with method chaining supporting select(), from(), where(), groupBy(), having(), orderBy(), limit() — returning this except for build().

Production Scenarios

  1. API Design: Design a NotificationService with overloaded send() methods for: basic (userId + message), typed (userId + message + type), scheduled (userId + message + Instant), and bulk (message + varargs userIds).
  2. Pass-by-Value Trap: You're code-reviewing a payment service method that takes a PaymentRequest and modifies its fields for normalization. Is this safe? What are the risks? How would you refactor?

Debugging Exercises

  1. What is wrong with this code?
    java public static void swap(String a, String b) { String temp = a; a = b; b = temp; } String x = "hello", y = "world"; swap(x, y); System.out.println(x + " " + y); // What prints?
  2. Why does this cause a StackOverflowError?
    java public int countdown(int n) { if (n == 0) return 0; return countdown(n - 1) + countdown(n - 1); } countdown(40); // Causes StackOverflowError — why?

Interview Challenges

  1. Prove Java is pass-by-value (not pass-by-reference) using a code example that demonstrates reassigning an object parameter doesn't affect the caller.
  2. You have a method process(Customer c, Order o, Payment p, Shipping s, Coupon coupon, boolean notify). How do you refactor this, and what principles does it violate?
  3. If overloading is resolved at compile time, what happens when you call an overloaded method through a supertype reference? Write a code example and explain the output.

Part 1

Concept Overview

An array in Java is a fixed-size, ordered, zero-indexed container that holds elements of a single type. Arrays are the most primitive collection structure in the language — no generics, no dynamic resizing, no built-in methods for searching or sorting beyond java.util.Arrays. Understanding arrays deeply is non-negotiable for a JVM architect because every higher-level collection (ArrayList, HashMap internal buckets, byte streams) ultimately reduces to arrays at the JVM layer.

Arrays in Java are objects. They live on the heap, are garbage-collected like any other object, and carry a length field as a built-in attribute of the array object itself (not a method call). This single distinction — array.length (field) vs String.length() (method) — is a perennial interview question and a genuine source of bugs in codebases.

Key properties of Java arrays:

Property Details
Fixed size Set at creation; cannot grow or shrink
Zero-indexed First element at index 0, last at length - 1
Type-safe All elements must be the same type (or subtypes for reference arrays)
Heap-allocated The array object lives on the heap regardless of where the reference is declared
Covariant String[] is a subtype of Object[] (this causes runtime bugs — covered in Part 7)
Default-initialized Numeric types → 0, boolean → false, references → null
Part 2

Historical Context and Motivation

Java inherited the array concept from C/C++ but added two critical safety guarantees that C arrays lack:

  1. Bounds checking — every array access is checked at runtime. Accessing arr[-1] or arr[arr.length] throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. In C, this is undefined behavior and the root of thousands of security vulnerabilities (buffer overflows). The JVM's bounds checking adds a small overhead but eliminates an entire class of CVEs.

  2. Null safety structure — Java arrays know their length. C arrays are just pointers; length is always tracked manually, leading to off-by-one errors. Java bakes length into the array object header.

Arrays were the only collection mechanism in Java 1.0. The Collections Framework (java.util) arrived in Java 1.2, and generics in Java 5. Today, arrays are primarily used for:

  • Low-level, performance-critical code (byte buffers, image pixel data, DSP)
  • Framework internals (Spring's Object[] varargs, JPA column mappings)
  • Interfacing with native/JNI code
  • Fixed-size data structures where resizing overhead is unacceptable

For application-layer code, prefer List<T>, Deque<T>, or Map<K,V> over raw arrays.

Part 3

Deep Dive

Declaration vs Initialization

// Declaration — allocates only the reference on the stack (or in the object field)
int[] arr;          // preferred style
int arr2[];         // C-style, legal but discouraged

// Initialization — allocates the array object on the heap
arr = new int[5];   // 5 ints, all defaulting to 0

// Declaration + initialization in one line
int[] scores = new int[10];

// Array literal (static initializer) — size inferred from values
int[] primes = {2, 3, 5, 7, 11};

// Explicit new with initializer
String[] names = new String[]{"Alice", "Bob", "Carol"};

The length Field

int[] arr = new int[5];
System.out.println(arr.length);    // 5   — field, not a method
System.out.println("hello".length()); // 5 — method on String, note the ()

length is a special pseudo-field defined by the JVM specification (JVMS §6.5 arraylength). It is not declared in source code; the JVM synthesizes it. It is final — you cannot assign to it.

Multi-Dimensional Arrays

Java does not have true 2D arrays — it has arrays of arrays (jagged arrays). This distinction matters for memory layout and performance:

// Rectangular (but still jagged internally)
int[][] matrix = new int[3][4];   // 3 rows, 4 columns each

// Jagged array — rows of different lengths
int[][] jagged = new int[3][];
jagged[0] = new int[2];
jagged[1] = new int[5];
jagged[2] = new int[1];

// 3D array
int[][][] cube = new int[2][3][4];

// Access
matrix[1][2] = 42;   // row 1, column 2

Default Values

int[]     ints    = new int[3];       // [0, 0, 0]
double[]  doubles = new double[3];    // [0.0, 0.0, 0.0]
boolean[] bools   = new boolean[3];   // [false, false, false]
char[]    chars   = new char[3];      // ['\u0000', '\u0000', '\u0000']
String[]  strs    = new String[3];    // [null, null, null]
Object[]  objs    = new Object[3];    // [null, null, null]
Part 4

ASCII Memory Diagram

Trace what happens when you execute int[] arr = new int[5];:

  STACK FRAME (main method)
  ┌──────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Local Variable Table            │
  │  ┌──────────┬──────────────────┐ │
  │  │  Slot 0  │  arr (reference) │ │
  │  │          │  0x7f3a2b10      │ │   ──┐
  │  └──────────┴──────────────────┘ │     │
  └──────────────────────────────────┘     │  reference points to heap
                                           │
  HEAP                                     │
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────▼──────────────────────────────┐
  │  Array Object @ 0x7f3a2b10                                            │
  │  ┌──────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  Object Header   │  mark word (8 bytes) + klass ptr (4/8 bytes)  │ │
  │  ├──────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │
  │  │  length field    │  5  (int, 4 bytes)                            │ │
  │  ├──────────────────┼────┬────┬────┬────┬────────────────────────── ┤ │
  │  │  Elements        │ 0  │ 0  │ 0  │ 0  │  0                        │ │
  │  │  (5 × 4 bytes)   │[0] │[1] │[2] │[3] │ [4]                       │ │
  │  └──────────────────┴────┴────┴────┴────┴───────────────────────────┘ │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Total heap allocation:
    Object header  ≈ 12–16 bytes (compressed oops)
    length field   =  4 bytes
    5 × int        = 20 bytes
    Padding        =  0–4 bytes (8-byte alignment)
    Total          ≈ 36–40 bytes

For a String[] array, each element slot holds a reference (4 or 8 bytes), not the String object itself. The String objects are separate heap allocations pointed to by those references.

  String[] names = new String[3];

  HEAP
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Array Object @ 0xA100                                          │
  │  header | length=3 | [null] [null] [null]                       │
  │                         │                                       │
  │  After names[0] = "Alice";                                      │
  │  header | length=3 | [0xB200] [null] [null]                     │
  │                          │                                      │
  │                          ▼                                      │
  │  String Object @ 0xB200                                         │
  │  char[] value = {'A','l','i','c','e'}   (or byte[] in Java 9+) │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Part 5

Iteration Patterns

Indexed for Loop

int[] arr = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50};

for (int i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) {
    System.out.println("Index " + i + ": " + arr[i]);
}

Use when: you need the index, you need to modify elements, you need to iterate in reverse, or you need to skip elements.

Enhanced for Loop (for-each)

for (int value : arr) {
    System.out.println(value);
}

Use when: you only need the value, not the index. Compiles to an iterator for Iterable types; for arrays, it compiles to a standard indexed loop — no iterator object is created, no heap allocation.

Performance Note

For primitive arrays (int[], long[], double[]), enhanced for and indexed for compile to equivalent bytecode. For Iterable collections (List<Integer>), enhanced for creates an Iterator object. Prefer arrays of primitives over List<Integer> in tight loops to avoid boxing overhead.

// Reverse iteration — only possible with indexed for
for (int i = arr.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
    System.out.println(arr[i]);
}

// Parallel index tracking — two arrays in lock-step
for (int i = 0; i < keys.length; i++) {
    map.put(keys[i], values[i]);
}
Part 6

Copying Arrays

Java provides four mechanisms for copying arrays, each with different performance and semantics:

1. System.arraycopy — Fastest

int[] src  = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
int[] dest = new int[5];

// System.arraycopy(src, srcPos, dest, destPos, length)
System.arraycopy(src, 0, dest, 0, src.length);
// dest = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

// Copy a sub-range
System.arraycopy(src, 1, dest, 0, 3);
// dest = [2, 3, 4, 0, 0]

System.arraycopy is a JVM intrinsic — the JIT replaces it with a native memcpy-equivalent instruction on x86 (REP MOVS). It is the fastest way to copy arrays in Java. Use in performance-critical paths.

2. Arrays.copyOf — Convenient, Handles Resizing

import java.util.Arrays;

int[] original = {1, 2, 3};
int[] copy = Arrays.copyOf(original, original.length);      // exact copy
int[] larger = Arrays.copyOf(original, 6);                  // [1, 2, 3, 0, 0, 0]
int[] smaller = Arrays.copyOf(original, 2);                 // [1, 2]

Internally calls System.arraycopy. Useful when you need to resize as you copy.

3. Arrays.copyOfRange — Sub-array Copy

int[] arr = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50};
int[] sub = Arrays.copyOfRange(arr, 1, 4);   // [20, 30, 40]

4. clone() — Shallow Copy

int[] arr = {1, 2, 3};
int[] copy = arr.clone();   // separate array, same values

For primitive arrays, clone() produces a true independent copy. For object arrays, it's a shallow copy — the new array holds the same object references as the original. Modifying an element in the clone modifies the original's element too (since both references point to the same object).

String[] strs = {"A", "B", "C"};
String[] clone = strs.clone();

// clone[0] is the same String object as strs[0]
// Strings are immutable, so this is safe, but for mutable objects:

int[][] matrix = {{1, 2}, {3, 4}};
int[][] matrixClone = matrix.clone();  // shallow!
matrixClone[0][0] = 99;
System.out.println(matrix[0][0]);      // 99 — original affected!
Part 7

Array Covariance (The Trap)

Java arrays are covariant: if B extends A, then B[] is assignable to A[]. This seems logical but creates a runtime type safety hole:

String[] strings = {"hello", "world"};
Object[] objects = strings;          // compiles — covariance

objects[0] = 42;                     // compiles — Object can hold Integer
// Throws ArrayStoreException at RUNTIME
// JVM checks that 42 (Integer) is compatible with String[] at runtime

Generics (List<String>) are invariant to avoid this exact problem — List<String> is NOT a List<Object>. This is why arrays and generics mix poorly:

// This won't compile — generic array creation is forbidden
List<String>[] arr = new List<String>[10];   // compile error

// You must use unchecked cast or List<List<String>>
Part 8

`java.util.Arrays` Utility Class

import java.util.Arrays;

int[] arr = {5, 3, 1, 4, 2};

// Sort (dual-pivot quicksort for primitives, timsort for objects)
Arrays.sort(arr);                           // [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

// Binary search — array MUST be sorted first
int idx = Arrays.binarySearch(arr, 3);      // 2 (index of value 3)

// Fill
Arrays.fill(arr, 0);                        // [0, 0, 0, 0, 0]

// Compare
int[] a = {1, 2, 3};
int[] b = {1, 2, 3};
System.out.println(Arrays.equals(a, b));    // true
System.out.println(a.equals(b));            // false (Object.equals — reference)
System.out.println(a == b);                 // false (different objects)

// Print
System.out.println(Arrays.toString(arr));        // [0, 0, 0, 0, 0]
System.out.println(Arrays.deepToString(matrix)); // [[1, 2], [3, 4]]

// Convert to List (fixed-size, backed by the array)
List<String> list = Arrays.asList("A", "B", "C");
// list.add("D");  // UnsupportedOperationException — fixed size!
// To get a mutable list:
List<String> mutable = new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList("A", "B", "C"));

// Stream from array (Java 8+)
int sum = Arrays.stream(arr).sum();
int[] doubled = Arrays.stream(arr).map(x -> x * 2).toArray();
Part 9

Common Mistakes and Edge Cases

// Mistake 1: Off-by-one in loop bounds
for (int i = 0; i <= arr.length; i++) {   // BUG: should be <, not <=
    System.out.println(arr[i]);           // ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException on last iter
}

// Mistake 2: Comparing arrays with ==
int[] a = {1, 2, 3};
int[] b = {1, 2, 3};
if (a == b) { ... }           // always false — different object references
if (Arrays.equals(a, b)) { } // correct

// Mistake 3: Null reference
int[] arr = null;
System.out.println(arr.length);   // NullPointerException

// Mistake 4: Empty array vs null
int[] empty = new int[0];
System.out.println(empty.length); // 0 — valid, no NPE
System.out.println(empty[0]);     // ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException

// Mistake 5: Shallow clone of object array
StringBuilder[] sbs = {new StringBuilder("A"), new StringBuilder("B")};
StringBuilder[] clone = sbs.clone();
clone[0].append("modified");
System.out.println(sbs[0]);  // "Amodified" — original affected!
Part 10

Performance Analysis

Operation Time Complexity Notes
Access arr[i] O(1) Direct memory offset calculation
Linear search O(n) No built-in; use a loop
Binary search (sorted) O(log n) Arrays.binarySearch
Arrays.sort (primitive) O(n log n) avg Dual-pivot quicksort
Arrays.sort (object) O(n log n) Timsort, stable
System.arraycopy O(n) Native memcpy, very fast
Insert/delete N/A Arrays are fixed size
Append N/A Must create new array

Memory: Primitive arrays are the most memory-efficient collection in Java. A int[1000] costs exactly ≈4016 bytes (header + length + 4000 bytes of ints). An ArrayList<Integer> holding the same 1000 integers costs roughly ≈20KB due to autoboxing (each Integer object = 16 bytes on heap) plus the Object[] internal array.

JVM Internals

Array Object Layout (HotSpot JVM)

┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Object Header                                         │
│  ┌──────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  mark word       │  8 bytes                      │  │
│  │  (GC, lock info) │  (lock state, hashCode, GC)   │  │
│  ├──────────────────┼───────────────────────────────┤  │
│  │  klass pointer   │  4 bytes (compressed oops on) │  │
│  │  (type info)     │  or 8 bytes (uncompressed)    │  │
│  ├──────────────────┼───────────────────────────────┤  │
│  │  array length    │  4 bytes (int)                │  │
│  └──────────────────┴───────────────────────────────┘  │
│  Padding to 8-byte boundary if needed                  │
│  Element data [...] — contiguous in memory             │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Bytecode for Array Operations

// Source: int[] arr = new int[5];
newarray 10      // opcode: creates int[] (type 10 = int)

// Source: arr[2] = 42;
iconst_2         // push index 2
bipush 42        // push value 42
iastore          // int array store — JVM checks bounds here

// Source: int x = arr[2];
iconst_2         // push index 2
iaload           // int array load — JVM checks bounds here

// Source: arr.length
arraylength      // dedicated opcode, not a field access in bytecode

Production Patterns

Pattern 1: Batch Processing with Fixed-Size Chunks

public class BatchProcessor {
    private static final int BATCH_SIZE = 1000;

    public void processRecords(List<Record> records) {
        // Convert to array once for faster indexed access in tight loops
        Record[] recordArray = records.toArray(new Record[0]);
        int total = recordArray.length;

        for (int batchStart = 0; batchStart < total; batchStart += BATCH_SIZE) {
            int batchEnd = Math.min(batchStart + BATCH_SIZE, total);
            processBatch(recordArray, batchStart, batchEnd);
        }
    }

    private void processBatch(Record[] records, int start, int end) {
        for (int i = start; i < end; i++) {
            // Process records[i]
        }
    }
}

Pattern 2: Ring Buffer (Circular Buffer)

A fixed-size array implementing a queue without shifting elements:

public class RingBuffer<T> {
    private final Object[] buffer;
    private int head = 0;
    private int tail = 0;
    private int size = 0;

    public RingBuffer(int capacity) {
        this.buffer = new Object[capacity];
    }

    public void enqueue(T item) {
        if (size == buffer.length) throw new IllegalStateException("Buffer full");
        buffer[tail] = item;
        tail = (tail + 1) % buffer.length;
        size++;
    }

    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    public T dequeue() {
        if (size == 0) throw new NoSuchElementException();
        T item = (T) buffer[head];
        buffer[head] = null;   // prevent memory leak
        head = (head + 1) % buffer.length;
        size--;
        return item;
    }
}

Pattern 3: Avoid Arrays for Dynamic Collections

// BAD — manual resizing, error-prone
int[] dynamic = new int[10];
int count = 0;

void add(int value) {
    if (count == dynamic.length) {
        dynamic = Arrays.copyOf(dynamic, dynamic.length * 2);  // O(n) copy
    }
    dynamic[count++] = value;
}

// GOOD — use ArrayList, which does this for you
List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>();
list.add(value);

@RequestParam with Arrays

Spring MVC binds repeated query parameters to arrays automatically:

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api")

    // GET /api/products?ids=1&ids=2&ids=3
    @GetMapping("/products")
    public List<Product> getProducts(@RequestParam Long[] ids) {

    // Optional with default value
    @GetMapping("/search")
    public List<Product> search(
        @RequestParam(defaultValue = "") String[] categories
    ) {

Part 14

Testing Arrays

import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.*;

class ArrayTest {

    @Test
    void arrayCopyIsIndependent() {
        int[] original = {1, 2, 3};
        int[] copy = Arrays.copyOf(original, original.length);

        copy[0] = 99;

        assertThat(original[0]).isEqualTo(1);       // original unchanged
        assertThat(copy[0]).isEqualTo(99);
    }

    @Test
    void arrayEquality() {
        int[] a = {1, 2, 3};
        int[] b = {1, 2, 3};

        assertThat(a).isNotSameAs(b);               // different objects
        assertThat(a).isEqualTo(b);                 // AssertJ checks content
        assertThat(Arrays.equals(a, b)).isTrue();   // explicit content check
    }

    @Test
    void outOfBoundsThrows() {
        int[] arr = new int[3];
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> arr[5])
            .isInstanceOf(ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.class);
    }
}

Anti-Patterns

Anti-Pattern Problem Fix

arr.equals(other) Inherited from Object, reference comparison Arrays.equals()

Part 17

Concurrency Considerations

Arrays are not thread-safe. Concurrent reads are safe, but concurrent reads and writes (or concurrent writes) require synchronization:

// Thread-unsafe — two threads writing to different indices can cause issues
// due to CPU cache and memory visibility
int[] shared = new int[100];

// Thread 1
shared[0] = 42;

// Thread 2 — may not see 42 without happens-before relationship

// Safe option 1: synchronized block
synchronized(shared) { shared[0] = 42; }

// Safe option 2: AtomicIntegerArray
AtomicIntegerArray atomicArr = new AtomicIntegerArray(100);
atomicArr.set(0, 42);
int val = atomicArr.get(0);

// Safe option 3: use concurrent collections
// CopyOnWriteArrayList for read-heavy scenarios
Part 18

Generics and Type Erasure Interaction

You cannot create a generic array directly:

// Compile error — generic array creation
T[] arr = new T[10];           // illegal
List<String>[] arr2 = new List<String>[10];  // illegal

// Workaround 1: unchecked cast
@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
T[] arr = (T[]) new Object[10];

// Workaround 2: use Array.newInstance via reflection
@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
T[] arr = (T[]) java.lang.reflect.Array.newInstance(clazz, 10);

// This is why ArrayList uses Object[] internally:
// private Object[] elementData;
Part 19

Java 11+ Enhancements

While arrays themselves haven't changed, working with arrays has become more ergonomic:

// Java 9: Arrays.mismatch — first index where two arrays differ
int[] a = {1, 2, 3, 4};
int[] b = {1, 2, 9, 4};
int mismatch = Arrays.mismatch(a, b);   // 2

// Java 9: Arrays.compare — lexicographic comparison
int cmp = Arrays.compare(a, b);         // negative (a < b at index 2)

// Java 11: toArray with IntFunction (from Collection)
List<String> list = List.of("a", "b", "c");
String[] arr = list.toArray(String[]::new);   // preferred over list.toArray(new String[0])
Part 20

Interview Preparation

Q1: What is the difference between array.length and String.length()?

array.length is a field — a property directly stored in the array object's header by the JVM. It requires no method invocation. String.length() is a method call that returns the count of characters (or more precisely, char values) in the string. The parentheses are the giveaway: method = (), field = no ().

Q2: What is the difference between an array and an ArrayList?

Aspect int[] / Object[] ArrayList<T>
Size Fixed at creation Dynamic (grows automatically)
Type Can hold primitives Holds only objects (autoboxing)
Performance Faster, no boxing Slightly slower, boxing overhead
Methods None (only Arrays.*) Rich API: add, remove, contains
Type safety Runtime (ArrayStoreException) Compile-time (generics)
Null elements Allowed Allowed
Covariance Yes (String[] → Object[]) No (List<String> ≠ List<Object>)

Q3: Is arr.clone() a deep copy or a shallow copy?

Shallow copy. For primitive arrays, the values are copied (primitives are values, not references, so it's effectively a deep copy for that case). For object arrays, the references are copied — both the original and the clone point to the same objects. Modifying a mutable object through the clone is visible through the original.

Q4: What does Arrays.asList return? Can you add elements?

Arrays.asList returns a java.util.Arrays$ArrayList — a fixed-size List backed by the original array. You can call set() (modify existing elements) but not add() or remove() — these throw UnsupportedOperationException. The backing array is the original, so mutations via set() are visible in the original array.

Q5: What is ArrayStoreException?

Thrown by the JVM when you try to store a value of the wrong type in an array. This happens due to array covariance: String[] can be assigned to Object[], but if you then try to store an Integer in it, the JVM's runtime type check fails and throws ArrayStoreException.

Part 21

Code Lab: Practical Exercises

// Exercise 1: Rotate array left by k positions
public static int[] rotateLeft(int[] arr, int k) {
    int n = arr.length;
    k = k % n;  // handle k > n
    int[] result = new int[n];
    System.arraycopy(arr, k, result, 0, n - k);
    System.arraycopy(arr, 0, result, n - k, k);
    return result;
}

// Exercise 2: Find maximum in array
public static int max(int[] arr) {
    if (arr == null || arr.length == 0)
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("Empty array");
    int max = arr[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < arr.length; i++) {
        if (arr[i] > max) max = arr[i];
    }
    return max;
}

// Exercise 3: Two-sum (unsorted, find indices)
public static int[] twoSum(int[] nums, int target) {
    Map<Integer, Integer> seen = new HashMap<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
        int complement = target - nums[i];
        if (seen.containsKey(complement)) {
            return new int[]{seen.get(complement), i};
        }
        seen.put(nums[i], i);
    }
    return new int[]{};
}

// Exercise 4: Merge two sorted arrays
public static int[] mergeSorted(int[] a, int[] b) {
    int[] result = new int[a.length + b.length];
    int i = 0, j = 0, k = 0;
    while (i < a.length && j < b.length) {
        result[k++] = (a[i] <= b[j]) ? a[i++] : b[j++];
    }
    while (i < a.length) result[k++] = a[i++];
    while (j < b.length) result[k++] = b[j++];
    return result;
}

When to use arrays vs alternatives:

Decision tree:

  int[], long[]        List.subList  List<T>
  double[], etc.       or Arrays.copyOfRange

Architect rules:

  • Never expose raw array fields in public API — return defensive copies
  • Use int[] / long[] / double[] for numeric computation pipelines to avoid boxing
  • Prefer List<T> in service/repository layers for flexibility
  • Use byte[] for binary I/O, serialization, cryptographic operations
  • Document whether array parameters are owned (caller must not modify) or borrowed
  • In multithreaded code, use AtomicIntegerArray or synchronize access
  • Profile before switching List<Integer> to int[] — the optimization may not matter at your scale

Coding Challenges

  1. Reverse in-place: Reverse an int array without using extra space.

Answers to Quick-Check

  1. false
  2. ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
  3. System.arraycopy — it's a JVM intrinsic compiled to a native memcpy instruction
  4. Generic array creation is forbidden (type erasure + covariance safety); raw List[] is allowed (unsafe, unchecked)
  5. Something like [I@1b6d3586 — arrays don't override toString(), so Object.toString() prints [I (type descriptor for int[]) + @ + hashCode

Part 1

Concept Overview

String is simultaneously the most used type in Java and one of the most misunderstood. It is not a primitive — it is a class (java.lang.String) — yet it receives special language-level treatment: a string literal syntax ("hello"), compile-time concatenation optimization, a dedicated memory region called the String Pool, and a special relationship with the + operator. Every Java developer writes strings from day one; most Java developers misuse them for years.

The three core facts that every architect must internalize:

  1. Strings are immutable — once created, the character data inside a String object never changes. Every "modification" creates a new object.
  2. String literals are interned — all string literals in your codebase are stored in the String Pool (a JVM-managed cache), and identical literals share the same object reference.
  3. String concatenation in loops is O(n²) — each + in a loop creates a new String object and copies all existing characters. Use StringBuilder in loops.

Understanding these three facts explains most string-related bugs, performance issues, and interview questions in Java.

Part 2

Historical Context and Motivation

Why Immutable?

Java's design team, drawing from lessons in distributed systems and concurrent programming, made String immutable in Java 1.0. The motivations were:

  1. Thread safety: Immutable objects can be shared freely between threads without synchronization — no thread can corrupt another's string view.
  2. Caching: The hash code of a String is expensive to compute (O(n) — must visit every character). With immutability, Java computes it once on first hashCode() call and caches it in an internal field. Every subsequent call is O(1).
  3. Security: String is used for file paths, network addresses, SQL queries, and passwords. If strings were mutable, a caller could pass a "safe" path string and then mutate it before the security check completes. Immutability closes this race window.
  4. String pool: Interning only makes sense if strings never change. If strings were mutable, two variables pointing to the same pooled object would interfere with each other.

Internal Representation Evolution

Java Version Internal Storage Notes
Java 1.0 – 8 char[] (UTF-16) Always 2 bytes per char
Java 9+ byte[] + coder field Latin-1 strings use 1 byte/char; UTF-16 for others

Java 9's Compact Strings (JEP 254) halved memory for ASCII/Latin-1 strings (the vast majority in most applications). A 100-character ASCII string dropped from 200 bytes to 100 bytes of character data. This was a transparent change — no API changes, same behavior.

Part 3

Deep Dive: Immutability

String s1 = "hello";
String s2 = s1.toUpperCase();   // creates a NEW String "HELLO"

System.out.println(s1);         // "hello" — unchanged
System.out.println(s2);         // "HELLO"

// Every "mutating" operation returns a new String
String s3 = "  trim me  ";
String s4 = s3.trim();          // new String "trim me", s3 unchanged

String s5 = "replace";
String s6 = s5.replace('e', 'a'); // new String "raplaca"

// Immutability is enforced by:
// 1. The char[]/byte[] field is private and final
// 2. String has no setter methods
// 3. String is declared 'final' — cannot be subclassed to add mutability

The final Field Chain

public final class String {
    private final byte[] value;   // Java 9+; char[] in Java 8
    private final byte coder;     // LATIN1 = 0, UTF16 = 1
    private int hash;             // cached hashCode (not final — lazy init)
    // ...
}

Even though hash is not final (it's computed lazily on first hashCode() call), this is safe because: (a) its default value 0 is also the sentinel for "not computed yet," and (b) writing the same computed value multiple times from multiple threads is idempotent — all threads compute the same hash, and writing an int is atomic on the JVM.

Part 4

ASCII Memory Diagram: String Pool and Heap Layout

String Pool Internals

The String Pool (also called the String Intern Pool or String Constant Pool) is a HashSet-like structure maintained by the JVM. In Java 7+, it lives in the heap (it was in PermGen in Java 6 and earlier). This matters for GC: pooled strings are now garbage-collected when no references remain.

SOURCE CODE:
  String a = "hello";
  String b = "hello";
  String c = new String("hello");
  String d = c.intern();

JVM MEMORY LAYOUT:

  STACK (main frame)
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  a  → 0xAA10  │  b  → 0xAA10  │             │
  │  c  → 0xBB20  │  d  → 0xAA10  │             │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  HEAP
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                    │
  │  ╔════════════════════════════════════════╗                        │
  │  ║       STRING POOL (in heap, Java 7+)  ║                        │
  │  ║                                        ║                        │
  │  ║  @ 0xAA10  ┌──────────────────────┐   ║                        │
  │  ║            │  String "hello"       │   ║                        │
  │  ║            │  value → byte[]{...} │   ║                        │
  │  ║            │  hash  = 99162322    │   ║                        │
  │  ║            └──────────────────────┘   ║                        │
  │  ╚════════════════════════════════════════╝                        │
  │                                                                    │
  │  Regular Heap (non-pool)                                           │
  │  @ 0xBB20  ┌──────────────────────┐                               │
  │            │  String "hello"       │  ← new String("hello")       │
  │            │  value → 0xCC30      │  (separate object)            │
  │            └──────────────────────┘                               │
  │  @ 0xCC30  ┌─────────────────────────┐                            │
  │            │  byte[] {'h','e','l',   │                            │
  │            │          'l','o'}       │                            │
  │            └─────────────────────────┘                            │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  a == b   → true   (same pool object @ 0xAA10)
  a == c   → false  (c is separate heap object @ 0xBB20)
  a == d   → true   (intern() returned the pool object)
  a.equals(c) → true (content is the same)
Part 5

`==` vs `.equals()` for Strings

This is the #1 String bug in Java codebases:

String s1 = "Java";
String s2 = "Java";
String s3 = new String("Java");
String s4 = "Ja" + "va";          // compile-time constant folding → pool
String s5 = "Ja";
String s6 = s5 + "va";            // runtime concatenation → new heap object

System.out.println(s1 == s2);     // true  — both from pool
System.out.println(s1 == s3);     // false — s3 bypasses pool
System.out.println(s1 == s4);     // true  — compiler folds literal concatenation
System.out.println(s1 == s6);     // false — s6 computed at runtime, on heap
System.out.println(s1.equals(s3));// true  — content comparison

// RULE: ALWAYS use .equals() to compare String content
// NEVER use == unless you explicitly need reference identity

Why Literal Concatenation Is Folded at Compile Time

String s = "Ja" + "va";
// The compiler sees two string literals at compile time.
// It folds them into "Java" before generating bytecode.
// Equivalent to: String s = "Java";
// This is a constant expression per the Java Language Specification.

When at least one operand is a variable or the result of a method call, folding cannot happen — concatenation happens at runtime, creating a new heap object.

Part 6

`intern()`

String.intern() manually adds a string to the pool (or returns the existing pooled instance if one already exists):

String pooled = new String("hello").intern();
String literal = "hello";

System.out.println(pooled == literal);  // true — both point to pool object

When to use intern():

  • When you read many duplicate strings from external data (CSV files, database columns with low cardinality values like status codes, country codes)
  • When you need == comparisons for performance (e.g., in a high-throughput state machine)
  • Be cautious: pooled strings are retained until GC — if you intern thousands of unique strings, you bloat the pool

When NOT to use intern():

  • On arbitrary user input (unbounded growth of pool)
  • As a general optimization without profiling (pool operations are slower than equals())
Part 7

String vs StringBuilder vs StringBuffer

The Core Problem: Concatenation in Loops

// TERRIBLE — O(n²) time and memory
String result = "";
for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) {
    result += "item" + i + "\n";  // creates a new String object every iteration
}

// Each iteration:
// 1. Create new StringBuilder (hidden by compiler)
// 2. Append existing result (copy all n chars)
// 3. Append "item"
// 4. Append i
// 5. Append "\n"
// 6. Call toString() → new String object
// 7. Old String object becomes garbage
// Total: O(1 + 2 + 3 + ... + n) = O(n²) character copies

// CORRECT — O(n) time
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) {
    sb.append("item").append(i).append('\n');
}
String result = sb.toString();   // one final String creation

Comparison Table

Feature String StringBuilder StringBuffer
Mutability Immutable Mutable Mutable
Thread-safe Yes (immutable) No Yes (synchronized)
Performance Slow for mutation Fast ~25-35% slower than SB
Pool support Yes No No
Java version 1.0 1.5 (replaced StringBuffer) 1.0
Use case General storage Single-thread building Multi-thread building
capacity() N/A Default 16, grows as needed Default 16, grows as needed

StringBuilder Internals

StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
// Internally: char[] buf = new char[16]; int count = 0;

sb.append("Hello");    // count = 5, buf = ['H','e','l','l','o',...]
sb.append(" World");   // count = 11

// When capacity exceeded, grows:
// newCapacity = (oldCapacity * 2) + 2
// new char[] created, System.arraycopy called — similar to ArrayList growth

// API
sb.insert(5, ",");          // insert at index
sb.delete(0, 5);            // remove chars 0 to 4
sb.reverse();               // reverse all chars
sb.replace(0, 3, "New");    // replace range
sb.deleteCharAt(0);         // remove single char
String result = sb.toString();  // new String from internal buffer

// Chaining — all mutating methods return 'this'
String result2 = new StringBuilder()
    .append("Hello")
    .append(" ")
    .append("World")
    .toString();

When to Use StringBuffer

Almost never in modern code. StringBuffer was the original mutable string class in Java 1.0, with every method synchronized. StringBuilder (Java 5) is its non-synchronized, faster replacement. Use StringBuffer only if:

  • You are maintaining code that must be thread-safe and you cannot refactor
  • You are building a string in a producer-consumer pattern across threads (rare — usually better design avoids this)

In practice, if you need thread-safe string building, build the string in a local StringBuilder (thread-confined) and publish the final immutable String.

Part 9

Text Blocks (Java 15+)

Text blocks (JEP 355, preview Java 13-14; standard Java 15+) are multi-line string literals that eliminate most backslashes and manual newline concatenation:

// Before text blocks — ugly, error-prone
String json = "{\n" +
              "  \"name\": \"Alice\",\n" +
              "  \"age\": 30\n" +
              "}";

// After text blocks — clean and readable
String json = """
        {
          "name": "Alice",
          "age": 30
        }
        """;

Text Block Rules

// The opening """ must be followed by a newline (not content)
// The closing """ position determines incidental whitespace removal

String block = """
        line one
        line two
        """;
// Content: "line one\nline two\n"
// The 8-space indent is stripped (aligns to closing """)

// Trailing whitespace on each line is stripped
// To preserve a trailing newline: place closing """ on its own line
// To omit trailing newline: place closing """ after last content character

String noTrailingNewline = """
        hello""";  // "hello" — no newline

// Escape sequences still work
String withEscapes = """
        tab:\there
        unicode: \u0041
        """;

// Template-like formatting
String sql = """
        SELECT u.id, u.name
        FROM   users u
        WHERE  u.active = true
          AND  u.role   = '%s'
        ORDER BY u.created_at DESC
        """.formatted("ADMIN");

Text Blocks for SQL and HTML in Spring Boot

public class UserRepository {

    private static final String FIND_ACTIVE_USERS_SQL = """
            SELECT u.id,
                   u.email,
                   u.created_at
            FROM   users u
            WHERE  u.active    = :active
              AND  u.tenant_id = :tenantId
            ORDER BY u.created_at DESC

Part 10

Performance Deep-Dive

Concatenation Optimization by the Compiler

The Java compiler (and JIT) optimize string concatenation, but the mechanism changed in Java 9:

Java 8 and earlier: s1 + s2 + s3 compiles to:

new StringBuilder().append(s1).append(s2).append(s3).toString()

A new StringBuilder is created for every concatenation expression. In a loop, a new StringBuilder is created on every iteration.

Java 9+ (invokedynamic + StringConcatFactory): s1 + s2 + s3 uses an invokedynamic call site that the JVM bootstraps with StringConcatFactory. This allows the JVM to use strategies like:
- MH_inline_sized_exact — computes the total needed size, allocates once, copies all parts (zero intermediate allocations)
- Eliminates intermediate StringBuilder for simple cases

This makes simple concatenation faster in Java 9+ than Java 8, but the loop problem remains:

// Java 9+ — STILL O(n²) — a new concatenation is bootstrapped each iteration
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    result += data[i];   // still creates a new String each time
}

Memory Profile: String vs StringBuilder

Building "ABCDE" from 5 single-character appends:

With String concatenation ("+=" loop):
  Iteration 1: "A"      — 1 char → 1 String on heap
  Iteration 2: "AB"     — 2 chars → 1 new String, old "A" is garbage
  Iteration 3: "ABC"    — 3 chars → 1 new String
  Iteration 4: "ABCD"   — 4 chars → 1 new String
  Iteration 5: "ABCDE"  — 5 chars → 1 new String
  Total copies: 1+2+3+4+5 = 15 character copies, 5 heap allocations

With StringBuilder:
  append("A")  → internal buf: "A______...______" (capacity 16)
  append("B")  → internal buf: "AB_____________"
  append("C")  → internal buf: "ABC____________"
  append("D")  → internal buf: "ABCD___________"
  append("E")  → internal buf: "ABCDE__________"
  toString()   → 1 new String("ABCDE")
  Total copies: 5 char copies (all into sb), 1 final String copy = 10 total
  Only 1 heap allocation (the final String)
Part 11

`String.format` vs `StringBuilder` vs `+` Performance

// Benchmark context: constructing "Hello, Alice! You have 5 messages."
// (microbenchmark — use JMH for real measurements)

// Option 1: String.format — convenient but slowest
String msg = String.format("Hello, %s! You have %d messages.", name, count);
// Parses format string at runtime; creates multiple objects

// Option 2: String.formatted (Java 15+) — same as String.format, just method syntax
String msg2 = "Hello, %s! You have %d messages.".formatted(name, count);

// Option 3: StringBuilder — fastest for runtime construction
String msg3 = new StringBuilder("Hello, ")
    .append(name).append("! You have ")
    .append(count).append(" messages.")
    .toString();

// Option 4: simple + — fine for small, non-loop concatenations
String msg4 = "Hello, " + name + "! You have " + count + " messages.";
// Java 9+ compiles this to invokedynamic — fast, close to StringBuilder

Architect guidance: Use + freely for non-loop code (readability). Use StringBuilder in loops, recursive string construction, or when the number of appends is dynamic. Use String.format/formatted for human-readable messages (logs, exceptions, UI), accepting the ~2-5x performance hit for clarity.

Part 13

Common `String` Methods in Production Code

Null-Safe Operations

// Problem: s.equals("expected") throws NPE if s is null
if (s.equals("expected")) { ... }         // NPE if s is null

// Safe patterns
if ("expected".equals(s)) { ... }        // "Yoda condition" — constant on left
if (Objects.equals(s, "expected")) { }   // Java 7+ — null-safe
if ("expected".equalsIgnoreCase(s)) { }  // null-safe if constant is on left

String Splitting and Parsing

// split returns String[] — be aware of edge cases
"a,b,c".split(",")         // ["a", "b", "c"]
"a,,b".split(",")          // ["a", "", "b"]
"a,b,c,".split(",")        // ["a", "b", "c"] — trailing empty strings removed!
"a,b,c,".split(",", -1)    // ["a", "b", "c", ""] — keep trailing empty strings

// For simple CSV-like parsing, be aware of limit parameter
String line = "Alice,30,Engineer";
String[] parts = line.split(",", 3);   // max 3 tokens: ["Alice", "30", "Engineer"]

// Prefer Apache Commons or dedicated CSV libraries for real CSV

String Interning in High-Throughput Systems

// Reading 10M rows from a database where "status" is one of 5 values
// Without intern: 10M distinct String objects for status column
// With intern: 5 String objects shared across all 10M rows

public List<Record> loadRecords(ResultSet rs) throws SQLException {
    List<Record> records = new ArrayList<>();
    while (rs.next()) {
        String status = rs.getString("status").intern();   // deduplicate
        records.add(new Record(status, rs.getLong("id")));
    }
    return records;
}

// Alternatively, use a manual cache (more control than intern()):
private final Map<String, String> statusCache = new HashMap<>();

private String deduplicate(String s) {
    return statusCache.computeIfAbsent(s, k -> k);
}

Part 15

String Security Considerations

Passwords Must NOT Be Stored as String

// WRONG — String stays in pool and memory dumps can expose it
String password = "secret123";
authenticateUser(username, password);

// CORRECT — char[] can be zeroed after use
char[] password = console.readPassword("Enter password: ");
try {
    authenticateUser(username, password);
} finally {
    Arrays.fill(password, '\0');   // zero out the array
}

// In Spring Security — use char[] or dedicated PasswordEncoder
// PasswordEncoder hashes before storage, never keeps plaintext

SQL Injection Prevention

// WRONG — string concatenation in SQL
String query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + userInput + "'";
// If userInput = "'; DROP TABLE users; --", the DB is compromised

// CORRECT — parameterized queries
PreparedStatement stmt = conn.prepareStatement(
    "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?"
);
stmt.setString(1, userInput);   // JDBC driver handles escaping
Part 16

`String` Interning: When it Helps, When it Hurts

How intern() Works Under the Hood

intern() algorithm:
  1. Compute hashCode of the String
  2. Look up in the String Pool (a native hash table in the JVM)
  3. If found: return the pooled reference (discard the caller's object)
  4. If not found: add the caller's String to the pool, return it

Pool capacity: starts small, grows with load factor
Pool location: Heap (Java 7+); PermGen (Java 6 and earlier)

Performance Characteristics

// intern() itself has overhead — native JVM call, lock contention possible
// Only worth it if:
//   1. You will compare with == (faster than equals)
//   2. You have high duplication (e.g., 10% unique, 90% repeated)

// Benchmark guide (approximate — run JMH for real numbers):
//   String.equals()            ~5ns    (constant time for mismatches, O(n) for matches)
//   String.intern() + ==       ~50-200ns (intern call overhead)
//   Objects.equals(s1, s2)     ~5-6ns  (null-safe equals)

// Rule of thumb: intern() is worth it only if you intern once and compare many times
Part 17

How Many String Objects Are Created?

This is the canonical Java interview question. Let's trace several cases:

// Case 1: String literal
String s = "hello";
// Objects created: 1 (in String pool, at class loading time)
// If pool already has "hello", zero new objects at runtime

// Case 2: new String()
String s = new String("hello");
// Objects created: 1 new heap String + 0 or 1 pool String
// = 1 if "hello" already in pool, 2 if not yet in pool

// Case 3: Concatenation of two literals
String s = "hello" + " " + "world";
// Compiler folds to "hello world" at compile time
// Objects created: 1 (one pool entry for "hello world")

// Case 4: Concatenation with variable
String a = "hello";
String b = " world";
String s = a + b;
// Runtime concatenation: creates 1 new heap String "hello world"
// (a and b already existed)

// Case 5: Mixed
String s = new String("hello") + new String(" world");
// "hello" may create 1-2 objects (literal + new)
// " world" may create 1-2 objects (literal + new)
// Final concatenation: 1 new heap String
// Total: 2-4 objects depending on pool state + 1 final = 3-5 objects

// Case 6: intern chain
String s = new String("test").intern();
// "test" literal: 1 pool object (at class load)
// new String("test"): 1 new heap object
// .intern(): returns pool object, new heap object becomes garbage
// Net: 1 live object (pool), 1 GC candidate
Part 18

String Comparisons: Complete Reference

String a = "hello";
String b = new String("hello");
String c = b.intern();

// Reference comparison
a == b          // false (different objects)
a == c          // true  (c is the pool object)

// Content comparison
a.equals(b)     // true
a.equals(null)  // false (equals handles null internally)
null == null    // true  (reference comparison)

// Null-safe comparison
Objects.equals(a, null)    // false
Objects.equals(null, null) // true
Objects.equals(null, b)    // false

// Ordering
a.compareTo("hello")       // 0 (same content)
a.compareTo("jello")       // negative (h < j)
a.compareTo("HELLO")       // positive (lowercase > uppercase in Unicode)
a.compareToIgnoreCase("HELLO")  // 0

// Collator for locale-aware comparison (for user-facing sort)
import java.text.Collator;
Collator collator = Collator.getInstance(Locale.GERMAN);
collator.compare("ä", "z");   // correct locale sort, not ASCII-based

"  hello  ".stripLeading()   // "hello  "
"  hello  ".stripTrailing()  // "  hello"
// trim() only strips ASCII whitespace (char <= ' ')
// strip() uses Character.isWhitespace() — handles non-breaking spaces etc.
