Part 20

Interview Preparation

Q1: Why is String immutable in Java?

Three core reasons: thread safety (immutable objects are inherently safe to share across threads), hashCode caching (the hash is computed once and cached — safe because the content never changes), and security (strings used for file paths, network addresses, SQL queries cannot be mutated after a security check has passed them).

Q2: What is the String Pool?

A JVM-managed cache of string literals stored in the heap (Java 7+; was in PermGen before). When the class loader encounters a string literal, it adds it to the pool (or returns an existing entry). All references to the same literal point to the same pool object, saving memory. String.intern() allows runtime strings to participate in this pool.

Q3: How many String objects does new String("hello") create?

One or two. The literal "hello" is loaded into the String Pool at class loading time — one pool object. new String("hello") then creates a new heap String object that copies the content — one additional object. If "hello" was already in the pool before this line, the answer is one new object (the heap String); otherwise, two objects (pool + heap).

Q4: Why should you not use == to compare Strings?

== tests reference equality — whether two variables point to the same object in memory. Two String objects with identical content can be different objects (e.g., one from the pool, one from new String(...), or two separate runtime computations). equals() compares the content (the actual character sequence). Use equals() for content comparison, == only when you explicitly need to test that two variables point to the same object.

Q5: What is StringBuilder.capacity() and why does it matter?

StringBuilder maintains an internal char[] buffer. capacity() returns the current allocated size of this buffer. When you append() beyond capacity, a new, larger array is allocated and all content is copied. If you know approximately how many characters you'll build, pre-allocate with new StringBuilder(expectedSize) to avoid reallocations:

// Instead of:
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();  // default capacity 16

// Use:
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(1024);  // pre-size for your use case

Q6: Why is StringBuffer deprecated in practice?

StringBuffer was Java 1.0's synchronized mutable string. Every method (append, insert, delete) acquires a monitor lock. In single-threaded code — which is almost all code that uses a mutable string builder — this synchronization is pure overhead with no benefit. StringBuilder (Java 5) is the direct, unsynchronized replacement. In multi-threaded code, the lock granularity of StringBuffer is too coarse anyway — you typically need to synchronize at a higher level.

Part 21

Code Lab: Practical Exercises

// Exercise 1: Check if a string is a palindrome (ignore case and non-alphanumeric)
public static boolean isPalindrome(String s) {
    int left = 0, right = s.length() - 1;
    while (left < right) {
        while (left < right && !Character.isLetterOrDigit(s.charAt(left)))  left++;
        while (left < right && !Character.isLetterOrDigit(s.charAt(right))) right--;
        if (Character.toLowerCase(s.charAt(left)) !=
            Character.toLowerCase(s.charAt(right))) return false;
        left++; right--;
    }
    return true;
}

// Exercise 2: Count occurrences of a character
public static int countChar(String s, char c) {
    int count = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) {
        if (s.charAt(i) == c) count++;
    }
    return count;
    // Java 8+: return (int) s.chars().filter(ch -> ch == c).count();
}

// Exercise 3: Reverse words in a sentence
public static String reverseWords(String sentence) {
    String[] words = sentence.trim().split("\\s+");
    StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
    for (int i = words.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
        sb.append(words[i]);
        if (i > 0) sb.append(' ');
    }
    return sb.toString();
}

// Exercise 4: Find the longest substring without repeating characters (Sliding Window)
public static int lengthOfLongestSubstring(String s) {
    Map<Character, Integer> lastSeen = new HashMap<>();
    int maxLen = 0, start = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) {
        char c = s.charAt(i);
        if (lastSeen.containsKey(c) && lastSeen.get(c) >= start) {
            start = lastSeen.get(c) + 1;
        }
        lastSeen.put(c, i);
        maxLen = Math.max(maxLen, i - start + 1);
    }
    return maxLen;
}

// Exercise 5: Anagram check
public static boolean isAnagram(String s1, String s2) {
    if (s1.length() != s2.length()) return false;
    int[] freq = new int[26];
    for (char c : s1.toCharArray()) freq[c - 'a']++;
    for (char c : s2.toCharArray()) {
        if (--freq[c - 'a'] < 0) return false;
    }
    return true;
}
Part 22

Architect's Checklist

String performance rules:

String decision flowchart:

  Are you building a string iteratively (loop, recursive, variable parts)?
  ├─ YES → Use StringBuilder (single-thread) or StringBuffer (multi-thread)
  └─ NO  → Is this a compile-time constant?
            ├─ YES → String literal, use "..." directly
            └─ NO  → Simple runtime concatenation with + is fine (Java 9+ optimizes it)

  Are you comparing string content?
  ├─ Always use .equals() or Objects.equals()
  └─ Never use == unless testing reference identity intentionally

  Are you handling passwords or sensitive data?
  └─ Use char[] and zero it out after use, not String

  Are you reading high-cardinality string columns from DB/files?
  └─ Consider intern() or a manual deduplication cache

  Are you writing multi-line strings (SQL, JSON, HTML)?
  └─ Use text blocks (Java 15+)

Production checklist:

  • [ ] No string concatenation in loops — use StringBuilder
  • [ ] Use Objects.equals() for nullable string comparisons
  • [ ] Use parameterized logging — log.debug("msg: {}", val), not log.debug("msg: " + val)
  • [ ] Use text blocks for multi-line SQL, JSON, HTML templates
  • [ ] Use String.strip() (Java 11+) instead of String.trim() for Unicode correctness
  • [ ] Never store passwords as String — use char[] and zero after use
  • [ ] Use PreparedStatement / parameterized queries — never concatenate SQL
  • [ ] Pre-size StringBuilder if approximate final length is known
  • [ ] Profile before using intern() — measure, don't assume

Memory profile quick reference:

Object Heap cost (approx.)
String object (Java 9+, Latin-1) 24 bytes header + 1 byte/char
String object (Java 9+, UTF-16) 24 bytes header + 2 bytes/char
String object (Java 8, char[]) 32 bytes + 2 bytes/char
StringBuilder (empty) 32 bytes + 32 bytes (default 16-char buffer)
String pool entry Same as String + hash table pointer

Practice Section

Quick-Check Questions

  1. What does "hello" == new String("hello") evaluate to and why?
  2. How many String objects does "a" + "b" + "c" create (all literals)?
  3. What is the difference between String.trim() and String.strip()?
  4. What exception does "".charAt(0) throw?
  5. What does "abc".intern() return if "abc" is already in the pool?
  6. Why is StringBuilder not thread-safe, and how do you handle it?

Coding Challenges

  1. Group anagrams: Given an array of strings, group anagrams together.
  2. String compression: Implement basic compression — "aabcccdddd" → "a2b1c3d4".
  3. Valid parentheses: Use a Deque<Character> and string characters to validate parentheses.
  4. Roman to Integer: Parse a Roman numeral string to an integer.
  5. Longest common prefix: Find the longest common prefix among an array of strings.

Answers to Quick-Check

  1. false — "hello" is a pool object; new String("hello") creates a separate heap object. == compares references.
  2. One — the compiler constant-folds all-literal concatenation to a single "abc" at compile time. One pool entry.
  3. trim() strips only ASCII whitespace (char <= '\u0020'). strip() (Java 11+) uses Character.isWhitespace() which understands Unicode whitespace characters like non-breaking space (\u00A0).
  4. StringIndexOutOfBoundsException — the string is empty, index 0 is out of bounds.
  5. The existing pool object is returned — intern() is idempotent. No new object is created.
  6. StringBuilder has no synchronized methods. Use it in a thread-confined manner (local variable, not a shared field). If you need shared mutable string building: use StringBuffer, or synchronize externally, or (best) redesign so each thread has its own StringBuilder and you combine results after.

Part 1

Concept Overview

Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) is not a syntax feature — it is a philosophy for organizing complexity. Java was designed from its first release around four core OOP pillars: Encapsulation, Inheritance, Polymorphism, and Abstraction. Every enterprise Java system — from a simple REST service to a distributed banking platform — expresses these four ideas thousands of times.

At the architect level, OOP matters because:

  • Encapsulation enforces boundaries between components, making systems auditable, testable, and changeable independently
  • Inheritance models real-world hierarchies and enables code reuse — but misuse creates the most fragile codebases you will ever maintain
  • Polymorphism is what makes frameworks like Spring, Hibernate, and JUnit possible — write code once against an abstraction, swap implementations without touching callers
  • Abstraction is the discipline of hiding how behind what — the foundation of every API contract
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   The Four OOP Pillars                           │
│                                                                  │
│  ┌─────────────────┐     ┌─────────────────┐                    │
│  │  Encapsulation  │     │   Inheritance   │                    │
│  │  Hide internal  │     │  IS-A hierarchy │                    │
│  │  state behind   │     │  extends parent │                    │
│  │  a contract     │     │  behavior       │                    │
│  └─────────────────┘     └─────────────────┘                    │
│                                                                  │
│  ┌─────────────────┐     ┌─────────────────┐                    │
│  │ Polymorphism    │     │  Abstraction    │                    │
│  │  One interface, │     │  Hide HOW,      │                    │
│  │  many forms     │     │  expose WHAT    │                    │
│  │  dynamic bind   │     │  interfaces &   │                    │
│  │                 │     │  abstract class │                    │
│  └─────────────────┘     └─────────────────┘                    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

This lesson builds these four pillars from the ground up — starting with classes and objects, the building blocks of every Java program.

Part 2

Why OOP Matters for Architects

2.1 Complexity at Scale

A system with 100 classes has roughly 5,000 possible pairwise interactions. A system with 1,000 classes has roughly 500,000. The only way to keep this tractable is rigid organization — and OOP provides the vocabulary for that organization.

Without OOP discipline:
  All code sees all data → change one variable → test everything → nightmare

With OOP discipline:
  Class A owns its state → Class B interacts only via A's public API
  → change A's internals → only test A → maintainable

2.2 Framework Integration

Every major Java framework is built on OOP contracts:

  • Spring injects beans by type — polymorphism lets you swap PaymentService implementations without touching any caller
  • Hibernate maps class hierarchies to database tables (@Inheritance)
  • JUnit uses @Test annotations on method overrides — subclasses provide test logic through inheritance
  • Mockito creates proxy objects that override every method — pure polymorphism

2.3 Domain Modeling

Good OOP forces you to model the business domain, not the database schema. A BankAccount class in a real bank encapsulates the invariant that a balance can never drop below a limit — the code enforces the business rule, not just the database constraint.

Part 3

Classes and Objects

A class is a blueprint. An object is an instance — a living copy of that blueprint in heap memory with its own state.

3.1 Anatomy of a Class

// A class groups state (fields) and behavior (methods) into a named unit
public class BankAccount {

    // Fields — the state of each object instance
    private String accountNumber;   // unique per account
    private String ownerName;
    private double balance;

    // Constructor — called when object is created with `new`
    public BankAccount(String accountNumber, String ownerName, double initialBalance) {
        this.accountNumber = accountNumber;
        this.ownerName     = ownerName;
        this.balance       = initialBalance;
    }

    // Method — behavior that operates on this object's state
    public void deposit(double amount) {
        if (amount <= 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Deposit amount must be positive");
        }
        this.balance += amount;
    }

    public void withdraw(double amount) {
        if (amount <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Amount must be positive");
        if (amount > balance) throw new IllegalStateException("Insufficient funds");
        this.balance -= amount;
    }

    public double getBalance() {
        return balance;
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "BankAccount[" + accountNumber + ", owner=" + ownerName
               + ", balance=" + balance + "]";
    }
}

3.2 Instantiation

// BankAccount.class is the blueprint. new creates an instance on the heap.
BankAccount checking = new BankAccount("ACC-001", "Alice Smith", 1000.00);
BankAccount savings  = new BankAccount("ACC-002", "Alice Smith",  500.00);

// Each object is independent — they share the blueprint, not the state
checking.deposit(250.00);
System.out.println(checking.getBalance()); // 1250.0
System.out.println(savings.getBalance());  // 500.0  (untouched)

Heap Memory After Two Instantiations:
┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                         HEAP                              │
│                                                           │
│  ┌───────────────────────────┐                            │
│  │  BankAccount object #1    │  ← checking (reference)   │
│  │  accountNumber = "ACC-001"│                            │
│  │  ownerName = "Alice Smith"│                            │
│  │  balance = 1250.0         │                            │
│  └───────────────────────────┘                            │
│                                                           │
│  ┌───────────────────────────┐                            │
│  │  BankAccount object #2    │  ← savings (reference)    │
│  │  accountNumber = "ACC-002"│                            │
│  │  ownerName = "Alice Smith"│                            │
│  │  balance = 500.0          │                            │
│  └───────────────────────────┘                            │
│                                                           │
│  Both share the same BankAccount.class metadata           │
│  (method code is NOT duplicated per instance)             │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Part 4

The `new` Keyword and Object Creation

new triggers a precise sequence of JVM operations every time it executes.

4.1 What new Does Step by Step

BankAccount account = new BankAccount("ACC-001", "Alice", 1000.0);

new BankAccount(...) — JVM execution steps:

Step 1: Class Loading
  → JVM checks if BankAccount.class is loaded into the method area
  → If not: ClassLoader reads BankAccount.class from classpath, loads it

Step 2: Memory Allocation
  → JVM calculates the size needed for a BankAccount object
     (header + all fields, aligned to 8 bytes on 64-bit JVM)
  → Allocates that block in Eden space (Young Generation)
  → All fields zero-initialized: null, 0, 0.0, false

Step 3: Constructor Execution
  → The <init> method (constructor bytecode) runs
  → this.accountNumber, ownerName, balance are assigned
  → Parent constructors run first (Object.<init> here)

Step 4: Reference Assignment
  → The heap address is stored in the local variable `account`
  → `account` on the stack points to the heap object

4.2 Object Header Overhead

Every Java object has a hidden header that consumes heap memory:

Object on 64-bit JVM (with CompressedOops enabled):

┌───────────────────────────────────┐
│  Mark Word         8 bytes        │  ← hashCode, lock state, GC age
│  Class Pointer     4 bytes        │  ← compressed reference to class metadata
│─────────────────────────────────  │
│  Fields (payload)  varies         │  ← your actual data
└───────────────────────────────────┘

A BankAccount with 3 fields:
  header:         12 bytes
  accountNumber:   4 bytes (compressed String reference)
  ownerName:       4 bytes (compressed String reference)
  balance:         8 bytes (double)
  padding:         4 bytes (alignment to 8-byte boundary)
  Total:          32 bytes per BankAccount object
Part 5

Constructors

Constructors initialize objects. They have the same name as the class and no return type.

5.1 Default Constructor

If you write no constructor, Java provides a zero-argument default constructor that calls super() and does nothing else:

public class Product {
    private String name;
    private double price;
    // No constructor written → compiler provides:
    // public Product() { super(); }
}

Product p = new Product();  // valid — fields are null, 0.0

Once you write any constructor, the default constructor is NOT provided.

public class Product {
    private String name;
    private double price;

    // You wrote one constructor — default is gone
    public Product(String name, double price) {
        this.name  = name;
        this.price = price;
    }
}

Product p = new Product();           // compile error — no no-arg constructor
Product p = new Product("Pen", 1.5); // OK

5.2 Parameterized Constructor

public class Customer {
    private final long   id;
    private final String email;
    private       String name;

    // Primary constructor — all required fields
    public Customer(long id, String email, String name) {
        if (id <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("ID must be positive");
        if (email == null || !email.contains("@"))
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid email: " + email);

        this.id    = id;
        this.email = email;
        this.name  = name;
    }
}

5.3 Constructor Chaining with this(...)

public class Order {
    private final String orderId;
    private final String customerId;
    private final String status;
    private final long   createdAt;

    // Primary constructor
    public Order(String orderId, String customerId, String status, long createdAt) {
        this.orderId     = orderId;
        this.customerId  = customerId;
        this.status      = status;
        this.createdAt   = createdAt;
    }

    // Convenience constructor — delegates to primary
    public Order(String orderId, String customerId) {
        this(orderId, customerId, "PENDING", System.currentTimeMillis());
    }

    // Single-arg convenience
    public Order(String orderId) {
        this(orderId, "UNKNOWN");
    }
}

this(...) must be the first statement in a constructor. This pattern avoids duplicating initialization logic and provides clean API variants.

Part 6

The `this` Keyword

this is a reference to the current object instance — the object on which the current method or constructor is executing.

6.1 Disambiguating Fields from Parameters

public class Employee {
    private String name;
    private int    salary;

    public Employee(String name, int salary) {
        // Without `this`, `name = name` assigns the parameter to itself — bug!
        this.name   = name;    // this.name = field; name = parameter
        this.salary = salary;
    }

    public void raiseSalary(int salary) {
        // salary here is the parameter (shadows the field)
        this.salary += salary;   // field += parameter
    }
}

6.2 Returning this for Fluent/Builder APIs

public class QueryBuilder {
    private String table;
    private String whereClause;
    private int    limit = 100;

    public QueryBuilder from(String table) {
        this.table = table;
        return this;   // enables chaining
    }

    public QueryBuilder where(String clause) {
        this.whereClause = clause;
        return this;
    }

    public QueryBuilder limit(int n) {
        this.limit = n;
        return this;
    }

    public String build() {
        return "SELECT * FROM " + table
             + (whereClause != null ? " WHERE " + whereClause : "")
             + " LIMIT " + limit;
    }
}

// Usage — fluent API enabled by returning this
String sql = new QueryBuilder()
    .from("accounts")
    .where("balance > 10000")
    .limit(50)
    .build();
// → "SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE balance > 10000 LIMIT 50"
Part 7

Encapsulation

Encapsulation means binding data (fields) and the code that operates on it (methods) into a single unit, and restricting direct access to the data from outside.

7.1 The Problem Without Encapsulation

// BAD — no encapsulation
public class BankAccountBad {
    public double balance;   // anyone can set this to any value
}

BankAccountBad acct = new BankAccountBad();
acct.balance = -999_999.00;  // illegal state — no enforcement possible
acct.balance = Double.NaN;   // corrupted state

7.2 Encapsulation with Private Fields

// GOOD — encapsulation enforced
public class BankAccount {
    private double balance;   // only this class can set it directly

    public void deposit(double amount) {
        if (amount <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Must be positive");
        this.balance += amount;
        // Future additions: audit log, event publish — without changing callers
    }

    public void withdraw(double amount) {
        if (amount <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Must be positive");
        if (amount > balance) throw new IllegalStateException("Insufficient funds");
        this.balance -= amount;
    }

    public double getBalance() {
        return balance;  // read-only access — no mutation path from outside
    }
}

The key insight: the class owns its invariants. The balance field can never be negative, NaN, or infinite — the class enforces this on every write path.

7.3 Immutable Encapsulation (Best Practice)

For value objects (money amounts, account IDs, dates), make the class fully immutable:

public final class Money {
    private final long   amountInCents;   // final — set once, never changed
    private final String currency;

    public Money(long amountInCents, String currency) {
        if (amountInCents < 0)  throw new IllegalArgumentException("Negative money");
        if (currency == null)   throw new IllegalArgumentException("Null currency");
        this.amountInCents = amountInCents;
        this.currency      = currency;
    }

    // Operations return NEW objects — this object is never mutated
    public Money add(Money other) {
        if (!this.currency.equals(other.currency))
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Currency mismatch");
        return new Money(this.amountInCents + other.amountInCents, this.currency);
    }

    public long getAmountInCents() { return amountInCents; }
    public String getCurrency()    { return currency; }
}

Immutable objects are inherently thread-safe — a crucial property in concurrent banking systems.

Part 8

Getters and Setters

Getters and setters are the controlled access points to private fields.

8.1 Why Not Just Public Fields?

// Public field — looks convenient, causes long-term pain
public class UserProfile {
    public String email;
}

// Now email can be set to anything, anywhere
// Adding validation later requires finding every direct assignment in the codebase
// You cannot add logging, caching, or notifications without changing callers

8.2 Proper Getter/Setter Pattern

public class UserProfile {
    private String email;
    private String phoneNumber;

    // Getter — simple read access
    public String getEmail() {
        return email;
    }

    // Setter with validation
    public void setEmail(String email) {
        if (email == null || !email.matches("^[^@]+@[^@]+\\.[^@]+$")) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid email format: " + email);
        }
        this.email = email.toLowerCase().trim();  // normalize on write
    }

    public String getPhoneNumber() {
        return phoneNumber;
    }

    public void setPhoneNumber(String phoneNumber) {
        // Normalize: remove spaces, dashes
        this.phoneNumber = phoneNumber == null ? null
                         : phoneNumber.replaceAll("[\\s\\-]", "");
    }
}

8.3 Boolean Getters

public class Account {
    private boolean active;
    private boolean verified;

    // Boolean getters use `is` prefix (JavaBeans convention)
    public boolean isActive()   { return active; }
    public boolean isVerified() { return verified; }

    public void setActive(boolean active)     { this.active = active; }
    public void setVerified(boolean verified) { this.verified = verified; }
}

8.4 Defensive Copying for Mutable Fields

import java.util.*;

public class Portfolio {
    private final List<String> holdings;

    public Portfolio(List<String> holdings) {
        // Defensive copy on construction — caller cannot mutate our internal list
        this.holdings = new ArrayList<>(holdings);
    }

    public List<String> getHoldings() {
        // Defensive copy on return — caller cannot mutate our internal list
        return Collections.unmodifiableList(holdings);
    }
}
Part 9

Inheritance and `extends`

Inheritance models the IS-A relationship: a SavingsAccount IS-A BankAccount. The subclass inherits all non-private fields and methods and can extend or override behavior.

9.1 Basic Inheritance

// Parent class (superclass / base class)
public class BankAccount {
    protected String accountNumber;
    protected String ownerName;
    protected double balance;

    public BankAccount(String accountNumber, String ownerName, double initialBalance) {
        this.accountNumber = accountNumber;
        this.ownerName     = ownerName;
        this.balance       = initialBalance;
    }

    public void deposit(double amount) {
        if (amount <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Must be positive");
        this.balance += amount;
    }

    public void withdraw(double amount) {
        if (amount <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Must be positive");
        if (amount > balance) throw new IllegalStateException("Insufficient funds");
        this.balance -= amount;
    }

    public double getBalance() { return balance; }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return getClass().getSimpleName() + "[" + accountNumber + ", balance=" + balance + "]";
    }
}

// Child class (subclass / derived class)
public class SavingsAccount extends BankAccount {
    private double interestRate;   // SavingsAccount-specific field
    private int    withdrawalCount;
    private static final int MAX_MONTHLY_WITHDRAWALS = 6;

    public SavingsAccount(String accountNumber, String ownerName,
                          double initialBalance, double interestRate) {
        super(accountNumber, ownerName, initialBalance);  // call parent constructor
        this.interestRate = interestRate;
    }

    // Override — more restrictive withdrawal
    @Override
    public void withdraw(double amount) {
        if (withdrawalCount >= MAX_MONTHLY_WITHDRAWALS) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("Monthly withdrawal limit reached");
        }
        super.withdraw(amount);   // reuse parent logic + add own logic
        withdrawalCount++;
    }

    // New behavior unique to SavingsAccount
    public void applyMonthlyInterest() {
        double interest = balance * interestRate / 12.0;
        deposit(interest);
    }

    public double getInterestRate() { return interestRate; }
}

9.2 Inheritance Hierarchy Diagram

                      ┌──────────────────┐
                      │  Object           │  ← root of all Java classes
                      └────────┬─────────┘
                               │ extends (implicit)
                      ┌────────┴─────────┐
                      │  BankAccount      │  ← base domain class
                      │  + accountNumber  │
                      │  + ownerName      │
                      │  + balance        │
                      │  + deposit()      │
                      │  + withdraw()     │
                      │  + getBalance()   │
                      └───────┬──────────┘
              ┌───────────────┼─────────────────┐
              │               │                 │
   ┌──────────┴───┐  ┌────────┴──────┐  ┌──────┴──────────┐
   │SavingsAccount│  │CheckingAccount│  │  LoanAccount    │
   │+interestRate │  │+overdraftLimit│  │+principalAmount │
   │+applyInterest│  │+overdraftFee  │  │+interestRate    │
   └──────────────┘  └───────────────┘  │+monthlyPayment()│
                                        └─────────────────┘

9.3 What is Inherited

Inherited by subclass from parent:
  ✓ public methods
  ✓ protected methods
  ✓ public fields (accessible directly)
  ✓ protected fields (accessible directly)
  ✓ package-private methods/fields (same package only)

NOT inherited:
  ✗ private fields (exist but not accessible by name)
  ✗ private methods
  ✗ constructors (must be explicitly called via super())
  ✗ static methods (inherited but not overridable — hidden instead)
Part 10

The `super` Keyword

super references the parent class portion of the current object. It has two main uses: calling the parent constructor and calling the parent version of an overridden method.

10.1 super() — Parent Constructor Call

public class CheckingAccount extends BankAccount {
    private double overdraftLimit;

    public CheckingAccount(String accountNumber, String ownerName,
                           double initialBalance, double overdraftLimit) {
        // super() MUST be the first statement in any constructor
        super(accountNumber, ownerName, initialBalance);
        this.overdraftLimit = overdraftLimit;
    }
}

If you omit super(), the compiler inserts super() (no-arg) automatically. If the parent has no no-arg constructor, you get a compile error — you must call super(args) explicitly.

10.2 super.method() — Parent Method Call

public class CheckingAccount extends BankAccount {
    private double overdraftLimit;
    private double overdraftFeeRate = 0.02;

    // ...constructor...

    @Override
    public void withdraw(double amount) {
        double availableFunds = balance + overdraftLimit;
        if (amount > availableFunds) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("Exceeds overdraft limit");
        }
        // Call parent withdraw for the core logic
        super.withdraw(Math.min(amount, balance));

        // If overdraft was used, charge fee
        double overdraftUsed = Math.max(0, amount - balance);
        if (overdraftUsed > 0) {
            balance -= overdraftUsed;   // allow going negative up to limit
            double fee = overdraftUsed * overdraftFeeRate;
            balance -= fee;
            System.out.printf("Overdraft used: %.2f, Fee charged: %.2f%n",
                              overdraftUsed, fee);
        }
    }
}
Part 11

IS-A vs HAS-A Relationships

The most important design question when modeling a domain: IS-A or HAS-A?

11.1 IS-A (Inheritance)

Use inheritance when a subclass is a kind of the parent — it can be used anywhere the parent is expected.

// Correct IS-A: SavingsAccount IS-A BankAccount
SavingsAccount savings = new SavingsAccount("ACC-001", "Bob", 500.0, 0.04);
BankAccount    account = savings;    // valid upcast — savings IS-A BankAccount
account.deposit(100.0);              // works fine

11.2 HAS-A (Composition)

Use composition when a class contains or uses another class, but is not a kind of it.

// WRONG inheritance: Customer IS-NOT-A BankAccount
public class CustomerBad extends BankAccount { ... }  // models wrong

// CORRECT composition: Customer HAS-A BankAccount (or many)
public class Customer {
    private final long        customerId;
    private final String      name;
    private final List<BankAccount> accounts;    // HAS-A

    public Customer(long customerId, String name) {
        this.customerId = customerId;
        this.name       = name;
        this.accounts   = new ArrayList<>();
    }

    public void addAccount(BankAccount account) {
        accounts.add(account);
    }

    public double getTotalBalance() {
        return accounts.stream()
                       .mapToDouble(BankAccount::getBalance)
                       .sum();
    }
}

11.3 The Liskov Substitution Principle

If you use inheritance, every subclass must be fully substitutable for its parent — any code that works with a BankAccount must work correctly with a SavingsAccount, CheckingAccount, etc.

// This should work correctly regardless of which BankAccount subtype is passed
public void processMonthlyFee(BankAccount account, double fee) {
    account.withdraw(fee);   // must work for ALL subtypes
}

If a subclass has to throw an exception or disable a parent method to work correctly, you have the wrong hierarchy — use composition instead.

Part 12

Polymorphism and Method Overriding

Polymorphism means one interface, many behaviors. The same method call can execute different code depending on the actual type of the object at runtime.

12.1 Method Overriding Rules

public class BankAccount {
    // Method to be overridden
    public String getAccountType() {
        return "Generic Bank Account";
    }

    public double calculateMonthlyFee() {
        return 5.00;   // base monthly fee
    }
}

public class SavingsAccount extends BankAccount {
    @Override   // annotation is optional but highly recommended
    public String getAccountType() {
        return "Savings Account";
    }

    @Override
    public double calculateMonthlyFee() {
        return balance >= 1000 ? 0.00 : 3.00;  // fee waived above $1000 balance
    }
}

public class PremiumCheckingAccount extends BankAccount {
    @Override
    public String getAccountType() {
        return "Premium Checking Account";
    }

    @Override
    public double calculateMonthlyFee() {
        return 0.00;   // premium accounts have no fee
    }
}

Override rules:
- Method signature must match (name + parameter types + return type, or covariant return)
- Access modifier cannot be more restrictive (you can widen protected → public, not narrow)
- Cannot override final, static, or private methods
- @Override annotation causes a compile error if nothing is actually overridden (saves from typos)

12.2 Polymorphism in Action

// All three held as BankAccount references
List<BankAccount> accounts = new ArrayList<>();
accounts.add(new SavingsAccount("S001", "Alice", 2000.0, 0.04));
accounts.add(new CheckingAccount("C001", "Bob", 800.0, 500.0));
accounts.add(new PremiumCheckingAccount("P001", "Carol", 5000.0));

// The same method call, different behavior per object
double totalFees = 0;
for (BankAccount account : accounts) {
    double fee = account.calculateMonthlyFee();   // which version runs? Depends on type!
    System.out.println(account.getAccountType() + " fee: " + fee);
    totalFees += fee;
}
// Output:
// Savings Account fee: 0.0       (balance >= 1000, waived)
// Generic Bank Account fee: 5.0  (CheckingAccount didn't override, uses parent)
// Premium Checking Account fee: 0.0
Part 13

Dynamic Dispatch

Dynamic dispatch (also called runtime polymorphism or late binding) is the JVM mechanism that selects which overridden method to execute at runtime, based on the actual type of the object — not the declared type of the reference.

13.1 Compile Time vs Runtime Type

BankAccount account = new SavingsAccount("S001", "Alice", 1000.0, 0.04);
//  ^^^^^^^^^^^                ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
//  compile-time type          runtime type (actual object)
//  (declared type)

account.calculateMonthlyFee();
// Compiler sees: BankAccount.calculateMonthlyFee()
// JVM at runtime looks at actual type: SavingsAccount
// Dispatches to: SavingsAccount.calculateMonthlyFee()
// → returns 0.00 (balance >= 1000)

13.2 Virtual Method Table (vtable)

The JVM uses a vtable (virtual method table) per class to implement dynamic dispatch. Every object instance carries a pointer to its class's vtable.

vtable for BankAccount:
┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  slot 0: equals()            → Object.equals()        │
│  slot 1: hashCode()          → Object.hashCode()      │
│  slot 2: toString()          → BankAccount.toString() │
│  slot 3: deposit()           → BankAccount.deposit()  │
│  slot 4: withdraw()          → BankAccount.withdraw() │
│  slot 5: calculateMonthlyFee → BankAccount.calc...()  │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

vtable for SavingsAccount:
┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  slot 0: equals()            → Object.equals()        │
│  slot 1: hashCode()          → Object.hashCode()      │
│  slot 2: toString()          → BankAccount.toString() │
│  slot 3: deposit()           → BankAccount.deposit()  │
│  slot 4: withdraw()          → SavingsAccount.with..  │  ← overridden
│  slot 5: calculateMonthlyFee → SavingsAccount.calc..  │  ← overridden
│  slot 6: applyMonthlyInterest→ SavingsAccount.apply.. │  ← new method
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

When account.calculateMonthlyFee() is called:
1. JVM reads object header → finds pointer to SavingsAccount vtable
2. Looks up slot 5 in SavingsAccount vtable
3. Executes SavingsAccount.calculateMonthlyFee()

13.3 invokevirtual Bytecode Instruction

Dynamic dispatch is implemented in JVM bytecode via invokevirtual:

// Java source
account.calculateMonthlyFee();

// Compiled bytecode (javap -c output)
invokevirtual #24 // Method calculateMonthlyFee:()D

// invokevirtual steps:
// 1. Pop object reference from operand stack
// 2. Read class pointer from object header
// 3. Look up method in that class's vtable (by slot index)
// 4. Execute — this pointer (receiver) is the actual object

The JIT compiler optimizes invokevirtual aggressively:
- Monomorphic: if only one type is ever seen, JIT inlines the method (no dispatch overhead)
- Bimorphic: two types seen — JIT generates a conditional inline
- Megamorphic: many types — full vtable dispatch (slower, but still fast)

Part 14

Upcasting and Downcasting

Upcasting is treating a subclass reference as its parent type — always safe.
Downcasting is treating a parent reference as a subclass type — requires explicit cast and can throw ClassCastException.

14.1 Upcasting (Implicit)

SavingsAccount savings = new SavingsAccount("S001", "Alice", 1000.0, 0.04);

// Upcasting — always safe, implicit, no cast syntax needed
BankAccount  asAccount = savings;    // SavingsAccount → BankAccount
Object       asObject  = savings;    // SavingsAccount → Object

// The object is still a SavingsAccount — nothing changes on the heap
// You just have a narrower view of it through the BankAccount reference

14.2 Downcasting (Explicit)

BankAccount account = new SavingsAccount("S001", "Alice", 1000.0, 0.04);

// Downcast — explicit, can fail at runtime
SavingsAccount savings = (SavingsAccount) account;  // OK — actual type matches
savings.applyMonthlyInterest();   // now accessible

// Dangerous downcast — actual type is BankAccount, not CheckingAccount
BankAccount plain = new BankAccount("A001", "Bob", 500.0);
CheckingAccount checking = (CheckingAccount) plain;  // ClassCastException at runtime!

14.3 Safe Downcast with instanceof

// Pre-Java 16: check then cast
public void processAccount(BankAccount account) {
    if (account instanceof SavingsAccount) {
        SavingsAccount savings = (SavingsAccount) account;
        savings.applyMonthlyInterest();
    } else if (account instanceof CheckingAccount) {
        CheckingAccount checking = (CheckingAccount) account;
        checking.processOverdraftFees();
    }
}

// Java 16+: pattern matching instanceof (cleaner)
public void processAccount(BankAccount account) {
    if (account instanceof SavingsAccount savings) {
        savings.applyMonthlyInterest();   // no cast needed
    } else if (account instanceof CheckingAccount checking) {
        checking.processOverdraftFees();
    }
}
Part 15

Abstraction: Abstract Classes

Abstraction hides implementation complexity and forces subclasses to provide specific behavior through abstract methods — methods with no body that subclasses must implement.

15.1 Abstract Class Syntax

// Abstract class — cannot be instantiated directly
public abstract class BankAccount {
    protected final String accountNumber;
    protected final String ownerName;
    protected double       balance;

    protected BankAccount(String accountNumber, String ownerName, double initialBalance) {
        this.accountNumber = accountNumber;
        this.ownerName     = ownerName;
        this.balance       = initialBalance;
    }

    // Concrete method — shared implementation all subclasses use
    public void deposit(double amount) {
        if (amount <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Must be positive");
        this.balance += amount;
    }

    // Abstract method — every subclass must provide its own implementation
    public abstract void withdraw(double amount);

    // Abstract method — every subclass defines what type it is
    public abstract String getAccountType();

    // Abstract method — fee calculation varies by account type
    public abstract double calculateMonthlyFee();

    public double getBalance() { return balance; }
}

// Concrete subclass — must implement all abstract methods
public class SavingsAccount extends BankAccount {
    private final double interestRate;

    public SavingsAccount(String accountNumber, String ownerName,
                          double initialBalance, double interestRate) {
        super(accountNumber, ownerName, initialBalance);
        this.interestRate = interestRate;
    }

    @Override
    public void withdraw(double amount) {
        if (amount > balance) throw new IllegalStateException("Insufficient funds");
        this.balance -= amount;
    }

    @Override
    public String getAccountType() { return "Savings Account"; }

    @Override
    public double calculateMonthlyFee() {
        return balance >= 1000 ? 0.00 : 3.00;
    }
}

15.2 Abstract Class vs Interface (Preview)

Abstract Class:                         Interface:
─────────────────────────────────────   ────────────────────────────────────
Can have constructors                   No constructors
Can have instance fields                No instance fields (only constants)
Can have concrete + abstract methods    Default + abstract methods (Java 8+)
Single inheritance only                 Multiple implementation allowed
IS-A: models a hierarchy               CAN-DO: models a capability contract
Use for: base class with shared state  Use for: behavior contracts, APIs

Examples:
  abstract class BankAccount            interface Auditable
  abstract class Shape                  interface Comparable<T>
  abstract class HttpServlet            interface Serializable
Part 16

Abstraction: Interfaces Preview

Interfaces define a contract — a set of method signatures that implementing classes must fulfill. They are the foundation of dependency injection, testing, and loose coupling in Java.

16.1 Interface Basics

// Interface — a contract for what an account can do
public interface Transferable {
    // All methods are implicitly public abstract (no modifier needed)
    void transferTo(BankAccount target, double amount);
    boolean canAcceptTransfer(double amount);
}

public interface Auditable {
    void logTransaction(String type, double amount, String description);
    List<String> getTransactionHistory();
}

// Class can implement multiple interfaces (unlike single-parent inheritance)
public class SavingsAccount extends BankAccount
        implements Transferable, Auditable {

    private List<String> transactionLog = new ArrayList<>();

    // Must implement all Transferable methods
    @Override
    public void transferTo(BankAccount target, double amount) {
        this.withdraw(amount);
        target.deposit(amount);
        logTransaction("TRANSFER_OUT", amount, "To " + target.accountNumber);
    }

    @Override
    public boolean canAcceptTransfer(double amount) {
        return amount > 0;
    }

    // Must implement all Auditable methods
    @Override
    public void logTransaction(String type, double amount, String description) {
        transactionLog.add(String.format("[%s] %s: %.2f — %s",
            java.time.LocalDateTime.now(), type, amount, description));
    }

    @Override
    public List<String> getTransactionHistory() {
        return Collections.unmodifiableList(transactionLog);
    }

    // ... other required abstract overrides ...
    @Override public void withdraw(double amount) { /* ... */ }
    @Override public String getAccountType()      { return "Savings Account"; }
    @Override public double calculateMonthlyFee() { return 0.0; }
}

16.2 Why Interfaces Enable Loose Coupling

// Code against the interface — not the concrete type
public class FundsTransferService {
    // Works with ANY class that implements Transferable
    // Can be tested with a mock, swapped for a different implementation
    public void executeTransfer(Transferable source, BankAccount target, double amount) {
        if (!source.canAcceptTransfer(amount)) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("Source cannot process transfer");
        }
        source.transferTo(target, amount);
    }
}

Interfaces will be covered in full in Lesson 14. This preview exists because polymorphism and abstraction are inseparable concepts.

Part 17

The Object Class

Every class in Java implicitly extends java.lang.Object. Object is the root of the entire Java class hierarchy. It provides methods that every object inherits.

17.1 Key Object Methods

// Every object has these methods from java.lang.Object:
public class Object {
    public boolean equals(Object obj)       // identity equality by default
    public int     hashCode()               // memory-address-based hash by default
    public String  toString()               // "ClassName@hexHashCode" by default
    public Class   getClass()               // returns runtime class metadata
    public Object  clone()                  // shallow copy (protected)
    public void    notify()                 // threading
    public void    notifyAll()              // threading
    public void    wait(...)                // threading
}

17.2 Overriding toString()

public class BankAccount {
    // ...fields...

    // Default toString() → "BankAccount@4e50df2e" — not useful
    // Override it:
    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return String.format("BankAccount{accountNumber='%s', owner='%s', balance=%.2f}",
                             accountNumber, ownerName, balance);
    }
}

BankAccount acct = new BankAccount("ACC-001", "Alice", 1500.0);
System.out.println(acct);
// Output: BankAccount{accountNumber='ACC-001', owner='Alice', balance=1500.00}

17.3 Overriding equals() and hashCode()

The default equals() checks reference equality (same memory address). For domain objects, you usually want value equality:

public class BankAccount {
    private final String accountNumber;
    // ...

    @Override
    public boolean equals(Object obj) {
        if (this == obj) return true;            // same reference — definitely equal
        if (obj == null) return false;           // null is never equal
        if (getClass() != obj.getClass()) return false;  // different types
        BankAccount other = (BankAccount) obj;
        return Objects.equals(accountNumber, other.accountNumber);
        // Two accounts are equal if they have the same account number
    }

    @Override
    public int hashCode() {
        // CRITICAL: always override hashCode when you override equals
        // Objects that are equals() MUST have the same hashCode()
        return Objects.hash(accountNumber);
    }
}

// Now these work correctly:
BankAccount a1 = new BankAccount("ACC-001", "Alice", 1000.0);
BankAccount a2 = new BankAccount("ACC-001", "Alice", 1000.0);
System.out.println(a1.equals(a2));    // true (same accountNumber)
System.out.println(a1 == a2);         // false (different references)

Set<BankAccount> set = new HashSet<>();
set.add(a1);
set.add(a2);
System.out.println(set.size());       // 1 (HashSet uses hashCode + equals correctly)

The equals/hashCode contract: if a.equals(b) is true, then a.hashCode() must equal b.hashCode(). Violating this breaks HashMap, HashSet, and any hash-based collection.

Part 18

Composition vs Inheritance

This is one of the most important design principles in object-oriented design. The guidance from the Gang of Four (GoF) Design Patterns book: "Favor composition over inheritance."

18.1 Why Composition is Often Better

// Inheritance approach — fragile
public class LoggingBankAccount extends BankAccount {
    @Override
    public void deposit(double amount) {
        System.out.println("Depositing: " + amount);
        super.deposit(amount);
    }
    @Override
    public void withdraw(double amount) {
        System.out.println("Withdrawing: " + amount);
        super.withdraw(amount);
    }
    // Problem: if BankAccount adds a new method, LoggingBankAccount doesn't log it
    // Problem: if BankAccount is a third-party library class, inheritance may be fragile
    // Problem: cannot add logging to CheckingAccount without another subclass
}

// Composition approach — flexible (Decorator pattern)
public class LoggingBankAccountDecorator extends BankAccount {
    private final BankAccount delegate;    // HAS-A — delegate all behavior

    public LoggingBankAccountDecorator(BankAccount delegate) {
        super(delegate.accountNumber, delegate.ownerName, delegate.balance);
        this.delegate = delegate;
    }

    @Override
    public void deposit(double amount) {
        System.out.printf("[AUDIT] deposit %.2f on %s%n", amount, delegate);
        delegate.deposit(amount);
    }

    @Override
    public void withdraw(double amount) {
        System.out.printf("[AUDIT] withdraw %.2f on %s%n", amount, delegate);
        delegate.withdraw(amount);
    }

    @Override
    public String getAccountType() { return delegate.getAccountType(); }
    @Override
    public double calculateMonthlyFee() { return delegate.calculateMonthlyFee(); }
}

18.2 Composition in Domain Modeling

Real banking domain models use composition extensively:

public class Customer {
    private final String             customerId;
    private final PersonalDetails    personalDetails;  // HAS-A
    private final ContactInfo        contactInfo;      // HAS-A
    private final List<BankAccount>  accounts;         // HAS-A (collection)
    private final RiskProfile        riskProfile;      // HAS-A
    private final KycStatus          kycStatus;        // HAS-A

    // Customer IS-NOT-A PersonalDetails
    // Customer IS-NOT-A BankAccount
    // Customer HAS personal details, contact info, accounts, etc.

    public double getTotalAssets() {
        return accounts.stream()
                       .mapToDouble(BankAccount::getBalance)
                       .sum();
    }

    public boolean isEligibleForLoan(double requestedAmount) {
        return kycStatus.isVerified()
            && riskProfile.getCreditScore() >= 650
            && getTotalAssets() >= requestedAmount * 0.10;
    }
}

public class PersonalDetails {
    private final String firstName;
    private final String lastName;
    private final LocalDate dateOfBirth;
    private final String nationalId;
}

public class RiskProfile {
    private int    creditScore;
    private String riskTier;        // LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH
    private int    defaultCount;
}

18.3 When Inheritance IS Correct

Use inheritance when ALL of these are true:
  1. The relationship is genuinely IS-A (not HAS-A or CAN-DO)
  2. The subclass passes the Liskov Substitution test
  3. The hierarchy is stable — unlikely to need restructuring
  4. You want to leverage polymorphism (override methods)
  5. The base class was designed for extension (not a library class)

Classic correct uses:
  Exception hierarchies:  IOException extends Exception
  UI components:          Button extends Component
  Domain hierarchy:       SavingsAccount extends BankAccount (stable, IS-A)
Part 19

JVM Internals: `invokevirtual` and Method Resolution

Understanding how the JVM resolves method calls at runtime is essential for writing performant polymorphic code and understanding framework proxies.

19.1 Four JVM Method Invocation Instructions

invokevirtual  — instance methods (virtual dispatch, supports override)
invokeinterface— interface methods (similar to invokevirtual, different vtable lookup)
invokespecial  — constructors, private methods, super calls (no virtual dispatch)
invokestatic   — static methods (no receiver, no virtual dispatch)
invokedynamic  — lambda/method references, dynamically typed (Java 7+)

19.2 Method Resolution Algorithm

When invokevirtual executes for account.withdraw(amount):

Step 1: Lookup the symbolic reference
  → In the constant pool: "BankAccount.withdraw:(D)V"
  → JVM resolves BankAccount.withdraw() during class loading

Step 2: Determine actual receiver type
  → Read object header of `account`
  → Class pointer → SavingsAccount.class

Step 3: vtable dispatch
  → Look in SavingsAccount's vtable for withdraw() slot
  → If SavingsAccount overrides: dispatch to SavingsAccount.withdraw()
  → If not overridden: follow parent chain until method found
  → Execute

Step 4: JIT optimization (C2 compiler)
  → Profile invokevirtual call sites
  → If always same type (monomorphic): inline the method, eliminate dispatch
  → If two types (bimorphic): generate if/else with two inline paths
  → If many types (megamorphic): full vtable dispatch each time

19.3 invokespecial for super Calls

// Java source
super.withdraw(amount);

// Bytecode
invokespecial #30 // Method BankAccount.withdraw:(D)V
// invokespecial does NOT do virtual dispatch
// It directly calls BankAccount.withdraw, bypassing the vtable
// This is why super.method() always calls the parent version, not a further override

19.4 Interface Method Dispatch (invokeinterface)

Transferable t = new SavingsAccount("S001", "Alice", 1000.0, 0.04);
t.transferTo(target, 200.0);  // compiled as invokeinterface

// invokeinterface:
// → Cannot use simple vtable index (class may implement many interfaces)
// → Searches the itable (interface table) of SavingsAccount for Transferable
// → Finds Transferable's method slot in SavingsAccount's itable
// → Dispatches
// → Slightly slower than invokevirtual in theory, but JIT often eliminates the cost
Part 20

Production Patterns: Domain Modeling in Banking

Let's see all four OOP pillars working together in a realistic production-style banking domain model.

20.1 Full Domain Model

// ─── Value Object (Immutable, encapsulated) ──────────────────────────────────
public final class Money {
    private final long   amountInCents;
    private final String currency;

    public Money(long amountInCents, String currency) {
        if (amountInCents < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Negative money");
        this.amountInCents = amountInCents;
        this.currency      = currency;
    }

    public Money add(Money other) {
        ensureSameCurrency(other);
        return new Money(this.amountInCents + other.amountInCents, this.currency);
    }

    public Money subtract(Money other) {
        ensureSameCurrency(other);
        if (other.amountInCents > this.amountInCents)
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Result would be negative");
        return new Money(this.amountInCents - other.amountInCents, this.currency);
    }

    public boolean isGreaterThan(Money other) {
        ensureSameCurrency(other);
        return this.amountInCents > other.amountInCents;
    }

    private void ensureSameCurrency(Money other) {
        if (!this.currency.equals(other.currency))
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Currency mismatch: "
                    + this.currency + " vs " + other.currency);
    }

    public long getAmountInCents() { return amountInCents; }
    public String getCurrency()    { return currency; }

    @Override public String toString() {
        return String.format("%s %.2f", currency, amountInCents / 100.0);
    }
}

// ─── Abstract Base Account ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
public abstract class Account {
    private final String accountId;
    private final String ownerId;
    private Money        balance;
    private AccountStatus status;

    protected Account(String accountId, String ownerId, Money initialBalance) {
        this.accountId = accountId;
        this.ownerId   = ownerId;
        this.balance   = initialBalance;
        this.status    = AccountStatus.ACTIVE;
    }

    public final void credit(Money amount) {      // final — cannot be overridden
        validateActive();
        validatePositive(amount);
        this.balance = this.balance.add(amount);
        onCredit(amount);                         // hook for subclasses
    }

    public final void debit(Money amount) {       // final — core logic locked
        validateActive();
        validatePositive(amount);
        validateSufficientFunds(amount);
        this.balance = this.balance.subtract(amount);
        onDebit(amount);                          // hook for subclasses
    }

    // Template method pattern — subclasses customize without changing the algorithm
    protected void onCredit(Money amount) { }     // default: do nothing
    protected void onDebit(Money amount)  { }     // default: do nothing

    protected void validateSufficientFunds(Money amount) {
        if (amount.isGreaterThan(balance))
            throw new InsufficientFundsException(accountId, amount, balance);
    }

    // Abstract — each account type defines its own
    public abstract Money calculateMonthlyFee();
    public abstract boolean isEligibleForOverdraft();

    private void validateActive() {
        if (status != AccountStatus.ACTIVE)
            throw new IllegalStateException("Account " + accountId + " is not active");
    }

    private void validatePositive(Money amount) {
        if (amount.getAmountInCents() <= 0)
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Amount must be positive");
    }

    public String getAccountId()  { return accountId; }
    public String getOwnerId()    { return ownerId; }
    public Money  getBalance()    { return balance; }
    public AccountStatus getStatus() { return status; }
}

// ─── Concrete Subtype ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
public class SavingsAccount extends Account {
    private final double annualInterestRate;
    private int          monthlyDebitCount;

    public SavingsAccount(String accountId, String ownerId,
                          Money initialBalance, double annualInterestRate) {
        super(accountId, ownerId, initialBalance);
        this.annualInterestRate = annualInterestRate;
    }

    @Override
    protected void onDebit(Money amount) {
        monthlyDebitCount++;
        if (monthlyDebitCount > 6) {
            // Regulation D: excessive transaction fee after 6
            Money fee = new Money(500, amount.getCurrency()); // $5.00 fee
            super.validateSufficientFunds(fee);
            getBalance();  // apply fee (simplified)
        }
    }

    @Override
    public Money calculateMonthlyFee() {
        Money minBalance = new Money(100_000, getBalance().getCurrency()); // $1000
        return getBalance().isGreaterThan(minBalance)
            ? new Money(0, getBalance().getCurrency())
            : new Money(300, getBalance().getCurrency());  // $3.00 fee
    }

    @Override
    public boolean isEligibleForOverdraft() {
        return false;  // savings accounts cannot overdraft
    }

    public void applyMonthlyInterest() {
        long cents    = getBalance().getAmountInCents();
        long interest = Math.round(cents * annualInterestRate / 12.0);
        credit(new Money(interest, getBalance().getCurrency()));
    }
}
Part 21

Spring Framework: `@Component` and Dependency Injection as Composition

Spring Boot is the dominant Java enterprise framework, and it is built entirely on OOP — specifically composition and polymorphism via dependency injection (DI).

21.1 Spring Beans are OOP Classes

// Spring @Component = "this class is managed by Spring's IoC container"
// Spring will create one instance (bean) and manage its lifecycle

@Component
public class AccountRepository {
    // Manages data access for Account objects
    private final Map<String, Account> store = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    public Optional<Account> findById(String accountId) {
        return Optional.ofNullable(store.get(accountId));
    }

    public void save(Account account) {
        store.put(account.getAccountId(), account);
    }
}

@Component
public class InterestCalculationService {
    public Money calculateInterest(Money balance, double annualRate) {
        long cents    = balance.getAmountInCents();
        long interest = Math.round(cents * annualRate / 12.0);
        return new Money(interest, balance.getCurrency());
    }
}

21.2 Dependency Injection IS Composition

When Spring injects one bean into another, it wires composition relationships:

// AccountService HAS-A AccountRepository (composition via DI)
// AccountService HAS-A InterestCalculationService (composition via DI)
@Service
public class AccountService {

    private final AccountRepository         accountRepository;       // HAS-A
    private final InterestCalculationService interestService;        // HAS-A
    private final AuditLogger               auditLogger;             // HAS-A

    // Constructor injection (recommended over field injection)
    @Autowired
    public AccountService(AccountRepository accountRepository,
                          InterestCalculationService interestService,
                          AuditLogger auditLogger) {
        this.accountRepository = accountRepository;
        this.interestService   = interestService;
        this.auditLogger       = auditLogger;
    }

    public void processMonthlyInterest(String accountId) {
        Account account = accountRepository.findById(accountId)
            .orElseThrow(() -> new AccountNotFoundException(accountId));

        if (account instanceof SavingsAccount savings) {
            savings.applyMonthlyInterest();
            accountRepository.save(savings);
            auditLogger.log("INTEREST_APPLIED", accountId);
        }
    }

    public void transfer(String fromId, String toId, Money amount) {
        Account from = accountRepository.findById(fromId)
            .orElseThrow(() -> new AccountNotFoundException(fromId));
        Account to   = accountRepository.findById(toId)
            .orElseThrow(() -> new AccountNotFoundException(toId));

        from.debit(amount);
        to.credit(amount);

        accountRepository.save(from);
        accountRepository.save(to);
        auditLogger.log("TRANSFER", fromId + " → " + toId + " : " + amount);
    }
}

21.3 Polymorphism in Spring: Interface-Based DI

The real power of Spring DI is programming to interfaces — enabling you to swap implementations without changing callers:

// Define a contract (interface)
public interface NotificationService {
    void notifyAccountHolder(String ownerId, String message);
}

// Multiple implementations
@Component("emailNotificationService")
public class EmailNotificationService implements NotificationService {
    @Override
    public void notifyAccountHolder(String ownerId, String message) {
        System.out.println("Sending EMAIL to " + ownerId + ": " + message);
    }
}

@Component("smsNotificationService")
public class SmsNotificationService implements NotificationService {
    @Override
    public void notifyAccountHolder(String ownerId, String message) {
        System.out.println("Sending SMS to " + ownerId + ": " + message);
    }
}

// Inject by interface — swap implementation in configuration, not here
@Service
public class TransferService {
    private final NotificationService notificationService;

    @Autowired
    public TransferService(
            @Qualifier("emailNotificationService")
            NotificationService notificationService) {
        this.notificationService = notificationService;
    }

    public void transfer(Account from, Account to, Money amount) {
        from.debit(amount);
        to.credit(amount);
        notificationService.notifyAccountHolder(from.getOwnerId(),
            "Transfer of " + amount + " completed");
    }
}

Practice — Lesson 10

Exercise 1: Banking Domain with All Four Pillars

Build a small banking domain that exercises all four OOP pillars:

  1. Create an abstract class Account with:
    - protected fields: accountId, ownerName, balance (double)
    - A constructor that validates non-negative initial balance
    - Concrete methods: deposit(double), getBalance()
    - Abstract methods: withdraw(double), getAccountType(), calculateMonthlyFee()

  2. Create two concrete subclasses:
    - SavingsAccount: enforces max 6 withdrawals/month; earns 4% annual interest (add applyMonthlyInterest())
    - CheckingAccount: allows overdraft up to a configurable limit; charges $35 overdraft fee per occurrence

  3. Create a class AccountManager that:
    - Holds a List<Account> (composition)
    - Has a method processMonthlyCycle() that calls calculateMonthlyFee() on each account (polymorphism)
    - Has a method totalBalance() that sums all balances
    - Has a method getAccountsByType(Class<?>) that filters using instanceof

Exercise 2: Encapsulation Enforcement

Create a class LoanAccount with these invariants enforced through encapsulation:
1. principalAmount must be positive and cannot change after creation (final)
2. interestRate must be between 0.01 and 0.30 (1%–30%) — validate in setter
3. remainingBalance starts at principalAmount and decreases only via makePayment(double amount)
4. makePayment() must: validate payment > 0, compute interest portion vs principal portion, update remainingBalance, throw LoanFullyPaidException when balance reaches 0
5. Override toString() to show: loan ID, remaining balance, next payment date

Exercise 3: Polymorphism and Dynamic Dispatch

  1. Create an interface Reportable with method generateReport(): String
  2. Make SavingsAccount, CheckingAccount, and LoanAccount all implement Reportable
  3. Write a class ReportingService that accepts a List<Reportable> and has method printAllReports() — it must not use any instanceof checks or casting
  4. Add a method countByType(Class<?>) that returns how many accounts are of each type — compare the clean polymorphic approach vs the instanceof approach

Exercise 4: Composition vs Inheritance

Demonstrate the fragile base class problem, then fix it with composition:

  1. Write StackWithLogging extends Stack<String> — override push() and pop() to log each call. Show that calling addAll() from Stack causes double-logging because addAll calls push internally. This is the fragile base class problem.
  2. Rewrite as LoggingStack using composition: private final Stack<String> delegate. Now addAll() behavior is stable regardless of what Stack does internally.

Exercise 5: Object equals/hashCode Contract

  1. Create a Transaction class with fields: transactionId (String), amount (double), timestamp (long)
  2. Implement equals() based only on transactionId (business key)
  3. Implement hashCode() consistently with equals()
  4. Demonstrate that two Transaction objects with the same transactionId but different amounts are equals() and produce the same hashCode()
  5. Add both to a HashSet<Transaction> and verify the set has size 1 (deduplication works)
  6. Break the contract intentionally (implement equals without hashCode), add to HashSet, and explain why the set now has size 2

Part 1

Concept Overview

Access modifiers are the gatekeepers of Java programs. They declare who is allowed to see what — enforcing the boundaries between components, layers, and modules. Without them, every field, every helper method, every internal constant becomes part of the public API, making change almost impossible without breaking callers.

Java provides four access levels, expressed through three keywords:

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    Java Access Levels (widest → narrowest)           │
│                                                                      │
│   public  ──────────────────────────────────────────── everyone      │
│   protected ──────────────── same package + subclasses               │
│   (default) ──────────────── same package only                       │
│   private   ──────────────── same class only                         │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The keyword default is not actually written in code — it is what you get when you write no modifier at all. Developers often call it package-private to make its meaning explicit in conversation.

At the language level, access modifiers apply to:

  • Top-level types (classes, interfaces, enums, annotations) — only public or package-private
  • Members (fields, methods, constructors, nested types) — all four levels

At the JVM level, access modifiers become access flags stored in the .class file binary. The JVM checks them at class loading and linking time, enforcing access rules before your code runs.

At the architecture level, access modifiers are your first line of defence against coupling. A system where everything is public is a system where everything depends on everything. A system where access is deliberately minimized is a system that can evolve.

Part 2

Why Access Modifiers Matter for Architects

2.1 The Cost of Unrestricted Access

Imagine a payments service with a TransactionProcessor class. Its buildAuditRecord() helper was public because a developer once needed it for a quick test. Two years later, six other services call it directly. When you need to change the audit record format, you cannot — the helper has become load-bearing.

This is accidental API surface — a routine failure mode in codebases that do not apply access control intentionally.

Accidental API surface growth:

  Week 1:  TransactionProcessor.buildAuditRecord()  [public — "just for testing"]
  Week 4:  ReportingService calls buildAuditRecord() directly
  Week 12: AuditExporter calls buildAuditRecord() directly
  Week 24: BillingAdapter calls buildAuditRecord() directly

  Now changing buildAuditRecord() breaks three services.
  Cost: high. Benefit of the original "public": zero.

2.2 Access as Contract

When you mark something public, you are making an implicit contract: this is intentional, this is stable, callers may depend on it. The contract is difficult to revoke. Narrower access levels are not restrictions — they are freedom to change internals without breaking callers.

2.3 Framework Implications

Spring, JPA, and other frameworks have specific expectations:

  • Spring can inject private fields via reflection (when @Autowired is on the field), but constructor injection is preferred precisely because it works through normal public contracts
  • JPA requires entity fields to be private with protected no-arg constructor for proxy generation
  • JUnit 5 allows package-private test methods — this is intentional so test helpers are not accidentally public API
Part 3

The Four Access Levels in Detail

3.1 private — Maximum Restriction

A private member is accessible only within the same class (including inner classes defined inside it). No subclass, no same-package class, no reflection without setAccessible(true) can read it through normal channels.

public class BankAccount {

    private double balance;          // only this class can touch this
    private String internalAuditId;  // implementation detail — hidden

    public void deposit(double amount) {
        validateAmount(amount);       // private helper — fine to call here
        this.balance += amount;
    }

    private void validateAmount(double amount) {    // private — not part of API
        if (amount <= 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Amount must be positive: " + amount);
        }
    }

    // Subclasses cannot call validateAmount() — they see none of this
}

When to use private: All fields (always). Helper methods that are implementation details. Constants used only within the class. The default choice — start private, relax only when needed.

3.2 Package-Private (Default) — No Keyword Written

A member with no modifier is visible to every class in the same package. This is more permissive than private but invisible to the outside world.

// File: com/example/payments/TransactionValidator.java
package com.example.payments;

class TransactionValidator {                  // package-private class — internal to package
    boolean validate(Transaction tx) {        // package-private method
        return tx.getAmount().compareTo(BigDecimal.ZERO) > 0;
    }
}

// File: com/example/payments/PaymentService.java
package com.example.payments;

public class PaymentService {
    private final TransactionValidator validator = new TransactionValidator(); // fine

    public void processPayment(Transaction tx) {
        if (!validator.validate(tx)) {        // allowed — same package
            throw new InvalidTransactionException(tx);
        }
        // ... rest of processing
    }
}

// File: com/example/api/PaymentController.java
package com.example.api;

public class PaymentController {
    // TransactionValidator validator = new TransactionValidator(); // COMPILE ERROR
    // Cannot access package-private class from a different package
}

When to use package-private: Internal implementation classes within a package. Utility helpers shared within a layer (e.g., all DAO helpers in com.example.repository). Classes that should be used via a public facade. This is massively underused — many architects leave things as public when package-private is exactly right.

3.3 protected — Package + Subclasses

A protected member is visible to:

  1. All classes in the same package (same as package-private)
  2. Subclasses, even in different packages — but only through the subclass reference
// File: com/example/core/BaseRepository.java
package com.example.core;

public abstract class BaseRepository<T, ID> {

    protected EntityManager entityManager;    // subclasses need this

    protected T findById(ID id, Class<T> type) {   // shared implementation
        return entityManager.find(type, id);
    }

    protected void persist(T entity) {         // shared persistence logic
        entityManager.persist(entity);
        entityManager.flush();
    }
}

// File: com/example/payments/PaymentRepository.java
package com.example.payments;  // DIFFERENT package

import com.example.core.BaseRepository;

public class PaymentRepository extends BaseRepository<Payment, Long> {

    public Payment findPaymentById(Long id) {
        return findById(id, Payment.class);    // allowed — subclass access to protected
    }

    public void save(Payment payment) {
        persist(payment);                      // allowed — subclass access to protected
    }
}

The protected subclass-only nuance: A subclass in a different package can access a protected member through its own reference (this.entityManager), but not through a reference to a sibling subclass. This is the source of one of Java's most-asked interview questions (covered in Part 15).

When to use protected: Template method pattern (base class defines skeleton, subclasses fill in steps). Framework extension points. Fields that subclasses legitimately need to read — though consider protected getters over protected fields to retain some encapsulation.

3.4 public — No Restriction

A public member is visible everywhere — same class, same package, subclasses, different packages, different modules (subject to module exports). It is a binding contract with every possible caller in the universe.

// This is your public API — treat it like a contract you cannot break
public class PaymentService {

    public PaymentResult processPayment(PaymentRequest request) {
        // This signature is now frozen — changing it breaks all callers
        validateRequest(request);           // private helper — can freely change
        Payment payment = buildPayment(request);  // private — can freely change
        return executeTransaction(payment);
    }
}

When to use public: Types intended for use outside their package. Methods that form the public API contract. Constants that external code legitimately needs. The minority of your codebase — not the majority.

Part 4

The Access Matrix

This table is the canonical reference. Memorize it. It appears in every Java interview at every level.

Access Level Same Class Same Package Subclass (diff pkg) Different Package
private ✅ Yes ❌ No ❌ No ❌ No
(default) ✅ Yes ✅ Yes ❌ No ❌ No
protected ✅ Yes ✅ Yes ✅ Yes ❌ No
public ✅ Yes ✅ Yes ✅ Yes ✅ Yes
