Part 6

Top-Level Type Visibility

Top-level classes (not nested inside another class) can only be public or package-private. The modifiers private and protected are illegal for top-level types.

// LEGAL: public top-level class — visible everywhere
public class PublicService { }

// LEGAL: package-private top-level class — only visible within package
class InternalHelper { }

// ILLEGAL: private top-level class — compiler error
// private class SecretClass { }   // Error: modifier private not allowed here

// ILLEGAL: protected top-level class — compiler error
// protected class SemiPublic { }  // Error: modifier protected not allowed here

One public class per file: A single .java file can contain multiple classes, but at most one may be public, and it must match the filename.

// File: PaymentService.java — one public class, plus internal helpers
public class PaymentService {       // filename must match
    // ... implementation
}

class PaymentServiceHelper {        // package-private — fine to coexist
    // ... helper implementation
}

class PaymentServiceConfig {        // package-private — fine to coexist
    // ... configuration
}
Part 7

Nested Classes and Access

Access rules interact with nested classes in powerful ways.

public class Outer {
    private int secret = 42;

    // Inner class — has full access to all Outer members including private!
    class Inner {
        void reveal() {
            System.out.println(secret);   // private field of Outer — accessible!
        }
    }

    // Static nested class — no implicit Outer instance, but still sees private
    static class StaticNested {
        void reveal(Outer outer) {
            System.out.println(outer.secret);  // accesses private via instance — legal!
        }
    }

    // Private nested class — only Outer can create/use it
    private class PrivateNested {
        void work() { }
    }
}

This is why the Builder pattern works so elegantly in Java: the Builder inner class can directly access all private fields of the outer class it constructs, keeping both encapsulated from the outside world.

Part 8

JVM: Access Flags in Class Files

Every Java access modifier becomes a binary flag in the .class file. The JVM reads these flags at class loading time and enforces them.

Class file structure (simplified):
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  ClassFile {                                     │
│    u4  magic;           // 0xCAFEBABE            │
│    u2  minor_version;                            │
│    u2  major_version;                            │
│    u2  access_flags;    // <── access modifiers! │
│    ...                                           │
│  }                                               │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

8.1 Class-Level Access Flags

Flag Hex Value Meaning
ACC_PUBLIC 0x0001 Class is public
ACC_FINAL 0x0010 Class cannot be subclassed
ACC_SUPER 0x0020 Treat invokespecial of superclass differently
ACC_INTERFACE 0x0200 Is an interface
ACC_ABSTRACT 0x0400 Is abstract
ACC_SYNTHETIC 0x1000 Generated by compiler
ACC_ENUM 0x4000 Is an enum

8.2 Field and Method Access Flags

Flag Hex Value Meaning
ACC_PUBLIC 0x0001 public
ACC_PRIVATE 0x0002 private
ACC_PROTECTED 0x0004 protected
ACC_STATIC 0x0008 static
ACC_FINAL 0x0010 final
ACC_SYNCHRONIZED 0x0020 synchronized
ACC_VOLATILE 0x0040 volatile (fields only)
ACC_BRIDGE 0x0040 Compiler-generated bridge method
ACC_NATIVE 0x0100 native
ACC_ABSTRACT 0x0400 abstract

No ACC_PACKAGE_PRIVATE flag: Package-private access is the absence of the ACC_PUBLIC, ACC_PRIVATE, and ACC_PROTECTED flags. The JVM infers package-private when none of the three access bits are set.

8.3 Inspecting Access Flags

You can verify access flags using javap -verbose:

$ javap -verbose BankAccount.class

Classfile BankAccount.class
  ...
  flags: (0x0021) ACC_PUBLIC, ACC_SUPER
  ...
  {
    private double balance;
      descriptor: D
      flags: (0x0002) ACC_PRIVATE

    public void deposit(double);
      descriptor: (D)V
      flags: (0x0001) ACC_PUBLIC

    private void validateAmount(double);
      descriptor: (D)V
      flags: (0x0002) ACC_PRIVATE
  }

8.4 Access Check Timing

The JVM checks access at:
1. Link time — when the class is first loaded and verified
2. Resolution time — when a symbolic reference to a field/method is resolved
3. Runtime (reflection) — Field.get() / Method.invoke() check access unless setAccessible(true) is called

setAccessible(true) bypasses the language-level access check — which is why frameworks like Spring use it to inject private fields. Java 9+ modules introduced a stronger barrier (--add-opens required) to protect even setAccessible paths.

Part 9

Access Modifiers and Inheritance Rules

When overriding a method in a subclass, you may broaden access but never narrow it.

public class Parent {
    protected void display() {
        System.out.println("Parent display");
    }
}

public class Child extends Parent {

    @Override
    public void display() {         // broadening protected → public: LEGAL
        System.out.println("Child display");
    }
}

public class BadChild extends Parent {

    // @Override
    // private void display() { }   // COMPILE ERROR: narrowing public to private illegal
}

The reason: callers that hold a Parent reference and call display() must always be able to call it. If a subclass could narrow access, the Liskov Substitution Principle would break — you could no longer substitute a subclass where a parent was expected.

Part 10

Constructors and Access Modifiers

Constructor visibility controls who can instantiate a class:

// Private constructor: Singleton pattern
public class ConfigurationManager {
    private static final ConfigurationManager INSTANCE = new ConfigurationManager();

    private ConfigurationManager() {    // prevents external instantiation
        loadProperties();
    }

    public static ConfigurationManager getInstance() {
        return INSTANCE;
    }
}

// Private constructor: Utility class (no instantiation intended)
public final class StringUtils {
    private StringUtils() {             // prevents instantiation of utility class
        throw new AssertionError("Utility class");
    }

    public static String toTitleCase(String s) { /* ... */ return s; }
    public static boolean isBlank(String s) { return s == null || s.trim().isEmpty(); }
}

// Package-private constructor: Force factory method usage
public class Payment {
    private final String paymentId;
    private final BigDecimal amount;

    Payment(String paymentId, BigDecimal amount) {  // package-private constructor
        this.paymentId = paymentId;
        this.amount    = amount;
    }

    // Only PaymentFactory (same package) can create instances
}
Part 11

`protected` and the Subclass Access Nuance

This is the subtlest rule in Java access control and a classic interview trap.

A subclass in a different package can access a protected member only through its own class reference, not through a sibling subclass reference:

// Package: com.example.core
public class Account {
    protected double balance;
}

// Package: com.example.savings
public class SavingsAccount extends Account {

    void adjust(SavingsAccount other) {
        this.balance  = 100.0;     // LEGAL: accessing own protected field
        other.balance = 100.0;     // LEGAL: same class, same subclass type

        Account acc = new Account();
        acc.balance  = 100.0;      // COMPILE ERROR: acc is not a SavingsAccount
                                   // different-package subclass cannot access
                                   // protected via a plain Account reference
    }
}

// Package: com.example.checking
public class CheckingAccount extends Account {

    void adjust(SavingsAccount savings) {
        savings.balance = 100.0;   // COMPILE ERROR: SavingsAccount is not in
                                   // the same package as CheckingAccount,
                                   // and CheckingAccount is not a subtype of SavingsAccount
    }
}

The rule summarized: In a different package, protected access is granted only when the access is through the subclass itself (or a reference of the same subclass type). This prevents cross-subclass access to protected state.

Part 12

Interfaces and Access Modifiers

Interface members have specific default access rules:

public interface PaymentProcessor {

    // All interface methods are implicitly public abstract
    // Writing public/abstract is optional (and often omitted)
    void processPayment(Payment payment);

    // Default methods: implicitly public
    default void validatePayment(Payment payment) {
        if (payment == null) throw new NullPointerException("Payment must not be null");
    }

    // Static methods: implicitly public
    static PaymentProcessor noOp() {
        return payment -> {};
    }

    // Constants: implicitly public static final
    int MAX_RETRY_COUNT = 3;   // equivalent to: public static final int MAX_RETRY_COUNT = 3

    // Private methods (Java 9+): allowed to share code between default methods
    private boolean isValidAmount(BigDecimal amount) {
        return amount != null && amount.compareTo(BigDecimal.ZERO) > 0;
    }
}

Cannot use protected in an interface: Interface members are part of a public contract. protected makes no semantic sense in an interface — there is no state, no package-level sharing to protect.

Part 13

Java 9+ Module System and Access

Java 9 introduced the module system (Project Jigsaw), which adds a third layer of access control above packages. Even public members can be inaccessible between modules if not explicitly exported.

// File: module-info.java (in module root)
module com.example.payments {

    // Export the public API package — other modules can use public types here
    exports com.example.payments.api;

    // Do NOT export internal package — even public types are invisible to other modules
    // com.example.payments.internal is invisible outside this module

    // Qualified export: only specific module can access this package
    exports com.example.payments.internal to com.example.reporting;

    // Opens package for deep reflection (e.g., Spring, Hibernate need this)
    opens com.example.payments.domain to org.springframework.core;

    // Require other modules
    requires java.sql;
    requires spring.context;
}

13.1 Module Access Matrix

Access Level Same Module Exported to All Exported to Module Not Exported
public in exported pkg ✅ ✅ ✅ (specific) ❌
public in unexported pkg ✅ ❌ ❌ ❌
protected ✅ (subclass) ❌ ❌ ❌
private ✅ (same class) ❌ ❌ ❌

13.2 Strong Encapsulation vs --add-opens

Before modules, frameworks used setAccessible(true) freely. Modules block this by default. You can re-open modules at JVM startup:

# Required for Spring on Java 17+
java --add-opens java.base/java.lang=ALL-UNNAMED \
     --add-opens java.base/java.util=ALL-UNNAMED \
     -jar myapp.jar

Spring Boot 3.x added these automatically. Understanding why they exist is an architect-level concern.

Part 14

Production Patterns: Minimizing Public Surface

14.1 Package-Private by Default

The single most impactful habit: make everything package-private unless it needs to be public.

// Mediocre: everything public — maximum coupling
public class OrderProcessor {
    public Order buildOrder(Cart cart) { ... }
    public void validateOrder(Order order) { ... }
    public BigDecimal calculateTax(Order order) { ... }
    public void applyDiscounts(Order order) { ... }
    public OrderResult submit(Order order) { ... }
}

// Better: only the entry point is public
public class OrderProcessor {
    public OrderResult submit(Cart cart) {     // one public method: the intended API
        Order order = buildOrder(cart);
        validateOrder(order);
        applyDiscounts(order);
        return executeSubmission(order);
    }

    Order buildOrder(Cart cart) { ... }        // package-private — testable, not API
    void validateOrder(Order order) { ... }    // package-private
    BigDecimal calculateTax(Order order) { ... }  // package-private
    void applyDiscounts(Order order) { ... }   // package-private
    private OrderResult executeSubmission(Order order) { ... }  // private
}

14.2 Layered Access Design

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  com.example.payments.api          (public types only)        │
│  └── PaymentService (public)                                  │
│  └── PaymentRequest (public)                                  │
│  └── PaymentResult  (public)                                  │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  com.example.payments.internal     (package-private types)    │
│  └── PaymentValidator  (package-private)                      │
│  └── FraudDetector     (package-private)                      │
│  └── AuditRecordBuilder (package-private)                     │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  com.example.payments.domain       (protected in base)        │
│  └── BasePayment (public abstract, protected hooks)           │
│  └── CardPayment extends BasePayment                          │
│  └── BankTransfer extends BasePayment                         │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

14.3 API Evolution

When you later need to change an internal helper, the access modifier tells you the blast radius:

  • private: change freely, only impacts this class
  • package-private: change impacts this package only — run package-level tests
  • protected: change impacts all subclasses, possibly in other modules — check all subclasses
  • public: change impacts every caller in the codebase and every external consumer — major version bump required
Part 15

Spring Framework Patterns

15.1 @VisibleForTesting

Guava's @VisibleForTesting annotation documents intent when you widen access for testability:

import com.google.common.annotations.VisibleForTesting;

public class FraudDetector {

    @VisibleForTesting
    static double computeRiskScore(Transaction tx) {   // package-private for testing
        return tx.getAmount().doubleValue() * RISK_MULTIPLIER;
    }
}

// In the test package (same package as FraudDetector)
class FraudDetectorTest {
    @Test
    void riskScoreIsHighForLargeAmount() {
        double score = FraudDetector.computeRiskScore(largeTransaction());
        assertThat(score).isGreaterThan(HIGH_RISK_THRESHOLD);
    }
}

15.2 Spring Component Scanning and Visibility

Spring discovers beans through package scanning. Bean classes must be accessible to Spring's component scanner:

@SpringBootApplication  // scans com.example.myapp and all sub-packages
public class MyApplication { }

// This bean WILL be found — public class in scanned package
@Service
public class PaymentService { }

// This class will NOT be found by default — package-private class
@Service
class InternalAuditHelper { }   // Spring can't instantiate without @Bean factory method

15.3 Module Boundary Enforcement with Spring Modulith

Spring Modulith enforces package-private access as module boundaries:

// Each top-level sub-package is a module
// com.example.orders      — Orders module
// com.example.payments    — Payments module
// com.example.inventory   — Inventory module

// Within com.example.orders:
public class OrderService { }      // public API of Orders module
class OrderValidator { }           // package-private — internal to Orders

// Spring Modulith test: verify no cross-module package-private access
@ApplicationModuleTest
class OrdersModuleTests {
    // Modulith verifies that Payments does not call internal Orders helpers
}
Part 16

Common Mistakes and Anti-Patterns

16.1 Making Everything Public "Just to Be Safe"

// Anti-pattern: everything public
public class UserService {
    public User loadFromDatabase(String id) { ... }        // needed by others
    public String hashPassword(String password) { ... }    // should be private!
    public boolean checkPasswordPolicy(String pwd) { ... } // should be private!
    public void sendWelcomeEmail(User user) { ... }        // should delegate to EmailService
}

16.2 Leaking Internal Types

// Anti-pattern: public method returns internal type
public InternalPaymentRecord processPayment(Request r) { ... }
//                            ^ InternalPaymentRecord forced to be public
//                              because it appears in a public method signature

// Better: use a public result DTO
public PaymentResult processPayment(Request r) { ... }
//     ^ PaymentResult is the intentional public API type

16.3 protected Fields Instead of protected Accessors

// Anti-pattern: protected field — subclasses bypass encapsulation
public abstract class BaseEntity {
    protected long id;           // subclass can set this to any value
    protected Timestamp created;
}

// Better: protected getter, private setter — subclasses read but don't corrupt
public abstract class BaseEntity {
    private long id;
    private Timestamp created;

    protected long getId() { return id; }
    protected Timestamp getCreated() { return created; }
}
Part 17

Records and Access Modifiers (Java 16+)

Java Records have specific access rules for their generated members:

public record PaymentRequest(
    String paymentId,
    BigDecimal amount,
    String currency
) {
    // Record components automatically get:
    //   public accessor methods: paymentId(), amount(), currency()
    //   public equals(), hashCode(), toString()
    //   private final fields

    // Compact constructor — always has the same access as the record
    public PaymentRequest {
        Objects.requireNonNull(paymentId, "paymentId");
        if (amount.compareTo(BigDecimal.ZERO) <= 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Amount must be positive");
        }
    }

    // Additional methods can have any access
    public String formattedAmount() {
        return amount + " " + currency;
    }
}

Records enforce: field-like accessor methods are always public. You cannot make them private or protected. The underlying fields are always private final.

Part 18

Enums and Access Modifiers

public enum PaymentStatus {

    PENDING, PROCESSING, COMPLETED, FAILED, REFUNDED;

    // Enum constructor is always package-private or private
    // (never public or protected — you cannot instantiate enums directly)
    PaymentStatus() { }

    private PaymentStatus(String description) {   // fine
        this.description = description;
    }

    // public enum constant — that's the whole point of an enum
    public static final PaymentStatus DEFAULT = PENDING;

    private final String description = name().toLowerCase();

    public String getDescription() { return description; }

    // Package-private helper
    boolean isTerminal() {
        return this == COMPLETED || this == FAILED || this == REFUNDED;
    }
}
Part 19

Access Modifiers in Annotations

// Annotation types are always implicitly public if declared public
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@Target(ElementType.METHOD)
public @interface Audited {

    // Annotation element methods are implicitly public abstract
    String action() default "UNKNOWN";
    boolean logRequest() default true;

    // Default values make elements optional
    // No access modifiers other than public are meaningful here
}
Part 20

Interview Deep Dives

Q1: What is the difference between protected and package-private?

Both allow same-package access. The difference is outside the package: protected additionally grants access to subclasses in any package, while package-private grants access to no one outside the package, regardless of inheritance.

Q2: Can a subclass in a different package call a protected method on an instance of a different sibling subclass?

No. In a different package, protected access is only granted when accessing through the subclass's own type. Consider:

// com.example.base
public class Animal { protected void breathe() { } }

// com.example.zoo
public class Dog extends Animal {
    void show(Cat cat) {
        this.breathe();   // LEGAL — through own type
        cat.breathe();    // COMPILE ERROR — Cat is not Dog or a supertype
    }
}
public class Cat extends Animal { }

Q3: What happens if you use setAccessible(true) to bypass private?

It works in non-modular code (Java 8 and below, or unnamed modules). In Java 9+ modules, setAccessible(true) on types in closed modules throws InaccessibleObjectException. You must use --add-opens at JVM startup or declare opens in module-info.java.

Q4: Can you override a package-private method in a subclass in a different package?

No. The subclass in a different package does not see the package-private method, so it cannot override it. If the subclass defines a method with the same name and signature, it is a completely new method — no @Override, no polymorphic dispatch through the parent type.

Part 21

Production Case Study: Payment Gateway API Design

A real payment gateway team redesigned their internal library to minimize public surface. Before:

// Before: 47 public classes, every internal detail exposed
public class PaymentGateway {
    public void configure(Config c) { ... }
    public void initializeConnection() { ... }
    public void warmConnectionPool() { ... }
    public Connection borrowConnection() { ... }
    public void returnConnection(Connection c) { ... }
    public void processPayment(Payment p) { ... }
    public void retryPayment(Payment p, int attempt) { ... }
    public void handleTimeout(Payment p) { ... }
    public void logFailure(Payment p, Exception e) { ... }
    public PaymentRecord buildRecord(Payment p, Result r) { ... }
}

After applying access discipline:

// After: 3 public classes, 44 internal classes made package-private
public class PaymentGateway {               // public: entry point
    public PaymentResult submit(PaymentRequest request) { ... }
    public void configure(GatewayConfig config) { ... }
    // All other methods become package-private or private
}

public class PaymentRequest { ... }         // public: input DTO
public class PaymentResult { ... }          // public: output DTO

// Everything else: package-private
class ConnectionPool { ... }
class RetryPolicy { ... }
class TimeoutHandler { ... }
class AuditLogger { ... }
class PaymentRecordBuilder { ... }

Result: refactored the connection pool completely (3 times over 2 years) without any caller needing to change. The public surface of 3 classes never changed.

Part 22

Summary Table

Concept Keyword Visible To JVM Flag Best Used For
Private private Same class only ACC_PRIVATE (0x0002) All fields; implementation helpers
Package-Private (none) Same package (no flag set) Internal classes, helpers; massively underused
Protected protected Same package + subclasses ACC_PROTECTED (0x0004) Template method hooks; base class fields (prefer accessors)
Public public Everyone ACC_PUBLIC (0x0001) Intentional API contracts; minority of your code
Top-level access public or none Package or all Class access_flags Only two options for top-level types
Access widening @Override Broaden only N/A Override protected → public legal; reverse illegal
Module system exports / opens Per-module N/A (module layer) Java 9+: control public API at module granularity
Reflection bypass setAccessible Bypasses language N/A Framework injection; blocked by strong encapsulation in modules
Interface members implicit public All callers ACC_PUBLIC All interface methods/constants are always public
Enum constructors private (implicit) N/A ACC_PRIVATE Enum construction always private
Record accessors public (implicit) All callers ACC_PUBLIC Record component accessors always public
Minimize surface Architecture rule N/A N/A Smaller public surface = easier evolution = lower coupling

Part 1

Concept Overview

A Java package is a named namespace that groups related types. It is simultaneously:

  • A naming mechanism — preventing collision between classes with the same name
  • An access control boundary — the unit of package-private visibility
  • A physical organization rule — the package name must mirror the directory structure on disk
  • A logical module boundary — the basis for separating concerns within a codebase
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    Package = Namespace + Directory + Boundary            │
│                                                                          │
│  com.example.payments                                                    │
│       │                                                                  │
│       ├── PaymentService.java          (public API)                      │
│       ├── PaymentRepository.java       (public API)                      │
│       ├── PaymentValidator.java        (package-private internal)        │
│       └── FraudDetector.java           (package-private internal)        │
│                                                                          │
│  Maps to filesystem:                                                     │
│  src/main/java/com/example/payments/PaymentService.java                  │
│                                                                          │
│  Enables:                                                                │
│  - com.example.payments.PaymentService  (fully qualified name)           │
│  - package-private access for PaymentValidator, FraudDetector            │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Without packages, every Java class in the world would compete for names in a single namespace. A class named Date would collide between the JDK's java.util.Date, java.sql.Date, org.joda.time.DateTime, and every application-defined date class ever written. Packages solve this.

At the architect level, packages are design decisions. A well-organized package structure is self-documenting architecture. A poorly organized one is a symptom of architectural confusion.

Part 2

Why Packages Matter for Architects

2.1 Packages as Architecture Diagrams

The package structure of a codebase tells the story of how it was designed — and how well:

Symptoms of a healthy package structure:
  com.example.orders.api        → clear inbound contract
  com.example.orders.domain     → domain model, no framework deps
  com.example.orders.repository → database access layer
  com.example.orders.service    → business logic
  com.example.orders.event      → event publishing/handling

Symptoms of an unhealthy package structure:
  com.example.models            → all DTOs from 12 different domains mixed together
  com.example.utils             → 200 unrelated utility classes
  com.example.service           → "service" but contains DAOs and controllers too
  com.example.stuff             → real example from production codebase at $COMPANY

2.2 Coupling Measurement

The number of cross-package dependencies is a measurable proxy for coupling. Tools like JDepend, ArchUnit, and Structure101 analyze package dependencies and detect cycles. A package that imports from 20 other packages is almost certainly doing too much.

2.3 Spring Boot Package Scanning

Spring Boot auto-configures component scanning based on the package of the @SpringBootApplication class. Getting the package structure wrong means beans are not found, or unwanted beans are loaded. This is one of the most common Spring Boot configuration mistakes for junior developers — and understanding why it happens requires understanding packages.

Part 3

Package Declaration

Every Java source file either belongs to a package or the default package (no declaration). Best practice: always declare a package. The default package cannot be imported from other packages.

// First statement in the file (before imports, before class declaration)
package com.example.payments.service;

// Then imports (if any)
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.List;

// Then the type declaration
public class PaymentService {
    // ...
}

3.1 Package Declaration Rules

  1. Must be the first non-comment statement in the file
  2. Only one package declaration per file
  3. The package name must match the directory path of the file
  4. Package names use all lowercase by convention
  5. Components are separated by dots: com.example.payments.service
  6. Cannot start with a digit or contain reserved words (though technically allowed, highly discouraged)
// LEGAL package declarations
package com.example.payments;
package org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.web;
package java.util.concurrent;

// ILLEGAL: starts with number
// package 1com.example;   // compile error

// LEGAL but terrible practice: camelCase components
// package Com.Example.Payments;  // technically valid, violates all conventions
Part 4

Directory Structure and Package-to-Folder Mapping

The Java compiler requires that the source file for class com.example.payments.PaymentService lives at the path com/example/payments/PaymentService.java relative to the source root.

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Source Root: src/main/java/                                             │
│                                                                          │
│  src/main/java/                                                          │
│  └── com/                                                                │
│      └── example/                                                        │
│          └── payments/                                                   │
│              ├── PaymentService.java     → package com.example.payments  │
│              ├── PaymentRepository.java  → package com.example.payments  │
│              └── service/                                                │
│                  └── FraudDetector.java  → package com.example.payments.service │
│                                                                          │
│  Compiled output: target/classes/                                        │
│  └── com/                                                                │
│      └── example/                                                        │
│          └── payments/                                                   │
│              ├── PaymentService.class                                    │
│              └── service/                                                │
│                  └── FraudDetector.class                                 │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The compiler does not create the directory — you must. In IDEs, creating a package creates the directory automatically. In javac on the command line, you must create directories manually.

4.1 Mismatch Between Declaration and Directory

If the package declaration does not match the directory path, the compiler produces an error:

// File at: src/com/example/api/Controller.java
// But declares: package com.example.payments;

error: class Controller is public, should be declared in a file named Controller.java
  Correction: move the file or change the package declaration
Part 5

Fully Qualified Names

A fully qualified name (FQN) uniquely identifies a type across all packages: packageName.ClassName.

// Using fully qualified names — no import needed
java.util.List<java.lang.String> names = new java.util.ArrayList<>();
java.time.LocalDate today = java.time.LocalDate.now();
java.sql.Date sqlDate = java.sql.Date.valueOf(today);

// The above is valid but verbose — imports exist to shorten this

Fully qualified names are necessary when:

  1. Resolving name conflicts — two imported classes have the same simple name
  2. Annotation processing — some tools require FQNs in configuration
  3. Reflection — Class.forName("com.example.payments.PaymentService")
  4. Spring configuration — @Bean(name = "com.example.payments.PaymentService")
// Classic conflict: java.util.Date vs java.sql.Date
import java.util.Date;

public class ReportService {
    public void generateReport() {
        Date utilDate = new Date();                    // java.util.Date from import
        java.sql.Date sqlDate = new java.sql.Date(0);  // FQN required for sql.Date
    }
}
Part 6

The `import` Statement

import statements let you use short simple names instead of fully qualified names.

package com.example.reports;

// Single-type import — most readable, most explicit
import java.util.List;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.time.LocalDate;
import com.example.payments.PaymentService;

public class ReportGenerator {
    private final PaymentService paymentService;   // no FQN needed

    public List<BigDecimal> getMonthlySummary(LocalDate from, LocalDate to) {
        List<BigDecimal> totals = new ArrayList<>();
        // ...
        return totals;
    }
}

6.1 Import Rules

  1. Imports appear after the package declaration, before the class declaration
  2. Imports are compile-time only — they generate no bytecode
  3. A used but unimported type causes a compile error (unless using FQN)
  4. An imported but unused type causes a warning (IDEs report it; javac does not by default)
  5. Multiple imports of the same type are allowed but pointless
Part 7

Wildcard Imports

A wildcard import (import package.*;) imports all public types from a package in one statement.

import java.util.*;     // imports List, ArrayList, HashMap, Set, Map, Date, ...
import java.time.*;     // imports LocalDate, LocalDateTime, ZonedDateTime, ...

public class PaymentProcessor {
    private Map<String, List<BigDecimal>> transactionsByAccount = new HashMap<>();
    // ...
}

7.1 Wildcard Import Rules and Pitfalls

Aspect Details
Depth java.util.* does NOT include java.util.concurrent.* — wildcard is one level only
Bytecode impact Zero — imports are purely compile-time hints
Ambiguity If two wildcard imports bring in same simple name, compiler requires FQN
Static members import java.util.*; does NOT import static members — need import static
Convention Many teams/style guides (Google, Sun) discourage wildcards for readability 
import java.util.*;
import java.sql.*;

// Both packages have a class named "Date"
public class ReportService {
    // Date date = new Date();  // COMPILE ERROR: ambiguous — java.util.Date or java.sql.Date?

    java.util.Date utilDate = new java.util.Date();   // FQN required to resolve
    java.sql.Date sqlDate   = new java.sql.Date(0);   // FQN required to resolve
}
Part 8

Static Imports

import static imports static members (fields and methods) so they can be used without the class name prefix.

import static java.lang.Math.PI;
import static java.lang.Math.sqrt;
import static java.lang.Math.pow;
import static java.util.Collections.unmodifiableList;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertEquals;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertThrows;
import static org.mockito.Mockito.when;
import static org.mockito.Mockito.verify;

public class CircleCalculator {
    public double area(double radius) {
        return PI * pow(radius, 2);   // no Math. prefix needed
    }

    public double circumference(double radius) {
        return 2 * PI * radius;
    }
}

// In tests — static imports keep test code fluent and readable
class PaymentServiceTest {
    @Test
    void shouldThrowForNegativeAmount() {
        assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class,
            () -> service.processPayment(new Payment(-1.0)));    // no Assertions. prefix

        verify(auditLogger).logFailure(any());                   // no Mockito. prefix
    }
}

8.1 Static Import Best Practices

Use static imports for:                    Avoid static imports for:
  - Test assertions (JUnit, AssertJ)         - General utility methods (confusing where they come from)
  - Math constants (PI, E)                   - Anything where the source is not obvious
  - Builder pattern constants                - Multiple static imports from same class (just import the class)
  - DSL-like fluent APIs (Mockito, etc.)
Part 9

`java.lang` and Auto-Import

The package java.lang is automatically imported by the compiler into every Java file. You never need to write import java.lang.String or import java.lang.System.

9.1 Key java.lang Types (Always Available)

Type Description
String Immutable character sequence — the most-used class in Java
Object Root of all class hierarchies
System System I/O (System.out.println), environment, GC
Math Mathematical functions — note: static members still need Math.sqrt()
Integer, Long, Double, etc. Wrapper types for primitives
Boolean, Character, Byte, Short, Float Remaining wrappers
StringBuilder, StringBuffer Mutable string builders
Thread, Runnable Threading fundamentals
Exception, RuntimeException, Error Exception hierarchy root
Enum Base class for all enum types
Record Base class for all record types (Java 16+)
Iterable for-each contract
Comparable Natural ordering contract
AutoCloseable try-with-resources contract
ClassLoader Class loading mechanism
Process, ProcessBuilder External process management 
// This compiles without ANY imports — all from java.lang
public class Example {
    public static void main(String[] args) {       // String from java.lang
        System.out.println("Hello");               // System from java.lang
        Object o = new Object();                   // Object from java.lang
        Integer i = Integer.valueOf(42);           // Integer from java.lang
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();   // StringBuilder from java.lang
        Thread t = new Thread(() -> {});           // Thread, Runnable from java.lang
    }
}
Part 10

Classpath and Package Resolution at Runtime

At runtime, the JVM resolves classes by searching the classpath for directories and JARs that contain the class file at the path matching the package name.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Classpath: /app/classes:/app/lib/spring-core-6.1.0.jar                 │
│                                                                         │
│  JVM needs: com.example.payments.PaymentService                         │
│                                                                         │
│  Step 1: Search /app/classes for                                        │
│          /app/classes/com/example/payments/PaymentService.class         │
│          → FOUND → load it                                              │
│                                                                         │
│  JVM needs: org.springframework.beans.factory.BeanFactory               │
│                                                                         │
│  Step 1: Search /app/classes for path... NOT FOUND                      │
│  Step 2: Open spring-core-6.1.0.jar, look for                           │
│          org/springframework/beans/factory/BeanFactory.class            │
│          → FOUND inside JAR → load it                                   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

10.1 Classpath Configuration

# Command line — colon separator on Unix, semicolon on Windows
java -cp /app/classes:/app/lib/mylib.jar com.example.Main

# Modern: use -classpath or --class-path
java --class-path /app/classes:/app/lib/*  com.example.Main

# Wildcard (Java 6+): includes all JARs in directory
java -cp /app/classes:/app/lib/*  com.example.Main

10.2 ClassLoader Hierarchy

Bootstrap ClassLoader (JVM built-in)
    └── loads: java.lang.*, java.util.*, JDK core classes from rt.jar / modules

Extension / Platform ClassLoader
    └── loads: java.se, java.xml, javax.* module classes

Application ClassLoader (your code)
    └── loads: everything on the -classpath / -cp
        └── your classes, framework JARs, library JARs

Optional: Custom ClassLoaders
    └── servlet containers (Tomcat, Jetty) load WARs in isolated classloaders
    └── OSGi loads bundles in isolated classloaders
    └── Java agents instrument classes at load time

10.3 ClassNotFoundException vs NoClassDefFoundError

ClassNotFoundException:
  - Thrown by Class.forName("...") or ClassLoader.loadClass("...")
  - Class literal not on classpath — checked exception
  - Fix: add the JAR to the classpath

NoClassDefFoundError:
  - Thrown when a class was found at compile time but missing at runtime
  - Often: JAR is on compile classpath but not runtime classpath
  - Also: class was loaded before but became unavailable (rare in apps, common in containers)
  - Fix: ensure runtime classpath matches compile classpath
Part 11

Naming Conventions: Reverse Domain

The universal Java package naming convention uses the reverse of your organization's internet domain name, followed by the project and module:

Convention:  com.{company}.{product}.{module}.{layer}

Examples:
  com.google.guava.collect
  org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.web
  io.netty.channel.socket.nio
  com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ser
  org.apache.kafka.clients.producer

11.1 Why Reverse Domain?

The reverse domain guarantees global uniqueness. If two separate organizations both write a class called StringUtils, they will have:
- com.example.StringUtils
- org.apache.commons.lang.StringUtils

These never collide, even when both are on the same classpath.

11.2 Real-World Package Naming Patterns

Enterprise application:
  com.acme.payments.api              ← REST controllers, DTOs
  com.acme.payments.domain           ← domain entities, value objects
  com.acme.payments.service          ← business logic
  com.acme.payments.repository       ← data access
  com.acme.payments.event            ← domain events
  com.acme.payments.config           ← Spring configuration
  com.acme.payments.exception        ← custom exception types
  com.acme.payments.util             ← truly shared utilities

Open-source library:
  io.example.sdk                     ← main entry points
  io.example.sdk.core                ← core abstractions
  io.example.sdk.internal            ← package-private internals (by convention)
  io.example.sdk.spi                 ← Service Provider Interface (extension points)
  io.example.sdk.test                ← test utilities for library users

11.3 Anti-Patterns in Naming

Anti-pattern: Technology-based organization
  com.example.controllers   ← mixes orders, payments, inventory controllers
  com.example.services      ← mixes all services
  com.example.models        ← mixes all domain objects

Better: Feature-based organization
  com.example.orders        ← everything for orders in one place
  com.example.payments      ← everything for payments in one place
  com.example.inventory     ← everything for inventory in one place
Part 12

Maven and Gradle Project Structure

Build tools enforce a standard directory layout that maps packages to source trees.

12.1 Maven Standard Directory Layout

my-project/
├── pom.xml
└── src/
    ├── main/
    │   ├── java/                           ← main source root
    │   │   └── com/example/payments/
    │   │       ├── PaymentService.java
    │   │       └── repository/
    │   │           └── PaymentRepository.java
    │   └── resources/                      ← classpath resources
    │       ├── application.properties
    │       └── db/
    │           └── migration/
    │               └── V1__create_payments.sql
    └── test/
        ├── java/                           ← test source root
        │   └── com/example/payments/
        │       ├── PaymentServiceTest.java
        │       └── repository/
        │           └── PaymentRepositoryTest.java
        └── resources/                      ← test classpath resources
            └── application-test.properties

12.2 Gradle Multi-Module Structure

enterprise-app/
├── settings.gradle
├── build.gradle
├── payments/                     ← :payments module
│   ├── build.gradle
│   └── src/main/java/com/example/payments/
├── orders/                       ← :orders module
│   ├── build.gradle
│   └── src/main/java/com/example/orders/
├── inventory/                    ← :inventory module
│   ├── build.gradle
│   └── src/main/java/com/example/inventory/
└── shared/                       ← :shared module
    ├── build.gradle
    └── src/main/java/com/example/shared/

// settings.gradle
rootProject.name = 'enterprise-app'

include ':payments'
include ':orders'
include ':inventory'
include ':shared'

// payments/build.gradle
dependencies {
    implementation project(':shared')      // depends on shared module
    testImplementation 'org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter:5.10.0'
}

12.3 Package-to-Module Alignment

Best practice: one module per top-level domain package:

Gradle module :payments → package root com.example.payments
Gradle module :orders   → package root com.example.orders

Benefit: Gradle module boundary = package boundary = access control boundary
         All three layers enforce the same separation
Part 13

The Default Package

The default package is the unnamed namespace for classes with no package declaration. Avoid it in any non-trivial code.

// File at: src/main/java/MyClass.java  (no subdirectory, no package declaration)
public class MyClass {       // default package — dangerous
    public void doSomething() { }
}

13.1 Why the Default Package is Dangerous

  1. Cannot be imported — types in the default package cannot be imported by types in named packages
  2. No access control — the package-private mechanism is useless; every class is in the same "package"
  3. Spring Boot fails — @SpringBootApplication in default package scans every class on the classpath, massively slowing startup and often causing errors
  4. JAR conflicts — default-package classes from multiple JARs conflict
// Named package class trying to import from default package
package com.example.service;

import MyClass;   // COMPILE ERROR: package name required

// Workaround: use reflection — but why are you here?
Class<?> clazz = Class.forName("MyClass");   // works at runtime
Part 14

`import` Conflict Resolution

When two types from different packages share the same simple name, you have three options:

import java.util.Date;
// import java.sql.Date;  // <-- conflict: cannot import both as "Date"

public class ReportService {

    // Option 1: Import the more commonly used one, use FQN for the other
    public void generateReport() {
        Date utilDate    = new Date();                  // java.util.Date
        java.sql.Date sqlDate = new java.sql.Date(0);   // FQN for the less common one
    }

    // Option 2: Use FQN for both (when both are equally common)
    public void updateDatabase() {
        java.util.Date now = new java.util.Date();
        java.sql.Date dbDate = new java.sql.Date(now.getTime());
    }

    // Option 3: Alias via local variable — (Java has no import alias like Kotlin/Python)
    // (Not available in Java — use FQN)
}

14.1 Common Name Conflict Pairs

Simple Name Conflict Between
Date java.util.Date vs java.sql.Date
List java.util.List vs java.awt.List
Optional java.util.Optional vs Spring's Optional annotations
Logger java.util.logging.Logger vs org.slf4j.Logger
Assert org.junit.Assert vs org.springframework.util.Assert
Path java.nio.file.Path vs javax.ws.rs.Path
Properties java.util.Properties vs test framework properties types
Part 15

JVM: How Packages Map to Class Loading

At the JVM level, there is no concept of a "package object." The package name is encoded directly into the class's binary name (internal name), which replaces dots with slashes.

Java name:    com.example.payments.PaymentService
Binary name:  com/example/payments/PaymentService
Descriptor:   Lcom/example/payments/PaymentService;

You see the binary name when reading bytecode with javap -verbose:

$ javap -verbose PaymentService.class

Classfile PaymentService.class
  Last modified ...
  MD5 checksum ...
  Compiled from "PaymentService.java"
public class com.example.payments.PaymentService   ← binary name with dots
  minor version: 0
  major version: 65  (Java 21)
  flags: (0x0021) ACC_PUBLIC, ACC_SUPER
  this_class: #7                          // com/example/payments/PaymentService
  super_class: #2                         // java/lang/Object
  ...

15.1 Package-Info Files

You can attach Javadoc and package-level annotations using a special package-info.java file:

// File: com/example/payments/package-info.java
/**
 * Payments domain — core payment processing logic.
 *
 * <p>Public API: {@link com.example.payments.PaymentService}
 * <p>All other types are package-private implementation details.
 *
 * @author payments-team
 * @since 2.0
 */
@NonNullApi                     // Apply annotation to all types in this package
@NonNullFields
package com.example.payments;

import org.springframework.lang.NonNullApi;
import org.springframework.lang.NonNullFields;
Part 16

Spring Boot Package Scanning Rules

Spring Boot's @SpringBootApplication combines three annotations: @Configuration, @EnableAutoConfiguration, and @ComponentScan. The @ComponentScan scans the package of the annotated class and all sub-packages.

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  @SpringBootApplication on com.example.payments.PaymentApplication   │
│                                                                      │
│  Scans:                                                              │
│    com.example.payments          ✅                                   │
│    com.example.payments.service  ✅ (sub-package)                    │
│    com.example.payments.domain   ✅ (sub-package)                    │
│    com.example.orders            ❌ (different top-level package)    │
│    com.example                   ❌ (parent package — not scanned)   │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

16.1 Placement of Main Class — The Golden Rule

// CORRECT: main class at root of your application's package
// Scans everything under com.example.myapp
package com.example.myapp;

@SpringBootApplication
public class MyApplication {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(MyApplication.class, args);
    }
}

// WRONG: main class in sub-package — sibling packages not scanned
package com.example.myapp.config;   // ← too deep!

@SpringBootApplication
public class MyApplication {
    // com.example.myapp.service will NOT be scanned!
    // com.example.myapp.domain will NOT be scanned!
}

16.2 Custom Scan Configuration

@SpringBootApplication(
    scanBasePackages = {
        "com.example.myapp",
        "com.example.shared"       // explicitly add additional packages
    }
)
public class MyApplication { }

// Or use the annotation directly:
@SpringBootApplication
@ComponentScan(basePackages = {"com.example.myapp", "com.example.shared"})
public class MyApplication { }

// Or scan specific classes (safer — refactoring-proof):
@ComponentScan(basePackageClasses = {PaymentService.class, OrderService.class})
public class MyApplication { }

16.3 Spring Modulith Package Structure

Spring Modulith enforces each direct sub-package of the application package as a module boundary:

com.example.myapp                  ← application root (Spring Boot main class here)
├── orders                         ← "orders" module (com.example.myapp.orders)
│   ├── OrderService.java          public API of orders module
│   ├── OrderRepository.java       public API of orders module
│   └── internal/                  package-private internals
│       └── OrderValidator.java
├── payments                       ← "payments" module
│   ├── PaymentService.java
│   └── internal/
│       └── FraudDetector.java
└── inventory                      ← "inventory" module
    └── InventoryService.java
Part 17

Subpackage Relationships (There Are None)

A common misconception: com.example.payments.service is a child of com.example.payments.

This is false. Java packages have no parent-child relationship at runtime. The dot is purely cosmetic — it is part of the name, not a hierarchy separator.

package com.example.payments;

class PackageInternals {
    // Accessible to classes in com.example.payments  ← YES
    // Accessible to classes in com.example.payments.service  ← NO
}

com.example.payments
    └── (package-private visibility)  ← applies ONLY to this exact package name

com.example.payments.service
    └── completely separate package — zero access to com.example.payments internals

This is NOT like a filesystem hierarchy where a directory sees its parent.

This surprises many developers. If you need shared package-private access, all classes must be in the exact same package string.

Part 18

Sealed Classes and Packages (Java 17+)

Java 17's sealed classes interact with packages in an interesting way:

// All permitted subclasses must be in the same package
// OR the same compilation unit
package com.example.payments;

public sealed class PaymentMethod
    permits CreditCardPayment, BankTransferPayment, CryptoPayment {
    public abstract BigDecimal getFee(BigDecimal amount);
}

// These must be in com.example.payments (same package)
final class CreditCardPayment extends PaymentMethod {
    @Override public BigDecimal getFee(BigDecimal amount) {
        return amount.multiply(new BigDecimal("0.029"));  // 2.9%
    }
}

final class BankTransferPayment extends PaymentMethod {
    @Override public BigDecimal getFee(BigDecimal amount) {
        return new BigDecimal("0.25");  // flat fee
    }
}

non-sealed class CryptoPayment extends PaymentMethod {
    @Override public BigDecimal getFee(BigDecimal amount) {
        return amount.multiply(new BigDecimal("0.01"));  // 1%
    }
}

Java 17+ allows permits classes in different packages (they just need to be public), but the most common pattern keeps them in the same package.

Part 19

Production Patterns and Real Codebases

19.1 Domain-Driven Design Package Structure

DDD aligns packages with bounded contexts:

com.example.banking
├── account                    ← Account bounded context
│   ├── Account.java           (aggregate root)
│   ├── AccountId.java         (value object)
│   ├── AccountService.java    (application service)
│   ├── AccountRepository.java (repository interface)
│   └── events/
│       ├── AccountOpened.java
│       └── AccountClosed.java
├── payment                    ← Payment bounded context
│   ├── Payment.java
│   ├── PaymentService.java
│   └── PaymentRepository.java
└── shared                     ← Shared kernel
    ├── Money.java             (value object shared across contexts)
    └── CustomerId.java

19.2 Hexagonal Architecture (Ports and Adapters)

com.example.payments
├── domain                     ← pure domain logic, no framework dependencies
│   ├── Payment.java
│   ├── PaymentService.java    (port: driven side)
│   └── PaymentRepository.java (port: driving side)
├── application                ← use cases, orchestration
│   └── ProcessPaymentUseCase.java
└── infrastructure             ← adapters: web, database, messaging
    ├── web
    │   └── PaymentController.java    (Spring REST adapter)
    ├── persistence
    │   └── JpaPaymentRepository.java (JPA adapter for PaymentRepository port)
    └── messaging
        └── KafkaPaymentPublisher.java

19.3 Naming Collision in Real Production

At a real payment company, two separate teams had both created a class TransactionStatus. One was in com.example.payments.TransactionStatus, the other in com.example.ledger.TransactionStatus. When a new service needed both, developers had to use FQNs everywhere, leading to 60+ occurrences of com.example.payments.TransactionStatus in a single file. The fix: rename one to LedgerTransactionStatus — a refactoring that took a day and touched 40 files.

Lesson: Package naming is cheap to get right upfront and expensive to fix later.

Part 20

Interview Deep Dives

Q1: Can two classes in different packages have the same simple name?

Yes — this is the entire purpose of packages. java.util.Date and java.sql.Date coexist. When using both in the same file, one is imported and the other used via FQN.

Q2: What does import java.util.* include?

All public top-level types in the java.util package. It does NOT include:
- Types in sub-packages (java.util.concurrent.* requires a separate import)
- Static members (need import static)
- Types that are package-private (they are invisible outside the package regardless)

Q3: You have import java.util.* and import java.awt.* in the same file. You use List. What happens?

java.util.List exists. java.awt.List also exists. The compiler detects ambiguity and raises a compile error: reference to List is ambiguous. Fix: replace the wildcard imports with single-type imports, or use FQN.

Q4: Why can't classes in com.example.payments.service see package-private types in com.example.payments?

Because they are different packages. The dot in the name is not a hierarchy separator. Package-private access requires membership in the exact same package string. com.example.payments.service and com.example.payments are completely unrelated namespaces.

Q5: What happens when @SpringBootApplication is placed in the default package?

Spring scans all classes on the entire classpath — including JDK classes, Spring itself, and every library JAR. The application either fails to start (context too large) or starts with thousands of spurious beans. Always place the main class in a named package at the root of your application's namespace.

Part 21

Production Case Study: Refactoring a Monolith Package Structure

A team inherited a 200k-line monolith with this package structure:

Before (technology-layered):
com.acme.app.controllers     (92 classes mixed from all domains)
com.acme.app.services        (78 classes mixed from all domains)
com.acme.app.dao             (65 classes mixed from all domains)
com.acme.app.models          (143 classes mixed from all domains)
com.acme.app.utils           (34 unrelated utility classes)

Problems: every class could see every other class. Adding a feature required reading hundreds of unrelated files to understand context. Test failures cascaded across unrelated domains.

Refactoring to feature-based packages (over 6 months, in parallel with feature development):

After (domain-layered):
com.acme.app.orders
  ├── OrderController        (public)
  ├── OrderService           (public)
  ├── OrderRepository        (public)
  ├── Order                  (public domain entity)
  └── internal/
      ├── OrderValidator     (package-private)
      └── OrderPricingEngine (package-private)

com.acme.app.payments
  ├── PaymentController      (public)
  ├── PaymentService         (public)
  └── internal/
      ├── PaymentValidator   (package-private)
      └── FraudDetector      (package-private)

... (6 more domains)

Outcome: team velocity doubled within 3 months of completing the refactoring. Onboarding time for new developers dropped from 3 weeks to 4 days (measured by time to first solo PR). Cross-team merge conflicts dropped by 80%.

Part 22

Summary Table

Concept Syntax Key Rule Common Mistake Architect's Take
Package declaration package com.example.foo; First statement; must match directory Wrong directory path Package = directory; enforce with IDE/build tool
Default package (no declaration) Cannot be imported from named packages Putting Main class here — breaks Spring scan Never use in production code
Single-type import import java.util.List; Compile-time only; no bytecode generated Importing unused types (just noise) Prefer explicit imports over wildcards
Wildcard import import java.util.*; Only one level deep; causes ambiguity if two packages share a name java.util.* + java.awt.* → List ambiguous Use sparingly; explicit imports are more readable
Static import import static java.lang.Math.PI; Imports static members Overuse obscures origin of identifiers Great for tests (JUnit/Mockito) and Math constants
java.lang auto-import (implicit) Always available; no import needed Explicitly importing java.lang.String (redundant) Know what's in java.lang — never waste an import
Fully qualified name java.util.Date d = ... Always unique; no import needed FQN everywhere when an import would suffice Use to resolve name conflicts, not as default style
Reverse domain naming com.company.product.module Globally unique com.utils, com.models (not unique, not descriptive) Package = architecture; name it to reflect domain
Subpackage isolation com.a.b ≠ com.a No parent-child access relationship Assuming subpackages share package-private access Each package is a fully independent namespace
Classpath lookup -cp dir:jar Dot → slash mapping for file path Missing JAR at runtime → NoClassDefFoundError Understand ClassLoader hierarchy for debugging
package-info.java package-info.java Package-level Javadoc + annotations Skipping it in library code Essential for @NonNullApi, package Javadoc
Maven layout src/main/java/ Standard; all tools expect it Putting Java files in src/ root Always use Maven standard layout
Spring scan root @SpringBootApplication package Scans own package + all sub-packages Main class too deep → beans not found Main class = root package of your application
Module exports exports com.example.api; Java 9+; controls public API at module boundary Not exporting needed package Module system = ultimate package boundary enforcement
Feature vs tech layers Domain-first organization Co-locate what changes together Technology layers (controllers, services, daos packages) Feature packages reduce coupling and cognitive load

Practice — Lesson 12

Easy Exercises

Exercise 1: Package Declaration and Directory Structure

Given the following source files, write the correct package declaration for each and describe the directory structure they should be placed in:

  1. A class OrderService in the order management domain of a company named techcorp.io, product platform, module orders
  2. A class DateUtils that is a shared utility across all modules
  3. A test class OrderServiceTest for the above OrderService
  4. A package-info.java for the orders package with Javadoc explaining the module purpose

Exercise 2: Import Resolution

Fix the compilation issues in this class:

package com.example.reporting;

import java.util.*;
import java.awt.*;
import java.sql.*;

public class ReportGenerator {
    List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();    // which List? which ArrayList?
    Date reportDate = new Date();              // which Date?
    Connection dbConn;                         // which Connection?
    Color headerColor = Color.RED;             // which Color?
}

Medium Exercises

Exercise 3: Package-Private Communication

Create a package com.example.notification with:
1. A public class NotificationService with one public method send(String recipient, String message)
2. A package-private class EmailDispatcher with method dispatch(String to, String body)
3. A package-private class SmsDispatcher with method dispatch(String phone, String text)
4. A package-private class NotificationRouter that decides whether to use email or SMS based on recipient format
5. NotificationService delegates through NotificationRouter to the appropriate dispatcher

Verify: code outside com.example.notification can only see NotificationService. All dispatching logic is hidden.

Exercise 4: Static Imports and Readability

Rewrite this test class to use appropriate static imports, making the test code more readable:

package com.example.orders;

public class OrderServiceTest {
    @org.junit.jupiter.api.Test
    void shouldThrowForEmptyOrder() {
        org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertThrows(
            IllegalArgumentException.class,
            () -> orderService.placeOrder(null)
        );
    }

    @org.junit.jupiter.api.Test
    void shouldCalculateCorrectTotal() {
        Order order = buildTestOrder();
        org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertEquals(
            new java.math.BigDecimal("100.00"),
            orderService.calculateTotal(order)
        );
        org.mockito.Mockito.verify(inventoryService)
            .decrementStock(org.mockito.ArgumentMatchers.any());
    }
}
