Part 1

Concept Overview

An enum (enumeration) is a special Java type used to define collections of constants. Introduced in Java 5 (2004), enums solved the "int constants" antipattern that plagued Java code for years. Rather than scattering public static final int STATUS_ACTIVE = 1; declarations across codebases, enums provide type-safe, self-documenting, feature-rich constant groups.

Java enums are far more powerful than their C/C++ counterparts. A Java enum is a full-blown class under the hood — it can have fields, constructors, methods, and implement interfaces. The JVM treats each enum constant as a singleton instance of the enum class, giving you compile-time safety, runtime introspection, and behavioral polymorphism in one construct.

Why Enums Matter for Architects

  • Type safety: the compiler rejects invalid values at compile time, no more if (status == 99) mystery bugs
  • Singleton guarantee: each constant is instantiated exactly once by the JVM class loader
  • Behavioral constants: constants can carry their own logic via methods (Strategy pattern)
  • Switch compatibility: works cleanly with switch expressions (Java 14+ enhanced switch)
  • Serialization safety: unlike int constants, enum names survive refactoring serialization concerns properly
Part 2

Basic Enum Declaration

The simplest enum is a list of named constants:

public enum Direction {
    NORTH, SOUTH, EAST, WEST;
}

Under the hood, each constant is an instance of Direction. Use it like:

Direction d = Direction.NORTH;
System.out.println(d);         // NORTH
System.out.println(d.name());  // NORTH
System.out.println(d.ordinal()); // 0

Core Instance Methods (from java.lang.Enum)

Method Return Type Description
name() String Declared name of the constant (same as toString() by default)
ordinal() int Zero-based position in declaration order
compareTo(E other) int Comparison by ordinal
equals(Object) boolean Identity equality (same instance)
hashCode() int Based on identity

Core Static Methods (compiler-generated)

Method Description
Direction.values() Returns Direction[] of all constants in declaration order
Direction.valueOf("NORTH") Returns the constant with that name; throws IllegalArgumentException if not found 
// Iterating all constants
for (Direction dir : Direction.values()) {
    System.out.println(dir.ordinal() + ": " + dir.name());
}
// Output:
// 0: NORTH
// 1: SOUTH
// 2: EAST
// 3: WEST

// Parsing from String
Direction parsed = Direction.valueOf("EAST");  // Direction.EAST
Direction bad    = Direction.valueOf("UP");    // throws IllegalArgumentException
Part 3

Enum with Fields, Constructors, and Methods

This is where Java enums diverge from all other languages. Each constant can carry data:

public enum Planet {
    MERCURY(3.303e+23, 2.4397e6),
    VENUS  (4.869e+24, 6.0518e6),
    EARTH  (5.976e+24, 6.37814e6),
    MARS   (6.421e+23, 3.3972e6);

    private final double mass;    // in kilograms
    private final double radius;  // in meters

    // Enum constructor is always package-private or private
    Planet(double mass, double radius) {
        this.mass   = mass;
        this.radius = radius;
    }

    static final double G = 6.67300E-11;

    public double surfaceGravity() {
        return G * mass / (radius * radius);
    }

    public double surfaceWeight(double otherMass) {
        return otherMass * surfaceGravity();
    }
}

Usage:

double earthWeight = 75.0;
double mass = earthWeight / Planet.EARTH.surfaceGravity();

for (Planet p : Planet.values()) {
    System.out.printf("Your weight on %s is %6.2f%n",
                      p, p.surfaceWeight(mass));
}

Key Rules for Enum Constructors

  • Always private or implicitly package-private — you cannot call new Planet(...) externally
  • Each constant's constructor arguments appear in parentheses after its name
  • The constructor runs during class loading, before any user code accesses the enum
Part 4

Enum with Abstract Methods (Constant-Specific Bodies)

Each constant can override an abstract method, implementing the Strategy pattern directly in the enum:

public enum Operation {
    PLUS("+") {
        @Override
        public double apply(double x, double y) { return x + y; }
    },
    MINUS("-") {
        @Override
        public double apply(double x, double y) { return x - y; }
    },
    TIMES("*") {
        @Override
        public double apply(double x, double y) { return x * y; }
    },
    DIVIDE("/") {
        @Override
        public double apply(double x, double y) { return x / y; }
    };

    private final String symbol;

    Operation(String symbol) { this.symbol = symbol; }

    public abstract double apply(double x, double y);

    @Override
    public String toString() { return symbol; }
}

Usage:

double x = 10, y = 3;
for (Operation op : Operation.values()) {
    System.out.printf("%.1f %s %.1f = %.1f%n", x, op, y, op.apply(x, y));
}
// 10.0 + 3.0 = 13.0
// 10.0 - 3.0 = 7.0
// 10.0 * 3.0 = 30.0
// 10.0 / 3.0 = 3.3

Each constant (PLUS, MINUS, etc.) is actually an anonymous subclass of Operation at the bytecode level.

Part 5

Enum Implementing Interfaces

public interface Describable {
    String describe();
}

public enum Season implements Describable {
    SPRING {
        @Override public String describe() { return "Flowers bloom, mild temperatures"; }
    },
    SUMMER {
        @Override public String describe() { return "Hot and sunny"; }
    },
    AUTUMN {
        @Override public String describe() { return "Leaves fall, cooling down"; }
    },
    WINTER {
        @Override public String describe() { return "Cold, snow possible"; }
    };
}

Or implement the interface uniformly in the enum body (one implementation for all constants):

public enum Status implements Describable {
    ACTIVE, INACTIVE, PENDING;

    @Override
    public String describe() {
        return "Status is: " + name().toLowerCase();
    }
}
Part 6

Switch on Enum

Traditional Switch (Java 5+)

Direction dir = Direction.NORTH;

switch (dir) {
    case NORTH:
        System.out.println("Go north");
        break;
    case SOUTH:
        System.out.println("Go south");
        break;
    default:
        System.out.println("Go east or west");
}

Switch Expression (Java 14+, production standard in Java 17+)

String message = switch (dir) {
    case NORTH -> "Heading northward";
    case SOUTH -> "Heading southward";
    case EAST  -> "Heading eastward";
    case WEST  -> "Heading westward";
};
// No default needed — compiler verifies exhaustiveness for enums!

The compiler verifies that all enum constants are covered in switch expressions, eliminating missed-case bugs. This is a major advantage over int-based switches.

Part 7

Singleton Pattern with Enum (Joshua Bloch)

Effective Java, Item 3: "A single-element enum type is often the best way to implement a singleton."

public enum AppConfig {
    INSTANCE;

    private final String databaseUrl;
    private final int maxConnections;

    AppConfig() {
        // Load from environment or config file
        this.databaseUrl    = System.getenv().getOrDefault("DB_URL", "jdbc:h2:mem:test");
        this.maxConnections = Integer.parseInt(
            System.getenv().getOrDefault("DB_MAX_CONN", "10"));
    }

    public String getDatabaseUrl()   { return databaseUrl; }
    public int getMaxConnections()   { return maxConnections; }
}

// Usage
AppConfig config = AppConfig.INSTANCE;
System.out.println(config.getDatabaseUrl());

Why Enum Singleton is Superior

Property synchronized getInstance volatile double-check Enum Singleton
Thread safe Yes Yes Yes
Serialization safe Manual readResolve() required Manual required Automatic
Reflection safe Vulnerable Vulnerable Immune
Lazy initialization Yes Yes No (class-load time)
Code complexity High Medium Minimal

The JVM guarantees that enum constants are instantiated exactly once, even under concurrent class loading. Serialization/deserialization returns the same instance — the readResolve() mechanism is built into java.io.ObjectInputStream for enums. Reflection cannot call newInstance() on an enum — it throws IllegalArgumentException.

Part 8

ASCII Diagram: Enum on the Heap

CLASS LOADING (happens once, when Direction.class is first referenced)
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  Method Area (Metaspace in Java 8+)
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Class: Direction  (extends java.lang.Enum<Direction>)       │
  │  ┌────────────────┐  ┌────────────────┐                      │
  │  │ static field:  │  │ static field:  │  ...                 │
  │  │ NORTH          │  │ SOUTH          │                      │
  │  │ (ref)─────┐    │  │ (ref)──────┐   │                      │
  │  └────────────│───┘  └────────────│───┘                      │
  │               │                   │                           │
  └───────────────│───────────────────│───────────────────────────┘
                  │                   │
  Heap            ▼                   ▼
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                               │
  │  ┌─────────────────┐    ┌─────────────────┐                  │
  │  │ Direction@1a2b  │    │ Direction@3c4d  │    ...            │
  │  │ name:  "NORTH"  │    │ name:  "SOUTH"  │                  │
  │  │ ordinal: 0      │    │ ordinal: 1      │                  │
  │  └─────────────────┘    └─────────────────┘                  │
  │                                                               │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  values() array (also static, created once):
  ┌──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┐
  │[0]   │[1]   │[2]   │[3]   │
  │NORTH │SOUTH │EAST  │WEST  │
  └──────┴──────┴──────┴──────┘

  Each enum constant is a SINGLETON on the heap.
  No user code can create additional instances.
Part 9

JVM Internals: What the Compiler Generates

Given:

public enum Color { RED, GREEN, BLUE; }

The compiler generates roughly:

// Conceptual decompilation — not actual source
public final class Color extends java.lang.Enum<Color> {

    public static final Color RED   = new Color("RED",   0);
    public static final Color GREEN = new Color("GREEN", 1);
    public static final Color BLUE  = new Color("BLUE",  2);

    private static final Color[] $VALUES = { RED, GREEN, BLUE };

    // Private constructor — cannot be called by user code
    private Color(String name, int ordinal) {
        super(name, ordinal);  // java.lang.Enum(String, int)
    }

    // Compiler synthesizes these:
    public static Color[] values() {
        return $VALUES.clone();  // defensive copy!
    }

    public static Color valueOf(String name) {
        return (Color) Enum.valueOf(Color.class, name);
    }
}

Key JVM facts:

  1. final class: cannot be subclassed (except by the enum's own constant bodies)
  2. extends java.lang.Enum<E>: you cannot extend anything else; interfaces are allowed
  3. $VALUES clone: values() always returns a fresh array — mutating the returned array does NOT affect the enum
  4. Static initializer block: all constants are created in <clinit> during class loading
  5. ACC_ENUM flag: set in the class file, used by reflection and serialization APIs
Part 10

EnumSet and EnumMap

Two specialized collections exist specifically for enums, offering significant performance advantages:

EnumSet — Bit-Vector Backed Set

import java.util.EnumSet;

EnumSet<Direction> cardinals = EnumSet.of(Direction.NORTH, Direction.SOUTH);
EnumSet<Direction> all       = EnumSet.allOf(Direction.class);
EnumSet<Direction> none      = EnumSet.noneOf(Direction.class);
EnumSet<Direction> complement = EnumSet.complementOf(cardinals);

cardinals.add(Direction.EAST);
System.out.println(cardinals.contains(Direction.NORTH)); // true

EnumSet uses a single long bitmask (for enums with ≤64 constants) — O(1) operations, no hashing, no boxing, minimal memory. For architects: always prefer EnumSet over HashSet<MyEnum>.

EnumMap — Array-Backed Map

import java.util.EnumMap;

EnumMap<Direction, String> labels = new EnumMap<>(Direction.class);
labels.put(Direction.NORTH, "N");
labels.put(Direction.SOUTH, "S");
labels.put(Direction.EAST,  "E");
labels.put(Direction.WEST,  "W");

System.out.println(labels.get(Direction.NORTH)); // N

EnumMap uses a plain array indexed by ordinal — faster than HashMap, no hashing overhead, iteration follows declaration order.

Collection Backed By contains put/get Memory
HashSet<Enum> Hash table O(1) avg O(1) avg High
EnumSet Bit vector O(1) exact O(1) exact Minimal
HashMap<Enum, V> Hash table — O(1) avg High
EnumMap Array — O(1) exact Low
Part 11

Production Patterns: Status Codes and State Machines

Pattern 1: Rich Status Enum with HTTP Codes

public enum OrderStatus {
    PENDING   (102, "Order received, awaiting payment"),
    CONFIRMED (200, "Payment confirmed"),
    SHIPPED   (201, "Order dispatched"),
    DELIVERED (200, "Order delivered successfully"),
    CANCELLED (410, "Order cancelled"),
    REFUNDED  (200, "Refund processed");

    private final int httpCode;
    private final String description;

    OrderStatus(int httpCode, String description) {
        this.httpCode    = httpCode;
        this.description = description;
    }

    public int    getHttpCode()    { return httpCode; }
    public String getDescription() { return description; }

    public boolean isTerminal() {
        return this == DELIVERED || this == CANCELLED || this == REFUNDED;
    }

    public boolean canTransitionTo(OrderStatus next) {
        return switch (this) {
            case PENDING    -> next == CONFIRMED || next == CANCELLED;
            case CONFIRMED  -> next == SHIPPED   || next == CANCELLED;
            case SHIPPED    -> next == DELIVERED;
            case DELIVERED,
                 CANCELLED,
                 REFUNDED   -> false; // terminal states
        };
    }
}

Pattern 2: State Machine

public class Order {
    private OrderStatus status = OrderStatus.PENDING;

    public void transition(OrderStatus newStatus) {
        if (!status.canTransitionTo(newStatus)) {
            throw new IllegalStateException(
                "Cannot transition from " + status + " to " + newStatus);
        }
        this.status = newStatus;
    }
}
Part 12

Critical Anti-Pattern: Never Use ordinal() for Persistence

// DANGER — DO NOT DO THIS
public enum Size { SMALL, MEDIUM, LARGE; }

// BAD: storing ordinal in database
db.save("size", size.ordinal()); // stores 0, 1, or 2

// If someone adds XS before SMALL:
public enum Size { XS, SMALL, MEDIUM, LARGE; }
// Now SMALL.ordinal() == 1, MEDIUM == 2, LARGE == 3
// All existing database rows are now WRONG!

// CORRECT: store the name
db.save("size", size.name()); // stores "SMALL", "MEDIUM", "LARGE"

// Or better: assign an explicit stable code
public enum Size {
    SMALL("S"), MEDIUM("M"), LARGE("L");
    private final String code;
    Size(String code) { this.code = code; }
    public String getCode() { return code; }
    public static Size fromCode(String code) {
        for (Size s : values()) {
            if (s.code.equals(code)) return s;
        }
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown size code: " + code);
    }
}

Architect rule: ordinal is positional metadata, not an identity. Use name() or a dedicated stable field for persistence.

Part 13

Spring Integration: @Enumerated and Jackson

JPA / Hibernate: @Enumerated

import jakarta.persistence.*;

@Entity
public class Product {

    @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)   // stores "SMALL", "MEDIUM", "LARGE"
    @Column(nullable = false)
    private Size size;

    // NEVER use EnumType.ORDINAL in production!
    // @Enumerated(EnumType.ORDINAL) -- stores 0, 1, 2 — fragile!
}

Jackson: JSON Serialization/Deserialization

import com.fasterxml.jackson.annotation.JsonCreator;
import com.fasterxml.jackson.annotation.JsonValue;

public enum Priority {
    LOW("low"), MEDIUM("medium"), HIGH("high"), CRITICAL("critical");

    private final String jsonValue;

    Priority(String jsonValue) { this.jsonValue = jsonValue; }

    @JsonValue
    public String getJsonValue() { return jsonValue; }  // serialized as "low", "high" etc.

    @JsonCreator
    public static Priority fromJson(String value) {
        for (Priority p : values()) {
            if (p.jsonValue.equalsIgnoreCase(value)) return p;
        }
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown priority: " + value);
    }
}

Without @JsonValue, Jackson serializes by name() (uppercase). With it, you control the wire format independently of the Java constant name.

Spring MVC: Enum as Request Parameter

@RestController
public class OrderController {

    @GetMapping("/orders")
    public List<Order> getOrders(
            @RequestParam(required = false) OrderStatus status) {
        // Spring auto-converts "PENDING" → OrderStatus.PENDING via valueOf()
        return orderService.findByStatus(status);
    }
}

For case-insensitive conversion, register a ConversionService or use @RequestParam with a custom Converter<String, OrderStatus>.

Part 14

Thread Safety of Enums

Enum constants are created during class initialization (<clinit>), which the JVM guarantees happens at most once per ClassLoader. The Java Language Specification (§12.4) ensures that class initialization is thread-safe via a per-class initialization lock.

Thread 1 accesses Direction.NORTH
       │
       ▼
  JVM checks: is Direction initialized?
       │
       ├── YES (already done) ──► return NORTH immediately
       │
       └── NO ──► acquire class init lock
                  execute <clinit> (creates NORTH, SOUTH, EAST, WEST)
                  release lock
                  return NORTH

Thread 2 tries simultaneously:
       │
       ▼
  JVM checks: is Direction initialized?
       │
       └── Blocked on init lock until Thread 1 finishes
           Then: already initialized, return NORTH immediately

Result: enum constants are inherently thread-safe. No synchronized, no volatile, no double-checked locking needed.

Part 15

Enum Serialization

Enums participate in Java serialization specially:

// For a regular class, deserialization creates a NEW object
// For an enum, the JVM uses Enum.valueOf() to look up the existing singleton

ObjectOutputStream out = new ObjectOutputStream(new FileOutputStream("data.bin"));
out.writeObject(Direction.NORTH);

ObjectInputStream in = new ObjectInputStream(new FileInputStream("data.bin"));
Direction d = (Direction) in.readObject();

System.out.println(d == Direction.NORTH); // true — same singleton!

The serial form of an enum constant is just its name(). The class field values are not serialized. This is safe and correct — but it means if you rename a constant, old serialized data breaks. Solution: use a separate stable identifier field (see ordinal anti-pattern above).

Part 16

Reflection and Enums

// Listing constants via reflection
Class<Direction> clazz = Direction.class;
System.out.println(clazz.isEnum()); // true

for (Direction d : clazz.getEnumConstants()) {
    System.out.println(d.name() + " ordinal=" + d.ordinal());
}

// Cannot create new instances via reflection
try {
    Constructor<Direction> c = Direction.class.getDeclaredConstructor(String.class, int.class);
    c.setAccessible(true);
    c.newInstance("UP", 4); // throws IllegalArgumentException: Cannot reflectively create enum objects
} catch (Exception e) {
    System.out.println(e.getMessage()); // Cannot reflectively create enum objects
}

This reflection protection is the key advantage of enum singletons over other singleton implementations.

Part 17

Java 21 Preview: Enum in Pattern Matching

// Java 21 sealed types + pattern matching (not yet full enum pattern, but close)
Object obj = OrderStatus.PENDING;

String msg = switch (obj) {
    case OrderStatus s when s.isTerminal() -> "Terminal: " + s;
    case OrderStatus s                     -> "Active: " + s;
    case String str                        -> "String: " + str;
    default                                -> "Unknown";
};

Future JEPs aim to allow deconstruction patterns on enums with fields, making switch on enums even more expressive.

Part 18

Common Mistakes and Pitfalls

Mistake 1: Comparing with == vs equals()

// Both work, but == is preferred and idiomatic
Direction d = Direction.NORTH;
if (d == Direction.NORTH) { }         // correct, idiomatic
if (d.equals(Direction.NORTH)) { }    // works but verbose

// equals() is final in java.lang.Enum — cannot be overridden
// == is safe because each constant is a singleton

Mistake 2: Calling valueOf() without try/catch

// From user input — always guard:
public static Optional<OrderStatus> parse(String input) {
    try {
        return Optional.of(OrderStatus.valueOf(input.toUpperCase().trim()));
    } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
        return Optional.empty();
    }
}

Mistake 3: Adding new constants in the middle

// Before
enum Level { LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH }   // ordinals: 0, 1, 2

// DON'T insert in the middle if ordinals are persisted anywhere
enum Level { LOW, MEDIUM_LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH }  // breaks ordinal-based data
// Always ADD at the end; never INSERT unless you own all data stores
Part 19

Full Production Example: Payment Gateway Integration

public enum PaymentProvider {
    STRIPE   ("stripe",   "https://api.stripe.com/v1",   true),
    PAYPAL   ("paypal",   "https://api.paypal.com/v2",   true),
    RAZORPAY ("razorpay", "https://api.razorpay.com/v1", false),
    MOCK     ("mock",     "http://localhost:8080/mock",   false);

    private final String code;
    private final String baseUrl;
    private final boolean prodReady;

    PaymentProvider(String code, String baseUrl, boolean prodReady) {
        this.code      = code;
        this.baseUrl   = baseUrl;
        this.prodReady = prodReady;
    }

    public String  getCode()      { return code; }
    public String  getBaseUrl()   { return baseUrl; }
    public boolean isProdReady()  { return prodReady; }

    public static PaymentProvider fromCode(String code) {
        for (PaymentProvider p : values()) {
            if (p.code.equalsIgnoreCase(code)) return p;
        }
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown payment provider: " + code);
    }

    public static EnumSet<PaymentProvider> productionProviders() {
        return EnumSet.of(STRIPE, PAYPAL);
    }
}
Part 20

Interview Deep Dives

Q1: What is the difference between enum and int constants?

Aspect int Constants Enum
Type safety None — any int is valid Compile-time checked
Namespace Pollutes class namespace Self-contained
Printability Prints number (meaningless) Prints name
Switch Yes Yes, with exhaustiveness check
Behavior Cannot have methods Can have fields/methods
Iteration Manual array needed values() built-in
Serialization Just a number Name-based

Q2: Is enum singleton thread-safe?

Yes. The JVM class initialization protocol (JLS §12.4.2) uses a per-class lock to ensure <clinit> runs exactly once. Enum constants are created in <clinit>, so they are guaranteed to be visible to all threads correctly without any additional synchronization.

Q3: Can an enum extend a class?

No. Every enum implicitly extends java.lang.Enum<E>, and Java does not support multiple inheritance of classes. An enum can implement multiple interfaces.

Q4: Can an enum be abstract?

An enum can declare abstract methods, forcing each constant to provide a body. The enum class itself is final (cannot be subclassed), but the anonymous constant-specific class bodies form internal subclasses.

Q5: What does values() return — can you modify it?

values() returns a clone of the internal $VALUES array each time it's called. Modifying the returned array has no effect. However, calling values() in a tight loop creates GC pressure — cache it:

private static final OrderStatus[] CACHED_VALUES = OrderStatus.values();
Part 21

Checklist: Architect's Enum Decision Guide

When to use enum:
  ✓ Fixed, known set of related constants
  ✓ Constants need associated behavior (methods)
  ✓ Constants need associated data (fields)
  ✓ Singleton with guaranteed thread safety and serialization
  ✓ Type-safe switch with exhaustiveness checking

When NOT to use enum:
  ✗ Open-ended sets that grow dynamically (use database table)
  ✗ Configuration values loaded at runtime
  ✗ Large numbers of constants with no structure (consider properties)

Persistence rules:
  ✓ Use @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING) — NEVER ORDINAL
  ✓ Or use a stable explicit code field
  ✗ Never use ordinal() as a persistent identifier

Collection rules:
  ✓ EnumSet instead of HashSet<MyEnum>
  ✓ EnumMap instead of HashMap<MyEnum, V>

API/serialization rules:
  ✓ Use @JsonValue/@JsonCreator for controlled wire format
  ✓ Guard valueOf() with try/catch for user input

Exercise 1 — Basic Enum

Define a DayOfWeek enum with constants MON through SUN. Add a isWeekend() method returning true for SAT and SUN. Iterate all days and print whether each is a weekend.

Part 1

Concept Overview

Java is a nearly object-oriented language — nearly, because its eight primitive types (boolean, byte, short, int, long, float, double, char) are not objects. They cannot be placed in collections, used as generic type arguments, stored in Optional, or passed where Object is expected. This gap is bridged by wrapper classes: eight corresponding classes in java.lang that box each primitive into a proper object.

Autoboxing (Java 5, 2004) made this largely transparent to developers — the compiler inserts conversion calls automatically. But transparency is not free. Wrapper classes carry object overhead (header, heap allocation, GC pressure) and introduce subtle traps: the famous Integer cache range, NPE from unboxing null, and performance degradation in tight loops.

A Java Solution Architect must understand wrapper classes deeply to:
- Explain the 127 == 127 but 128 != 128 puzzle (one of the most common interview questions)
- Make the correct primitive-vs-wrapper choice in performance-sensitive code
- Diagnose NPEs that appear to come from arithmetic operations
- Configure libraries and frameworks that interact with boxed types (JPA, Jackson, Spring, Hibernate)

Part 2

The Eight Wrapper Classes

Primitive Wrapper Class Size Range
boolean Boolean 1 bit (JVM uses 32-bit slot) true / false
byte Byte 8 bits -128 to 127
short Short 16 bits -32,768 to 32,767
int Integer 32 bits -2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647
long Long 64 bits -9.2×10¹⁸ to 9.2×10¹⁸
float Float 32 bits (IEEE 754) ~±3.4×10³⁸
double Double 64 bits (IEEE 754) ~±1.8×10³⁰⁸
char Character 16 bits (unsigned) '\u0000' to '\uFFFF'

All wrapper classes:
- Reside in java.lang (auto-imported)
- Are final — cannot be subclassed
- Are immutable — once created, value cannot change
- Implement Comparable<T> and Serializable
- Extend Number (except Boolean and Character)

Part 3

Boxing and Unboxing (Manual, Pre-Java 5)

Before autoboxing, conversion was explicit:

// Manual boxing (wrapping a primitive in an object)
int primitiveInt = 42;
Integer boxedInt = Integer.valueOf(primitiveInt);   // preferred
Integer oldWay   = new Integer(primitiveInt);        // deprecated since Java 9, removed Java 17

// Manual unboxing (extracting primitive from object)
int backToPrimitive = boxedInt.intValue();

// Other type conversions from Integer
double asDouble = boxedInt.doubleValue();
long   asLong   = boxedInt.longValue();
float  asFloat  = boxedInt.floatValue();

new Integer(42) is deprecated and removed in Java 17 because it bypasses the cache and always allocates a new object. Always use Integer.valueOf(42) or let autoboxing do it.

Part 4

Autoboxing and Unboxing (Java 5+)

Autoboxing: the compiler automatically wraps a primitive as its wrapper when an object is expected.
Unboxing: the compiler automatically extracts the primitive from a wrapper when a primitive is expected.

// Autoboxing — compiler inserts Integer.valueOf(42)
Integer boxed = 42;

// Unboxing — compiler inserts boxed.intValue()
int unboxed = boxed;

// In a collection (requires object)
List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>();
list.add(7);    // autoboxing: Integer.valueOf(7)
int x = list.get(0);  // unboxing: list.get(0).intValue()

// Arithmetic triggers unboxing
Integer a = 10, b = 20;
Integer sum = a + b;  // a.intValue() + b.intValue() → Integer.valueOf(result)

What the Compiler Actually Generates

// Your code:
Integer i = 100;
int j = i + 5;

// Compiled equivalent:
Integer i = Integer.valueOf(100);
int j = i.intValue() + 5;
Part 5

The Integer Cache: -128 to 127

This is arguably the most famous Java interview trap. The JVM caches Integer objects for values in the range -128 to 127 (inclusive). When you call Integer.valueOf(n) for any n in this range, you get back the same cached object every time.

Integer a = 127;
Integer b = 127;
System.out.println(a == b);    // true  — same cached object

Integer c = 128;
Integer d = 128;
System.out.println(c == d);    // false — different objects!
System.out.println(c.equals(d)); // true  — same value

ASCII Diagram: Integer Cache

Integer.valueOf() call flow:
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  Input value n
       │
       ▼
  n >= -128 AND n <= 127?
       │
  YES  │                    NO
  ─────┤                    ├──────────────────────────────
       │                    │
       ▼                    ▼
  IntegerCache.cache[]    new Integer(n)
  ┌────────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────┐
  │ [0] → Integer(-128)│  │  Integer@7f3a    │  (new heap object)
  │ [1] → Integer(-127)│  │  value: 200      │
  │ ...                │  └─────────────────┘
  │[255] → Integer(127)│       returned
  └────────────────────┘
       │
       ▼
  return cache[n + 128]  ◄── SAME object reference every time


  Example:
  Integer.valueOf(42)  → cache[170]  → Integer@abc (always this one)
  Integer.valueOf(42)  → cache[170]  → Integer@abc (same!)
  Integer.valueOf(200) → new Integer → Integer@def
  Integer.valueOf(200) → new Integer → Integer@ghi  (different!)

Why This Range?

The cache range -128 to 127 is specified in the JLS (§5.1.7) as mandatory minimum. The upper bound can be increased via JVM flag:

java -XX:AutoBoxCacheMax=1000 MyApp
# Now Integer.valueOf(n) caches up to n=1000

The same caching applies to:
- Byte — always caches all 256 values (-128 to 127, full range)
- Short — caches -128 to 127
- Long — caches -128 to 127
- Character — caches 0 to 127
- Boolean — caches Boolean.TRUE and Boolean.FALSE always (only two values exist)

Boolean t1 = true;
Boolean t2 = true;
System.out.println(t1 == t2);  // true — Boolean.TRUE is always the same object

Long l1 = 100L;
Long l2 = 100L;
System.out.println(l1 == l2);  // true (in cache range)

Long l3 = 200L;
Long l4 = 200L;
System.out.println(l3 == l4);  // false (outside cache range)

Golden rule: always use equals() to compare wrapper values. Never use == unless you specifically need reference identity.

Part 6

Key Static Methods

Integer

// Parsing strings to primitives
int parsed   = Integer.parseInt("42");         // int 42
int hex      = Integer.parseInt("2A", 16);     // int 42 (hex)
int octal    = Integer.parseInt("52", 8);      // int 42 (octal)

// Factory (cached)
Integer boxed = Integer.valueOf(42);

// Arithmetic utilities
int max  = Integer.max(10, 20);        // 20
int min  = Integer.min(10, 20);        // 10
int sum  = Integer.sum(10, 20);        // 30  (useful as method reference)

// Bit manipulation
int bits     = Integer.bitCount(255);       // 8
int highest  = Integer.highestOneBit(100);  // 64
int reversed = Integer.reverse(1);          // 2147483648

// Comparison (avoids overflow vs subtraction)
int cmp = Integer.compare(10, 20);  // negative (10 < 20)

// String representation
String binary = Integer.toBinaryString(42);   // "101010"
String hex2   = Integer.toHexString(42);      // "2a"
String octal2 = Integer.toOctalString(42);    // "52"

// Constants
System.out.println(Integer.MAX_VALUE);  // 2147483647
System.out.println(Integer.MIN_VALUE);  // -2147483648
System.out.println(Integer.SIZE);       // 32 (bits)
System.out.println(Integer.BYTES);      // 4

Double

double parsed  = Double.parseDouble("3.14");
boolean isNaN  = Double.isNaN(0.0 / 0.0);           // true
boolean isInf  = Double.isInfinite(1.0 / 0.0);      // true
boolean finite = Double.isFinite(3.14);              // true
long bits      = Double.doubleToLongBits(3.14);      // bit representation
int cmp        = Double.compare(3.14, 2.71);         // positive

Character

char c = 'A';
Character.isLetter(c);      // true
Character.isDigit('5');     // true
Character.isWhitespace(' ');// true
Character.isUpperCase('A'); // true
Character.toLowerCase('A'); // 'a'
Character.toUpperCase('a'); // 'A'
int numeric = Character.getNumericValue('9'); // 9
Part 7

NullPointerException from Unboxing

This is one of the most insidious bugs in Java. When the JVM unboxes a null wrapper, it throws NPE at the arithmetic/assignment point — which looks like the error is in the math, not in a null reference.

Integer maybeNull = null;  // legal — Integer is an object

// This throws NPE, NOT because of division, but because of unboxing:
int value = maybeNull;  // compiler: maybeNull.intValue() → NPE!

// More dangerous — hidden unboxing in conditions:
Integer score = getScoreFromDatabase(); // might return null

if (score > 100) {  // NPE if score is null! (score.intValue() > 100)
    System.out.println("Perfect score");
}

Common NPE Patterns

// Pattern 1: Method returns Integer, used as int
public Integer computeScore(String key) {
    return cache.get(key);  // returns null if not found
}

int score = computeScore("nonexistent");  // NPE!

// Pattern 2: Ternary with mixed types
Integer x = null;
int result = (x != null) ? x : 0;  // SAFE
int bad    = (x != null) ? x : 0;  // Wait, this IS safe with ternary
// But this is NOT:
int bad2 = condition ? x : defaultInt;  // if x is null and chosen, NPE

// Pattern 3: Arithmetic on null wrapper in collections
Map<String, Integer> counts = new HashMap<>();
counts.put("a", 5);
int total = counts.get("a") + counts.get("b");  // get("b") returns null → NPE

// Fix: use getOrDefault
int total2 = counts.getOrDefault("a", 0) + counts.getOrDefault("b", 0);

Safe Unboxing Patterns

// Option 1: Null check
Integer boxed = getFromSomewhere();
int primitive = (boxed != null) ? boxed : 0;

// Option 2: Optional
Optional<Integer> opt = Optional.ofNullable(getFromSomewhere());
int value = opt.orElse(0);

// Option 3: Objects.requireNonNullElse (Java 9+)
int val = Objects.requireNonNullElse(getFromSomewhere(), 0);
Part 8

Performance Cost of Autoboxing

Autoboxing is not free. Every box operation:
1. Allocates a new object on the heap (if outside cache range)
2. Writes two fields (header + value)
3. Adds a reference for the GC to track

In hot paths (tight loops, data pipelines, game engines), this matters:

// SLOW: autoboxing in loop
long start = System.nanoTime();
Long sum = 0L;
for (long i = 0; i < 10_000_000L; i++) {
    sum += i;  // unbox sum, add i, rebox result — 10M allocations!
}
long elapsed = System.nanoTime() - start;
System.out.println("Boxed sum: " + sum + " in " + elapsed/1_000_000 + "ms");
// Typical: ~500–800ms

// FAST: no boxing
start = System.nanoTime();
long sumPrimitive = 0L;
for (long i = 0; i < 10_000_000L; i++) {
    sumPrimitive += i;  // pure primitive arithmetic
}
elapsed = System.nanoTime() - start;
System.out.println("Primitive sum: " + sumPrimitive + " in " + elapsed/1_000_000 + "ms");
// Typical: ~5–15ms — 50–100x faster!

ASCII: Memory Layout Comparison

Primitive int on stack:
  ┌────────────────┐
  │   int: 42      │   4 bytes, zero overhead
  └────────────────┘

Boxed Integer on heap:
  Stack reference:        Heap object:
  ┌───────────────┐       ┌───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ref ─────────┼──────►│  Object header (mark word)  8 bytes│
  └───────────────┘       │  Class pointer              4 bytes│
   8 bytes (64-bit)        │  int value                  4 bytes│
                           └───────────────────────────────────┘
                                        16 bytes total

Cost of boxing:
  - 16 bytes heap allocation (vs 4 bytes)
  - GC root tracking
  - Cache-miss risk (Integer on heap vs int on stack/register)
  - JIT debox optimization sometimes (but not always)

When to Use Primitives vs Wrappers

Scenario Use Reason
Local variable computation int, double, etc. Zero overhead
Hot-path arithmetic (loops) Primitives Avoid GC, maximize CPU throughput
Collection element type Integer, Double, etc. Collections require objects
Generic type argument Wrapper (required) Generics erase to Object
Field that can be null / absent Wrapper int cannot represent "not set"
Method parameter from reflection Wrapper Reflection uses Object
JPA entity numeric field, nullable Integer DB nullable column needs null
JPA entity numeric field, not null int Use primitive, map nullable=false
Part 9

Number Hierarchy and Numeric Utilities

java.lang.Object
    └── java.lang.Number  (abstract)
            ├── Integer
            ├── Long
            ├── Double
            ├── Float
            ├── Short
            ├── Byte
            └── java.math.BigInteger, BigDecimal (not wrapper classes but extend Number)

java.lang.Comparable<T>  (implemented by all wrappers)
java.io.Serializable      (implemented by all wrappers)

Number defines abstract methods: intValue(), longValue(), floatValue(), doubleValue(), byteValue(), shortValue().

Number n = Integer.valueOf(42);
System.out.println(n.intValue());    // 42
System.out.println(n.doubleValue()); // 42.0
System.out.println(n.longValue());   // 42L
Part 10

String Conversion Utilities

// Primitives/Wrappers to String
String s1 = String.valueOf(42);        // "42"
String s2 = Integer.toString(42);      // "42"
String s3 = "" + 42;                   // "42" (least preferred — uses StringBuilder)

String s4 = Integer.toString(42, 16);  // "2a" (base 16)
String s5 = Integer.toBinaryString(42);// "101010"
String s6 = Integer.toHexString(42);   // "2a"
String s7 = Integer.toOctalString(42); // "52"

// String to primitives
int    i = Integer.parseInt("42");
double d = Double.parseDouble("3.14");
boolean b = Boolean.parseBoolean("true");   // case-insensitive
long   l  = Long.parseLong("9876543210");

// Parsing with radix
int hex  = Integer.parseInt("FF", 16);  // 255
int bin  = Integer.parseInt("1010", 2); // 10

// TRAP: parseInt vs valueOf
int primitive = Integer.parseInt("42");   // returns int
Integer boxed = Integer.valueOf("42");    // returns Integer (cached if in range)

parseXxx vs valueOf

Method Returns Notes
Integer.parseInt(s) int (primitive) Never allocates
Integer.valueOf(s) Integer (object) Uses cache
new Integer(s) Integer (object) Deprecated, always allocates

If you only need the primitive value, use parseInt — it avoids boxing entirely.

Part 11

Comparisons and Ordering

// Safe numeric comparison — avoids integer overflow!
// WRONG (overflow risk when values are very large/small):
// int cmp = a - b; // if a=MAX_VALUE, b=-1, this overflows!

// CORRECT:
int result = Integer.compare(a, b);  // returns negative, 0, or positive

// As Comparator (method reference style)
List<Integer> nums = Arrays.asList(5, 3, 8, 1, 9, 2);
nums.sort(Integer::compare);  // ascending
nums.sort(Comparator.reverseOrder()); // descending

// Min/Max without branching
int maximum = Integer.max(10, 20);  // 20
int minimum = Integer.min(10, 20);  // 10

// Unsigned operations (Java 8+)
int unsigned = Integer.compareUnsigned(-1, 1);  // -1 as unsigned is MAX_VALUE
String unsignedStr = Integer.toUnsignedString(-1); // "4294967295"
long unsignedLong  = Integer.toUnsignedLong(-1);   // 4294967295L
Part 12

JVM Internals: Autoboxing Bytecode

Consider this Java code:

Integer a = 42;
int b = a + 1;

The compiled bytecode is roughly:

bipush 42                    // push int 42 onto operand stack
invokestatic Integer.valueOf:(I)Ljava/lang/Integer;  // box it
astore_1                     // store reference in variable 'a'

aload_1                      // load 'a' (Integer reference)
invokevirtual Integer.intValue:()I   // unbox: call intValue()
iconst_1                     // push int 1
iadd                         // add two ints
invokestatic Integer.valueOf:(I)Ljava/lang/Integer;  // box result
astore_2                     // store in 'b'

Every autoboxing operation is an invokestatic Integer.valueOf call. Every unboxing is an invokevirtual intValue() call. These are real method calls — not free conversions.

JIT Optimization: Scalar Replacement

The JIT compiler can eliminate some boxing allocations through scalar replacement (a form of escape analysis): if a boxed value never escapes the current method, the JIT may keep it as a register value. But this optimization is fragile and cannot be relied upon in production code that matters.

Part 13

ASCII Diagram: Autoboxing Flow Through JVM

Java Source: Integer i = 42;  List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>();  list.add(i + 1);
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  Compile time (javac)
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Integer i = Integer.valueOf(42);                                     │
  │ list.add(Integer.valueOf(i.intValue() + 1));                         │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                  │
                  ▼
  Runtime: Integer.valueOf(42)
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  n=42, in cache range (-128..127)?   YES                            │
  │                                                                      │
  │  IntegerCache.cache[42+128] = IntegerCache.cache[170]               │
  │                                                                      │
  │  ┌───────────────────┐                                              │
  │  │ Integer@cafebabe  │  ← pre-allocated, shared                     │
  │  │ value: 42         │                                              │
  │  └───────────────────┘                                              │
  │  return cache[170]  (no new allocation)                              │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                  │
                  ▼
  Runtime: i.intValue() → 42  (unboxing)
  Runtime: 42 + 1 → 43        (primitive addition)
  Runtime: Integer.valueOf(43) → cache[171] → Integer@deadbeef (cached)
                  │
                  ▼
  list.add(Integer@deadbeef)  ← adds object reference to ArrayList
Part 14

Optional with Wrapper Classes

// Spring / Service layer patterns
public Optional<Integer> findUserAge(long userId) {
    User user = userRepo.findById(userId).orElse(null);
    return user == null ? Optional.empty() : Optional.ofNullable(user.getAge());
}

// Usage
int age = findUserAge(123L).orElse(0);
int ageOrThrow = findUserAge(123L).orElseThrow(() ->
    new UserNotFoundException("User 123 not found"));

// Stream with wrapper classes
OptionalInt streamMin = IntStream.of(5, 3, 8, 1).min();
int minVal = streamMin.getAsInt();

// Primitive streams avoid boxing
IntStream.range(0, 1_000_000)
         .filter(n -> n % 2 == 0)
         .sum();  // no Integer objects created

// vs boxed stream (avoid in hot paths)
Stream.iterate(0, n -> n + 1)
      .limit(1_000_000)
      .filter(n -> n % 2 == 0)  // n is Integer — boxing!
      .mapToInt(Integer::intValue)
      .sum();

OptionalInt, OptionalLong, OptionalDouble

The JDK provides primitive-specialized Optional variants to avoid boxing in stream terminal operations:

OptionalInt    optInt    = IntStream.of(1, 2, 3).max();
OptionalLong   optLong   = LongStream.of(1L, 2L).min();
OptionalDouble optDouble = DoubleStream.of(1.5, 2.5).average();

int    v1 = optInt.getAsInt();
long   v2 = optLong.getAsLong();
double v3 = optDouble.getAsDouble();
Part 15

Primitive Streams vs Object Streams

Java provides specialized primitive stream types that eliminate boxing:

Stream Type Primitive Equivalent Object Stream
IntStream int Stream<Integer>
LongStream long Stream<Long>
DoubleStream double Stream<Double> 
// PREFER: IntStream — no boxing
int sum = IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 100).sum();  // Gauss's formula check: 5050

// AVOID in hot paths: Stream<Integer> — boxing overhead
int sumBoxed = Stream.iterate(1, n -> n <= 100, n -> n + 1)
                     .mapToInt(Integer::intValue)
                     .sum();

// Converting between primitive and boxed streams
IntStream intStream = IntStream.of(1, 2, 3);
Stream<Integer> boxedStream = intStream.boxed();  // explicit boxing

Stream<Integer> objectStream = Stream.of(1, 2, 3);
IntStream backToPrimitive = objectStream.mapToInt(Integer::intValue); // unboxing
Part 16

Production Patterns and Anti-Patterns

Pattern 1: Avoiding Unboxing NPE in Data Processing

// Assume records from CSV/DB may have null numeric fields
public class SalesRecord {
    private Integer units;     // nullable — wrapper
    private Double unitPrice;  // nullable — wrapper

    public double getTotalRevenue() {
        if (units == null || unitPrice == null) {
            return 0.0;
        }
        return units * unitPrice;  // safe unboxing after null check
    }
}

Pattern 2: JPA Entity Design

@Entity
public class Employee {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue
    private Long id;  // wrapper: JPA ID can be null before persist

    @Column(nullable = false)
    private int salary;  // primitive: always present, not null

    @Column(nullable = true)
    private Integer bonusMultiplier;  // wrapper: nullable DB column

    @Column(nullable = false)
    private boolean active;  // primitive: boolean maps to BIT/BOOLEAN not null
}

Pattern 3: DTO / API Boundary

// At API boundaries (JSON input), use wrappers to distinguish "not provided" from 0/false
public class UpdateProfileRequest {
    private Integer age;        // null = "not provided", don't update
    private String name;
    private Boolean newsletter; // null = "not provided", preserve existing

    // Getters, setters...
}

// In service layer, use primitives for internal computation
public void processOrder(int quantity, double price) {
    double total = quantity * price;
    // ...
}

Anti-Pattern: Wrapper in Hot Loop

// BAD — measures from real profiling sessions show 10–100x slowdown
public long computeSum(List<Integer> data) {
    Long sum = 0L;
    for (Integer value : data) {  // unbox each element
        sum += value;             // unbox sum, unbox value, add, rebox sum
    }
    return sum;  // unbox for return
}

// GOOD — convert once, compute with primitives
public long computeSum(List<Integer> data) {
    long sum = 0L;
    for (Integer value : data) {
        sum += value;  // one unbox per element, sum stays primitive
    }
    return sum;
}

// BEST for large datasets — parallel primitive stream
public long computeSum(List<Integer> data) {
    return data.stream()
               .mapToLong(Integer::longValue)  // unbox once, stay primitive
               .sum();
}
Part 17

Spring Framework Specifics

@RequestParam with Wrapper Types (Optional Parameters)

@RestController
public class ReportController {

    // int: parameter is REQUIRED — Spring throws 400 if missing
    @GetMapping("/report")
    public Report getReport(@RequestParam int year) { ... }

    // Integer: parameter is OPTIONAL — Spring passes null if missing
    @GetMapping("/report2")
    public Report getReport2(@RequestParam(required = false) Integer year) {
        int effectiveYear = (year != null) ? year : LocalDate.now().getYear();
        return generateReport(effectiveYear);
    }

    // Even cleaner with defaultValue:
    @GetMapping("/report3")
    public Report getReport3(
            @RequestParam(defaultValue = "#{T(java.time.Year).now().getValue()}")
            int year) { ... }
}

Optional<Integer> vs int in Service Layer

@Service
public class UserService {

    // Use Optional to signal "might not exist"
    public Optional<Integer> getUserLevel(long userId) {
        return userRepo.findById(userId)
                       .map(User::getLevel);
    }

    // Use int for computed values that always exist
    public int calculateTotalPoints(long userId) {
        return transactionRepo.sumPointsByUserId(userId)
                              .orElse(0);  // sum returns Optional<Integer>
    }
}

Jackson Serialization of Wrappers

public class ProductDto {
    private Integer price;    // serialized as number or null in JSON
    private Integer discount; // null → "discount": null (or omit with annotation)

    @JsonInclude(JsonInclude.Include.NON_NULL)
    private Integer optionalRating; // omitted from JSON if null
}

// Output for price=100, discount=null, optionalRating=null:
// { "price": 100, "discount": null }
// (optionalRating omitted due to @JsonInclude)
Part 18

Common Interview Scenarios with Code

Scenario 1: The Classic 127 vs 128 Question

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Integer a = 127, b = 127;
        Integer c = 128, d = 128;

        System.out.println(a == b);      // true  (cached)
        System.out.println(c == d);      // false (not cached)
        System.out.println(c.equals(d)); // true  (always use equals for value comparison)
    }
}

Explain it in an interview: "Java's Integer.valueOf() caches instances for values -128 to 127. Both a and b reference the same cached object, so == is true. For 128, two separate heap objects are created, so == is false, but equals() compares values and is true."

Scenario 2: The Unboxing NPE Puzzle

public class Score {
    private Integer value;

    public boolean isHighScore() {
        return value > 100;  // NPE if value is null!
    }
}

"The > operator triggers unboxing: value.intValue() > 100. If value is null, intValue() throws NPE."

Scenario 3: The Switch Unboxing

Integer x = null;
switch (x) {  // NPE here — x is unboxed before switch
    case 1: System.out.println("one"); break;
    default: System.out.println("other");
}

Scenario 4: The Ternary Type Promotion

Integer i = null;
double d = true ? i : 9.0;  // NPE!
// The ternary has type double (numeric promotion).
// The compiler inserts: (double) i.intValue() → NPE
Part 19

Memory and GC Impact

Object Size of Wrapper Classes

On a 64-bit JVM with compressed OOPs (standard configuration):

Type Primitive Size Wrapper Object Size Overhead
byte / Byte 1 byte 16 bytes 16x
int / Integer 4 bytes 16 bytes 4x
long / Long 8 bytes 24 bytes 3x
double / Double 8 bytes 24 bytes 3x
boolean / Boolean 1 bit (4 bytes in JVM slot) 16 bytes ~16x

A List<Integer> with 1 million elements:
- The list's object array: ~4 MB (8 bytes per reference × 1M)
- The Integer objects themselves: ~16 MB (16 bytes × 1M)
- Total: ~20 MB

An int[] with 1 million elements:
- 4 MB flat array — no references, no GC tracking, cache-friendly

GC Pressure

Boxed collections generate GC pressure. For Long sum = 0L; sum += i in a loop with N iterations, you create N temporary Long objects. Young generation fills quickly, triggering frequent minor GCs.

Mitigation strategies:
1. Use primitive arrays or int[] / long[] instead of ArrayList<Integer>
2. Use IntStream, LongStream, DoubleStream for aggregations
3. Use specialized libraries: Eclipse Collections, Trove, or Koloboke for primitive collections
4. Use primitive-typed fields in tight classes (cache locality)

Part 20

Java 8+ Functional Interfaces for Primitives

The JDK provides primitive-specialized functional interfaces to avoid boxing in lambdas:

Primitive Consumer Function Supplier Predicate
int IntConsumer IntFunction<R>, IntUnaryOperator IntSupplier IntPredicate
long LongConsumer LongFunction<R>, LongUnaryOperator LongSupplier LongPredicate
double DoubleConsumer DoubleFunction<R>, DoubleUnaryOperator DoubleSupplier DoublePredicate 
// Boxing version (avoid in hot paths)
Function<Integer, String> boxed = i -> "value: " + i;

// Primitive version (preferred)
IntFunction<String> primitive = i -> "value: " + i;

// Applying
String r1 = boxed.apply(42);     // boxes 42 into Integer
String r2 = primitive.apply(42); // no boxing

// IntUnaryOperator (int → int, no boxing at all)
IntUnaryOperator doubler = x -> x * 2;
int doubled = doubler.applyAsInt(21);  // 42, no Integer created
Part 21

Checklist: Architect's Wrapper Class Decision Guide

Primitive vs Wrapper Decision:
  Use PRIMITIVES when:
    ✓ Local variable in method body
    ✓ Arithmetic-heavy computation
    ✓ Array element type (int[], double[])
    ✓ JPA field with NOT NULL constraint
    ✓ Performance-critical code path (loops, streams)

  Use WRAPPERS when:
    ✓ Collection element type (List, Set, Map)
    ✓ Generic type parameter
    ✓ Value can be null/absent (nullable DB column, optional API field)
    ✓ Need to call methods (parseInt, valueOf, toString)
    ✓ Reflection or serialization context

Comparison rules:
  ✓ ALWAYS use .equals() to compare wrapper values
  ✗ NEVER use == to compare wrapper values (except Boolean)
  ✓ Use Integer.compare(a, b) for ordering (avoids overflow)

Null safety:
  ✓ Always null-check before unboxing
  ✓ Use getOrDefault() on maps returning Integer
  ✓ Use Optional.orElse(defaultValue) for service layer
  ✗ Never unbox a wrapper that may be null directly in arithmetic

Performance:
  ✓ Profile before optimizing boxing hotspots
  ✓ Use primitive streams (IntStream) for numeric aggregations
  ✓ Prefer int[] over List<Integer> for large numeric data
  ✓ Cache Integer.valueOf() awareness: -128..127 range
Part 22

Summary Table

Feature Detail
Count 8 wrapper classes, one per primitive
Package java.lang (auto-imported)
Introduced Java 1.0; autoboxing in Java 5
Mutability Immutable (final value field)
Superclass Number (except Boolean, Character)
Interfaces Comparable<T>, Serializable
Integer cache range -128 to 127 (adjustable via -XX:AutoBoxCacheMax)
Boolean cache Always — only TRUE and FALSE exist
== on wrappers Unreliable outside cache range — use equals()
Unboxing null Throws NullPointerException
Integer.parseInt Returns int — no allocation
Integer.valueOf Returns Integer — uses cache
new Integer() Deprecated Java 9, removed Java 17
Memory overhead 16–24 bytes vs 1–8 bytes for primitive
JPA mapping Use wrapper for nullable, primitive for not-null
Stream best practice IntStream/LongStream over Stream<Integer>
Functional interfaces Use IntFunction, IntPredicate to avoid boxing

Practice

Exercise 1 — Cache Boundary Test

Write a program that tests == for Integer values from 126 to 129. Print each comparison result. Explain why each result is true or false. Then repeat using equals().

Exercise 2 — NPE Diagnosis

Given the following code, identify every place an NPE can occur and fix them:

Map<String, Integer> scores = new HashMap<>();
scores.put("Alice", 95);
scores.put("Bob", null);

int aliceScore = scores.get("Alice");
int bobScore   = scores.get("Bob");
int charlieScore = scores.get("Charlie");
int total = aliceScore + bobScore + charlieScore;

Exercise 3 — Performance Benchmark

Write a microbenchmark (avoid JMH for simplicity, use System.nanoTime()) comparing:
a) Summing 10 million values with Long sum = 0L; sum += i;
b) Summing 10 million values with long sum = 0L; sum += i;
c) Using LongStream.rangeClosed(1, 10_000_000).sum()

Record the timing and explain the differences.

Exercise 4 — Safe Parsing Utility

Write a utility class SafeParse with static methods:
- parseInt(String s, int defaultValue) — returns default on null/invalid input
- parseDouble(String s, double defaultValue) — same for double
- parseBoolean(String s, boolean defaultValue) — same for boolean

Handle null input, NumberFormatException, and empty strings.

Exercise 5 — JPA Entity Design

Design a Contract JPA entity with these fields and choose the appropriate type (primitive vs wrapper) for each, justifying your choice:
- id — auto-generated, nullable before persist
- contractValue — monetary amount in cents, never null
- bonusPercentage — optional, may not be set
- active — flag, always set
- reviewerCount — always present, defaults to 0
- expiryDays — may be absent (perpetual contracts)

Exercise 6 — Stream Optimization

Refactor this code to eliminate all unnecessary boxing:

List<String> prices = Arrays.asList("10.5", "20.0", "15.75", "8.25");
Double total = prices.stream()
                     .map(Double::valueOf)
                     .reduce(0.0, Double::sum);
System.out.println("Total: " + total);
