Part 1

Why Generics Exist

Before Java 5, every collection stored Object. You retrieved elements and cast them manually. This was error-prone, verbose, and unsafe — ClassCastException was a runtime surprise.

// Pre-generics (Java 1.4 and earlier)
List names = new ArrayList();
names.add("Alice");
names.add(42);               // compiles — no type safety
String s = (String) names.get(1);  // ClassCastException at runtime

Generics solve this by moving the type check from runtime to compile time:

// Post-generics (Java 5+)
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
names.add("Alice");
names.add(42);               // COMPILE ERROR — caught immediately
String s = names.get(0);     // no cast needed

Three core benefits:
1. Type safety — the compiler enforces correct types
2. Eliminate casts — cleaner, less boilerplate code
3. Enable generic algorithms — write one sort/search that works for any type

Part 2

Type Parameter Conventions

Java uses single-letter type parameter names by convention. These are not enforced by the language but are universally followed:

Parameter Meaning Typical Location
T Type (generic) class Box<T>, <T> T get()
E Element List<E>, Set<E>
K Key Map<K, V>
V Value Map<K, V>
N Number class Counter<N extends Number>
R Return type Function<T, R>
A Accumulator Collector<T, A, R>
S,U,W Second, third, fourth types Multi-type-param contexts

Multiple parameters use commas: Map<K, V>, BiFunction<T, U, R>.

Part 3

Generic Classes

A generic class declares one or more type parameters in angle brackets after the class name. The type parameter is a placeholder resolved when the class is instantiated.

public class Box<T> {
    private T value;

    public Box(T value) {
        this.value = value;
    }

    public T getValue() {
        return value;
    }

    public void setValue(T value) {
        this.value = value;
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "Box[" + value + "]";
    }
}

Usage:

Box<String>  stringBox  = new Box<>("hello");
Box<Integer> intBox     = new Box<>(42);
Box<Double>  doubleBox  = new Box<>(3.14);

String s = stringBox.getValue();   // no cast
int    n = intBox.getValue();      // auto-unboxed

Diamond operator (<>) — since Java 7, the right-hand type argument can be inferred:

Box<String> box = new Box<>("hi");   // compiler infers String

Multiple type parameters:

public class Pair<A, B> {
    private final A first;
    private final B second;

    public Pair(A first, B second) {
        this.first  = first;
        this.second = second;
    }

    public A getFirst()  { return first;  }
    public B getSecond() { return second; }

    public static <X, Y> Pair<X, Y> of(X x, Y y) {
        return new Pair<>(x, y);
    }
}

Pair<String, Integer> entry = Pair.of("Alice", 30);
Part 4

Generic Interfaces

Interfaces can also be parameterized. Implementing classes either fix the type or stay generic:

public interface Repository<T, ID> {
    Optional<T> findById(ID id);
    List<T> findAll();
    T save(T entity);
    void deleteById(ID id);
}

// Fix both type params — concrete implementation
public class UserRepository implements Repository<User, Long> {
    public Optional<User> findById(Long id) { ... }
    // ...
}

// Stay generic — still abstract
public abstract class BaseRepository<T, ID> implements Repository<T, ID> {
    // partial implementation
}

The standard library is full of generic interfaces: Comparable<T>, Iterable<T>, Iterator<T>, Callable<V>, Supplier<T>, Consumer<T>, Function<T,R>, Predicate<T>, and so on.

Part 5

Generic Methods

A method can introduce its own type parameters independent of the class's parameters. The type parameter is declared before the return type:

public class Utils {

    // Generic static method
    public static <T> void swap(T[] arr, int i, int j) {
        T temp = arr[i];
        arr[i] = arr[j];
        arr[j] = temp;
    }

    // Type param with bound
    public static <T extends Comparable<T>> T max(T a, T b) {
        return a.compareTo(b) >= 0 ? a : b;
    }

    // Multiple bounds
    public static <T extends Cloneable & Serializable> T copyAndSerialize(T obj) {
        // ...
    }
}

Type inference at call sites:

Integer[] nums = {3, 1, 4, 1, 5};
Utils.swap(nums, 0, 4);                     // T inferred as Integer
String result = Utils.max("apple", "zebra"); // T inferred as String

// Explicit type witness (rarely needed)
String r = Utils.<String>max("a", "b");
Part 6

Bounded Type Parameters

Upper Bound — extends

Restricts T to a type or any subtype:

public class NumberBox<T extends Number> {
    private T value;

    public NumberBox(T value) { this.value = value; }

    public double doubled() {
        return value.doubleValue() * 2;  // Number methods available
    }
}

NumberBox<Integer> i = new NumberBox<>(5);    // ok
NumberBox<Double>  d = new NumberBox<>(3.14); // ok
NumberBox<String>  s = new NumberBox<>("hi"); // COMPILE ERROR

Multiple Bounds

T extends ClassBound & Interface1 & Interface2 — at most one class, interfaces after:

public <T extends Number & Comparable<T> & Serializable> T clamp(T val, T min, T max) {
    if (val.compareTo(min) < 0) return min;
    if (val.compareTo(max) > 0) return max;
    return val;
}

Why extends, not implements?

Java uses extends for both class and interface bounds in generics for uniformity. <T extends Runnable> is the syntax even though Runnable is an interface.

Part 7

Wildcards: The Three Forms

Wildcards (?) appear in variable declarations, method parameters, and return types — not in class/method definitions. They represent an unknown type.

? alone          — unbounded wildcard
? extends Type   — upper-bounded wildcard (covariant)
? super Type     — lower-bounded wildcard (contravariant)

Unbounded Wildcard ?

Use when you need a collection of any type and only call methods that don't depend on the element type:

public static void printList(List<?> list) {
    for (Object o : list) {
        System.out.println(o);   // safe: every type is an Object
    }
}

printList(new ArrayList<String>());
printList(new ArrayList<Integer>());

You cannot add to List<?> (except null) because the exact type is unknown.

Part 8

PECS Principle (Producer Extends, Consumer Super)

This is one of the most important rules in generic API design:

If a generic structure PRODUCES values you read → use ? extends T
If a generic structure CONSUMES values you write → use ? super T

Upper-bounded wildcard ? extends T — Producer

// source is a producer — we read from it
public static <T> void copy(List<? extends T> source, List<T> dest) {
    for (T item : source) {
        dest.add(item);
    }
}

List<Integer> ints    = List.of(1, 2, 3);
List<Number>  numbers = new ArrayList<>();
copy(ints, numbers);  // works: Integer extends Number

You can read but not add to List<? extends T>.

Lower-bounded wildcard ? super T — Consumer

// dest is a consumer — we write into it
public static <T> void fill(List<? super T> dest, T value, int count) {
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        dest.add(value);
    }
}

List<Number> numbers = new ArrayList<>();
fill(numbers, 42, 5);   // works: Integer super-typed by Number

You can add but only read as Object from List<? super T>.

PECS Mnemonic Diagram

                    PECS
        ┌───────────────────────────────┐
        │                               │
  Producer                         Consumer
(you read from it)            (you write into it)
        │                               │
  ? extends T                     ? super T
  (covariant)                   (contravariant)
        │                               │
  List<? extends Number>      List<? super Integer>
  can hold Integer, Double     can hold Number, Object
  READ  ✓   WRITE ✗           READ as Object ✓  WRITE Integer ✓
        │                               │
        └───────────────────────────────┘
              When in doubt: if both, use T directly

Real-world example — Collections.copy:

// From java.util.Collections
public static <T> void copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src) {
    // src is producer (extends), dest is consumer (super)
    int srcSize = src.size();
    for (int i = 0; i < srcSize; i++)
        dest.set(i, src.get(i));
}
Part 9

Type Erasure: What Happens at Runtime

Java generics are a compile-time feature only. The JVM has no knowledge of type parameters. During compilation, the compiler:

  1. Replaces all type parameters with their bounds (or Object if unbounded)
  2. Inserts casts where needed
  3. Generates bridge methods to maintain polymorphism

Compile Time vs Runtime Type Diagram

  SOURCE CODE (compile time)           BYTECODE (runtime)
  ─────────────────────────────        ─────────────────────────────

  class Box<T> {                       class Box {
      T value;                             Object value;
      T getValue() {                       Object getValue() {
          return value;                        return value;
      }                                    }
  }                                    }

  Box<String> b = new Box<>();         Box b = new Box();
  b.setValue("hello");                 b.setValue("hello");
  String s = b.getValue();            String s = (String) b.getValue();
                                                  ↑
                                          cast inserted by compiler

  ─────────────────────────────        ─────────────────────────────
  List<String>  ──────────────────►   List        (same class)
  List<Integer> ──────────────────►   List        (same class)
  List<Double>  ──────────────────►   List        (same class)

  List<String>.class == List<Integer>.class  →  TRUE at runtime

What type erasure means in practice:

List<String> strings  = new ArrayList<>();
List<Integer> ints    = new ArrayList<>();

// At runtime both are just ArrayList
System.out.println(strings.getClass() == ints.getClass()); // true

// Cannot use instanceof with generic type
if (obj instanceof List<String>) { }  // COMPILE ERROR

// Cannot create generic array
T[] arr = new T[10];     // COMPILE ERROR (covered in Part 11)

// Cannot catch generic exception type
catch (SomeException<String> e) { }  // COMPILE ERROR
Part 10

Bridge Methods

Bridge methods are synthetic methods the compiler generates to preserve polymorphism after type erasure. They arise when a class implements or extends a generic type.

public interface Processor<T> {
    void process(T item);
}

public class StringProcessor implements Processor<String> {
    @Override
    public void process(String item) {
        System.out.println(item.toUpperCase());
    }
}

After erasure, Processor<T> becomes Processor with void process(Object item). But StringProcessor has void process(String item). These don't match — so the compiler generates a bridge method:

// Synthetic bridge method generated by compiler
public void process(Object item) {
    process((String) item);   // delegates with cast
}

You can see bridge methods in the bytecode:

javap -c -verbose StringProcessor.class
# Look for: Flags: ACC_PUBLIC, ACC_BRIDGE, ACC_SYNTHETIC
Part 11

Generic Array Limitation

You cannot create arrays of parameterized types because arrays are covariant while generics are invariant, and combining them would break type safety.

// Cannot do this:
List<String>[] arr = new List<String>[10];   // COMPILE ERROR
T[] arr = new T[10];                          // COMPILE ERROR

// Why? Consider what would happen if allowed:
List<String>[] stringLists = new List<String>[1];  // hypothetically allowed
Object[] objects = stringLists;              // arrays are covariant — OK
objects[0] = new ArrayList<Integer>();       // ArrayStoreException NOT thrown (no runtime check)
String s = stringLists[0].get(0);           // ClassCastException at runtime

Workarounds:

// Option 1: Use List<List<String>> instead of List<String>[]
List<List<String>> listOfLists = new ArrayList<>();

// Option 2: Use raw type array and suppress warning (known safe contexts)
@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
List<String>[] arr = (List<String>[]) new List[10];

// Option 3: Use Array.newInstance with reflection
@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
T[] arr = (T[]) Array.newInstance(componentType, size);

Varargs with generics — this is where @SafeVarargs comes in:

@SafeVarargs
public static <T> List<T> listOf(T... elements) {
    return Arrays.asList(elements);
}

The annotation tells the compiler that the varargs usage is safe (you don't write to the backing array).

Part 12

Raw Types and Warnings

A raw type is using a generic class without type arguments. Raw types exist for backward compatibility with pre-Java-5 code.

List raw = new ArrayList();    // raw type
raw.add("hello");
raw.add(42);

String s = (String) raw.get(1); // ClassCastException at runtime

Using raw types disables all generic type checking in that expression. The compiler issues unchecked warnings:

Note: MyClass.java uses unchecked or unsafe operations.
Note: Recompile with -Xlint:unchecked for details.

Rules for production code:

// BAD: raw type
List list = new ArrayList();
Map map  = new HashMap();

// GOOD: always parameterize
List<String>          list = new ArrayList<>();
Map<String, Integer>  map  = new HashMap<>();

// If type genuinely unknown, use wildcard — not raw
List<?> unknown = getListFromSomewhere();

Heap pollution — when a variable of parameterized type refers to an object that is not of that type, caused by mixing raw and generic code:

@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
static void heapPollution() {
    List<String> strings = new ArrayList<>();
    List raw = strings;
    raw.add(42);                     // heap pollution: Integer in List<String>
    String s = strings.get(0);      // ClassCastException
}
Part 13

Generics and Inheritance

Generic types are invariant — List<Dog> is NOT a subtype of List<Animal> even if Dog extends Animal.

     Animal
       │
      Dog

  List<Animal>    List<Dog>
       │               │
  NOT related!    NOT related!

This is by design: if List<Dog> were a List<Animal>, you could add a Cat through the List<Animal> reference and corrupt the List<Dog>.

List<Dog>    dogs    = new ArrayList<>();
List<Animal> animals = dogs;          // COMPILE ERROR — invariant

// Wildcards restore flexibility at the cost of read/write restrictions:
List<? extends Animal> animals2 = dogs;   // OK (read-only)

Arrays are covariant (legacy behavior, pre-generics design):

Dog[]    dogs    = new Dog[3];
Animal[] animals = dogs;       // OK — covariant (but dangerous!)
animals[0] = new Cat();        // ArrayStoreException at runtime
Part 14

Recursive Type Bounds

A type parameter can refer to itself — common for Comparable-based APIs:

// T must be comparable to itself
public static <T extends Comparable<T>> T max(List<T> list) {
    return list.stream().max(Comparator.naturalOrder()).orElseThrow();
}

// Self-referential generic class (builder pattern)
public abstract class Builder<T, B extends Builder<T, B>> {
    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    public B withName(String name) {
        this.name = name;
        return (B) this;    // returns concrete subtype
    }
    public abstract T build();
}

public class PersonBuilder extends Builder<Person, PersonBuilder> {
    public Person build() { return new Person(name); }
}

Person p = new PersonBuilder().withName("Alice").build(); // fluent, type-safe
Part 15

Bounded Wildcards vs Bounded Type Parameters

These look similar but serve different purposes:

// Bounded TYPE PARAMETER — use when return type or multiple params depend on T
public <T extends Number> void process(List<T> list, T defaultVal) {
    // T appears in two places — must be consistent
}

// Bounded WILDCARD — use when no relationship between params needed
public void printNumbers(List<? extends Number> list) {
    // just iterating, no cross-param constraint
}

Rule of thumb: If the type parameter appears only once in the method signature, prefer a wildcard. If it appears multiple times (especially as return type), use a type parameter.

// Prefer wildcard (T appears once, return is void):
public void printAll(List<?> list) { ... }

// Need type param (T in param and return):
public <T> T firstOrDefault(List<T> list, T defaultVal) { ... }
Part 16

Generic Type Tokens and Class Literals

Since type information is erased, you sometimes need to pass the class explicitly — called a type token:

public class TypeSafeMap {
    private Map<Class<?>, Object> map = new HashMap<>();

    public <T> void put(Class<T> type, T value) {
        map.put(type, value);
    }

    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    public <T> T get(Class<T> type) {
        return type.cast(map.get(type));
    }
}

TypeSafeMap tsm = new TypeSafeMap();
tsm.put(String.class, "hello");
tsm.put(Integer.class, 42);

String  s = tsm.get(String.class);   // type-safe, no cast needed
Integer i = tsm.get(Integer.class);

For complex generic types like List<String>, use Guava's TypeToken or Jackson's TypeReference:

// Jackson TypeReference — captures generic type at compile time via anonymous class
TypeReference<List<String>> ref = new TypeReference<List<String>>() {};
List<String> result = objectMapper.readValue(json, ref);
Part 17

Comparable and Comparator with Generics

public class Temperature implements Comparable<Temperature> {
    private final double celsius;

    public Temperature(double celsius) { this.celsius = celsius; }

    @Override
    public int compareTo(Temperature other) {
        return Double.compare(this.celsius, other.celsius);
    }
}

// Usage with generic methods
List<Temperature> temps = List.of(
    new Temperature(100), new Temperature(0), new Temperature(37)
);

Temperature max = Collections.max(temps);   // uses Comparable<Temperature>

// Comparator chains — fully generic
Comparator<String> byLength = Comparator.comparingInt(String::length)
    .thenComparing(Comparator.naturalOrder());

List<String> words = Arrays.asList("banana", "apple", "fig");
words.sort(byLength);
Part 18

Generic Exceptions (Limitations)

Java allows generic checked exceptions in method signatures but not as new throw types or in catch blocks:

// Allowed: declare a generic checked exception
public interface Task<T, E extends Exception> {
    T execute() throws E;
}

public class FileTask implements Task<String, IOException> {
    public String execute() throws IOException {
        return Files.readString(Path.of("file.txt"));
    }
}

// Not allowed: catch clause
catch (SomeException<String> e) { }   // COMPILE ERROR — type erased

// Not allowed: throw new T() — T is erased, can't instantiate
public <T extends Exception> void doThrow() throws T {
    throw new T();   // COMPILE ERROR
}
Part 19

Spring Framework Generics

Spring uses generics extensively. Understanding them is essential for production Java.

RestTemplate — parameterized responses

@Service
public class UserService {
    private final RestTemplate restTemplate;

    public UserService(RestTemplate restTemplate) {
        this.restTemplate = restTemplate;
    }

    // Simple type
    public User getUser(Long id) {
        return restTemplate.getForObject("/users/{id}", User.class, id);
    }

    // Generic list — need ParameterizedTypeReference (like TypeReference)
    public List<User> getAllUsers() {
        ResponseEntity<List<User>> response = restTemplate.exchange(
            "/users",
            HttpMethod.GET,
            null,
            new ParameterizedTypeReference<List<User>>() {}
        );
        return response.getBody();
    }
}

ResponseEntity\<T>

@RestController
public class UserController {

    @GetMapping("/users/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<User> getUser(@PathVariable Long id) {
        return userService.findById(id)
            .map(ResponseEntity::ok)
            .orElse(ResponseEntity.notFound().build());
    }

    @GetMapping("/users")
    public ResponseEntity<List<User>> getAllUsers() {
        List<User> users = userService.findAll();
        return ResponseEntity.ok(users);
    }

    @PostMapping("/users")
    public ResponseEntity<User> createUser(@RequestBody User user) {
        User saved = userService.save(user);
        URI location = URI.create("/users/" + saved.getId());
        return ResponseEntity.created(location).body(saved);
    }
}

Spring Data JpaRepository\<T, ID>

// Spring generates the implementation at runtime via proxies
public interface UserRepository extends JpaRepository<User, Long> {
    // JpaRepository provides: save, findById, findAll, deleteById, ...
    Optional<User> findByEmail(String email);
    List<User> findByAgeGreaterThan(int age);
    Page<User> findByCity(String city, Pageable pageable);
}

// Service layer
@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class UserService {
    private final UserRepository userRepository;

    public User createUser(User user) {
        return userRepository.save(user);          // returns User (T)
    }

    public Optional<User> findUser(Long id) {
        return userRepository.findById(id);        // Optional<T> = Optional<User>
    }
}

Custom generic base repository pattern:

@NoRepositoryBean
public interface BaseRepository<T extends BaseEntity, ID>
        extends JpaRepository<T, ID> {

    List<T> findByCreatedAtAfter(LocalDateTime date);
    List<T> findByCreatedBy(String username);
}

public interface UserRepository extends BaseRepository<User, Long> {
    Optional<User> findByEmail(String email);
}
Part 20

Kafka Generics: ConsumerRecord\&lt;K, V&gt;

Kafka's Java client uses generics pervasively:

// Consumer setup with typed deserializers
Properties props = new Properties();
props.put(ConsumerConfig.KEY_DESERIALIZER_CLASS_CONFIG,
          StringDeserializer.class.getName());
props.put(ConsumerConfig.VALUE_DESERIALIZER_CLASS_CONFIG,
          JsonDeserializer.class.getName());

KafkaConsumer<String, OrderEvent> consumer = new KafkaConsumer<>(props);
consumer.subscribe(List.of("orders"));

while (true) {
    ConsumerRecords<String, OrderEvent> records = consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(100));
    for (ConsumerRecord<String, OrderEvent> record : records) {
        String     key   = record.key();     // K = String
        OrderEvent order = record.value();   // V = OrderEvent
        long       offset = record.offset();
        System.out.printf("offset=%d key=%s order=%s%n", offset, key, order);
    }
}

Spring Kafka — cleaner with @KafkaListener:

@Component
public class OrderConsumer {

    @KafkaListener(topics = "orders", groupId = "order-service")
    public void consume(ConsumerRecord<String, OrderEvent> record) {
        String key        = record.key();
        OrderEvent event  = record.value();
        processOrder(key, event);
    }

    // Or directly with the value type
    @KafkaListener(topics = "notifications")
    public void handleNotification(Notification notification) {
        // Spring Kafka deserializes and passes the typed value
        sendEmail(notification);
    }
}

Producer with generics:

@Service
public class OrderProducer {
    private final KafkaTemplate<String, OrderEvent> kafkaTemplate;

    public OrderProducer(KafkaTemplate<String, OrderEvent> kafkaTemplate) {
        this.kafkaTemplate = kafkaTemplate;
    }

    public void publishOrder(OrderEvent event) {
        kafkaTemplate.send("orders", event.getOrderId(), event);
    }
}
Part 21

Interview Questions and Deep Dives

Q1: What is type erasure? Why does Java use it?

Answer: Type erasure is the process by which the compiler removes all generic type information after type checking. At runtime, List<String> and List<Integer> are both just List. Java chose erasure for backward compatibility with pre-Java-5 code — existing JVMs and libraries didn't need to change. The cost is that generic type info is unavailable at runtime.

Follow-up traps:

// Does this compile?
List<String> a = new ArrayList<>();
List<Integer> b = new ArrayList<>();
System.out.println(a.getClass() == b.getClass()); // TRUE — both are ArrayList.class

Q2: Why can't generics use primitive types?

Answer: Because of type erasure. After erasure, T becomes Object. Primitives (int, double, etc.) are not Object — they live on the stack, not the heap. You must use wrapper types: Integer, Double, etc. Autoboxing handles the conversion automatically but incurs overhead.

List<int>     illegal = new ArrayList<>();     // COMPILE ERROR
List<Integer> legal   = new ArrayList<>();     // OK, autoboxed

// Performance implication
List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>();
for (int i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++) {
    list.add(i);  // autoboxing: int → Integer, allocation each time
}

> Future: Project Valhalla (JEP drafts) aims to add value types and eventually List<int>. Not yet in stable Java as of Java 21.

Q3: Explain PECS with an example.

Answer: PECS — Producer Extends, Consumer Super. When a collection produces values (you read from it), use ? extends T. When it consumes values (you write to it), use ? super T.

// Copy integers (or any Number subtype) into a List<Number>
public static <T> void copy(List<? extends T> src, List<? super T> dst) {
    src.forEach(dst::add);
}

List<Integer> ints    = List.of(1, 2, 3);
List<Number>  numbers = new ArrayList<>();
copy(ints, numbers);   // ints is producer (extends), numbers is consumer (super)

Q4: What is heap pollution?

Answer: Heap pollution occurs when a variable of a parameterized type refers to an object that is not of that type. It happens when raw types or unchecked operations mix with generic code, and it results in a ClassCastException from a line that doesn't contain a cast.

@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
static void pollute() {
    List<String> strings = new ArrayList<>();
    List raw = strings;    // raw type reference
    raw.add(42);           // Integer sneaks in
    String s = strings.get(0); // ClassCastException — the cast is inserted by compiler
}

Q5: What are bridge methods?

Answer: Bridge methods are synthetic methods generated by the compiler to maintain proper polymorphism after type erasure. When a class implements a generic interface and specializes the type, the compiler generates a method with the erased signature that delegates to the type-specific one.

interface Processor<T> { void process(T t); }

class IntProcessor implements Processor<Integer> {
    public void process(Integer i) { System.out.println(i * 2); }
    // Compiler generates: void process(Object t) { process((Integer) t); }
}

Q6: Is List<Object> a supertype of List<String>?

Answer: No. Due to invariance, List<Object> is not a supertype of List<String>. Only List<?> or List<? extends Object> accepts any List. This is fundamental to why PECS wildcards exist.

Q7: What does @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") mean?

Answer: It suppresses compiler warnings for unchecked casts and unchecked calls related to generics. Use it sparingly and locally — never on a whole class. Always add a comment explaining why it's safe.

@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")  // safe: we control the put, class token guarantees T
public <T> T get(Class<T> type) {
    return (T) map.get(type);
}

Generic Construct Master Reference

Construct Syntax Reads Writes Use Case

Generic interface interface Repo<T,ID> ✓ ✓ API contracts

Multiple bounds <T extends A & B> A, B ✓ Combined constraints

Type Erasure Effects

Feature Compile Time Runtime
List<String> vs List<Integer> Different types Same class (List)
instanceof List<String> Allowed check Not possible — compile error
new T() / new T[] Rejected N/A
Generic type in catch Not allowed N/A

PECS Quick Reference

Scenario Wildcard Can Read Can Write
Read from collection ? extends T As T ✗
Write to collection ? super T As Object As T
Read and write T (type param) As T As T
Don't care about type ? As Object ✗

Common Generic Patterns in Production

Pattern Example Purpose
Type token Class<T> param Runtime type ops after erasure
Fluent builder Builder<T, B extends Builder<T,B>> Typed chaining

Practice

Quick Exercises

  1. Generic Stack — Implement a Stack<T> class with push(T), pop(), peek(), isEmpty(). Add a <T extends Comparable<T>> T max() method that returns the largest element.

  2. Bounded pair — Write NumberPair<A extends Number, B extends Number> with a sum() method returning double.

  3. PECS practice — Write mergeInto(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src) that copies all elements from src into dest. Call it with List<Integer> → List<Number>.

  4. Type-safe heterogeneous container — Implement a Container class with <T> void put(Class<T> type, T value) and <T> T get(Class<T> type). Make it reject nulls.

  5. Wildcard analysis — For each method signature, determine whether it compiles and explain why:
    java List<? extends Number> a = new ArrayList<Integer>(); // ? List<? super Integer> b = new ArrayList<Number>(); // ? List<Number> c = new ArrayList<Integer>(); // ?

Code Reading Challenge

Trace through the following and predict the output. Explain every cast:

public class Challenge {
    static <T> List<T> repeat(T val, int n) {
        List<T> result = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) result.add(val);
        return result;
    }

    static <T extends Comparable<T>> T middle(List<T> list) {
        Collections.sort(list);
        return list.get(list.size() / 2);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Integer> nums = repeat(5, 4);
        List<String>  strs = repeat("hi", 3);
        System.out.println(nums);
        System.out.println(strs);
        System.out.println(middle(List.of(3, 1, 4, 1, 5)));
        System.out.println(middle(List.of("banana", "apple", "cherry")));
    }
}

Part 1

Concept Overview

Annotations are a form of metadata — data about data. They allow you to attach structured information to Java code elements (classes, methods, fields, parameters, packages, and more) without changing their runtime behaviour unless a tool or framework explicitly reads and acts on them.

Introduced in Java 5 (2004), annotations replaced many fragile conventions: @throws Javadoc tags, marker interfaces, and XML descriptor files (e.g., old EJB 2.x ejb-jar.xml). Today, every major Java framework — Spring, Hibernate, Jackson, JUnit, CDI — is driven almost entirely by annotations.

Three phases of annotation processing

Source Code (.java)
       |
       v
  [Annotation Processor] ← javac pluggable AP (compile-time)
       |  generates new .java / .class / resources
       v
  Bytecode (.class)      ← CLASS-retained annotations baked in
       |
       v
  JVM Runtime            ← RUNTIME-retained annotations readable
       |                    via java.lang.reflect.*
       v
  Framework/Library
  (Spring, Hibernate …)  reads RUNTIME annotations, acts on them

Key insight for architects: annotations are passive — they are just markers. The behaviour comes from whoever reads them: the compiler, an annotation processor, or runtime reflection.

Part 2

Core Syntax

An annotation type is declared with @interface:

public @interface MyAnnotation {
    String value() default "hello";
    int count() default 1;
}

An annotation with a single element named value can use the shorthand syntax:

@MyAnnotation("world")          // equivalent to @MyAnnotation(value = "world")
public class Foo { }

Multiple elements require named syntax:

@MyAnnotation(value = "world", count = 3)
public class Foo { }

Element types allowed in annotations

Type Example
Primitive int, long, boolean, …
String String name()
Class<?> Class<?> target()
Another annotation @SomeOther nested()
Enum RetentionPolicy policy()
Array of any of the above String[] roles()

> Annotations cannot have elements of type Object, collections, generics, or void.

Part 3

Built-in Annotations

Java ships with a small set of standard annotations you will use every day.

@Override

public class Animal {
    public String sound() { return "..."; }
}

public class Dog extends Animal {
    @Override
    public String sound() { return "Woof"; }   // compiler verifies override is valid
}

@Override has retention SOURCE — it exists only to ask the compiler to verify that the method genuinely overrides or implements a supertype method. Without it, a typo like souund() compiles silently as a new method; with it, you get a compile error.

@Deprecated

/**
 * @deprecated Use {@link #newMethod()} instead.
 */
@Deprecated(since = "11", forRemoval = true)
public void oldMethod() { ... }

Since Java 9, @Deprecated has since and forRemoval attributes. IDEs and javac emit warnings when deprecated code is used.

@SuppressWarnings

@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
public <T> List<T> legacyLoad(Class<T> type) {
    return (List<T>) rawList;  // no unchecked cast warning
}

Common tokens: "unchecked", "deprecation", "rawtypes", "unused", "all". Avoid "all" — it can mask real bugs.

@FunctionalInterface

@FunctionalInterface
public interface Transformer<T, R> {
    R transform(T input);
    // adding a second abstract method → compile error
}

Signals intent and enforces the single-abstract-method constraint. The compiler rejects the interface if it does not qualify. Essential for lambda compatibility.

@SafeVarargs

@SafeVarargs
public final <T> List<T> listOf(T... elements) {
    return Arrays.asList(elements);
}

Suppresses heap-pollution warnings on generic varargs. Can only be applied to final or static methods (and constructors), because it promises the implementation does not expose the underlying array.

Part 4

Meta-Annotations

Meta-annotations annotate annotation declarations themselves. Java defines five in java.lang.annotation.

@Retention

Controls how long the annotation survives the compilation/execution lifecycle.

@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
public @interface Auditable { ... }
Policy Available at Use case
SOURCE Source code only @Override, @SuppressWarnings, Lombok
CLASS Bytecode (default) Bytecode analysis tools, ProGuard rules
RUNTIME JVM runtime via reflection Spring, Hibernate, JUnit, Jackson

@Target

Restricts where the annotation can be placed.

@Target({ElementType.METHOD, ElementType.TYPE})
public @interface Transactional { ... }
ElementType Placement
TYPE Class, interface, enum, annotation
FIELD Instance/static field
METHOD Method
PARAMETER Method parameter
CONSTRUCTOR Constructor
LOCAL_VARIABLE Local variable (SOURCE only, typically)
ANNOTATION_TYPE Annotation type (meta-annotations)
PACKAGE Package declaration
TYPE_PARAMETER Generic type parameter (Java 8+)
TYPE_USE Any use of a type (Java 8+)

@Documented

@Documented
public @interface PublicApi { }

When present, the annotation appears in the generated Javadoc of annotated elements. Without it, the annotation is invisible in documentation.

@Inherited

@Inherited
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@Target(ElementType.TYPE)
public @interface Component { }

@Component
public class BaseService { }

public class OrderService extends BaseService { }
// OrderService.class.isAnnotationPresent(Component.class) → true

@Inherited applies only to class-level annotations. Annotations on interfaces, methods, and fields are never inherited automatically.

@Repeatable (Java 8+)

@Repeatable(Schedules.class)
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
public @interface Schedule {
    String cron();
}

@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
public @interface Schedules {
    Schedule[] value();
}

@Schedule(cron = "0 0 * * * ?")
@Schedule(cron = "0 30 8 * * MON-FRI")
public void runJob() { ... }

Without @Repeatable, you can only apply an annotation once. The container annotation (Schedules) holds the array. Under the hood, the compiler wraps the repeated annotations inside the container.

Part 5

Retention Deep Dive

Understanding retention is critical for architects deciding whether to use compile-time processing or runtime reflection.

Source (.java)
  │
  │  javac  ──► Annotation Processors run HERE  ← SOURCE + CLASS annotations visible
  │
  ▼
Bytecode (.class)
  │    ← CLASS-retained: baked into bytecode as attributes, invisible to JVM reflection
  │
  │  classloader
  │
  ▼
Loaded Class
       ← RUNTIME-retained: accessible via Class.getAnnotation(), Method.getAnnotations(), etc.

Why SOURCE retention matters (Lombok)

Lombok annotations like @Data have RetentionPolicy.SOURCE. The Lombok annotation processor runs at compile time, generates synthetic methods (equals, hashCode, toString, getters, setters), and the annotation itself disappears from the class file. Zero runtime overhead.

Why RUNTIME retention matters (Spring)

Spring's @Autowired has RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME. When the application context starts, Spring uses reflection to scan every class for @Autowired fields and methods, then injects dependencies. If retention were CLASS, Spring could not read it at runtime and injection would silently fail.

Part 6

Custom Annotation: Full Example

Design a reusable @AuditLog annotation for a financial system.

// Step 1: Define the annotation
package com.example.audit;

import java.lang.annotation.*;

@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)       // needs runtime reading
@Target({ElementType.METHOD})             // only on methods
@Documented                               // show in Javadoc
public @interface AuditLog {
    String action();                      // required element
    String resource() default "";         // optional, default empty
    boolean captureArgs() default false;  // capture method arguments?
    AuditLevel level() default AuditLevel.INFO;
}

// Step 2: Supporting enum
public enum AuditLevel { INFO, WARN, CRITICAL }

// Step 3: Apply it
public class PaymentService {

    @AuditLog(action = "PAYMENT_PROCESS", resource = "payments",
              captureArgs = true, level = AuditLevel.CRITICAL)
    public Receipt processPayment(Payment payment) {
        // business logic
        return new Receipt(...);
    }
}

// Step 4: Read it at runtime (e.g., in an AOP aspect or interceptor)
Method method = PaymentService.class.getMethod("processPayment", Payment.class);
AuditLog audit = method.getAnnotation(AuditLog.class);

if (audit != null) {
    System.out.println("Action: " + audit.action());         // PAYMENT_PROCESS
    System.out.println("Resource: " + audit.resource());     // payments
    System.out.println("Level: " + audit.level());           // CRITICAL
    System.out.println("Capture args: " + audit.captureArgs()); // true
}
Part 7

Annotation Processing Pipeline (Compile-Time)

The javax.annotation.processing API allows you to write processors that run inside javac. This is how Lombok, Dagger, MapStruct, and AutoValue work.

javac invoked
    │
    ├─► [RoundEnvironment] ← set of all source elements
    │         │
    │         ▼
    │   [AbstractProcessor.process()]
    │         │
    │         ├── generate new .java files (Filer API)
    │         ├── emit compiler warnings/errors (Messager API)
    │         └── read type information (Types, Elements APIs)
    │
    └─► repeat rounds until no new files generated

Minimal processor skeleton

@SupportedAnnotationTypes("com.example.audit.AuditLog")
@SupportedSourceVersion(SourceVersion.RELEASE_17)
public class AuditLogProcessor extends AbstractProcessor {

    @Override
    public boolean process(Set<? extends TypeElement> annotations,
                           RoundEnvironment roundEnv) {
        for (Element el : roundEnv.getElementsAnnotatedWith(AuditLog.class)) {
            AuditLog a = el.getAnnotation(AuditLog.class);
            processingEnv.getMessager()
                .printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.NOTE,
                    "Audit log found: " + a.action(), el);
        }
        return true; // claim these annotations
    }
}

Register via META-INF/services/javax.annotation.processing.Processor.

Architect note: Prefer compile-time processing over runtime reflection for performance-critical paths. Dagger (compile-time DI) is significantly faster to start than Spring's reflection-based DI for serverless/cold-start scenarios.

Part 8

Annotations in Spring Framework

Spring's entire programming model is annotation-driven.

Stereotype Annotations (component scanning)

@Component          // generic Spring-managed bean
@Service            // service-layer bean (semantic alias of @Component)
@Repository         // DAO/persistence bean (adds exception translation)
@Controller         // MVC controller
@RestController     // @Controller + @ResponseBody combined

All four are specialisations of @Component. During context initialisation, Spring scans the classpath for all @Component-annotated classes and registers them as beans.

Dependency Injection

@Service
public class OrderService {

    private final PaymentGateway gateway;

    @Autowired                         // constructor injection (preferred)
    public OrderService(PaymentGateway gateway) {
        this.gateway = gateway;
    }
}

Since Spring 4.3, @Autowired on a single constructor is optional — Spring injects automatically. For field injection (@Autowired on a field), the field can be private because Spring uses setAccessible(true) via reflection.

Web Layer

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/v1/orders")
public class OrderController {

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<Order> getOrder(@PathVariable Long id) { ... }

    @PostMapping
    public ResponseEntity<Order> createOrder(@RequestBody @Valid OrderRequest req) { ... }
}

@RequestMapping, @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @DeleteMapping, @PatchMapping are all meta-annotated with @RequestMapping — they are convenience aliases.

Configuration

@Configuration
public class AppConfig {

    @Bean
    @Scope("prototype")
    public EmailSender emailSender(@Value("${smtp.host}") String host) {
        return new SmtpEmailSender(host);
    }
}

Spring Annotation Hierarchy

@Component
    ├── @Service
    ├── @Repository
    └── @Controller
            └── @RestController  (@Controller + @ResponseBody)
Part 9

Annotations in Hibernate / JPA

JPA is the standard ORM specification; Hibernate is the most popular implementation. Both are driven by javax.persistence (now jakarta.persistence) annotations.

@Entity
@Table(name = "orders", schema = "sales",
       indexes = @Index(name = "idx_created_at", columnList = "created_at"))
public class Order {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;

    @Column(name = "order_number", nullable = false, unique = true, length = 30)
    private String orderNumber;

    @Column(name = "total_amount", precision = 19, scale = 4)
    private BigDecimal totalAmount;

    @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)
    @Column(nullable = false)
    private OrderStatus status;

    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
    @JoinColumn(name = "customer_id")
    private Customer customer;

    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "order", cascade = CascadeType.ALL, orphanRemoval = true)
    private List<OrderItem> items = new ArrayList<>();

    @CreationTimestamp
    @Column(name = "created_at", updatable = false)
    private LocalDateTime createdAt;
}

Key JPA Annotations

Annotation Purpose
@Entity Marks class as a JPA entity (table-mapped)
@Table Specifies table name, schema, indexes, unique constraints
@Id Marks primary key field
@GeneratedValue Auto-generation strategy (IDENTITY, SEQUENCE, AUTO, TABLE)
@Column Column mapping, nullable, length, unique
@ManyToOne, @OneToMany Relationship cardinality
@JoinColumn FK column for relationships
@Enumerated How to persist enums (ORDINAL vs STRING — always prefer STRING)
@Transient Exclude field from persistence
@Version Optimistic locking version column
Part 10

Lombok Annotations Preview

Lombok uses SOURCE-retained annotations processed at compile time to generate boilerplate.

@Data                      // getters, setters, equals, hashCode, toString
@Builder                   // builder pattern
@NoArgsConstructor         // no-arg constructor
@AllArgsConstructor        // all-args constructor
@Slf4j                     // injects: private static final Logger log = ...
public class Customer {
    private Long id;
    private String name;
    private String email;
}

What @Data generates:

// Lombok generates these (conceptually):
public Long getId() { return id; }
public void setId(Long id) { this.id = id; }
// ... getters/setters for all fields ...
public boolean equals(Object o) { ... }  // based on all non-transient fields
public int hashCode() { ... }
public String toString() { ... }

What @Builder generates:

Customer customer = Customer.builder()
    .id(1L)
    .name("Alice")
    .email("alice@example.com")
    .build();

Architect caution with @Data and JPA: @Data generates equals/hashCode on all fields including the @Id. This can cause issues with Hibernate's first-level cache and HashSet collections because the id changes from null to a generated value after persist(). Use @EqualsAndHashCode(onlyExplicitlyIncluded = true) on JPA entities.

Part 11

Annotation-Based Validation (Bean Validation / JSR-380)

public class UserRegistrationRequest {

    @NotBlank(message = "Username is required")
    @Size(min = 3, max = 50)
    private String username;

    @Email(message = "Must be a valid email")
    @NotNull
    private String email;

    @NotNull
    @Min(value = 0, message = "Age must be non-negative")
    @Max(value = 150)
    private Integer age;

    @Pattern(regexp = "^(?=.*[A-Z])(?=.*\\d).{8,}$",
             message = "Password must be 8+ chars with uppercase and digit")
    private String password;
}

In Spring Boot, add @Valid or @Validated to a controller parameter to trigger validation automatically.

Custom Validator Annotation

// Step 1: Define annotation
@Documented
@Constraint(validatedBy = UniqueUsernameValidator.class)
@Target(ElementType.FIELD)
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
public @interface UniqueUsername {
    String message() default "Username already exists";
    Class<?>[] groups() default {};
    Class<? extends Payload>[] payload() default {};
}

// Step 2: Implement validator
public class UniqueUsernameValidator
        implements ConstraintValidator<UniqueUsername, String> {

    @Autowired
    private UserRepository userRepository;

    @Override
    public boolean isValid(String username, ConstraintValidatorContext ctx) {
        if (username == null) return true; // @NotNull handles null
        return !userRepository.existsByUsername(username);
    }
}

// Step 3: Use it
public class UserRegistrationRequest {
    @UniqueUsername
    private String username;
}

Part 13

Annotations vs Other Mechanisms

Mechanism Pros Cons Best for
Annotations Co-located with code, IDE support, type-safe Couples code to framework Most framework integration
XML config Externalisable, no recompile Verbose, no type-safety, hard to refactor Legacy apps, environment-specific config
Programmatic API Full Java power, testable More boilerplate Dynamic/conditional configuration
Marker interfaces Checked at compile time Pollute type hierarchy Historical (e.g., Serializable)

Spring supports all three: annotations, XML, and @Configuration programmatic — they can be mixed.

Part 14

Pitfalls and Anti-Patterns

1. Using RUNTIME retention when SOURCE suffices

Unnecessary runtime annotations slow class loading and increase memory footprint at scale. Audit retention policies when designing libraries.

2. Annotation overload on entities

// Too much — hard to read, hard to maintain
@NotNull @Size(min=1,max=50) @Pattern(regexp="[A-Za-z]+")
@Column(nullable=false, length=50)
@Index(name="idx_name")
private String name;

Split validation from persistence mapping. Consider separate DTO + entity layers.

3. Inheriting annotations on interfaces

@Transactional   // on interface
public interface OrderService {
    void placeOrder(Order o);
}

@Inherited only works on class annotations. Interface annotations are not inherited by implementing classes. Spring's @Transactional works anyway because Spring's proxy mechanism scans the interface chain explicitly — but this is framework magic, not standard Java inheritance.

4. @SuppressWarnings hiding real bugs

Never use @SuppressWarnings("all") or suppress warnings without a comment explaining why it is safe.

Part 17

Annotations and Proxies

Spring AOP and @Transactional work via proxies — the container wraps your bean in a generated class. This has an important implication:

@Service
public class InvoiceService {

    @Transactional
    public void createInvoice(Invoice inv) {
        save(inv);
        sendNotification(inv);  // calls self — bypasses proxy!
    }

    @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)
    public void sendNotification(Invoice inv) {
        // This @Transactional is IGNORED when called from createInvoice()
        // because it's a self-call — the proxy is bypassed
    }
}

Fix: Inject self via @Autowired InvoiceService self (Spring), or use AopContext.currentProxy(), or refactor into a separate bean.

@Repeatable Deep Dive

// Container annotation
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@Target(ElementType.METHOD)
public @interface RateLimits {
    RateLimit[] value();
}

// Repeatable annotation
@Repeatable(RateLimits.class)
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@Target(ElementType.METHOD)
public @interface RateLimit {
    String plan();
    int requestsPerMinute();
}

// Usage
@RateLimit(plan = "FREE", requestsPerMinute = 10)
@RateLimit(plan = "PRO", requestsPerMinute = 100)
@RateLimit(plan = "ENTERPRISE", requestsPerMinute = 1000)
public Response search(SearchRequest req) { ... }

// Reading repeatable annotations
RateLimit[] limits = method.getAnnotationsByType(RateLimit.class);
// OR
RateLimits container = method.getAnnotation(RateLimits.class);

Part 20

Architect Perspective: Performance Considerations

Concern Impact Mitigation
Reflection to read RUNTIME annotations Slow first call, JIT-cached subsequently Frameworks cache Method objects; architect's code should too
Annotation scanning at startup Slower cold start Use compile-time processing (Quarkus/Micronaut vs Spring)
Proxy creation for AOP annotations Additional heap objects Use class-level annotations to reduce proxy depth
@Repeatable container wrapping Extra array allocation Negligible at modern JVM scales

Quarkus/Micronaut approach: Move annotation processing to build time using GraalVM metadata. @ApplicationScoped in Quarkus is processed at compile time via Jandex, enabling near-instant startup — a major architectural difference from Spring's runtime scanning.

Part 21

Common Interview Questions

Q: What is the difference between RetentionPolicy.CLASS and RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME?

A: Both are retained in the bytecode (.class file), but CLASS annotations are not loaded into the JVM's method area and cannot be accessed via java.lang.reflect. RUNTIME annotations are loaded and queryable at runtime. Bytecode manipulation tools (ASM, ByteBuddy) can read CLASS-retained annotations without loading the class.

Q: Why does @Inherited not work on interfaces?

A: @Inherited is defined only for class hierarchies (extends). Java interfaces support multiple inheritance, and applying annotation inheritance through interfaces could create ambiguity when a class implements two annotated interfaces with conflicting annotation values. The spec chose to exclude it.

Q: How would you create a custom validation annotation?

A: (1) Define the annotation with @Constraint(validatedBy = MyValidator.class), @Retention(RUNTIME), @Target, and the required message(), groups(), and payload() elements. (2) Implement ConstraintValidator<MyAnnotation, TargetType> with the isValid() logic. (3) Apply @Valid on the controller parameter to trigger validation.

Q: How does Spring discover beans annotated with @Component?

A: Spring's ClassPathBeanDefinitionScanner scans the classpath using ASM (not reflection) to read CLASS-level annotations without loading every class. When it finds @Component (or a meta-annotated stereotype), it registers a BeanDefinition. On first getBean(), the bean is instantiated and RUNTIME annotations drive injection, proxy creation, and lifecycle callbacks.

Part 1

Concept Overview

Reflection is the ability of a running program to inspect and manipulate its own structure. In Java, reflection means examining classes, methods, fields, constructors, and their annotations at runtime, and invoking them dynamically — without knowing their names at compile time.

The Java Reflection API lives in java.lang.reflect and has been part of the language since Java 1.1 (1997). Every major Java framework relies on it:

  • Spring — discovers beans, injects dependencies, creates AOP proxies
  • Hibernate — reads entity field values, sets them after a database query
  • Jackson — serialises/deserialises private fields to/from JSON
  • JUnit — discovers @Test methods without you registering them
  • Mockito — creates dynamic proxy subclasses, intercepts calls

Understanding reflection at the architecture level means understanding why frameworks work, where the performance cost lies, and what the safer modern alternatives are.

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   Reflection Universe                    │
│                                                          │
│  Class<?>   ──► Method[]      ──► Method.invoke()       │
│             ──► Field[]       ──► Field.get() / .set()  │
│             ──► Constructor[] ──► Constructor.newInstance│
│             ──► Annotation[]  ──► getAnnotation()       │
│             ──► Class[]       ──► getInterfaces()        │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Part 2

The `Class<?>` Object

Every loaded type in the JVM has exactly one Class<T> object in the method area. It is the entry point for all reflection.

Three ways to obtain a Class<?> object

// 1. Compile-time literal — preferred, fastest, type-safe
Class<String> strClass = String.class;

// 2. From an instance — when you have an object
String s = "hello";
Class<?> runtimeClass = s.getClass();   // returns String.class

// 3. Dynamic name lookup — for truly dynamic code
Class<?> dynamic = Class.forName("com.example.OrderService");
// throws ClassNotFoundException if not on classpath
// also runs static initialiser blocks!

Class.forName variants

// Load with current classloader (runs static initialisers)
Class<?> c1 = Class.forName("com.example.Foo");

// Explicit classloader, control initialisation
ClassLoader loader = Thread.currentThread().getContextClassLoader();
Class<?> c2 = Class.forName("com.example.Foo", true, loader);
//                                              ^ initialize = true

Architect note: Class.forName is used extensively in JDBC drivers — Class.forName("com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver") triggered static initialisation that registered the driver with DriverManager.

Class hierarchy navigation

Class<?> clazz = OrderService.class;

clazz.getSuperclass();           // direct superclass
clazz.getInterfaces();           // directly implemented interfaces
clazz.getGenericInterfaces();    // with generic type parameters
clazz.isInterface();
clazz.isEnum();
clazz.isAnnotation();
clazz.isArray();
clazz.isPrimitive();
clazz.getModifiers();            // int bitmask, decoded by java.lang.reflect.Modifier
clazz.getPackageName();          // Java 9+
clazz.getSimpleName();
clazz.getCanonicalName();
Part 3

Inspecting Methods

Class<?> clazz = PaymentService.class;

// getDeclaredMethods() — all methods declared in THIS class (any visibility)
// getMethods()         — all PUBLIC methods, including inherited ones
Method[] declared = clazz.getDeclaredMethods();
Method[] publicInherited = clazz.getMethods();

// Retrieve a specific method by name + parameter types
Method processPayment = clazz.getDeclaredMethod("processPayment", Payment.class);

// Method metadata
processPayment.getName();                    // "processPayment"
processPayment.getReturnType();              // Receipt.class
processPayment.getParameterCount();          // 1
processPayment.getParameterTypes();          // [Payment.class]
processPayment.getExceptionTypes();          // checked exceptions declared
processPayment.getModifiers();               // Modifier bitmask
processPayment.getAnnotations();             // runtime-retained annotations
processPayment.getAnnotation(AuditLog.class);
Modifier.isPublic(processPayment.getModifiers());   // true/false

Parameter names (Java 8+ with -parameters flag)

for (Parameter p : processPayment.getParameters()) {
    System.out.println(p.getName());        // "payment" (if -parameters was set)
    System.out.println(p.getType());        // Payment.class
    System.out.println(p.getAnnotations()); // annotations on the parameter
}
Part 4

Invoking Methods Dynamically

PaymentService service = new PaymentService();
Method method = PaymentService.class
    .getDeclaredMethod("processPayment", Payment.class);

Payment payment = new Payment(BigDecimal.TEN, "USD");

// Invoke the method: method.invoke(target, args...)
Receipt receipt = (Receipt) method.invoke(service, payment);

Invoking static methods

Method staticMethod = MathUtils.class.getDeclaredMethod("add", int.class, int.class);
Integer result = (Integer) staticMethod.invoke(null, 3, 4);  // null target for statics

Handling checked exceptions

Method.invoke wraps any exception thrown by the target method in InvocationTargetException:

try {
    method.invoke(target, args);
} catch (InvocationTargetException e) {
    Throwable cause = e.getCause();     // the real exception from the method
    if (cause instanceof PaymentException) {
        throw (PaymentException) cause;
    }
    throw new RuntimeException("Unexpected error", cause);
} catch (IllegalAccessException e) {
    throw new RuntimeException("Cannot access method", e);
} catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
    throw new RuntimeException("Wrong arguments", e);
}
Part 5

Inspecting and Manipulating Fields

Class<?> clazz = User.class;

// getDeclaredFields() — all fields in THIS class (any visibility)
// getFields()         — only PUBLIC fields, including inherited
Field[] fields = clazz.getDeclaredFields();

Field nameField = clazz.getDeclaredField("name");

nameField.getName();           // "name"
nameField.getType();           // String.class
nameField.getModifiers();      // includes private, final, etc.
nameField.getAnnotations();    // runtime-retained annotations

Reading and writing field values

User user = new User(1L, "Alice", "alice@example.com");

Field nameField = User.class.getDeclaredField("name");
nameField.setAccessible(true);          // bypass private access modifier

String name = (String) nameField.get(user);   // read: "Alice"
nameField.set(user, "Bob");                    // write: changes name to "Bob"

// Static fields: pass null as instance
Field constantField = Config.class.getDeclaredField("MAX_RETRY");
constantField.setAccessible(true);
int maxRetry = (int) constantField.get(null);

Critical security note: Since Java 9, setAccessible(true) is restricted by the module system. Strong encapsulation means accessing private fields across module boundaries requires the module to declare opens in module-info.java, or the JVM must be started with --add-opens.

Part 6

`setAccessible(true)` — Breaking Encapsulation

// This works for classes in the unnamed module (classpath)
field.setAccessible(true);

// For named modules, the module must declare:
// module my.framework {
//     requires java.base;
// }
// AND the target module must declare:
// opens com.example.internal to my.framework;

The hidden cost of setAccessible

Field.get() WITHOUT setAccessible  →  security check per call (slow)
Field.get() WITH setAccessible     →  security check once, then fast(er)
                                      but still slower than direct access

JVM flag to observe reflective access:

java --illegal-access=warn MyApp   # Java 9-15 (deprecated)
java --add-opens java.base/java.lang=ALL-UNNAMED MyApp  # explicit open

Why frameworks use it

Hibernate must populate private id fields after a SELECT. Jackson must read private name fields during JSON serialization. Both call setAccessible(true) internally. This is a well-known, accepted trade-off — but it is why the Java module system's opens directive exists.

Part 7

Constructors via Reflection

Class<?> clazz = Customer.class;

// No-arg constructor
Constructor<?> noArg = clazz.getDeclaredConstructor();
Customer c1 = (Customer) noArg.newInstance();

// Parameterised constructor
Constructor<?> paramCtor = clazz.getDeclaredConstructor(Long.class, String.class);
Customer c2 = (Customer) paramCtor.newInstance(1L, "Alice");

// Private constructor (e.g., Singleton)
Constructor<?> privateCtor = clazz.getDeclaredConstructor();
privateCtor.setAccessible(true);
Singleton singleton = (Singleton) privateCtor.newInstance();

Class.newInstance() is deprecated

Class.newInstance() (removed in Java 17) silently propagated checked exceptions. Always use Constructor.newInstance() which wraps them in InvocationTargetException.

Part 8

Generic Type Information at Runtime

Java generics use type erasure — generic type parameters are removed from bytecode. However, declaration-site generic information is retained in the Signature bytecode attribute, readable via reflection.

public class Container<T> {
    private List<String> items;            // field generic type retained
    public Map<String, List<Integer>> getMap() { return null; }
}

// Reading generic field type
Field items = Container.class.getDeclaredField("items");
Type genericType = items.getGenericType();   // ParameterizedType
if (genericType instanceof ParameterizedType pt) {
    Type[] typeArgs = pt.getActualTypeArguments();
    System.out.println(typeArgs[0]);   // class java.lang.String
}

// Reading generic return type
Method getMap = Container.class.getDeclaredMethod("getMap");
ParameterizedType returnType = (ParameterizedType) getMap.getGenericReturnType();
// returnType.getRawType()              → Map.class
// returnType.getActualTypeArguments()  → [String, ParameterizedType(List<Integer>)]

Jackson uses this to know the element type of List<Order> when deserialising. Spring uses it to resolve the element type of @Autowired List<Service> beans.

Part 9

Performance Cost of Reflection

Reflection is measurably slower than direct code — understanding where the cost comes from is essential for architects.

Cost breakdown

Direct method call:          ~1 ns      (JIT-compiled, inline-able)
Reflected method (1st call): ~100-500 ns (security check, method lookup)
Reflected method (cached):   ~10-50 ns  (Method object reused, no lookup)
                                         (JIT inflation kicks in after ~15 calls)

JVM inflation mechanism

The JVM uses two strategies for reflective calls:

First ~15 calls:  NativeMethodAccessorImpl  (JNI, slower, no JIT)
After 15 calls:   GeneratedMethodAccessorImpl (bytecode generated, JIT-able)
                  ← controlled by sun.reflect.inflationThreshold

Best practices to minimise reflection overhead

// BAD: look up Method on every call
public void invokeHandler(Object target, String methodName, Object arg) {
    Method m = target.getClass().getDeclaredMethod(methodName, arg.getClass()); // every time!
    m.invoke(target, arg);
}

// GOOD: cache the Method object
private static final Map<String, Method> METHOD_CACHE = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

public void invokeHandler(Object target, String methodName, Object arg) {
    Method m = METHOD_CACHE.computeIfAbsent(
        target.getClass().getName() + "#" + methodName,
        k -> {
            try {
                Method found = target.getClass().getDeclaredMethod(methodName, arg.getClass());
                found.setAccessible(true);
                return found;
            } catch (NoSuchMethodException e) { throw new RuntimeException(e); }
        }
    );
    m.invoke(target, arg);
}
Part 10

MethodHandle: The Modern Alternative

Introduced in Java 7 as part of java.lang.invoke, MethodHandle is a low-level, type-safe, JIT-friendly way to perform reflective-style invocations. It is faster than Method.invoke because it can be optimised by the JIT compiler and inlined like a normal method call.

Comparison

Method.invoke()      — reflection API, argument boxing, wraps exceptions
MethodHandle         — direct invocation after lookup, JIT-optimisable
VarHandle            — field read/write equivalent of MethodHandle (Java 9+)
LambdaMetafactory    — creates lambdas from MethodHandles at runtime (fastest)

MethodHandle example

import java.lang.invoke.*;

MethodHandles.Lookup lookup = MethodHandles.lookup();

// Find a method handle for String.length()
MethodType mt = MethodType.methodType(int.class);
MethodHandle mh = lookup.findVirtual(String.class, "length", mt);

int len = (int) mh.invoke("hello");  // 5

// Private field access via VarHandle
VarHandle vh = MethodHandles.privateLookupIn(User.class, lookup)
    .findVarHandle(User.class, "name", String.class);

User user = new User(1L, "Alice");
String name = (String) vh.get(user);        // "Alice"
vh.set(user, "Bob");                        // sets name to "Bob"

LambdaMetafactory — the fastest approach

// Create a functional interface instance backed by a MethodHandle
// This is what the JVM does internally for lambda expressions
MethodHandles.Lookup lookup = MethodHandles.lookup();
MethodHandle target = lookup.findVirtual(String.class, "toUpperCase",
    MethodType.methodType(String.class));

// Create a Function<String,String> that delegates to toUpperCase
CallSite site = LambdaMetafactory.metafactory(
    lookup,
    "apply",
    MethodType.methodType(Function.class),
    MethodType.methodType(Object.class, Object.class),
    target,
    MethodType.methodType(String.class, String.class)
);

@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
Function<String, String> fn = (Function<String, String>) site.getTarget().invoke();
String result = fn.apply("hello");  // "HELLO"
// → as fast as a regular method call after JIT

When to prefer MethodHandle over reflection

Scenario Use
Hot path called >1000/sec MethodHandle or LambdaMetafactory
Framework startup (cold path) Method.invoke with caching is fine
Need checked exception suppression MethodHandle propagates as-is
Module system private access MethodHandles.privateLookupIn()
GraalVM native image MethodHandle is AOT-friendly; Method.invoke needs reflection config
Part 11

How Spring Uses Reflection to Create Beans

Understanding this end-to-end is a favourite senior interview topic.

Application starts
       │
       ▼
ClassPathBeanDefinitionScanner
  ├─ uses ASM (not reflection!) to read bytecode metadata
  ├─ finds @Component, @Service, @Repository, @Controller
  └─ registers BeanDefinition objects (no instantiation yet)
       │
       ▼
DefaultListableBeanFactory
  ├─ resolves BeanDefinition dependencies
  └─ for each bean definition when first requested:
       │
       ▼
  SimpleInstantiationStrategy
  ├─ Class.forName(beanClassName)
  ├─ finds @Autowired constructor via getDeclaredConstructors()
  ├─ Constructor.newInstance(resolvedDeps...)
  └─ returns raw instance
       │
       ▼
  AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor
  ├─ getDeclaredFields() → finds @Autowired fields
  ├─ field.setAccessible(true)
  ├─ field.set(beanInstance, resolvedDependency)
  ├─ getDeclaredMethods() → finds @Autowired setter methods
  └─ method.invoke(beanInstance, resolvedDependency)
       │
       ▼
  BeanPostProcessors (AOP)
  ├─ scans methods for @Transactional, @Cacheable, etc.
  ├─ creates CGLIB or JDK dynamic proxy if needed
  └─ replaces raw bean with proxy in the context
       │
       ▼
  Fully initialised, injectable bean

JDK Dynamic Proxy vs CGLIB

// JDK Proxy: target must implement an interface
// Spring creates a class that implements the same interface
InvocationHandler handler = (proxy, method, args) -> {
    // before advice
    Object result = method.invoke(target, args);  // reflection!
    // after advice
    return result;
};
Object proxy = Proxy.newProxyInstance(
    target.getClass().getClassLoader(),
    target.getClass().getInterfaces(),
    handler
);

// CGLIB Proxy: subclasses the concrete class (no interface required)
// Spring Boot uses CGLIB by default for @Configuration classes
Part 12

How Hibernate Uses Reflection

SessionFactory starts
       │
       ▼
  reads @Entity, @Table → maps to table name
  reads @Id            → identifies primary key field
  reads @Column        → column name, nullable, length constraints
  reads @ManyToOne     → builds association graph
       │
       ▼
  EntityPersister built per @Entity class
  (caches Field objects, Constructor, column mappings)
       │
       ▼
  Query executes (SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = ?)
       │
       ▼
  ResultSet row → BeanReflector
  ├─ Constructor.newInstance()         → create empty entity
  ├─ field.setAccessible(true)         → open private fields
  ├─ id_field.set(entity, rs.getLong)  → set id
  ├─ name_field.set(entity, rs.getString) → set name
  └─ return populated entity

Hibernate uses ByteBuddy (formerly Javassist) to generate subclasses for lazy loading proxies. When you access order.getCustomer() and it is a lazy proxy, Hibernate intercepts the call via the generated subclass, fires a SQL query, and returns the real object.

Part 13

Jackson and Reflection

ObjectMapper mapper = new ObjectMapper();

// Serialisation: POJO → JSON
Order order = new Order(1L, "ORD-001", BigDecimal.TEN);
String json = mapper.writeValueAsString(order);
// Jackson: getClass() → getDeclaredFields() → setAccessible(true) → field.get(order)

// Deserialisation: JSON → POJO
Order restored = mapper.readValue(json, Order.class);
// Jackson: getDeclaredConstructor() → newInstance() → field.set(restored, value)

Jackson actually uses MethodHandle internally since version 2.12+ for better performance. It also respects @JsonProperty, @JsonIgnore, @JsonCreator annotations read via getAnnotation().

Part 14

Security: Module System and `opens`

Java 9's module system (JPMS) introduced strong encapsulation. By default, a module's packages are not accessible via deep reflection.

// module-info.java of the framework module
module my.framework {
    requires java.base;
    // can NOT reflectively access private members of other modules by default
}

// module-info.java of the application module
module com.myapp {
    requires my.framework;

    // Allow my.framework to do deep reflection on this package:
    opens com.myapp.model to my.framework;

    // Allow anyone to do deep reflection:
    opens com.myapp.internal;
}

Command-line workaround (migration period)

java --add-opens java.base/java.lang=ALL-UNNAMED \
     --add-opens java.base/java.util=ALL-UNNAMED \
     -jar myapp.jar

Spring Boot's spring-boot-maven-plugin adds these flags automatically for legacy compatibility. A fully modular Spring application would use opens declarations instead.

IllegalAccessException flow

field.setAccessible(true)
       │
       ▼
  AccessController.checkPermission()
       │
       ├── if caller module ≠ declaring module AND package not opened
       │   └── throws InaccessibleObjectException (Java 9+)
       │       extends RuntimeException
       │
       └── if permitted (same module, or opened)
           └── marks Field as accessible, skips future access checks

ASCII Architecture: Full Reflection Pipeline

│  class OrderService { private Payment p; ... }                      │

│  │  ├── String name = "OrderService"      │                        │
