│  │  ├── Field[] declaredFields            │  ◄── getDeclaredFields │
│  │  ├── Method[] declaredMethods          │  ◄── getDeclaredMethods│
│  │  ├── Constructor[] constructors        │  ◄── getConstructors   │
│  │  └── Annotation[] annotations          │  ◄── getAnnotations    │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────┘                        │
│         │                                                           │
│         ▼                                                           │
│  Reflection API (java.lang.reflect)                                 │
│  ├── Class.forName()    → Class<?>                                  │
│  ├── .getDeclaredField() → Field → .setAccessible(true) → .get/.set│
│  ├── .getDeclaredMethod() → Method → .setAccessible(true) → .invoke│
│  └── .getDeclaredConstructor() → Constructor → .newInstance()      │
│         │                                                           │
│         ▼                                                           │
│  Frameworks: Spring / Hibernate / Jackson / JUnit                  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Part 16

Reflection vs MethodHandle vs Direct Code

Performance (faster → slower):
  Direct call → LambdaMetafactory → MethodHandle → Method.invoke (cached) → Method.invoke (uncached)

Safety (safer → less safe):
  Direct call → MethodHandle (type-safe) → Method.invoke (runtime ClassCastException risk)

GraalVM Native Image compatibility:
  Direct call → MethodHandle → Method.invoke (requires reflect-config.json)

Module system friendliness:
  Direct call → MethodHandle (privateLookupIn) → Method.invoke (setAccessible, needs opens)

Practical decision tree

Need to invoke a method dynamically?
    │
    ├── Is it in a hot loop (>10k calls/sec)?
    │       └── YES → MethodHandle or LambdaMetafactory
    │
    ├── Is it a framework startup one-time setup?
    │       └── YES → Method.invoke with caching is fine
    │
    ├── Targeting GraalVM native image?
    │       └── YES → MethodHandle (no reflect-config needed)
    │
    └── Need to access private members across modules?
            └── YES → MethodHandles.privateLookupIn() + VarHandle
Part 17

Dynamic Proxy Pattern

The JDK's java.lang.reflect.Proxy creates an implementation of an interface at runtime. Spring AOP, RMI stubs, and Mockito all use this.

public interface UserRepository {
    User findById(Long id);
    void save(User user);
}

// Create a logging proxy
UserRepository proxy = (UserRepository) Proxy.newProxyInstance(
    UserRepository.class.getClassLoader(),
    new Class<?>[]{ UserRepository.class },
    new InvocationHandler() {
        private final UserRepository delegate = new JdbcUserRepository();

        @Override
        public Object invoke(Object proxy, Method method, Object[] args) throws Throwable {
            long start = System.nanoTime();
            try {
                return method.invoke(delegate, args);
            } finally {
                long elapsed = System.nanoTime() - start;
                System.out.printf("Method %s took %d ns%n", method.getName(), elapsed);
            }
        }
    }
);

proxy.findById(1L);  // logs: "Method findById took 142300 ns"
Part 18

Annotations + Reflection: Building a Mini-Framework

Combining Lessons 16 and 17: build a tiny dependency injection container.

// Annotation
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@Target(ElementType.FIELD)
public @interface Inject {}

// Mini DI container
public class SimpleContainer {
    private final Map<Class<?>, Object> registry = new HashMap<>();

    public void register(Object instance) {
        registry.put(instance.getClass(), instance);
    }

    public void inject(Object target) throws Exception {
        for (Field field : target.getClass().getDeclaredFields()) {
            if (field.isAnnotationPresent(Inject.class)) {
                Object dep = registry.get(field.getType());
                if (dep == null) {
                    throw new RuntimeException("No bean for: " + field.getType());
                }
                field.setAccessible(true);
                field.set(target, dep);
            }
        }
    }
}

// Usage
SimpleContainer container = new SimpleContainer();
container.register(new EmailSender());
container.register(new SmsNotifier());

OrderService service = new OrderService();  // @Inject EmailSender emailSender;
container.inject(service);
// service.emailSender is now populated — like Spring @Autowired
Part 19

Reflection in Testing: Mockito

Mockito creates mock objects using ByteBuddy (a bytecode generation library) to generate subclasses at runtime. When you call Mockito.mock(OrderService.class), here is what happens:

Mockito.mock(OrderService.class)
       │
       ▼
  ByteBuddy creates a subclass:
  class OrderService$MockitoMock$xxx extends OrderService {
      @Override
      public Receipt processPayment(Payment p) {
          return (Receipt) handler.handle(this, "processPayment", new Object[]{p});
      }
      // all other methods overridden similarly
  }
       │
       ▼
  Constructor reflectively called to create instance
  (Constructor.newInstance)
       │
       ▼
  when(mock.processPayment(any()))
    .thenReturn(new Receipt(...))
  → stub registered in MockitoInvocationHandler
       │
       ▼
  mock.processPayment(payment)
  → intercepted → returns stub → no real code runs

This is why Mockito cannot mock final classes (by default) — you cannot subclass a final class. The mockito-inline extension uses Java instrumentation (java.lang.instrument) and a Java agent to transform bytecode at load time, enabling final class mocking.

Part 20

Performance Benchmarks: Reflection vs Direct

These are approximate JMH benchmark results (JDK 21, server JVM):

Benchmark                          Mode   Score    Units
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DirectMethodCall                   avgt    1.2     ns/op
MethodHandle_invokeExact           avgt    1.8     ns/op
MethodHandle_invoke                avgt    4.2     ns/op  (polymorphic signature)
LambdaMetafactory                  avgt    2.1     ns/op  (after JIT warm-up)
Method_invoke_cached               avgt   18.0     ns/op  (after inflation)
Method_invoke_uncached             avgt  380.0     ns/op  (includes lookup)
Field_get_setAccessible_cached     avgt   22.0     ns/op
VarHandle_get                      avgt    2.4     ns/op
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Architect takeaway: Cached Method.invoke is ~15× slower than a direct call, but at 18 ns/op this is imperceptible for most business logic. The danger is uncached reflection or reflection in tight loops — both are 100–400× slower.

Part 21

Common Interview Questions

Q: How does Spring create beans via reflection?

A: Spring uses Class.forName() or direct class references from its metadata to load the bean class. It inspects the class with getDeclaredConstructors() to find the @Autowired constructor (or a no-arg constructor). It calls Constructor.newInstance(dependencies...) to create the instance. Then AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor scans getDeclaredFields() and getDeclaredMethods() for @Autowired, calls setAccessible(true), and injects dependencies. Finally, BeanPostProcessors wrap the bean in a CGLIB or JDK proxy if AOP annotations (@Transactional, @Cacheable) are present.

Q: What is the difference between Method.invoke and MethodHandle?

A: Both invoke methods dynamically, but MethodHandle is lower-level and can be fully optimised by the JIT compiler — including inlining — so it approaches the performance of a direct call after warm-up. Method.invoke involves argument boxing/unboxing to Object[], is checked by AccessController on every call unless setAccessible is used, and wraps exceptions in InvocationTargetException. MethodHandle performs a single permission check at lookup time and has better module system integration via MethodHandles.privateLookupIn().

Q: What happens if you call setAccessible(true) on a private field in Java 17?

A: For classes in the unnamed module (classpath, not in a named module), it succeeds with a warning (or silently, depending on JVM flags). For classes in a named module, it throws InaccessibleObjectException unless the field's package is opened to the calling module via opens in module-info.java, or the JVM is started with --add-opens.

Q: Why can Mockito not mock final classes by default?

A: Mockito's standard implementation uses ByteBuddy to generate a subclass of the target. Since final classes cannot be subclassed, the generated class cannot override their methods. The mockito-inline extension uses a Java agent and java.lang.instrument.Instrumentation to redefine the class bytecode at load time, removing the final flag from the mock's copy of the class.

Q: How does Jackson deserialise private fields without setters?

A: Jackson's ObjectMapper (when configured with MapperFeature.CAN_OVERRIDE_ACCESS_MODIFIERS, which is enabled by default) calls field.setAccessible(true) on private fields. It then uses field.set(instance, value) to populate them. Since Jackson 2.12, it uses MethodHandle and VarHandle for better performance on supported JVM versions.

Practice — Lesson 17

Easy

  1. What are the three ways to obtain a Class<?> object in Java?
  2. What is the difference between getDeclaredMethods() and getMethods()?
  3. What exception does Method.invoke() throw when the target method throws an exception?
  4. Why is Class.newInstance() deprecated? What should you use instead?
  5. What does setAccessible(true) do and what restriction does Java 9+ add?

Medium

  1. Write a method printAllFields(Object obj) that uses reflection to print every field name and value of the given object, including private ones.
  2. Write a deepCopy(Object source) method that uses reflection to create a shallow copy of any object.
  3. Given class Box<T> { private List<T> items; }, write code to retrieve the generic type argument of the items field at runtime.
  4. Implement a @ToString annotation processor (runtime) that reads field values via reflection and generates a formatted string, replacing Object.toString().
  5. Explain why proxy.getClass() does not return UserRepository.class when using Proxy.newProxyInstance.

Advanced

  1. Implement a MethodCache class that caches MethodHandle objects keyed by (Class<?>, String methodName) using MethodHandles.lookup() and reuses them across calls.
  2. Build a mini ORM: given an @Entity class and a ResultSet, use reflection to create and populate an instance with values from the result set.
  3. Compare Method.invoke vs MethodHandle.invokeExact vs LambdaMetafactory in terms of performance characteristics and explain when each is appropriate.
  4. Explain how ByteBuddy differs from java.lang.reflect.Proxy and why Mockito switched from using JDK proxies to ByteBuddy.

Production

  1. Your Spring Boot service at 100 RPS is profiling 8% CPU in sun.reflect.NativeMethodAccessorImpl. Diagnose and fix.
  2. After upgrading from Java 8 to Java 17, your framework gets InaccessibleObjectException on startup. List all strategies to fix this without downgrading.
  3. You need to build a plugin system where plugins are loaded from JARs at runtime. Design the Class.forName strategy, ClassLoader hierarchy, and module isolation.
  4. A GraalVM native image build fails with Missing reflection config for com.example.OrderService. How do you fix this without switching away from reflection?

Debugging

@Service
public class ReportService {

    public void init() throws Exception {
        Field f = ReportService.class.getDeclaredField("repo");
        // Bug: setAccessible not called
        f.set(this, new JdbcReportRepository());

Identify the bug, explain the exception thrown, and provide the fix. Then explain why this pattern is an anti-pattern in a Spring application.

Part 1

Concept Overview

Java Records (finalized in Java 16, previewed in Java 14–15) are a special kind of class designed to be transparent carriers of immutable data. They dramatically reduce the boilerplate required to define data-holding classes while communicating clear design intent: this type exists purely to store and expose values.

Before records, writing a simple data class in plain Java required:

  • A private final field per component
  • A constructor to initialize all fields
  • equals() and hashCode() implementations
  • A toString() implementation
  • Getter methods for each field

Records collapse all of that into a single, concise declaration.

// Before records
public final class Point {
    private final int x;
    private final int y;

    public Point(int x, int y) {
        this.x = x;
        this.y = y;
    }

    public int x() { return x; }
    public int y() { return y; }

    @Override
    public boolean equals(Object o) {
        if (this == o) return true;
        if (!(o instanceof Point)) return false;
        Point p = (Point) o;
        return x == p.x && y == p.y;
    }

    @Override
    public int hashCode() {
        return Objects.hash(x, y);
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "Point[x=" + x + ", y=" + y + "]";
    }
}

// After records — same semantics, one line
public record Point(int x, int y) {}

Records are not simply syntactic sugar — they carry semantic guarantees that the compiler and runtime can rely upon, enabling future optimizations (e.g., value types in Project Valhalla).

Part 2

Record Syntax and Anatomy

The complete syntax of a record declaration:

[modifiers] record RecordName(ComponentList) [implements InterfaceList] {
    [additional members]
}

Component list — the parenthesized parameters after the record name — defines the record components, which simultaneously declare:

  1. A private final field with the same name and type
  2. A public accessor method with the same name (no get prefix)
  3. A parameter in the canonical constructor
public record Employee(
    long id,
    String name,
    String department,
    double salary
) {}

This generates:

// Compiler-generated (conceptual desugaring)
public final class Employee extends Record {
    private final long id;
    private final String name;
    private final String department;
    private final double salary;

    public Employee(long id, String name, String department, double salary) {
        this.id = id;
        this.name = name;
        this.department = department;
        this.salary = salary;
    }

    public long id()         { return id; }
    public String name()     { return name; }
    public String department() { return department; }
    public double salary()   { return salary; }

    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) { /* component-wise */ }
    @Override public int hashCode()           { /* component-wise */ }
    @Override public String toString()        { /* component-wise */ }
}
Part 3

Canonical Constructor

The canonical constructor has exactly the same parameter list as the record components, in the same order. The compiler generates one automatically, but you can define it explicitly when you need validation or normalization:

public record Range(int min, int max) {

    // Explicit canonical constructor — full form
    public Range(int min, int max) {
        if (min > max) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException(
                "min (%d) must be <= max (%d)".formatted(min, max)
            );
        }
        this.min = min;  // must assign all fields manually in full form
        this.max = max;
    }
}

Compact Constructor

The compact constructor is unique to records. It omits the parameter list (they are implicitly available) and the compiler automatically appends the field assignments after the body:

public record Range(int min, int max) {

    // Compact constructor — no parameter list, no field assignments needed
    public Range {
        if (min > max) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException(
                "min (%d) must be <= max (%d)".formatted(min, max)
            );
        }
        // Compiler adds: this.min = min; this.max = max;
    }
}

Compact constructors are the preferred style for validation and normalization because they are concise and prevent forgetting field assignment.

Normalization example:

public record EmailAddress(String value) {

    public EmailAddress {
        Objects.requireNonNull(value, "email must not be null");
        value = value.strip().toLowerCase();  // normalize before assignment
    }
}
Part 4

Auto-Generated Members

Records automatically generate the following for all components:

Member Behavior
equals(Object) True if same type and all components are equal (using component equals)
hashCode() Derived from all components using Objects.hash(...) logic
toString() ClassName[comp1=val1, comp2=val2, ...] format
Accessor methods public T componentName() — no get prefix

Key nuance with arrays: Array components use identity-based equals and hashCode by default, which is often a bug:

public record DataPacket(byte[] payload) {}

var a = new DataPacket(new byte[]{1, 2, 3});
var b = new DataPacket(new byte[]{1, 2, 3});
a.equals(b); // FALSE — array identity comparison!

Fix: Override equals and hashCode explicitly, or use a List<Byte> component instead.

Part 5

Immutability and Constraints

Records enforce a specific set of constraints that give them their semantic guarantees:

What records CANNOT do:

  • Extend any class (they implicitly extend java.lang.Record)
  • Be extended (they are implicitly final)
  • Declare instance fields outside the component list
  • Have mutable components (components are always private final)

What records CAN do:

  • Implement interfaces — a powerful composition pattern
  • Define static fields and methods
  • Define additional constructors (must delegate to canonical)
  • Define instance methods (including overriding generated ones)
  • Be generic
  • Have annotations on components
  • Be nested inside classes or other records
// Records implementing interfaces
public interface Identifiable {
    long id();
}

public record Customer(long id, String name, String email)
    implements Identifiable {}

// Generic record
public record Pair<A, B>(A first, B second) {
    public Pair<B, A> swap() {
        return new Pair<>(second, first);
    }
}

// Static factory and utility methods
public record Money(BigDecimal amount, Currency currency) {

    public static Money of(String amount, String currencyCode) {
        return new Money(
            new BigDecimal(amount),
            Currency.getInstance(currencyCode)
        );
    }

    public Money add(Money other) {
        if (!currency.equals(other.currency)) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Currency mismatch");
        }
        return new Money(amount.add(other.amount), currency);
    }

    public boolean isPositive() {
        return amount.compareTo(BigDecimal.ZERO) > 0;
    }
}

JVM HEAP — Object Layout (64-bit, compressed oops)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Mark Word           (8 bytes)                  │
  │  Class Pointer       (4 bytes compressed)       │
  │  int x               (4 bytes)                 │
  │  int y               (4 bytes)                 │
  │  [padding]           (4 bytes alignment)        │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  Total: 24 bytes — same as equivalent hand-written class

INVOKEDYNAMIC for equals/hashCode/toString
────────────────────────────────────────────
  Bootstrap method: ObjectMethods.bootstrap(...)
  Linked at class-load time to a MethodHandle chain
  → No reflection overhead at runtime
  → Equivalent performance to hand-written code
Part 7

JVM Internals

At the JVM level, records are implemented with three key JVM mechanisms:

1. final class extending java.lang.Record

The Record abstract class lives in java.lang and provides no concrete behavior — it is simply a marker for the type system. The JVM knows a class is a record because it extends Record AND has the ACC_RECORD flag set in its class file.

2. Private Final Fields

All component fields are private final. This means:
- No subclass can access them directly
- The JVM can optimize field access aggressively
- The fields are assigned exactly once, in the constructor

3. invokedynamic for equals/hashCode/toString

This is the key JVM optimization. Rather than generating bytecode for these methods at compile time, the compiler emits invokedynamic instructions that are lazily linked at class-load time using java.lang.runtime.ObjectMethods.bootstrap. This:
- Keeps the class file small
- Allows the JVM to optimize the linked implementation
- Avoids reflection overhead after the first invocation

// Reflective inspection of a record
Point p = new Point(3, 4);

// RecordComponent API (Java 16+)
for (RecordComponent rc : Point.class.getRecordComponents()) {
    System.out.println(rc.getName() + " : " + rc.getType().getSimpleName());
    // Invoke the accessor
    Object value = rc.getAccessor().invoke(p);
    System.out.println("  value = " + value);
}
// Output:
// x : int
//   value = 3
// y : int
//   value = 4
Part 8

Records vs Classes vs Lombok @Value

Understanding when to use each option is a critical architectural decision:

Aspect Plain Class Record (Java 16+) Lombok @Value
Boilerplate High None Low (annotation)
Immutability Manual Enforced Enforced
Extends other class Yes No (extends Record) Yes
Mutable fields Yes No No
Custom constructor logic Full control Compact constructor @NonNull, @ConstructorProperties
wither / copy-with Manual Manual or library @With annotation
Serialization Jackson standard Needs config or Jackson 2.12+ Works with Jackson
Compile-time Standard Standard Annotation processing
IDE support Native Native Plugin required
Reflection API Standard getRecordComponents() Standard
Semantic clarity Low High ("this is data") Medium
JVM optimization potential Standard Valhalla-ready Standard

Decision Guideline

Is the class a pure data carrier with no mutable state?
    └─ YES → Is Java 16+ available?
                └─ YES → Use record
                └─ NO  → Use Lombok @Value or hand-written class
    └─ NO  → Does it extend a class?
                └─ YES → Hand-written class (possibly with Lombok)
                └─ NO  → Hand-written class with selective mutability
Part 9

Custom Methods and Nested Records

Records support rich additional behavior while maintaining their data-carrier character:

public record HttpRequest(
    String method,
    URI uri,
    Map<String, List<String>> headers,
    byte[] body
) {
    // Compact constructor for validation
    public HttpRequest {
        Objects.requireNonNull(method, "method");
        Objects.requireNonNull(uri, "uri");
        method = method.toUpperCase();
        headers = headers == null
            ? Map.of()
            : Collections.unmodifiableMap(new LinkedHashMap<>(headers));
        body = body == null ? new byte[0] : body.clone();
    }

    // Instance methods
    public boolean hasBody() {
        return body.length > 0;
    }

    public Optional<String> firstHeader(String name) {
        return Optional.ofNullable(headers.get(name.toLowerCase()))
            .flatMap(list -> list.stream().findFirst());
    }

    public String contentType() {
        return firstHeader("content-type").orElse("application/octet-stream");
    }

    // Static factory methods
    public static HttpRequest get(URI uri) {
        return new HttpRequest("GET", uri, null, null);
    }

    public static HttpRequest post(URI uri, byte[] body) {
        return new HttpRequest("POST", uri, null, body);
    }

    // Nested record for structured header
    public record Header(String name, String value) {
        public Header {
            name = name.strip().toLowerCase();
            value = value.strip();
        }
    }
}
Part 10

"Wither" Pattern (Copy-With Modification)

Records are immutable, so "updating" a record means creating a new instance. The wither pattern makes this ergonomic:

public record UserProfile(
    long id,
    String username,
    String email,
    boolean active
) {
    // Wither methods — return new instance with one field changed
    public UserProfile withEmail(String newEmail) {
        return new UserProfile(id, username, newEmail, active);
    }

    public UserProfile withActive(boolean newActive) {
        return new UserProfile(id, username, email, newActive);
    }

    public UserProfile deactivate() {
        return withActive(false);
    }
}

// Usage
var user = new UserProfile(1L, "alice", "alice@old.com", true);
var updated = user.withEmail("alice@new.com").deactivate();

For records with many components, a builder wither is more maintainable:

public record Config(
    String host, int port, boolean tls,
    Duration timeout, int maxConnections
) {
    public Builder toBuilder() {
        return new Builder(this);
    }

    public static class Builder {
        private String host;
        private int port;
        private boolean tls;
        private Duration timeout;
        private int maxConnections;

        public Builder(Config base) {
            this.host = base.host;
            this.port = base.port;
            this.tls = base.tls;
            this.timeout = base.timeout;
            this.maxConnections = base.maxConnections;
        }

        public Builder host(String h) { host = h; return this; }
        public Builder port(int p) { port = p; return this; }
        public Builder tls(boolean t) { tls = t; return this; }

        public Config build() {
            return new Config(host, port, tls, timeout, maxConnections);
        }
    }
}

// Usage
var newConfig = config.toBuilder().host("newhost.com").port(443).tls(true).build();
Part 11

Serialization

Java Serialization

Records support Java serialization out of the box. The serialization mechanism uses the canonical constructor for deserialization (not field manipulation), which is safer:

public record Point(int x, int y) implements Serializable {}

// Serialization works normally
var point = new Point(3, 4);
// ObjectOutputStream → ObjectInputStream
// Deserialization invokes Point(int, int) canonical constructor

Note: Records cannot define readObject, writeObject, or readResolve — the compact constructor handles all validation on deserialization automatically, preventing invariant violations.

Jackson Serialization (REST APIs)

Jackson 2.12+ handles records natively with no configuration:

// pom.xml: jackson-databind 2.12+
@RestController
public class ProductController {

    public record CreateProductRequest(
        String name,
        String description,
        BigDecimal price,
        String category
    ) {}

    public record ProductResponse(
        long id,
        String name,
        BigDecimal price,
        String category,
        Instant createdAt
    ) {}

    @PostMapping("/products")
    public ResponseEntity<ProductResponse> create(
            @RequestBody CreateProductRequest req) {
        // Jackson deserializes JSON → record via canonical constructor
        // Jackson serializes record → JSON via accessor methods
        var product = productService.create(req);
        return ResponseEntity.ok(new ProductResponse(
            product.id(), product.name(), product.price(),
            product.category(), product.createdAt()
        ));
    }
}

Jackson with older versions (pre-2.12): Add @JsonCreator and @JsonProperty:

public record Point(
    @JsonProperty("x") int x,
    @JsonProperty("y") int y
) {
    @JsonCreator
    public Point(
        @JsonProperty("x") int x,
        @JsonProperty("y") int y
    ) {
        this.x = x;
        this.y = y;
    }
}
Part 12

Records with Pattern Matching

Records integrate seamlessly with Java 16+ instanceof pattern matching and Java 21+ pattern matching in switch:

sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Rectangle, Triangle {}
record Circle(double radius) implements Shape {}
record Rectangle(double width, double height) implements Shape {}
record Triangle(double base, double height) implements Shape {}

double area(Shape shape) {
    return switch (shape) {
        case Circle(var r)             -> Math.PI * r * r;
        case Rectangle(var w, var h)   -> w * h;
        case Triangle(var b, var h)    -> 0.5 * b * h;
    };
}

Record patterns (Java 21, JEP 440) allow destructuring records directly in instanceof and switch:

// Record pattern in instanceof
Object obj = new Point(3, 4);
if (obj instanceof Point(int x, int y)) {
    System.out.println("Point at " + x + ", " + y);
}

// Nested record patterns
record Line(Point start, Point end) {}

void describe(Object obj) {
    if (obj instanceof Line(Point(var x1, var y1), Point(var x2, var y2))) {
        System.out.printf("Line from (%d,%d) to (%d,%d)%n", x1, y1, x2, y2);
    }
}

Records as @RequestBody and @ResponseBody

Part 14

Kafka Event Modeling with Records

Records are excellent for Kafka event schemas — they are immutable, self-documenting, and serialize cleanly:

// Event hierarchy using records
public sealed interface DomainEvent permits
    OrderPlaced, OrderShipped, OrderCancelled {}

public record OrderPlaced(
    String orderId,
    String customerId,
    List<OrderLine> lines,
    BigDecimal total,
    Instant occurredAt
) implements DomainEvent {
    public record OrderLine(String productId, int qty, BigDecimal unitPrice) {}
}

public record OrderShipped(
    String orderId,
    String trackingNumber,
    String carrier,
    Instant shippedAt
) implements DomainEvent {}

public record OrderCancelled(
    String orderId,
    String reason,
    Instant cancelledAt
) implements DomainEvent {}

// Kafka producer
@Service
public class OrderEventProducer {
    private final KafkaTemplate<String, DomainEvent> kafka;

    public void publish(DomainEvent event) {
        String key = switch (event) {
            case OrderPlaced e    -> e.orderId();
            case OrderShipped e   -> e.orderId();
            case OrderCancelled e -> e.orderId();
        };
        kafka.send("order-events", key, event);
    }
}
Part 15

Production Patterns and Anti-Patterns

Good Production Uses of Records

1. API Request/Response DTOs

public record PagedResponse<T>(
    List<T> content,
    int page,
    int size,
    long totalElements,
    int totalPages,
    boolean last
) {
    public static <T> PagedResponse<T> from(Page<T> page) {
        return new PagedResponse<>(
            page.getContent(), page.getNumber(), page.getSize(),
            page.getTotalElements(), page.getTotalPages(), page.isLast()
        );
    }
}

2. Value Objects in Domain Model

public record CustomerId(UUID value) {
    public CustomerId {
        Objects.requireNonNull(value, "Customer ID must not be null");
    }

    public static CustomerId generate() {
        return new CustomerId(UUID.randomUUID());
    }

    public static CustomerId of(String uuidStr) {
        return new CustomerId(UUID.fromString(uuidStr));
    }
}

public record Money(BigDecimal amount, String currencyCode) {
    public Money {
        Objects.requireNonNull(amount);
        Objects.requireNonNull(currencyCode);
        if (amount.scale() > 2)
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Amount has too many decimal places");
    }

    public Money add(Money other) {
        if (!currencyCode.equals(other.currencyCode))
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Cannot add different currencies");
        return new Money(amount.add(other.amount), currencyCode);
    }
}

3. Query Result Projections (Spring Data)

public interface ProductRepository extends JpaRepository<Product, Long> {
    // Spring Data interface projection
    interface ProductSummary {
        Long getId();
        String getName();
        BigDecimal getPrice();
    }

    // Or use a record class-based projection (Spring Data 3+)
    List<ProductSummaryRecord> findByCategory(String category);

    record ProductSummaryRecord(Long id, String name, BigDecimal price) {}
}

Anti-Patterns to Avoid

// ❌ Anti-pattern: Record with mutable collection component
public record BadOrder(List<String> items) {}
var order = new BadOrder(new ArrayList<>());
order.items().add("hacked"); // Mutates internal state!

// ✅ Fix: Defensive copy and wrap in unmodifiable
public record GoodOrder(List<String> items) {
    public GoodOrder {
        items = List.copyOf(items); // Unmodifiable + defensive copy
    }
}

// ❌ Anti-pattern: Using record for entities (needs identity, mutable)
public record UserEntity(long id, String name) {} // Wrong!

// ✅ Fix: Use @Entity class for JPA entities
@Entity
public class User {
    @Id private Long id;
    private String name;
    // getters/setters...
}

// ❌ Anti-pattern: Record extending a class
// public record Foo(int x) extends AbstractFoo {} // Compile error!
Part 16

Generic Records

Records can be parameterized with type parameters:

// Result monad as a record
public sealed interface Result<T> permits Result.Success, Result.Failure {

    record Success<T>(T value) implements Result<T> {}
    record Failure<T>(String message, Throwable cause) implements Result<T> {
        public Failure(String message) {
            this(message, null);
        }
    }

    static <T> Result<T> success(T value) {
        return new Success<>(value);
    }

    static <T> Result<T> failure(String message) {
        return new Failure<>(message);
    }

    default boolean isSuccess() {
        return this instanceof Success;
    }

    default T getOrThrow() {
        return switch (this) {
            case Success<T> s  -> s.value();
            case Failure<T> f  -> throw new RuntimeException(f.message(), f.cause());
        };
    }
}

// Usage
Result<User> result = userService.findById(42L);
User user = result.getOrThrow();
Part 17

Records and Interfaces

Records can implement multiple interfaces, enabling powerful composition:

public interface Auditable {
    Instant createdAt();
    String createdBy();
}

public interface Versioned {
    long version();
}

public interface Identifiable<ID> {
    ID id();
}

public record AuditedOrder(
    UUID id,
    String customerId,
    BigDecimal total,
    Instant createdAt,
    String createdBy,
    long version
) implements Identifiable<UUID>, Auditable, Versioned {}
Part 18

Reflection and Serialization Frameworks

// Using the RecordComponent API
public class RecordSerializer {
    public static Map<String, Object> toMap(Record record)
            throws ReflectiveOperationException {
        var map = new LinkedHashMap<String, Object>();
        for (var rc : record.getClass().getRecordComponents()) {
            map.put(rc.getName(), rc.getAccessor().invoke(record));
        }
        return map;
    }

    public static boolean isRecord(Class<?> clazz) {
        return clazz.isRecord();
    }
}

// Test
var point = new Point(3, 4);
var map = RecordSerializer.toMap(point);
// {x=3, y=4}
Part 19

Records in Multi-Threading

Because records are immutable (assuming immutable components), they are inherently thread-safe with no synchronization needed:

// Safe to share across threads without synchronization
public record CacheEntry<V>(
    String key,
    V value,
    Instant expiresAt
) {
    public boolean isExpired() {
        return Instant.now().isAfter(expiresAt);
    }
}

// Concurrent cache using records as values
private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, CacheEntry<User>> cache
    = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

public Optional<User> getUser(String id) {
    return Optional.ofNullable(cache.get(id))
        .filter(Predicate.not(CacheEntry::isExpired))
        .map(CacheEntry::value);
}
Part 20

Testing Records

Records simplify testing significantly because of their value-based equals:

class OrderResponseTest {

    @Test
    void should_create_order_response() {
        var response = new OrderResponse(
            "order-123", "CONFIRMED",
            new BigDecimal("99.99"), Instant.parse("2024-01-15T10:00:00Z")
        );

        // Direct equality — no custom matcher needed
        var expected = new OrderResponse(
            "order-123", "CONFIRMED",
            new BigDecimal("99.99"), Instant.parse("2024-01-15T10:00:00Z")
        );

        assertThat(response).isEqualTo(expected);
    }

    @Test
    void should_validate_in_compact_constructor() {
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> new Range(10, 5))
            .isInstanceOf(IllegalArgumentException.class)
            .hasMessageContaining("min");
    }

    @Test
    void should_serialize_to_json() throws Exception {
        var mapper = new ObjectMapper();
        var point = new Point(3, 4);
        var json = mapper.writeValueAsString(point);
        assertThat(json).isEqualToIgnoringWhitespace("""
            {"x":3,"y":4}
            """);
    }
}
Part 21

Common Interview Questions

Q1: What is a Java record and when would you use one?

A record is a special class designed to be an immutable data carrier. Use it when modeling data-transfer objects, value objects, query results, or any structure where the primary purpose is holding named, typed values with no mutable state.

Q2: Can a record extend another class?

No. Records implicitly extend java.lang.Record, and Java supports only single-class inheritance, so records cannot extend any other class. They can, however, implement interfaces.

Q3: Can a record implement an interface?

Yes. Records can implement any number of interfaces, which is the primary mechanism for composing record types into type hierarchies.

Q4: How does serialization work with records?

Java serialization uses the canonical constructor for deserialization rather than field manipulation, making it safer than regular classes. Jackson 2.12+ handles records natively. The compact constructor runs during deserialization, so validation logic is always enforced.

Q5: What is the difference between a compact constructor and a canonical constructor?

The canonical constructor matches the full component parameter list. The compact constructor omits the parameter list and field assignment — the compiler implicitly adds them at the end, making it ideal for validation and normalization.

Q6: Are records thread-safe?

Records are immutable by design (fields are private final), so they are inherently thread-safe as long as all component types are also immutable or thread-safe.

Q7: Can you add mutable state to a record?

You cannot add instance fields outside the component list. However, static fields can be mutable. To prevent mutation through mutable component types, use defensive copies and unmodifiable wrappers in the compact constructor.

Q8: How do records compare to Lombok's @Value?

Both produce immutable value classes. Records are a JVM/language feature (no tooling required, IDE-native, Valhalla-ready), while @Value requires annotation processing and works on older Java versions. Records cannot extend classes; @Value classes can. Lombok offers @With for withers; records require manual wither methods.

Part 1

Concept Overview

Java Sealed Classes (finalized in Java 17, previewed in Java 15–16) give developers the ability to explicitly restrict which classes or interfaces can extend or implement a given type. They close a previously open inheritance hierarchy and declare its complete membership at the point of definition.

Before sealed classes, abstract classes and interfaces were completely open: any class anywhere in the codebase — or even a different module — could extend them. This was problematic for two reasons:

  1. Modeling: A domain type often has a finite, known set of subtypes. Leaving inheritance open misrepresents the domain and allows invalid extensions.
  2. Exhaustiveness: Pattern matching and switch could never be exhaustive over a type hierarchy without full knowledge of all subtypes at compile time.

Sealed classes solve both problems:

// Open hierarchy — anyone can extend
public abstract class Shape {} // Bad for modeling closed domains

// Sealed hierarchy — exactly three subtypes, forever
public sealed class Shape permits Circle, Rectangle, Triangle {}

public final class Circle    extends Shape { double radius; }
public final class Rectangle extends Shape { double width, height; }
public final class Triangle  extends Shape { double base, height; }

With this declaration, the compiler knows at compile time that Shape has exactly three subtypes — enabling exhaustive switch expressions without a default branch.

Part 2

The Three Keywords: `sealed`, `permits`, `non-sealed`

sealed

Marks a class or interface as sealed. The subtype set must be declared with permits.

public sealed interface Expr permits Num, Add, Mul, Neg {}

permits

Lists the allowed direct subtypes. These must be in the same compilation unit (same package, or explicitly named when in different packages/modules). Rules:

  • Every listed type must directly extend/implement the sealed type
  • Every listed type must be in the same package (or same module with accessible package)
  • Every permitted subtype must be final, sealed, or non-sealed

non-sealed

A permitted subtype that re-opens itself to unrestricted extension. This is an escape hatch — use sparingly:

public sealed interface Vehicle permits Car, Truck, SpecialVehicle {}

public final class Car implements Vehicle {}
public final class Truck implements Vehicle {}
public non-sealed class SpecialVehicle implements Vehicle {}

// SpecialVehicle is now open — anything can extend it
public class EmergencyVehicle extends SpecialVehicle {} // OK
Part 3

Subtype Constraint Rules

Every permitted subtype must satisfy exactly one of three constraints:

Constraint Meaning
final Cannot be further extended. Leaf node in hierarchy.
sealed Can be extended, but only by its own permits list. Intermediate node.
non-sealed Open for extension again. Escape hatch; breaks exhaustiveness locally. 
// Multi-level sealed hierarchy
public sealed interface JsonValue
    permits JsonNull, JsonBool, JsonNumber, JsonString, JsonArray, JsonObject {}

public record JsonNull()    implements JsonValue {}
public record JsonBool(boolean value) implements JsonValue {}
public record JsonNumber(double value) implements JsonValue {}
public record JsonString(String value) implements JsonValue {}
public record JsonArray(List<JsonValue> elements) implements JsonValue {}
public record JsonObject(Map<String, JsonValue> fields) implements JsonValue {}

// Intermediate node: JsonNumber is itself sealed
public sealed interface Payment permits CreditCard, BankTransfer, Crypto {}

public final class CreditCard  extends Payment {}
public sealed class BankTransfer extends Payment
    permits DomesticTransfer, InternationalTransfer {}

public final class DomesticTransfer      extends BankTransfer {}
public final class InternationalTransfer extends BankTransfer {}

public non-sealed class Crypto extends Payment {} // third-party crypto implementations allowed
Part 4

Sealed Interfaces

Sealed works on both classes and interfaces. Sealed interfaces are often the better choice because they allow permitted subtypes to be records or any class type without the single-inheritance restriction:

// Sealed interface — permits records, final classes, other sealed interfaces
public sealed interface Command permits
    CreateUser, UpdateUser, DeleteUser, BulkCommand {}

public record CreateUser(String username, String email) implements Command {}
public record UpdateUser(long id, String newEmail) implements Command {}
public record DeleteUser(long id) implements Command {}

public sealed interface BulkCommand extends Command
    permits BulkCreate, BulkDelete {}

public record BulkCreate(List<CreateUser> commands) implements BulkCommand {}
public record BulkDelete(List<Long> ids) implements BulkCommand {}
Part 5

Exhaustive Pattern Matching with Switch

This is the killer feature of sealed classes. Because the compiler knows the complete set of permitted subtypes, a switch expression over a sealed type can be exhaustive without a default branch:

public sealed interface Notification
    permits EmailNotification, SmsNotification, PushNotification {}

public record EmailNotification(String to, String subject, String body)
    implements Notification {}
public record SmsNotification(String phone, String message)
    implements Notification {}
public record PushNotification(String deviceToken, String title, String body)
    implements Notification {}

// Exhaustive switch — no default needed
public String describe(Notification n) {
    return switch (n) {
        case EmailNotification e ->
            "Email to %s: %s".formatted(e.to(), e.subject());
        case SmsNotification s ->
            "SMS to %s: %s".formatted(s.phone(), s.message());
        case PushNotification p ->
            "Push to %s: %s".formatted(p.deviceToken(), p.title());
        // No default — compiler verifies exhaustiveness
    };
}

Compile-time safety: If a new type is added to the permits list — say InAppNotification — every exhaustive switch over Notification fails to compile until it handles the new case. This is refactoring safety that instanceof chains and abstract methods cannot provide.

Guarded Patterns

public double calculateFee(Payment payment) {
    return switch (payment) {
        case CreditCard cc when cc.isInternational() -> 0.035;
        case CreditCard cc                           -> 0.015;
        case BankTransfer bt when bt.amount() > 10_000 -> 0.005;
        case BankTransfer bt                           -> 0.002;
        case Crypto c                                  -> 0.01;
    };
}

Nested Record Patterns in Switch

public record Order(String id, Payment payment, Money total) {}

String receipt(Order order) {
    return switch (order) {
        case Order(var id, CreditCard(var num, var exp), var total) ->
            "Order %s paid by card ending %s, total %s".formatted(
                id, num.substring(num.length() - 4), total
            );
        case Order(var id, BankTransfer(var iban), var total) ->
            "Order %s paid via bank transfer to %s, total %s"
                .formatted(id, iban, total);
        case Order(var id, Crypto(var wallet, var coin), var total) ->
            "Order %s paid %s %s to wallet %s".formatted(id, total, coin, wallet);
    };
}

ASCII Diagram: Sealed Class Hierarchy

SEALED HIERARCHY TAXONOMY
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  sealed interface Shape
  permits Circle, Polygon, CompositeShape
  │
  ├─── final class Circle                   [LEAF — cannot extend]
  │    └── double radius
  │
  ├─── sealed class Polygon                  [INTERMEDIATE — further sealed]
  │    permits Triangle, Quadrilateral
  │    │
  │    ├─── final class Triangle            [LEAF]
  │    │    └── double base, height
  │    │
  │    └─── sealed class Quadrilateral      [INTERMEDIATE]
  │         permits Rectangle, Parallelogram
  │         │
  │         ├─── final class Rectangle     [LEAF]
  │         └─── final class Parallelogram [LEAF]
  │
  └─── non-sealed class CompositeShape      [OPEN — anyone can extend]
       └── List<Shape> parts
            │
            ├─── class Arrow extends CompositeShape    (external)
            └─── class Star  extends CompositeShape    (external)


COMPILER KNOWLEDGE MAP
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  switch(shape) exhaustive check:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  case Circle           → ✅ covered                  │
  │  case Triangle         → ✅ covered (via Polygon)    │
  │  case Rectangle        → ✅ covered (via Polygon)    │
  │  case Parallelogram    → ✅ covered (via Polygon)    │
  │  case CompositeShape   → ✅ covered (non-sealed:     │
  │                           one arm covers all exts)   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

PERMITS CLAUSE SCOPE RULES
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  Same file (unnamed module):
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Shape.java  →  Circle.java  ✅ (same package)      │
  │  Shape.java  →  other.pkg.X  ❌ (different package) │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Named module:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  module-info exports com.example.shapes              │
  │  Shape in com.example.shapes                         │
  │  Circle can be in com.example.shapes.impl ✅         │
  │  (if module exports or opens correctly)              │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Domain Modeling: Payment Type Hierarchy

A sealed class hierarchy for payment types is a canonical production example:

// Domain: Payment processing system
public sealed interface PaymentMethod
    permits CardPayment, BankPayment, WalletPayment {}

public sealed interface CardPayment extends PaymentMethod
    permits CreditCardPayment, DebitCardPayment {}

public record CreditCardPayment(
    String cardNumber,
    String cardholderName,
    YearMonth expiryDate,
    String cvv,
    boolean international
) implements CardPayment {
    public CreditCardPayment {
        Objects.requireNonNull(cardNumber);
        if (!cardNumber.matches("\\d{16}"))
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid card number format");
    }

    public String maskedNumber() {
        return "**** **** **** " + cardNumber.substring(12);
    }
}

public record DebitCardPayment(
    String cardNumber,
    String pin,
    String bankCode
) implements CardPayment {}

public sealed interface BankPayment extends PaymentMethod
    permits ACHPayment, WireTransfer, SEPAPayment {}

public record ACHPayment(
    String routingNumber,
    String accountNumber,
    boolean savings
) implements BankPayment {}

public record WireTransfer(
    String swiftCode,
    String iban,
    String beneficiaryName
) implements BankPayment {}

public record SEPAPayment(
    String iban,
    String bic,
    String reference
) implements BankPayment {}

public sealed interface WalletPayment extends PaymentMethod
    permits PayPalPayment, CryptoPayment {}

public record PayPalPayment(String email, String token) implements WalletPayment {}
public record CryptoPayment(
    String walletAddress,
    String coinSymbol,
    BigDecimal amount
) implements WalletPayment {}

// Payment processor using exhaustive switch
@Service
public class PaymentProcessor {

    public PaymentResult process(PaymentMethod payment) {
        return switch (payment) {
            case CreditCardPayment cc -> processCard(cc, true);
            case DebitCardPayment dc  -> processCard(dc, false);
            case ACHPayment ach       -> processACH(ach);
            case WireTransfer wire    -> processWire(wire);
            case SEPAPayment sepa     -> processSEPA(sepa);
            case PayPalPayment pp     -> processPayPal(pp);
            case CryptoPayment crypto -> processCrypto(crypto);
        };
    }

    private PaymentResult processCard(CreditCardPayment cc, boolean credit) {
        // delegate to card processor
    }
    // ... other methods
}
Part 8

Sealed Classes vs Enum vs Abstract Class

This decision matrix is essential for Java Solution Architects:

Aspect Enum Sealed Class Abstract Class
Instances Singleton per constant Multiple instances per subtype Multiple instances per subtype
State Limited (fields per constant) Rich state per subtype Rich state per subtype
Behavior Methods on enum body Separate class per subtype Override in each subtype
Type differentiation Identity-based Type-based (instanceof/switch) Type-based
Exhaustiveness Java 21+ switch Java 17+ switch No (must use default)
New variants Add constant (source break) Add to permits (compile break in switch) Add subclass (no break)
External extension No No (unless non-sealed) Yes
Serialization Built-in (ordinal/name) Custom (Jackson, Java Serialization) Custom
Pattern matching Java 21 Java 17+ No exhaustiveness
Inheritance Cannot extend Extends exactly one Extends exactly one
Use case Named constants, singleton behavior Data variants with different structure Shared behavior, open extension

Decision Flowchart

Does the type represent a FIXED SET of variants?
    └─ YES → Do all variants have the SAME structure/fields?
                └─ YES → Enum (possibly with abstract methods)
                └─ NO  → Do variants have DIFFERENT field sets?
                            └─ YES → Sealed class/interface with records
                            └─ NO  → Sealed abstract class
    └─ NO  → Abstract class (open hierarchy)

Is exhaustive pattern matching required at compile time?
    └─ YES → Sealed class (or Enum in Java 21+)
    └─ NO  → Abstract class is fine
Part 9

State Machine Modeling

Sealed classes are ideal for state machines because the state set is finite and transitions can be validated at compile time:

// Order state machine
public sealed interface OrderState
    permits OrderState.Draft, OrderState.Confirmed,
            OrderState.Shipped, OrderState.Delivered,
            OrderState.Cancelled {}

public sealed interface OrderState {

    record Draft(Instant createdAt) implements OrderState {}

    record Confirmed(
        Instant confirmedAt,
        String confirmationCode
    ) implements OrderState {}

    record Shipped(
        Instant shippedAt,
        String trackingNumber,
        String carrier
    ) implements OrderState {}

    record Delivered(
        Instant deliveredAt,
        String signedBy
    ) implements OrderState {}

    record Cancelled(
        Instant cancelledAt,
        String reason,
        boolean refundIssued
    ) implements OrderState {}
}

// State transition logic — exhaustive and type-safe
public class OrderStateMachine {

    public OrderState confirm(OrderState current, String code) {
        return switch (current) {
            case OrderState.Draft d ->
                new OrderState.Confirmed(Instant.now(), code);
            case OrderState.Confirmed c ->
                throw new IllegalStateException("Already confirmed");
            case OrderState.Shipped s, OrderState.Delivered s2 ->
                throw new IllegalStateException("Cannot confirm: already processed");
            case OrderState.Cancelled c ->
                throw new IllegalStateException("Cannot confirm: cancelled");
        };
    }

    public OrderState ship(OrderState current, String tracking, String carrier) {
        return switch (current) {
            case OrderState.Confirmed c ->
                new OrderState.Shipped(Instant.now(), tracking, carrier);
            case OrderState.Draft d ->
                throw new IllegalStateException("Must confirm before shipping");
            case OrderState.Shipped s ->
                throw new IllegalStateException("Already shipped");
            case OrderState.Delivered d ->
                throw new IllegalStateException("Already delivered");
            case OrderState.Cancelled c ->
                throw new IllegalStateException("Order is cancelled");
        };
    }

    public String describeState(OrderState state) {
        return switch (state) {
            case OrderState.Draft(var at) ->
                "Draft (created: " + at + ")";
            case OrderState.Confirmed(var at, var code) ->
                "Confirmed at " + at + " [" + code + "]";
            case OrderState.Shipped(var at, var tracking, var carrier) ->
                "In transit via " + carrier + " (" + tracking + ")";
            case OrderState.Delivered(var at, var sig) ->
                "Delivered at " + at + " (signed: " + sig + ")";
            case OrderState.Cancelled(var at, var reason, var refund) ->
                "Cancelled: " + reason + (refund ? " [refunded]" : "");
        };
    }
}
Part 10

Expression Trees and ASTs

Sealed classes with records are the canonical representation for expression trees and abstract syntax trees (ASTs):

// A mini expression language
public sealed interface Expr
    permits Expr.Num, Expr.Var, Expr.Add, Expr.Mul,
            Expr.Neg, Expr.Let, Expr.Cond {}

public sealed interface Expr {
    record Num(double value) implements Expr {}
    record Var(String name) implements Expr {}
    record Add(Expr left, Expr right) implements Expr {}
    record Mul(Expr left, Expr right) implements Expr {}
    record Neg(Expr expr) implements Expr {}
    record Let(String name, Expr value, Expr body) implements Expr {}
    record Cond(Expr condition, Expr then, Expr otherwise) implements Expr {}
}

// Evaluator — exhaustive, recursive, compile-safe
public class Evaluator {
    public double eval(Expr expr, Map<String, Double> env) {
        return switch (expr) {
            case Expr.Num(var v)               -> v;
            case Expr.Var(var name)            -> env.getOrDefault(name, 0.0);
            case Expr.Add(var l, var r)        -> eval(l, env) + eval(r, env);
            case Expr.Mul(var l, var r)        -> eval(l, env) * eval(r, env);
            case Expr.Neg(var e)               -> -eval(e, env);
            case Expr.Let(var name, var v, var body) -> {
                var newEnv = new HashMap<>(env);
                newEnv.put(name, eval(v, env));
                yield eval(body, newEnv);
            }
            case Expr.Cond(var cond, var then, var other) ->
                eval(cond, env) != 0.0 ? eval(then, env) : eval(other, env);
        };
    }
}

// Pretty printer — second exhaustive visitor over same type
public class PrettyPrinter {
    public String print(Expr expr) {
        return switch (expr) {
            case Expr.Num(var v)        -> String.valueOf(v);
            case Expr.Var(var name)     -> name;
            case Expr.Add(var l, var r) -> "(" + print(l) + " + " + print(r) + ")";
            case Expr.Mul(var l, var r) -> "(" + print(l) + " * " + print(r) + ")";
            case Expr.Neg(var e)        -> "-" + print(e);
            case Expr.Let(var n, var v, var b) ->
                "let %s = %s in %s".formatted(n, print(v), print(b));
            case Expr.Cond(var c, var t, var e) ->
                "if %s then %s else %s".formatted(print(c), print(t), print(e));
        };
    }
}

REST API Error Hierarchy

// Typed API errors — exhaustive handling in exception handler
public sealed interface ApiError
    permits ApiError.NotFound, ApiError.Validation,
            ApiError.Unauthorized, ApiError.Conflict,
            ApiError.RateLimit, ApiError.Internal {}

public sealed interface ApiError {
    record NotFound(String resource, String id) implements ApiError {}
    record Validation(Map<String, String> fieldErrors) implements ApiError {}
    record Unauthorized(String reason) implements ApiError {}
    record Conflict(String resource, String detail) implements ApiError {}
    record RateLimit(int limit, Duration retryAfter) implements ApiError {}
    record Internal(String correlationId, String detail) implements ApiError {}
}

@RestControllerAdvice
public class GlobalExceptionHandler {

    @ExceptionHandler(DomainException.class)
    public ResponseEntity<ErrorResponse> handle(DomainException ex) {
        ApiError error = ex.toApiError();

        var status = switch (error) {
            case ApiError.NotFound n         -> HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND;
            case ApiError.Validation v       -> HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST;
            case ApiError.Unauthorized u     -> HttpStatus.UNAUTHORIZED;
            case ApiError.Conflict c         -> HttpStatus.CONFLICT;
            case ApiError.RateLimit r        -> HttpStatus.TOO_MANY_REQUESTS;
            case ApiError.Internal i         -> HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR;
        };

        var body = switch (error) {
            case ApiError.NotFound(var res, var id) ->
                new ErrorResponse(status.value(),
                    "%s with id '%s' not found".formatted(res, id));
            case ApiError.Validation(var fields) ->
                new ValidationErrorResponse(status.value(), fields);
            case ApiError.Unauthorized(var reason) ->
                new ErrorResponse(status.value(), reason);
            case ApiError.Conflict(var res, var detail) ->
                new ErrorResponse(status.value(),
                    "Conflict on %s: %s".formatted(res, detail));
            case ApiError.RateLimit(var limit, var retry) ->
                new RateLimitErrorResponse(status.value(), limit,
                    retry.toSeconds());
            case ApiError.Internal(var corrId, var detail) ->
                new ErrorResponse(status.value(),
                    "Internal error [" + corrId + "]");
        };

        return ResponseEntity.status(status).body(body);
    }
}

Kafka Event Hierarchies

// Kafka event schema for an e-commerce platform
public sealed interface ProductEvent
    permits ProductCreated, ProductUpdated, ProductPriceChanged,
            ProductStockUpdated, ProductDiscontinued {}

public record ProductCreated(
    String productId, String name, String category,
    BigDecimal price, int stock, Instant occurredAt
) implements ProductEvent {}

public record ProductUpdated(
    String productId, String name, String description,
    Instant occurredAt
) implements ProductEvent {}

public record ProductPriceChanged(
    String productId, BigDecimal oldPrice, BigDecimal newPrice,
    String reason, Instant occurredAt
) implements ProductEvent {}

public record ProductStockUpdated(
    String productId, int previousStock, int newStock,
    String warehouse, Instant occurredAt
) implements ProductEvent {}

public record ProductDiscontinued(
    String productId, String reason, Instant occurredAt
) implements ProductEvent {}

// Kafka consumer with exhaustive processing
@Component
public class ProductEventConsumer {

    @KafkaListener(topics = "product-events")
    public void consume(ProductEvent event) {
        switch (event) {
            case ProductCreated c -> {
                searchIndexer.index(c.productId(), c.name(), c.category());
                inventoryService.initialize(c.productId(), c.stock());
            }
            case ProductUpdated u -> {
                searchIndexer.update(u.productId(), u.name(), u.description());
                cacheEviction.evict("product:" + u.productId());
            }
            case ProductPriceChanged pc -> {
                pricingHistory.record(pc.productId(), pc.oldPrice(), pc.newPrice());
                alertService.notifyPriceWatchers(pc.productId(), pc.newPrice());
            }
            case ProductStockUpdated su -> {
                if (su.newStock() == 0)
                    alertService.notifyOutOfStock(su.productId());
                inventoryService.update(su.productId(), su.newStock());
            }
            case ProductDiscontinued d -> {
                searchIndexer.remove(d.productId());
                inventoryService.markDiscontinued(d.productId());
            }
        }
    }
}
Part 13

JVM Internals of Sealed Classes

Class File Flags and Attributes

The JVM represents sealed classes through two additions to the class file format (JEP 360):

  1. ACC_SEALED flag — set on the sealed class/interface
  2. PermittedSubclasses attribute — lists the internal names of permitted subtypes
ClassFile {
    access_flags: ACC_PUBLIC | ACC_ABSTRACT | ACC_SEALED
    ...
    attributes: [
        PermittedSubclasses {
            classes: [
                "com/example/Circle",
                "com/example/Rectangle",
                "com/example/Triangle"
            ]
        }
    ]
}

Reflection API

// Inspecting sealed hierarchy at runtime
Class<?> shapeClass = Shape.class;

System.out.println(shapeClass.isSealed()); // true

Class<?>[] permitted = shapeClass.getPermittedSubclasses();
for (Class<?> sub : permitted) {
    System.out.println(sub.getSimpleName() + " → " +
        (sub.isRecord() ? "record" :
         sub.isSealed() ? "sealed" :
         Modifier.isFinal(sub.getModifiers()) ? "final" : "non-sealed")
    );
}
// Circle     → final
// Rectangle  → final
// Triangle   → final

// Check if a class is a permitted subtype of another
boolean isPermitted = Arrays.stream(shapeClass.getPermittedSubclasses())
    .anyMatch(c -> c == Circle.class);

Exhaustiveness Checking in the JVM

Exhaustiveness in switch over sealed types is checked by the compiler, not the JVM. At runtime, the JVM sees a standard tableswitch or lookupswitch bytecode. However:

  • The compiler generates a synthetic default that throws MatchException (Java 21+) or IncompatibleClassChangeError to guard against class-loading inconsistencies (e.g., a class compiled against an older version of the sealed type).
  • This makes sealed-class switches robust against binary compatibility issues.
Part 14

Module System Integration

Sealed classes interact with the module system (JPMS) to provide strong encapsulation:

// module-info.java for the shapes module
module com.example.shapes {
    exports com.example.shapes.api;           // exports sealed interface
    // Does NOT export com.example.shapes.impl — permitted subtypes are module-internal
}

// com.example.shapes.api
public sealed interface Shape
    permits com.example.shapes.impl.Circle,
            com.example.shapes.impl.Rectangle {}

// com.example.shapes.impl (not exported)
public final class Circle extends Shape { ... }
public final class Rectangle extends Shape { ... }

This pattern lets you expose the sealed type publicly while keeping the concrete implementations module-private — API consumers can match on the sealed type but cannot instantiate or extend the implementations.

Part 15

Sealed Classes and the Visitor Pattern

Sealed classes + pattern matching in switch effectively replace the Visitor pattern in modern Java:

// Classic Visitor — boilerplate-heavy
interface ShapeVisitor<R> {
    R visitCircle(Circle c);
    R visitRectangle(Rectangle r);
    R visitTriangle(Triangle t);
}

abstract class Shape {
    abstract <R> R accept(ShapeVisitor<R> visitor);
}

// Modern alternative: sealed + switch — no visitor interface needed
sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Rectangle, Triangle {}
record Circle(double radius) implements Shape {}
record Rectangle(double w, double h) implements Shape {}
record Triangle(double base, double height) implements Shape {}

// Multiple "visitors" — just switch expressions
double area(Shape s) {
    return switch (s) {
        case Circle(var r)       -> Math.PI * r * r;
        case Rectangle(var w, var h) -> w * h;
        case Triangle(var b, var h)  -> 0.5 * b * h;
    };
}

String describe(Shape s) {
    return switch (s) {
        case Circle c    -> "A circle with radius " + c.radius();
        case Rectangle r -> "A %s×%s rectangle".formatted(r.w(), r.h());
        case Triangle t  -> "A triangle";
    };
}

The sealed + switch approach is more concise, equally type-safe, and removes the double-dispatch ceremony of the traditional Visitor.

Part 16

Sealed Classes: Permits Clause Rules Deep Dive

// Rule 1: All permitted subtypes must be accessible from the sealed type
// ✅ Same package
package com.example;
public sealed class Animal permits Dog, Cat {}
final class Dog extends Animal {} // same package — OK
final class Cat extends Animal {} // same package — OK

// ✅ Same compilation unit (can be in the same file, unnamed permits)
public sealed class Color permits Color.Red, Color.Green, Color.Blue {
    public final class Red   extends Color {}
    public final class Green extends Color {}
    public final class Blue  extends Color {}
}

// ✅ Permits can be omitted if all subtypes are in the same file
public sealed class Token {
    public final class Keyword extends Token {}
    public final class Identifier extends Token {}
    public final class Literal extends Token {}
    // No permits clause — compiler infers from subtypes in same file
}

// ❌ INVALID: Permitted subtype in wrong package without explicit module setup
package com.example.shapes;
public sealed interface Shape permits com.other.pkg.Circle {} // compile error!

// Rule 2: Every permitted subtype must directly extend/implement the sealed type
public sealed class A permits B {}
public sealed class B extends A permits C {} // OK — B directly extends A
public final class C extends B {} // OK — C directly extends B (sealed)
// public final class D extends A {} // ERROR — not in A's permits list
Part 17

Combining Sealed Classes with Generics

// Generic sealed interface for typed results
public sealed interface Validation<T>
    permits Validation.Valid, Validation.Invalid {}

public sealed interface Validation<T> {
    record Valid<T>(T value) implements Validation<T> {}
    record Invalid<T>(List<String> errors) implements Validation<T> {}

    static <T> Validation<T> valid(T value) {
        return new Valid<>(value);
    }

    static <T> Validation<T> invalid(String... errors) {
        return new Invalid<>(List.of(errors));
    }

    default boolean isValid() {
        return this instanceof Valid;
    }

    default <U> Validation<U> map(java.util.function.Function<T, U> f) {
        return switch (this) {
            case Valid<T>(var v)    -> new Valid<>(f.apply(v));
            case Invalid<T>(var e)  -> new Invalid<>(e);
        };
    }

    default Validation<T> and(Validation<T> other) {
        return switch (this) {
            case Valid<T> v         -> other;
            case Invalid<T>(var e1) -> switch (other) {
                case Valid<T> v2        -> this;
                case Invalid<T>(var e2) -> {
                    var combined = new ArrayList<>(e1);
                    combined.addAll(e2);
                    yield new Invalid<>(combined);
                }
            };
        };
    }
}

// Usage in validation pipeline
Validation<CreateUserRequest> validate(CreateUserRequest req) {
    var nameCheck = req.username().length() >= 3
        ? Validation.valid(req)
        : Validation.invalid("Username must be at least 3 characters");

    var emailCheck = req.email().contains("@")
        ? Validation.valid(req)
        : Validation.invalid("Invalid email format");

    return nameCheck.and(emailCheck);
}

Part 19

Anti-Patterns and Pitfalls

Anti-Pattern 1: Overusing non-sealed

// ❌ Bad: non-sealed defeats the purpose
public sealed interface Strategy permits StrategyA, StrategyB, ThirdParty {}
public non-sealed class ThirdParty implements Strategy {}
// Now external code can add strategies that won't be caught by exhaustive switch
// A switch over Strategy without a default will still compile
// but new ThirdParty subclasses hit the synthetic throw at runtime

// ✅ Better: use a separate open interface for truly extensible strategies
public sealed interface BuiltInStrategy permits StrategyA, StrategyB {}
public interface CustomStrategy {} // open
public interface Strategy extends BuiltInStrategy, CustomStrategy {} // not sealed

Anti-Pattern 2: Treating Sealed Classes as Enums

// ❌ Bad: modeling things with no differing structure as sealed classes
public sealed interface Direction permits North, South, East, West {}
public record North() implements Direction {} // Pointless records for singletons

// ✅ Better: enum is simpler and has built-in singleton semantics
public enum Direction { NORTH, SOUTH, EAST, WEST }

Anti-Pattern 3: Missing Permits in Wrong Package

// ❌ Bad: permitted class in separate package without module configuration
// package a: public sealed class Base permits b.Child {}
// package b: public final class Child extends Base {}
// This is a compile error without explicit module setup.

Anti-Pattern 4: Forgetting non-sealed on intermediate abstract class

// ❌ Bad: won't compile — BankTransfer must be final, sealed, or non-sealed
public sealed interface Payment permits CreditCard, BankTransfer {}
public abstract class BankTransfer implements Payment {} // compile error!

// ✅ Fix:
public sealed abstract class BankTransfer implements Payment
    permits ACH, Wire {}
Part 20

Sealed Interfaces vs Sealed Abstract Classes

Aspect Sealed Interface Sealed Abstract Class
Permitted subtypes can Extend any class AND implement the interface Only extend this class (single inheritance)
State No state (default methods only) Can have state, constructors
Multiple implementation Permitted type can implement multiple interfaces Permitted type occupies one extends slot
Records as subtypes Yes — records can implement interfaces Yes — records can extend abstract classes (but cannot have fields)
Use when Variants have unrelated structure/hierarchy Variants share common fields/behavior 
// When to use sealed interface:
// Variants need to implement OTHER interfaces too
public sealed interface Event permits Created, Updated, Deleted {}
public record Created(String id, Instant at) implements Event, Auditable {}
public record Updated(String id, Instant at) implements Event, Auditable {}
public record Deleted(String id, Instant at) implements Event, Auditable {}

// When to use sealed abstract class:
// Variants share a common field (e.g., id, timestamp)
public sealed abstract class BaseEvent
    permits Created, Updated, Deleted {
    private final String id;
    private final Instant occurredAt;

    protected BaseEvent(String id, Instant occurredAt) {
        this.id = id;
        this.occurredAt = occurredAt;
    }

    public String id() { return id; }
    public Instant occurredAt() { return occurredAt; }
}
Part 21

Common Interview Questions

Q1: What is a sealed class in Java and what problem does it solve?

A sealed class restricts which classes can extend or implement it via the permits clause. It solves two problems: domain modeling (expressing that a type has a finite, known set of variants) and exhaustiveness (enabling the compiler to verify that switch expressions cover all cases without a default branch).

Q2: What is the difference between sealed, final, and non-sealed?

sealed restricts inheritance to the listed permits set. final forbids all extension. non-sealed is used on a permitted subtype to re-open it for unrestricted extension — it is an escape hatch that breaks local exhaustiveness for that branch.

Q3: What rules must a permitted subtype follow?

A permitted subtype must: (1) directly extend/implement the sealed type, (2) be in the same package or named module as the sealed type, and (3) be declared as final, sealed, or non-sealed.

Q4: How do sealed classes enable exhaustive pattern matching?

Because the compiler knows the complete set of permitted subtypes at compile time, it can verify that a switch expression covers all subtypes. If a new subtype is added to the permits list, all exhaustive switches fail to compile until updated. This provides refactoring safety impossible with open hierarchies.

Q5: Can a sealed class extend another class?

Yes. A sealed class can extend any class (as long as that parent class either is non-sealed, non-final, or the sealed class is in its permits list). A sealed interface can extend other interfaces.

Q6: What happens at the JVM level with sealed classes?

The JVM uses the PermittedSubclasses class file attribute and an ACC_SEALED access flag. The exhaustiveness check happens at compile time. At runtime, the JVM generates a synthetic default in exhaustive switches that throws MatchException to guard against stale compiled code.

Q7: How do sealed classes compare to the Visitor pattern?

Sealed classes with switch pattern matching achieve the same typed dispatch as the Visitor pattern but with far less boilerplate. No visitor interface, no accept method, no double dispatch. Each "visitor" is a switch expression. The downside is that adding new operations is easy (new switch), but adding new subtypes requires updating all switches — the same trade-off as Visitor.

Q8: Can records be permitted subtypes of a sealed interface?

Yes. Records implementing a sealed interface is the most common and idiomatic combination in modern Java. Records are final by default, satisfying the sealed subtype constraint.

Part 22

Summary Table

Feature Detail
Since Java 17 (preview: 15, 16)
Keywords sealed, permits, non-sealed
Applies to Classes and interfaces
Permitted subtype must be final, sealed, or non-sealed
Permitted subtype location Same package (unnamed module) or accessible in named module
Exhaustive switch Yes — no default needed if all subtypes covered
Compiler check Exhaustiveness at compile time; synthetic throw at runtime
JVM representation ACC_SEALED flag + PermittedSubclasses attribute
Reflection API Class.isSealed(), Class.getPermittedSubclasses()
Records compatibility Records can be permitted subtypes (they are final)
Generics Supported — sealed interface Result<T>
Visitor pattern Replaced by sealed + switch in modern Java
Module integration Strong encapsulation — can hide implementations
Pattern matching Full record patterns + guards in Java 21
vs Enum Use sealed when variants have different structures/fields
vs Abstract class Sealed when hierarchy must be closed; abstract when open
Anti-patterns Overusing non-sealed; using sealed for singleton-like types

Kafka uses Event type routing, consumer dispatch, schema modeling

Practice Section

Exercise 1 — Basic Sealed Interface

Define a sealed interface Shape with three permitted records: Circle(double radius), Rectangle(double width, double height), and Triangle(double a, double b, double c). Write three exhaustive switch methods: area(Shape), perimeter(Shape), and describe(Shape).

Exercise 2 — State Machine

Model a TrafficLight state machine with a sealed interface and three states: Red, Yellow, Green (each with a Duration duration). Implement a next(TrafficLight.State current) method that returns the next state in cycle, and a canCross(TrafficLight.State state) method.

Exercise 3 — Nested Hierarchy

Create a sealed interface MediaContent with subtypes: Image(String url, int width, int height), Video(String url, Duration length, String codec), and a sealed subtype Document with permits PdfDocument(String url, int pages) and SpreadsheetDocument(String url, int rows, int cols). Write an exhaustive renderHtml(MediaContent content) method.

Exercise 4 — Spring Integration

Build a REST API for a payment gateway. Define a sealed PaymentRequest hierarchy (card, bank, wallet). Write a @PostMapping endpoint that accepts a PaymentRequest, dispatches via exhaustive switch, and returns a sealed PaymentResult (success or failure variants as records). Include @RestControllerAdvice using exhaustive switch on ApiError for error responses.

Exercise 5 — Generic Validation

Implement a Validated<T> sealed interface with Valid<T>(T value) and Invalid<T>(List<ValidationError> errors) records. Add map, flatMap, and, and orElseThrow methods. Use this to validate a UserRegistrationRequest through a pipeline of validation functions.

Challenge — Expression Interpreter

Build a complete expression interpreter using sealed interfaces:
- Expr: Num, Str, Bool, Add, Sub, Mul, Div, Concat, And, Or, Not, If, Var, Let
- Implement eval(Expr, Map<String, Object> env) returning Object
- Implement typeCheck(Expr, Map<String, Class<?>> typeEnv) returning Class<?>
- Implement prettyPrint(Expr) returning formatted string

Both eval and typeCheck must be exhaustive switches — no default clause permitted.
