Part 1

What Is JPMS and Why It Exists

The Java Platform Module System (JPMS), introduced in Java 9 as part of Project Jigsaw, is a code-organization mechanism that goes beyond packages. Before JPMS, Java had exactly two units of deployment: classes and JARs. JARs were just zip files with no enforced boundaries — any code could reach into any other JAR's internals if it had the right classpath entry. The JDK itself suffered from this: developers relied heavily on internal APIs like sun.misc.Unsafe, com.sun.misc.*, and sun.reflect.* that were never intended for public use.

JPMS solves three problems:

  1. Reliable configuration — missing dependencies are detected at startup, not at runtime when a class is first needed.
  2. Strong encapsulation — internal packages are hidden by default; only explicitly exported packages are visible to other modules.
  3. Scalable platform — the JDK itself was split into modules, enabling jlink to build minimal custom runtimes that ship only what your application needs.

Java 9 modularized the entire JDK into ~70 modules. java.base is the root module every module implicitly requires. You can list all platform modules with:

java --list-modules
Part 2

The `module-info.java` File

A module is declared by placing a module-info.java file at the root of the source tree (not inside a package directory). The file is compiled into module-info.class and embedded in the JAR or module directory.

Minimal module declaration:

module com.example.myapp {
}

Full directive showcase:

module com.example.myapp {
    // Compile-time AND runtime dependency
    requires java.sql;

    // Compile-time only (not needed at runtime)
    requires static java.annotation;

    // Re-export everything you read from java.logging
    requires transitive java.logging;

    // Make this package visible to all other modules
    exports com.example.myapp.api;

    // Make this package visible ONLY to a specific module
    exports com.example.myapp.internal to com.example.otherplugin;

    // Deep reflection (for frameworks like Spring, Hibernate)
    opens com.example.myapp.model;

    // Deep reflection to a specific module only
    opens com.example.myapp.config to spring.core;

    // Declare that this module uses a service interface
    uses com.example.myapp.spi.DataProcessor;

    // Declare that this module provides an implementation
    provides com.example.myapp.spi.DataProcessor
        with com.example.myapp.impl.FastDataProcessor;
}

The file lives at the project root, not inside a package:

src/
  module-info.java          ← here
  com/
    example/
      myapp/
        api/
          MyService.java
        internal/
          InternalHelper.java
        model/
          User.java
Part 3

The Six Module Directives

Directive Direction Effect
requires M Inbound This module depends on module M
requires transitive M Inbound + propagation Dependents of this module also implicitly read M
requires static M Inbound, compile-time M must be present at compile time; optional at runtime
exports P Outbound Package P is accessible to all modules
exports P to M Outbound, qualified Package P is accessible only to module M
opens P Outbound, reflective Package P allows deep reflection by all modules
opens P to M Outbound, qualified reflective Package P allows deep reflection only by module M
uses S Service consumer This module consumes service interface S via ServiceLoader
provides S with I Service provider This module provides implementation I for service S

exports vs opens — The Critical Difference

exports grants compile-time and normal runtime access (public types and members only). Code in other modules can import and call exported classes.

opens grants deep reflective access at runtime — setAccessible(true), reading private fields, invoking private methods. It does NOT grant compile-time access. This is what Spring, Hibernate, Jackson, and JUnit need.

// exports: other modules can call MyService.doWork() at compile + runtime
exports com.example.api;

// opens: frameworks can reflect on User's private fields at runtime
opens com.example.model;

// opens + exports: both compile-time API and reflective access
exports com.example.dto;
opens com.example.dto;
Part 4

Named, Automatic, and Unnamed Modules

JPMS defines three kinds of modules to handle the reality that most existing JARs have no module-info.java.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                      MODULE TAXONOMY                        │
│                                                             │
│  ┌────────────────┐  ┌────────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐  │
│  │  Named Module  │  │Automatic Module│  │Unnamed Module│  │
│  │                │  │                │  │              │  │
│  │ Has module-    │  │ Regular JAR on │  │ Everything   │  │
│  │ info.java      │  │ --module-path  │  │ on classpath │  │
│  │                │  │                │  │              │  │
│  │ Explicit name  │  │ Name derived   │  │ No name      │  │
│  │ Explicit deps  │  │ from JAR name  │  │ Reads all    │  │
│  │ Controlled     │  │ Exports ALL    │  │ named modules│  │
│  │ exports        │  │ packages       │  │ Exports all  │  │
│  │                │  │ Opens nothing  │  │ packages     │  │
│  └────────────────┘  └────────────────┘  └──────────────┘  │
│       ↑ on --module-path   ↑ on --module-path  ↑ classpath  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Named Module

A JAR with a module-info.class. Has an explicit name declared in source. Precise control over what it exports and what it requires.

Automatic Module

A plain JAR (no module-info) placed on the module path (--module-path). The JVM gives it an automatic name derived from the JAR filename (stripping version numbers and replacing hyphens with dots). An automatic module:
- Reads every other module on the module path
- Exports all its packages to all other modules
- Can be requires-ed by named modules

Automatic module name derivation:

jackson-databind-2.15.2.jar  →  jackson.databind
my-util-lib-1.0.jar          →  my.util.lib
slf4j-api-2.0.9.jar          →  slf4j.api

A JAR author can set a stable name via Automatic-Module-Name in MANIFEST.MF:

Automatic-Module-Name: com.fasterxml.jackson.databind

Unnamed Module

All JARs on the classpath become part of the single unnamed module. The unnamed module:
- Reads every named module (so classpath code can always use the JDK)
- Exports all packages (but named modules cannot require it — it has no name)
- Is essentially the "legacy compatibility" container

Key constraint: named modules cannot requires the unnamed module. This is why you can't cleanly depend on a classpath-only library from a named module without either: (a) moving it to the module path as an automatic module, or (b) using --add-reads.

Part 5

Classpath vs Module Path

Understanding where JARs are placed determines how they are treated:

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              CLASSPATH  vs  MODULE PATH                          │
│                                                                  │
│  --class-path (-cp)              --module-path (-p)              │
│  ─────────────────────           ────────────────────            │
│  All JARs → unnamed module       JARs with module-info           │
│                                  → named modules                 │
│  No encapsulation                JARs without module-info        │
│  No dependency checking          → automatic modules             │
│                                                                  │
│  java.lang.ClassLoader           Module system + ClassLoader     │
│  flat classpath                  hierarchical layer              │
│                                                                  │
│  Legacy behavior                 Strong encapsulation            │
│  Works for all old JARs          Dependency graph verified       │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Command-line example:

# Old way: everything on classpath
java -cp lib/spring.jar:lib/myapp.jar com.example.Main

# New way: modules on module path
java --module-path lib --module com.example.myapp/com.example.Main

# Mixed: some modules + classpath libs
java --module-path mods \
     --class-path lib/legacy.jar \
     --module com.example.myapp/com.example.Main

You can abbreviate: -p is --module-path, -m is --module.

Part 6

Module Dependency Graph

The module system builds a readability graph at startup. Each requires directive adds a directed edge. Transitive requires propagate readability to downstream modules.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    MODULE DEPENDENCY GRAPH                      │
│                                                                 │
│           com.example.app                                       │
│          /               \                                      │
│         ↓                 ↓                                     │
│  com.example.api     com.example.db                             │
│         \                 /                                     │
│          ↓               ↓                                      │
│       java.base      java.sql                                   │
│                          |                                      │
│                          ↓  (requires transitive)               │
│                     java.logging                                │
│                                                                 │
│  ← All modules implicitly require java.base →                   │
│                                                                 │
│  com.example.app reads java.logging transitively                │
│  because java.sql declares: requires transitive java.logging    │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

requires transitive propagation rule: if module A requires transitive B, then any module that requires A also reads B automatically. This is how java.sql exposes java.logging — consumers of java.sql can use java.util.logging without declaring it themselves.

Part 7

Strong Encapsulation in Practice

Before Java 9, internal JDK APIs were freely accessible:

// This worked on Java 8 and earlier — accessing JDK internals
import sun.misc.Unsafe;
import com.sun.misc.BASE64Encoder;
import sun.reflect.Reflection;

Unsafe unsafe = Unsafe.getUnsafe();  // No longer accessible by default

From Java 9+, the JDK is fully modular. sun.misc.Unsafe lives in jdk.unsupported which is not exported. com.sun.* and sun.* packages are internal to java.base and similar modules.

What happens when you access internal APIs:

ERROR: package sun.misc is not visible
  (package sun.misc is declared in module java.base,
   which does not export it)

The --add-opens and --add-exports Escape Hatches

For migration scenarios, the JVM provides command-line flags to override module encapsulation:

# Allow ALL modules to open java.lang to all unnamed modules
--add-opens java.base/java.lang=ALL-UNNAMED

# Allow a specific module to read an unexported package
--add-exports java.base/sun.misc=ALL-UNNAMED

# Grant specific module access
--add-opens java.base/java.lang.reflect=com.example.myapp

These flags appear in many Spring Boot and Hibernate startup scripts for Java 16+ compatibility. They are a migration tool, not a permanent solution.

Spring Boot 2.x typical JVM args for Java 17:

--add-opens java.base/java.lang=ALL-UNNAMED
--add-opens java.base/java.util=ALL-UNNAMED
--add-opens java.base/java.io=ALL-UNNAMED
Part 8

The Service Loader Pattern

JPMS first-class supports the service provider interface (SPI) pattern via uses and provides directives. This allows loose coupling between a service interface and its implementations.

Service interface (in module com.example.spi):

// com/example/spi/DataProcessor.java
package com.example.spi;

public interface DataProcessor {
    String process(String input);
}

Service provider (in module com.example.fast):

// module-info.java
module com.example.fast {
    requires com.example.spi;
    provides com.example.spi.DataProcessor
        with com.example.fast.impl.FastDataProcessor;
}

// com/example/fast/impl/FastDataProcessor.java
package com.example.fast.impl;

import com.example.spi.DataProcessor;

public class FastDataProcessor implements DataProcessor {
    @Override
    public String process(String input) {
        return input.toUpperCase(); // fast, obviously
    }
}

Service consumer (in module com.example.app):

// module-info.java
module com.example.app {
    requires com.example.spi;
    uses com.example.spi.DataProcessor;
}

// Usage
import java.util.ServiceLoader;
import com.example.spi.DataProcessor;

ServiceLoader<DataProcessor> loader = ServiceLoader.load(DataProcessor.class);
loader.forEach(processor -> System.out.println(processor.process("hello")));

The ServiceLoader finds all providers declared via provides in modules on the module path. No manual registration needed — it's declaration-driven at the module level.

Part 9

Building a Modular Project

A real multi-module project has a directory structure that mirrors the module graph:

myproject/
├── com.example.api/
│   ├── module-info.java
│   └── com/example/api/
│       └── UserService.java
├── com.example.impl/
│   ├── module-info.java
│   └── com/example/impl/
│       └── UserServiceImpl.java
└── com.example.app/
    ├── module-info.java
    └── com/example/app/
        └── Main.java

com.example.api module:

// com.example.api/module-info.java
module com.example.api {
    exports com.example.api;
}

// com/example/api/UserService.java
package com.example.api;

public interface UserService {
    String getUser(long id);
}

com.example.impl module:

// com.example.impl/module-info.java
module com.example.impl {
    requires com.example.api;
    provides com.example.api.UserService
        with com.example.impl.UserServiceImpl;
}

// com/example/impl/UserServiceImpl.java
package com.example.impl;

import com.example.api.UserService;

public class UserServiceImpl implements UserService {
    @Override
    public String getUser(long id) {
        return "User#" + id;
    }
}

com.example.app module:

// com.example.app/module-info.java
module com.example.app {
    requires com.example.api;
    uses com.example.api.UserService;
}

// com/example/app/Main.java
package com.example.app;

import com.example.api.UserService;
import java.util.ServiceLoader;

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ServiceLoader.load(UserService.class)
            .findFirst()
            .ifPresent(svc -> System.out.println(svc.getUser(42)));
    }
}

Compile all modules:

javac --module-source-path myproject \
      -d mods \
      $(find myproject -name "*.java")

Run the app:

java --module-path mods \
     --module com.example.app/com.example.app.Main
Part 10

jlink: Custom Runtime Images

jlink is a tool introduced in Java 9 that creates a minimal custom runtime image — a self-contained JRE that includes only the modules your application actually uses.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     JLINK WORKFLOW                              │
│                                                                 │
│  Full JDK (~300MB)          Custom Runtime Image (~30MB)        │
│  ─────────────────           ─────────────────────────         │
│  java.base          ──┐      java.base                         │
│  java.desktop       ──┤      java.sql           ← only         │
│  java.sql           ──┼─────→java.logging         what you     │
│  java.logging       ──┤      com.example.myapp    need         │
│  java.xml           ──┤                                        │
│  jdk.compiler       ──┤      + embedded launcher               │
│  jdk.jshell         ──┤      + no JDK overhead                 │
│  ... 65+ more       ──┘                                        │
│                                                                 │
│          jlink --module-path $JAVA_HOME/jmods:mods             │
│                --add-modules com.example.myapp                  │
│                --output myapp-runtime                           │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Full jlink example:

jlink \
  --module-path $JAVA_HOME/jmods:mods \
  --add-modules com.example.myapp \
  --launcher myapp=com.example.myapp/com.example.Main \
  --compress=2 \
  --strip-debug \
  --no-header-files \
  --no-man-pages \
  --output myapp-runtime

Run the custom runtime:

./myapp-runtime/bin/myapp
# or
./myapp-runtime/bin/java --module com.example.myapp/com.example.Main

Typical size comparison:

Image type Size
Full JDK 21 ~290 MB
JRE (no compiler) ~175 MB
jlink for simple app 30–60 MB
jlink for minimal CLI ~15 MB

jlink only works with named modules. Applications on the classpath (unnamed module) cannot be linked. This is the primary incentive to modularize libraries — enabling downstream users to jlink.

Part 11

Module Layers

For advanced use cases (plugins, application servers, IDEs), JPMS supports module layers — multiple independent module graphs loaded by the same JVM.

┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    MODULE LAYERS                               │
│                                                                │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │                    Boot Layer                           │  │
│  │   java.base, java.sql, java.logging, ...                │  │
│  │   (loaded at JVM startup by bootstrap loader)           │  │
│  └──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                         │ parent                               │
│          ┌──────────────┴──────────────┐                      │
│          ↓                             ↓                       │
│  ┌───────────────┐           ┌───────────────┐                │
│  │  Plugin A     │           │  Plugin B     │                │
│  │  Layer        │           │  Layer        │                │
│  │               │           │               │                │
│  │  Reads boot   │           │  Reads boot   │                │
│  │  layer        │           │  layer        │                │
│  │  (isolated    │           │  (isolated    │                │
│  │   versions)   │           │   versions)   │                │
│  └───────────────┘           └───────────────┘                │
│                                                                │
│  Each plugin can have its own version of a dependency          │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

// Programmatic layer creation
ModuleFinder finder = ModuleFinder.of(pluginPath);
ModuleLayer parent = ModuleLayer.boot();
Configuration config = parent.configuration()
    .resolve(finder, ModuleFinder.of(), Set.of("com.example.plugin"));

ModuleLayer layer = parent.defineModulesWithOneLoader(
    config,
    ClassLoader.getSystemClassLoader()
);

Class<?> pluginClass = layer.findLoader("com.example.plugin")
    .loadClass("com.example.plugin.PluginImpl");

Layers are used by IDEs (IntelliJ, Eclipse) and application servers to load extensions in isolation.

Part 12

jdeps: Analyzing Dependencies

jdeps (shipped with the JDK) analyzes class files and reports dependencies. It is the primary tool for migration analysis — understanding what JDK-internal APIs your code uses before upgrading to modules.

# Analyze a JAR for JDK internal API usage
jdeps --jdk-internals myapp.jar

# Show module-level summary
jdeps --module-path mods -m com.example.myapp

# Generate module-info.java recommendations
jdeps --generate-module-info . myapp.jar

# Check for split packages (fatal for modules)
jdeps --check myapp.jar

# Full dependency tree
jdeps -recursive --module-path $JAVA_HOME/jmods myapp.jar

Sample jdeps output showing internal API usage:

myapp.jar -> java.base
myapp.jar -> jdk.unsupported
   com.example.MyClass    -> sun.misc.Unsafe    JDK internal API (jdk.unsupported)
   com.example.OldUtil    -> sun.reflect.Reflection  JDK internal API (java.base)

This output tells you exactly which classes to refactor before full modularization.

Part 13

Migrating from Classpath to Modules

Migration is a three-stage process. Most production applications stop at stage 1 or 2.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│               MIGRATION STAGES                                  │
│                                                                 │
│  Stage 0: Legacy                                                │
│  ──────────────                                                 │
│  All JARs on --class-path                                       │
│  Unnamed module                                                 │
│  No encapsulation                                               │
│         │                                                       │
│         ↓                                                       │
│  Stage 1: Module path, no module-info (Automatic modules)       │
│  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────      │
│  Move JARs to --module-path                                     │
│  All become automatic modules                                   │
│  --add-opens flags for reflection                               │
│         │                                                       │
│         ↓                                                       │
│  Stage 2: Add module-info to your app (Named module)            │
│  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────            │
│  Write module-info.java                                         │
│  Declare all requires, exports, opens                           │
│  Third-party libs may still be automatic                        │
│         │                                                       │
│         ↓                                                       │
│  Stage 3: Full modularization (All named modules)               │
│  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────              │
│  All deps have module-info                                      │
│  jlink available                                                │
│  Maximum encapsulation                                          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Common Migration Problems

Split packages — the same package exists in two different JARs. Modules forbid this entirely. The module system will refuse to load if two named modules export the same package.

# Detecting split packages
jdeps --check myapp.jar lib/dependency.jar

Reflective access warnings (Java 9–15):

WARNING: An illegal reflective access operation has occurred
WARNING: Please consider reporting this to the maintainers of ...

These became errors in Java 16+. Fix them with --add-opens or upgrade to module-aware versions of the library.

Missing Automatic-Module-Name — if a library JAR has no Automatic-Module-Name manifest entry and you requires it by the derived name, renaming or versioning the JAR breaks your build. Always prefer libraries that declare Automatic-Module-Name.

Part 14

Spring Boot and JPMS in Production

Spring Boot applications in production almost universally use the classpath (unnamed module), not named modules. This is a deliberate and practical choice, not a shortcoming.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│          SPRING BOOT + JPMS REALITY CHECK                       │
│                                                                 │
│  Typical Spring Boot App                                        │
│  ─────────────────────────                                      │
│  java -jar myapp.jar                                            │
│         ↓                                                       │
│  Executable JAR (fat JAR)                                       │
│  All classes on classpath                                       │
│  Unnamed module                                                 │
│  Spring's heavy reflection works without --add-opens            │
│                                                                 │
│  Why not named modules?                                         │
│  ───────────────────────                                        │
│  • Fat JARs contain nested JARs (Spring Boot Loader)            │
│  • Split packages across Spring's own modules                   │
│  • Deep reflection on user classes is fundamental to Spring     │
│  • Most third-party libs lack proper module-info                │
│  • Limited gain: server JVM doesn't benefit from jlink          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Spring Boot 3 and Modular JDK

Spring Boot 3 targets Java 17+ and uses the modular JDK. Even though the application runs unnamed, it must handle a modular JDK. The framework itself is compiled against the modular JDK.

Common Spring Boot 3 JVM args for modular JDK compatibility:

# In application startup script or JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
--add-opens java.base/java.lang=ALL-UNNAMED
--add-opens java.base/java.lang.invoke=ALL-UNNAMED
--add-opens java.base/java.util=ALL-UNNAMED
--add-opens java.base/java.io=ALL-UNNAMED
--add-opens java.rmi/sun.rmi.transport=ALL-UNNAMED

These are typically set in JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS in containers or in the Gradle/Maven build file.

When Named Modules Make Sense for Spring Boot

A Spring Boot application as a named module is possible but uncommon. The effort pays off when:
- You're building a library that others will consume (especially for jlink)
- You want the JVM to fail fast on missing or unexpected dependencies
- Your app is small and self-contained (microservice with few deps)
- You're deploying with jlink to reduce container image size

Part 15

When to Adopt Modules: Libraries vs Applications

The decision is different for library authors versus application developers.

Library Authors — Adopt Modules

If you publish a library on Maven Central, adding module-info.java is strongly recommended:

// Good library module-info
module com.example.mylib {
    requires transitive com.google.gson;   // transitive: users need it too
    requires static org.slf4j;             // optional logging support
    exports com.example.mylib;             // public API
    exports com.example.mylib.util;        // utility API
    // NOT exporting com.example.mylib.internal — it's hidden
}

Benefits for library authors:
- Consumers using jlink can include your library
- Internal implementation details are truly hidden
- Accidental API usage of internal packages becomes a compile error
- Automatic-Module-Name in MANIFEST.MF as a minimum — prevents name instability

Application Developers — Be Pragmatic

For applications (especially server-side Spring/Micronaut/Quarkus apps):

ADOPT MODULES IF:                     STAY ON CLASSPATH IF:
────────────────────                  ─────────────────────
Building CLI tool for distribution    Large enterprise app (many deps)
Deploying to constrained devices      Spring Boot fat JAR deployment
Building a plugin framework           Many reflection-heavy frameworks
All deps have module-info             Any dep lacks module-info
Team understands JPMS well            Team is new to JPMS
Part 16

Multi-Release JARs and Modules

Multi-release JARs (MR-JARs, introduced Java 9) can contain different class implementations for different Java versions. They complement JPMS — you can add a module-info.class only for Java 9+ while keeping compatibility for Java 8 in the base JAR.

mrjar.jar
├── META-INF/
│   └── versions/
│       └── 9/
│           └── module-info.class    ← used on Java 9+
├── com/example/MyClass.class        ← used on Java 8
└── META-INF/MANIFEST.MF
    Multi-Release: true

Build with Maven:

<plugin>
    <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
    <artifactId>maven-compiler-plugin</artifactId>
    <executions>
        <execution>
            <id>compile-java9</id>
            <goals><goal>compile</goal></goals>
            <configuration>
                <release>9</release>
                <compileSourceRoots>
                    <compileSourceRoot>src/main/java9</compileSourceRoot>
                </compileSourceRoots>
                <multiReleaseOutput>true</multiReleaseOutput>
            </configuration>
        </execution>
    </executions>
</plugin>

This is how libraries like Guava and Jackson added module support without dropping Java 8 compatibility.

Part 17

Module System Internals: The Readability Graph

At JVM startup, the module system performs the following sequence:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│          JVM MODULE RESOLUTION SEQUENCE                         │
│                                                                 │
│  1. Parse --module-path entries                                 │
│     → build map: module-name → ModuleDescriptor                 │
│                                                                 │
│  2. Parse --add-modules, --module (root modules)                │
│                                                                 │
│  3. Transitive closure resolution                               │
│     → BFS from root modules following requires edges            │
│     → Error if required module not found                        │
│                                                                 │
│  4. Uniqueness check                                            │
│     → No two modules with same name                             │
│     → No split packages between named modules                   │
│                                                                 │
│  5. Build readability graph                                     │
│     → each requires → edge A reads B                            │
│     → requires transitive → propagate readability               │
│                                                                 │
│  6. Build export/open sets                                      │
│     → map: (package, module) → accessible?                      │
│                                                                 │
│  7. Enforce at every class load                                 │
│     → AccessControlException if encapsulation violated          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The enforcement is done in ClassLoader, java.lang.reflect, and in the Module class itself. Every field access and method invocation can be checked against module boundaries at runtime.

Part 18

Compile and Runtime Module Flags Reference

A complete reference for module-related JVM and javac flags:

Flag Tool Purpose
--module-path / -p javac, java Specify module path
--module / -m java Root module and main class
--module-source-path javac Source root for multi-module compilation
--add-modules java Add modules not directly required
--add-reads M=N java Module M reads module N (bypasses requires)
--add-exports M/P=N java, javac Package P of M exported to N (bypasses exports)
--add-opens M/P=N java Package P of M opened to N for reflection
--list-modules java List all observable modules and exit
--describe-module M java Print module descriptor for M
--validate-modules java Check all observable modules for errors
--patch-module M=path java Inject classes/resources into module M
--limit-modules java Limit universe of observable modules

Common ALL-UNNAMED usage:

# Open java.base/java.lang to ALL classpath code
--add-opens java.base/java.lang=ALL-UNNAMED

# Equivalent for reads
--add-reads java.base=ALL-UNNAMED
Part 19

Testing Modular Code

Testing introduces a wrinkle: test code must access production package internals, which conflicts with encapsulation.

Option 1: Open the package to the test runner in module-info:

module com.example.myapp {
    exports com.example.myapp.api;

    // For testing only — open internal package to JUnit
    opens com.example.myapp.internal to org.junit.platform.commons;
}

Option 2: Patch the module at test runtime (Maven Surefire):

<plugin>
    <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
    <artifactId>maven-surefire-plugin</artifactId>
    <configuration>
        <argLine>
            --add-opens com.example.myapp/com.example.myapp.internal=ALL-UNNAMED
        </argLine>
    </configuration>
</plugin>

Option 3: Use a separate test module-info (Gradle):

src/
  test/
    java/
      module-info.java   ← test-specific module descriptor

// src/test/java/module-info.java
open module com.example.myapp {   // "open" opens ALL packages
    requires com.example.myapp;
    requires org.junit.jupiter.api;
}

The open module keyword (without specifying a package) is an open module — it makes all packages reflectively accessible.

Part 20

Real-World Module Decisions at the JDK Level

The JDK itself is an example of JPMS in production. Understanding how Oracle modularized the JDK teaches patterns:

java.base               ← core: Object, String, Collections, IO
    ↑ required by all
java.sql                ← JDBC: requires java.logging transitively
java.logging            ← java.util.logging
java.xml                ← DOM, SAX, StAX, XSLT
java.desktop            ← AWT, Swing (huge, ~40MB)
java.management         ← JMX
jdk.compiler            ← javac
jdk.jshell              ← JShell REPL
jdk.unsupported         ← sun.misc.Unsafe (backwards compat)
jdk.incubator.*         ← preview features

java.base exports ~100 packages, opens ~0. Everything in java.base requires --add-opens for deep reflection since Java 16 strict mode.

jdk.unsupported exists specifically to preserve sun.misc.Unsafe access. It exports sun.misc — so code that depends on Unsafe still works on the module path if you add jdk.unsupported to your module path. But jdk.unsupported is NOT part of the Java SE specification and may be removed in a future LTS.

Part 21

Interview Deep-Dive: JPMS Questions

Q1: What is the difference between exports and opens?

exports com.example.api grants compile-time and normal runtime access to public types in that package — other modules can import and call those classes. opens com.example.model grants deep reflective access at runtime — frameworks can call setAccessible(true) on private fields and constructors. exports is for your API surface; opens is for framework introspection. A package can be both exported and opened.

Q2: How is an automatic module named?

The name is derived from the JAR filename by stripping version suffixes (e.g., -1.2.3, -SNAPSHOT) and replacing hyphens and dots according to the naming rules. jackson-databind-2.15.jar → jackson.databind. If the JAR's MANIFEST.MF contains Automatic-Module-Name: com.fasterxml.jackson.databind, that name is used instead. The manifest entry is preferred because derived names are fragile — a version bump changes the name.

Q3: When would you use requires transitive?

When your module's public API returns or accepts types from another module. Example: if com.example.api exports a method UserService.getConnection() that returns java.sql.Connection, then com.example.api should declare requires transitive java.sql. Consumers of com.example.api automatically read java.sql and can use Connection without their own requires java.sql.

Q4: What is a split package and why is it fatal?

A split package is when the same package name exists in two different modules. For example, com.example.util in both com.example.core and com.example.legacy. JPMS forbids this because class loading would be ambiguous — which module's com.example.util.Helper should be loaded? The JVM refuses to start with a split package error. This is the most common migration problem and requires package renaming or consolidation.

Q5: Why can't a named module requires the unnamed module?

The unnamed module has no name — you can't reference it in a requires directive. Named modules can only depend on other named modules (or automatic modules). This prevents new modular code from having uncontrolled dependencies on "classpath soup." You can work around this with --add-reads mymodule=ALL-UNNAMED at the command line, but this bypasses the module system's guarantees.

Q6: What does --add-opens do and when should you use it?

--add-opens module/package=target makes package in module reflectively accessible to target at runtime, as if the module had declared opens package to target. Use it as a temporary migration workaround when a library needs reflective access to JDK internals (common with older Spring, Hibernate, or serialization frameworks). It should not be a permanent solution — the proper fix is to upgrade to module-aware library versions or refactor away from internal API usage.

Q7: Can you jlink an application that uses the classpath?

No. jlink requires all application code to be in named modules on the module path. Classpath code lives in the unnamed module, which jlink cannot include in a custom runtime. To jlink your app, you must create a proper module-info.java for your own code and ensure all dependencies are either named modules or automatic modules (JARs on the module path).

Part 22

Summary Table and Phase 1 Completion

Module Directives Master Reference

Directive Syntax Access granted When to use
requires requires M; Compile + runtime reads Standard dependency
requires transitive requires transitive M; + propagates to consumers Public API uses M's types
requires static requires static M; Compile-time only Optional runtime dep
exports exports P; Public access to all Public API package
exports to exports P to M; Public access to M only Friend-module pattern
opens opens P; Reflection to all Framework introspection
opens to opens P to M; Reflection to M only Specific framework support
uses uses S; Consume service S SPI consumer
provides provides S with I; Register impl I SPI provider

Module Types Quick Reference

Type Source Name Exports Requires
Named module-info.java Declared in source Only what's exports-ed Only what's requires-ed
Automatic JAR on --module-path Derived from filename or Automatic-Module-Name All packages All other modules
Unnamed JAR on --class-path None (no name) All packages All named modules

Key JPMS Rules

  1. A named module can only access packages that are exported to it
  2. Reflection requires either opens or --add-opens
  3. Split packages between named modules are forbidden
  4. Named modules cannot requires the unnamed module
  5. jlink requires all modules to be named modules
  6. requires transitive propagates readability to consumers

Part 1

Why the Collection Framework Exists

Before Java 1.2, developers managed groups of objects using raw arrays, homegrown linked-list classes, and ad-hoc utility methods. Every project reinvented the wheel. Arrays are fixed-size, lack search/sort helpers, and offer no type safety before generics. The Java Collections Framework (JCF), introduced in Java 1.2 and significantly matured with generics in Java 5, solved all of this in one cohesive design:

  • Uniform API — every collection shares a common set of operations (add, remove, contains, size, iterator).
  • Interoperability — algorithms in java.util.Collections work on any Collection<E>.
  • Performance contracts — each implementation documents its Big-O complexity.
  • Thread-safety options — java.util.concurrent adds concurrent siblings for every structure.
  • Reduced programming effort — no wheel reinvention; use battle-tested, JVM-optimized implementations.

A Java Solution Architect must choose the right collection for each use case. A wrong choice (e.g., LinkedList for random access, ArrayList for concurrent writes) causes subtle bugs, high GC pressure, or OutOfMemoryError under load.

Part 2

The Two Root Interfaces

The JCF is built on two completely separate hierarchies:

Root Package Purpose
Collection<E> java.util Groups of individual elements (List, Set, Queue)
Map<K,V> java.util Key-value pairs; intentionally not a Collection

Map is not a Collection because it stores pairs, not single elements. However, Map participates in the framework through view methods: keySet() returns a Set<K>, values() returns a Collection<V>, and entrySet() returns a Set<Map.Entry<K,V>>.

The super-interface of Collection is Iterable<E>, which provides the iterator() method and enables the enhanced for-each loop.

Part 4

The `Collection<E>` Interface Methods

Every class that implements Collection must provide (or inherit) these operations:

public interface Collection<E> extends Iterable<E> {
    // Query operations
    int     size();
    boolean isEmpty();
    boolean contains(Object o);
    Iterator<E> iterator();
    Object[] toArray();
    <T> T[] toArray(T[] a);

    // Modification operations
    boolean add(E e);
    boolean remove(Object o);

    // Bulk operations
    boolean containsAll(Collection<?> c);
    boolean addAll(Collection<? extends E> c);
    boolean removeAll(Collection<?> c);
    boolean retainAll(Collection<?> c);
    void    clear();

    // Java 8+ default methods
    default boolean removeIf(Predicate<? super E> filter) { ... }
    default Stream<E> stream()                            { ... }
    default Stream<E> parallelStream()                    { ... }
    default void forEach(Consumer<? super E> action)      { ... }
    default Spliterator<E> spliterator()                  { ... }
}

Key insight: remove(Object o) accepts Object, not E. This is intentional for backward compatibility; you can remove a String from a Collection<Integer> without compile error (it simply returns false).

Part 5

The `List<E>` Interface at a Glance

List adds positional access and ordered duplicates to Collection:

public interface List<E> extends Collection<E> {
    E       get(int index);
    E       set(int index, E element);
    void    add(int index, E element);
    E       remove(int index);
    int     indexOf(Object o);
    int     lastIndexOf(Object o);
    ListIterator<E> listIterator();
    List<E> subList(int fromIndex, int toIndex);
    // Java 9+
    static <E> List<E> of(E... elements);        // immutable
    static <E> List<E> copyOf(Collection<? extends E> c); // immutable copy
}

Implementations: ArrayList, LinkedList, Vector (legacy), Stack (legacy), CopyOnWriteArrayList.

Part 6

The `Set<E>` Interface at a Glance

Set enforces uniqueness — no two elements where e1.equals(e2). The add() method returns false if the element already exists.

Ordered?        | No           → HashSet<E>         (O(1) add/remove/contains, random order)
Insertion order | Yes          → LinkedHashSet<E>   (O(1) ops, insertion-order iteration)
Sorted order?   | Natural/Comp → TreeSet<E>         (O(log n) ops, NavigableSet API)
Enum elements?  |              → EnumSet<E>         (bit-vector, O(1), must be enum)

The contract: if you override equals() you MUST override hashCode(). A broken contract causes silent duplicate insertion into HashSet.

Part 7

The `Queue<E>` and `Deque<E>` Interfaces

Queue models a first-in-first-out structure. It has two sets of methods: one throws exceptions, the other returns special values:

Operation Throws Exception Returns Special Value
Insert add(e) offer(e) → false
Remove remove() poll() → null
Examine element() peek() → null

Deque (Double-Ended Queue) extends Queue with both-end access:

// Deque as stack (LIFO)
Deque<String> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
stack.push("A");   // addFirst
stack.pop();       // removeFirst

// Deque as queue (FIFO)
Deque<String> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();
queue.offer("A");  // addLast
queue.poll();      // removeFirst

Prefer ArrayDeque over Stack and LinkedList for both stack and queue use cases — it has better cache locality and no synchronization overhead.

Part 8

The `Map<K,V>` Interface at a Glance

public interface Map<K,V> {
    // Query
    int     size();
    boolean isEmpty();
    boolean containsKey(Object key);
    boolean containsValue(Object value);
    V       get(Object key);
    // Modification
    V       put(K key, V value);
    V       remove(Object key);
    void    putAll(Map<? extends K, ? extends V> m);
    void    clear();
    // Views
    Set<K>          keySet();
    Collection<V>   values();
    Set<Map.Entry<K,V>> entrySet();
    // Java 8+ defaults
    V       getOrDefault(Object key, V defaultValue);
    V       putIfAbsent(K key, V value);
    boolean remove(Object key, Object value);
    V       replace(K key, V value);
    V       computeIfAbsent(K key, Function<? super K, ? extends V> mappingFn);
    V       computeIfPresent(K key, BiFunction<K, V, V> remappingFn);
    V       compute(K key, BiFunction<K, V, V> remappingFn);
    V       merge(K key, V value, BiFunction<V, V, V> remappingFn);
}

Part 11

Fail-Fast vs Fail-Safe Iterators

One of the most critical concepts for production code and interviews.

Fail-Fast Iterator

A fail-fast iterator detects structural modifications made to the collection while iterating and immediately throws ConcurrentModificationException. It does this by checking an internal modCount counter.

List<String> list = new ArrayList<>(List.of("a", "b", "c"));
Iterator<String> it = list.iterator();
while (it.hasNext()) {
    String s = it.next();
    list.add("d");  // ← modifies list during iteration
    // Throws ConcurrentModificationException on next it.next() call
}

// Correct way to remove during iteration:
Iterator<String> it2 = list.iterator();
while (it2.hasNext()) {
    if (it2.next().equals("b")) {
        it2.remove();  // ← safe; uses iterator's own remove
    }
}

Collections that are fail-fast: ArrayList, LinkedList, HashSet, HashMap, TreeMap, TreeSet, and most non-concurrent collections.

Fail-Safe Iterator (Snapshot Iterators)

A fail-safe iterator operates on a copy (snapshot) of the collection, so structural changes during iteration are invisible and no exception is thrown. The downside: you may iterate over stale data.

CopyOnWriteArrayList<String> cowList = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(List.of("a", "b", "c"));
for (String s : cowList) {
    cowList.add("d");  // ← writes create new copy; iterator sees original snapshot
    System.out.println(s);  // Prints a, b, c — no CME
}

Collections that are fail-safe: CopyOnWriteArrayList, CopyOnWriteArraySet, ConcurrentHashMap, ConcurrentSkipListMap.

Comparison Table

Feature Fail-Fast Fail-Safe
Exception on modification ConcurrentModificationException None
Operates on Original collection Snapshot copy
Memory overhead Low Higher (copy)
Reflects concurrent changes No (throws) No (stale)
Examples ArrayList, HashMap CopyOnWriteArrayList, ConcurrentHashMap
Part 12

The `equals()` and `hashCode()` Contract

Collections like HashSet and HashMap rely on equals() and hashCode() correctness. The contract:

  1. If a.equals(b) is true, then a.hashCode() == b.hashCode() MUST be true.
  2. If a.hashCode() == b.hashCode(), a.equals(b) may be true (hash collision is allowed).
  3. hashCode() must be consistent — same result for the same object across calls (unless fields change).

What happens when the contract is broken?

class BadKey {
    int id;
    BadKey(int id) { this.id = id; }

    @Override
    public boolean equals(Object o) {
        return o instanceof BadKey bk && bk.id == this.id;
    }
    // MISSING hashCode override!
}

Map<BadKey, String> map = new HashMap<>();
BadKey k1 = new BadKey(1);
map.put(k1, "one");

BadKey k2 = new BadKey(1);
System.out.println(map.get(k2));  // Prints null! Should print "one"
// k1.equals(k2) is true, but k1.hashCode() != k2.hashCode()
// → they land in different buckets → lookup fails

Rule for architects: Any class used as a Map key or Set element MUST override both equals() and hashCode() consistently. Use Objects.equals() and Objects.hash() for field-based implementations, or use Java 16+ records which provide them automatically.

record Point(int x, int y) {}  // equals, hashCode, toString auto-generated

Set<Point> points = new HashSet<>();
points.add(new Point(1, 2));
System.out.println(points.contains(new Point(1, 2)));  // true ✓
Part 13

`Comparable` vs `Comparator` in Collections

Sorted collections (TreeSet, TreeMap, PriorityQueue) require elements to have a defined order.

Comparable<T> — natural ordering, implemented in the element class:

class Employee implements Comparable<Employee> {
    String name;
    int salary;
    @Override
    public int compareTo(Employee other) {
        return Integer.compare(this.salary, other.salary);
    }
}
TreeSet<Employee> byNaturalOrder = new TreeSet<>(); // uses compareTo

Comparator<T> — external ordering, passed at construction:

TreeSet<Employee> byName = new TreeSet<>(Comparator.comparing(e -> e.name));
TreeSet<Employee> multiSort = new TreeSet<>(
    Comparator.comparing((Employee e) -> e.salary).reversed()
              .thenComparing(e -> e.name)
);

Rule: If an element class already has a natural order that all callers agree on, implement Comparable. Use Comparator for alternate orderings or third-party classes you cannot modify.

Part 14

`Collections` Utility Class (not `Collection`)

java.util.Collections provides static algorithms over Collection and List:

// Sorting
Collections.sort(list);                   // O(n log n), natural order
Collections.sort(list, comparator);

// Searching (list must be sorted)
int idx = Collections.binarySearch(list, "target");  // O(log n)

// Shuffling / Rotating
Collections.shuffle(list);
Collections.rotate(list, 2);  // rotate right by 2 positions

// Min / Max
String min = Collections.min(collection);
String max = Collections.max(collection, comparator);

// Frequency / Disjoint
int freq = Collections.frequency(collection, "value");
boolean noCommon = Collections.disjoint(c1, c2);

// Unmodifiable wrappers (views)
List<String> immutable = Collections.unmodifiableList(list);

// Synchronized wrappers (deprecated pattern — prefer java.util.concurrent)
List<String> syncList = Collections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>());

// Singleton / Empty collections
List<String> one    = Collections.singletonList("x");
Set<String>  empty  = Collections.emptySet();
Map<K,V>     emptyM = Collections.emptyMap();

// Fill / Copy / Swap / Reverse
Collections.fill(list, "default");
Collections.copy(dest, src);
Collections.swap(list, i, j);
Collections.reverse(list);

Java 9+ factory methods on the interfaces themselves (preferred for immutability):

List<String>    l = List.of("a", "b", "c");       // immutable
Set<Integer>    s = Set.of(1, 2, 3);               // immutable, no duplicates
Map<String,Int> m = Map.of("k1", 1, "k2", 2);     // immutable, ≤10 entries
Map<String,Int> m2 = Map.ofEntries(
    Map.entry("k1", 1), Map.entry("k2", 2)         // immutable, unlimited entries
);

Immutable vs Unmodifiable Collections

A common architect confusion:

Property Collections.unmodifiableList(list) List.of(...)
Mutation through wrapper Throws UnsupportedOperationException Throws UnsupportedOperationException
Mutation through original Reflected in wrapper N/A (no backing collection)
Truly immutable No Yes
Null elements Allowed if backing allows Throws NullPointerException
Serializable Only if backing is Yes 
List<String> mutable = new ArrayList<>(List.of("a", "b"));
List<String> view    = Collections.unmodifiableList(mutable);

Concurrent Collections Overview

java.util.concurrent provides thread-safe collections without the bottleneck of full synchronization:

Concurrent Class Replaces Key Technique
ConcurrentHashMap Hashtable, synchronizedMap Segment/bucket-level locking (Java 8+: CAS + fine-grain sync)
CopyOnWriteArrayList synchronizedList Copy-on-write; reads lock-free
CopyOnWriteArraySet synchronizedSet Backed by CopyOnWriteArrayList
ConcurrentSkipListMap synchronizedSortedMap Skip list; sorted, lock-free reads
ConcurrentSkipListSet synchronizedSortedSet Backed by ConcurrentSkipListMap
LinkedBlockingQueue N/A Bounded/unbounded blocking FIFO
ArrayBlockingQueue N/A Bounded, array-backed blocking FIFO
PriorityBlockingQueue N/A Blocking heap-based priority queue
ConcurrentLinkedQueue N/A Lock-free FIFO via CAS 
// ConcurrentHashMap — atomically compute-if-absent
ConcurrentHashMap<String, List<String>> graph = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
graph.computeIfAbsent("node1", k -> new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>()).add("node2");

// ConcurrentHashMap — atomic merge for counters
ConcurrentHashMap<String, Long> wordCount = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
wordCount.merge("hello", 1L, Long::sum);  // thread-safe increment

Part 18

Choosing the Right Collection: Decision Tree

Need key-value pairs?
    └─ Yes → Map
           ├─ Sorted by key?      → TreeMap (NavigableMap API)
           ├─ Insertion order?    → LinkedHashMap
           ├─ Enum keys?          → EnumMap
           ├─ Concurrent access?  → ConcurrentHashMap
           └─ Default             → HashMap

Need unique elements (no duplicates)?
    └─ Yes → Set
           ├─ Sorted?             → TreeSet
           ├─ Insertion order?    → LinkedHashSet
           ├─ Enum elements?      → EnumSet
           ├─ Concurrent?         → ConcurrentSkipListSet / CopyOnWriteArraySet
           └─ Default             → HashSet

Need ordered elements with duplicates?
    └─ Yes → List
           ├─ Random access by index?     → ArrayList (default)
           ├─ Frequent insert/remove at head/tail? → LinkedList
           ├─ Concurrent read-heavy?      → CopyOnWriteArrayList
           └─ Default                    → ArrayList

Need FIFO or LIFO processing?
    └─ Yes → Queue / Deque
           ├─ Priority-based?     → PriorityQueue
           ├─ Blocking (producer/consumer)? → LinkedBlockingQueue / ArrayBlockingQueue
           └─ Default general-purpose Deque → ArrayDeque
Part 19

Spring Framework Integration

Injecting All Beans of a Type

Spring's ApplicationContext can inject all beans implementing an interface into a List or Set:

public interface NotificationService {
    void send(String message);
}

@Component
public class EmailNotification implements NotificationService { ... }

@Component
public class SmsNotification implements NotificationService { ... }

@Service
public class NotificationDispatcher {
    private final List<NotificationService> services;

    public NotificationDispatcher(List<NotificationService> services) {
        this.services = services;  // Spring injects all beans implementing NotificationService
    }

    public void dispatch(String msg) {
        services.forEach(s -> s.send(msg));
    }
}

Controlling Bean Order with @Order and Ordered

@Component
@Order(1)  // Lower number = higher priority
public class PrimaryNotification implements NotificationService { ... }

@Component
@Order(2)
public class FallbackNotification implements NotificationService { ... }

// Or implement org.springframework.core.Ordered:
@Component
public class AuditNotification implements NotificationService, Ordered {
    @Override
    public int getOrder() { return Ordered.LOWEST_PRECEDENCE; }
}

@Qualifier with List Injection

@Bean
@Qualifier("highPriority")
public NotificationService smsService() { return new SmsNotification(); }

@Autowired
@Qualifier("highPriority")
private List<NotificationService> priorityServices;  // Only beans with the qualifier
Part 20

Production Pitfalls and Best Practices

1. NullPointerException in sorted collections

TreeSet, TreeMap, PriorityQueue do NOT allow null because they call compareTo/compare during insertion. Always validate inputs before inserting into sorted collections.

2. Mutable keys in HashMap

List<String> mutableKey = new ArrayList<>(List.of("a"));
Map<List<String>, String> map = new HashMap<>();
map.put(mutableKey, "value");
mutableKey.add("b");  // hashCode changes!
System.out.println(map.get(mutableKey));  // null — key is lost in wrong bucket

Rule: Use only immutable objects (String, Integer, record, etc.) as Map keys.

3. Iterating and removing

Use Iterator.remove(), removeIf(), or collect-then-remove patterns. Never remove from a list/set while iterating with for-each.

// Wrong: ConcurrentModificationException
for (String s : list) {
    if (s.startsWith("x")) list.remove(s);
}

// Right — removeIf (Java 8+)
list.removeIf(s -> s.startsWith("x"));

// Right — collect then remove
Set<String> toRemove = list.stream()
    .filter(s -> s.startsWith("x"))
    .collect(Collectors.toSet());
list.removeAll(toRemove);

4. Initial capacity for HashMap

Default capacity is 16, load factor 0.75 → resize (rehash) at 12 elements. If you know the size up front:

// Capacity to avoid resize: ceil(expectedSize / loadFactor) + 1
int expectedSize = 1000;
Map<String, String> map = new HashMap<>(1334);  // no resize up to 1000 entries
// Or use Guava: Maps.newHashMapWithExpectedSize(1000)

5. SubList and SubSet are views

List<String> sub = list.subList(1, 4);  // view, not copy
sub.clear();  // clears elements 1-3 from original list!
Part 21

Interview Deep Dive

Q1: What is the difference between Collection, Collections, and concurrent collections?

  • Collection<E> — interface in java.util; root of List/Set/Queue hierarchy.
  • Collections — utility class with static methods (sort, shuffle, unmodifiableList, etc.).
  • Concurrent collections — classes in java.util.concurrent designed for thread-safe concurrent access (ConcurrentHashMap, CopyOnWriteArrayList, etc.).

Q2: Why doesn't Map extend Collection?

Map stores key-value pairs — two objects per entry. Collection stores single elements. There's no conceptual fit; a Map.Entry<K,V> is the atomic unit, which doesn't match Collection<E>. The designers made this explicit. Maps participate through views: map.entrySet(), map.keySet(), map.values().

Q3: When does HashSet.add() return false?

When the element already exists in the set (based on equals() and hashCode()). Return value matters for deduplication logic — always check it in production code.

Q4: What is the modCount field?

An internal counter in AbstractList (and similar) incremented on every structural modification. The iterator saves the modCount at creation time; on each next(), it compares the current modCount. If they differ, a ConcurrentModificationException is thrown. This is a best-effort detection, not a strict guarantee — it's not thread-safe.

Q5: What is the performance of contains() for different collections?

Collection contains() Reason
ArrayList O(n) Linear scan
HashSet O(1) avg Hash bucket lookup
TreeSet O(log n) BST traversal
EnumSet O(1) Bit-mask check
LinkedList O(n) Linear scan

Practice — Lesson 21

Easy

  1. Write a method that accepts a Collection<String> (not a concrete type) and prints each element using a for-each loop.
  2. Create a HashSet<String> and demonstrate that add() returns false for a duplicate element.
  3. Demonstrate Collections.sort() and Collections.binarySearch() on an ArrayList<Integer>.
  4. Create an unmodifiable view of a List and verify that modifying the original list is reflected in the view.

Medium

  1. Implement a method that removes all strings starting with "temp" from an ArrayList<String> without a ConcurrentModificationException. Use three different approaches (iterator, removeIf, stream).
  2. Create a LinkedHashMap<String, Integer> that functions as an LRU cache (size ≤ 5) by overriding removeEldestEntry.
  3. Write a class Point(int x, int y) that properly overrides equals and hashCode, then use it as a HashSet element and HashMap key to verify correctness.
  4. Demonstrate fail-fast behavior: show the ConcurrentModificationException and then fix it using CopyOnWriteArrayList.

Advanced

  1. Implement a WordFrequencyCounter that reads a list of strings and returns a Map<String, Long> sorted by frequency descending, then alphabetically for ties. Use TreeMap with a custom comparator backed by a HashMap for counting.
  2. Implement a thread-safe event bus using ConcurrentHashMap<String, CopyOnWriteArrayList<Runnable>> where subscribers can register for named events and publishers can fire all subscribers concurrently.
  3. Demonstrate the mutable-key HashMap bug: put a List<String> as key, mutate the list, and show the value becomes unreachable. Then fix using an immutable record key.

Production

  1. You have a service receiving 10,000 products per second. Each product has a unique SKU (String) and a price. Design the collection strategy: (a) fast lookup by SKU, (b) top-10 most expensive products (maintained live), (c) products sorted by name for pagination. Justify each collection choice with Big-O reasoning.
  2. A Spring service injects List<PaymentProcessor> beans. Add three processors with different priorities. Write a unit test that verifies ordering using @Order annotations and the Spring TestContext.
  3. You inherit a legacy service using Hashtable<String, UserSession> (synchronized on every get/put). Migrate it to ConcurrentHashMap and explain which atomic operations (putIfAbsent, computeIfAbsent, merge) replace manual synchronized blocks.

Debugging

  1. The following code throws ConcurrentModificationException intermittently in production (not in tests). Identify why and fix it:
    java public void processQueue(List<Task> tasks) { for (Task t : tasks) { if (t.isComplete()) tasks.remove(t); else executor.submit(t::run); } }
  2. A HashSet<User> contains duplicate users after a refactor. The User class was changed from a POJO to a JPA @Entity. Explain why duplicates appeared and how to fix.

Interview

  1. Explain the contract between equals() and hashCode(). What happens if only equals() is overridden? What if only hashCode() is overridden?
  2. Describe the internal structure of HashMap (array of buckets, linked list / red-black tree after Java 8 for chains ≥ 8). What is the significance of the load factor?
  3. "ConcurrentHashMap is always better than HashMap in a multi-threaded environment." Evaluate this statement. When would you still use HashMap?
  4. What is the difference between Iterator.remove() and Collection.remove()? Which is safe during iteration and why?
