Part 1

What Is a Queue and Why It Exists

A Queue is a collection designed for holding elements prior to processing, where the order of processing is defined by the queue's policy. The canonical policy is FIFO (First-In, First-Out): the element that has waited the longest is processed next. This mirrors real-world queues — a print spooler, a web server's request backlog, a task scheduler's work queue.

The java.util.Queue<E> interface extends java.util.Collection<E> and represents the general contract: elements enter at the tail, leave from the head. The interface makes no mandate about ordering — implementations may use FIFO, priority ordering, LIFO, or any other policy.

Why Java provides multiple Queue implementations:

Need Implementation
FIFO, single-threaded, fast ArrayDeque
Elements processed by priority PriorityQueue
Thread-safe producer-consumer, bounded ArrayBlockingQueue
Thread-safe producer-consumer, unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue
Thread-safe, priority-ordered, concurrent PriorityBlockingQueue
Zero-latency handoff between threads SynchronousQueue
Delayed task execution DelayQueue
Lock-free, non-blocking FIFO ConcurrentLinkedQueue

Queues are the backbone of concurrent systems. Understanding their contracts, blocking semantics, and ordering guarantees is essential for building correct producer-consumer pipelines, thread pools, and task schedulers.

Part 2

The `Queue` Interface: Two Method Families

Queue defines six methods organized into two families distinguished by their failure behavior:

public interface Queue<E> extends Collection<E> {

    // ── Throws exception on failure ─────────────────────────
    boolean add(E e);     // insert; throws IllegalStateException if full
    E       remove();     // retrieve & remove head; throws NoSuchElementException if empty
    E       element();    // peek head; throws NoSuchElementException if empty

    // ── Returns special value on failure ────────────────────
    boolean offer(E e);   // insert; returns false if full (preferred for bounded queues)
    E       poll();       // retrieve & remove head; returns null if empty
    E       peek();       // peek head; returns null if empty
}

Which family to use:

Scenario Use
Bounded queue where full = logic error add (exception alerts you)
Bounded queue where full = expected condition offer (check return value)
Empty queue = expected condition poll / peek (null-check)
Empty queue = bug remove / element (exception alerts you)

ASCII: Queue Operation Diagram

FIFO Queue — elements enter at TAIL, leave from HEAD

  offer("A")         offer("B")         offer("C")
     │                  │                  │
     ▼                  ▼                  ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  HEAD                          TAIL      │
  │  [A]   ←  [B]   ←  [C]                  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────┘
     │
  poll() → returns "A", queue becomes [B] ← [C]
  peek() → returns "B" without removing

  After poll():
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  HEAD                TAIL                │
  │  [B]   ←  [C]                            │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────┘
Part 3

`ArrayDeque` as a FIFO Queue

For single-threaded FIFO queue needs, ArrayDeque is the recommended choice over LinkedList. Despite implementing Deque (double-ended queue), ArrayDeque used with only offer/poll behaves as a standard FIFO queue.

Why ArrayDeque beats LinkedList for queues:
- Memory: No per-element Node objects. Uses a resizable circular array — each element is a raw reference, saving 2 pointers and an object header per entry.
- CPU cache: Array elements are contiguous in memory; iterating is cache-friendly. Linked list nodes are scattered on the heap.
- GC pressure: Fewer objects means fewer GC roots and less allocation pressure.

ArrayDeque internal layout (circular array of capacity 16):

  head=4, tail=8, size=4
  elements: [null, null, null, null, "A", "B", "C", "D", null, ...]
                                     ▲head                ▲tail

  offer("E"):  elements[8]="E", tail=9
  poll():      returns elements[4]="A", head=5

  Wrap-around: when tail reaches end of array, it wraps to index 0
  Resize: when head==tail (full), double capacity and copy

Queue<String> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();

// Enqueue
queue.offer("first");
queue.offer("second");
queue.offer("third");

// Dequeue — FIFO order
System.out.println(queue.poll()); // "first"
System.out.println(queue.poll()); // "second"
System.out.println(queue.peek()); // "third" (not removed)
System.out.println(queue.size()); // 1

// Drain the queue
while (!queue.isEmpty()) {
    process(queue.poll());
}
Part 4

`PriorityQueue`: Heap-Based Priority Ordering

PriorityQueue<E> stores elements such that poll() always returns the smallest element according to natural ordering or a supplied Comparator. It is backed by a binary min-heap — a complete binary tree stored in an array where every parent is smaller than its children.

Binary min-heap properties:
- Root (index 0) is always the minimum element.
- For node at index i: left child at 2i+1, right child at 2i+2, parent at (i-1)/2.
- offer (sift-up): insert at end, bubble up to restore heap property — O(log n).
- poll (sift-down): remove root, move last element to root, bubble down — O(log n).
- peek: read root without removal — O(1).

ASCII: Priority Heap (min-heap) containing {1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 4, 6}

         Tree view:            Array representation:
              1                [1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 4, 6]
            /   \               0  1  2  3  4  5  6
           3     5
          / \   / \
         7   9 4   6

  offer(2):
    Insert at end: [1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 4, 6, 2]
    Sift up: 2 < parent(7) → swap → 2 < parent(3) → swap
    Result: [1, 2, 5, 3, 9, 4, 6, 7]
              1
            /   \
           2     5
          / \   / \
         3   9 4   6
        /
       7

  poll():
    Remove root (1), move last (7) to root
    Sift down: 7 > min(2,5) → swap with 2
    Result: [2, 3, 5, 7, 9, 4, 6]

// Natural ordering (min-heap)
PriorityQueue<Integer> pq = new PriorityQueue<>();
pq.offer(5);
pq.offer(1);
pq.offer(3);
pq.offer(2);
pq.offer(4);

while (!pq.isEmpty()) {
    System.out.print(pq.poll() + " "); // 1 2 3 4 5 — ascending order
}

// Custom ordering: max-heap (largest first)
PriorityQueue<Integer> maxHeap = new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.reverseOrder());
maxHeap.offer(5); maxHeap.offer(1); maxHeap.offer(3);
System.out.println(maxHeap.poll()); // 5

// Task scheduling: highest priority (lowest number) first
record Task(int priority, String name) implements Comparable<Task> {
    @Override public int compareTo(Task o) {
        return Integer.compare(this.priority, o.priority);
    }
}

PriorityQueue<Task> taskQueue = new PriorityQueue<>();
taskQueue.offer(new Task(3, "low-priority job"));
taskQueue.offer(new Task(1, "critical alert"));
taskQueue.offer(new Task(2, "normal job"));

System.out.println(taskQueue.poll().name()); // "critical alert"
System.out.println(taskQueue.poll().name()); // "normal job"

Important caveat: PriorityQueue does NOT guarantee ordering when iterating with a for-each loop or using toString(). Only poll() gives you elements in priority order.

Part 5

`BlockingQueue`: The Concurrent Queue Family

BlockingQueue<E> extends Queue with blocking and timed operations for thread-safe producer-consumer patterns. It is the foundation of Java's executor service thread pools.

public interface BlockingQueue<E> extends Queue<E> {

    // ── Blocks indefinitely ──────────────────────────────────
    void put(E e) throws InterruptedException;    // blocks if full
    E    take()   throws InterruptedException;    // blocks if empty

    // ── Blocks with timeout ──────────────────────────────────
    boolean offer(E e, long timeout, TimeUnit unit) throws InterruptedException;
    E       poll(long timeout, TimeUnit unit)        throws InterruptedException;

    // ── Non-blocking (inherited from Queue) ─────────────────
    boolean offer(E e);
    E       poll();

    // ── Capacity ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    int remainingCapacity();  // Integer.MAX_VALUE for unbounded queues
    int drainTo(Collection<? super E> c);  // bulk-remove
}

The four method behaviors at a glance:

Action Throws exception Returns special value Blocks Times out
Insert add(e) offer(e) put(e) offer(e, t, u)
Remove remove() poll() take() poll(t, u)
Examine element() peek() — —
Part 6

`ArrayBlockingQueue`: Bounded FIFO with Lock

ArrayBlockingQueue<E> is a bounded, array-backed FIFO queue protected by a single ReentrantLock with two Condition objects (notEmpty, notFull).

Architecture:

ArrayBlockingQueue (capacity = 4)

  ReentrantLock
  ├── Condition: notFull  (producers wait here when full)
  └── Condition: notEmpty (consumers wait here when empty)

  Circular array: [  A  |  B  |  C  |     ]
                  ▲head              ▲tail

  put("D") when full:
    lock acquired → queue is full → notFull.await()
    [producer thread parks here, lock released]
    consumer calls take() → removes "A", signals notFull
    producer wakes up → inserts "D" → releases lock

  take() when empty:
    lock acquired → queue is empty → notEmpty.await()
    [consumer thread parks here, lock released]
    producer calls put() → inserts element, signals notEmpty
    consumer wakes up → removes element → releases lock

// Classic producer-consumer with ArrayBlockingQueue
BlockingQueue<String> queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(10);

// Producer thread
Thread producer = new Thread(() -> {
    try {
        for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) {
            queue.put("task-" + i);   // blocks if queue is full
            System.out.println("Produced: task-" + i);
        }
        queue.put("POISON_PILL");     // signal completion
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
    }
});

// Consumer thread
Thread consumer = new Thread(() -> {
    try {
        while (true) {
            String task = queue.take();  // blocks if queue is empty
            if ("POISON_PILL".equals(task)) break;
            System.out.println("Consumed: " + task);
            processTask(task);
        }
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
    }
});

producer.start();
consumer.start();
Part 7

`LinkedBlockingQueue`: Optionally Bounded with Two Locks

LinkedBlockingQueue<E> is a linked-node FIFO queue that uses separate locks for put and take operations (putLock and takeLock), enabling higher throughput in high-contention scenarios by allowing a producer and consumer to operate simultaneously.

LinkedBlockingQueue (capacity = Integer.MAX_VALUE by default)

  putLock  → guards: tail pointer, putCount
  takeLock → guards: head pointer, takeCount

  head → [dummy] → [A] → [B] → [C] → tail

  Producer calling put():
    acquires putLock
    creates new Node("D"), tail.next = new node, tail = new node
    signals notEmpty if count was 0
    releases putLock

  Consumer calling take():
    acquires takeLock
    head = head.next (dummy advances), returns first real element
    signals notFull if count was capacity
    releases takeLock

  Producer and Consumer CAN execute simultaneously (different locks)!
  → Higher throughput than ArrayBlockingQueue under high contention

// Unbounded (logically bounded by available heap)
BlockingQueue<Runnable> taskQueue = new LinkedBlockingQueue<>();

// Bounded (explicitly capped)
BlockingQueue<LogEvent> logQueue = new LinkedBlockingQueue<>(1000);

// This is exactly what ThreadPoolExecutor uses internally:
ExecutorService pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
    4, 8, 60L, TimeUnit.SECONDS,
    new LinkedBlockingQueue<>(500)  // task buffer between core and max pool
);

ArrayBlockingQueue vs LinkedBlockingQueue:

Aspect ArrayBlockingQueue LinkedBlockingQueue
Backing Array (preallocated) Linked nodes
Bounded? Always (required) Optional
Locks One lock (put + take share) Two locks (put lock ≠ take lock)
Throughput Lower under high contention Higher under high contention
Memory Fixed, predictable Variable, GC pressure
Capacity Specified at construction Integer.MAX_VALUE by default
Part 8

`offer`/`poll` vs `add`/`remove`: When Each Matters

This distinction matters most in bounded queues where overflow is expected behavior:

BlockingQueue<String> bounded = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(3);
bounded.add("a");
bounded.add("b");
bounded.add("c");

// Queue is now full (capacity=3)

// Option 1: add() — throws IllegalStateException
try {
    bounded.add("d"); // throws! Queue full
} catch (IllegalStateException e) {
    System.out.println("Queue full");
}

// Option 2: offer() — returns false silently
boolean accepted = bounded.offer("d");
System.out.println(accepted); // false — caller decides what to do

// Option 3: offer() with timeout
boolean accepted2 = bounded.offer("d", 100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
// waits up to 100ms for space, returns false if still full

// remove() vs poll() — symmetric for empty queue
Queue<String> empty = new ArrayDeque<>();
try {
    empty.remove(); // throws NoSuchElementException
} catch (NoSuchElementException e) { ... }

String val = empty.poll(); // returns null — no exception

Design guidance:
- In application code working with bounded queues, prefer offer/poll — they make the "queue full" and "queue empty" cases explicit in your control flow without exception overhead.
- In thread-pool and system-level code where blocking is intentional, use put/take.
- Use add/remove when the exception represents a genuine programming error.

Part 9

`SynchronousQueue`: Zero-Capacity Handoff

SynchronousQueue<E> is a special-purpose queue with zero internal capacity. Every put operation blocks until a corresponding take arrives (and vice versa). It is a rendezvous mechanism — a direct handoff between threads with no buffering.

SynchronousQueue

  Producer                    Consumer
     │                            │
     │ put("task")                │
     │ ── waits ──────────────────┤ take()
     │                            │
     │ ◄─── handoff complete ────►│
     │                            │
  unblocks                    unblocks

  No internal array. No nodes. No buffering.
  put() and take() must rendezvous simultaneously.

// This is what Executors.newCachedThreadPool() uses:
ExecutorService cached = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
    0, Integer.MAX_VALUE, 60L, TimeUnit.SECONDS,
    new SynchronousQueue<>()
);
// Each submitted task either goes to an existing idle thread immediately
// or spawns a new thread — the SynchronousQueue prevents buffering

SynchronousQueue is ideal when you want maximum throughput in cached thread pools, where buffering would hide the need for new threads.

Part 10

`PriorityBlockingQueue`: Concurrent Priority Queue

PriorityBlockingQueue<E> combines the min-heap behavior of PriorityQueue with the blocking semantics of BlockingQueue. It is unbounded (grows as needed) and therefore put never blocks — only take can block (when empty).

PriorityBlockingQueue<Task> priorityQueue =
    new PriorityBlockingQueue<>(11, Comparator.comparingInt(Task::priority));

// Multiple producer threads
Runnable producer = () -> {
    for (int i = 0; i < 50; i++) {
        int priority = ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt(1, 10);
        priorityQueue.put(new Task(priority, "task-" + i));
    }
};

// Consumer always gets highest-priority task
Runnable consumer = () -> {
    while (!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) {
        try {
            Task task = priorityQueue.take(); // blocks if empty
            System.out.println("Processing priority=" + task.priority()
                               + " " + task.name());
        } catch (InterruptedException e) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        }
    }
};
Part 11

`DelayQueue`: Time-Based Priority

DelayQueue<E extends Delayed> is an unbounded blocking queue where elements become available only after their delay has expired. Elements must implement java.util.concurrent.Delayed:

interface Delayed extends Comparable<Delayed> {
    long getDelay(TimeUnit unit);
}

// Scheduled task with expiry
class ScheduledTask implements Delayed {
    private final String name;
    private final long executeAt; // epoch millis

    ScheduledTask(String name, long delayMs) {
        this.name = name;
        this.executeAt = System.currentTimeMillis() + delayMs;
    }

    @Override
    public long getDelay(TimeUnit unit) {
        return unit.convert(executeAt - System.currentTimeMillis(),
                            TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
    }

    @Override
    public int compareTo(Delayed o) {
        return Long.compare(executeAt,
                            ((ScheduledTask) o).executeAt);
    }
}

DelayQueue<ScheduledTask> scheduler = new DelayQueue<>();
scheduler.put(new ScheduledTask("job-1", 5000)); // executes in 5 seconds
scheduler.put(new ScheduledTask("job-2", 1000)); // executes in 1 second
scheduler.put(new ScheduledTask("job-3", 3000)); // executes in 3 seconds

// Worker thread
while (true) {
    ScheduledTask task = scheduler.take(); // blocks until earliest task is ready
    System.out.println("Executing: " + task.name); // job-2 → job-3 → job-1
}

DelayQueue underpins ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor internally.

Part 12

`ConcurrentLinkedQueue`: Lock-Free FIFO

ConcurrentLinkedQueue<E> is a non-blocking, thread-safe FIFO queue using the Michael-Scott queue algorithm based on CAS (Compare-And-Swap) atomic operations. No locks, no blocking, no waiting.

Michael-Scott Queue (CAS-based)

  head → [dummy] →CAS→ [A] →CAS→ [B] →CAS→ [C] ← tail

  offer("D") — lock-free:
    1. Read current tail
    2. CAS: tail.next from null to new Node("D")
    3. If CAS wins → update tail pointer
    4. If CAS fails → another thread beat us → retry

  poll() — lock-free:
    1. Read current head
    2. CAS: head from current to head.next
    3. If CAS wins → return element
    4. If CAS fails → retry

ConcurrentLinkedQueue<String> clq = new ConcurrentLinkedQueue<>();

// Safe for concurrent use without synchronization
clq.offer("a");
clq.offer("b");

// size() is O(n) — traverse the whole list! Avoid in hot paths
int size = clq.size(); // expensive

// isEmpty() is O(1) — preferred
if (!clq.isEmpty()) {
    String head = clq.poll();
}

Key caveat: size() on ConcurrentLinkedQueue traverses the entire queue — O(n). Never call it in a tight loop. Use isEmpty() instead.

Part 14

Production Pattern: Task Queue with Worker Pool

The producer-consumer pattern using a BlockingQueue as a work buffer between a producer thread and a fixed thread pool is one of the most common patterns in Java backend services:

@Component
public class TaskProcessingService {

    private final BlockingQueue<ProcessingTask> taskQueue;
    private final ExecutorService workerPool;
    private volatile boolean running = true;

    public TaskProcessingService(
            @Value("${task.queue.capacity:1000}") int capacity,
            @Value("${task.worker.threads:4}")    int workers) {
        this.taskQueue  = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(capacity);
        this.workerPool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(workers);

        // Start worker threads
        for (int i = 0; i < workers; i++) {
            workerPool.submit(this::workerLoop);
        }
    }

    // Called by producers (e.g. REST endpoint, Kafka consumer)
    public boolean submit(ProcessingTask task) {
        return taskQueue.offer(task, 100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
        // returns false if queue is full after 100ms → apply backpressure
    }

    private void workerLoop() {
        while (running && !Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) {
            try {
                ProcessingTask task = taskQueue.poll(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
                if (task != null) {
                    processTask(task);
                }
            } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
                break;
            }
        }
    }

    @PreDestroy
    public void shutdown() {
        running = false;
        workerPool.shutdown();
        try {
            workerPool.awaitTermination(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
        } catch (InterruptedException e) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
            workerPool.shutdownNow();
        }
    }
}
Part 15

Production Pattern: Rate-Limiting Buffer

A bounded BlockingQueue naturally provides backpressure — a mechanism to slow down producers when consumers can't keep up:

@Service
public class RateLimitedEmailSender {

    // Buffer max 500 pending emails; producers block/reject beyond this
    private final BlockingQueue<EmailJob> emailBuffer =
        new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(500);

    private final ScheduledExecutorService scheduler =
        Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor();

    @PostConstruct
    public void startSender() {
        // Send at most 100 emails/second using a fixed-rate schedule
        scheduler.scheduleAtFixedRate(this::sendBatch,
            0, 10, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);  // every 10ms → ~100/sec
    }

    public boolean enqueue(EmailJob job) {
        boolean accepted = emailBuffer.offer(job);
        if (!accepted) {
            metrics.increment("email.queue.rejected");
            // Return 429 Too Many Requests to caller
        }
        return accepted;
    }

    private void sendBatch() {
        List<EmailJob> batch = new ArrayList<>(10);
        emailBuffer.drainTo(batch, 10);  // drain up to 10 at once
        batch.forEach(this::sendEmail);
    }
}
Part 16

Production Pattern: Priority Work Queue

public class PriorityTaskExecutor {

    private final PriorityBlockingQueue<PriorityTask> queue =
        new PriorityBlockingQueue<>(100,
            Comparator.comparingInt(PriorityTask::getPriority)
                      .thenComparingLong(PriorityTask::getSubmittedAt));

    public void submit(PriorityTask task) {
        queue.offer(task);
        metrics.gauge("priority.queue.size", queue.size());
    }

    // Worker: always picks highest-priority pending task
    private void workerLoop() {
        while (!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) {
            try {
                PriorityTask task = queue.take();
                try {
                    task.execute();
                } catch (Exception e) {
                    if (task.canRetry()) {
                        // Requeue with lower priority to avoid starvation
                        task.decrementPriority();
                        queue.offer(task);
                    } else {
                        deadLetterQueue.publish(task);
                    }
                }
            } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
            }
        }
    }
}

Spring Integration and Spring Batch

Spring Integration: QueueChannel

Spring Integration models asynchronous message passing using a QueueChannel, which wraps a BlockingQueue:

@Configuration
public class IntegrationConfig {

    // Backed by a LinkedBlockingQueue with capacity 100
    @Bean
    public QueueChannel orderChannel() {
        return new QueueChannel(100);
    }

    @Bean
    public IntegrationFlow orderProcessingFlow() {
        return IntegrationFlow
            .from("orderChannel")
            .handle(orderService::processOrder)
            .get();
    }
}

// Sending messages
@Autowired
private QueueChannel orderChannel;

public void submitOrder(Order order) {
    boolean sent = orderChannel.send(
        MessageBuilder.withPayload(order).build(),
        5000  // timeout 5 seconds
    );
    if (!sent) {
        throw new ServiceUnavailableException("Order queue full");
    }
}

Spring Batch: Step-scoped chunk processing uses bounded queues internally

The SimpleAsyncTaskExecutor and TaskExecutorRepeatTemplate in Spring Batch coordinate between reader and writer steps using BlockingQueue semantics to buffer chunks.

Spring's ThreadPoolTaskExecutor queue:

@Bean
public ThreadPoolTaskExecutor taskExecutor() {
    ThreadPoolTaskExecutor executor = new ThreadPoolTaskExecutor();
    executor.setCorePoolSize(4);
    executor.setMaxPoolSize(8);
    executor.setQueueCapacity(200);     // ArrayBlockingQueue(200) internally
    executor.setRejectedExecutionHandler(new CallerRunsPolicy());
    executor.initialize();
    return executor;
}
Part 18

Kafka as a Distributed Queue: The Contrast

Understanding BlockingQueue in the JVM helps you appreciate what Apache Kafka does at the distributed level:

Aspect BlockingQueue (JVM) Apache Kafka
Scope Single JVM process Distributed cluster
Durability Memory only (lost on crash) Persisted to disk
Consumers Multiple threads, single process Consumer groups across services
Ordering FIFO / priority within queue Per-partition ordering
Backpressure put blocks or offer rejects Producer blocks, consumer lag
Replay Not possible Configurable retention period
Throughput Millions/sec (in-memory) Hundreds of thousands/sec (network)
Failure recovery None (in-memory) Replication, leader election

Typical architecture: Kafka consumers write to an in-process BlockingQueue to decouple Kafka polling from business logic:

@KafkaListener(topics = "orders")
public void onMessage(ConsumerRecord<String, Order> record) {
    // Fast Kafka poll loop — just enqueue
    boolean accepted = internalQueue.offer(record.value(), 100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
    if (!accepted) {
        // Pause Kafka consumption — apply backpressure upstream
        consumer.pause(Collections.singleton(record.partition()));
        metrics.increment("kafka.consumer.paused");
    }
}
Part 19

Queue vs Stack: Conceptual and Practical Contrast

Q: What is the difference between a Queue and a Stack?

Aspect Queue (FIFO) Stack (LIFO)
Insertion Tail (offer/add) Top (push)
Removal Head (poll/remove) Top (pop)
Order First in, first out Last in, first out
Use case Task queues, BFS, buffers DFS, undo/redo, call stack
Java interface Queue<E> Deque<E> (use push/pop)
Recommended impl ArrayDeque ArrayDeque 
Queue (FIFO):                  Stack (LIFO):
  offer A, B, C                  push A, B, C
  ┌───────────────┐               ┌───┐
  │ A → B → C    │               │ C │ ← top (pop returns C first)
  └───────────────┘               │ B │
  poll → A first                  │ A │
                                  └───┘

BFS (Queue): explore level by level
DFS (Stack): explore branch fully before backtracking

// Stack using ArrayDeque (preferred over legacy java.util.Stack)
Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
stack.push(1);
stack.push(2);
stack.push(3);
System.out.println(stack.pop()); // 3 — LIFO
System.out.println(stack.pop()); // 2

Why not use java.util.Stack? It extends Vector, which is synchronized and largely obsolete. ArrayDeque is faster, unsynchronized (use LinkedBlockingDeque if you need concurrent LIFO), and the recommended replacement.

Part 20

Interview Deep Dive: PriorityQueue Ordering

Q: How does PriorityQueue order elements?

A: By default, PriorityQueue uses the natural ordering of elements (requires Comparable). The smallest element (minimum compareTo) is at the head and returned first by poll(). You can provide a Comparator at construction to override this. Internally it uses a binary min-heap stored in an array.

Q: Why doesn't iterating a PriorityQueue yield elements in priority order?

A: The internal array is heap-ordered, not fully sorted. Only the root (index 0) is guaranteed to be the minimum. Elements at other positions satisfy the heap property (parent ≤ children) but siblings are not ordered relative to each other. Iteration visits array positions in order, not in heap-priority order.

PriorityQueue<Integer> pq = new PriorityQueue<>(Arrays.asList(5, 1, 3, 2, 4));
System.out.println(pq);            // may print [1, 2, 3, 5, 4] — heap internal layout
pq.forEach(System.out::print);     // NOT sorted order
while (!pq.isEmpty()) System.out.print(pq.poll() + " "); // 1 2 3 4 5 — correct

Q: How would you implement a k-way merge using PriorityQueue?

// Merge k sorted lists
public List<Integer> mergeKSortedLists(List<List<Integer>> lists) {
    // Min-heap: (value, listIndex, elementIndex)
    PriorityQueue<int[]> heap = new PriorityQueue<>(
        Comparator.comparingInt(arr -> arr[0])
    );

    // Initialize heap with first element from each list
    for (int i = 0; i < lists.size(); i++) {
        if (!lists.get(i).isEmpty()) {
            heap.offer(new int[]{lists.get(i).get(0), i, 0});
        }
    }

    List<Integer> result = new ArrayList<>();
    while (!heap.isEmpty()) {
        int[] curr = heap.poll();
        result.add(curr[0]);
        int listIdx = curr[1], elemIdx = curr[2];
        if (elemIdx + 1 < lists.get(listIdx).size()) {
            heap.offer(new int[]{
                lists.get(listIdx).get(elemIdx + 1), listIdx, elemIdx + 1
            });
        }
    }
    return result;
}

Q: What is starvation in a PriorityQueue-based task queue and how do you prevent it?

A: Low-priority tasks may never be processed if high-priority tasks arrive continuously. Prevention strategies:
1. Aging: Increase priority as wait time increases (e.g., priority = basePriority - waitTimeInSeconds).
2. Separate queues: Maintain multiple queues with round-robin or weighted scheduling between them.
3. Bounded priority range: Cap priority levels (e.g., 1-5) and use a round-robin within each level.

Part 21

Interview Deep Dive: Blocking, Capacity, and Concurrency

Q: What is the difference between ArrayBlockingQueue and LinkedBlockingQueue?

A: ArrayBlockingQueue uses a single ReentrantLock shared between producers and consumers, backed by a preallocated array. LinkedBlockingQueue uses separate put/take locks, enabling producers and consumers to operate concurrently on different ends. This makes LinkedBlockingQueue higher throughput under high contention. ArrayBlockingQueue has predictable, bounded memory; LinkedBlockingQueue incurs per-node object allocation.

Q: When would you use SynchronousQueue?

A: When you want a direct handoff with no buffering — the producer blocks until a consumer is ready. This is used in Executors.newCachedThreadPool() because buffering would prevent the pool from detecting that it needs a new thread. If a task can immediately hand off to an idle thread, it does. If not, a new thread is spawned.

Q: Can a PriorityQueue have duplicate priorities?

A: Yes. The heap property only requires parent ≤ children; it does not require uniqueness. Two tasks with equal priority may be returned in any order. To create a stable ordering for equal-priority elements, add a secondary comparator on a monotonically increasing sequence number:

AtomicLong seq = new AtomicLong();
PriorityQueue<Task> pq = new PriorityQueue<>(
    Comparator.comparingInt(Task::priority)
              .thenComparingLong(Task::sequenceNumber)
);
// Now tasks with equal priority are ordered by submission time

Q: What happens when you call size() on a ConcurrentLinkedQueue in a hot path?

A: size() traverses the entire linked list — O(n). This is documented behavior. In a concurrent context with millions of elements, this is catastrophic for performance. Use isEmpty() (O(1)) for empty checks, or maintain a separate AtomicLong counter if you need approximate sizes.

Part 22

Summary Table

Implementation Ordering Bounded Thread-Safe Blocking Best For
ArrayDeque FIFO No No No General-purpose FIFO, single-threaded
PriorityQueue Min-heap No No No Priority-based processing, single-threaded
LinkedList FIFO No No No Legacy code, rarely preferred
ArrayBlockingQueue FIFO Required Yes Yes Bounded producer-consumer, low memory variance
LinkedBlockingQueue FIFO Optional Yes Yes High-throughput producer-consumer
PriorityBlockingQueue Min-heap No Yes Yes (empty) Concurrent priority processing
SynchronousQueue N/A 0 Yes Always Thread handoff, cached pools
DelayQueue Delay+Heap No Yes Yes Scheduled/delayed execution
ConcurrentLinkedQueue FIFO No Yes (CAS) No Lock-free concurrent reads

Core takeaways:
- ArrayDeque is the default FIFO queue for single-threaded use — prefer it over LinkedList.
- PriorityQueue is a min-heap: poll() always returns the smallest element; iteration is NOT ordered.
- BlockingQueue variants (ArrayBlockingQueue, LinkedBlockingQueue) are the foundation of producer-consumer and thread-pool patterns.
- Prefer offer/poll over add/remove in bounded-queue production code.
- SynchronousQueue enables zero-buffer direct thread handoff.
- ConcurrentLinkedQueue.size() is O(n) — never call it in hot paths.
- Understand that Kafka is essentially a distributed BlockingQueue with durability, replay, and consumer groups added.

Practice

Exercise 1 — Round-Robin Scheduler

Implement a RoundRobinScheduler<T> that accepts a list of tasks and cycles through them repeatedly using a Queue. Each call to next() should return the next task in round-robin order (wrapping back to the start after the last task).

public class RoundRobinScheduler<T> {
    private final Queue<T> queue;

    public RoundRobinScheduler(List<T> tasks) {
        this.queue = new ArrayDeque<>(tasks);
    }

    public T next() {
        T task = queue.poll();   // take from head
        queue.offer(task);       // put back at tail
        return task;
    }
}

// Usage
RoundRobinScheduler<String> scheduler =
    new RoundRobinScheduler<>(List.of("server-1", "server-2", "server-3"));
for (int i = 0; i < 6; i++) {
    System.out.println(scheduler.next()); // 1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3
}

Exercise 2 — BFS Using Queue

Implement Breadth-First Search on a binary tree using a Queue. Return all nodes level by level:

record TreeNode(int val, TreeNode left, TreeNode right) {
    TreeNode(int val) { this(val, null, null); }
}

public List<List<Integer>> levelOrder(TreeNode root) {
    List<List<Integer>> result = new ArrayList<>();
    if (root == null) return result;

    Queue<TreeNode> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();
    queue.offer(root);

    while (!queue.isEmpty()) {
        int levelSize = queue.size();
        List<Integer> level = new ArrayList<>(levelSize);

        for (int i = 0; i < levelSize; i++) {
            TreeNode node = queue.poll();
            level.add(node.val());
            if (node.left()  != null) queue.offer(node.left());
            if (node.right() != null) queue.offer(node.right());
        }
        result.add(level);
    }
    return result;
}

Exercise 3 — PriorityQueue Median Finder

Use two PriorityQueues (a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half) to find the running median as numbers are added one at a time:

public class MedianFinder {
    private final PriorityQueue<Integer> lower = // max-heap
        new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.reverseOrder());
    private final PriorityQueue<Integer> upper = // min-heap
        new PriorityQueue<>();

    public void addNum(int num) {
        lower.offer(num);
        upper.offer(lower.poll());   // balance: upper gets smallest of lower
        if (upper.size() > lower.size()) {
            lower.offer(upper.poll()); // keep lower.size >= upper.size
        }
    }

    public double findMedian() {
        return lower.size() > upper.size()
            ? lower.peek()
            : (lower.peek() + upper.peek()) / 2.0;
    }
}

Exercise 4 — Bounded Work Queue with Backpressure

Implement a BoundedWorkQueue that accepts Runnable tasks and processes them with a configurable number of worker threads. If the queue is full, submit() should return false (non-blocking rejection). Include a graceful shutdown() method that drains remaining tasks before stopping workers.

public class BoundedWorkQueue {
    private final BlockingQueue<Runnable> queue;
    private final List<Thread> workers;
    private volatile boolean running = true;

    public BoundedWorkQueue(int capacity, int workerCount) {
        this.queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(capacity);
        this.workers = new ArrayList<>(workerCount);
        for (int i = 0; i < workerCount; i++) {
            Thread t = new Thread(this::workerLoop, "worker-" + i);
            t.setDaemon(false);
            t.start();
            workers.add(t);
        }
    }

    public boolean submit(Runnable task) {
        return queue.offer(task);  // non-blocking: false if full
    }

    private void workerLoop() {
        while (running || !queue.isEmpty()) {
            try {
                Runnable task = queue.poll(100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
                if (task != null) task.run();
            } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
                break;
            }
        }
    }

    public void shutdown() throws InterruptedException {
        running = false;
        for (Thread t : workers) t.join(5000);
    }
}

Part 1

What Is a Deque?

A Deque (pronounced "deck") stands for Double-Ended Queue. It is a linear data structure that allows insertion and removal of elements from both ends — the front (head) and the back (tail). This makes it a strict superset of both Queue (FIFO) and Stack (LIFO): you can use a single Deque instance to model either, or combine both behaviors.

In Java, Deque<E> is an interface in java.util, extending Queue<E>, which itself extends Collection<E>. The hierarchy looks like this:

Iterable<E>
  └── Collection<E>
        └── Queue<E>
              └── Deque<E>
                    ├── ArrayDeque<E>    (resizable circular array — preferred)
                    └── LinkedList<E>   (doubly-linked list — also implements List<E>)

The two primary concrete implementations are:

Class Internal Structure Thread-Safe? Null Elements?
ArrayDeque Resizable circular array No No
LinkedList Doubly-linked list No Yes

There is also java.util.concurrent.LinkedBlockingDeque, a thread-safe bounded deque used in concurrent pipelines — covered briefly in Part 14.

The Deque interface was introduced in Java 6 (2006). Before that, developers relied on the legacy Stack class (introduced in Java 1.0) or manually managed a LinkedList. Today, ArrayDeque is the idiomatic, recommended replacement for both Stack and Queue in single-threaded code.

Part 2

The Deque Interface: Full API Surface

Deque<E> exposes a rich, symmetric API. Operations come in three flavours for each end:

  1. Throws exception on failure (capacity violation or empty deque)
  2. Returns special value (null or false) on failure — safer in most application code
  3. Blocks (only on BlockingDeque implementations — see Part 14)

Head (Front) Operations

Action Throws Exception Returns Special Value
Insert at head addFirst(e) offerFirst(e) → boolean
Remove from head removeFirst() pollFirst() → E or null
Inspect head getFirst() peekFirst() → E or null

Tail (Back) Operations

Action Throws Exception Returns Special Value
Insert at tail addLast(e) offerLast(e) → boolean
Remove from tail removeLast() pollLast() → E or null
Inspect tail getLast() peekLast() → E or null

Queue-Equivalent Methods (delegating to tail insert / head remove)

Queue Method Deque Equivalent
add(e) addLast(e)
offer(e) offerLast(e)
remove() removeFirst()
poll() pollFirst()
element() getFirst()
peek() peekFirst()

Stack-Equivalent Methods (delegating to head insert / head remove)

Stack Method Deque Equivalent
push(e) addFirst(e)
pop() removeFirst()
peek() peekFirst()

Understanding these delegations is crucial: push puts elements at the front, so the deque acts as a LIFO stack. offer puts elements at the back, so the deque acts as a FIFO queue. Both behaviors are supported simultaneously.

Part 3

ArrayDeque: The Circular Buffer Internals

ArrayDeque stores elements in a resizable circular array. The key insight: instead of shifting elements on every insertion or removal (O(n)), a pair of integer pointers — head and tail — track the logical front and back of the data. Both pointers wrap around when they reach the end of the physical array, giving the "circular" effect.

ASCII Diagram: ArrayDeque Circular Buffer

Initial state after addLast(A), addLast(B), addLast(C):

Physical array (capacity = 8):
 Index:  0    1    2    3    4    5    6    7
        [ ]  [A]  [B]  [C]  [ ]  [ ]  [ ]  [ ]
              ↑                   ↑
            head                tail
            (1)                 (4)

Logical sequence: A → B → C

After addFirst(Z) (insert at front, head moves left by 1):

 Index:  0    1    2    3    4    5    6    7
        [ ]  [A]  [B]  [C]  [ ]  [ ]  [ ]  [ ]
         ↑    ↑                   ↑
       new   old-head            tail
       head

 Index:  0    1    2    3    4    5    6    7
        [Z]  [A]  [B]  [C]  [ ]  [ ]  [ ]  [ ]
         ↑                   ↑
        head                tail

Logical sequence: Z → A → B → C

After pollFirst() (remove from front, head moves right):

 Index:  0    1    2    3    4    5    6    7
        [ ]  [A]  [B]  [C]  [ ]  [ ]  [ ]  [ ]
              ↑              ↑
            head            tail

Logical sequence: A → B → C

Wrap-around scenario — after many operations where head is near the end:

 Index:  0    1    2    3    4    5    6    7
        [E]  [F]  [ ]  [ ]  [ ]  [B]  [C]  [D]
                   ↑              ↑
                  tail           head

Logical sequence: B → C → D → E → F
(reading from head, wrapping around the physical boundary)

Resizing

When head == tail after an insertion (array is full), ArrayDeque doubles the capacity and copies elements into the new array, resetting head = 0. This amortized resize is identical in cost to ArrayList resizing — O(n) for the copy itself, but O(1) amortized over many operations.

Initial default capacity is 16 in OpenJDK. The capacity is always a power of two, enabling fast modulo via bitmasking: (head - 1) & (elements.length - 1) instead of (head - 1) % length.

Part 4

ArrayDeque vs LinkedList: When to Choose What

Both implement Deque<E>, but their performance profiles are very different.

Memory Layout

ArrayDeque stores all elements contiguously in one array. Modern CPUs prefetch cache lines ahead of the program counter, so iterating an ArrayDeque is cache-friendly — the next element is almost always already in L1/L2 cache.

LinkedList allocates a separate Node object for every element. Each node holds item, prev, and next references. A list of 1,000 integers creates 1,000 Node objects scattered across the heap. Traversal causes frequent cache misses as the CPU chases pointers to random heap addresses.

Performance Comparison

Operation ArrayDeque LinkedList
addFirst / addLast O(1) amortized O(1)
pollFirst / pollLast O(1) O(1)
peekFirst / peekLast O(1) O(1)
Random access (get(i)) O(n) — no index support O(n)
Memory per element ~4–8 bytes (array slot) ~32–48 bytes (Node object)
Cache friendliness Excellent Poor
Null elements Not allowed Allowed
Also implements List No Yes

Decision Rule

  • Default choice: ArrayDeque. Better cache behaviour, lower memory overhead, faster in benchmarks for typical push/pop/enqueue/dequeue workloads.
  • Use LinkedList when: you need a List interface and a Deque interface simultaneously, or you need null elements in the deque (rare and usually a design smell).
  • Never use LinkedList as a general-purpose queue. Its O(1) tail operations come with severe cache miss overhead that makes it consistently slower than ArrayDeque in practice.
Part 5

Using Deque as a Stack

The legacy java.util.Stack class (Java 1.0) extends Vector, which is synchronized. Every push, pop, and peek acquires a lock, even in single-threaded code. This is unnecessary overhead and the class carries decades of design baggage (it inherits Vector's get(int), set(int, E), etc., none of which belong to a stack abstraction).

The official recommendation since Java 6: use ArrayDeque as a stack.

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

// Stack usage pattern
Deque<String> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();

// Push — inserts at front
stack.push("first");
stack.push("second");
stack.push("third");
// Internal state (front → back): third, second, first

// Peek — read top without removing
System.out.println(stack.peek());   // "third"

// Pop — remove from front (LIFO order)
System.out.println(stack.pop());    // "third"
System.out.println(stack.pop());    // "second"
System.out.println(stack.pop());    // "first"

// Safe pop (returns null instead of throwing NoSuchElementException)
String top = stack.pollFirst();     // null (stack is empty)

Why push Inserts at the Front

It might seem counterintuitive that push calls addFirst. But think of a physical stack of plates: you always place the new plate on top (the front/accessible end), and you always take from the top. The "front" of the ArrayDeque is the top of the stack. push = addFirst, pop = removeFirst.

Legacy Stack Class — What Not to Do

// AVOID — legacy, synchronized unnecessarily, poor abstraction
import java.util.Stack;
Stack<Integer> legacyStack = new Stack<>();
legacyStack.push(1);
legacyStack.push(2);
legacyStack.pop(); // 2

// PREFER
Deque<Integer> modernStack = new ArrayDeque<>();
modernStack.push(1);
modernStack.push(2);
modernStack.pop(); // 2

The Stack class is not formally deprecated in the JDK as of Java 21, but every major style guide (Google, Oracle, Effective Java) explicitly recommends against using it.

Part 6

Using Deque as a Queue

When you want FIFO behaviour, offer at the tail and poll from the head:

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

Deque<String> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();

// Enqueue — add to back/tail
queue.offerLast("task-1");
queue.offerLast("task-2");
queue.offerLast("task-3");

// Dequeue — remove from front/head (FIFO order)
System.out.println(queue.pollFirst()); // "task-1"
System.out.println(queue.pollFirst()); // "task-2"
System.out.println(queue.pollFirst()); // "task-3"

// Via Queue interface alias methods (same behaviour)
Deque<Integer> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
q.offer(10);    // addLast under the hood
q.offer(20);
q.poll();       // 10 — removes from front
q.peek();       // 20 — inspects front, does not remove

This is identical in behaviour to using LinkedList as a queue, but significantly faster in practice.

Part 7

Using Deque as a Double-Ended Queue

The full power of Deque is when you need to insert and remove from both ends in the same algorithm — the feature that gives it the name.

Example: Sliding Window Maximum (Classic Interview Problem)

Given an array and a window size k, find the maximum element in every window of size k as the window slides across the array.

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

public class SlidingWindowMax {

    public static int[] maxSlidingWindow(int[] nums, int k) {
        if (nums == null || nums.length == 0) return new int[0];

        int n = nums.length;
        int[] result = new int[n - k + 1];
        // Deque stores INDICES; front always holds index of current window max
        Deque<Integer> deque = new ArrayDeque<>();

        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            // Remove indices that fall outside the current window from the front
            while (!deque.isEmpty() && deque.peekFirst() < i - k + 1) {
                deque.pollFirst();
            }

            // Remove indices from the back whose values are less than nums[i]
            // (they can never be the max while nums[i] is in the window)
            while (!deque.isEmpty() && nums[deque.peekLast()] < nums[i]) {
                deque.pollLast();
            }

            deque.offerLast(i);

            // Window is fully formed; record the maximum
            if (i >= k - 1) {
                result[i - k + 1] = nums[deque.peekFirst()];
            }
        }
        return result;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[] nums = {1, 3, -1, -3, 5, 3, 6, 7};
        int k = 3;
        int[] maxes = maxSlidingWindow(nums, k);
        // Output: [3, 3, 5, 5, 6, 7]
        for (int m : maxes) System.out.print(m + " ");
    }
}

This algorithm runs in O(n) time because each element is added and removed from the deque at most once. Without Deque's O(1) operations on both ends, the naive approach is O(n × k).

Part 8

Production Use Case: Undo/Redo Stack

Text editors, drawing apps, IDEs, and spreadsheets all implement undo/redo. The classic implementation uses two stacks: one for undoable actions and one for redoable actions.

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

public class UndoRedoManager<T> {

    private final Deque<T> undoStack = new ArrayDeque<>();
    private final Deque<T> redoStack = new ArrayDeque<>();

    /** Record a new action; clears redo history (as in most editors). */
    public void execute(T action) {
        undoStack.push(action);
        redoStack.clear();  // New action invalidates redo history
    }

    /** Undo the most recent action. */
    public T undo() {
        if (undoStack.isEmpty()) throw new IllegalStateException("Nothing to undo");
        T action = undoStack.pop();
        redoStack.push(action);
        return action;
    }

    /** Redo the most recently undone action. */
    public T redo() {
        if (redoStack.isEmpty()) throw new IllegalStateException("Nothing to redo");
        T action = redoStack.pop();
        undoStack.push(action);
        return action;
    }

    public boolean canUndo() { return !undoStack.isEmpty(); }
    public boolean canRedo() { return !redoStack.isEmpty(); }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        UndoRedoManager<String> editor = new UndoRedoManager<>();
        editor.execute("type 'Hello'");
        editor.execute("type ' World'");
        editor.execute("bold selection");

        System.out.println(editor.undo());  // "bold selection"
        System.out.println(editor.undo());  // "type ' World'"
        System.out.println(editor.redo());  // "type ' World'"
        editor.execute("italic selection"); // Clears redo stack
    }
}

Why ArrayDeque, Not Stack?

  1. No unnecessary synchronization — Stack locks on every operation.
  2. Clean interface — Deque exposes only push/pop/peek; Stack leaks Vector methods that make no semantic sense on a stack.
  3. Better performance — measurably faster in benchmarks, especially under JIT compilation.
Part 9

Production Use Case: BFS with a Deque

Breadth-First Search (BFS) for graph/tree traversal is naturally expressed with a queue. The standard BFS loop uses a Deque operating in queue mode (FIFO):

import java.util.*;

public class BfsExample {

    static Map<Integer, List<Integer>> graph = new HashMap<>();

    static {
        graph.put(1, List.of(2, 3));
        graph.put(2, List.of(4, 5));
        graph.put(3, List.of(6));
        graph.put(4, Collections.emptyList());
        graph.put(5, Collections.emptyList());
        graph.put(6, Collections.emptyList());
    }

    public static List<Integer> bfs(int start) {
        List<Integer> visited = new ArrayList<>();
        Set<Integer> seen = new HashSet<>();
        Deque<Integer> frontier = new ArrayDeque<>();

        frontier.offerLast(start);
        seen.add(start);

        while (!frontier.isEmpty()) {
            int node = frontier.pollFirst();  // FIFO — process oldest first
            visited.add(node);

            for (int neighbor : graph.getOrDefault(node, Collections.emptyList())) {
                if (!seen.contains(neighbor)) {
                    seen.add(neighbor);
                    frontier.offerLast(neighbor);
                }
            }
        }
        return visited;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(bfs(1)); // [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
    }
}

Changing pollFirst() to pollLast() (and offerLast to offerFirst) converts BFS to an iterative DFS with a stack — demonstrating how a single Deque can implement both traversal strategies.

Part 10

Deque Iterator and Descendingiterator

Deque provides two iterators:

  • iterator() — traverses from head to tail (front to back).
  • descendingIterator() — traverses from tail to head (back to front).
import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;
import java.util.Iterator;

Deque<String> dq = new ArrayDeque<>(List.of("A", "B", "C", "D"));

// Forward iteration: A B C D
System.out.print("Forward:    ");
for (String s : dq) System.out.print(s + " ");

// Reverse iteration using descendingIterator
System.out.print("\nDescending: ");
Iterator<String> desc = dq.descendingIterator();
while (desc.hasNext()) System.out.print(desc.next() + " ");
// Output: D C B A

ArrayDeque does not implement List, so there is no get(int index) or listIterator(int index). If you need indexed random access, use ArrayList. If you need both deque operations and indexed access, LinkedList technically provides both — but its poor cache performance makes it a mediocre choice for either.

Part 11

Exception-Throwing vs. Value-Returning Methods: When to Use Each

This is a common source of bugs. The rule is simple:

Use the exception-throwing variant when an empty deque or capacity overflow is a programming error.

Deque<String> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
// ...load stack with data...

// CORRECT: pop() in a context where we KNOW there's data
// If the stack is unexpectedly empty, NoSuchElementException reveals the bug immediately.
String top = stack.pop();

Use the value-returning variant when absence of an element is an expected, normal condition.

Deque<Task> taskQueue = new ArrayDeque<>();
// ...

// CORRECT: pollFirst() in a work-loop where queue may legitimately be empty
Task next = taskQueue.pollFirst();
if (next != null) {
    process(next);
} else {
    idle();
}

Common mistake: mixing up exception-throwing methods with silent value-returning methods.

// BUG: using peek() (returns null) but treating null as a valid task
Task t = taskQueue.peek();
t.run(); // NullPointerException if queue is empty!

// FIX: check for null, or use getFirst() + isEmpty() guard
if (!taskQueue.isEmpty()) {
    taskQueue.peek().run();
}
Part 12

ArrayDeque: Key Behaviours and Edge Cases

Null Elements Are Prohibited

ArrayDeque does not permit null elements. This is intentional: the poll* and peek* methods use null as a sentinel value to signal "empty deque". If nulls were allowed, you could not distinguish between "element is null" and "deque is empty".

Deque<String> dq = new ArrayDeque<>();
dq.push(null); // NullPointerException

If you need null in a deque, use LinkedList — but first ask whether null is really meaningful data or a design smell.

Size and isEmpty

Deque<Integer> dq = new ArrayDeque<>();
dq.push(1); dq.push(2); dq.push(3);

System.out.println(dq.size());    // 3
System.out.println(dq.isEmpty()); // false
dq.clear();
System.out.println(dq.isEmpty()); // true

Deque Is Not Thread-Safe

ArrayDeque has no synchronization. Concurrent modification from multiple threads leads to ConcurrentModificationException or silent data corruption. Use LinkedBlockingDeque or ConcurrentLinkedDeque for concurrent scenarios (see Part 14).

Converting Between Deque and List

Deque<String> dq = new ArrayDeque<>(List.of("X", "Y", "Z"));
List<String> list = new ArrayList<>(dq); // [X, Y, Z] — head-to-tail order
Part 13

Performance Benchmarks: ArrayDeque vs Stack vs LinkedList

The performance difference between ArrayDeque and Stack/LinkedList is not theoretical — it is measurable and significant in real applications.

Microbenchmark Summary (JMH, OpenJDK 21, typical hardware)

Operation (1M iterations) ArrayDeque Stack (synchronized) LinkedList
push + pop (stack) ~28 ms ~85 ms ~95 ms
offer + poll (queue) ~30 ms N/A ~90 ms
Mixed push/pop 50/50 ~27 ms ~88 ms ~92 ms
Memory (1M String refs) ~8 MB ~8 MB ~56 MB

Key observations:

  1. Stack is ~3× slower than ArrayDeque purely due to synchronized method overhead.
  2. LinkedList is ~3× slower due to per-node heap allocation and cache miss overhead.
  3. Memory usage of LinkedList is ~7× higher due to Node wrapper objects.
  4. Under a low-contention multi-threaded scenario, Stack's synchronization still adds disproportionate cost versus using an explicit external lock or a concurrent collection.

Why Cache Matters

When the JIT-compiled code accesses ArrayDeque's backing array, sequential elements are on the same or adjacent 64-byte cache lines. Each cache line holds 8–16 references on a 64-bit JVM. Iteration and sequential push/pop operations hit the CPU cache with very high hit rates.

LinkedList node chains are allocated at arbitrary heap addresses. Even with a generational GC keeping young objects close together after a minor GC, pointer chasing rapidly defeats the CPU's prefetch unit. This effect amplifies as the deque grows larger than the L3 cache.

Part 14

BlockingDeque: Concurrent Preview

java.util.concurrent.BlockingDeque<E> extends both Deque<E> and BlockingQueue<E>. It adds blocking operations that wait (with optional timeout) when the deque is empty or full:

Method Behaviour
putFirst(e) / putLast(e) Block indefinitely until space is available
takeFirst() / takeLast() Block indefinitely until an element is available
offerFirst(e, timeout, unit) Block up to timeout; return false if still full
pollFirst(timeout, unit) Block up to timeout; return null if still empty

Primary Implementation: LinkedBlockingDeque

import java.util.concurrent.LinkedBlockingDeque;
import java.util.concurrent.BlockingDeque;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;

BlockingDeque<String> bdeque = new LinkedBlockingDeque<>(100); // capacity 100

// Producer thread
bdeque.putLast("work-item");

// Consumer thread
String item = bdeque.pollFirst(500, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); // wait up to 500ms
if (item != null) process(item);

LinkedBlockingDeque uses two ReentrantLock instances (one for head, one for tail) with Condition variables, allowing concurrent head and tail operations to proceed in parallel under low contention.

Work-Stealing Deque (ForkJoinPool Preview)

The ForkJoinPool (Java 7+) implements the work-stealing algorithm. Each worker thread maintains a private work-stealing deque (a WorkQueue internally). The owning thread operates on its deque's tail (LIFO — newest tasks first, for better cache locality with recursive decomposition). Idle threads steal from other workers' deque heads (oldest tasks first), minimising contention.

This is not ArrayDeque but a specialized lock-free data structure. The deque interface concepts are identical: add/remove from both ends with different ownership semantics. You will revisit this in detail in the Concurrency phase.

Part 15

Deque in Recursive Algorithm Simulation

Many recursive algorithms can be converted to iterative form using an explicit stack (a Deque in stack mode). This avoids StackOverflowError for deep recursion and gives you manual control over the call stack.

Example: Iterative Tree Postorder Traversal

import java.util.*;

public class TreeTraversal {

    record TreeNode(int val, TreeNode left, TreeNode right) {}

    // Recursive version — can overflow for deep trees
    static List<Integer> postorderRecursive(TreeNode root) {
        List<Integer> res = new ArrayList<>();
        if (root == null) return res;
        res.addAll(postorderRecursive(root.left));
        res.addAll(postorderRecursive(root.right));
        res.add(root.val);
        return res;
    }

    // Iterative version using explicit Deque stack
    static List<Integer> postorderIterative(TreeNode root) {
        LinkedList<Integer> result = new LinkedList<>();
        if (root == null) return result;

        Deque<TreeNode> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
        stack.push(root);

        while (!stack.isEmpty()) {
            TreeNode node = stack.pop();
            result.addFirst(node.val); // Insert at head — reverses order to postorder

            if (node.left != null) stack.push(node.left);
            if (node.right != null) stack.push(node.right);
        }
        return result;
    }
}

This pattern — using a Deque as an explicit call stack for DFS/postorder/preorder traversals — appears frequently in both production code and technical interviews.

Part 16

Deque as a Monotonic Stack

A monotonic stack maintains elements in strictly increasing or decreasing order. It is the foundation of algorithms like "Next Greater Element," "Largest Rectangle in Histogram," and "Trapping Rain Water."

Example: Next Greater Element

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

public class NextGreaterElement {

    /**
     * For each element in nums, find the first element to its right that is greater.
     * Returns -1 if no such element exists.
     * Time: O(n), Space: O(n)
     */
    public static int[] nextGreater(int[] nums) {
        int n = nums.length;
        int[] result = new int[n];
        Arrays.fill(result, -1);

        // Stack holds INDICES; elements in stack are in decreasing order of value
        Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();

        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            // Pop all elements smaller than nums[i] — nums[i] is their next greater
            while (!stack.isEmpty() && nums[stack.peekFirst()] < nums[i]) {
                int idx = stack.pollFirst();
                result[idx] = nums[i];
            }
            stack.push(i);
        }
        return result;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[] nums = {4, 1, 2, 3};
        System.out.println(Arrays.toString(nextGreater(nums)));
        // Output: [-1, 2, 3, -1]
    }
}

The invariant: elements remain in the stack only while their "next greater" hasn't been found. Each element is pushed once and popped once → O(n) total.

Part 17

Deque in Palindrome Checking

A deque provides an elegant O(n) palindrome checker by consuming characters from both ends simultaneously:

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

public class PalindromeChecker {

    public static boolean isPalindrome(String s) {
        // Normalize: lowercase, letters and digits only
        String cleaned = s.toLowerCase().replaceAll("[^a-z0-9]", "");

        Deque<Character> dq = new ArrayDeque<>();
        for (char c : cleaned.toCharArray()) dq.offerLast(c);

        while (dq.size() > 1) {
            if (!dq.pollFirst().equals(dq.pollLast())) return false;
        }
        return true;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(isPalindrome("A man, a plan, a canal: Panama")); // true
        System.out.println(isPalindrome("race a car"));                      // false
        System.out.println(isPalindrome("Was it a car or a cat I saw?"));   // true
    }
}

While a simple charAt comparison also works for this problem, the deque approach generalises naturally to stream-based palindrome checking where characters arrive one at a time.

Part 18

Deque Serialization and Copying

ArrayDeque implements Cloneable and Serializable.

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

Deque<String> original = new ArrayDeque<>(List.of("A", "B", "C"));

// Shallow copy — same String references, new ArrayDeque instance
ArrayDeque<String> copy = ((ArrayDeque<String>) original).clone();

// Construct a new deque from any Collection (preserves iteration order: head → tail)
Deque<String> copy2 = new ArrayDeque<>(original);

// Convert to array (head → tail order)
Object[] arr = original.toArray();           // [A, B, C]
String[] typed = original.toArray(new String[0]); // [A, B, C]

Note on clone(): The clone is a shallow copy. If elements are mutable objects, both the original and the clone share the same element references. Mutating an element through one deque affects the other. For a deep copy, iterate and copy each element manually.

Part 19

Common Bugs and Pitfalls

Bug 1: Expecting FIFO from push/pop

Deque<Integer> dq = new ArrayDeque<>();
dq.push(1); dq.push(2); dq.push(3);

// Mistake: expecting 1, 2, 3 (FIFO)
while (!dq.isEmpty()) System.out.print(dq.pop() + " ");
// Actual output: 3 2 1 — because push/pop is LIFO (stack semantics)

// For FIFO: use offerLast + pollFirst

Bug 2: Using peek() on an Empty Deque with the Wrong Method

Deque<String> dq = new ArrayDeque<>();
String s = dq.element(); // NoSuchElementException — use peek() for safe version
String safe = dq.peek(); // null — no exception

Bug 3: Modifying Deque During Iteration

Deque<Integer> dq = new ArrayDeque<>(List.of(1, 2, 3, 4, 5));
for (Integer i : dq) {
    if (i % 2 == 0) dq.remove(i); // ConcurrentModificationException!
}

// Fix: use iterator's remove method or collect and then remove
Iterator<Integer> it = dq.iterator();
while (it.hasNext()) {
    if (it.next() % 2 == 0) it.remove(); // Safe
}

Bug 4: Confusing addFirst/addLast with Stack semantics

Deque<String> dq = new ArrayDeque<>();
dq.addLast("A");
dq.addLast("B");
dq.push("C"); // addFirst — C is now at the FRONT

// State (front → back): C, A, B
System.out.println(dq.pop()); // C — not A!

When mixing push/pop (stack) and offerLast/pollFirst (queue) on the same deque, the mental model must be clear about which end each operation touches.

Bug 5: Using Stack Class in New Code

// This is the most common legacy bug in Java interview codebases
Stack<Integer> s = new Stack<>(); // Never do this in new code

The Stack class inherits Vector.insertElementAt(E, int), Vector.removeElementAt(int), and Vector.elementAt(int). None of these belong to a stack. Use ArrayDeque.

Part 20

Interview Preparation: Key Questions

Q1: What is the difference between ArrayDeque and Stack?

Answer: Stack extends Vector (synchronized) and is a legacy class from Java 1.0. It incurs synchronization overhead even in single-threaded code and exposes inappropriate Vector methods on a stack abstraction. ArrayDeque is a modern (Java 6+), unsynchronized, faster implementation of the stack abstraction via the Deque interface. It uses a resizable circular array for O(1) amortized push/pop/peek. Prefer ArrayDeque over Stack in all new code.

Q2: When would you choose LinkedList over ArrayDeque as a deque?

Answer: Only when you simultaneously need the List interface and Deque interface on the same object, or when you require null elements in the deque. In virtually all other cases, ArrayDeque is faster (cache-friendly array access vs pointer-chasing), uses less memory (no Node wrapper per element), and has simpler failure semantics (null-safe sentinels).

Q3: How does ArrayDeque achieve O(1) operations at both ends?

Answer: ArrayDeque maintains a circular array with head and tail integer indices. addFirst decrements head (wrapping around using bitmask arithmetic), addLast places the element at tail and increments tail. Both are constant-time array index operations. Resizing doubles the capacity and is O(n) for the copy itself, but O(1) amortized over all insertions.

Q4: Explain the sliding window maximum algorithm using a Deque.

Answer: Maintain a deque of indices such that the corresponding values are in decreasing order (monotonic deque). For each new element, pop from the back while the back element is smaller (it can never be the window max while the new element is present). Pop from the front when that index falls outside the current window. The front always holds the index of the current window maximum. Each element is enqueued and dequeued at most once → O(n) total.

Q5: Why doesn't ArrayDeque allow null elements?

Answer: The poll* and peek* family of methods returns null to signal "deque is empty." If nulls were permitted as valid elements, this sentinel-based signalling would be ambiguous — you could not distinguish "deque is empty" from "the front element is null." LinkedList allows nulls because it uses a separate size counter and explicit node checks rather than null-as-sentinel.

Q6: How is a Deque used in ForkJoinPool?

Answer: ForkJoinPool gives each worker thread a private work-stealing deque. The owning thread pushes and pops tasks from the tail (LIFO — processes recently forked subtasks first, maximising spatial locality and reducing unnecessary task migration). Idle threads steal tasks from other workers' heads (FIFO — steal the oldest, largest chunks of work, which keeps stolen work coarse-grained and minimises steal frequency). This dual-end access pattern is exactly what Deque is designed for.

Q7: What is the difference between offer and add on a Deque?

Answer: Both insert an element; the difference is failure behavior. add (and addFirst/addLast) throws IllegalStateException if the deque is capacity-constrained and full. offer (and offerFirst/offerLast) returns false instead of throwing. ArrayDeque is unbounded (grows dynamically), so both are effectively equivalent for ArrayDeque. For bounded BlockingDeque implementations, the distinction is meaningful.

Part 21

Real-World Production Patterns

Pattern 1: Bounded History Buffer (Recent N Items)

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

/**
 * Keeps the last N items in O(1) per insertion.
 * Useful for: browser history, command history, recent file list.
 */
public class BoundedHistory<T> {
    private final Deque<T> history = new ArrayDeque<>();
    private final int maxSize;

    public BoundedHistory(int maxSize) {
        this.maxSize = maxSize;
    }

    public void record(T item) {
        if (history.size() == maxSize) {
            history.pollLast(); // Remove oldest entry (tail)
        }
        history.offerFirst(item); // Most recent at front
    }

    public List<T> getHistory() {
        return new ArrayList<>(history); // Front = most recent
    }
}

Pattern 2: Task Scheduler with Priority Lanes

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

public class PriorityTaskScheduler {
    private final Deque<Runnable> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();

    /** Normal priority — add to back (processed after existing tasks). */
    public void schedule(Runnable task) {
        queue.offerLast(task);
    }

    /** High priority — add to front (processed before existing tasks). */
    public void scheduleUrgent(Runnable task) {
        queue.offerFirst(task);
    }

    public void runAll() {
        while (!queue.isEmpty()) {
            queue.pollFirst().run();
        }
    }
}

Pattern 3: LRU Cache Eviction Order Tracking

In a Least-Recently-Used cache, when an element is accessed, it is moved to the "most recently used" end. When the cache is full, the element at the "least recently used" end is evicted. A Deque (combined with a HashMap for O(1) lookup) is the building block of the standard LRU cache:

HashMap<Key, Node>  →  O(1) lookup
LinkedList/Deque    →  O(1) move-to-front, O(1) evict-from-tail

The LinkedHashMap with accessOrder = true encapsulates this pattern; internally it maintains a doubly-linked list equivalent to a deque for eviction ordering.

Part 22

Summary Table

Deque Quick Reference

Topic Key Point
Interface java.util.Deque<E> — extends Queue<E>
Primary impl ArrayDeque — circular array, O(1) amortized both ends
Secondary impl LinkedList — doubly-linked, also implements List
Stack methods push(e) = addFirst(e), pop() = removeFirst(), peek() = peekFirst()
Queue methods offer(e) = offerLast(e), poll() = pollFirst(), peek() = peekFirst()
Null allowed ArrayDeque: No. LinkedList: Yes
Thread-safe Neither. Use LinkedBlockingDeque for concurrency
Resizing ArrayDeque doubles on full; always power-of-two capacity
Legacy to avoid java.util.Stack — extends Vector, synchronized, design flaws
Concurrent variant LinkedBlockingDeque, ConcurrentLinkedDeque
Work-stealing ForkJoinPool uses internal deque — owner pops tail, stealer polls head

Method Symmetry Cheat Sheet

             HEAD (front)              TAIL (back)
           ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  throws   │  addFirst(e)      ←→      addLast(e)     │
exception  │  removeFirst()    ←→      removeLast()   │
           │  getFirst()       ←→      getLast()      │
           ├──────────────────────────────────────────┤
  returns  │  offerFirst(e)    ←→      offerLast(e)   │
  null/    │  pollFirst()      ←→      pollLast()     │
  false    │  peekFirst()      ←→      peekLast()     │
           └──────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Stack mode:  push(e) = addFirst(e)    pop() = removeFirst()
  Queue mode:  offer(e) = offerLast(e)  poll() = pollFirst()

Choosing the Right Tool

Need a stack (LIFO)?
  └── Use ArrayDeque.push() / .pop()

Need a queue (FIFO)?
  └── Use ArrayDeque.offerLast() / .pollFirst()

Need both ends in the same algorithm?
  └── Use ArrayDeque (full Deque API)

Need thread-safety?
  └── Use LinkedBlockingDeque (bounded) or ConcurrentLinkedDeque (unbounded)

Already using Stack class?
  └── Migrate to ArrayDeque — it is a drop-in replacement for push/pop/peek

Practice Problems

Beginner

  1. Browser Back/Forward: Implement a browser navigation history using two ArrayDeque instances — one for the back stack and one for the forward stack. Support visit(url), back(), forward(), and currentUrl().

  2. Deque Rotation: Given a deque of integers and a rotation count k, rotate the deque to the right by k positions using only pollFirst() and offerLast().

  3. Print Deque in Reverse: Given any Deque<String>, print its contents from tail to head without using descendingIterator().

Intermediate

  1. Sliding Window Minimum: Adapt the sliding window maximum algorithm from Part 7 to find the minimum instead. What change is needed in the monotonic invariant?

  2. Valid Parentheses with Deque: Use an ArrayDeque as a stack to check whether a string of ()[]{} parentheses is valid. Handle nested and interleaved brackets.

  3. Implement a Queue using Two Stacks: Using only two ArrayDeque instances operating as stacks, implement a Queue with enqueue(e), dequeue(), and peek(). What is the amortized time complexity of dequeue()?

  4. Bounded Deque: Implement a BoundedDeque<T> that wraps ArrayDeque and throws IllegalStateException on addFirst/addLast when at capacity, and NoSuchElementException on pollFirst/pollLast when empty.

Advanced

  1. Largest Rectangle in Histogram: Given an array of bar heights, find the area of the largest rectangle. Use a monotonic stack (ArrayDeque) approach for an O(n) solution.

  2. Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation: Use an ArrayDeque as an operand stack to evaluate an expression given as a String[] of tokens ("2", "3", "+", etc.).

  3. Maximum Sum Subarray of Length K: Given an array and size k, use a deque to compute the maximum subarray sum for every contiguous window of size k in O(n).

  4. Serialise / Deserialise Binary Tree using Deque: Implement level-order serialisation of a binary tree using a Deque and reconstruct the tree from the serialised string. Demonstrate that the deque naturally models the BFS frontier.

End of Lesson 25 — Deque
