Part 1

Why Ordering Matters in Java Collections

Java's collection framework is built around two orthogonal concerns: storage (how elements are kept in memory) and ordering (how elements are ranked relative to one another). These two concerns are intentionally separated in the design.

Many of the most powerful data structures in Java require a well-defined comparison strategy for their elements:

  • TreeSet and TreeMap maintain elements in sorted order — they cannot function without knowing how to compare elements.
  • PriorityQueue serves its highest- (or lowest-) priority element first — comparison defines priority.
  • Collections.sort() and Arrays.sort() need to rank elements against each other.
  • Stream operations like .sorted() and .min() / .max() need comparison semantics.
  • BinarySearch requires a sorted collection and a consistent comparison strategy.

Without a clear, consistent ordering strategy, all of these fail — either with a ClassCastException at runtime or with subtly incorrect behavior that is hard to debug in production.

Java solves this with two complementary interfaces:

  1. Comparable<T> — the element itself knows how to compare to another element of the same type. This is called the natural ordering of the class.
  2. Comparator<T> — an external strategy object that compares two instances of any type. This is called a total ordering or custom ordering, and it is decoupled entirely from the class being sorted.

The distinction is architectural, not just syntactic. Comparable embeds ordering into the domain model; Comparator externalizes it. Both approaches have clear use cases, and experienced architects know when to use each.

              Ordering in Java
              ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
              ┌─────────────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
              │     Comparable<T>       │  │       Comparator<T>          │
              │                         │  │                              │
              │  • Implemented ON       │  │  • External strategy object  │
              │    the class itself     │  │  • Separate from the class   │
              │  • Single natural       │  │  • Multiple orderings        │
              │    ordering             │  │    supported simultaneously  │
              │  • compareTo(T other)   │  │  • compare(T o1, T o2)       │
              │  • java.lang package    │  │  • java.util package         │
              └─────────────────────────┘  └──────────────────────────────┘
                       "natural"                      "custom"

              Examples:
              • String, Integer,          • Comparator.comparing()
                LocalDate all implement   • lambda (a, b) -> ...
                Comparable naturally      • Comparator.reverseOrder()

Both interfaces are deeply integrated into the Java standard library and frameworks like Spring Data, Hibernate, and Apache Commons Collections.

Part 2

The `Comparable<T>` Interface

Interface Declaration

package java.lang;

public interface Comparable<T> {
    int compareTo(T other);
}

The single method compareTo(T other) returns an integer whose sign (not magnitude) determines the ordering:

Return Value Meaning
Negative integer this is less than other
Zero (0) this is equal to other
Positive integer this is greater than other

Only the sign matters. The actual magnitude is irrelevant for most sorting algorithms. Common conventions are:
- Return exactly -1, 0, or 1 for clarity
- Return the difference of two integers (with important caveats — see Part 6)
- Use Integer.compare(a, b) or Double.compare(a, b) for numeric types

A Minimal Example

public class Temperature implements Comparable<Temperature> {
    private final double celsius;

    public Temperature(double celsius) {
        this.celsius = celsius;
    }

    @Override
    public int compareTo(Temperature other) {
        return Double.compare(this.celsius, other.celsius);
    }

    @Override
    public boolean equals(Object obj) {
        if (this == obj) return true;
        if (!(obj instanceof Temperature t)) return false;
        return Double.compare(celsius, t.celsius) == 0;
    }

    @Override
    public int hashCode() {
        return Double.hashCode(celsius);
    }
}

Now Temperature objects can be sorted in any collection that requires Comparable:

List<Temperature> temps = new ArrayList<>(List.of(
    new Temperature(37.5),
    new Temperature(36.1),
    new Temperature(38.9)
));

Collections.sort(temps);
// Results in: [36.1, 37.5, 38.9]

TreeSet<Temperature> treeSet = new TreeSet<>(temps);
// Stored in sorted order automatically

Classes in the JDK that Implement Comparable

Class Natural Order
Integer Numeric ascending
String Lexicographic (Unicode code point)
LocalDate Chronological (earlier = less than)
BigDecimal Numeric value ascending
Enum subclass Declaration order in source
UUID Lexicographic of string representation
File Platform-dependent pathname
Part 3

The `compareTo` Contract

The Comparable Javadoc specifies a mathematical contract that all implementations must uphold. Violating any property leads to subtle bugs, undefined sort behavior, and broken tree structures.

The Three Properties

1. Antisymmetry

sgn(x.compareTo(y)) == -sgn(y.compareTo(x))

If x is greater than y, then y must be less than x. This seems obvious but is easy to break when dealing with nullable fields or floating-point arithmetic.

2. Transitivity

if x.compareTo(y) > 0  AND  y.compareTo(z) > 0
then x.compareTo(z) > 0

If A > B and B > C, then A > C. TimSort and merge sort algorithms rely on transitivity to produce correct results. Violating transitivity can cause infinite loops or incorrect sorted output.

3. Consistency with equals (strongly recommended)

x.compareTo(y) == 0  ⟺  x.equals(y)

This is not required by Comparable, but strongly recommended by the Javadoc. TreeSet and TreeMap use compareTo for equality checks (not equals), so if these diverge, elements that are equals() can appear multiple times in a TreeSet, or the same key can be stored twice in a TreeMap.

Notable exception: BigDecimal intentionally violates this. new BigDecimal("1.0") and new BigDecimal("1.00") are equals() to each other? No — they are NOT equal via equals(), but compareTo() returns 0. This means a TreeSet<BigDecimal> treats them as duplicates, while a HashSet<BigDecimal> stores both.

Contract Violation Example — The Transitivity Bug

// BAD: Comparator that violates transitivity
public class BrokenComparator implements Comparator<String> {
    @Override
    public int compare(String a, String b) {
        if (a.length() < b.length()) return -1;
        if (a.length() > b.length()) return 1;
        // If equal length, compare lexicographically
        // BUT this creates transitivity issues:
        // "abc" == "xyz" (same length), "xyz" == "abc"
        // but also "abc" < "abcd" and "abcd" < "abcde"
        // OK so far — this is actually fine
        return 0; // ties treated as equal regardless of content
    }
}
// "cat" == "dog" by this comparator (same length)
// but "cat".equals("dog") is false
// TreeSet will only store one of them!

The subtle consequence: placing "cat" and "dog" (both length 3) into a TreeSet with this comparator results in only one being stored, because compare("cat","dog") == 0 means they are considered duplicates.

Part 4

The `Comparator<T>` Interface

Interface Declaration

package java.util;

@FunctionalInterface
public interface Comparator<T> {
    int compare(T o1, T o2);

    // default methods:
    default Comparator<T> reversed() { ... }
    default Comparator<T> thenComparing(Comparator<? super T> other) { ... }
    default <U extends Comparable<? super U>> Comparator<T>
        thenComparing(Function<? super T, ? extends U> keyExtractor) { ... }

    // static factory methods:
    static <T, U extends Comparable<? super U>> Comparator<T>
        comparing(Function<? super T, ? extends U> keyExtractor) { ... }
    static <T> Comparator<T> naturalOrder() { ... }
    static <T> Comparator<T> reverseOrder() { ... }
    static <T> Comparator<T> nullsFirst(Comparator<? super T> comparator) { ... }
    static <T> Comparator<T> nullsLast(Comparator<? super T> comparator) { ... }
}

Comparator is a @FunctionalInterface, meaning it can be expressed as a lambda:

Comparator<String> byLength = (a, b) -> Integer.compare(a.length(), b.length());

The key differences from Comparable:

Aspect Comparable<T> Comparator<T>
Location Inside the class External to the class
Method compareTo(T other) compare(T o1, T o2)
Parameters One (compare to this) Two (both objects passed in)
Orderings per class One (natural) Unlimited (compose as needed)
FunctionalInterface No Yes (lambda-friendly)
Package java.lang java.util
Part 5

`Comparator` Factory Methods (Java 8+)

Java 8 added powerful static factory methods to Comparator that make multi-field sorting expressive and readable.

Comparator.comparing()

Extracts a sort key from the object using a key extractor function:

Comparator<Employee> byLastName = Comparator.comparing(Employee::getLastName);
Comparator<Employee> bySalary   = Comparator.comparingDouble(Employee::getSalary);
Comparator<Employee> byAge      = Comparator.comparingInt(Employee::getAge);

Specializations exist for primitives to avoid boxing:
- comparingInt(ToIntFunction)
- comparingLong(ToLongFunction)
- comparingDouble(ToDoubleFunction)

thenComparing() — Chaining

When the primary key comparison results in 0 (tie), thenComparing applies the secondary key:

Comparator<Employee> byDeptThenSalaryDescThenName =
    Comparator.comparing(Employee::getDepartment)
              .thenComparingDouble(Employee::getSalary).reversed() // watch out — reversed() applies to entire chain!
              .thenComparing(Employee::getLastName);

// Safer approach for partial reversal:
Comparator<Employee> byDeptThenSalaryDescThenName =
    Comparator.comparing(Employee::getDepartment)
              .thenComparing(Comparator.comparingDouble(Employee::getSalary).reversed())
              .thenComparing(Employee::getLastName);

reversed()

Returns a comparator that imposes the reverse of the original ordering:

Comparator<String> descLength = Comparator.comparingInt(String::length).reversed();
List<String> words = Arrays.asList("ant", "elephant", "bee", "rhinoceros");
words.sort(descLength);
// ["rhinoceros", "elephant", "ant", "bee"]

naturalOrder() and reverseOrder()

List<Integer> nums = Arrays.asList(5, 2, 8, 1, 9);
nums.sort(Comparator.naturalOrder());   // [1, 2, 5, 8, 9]
nums.sort(Comparator.reverseOrder());   // [9, 8, 5, 2, 1]
Part 6

The Subtraction Anti-Pattern

A common mistake when implementing compareTo or compare for integer fields:

// DANGEROUS — integer overflow bug
@Override
public int compareTo(MyObj other) {
    return this.value - other.value; // WRONG!
}

If this.value = Integer.MIN_VALUE (-2147483648) and other.value = 1, the subtraction overflows to a large positive number — incorrectly reporting this > other when in fact this < other.

Always use the comparison helpers instead:

// CORRECT
return Integer.compare(this.value, other.value);
return Long.compare(this.longValue, other.longValue);
return Double.compare(this.doubleValue, other.doubleValue);

// Or for reference types with natural ordering:
return this.name.compareTo(other.name);
return this.date.compareTo(other.date);

The helper methods are branch-free, overflow-safe, and JIT-friendly.

Part 7

`TreeSet` and `TreeMap`: Sorted Collection Integration

TreeSet and TreeMap are the primary consumers of comparison in Java's collection framework. They maintain elements in a Red-Black tree, always sorted according to the active comparison strategy.

Two Ways to Provide Ordering to TreeSet/TreeMap

Option 1: Element implements Comparable (natural ordering)

TreeSet<String> names = new TreeSet<>();
names.add("Charlie");
names.add("Alice");
names.add("Bob");
// Stored as: [Alice, Bob, Charlie]

Option 2: Provide an explicit Comparator at construction time

Comparator<String> caseInsensitive = String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER;
TreeSet<String> ci = new TreeSet<>(caseInsensitive);
ci.add("banana");
ci.add("Apple");
ci.add("cherry");
// Stored as: [Apple, banana, cherry]

// TreeMap with custom comparator:
TreeMap<String, Integer> wordCount = new TreeMap<>(String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER);
wordCount.put("Hello", 1);
wordCount.put("hello", 2); // Updates the same entry! comparator says they're equal
System.out.println(wordCount.get("HELLO")); // 2

Critical Behavior: compareTo for Equality in TreeSet/TreeMap

TreeSet and TreeMap use compareTo() (or compare()) to determine equality — not equals() and not hashCode(). This surprises many developers:

class Product implements Comparable<Product> {
    String sku;
    String name;
    double price;

    @Override
    public int compareTo(Product other) {
        return this.sku.compareTo(other.sku); // Sort only by SKU
    }

    // equals() uses all fields — INCONSISTENT with compareTo!
    @Override
    public boolean equals(Object obj) { ... uses sku+name+price ... }
}

TreeSet<Product> catalog = new TreeSet<>();
Product p1 = new Product("SKU001", "Widget", 9.99);
Product p2 = new Product("SKU001", "Widget Pro", 19.99); // same SKU, different name/price

catalog.add(p1);
catalog.add(p2); // NOT ADDED — compareTo returns 0 for same SKU
System.out.println(catalog.size()); // 1, NOT 2!

This is the consistency with equals requirement from Part 3 — violating it causes exactly this kind of confusion.

Part 8

ASCII Diagram: TimSort Flow

Java uses TimSort for Collections.sort(), Arrays.sort() on object arrays, and stream .sorted(). TimSort is a hybrid algorithm combining merge sort and insertion sort, with O(n log n) worst case and O(n) best case (already-sorted data).

TimSort: How Comparison is Used
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Input:  [ 5, 2, 8, 1, 9, 3, 7, 4, 6 ]

Step 1: Identify "Runs" (naturally sorted or reverse-sorted sub-sequences)
        ┌──────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐
        │ 2, 5 │ │ 1, 8     │ │ 3, 9  │ │ 4, 6, 7│
        └──────┘ └──────────┘ └────────┘ └────────┘
        (each run needs minimum size, padded with insertion sort)

Step 2: Merge runs pairwise using compare() at each merge step
        Merge pass 1:
        ┌────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐
        │ 1, 2, 5, 8 │  │  3, 4, 6, 7, 9 │
        └────────────┘  └──────────────┘

        Merge pass 2:
        ┌──────────────────────────────┐
        │  1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9  │
        └──────────────────────────────┘

Each comparison step calls:
        comparator.compare(element_a, element_b)
              OR
        ((Comparable) element_a).compareTo(element_b)

Return value sign determines which element advances left pointer.

Complexity: O(n log n) worst case, O(n) best case (pre-sorted input)
Stability: YES — equal elements maintain original relative order
           (requires compareTo/compare to return 0 for equal keys)
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Stability note: Because TimSort is stable, elements that compare as equal retain their original relative order. This makes multi-field sorting composed via thenComparing() work correctly — the secondary sort is only applied when the primary sort produces a tie, and stability ensures tertiary sorts preserve secondary sort order.

Part 9

Multi-Field Sorting in Production

Real-world domain objects almost always require multi-field sorting. Here is a complete production-quality example:

public class Employee {
    private final String department;
    private final String lastName;
    private final String firstName;
    private final double salary;
    private final LocalDate hireDate;

    // Constructor, getters...
}

Building the Comparator Chain

// Sort by: department ASC → salary DESC → lastName ASC → firstName ASC
Comparator<Employee> payrollOrder =
    Comparator.comparing(Employee::getDepartment)
              .thenComparing(Comparator.comparingDouble(Employee::getSalary).reversed())
              .thenComparing(Employee::getLastName)
              .thenComparing(Employee::getFirstName);

List<Employee> employees = fetchAllEmployees();
employees.sort(payrollOrder);

Reusable Comparator Constants

In production code, declare commonly used comparators as static constants:

public final class EmployeeComparators {
    private EmployeeComparators() {}

    public static final Comparator<Employee> BY_DEPARTMENT =
        Comparator.comparing(Employee::getDepartment);

    public static final Comparator<Employee> BY_SALARY_DESC =
        Comparator.comparingDouble(Employee::getSalary).reversed();

    public static final Comparator<Employee> BY_HIRE_DATE =
        Comparator.comparing(Employee::getHireDate);

    public static final Comparator<Employee> PAYROLL_ORDER =
        BY_DEPARTMENT
            .thenComparing(BY_SALARY_DESC)
            .thenComparing(Comparator.comparing(Employee::getLastName));
}

Using static constants makes code readable and testable:

employees.sort(EmployeeComparators.PAYROLL_ORDER);

// Unit test
Employee senior = new Employee("Engineering", "Smith", "Alice", 120_000, LocalDate.of(2018, 1, 1));
Employee junior = new Employee("Engineering", "Smith", "Bob",  80_000, LocalDate.of(2022, 3, 1));
assertTrue(EmployeeComparators.BY_SALARY_DESC.compare(senior, junior) < 0); // senior first
Part 10

Null-Safe Comparators

Comparator.compareTo() throws NullPointerException if either argument is null, and most natural orderings (like String.compareTo()) also throw NPE. In production where data may be null (nullable database columns, optional fields), use Comparator.nullsFirst() or Comparator.nullsLast().

// nullsFirst: nulls sort before non-null values
Comparator<String> nullsSafeAsc =
    Comparator.nullsFirst(Comparator.naturalOrder());

// nullsLast: nulls sort after non-null values
Comparator<String> nullsSafeDesc =
    Comparator.nullsLast(Comparator.reverseOrder());

List<String> data = Arrays.asList("Charlie", null, "Alice", null, "Bob");
data.sort(nullsSafeAsc);
// [null, null, Alice, Bob, Charlie]
data.sort(nullsSafeDesc);
// [Charlie, Bob, Alice, null, null]

Null-Safe Multi-Field Comparator

Comparator<Employee> nullSafeOrder =
    Comparator.comparing(
        Employee::getMiddleName,
        Comparator.nullsLast(Comparator.naturalOrder())   // nullable field
    ).thenComparing(Employee::getLastName);

The two-argument form of comparing(keyExtractor, keyComparator) is the cleanest approach when a specific field may be null.

Part 11

Comparator Composition Deep Dive

The reversed() Pitfall

reversed() reverses the entire chain accumulated so far, not just the last step. This is a common source of bugs:

// WRONG — reversed() applies to the whole chain
Comparator<Employee> wrong =
    Comparator.comparing(Employee::getDepartment)
              .thenComparingDouble(Employee::getSalary)
              .reversed(); // NOW both department AND salary are reversed!

// CORRECT — reverse only salary
Comparator<Employee> correct =
    Comparator.comparing(Employee::getDepartment)
              .thenComparing(
                  Comparator.comparingDouble(Employee::getSalary).reversed()
              );

Composing Comparator with Function

For complex key transformations:

// Sort by length of last name, then alphabetically
Comparator<Employee> byNameLengthThenAlpha =
    Comparator.comparingInt((Employee e) -> e.getLastName().length())
              .thenComparing(Employee::getLastName);

Using Comparator with Map.Entry

A common production pattern — sort a map by its values:

Map<String, Long> wordFrequency = computeFrequencies(text);

List<Map.Entry<String, Long>> sorted = wordFrequency.entrySet()
    .stream()
    .sorted(Map.Entry.<String, Long>comparingByValue().reversed())
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
Part 12

Implementing `Comparable` on Domain Objects

Full Production-Quality Implementation

public final class Invoice implements Comparable<Invoice> {
    private final String invoiceId;
    private final LocalDate issueDate;
    private final BigDecimal amount;
    private final String customerId;

    public Invoice(String invoiceId, LocalDate issueDate,
                   BigDecimal amount, String customerId) {
        this.invoiceId  = Objects.requireNonNull(invoiceId);
        this.issueDate  = Objects.requireNonNull(issueDate);
        this.amount     = Objects.requireNonNull(amount);
        this.customerId = Objects.requireNonNull(customerId);
    }

    /**
     * Natural ordering: newest first, then highest amount first, then by ID.
     * Consistent with equals.
     */
    @Override
    public int compareTo(Invoice other) {
        Objects.requireNonNull(other, "Cannot compare with null Invoice");

        int cmp = other.issueDate.compareTo(this.issueDate); // reversed: newest first
        if (cmp != 0) return cmp;

        cmp = other.amount.compareTo(this.amount); // reversed: highest first
        if (cmp != 0) return cmp;

        return this.invoiceId.compareTo(other.invoiceId); // tiebreaker
    }

    @Override
    public boolean equals(Object obj) {
        if (this == obj) return true;
        if (!(obj instanceof Invoice inv)) return false;
        return invoiceId.equals(inv.invoiceId)
            && issueDate.equals(inv.issueDate)
            && amount.compareTo(inv.amount) == 0
            && customerId.equals(inv.customerId);
    }

    @Override
    public int hashCode() {
        return Objects.hash(invoiceId, issueDate, amount, customerId);
    }

    // getters...
}

Design Guidelines for Comparable on Domain Objects

  1. Make the natural ordering obvious from the class name or Javadoc — developers should not have to read the implementation to understand what "natural order" means for your type.
  2. If no single obvious ordering exists, do NOT implement Comparable — use Comparator instead.
  3. Ensure consistency with equals — mismatch between compareTo and equals is a notorious source of bugs in TreeSet/TreeMap.
  4. Make the class final if it implements Comparable — subclasses cannot extend the ordering contract without violating transitivity.
Part 13

Records and Comparable

Java records (introduced in Java 16) can implement Comparable:

public record Point(int x, int y) implements Comparable<Point> {

    @Override
    public int compareTo(Point other) {
        int cmp = Integer.compare(this.x, other.x);
        if (cmp != 0) return cmp;
        return Integer.compare(this.y, other.y);
    }
}

// Records generate equals/hashCode from components automatically
// compareTo above is consistent with equals (same x and y = equal)
List<Point> points = List.of(new Point(3,1), new Point(1,5), new Point(1,2));
points.stream().sorted().forEach(System.out::println);
// Point[x=1, y=2]
// Point[x=1, y=5]
// Point[x=3, y=1]

Records are a natural fit for Comparable because their equality semantics are already tied to their components — making it straightforward to write a compareTo that is consistent with equals.

Part 14

Streams and `sorted()`

Stream's .sorted() method accepts an optional Comparator:

// Natural order (elements must implement Comparable)
list.stream().sorted()

// Explicit comparator
list.stream().sorted(Comparator.comparing(Employee::getSalary))

// Reverse natural order
list.stream().sorted(Comparator.reverseOrder())

// Min and max
Optional<Employee> highest = employees.stream()
    .max(Comparator.comparingDouble(Employee::getSalary));

Optional<Employee> earliest = employees.stream()
    .min(Comparator.comparing(Employee::getHireDate));

Performance note: stream().sorted() collects all elements internally before sorting, so it is not streaming-friendly for very large datasets. For large in-memory sorts, Collections.sort() on a List is preferable (sorts in-place, avoids intermediate collection).

Part 15

Spring Data: `Sort.by()` and `Pageable`

Spring Data's Sort class wraps comparator logic in a query-compatible form:

// Simple single-field sort
Sort byName = Sort.by("lastName");
Sort bySalaryDesc = Sort.by(Sort.Direction.DESC, "salary");

// Multi-field sort
Sort multiSort = Sort.by("department")
                     .and(Sort.by(Sort.Direction.DESC, "salary"))
                     .and(Sort.by("lastName"));

Using Sort with Pageable

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/employees")
public class EmployeeController {

    @GetMapping
    public Page<Employee> getEmployees(
            @RequestParam(defaultValue = "0")  int page,
            @RequestParam(defaultValue = "20") int size,
            @RequestParam(defaultValue = "lastName") String sortBy,
            @RequestParam(defaultValue = "ASC") String direction) {

        Sort sort = Sort.by(Sort.Direction.fromString(direction), sortBy);
        Pageable pageable = PageRequest.of(page, size, sort);
        return employeeRepository.findAll(pageable);
    }
}

Spring Data JPA Repository with Custom Sort

public interface EmployeeRepository extends JpaRepository<Employee, Long> {

    List<Employee> findByDepartment(String department, Sort sort);

    Page<Employee> findBySalaryGreaterThan(double minSalary, Pageable pageable);
}

// Service usage:
Sort sort = Sort.by("salary").descending().and(Sort.by("lastName").ascending());
List<Employee> result = repository.findByDepartment("Engineering", sort);

Important: Spring Data Sort field names refer to entity property names, not database column names. If you use a custom @Column(name = "last_name"), the Sort field is still "lastName" (the Java property).

Part 16

`Collections` Utility Methods

java.util.Collections provides utility methods that use comparison:

List<Integer> nums = new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList(5, 2, 8, 1, 9, 3));

// Sort in natural order
Collections.sort(nums);

// Sort with comparator
Collections.sort(nums, Comparator.reverseOrder());

// Binary search (list must be sorted first!)
int idx = Collections.binarySearch(nums, 5); // requires natural ordering
int idx2 = Collections.binarySearch(nums, 5, Comparator.reverseOrder()); // with comparator

// Min and max
Integer max = Collections.max(nums);
Integer min = Collections.min(nums, Comparator.reverseOrder()); // "min" by custom order

// Frequency and disjoint don't use ordering, but are useful companions
int freq = Collections.frequency(nums, 5);

Comparator with Arrays

String[] words = {"banana", "Apple", "cherry"};
Arrays.sort(words, String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER);
// [Apple, banana, cherry]

int pos = Arrays.binarySearch(words, "apple", String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER);
// Found at some index
Part 17

Performance Considerations

Operation Time Complexity Notes
Collections.sort() / Arrays.sort() O(n log n) TimSort, stable, fast for near-sorted
TreeSet.add() / TreeMap.put() O(log n) Red-Black tree insertion
TreeSet.contains() / TreeMap.get() O(log n) Tree traversal using compareTo
PriorityQueue.offer() O(log n) Binary heap sift-up
PriorityQueue.poll() O(log n) Binary heap sift-down
stream().sorted().findFirst() O(n log n) Must sort all elements first
stream().min() / .max() O(n) Single pass, no full sort
Collections.binarySearch() O(log n) Requires pre-sorted list

Comparator caching: Building a comparator chain with Comparator.comparing().thenComparing()... is done once at construction time. The resulting Comparator object is cheap to invoke. Never rebuild comparator chains inside hot loops.

Method references vs lambdas: Comparator.comparing(Employee::getSalary) using a method reference is slightly more efficient than e -> e.getSalary() in some JVM configurations because method references can be inlined more aggressively. The difference is negligible for most use cases.

Part 18

Breaking the Contract: Real Bug Examples

Bug 1: Non-Transitive Comparator Causing Infinite Loop

In Java 6 and earlier, some Arrays.sort() implementations could enter infinite loops with non-transitive comparators. Java 7+ TimSort throws IllegalArgumentException: Comparison method violates its general contract! — protecting users from this silent corruption.

// This triggers IllegalArgumentException with TimSort:
Comparator<Integer> broken = (a, b) -> {
    if (a == 1 && b == 2) return -1; // 1 < 2
    if (a == 2 && b == 3) return -1; // 2 < 3
    if (a == 1 && b == 3) return  1; // 1 > 3  — VIOLATES TRANSITIVITY
    return 0;
};
List<Integer> list = Arrays.asList(1, 2, 3);
Collections.sort(list, broken); // throws IllegalArgumentException

Bug 2: Comparator Using Mutable State

// BAD: mutable threshold affects sorting outcome
class ThresholdComparator implements Comparator<Integer> {
    private int threshold = 5;

    @Override
    public int compare(Integer a, Integer b) {
        boolean aAbove = a > threshold;
        boolean bAbove = b > threshold;
        if (aAbove == bAbove) return Integer.compare(a, b);
        return aAbove ? 1 : -1; // above-threshold sorts last
    }

    public void setThreshold(int t) { this.threshold = t; }
}
// If threshold changes mid-sort, the sort result is undefined

Bug 3: Overflow in Subtraction

// BUG: overflow corrupts sort order
int[] arr = {Integer.MIN_VALUE, Integer.MAX_VALUE, 0};
Arrays.sort(arr); // OK — primitive sort uses numeric comparison

// But with a custom boxed comparator:
Comparator<Integer> overflow = (a, b) -> a - b; // OVERFLOW BUG
List<Integer> boxed = Arrays.asList(Integer.MIN_VALUE, Integer.MAX_VALUE, 0);
Collections.sort(boxed, overflow); // Wrong result
Part 19

Thread Safety

Comparator and Comparable implementations are stateless in most cases, making them inherently thread-safe. However, there are two hazards to be aware of:

1. Stateful Comparators: If a Comparator reads from mutable shared state (like a locale setting, threshold, or configuration object), concurrent modification of that state while a sort is in progress will produce undefined results.

2. Sorting Shared Lists: Collections.sort() and list.sort() modify the list in place. Sorting a shared List from multiple threads without external synchronization causes data corruption. Sort into a copy, or sort under a lock.

// Thread-safe pattern: sort a private copy
List<Employee> snapshot;
synchronized (sharedList) {
    snapshot = new ArrayList<>(sharedList);
}
snapshot.sort(EmployeeComparators.PAYROLL_ORDER);
return Collections.unmodifiableList(snapshot);
Part 20

`Enum` Ordering

Java enum types automatically implement Comparable, with the natural order being the declaration order in source code:

public enum Priority {
    LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, CRITICAL // ordinals: 0, 1, 2, 3
}

Priority p1 = Priority.LOW;
Priority p2 = Priority.HIGH;
System.out.println(p1.compareTo(p2)); // negative: LOW < HIGH
System.out.println(p1.ordinal());     // 0
System.out.println(p2.ordinal());     // 2

// Enums work naturally in TreeSet, PriorityQueue, etc.
TreeSet<Priority> set = new TreeSet<>();
set.addAll(List.of(Priority.CRITICAL, Priority.LOW, Priority.MEDIUM));
System.out.println(set); // [LOW, MEDIUM, CRITICAL]

Best practice: When enum values have a logical ordering, declare them in that order (LOW → HIGH) so that natural ordering is intuitive. If ordering requirements change, update both the declaration order and any documentation.

Part 21

Sorting in Java 8+ Streams vs Legacy APIs

Feature Legacy (Collections.sort) Stream .sorted()
In-place modification Yes (modifies the original list) No (produces a new stream)
Returns void Stream<T> (lazy)
Requires List Yes No (any Stream)
Supports Comparator Yes Yes
Stable sort Yes (TimSort) Yes (TimSort underneath)
Parallel sort support Via Arrays.parallelSort() Via parallelStream().sorted()
Early termination No Yes (with findFirst(), limit())
Best for Sorting and using the same list Sort-and-transform pipelines 
// Legacy: sort the list itself
List<Employee> mutable = new ArrayList<>(employees);
Collections.sort(mutable, Comparator.comparing(Employee::getSalary));

// Stream: sort in a pipeline (original list unchanged)
List<Employee> topEarners = employees.stream()
    .sorted(Comparator.comparingDouble(Employee::getSalary).reversed())
    .limit(10)
    .collect(Collectors.toList());

// Parallel sort for large arrays (primitives only — use with care)
int[] largeArray = fetchLargeDataset();
Arrays.parallelSort(largeArray);
Part 22

Summary Table

Concept Key Points
Comparable<T> Natural ordering; compareTo(T other); one ordering per class; in java.lang
Comparator<T> Custom ordering; compare(T o1, T o2); multiple per class; @FunctionalInterface
compareTo contract Antisymmetric + Transitive + (ideally) Consistent with equals
Subtraction anti-pattern a - b overflows; use Integer.compare(a, b) instead
TreeSet / TreeMap equality Use compareTo, NOT equals — must be consistent or duplicates slip in
Comparator.comparing() Key extractor; primitives: comparingInt, comparingLong, comparingDouble
thenComparing() Secondary, tertiary sort keys; applied only when primary returns 0
reversed() Reverses entire chain so far — not just last step; isolate with wrapping to reverse one key
Null-safe sorting Comparator.nullsFirst() / nullsLast() wraps any comparator
TimSort Stable; O(n log n) worst, O(n) best; throws on contract violation
Spring Sort.by() Wraps Comparator for Spring Data queries; field names are Java properties
Enum ordering Natural order = declaration order; auto-implements Comparable
Records + Comparable Clean fit; components map to comparison fields; consistency with auto-generated equals
Thread safety Stateless comparators are safe; sorting shared mutable lists requires synchronization

Practice Section

Exercises

Exercise 28.1 — Implement Comparable<Product> for a Product record with fields category, price, and productId. Natural order: by category ascending, then price descending, then productId ascending. Write a test that places products in a TreeSet and verifies the iteration order.

Exercise 28.2 — Write a null-safe, multi-field Comparator<Customer> that sorts by lastName (nulls last), then firstName (nulls last), then registrationDate ascending. Verify with a list that contains several null last names.

Exercise 28.3 — Demonstrate the "reversed() applies to whole chain" bug: create a comparator that sorts employees by department ascending, then salary descending. Show the wrong approach and the correct approach side-by-side, and write a unit test that catches the bug.

Exercise 28.4 — Reproduce the IllegalArgumentException: Comparison method violates its general contract! error by creating a deliberately non-transitive comparator and sorting a list of 3 or more elements with it.

Exercise 28.5 — Use Comparator.comparing(Map.Entry::getValue).reversed() to produce a sorted list of the top-10 most frequent words from a given text.

Interview Questions

Q: What is the difference between Comparable and Comparator?
A: Comparable defines the natural ordering of a class and is implemented on the class itself via compareTo(T other). Comparator is an external strategy that compares two objects via compare(T o1, T o2), supports multiple orderings, and is a @FunctionalInterface. Use Comparable when there is one obvious natural ordering; use Comparator for custom or context-dependent orderings.

Q: What are the three properties of the compareTo contract?
A: (1) Antisymmetry: sgn(x.compareTo(y)) == -sgn(y.compareTo(x)); (2) Transitivity: if x > y and y > z then x > z; (3) Consistency with equals (recommended): x.compareTo(y) == 0 if and only if x.equals(y).

Q: Why should you never use subtraction to implement compareTo for integers?
A: Integer subtraction overflows. Integer.MIN_VALUE - 1 wraps around to Integer.MAX_VALUE, making a very small number appear greater than a very large number. Use Integer.compare(a, b) instead.

Q: TreeSet contains one element after adding two objects that are not equals(). Why?
A: TreeSet uses compareTo() (or compare()) to determine membership — not equals(). If both objects return 0 from compareTo(), the TreeSet treats them as equal and only stores the first one. The fix is to make compareTo() consistent with equals().

Q: How does Comparator.reversed() behave in a chain?
A: It reverses the entire comparator accumulated so far, not just the last step. To reverse only one key in a chain, wrap that key's comparator separately: .thenComparing(Comparator.comparing(Employee::getSalary).reversed()).

Q: What does Spring Data's Sort.by() represent, and how is it different from Comparator?
A: Sort.by() describes field-based sorting that Spring Data translates into SQL ORDER BY clauses. It uses Java property names (not DB column names) and does not execute JVM-level comparison. Comparator is a JVM construct for in-memory sorting only.

Part 1

Why Immutability Matters in Collection Design

Mutable shared state is one of the most persistent sources of bugs in concurrent and multi-layered applications. When a collection is passed between methods, layers, or threads, any receiver can modify it — breaking invariants, corrupting caches, or producing subtle race conditions that are nearly impossible to reproduce.

Immutable collections solve this by making mutation structurally impossible. An immutable collection cannot be added to, removed from, or have its elements replaced — any such attempt throws UnsupportedOperationException at runtime (or is prevented at compile time with proper API design).

Mutable Collection Problem
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  Service A                  Service B
  ─────────                  ─────────
  List<String> tags = new ArrayList<>();
  tags.add("java");

  processAsync(tags);   ──►  void processAsync(List<String> tags) {
  tags.add("jvm");  ◄──        // Concurrent modification!
                               tags.clear(); // mutates caller's list
                             }

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  With Immutable Collection:

  List<String> tags = List.of("java", "jvm");
  processAsync(tags); // Safe: any mutation attempt throws immediately

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Immutable collections also enable sharing without copying, structural sharing in functional data structures, safe caching, and thread-safe reads without synchronization.

Part 2

Three Levels of "Immutability" in Java

Java's ecosystem offers three distinct levels of protection, which are frequently confused:

Level Mechanism Can existing elements be mutated? Can structure be changed?
Unmodifiable view Collections.unmodifiableList() Yes (via original reference) No (via wrapper)
Truly immutable List.of(), List.copyOf() No No
Deep immutable Immutable elements + immutable structure No No

Only level 3 is "truly" immutable in the sense that no mutation is possible from any reference. Java's built-in List.of() is level 2 — the list structure is immutable, but if the elements themselves are mutable (e.g., List<Employee>), the employee objects can still be modified.

Part 3

`Collections.unmodifiableXxx` — The Legacy Approach

Before Java 9, the standard way to prevent structural mutation was to wrap a mutable collection in an unmodifiable view:

List<String> mutable = new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList("a", "b", "c"));
List<String> view = Collections.unmodifiableList(mutable);

view.add("d"); // throws UnsupportedOperationException — good
mutable.add("d"); // succeeds — and view sees the change!

System.out.println(view); // [a, b, c, d] — the "immutable" view mutated!

This is the wrapper / unmodifiable view pattern. It provides a restricted API but does not prevent mutation through the original reference. The view and the original list share the same underlying array.

Available wrapper methods:

Method Returns
Collections.unmodifiableList(list) Unmodifiable List<E> view
Collections.unmodifiableSet(set) Unmodifiable Set<E> view
Collections.unmodifiableSortedSet(set) Unmodifiable SortedSet<E> view
Collections.unmodifiableMap(map) Unmodifiable Map<K,V> view
Collections.unmodifiableSortedMap(map) Unmodifiable SortedMap<K,V> view
Collections.unmodifiableCollection(c) Unmodifiable Collection<E> view

When to use: When you receive a mutable collection from a library/framework and need to pass a read-only view downward without copying. Always document that the view is not truly immutable.

Part 4

`List.of()`, `Set.of()`, `Map.of()` — Java 9 Immutable Factories

Java 9 (JEP 269) introduced factory methods that create truly immutable collections — not views, but new independent objects that can never be mutated through any reference.

List.of()

List<String> languages = List.of("Java", "Kotlin", "Scala");
languages.add("Groovy");    // UnsupportedOperationException
languages.set(0, "Python"); // UnsupportedOperationException
languages.remove(0);        // UnsupportedOperationException

Overloads from 0 to 10 elements are defined for performance (avoiding varargs array allocation). A varargs overload handles 11+:

List<String> empty  = List.of();
List<String> single = List.of("only");
List<String> pair   = List.of("a", "b");
// ... up to List.of(e1, e2, e3, e4, e5, e6, e7, e8, e9, e10)
List<String> large  = List.of("a", "b", "c", "d", "e", "f",
                               "g", "h", "i", "j", "k"); // varargs

Set.of()

Set<Integer> primes = Set.of(2, 3, 5, 7, 11);
primes.add(13);   // UnsupportedOperationException

Important: Set.of() does not guarantee iteration order — unlike List.of(), the order may differ between JVM runs. Also, duplicate elements throw IllegalArgumentException at creation time (not silently ignored).

Set<String> bad = Set.of("a", "b", "a"); // IllegalArgumentException: duplicate element

Map.of()

Map<String, Integer> httpCodes = Map.of(
    "OK",        200,
    "Not Found", 404,
    "Error",     500
);

Map.of() accepts alternating key-value pairs up to 10 pairs maximum. For more entries, use Map.ofEntries().

Map.ofEntries() — Unlimited Map Entries

Map<String, String> config = Map.ofEntries(
    Map.entry("host",     "localhost"),
    Map.entry("port",     "8080"),
    Map.entry("db",       "postgres"),
    Map.entry("user",     "admin"),
    Map.entry("timeout",  "30"),
    Map.entry("pool",     "10"),
    Map.entry("ssl",      "false"),
    Map.entry("schema",   "public"),
    Map.entry("charset",  "UTF-8"),
    Map.entry("timezone", "UTC"),
    Map.entry("locale",   "en_US") // 11th entry — would fail with Map.of()
);

Map.entry(k, v) creates an immutable Map.Entry<K,V>. Neither key nor value can be null.

Part 5

`List.copyOf()`, `Set.copyOf()`, `Map.copyOf()` — Defensive Copies

Java 10 added copyOf() factory methods that create a new immutable collection from any existing collection:

List<String> mutable = new ArrayList<>(List.of("a", "b", "c"));
List<String> snapshot = List.copyOf(mutable); // immutable copy

mutable.add("d");
System.out.println(snapshot); // [a, b, c] — unaffected

copyOf() is the defensive copy pattern formalized. It is significantly safer than wrapping with Collections.unmodifiableList() because the snapshot is independent of the original.

Behavior with already-immutable input:

List<String> original = List.of("x", "y");
List<String> copy = List.copyOf(original);
System.out.println(original == copy); // true (JVM optimization: same object returned)

When the input is already an unmodifiable List created by List.of(), the JVM may return the same object — making copyOf() zero-cost in the common case.

Part 6

ASCII Diagram: Unmodifiable Wrapper vs Truly Immutable

UNMODIFIABLE WRAPPER (Collections.unmodifiableList)
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  originalList (ArrayList)         unmodifiableView
  ┌─────────────────────────┐      ┌─────────────────────────┐
  │  [0] "Java"             │◄─────│  delegate → originalList│
  │  [1] "Kotlin"           │      │  add()  → throws UOE    │
  │  [2] "Scala"            │      │  set()  → throws UOE    │
  └─────────────────────────┘      │  get()  → delegates ✓   │
          ▲                        └─────────────────────────┘
          │
  originalList.add("Groovy")  ←── Still works! View sees the change.

  Both references → SAME backing array

════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

TRULY IMMUTABLE (List.of / List.copyOf)
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  List.of("Java", "Kotlin", "Scala")

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ImmutableCollections$List12 (internal) │
  │                                         │
  │  e0 = "Java"   (final field)            │
  │  e1 = "Kotlin" (final field)            │
  │  e2 = "Scala"  (final field)            │
  │                                         │
  │  add()    → throws UOE immediately      │
  │  set()    → throws UOE immediately      │
  │  remove() → throws UOE immediately      │
  │  get()    → direct field access ✓       │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────┘

  No other reference → original mutable backing structure.
  Elements stored directly as final fields for 1–2 elements,
  as a final Object[] for 3+ elements (array itself is final,
  cannot be swapped — but elements within are Object refs).

════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
Part 7

Null Rejection Policy

A critical and interview-relevant behavioral difference: List.of(), Set.of(), and Map.of() reject null elements immediately at creation time.

List.of("a", null, "b");       // NullPointerException
Set.of("x", null);             // NullPointerException
Map.of("key", null);           // NullPointerException
Map.of(null, "value");         // NullPointerException

This is a design decision — immutable collections are intended as "value" containers, and null is a placeholder for absence of value, not a value itself. Forcing null rejection at creation time causes failures fast (at the source) rather than silently at use time.

Contrast with Collections.unmodifiableList():

List<String> nullAllowed = new ArrayList<>();
nullAllowed.add(null);
List<String> view = Collections.unmodifiableList(nullAllowed); // Works
System.out.println(view.get(0)); // null — allowed

And Arrays.asList():

List<String> withNull = Arrays.asList("a", null, "b"); // Allowed, fixed-size

Interview key point: If your data may contain null and you need an immutable-like collection, use Collections.unmodifiableList(new ArrayList<>(source)) after filtering nulls, or use List.copyOf() after ensuring no nulls are present.

Part 8

`Map.of()` 10-Pair Limit

Map.of() is defined with specific overloads for 0 through 10 key-value pairs:

static <K,V> Map<K,V> of()
static <K,V> Map<K,V> of(K k1, V v1)
static <K,V> Map<K,V> of(K k1, V v1, K k2, V v2)
// ... up to 10 pairs
static <K,V> Map<K,V> of(K k1, V v1, ..., K k10, V v10)

This design choice (varargs Object... would require unsafe casts and lose compile-time type checking) means exceeding 10 pairs requires Map.ofEntries().

// At compile time, no error. At runtime:
// Map.of(k1,v1, k2,v2, ...) — limited to 10 pairs
// For 11+, always use:
Map.ofEntries(
    Map.entry("k1", "v1"),
    // ... as many as needed
);
Part 9

Internal Implementation Details

The JDK implements immutable collections with highly optimized internal classes that are not ArrayList, HashSet, or HashMap:

List.of() Internal Classes (OpenJDK)
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  List.of()          →  ImmutableCollections.List0
  List.of(e1)        →  ImmutableCollections.List1
  List.of(e1,e2)     →  ImmutableCollections.List12
  List.of(e1..eN)    →  ImmutableCollections.ListN

  Set.of()           →  ImmutableCollections.Set0  
  Set.of(e1)         →  ImmutableCollections.Set1
  Set.of(e1,e2)      →  ImmutableCollections.Set12
  Set.of(e1..eN)     →  ImmutableCollections.SetN (hash-based)

  Map.of()           →  ImmutableCollections.Map0
  Map.of(k,v)        →  ImmutableCollections.Map1
  Map.of(k,v,k,v)    →  ImmutableCollections.MapN

These classes:
- Store elements in final fields or a final array (cannot be reassigned)
- Override all mutating methods to throw UnsupportedOperationException
- Are Serializable (since Java 9)
- Produce a compact, cache-friendly memory layout (no Node/Entry objects for small sizes)
- Are not guaranteed to be the same class across JVM implementations or versions

Never depend on the concrete type:

List<String> list = List.of("a", "b");
// WRONG: instanceof checks on internal classes are fragile
if (list instanceof ArrayList) { ... }
// RIGHT: program to the interface
if (list instanceof List) { ... }
Part 10

`Arrays.asList()` — The Partially Mutable Pitfall

Arrays.asList() is frequently confused with immutable collections:

List<String> list = Arrays.asList("a", "b", "c");
list.set(0, "z");        // Works! — structural immutability only
list.add("d");           // UnsupportedOperationException
list.remove(0);          // UnsupportedOperationException

Arrays.asList() returns a fixed-size list backed by the array — you can replace elements (change values) but cannot add or remove (change size). It is neither unmodifiable nor truly immutable.

Arrays.asList() vs List.of()
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
│ Operation   │ Arrays.asList() │ List.of()          │
│─────────────│─────────────────│────────────────────│
│ get(i)      │ ✓               │ ✓                  │
│ set(i, e)   │ ✓               │ ✗ UOE              │
│ add(e)      │ ✗ UOE           │ ✗ UOE              │
│ remove(i)   │ ✗ UOE           │ ✗ UOE              │
│ null        │ ✓ allowed       │ ✗ NPE at creation  │
│ backed by   │ original array  │ new internal object│
│ array sync  │ yes (both views)│ no                 │
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
Part 11

Guava Immutable Collections (Preview)

Google's Guava library provides a battle-tested set of truly immutable collections with richer builder APIs and additional guarantees:

// Maven/Gradle dependency:
// com.google.guava:guava:32.x.x-jre

import com.google.common.collect.ImmutableList;
import com.google.common.collect.ImmutableSet;
import com.google.common.collect.ImmutableMap;

ImmutableList<String> list = ImmutableList.of("a", "b", "c");

ImmutableList<String> built = ImmutableList.<String>builder()
    .add("x")
    .add("y")
    .addAll(existingCollection)
    .build();

ImmutableMap<String, Integer> map = ImmutableMap.<String, Integer>builder()
    .put("one", 1)
    .put("two", 2)
    .buildOrThrow(); // throws on duplicate keys (vs silently overwriting)

Guava advantages over JDK List.of():

Feature JDK List.of() Guava ImmutableList
Builder pattern No Yes
addAll from collection No Yes
Serialization-stable type Partially Yes (guaranteed)
Null rejection Yes Yes
Sorted variant No ImmutableSortedSet, ImmutableSortedMap
Multimap, Multiset No ImmutableMultimap, ImmutableMultiset
asList() on Set No Yes
inverse() on BiMap No ImmutableBiMap.inverse()

For new projects using Java 9+, prefer JDK immutable factories for simple cases. Use Guava when you need builders, sorted variants, or Guava-specific collection types.

Part 12

Defensive Programming with Immutable Collections

The canonical use of immutable collections in API design is defensive copying at boundaries.

Anti-pattern: Exposing Internal Mutable State

public class CustomerProfile {
    private final List<String> roles = new ArrayList<>();

    public List<String> getRoles() {
        return roles; // DANGEROUS: caller can mutate internal state
    }
}

profile.getRoles().add("ADMIN"); // Modifies internal state!

Pattern 1: Return Immutable View (low cost, still mutable via internal reference)

public List<String> getRoles() {
    return Collections.unmodifiableList(roles);
}

Pattern 2: Return Defensive Copy (safe, allocates new list)

public List<String> getRoles() {
    return new ArrayList<>(roles); // caller has own mutable copy
}

Pattern 3: Return Truly Immutable Copy (preferred in modern Java)

public List<String> getRoles() {
    return List.copyOf(roles); // truly immutable snapshot
}

Constructor Defensive Copy (input validation)

public class ImmutableRoute {
    private final List<String> waypoints;

    public ImmutableRoute(List<String> waypoints) {
        // Defensive copy: don't trust caller not to mutate their list later
        this.waypoints = List.copyOf(waypoints); // also validates no nulls
    }

    public List<String> getWaypoints() {
        return waypoints; // already immutable — safe to return directly
    }
}
Part 13

Records + Immutable Collections

Java Records (Java 16+) are immutable value carriers by design. Pairing them with immutable collections produces genuinely immutable domain objects.

public record ApiResponse<T>(
    int statusCode,
    T body,
    List<String> headers,
    Map<String, String> metadata
) {
    // Compact constructor — validate and defensively copy
    public ApiResponse {
        headers  = List.copyOf(headers);   // immutable snapshot
        metadata = Map.copyOf(metadata);   // immutable snapshot
    }
}

List<String> hdrs = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Content-Type: application/json"));
ApiResponse<String> response = new ApiResponse<>(200, "OK", hdrs, Map.of());

hdrs.add("X-Custom: evil"); // mutate the original
System.out.println(response.headers()); // [Content-Type: application/json] — safe!

The compact constructor pattern with List.copyOf() / Map.copyOf() is the idiomatic way to create immutable records with collection fields.

Part 14

Immutable Collections in Concurrent Code

Because immutable collections allow no structural mutation, they are inherently thread-safe for reads — no synchronization is needed.

// Computed once at startup, shared across all threads
private static final Map<String, Handler> ROUTE_TABLE = Map.ofEntries(
    Map.entry("/api/users",    new UserHandler()),
    Map.entry("/api/products", new ProductHandler()),
    Map.entry("/api/orders",   new OrderHandler())
);

// Safe to call from any thread simultaneously — no lock needed
public Handler resolve(String path) {
    return ROUTE_TABLE.get(path);
}

Compare with a mutable HashMap shared across threads (requires ConcurrentHashMap or explicit locking for correctness).

Thread Safety Comparison
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  Collection Type          Read   Write   Lock Needed?
  ───────────────────────  ─────  ──────  ─────────────
  ArrayList                ✓      ✓       Yes (both ops)
  HashMap                  ✓      ✓       Yes (both ops)
  Collections.unmodifiable ✓      ✗ UOE   No (reads safe)
  List.of() / Map.of()     ✓      ✗ UOE   No (reads safe)
  ConcurrentHashMap        ✓      ✓       No (built-in)
  CopyOnWriteArrayList     ✓      ✓       No (built-in)
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
Part 15

Iteration Order Guarantees

Iteration order behavior differs between factory methods:

Factory Iteration Order
List.of(e1, e2, e3) Guaranteed: insertion order
Set.of(e1, e2, e3) Not guaranteed: may vary between JVM runs
Map.of(k1,v1, k2,v2) Not guaranteed: may vary between JVM runs
Map.ofEntries(...) Not guaranteed: may vary between JVM runs
List.copyOf(collection) Iteration order of source
Set.copyOf(collection) Not guaranteed
Map.copyOf(map) Not guaranteed

The JDK intentionally does not guarantee Set.of() / Map.of() iteration order and may randomize it per-run to deter code that accidentally depends on it. This is a stronger contract than HashSet (which has deterministic but undocumented order per JVM session).

Part 16

Converting Between Mutable and Immutable

// Immutable → Mutable (when you need to add elements)
List<String> immutable = List.of("a", "b", "c");
List<String> mutable   = new ArrayList<>(immutable);
mutable.add("d");

Set<String>  mutableSet = new HashSet<>(Set.of("x", "y"));
Map<String,Integer> mutableMap = new HashMap<>(Map.of("k", 1));

// Mutable → Immutable (snapshot / seal)
List<String> frozen  = List.copyOf(mutableList);
Set<String>  frozenS = Set.copyOf(mutableSet);
Map<K,V>    frozenM  = Map.copyOf(mutableMap);

Stream → Immutable Collection (Java 10+):

List<String> immutableResult = Stream.of("a", "b", "c")
    .filter(s -> !s.isEmpty())
    .collect(Collectors.toUnmodifiableList()); // Java 10

// Java 16+ — toList() returns unmodifiable list
List<String> toList = Stream.of("x", "y").toList();

Collectors.toUnmodifiableList() / toUnmodifiableSet() / toUnmodifiableMap() were added in Java 10. Stream.toList() shorthand was added in Java 16 and returns an unmodifiable but not necessarily truly immutable list (implementation-defined).

Part 17

Sorted Immutable Collections

The JDK does not provide sorted immutable collection factories directly. For a sorted immutable List, sort then freeze:

List<String> sortedImmutable = Stream.of("Charlie", "Alice", "Bob")
    .sorted()
    .collect(Collectors.toUnmodifiableList());
// or
List<String> sorted = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Charlie", "Alice", "Bob"));
Collections.sort(sorted);
List<String> immutableSorted = List.copyOf(sorted);

For sorted immutable Set or Map, Guava provides ImmutableSortedSet and ImmutableSortedMap:

ImmutableSortedSet<String> sortedSet = ImmutableSortedSet.of("c", "a", "b");
// Iteration: a, b, c (natural order)
Part 18

Production Anti-Patterns to Avoid

Anti-Pattern 1 — Using Collections.unmodifiableList and Leaking the Original

// In a service
private List<String> allowedOrigins = new ArrayList<>();

public List<String> getAllowedOrigins() {
    return Collections.unmodifiableList(allowedOrigins);
}

// In a test or subclass — bypasses the protection
((ArrayList<String>) ((List) allowedOrigins)).add("evil.com"); // reflection hack
// OR simply via the field reference before wrapping

Fix: Use List.copyOf() in the getter, or store allowedOrigins as List.copyOf() from the start.

Anti-Pattern 2 — Assuming List.of() Elements Are Immutable

List<List<String>> nested = List.of(
    new ArrayList<>(List.of("a", "b")),
    new ArrayList<>(List.of("c", "d"))
);

nested.add(new ArrayList<>()); // UOE — outer list is immutable
nested.get(0).add("injected"); // Works! — inner lists are mutable

True deep immutability requires immutable elements throughout the entire object graph.

Anti-Pattern 3 — Ignoring Map.of() 10-Entry Limit

// This compiles only with Map.of() overloads up to 10 pairs
Map<String, String> config = Map.of(
    "a","1","b","2","c","3","d","4","e","5",
    "f","6","g","7","h","8","i","9","j","10",
    "k","11" // ← COMPILE ERROR: no matching overload!
);
// Fix: use Map.ofEntries()

Anti-Pattern 4 — Sorting or Searching Unmodifiable Collections Without Copying

List<String> view = Collections.unmodifiableList(mutableList);
Collections.sort(view);         // UnsupportedOperationException!
Collections.shuffle(view);      // UnsupportedOperationException!
// These methods require a modifiable list — always sort the mutable original
Part 19

Performance Characteristics

Memory Layout Comparison
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  Collection             Overhead per element   Notes
  ────────────────────── ──────────────────────  ────────────────────
  ArrayList              ~16 bytes (Object ref + Object header)
  List.of(e1)            0 (element in final field directly)
  List.of(e1..eN)        Object[] + header (~12 bytes + 4/ref)
  HashMap                ~48 bytes (Node: hash, key, val, next)
  Map.of(k,v)            ~12 bytes (flat key+value array slot pair)
  HashSet                ~48 bytes (uses HashMap internally)
  Set.of(e1..eN)         ~8 bytes (flat array slot)
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

For small immutable collections (< 20 elements), List.of() / Map.of() are more memory-efficient than their mutable counterparts due to the compact flat-array storage and absence of load-factor overhead.

For read-heavy workloads, immutable collections are also cache-friendly — no concurrent modification checks, no volatile reads, predictable layout.

Part 20

Spring Boot Integration

Configuration Properties with Immutable Collections

@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "app.security")
public record SecurityConfig(
    List<String> allowedOrigins,
    Set<String>  allowedMethods,
    Map<String, String> headers
) {}

Spring Boot 2.2+ supports binding configuration to records. The bound values are not List.of() instances — they are regular mutable lists. If you need immutable semantics, copy in the constructor:

public SecurityConfig {
    allowedOrigins = List.copyOf(allowedOrigins);
    allowedMethods = Set.copyOf(allowedMethods);
    headers        = Map.copyOf(headers);
}

Return Immutable Collections from REST Responses

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/products")
public class ProductController {

    private final ProductService productService;

    @GetMapping
    public List<ProductDto> getAll() {
        // Return immutable — no caller can accidentally mutate the response list
        return List.copyOf(productService.findAll());
    }

    @GetMapping("/tags")
    public Set<String> getAllTags() {
        return Set.copyOf(productService.findAllTags());
    }
}

Jackson (JSON serialization) serializes immutable collections identically to their mutable counterparts — List.of() becomes a JSON array, Map.of() becomes a JSON object.

Scenario Collections.unmodifiableList() List.of() List.copyOf()
Null elements Allowed NPE at creation NPE at creation
Mutation via original Yes N/A (no original) No (independent copy)
Element replacement (set) UOE UOE UOE
Memory allocation Wrapper only New internal object New internal object
Serialize stable Yes Yes (since Java 9) Yes
Available since Java 1.2 Java 9 Java 10
Duplicate detection (Set) No (at wrap time) IAE at creation IAE at creation
Empty singleton Yes Yes Yes

Practice

Exercise 1 — Spot the Bug

Identify all problems in this code and explain why each is a bug:

public class UserService {
    private List<String> adminUsers = new ArrayList<>(List.of("alice", "bob"));

    public List<String> getAdmins() {
        return Collections.unmodifiableList(adminUsers);
    }

    public void addAdmin(String user) {
        adminUsers.add(user);
    }
}

// In a test:
List<String> admins = service.getAdmins();
service.addAdmin("carol");
System.out.println(admins.contains("carol")); // What does this print?

Exercise 2 — Immutable Record

Create a Route record with a List<Waypoint> field where Waypoint is another record with String name and double lat, double lon. Ensure the Route is deeply immutable — the list cannot be modified, but also ensure the caller gets a meaningful exception message if they pass null waypoints.

Exercise 3 — Map Building

Create a Map<String, List<String>> representing HTTP method to allowed paths (e.g., GET → [/api/users, /api/products], POST → [/api/orders]). Use Map.ofEntries() and List.of() throughout. Verify that neither the outer map nor any inner list can be mutated.

Exercise 4 — Stream to Immutable

Given a List<Employee> where some employees have null department fields, write a stream pipeline that:
1. Filters out employees with null departments
2. Groups them by department into a Map<String, List<Employee>>
3. Returns an unmodifiable view of the result

Use Collectors.toUnmodifiableMap() and handle the case where multiple employees share a department.

Exercise 5 — Spring Boot Configuration

Write a @ConfigurationProperties record called AllowlistConfig with a List<String> field trustedHosts. Demonstrate in a compact constructor how to:
1. Validate the list is not empty
2. Ensure all entries are non-null and non-blank
3. Store an immutable copy

Interview Questions

Q1: What is the difference between Collections.unmodifiableList() and List.of()?
Collections.unmodifiableList() returns a view over a mutable list — it prevents mutation through the view but the underlying list can still be mutated via the original reference. List.of() creates a truly independent immutable object — no other reference can mutate it. Additionally, List.of() rejects null elements with NullPointerException, while unmodifiableList() allows them if the underlying list contains them.

Q2: Why does List.of() throw NullPointerException for null elements?
By design — immutable collections are intended as "value objects" where null has no place. Failing at creation time (fast-fail) is preferable to a NullPointerException thrown later during usage, making debugging easier. If null support is needed, use Collections.unmodifiableList(new ArrayList<>(source)).

Q3: What is the maximum number of key-value pairs Map.of() accepts? Why?
10 pairs maximum. The API provides specific overloads from 0 to 10 key-value parameters to maintain compile-time type safety (an Object... varargs approach would lose type safety). For more than 10 pairs, Map.ofEntries(Map.entry(k,v), ...) must be used.

Q4: Does List.of() guarantee iteration order?
Yes — List has a defined insertion order and List.of() preserves it. However, Set.of() and Map.of() do not guarantee iteration order and may randomize it between JVM runs to prevent accidental dependencies on ordering.

Q5: Is List.copyOf(List.of("a","b","c")) guaranteed to return the same object?
It may — the JVM is allowed to return the same object if the source is already an immutable List. In OpenJDK, List.copyOf() checks if the source is already an ImmutableCollections instance and returns it directly. This is an optimization, not a guaranteed contract — code should not rely on reference equality.

Q6: Can you modify elements inside a List.of() if those elements are mutable objects?
Yes — List.of() provides structural immutability (you cannot add/remove/replace elements), but it does not provide deep immutability. If you have List<Employee> returned by List.of(), you cannot call list.set(0, newEmployee), but you can call list.get(0).setName("new name") if Employee is mutable. True deep immutability requires immutable elements throughout.
