Part 1

Concept

When multiple threads read from and write to a plain ArrayList, HashMap, or HashSet without external synchronization, the results are unpredictable:

  • A HashMap resize can lose entries permanently (infinite loop in Java 6, silent data loss in Java 7).
  • An ArrayList iterator throws ConcurrentModificationException if another thread modifies the list mid-iteration.
  • Counter updates (map.put(k, map.get(k) + 1)) silently drop increments under contention.

These are not edge cases. Every web server, message broker, and microservice runs code paths that share in-memory state across threads. Thread-safe collections solve this without forcing every caller to hold a lock manually.

The Three Design Goals

Goal Description
Correctness No data corruption or lost updates under any interleaving
Liveness No global lock that serializes all threads; allow concurrent readers
Usability Standard java.util interfaces — drop-in replacements where possible

The java.util.concurrent package (JSR-166, Java 5) and its Java 8 enhancements deliver all three through a combination of CAS (Compare-And-Swap) hardware instructions, lock striping, and copy-on-write snapshot semantics.

Part 2

The Synchronized Wrapper Approach

Before java.util.concurrent existed, the only option was Collections.synchronizedXxx():

Map<String, Integer> syncMap = Collections.synchronizedMap(new HashMap<>());
List<String>         syncList = Collections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>());
Set<String>          syncSet  = Collections.synchronizedSet(new HashSet<>());

How Wrappers Work

Each mutating and read method is wrapped in a synchronized(mutex) block where mutex is the wrapper object itself. All threads lock on the single object — this is coarse-grained locking.

Thread A (put)    ──► acquires syncMap lock ──► holds ──► releases
Thread B (get)    ──► BLOCKED           ──►           ──► acquires ──► ...
Thread C (size)   ──► BLOCKED           ──► BLOCKED   ──►           ──► ...

Critical Compound-Action Trap

Even with the wrapper, compound operations are not atomic:

// BROKEN — check-then-act is not atomic even with synchronizedMap
if (!syncMap.containsKey("x")) {       // ← lock acquired then released
    syncMap.put("x", compute());       // ← different lock acquisition
}

// ALSO BROKEN — iteration requires manual external lock
synchronized (syncMap) {               // ← caller must hold the map's lock
    for (Map.Entry<String, Integer> e : syncMap.entrySet()) {
        process(e);
    }
}

Synchronized Wrapper Limitations

Issue Impact
Single lock for all operations No read concurrency
Compound operations not atomic Race conditions without external synchronized
Iterator not thread-safe by default Must manually lock entire iteration
No putIfAbsent, computeIfAbsent Atomic conditional puts require external sync
Part 3

ConcurrentHashMap — Architecture

ConcurrentHashMap replaces the single-lock model with lock striping — a technique where the internal array is divided into independently-lockable segments, and only the segment containing the relevant bucket is locked during a write.

Java 5–7: Segment-Based Lock Striping

ConcurrentHashMap (concurrencyLevel=16)
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Segment[0]     Segment[1]   ...   Segment[15]                  │
│  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐       ┌──────────┐                  │
│  │ ReentLock│  │ ReentLock│       │ ReentLock│                   │
│  │ HashTable│  │ HashTable│       │ HashTable│                   │
│  │ [bucket] │  │ [bucket] │       │ [bucket] │                   │
│  │ [bucket] │  │ [bucket] │       │ [bucket] │                   │
│  └──────────┘  └──────────┘       └──────────┘                  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  Thread A holds Segment[0] lock → Thread B can operate on Segment[3]

Writes to different segments proceed truly in parallel. Reads required no lock at all because segment entries used volatile fields.

Java 8+: Bucket-Level Locking with CAS

Java 8 eliminated the Segment class entirely and moved to a flat Node[] array with per-bucket synchronization:

Internal Node[] table (resizes dynamically)

Index:  0       1       2       3   ...   N-1
       ┌───┐  ┌───┐  ┌───┐  ┌───┐       ┌───┐
table: │nil│  │ N │  │nil│  │ N │       │ N │
       └───┘  └───┴─►└───┘  └─┬─┘       └───┘
                 │              │
               Node            Node──►Node──►Node
              (head)           (head of chain / tree)

Lock granularity: synchronized(table[i]) — only the head node
CAS:              used for null-bucket insertions (no lock needed)
Part 4

ConcurrentHashMap — Java 8+ Internals

Bin Structure Evolution

Each bucket (bin) starts as a linked list. When a bin's chain grows beyond TREEIFY_THRESHOLD (8) and the table has at least 64 slots, the chain is converted to a red-black tree (TreeBin). This bounds worst-case lookup to O(log n) even with many hash collisions.

LINKED LIST BIN                    RED-BLACK TREE BIN
(chain length ≤ 8)                 (chain length > 8, table size ≥ 64)

 [head Node]                        [TreeBin root]
     │                               /           \
     ▼                          [TreeNode]    [TreeNode]
 [Node k=A]                        /    \
     │                        [TN]     [TN]
     ▼
 [Node k=B]
     │
     ▼
  null

Lookup: O(n) worst case          Lookup: O(log n) worst case

CAS for Empty Buckets

// Simplified insert into empty bucket (no lock needed)
if (casTabAt(tab, i, null, new Node<>(hash, key, value, null)))
    break;   // successful CAS — atomically wrote the first node

// Insert into occupied bucket (synchronized on head node)
synchronized (f) {           // f = first node in bin
    if (tabAt(tab, i) == f) {
        // traverse chain, append or update
    }
}

Size Tracking: LongAdder-Style Cells

ConcurrentHashMap.size() is approximate. Internally, size is tracked via a baseCount long plus a CounterCell[] array (analogous to LongAdder). Under contention, threads increment their own cell; size() sums all cells. This means:

  • size() is not atomic relative to ongoing puts/removes.
  • It reflects a weakly consistent snapshot.
  • mappingCount() returns long — prefer it over size() for large maps.
Part 5

ConcurrentHashMap — Key Operations

ConcurrentHashMap<String, Integer> map = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

// Basic operations — all thread-safe
map.put("requests", 0);
Integer val = map.get("requests");
map.remove("requests");

// Atomic conditional operations
map.putIfAbsent("host", "localhost");           // only inserts if absent
map.replace("host", "localhost", "127.0.0.1"); // only replaces if value matches
boolean removed = map.remove("host", "127.0.0.1"); // conditional remove

// putIfAbsent vs computeIfAbsent
// putIfAbsent always evaluates the value argument
// computeIfAbsent evaluates lazily — value function called only when key absent
map.computeIfAbsent("cache", k -> new ArrayList<>());

// Bulk read operations (weakly consistent)
map.forEach((k, v) -> System.out.println(k + "=" + v));
map.forEachKey(parallelismThreshold, System.out::println);
long total = map.reduceValues(1, Integer::sum);

Null Restrictions

ConcurrentHashMap does not permit null keys or null values. This is intentional: map.get(key) == null is unambiguous — the key is absent. A HashMap cannot make this guarantee (it allows null values), leading to ambiguous get results in concurrent code.

Part 6

ConcurrentHashMap — Compute & Merge Methods

Java 8 added atomic compute operations that eliminate the check-then-act race condition entirely. The entire compute lambda runs under the bin lock.

ConcurrentHashMap<String, Integer> counts = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

// compute — always called, receives current value (may be null)
counts.compute("pageviews", (k, v) -> (v == null) ? 1 : v + 1);

// computeIfAbsent — called only when key is absent
counts.computeIfAbsent("newKey", k -> expensiveInit(k));

// computeIfPresent — called only when key exists and value is non-null
counts.computeIfPresent("pageviews", (k, v) -> v > 1000 ? null : v + 1);
// returning null from compute removes the entry

// merge — combines existing value with a new one using a BiFunction
counts.merge("errors", 1, Integer::sum);
// merge("errors", 1, sum) means:
//   if absent  → put("errors", 1)
//   if present → put("errors", existing + 1)

// Practical: word frequency counter (thread-safe, no external sync)
String[] words = text.split("\\s+");
Arrays.stream(words).parallel()
      .forEach(w -> frequency.merge(w, 1, Integer::sum));

compute vs merge vs putIfAbsent

Method When key absent When key present Removes on null return
putIfAbsent(k, v) inserts no-op No
computeIfAbsent(k, fn) inserts fn(k) no-op No
computeIfPresent(k, fn) no-op applies fn Yes
compute(k, fn) applies fn(k,null) applies fn Yes
merge(k, v, fn) inserts v applies fn(old,v) Yes
Part 7

CopyOnWriteArrayList

CopyOnWriteArrayList (COW) takes a radically different approach: every mutating operation creates a brand-new copy of the underlying array, performs the mutation on the copy, then atomically swaps the reference.

Initial:  array ref ──► [A, B, C]

Thread 1 calls add("D"):
  1. Lock acquired
  2. Copy: newArr = [A, B, C, D]
  3. Atomic reference swap: array ref ──► [A, B, C, D]
  4. Lock released

Thread 2 was iterating over [A, B, C] — sees old snapshot, no CME

CopyOnWriteArrayList<String> cowList = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();

cowList.add("handler-A");
cowList.add("handler-B");

// Safe iteration — snapshot taken at iterator creation time
for (String handler : cowList) {
    dispatch(handler);   // another thread may add/remove — no CME
}

// Bulk add is more efficient than multiple single adds
cowList.addAllAbsent(List.of("handler-C", "handler-D"));

// Safe removal — no ConcurrentModificationException
cowList.removeIf(h -> h.startsWith("deprecated-"));

When to Use COW Collections

Characteristic Implication
Reads vastly outnumber writes Read path is lock-free (just array deref)
Iteration is the hot path Snapshot semantics prevent CME without external sync
Write frequency is low Array copy overhead is acceptable
Collection is small Copying 10 elements ≠ copying 10 million elements

Ideal use cases: event listener registries, plugin handler lists, infrequently-changing allow/deny lists, Spring's ApplicationListener registry.

Avoid when: writes are frequent, or the list is large (copying is O(n) per write).

Part 8

CopyOnWriteArraySet

CopyOnWriteArraySet is backed by a CopyOnWriteArrayList and uses linear scan for uniqueness (no hash table). This makes it appropriate only for small sets.

CopyOnWriteArraySet<String> activeTopics = new CopyOnWriteArraySet<>();

activeTopics.add("orders");
activeTopics.add("payments");
activeTopics.add("orders");   // duplicate — ignored (linear scan)

System.out.println(activeTopics.size());  // 2

// Safe iteration while another thread may be adding topics
activeTopics.forEach(topic -> subscribe(topic));

Trade-offs vs ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet():
- CopyOnWriteArraySet: O(n) add/contains, lock-free reads, snapshot iteration
- ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet(): O(1) average add/contains, weakly consistent iteration, no snapshot

Use CopyOnWriteArraySet only when iteration order matters and the set is small (< ~100 elements).

Part 9

ConcurrentLinkedQueue

ConcurrentLinkedQueue is an unbounded, thread-safe FIFO queue based on the Michael-Scott non-blocking algorithm. It uses CAS operations exclusively — no locks at all.

Internal structure (singly-linked):

  head ──► [sentinel] ──► [item=A] ──► [item=B] ──► [item=C] ──► null
                                                                    ▲
                                                                   tail

offer("D"):
  1. CAS tail.next from null to new Node("D")
  2. Advance tail pointer (may lag one node — lazy update)

poll():
  1. Read head.next (first real item)
  2. CAS head to head.next (advance sentinel)
  3. Return old head.next.item, set its item to null (GC help)

ConcurrentLinkedQueue<Task> taskQueue = new ConcurrentLinkedQueue<>();

// Producer (any thread)
taskQueue.offer(new Task("job-1"));

// Consumer (any thread)
Task t = taskQueue.poll();   // returns null if empty — NON-BLOCKING
if (t != null) process(t);

// Peek without removal
Task peek = taskQueue.peek();

// IMPORTANT: size() is O(n) — traverses the whole queue
// Do NOT use size() in performance-sensitive code
// Use isEmpty() or keep a separate AtomicInteger counter

ConcurrentLinkedQueue is ideal for non-blocking producer-consumer patterns where producers must never block (e.g., event collection, log buffering).

Part 10

ConcurrentLinkedDeque

ConcurrentLinkedDeque extends the non-blocking approach to a doubly-linked deque — insertions and removals from both ends using CAS.

ConcurrentLinkedDeque<String> deque = new ConcurrentLinkedDeque<>();

// Deque operations — all non-blocking
deque.offerFirst("priority-task");
deque.offerLast("normal-task");

String first = deque.pollFirst();
String last  = deque.pollLast();
String peekF = deque.peekFirst();

// Work-stealing pattern: workers take from their own tail,
// steal from other workers' heads when idle

ConcurrentLinkedDeque vs ConcurrentLinkedQueue:

ConcurrentLinkedQueue ConcurrentLinkedDeque
Ends Head/tail (FIFO only) Both ends (FIFO + LIFO)
Algorithm Michael-Scott (singly-linked CAS) CAS on doubly-linked nodes
Use case Simple FIFO Work-stealing, LRU caches
Overhead Lower Slightly higher
Part 11

BlockingQueue Family — Overview

BlockingQueue extends Queue with blocking semantics: producers wait when the queue is full, consumers wait when the queue is empty. This is the backbone of the classic thread-pool and producer-consumer pattern.

The Four Operation Groups

Action Throws exception Returns special value Blocks Times out
Insert add(e) offer(e) put(e) offer(e, t, unit)
Remove remove() poll() take() poll(t, unit)
Examine element() peek() — — 
BlockingQueue<String> queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(10);

// Producer thread
void produce(String item) throws InterruptedException {
    queue.put(item);   // blocks if queue is full
}

// Consumer thread
void consume() throws InterruptedException {
    String item = queue.take();   // blocks if queue is empty
    process(item);
}

// Non-blocking with timeout
boolean added    = queue.offer(item, 100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
String  polled   = queue.poll(100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);

BlockingQueue Hierarchy

          «interface»
          BlockingQueue<E>
               │
    ┌──────────┼──────────────────────┐
    │          │                      │
ArrayBQ  LinkedBQ             «interface»
                             TransferQueue<E>
                                    │
                              LinkedTransferQueue

          SynchronousQueue
          PriorityBlockingQueue
          DelayQueue
Part 12

ArrayBlockingQueue & LinkedBlockingQueue

ArrayBlockingQueue

Bounded, backed by a fixed-size array. A single ReentrantLock with two conditions (notFull, notEmpty) serializes all access.

// Capacity fixed at construction — cannot grow
ArrayBlockingQueue<Integer> abq = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(100);

// Optional fairness — FIFO among waiting threads (lower throughput)
ArrayBlockingQueue<Integer> fair = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(100, true);

abq.put(42);        // blocks if 100 items already in queue
int v = abq.take(); // blocks if empty

// Drain to another collection (atomic bulk removal)
List<Integer> batch = new ArrayList<>();
abq.drainTo(batch, 20);  // removes up to 20 items

Memory layout: contiguous array, better cache locality, predictable GC behavior. Use when capacity is known and bounded throughput is acceptable.

LinkedBlockingQueue

Optionally bounded (defaults to Integer.MAX_VALUE), backed by a linked-node chain. Uses two locks — one for puts, one for takes — allowing a producer and consumer to proceed simultaneously when the queue is non-empty and non-full.

LinkedBlockingQueue<String> lbq = new LinkedBlockingQueue<>(1000);  // bounded
LinkedBlockingQueue<String> unbounded = new LinkedBlockingQueue<>(); // capacity = MAX_VALUE

// Two-lock design: put lock + take lock
// Producer and consumer can run truly in parallel
lbq.put("message");
String msg = lbq.take();

// Executor service uses LinkedBlockingQueue internally
ExecutorService pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
    4, 4, 0, TimeUnit.SECONDS, new LinkedBlockingQueue<>(500)
);

ArrayBlockingQueue vs LinkedBlockingQueue

ArrayBlockingQueue LinkedBlockingQueue
Capacity Fixed at construction Optionally bounded
Locking Single lock Two locks (put/take)
Throughput Lower under contention Higher under contention
Memory Contiguous array Linked nodes (GC pressure)
Fairness option Yes No
Typical use Fixed-size work queues Executors, pipelines
Part 13

SynchronousQueue & DelayQueue

SynchronousQueue

Has zero capacity. Every put must rendezvous directly with a take. There is no buffering — threads pair up handoff-style.

SynchronousQueue<Runnable> sq = new SynchronousQueue<>();

// Direct handoff executor — no task queuing, new threads spawned immediately
ExecutorService handoff = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
    0, Integer.MAX_VALUE, 60L, TimeUnit.SECONDS, new SynchronousQueue<>()
);
// This is exactly how Executors.newCachedThreadPool() works

// Manual use
Thread producer = new Thread(() -> {
    try { sq.put(task); }   // blocks until a consumer calls take()
    catch (InterruptedException e) { ... }
});

Thread consumer = new Thread(() -> {
    try { Runnable r = sq.take(); r.run(); }
    catch (InterruptedException e) { ... }
});

Use SynchronousQueue when you want strict one-to-one thread handoff with no latency buffering.

DelayQueue

Unbounded blocking queue where each element must implement Delayed. An element is only dequeue-able after its delay has expired.

class ScheduledTask implements Delayed {
    private final long executeAt;   // epoch millis
    private final Runnable task;

    public ScheduledTask(Runnable task, long delayMs) {
        this.executeAt = System.currentTimeMillis() + delayMs;
        this.task = task;
    }

    @Override
    public long getDelay(TimeUnit unit) {
        return unit.convert(executeAt - System.currentTimeMillis(), TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
    }

    @Override
    public int compareTo(Delayed other) {
        return Long.compare(getDelay(TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS), other.getDelay(TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS));
    }
}

DelayQueue<ScheduledTask> delayQueue = new DelayQueue<>();
delayQueue.put(new ScheduledTask(() -> evictCache(), 30_000));  // fires in 30s

// Consumer
ScheduledTask task = delayQueue.take();  // blocks until earliest delay expires
task.getTask().run();

Use cases: TTL cache eviction, retry scheduling with backoff, session expiry, circuit-breaker reset timers.

Part 14

ConcurrentSkipListMap & ConcurrentSkipListSet

Skip lists are probabilistic data structures that maintain sorted order while supporting O(log n) average-case put, get, and remove — all without locks, using only CAS.

Skip List Structure

Level 3:  head ──────────────────────────────────► [50] ──► null
Level 2:  head ──────────► [20] ──────────────► [50] ──► [80] ──► null
Level 1:  head ──► [10] ──► [20] ──► [30] ──► [50] ──► [80] ──► null
Level 0:  head ──► [10] ──► [20] ──► [30] ──► [40] ──► [50] ──► [60] ──► [80] ──► null
           (base sorted list)

Search for 40: Start high (Level 3), skip large ranges,
               descend when overshot → O(log n) expected hops

ConcurrentSkipListMap<String, Integer> skipMap = new ConcurrentSkipListMap<>();

skipMap.put("banana", 2);
skipMap.put("apple", 1);
skipMap.put("cherry", 3);

// NavigableMap operations — all thread-safe
System.out.println(skipMap.firstKey());         // "apple" (sorted)
System.out.println(skipMap.lastKey());          // "cherry"
System.out.println(skipMap.floorKey("blueberry")); // "banana"
System.out.println(skipMap.ceilingKey("avocado")); // "banana"

// Submap views — live, thread-safe, sorted
ConcurrentNavigableMap<String, Integer> sub = skipMap.subMap("apple", "cherry");

// ConcurrentSkipListSet — backed by ConcurrentSkipListMap
ConcurrentSkipListSet<Integer> sortedSet = new ConcurrentSkipListSet<>();
sortedSet.add(5); sortedSet.add(1); sortedSet.add(3);
System.out.println(sortedSet.first());  // 1
System.out.println(sortedSet.last());   // 5

ConcurrentSkipListMap vs ConcurrentHashMap

ConcurrentHashMap ConcurrentSkipListMap
Ordering None Natural / Comparator
Time complexity O(1) average O(log n) average
NavigableMap ops No Yes (floor, ceiling, range)
Lock-free Partial (CAS + bin lock) Fully CAS-based
Use case General key-value cache Leaderboards, time-ordered data
Part 15

Weakly Consistent Iterators

All iterators in java.util.concurrent collections are weakly consistent — a term with a precise meaning:

  1. They will never throw ConcurrentModificationException.
  2. They reflect the state of the collection at or after iterator creation.
  3. They may reflect modifications made after iterator creation, but are not required to.
ConcurrentHashMap<String, String> map = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
map.put("a", "1");
map.put("b", "2");

Iterator<String> it = map.keySet().iterator();

// Another thread adds "c" while iterating
// Iterator may or may not return "c" — both behaviors are valid
map.put("c", "3");

while (it.hasNext()) {
    System.out.println(it.next());
}

// CopyOnWriteArrayList: iteration is over a snapshot
// Elements added after iterator creation are NEVER seen
CopyOnWriteArrayList<String> cowList = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(List.of("x", "y"));
Iterator<String> cowIt = cowList.iterator();
cowList.add("z");          // adds to new copy
while (cowIt.hasNext()) {
    System.out.println(cowIt.next());   // prints x, y — never z
}

Practical Implications

  • Never rely on size() being consistent with iteration in concurrent maps.
  • Bulk operations (forEach, replaceAll, compute) on ConcurrentHashMap are atomic per entry, not across the whole map.
  • For a point-in-time consistent snapshot, copy to a new collection: new HashMap<>(concurrentMap).
Part 16

Master Comparison Table

Collection Ordering Null keys/vals Thread-safety mechanism Iteration Blocking Bounded
ConcurrentHashMap None No / No CAS + bin-level sync Weakly consistent No No
ConcurrentSkipListMap Sorted No / No CAS (lock-free) Weakly consistent No No
CopyOnWriteArrayList Insertion Yes Copy-on-write + lock Snapshot No No
CopyOnWriteArraySet Insertion Yes COW (backed by list) Snapshot No No
ConcurrentLinkedQueue FIFO No CAS (Michael-Scott) Weakly consistent No No
ConcurrentLinkedDeque Deque No CAS (doubly-linked) Weakly consistent No No
ArrayBlockingQueue FIFO No Single ReentrantLock Weakly consistent Yes Yes
LinkedBlockingQueue FIFO No Two ReentrantLocks Weakly consistent Yes Optional
SynchronousQueue N/A No CAS (handoff) Empty always Yes Zero
DelayQueue Delay-expiry No ReentrantLock Weakly consistent Yes No
PriorityBlockingQueue Priority No Single ReentrantLock Weakly consistent Yes No
ConcurrentSkipListSet Sorted No CAS (lock-free) Weakly consistent No No
Collections.synchronizedMap Depends Depends Single object lock Unsafe (needs external sync) No No
Part 17

Production — Shared Caches & Metrics Registries

Pattern 1: Application-Level Cache with ConcurrentHashMap

// Thread-safe cache with lazy initialization and TTL
public class SimpleCache<K, V> {

    private record CacheEntry<V>(V value, long expiresAt) {}

    private final ConcurrentHashMap<K, CacheEntry<V>> store = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final long ttlMillis;

    public SimpleCache(long ttlMillis) {
        this.ttlMillis = ttlMillis;
    }

    public V get(K key, Function<K, V> loader) {
        long now = System.currentTimeMillis();
        CacheEntry<V> entry = store.computeIfAbsent(key,
            k -> new CacheEntry<>(loader.apply(k), now + ttlMillis));

        // TTL check — replace expired entry atomically
        if (entry.expiresAt() < now) {
            CacheEntry<V> fresh = new CacheEntry<>(loader.apply(key), now + ttlMillis);
            store.replace(key, entry, fresh);   // only replaces if still same entry
            return fresh.value();
        }
        return entry.value();
    }

    public void invalidate(K key) { store.remove(key); }
}

Pattern 2: Metrics Registry with Atomic Counters

// High-throughput metrics registry — no blocking, no lock contention
public class MetricsRegistry {

    // LongAdder outperforms AtomicLong under contention (striped cells)
    private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, LongAdder> counters = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    public void increment(String metric) {
        counters.computeIfAbsent(metric, k -> new LongAdder()).increment();
    }

    public void increment(String metric, long delta) {
        counters.computeIfAbsent(metric, k -> new LongAdder()).add(delta);
    }

    public long get(String metric) {
        LongAdder adder = counters.get(metric);
        return adder == null ? 0L : adder.sum();
    }

    // Snapshot all metrics (eventual consistency — reads sum at call time)
    public Map<String, Long> snapshot() {
        Map<String, Long> snap = new HashMap<>();
        counters.forEach((k, v) -> snap.put(k, v.sum()));
        return Collections.unmodifiableMap(snap);
    }
}

Pattern 3: Request Deduplication Cache

// In-flight deduplication: ensure idempotent external calls
public class DeduplicationCache {

    private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, CompletableFuture<Response>> inflight =
        new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    public CompletableFuture<Response> deduplicate(String requestId,
                                                    Supplier<CompletableFuture<Response>> action) {
        return inflight.computeIfAbsent(requestId, k -> {
            CompletableFuture<Response> future = action.get();
            future.whenComplete((r, e) -> inflight.remove(k));   // cleanup on completion
            return future;
        });
        // All concurrent calls with same requestId get the SAME future
    }
}
Part 18

Production — Event Buffers in Microservices

Pattern 4: Non-Blocking Event Buffer with ConcurrentLinkedQueue

// High-throughput audit log — no blocking on hot path
public class AuditBuffer {

    private final ConcurrentLinkedQueue<AuditEvent> buffer = new ConcurrentLinkedQueue<>();
    private final int maxSize;
    private final AtomicInteger size = new AtomicInteger(0);

    public AuditBuffer(int maxSize) { this.maxSize = maxSize; }

    // Hot path — called on every request (zero blocking)
    public boolean record(AuditEvent event) {
        if (size.get() >= maxSize) return false;    // drop if full (backpressure signal)
        buffer.offer(event);
        size.incrementAndGet();
        return true;
    }

    // Background flush — drains to DB/Kafka in batches
    public List<AuditEvent> drainBatch(int batchSize) {
        List<AuditEvent> batch = new ArrayList<>(batchSize);
        AuditEvent e;
        int count = 0;
        while (count < batchSize && (e = buffer.poll()) != null) {
            batch.add(e);
            size.decrementAndGet();
            count++;
        }
        return batch;
    }
}

Pattern 5: Rate Limiter with CopyOnWriteArrayList

// Read-heavy rate limiter config — rules updated rarely, checked on every request
public class RateLimiterConfig {

    // Rules read on every API call; written only on config reload
    private final CopyOnWriteArrayList<RateRule> rules = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();

    // Called on every inbound request — lock-free array read
    public Optional<RateRule> findMatchingRule(String endpoint) {
        for (RateRule rule : rules) {               // snapshot iteration — no CME
            if (rule.matches(endpoint)) return Optional.of(rule);
        }
        return Optional.empty();
    }

    // Called only during config reload (rare)
    public void updateRules(List<RateRule> newRules) {
        rules.clear();
        rules.addAll(newRules);   // both ops create new array copies
    }
}

Pattern 6: Producer-Consumer with LinkedBlockingQueue

// Classic thread-pool task pipeline
public class TaskPipeline {

    private final LinkedBlockingQueue<Runnable> taskQueue = new LinkedBlockingQueue<>(10_000);
    private final List<Thread> workers = new ArrayList<>();

    public TaskPipeline(int workerCount) {
        for (int i = 0; i < workerCount; i++) {
            Thread worker = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> {
                while (!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) {
                    try {
                        Runnable task = taskQueue.take();   // blocks when empty
                        task.run();
                    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
                    }
                }
            });
            workers.add(worker);
        }
    }

    public boolean submit(Runnable task) {
        return taskQueue.offer(task);   // non-blocking offer; returns false if full
    }
}
Part 19

Spring Integration

@Cacheable with ConcurrentHashMap

Spring Cache abstraction supports ConcurrentMapCacheManager backed by ConcurrentHashMap out of the box — no Redis or Caffeine required for simple use cases:

@Configuration
@EnableCaching
public class CacheConfig {

    @Bean
    public CacheManager cacheManager() {
        ConcurrentMapCacheManager manager = new ConcurrentMapCacheManager();
        // Optionally pre-create named caches
        manager.setCacheNames(List.of("users", "products", "configs"));
        return manager;
    }
}

@Service
public class UserService {

    @Cacheable(value = "users", key = "#userId")
    public User findUser(String userId) {
        return userRepository.findById(userId).orElseThrow();
        // First call: hits DB, stores in ConcurrentHashMap
        // Subsequent calls: served from cache (no DB)
    }

    @CacheEvict(value = "users", key = "#user.id")
    public User updateUser(User user) {
        return userRepository.save(user);
        // Evicts entry from ConcurrentHashMap after save
    }

    @CachePut(value = "users", key = "#result.id")
    public User createUser(User user) {
        return userRepository.save(user);
        // Always updates the cache entry with the return value
    }
}

Concurrent Bean Registries

Spring's DefaultListableBeanFactory uses ConcurrentHashMap internally for its bean definition registry. Custom plugin registries should follow the same pattern:

@Component
public class HandlerRegistry {

    // Registered at startup, read on every request
    private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, MessageHandler> handlers = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    @PostConstruct
    public void init() {
        // Register all handlers once at startup
    }

    // Called on every inbound message (hot path)
    public Optional<MessageHandler> resolve(String messageType) {
        return Optional.ofNullable(handlers.get(messageType));
    }

    // Dynamic registration at runtime (rare)
    public void register(String type, MessageHandler handler) {
        handlers.putIfAbsent(type, handler);
    }
}

Spring's ApplicationListener Registry (CopyOnWriteArrayList)

// Spring internally uses COW for its listener list
// org.springframework.context.support.AbstractApplicationEventMulticaster
// stores ApplicationListeners in a CopyOnWriteArrayList equivalent

// Your own event bus should do the same:
@Component
public class DomainEventBus {

    private final CopyOnWriteArrayList<DomainEventListener> listeners =
        new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();

    public void subscribe(DomainEventListener listener) {
        listeners.addIfAbsent(listener);   // idempotent registration
    }

    public void unsubscribe(DomainEventListener listener) {
        listeners.remove(listener);
    }

    // Called on every domain event — lock-free snapshot iteration
    public void publish(DomainEvent event) {
        for (DomainEventListener listener : listeners) {
            listener.onEvent(event);
        }
    }
}
Part 20

Kafka Consumer Offset Tracking Patterns

Kafka consumers operate in a multi-threaded environment where offset tracking, partition assignment, and rebalancing require careful concurrency management.

Pattern: Per-Partition Offset Tracking

// Track the highest committed offset per partition
// Multiple consumer threads update this; a single committer thread reads it
public class OffsetTracker {

    // Partition → Offset. ConcurrentHashMap for thread-safe per-partition updates
    private final ConcurrentHashMap<TopicPartition, Long> pendingOffsets =
        new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    // Called by processing threads after successful message handling
    public void markProcessed(TopicPartition partition, long offset) {
        pendingOffsets.merge(partition, offset, Math::max);
        // merge: if no entry → put offset; if entry exists → keep the higher one
        // Ensures we never commit a lower offset than already processed
    }

    // Called by commit thread on schedule (e.g., every 5 seconds)
    public Map<TopicPartition, OffsetAndMetadata> drainCommittable() {
        Map<TopicPartition, OffsetAndMetadata> toCommit = new HashMap<>();
        pendingOffsets.forEach((partition, offset) -> {
            toCommit.put(partition, new OffsetAndMetadata(offset + 1));
        });
        pendingOffsets.clear();
        return toCommit;
    }
}

Pattern: In-Flight Message Registry

// Track messages currently being processed (for exactly-once guarantees)
public class InFlightRegistry {

    private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, Long> inFlight = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final ConcurrentSkipListSet<Long> completedOffsets = new ConcurrentSkipListSet<>();

    public void register(String messageId, long offset) {
        inFlight.put(messageId, offset);
    }

    public void complete(String messageId) {
        Long offset = inFlight.remove(messageId);
        if (offset != null) completedOffsets.add(offset);
    }

    // Find the highest offset where all prior messages are complete
    public long safeCommitOffset() {
        if (completedOffsets.isEmpty()) return -1;
        // Gaps in completedOffsets indicate in-flight messages
        // Only advance past a contiguous run from the bottom
        long contiguous = completedOffsets.first();
        for (Long offset : completedOffsets) {
            if (offset == contiguous) contiguous++;
            else break;
        }
        return contiguous - 1;
    }
}

Pattern: Rebalance-Aware Partition Map

// On rebalance, reassign partitions atomically
public class PartitionManager implements ConsumerRebalanceListener {

    private volatile Map<TopicPartition, PartitionProcessor> activeProcessors =
        Collections.emptyMap();

    @Override
    public void onPartitionsRevoked(Collection<TopicPartition> partitions) {
        // Flush and stop processors for revoked partitions
        partitions.forEach(p -> {
            PartitionProcessor proc = activeProcessors.get(p);
            if (proc != null) proc.flush();
        });
    }

    @Override
    public void onPartitionsAssigned(Collection<TopicPartition> partitions) {
        // Build new map — replace atomically with volatile write
        Map<TopicPartition, PartitionProcessor> newMap = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
        partitions.forEach(p -> newMap.put(p, new PartitionProcessor(p)));
        activeProcessors = Collections.unmodifiableMap(newMap);
    }
}
Part 21

Interview Questions & Answers

Q1: How does ConcurrentHashMap differ from Collections.synchronizedMap(new HashMap())?

Answer:

Collections.synchronizedMap wraps every method in synchronized(this) — a single lock shared by all readers and writers. Only one thread can operate on the map at a time, making it effectively single-threaded under contention.

ConcurrentHashMap uses per-bucket locking (Java 8+): writes to different buckets proceed in parallel, and reads are lock-free (volatile reads). Additionally, ConcurrentHashMap provides atomic compound operations (computeIfAbsent, merge, putIfAbsent) that synchronizedMap cannot offer safely.

Iteration with synchronizedMap requires the caller to externally synchronized(map) for the entire iteration; ConcurrentHashMap iterators are weakly consistent and never throw ConcurrentModificationException.

Q2: Is ConcurrentHashMap.size() accurate?

Answer: No, not in the absolute sense. size() returns an approximate count by summing a baseCount field and a CounterCell[] array (similar to LongAdder). Since these counters are updated without a global lock, the returned value may not reflect the exact current count under concurrent modifications. For maps that may exceed Integer.MAX_VALUE, use mappingCount() which returns long. If you need a consistent count, either use an external AtomicLong maintained alongside the map, or accept that the count is an approximation.

Q3: What does "weakly consistent iterator" mean in practice?

Answer: A weakly consistent iterator guarantees:
1. It never throws ConcurrentModificationException.
2. Each element it returns existed at some point during the iterator's lifetime.
3. It may or may not reflect modifications (inserts, removes) made after the iterator was created.

In practice: if thread A is iterating ConcurrentHashMap and thread B removes a key, the iterator may or may not return that key. If thread B adds a new key, the iterator may or may not return it. The iterator is safe to use but does not represent a point-in-time snapshot.

CopyOnWriteArrayList iterators are a special case: they always return a snapshot of the array at iterator creation — they are snapshot-consistent, not just weakly consistent.

Q4: When would you choose CopyOnWriteArrayList over ConcurrentLinkedQueue?

Answer:
- Iteration semantics matter: CopyOnWriteArrayList supports indexed access and ListIterator; ConcurrentLinkedQueue does not.
- Read-to-write ratio is very high: COW reads are a single array pointer dereference — faster than queue traversal.
- No consumer/producer pattern: COW is not a queue; it has no take/poll with blocking. Use ConcurrentLinkedQueue for producer-consumer.
- Small collection: COW's O(n) write cost is acceptable for small lists (listener registries, handler chains).

Choose ConcurrentLinkedQueue when elements are consumed in order and removed after processing.

Q5: What is the time complexity of ConcurrentSkipListMap.get() vs ConcurrentHashMap.get()?

Answer: ConcurrentHashMap.get() is O(1) amortized (hash lookup, possibly O(log n) for a treeified bin under heavy collisions). ConcurrentSkipListMap.get() is O(log n) expected because it traverses skip list levels. Use ConcurrentHashMap for pure key-value lookup; use ConcurrentSkipListMap when you need sorted order, range queries (subMap, headMap, tailMap), or floor/ceiling navigation.

Q6: Why does ConcurrentHashMap forbid null keys and values?

Answer: If null values were allowed, map.get(key) == null would be ambiguous — it could mean the key is absent, or that the key maps to null. In a single-threaded HashMap, you can disambiguate with containsKey. In a concurrent map, the containsKey+get pair is not atomic — the key could be removed between the two calls. By forbidding null, ConcurrentHashMap guarantees that get returning null unambiguously means "key absent," enabling safe atomic patterns like computeIfAbsent.

Q7: How do compute, merge, and putIfAbsent differ?

Answer:
- putIfAbsent(k, v): Insert only if absent. Value v is always evaluated (eager). Returns old value or null.
- computeIfAbsent(k, fn): Insert fn(k) only if absent. Function evaluated lazily (only when needed). Use for expensive initialization.
- compute(k, fn): Always calls fn(k, oldValue). If function returns null, the entry is removed. Runs atomically under bin lock.
- merge(k, v, fn): If absent, inserts v. If present, replaces with fn(existing, v). Null result removes entry. Ideal for counters and accumulators.

Q8: What is the difference between ArrayBlockingQueue and LinkedBlockingQueue in a thread pool?

Answer: ArrayBlockingQueue has a fixed capacity and uses a single lock, which can cause more contention under load. LinkedBlockingQueue defaults to Integer.MAX_VALUE capacity (effectively unbounded) and uses two separate locks (one for put, one for take), allowing a producer and consumer to proceed simultaneously. ThreadPoolExecutor with an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue as the work queue is a common pattern — but beware: an unbounded queue means the thread pool's maximum thread count is never reached (only core threads are used), and the queue can grow without bound under sustained overload.

Practice — Lesson 30

Easy Exercises

Write a method that accepts a List<String> of words and, using parallel streams and ConcurrentHashMap.merge, returns a Map<String, Long> of word frequencies. Verify correctness using a sequential stream as a reference.

public Map<String, Long> wordFrequency(List<String> words) {
    ConcurrentHashMap<String, Long> freq = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    words.parallelStream()
         .forEach(w -> freq.merge(w.toLowerCase(), 1L, Long::sum));
    return freq;
}

Exercise 2 — Fixed-Size LRU Cache

Implement a thread-safe LRU cache with a fixed capacity using ConcurrentHashMap and ConcurrentLinkedDeque. The get operation should promote the accessed key to the most-recently-used position, and on put when at capacity, the least-recently-used key should be evicted.

Hint: The deque tracks insertion/access order. ConcurrentLinkedDeque.remove(element) is O(n) — for a production LRU, combine ConcurrentHashMap with LinkedHashMap guarded by ReadWriteLock.

Exercise 3 — Bounded Event Buffer

Implement an EventBuffer class backed by ArrayBlockingQueue with capacity 1000. It must expose:
- boolean publish(Event e) — non-blocking (return false if full)
- Event consume(long timeoutMs) — blocking with timeout
- List<Event> drain(int max) — drain up to max events into a list

public class EventBuffer {
    private final ArrayBlockingQueue<Event> queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(1000);

    public boolean publish(Event e) { return queue.offer(e); }

    public Event consume(long timeoutMs) throws InterruptedException {
        return queue.poll(timeoutMs, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
    }

    public List<Event> drain(int max) {
        List<Event> batch = new ArrayList<>(max);
        queue.drainTo(batch, max);
        return batch;
    }
}

Exercise 4 — ConcurrentSkipListMap Leaderboard

Build a concurrent leaderboard that maintains the top-10 players by score. Use ConcurrentSkipListMap<Long, String> with the score as the key (descending) and player name as the value. Implement:
- void updateScore(String player, long score)
- List<String> topTen()

Challenge: What happens if two players have the same score? How would you modify the key to allow ties without losing entries?

Exercise 5 — Audit Log with DelayQueue

Design a DelayedAuditLog where audit entries are queued but only visible (dequeue-able) after a 5-second delay. This models a write-ahead log where entries are confirmed only after a persistence timeout. Use DelayQueue<AuditEntry> where AuditEntry implements Delayed.

  2. What is the TREEIFY_THRESHOLD and why is it set to 8?

Part 1

Concept

Java 8, released on March 18, 2014, is widely regarded as the most consequential release in Java's history since Java 5 (generics, 2004). It did not merely add new syntax; it introduced an entirely new programming paradigm to the Java ecosystem — functional programming — while preserving backward compatibility with every byte of existing code.

The core insight behind Java 8 was that modern hardware had changed. Moore's Law no longer delivered faster single-core processors; instead, CPUs multiplied their core counts. Parallelizing work across those cores with traditional imperative loops required explicit thread management, synchronization, and error-prone bookkeeping. Functional programming — where computations are expressed as transformations of immutable data through composable functions — maps naturally to parallel execution without locks.

The Six Pillars of Java 8

Pillar Primary API / Syntax Impact Area
Lambda expressions (x) -> x * 2 syntax Concise anonymous behavior
Stream API java.util.stream.Stream<T> Bulk data processing, parallelism
Optional java.util.Optional<T> Explicit null-safety at the type level
Date/Time API java.time.* (JSR-310) Replace broken java.util.Date
Default & static interface methods default keyword Interface evolution without breaking
CompletableFuture java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture<T> Async pipeline composition

Together, these six pillars transform how Java developers design collections processing, asynchronous workflows, date calculations, and API contracts. Every enterprise Java codebase written after 2016 uses at least four of them daily.

Part 2

The Historical Context: Why 2014?

Java Version Timeline (Paradigm Shifts)

1996  Java 1.0   ── OOP, applets, JVM
1997  Java 1.1   ── Inner classes, JDBC, reflection
1998  Java 1.2   ── Collections framework, Swing
2000  Java 1.3   ── HotSpot JIT (speed leap)
2002  Java 1.4   ── assert, NIO (non-blocking I/O)
2004  Java 5.0   ── Generics, annotations, enums, autoboxing ◄─── PARADIGM SHIFT #1
2006  Java 6     ── Scripting API, JDBC 4
2011  Java 7     ── try-with-resources, diamond, NIO.2, invokedynamic
2014  Java 8     ── Lambdas, Streams, Optional, java.time ◄────── PARADIGM SHIFT #2
2017  Java 9     ── JPMS modules, JShell
2018  Java 10/11 ── var, HTTP client, LTS release (6-month cadence begins)
2021  Java 17    ── Sealed classes, records, pattern matching (LTS) ◄── PARADIGM SHIFT #3
2023  Java 21    ── Virtual threads (Project Loom), sequenced collections (LTS)

Java 7 had deliberately deferred the lambda feature (Project Lambda was actively scoped out of Java 7 at the last moment to avoid delaying the release). Brian Goetz, Java Language Architect, spent 2008–2013 designing the lambda specification under JSR-335. The decision to base lambdas on functional interfaces rather than introducing a new function type was pivotal — it preserved full compatibility with existing Runnable, Comparator, and all callback-based APIs.

The Multicore Problem

2005 Intel Pentium 4:    1 core,  3.8 GHz
2007 Intel Core 2 Quad:  4 cores, 2.4 GHz
2012 Intel Core i7:      8 cores, 3.5 GHz
2014 Intel Xeon E5:     16 cores, 2.8 GHz
2020 AMD Ryzen 9:       16 cores, 3.7 GHz (32 threads)
2023 Intel Core i9:     24 cores (8P+16E), 5.8 GHz

A single-threaded for loop over a million items uses one core while 15 sit idle. Stream API's parallelStream() transparently distributes work across the common ForkJoinPool with a single method call change. This was the economic argument Oracle made to enterprise customers to justify migrating from Java 7.

Part 3

Before and After: Code Style Comparison

The most visceral way to understand Java 8 is to see the same task written in the pre-Java 8 style versus the modern idiomatic style.

Example: Filter-Sort-Transform a List of Orders

PRE-JAVA 8 STYLE (Java 7 / imperative)
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
List<Order> pending = new ArrayList<>();
for (Order o : allOrders) {
    if (o.getStatus() == Status.PENDING) {
        pending.add(o);
    }
}
Collections.sort(pending, new Comparator<Order>() {
    @Override
    public int compare(Order a, Order b) {
        return a.getAmount().compareTo(b.getAmount());
    }
});
List<String> ids = new ArrayList<>();
for (Order o : pending) {
    ids.add(o.getId());
}
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

JAVA 8 STYLE (declarative / functional)
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
List<String> ids = allOrders.stream()
    .filter(o -> o.getStatus() == Status.PENDING)
    .sorted(Comparator.comparing(Order::getAmount))
    .map(Order::getId)
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Observations:
- The Java 8 version is 1 line of business logic vs. 15 lines of boilerplate.
- Intent is self-documenting: filter → sort → map → collect.
- The anonymous Comparator inner class is replaced by a method reference.
- No mutable intermediate List is needed.
- Switching to parallel processing requires only changing .stream() to .parallelStream().

Date Calculation Comparison

PRE-JAVA 8 (java.util.Date + Calendar — bug-prone)
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
Calendar cal = Calendar.getInstance();
cal.add(Calendar.DAY_OF_MONTH, 30);
Date thirtyDaysLater = cal.getTime();   // mutable, not thread-safe

SimpleDateFormat sdf = new SimpleDateFormat("yyyy-MM-dd");
String formatted = sdf.format(thirtyDaysLater);  // not thread-safe!

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
JAVA 8 (java.time — immutable, thread-safe)
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
LocalDate thirtyDaysLater = LocalDate.now().plusDays(30);
String formatted = thirtyDaysLater.format(
    DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("yyyy-MM-dd"));    // thread-safe
Part 4

Lambda Expressions

A lambda expression is an anonymous function: a block of code with parameters, a body, and no name or class declaration. In Java, every lambda expression is an instance of a functional interface (an interface with exactly one abstract method).

Syntax Forms

// Form 1: Single parameter, expression body
Runnable r = () -> System.out.println("hello");

// Form 2: Single parameter (parens optional)
Consumer<String> print = s -> System.out.println(s);

// Form 3: Multiple parameters
BiFunction<Integer, Integer, Integer> add = (a, b) -> a + b;

// Form 4: Block body with explicit return
Function<String, Integer> length = s -> {
    String trimmed = s.trim();
    return trimmed.length();
};

// Form 5: Throwing checked exceptions (must handle or wrap)
Function<String, Integer> parse = s -> {
    try {
        return Integer.parseInt(s);
    } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
        throw new RuntimeException(e);
    }
};

Variable Capture Rules

int multiplier = 3;  // effectively final — OK to capture
// multiplier = 4;   // ← uncommenting this breaks compilation

Function<Integer, Integer> times = x -> x * multiplier;  // captures multiplier

// Instance fields and static fields can be read AND written
class Processor {
    private int count = 0;
    void process(List<String> items) {
        items.forEach(item -> {
            doWork(item);
            count++;  // OK — 'this' reference is captured (effectively final)
        });
    }
}

Rule: Lambda expressions can capture local variables only if those variables are final or effectively final. Instance and static field access is always permitted because this (effectively final) is captured.

Part 5

The Stream API

java.util.stream.Stream<T> is a sequence of elements supporting sequential and parallel aggregate operations. A stream is not a data structure — it doesn't store elements. It is a pipeline of transformations lazily applied to a source.

Stream Pipeline Anatomy

SOURCE          INTERMEDIATE OPERATIONS        TERMINAL OPERATION
────────────    ──────────────────────────     ──────────────────
collection      filter(predicate)              collect(collector)
array           map(function)                  forEach(consumer)
generator       flatMap(function)              reduce(identity, op)
I/O channel     sorted(comparator)             count()
                distinct()                     findFirst()
                limit(n)                       anyMatch(predicate)
                peek(consumer)                 toList() [Java 16+]

─────── LAZY ────────────────────────────────── EAGER ────────────
(not executed until terminal operation is called)

Key Stream Operations

List<Employee> employees = getEmployees();

// map: transform each element
List<String> names = employees.stream()
    .map(Employee::getName)           // T → R
    .collect(Collectors.toList());

// flatMap: flatten nested structures
List<String> allSkills = employees.stream()
    .flatMap(e -> e.getSkills().stream())  // T → Stream<R>
    .distinct()
    .sorted()
    .collect(Collectors.toList());

// reduce: combine all elements
Optional<BigDecimal> totalSalary = employees.stream()
    .map(Employee::getSalary)
    .reduce(BigDecimal::add);

// groupingBy Collector
Map<Department, List<Employee>> byDept = employees.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::getDepartment));

// Statistics
IntSummaryStatistics stats = employees.stream()
    .mapToInt(e -> e.getSalary().intValue())
    .summaryStatistics();
// stats.getAverage(), getMax(), getMin(), getSum(), getCount()

// Parallel stream
long seniorCount = employees.parallelStream()
    .filter(e -> e.getYearsExp() > 5)
    .count();

Stream Laziness in Action

// Only ONE element is fetched from DB — laziness stops after findFirst()
Optional<Order> firstExpensive = orderRepository.stream()
    .filter(o -> o.getAmount().compareTo(new BigDecimal("10000")) > 0)
    .peek(o -> System.out.println("Examining: " + o.getId()))
    .findFirst();
// Without findFirst(), filter+peek execute on ALL orders
// With findFirst(), execution stops at the first match
Part 6

Optional\&lt;T\&gt;

Optional<T> is a container that explicitly models the possible absence of a value. It forces the caller to handle the "absent" case at compile time rather than discovering a NullPointerException at runtime.

Optional Creation and Usage

// Creation
Optional<String> present = Optional.of("hello");      // throws NPE if null
Optional<String> nullable = Optional.ofNullable(null); // safe
Optional<String> empty    = Optional.empty();

// Reading values
String value = present.get();                        // throws if empty — avoid
String safe  = present.orElse("default");            // fallback value
String lazy  = present.orElseGet(() -> compute());   // lazy fallback
String boom  = present.orElseThrow(
    () -> new NotFoundException("Not found"));        // custom exception

// Transformation
Optional<Integer> length = present.map(String::length);          // T → U
Optional<String>  trimmed = present.flatMap(s ->
    s.isBlank() ? Optional.empty() : Optional.of(s.trim()));     // T → Optional<U>

Optional<String> upper = present.filter(s -> s.length() > 3)
                                 .map(String::toUpperCase);
// Returns Optional.empty() if filter fails

// Conditional action
present.ifPresent(s -> System.out.println("Got: " + s));
present.ifPresentOrElse(                              // Java 9+
    s -> System.out.println("Got: " + s),
    () -> System.out.println("Empty!"));

Optional Anti-Patterns

// ANTI-PATTERN 1: Optional as method parameter
// Never do this — just use @Nullable or overloading
void process(Optional<String> name) { ... }  // BAD

// ANTI-PATTERN 2: Optional.get() without isPresent()
String val = opt.get();  // BAD — NPE equivalent

// ANTI-PATTERN 3: Optional in collections
Map<String, Optional<User>> map = ...;  // BAD — use Map.getOrDefault() instead

// ANTI-PATTERN 4: Optional for primitives
Optional<Integer> count = ...;  // BAD — use OptionalInt instead
OptionalInt count = ...;        // GOOD — avoids boxing
Part 7

The java.time API (JSR-310)

java.util.Date and java.util.Calendar were broken from the start: Date is mutable, months are 0-indexed, SimpleDateFormat is not thread-safe. JSR-310, designed by Stephen Colebourne (creator of Joda-Time), replaced them entirely in Java 8.

Core Types

java.time package hierarchy
│
├── LocalDate          — date only, no time, no timezone (2024-03-15)
├── LocalTime          — time only, no date, no timezone (14:30:00.123)
├── LocalDateTime      — date + time, no timezone (2024-03-15T14:30:00)
│
├── ZonedDateTime      — date + time + timezone (2024-03-15T14:30:00+05:30[Asia/Kolkata])
├── OffsetDateTime     — date + time + UTC offset (2024-03-15T14:30:00+05:30)
├── Instant            — machine time (nanoseconds since epoch, always UTC)
│
├── Duration           — time-based amount (hours, minutes, seconds, nanos)
├── Period             — date-based amount (years, months, days)
│
├── DateTimeFormatter  — thread-safe formatting/parsing
├── ZoneId             — IANA timezone database (e.g., "Asia/Kolkata")
└── ZoneOffset         — raw offset from UTC (e.g., +05:30)

Common Operations

// Today
LocalDate today = LocalDate.now();
LocalDate nextMonth = today.plusMonths(1);
long daysBetween = ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(today, nextMonth);

// Business date calculation
LocalDate dueDate = LocalDate.of(2024, Month.MARCH, 15)
    .with(TemporalAdjusters.nextOrSame(DayOfWeek.MONDAY)); // skip weekends

// Parsing and formatting (thread-safe)
DateTimeFormatter fmt = DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("dd-MMM-yyyy", Locale.ENGLISH);
LocalDate parsed   = LocalDate.parse("15-Mar-2024", fmt);
String    formatted = parsed.format(fmt);  // "15-Mar-2024"

// Timezone-aware timestamp
ZonedDateTime nowInKolkata = ZonedDateTime.now(ZoneId.of("Asia/Kolkata"));
ZonedDateTime nowInNYC     = nowInKolkata.withZoneSameInstant(ZoneId.of("America/New_York"));

// Instant for DB/API storage
Instant timestamp = Instant.now();
ZonedDateTime asLocal = timestamp.atZone(ZoneId.systemDefault());
Part 8

Default and Static Interface Methods

Before Java 8, interfaces could only contain abstract method declarations. Adding a new method to a published interface was a breaking change — every implementing class had to be updated. Java 8 solved this with default methods.

Default Methods

public interface Collection<E> {
    // ... existing abstract methods ...

    // Java 8 default method — existing implementations inherit this
    default Stream<E> stream() {
        return StreamSupport.stream(spliterator(), false);
    }

    default Stream<E> parallelStream() {
        return StreamSupport.stream(spliterator(), true);
    }

    default void forEach(Consumer<? super E> action) {
        Objects.requireNonNull(action);
        for (E e : this) {
            action.accept(e);
        }
    }
}

Oracle added stream(), parallelStream(), forEach(), removeIf(), and spliterator() to Collection as default methods without breaking the tens of thousands of existing Collection implementations.

The Diamond Problem with Default Methods

interface A {
    default String name() { return "A"; }
}

interface B extends A {
    default String name() { return "B"; }
}

// Class must override — cannot inherit two conflicting defaults
class C implements A, B {
    @Override
    public String name() {
        return B.super.name();  // explicitly choose B's implementation
    }
}

// Rule: Class implementation wins > more specific interface > must override if equal

Static Interface Methods

public interface Validator<T> {
    boolean validate(T value);

    // Factory / utility method — called on the interface, not an instance
    static <T> Validator<T> noOp() {
        return value -> true;
    }

    static Validator<String> nonEmpty() {
        return s -> s != null && !s.isEmpty();
    }
}

// Usage
Validator<String> v = Validator.nonEmpty();
boolean valid = v.validate("hello");  // true
Part 9

CompletableFuture

CompletableFuture<T> (Java 8) is the answer to async programming limitations of Future<T> (Java 5). Future.get() blocks the calling thread; it provides no way to compose multiple async operations or attach callbacks. CompletableFuture solves all of this.

CompletableFuture vs Future

java.util.concurrent.Future<T>          java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture<T>
─────────────────────────────           ──────────────────────────────────────────
get() always blocks                     thenApply/thenAccept are non-blocking
No chaining                             Full pipeline composition
No exception transformation             exceptionally() / handle()
No combining multiple futures           allOf(), anyOf(), thenCombine()
Cannot be completed externally          complete(T), completeExceptionally(ex)

Async Pipeline Example

// Scenario: fetch user, then fetch orders, then send notification
CompletableFuture<Void> pipeline =
    CompletableFuture
        .supplyAsync(() -> userService.findById(userId),      executor)  // async
        .thenApplyAsync(user -> orderService.findByUser(user), executor) // chain
        .thenApplyAsync(orders -> notificationService
                                       .send(userId, orders), executor)
        .exceptionally(ex -> {
            log.error("Pipeline failed", ex);
            return null;
        });

// Combine two independent async calls
CompletableFuture<User>    userFuture    = fetchUserAsync(userId);
CompletableFuture<Profile> profileFuture = fetchProfileAsync(userId);

CompletableFuture<UserWithProfile> combined =
    userFuture.thenCombine(profileFuture,
        (user, profile) -> new UserWithProfile(user, profile));

// Wait for multiple independent tasks
CompletableFuture<Void> all = CompletableFuture.allOf(
    sendEmailAsync(), updateCacheAsync(), logAuditAsync());
all.join();  // blocks until all three complete
Part 10

Method References

Method references are a shorthand notation for lambdas that do nothing but call a single existing method. They improve readability by eliminating syntactic noise.

Four Types of Method References

// Type 1: Static method reference  ClassName::staticMethod
Function<String, Integer> parseInt = Integer::parseInt;
// equivalent: s -> Integer.parseInt(s)

// Type 2: Instance method on a specific instance  instance::method
String prefix = "ID-";
Predicate<String> startsWith = prefix::startsWith;
// equivalent: s -> prefix.startsWith(s)

// Type 3: Instance method on an arbitrary instance of a type  ClassName::instanceMethod
Function<String, String> toUpper = String::toUpperCase;
// equivalent: s -> s.toUpperCase()

// Type 4: Constructor reference  ClassName::new
Supplier<ArrayList<String>> listFactory = ArrayList::new;
// equivalent: () -> new ArrayList<>()

BiFunction<String, Integer, String> repeat = String::repeat; // Java 11+
// equivalent: (s, n) -> s.repeat(n)

The java.util.function Package

Java 8 ships with 43 functional interface types in java.util.function. The four root types and their compositions cover virtually all use cases:

Core Functional Interfaces
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
Supplier<T>          ()         → T     "produces a value"
Consumer<T>          T          → void  "consumes a value"
Function<T,R>        T          → R     "transforms a value"
Predicate<T>         T          → bool  "tests a value"
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
BiFunction<T,U,R>    (T,U)      → R
BiConsumer<T,U>      (T,U)      → void
BiPredicate<T,U>     (T,U)      → bool
UnaryOperator<T>     T          → T     (special Function<T,T>)
BinaryOperator<T>    (T,T)      → T     (special BiFunction<T,T,T>)
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
IntSupplier          ()         → int   (avoids Integer boxing)
IntConsumer          int        → void
IntFunction<R>       int        → R
IntPredicate         int        → bool
IntUnaryOperator     int        → int
IntBinaryOperator    (int,int)  → int
(same for Long*, Double*)
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Part 12

Nashorn JavaScript Engine

Java 8 shipped with Nashorn, a high-performance JavaScript engine built on invokedynamic. It replaced the older Rhino engine.

ScriptEngine engine = new ScriptEngineManager().getEngineByName("nashorn");
engine.eval("print('Hello from JavaScript')");

// Bidirectional Java-JS interop
engine.put("list", List.of(1, 2, 3, 4, 5));
engine.eval("var sum = 0; list.forEach(function(x) { sum += x; });");
Integer sum = (Integer) engine.get("sum");  // 15

Important: Nashorn was deprecated in Java 11 and removed in Java 15. GraalVM's Polyglot API is the modern replacement. Do not build new features on Nashorn.

sj.add("alpha");
sj.add("beta");

System.out.println(sj);  // [alpha, beta, gamma]

Arrays Enhancements

Arrays.parallelSort

int[] arr = {5, 3, 1, 4, 2, 8, 6, 7};

// Java 8: parallel merge-sort using common ForkJoinPool
Arrays.parallelSort(arr);  // faster than Arrays.sort() for arrays > ~8192 elements

// parallelSetAll — parallel array initialization
double[] data = new double[1_000_000];
Arrays.parallelSetAll(data, i -> Math.sin(i * 0.001));

// parallelPrefix — parallel cumulative operations
int[] values = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
Arrays.parallelPrefix(values, Integer::sum);
// values is now {1, 3, 6, 10, 15}  (prefix sums)

Part 16

Migration from Java 7 to Java 8 in Banks

Typical Banking Migration Pattern

// ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
// BEFORE (Java 7): Transaction summary report in a trading bank
// ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
public TransactionSummary buildSummary(List<Transaction> txns) {
    BigDecimal totalCredit = BigDecimal.ZERO;
    BigDecimal totalDebit  = BigDecimal.ZERO;
    List<Transaction> failed = new ArrayList<>();

    for (Transaction t : txns) {
        if (t.getStatus() == TransactionStatus.FAILED) {
            failed.add(t);
        } else if (t.getType() == TransactionType.CREDIT) {
            totalCredit = totalCredit.add(t.getAmount());
        } else {
            totalDebit = totalDebit.add(t.getAmount());
        }
    }
    Collections.sort(failed, new Comparator<Transaction>() {
        public int compare(Transaction a, Transaction b) {
            return b.getTimestamp().compareTo(a.getTimestamp());
        }
    });
    return new TransactionSummary(totalCredit, totalDebit, failed);
}

// ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
// AFTER (Java 8): Same logic, declarative and concise
// ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
public TransactionSummary buildSummary(List<Transaction> txns) {
    Map<Boolean, List<Transaction>> partitioned =
        txns.stream()
            .collect(Collectors.partitioningBy(
                t -> t.getStatus() == TransactionStatus.FAILED));

    List<Transaction> failed = partitioned.get(true).stream()
        .sorted(Comparator.comparing(Transaction::getTimestamp).reversed())
        .collect(Collectors.toList());

    Map<TransactionType, BigDecimal> totals = partitioned.get(false).stream()
        .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
            Transaction::getType,
            Collectors.reducing(BigDecimal.ZERO,
                                Transaction::getAmount, BigDecimal::add)));

    return new TransactionSummary(
        totals.getOrDefault(TransactionType.CREDIT, BigDecimal.ZERO),
        totals.getOrDefault(TransactionType.DEBIT,  BigDecimal.ZERO),
        failed);
}

Bank Migration Challenges

Challenge Java 7 Pain Java 8 Solution
Date arithmetic (maturity dates, accruals) Calendar bugs, not thread-safe LocalDate, Period, ChronoUnit
Async notification (SMS, email after trade) Future.get() blocks threads CompletableFuture chains
Null counterparty references NullPointerException in prod Optional explicit null-safety
Reporting aggregations Triple-nested for loops Collectors.groupingBy, summingLong
Risk model parallel computation Manual ForkJoinTask parallelStream()

Spring Boot and Java 8

Spring Boot 2.0 (February 2018) requires Java 8 as the minimum. This was a watershed moment: enterprises that wanted to use Spring Boot 2.x (and later) had no choice but to migrate to Java 8.

Spring Features Enabled by Java 8

// 1. Functional bean registration (Spring 5+)
SpringApplication app = new SpringApplication(Application.class);
app.addInitializers(ctx -> {
    ctx.registerBean(OrderService.class, () -> new OrderService(ctx.getBean(OrderRepository.class)));
});

// 2. Java 8 Time types in Spring Data / JPA
@Entity
public class Order {
    @Column
    private LocalDate orderDate;          // maps to DATE
    private Instant  createdAt;           // maps to TIMESTAMP
    private Duration processingTime;      // maps to BIGINT (nanoseconds)
}

// 3. Optional in Spring MVC repository methods
public interface UserRepository extends JpaRepository<User, Long> {
    Optional<User> findByEmail(String email);  // no null returns
}

// 4. Lambda in @Configuration
@Bean
public FilterRegistrationBean<AuditFilter> auditFilter() {
    return new FilterRegistrationBean<>(new AuditFilter());
}

// 5. Reactive streams (Spring WebFlux) built on CompletableFuture concepts
@GetMapping("/orders/{id}")
public Mono<Order> getOrder(@PathVariable Long id) {
    return orderService.findById(id);
}
Part 18

Collectors Deep Dive

java.util.stream.Collectors provides 40+ factory methods for terminal collection operations:

List<Employee> employees = ...;

// toList, toSet, toUnmodifiableList
List<String>          names   = employees.stream().map(Employee::getName).collect(toList());
Set<Department>       depts   = employees.stream().map(Employee::getDept).collect(toSet());

// groupingBy with downstream collector
Map<Department, Long> countByDept = employees.stream()
    .collect(groupingBy(Employee::getDept, counting()));

Map<Department, DoubleSummaryStatistics> salaryStats = employees.stream()
    .collect(groupingBy(Employee::getDept,
             summarizingDouble(e -> e.getSalary().doubleValue())));

// partitioningBy
Map<Boolean, List<Employee>> seniorVsJunior = employees.stream()
    .collect(partitioningBy(e -> e.getYearsExp() >= 5));

// toMap — careful with duplicate keys
Map<Long, Employee> byId = employees.stream()
    .collect(toMap(Employee::getId, e -> e,
                   (existing, replacement) -> existing));  // merge function for dups

// joining
String employeeList = employees.stream()
    .map(Employee::getName)
    .collect(joining(", ", "Employees: [", "]"));

// teeing (Java 12+) — two collectors, one pass
record MinMax(Employee min, Employee max) {}
MinMax result = employees.stream()
    .collect(teeing(
        minBy(Comparator.comparing(Employee::getSalary)),
        maxBy(Comparator.comparing(Employee::getSalary)),
        (min, max) -> new MinMax(min.orElseThrow(), max.orElseThrow())));
Part 19

JVM Internals: invokedynamic and Lambda Metafactory

Java 8 lambdas do not create anonymous inner class .class files at compile time (contrary to what many believe). The compiler generates a single invokedynamic bytecode instruction. At runtime, LambdaMetafactory dynamically generates the functional interface implementation using MethodHandles and ASM.

COMPILE TIME (javac):
  Lambda source code → invokedynamic instruction in bytecode

  invokedynamic #42, "apply", MethodType(Function)
    Bootstrap: LambdaMetafactory.metafactory(...)

RUNTIME (JVM, first call only):
  LambdaMetafactory generates an inner class bytecode IN MEMORY
  JVM spins up the class: MyClass$$Lambda$1/0x...
  Subsequent calls: direct method call (no class generation overhead)

RESULT:
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Heap allocation: ONE instance (often) │
  │  Startup: ~microseconds first call     │
  │  Subsequent: as fast as virtual call   │
  └────────────────────────────────────────┘

This approach is far more efficient than the Java 7 anonymous inner class pattern (which creates a .class file per lambda, loaded at JVM startup).

Part 20

Common Java 8 Pitfalls

Pitfall 1: Parallel Stream Overhead

// WRONG: parallelStream on small lists incurs ForkJoinPool overhead
List<String> names = List.of("Alice", "Bob");
names.parallelStream().map(String::toUpperCase).collect(toList());  // slower!

// RIGHT: parallel only for CPU-intensive work on large datasets (> ~10,000 elements)
IntStream.range(0, 1_000_000)
    .parallel()
    .mapToDouble(i -> Math.pow(Math.sin(i), 2))
    .sum();

Pitfall 2: Stream Reuse

Stream<String> stream = List.of("a","b","c").stream();
long count = stream.count();
stream.forEach(System.out::println);  // IllegalStateException: stream already closed!
// Streams are single-use — create a new stream for each terminal operation

Pitfall 3: Optional.get() Without Check

// WRONG — NPE equivalent
String val = Optional.ofNullable(map.get("key")).get();

// RIGHT
String val = Optional.ofNullable(map.get("key")).orElse("default");

Pitfall 4: Checked Exceptions in Lambdas

// WRONG — won't compile: IOException is checked
List<String> lines = paths.stream()
    .map(p -> Files.readString(p))  // ← IOException not handled
    .collect(toList());

// RIGHT — wrap in unchecked, or use utility wrapper
@FunctionalInterface
interface ThrowingFunction<T, R> {
    R apply(T t) throws Exception;
}
static <T, R> Function<T, R> wrap(ThrowingFunction<T, R> f) {
    return t -> { try { return f.apply(t); } catch (Exception e) { throw new RuntimeException(e); } };
}
List<String> lines = paths.stream()
    .map(wrap(p -> Files.readString(p)))
    .collect(toList());
Part 21

Performance Characteristics

Stream vs For-Loop Benchmark Context

Benchmark (JMH, 1M integers, sum):
──────────────────────────────────────────────────
Operation                      Throughput (ops/s)
──────────────────────────────────────────────────
for loop (int[])               ~2,100,000
IntStream.of(int[]).sum()      ~2,050,000   (~same)
Stream<Integer>.mapToInt.sum() ~  850,000   (~2.5x slower — boxing)
parallelStream (1M, 8 cores)   ~5,200,000   (~2.5x faster than sequential)
parallelStream (1K, 8 cores)   ~  400,000   (~5x SLOWER — FJP overhead)
──────────────────────────────────────────────────

Key insight: Use primitive streams (IntStream, LongStream, DoubleStream) wherever possible to avoid boxing overhead. Parallel streams are beneficial only for CPU-bound work on large datasets.

Easy Exercises

Exercise 1 — Stream Filter-Map-Collect

Given List<String> words = List.of("apple","banana","cherry","avocado","blueberry","apricot"), use a single stream pipeline to return a sorted list of all words that start with the letter 'a', converted to uppercase.

List<String> result = words.stream()
    .filter(w -> w.startsWith("a"))
    .map(String::toUpperCase)
    .sorted()
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
// Expected: [APPLE, APRICOT, AVOCADO]

Exercise 2 — Optional Chain

Write a method String getCountryCode(User user) that safely navigates user → address → country → code where any step can be null. Return "UNKNOWN" if any step is absent. Use Optional.

public String getCountryCode(User user) {
    return Optional.ofNullable(user)
        .map(User::getAddress)
        .map(Address::getCountry)
        .map(Country::getCode)
        .orElse("UNKNOWN");
}

Exercise 3 — LocalDate Business Logic

Calculate the number of working days (Monday–Friday) between two LocalDate values.

public long workingDaysBetween(LocalDate start, LocalDate end) {
    return start.datesUntil(end)   // Java 9+ Stream<LocalDate>
        .filter(d -> {
            DayOfWeek dow = d.getDayOfWeek();
            return dow != DayOfWeek.SATURDAY && dow != DayOfWeek.SUNDAY;
        })
        .count();
}

Medium Exercises

Exercise 4 — CompletableFuture Fan-Out

Implement Map<String, Double> fetchAllPrices(List<String> symbols) that fires one CompletableFuture per stock symbol concurrently, waits for all results, and returns a map of symbol → price. Use a custom ExecutorService with 4 threads.

public Map<String, Double> fetchAllPrices(List<String> symbols) {
    ExecutorService exec = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4);
    List<CompletableFuture<Map.Entry<String, Double>>> futures = symbols.stream()
        .map(sym -> CompletableFuture
            .supplyAsync(() -> Map.entry(sym, priceService.fetch(sym)), exec))
        .collect(Collectors.toList());

    return CompletableFuture.allOf(futures.toArray(new CompletableFuture[0]))
        .thenApply(v -> futures.stream()
            .map(CompletableFuture::join)
            .collect(Collectors.toMap(Map.Entry::getKey, Map.Entry::getValue)))
        .join();
}

Debugging Exercises

Exercise 10 — Stream Terminal Operation Bug

// What is wrong with this code?
Stream<Order> stream = orderRepo.findAll().stream()
    .filter(o -> o.getStatus() == Status.ACTIVE);
long count  = stream.count();
List<Order> list = stream.collect(Collectors.toList()); // line B

Answer: Line B throws IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed. Streams are single-use. Fix: call orderRepo.findAll().stream() again before collecting.

Exercise 11 — Default Method Diamond

interface Flyable  { default String move() { return "fly"; } }
interface Swimmable { default String move() { return "swim"; } }
class Duck implements Flyable, Swimmable { }
// Does this compile? What error? How do you fix it?

Answer: Compile error — Duck inherits two conflicting move() defaults. Fix: override move() in Duck and explicitly call Flyable.super.move() or Swimmable.super.move().

Interview Questions

Q1: What are the six major features introduced in Java 8?
Lambdas, Stream API, Optional, java.time (JSR-310), default/static interface methods, and CompletableFuture.

Q2: How are lambda expressions implemented at the JVM level?
The compiler emits an invokedynamic instruction with LambdaMetafactory as the bootstrap method. At runtime (first invocation), the JVM dynamically generates a class implementing the functional interface using MethodHandles. Subsequent invocations use the cached class — no .class file is written to disk.

Q3: What is the diamond problem with default methods and how is it resolved?
When a class implements two interfaces that both define a default method with the same signature, the class must override the method. Inside the override, InterfaceA.super.method() syntax explicitly selects the desired implementation.

Q4: Why is java.util.Date considered broken and what replaces it?
Date is mutable (thread-unsafe), months are 0-indexed (bug-prone), SimpleDateFormat is not thread-safe, and timezone handling is opaque. Java 8's java.time package (JSR-310) provides immutable, thread-safe classes: LocalDate, ZonedDateTime, Instant, DateTimeFormatter.

Q5: When should you NOT use parallelStream()?
When the dataset is small (< ~10,000 elements), when the operations have side effects, when the source is not efficiently splittable (e.g., LinkedList), or when ordering matters and the overhead of re-ordering is significant. Also avoid when the computation is I/O-bound — parallel streams use CPU threads, not async I/O.

Q6: What is the difference between map and flatMap in streams?
map transforms each element to exactly one element (T → R). flatMap transforms each element to a stream of zero or more elements (T → Stream<R>) and flattens the resulting streams into a single stream.

Q7: Why does Spring Boot 2.0 require Java 8?
Spring Boot 2 is built on Spring Framework 5, which uses Java 8 features extensively: lambda-based @Bean registration, Optional return types in @Repository methods, CompletableFuture in @Async, LocalDate/Instant in JPA/Jackson, and reactive programming via Project Reactor (built on functional interfaces).
