Part 1

Concept

A functional interface is the cornerstone of Java's functional programming model. Every lambda expression you write is — at the JVM level — an instance of a functional interface. Understanding what functional interfaces are, how the compiler and runtime handle them, and which built-in ones the JDK provides is the foundation for everything in Phase 3.

Definition

A functional interface is an interface with exactly one abstract method (SAM — Single Abstract Method). It may contain any number of default methods, static methods, and methods inherited from java.lang.Object, but only one abstract method.

// This is a functional interface — exactly ONE abstract method
@FunctionalInterface
public interface Transformer<T, R> {
    R transform(T input);                      // SAM

    default Transformer<T, R> logging() {      // default — does not break SAM rule
        return input -> {
            System.out.println("Input: " + input);
            return transform(input);
        };
    }

    static <T> Transformer<T, T> identity() { // static — does not break SAM rule
        return t -> t;
    }
}

// This is NOT a functional interface — two abstract methods
public interface TwoMethods {
    void methodA();
    void methodB();   // ← compiler error if @FunctionalInterface is present
}

Why SAM?

Java's designers deliberately chose not to create a new function type. Instead, they made any single-method interface compatible with lambda syntax. This decision preserved backward compatibility: Runnable, Callable, Comparator, and every existing callback interface became lambda-compatible without any changes.

Part 2

The @FunctionalInterface Annotation

@FunctionalInterface is a marker annotation from java.lang. It causes the compiler to verify that the annotated interface satisfies the SAM constraint. If you add a second abstract method by mistake, the compiler immediately flags it.

@FunctionalInterface
public interface Validator<T> {
    boolean validate(T value);
    // boolean validate2(T value);  // ← compile error: Multiple non-overriding abstract methods
}

When Is @FunctionalInterface Mandatory?

It is not mandatory — any interface that happens to have exactly one abstract method can be used as a lambda target, even without the annotation. But annotating your intent:
- Documents that the interface is designed for lambda use.
- Prevents accidental addition of a second abstract method by future maintainers.
- Enables IDE tooling to provide better lambda completion.

Rule: Always add @FunctionalInterface to any interface you intentionally design as a lambda target.

Object Methods Do Not Count

Methods declared in java.lang.Object do not count as abstract methods for the SAM rule, even if the interface redeclares them:

@FunctionalInterface
public interface MyComparator<T> {
    int compare(T a, T b);           // SAM — this is the abstract method

    boolean equals(Object obj);      // redeclares Object.equals — does NOT count
    String  toString();              // redeclares Object.toString — does NOT count
}
// Valid — still a functional interface because Object methods are excluded
Part 3

Predicate\&lt;T\&gt;

Predicate<T> represents a boolean-valued function of one argument: T → boolean. It is the go-to interface for filtering operations.

@FunctionalInterface
public interface Predicate<T> {
    boolean test(T t);                                      // SAM

    default Predicate<T> and(Predicate<? super T> other);  // logical AND
    default Predicate<T> or(Predicate<? super T> other);   // logical OR
    default Predicate<T> negate();                         // logical NOT
    static <T> Predicate<T> not(Predicate<? super T> target); // Java 11
    static <T> Predicate<T> isEqual(Object targetRef);     // null-safe equality
}

Predicate Composition

Predicate<String> notNull   = s -> s != null;
Predicate<String> notEmpty  = s -> !s.isEmpty();
Predicate<String> startsA   = s -> s.startsWith("A");
Predicate<Integer> isAdult  = age -> age >= 18;
Predicate<Integer> isSenior = age -> age >= 65;

// Compose: not null AND not empty AND starts with A
Predicate<String> validName = notNull.and(notEmpty).and(startsA);
boolean result = validName.test("Alice");   // true
boolean result2 = validName.test("");       // false

// Compose: adult OR senior (redundant but illustrative)
Predicate<Integer> eligible = isAdult.or(isSenior);

// Negate
Predicate<String> isEmpty = notEmpty.negate();

// Predicate.not (Java 11+) — great for method reference negation
List<String> nonBlanks = List.of("hello", "  ", "world", "")
    .stream()
    .filter(Predicate.not(String::isBlank))
    .collect(Collectors.toList());  // [hello, world]

// Predicate.isEqual
Predicate<String> isHello = Predicate.isEqual("hello");
isHello.test("hello");  // true
isHello.test(null);     // false (null-safe)

Stream.filter Uses Predicate

List<Employee> seniors = employees.stream()
    .filter(e -> e.getAge() >= 60)        // Predicate<Employee>
    .collect(Collectors.toList());

// Using a pre-built Predicate for reuse across multiple streams
Predicate<Employee> isSenior = e -> e.getAge() >= 60;
long count  = employees.stream().filter(isSenior).count();
List<Employee> list = employees.stream().filter(isSenior).collect(toList());
Part 4

Function\&lt;T, R\&gt;

Function<T, R> represents a function that accepts one argument of type T and produces a result of type R. It is the primary transformation interface.

@FunctionalInterface
public interface Function<T, R> {
    R apply(T t);                                              // SAM

    default <V> Function<T, V> andThen(Function<? super R, ? extends V> after);
    default <V> Function<V, R> compose(Function<? super V, ? extends T> before);
    static <T> Function<T, T> identity();
}

Function Composition

Function<String, Integer> length    = String::length;
Function<Integer, Boolean> isEven   = n -> n % 2 == 0;
Function<String, String>  toUpper   = String::toUpperCase;

// andThen: apply length first, then isEven
Function<String, Boolean> isEvenLength = length.andThen(isEven);
isEvenLength.test("hello");   // 5 → false
isEvenLength.test("java");    // 4 → true

// compose: apply toUpper first, then length
Function<String, Integer> upperLength = length.compose(toUpper);
upperLength.apply("hello");  // "HELLO" → 5  (same result, compose reverses order)

// Building processing pipelines
Function<String, String> pipeline = Function.<String>identity()
    .andThen(String::trim)
    .andThen(String::toLowerCase)
    .andThen(s -> s.replaceAll("\\s+", "-"));

pipeline.apply("  Hello World  ");   // "hello-world"

Function in Stream.map

List<Integer> nameLengths = employees.stream()
    .map(Employee::getName)       // Function<Employee, String>
    .map(String::length)          // Function<String, Integer>
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
Part 5

Consumer\&lt;T\&gt;

Consumer<T> represents an operation that accepts a single argument and returns no result. It is used for side effects: printing, logging, persisting, sending events.

@FunctionalInterface
public interface Consumer<T> {
    void accept(T t);                                       // SAM

    default Consumer<T> andThen(Consumer<? super T> after); // chain consumers
}

Consumer Usage

Consumer<String> print   = System.out::println;
Consumer<String> log     = s -> logger.info("Processing: {}", s);
Consumer<String> persist = s -> repository.save(s);

// Chain consumers: log THEN persist
Consumer<String> logAndPersist = log.andThen(persist);
logAndPersist.accept("order-123");  // logs, then persists

// forEach uses Consumer
List.of("a", "b", "c").forEach(s -> System.out.println(s.toUpperCase()));
List.of("a", "b", "c").forEach(print);  // method reference

// Map.forEach uses BiConsumer
Map<String, Integer> scores = Map.of("Alice", 95, "Bob", 87);
scores.forEach((name, score) -> System.out.printf("%s: %d%n", name, score));
Part 6

Supplier\&lt;T\&gt;

Supplier<T> represents a supplier of results. It takes no argument and returns a T. It is the factory / lazy-initialization interface.

@FunctionalInterface
public interface Supplier<T> {
    T get();  // SAM — no other default methods
}

Supplier Usage Patterns

// Factory / lazy initialization
Supplier<List<String>> listFactory = ArrayList::new;
List<String> list = listFactory.get();  // new ArrayList<>() each call

// Lazy computation — avoid computing until needed
Supplier<ExpensiveObject> lazyObj = () -> {
    System.out.println("Computing expensive object...");
    return new ExpensiveObject();
};
// Not computed yet!
ExpensiveObject obj = lazyObj.get();  // computed now

// Optional.orElseGet uses Supplier (lazy fallback)
String result = Optional.<String>empty()
    .orElseGet(() -> computeDefault());  // only called if empty

// vs Optional.orElse (eager fallback — always evaluates argument)
String result2 = Optional.<String>empty()
    .orElse(computeDefault());  // computeDefault() called EVEN IF value present!

// Exception supplier in orElseThrow
User user = Optional.ofNullable(map.get("id"))
    .orElseThrow(() -> new NotFoundException("User not found"));

// Supplier-based caching (memoization pattern)
public class Lazy<T> {
    private final Supplier<T> supplier;
    private T value;

    public Lazy(Supplier<T> supplier) { this.supplier = supplier; }

    public T get() {
        if (value == null) value = supplier.get();
        return value;
    }
}
Part 7

BiFunction, BiConsumer, BiPredicate

The Bi* variants accept two arguments instead of one. Java provides no TriFunction — for three+ argument functions, use custom functional interfaces or method handles.

// BiFunction<T, U, R> — two inputs, one output
BiFunction<String, Integer, String> repeat = String::repeat;  // (s, n) → s repeated n times
repeat.apply("ab", 3);  // "ababab"

BiFunction<String, String, String> concat = String::concat;
BiFunction<Integer, Integer, Integer> add = Integer::sum;

// andThen — transform the result
BiFunction<String, String, Integer> concatLength =
    concat.andThen(String::length);
concatLength.apply("hello", "world");  // 10

// BiConsumer<T, U> — two inputs, void output
BiConsumer<String, Integer> printRepeat =
    (s, n) -> System.out.println(s.repeat(n));
printRepeat.accept("Hi! ", 3);  // "Hi! Hi! Hi! "

// Map.forEach signature uses BiConsumer<K, V>
Map<String, List<Order>> ordersByCustomer = ...;
ordersByCustomer.forEach((customer, orders) ->
    orderService.notifyCustomer(customer, orders));

// BiPredicate<T, U> — two inputs, boolean output
BiPredicate<String, Integer> longerThan = (s, n) -> s.length() > n;
longerThan.test("hello", 3);  // true
longerThan.test("hi",    3);  // false
Part 8

UnaryOperator and BinaryOperator

These are specializations of Function and BiFunction where input and output types are identical. They express in-place transformations.

// UnaryOperator<T> extends Function<T, T>
// Input type == Output type
UnaryOperator<String> trim     = String::trim;
UnaryOperator<String> toUpper  = String::toUpperCase;
UnaryOperator<Integer> square  = n -> n * n;

// Chain via andThen (inherited from Function)
UnaryOperator<String> normalize = trim.andThen(toUpper)::apply;
// Note: andThen returns Function<T,T> not UnaryOperator<T> — cast or wrap as needed

// List.replaceAll uses UnaryOperator<E>
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(List.of("  alice ", " bob", "charlie "));
names.replaceAll(String::trim);                    // modifies in-place
names.replaceAll(s -> s.substring(0, 1).toUpperCase() + s.substring(1));

// BinaryOperator<T> extends BiFunction<T, T, T>
// Both inputs AND output are the same type
BinaryOperator<Integer> max = Integer::max;
BinaryOperator<String>  join = (a, b) -> a + "," + b;

// Stream.reduce uses BinaryOperator
Optional<Integer> total = IntStream.range(1, 6).boxed()
    .reduce(Integer::sum);            // BinaryOperator<Integer>

int product = IntStream.range(1, 6).boxed()
    .reduce(1, (a, b) -> a * b);     // identity + BinaryOperator

// BinaryOperator utility methods
BinaryOperator<Integer> minOp = BinaryOperator.minBy(Comparator.naturalOrder());
BinaryOperator<Integer> maxOp = BinaryOperator.maxBy(Comparator.naturalOrder());

Part 10

Primitive Specializations: Why They Exist

Generic types in Java use type erasure — at runtime, Function<Integer, Boolean> is just Function. Every Integer passed to apply(T t) must be boxed from int, and every Boolean result must be boxed from boolean. This means:

Without primitive specialization:
  int primitiveValue        → autobox    → Integer heap object
  Integer heap object       → unbox      → int primitiveValue

For 1,000,000 stream elements:
  1,000,000 Integer objects allocated
  1,000,000 objects eligible for GC
  Cache pressure from scattered heap allocations

With IntPredicate, IntFunction<R>, IntStream, etc., the JVM passes raw int values in CPU registers — no heap allocation, no GC pressure.

// SLOW — boxing overhead
Function<Integer, Boolean> isEvenBoxed = n -> n % 2 == 0;
Stream<Integer> integerStream = IntStream.range(0, 1_000_000).boxed();
integerStream.map(isEvenBoxed).count();

// FAST — no boxing
IntPredicate isEvenPrimitive = n -> n % 2 == 0;
long count = IntStream.range(0, 1_000_000)
    .filter(isEvenPrimitive)   // IntPredicate — no boxing
    .count();

// Cross-type: int → double (no boxing of int or double)
IntToDoubleFunction sqrtOf = n -> Math.sqrt(n);
double result = sqrtOf.applyAsDouble(16);  // 4.0

// ToIntFunction: T → int (unboxed output)
ToIntFunction<String> length = String::length;
int len = length.applyAsInt("hello");  // 5 — no Integer boxing

When to Use Primitive Specializations

Scenario Use Instead Of
Stream of int/long/double values Stream<Integer>, Stream<Long>
Extracting numeric field for sorting/summing Function<T, Integer>
Numeric predicate (age check, threshold) Predicate<Integer>
Numeric generator / sequence Supplier<Integer>

Always prefer IntStream, LongStream, DoubleStream and their associated primitive functional interfaces for numeric pipelines.

Part 11

Composing Functional Interfaces

All four root interfaces provide default composition methods. This enables building complex behavior from simple pieces without creating new classes.

Composition Methods by Interface
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
Predicate<T>
  and(Predicate<T>)     → Predicate<T>   logical AND
  or(Predicate<T>)      → Predicate<T>   logical OR
  negate()              → Predicate<T>   logical NOT
  not(Predicate<T>)     → Predicate<T>   static factory for negate

Function<T,R>
  andThen(Function<R,V>)→ Function<T,V>  apply this, then the after function
  compose(Function<V,T>)→ Function<V,R>  apply the before function, then this
  identity()            → Function<T,T>  static factory for identity function

Consumer<T>
  andThen(Consumer<T>)  → Consumer<T>    execute this, then the after consumer

BinaryOperator<T>
  minBy(Comparator)     → BinaryOperator<T>  static: returns the lesser of two
  maxBy(Comparator)     → BinaryOperator<T>  static: returns the greater of two
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Real-World Composition Example

// Build a validation pipeline from composable Predicates
public class OrderValidator {
    private static final Predicate<Order> isAmountPositive =
        o -> o.getAmount().compareTo(BigDecimal.ZERO) > 0;

    private static final Predicate<Order> isCustomerActive =
        o -> o.getCustomer().isActive();

    private static final Predicate<Order> hasShippingAddress =
        o -> o.getShippingAddress() != null;

    // Compose all three — order must pass ALL checks
    public static final Predicate<Order> isValid =
        isAmountPositive
            .and(isCustomerActive)
            .and(hasShippingAddress);

    // Compose a "fast reject" predicate — reject if ANY check fails
    public static final Predicate<Order> isInvalid = isValid.negate();

    public List<Order> filterValid(List<Order> orders) {
        return orders.stream()
            .filter(isValid)
            .collect(Collectors.toList());
    }
}

Function Pipeline Pattern

// Data transformation pipeline for an ETL process
Function<RawRecord, NormalizedRecord> normalize = RawRecord::normalize;
Function<NormalizedRecord, EnrichedRecord> enrich = r -> enricher.enrich(r);
Function<EnrichedRecord, DBRecord> toDbRecord = DBRecord::from;

// Compose into a single end-to-end function
Function<RawRecord, DBRecord> etlPipeline =
    normalize.andThen(enrich).andThen(toDbRecord);

// Apply to a batch
List<DBRecord> dbRecords = rawRecords.stream()
    .map(etlPipeline)
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
Part 12

Method Reference Types (Preview)

Method references are the most concise form of lambda. They delegate to an existing method. There are four kinds:

METHOD REFERENCE TYPES
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
Kind                   Syntax                   Equivalent Lambda
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
Static method          Integer::parseInt        s -> Integer.parseInt(s)
                       Math::abs                n -> Math.abs(n)

Bound instance         "hello"::toUpperCase     () -> "hello".toUpperCase()
                       System.out::println      s -> System.out.println(s)

Unbound instance       String::toUpperCase      s -> s.toUpperCase()
                       String::length           s -> s.length()

Constructor            ArrayList::new           () -> new ArrayList<>()
                       User::new                (n,e) -> new User(n,e)
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

// All four types assigned to matching functional interfaces
Function<String, Integer>  parseF      = Integer::parseInt;        // static
Supplier<String>           upperBound  = "hello"::toUpperCase;     // bound instance
Function<String, String>   upperUnbound= String::toUpperCase;      // unbound instance
Supplier<List<String>>     listCtor    = ArrayList::new;           // constructor

// Selecting the right type
List<String> names = employees.stream()
    .map(Employee::getName)           // unbound instance: Employee → String
    .filter(Predicate.not(String::isBlank))  // unbound instance: String → boolean
    .sorted(String::compareTo)        // unbound instance used as Comparator<String>
    .collect(Collectors.toList());

Lesson 33 covers method references in full detail including overload resolution and ambiguity.

Part 13

Custom Functional Interfaces

When none of the 43 built-in interfaces fit your use case, define your own. The most common reason: arity (more than two inputs) or checked exceptions.

// Three-argument function — no built-in equivalent
@FunctionalInterface
public interface TriFunction<A, B, C, R> {
    R apply(A a, B b, C c);

    default <V> TriFunction<A, B, C, V> andThen(Function<? super R, ? extends V> after) {
        Objects.requireNonNull(after);
        return (a, b, c) -> after.apply(apply(a, b, c));
    }
}

// Usage
TriFunction<String, Integer, Boolean, String> formatter =
    (name, age, active) ->
        String.format("%s (%d) — %s", name, age, active ? "active" : "inactive");

String result = formatter.apply("Alice", 30, true);
// "Alice (30) — active"

// Domain-specific functional interface
@FunctionalInterface
public interface RiskEvaluator {
    RiskScore evaluate(Portfolio portfolio, MarketConditions conditions);
}
// Used as: RiskEvaluator simple = (p, m) -> RiskScore.of(p.getVolatility() * m.getVIX());
Part 14

Handling Checked Exceptions in Functional Interfaces

Java's built-in functional interfaces do not declare checked exceptions in their SAM signatures. This means lambdas that call checked-exception methods require either a try-catch block or a wrapper utility.

The Problem

// IOException is checked — this does NOT compile
Function<Path, String> reader = Files::readString;
// Error: Unhandled exception: java.io.IOException

Solution 1: Inline try-catch (verbose)

Function<Path, String> reader = path -> {
    try {
        return Files.readString(path);
    } catch (IOException e) {
        throw new UncheckedIOException(e);
    }
};

Solution 2: Throwing Wrapper Utility (clean, reusable)

@FunctionalInterface
public interface ThrowingFunction<T, R> {
    R apply(T t) throws Exception;

    static <T, R> Function<T, R> wrap(ThrowingFunction<T, R> f) {
        return t -> {
            try {
                return f.apply(t);
            } catch (RuntimeException e) {
                throw e;
            } catch (Exception e) {
                throw new RuntimeException(e);
            }
        };
    }
}

// Usage — clean at the call site
List<String> lines = paths.stream()
    .map(ThrowingFunction.wrap(Files::readString))   // no inline try-catch
    .collect(Collectors.toList());

Solution 3: Checked-Exception-Aware Functional Interfaces (library approach)

Libraries like Vavr and Guava provide CheckedFunction, Try<T>, etc. for fully typed checked-exception handling in functional pipelines:

// Vavr CheckedFunction example
CheckedFunction1<Path, String> reader = Files::readString;
Function<Path, String> safe = reader.unchecked();   // wraps to RuntimeException
Part 15

invokedynamic and Lambda Metafactory

Understanding how the JVM actually executes a lambda requires knowing about invokedynamic — the bytecode instruction added in Java 7 (for dynamic languages) and repurposed for Java 8 lambdas.

Compile-Time: What javac Produces

Source:
  Function<String, Integer> fn = String::length;

Bytecode (simplified):
  invokedynamic #25, "apply", ()LFunction;
    Bootstrap: java/lang/invoke/LambdaMetafactory.metafactory(
      MethodHandles$Lookup, String, MethodType, MethodType, MethodHandle, MethodType)
    Target:   java/lang/String.length()I   (the actual method)
    Interface:java/util/function/Function.apply(Object)Object

At compile time, javac:
1. Does not generate a Foo$$Lambda$1.class file.
2. Emits a single invokedynamic instruction.
3. Records the bootstrap method (LambdaMetafactory.metafactory) and the target method handle.

Runtime: Lambda Metafactory

FIRST CALL TO invokedynamic INSTRUCTION:
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  JVM hits invokedynamic — calls bootstrap method                  │
│  LambdaMetafactory.metafactory(lookup, name, type, ...)           │
│    ↓                                                              │
│  ASM generates bytecode for an inner class at runtime:            │
│    class Foo$$Lambda$1 implements Function {                       │
│        public Object apply(Object s) {                             │
│            return ((String) s).length();                           │
│        }                                                           │
│    }                                                               │
│    ↓                                                              │
│  JVM loads this class into memory (no .class file on disk)        │
│  JVM creates a CallSite (ConstantCallSite) linking to the class   │
│  Returns a single INSTANCE of Foo$$Lambda$1                       │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

SUBSEQUENT CALLS:
  CallSite is already linked → direct dispatch (no bootstrap overhead)
  For non-capturing lambdas: same instance reused (singleton)
  For capturing lambdas: new instance per call (captures state)

Non-Capturing vs Capturing Lambdas

// NON-CAPTURING — does not reference any local variable from outer scope
Function<String, Integer> len = String::length;
// JVM can reuse a single instance — no heap allocation after first call

// CAPTURING — captures local variable 'prefix' from outer scope
String prefix = "Hello-";
Function<String, String> prepend = s -> prefix + s;
// New instance allocated per lambda creation (to hold 'prefix')
// But: 'prefix' must be effectively final

This distinction matters for performance in hot code paths — avoid capturing lambdas inside tight loops.

Part 16

Spring: Functional Bean Registration

Spring Framework 5+ allows registering beans via Supplier<T> (functional style) instead of @Component/@Bean annotations. This eliminates classpath scanning overhead and is useful in serverless/GraalVM environments.

// Traditional @Bean approach
@Configuration
public class AppConfig {
    @Bean
    public OrderService orderService(OrderRepository repo) {
        return new OrderService(repo);
    }
}

// Functional registration (Spring 5 / Spring Boot 2+)
SpringApplication app = new SpringApplication(Application.class);
app.addInitializers((GenericApplicationContext ctx) -> {
    ctx.registerBean(
        OrderRepository.class,
        () -> new JdbcOrderRepository(ctx.getBean(DataSource.class))
    );
    ctx.registerBean(
        OrderService.class,
        () -> new OrderService(ctx.getBean(OrderRepository.class))
    );
});
app.run(args);

Spring WebFlux Functional Routing

// RouterFunction uses Function<ServerRequest, Mono<ServerResponse>>
@Bean
public RouterFunction<ServerResponse> routes(OrderHandler handler) {
    return RouterFunctions.route()
        .GET("/orders",       handler::listOrders)
        .GET("/orders/{id}",  handler::getOrder)
        .POST("/orders",      handler::createOrder)
        .build();
}
Part 17

Spring: Predicate-Based Filtering

Predicate<T> is extensively used in Spring for conditional logic in batch processing, security, and data filtering.

// Spring Batch: ItemProcessor with Predicate filter
@Bean
public ItemProcessor<Order, Order> orderProcessor() {
    Predicate<Order> isValid = o -> o.getAmount().compareTo(BigDecimal.ZERO) > 0;
    Predicate<Order> isActive = o -> o.getCustomer().isActive();

    return order -> isValid.and(isActive).test(order) ? order : null;
}

// Spring Security: RequestMatcher as Predicate
HttpSecurity http = ...;
http.authorizeRequests()
    .requestMatchers(request ->
        request.getServletPath().startsWith("/api/") &&
        !request.getServletPath().equals("/api/health"))
    .authenticated();

// Custom repository filter using Specification (Predicate-like)
Specification<User> isActive = (root, query, cb) ->
    cb.equal(root.get("active"), true);
Specification<User> hasRole  = (root, query, cb) ->
    cb.equal(root.get("role"), "ADMIN");

List<User> admins = userRepo.findAll(isActive.and(hasRole));

// Spring Events with Predicate conditions
@EventListener(condition = "#event.priority == 'HIGH'")
public void handleHighPriority(OrderCreatedEvent event) {
    // only invoked when condition is true
}
Part 18

Functional Interfaces in Standard Library APIs

Beyond java.util.function, functional interfaces are used pervasively across the JDK:

// Comparator — also a @FunctionalInterface
Comparator<Employee> byAge  = Comparator.comparing(Employee::getAge);
Comparator<Employee> bySal  = Comparator.comparing(Employee::getSalary).reversed();
Comparator<Employee> complex = byAge.thenComparing(bySal);

// Runnable and Callable — pre-Java 8 @FunctionalInterfaces
Runnable task     = () -> processOrder(order);
Callable<Result>  call = () -> { return computeResult(); };

// Iterable.forEach(Consumer<T>)
list.forEach(System.out::println);

// Map.forEach(BiConsumer<K,V>)
map.forEach((k, v) -> audit(k, v));

// Map.compute/merge use BiFunction
map.compute("count", (key, val) -> val == null ? 1 : val + 1);
map.merge("count", 1, Integer::sum);

// Map.replaceAll uses BiFunction<K,V,V>
map.replaceAll((key, val) -> val.toUpperCase());

// List.removeIf uses Predicate<E>
list.removeIf(s -> s.startsWith("DELETED_"));

// List.sort uses Comparator
list.sort(Comparator.comparing(Employee::getName));

// Optional methods
opt.filter(Predicate)  // Predicate<T>
opt.map(Function)      // Function<T,R>
opt.flatMap(Function)  // Function<T, Optional<R>>
opt.ifPresent(Consumer)// Consumer<T>
opt.orElseGet(Supplier)// Supplier<T>
Part 19

Testing Functional Interfaces

Functional interfaces are trivially testable because they are pure functions with single-method contracts.

class OrderValidatorTest {
    private final Predicate<Order> validator = OrderValidator.isValid;

    @Test
    void validOrder_passes() {
        Order order = Order.builder()
            .amount(new BigDecimal("100"))
            .customer(activeCustomer())
            .shippingAddress(address())
            .build();
        assertTrue(validator.test(order));
    }

    @Test
    void zeroAmountOrder_fails() {
        Order order = Order.builder()
            .amount(BigDecimal.ZERO)
            .customer(activeCustomer())
            .shippingAddress(address())
            .build();
        assertFalse(validator.test(order));
    }

    @Test
    void composedPredicate_and_semantics() {
        Predicate<Integer> greaterThan5 = n -> n > 5;
        Predicate<Integer> lessThan10   = n -> n < 10;
        Predicate<Integer> between5and10 = greaterThan5.and(lessThan10);

        assertTrue(between5and10.test(7));
        assertFalse(between5and10.test(3));
        assertFalse(between5and10.test(12));
    }
}
Part 20

Common Pitfalls

Pitfall 1: Using Functional Interfaces for Stateful Operations

// WRONG — stateful lambda in parallel stream: race condition
List<String> results = new ArrayList<>();
items.parallelStream().forEach(results::add);  // ArrayList is not thread-safe!

// RIGHT — use collect instead
List<String> results = items.parallelStream().collect(Collectors.toList());

Pitfall 2: Overloading and Ambiguous Method References

class Printer {
    static void print(Object o)  { ... }
    static void print(String s)  { ... }
}
// Ambiguous: which overload does this refer to?
Consumer<String> c = Printer::print;  // compile error — ambiguous

// Fix: use explicit lambda
Consumer<String> c = s -> Printer.print(s);  // unambiguous — picks String overload

Pitfall 3: Ignoring the Return Type Mismatch

// WRONG: Consumer ignores the return value of a Function
Consumer<String> c = String::toUpperCase;   // compile error — Consumer expects void SAM
// String::toUpperCase returns String, not void

// RIGHT
Function<String, String> fn = String::toUpperCase;
Consumer<String> c = s -> System.out.println(s.toUpperCase());

Pitfall 4: @FunctionalInterface on a class

@FunctionalInterface
class NotAnInterface {   // compile error — @FunctionalInterface only applies to interfaces
    void doSomething();
}
Part 21

Performance Considerations

Lambda Allocation

Non-capturing lambda (no captured variables):
  Created ONCE by LambdaMetafactory on first call
  Reused as singleton on subsequent calls
  → Zero allocation overhead after JIT warm-up

Capturing lambda (captures effectively-final local variable):
  New object allocated on each lambda creation site
  → Small allocation per call if in a loop — use with care in hot paths

Instance method reference on a specific instance (bound):
  Behaves like capturing (holds a reference to the instance)
  → Same allocation pattern as capturing lambda

Functional Interface vs Direct Call

JMH Benchmark: 10M calls to a simple increment function
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Direct method call:          ~85 ns/op
Lambda (non-capturing):      ~87 ns/op      (effectively same after JIT)
Lambda (capturing, warm):    ~92 ns/op      (tiny allocation overhead)
Anonymous inner class:        ~87 ns/op     (same as lambda after JIT)
Reflection (Method.invoke):  ~950 ns/op    (~11x slower — avoid in hot paths)
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Conclusion: Lambdas are NOT slower than direct calls after JIT warm-up.

InliningBehavior

Modern JVMs (HotSpot/OpenJ9) inline monomorphic lambda call sites: if a Predicate<T> field always holds the same lambda implementation, the JIT devirtualizes the call and inlines the lambda body — resulting in performance identical to a direct method call.

Practice — Lesson 32

Easy Exercises

Exercise 1 — Write Functional Interfaces

Implement each of the following using a lambda expression assigned to the correct built-in functional interface type:

// a) A Predicate that tests if an integer is a perfect square
Predicate<Integer> isPerfectSquare = n -> {
    int sqrt = (int) Math.sqrt(n);
    return sqrt * sqrt == n;
};

// b) A Function that converts a comma-separated String to a List<String>
Function<String, List<String>> splitCsv =
    s -> Arrays.asList(s.split(","));

// c) A Supplier of the current timestamp as an Instant
Supplier<Instant> now = Instant::now;

// d) A Consumer that prints an object in JSON format via ObjectMapper
Consumer<Object> printJson = obj -> {
    try { System.out.println(mapper.writeValueAsString(obj)); }
    catch (JsonProcessingException e) { throw new RuntimeException(e); }
};

// e) A BinaryOperator that returns the longer of two strings
BinaryOperator<String> longer = (a, b) -> a.length() >= b.length() ? a : b;

Exercise 2 — @FunctionalInterface Validity

Determine which of the following are valid functional interfaces and explain why:

// A — valid or not?
@FunctionalInterface
interface A { void run(); }

// B — valid or not?
@FunctionalInterface
interface B { void run(); default void log() {} }

// C — valid or not?
@FunctionalInterface
interface C { void run(); void stop(); }

// D — valid or not?
@FunctionalInterface
interface D extends Runnable { boolean equals(Object o); }

// E — valid or not?
@FunctionalInterface
interface E<T> extends Comparable<T> { }

Answers:
- A: Valid — one abstract method.
- B: Valid — default methods don't count.
- C: Invalid — two abstract methods.
- D: Valid — equals redeclares Object method (doesn't count); inherits run() from Runnable.
- E: Invalid — compareTo from Comparable is abstract; E adds no method of its own but inherits one — valid! Actually, E is valid if Comparable's compareTo is the SAM. Wait — E does have exactly one SAM from Comparable. Valid.

Medium Exercises

Exercise 3 — Predicate Composition for Order Routing

Build a OrderRouter that routes orders to different processors based on composed Predicate<Order> rules. Define at least three predicates and compose them with and, or, negate to determine routing:

  • Premium orders: amount > 10,000 AND customer tier == "GOLD"
  • Express orders: amount < 500 OR delivery == "EXPRESS"
  • Standard orders: all others (negate of premium.or(express))
Predicate<Order> isPremium = o ->
    o.getAmount().compareTo(new BigDecimal("10000")) > 0 &&
    "GOLD".equals(o.getCustomer().getTier());

Predicate<Order> isExpress = o ->
    o.getAmount().compareTo(new BigDecimal("500")) < 0 ||
    "EXPRESS".equals(o.getDeliveryType());

Predicate<Order> isStandard = isPremium.or(isExpress).negate();

public Processor route(Order order) {
    if (isPremium.test(order))  return premiumProcessor;
    if (isExpress.test(order))  return expressProcessor;
    return standardProcessor;
}

Exercise 4 — Function Pipeline for Data Normalization

Build a Function<RawInput, NormalizedOutput> pipeline from three composable functions:
1. sanitize: trim whitespace, remove control characters
2. validate: throw IllegalArgumentException if input is blank after sanitization
3. transform: convert to a NormalizedOutput record

Function<String, String> sanitize = s ->
    s.trim().replaceAll("[\\p{Cntrl}]", "");

Function<String, String> validate = s -> {
    if (s.isBlank()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Input is blank after sanitization");
    return s;
};

Function<String, NormalizedOutput> transform = NormalizedOutput::from;

Function<String, NormalizedOutput> pipeline = sanitize.andThen(validate).andThen(transform);

Advanced Exercises

Exercise 5 — Custom ThrowingPredicate

Implement a ThrowingPredicate<T> functional interface that declares boolean test(T t) throws Exception, along with a static wrap method that converts it to a standard Predicate<T> by wrapping checked exceptions in RuntimeException. Write unit tests covering both successful evaluation and exception wrapping.

Exercise 6 — Memoizing Function

Implement a Function<T, R> wrapper that memoizes results in a ConcurrentHashMap, so repeated calls with the same argument return the cached result without re-computing:

public static <T, R> Function<T, R> memoize(Function<T, R> fn) {
    ConcurrentHashMap<T, R> cache = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    return input -> cache.computeIfAbsent(input, fn);
}

// Usage
Function<Integer, Long> fib = memoize(n -> computeFib(n));

Challenge: Extend to support recursive memoization (where the memoized function calls itself).

Production Exercises

Exercise 7 — Spring Batch Item Processor

Implement a Spring Batch ItemProcessor<RawTransaction, ProcessedTransaction> using composed functional interfaces:
- A Predicate<RawTransaction> for validity check
- A Function<RawTransaction, ProcessedTransaction> for transformation
- A Consumer<RawTransaction> for audit logging of rejected transactions

Use Predicate.and() composition for the validity check (amount > 0, currency code not null, timestamp not null).

Exercise 8 — Functional Rule Engine

Design a RuleEngine<T> that accepts a List<Predicate<T>> and a Consumer<T> for matched cases and a Consumer<T> for unmatched cases. Provide:
- void applyAll(List<T> items) — applies all rules to each item
- boolean matchesAll(T item) — returns true if item matches all rules

Debugging Exercises

Exercise 9 — Identify the Bug

// What is wrong? Will this compile? What happens at runtime?
@FunctionalInterface
interface Greeter {
    String greet(String name);
}

Greeter g = name -> {
    if (name == null) return;  // BUG
    return "Hello, " + name;
};

Answer: return; in a non-void method is a compile error. The SAM greet returns String, so all code paths must return a String. Fix: return "Hello, stranger"; or throw an exception.

Exercise 10 — Primitive Specialization Bug

// This compiles but has a performance problem. Identify and fix it.
Function<Integer, Integer> doubler = n -> n * 2;
List<Integer> result = IntStream.range(0, 1_000_000)
    .mapToObj(doubler::apply)
    .collect(Collectors.toList());

Answer: mapToObj(doubler::apply) boxes each int to Integer to call doubler.apply(Integer), then doubler immediately unboxes to multiply, then returns a boxed Integer. Two boxing operations per element. Fix:

IntUnaryOperator doubler = n -> n * 2;
List<Integer> result = IntStream.range(0, 1_000_000)
    .map(doubler)          // stays as IntStream (no boxing)
    .boxed()               // single boxing at the end
    .collect(Collectors.toList());

Interview Questions

Q1: What is a functional interface? What is the SAM rule?
A functional interface is an interface with exactly one abstract method (SAM — Single Abstract Method). default methods, static methods, and Object-inherited method redeclarations do not count toward the SAM constraint. The @FunctionalInterface annotation enforces this at compile time.

Q2: Can a functional interface extend another functional interface?
Yes, if the extending interface does not add any new abstract methods. Example: UnaryOperator<T> extends Function<T, T> and adds no new abstract methods — it inherits apply(T) as its SAM.

Q3: Why can't java.lang.Object methods break the SAM rule?
Because every class implicitly provides implementations of Object methods (equals, hashCode, toString, etc.). Redeclaring them in an interface does not require implementing classes to provide any additional implementation — the Object implementation is always present.

Q4: What is the difference between Function<T,T> and UnaryOperator<T>?
UnaryOperator<T> extends Function<T,T> — they are functionally equivalent. UnaryOperator<T> is more expressive when the input and output types are the same (e.g., List.replaceAll(UnaryOperator<E>)). Using UnaryOperator signals to the reader that the transformation preserves the type.

Q5: Why are there 43 functional interfaces instead of just the 4 root ones?
To avoid boxing/unboxing overhead for primitive types (int, long, double). Generic type parameters in Java always use reference types (Object wrappers). Primitive specializations like IntPredicate, LongFunction, and DoubleSupplier pass and return raw primitive values — no heap allocation, no GC pressure. For high-throughput numeric pipelines, this difference is significant.

Q6: How does invokedynamic relate to lambda expressions?
The Java compiler emits an invokedynamic instruction at the lambda creation site instead of generating an anonymous inner class file. At runtime (first call), LambdaMetafactory.metafactory dynamically generates and loads a class implementing the functional interface. Subsequent calls reuse the generated class. For non-capturing lambdas, the generated instance is a singleton — no allocation on hot paths.

Q7: Why is Optional.orElseGet(Supplier<T>) preferred over Optional.orElse(T) for expensive fallbacks?
orElse(T) eagerly evaluates its argument — the expression is computed whether or not the Optional is empty. orElseGet(Supplier<T>) is lazy — the Supplier's get() method is only called when the Optional is empty. For expensive computations or side-effectful fallbacks (like a DB query), orElseGet avoids unnecessary work.

Q8: What happens if you annotate a class (not interface) with @FunctionalInterface?
It is a compile error. @FunctionalInterface is only applicable to interface declarations. Attempting to annotate a class, abstract class, or enum with it causes: @FunctionalInterface is not applicable to this type of declaration.

Part 1

Concept

A lambda expression is an anonymous function — a block of code with parameters and a body — that can be assigned to a variable, passed as an argument, or returned from a method. Lambda expressions are the primary mechanism by which Java became a functional-style language in Java 8.

Before Java 8, every time you needed to express behavior you had to create a class (often an anonymous inner class). Lambda expressions eliminate that ceremony. They are syntactic sugar backed by the invokedynamic JVM instruction, and they implement functional interfaces — interfaces with exactly one abstract method.

Why Lambdas Matter for Architects

Problem (pre-Java 8) Lambda Solution
Anonymous inner classes for every callback Inline lambda, zero ceremony
Comparator required a full class (a, b) -> a.getName().compareTo(b.getName())
Runnable boilerplate in thread creation new Thread(() -> doWork()).start()
Strategy pattern needed interface + class Pass lambda as strategy directly
Event listener verbosity Spring/event listener as single-line lambda
Part 2

Syntax Reference

2.1 Basic Forms

// No parameters
Runnable r = () -> System.out.println("Hello");

// One parameter — parentheses optional
Consumer<String> printer = s -> System.out.println(s);

// Multiple parameters — parentheses required
Comparator<String> cmp = (a, b) -> a.compareTo(b);

// Block body — braces required when multiple statements or return needed
Function<Integer, Integer> factorial = n -> {
    int result = 1;
    for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++) result *= i;
    return result;
};

2.2 Syntax Grammar

LambdaExpression:
    LambdaParameters  ->  LambdaBody

LambdaParameters:
    Identifier                          // single param, no parens
  | ( )                                 // zero params
  | ( ParameterList )                   // one or more params

LambdaBody:
    Expression                          // implicit return
  | Block                               // explicit return required

2.3 ASCII: Lambda Forms at a Glance

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              LAMBDA EXPRESSION ANATOMY                          │
│                                                                 │
│  (String s, int n)  ->  s.repeat(n)                            │
│  └──────────────┘   ││  └────────┘                             │
│    Parameter List   ││  Expression Body (implicit return)       │
│                     ││                                          │
│                     └┴─ Arrow token                             │
│                                                                 │
│  (String s, int n)  ->  { return s.repeat(n); }                │
│                         └──────────────────────┘               │
│                           Block Body (explicit return)          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Part 3

Type Inference

The compiler infers the types of lambda parameters from the target type — the functional interface the lambda is being assigned to or passed into.

// Explicit types — always valid
BiFunction<String, Integer, String> f1 = (String s, Integer n) -> s.repeat(n);

// Inferred types — compiler reads BiFunction generic args
BiFunction<String, Integer, String> f2 = (s, n) -> s.repeat(n);

// Mixed types — NOT allowed
// BiFunction<String, Integer, String> f3 = (String s, n) -> s.repeat(n); // compile error

How the Compiler Determines the Target Type

Target type determination order:
  1. Variable assignment:  Predicate<String> p = s -> s.isEmpty();
  2. Method argument:      list.removeIf(s -> s.isEmpty());
  3. Return statement:     return (a, b) -> a + b;
  4. Cast:                 ((Comparator<String>) (a, b) -> a.compareTo(b));
  5. Conditional ternary:  cond ? (Runnable) () -> a() : () -> b()

Type Inference with var (Java 11+)

// var cannot be the target type of a lambda directly
// var f = s -> s.isEmpty(); // COMPILE ERROR — ambiguous target type

// But var works for already-typed lambda references
Predicate<String> pred = s -> s.isEmpty();
var p = pred; // fine — type is Predicate<String>
Part 4

Effectively Final Variables

A lambda can capture variables from the enclosing scope, but those variables must be effectively final — either declared final or never reassigned after the point of capture.

String prefix = "Hello, ";          // effectively final

// Captured in lambda — OK
Function<String, String> greeter = name -> prefix + name;

// Attempting to mutate after capture — compile error
// prefix = "Hi, ";                 // Error: variable used in lambda should be final or effectively final

int counter = 0;
Runnable broken = () -> counter++;  // COMPILE ERROR

Why the Effectively Final Rule Exists

Lambdas may be executed on a different thread or at a later time. If the captured variable could change after capture, the lambda would see inconsistent state. The effectively-final rule is the language's way of guaranteeing that the captured value is stable for the lifetime of the lambda.

Thread A (captures x=5)       Thread B (mutates x to 10)
      │                               │
      ▼                               ▼
  lambda runs: sees x=5 ????   or x=10 ????
         UNDEFINED BEHAVIOR — compiler prevents this

Workaround Patterns

// Pattern 1: copy to a local effectively-final variable
int mutableCounter = computeCounter();
int snapshot = mutableCounter;             // snapshot is effectively final
Supplier<Integer> s = () -> snapshot * 2;

// Pattern 2: use an AtomicInteger for mutation inside a lambda
AtomicInteger counter = new AtomicInteger(0);
Runnable r = () -> counter.incrementAndGet(); // the reference to counter is final
Part 5

Lambda vs. Anonymous Inner Class

These two produce the same observable behavior but differ in implementation significantly.

Syntactic Comparison

// Anonymous inner class (pre-Java 8)
Runnable r1 = new Runnable() {
    @Override
    public void run() {
        System.out.println("AIC");
    }
};

// Lambda equivalent
Runnable r2 = () -> System.out.println("Lambda");

Semantic Differences

Aspect Anonymous Inner Class Lambda
this reference Refers to AIC instance Refers to enclosing class
super reference Refers to AIC's superclass Refers to enclosing class superclass
Can declare state Yes (fields) No (stateless)
Shadowing outer vars Yes (field can shadow outer) No (cannot shadow outer locals)
instanceof check Has a specific class type Not a specific class; is functional interface type
Serialization Only if Serializable extended Only if target interface is Serializable

ASCII: No .class File for Lambda

javac compilation output:

  Anonymous Inner Class:                Lambda:
  ┌───────────────────┐                 ┌───────────────────┐
  │ MyClass.class     │                 │ MyClass.class     │
  │ MyClass$1.class   │  ← extra file!  │   (no extra file) │
  └───────────────────┘                 └───────────────────┘

  Each AIC = one .class file loaded at class-loading time
  Each lambda = one bootstrap call to LambdaMetafactory at runtime

This difference matters in large codebases: eliminating AIC .class files reduces classloader memory pressure and startup time.

Part 6

Capturing vs. Non-Capturing Lambdas

Non-Capturing Lambda

Does not reference any variables from the enclosing scope (only parameters).

// Non-capturing — no closure over outer variables
Comparator<String> cmp = (a, b) -> Integer.compare(a.length(), b.length());

The JVM can allocate a single instance and reuse it for every invocation. The lambda is essentially a static method.

Capturing Lambda

References at least one variable from the enclosing scope.

String separator = ", ";
Function<List<String>, String> joiner = list -> String.join(separator, list);
// 'separator' is captured — each time this scope executes a new lambda instance may be created

Performance Implication

Non-capturing lambda:
  First call  → LambdaMetafactory creates instance, caches it
  Subsequent → same cached instance reused (zero allocation)

Capturing lambda:
  Each capture-site evaluation may create a new instance
  (JVM is allowed to optimize, but not guaranteed)
Part 7

Under the Hood: `invokedynamic` and LambdaMetafactory

ASCII: Lambda Desugaring Flow

SOURCE CODE:
  Runnable r = () -> System.out.println("Hi");

                         │
                         ▼ javac
BYTECODE (simplified):
  INVOKEDYNAMIC run()Ljava/lang/Runnable;
     BootstrapMethod: LambdaMetafactory.metafactory(...)
     implMethod: MyClass.lambda$main$0()V   ← synthetic static method

                         │
                         ▼ first execution (JVM bootstrap)
RUNTIME:
  LambdaMetafactory.metafactory() called once per call site
       │
       ├─ generates a class implementing Runnable at runtime
       ├─ links lambda body to the generated run() method
       └─ returns CallSite that directly invokes generated class

                         │
                         ▼ subsequent executions
  CallSite already linked → direct dispatch, no bootstrap overhead

Key Classes in the Lambda Machinery

Class/Method Role
java.lang.invoke.LambdaMetafactory Bootstrap method factory; generates lambda implementation
java.lang.invoke.MethodHandles Provides lookup objects for method handle resolution
java.lang.invoke.CallSite Represents a linked call site (re-used after first link)
invokedynamic JVM instruction Defers linkage to bootstrap; enables lazy class generation

Decompiling to See the Synthetic Method

javap -p -c MyClass.class

You will see a synthetic static method like:

private static void lambda$main$0();
  Code:
    getstatic java/lang/System.out
    ldc "Hi"
    invokevirtual java/io/PrintStream.println:(Ljava/lang/String;)V
    return

The lambda body is compiled into this private static method; LambdaMetafactory wires it to the functional interface.

Part 8

Functional Interfaces Compatible with Lambdas

Lambdas only work with functional interfaces (exactly one abstract method). The standard java.util.function package provides the most common ones:

Interface Signature Use Case
Runnable () -> void Background tasks, threads
Callable<V> () -> V Tasks returning a value
Supplier<T> () -> T Lazy value provider
Consumer<T> T -> void Side-effecting operations
BiConsumer<T,U> (T, U) -> void Two-arg side effects
Function<T,R> T -> R Transformation
BiFunction<T,U,R> (T, U) -> R Two-arg transformation
Predicate<T> T -> boolean Boolean test / filtering
BiPredicate<T,U> (T, U) -> boolean Two-arg boolean test
UnaryOperator<T> T -> T Same-type transformation
BinaryOperator<T> (T, T) -> T Reduction, combine
Comparator<T> (T, T) -> int Sorting
Part 9

Lambda Composition

Functional interfaces in java.util.function provide default methods for composing lambdas:

Function Composition

Function<String, String> trim  = String::trim;      // method ref — see Lesson 34
Function<String, String> upper = String::toUpperCase;
Function<String, String> shout = String::trim.andThen(String::toUpperCase); // compose
// andThen: f.andThen(g) = x -> g(f(x))
// compose: f.compose(g) = x -> f(g(x))

Function<String, String> pipeline = trim.andThen(upper);
System.out.println(pipeline.apply("  hello  ")); // "HELLO"

Predicate Composition

Predicate<String> nonNull  = s -> s != null;
Predicate<String> nonEmpty = s -> !s.isEmpty();

Predicate<String> valid = nonNull.and(nonEmpty);
Predicate<String> either = nonNull.or(nonEmpty);
Predicate<String> isNull = nonNull.negate();

Consumer Chaining

Consumer<String> logger  = s -> log.info(s);
Consumer<String> auditor = s -> audit.record(s);

Consumer<String> both = logger.andThen(auditor);
both.accept("Order placed"); // logs, then records
Part 10

Exception Handling in Lambdas

Checked exceptions are a pain point with lambdas. Functional interfaces in java.util.function do not declare checked exceptions.

The Problem

// IOException is checked — this DOES NOT COMPILE
Function<String, String> reader = path -> Files.readString(Path.of(path)); // compile error

Pattern 1: Wrap in a try-catch inside the lambda

Function<String, String> reader = path -> {
    try {
        return Files.readString(Path.of(path));
    } catch (IOException e) {
        throw new RuntimeException(e);  // wrap as unchecked
    }
};

Pattern 2: Create a Checked Functional Interface

@FunctionalInterface
public interface CheckedFunction<T, R> {
    R apply(T t) throws Exception;
}

// Adapter to wrap it
public static <T, R> Function<T, R> unchecked(CheckedFunction<T, R> f) {
    return t -> {
        try {
            return f.apply(t);
        } catch (Exception e) {
            throw new RuntimeException(e);
        }
    };
}

// Usage
Function<String, String> reader = unchecked(path -> Files.readString(Path.of(path)));

Pattern 3: Use a library (Vavr, Failsafe)

// Vavr's CheckedFunction1
CheckedFunction1<String, String> f = path -> Files.readString(Path.of(path));
Function<String, String> safe = f.unchecked();
Part 11

Lambdas and `this` Reference

One of the most common gotchas when migrating from anonymous inner classes:

public class EventHandler {
    private String name = "Handler";

    public void register() {
        // Anonymous inner class: 'this' = the AIC instance
        Runnable aic = new Runnable() {
            @Override public void run() {
                System.out.println(this.getClass().getName()); // prints AIC class name
            }
        };

        // Lambda: 'this' = the enclosing EventHandler instance
        Runnable lambda = () -> {
            System.out.println(this.name); // prints "Handler"
        };
    }
}

Rule: In a lambda, this always refers to the enclosing class instance, never the lambda itself.

Part 12

Lambdas with Generics and Wildcards

// Generic method accepting a functional interface
public <T> List<T> filter(List<T> list, Predicate<? super T> pred) {
    return list.stream().filter(pred).collect(Collectors.toList());
}

// Bounded wildcards
Predicate<? super Number> isPositive = n -> n.doubleValue() > 0;
filter(List.of(1, -2, 3), isPositive); // works with Integer, Long, Double...

Wildcards with lambdas follow the same rules as generic wildcards in any other context. The compiler uses the wildcard bounds to verify the lambda parameter types.

Part 13

Performance: Lambda vs. Anonymous Class

Benchmark Summary (representative JMH results)

Benchmark                                    Mode  Score   Units
LambdaBench.runnable_lambda                  thrpt  458.2  ops/ms
LambdaBench.runnable_anonymous_class         thrpt  441.7  ops/ms
LambdaBench.non_capturing_lambda             thrpt  612.4  ops/ms  ← reused instance
LambdaBench.capturing_lambda                 thrpt  389.1  ops/ms  ← new instance each time

Key takeaways:
- Non-capturing lambdas are often faster than equivalent AIC due to instance reuse.
- Capturing lambdas carry allocation overhead similar to AIC.
- JIT compilation often inlines simple lambdas, eliminating virtual dispatch entirely.
- Do not premature-optimize by avoiding lambdas; profile first.

JIT Inlining of Lambdas

The JIT compiler treats the lambda body as a regular method call and will inline it when:
- The call site is monomorphic (only one lambda type flows through it).
- The lambda body is small enough to inline without code size explosion.

Part 14

Lambdas in Streams

Lambdas are the bread-and-butter of the Streams API (covered in Lesson 35), but a preview:

List<Order> orders = getOrders();

// Pipeline: filter → map → collect
List<String> premiumIds = orders.stream()
    .filter(o -> o.getTotal() > 1000.0)          // Predicate<Order>
    .sorted((a, b) -> Double.compare(b.getTotal(), a.getTotal())) // Comparator<Order>
    .map(o -> o.getId())                          // Function<Order, String>
    .collect(Collectors.toList());

Each step accepts a functional interface — all implemented here as lambdas.

Part 15

Lambdas in Comparators

Comparator is one of the most lambda-friendly interfaces in the JDK:

List<Employee> employees = getEmployees();

// Single field sort
employees.sort((a, b) -> a.getLastName().compareTo(b.getLastName()));

// Multi-field sort using Comparator.comparing factory (returns Comparator)
employees.sort(
    Comparator.comparing(Employee::getLastName)        // method ref — Lesson 34
              .thenComparing(Employee::getFirstName)
              .thenComparingInt(Employee::getAge)
);

// Reversed
employees.sort(Comparator.comparing(Employee::getSalary).reversed());
Part 16

Production Patterns

Pattern 1: Replace Runnable/Callable Boilerplate

// Before
ExecutorService exec = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4);
exec.submit(new Callable<Integer>() {
    @Override public Integer call() throws Exception {
        return computeValue();
    }
});

// After
exec.submit(() -> computeValue());

Pattern 2: Strategy Pattern without Extra Classes

// Define strategy interface
@FunctionalInterface
interface PricingStrategy {
    double apply(double basePrice, int quantity);
}

// Strategies as lambdas — no extra class files
PricingStrategy bulk      = (price, qty) -> qty > 100 ? price * 0.85 : price;
PricingStrategy premium   = (price, qty) -> price * 1.2;
PricingStrategy clearance = (price, qty) -> price * 0.5;

// Use
double finalPrice = bulk.apply(49.99, 120);

Pattern 3: Builder with Lambda Configuration

// HttpClient-style builder using lambda configuration
ServerConfig config = ServerConfig.builder()
    .port(8080)
    .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(30))
    .onError(e -> log.error("Server error", e))   // Consumer<Throwable>
    .onStart(() -> log.info("Server started"))     // Runnable
    .build();

Pattern 4: Retry with Lambda Supplier

public static <T> T withRetry(int maxAttempts, Supplier<T> action) {
    for (int i = 0; i < maxAttempts; i++) {
        try {
            return action.get();
        } catch (Exception e) {
            if (i == maxAttempts - 1) throw e;
            sleep(backoff(i));
        }
    }
    throw new IllegalStateException("unreachable");
}

// Usage
String result = withRetry(3, () -> httpClient.get("/api/data"));
Part 17

Spring Framework Integration

Lambda in @Bean Method

@Configuration
public class AppConfig {

    @Bean
    public Comparator<Product> productComparator() {
        return (a, b) -> a.getName().compareTo(b.getName());
    }

    @Bean
    public Predicate<Order> highValueOrder() {
        return order -> order.getTotal() > 500.0;
    }
}

Lambda Event Listeners

@Component
public class OrderService {

    private final ApplicationEventPublisher publisher;

    public OrderService(ApplicationEventPublisher publisher) {
        this.publisher = publisher;
    }

    // Spring 4.2+ functional event listener
    @Bean
    public ApplicationListener<OrderCreatedEvent> onOrderCreated() {
        return event -> sendConfirmationEmail(event.getOrder());
    }
}

Spring WebFlux with Lambdas

@Configuration
public class RouterConfig {

    @Bean
    public RouterFunction<ServerResponse> routes(OrderHandler handler) {
        return RouterFunctions.route()
            .GET("/orders",      handler::listOrders)
            .POST("/orders",     handler::createOrder)
            .GET("/orders/{id}", handler::getOrder)
            .build();
    }
}
Part 18

Lambda Serialization

Lambdas can be serialized, but with caveats:

// Serialize a lambda — target interface must extend Serializable
Comparator<String> cmp = (Comparator<String> & Serializable) (a, b) -> a.compareTo(b);

// Write
try (ObjectOutputStream oos = new ObjectOutputStream(new FileOutputStream("cmp.ser"))) {
    oos.writeObject(cmp);
}

// Read
try (ObjectInputStream ois = new ObjectInputStream(new FileInputStream("cmp.ser"))) {
    Comparator<String> restored = (Comparator<String>) ois.readObject();
}

Pitfalls

  • Serialized lambda depends on the host class name and method signature — brittle across refactors.
  • Avoid serializing lambdas across network boundaries; prefer serializing data and reconstructing lambdas.
  • Spring's @Bean lambdas are not serialized by the container; session-scoped beans use proxy, not lambda serialization.
Part 19

Common Mistakes and Anti-Patterns

Mistake 1: Mutating external state inside a lambda

List<String> results = new ArrayList<>();
list.stream()
    .filter(s -> s.length() > 3)
    .forEach(s -> results.add(s));  // mutation — breaks parallel streams!

// Correct
List<String> results = list.stream()
    .filter(s -> s.length() > 3)
    .collect(Collectors.toList());

Mistake 2: Ignoring checked exceptions silently

// Silent swallow — terrible
list.forEach(item -> {
    try { process(item); } catch (Exception e) { /* swallowed */ }
});

// Better — propagate
list.forEach(item -> unchecked(() -> process(item)));

Mistake 3: Using a lambda where a method reference is clearer

// Noisy lambda
list.stream().map(s -> s.toUpperCase()).collect(toList());

// Cleaner — use method reference (Lesson 34)
list.stream().map(String::toUpperCase).collect(toList());

Mistake 4: Over-nesting lambdas

// Hard to read
Function<String, Function<Integer, String>> curried = s -> n -> s.repeat(n);

// Better: named intermediate types or plain method

Mistake 5: Capturing this unintentionally in Android/UI contexts

// In Android — captures Activity, preventing GC
button.setOnClickListener(v -> {
    startActivity(new Intent(this, NextActivity.class)); // 'this' = Activity!
});
// Use weak references or lifecycle-aware components
Part 20

Advanced: Currying and Partial Application

// Currying: convert BiFunction into chain of Functions
public static <A, B, R> Function<A, Function<B, R>> curry(BiFunction<A, B, R> f) {
    return a -> b -> f.apply(a, b);
}

BiFunction<Integer, Integer, Integer> add = (a, b) -> a + b;
Function<Integer, Function<Integer, Integer>> curriedAdd = curry(add);

Function<Integer, Integer> add5 = curriedAdd.apply(5);
System.out.println(add5.apply(3));  // 8
System.out.println(add5.apply(7));  // 12

// Partial application
BiFunction<String, String, String> format = (template, value) -> template.formatted(value);
Function<String, String> jsonWrap = value -> format.apply("{\"data\":\"%s\"}", value);
Part 21

Interview Preparation

Q1: What is "effectively final" and why does Java require it for lambda captures?

Answer: A variable is effectively final if it is never assigned after its initial assignment. Java requires captured variables to be effectively final because lambdas may execute asynchronously or at a later time. If the captured variable could change, the lambda might observe inconsistent state, introducing race conditions. The compiler enforces this at compile time.

Q2: How does a lambda differ from an anonymous inner class in terms of this?

Answer: In an anonymous inner class, this refers to the AIC instance itself. In a lambda, this refers to the enclosing class instance. This is because a lambda is not a new class; it is a method of the enclosing class compiled into a synthetic static (or instance) method.

Q3: Why don't lambdas generate .class files?

Answer: Instead of compiling to a separate .class file, lambdas use the invokedynamic JVM instruction. The first time the lambda call site is hit, the JVM calls LambdaMetafactory.metafactory(), which generates a class at runtime and links the call site. Subsequent executions reuse the linked call site directly, with no additional class loading.

Q4: When is a lambda serializable?

Answer: A lambda is serializable only when its target functional interface also extends java.io.Serializable. You can use an intersection cast: (Runnable & Serializable) () -> doWork(). However, serialized lambdas are fragile and should not be used across JVM boundaries or after refactoring.

Q5: What is a non-capturing lambda and why is it more performant?

Answer: A non-capturing lambda does not close over any variables from the enclosing scope; it only uses its own parameters. The JVM can allocate a single instance at the first call and reuse it for every subsequent invocation. A capturing lambda may require a new instance per evaluation to hold the captured values.

Q6: Can a lambda throw checked exceptions?

Answer: Only if the target functional interface's abstract method declares the checked exception. java.util.function.* interfaces do not declare checked exceptions, so lambdas used with them cannot throw checked exceptions directly. The common workaround is to wrap checked exceptions in unchecked exceptions inside the lambda body, or to define a custom functional interface that declares the checked exception.

Part 22

Summary Table

Topic Key Point
Syntax (params) -> expr or (params) -> { block; return val; }
Target type Must be a functional interface (exactly one abstract method)
Type inference Compiler infers param types from target interface generics

this in lambda Refers to enclosing class, not the lambda itself
No .class file Backed by invokedynamic + LambdaMetafactory at runtime
Non-capturing Single reused instance; faster; no closure
Capturing May allocate per evaluation; holds captured state
Composition andThen, compose, and, or, negate on functional interfaces
Checked exceptions Must wrap in unchecked or use custom checked functional interface
Serialization Needs Serializable intersection cast; fragile across refactors

Spring use @Bean, event listeners, WebFlux routing, security config

  3. A Comparator<String> that sorts strings by length descending, then alphabetically ascending for ties.

int base = 10;
IntUnaryOperator doubler = n -> n * base;
base = 20;  // error here
System.out.println(doubler.applyAsInt(5));
