Part 1

Concept

A method reference is a shorthand notation for a lambda expression that calls an existing method by name. Instead of writing a lambda body that does nothing but delegate to a method, you can replace it with a concise ClassName::methodName or object::methodName syntax.

Method references are not a new feature in addition to lambdas — they are compiled using the exact same invokedynamic + LambdaMetafactory mechanism. They are purely a readability improvement: the compiler converts a method reference into the equivalent lambda at compile time.

The Core Motivation

// Lambda that does nothing but call one method:
list.stream().map(s -> s.toUpperCase()).collect(toList());

// Method reference — same thing, less noise:
list.stream().map(String::toUpperCase).collect(toList());

When a lambda is a single method call with its parameter(s) forwarded directly, a method reference is preferred. When the lambda does any additional computation, keep the lambda.

Why Architects Care

  • Readability at scale: codebases with hundreds of stream pipelines become dramatically more scannable.
  • Method references bind to named methods — easier to grep, refactor, and trace in stack traces.
  • The four types of method references map to four distinct patterns in production code, each solving a common problem.
Part 2

The Four Types: Overview

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   FOUR TYPES OF METHOD REFERENCES                           │
│                                                                             │
│  Type 1 — Static Method                                                     │
│    Syntax:   ClassName::staticMethod                                        │
│    Lambda:   (args) -> ClassName.staticMethod(args)                         │
│    Example:  Integer::parseInt                                              │
│                                                                             │
│  Type 2 — Instance Method of a Particular Object                           │
│    Syntax:   object::instanceMethod                                         │
│    Lambda:   (args) -> object.instanceMethod(args)                          │
│    Example:  System.out::println                                            │
│                                                                             │
│  Type 3 — Instance Method of an Arbitrary Object of a Particular Type      │
│    Syntax:   ClassName::instanceMethod                                      │
│    Lambda:   (obj, args) -> obj.instanceMethod(args)                        │
│    Example:  String::toUpperCase                                            │
│                                                                             │
│  Type 4 — Constructor Reference                                             │
│    Syntax:   ClassName::new                                                 │
│    Lambda:   (args) -> new ClassName(args)                                  │
│    Example:  ArrayList::new                                                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Part 3

Type 1: Static Method Reference

Syntax

ClassName::staticMethod

Equivalent Lambda

(args) -> ClassName.staticMethod(args)

Mechanics

The compiler expects the method reference to match the signature of the target functional interface. For a static method reference, the parameter list of the static method must exactly match the parameter list of the functional interface's abstract method.

Functional Interface:   Function<String, Integer>
Abstract method:        Integer apply(String s)

Static method:          static Integer Integer.parseInt(String s)
                                        └─────────────────────┘
                                        matches apply(String) → Integer ✓

Examples

// Integer::parseInt as Function<String, Integer>
Function<String, Integer> parser = Integer::parseInt;
System.out.println(parser.apply("42")); // 42

// Integer::parseInt as UnaryOperator? No — types don't match
// UnaryOperator<String> bad = Integer::parseInt; // compile error

// Math::abs as IntUnaryOperator
IntUnaryOperator abs = Math::abs;
System.out.println(abs.applyAsInt(-7)); // 7

// Math::max as IntBinaryOperator
IntBinaryOperator max = Math::max;
System.out.println(max.applyAsInt(3, 9)); // 9

// String::valueOf for various types
Function<Boolean, String> boolToStr = String::valueOf;
Function<Long,    String> longToStr  = String::valueOf;  // overload resolved by target type

// Collections::sort as Consumer<List<Comparable>>
Consumer<List<Integer>> sorter = Collections::sort;
List<Integer> nums = new ArrayList<>(List.of(3, 1, 2));
sorter.accept(nums); // [1, 2, 3]

In Streams

List<String> numbers = List.of("1", "2", "3", "4");

// Static ref in map
List<Integer> parsed = numbers.stream()
    .map(Integer::parseInt)
    .collect(Collectors.toList());

// Static ref in filter
List<Integer> nonNegative = Stream.of(-1, 0, 2, -3, 5)
    .filter(n -> n >= 0)               // lambda needed — comparison, not single method call
    .collect(Collectors.toList());

// Static ref in reduce
OptionalInt sum = IntStream.of(1, 2, 3).reduce(Integer::sum);
Part 4

Type 2: Instance Method Reference (Particular Object)

Syntax

object::instanceMethod

Equivalent Lambda

(args) -> object.instanceMethod(args)

Mechanics

Here, object is a specific, already-existing instance captured at the point of reference creation. The method is dispatched on that single object for every invocation.

object:           System.out          (a PrintStream instance)
instance method:  println(String s)
target interface: Consumer<String>    (void accept(String s))

Result: every call to accept(s) → System.out.println(s)

Examples

// System.out::println as Consumer<String>
Consumer<String> print = System.out::println;
print.accept("Hello"); // Hello

// String instance method on a specific string
String prefix = "PREFIX:";
Function<String, String> adder = prefix::concat;
System.out.println(adder.apply(" value")); // "PREFIX: value"

// Logger instance
Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(MyClass.class);
Consumer<String> logger = log::info;
logger.accept("Application started");

// Comparator from a specific Collator instance
Comparator<String> localeSort = Collator.getInstance(Locale.FRANCE)::compare;
List<String> words = new ArrayList<>(List.of("été", "abc", "çà"));
words.sort(localeSort);

// StringBuilder append as Consumer<String>
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
Consumer<String> appender = sb::append;
List.of("Hello", ", ", "World").forEach(appender);
System.out.println(sb); // "Hello, World"

ASCII: Capturing the Object Reference

At reference creation time:

  Consumer<String> logger = log::info;
                            │
                            ├── 'log' reference captured HERE (like a capturing lambda)
                            └── bound to the CallSite

Every accept(s) call:
  → log.info(s)   using the SAME 'log' instance captured at creation

This is a capturing reference — the bound instance is captured, similar to a capturing lambda.

Part 5

Type 3: Instance Method Reference (Arbitrary Object)

Syntax

ClassName::instanceMethod

Equivalent Lambda

(obj, args) -> obj.instanceMethod(args)

Mechanics — The Key Distinction from Type 2

This is the most commonly confused type. The method reference looks syntactically like a static reference (ClassName::method) but it calls an instance method. The crucial difference: the first parameter to the functional interface's abstract method becomes the receiver (the object the method is called on).

Functional Interface:   Function<String, String>
Abstract method:        String apply(String s)

Method reference:       String::toUpperCase
Instance method:        String toUpperCase()   (no parameters)

Compiler binding:
  apply(s)  →  s.toUpperCase()
  └─ first param becomes receiver

Examples

// String::toUpperCase — no additional args
Function<String, String> upper = String::toUpperCase;
System.out.println(upper.apply("hello")); // "HELLO"

// String::trim
UnaryOperator<String> trimmer = String::trim;

// String::length — String → int
ToIntFunction<String> length = String::length;

// String::compareTo — (String, String) → int — the Comparator pattern
Comparator<String> lexOrder = String::compareTo;
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Charlie", "Alice", "Bob"));
names.sort(lexOrder); // [Alice, Bob, Charlie]

// String::startsWith with one argument — BiPredicate pattern
BiPredicate<String, String> startsWith = String::startsWith;
System.out.println(startsWith.test("Hello World", "Hello")); // true

// List::contains — BiPredicate<List<String>, String>
BiPredicate<List<String>, String> contains = List::contains;

The Arity Rule

Instance method signature Functional interface (one param) Functional interface (two params)
T method() Function<T, R> / Supplier<R> N/A
T method(A a) BiFunction<T, A, R> If T is receiver
void method() Consumer<T> N/A
void method(A a) BiConsumer<T, A> N/A
boolean method() Predicate<T> (result ignored) N/A

The receiver object always fills the first parameter slot of the functional interface.

In Streams

List<String> words = List.of("  hello  ", "  world  ", "  java  ");

// All three are Type 3 method references
List<String> cleaned = words.stream()
    .map(String::trim)              // String::trim  — Function<String, String>
    .map(String::toUpperCase)       // String::upper — Function<String, String>
    .sorted(String::compareTo)      // String::compareTo — Comparator<String>
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
// Result: [HELLO, JAVA, WORLD]
Part 6

Type 4: Constructor Reference

Syntax

ClassName::new

Equivalent Lambda

(args) -> new ClassName(args)

Mechanics

Constructor references let you treat a constructor as a factory function. The compiler matches the constructor's parameter list to the functional interface's abstract method. If multiple constructors exist, the one matching the target interface is chosen.

Functional Interface:   Supplier<ArrayList<String>>
Abstract method:        ArrayList<String> get()

Constructor:            new ArrayList<String>()  (no-arg constructor)
Binding:                get() → new ArrayList<String>()

Examples

// No-arg constructor — Supplier
Supplier<ArrayList<String>> listFactory = ArrayList::new;
ArrayList<String> list = listFactory.get();

// Single-arg constructor — Function
Function<String, StringBuilder> sbFactory = StringBuilder::new;
StringBuilder sb = sbFactory.apply("initial content");

// Two-arg constructor — BiFunction
BiFunction<String, Integer, String> repeatFactory =
    (s, n) -> s.repeat(n); // lambda needed — String has no (String, int) constructor
    // String::new takes (String) or (char[]) or (byte[],Charset)...
    // so this particular two-arg pattern needs a lambda

// Custom class constructor
record Point(double x, double y) {}
BiFunction<Double, Double, Point> pointFactory = Point::new;
Point p = pointFactory.apply(3.0, 4.0);

// Supplier for a concrete type to inject dependencies
Supplier<HttpClient> clientFactory = HttpClient::newHttpClient; // static factory — Type 1

Arrays::new — Array Constructor Reference

The only way to create array constructor references:

// IntFunction<int[]> — takes size, returns array
IntFunction<int[]> intArrayFactory = int[]::new;
int[] arr = intArrayFactory.apply(10); // int[10]

// IntFunction<String[]>
IntFunction<String[]> strArrayFactory = String[]::new;
String[] strs = strArrayFactory.apply(5); // String[5]

This is particularly important with streams:

// Stream.toArray() requires an IntFunction<T[]>
String[] result = Stream.of("a", "b", "c")
    .toArray(String[]::new);   // correct — uses constructor reference
    // .toArray(n -> new String[n]); — equivalent lambda

Factory Method Pattern with Constructor References

// Map of type name → factory
Map<String, Supplier<Shape>> shapeFactories = Map.of(
    "circle",    Circle::new,
    "rectangle", Rectangle::new,
    "triangle",  Triangle::new
);

Shape shape = shapeFactories.get(shapeName).get();
Part 7

Disambiguation: Type 1 vs. Type 3

The hardest distinction in method references is between Type 1 (static) and Type 3 (instance of arbitrary object). Both use ClassName::method syntax. The compiler resolves ambiguity by looking at the method name:

ClassName::method

  If 'method' is static in ClassName  →  Type 1 (static reference)
  If 'method' is an instance method   →  Type 3 (arbitrary instance reference)
  If both exist (overloaded)          →  target type determines which

Example: Overloaded Method Resolution

// String.valueOf is both static (String.valueOf(Object)) and... wait, no — valueOf is always static.
// But consider a class where both exist:

class Processor {
    static String process(String s) { return "static:" + s; }
    String process()                { return "instance:" + this; }
}

Function<String, String>  f1 = Processor::process; // Type 1 — static, takes String
Supplier<String>          f2 = new Processor()::process; // Type 2 — particular instance, no args
Function<Processor, String> f3 = Processor::process; // Type 3 — instance method, receiver is first arg
Part 8

Method References and Functional Interface Compatibility

Method references must be compatible with the target functional interface. Compatibility means:

  1. Parameter count: number of params in abstract method = number of params in referenced method (or receiver + params for Type 3).
  2. Parameter types: each parameter type must be assignment-compatible (after auto-boxing/unboxing).
  3. Return type: return type of method must be assignment-compatible with the return type of the abstract method (or void-compatible).

Compatibility Matrix

Method Signature            →  Compatible Interfaces
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
static void foo()           →  Runnable
static void foo(T t)        →  Consumer<T>
static T foo()              →  Supplier<T>
static R foo(T t)           →  Function<T,R>, UnaryOperator<T> (if T==R)
static R foo(T t, U u)      →  BiFunction<T,U,R>
static boolean foo(T t)     →  Predicate<T>
static int foo(T t, T u)    →  Comparator<T>

instance void foo()         →  Consumer<OwnerType>           (Type 3)
instance R foo()            →  Function<OwnerType, R>        (Type 3)
instance R foo(A a)         →  BiFunction<OwnerType, A, R>   (Type 3)
Part 9

ASCII Deep Dive: All Four Types Side-by-Side

┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  TYPE 1 — Static                                                               │
│                                                                                │
│  Integer::parseInt                                                             │
│  ┌─────────┐     ┌──────────────────┐                                         │
│  │  "123"  │────▶│ Integer.parseInt  │────▶  123                              │
│  └─────────┘     └──────────────────┘                                         │
│  Function<String, Integer>                                                     │
│                                                                                │
│  TYPE 2 — Particular Instance                                                  │
│                                                                                │
│  System.out::println                                                           │
│  ┌───────────┐     ┌──────────────────────────────┐                           │
│  │ "message" │────▶│ System.out.println("message")│────▶  (side effect)       │
│  └───────────┘     └──────────────────────────────┘                           │
│  Consumer<String>                (System.out bound at creation)                │
│                                                                                │
│  TYPE 3 — Arbitrary Instance                                                   │
│                                                                                │
│  String::toUpperCase                                                           │
│  ┌──────────┐     ┌────────────────────────────────┐                          │
│  │ "hello"  │────▶│ ("hello").toUpperCase()        │────▶  "HELLO"            │
│  └──────────┘     └────────────────────────────────┘                          │
│  Function<String, String>        (first param becomes receiver)                │
│                                                                                │
│  TYPE 4 — Constructor                                                          │
│                                                                                │
│  ArrayList::new                                                                │
│  ┌───────────┐     ┌───────────────────────────────┐                          │
│  │   (void)  │────▶│ new ArrayList<>()             │────▶  []                 │
│  └───────────┘     └───────────────────────────────┘                          │
│  Supplier<ArrayList>                                                           │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Part 10

Under the Hood: Compilation and Bytecode

Method references compile to the same invokedynamic + LambdaMetafactory mechanism as lambdas:

SOURCE:   list.stream().map(String::toUpperCase)

BYTECODE (simplified):
  INVOKEDYNAMIC apply()Ljava/util/function/Function;
    BootstrapMethod: LambdaMetafactory.metafactory(
        MethodHandles.Lookup lookup,
        String invokedName,        // "apply"
        MethodType invokedType,    // ()Function
        MethodType samMethodType,  // (Object)Object
        MethodHandle implMethod,   // String::toUpperCase
        MethodType instantiatedMethodType  // (String)String
    )

The implMethod handle for a Type 3 reference points directly to String.toUpperCase(). The LambdaMetafactory generates a class that does:

// Generated class (conceptual)
class $Lambda$1 implements Function<String, String> {
    public String apply(String s) {
        return s.toUpperCase();  // first param is the receiver
    }
}

For a Type 2 reference (object::method), the generated class captures the bound object:

// Generated class for System.out::println
class $Lambda$2 implements Consumer<String> {
    private final PrintStream boundInstance;
    $Lambda$2(PrintStream ps) { this.boundInstance = ps; }
    public void accept(String s) {
        boundInstance.println(s);
    }
}
Part 11

Method References in Streams Pipelines

Method references shine brightest in stream pipelines. They make pipeline stages read like a sequence of English verbs:

String Processing Pipeline

List<String> rawInput = List.of("  Alice  ", "  BOB  ", "  charlie  ", "");

List<String> processed = rawInput.stream()
    .map(String::trim)               // Type 3 — trim whitespace
    .filter(Predicate.not(String::isEmpty))  // Type 3 — remove blanks
    .map(String::toLowerCase)        // Type 3 — normalize case
    .distinct()
    .sorted(String::compareTo)       // Type 3 — lexicographic sort
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
// Result: [alice, bob, charlie]

Object Transformation Pipeline

record Employee(String name, String dept, double salary) {}

List<String> seniorDevNames = employees.stream()
    .filter(e -> e.dept().equals("Engineering"))    // lambda — field access + comparison
    .filter(e -> e.salary() > 100_000)              // lambda — comparison
    .map(Employee::name)                            // Type 3 — record accessor
    .sorted(String::compareToIgnoreCase)            // Type 3 — case-insensitive sort
    .collect(Collectors.toList());

Collecting with Constructor References

// Collect to a TreeSet (sorted) using constructor reference
TreeSet<String> sorted = words.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.toCollection(TreeSet::new));  // Type 4 — TreeSet::new as Supplier

// Collect into a custom result
List<String> names = employees.stream()
    .map(Employee::name)
    .collect(Collectors.toList());

Grouping with Method References

// Group employees by department using method reference
Map<String, List<Employee>> byDept = employees.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::dept));

// Count per group
Map<String, Long> countByDept = employees.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::dept, Collectors.counting()));
Part 12

Method References in Comparators

Comparator.comparing is specifically designed to work with method references:

List<Employee> employees = getEmployees();

// Single key — Type 3 reference to accessor method
employees.sort(Comparator.comparing(Employee::name));

// Descending
employees.sort(Comparator.comparing(Employee::salary).reversed());

// Multi-level: dept ASC, salary DESC within dept
employees.sort(
    Comparator.comparing(Employee::dept)
              .thenComparing(Comparator.comparing(Employee::salary).reversed())
);

// Natural order comparator from method reference
Comparator<String> natural = Comparator.naturalOrder();
Comparator<String> byLength = Comparator.comparingInt(String::length);
Comparator<String> byLengthThenAlpha = byLength.thenComparing(Comparator.naturalOrder());
Part 13

Production Patterns

Pattern 1: Repository Factory with Constructor References

@FunctionalInterface
interface EntityFactory<T> {
    T create(Map<String, Object> attributes);
}

// Hypothetical entity with Map constructor
EntityFactory<Order> orderFactory = Order::new;
EntityFactory<Product> productFactory = Product::new;

Map<String, EntityFactory<?>> registry = Map.of(
    "order",   Order::new,
    "product", Product::new,
    "user",    User::new
);

// Deserializer using factory registry
Entity deserialize(String type, Map<String, Object> attrs) {
    EntityFactory<?> factory = registry.get(type);
    if (factory == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown type: " + type);
    return (Entity) factory.create(attrs);
}

Pattern 2: Event Bus Dispatch with Method References

class EventBus {
    private final Map<Class<?>, List<Consumer<Object>>> handlers = new HashMap<>();

    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    public <T> void subscribe(Class<T> eventType, Consumer<T> handler) {
        handlers.computeIfAbsent(eventType, k -> new ArrayList<>())
                .add((Consumer<Object>) handler);
    }

    public void publish(Object event) {
        handlers.getOrDefault(event.getClass(), List.of())
                .forEach(h -> h.accept(event));
    }
}

// Usage — Type 2: particular instance methods as handlers
eventBus.subscribe(OrderCreatedEvent.class,  orderService::onOrderCreated);
eventBus.subscribe(PaymentEvent.class,       paymentService::onPayment);
eventBus.subscribe(ShipmentEvent.class,      shipmentService::onShipment);

Pattern 3: Pipeline Builder with Method References

class Pipeline<T> {
    private final List<Function<T, T>> stages = new ArrayList<>();

    public Pipeline<T> addStage(Function<T, T> stage) {
        stages.add(stage);
        return this;
    }

    public T execute(T input) {
        T result = input;
        for (Function<T, T> stage : stages) result = stage.apply(result);
        return result;
    }
}

// Method references as pipeline stages — all Type 3
Pipeline<String> textPipeline = new Pipeline<String>()
    .addStage(String::trim)
    .addStage(String::toLowerCase)
    .addStage(StringUtils::removeSpecialChars)  // static utility — Type 1
    .addStage(normalizer::normalize);            // bound instance — Type 2

String result = textPipeline.execute("  Hello, World!  ");

Pattern 4: Validation Framework

@FunctionalInterface
interface Validator<T> {
    Optional<String> validate(T value);  // empty = valid, present = error message
}

class ValidatorChain<T> {
    private final List<Validator<T>> validators = new ArrayList<>();

    public ValidatorChain<T> add(Validator<T> v) {
        validators.add(v);
        return this;
    }

    public List<String> validateAll(T value) {
        return validators.stream()
            .map(v -> v.validate(value))
            .filter(Optional::isPresent)        // Type 3 — Optional::isPresent
            .map(Optional::get)                 // Type 3 — Optional::get
            .collect(Collectors.toList());
    }
}

ValidatorChain<String> emailValidator = new ValidatorChain<String>()
    .add(EmailValidators::notNull)              // Type 1 static validators
    .add(EmailValidators::notEmpty)
    .add(EmailValidators::hasAtSign)
    .add(domainValidator::isValidDomain);       // Type 2 — particular instance
Part 14

Spring Framework Integration

Spring Data Repository Queries with Method References

@Service
public class ProductService {
    private final ProductRepository repo;

    // Method reference to repository — Type 2
    private final Function<Long, Optional<Product>> findById;
    private final Consumer<Product> saveProduct;

    public ProductService(ProductRepository repo) {
        this.repo = repo;
        this.findById    = repo::findById;      // Type 2
        this.saveProduct = repo::save;          // Type 2
    }

    public Product getOrThrow(Long id) {
        return findById.apply(id)
            .orElseThrow(() -> new ProductNotFoundException(id));
    }
}

Spring Security with Method References

@Configuration
@EnableWebSecurity
public class SecurityConfig {

    @Bean
    public SecurityFilterChain filterChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        http.authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
                .requestMatchers("/public/**").permitAll()
                .anyRequest().authenticated()
            )
            .formLogin(Customizer.withDefaults())
            .logout(logout -> logout.logoutSuccessHandler(this::onLogoutSuccess));
        return http.build();
    }

    // Type 2 reference — instance method as handler
    private void onLogoutSuccess(HttpServletRequest req,
                                  HttpServletResponse res,
                                  Authentication auth) throws IOException {
        res.sendRedirect("/login?logout");
    }
}

Spring Boot ApplicationRunner with Method References

@SpringBootApplication
public class App {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(App.class, args);
    }

    @Bean
    ApplicationRunner loadData(DataLoader loader) {
        return loader::loadInitialData;  // Type 2 — ApplicationRunner is functional interface
    }
}
Part 15

Method References vs. Lambdas: Decision Guide

ASCII: Decision Flowchart

Is the lambda body a single method call?
           │
          YES
           │
           ▼
Does the lambda just forward its param(s) directly to the method?
           │
          YES
           │
           ▼
    ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │  Use a method reference                              │
    │  • Clearer intent                                    │
    │  • Easier to grep/navigate                           │
    │  • Better stack traces (named method appears in JIT) │
    └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Does the lambda need to do computation beyond forwarding?
           │
          YES
           │
           ▼
    ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │  Use a lambda                                        │
    │  • Additional computation: s -> s.trim() + "!"      │
    │  • Null check: s -> s == null ? "" : s.trim()       │
    │  • Multiple method calls                             │
    │  • Conditional logic                                 │
    └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Side-by-Side Comparison

Scenario Method Reference Lambda Alternative
Map String → uppercase String::toUpperCase s -> s.toUpperCase()
Filter non-empty strings Predicate.not(String::isEmpty) s -> !s.isEmpty()
Print each element System.out::println s -> System.out.println(s)
Parse String to int Integer::parseInt s -> Integer.parseInt(s)
Sort by name Comparator.comparing(Person::getName) (a,b) -> a.getName().compareTo(b.getName())
Create ArrayList ArrayList::new () -> new ArrayList<>()
Trim + uppercase (two ops) not possible in one ref s -> s.trim().toUpperCase()
Add prefix before printing not possible in one ref s -> System.out.println("X:" + s)
Part 16

Performance Considerations

Method references and equivalent lambdas compile to the same bytecode mechanism, so there is no performance difference between a method reference and its equivalent lambda. The JVM does not distinguish them after compilation.

JIT Inlining

Both method references and lambdas are eligible for JIT inlining when:
- The call site is monomorphic (one type of lambda/ref flowing through it).
- The referenced method is small enough to inline.

hotspot JIT view:

  list.stream().map(String::toUpperCase).collect(...)
                      │
                      ▼
  [Compiled code — JIT inlines String.toUpperCase() directly]
  [No virtual dispatch overhead at steady state]

Startup Performance

Method references to static methods (Type 1) are slightly advantageous at startup because the LambdaMetafactory can resolve the method handle more quickly for static targets versus instance methods. The difference is sub-microsecond and only matters for applications that create millions of lambdas/refs during startup.

Part 17

Advanced: Method References to Inherited Methods

class Animal {
    public String speak() { return "..."; }
}

class Dog extends Animal {
    @Override
    public String speak() { return "Woof"; }
}

// Method reference binds to the declared type
Function<Dog, String> dogSpeaker = Dog::speak;      // calls Dog.speak()
Function<Animal, String> anyAnimal = Animal::speak;  // virtual — calls actual runtime type's speak()

Dog d = new Dog();
System.out.println(anyAnimal.apply(d)); // "Woof" — virtual dispatch!

Even with Animal::speak, the JVM uses virtual dispatch, so the overridden method in Dog is called. This is consistent with normal Java polymorphism.

Part 18

Generics and Method References

Generic Method References

// Generic static method
public static <T extends Comparable<T>> T max(T a, T b) {
    return a.compareTo(b) >= 0 ? a : b;
}

// Reference to generic method — type inferred from context
BinaryOperator<String>  strMax = Utils::max;
BinaryOperator<Integer> intMax = Utils::max;

Bounded Type Parameters

public static <T extends Number> double sum(T a, T b) {
    return a.doubleValue() + b.doubleValue();
}

// Compiler infers T = Integer from context
BiFunction<Integer, Integer, Double> intSum = MathUtils::sum;

Wildcard Interaction

// Type 3 reference with wildcards
Function<? extends Number, Double> toDouble = Number::doubleValue;
// Works for Integer, Long, Double, etc.
Part 19

Common Mistakes and Anti-Patterns

Mistake 1: Using a lambda when a method reference is clearer

// Noisy
list.stream().map(s -> s.toUpperCase()).collect(toList());

// Clean
list.stream().map(String::toUpperCase).collect(toList());

Mistake 2: Confusing Type 2 and Type 3

String value = "hello";

// Type 2 — bound to 'value', returns substring of "hello"
Function<Integer, String> f2 = value::substring;
f2.apply(2); // "llo" (always "hello".substring(2))

// Type 3 — works on arbitrary String passed as arg
Function<String, String> f3_WRONG = String::substring; // COMPILE ERROR
// String.substring(int) takes the String as receiver, but also needs int param
BiFunction<String, Integer, String> f3 = String::substring;
f3.apply("hello", 2); // "llo" (any string's substring)

Mistake 3: Null dereference in Type 2 reference

Printer printer = null;
Consumer<String> c = printer::print; // Compiles!
c.accept("test"); // NullPointerException at invocation time

The null check for Type 2 references must be done before creating the reference, not at invocation.

Mistake 4: Assuming method reference is always more readable

// Sometimes the lambda is clearer
list.stream()
    .map(s -> s.substring(0, Math.min(s.length(), 50))) // clearly truncates to 50 chars
    .collect(toList());

// A contrived method reference version would require an extracted method
// — not worth it just to avoid the lambda

Mistake 5: Constructor reference with wrong arity

// ArrayList has a constructor taking initial capacity (int)
// and a constructor taking a Collection
Function<Integer, ArrayList<String>> withCapacity = ArrayList::new;   // int constructor ✓
Function<Collection<String>, ArrayList<String>> fromCollection = ArrayList::new; // Collection constructor ✓

// Which constructor? Resolved by the target functional interface's parameter type
Part 20

Interview Preparation

Q1: What are the four types of method references? Give an example of each.

Answer:
1. Static: Integer::parseInt — equivalent to s -> Integer.parseInt(s)
2. Particular instance: System.out::println — equivalent to s -> System.out.println(s)
3. Arbitrary instance: String::toUpperCase — equivalent to s -> s.toUpperCase()
4. Constructor: ArrayList::new — equivalent to () -> new ArrayList<>()

Q2: What is the difference between String::toUpperCase (Type 3) and myString::toUpperCase (Type 2)?

Answer: String::toUpperCase is a Type 3 reference — the object it operates on is passed as the first argument to the functional interface at invocation time. It fits Function<String, String>. myString::toUpperCase is a Type 2 reference — it is bound to the specific myString instance at reference-creation time, and always calls toUpperCase() on that specific object. It fits Supplier<String>.

Q3: When should you prefer a lambda over a method reference?

Answer: Prefer a lambda when the lambda body does more than forward parameters to a single method: additional computation, null checks, conditional logic, multiple method calls, or when the equivalent method reference would require extracting a helper method just to use the reference syntax. Method references are best when the lambda body is literally (args) -> method(args) or (obj, args) -> obj.method(args).

Q4: Can a method reference throw checked exceptions?

Answer: A method reference can effectively throw checked exceptions only if the target functional interface's abstract method declares those checked exceptions. If using java.util.function interfaces (which declare no checked exceptions), the referenced method must not throw checked exceptions, or you must wrap them. The same rule applies to lambdas.

Q5: How does Arrays::new differ from new int[n]?

Answer: Arrays::new (or int[]::new) is a constructor reference that produces an IntFunction<int[]>. It takes the array size as an argument at invocation time. new int[n] creates a single array of size n immediately. The constructor reference is used when you need a factory that will create arrays of different sizes lazily or inside a higher-order function, such as Stream.toArray(String[]::new).

Q6: Are method references more performant than lambdas?

Answer: No — they compile to the same invokedynamic + LambdaMetafactory mechanism. The JVM cannot distinguish a method reference from an equivalent lambda after compilation. Both are equally eligible for JIT inlining. The choice between them is purely a code readability decision.

Q7: What happens if you create a Type 2 reference to a method on a null object?

Answer: The null dereference does not occur at reference-creation time. The JVM captures the reference to the null object. The NullPointerException is thrown at invocation time when the method is actually called on the null object.

Part 1

Concept: What Is a Stream?

A Stream (introduced in Java 8 via java.util.stream) is a sequence of elements supporting sequential and parallel aggregate operations. A stream is not a data structure — it does not store elements. Instead, it is a pipeline of computations over a data source (collection, array, I/O channel, or generator function).

The central mental model:

Data Source → [Intermediate Ops] → Terminal Op → Result

Key properties of streams:

Property Description
Not a data structure No storage; pulls elements from source on demand
Functional in nature Operations produce new streams; source is never mutated
Lazy Intermediate operations are not evaluated until a terminal op is invoked
Possibly unbounded Can represent infinite sequences; short-circuit ops terminate early
Consumable A stream can be traversed only once; reuse requires a new stream

Why Streams?

Before Java 8, processing collections required verbose imperative loops:

// Pre-streams: filter and transform a list
List<String> result = new ArrayList<>();
for (String name : names) {
    if (name.startsWith("A")) {
        result.add(name.toUpperCase());
    }
}

With streams, the same logic becomes a declarative pipeline:

List<String> result = names.stream()
    .filter(name -> name.startsWith("A"))
    .map(String::toUpperCase)
    .collect(Collectors.toList());

The stream version expresses what to compute, not how to compute it — enabling the JVM to optimize execution order, apply lazy evaluation, and parallelize transparently.

Part 2

Stream Pipeline Architecture

Every stream pipeline has exactly three layers:

╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║                    STREAM PIPELINE ARCHITECTURE                      ║
╠══════════════╦═══════════════════════════════╦═══════════════════════╣
║   SOURCE     ║   INTERMEDIATE OPERATIONS     ║   TERMINAL OPERATION  ║
║              ║   (lazy, return Stream<T>)    ║   (eager, triggers    ║
║  Collection  ║                               ║    evaluation)        ║
║  Array       ║  filter()   → Stream<T>       ║                       ║
║  Range       ║  map()      → Stream<R>       ║  collect()            ║
║  Generator   ║  flatMap()  → Stream<R>       ║  forEach()            ║
║  I/O         ║  distinct() → Stream<T>       ║  reduce()             ║
║              ║  sorted()   → Stream<T>       ║  count()              ║
║              ║  peek()     → Stream<T>       ║  min() / max()        ║
║              ║  limit()    → Stream<T>       ║  findFirst()          ║
║              ║  skip()     → Stream<T>       ║  anyMatch()           ║
║              ║                               ║  toArray()            ║
╚══════════════╩═══════════════════════════════╩═══════════════════════╝
         │                    │                          │
         ▼                    ▼                          ▼
    Provides               Builds the              Pulls elements
    Spliterator            pipeline DAG            through pipeline

Pipeline execution flow:

  1. Source creates a Spliterator — the underlying iterator mechanism.
  2. Each intermediate operation wraps the previous stage in a StatelessOp or StatefulOp.
  3. The terminal operation calls evaluate() or forEach() on the final stage, which pulls elements one by one (or in batches for parallel) backward through the chain.

The pipeline is not executed at all until the terminal operation is called. This is the foundation of lazy evaluation.

Part 3

Creating Streams (Sources)

There are multiple ways to obtain a stream:

From Collections

List<String> list = List.of("alpha", "beta", "gamma");
Stream<String> s1 = list.stream();          // sequential
Stream<String> s2 = list.parallelStream();  // parallel

From Arrays

String[] arr = {"x", "y", "z"};
Stream<String> s = Arrays.stream(arr);
// partial range:
Stream<String> partial = Arrays.stream(arr, 0, 2); // "x", "y"

From Values (varargs)

Stream<Integer> s = Stream.of(1, 2, 3, 4, 5);
Stream<String> single = Stream.of("only");
Stream<Object> empty = Stream.empty();

From Generators (Infinite Streams)

// iterate: seed, then apply f repeatedly
Stream<Long> evens = Stream.iterate(0L, n -> n + 2); // 0, 2, 4, 6, ...

// iterate with predicate (Java 9+): finite by condition
Stream<Integer> bounded = Stream.iterate(1, n -> n <= 100, n -> n * 2);

// generate: stateless supplier
Stream<Double> randoms = Stream.generate(Math::random);

From Primitive Ranges

IntStream range     = IntStream.range(0, 10);       // [0, 10)
IntStream rangeClosed = IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 5); // [1, 5]
LongStream longs    = LongStream.range(0L, 1_000_000L);

From I/O

// Each line becomes a stream element
try (Stream<String> lines = Files.lines(Path.of("data.txt"))) {
    lines.filter(l -> !l.isBlank()).forEach(System.out::println);
}

> Critical: Streams backed by I/O must be closed. Use try-with-resources — Stream implements AutoCloseable.

From String

IntStream chars = "hello".chars();    // Unicode code points as IntStream
Stream<String> parts = "a,b,c".chars()
    .mapToObj(c -> String.valueOf((char) c));
Part 4

Lazy Evaluation Deep Dive

Lazy evaluation is the most important behavioral characteristic of streams. Intermediate operations are descriptors — they build a pipeline DAG, they do not iterate.

List<String> names = List.of("Alice", "Bob", "Charlie", "David", "Eve");

Stream<String> pipeline = names.stream()
    .filter(n -> {
        System.out.println("filter: " + n);
        return n.length() > 3;
    })
    .map(n -> {
        System.out.println("map: " + n);
        return n.toUpperCase();
    });

// Nothing printed yet — no terminal op

System.out.println("--- triggering ---");
List<String> result = pipeline.collect(Collectors.toList());

Output:

--- triggering ---
filter: Alice
map: Alice
filter: Bob
filter: Charlie
map: Charlie
filter: David
map: David
filter: Eve
map: Eve

Observation: each element flows through all stages before the next element is processed. This is vertical (depth-first) execution, not horizontal (breadth-first). The stream does not first filter all elements and then map all results — it does both in one pass per element.

Why Lazy Evaluation Matters

  1. Short-circuiting: findFirst(), anyMatch(), limit() can terminate after processing far fewer elements than the source contains.
  2. Single-pass optimization: Filter + map + collect = one pass over the data, not three.
  3. Infinite sources: Without laziness, Stream.generate() would immediately attempt to generate infinitely many elements.
Part 5

Short-Circuiting Operations

Short-circuit operations allow the pipeline to terminate before consuming all source elements.

Short-Circuit Terminal Operations

List<Integer> numbers = List.of(1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 2, 4, 6);

// findFirst — stops at first match
Optional<Integer> first = numbers.stream()
    .filter(n -> n % 2 == 0)
    .findFirst();   // processes: 1,3,5,7,9,2 — stops at 2

// findAny — stops at any match (non-deterministic in parallel)
Optional<Integer> any = numbers.parallelStream()
    .filter(n -> n > 5)
    .findAny();

// anyMatch — stops at first true
boolean hasEven = numbers.stream().anyMatch(n -> n % 2 == 0); // true, stops at 2

// allMatch — stops at first false
boolean allOdd = numbers.stream().allMatch(n -> n % 2 != 0);  // false, stops at 2

// noneMatch — stops at first true
boolean noneNeg = numbers.stream().noneMatch(n -> n < 0);     // true, scans all

Short-Circuit Intermediate Operations

// limit — at most N elements
Stream.iterate(1, n -> n + 1)
    .limit(5)
    .forEach(System.out::println); // prints 1,2,3,4,5 — infinite source, finite output

Infinite Source
      │
   generate(...)
      │
   ┌──▼──┐
   │limit│ ← short-circuit: closes upstream after N elements
   └──┬──┘
      │ N elements
   terminal
Part 6

Intermediate Operations: filter and map

filter(Predicate<T>)

Retains elements matching the predicate; discards the rest.

List<String> words = List.of("stream", "is", "a", "powerful", "api", "in", "java");

List<String> longWords = words.stream()
    .filter(w -> w.length() >= 4)
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
// [stream, powerful, java]

Filters are stateless — no shared mutable state between elements. Each element is evaluated independently.

map(Function<T, R>)

Transforms each element from type T to type R. The stream changes its element type.

List<String> names = List.of("alice", "bob", "carol");

List<Integer> lengths = names.stream()
    .map(String::length)     // Stream<String> → Stream<Integer>
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
// [5, 3, 5]

Method references (String::length) are preferred over lambdas when they directly reference an existing method — they are cleaner and often more performant.

Primitive-Specialized map variants

// mapToInt avoids boxing Integer objects
int total = names.stream()
    .mapToInt(String::length)   // Stream<String> → IntStream
    .sum();

// mapToLong, mapToDouble similarly
double avg = names.stream()
    .mapToDouble(String::length)
    .average()
    .orElse(0.0);

> Performance note: mapToInt() returns an IntStream of primitives. Prefer this over map(String::length) which boxes each int to Integer.

Part 7

flatMap: One-to-Many Transformation

flatMap(Function<T, Stream<R>>) applies a function that returns a stream for each element, then flattens those streams into a single stream.

Element A  →  Stream[A1, A2]  ─┐
Element B  →  Stream[B1]      ─┤  flatMap  →  [A1, A2, B1, C1, C2, C3]
Element C  →  Stream[C1,C2,C3]─┘

Example: Words in sentences

List<String> sentences = List.of("hello world", "java streams are great");

List<String> words = sentences.stream()
    .flatMap(s -> Arrays.stream(s.split(" ")))
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
// [hello, world, java, streams, are, great]

Example: Nested collections

List<List<Integer>> matrix = List.of(
    List.of(1, 2, 3),
    List.of(4, 5, 6),
    List.of(7, 8, 9)
);

List<Integer> flat = matrix.stream()
    .flatMap(Collection::stream)
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
// [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9]

map vs flatMap

Scenario Use
1-to-1 transformation map
1-to-many expansion flatMap
Unwrap Optional in stream flatMap(Optional::stream) (Java 9+)
Flatten nested collections flatMap(Collection::stream) 
// Filtering out empty Optionals (Java 9+)
List<Optional<String>> opts = List.of(Optional.of("a"), Optional.empty(), Optional.of("b"));
List<String> values = opts.stream()
    .flatMap(Optional::stream)
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
// [a, b]
Part 8

distinct, sorted, peek, limit, skip

distinct()

Returns a stream of unique elements based on equals()/hashCode().

List<Integer> nums = List.of(1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4);
List<Integer> unique = nums.stream().distinct().collect(Collectors.toList());
// [1, 2, 3, 4]

> Stateful operation: distinct() must track which elements have been seen. For ordered sequential streams, it maintains insertion order. This has memory overhead proportional to distinct elements.

sorted()

Returns a stream with elements sorted in natural order. Requires Comparable. An overload accepts Comparator.

List<String> sorted = Stream.of("banana", "apple", "cherry")
    .sorted()
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
// [apple, banana, cherry]

// Custom comparator
List<String> byLength = Stream.of("banana", "apple", "cherry")
    .sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(String::length))
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
// [apple, banana, cherry]

// Multi-level sort
List<String> byLengthThenAlpha = Stream.of("dog", "cat", "ant", "bee")
    .sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(String::length)
                      .thenComparing(Comparator.naturalOrder()))
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
// [ant, bee, cat, dog]

> Stateful operation: sorted() must see all elements before emitting any — it buffers the entire stream.

peek(Consumer<T>)

Performs an action on each element as it passes through, without modifying elements. Primarily a debugging tool.

List<Integer> result = IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 5)
    .boxed()
    .peek(n -> System.out.println("before filter: " + n))
    .filter(n -> n % 2 == 0)
    .peek(n -> System.out.println("after filter: " + n))
    .collect(Collectors.toList());

> Warning: Never use peek for side effects in production code. Its behavior with parallel streams or optimized pipelines is not guaranteed. Use forEach if you need side effects at the terminal.

limit(long n) and skip(long n)

// limit: take first N elements
List<Integer> first5 = IntStream.iterate(1, i -> i + 1)
    .limit(5)
    .boxed()
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
// [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

// skip: discard first N elements
List<Integer> skip3 = IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 7)
    .skip(3)
    .boxed()
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
// [4, 5, 6, 7]

// pagination pattern
int page = 2, pageSize = 10;
List<Item> page2 = items.stream()
    .skip((long) page * pageSize)
    .limit(pageSize)
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
Part 9

Terminal Operations: collect and forEach

collect(Collector<T, A, R>)

The most powerful terminal operation. Performs a mutable reduction — accumulates elements into a result container.

// Basic collectors
List<String>  list = stream.collect(Collectors.toList());
Set<String>   set  = stream.collect(Collectors.toSet());
String joined = Stream.of("a","b","c").collect(Collectors.joining(", ", "[", "]"));
// "[a, b, c]"

// Grouping
Map<Integer, List<String>> byLength = names.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(String::length));

// Counting per group
Map<Integer, Long> countByLength = names.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(String::length, Collectors.counting()));

// Partitioning (binary grouping by predicate)
Map<Boolean, List<Integer>> oddEven = IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 10)
    .boxed()
    .collect(Collectors.partitioningBy(n -> n % 2 == 0));

The Collector interface involves three steps:
1. Supplier: creates the mutable result container (ArrayList::new)
2. Accumulator: folds an element into the container (List::add)
3. Combiner: merges two containers (used in parallel: list1.addAll(list2))

forEach(Consumer<T>)

Performs an action for each element. Unlike collect, it produces no return value.

names.stream().forEach(System.out::println);

// forEachOrdered — guarantees encounter order even in parallel streams
names.parallelStream().forEachOrdered(System.out::println);

> Side-effect warning: forEach is intentionally the "escape hatch" for side effects. Avoid mutating external state inside forEach in parallel streams — use thread-safe structures or prefer collect.

Part 10

Terminal Operations: reduce, count, min/max, toArray

reduce

Combines elements using an associative accumulation function.

// Identity + accumulator → T
int sum = IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 10)
    .reduce(0, Integer::sum); // 55

// No identity → Optional<T> (handles empty stream)
Optional<Integer> product = Stream.of(1, 2, 3, 4)
    .reduce((a, b) -> a * b);   // Optional[24]

// Three-arg form: identity, accumulator, combiner (for parallel)
int parallelSum = Stream.of(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
    .reduce(0, Integer::sum, Integer::sum); // 15

count()

long count = names.stream().filter(n -> n.startsWith("A")).count();

min() and max()

Optional<String> shortest = names.stream()
    .min(Comparator.comparingInt(String::length));

Optional<Integer> max = Stream.of(3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2)
    .max(Integer::compareTo);

toArray()

Object[]  arr1 = stream.toArray();
String[]  arr2 = names.stream().toArray(String[]::new);

Summary of Terminal Operations

Operation Return Type Notes
collect(collector) R Mutable reduction; most flexible
forEach(action) void Side effects
forEachOrdered(action) void Ordered in parallel
reduce(identity, acc) T Immutable fold
reduce(acc) Optional<T> No identity; handles empty
count() long
min(comparator) Optional<T>
max(comparator) Optional<T>
findFirst() Optional<T> Short-circuit
findAny() Optional<T> Non-deterministic in parallel
anyMatch(pred) boolean Short-circuit
allMatch(pred) boolean Short-circuit
noneMatch(pred) boolean Short-circuit
toArray() Object[] / T[]
Part 11

Primitive Streams: IntStream, LongStream, DoubleStream

Boxing int to Integer is expensive — each Integer object costs ~16 bytes plus GC pressure vs a 4-byte int primitive. Java provides specialized stream types to avoid this.

The Three Primitive Stream Types

Stream<Integer>   →  boxing overhead (avoid for numeric computation)
IntStream         →  int primitives (range, sum, average, min, max)
LongStream        →  long primitives
DoubleStream      →  double primitives

Creating Primitive Streams

IntStream r1 = IntStream.range(0, 100);           // [0, 100)
IntStream r2 = IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 100);     // [1, 100]
IntStream r3 = IntStream.of(1, 2, 3, 4, 5);
IntStream r4 = "hello".chars();                    // Unicode code points

LongStream ls = LongStream.range(0L, 1_000_000L);
DoubleStream ds = DoubleStream.of(1.1, 2.2, 3.3);

Specialized Terminal Operations

Primitive streams expose numeric aggregations that Stream<T> lacks:

IntStream ints = IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 100);

int     sum  = ints.sum();      // 5050
OptionalDouble avg  = IntStream.rangeClosed(1,100).average(); // 50.5
OptionalInt    min  = IntStream.of(3,1,4,1,5).min();
OptionalInt    max  = IntStream.of(3,1,4,1,5).max();
IntSummaryStatistics stats = IntStream.rangeClosed(1,100).summaryStatistics();
// count=100, sum=5050, min=1, max=100, average=50.5

Conversion Between Stream Types

// Stream<T> → IntStream
Stream<String> names = Stream.of("alice","bob","carol");
IntStream lengths = names.mapToInt(String::length);

// IntStream → Stream<Integer>  (boxing)
Stream<Integer> boxed = IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 5).boxed();

// IntStream → Stream<String>
Stream<String> mapped = IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 5)
    .mapToObj(i -> "item-" + i);

// IntStream → LongStream / DoubleStream
LongStream longs   = IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 5).asLongStream();
DoubleStream doubles = IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 5).asDoubleStream();
Part 12

Internal Mechanics: Pipeline Stages and StreamOp Flags

Understanding how streams are implemented in java.util.stream reveals why they are efficient.

The AbstractPipeline

Every stream is backed by an AbstractPipeline chain:

ReferencePipeline$Head  (source stage)
        │
ReferencePipeline$StatelessOp  (filter, map, peek)
        │
ReferencePipeline$StatefulOp   (sorted, distinct, limit)
        │
        ▼
TerminalOp (collect, reduce, forEach...)

The terminal op calls evaluate() on the last pipeline stage, which walks backward to the head, connecting Sink objects in a chain.

Sink Chain Execution

Source Spliterator
       │  push elements
       ▼
  FilterSink.accept(e)  → if predicate passes → delegate to next sink
       │
       ▼
  MapSink.accept(e)     → apply function       → delegate to next sink
       │
       ▼
  CollectSink.accept(e) → accumulate into list

Each Sink has three methods:
- begin(size) — prepare (called once before elements flow)
- accept(T) — process one element
- end() — finalize (called after all elements)

StreamOp Flags

Flags are bit-masks on StreamOpFlag that describe element characteristics. They enable optimizations:

Flag Meaning Example
ORDERED Elements have a defined encounter order List source
DISTINCT All elements are distinct After .distinct()
SORTED Elements are sorted After .sorted()
SIZED Size is known From Collection
SHORT_CIRCUIT Terminal may not need all elements findFirst, limit

When DISTINCT is set upstream, a downstream .distinct() call can be elided entirely. When SIZED is known, count() can short-circuit to just returning the known size without iterating.

Part 13

Spliterator: The Underlying Iterator

Spliterator<T> (introduced in Java 8) is the parallel-aware iterator that underpins streams.

         ┌──────────────────────────────┐
         │        Spliterator<T>        │
         │                              │
         │  tryAdvance(Consumer)  ──────┼──► process one element
         │  forEachRemaining(Consumer) ─┼──► process all remaining
         │  trySplit()  ────────────────┼──► split half for parallel
         │  estimateSize()  ────────────┼──► hint for parallel sizing
         │  characteristics() ──────────┼──► ORDERED, DISTINCT, etc.
         └──────────────────────────────┘

How Parallel Splitting Works

Original Spliterator [1..1000]
        │
   trySplit()
   ┌─────┴─────┐
[1..500]   [501..1000]
   │              │
trySplit()   trySplit()
[1..250] [251..500] [501..750] [751..1000]
   │        │         │          │
  T1        T2        T3         T4   (ForkJoinPool workers)

Each sub-spliterator is processed by a separate worker thread. Results are combined using the Collector's combiner or the reduce combiner function.

Custom Spliterator

public class RangeSpliterator implements Spliterator<Integer> {
    private int current;
    private final int end;

    RangeSpliterator(int start, int end) { this.current = start; this.end = end; }

    @Override
    public boolean tryAdvance(Consumer<? super Integer> action) {
        if (current < end) { action.accept(current++); return true; }
        return false;
    }

    @Override
    public Spliterator<Integer> trySplit() {
        int mid = (current + end) >>> 1;
        if (mid == current) return null;
        int lo = current; current = mid;
        return new RangeSpliterator(lo, mid);
    }

    @Override public long estimateSize() { return end - current; }
    @Override public int characteristics() { return ORDERED | SIZED | SUBSIZED | IMMUTABLE; }
}
Part 14

parallelStream() and the ForkJoinPool

parallelStream() returns a parallel stream backed by the ForkJoinPool common pool by default.

How parallelStream Works

list.parallelStream()
        │
   Creates parallel pipeline
        │
   TerminalOp triggers parallel evaluate()
        │
   ForkJoinTask submitted to common pool
        │
   Spliterator.trySplit() recursively partitions data
        │
   Worker threads process chunks concurrently
        │
   Combiner function merges partial results
        │
   Final result returned to calling thread

The Common Pool

The common ForkJoinPool is shared across the JVM:
- Default parallelism = Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() - 1
- Set via system property: -Djava.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool.common.parallelism=N

// Check parallelism level
System.out.println(ForkJoinPool.commonPool().getParallelism());

Custom ForkJoinPool

To avoid starving other tasks on the common pool, submit to a custom pool:

ForkJoinPool pool = new ForkJoinPool(4);
List<Integer> result = pool.submit(
    () -> IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 1_000_000)
                   .parallel()
                   .filter(n -> n % 2 == 0)
                   .boxed()
                   .collect(Collectors.toList())
).get();
pool.shutdown();

When Parallel Is Beneficial

Factor Sequential Parallel
Data size Small (<1000 elements) Large (>10,000 elements)
Per-element cost Low (simple filter/map) High (CPU-intensive)
Source splittability Poor (LinkedList) Good (ArrayList, array)
Ordering requirements Ordered Unordered
Statefulness N/A Stateless ops preferred
Part 15

Parallel Stream Pitfalls

Parallel streams can silently produce wrong results when misused.

Pitfall 1: Mutable Shared State

// BROKEN — race condition
List<Integer> results = new ArrayList<>();
IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 1000)
    .parallel()
    .filter(n -> n % 2 == 0)
    .forEach(results::add);  // ArrayList is not thread-safe!
// results.size() is unpredictable; may corrupt internal state

// CORRECT — use thread-safe terminal op
List<Integer> correct = IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 1000)
    .parallel()
    .filter(n -> n % 2 == 0)
    .boxed()
    .collect(Collectors.toList());  // combiner merges safely

Pitfall 2: Ordered Operations on Parallel Streams

// forEachOrdered serializes output — negates parallel benefit
IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 10)
    .parallel()
    .forEachOrdered(System.out::println); // sequential output but parallel overhead

Pitfall 3: Stateful Lambda Referencing External State

int[] counter = {0};
// BROKEN — stateful lambda
Stream.of(1,2,3,4,5).parallel().forEach(n -> counter[0]++); // data race
// counter[0] will not reliably be 5

Pitfall 4: Poor Splittability

// LinkedList splits poorly — parallel is slower than sequential here
LinkedList<Integer> linked = new LinkedList<>(largeList);
linked.parallelStream().map(expensiveOp).collect(toList()); // avoid

Pitfall 5: Blocking Operations in Parallel Streams

// Blocking I/O inside parallel stream starves ForkJoinPool common pool
urls.parallelStream()
    .map(url -> httpClient.get(url))  // blocking! ties up FJ worker threads
    .collect(toList());
// Use CompletableFuture or dedicated executor instead
Part 16

Stateful vs Stateless Operations

Operations are classified by whether they require knowledge of other elements in the stream.

STATELESS OPERATIONS          STATEFUL OPERATIONS
─────────────────────         ──────────────────────────
filter(pred)                  distinct()   ← needs seen-set
map(fn)                       sorted()     ← needs all elements
flatMap(fn)                   limit(n)     ← needs count
peek(action)                  skip(n)      ← needs count
mapToInt/Long/Double          (note: limit/skip are ORDER-sensitive)

Why This Matters

Stateless ops can run element-by-element without buffering — perfectly suited for parallel execution.

Stateful ops introduce barriers:
- sorted() must buffer the entire stream before emitting anything.
- distinct() must maintain a seen-set (HashSet internally), growing with distinct elements.
- In parallel streams, stateful ops require synchronization or a gather-and-sort phase.

Ordering and Parallel Streams

Some ops preserve encounter order; others do not:

// unordered() hint can improve parallel performance
List<Integer> nums = IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 1_000_000)
    .parallel()
    .unordered()         // release ordering constraint
    .filter(n -> n % 3 == 0)
    .limit(100)          // limit on unordered parallel is much faster
    .boxed()
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
Part 17

When NOT to Use Streams

Streams are powerful but are not always the best tool. Understanding their costs enables good judgment.

Use a Simple Loop Instead When:

1. You need to modify loop indices or external counters:

// Awkward with streams
for (int i = 0; i < list.size(); i++) {
    if (list.get(i).equals(list.get(i + 1))) {  // peek at neighbors — stream can't do this
        process(i);
    }
}

2. You need to break/continue with complex logic:

// Stream short-circuiting is limited to specific ops
// Nested labeled break/continue is impossible in streams
outer:
for (A a : listA) {
    for (B b : listB) {
        if (someCondition(a, b)) break outer;
    }
}

3. Performance-critical tight loops:

// Stream overhead is measurable for micro-tight loops
// Lambda invocation + boxing + pipeline overhead adds up
// For hot paths processing millions of primitives, manual loops may win
int sum = 0;
for (int n : arr) sum += n;  // simpler, predictable, JIT-friendly

4. You need checked exceptions:

// This does not compile without try-catch wrapping
names.stream().map(Files::readString);  // readString throws IOException
// Must wrap in unchecked or use try-catch inside lambda — ugly

5. You need to track multiple accumulators simultaneously:

// Computing min, max, and sum in one pass is ugly with streams
// A single loop with three accumulators is clearer

6. Debugging is critical: Stepping through a stream pipeline in a debugger is far harder than stepping through a loop. For exploratory or diagnostic code, prefer clarity.

Streams Are Wrong Here: Performance-Critical JVM Code

  • Object creation per element (boxing, lambda captures) triggers GC
  • Spliterator overhead for small collections
  • Method dispatch overhead vs inlined loop body
  • Use JMH to benchmark before assuming streams are fast
Part 18

Advanced Patterns

Collecting to Immutable Collections (Java 10+)

// Java 10+
List<String> immutable = names.stream()
    .filter(n -> n.length() > 3)
    .collect(Collectors.toUnmodifiableList());

// Java 16+ — toList() collector shorthand
List<String> toList = names.stream()
    .filter(n -> n.length() > 3)
    .toList();  // returns unmodifiable List

Stream.Builder

Stream.Builder<String> builder = Stream.builder();
builder.add("a");
if (condition) builder.add("b");
builder.add("c");
Stream<String> s = builder.build();

Chained flatMap for Optional

// Flattening Optional chains
Optional<User> user = findUser(id);
Optional<String> city = user
    .flatMap(User::getAddress)
    .flatMap(Address::getCity);

takeWhile / dropWhile (Java 9+)

// takeWhile — take elements while predicate holds; stop at first false
List<Integer> ascending = List.of(1,2,3,4,5,3,2);
List<Integer> taken = ascending.stream()
    .takeWhile(n -> n < 4)
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
// [1, 2, 3]

// dropWhile — skip while predicate holds; take rest
List<Integer> dropped = ascending.stream()
    .dropWhile(n -> n < 4)
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
// [4, 5, 3, 2]

Stream.ofNullable (Java 9+)

// Safe single-element stream from nullable value
String value = possiblyNull();
long count = Stream.ofNullable(value).count(); // 0 or 1
Part 19

Spring Integration

Repository Methods Returning Stream

Spring Data JPA supports streaming large result sets to avoid loading everything into memory:

// Repository interface
public interface UserRepository extends JpaRepository<User, Long> {

    @Query("SELECT u FROM User u WHERE u.active = true")
    Stream<User> findAllActiveUsers();
}

// Service layer — must be within a transaction
@Service
@Transactional(readOnly = true)
public class UserExportService {

    @Autowired
    private UserRepository userRepository;

    public void exportActiveUsers(OutputStream out) {
        try (Stream<User> users = userRepository.findAllActiveUsers()) {
            users.map(UserDTO::from)
                 .forEach(dto -> writeToOutput(out, dto));
        }
        // Stream MUST be closed — it holds a cursor to the DB
    }
}

> Critical: A Stream<T> from Spring Data holds an open database cursor. It must be closed (use try-with-resources) and must run within a @Transactional method — the connection stays open for the duration of the stream.

Streams vs. Reactive (Preview)

Streams (java.util.stream)          Reactive (Project Reactor / RxJava)
────────────────────────────────    ────────────────────────────────────
Pull-based                          Push-based (or pull via backpressure)
Synchronous (sequential/parallel)   Asynchronous, non-blocking
Finite or infinite (lazy)           Infinite, event-driven
In-memory data                      Network I/O, DB, events
Stream<T>                           Flux<T> / Mono<T>
collect() terminal                  subscribe() terminal
Blocking terminal op                Non-blocking throughout

Reactive streams are the subject of a dedicated lesson. Streams provide a mental model that transfers well: both use pipeline-based transformations with lazy evaluation.

Part 20

Interview Deep Dive

Q1: Demonstrate lazy evaluation

// Classic interview demo
List<String> list = List.of("a","bb","ccc","dddd","eeeee");

// This pipeline never executes map() or filter() more than needed
Optional<String> result = list.stream()
    .filter(s -> {
        System.out.println("FILTER: " + s);
        return s.length() >= 3;
    })
    .map(s -> {
        System.out.println("MAP: " + s);
        return s.toUpperCase();
    })
    .findFirst();

// Output:
// FILTER: a
// FILTER: bb
// FILTER: ccc   ← first match
// MAP: ccc       ← map applied only to first match
// result = Optional[CCC]
// "dddd" and "eeeee" never touched

Key insight: findFirst() short-circuits, so after finding the first element that passes filter, the stream stops. map is applied only to that one element.

Q2: Parallel stream pitfalls

// Pitfall 1: Wrong result from shared mutable state
List<Integer> unsafe = new ArrayList<>();
IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 1000).parallel().forEach(unsafe::add);
System.out.println(unsafe.size()); // NOT guaranteed to be 1000

// Pitfall 2: forEach vs forEachOrdered ordering
IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 5).parallel().forEach(System.out::print);
// May print: 3 1 4 2 5 (any order)

IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 5).parallel().forEachOrdered(System.out::print);
// Always prints: 1 2 3 4 5 (but loses parallelism benefit for ordering)

Q3: Stateful vs stateless — identify the bug

// Which operation makes this parallel stream potentially incorrect?
List<Integer> list = IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 20)
    .parallel()
    .sorted()           // STATEFUL — must gather all elements first
    .limit(5)           // STATEFUL — order-dependent
    .boxed()
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
// sorted() + limit() on parallel may be slower than sequential
// but produces correct results because sorted() gathers all before limit

Q4: Stream vs Iterator

Aspect Stream Iterator
Traversal Internal (push to lambda) External (caller pulls)
Parallel Built-in parallelStream() Manual thread management
Lazy Yes No
Reusable No (single-use) Yes (new iterator per use)
Composable Yes (chained ops) No

Q5: Why is collect() more efficient than reduce() for mutable containers?

reduce() creates a new immutable result at each step (copying):

// reduce on strings: creates new String object each step
String result = Stream.of("a","b","c","d")
    .reduce("", String::concat); // 4 intermediate String objects

collect() mutates a single container:

// collect: mutates one StringBuilder throughout
String result = Stream.of("a","b","c","d")
    .collect(Collectors.joining()); // one StringBuilder, one toString()
Part 21

Code: Complete Production Example

A realistic example combining multiple stream features in a production context:

import java.util.*;
import java.util.stream.*;
import java.util.function.*;

public class OrderAnalytics {

    record Order(String customerId, String category, double amount, boolean fulfilled) {}

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        List<Order> orders = List.of(
            new Order("C1", "Electronics", 299.99, true),
            new Order("C2", "Books",       49.99,  true),
            new Order("C1", "Electronics", 149.99, false),
            new Order("C3", "Books",       19.99,  true),
            new Order("C2", "Electronics", 599.99, true),
            new Order("C3", "Clothing",    89.99,  false),
            new Order("C1", "Books",       39.99,  true)
        );

        // 1. Total revenue from fulfilled orders
        double totalRevenue = orders.stream()
            .filter(Order::fulfilled)
            .mapToDouble(Order::amount)
            .sum();
        System.out.printf("Total Revenue: $%.2f%n", totalRevenue); // $1009.96

        // 2. Revenue by category (fulfilled only)
        Map<String, Double> revenueByCategory = orders.stream()
            .filter(Order::fulfilled)
            .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
                Order::category,
                Collectors.summingDouble(Order::amount)
            ));
        revenueByCategory.forEach((cat, rev) ->
            System.out.printf("  %s: $%.2f%n", cat, rev));

        // 3. Top customer by fulfilled order count
        Optional<Map.Entry<String, Long>> topCustomer = orders.stream()
            .filter(Order::fulfilled)
            .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Order::customerId, Collectors.counting()))
            .entrySet().stream()
            .max(Map.Entry.comparingByValue());
        topCustomer.ifPresent(e ->
            System.out.printf("Top customer: %s (%d orders)%n", e.getKey(), e.getValue()));

        // 4. Categories with unfulfilled orders
        List<String> unfulfilled = orders.stream()
            .filter(o -> !o.fulfilled())
            .map(Order::category)
            .distinct()
            .sorted()
            .collect(Collectors.toList());
        System.out.println("Unfulfilled categories: " + unfulfilled);

        // 5. Average order value per customer (all orders)
        Map<String, OptionalDouble> avgPerCustomer = orders.stream()
            .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
                Order::customerId,
                Collectors.collectingAndThen(
                    Collectors.toList(),
                    list -> list.stream().mapToDouble(Order::amount).average()
                )
            ));
        avgPerCustomer.forEach((cust, avg) ->
            avg.ifPresent(v -> System.out.printf("  %s avg: $%.2f%n", cust, v)));

        // 6. Flat list of all customer-category pairs
        List<String> pairs = orders.stream()
            .map(o -> o.customerId() + ":" + o.category())
            .distinct()
            .sorted()
            .collect(Collectors.toList());
        System.out.println("Customer-Category pairs: " + pairs);
    }
}

Practice — Lesson 35

Exercise 1: Pipeline Construction

Given a list of employee records with fields name, department, salary (double), and active (boolean), write a stream pipeline that:
- Filters to active employees only
- Groups by department
- For each department, computes the average salary
- Returns a Map<String, Double> of department → average salary

Challenge: Do it in a single collect call using Collectors.groupingBy + Collectors.averagingDouble.

record Employee(String name, String department, double salary, boolean active) {}

Map<String, Double> avgSalaryByDept = employees.stream()
    .filter(Employee::active)
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
        Employee::department,
        Collectors.averagingDouble(Employee::salary)
    ));

Exercise 2: Lazy Evaluation Trace

Predict the exact console output of this code before running it:

List<Integer> list = List.of(1, 2, 3, 4, 5);
Optional<Integer> result = list.stream()
    .filter(n -> { System.out.println("F:" + n); return n > 2; })
    .map(n    -> { System.out.println("M:" + n); return n * 10; })
    .findFirst();
System.out.println("Result: " + result.orElse(-1));

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

F:1
F:2
F:3
M:3
Result: 30

Explanation: Elements flow vertically through the pipeline. findFirst() short-circuits after the first element passes filter and gets mapped. Elements 4 and 5 are never processed.
</details>

Exercise 3: Parallel vs Sequential Performance

Write a benchmark (conceptual — without JMH) comparing:
- Sequential stream summing 10M random integers
- Parallel stream summing the same 10M integers
- Manual for-loop summing the same 10M integers

Predict: which is fastest and why? What does this tell you about choosing parallel streams?

Expected insight: For a simple sum of boxed Integer objects, the parallel overhead of splitting and combining may not outperform sequential. For primitives (IntStream), the sequential IntStream.sum() is very fast. Parallelism shines when per-element work is CPU-intensive and the array is large enough to amortize split/combine overhead.

Exercise 4: FlatMap Mastery

Given a list of sentences, write a stream pipeline that:
1. Splits each sentence into words
2. Converts all words to lowercase
3. Removes duplicates
4. Sorts alphabetically
5. Returns the top 5 most frequent words (hint: use Collectors.groupingBy + Collectors.counting(), then sort the resulting map)

List<String> sentences = /* ... */;

// Step 1-4: unique sorted words
List<String> uniqueWords = sentences.stream()
    .flatMap(s -> Arrays.stream(s.toLowerCase().split("\\W+")))
    .filter(w -> !w.isBlank())
    .distinct()
    .sorted()
    .collect(Collectors.toList());

// Step 5: frequency count, top 5
Map<String, Long> freq = sentences.stream()
    .flatMap(s -> Arrays.stream(s.toLowerCase().split("\\W+")))
    .filter(w -> !w.isBlank())
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Function.identity(), Collectors.counting()));

List<String> top5 = freq.entrySet().stream()
    .sorted(Map.Entry.<String, Long>comparingByValue().reversed())
    .limit(5)
    .map(Map.Entry::getKey)
    .collect(Collectors.toList());

Exercise 5: Identify the Bug

What is wrong with each of the following, and how would you fix it?

Bug A:

Stream<String> stream = names.stream().filter(n -> n.length() > 3);
long count1 = stream.count();
long count2 = stream.count(); // ???

Bug: A stream can only be consumed once. Second count() throws IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed. Fix: create two separate streams from names.

Bug B:

List<String> results = new ArrayList<>();
names.parallelStream().filter(n -> n.length() > 3).forEach(results::add);

Bug: ArrayList is not thread-safe. Concurrent add can corrupt internal state. Fix: use collect(Collectors.toList()) instead of forEach with shared mutable list.

Bug C:

try (Stream<String> lines = Files.lines(Path.of("data.txt"))) {
    Stream<String> filtered = lines.filter(l -> !l.isBlank());
    // stream used later after try block...
}
// filtered used here
filtered.forEach(System.out::println); // ???

Bug: filtered is a view on lines. After the try block closes lines, using filtered throws IllegalStateException. Fix: collect into a List<String> inside the try block.
