Part 1

Concept: What Are Collectors?

A Collector is the bridge between a stream pipeline and a mutable result container. When you call stream.collect(collector), you are handing control to the collector, which knows how to create a container, fold each element into it, and — in parallel mode — merge sub-containers into the final result.

The Collectors utility class (introduced in Java 8 as java.util.stream.Collectors) provides over 40 factory methods producing ready-to-use Collector implementations for the most common aggregation patterns: grouping, partitioning, joining strings, producing maps, computing statistics, and more.

The mental model:

stream.collect(Collectors.toList())
       │             │
       │             └── Collector: knows HOW to accumulate
       └── Stream: provides elements one by one

Unlike reduce(), which works best with immutable accumulation (producing a scalar), collect() is designed for mutable reduction — folding elements into a List, Map, Set, StringBuilder, or any custom container efficiently.

Key distinctions:

Aspect reduce() collect()
Container Immutable intermediate values Mutable result container
Best for Scalars, summation, concatenation Lists, Maps, Sets, grouped results
Parallel merge Identity + combiner function Combiner merges sub-containers
Type T → T → T fold Supplier + BiConsumer + BinaryOperator
Part 2

The Collector Interface: Four Functional Components

Collector<T, A, R> is a parameterized interface with three type parameters:

  • T — the type of input elements from the stream
  • A — the mutable accumulation type (the intermediate container, often hidden from callers)
  • R — the result type after optional finisher transformation
public interface Collector<T, A, R> {
    Supplier<A>          supplier();      // creates new empty container
    BiConsumer<A, T>     accumulator();   // folds one element into container
    BinaryOperator<A>    combiner();      // merges two containers (parallel)
    Function<A, R>       finisher();      // converts container to final result
    Set<Characteristics> characteristics(); // hints (CONCURRENT, UNORDERED, IDENTITY_FINISH)
}

Visualising the Four Components

╔═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║              COLLECTOR EXECUTION MODEL                                ║
╠═══════════════╦═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║  1. supplier  ║  () → A                                               ║
║               ║  Creates the mutable container before processing      ║
║               ║  Example: () -> new ArrayList<>()                     ║
╠═══════════════╬═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║  2. accumu-   ║  (A, T) → void                                        ║
║     lator     ║  Folds one stream element T into container A          ║
║               ║  Example: (list, elem) -> list.add(elem)              ║
╠═══════════════╬═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║  3. combiner  ║  (A, A) → A                                           ║
║               ║  Merges two partial containers (parallel streams)      ║
║               ║  Example: (a, b) -> { a.addAll(b); return a; }        ║
╠═══════════════╬═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║  4. finisher  ║  A → R                                                ║
║               ║  Post-processes container into final result           ║
║               ║  Example: Collections::unmodifiableList               ║
║               ║  If A == R: IDENTITY_FINISH characteristic skips this ║
╚═══════════════╩═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝

Characteristics

enum Characteristics {
    CONCURRENT,       // accumulator can be called from multiple threads simultaneously
    UNORDERED,        // result does not depend on encounter order of elements
    IDENTITY_FINISH   // finisher is identity fn; cast A to R directly, skip call
}

toList() has IDENTITY_FINISH. toSet() has UNORDERED | IDENTITY_FINISH. groupingBy has none by default (order matters for the outer map).

Part 3

Basic Collectors: toList, toSet, toUnmodifiableList, toCollection

toList and toUnmodifiableList

import java.util.stream.Collectors;

List<String> names = List.of("Alice", "Bob", "Charlie", "Diana");

// Java 8-15: returns mutable ArrayList
List<String> mutableList = names.stream()
    .filter(n -> n.length() > 3)
    .collect(Collectors.toList());

// Java 10+: guaranteed unmodifiable
List<String> immutableList = names.stream()
    .filter(n -> n.length() > 3)
    .collect(Collectors.toUnmodifiableList());

// Java 16+: shorthand terminal operation (not a Collector)
List<String> java16List = names.stream()
    .filter(n -> n.length() > 3)
    .toList();   // unmodifiable, null-safe

> Note: Collectors.toList() does NOT guarantee mutability, ordering, or nulls per the spec — it just happens to return ArrayList in the OpenJDK implementation. For guaranteed contract, use toCollection(ArrayList::new).

toSet

Set<String> uniqueDepts = employees.stream()
    .map(Employee::department)
    .collect(Collectors.toSet());   // HashSet, UNORDERED

// Guaranteed LinkedHashSet (insertion-order):
Set<String> ordered = employees.stream()
    .map(Employee::department)
    .collect(Collectors.toCollection(LinkedHashSet::new));

toCollection

// When you need a specific collection type:
TreeSet<String> sorted = names.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.toCollection(TreeSet::new));

ArrayDeque<String> deque = names.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.toCollection(ArrayDeque::new));
Part 4

toMap: Basic Usage, Merge Functions, and Null Traps

toMap collects stream elements into a Map<K, V> using two functions: a key mapper and a value mapper.

Basic toMap

record Product(String sku, String name, double price) {}

List<Product> catalog = List.of(
    new Product("A1", "Widget",  9.99),
    new Product("B2", "Gadget", 19.99),
    new Product("C3", "Doohickey", 4.99)
);

// Map<SKU, Product>
Map<String, Product> bySku = catalog.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.toMap(
        Product::sku,     // key mapper
        p -> p            // value mapper (Function.identity() also works)
    ));

// Map<SKU, price>
Map<String, Double> priceBySku = catalog.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.toMap(Product::sku, Product::price));

The Duplicate Key Problem and Merge Function

If two elements map to the same key, toMap throws IllegalStateException: Duplicate key. Use the three-argument overload with a merge function:

// Employees by department — keep only the highest-paid per department
Map<String, Employee> topEarnerByDept = employees.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.toMap(
        Employee::department,                   // key
        e -> e,                                 // value
        (existing, incoming) ->                 // merge: keep higher salary
            existing.salary() >= incoming.salary() ? existing : incoming
    ));

// Sum all salaries per department (merge as arithmetic)
Map<String, Double> totalSalaryByDept = employees.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.toMap(
        Employee::department,
        Employee::salary,
        Double::sum                             // merge: add duplicates
    ));

Controlling Map Type (Fourth Argument)

// LinkedHashMap to preserve insertion order
Map<String, Product> linkedMap = catalog.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.toMap(
        Product::sku,
        p -> p,
        (a, b) -> a,            // keep first on collision
        LinkedHashMap::new      // map factory
    ));

The Null Value Trap

// This THROWS NullPointerException even though Optional.empty() is valid:
Map<String, String> map = users.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.toMap(
        User::id,
        u -> u.email()  // if email() returns null → NPE!
    ));

// Fix: use toMap with null handling via Optional or a sentinel
Map<String, Optional<String>> safeMap = users.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.toMap(
        User::id,
        u -> Optional.ofNullable(u.email())
    ));

> Interview Critical: toMap calls HashMap.merge() internally, which explicitly throws NullPointerException if the value is null. This is a known design decision — HashMap supports null values, but Collectors.toMap uses Map.merge() which does not.

Part 5

Counting, Summing, Averaging, and Summarizing Collectors

These are the numeric aggregation collectors — most useful as downstream collectors inside groupingBy.

// Stand-alone counting (use stream.count() instead for simple cases)
long count = employees.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.counting());

// Summing
long totalSalary = employees.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.summingLong(e -> (long) e.salary()));

double totalSalaryD = employees.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.summingDouble(Employee::salary));

// Averaging
double avgSalary = employees.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.averagingDouble(Employee::salary));

// Summary statistics — min, max, count, sum, average in one pass
DoubleSummaryStatistics stats = employees.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.summarizingDouble(Employee::salary));

System.out.printf("Count=%d  Min=%.2f  Max=%.2f  Avg=%.2f%n",
    stats.getCount(), stats.getMin(), stats.getMax(), stats.getAverage());

As Downstream Collectors

// Average salary by department — a very common pattern
Map<String, Double> avgSalaryByDept = employees.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
        Employee::department,
        Collectors.averagingDouble(Employee::salary)
    ));

// Count employees per department
Map<String, Long> countByDept = employees.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
        Employee::department,
        Collectors.counting()
    ));
Part 6

joining Collector: String Assembly

Collectors.joining() is the stream-equivalent of String.join() and StringJoiner, but composable into pipelines.

List<String> words = List.of("alpha", "beta", "gamma", "delta");

// No separator
String plain = words.stream().collect(Collectors.joining());
// "alphabetagammadelta"

// Delimiter only
String csv = words.stream().collect(Collectors.joining(", "));
// "alpha, beta, gamma, delta"

// Delimiter + prefix + suffix
String json = words.stream().collect(Collectors.joining(
    "\", \"",   // delimiter
    "[\"",      // prefix
    "\"]"       // suffix
));
// ["alpha", "beta", "gamma", "delta"]

// Practical: build a SQL IN-clause
String ids = userIds.stream()
    .map(String::valueOf)
    .collect(Collectors.joining(", ", "(", ")"));
// (1, 2, 3, 42)
Part 7

groupingBy: Single-Level Grouping

groupingBy is the most powerful collector in the toolkit — it mirrors SQL GROUP BY, producing a Map<K, List<T>> (or any downstream accumulation).

// Default: Map<Department, List<Employee>>
Map<String, List<Employee>> byDept = employees.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::department));

// Custom classifier function
Map<String, List<Employee>> bySalaryBracket = employees.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(e -> {
        if (e.salary() < 50_000)  return "Junior";
        if (e.salary() < 100_000) return "Mid";
        return "Senior";
    }));

// Controlling map type: TreeMap for sorted keys
Map<String, List<Employee>> sorted = employees.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
        Employee::department,
        TreeMap::new,          // map factory
        Collectors.toList()    // downstream
    ));

> groupingBy always produces a HashMap<K, List<T>> unless you supply a map factory. The inner list is always ArrayList unless you specify a downstream.

Part 8

groupingBy with Downstream Collectors: Multi-Level Grouping

The real power of groupingBy comes from its downstream collector parameter. Any collector can be nested inside, including another groupingBy — enabling multi-level aggregation trees.

record Transaction(String accountId, String category,
                   double amount, LocalDate date) {}

// Level 1: group by account, then by category, collect amounts
Map<String, Map<String, List<Double>>> grouped = transactions.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
        Transaction::accountId,
        Collectors.groupingBy(
            Transaction::category,
            Collectors.mapping(Transaction::amount, Collectors.toList())
        )
    ));

// Level 1: group by account → Level 2: total amount per category
Map<String, Map<String, Double>> totalByAccountAndCategory =
    transactions.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
            Transaction::accountId,
            Collectors.groupingBy(
                Transaction::category,
                Collectors.summingDouble(Transaction::amount)
            )
        ));

// Multi-level with count and max: most common pattern in reporting
Map<String, DoubleSummaryStatistics> statsByDept = employees.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
        Employee::department,
        Collectors.summarizingDouble(Employee::salary)
    ));

// Produce a Map<Dept, Set<String>> of names (not List)
Map<String, Set<String>> namesByDept = employees.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
        Employee::department,
        Collectors.mapping(Employee::name, Collectors.toSet())
    ));

Banking Use Case: Monthly Transaction Summary per Account

// Real-world: monthly spend per account per category
Map<String, Map<YearMonth, Double>> monthlySpend = transactions.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
        Transaction::accountId,
        Collectors.groupingBy(
            t -> YearMonth.from(t.date()),
            Collectors.summingDouble(Transaction::amount)
        )
    ));

monthlySpend.forEach((account, monthMap) -> {
    System.out.println("Account: " + account);
    monthMap.entrySet().stream()
        .sorted(Map.Entry.comparingByKey())
        .forEach(e -> System.out.printf("  %s: $%.2f%n", e.getKey(), e.getValue()));
});
Part 9

partitioningBy: Boolean Grouping

partitioningBy is a specialised groupingBy for boolean predicates — it always produces exactly two entries in the map: true and false.

// Split employees: passing threshold vs not
Map<Boolean, List<Employee>> partition = employees.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.partitioningBy(e -> e.salary() >= 75_000));

List<Employee> highEarners = partition.get(true);
List<Employee> lowEarners  = partition.get(false);

// With downstream: count in each partition
Map<Boolean, Long> counts = employees.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.partitioningBy(
        e -> e.salary() >= 75_000,
        Collectors.counting()
    ));

System.out.println("High earners: " + counts.get(true));
System.out.println("Low  earners: " + counts.get(false));

partitioningBy vs groupingBy

Feature partitioningBy groupingBy
Key type Boolean only Any K
Map size Always 2 entries One per distinct key
Null keys Not applicable Not allowed (NPE)
Performance Slightly faster (no hashCode) General purpose
Use when Binary split by predicate N-way classification
Part 10

mapping, flatMapping, and filtering Collectors

These three adapters transform elements before downstream accumulation, decoupling the transformation from the collection target.

mapping

// Collect only names (not full Employee) grouped by department
Map<String, List<String>> namesByDept = employees.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
        Employee::department,
        Collectors.mapping(Employee::name, Collectors.toList())
    ));

// Equivalent without mapping (more verbose):
Map<String, List<String>> namesByDeptV2 = employees.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
        Employee::department,
        Collectors.toList()   // would give List<Employee>, not List<String>
    ));
// ↑ This is WRONG — need mapping() to transform inside the group

flatMapping (Java 9+)

flatMapping applies a function returning a Stream<U> to each element, then flattens and collects.

record Order(String customerId, List<String> productSkus) {}

// All SKUs per customer (flat list, not list-of-lists)
Map<String, Set<String>> skusByCustomer = orders.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
        Order::customerId,
        Collectors.flatMapping(
            o -> o.productSkus().stream(),    // flatten per order
            Collectors.toSet()                // unique SKUs per customer
        )
    ));

filtering (Java 9+)

filtering applies a predicate inside the downstream accumulation — different from stream.filter() because it preserves empty groups in the map.

// WITHOUT filtering: departments with no high earners are ABSENT from map
Map<String, List<Employee>> mapA = employees.stream()
    .filter(e -> e.salary() > 80_000)
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::department));

// WITH filtering: all departments appear; empty ones map to empty list
Map<String, List<Employee>> mapB = employees.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
        Employee::department,
        Collectors.filtering(
            e -> e.salary() > 80_000,
            Collectors.toList()
        )
    ));

// mapA may be missing "HR" (if no HR employee earns > 80k)
// mapB will always have "HR" → [] (empty list)
Part 11

collectingAndThen: Post-Processing the Result

collectingAndThen(downstream, finisher) wraps another collector and applies a final transformation to its result.

// Collect to list, then make it unmodifiable
List<String> names = employees.stream()
    .map(Employee::name)
    .collect(Collectors.collectingAndThen(
        Collectors.toList(),
        Collections::unmodifiableList
    ));

// Collect to list, get the max element
Optional<Employee> topEarner = employees.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.collectingAndThen(
        Collectors.toList(),
        list -> list.stream().max(Comparator.comparingDouble(Employee::salary))
    ));

// Collect, then wrap in custom DTO
Map<String, DepartmentReport> reports = employees.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
        Employee::department,
        Collectors.collectingAndThen(
            Collectors.toList(),
            list -> new DepartmentReport(
                list.size(),
                list.stream().mapToDouble(Employee::salary).average().orElse(0)
            )
        )
    ));
Part 12

teeing Collector (Java 12+)

teeing(downstream1, downstream2, merger) fans out the same stream of elements to two independent collectors simultaneously, then merges their results.

// Compute min and max salary in a single pass
record SalaryRange(double min, double max) {}

SalaryRange range = employees.stream()
    .map(Employee::salary)
    .collect(Collectors.teeing(
        Collectors.minBy(Comparator.naturalOrder()),   // downstream 1
        Collectors.maxBy(Comparator.naturalOrder()),   // downstream 2
        (min, max) -> new SalaryRange(                 // merger
            min.orElse(0.0),
            max.orElse(0.0)
        )
    ));

// Compute both count and sum (average = sum/count) in one pass
record Stats(long count, double sum) {
    double average() { return count == 0 ? 0 : sum / count; }
}

Stats stats = employees.stream()
    .map(Employee::salary)
    .collect(Collectors.teeing(
        Collectors.counting(),
        Collectors.summingDouble(Double::doubleValue),
        Stats::new
    ));

// Partition AND count simultaneously
record Partition<T>(List<T> matching, List<T> notMatching) {}

Partition<Employee> result = employees.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.teeing(
        Collectors.filtering(e -> e.salary() > 80_000, Collectors.toList()),
        Collectors.filtering(e -> e.salary() <= 80_000, Collectors.toList()),
        Partition::new
    ));

> Why teeing matters: before Java 12, producing two independent aggregates from the same stream required either two separate stream passes over the data or a custom collector. teeing eliminates that overhead.

Part 13

Custom Collector Implementation

When built-in collectors are insufficient, implement Collector<T, A, R> directly.

// Custom: collect into an ImmutableList (Guava-style example)
public class ImmutableListCollector<T>
        implements Collector<T, List<T>, List<T>> {

    @Override
    public Supplier<List<T>> supplier() {
        return ArrayList::new;
    }

    @Override
    public BiConsumer<List<T>, T> accumulator() {
        return List::add;
    }

    @Override
    public BinaryOperator<List<T>> combiner() {
        return (a, b) -> { a.addAll(b); return a; };
    }

    @Override
    public Function<List<T>, List<T>> finisher() {
        return Collections::unmodifiableList;
    }

    @Override
    public Set<Characteristics> characteristics() {
        return Set.of();  // no special characteristics
    }

    public static <T> ImmutableListCollector<T> toImmutableList() {
        return new ImmutableListCollector<>();
    }
}

// Usage:
List<String> immutable = names.stream()
    .filter(n -> n.startsWith("A"))
    .collect(ImmutableListCollector.toImmutableList());

Simpler: Collector.of Factory

// Use Collector.of() instead of implementing the interface
Collector<String, StringBuilder, String> joiner =
    Collector.of(
        StringBuilder::new,                          // supplier
        StringBuilder::append,                       // accumulator
        StringBuilder::append,                       // combiner (parallel)
        StringBuilder::toString,                     // finisher
        Collector.Characteristics.IDENTITY_FINISH    // NOT here; finisher needed
    );

// Better approach using Collector.of for a word-frequency map:
Collector<String, Map<String, Long>, Map<String, Long>> frequencyCollector =
    Collector.of(
        HashMap::new,
        (map, word) -> map.merge(word, 1L, Long::sum),
        (a, b) -> { b.forEach((k, v) -> a.merge(k, v, Long::sum)); return a; },
        Collector.Characteristics.IDENTITY_FINISH
    );
Part 14

Concurrent Collectors

Two collectors are thread-safe for parallel stream accumulation into a shared container:

// toConcurrentMap: thread-safe map accumulation in parallel
Map<String, Employee> concMap = employees.parallelStream()
    .collect(Collectors.toConcurrentMap(
        Employee::id,
        e -> e,
        (a, b) -> a    // merge on duplicate (keep first)
    ));

// groupingByConcurrent: parallel grouping without split/merge overhead
Map<String, List<Employee>> groups = employees.parallelStream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingByConcurrent(Employee::department));

Concurrent vs Standard in Parallel

Collector Parallel Strategy Order Preserved
toMap Split→accumulate separately→merge maps Yes (encounter order)
toConcurrentMap Single ConcurrentHashMap, all threads accumulate directly No (UNORDERED)
groupingBy Split→group separately→merge maps Yes
groupingByConcurrent Single ConcurrentHashMap, no merge step No (UNORDERED)

> Use groupingByConcurrent with parallelStream() when you have a large dataset and do not need encounter-order preservation. It avoids the expensive merge-maps step.

Part 16

Common Pitfalls and Anti-Patterns

Pitfall 1: toMap With Duplicate Keys

// THROWS: IllegalStateException: Duplicate key Alice
Map<String, Integer> wordLengths = List.of("Alice", "Alice", "Bob")
    .stream()
    .collect(Collectors.toMap(s -> s, String::length));
// Fix: add merge function
Map<String, Integer> safe = List.of("Alice", "Alice", "Bob")
    .stream()
    .collect(Collectors.toMap(s -> s, String::length, (a, b) -> a));

Pitfall 2: Null Value in toMap

// NPE even though null values are valid in HashMap
Map<String, String> map = users.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.toMap(User::id, User::nickname)); // NPE if nickname is null
// Fix: wrap or filter
Map<String, Optional<String>> safe = users.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.toMap(User::id, u -> Optional.ofNullable(u.nickname())));

Pitfall 3: Mutable State in Lambdas

// WRONG: shared mutable accumulator — race condition in parallel
List<String> accumulator = new ArrayList<>();
names.parallelStream().collect(Collectors.toList())
    .forEach(accumulator::add);  // data race if on parallel streams

// RIGHT: collectors manage their own containers
List<String> safe = names.parallelStream()
    .collect(Collectors.toList());

Pitfall 4: groupingBy With Null Keys

// NPE: groupingBy does not allow null classifier result
employees.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(e -> e.department())); // NPE if department() is null
// Fix: provide default for null
employees.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
        e -> e.department() != null ? e.department() : "Unknown"
    ));
Part 17

Performance Considerations

Collector Time Complexity Notes
toList() O(n) ArrayList grow-and-copy
toSet() O(n) avg HashSet, O(n²) worst (hash collisions)
toMap() O(n) avg HashMap, NPE on null value
groupingBy() O(n) One pass; inner lists amortised O(1) add
counting() O(n) Just an accumulating long
joining() O(n) StringJoiner internals
sorted() + toList() O(n log n) sorted is stateful — buffers all

Prefer toList() over Collectors.toList() in Java 16+ — the stream terminal toList() avoids creating a Collector object entirely and can be optimised by the JVM more aggressively.

Avoid collectingAndThen(..., Collections::unmodifiableList) on hot paths — toList() in Java 16+ is already unmodifiable with zero overhead.

Java Version Evolution

Version Addition

Java 9 flatMapping, filtering
Java 10 toUnmodifiableList, toUnmodifiableSet, toUnmodifiableMap
Java 12 teeing
Java 16 Stream.toList() (terminal op, not a Collector)
Part 19

Production Pattern: Aggregation Reports

Real-world aggregation pipelines are the primary use case for collectors in enterprise applications.

// ─── Domain ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
record Trade(String accountId, String instrument,
             String side, double quantity, double price, LocalDate tradeDate) {
    double notional() { return quantity * price; }
}

// ─── Report DTOs ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
record InstrumentSummary(long trades, double totalNotional, double avgPrice) {}
record DailyReport(String accountId, Map<String, InstrumentSummary> byInstrument) {}

// ─── Service Layer ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
@Service
public class TradingReportService {

    public Map<String, DailyReport> buildDailyReport(
            List<Trade> trades, LocalDate forDate) {

        return trades.stream()
            .filter(t -> t.tradeDate().equals(forDate))
            .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
                Trade::accountId,
                Collectors.collectingAndThen(
                    Collectors.groupingBy(
                        Trade::instrument,
                        Collectors.teeing(
                            Collectors.counting(),
                            Collectors.summarizingDouble(Trade::notional),
                            (count, stats) -> new InstrumentSummary(
                                count,
                                stats.getSum(),
                                stats.getAverage()
                            )
                        )
                    ),
                    instrumentMap -> new DailyReport(/* accountId from outer */ null, instrumentMap)
                )
            ));
    }

    // Simpler pattern: top 5 instruments by total volume
    public List<String> topInstrumentsByVolume(List<Trade> trades) {
        return trades.stream()
            .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
                Trade::instrument,
                Collectors.summingDouble(Trade::notional)
            ))
            .entrySet().stream()
            .sorted(Map.Entry.<String, Double>comparingByValue().reversed())
            .limit(5)
            .map(Map.Entry::getKey)
            .collect(Collectors.toList());
    }
}

Spring Integration: Collectors in the Service Layer

Collecting Spring Data Results

@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class UserService {

    private final UserRepository userRepository;

    // Convert JPA entities to DTOs grouped by role
    public Map<String, List<UserDto>> getUsersByRole() {
        return userRepository.findAll().stream()
            .map(this::toDto)
            .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(UserDto::role));
    }

    // Build a quick-lookup map from ID to entity
    public Map<Long, User> getUserLookupMap(List<Long> ids) {
        return userRepository.findAllById(ids).stream()
            .collect(Collectors.toMap(User::getId, u -> u));
    }

    // Page result mapping (Spring Data Page<T>)
    public Page<UserDto> toDto(Page<User> page, Pageable pageable) {
        List<UserDto> dtos = page.getContent().stream()
            .map(this::toDto)
            .collect(Collectors.toList());
        return new PageImpl<>(dtos, pageable, page.getTotalElements());
    }

    // Collect active users, then group by subscription tier
    public Map<String, Long> activeUserCountByTier() {
        return userRepository.findByActiveTrue().stream()
            .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
                User::getSubscriptionTier,
                Collectors.counting()
            ));
    }

    private UserDto toDto(User user) { /* ... */ return null; }
}

ResponseEntity Mapping Pattern

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/reports")
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class ReportController {

    private final ReportService reportService;

    @GetMapping("/summary")
    public ResponseEntity<Map<String, DepartmentStats>> summary() {
        Map<String, DepartmentStats> result =
            reportService.findAllEmployees().stream()
                .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
                    EmployeeDto::department,
                    Collectors.collectingAndThen(
                        Collectors.toList(),
                        list -> new DepartmentStats(
                            list.size(),
                            list.stream().mapToDouble(EmployeeDto::salary).average().orElse(0),
                            list.stream().mapToDouble(EmployeeDto::salary).max().orElse(0)
                        )
                    )
                ));
        return ResponseEntity.ok(result);
    }
}
Part 21

Interview Deep Dive

Q1: What happens with duplicate keys in toMap without a merge function?

Answer: IllegalStateException: Duplicate key <value>. Internally, toMap uses Map.merge(key, value, mergeFunction). Without a merge function, the default merge throws on collision. Always provide a merge function for data where duplicate keys are possible.

Q2: What is the difference between toMap and toConcurrentMap?

Answer: toMap uses HashMap and is designed for sequential or parallel streams where each thread accumulates into a separate container, then containers are merged. toConcurrentMap uses ConcurrentHashMap with the CONCURRENT and UNORDERED characteristics, meaning all threads share a single map and accumulate directly — no merge step. toConcurrentMap is faster for large parallel workloads where ordering is not required, but result order is non-deterministic.

Q3: Why does Collectors.toMap throw NullPointerException when a value is null, even though HashMap supports null values?

Answer: toMap is implemented using Map.merge(key, value, merger). The contract of Map.merge explicitly states it throws NullPointerException if the value is null. This is a deliberate design decision — it forces callers to be explicit about null handling rather than silently storing nulls in maps. Workarounds: wrap values in Optional, use a custom collector, or post-process with computeIfAbsent.

Q4: What is the practical difference between groupingBy (sequential) vs groupingByConcurrent (parallel)?

Answer: groupingBy with parallelStream() splits the stream into chunks, groups each chunk into a separate HashMap, then merges the per-chunk maps at the end. groupingByConcurrent has CONCURRENT characteristic — all threads accumulate into a single shared ConcurrentHashMap, eliminating the merge step. groupingByConcurrent is more memory-efficient (one map, not N maps) but loses encounter-order guarantees. Use groupingByConcurrent when processing large parallel streams where order doesn't matter.

Q5: What is teeing and when would you use it over two separate stream pipelines?

Answer: teeing(d1, d2, merger) fans one stream into two independent collectors simultaneously. Use it instead of two separate stream traversals when the source is a one-time resource (file, JDBC ResultSet), when you need two different aggregates from the same pass (min+max, count+sum), or to avoid reading large collections into memory twice. Performance is the same as one traversal rather than two.

Q6: Explain collectingAndThen and give a production use case.

Answer: collectingAndThen(downstream, finisher) applies a function to the result of another collector. Common uses: wrap a toList() result in Collections.unmodifiableList(); apply a constructor to the grouped list to produce a DTO; convert a collected List<T> to Optional<T> for "find single result or empty" patterns. It is a finisher adapter — no element-level transformation, only result-level.

Summary Table

Collector Input Output Notes

toUnmodifiableList() T List<T> Immutable; Java 10+
toSet() T Set<T> HashSet; UNORDERED
toUnmodifiableSet() T Set<T> Immutable; Java 10+

toMap(k, v) T Map<K,V> Throws on duplicate key
toMap(k, v, merge) T Map<K,V> Resolves duplicate keys
toMap(k, v, merge, factory) T Map<K,V> Custom map type
toConcurrentMap(...) T ConcurrentMap<K,V> Thread-safe, CONCURRENT
groupingBy(fn) T Map<K,List<T>> Default downstream = toList

groupingBy(fn, factory, downstream) T M<K,R> Custom map type
groupingByConcurrent(fn) T ConcurrentMap<K,List<T>> Parallel; CONCURRENT

partitioningBy(pred, downstream) T Map<Boolean,R> Any downstream
counting() T Long Count elements
summingInt/Long/Double(fn) T Integer/Long/Double Sum numeric projection
averagingInt/Long/Double(fn) T Double Average numeric projection

minBy(cmp) T Optional<T> Minimum by comparator
maxBy(cmp) T Optional<T> Maximum by comparator

joining(delim,pre,suf) CharSequence String With wrapping

reducing(op) T Optional<T> No identity version

Practice — Lesson 36

Easy

E1. Given List<String> fruits = List.of("apple", "banana", "cherry", "apricot", "blueberry", "avocado"), use a collector to build a Map<Character, List<String>> grouping fruits by their first letter.

Map<Character, List<String>> byFirstLetter = fruits.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(s -> s.charAt(0)));

E2. From a List<Integer>, collect even numbers into a LinkedHashSet preserving encounter order.

Set<Integer> evens = numbers.stream()
    .filter(n -> n % 2 == 0)
    .collect(Collectors.toCollection(LinkedHashSet::new));

E3. Build a comma-separated string of all employee names, sorted alphabetically, wrapped in square brackets.

String result = employees.stream()
    .map(Employee::name)
    .sorted()
    .collect(Collectors.joining(", ", "[", "]"));

Medium

M1. Given a list of transactions (fields: userId, amount), produce a Map<String, DoubleSummaryStatistics> — per-user statistics in one stream pass.

Map<String, DoubleSummaryStatistics> stats = transactions.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
        Transaction::userId,
        Collectors.summarizingDouble(Transaction::amount)
    ));

M2. Use partitioningBy to split a list of words into those ≥ 5 characters and those < 5 characters, then get a count of each partition.

Map<Boolean, Long> counts = words.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.partitioningBy(
        w -> w.length() >= 5,
        Collectors.counting()
    ));
System.out.println("Long words: " + counts.get(true));
System.out.println("Short words: " + counts.get(false));

M3. Use mapping inside groupingBy to produce Map<String, Set<String>> — department → unique employee names.

Map<String, Set<String>> namesByDept = employees.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
        Employee::department,
        Collectors.mapping(Employee::name, Collectors.toSet())
    ));

Advanced

A1. Implement a Collector<String, ?, Map<Integer, List<String>>> that groups strings by their length using Collector.of().

Collector<String, Map<Integer, List<String>>, Map<Integer, List<String>>> byLength =
    Collector.of(
        HashMap::new,
        (map, s) -> map.computeIfAbsent(s.length(), k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(s),
        (a, b) -> {
            b.forEach((k, v) -> a.merge(k, v, (l1, l2) -> { l1.addAll(l2); return l1; }));
            return a;
        },
        Collector.Characteristics.IDENTITY_FINISH
    );

A2. Use teeing to compute both the List<Employee> above-average salary employees and List<Employee> below-average salary employees in a single stream pass without knowing the average upfront. (Hint: compute average first, then teeing in a second pass, OR use a custom collector.)

Production

P1. You have a List<Order> where each Order has a customerId, status (PENDING/SHIPPED/DELIVERED/CANCELLED), and totalAmount. Build a report map: Map<String, Map<OrderStatus, DoubleSummaryStatistics>> — per customer, per status, order amount statistics — in a single collect call.

Map<String, Map<OrderStatus, DoubleSummaryStatistics>> report =
    orders.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
            Order::customerId,
            Collectors.groupingBy(
                Order::status,
                Collectors.summarizingDouble(Order::totalAmount)
            )
        ));

P2. A high-frequency trading system receives a Stream<Tick> (symbol, bid, ask, timestamp). Write a collector that produces Map<String, TickStats> (per symbol: min bid, max ask, tick count) from a single parallel pass. Ensure the implementation is thread-safe.

Debugging

D1. Identify the bug:

List<String> names = List.of("Alice", "Alice", "Bob");
Map<String, Integer> lengths = names.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.toMap(s -> s, String::length));

Bug: Duplicate key "Alice" causes IllegalStateException. Fix: Add merge function (a, b) -> a.

D2. Identify the bug:

Map<String, String> emailById = users.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.toMap(User::id, User::email));
// NullPointerException at runtime

Bug: User::email may return null; toMap uses Map.merge which rejects null values. Fix: u -> Objects.toString(u.email(), "") or wrap in Optional.

D3. Identify the bug:

employees.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(e -> e.getManager())); // manager can be null for CEO

Bug: groupingBy throws NullPointerException when classifier returns null. Fix: e -> e.getManager() != null ? e.getManager() : "None".

Interview

I1. "Explain the difference between groupingBy and partitioningBy. When would you choose one over the other?"

partitioningBy is a specialised groupingBy restricted to a boolean predicate — always producing exactly two entries. Choose partitioningBy for binary splits (pass/fail, active/inactive) — it is self-documenting, avoids accidental null keys, and is marginally faster for boolean classification. Choose groupingBy for N-way classification by any key type.

I2. "How does teeing differ from calling collect twice on the same list?"

teeing processes elements once, simultaneously feeding two downstream collectors. Two separate collect() calls iterate the source twice — problematic for one-shot streams (I/O, JDBC), and twice as slow for large collections. Use teeing whenever you need two independent aggregates from a single source traversal.

I3. "A colleague says Collectors.toList() returns an immutable list in Java 16+. Are they correct?"

Partially. Collectors.toList() still returns a mutable ArrayList in all Java versions per the Javadoc ("There are no guarantees on mutability, serializability, or thread safety"). What changed in Java 16 is Stream.toList() — the terminal operation (not a Collector) — which returns an unmodifiable list. The colleague is confusing Collectors.toList() with Stream.toList().

End of Lesson 36 — Collectors

Part 1

Concept: What Is Optional?

Optional<T> (introduced in Java 8 via java.util.Optional) is a container object that may or may not hold a non-null value. It provides a type-safe, null-free way to represent "value or absence of value" — the same concept as Haskell's Maybe monad or Scala's Option[T].

The primary motivation is to eliminate NullPointerException by making the possibility of absence explicit at the type level, rather than using the hidden convention that null means "no value."

Without Optional:
  String result = findEmail(userId);
  // Is null a valid return? An error? Does the user not exist?
  // The type String gives you no information.
  result.toUpperCase();  // NullPointerException if not found

With Optional:
  Optional<String> result = findEmail(userId);
  // The type explicitly says: "this might be empty"
  result.map(String::toUpperCase).orElse("NO EMAIL");

Optional is a value-based class — do not use == for equality, do not use it in synchronized blocks, and do not use it in serializable data structures (more on this in Part 12).

What Optional Is NOT

Optional is not a replacement for all null checks. The Java API design team intended Optional specifically for method return types where no result is a legitimate outcome — not for parameters, not for fields, not for collections.

Part 2

Creating Optional Values: of, ofNullable, empty

Three factory methods cover all creation scenarios:

import java.util.Optional;

// Optional.of(value): value MUST be non-null
Optional<String> definiteValue = Optional.of("hello");
// Optional.of(null) → throws NullPointerException immediately

// Optional.ofNullable(value): value may or may not be null
String maybeNull = getFromExternalSource();  // might return null
Optional<String> nullable = Optional.ofNullable(maybeNull);
// If maybeNull == null → Optional.empty()
// If maybeNull != null → Optional.of(maybeNull)

// Optional.empty(): explicit absence
Optional<String> nothing = Optional.empty();

When to Use Each

Factory Use When
Optional.of(v) You are certain value is non-null (post-assertion, from constructor)
Optional.ofNullable(v) Wrapping legacy code, external APIs, or any value that might be null
Optional.empty() Returning "not found", "not applicable" from a method 
// Typical repository method pattern
public Optional<User> findById(Long id) {
    User user = userDao.selectById(id);
    return Optional.ofNullable(user);  // null from DAO → empty Optional
}

// Certain value from logic
public Optional<BigDecimal> getDiscount(Customer customer) {
    if (!customer.isPremium()) return Optional.empty();
    BigDecimal discount = rateTable.get(customer.tier());
    return Optional.of(discount);  // we know rateTable never returns null
}
Part 3

Checking and Extracting: isPresent, isEmpty, get

Optional<String> opt = Optional.ofNullable(getValue());

// Check presence
boolean present = opt.isPresent();   // true if value exists
boolean empty   = opt.isEmpty();     // true if no value (Java 11+)

// Unsafe extraction — AVOID in production code
String value = opt.get();
// If Optional is empty, get() throws: NoSuchElementException

Why get() Is Considered a Code Smell

opt.get() without a prior opt.isPresent() check is no better than dereferencing a potentially-null reference — it just throws a different exception. The Optional API is designed so that you never need to call get() directly in idiomatic code. Use the transformation and default-providing methods instead.

// Anti-pattern — defeats the purpose of Optional
if (opt.isPresent()) {
    String v = opt.get();
    process(v);
}

// Idiomatic — use ifPresent or map
opt.ifPresent(v -> process(v));

The IntelliJ IDEA and SonarQube rulesets both flag opt.get() without isPresent() as a critical issue. Treat get() as deprecated in style — use orElse, orElseGet, orElseThrow, or the functional transformation methods.

Part 4

Providing Defaults: orElse, orElseGet, orElseThrow

These three methods cover the "empty Optional" case with different strategies:

orElse(defaultValue)

// Return the value, or the provided default if empty
String email = userOpt.map(User::email).orElse("unknown@example.com");
int count = countOpt.orElse(0);

Critical: orElse(T) evaluates the default expression eagerly — the argument is computed regardless of whether the Optional is empty.

// This creates a new object EVEN IF Optional is present:
User user = userOpt.orElse(new User("default"));  // new User() always called!

orElseGet(Supplier)

// Return the value, or invoke the supplier only if empty
User user = userOpt.orElseGet(() -> createDefaultUser());
// createDefaultUser() is called ONLY if userOpt is empty

// Prefer orElseGet for expensive defaults:
Config config = configOpt.orElseGet(() -> loadConfigFromDisk());

orElseThrow

// Java 8: throw a custom exception if empty
User user = userOpt.orElseThrow(() ->
    new UserNotFoundException("User not found: " + userId));

// Java 10+: no-arg overload throws NoSuchElementException
User user = userOpt.orElseThrow();

Decision Guide

Is the default value always available and cheap to compute?
  YES → orElse(value)

Is the default value expensive (DB call, file I/O, object creation)?
  YES → orElseGet(supplier)   ← lazy evaluation, only runs if empty

Is absence an error condition that should throw?
  YES → orElseThrow(exceptionSupplier)
Part 5

Transforming: map and flatMap

Optional supports transformation without extracting the value, keeping the pipeline null-safe.

map

map(Function<T, U>) applies the function if the Optional is present; returns Optional.empty() if it was already empty or if the function returns null.

Optional<String> emailOpt = userOpt.map(User::email);
// If userOpt is empty → Optional.empty()
// If user.email() is null → Optional.empty()
// Otherwise → Optional.of(email)

// Chain transformations
Optional<String> upperDomain = userOpt
    .map(User::email)
    .map(email -> email.split("@")[1])
    .map(String::toUpperCase);
// Any null/empty at any step → Optional.empty() propagates through

flatMap

flatMap(Function<T, Optional<U>>) is used when the mapping function itself returns an Optional — prevents wrapping an Optional inside another Optional.

// If User.findAddress() returns Optional<Address>:
Optional<String> city = userOpt
    .flatMap(User::findAddress)        // Optional<Address>
    .flatMap(Address::findCity)        // Optional<String>
    .map(String::toUpperCase);

// WITHOUT flatMap (wrong — wraps Optional<Optional<Address>>):
Optional<Optional<Address>> wrong = userOpt.map(User::findAddress);

// WITH flatMap (correct — stays as Optional<Address>):
Optional<Address> correct = userOpt.flatMap(User::findAddress);

map vs flatMap Summary

Method Function signature Use when
map(fn) T → U fn returns a plain value
flatMap(fn) T → Optional<U> fn returns an Optional itself
Part 6

Filtering: filter

filter(Predicate<T>) tests the value if present. If the predicate returns false, Optional.empty() is returned. If the Optional was already empty, it remains empty.

Optional<User> adultUser = userOpt
    .filter(u -> u.age() >= 18);
// Present adult → Optional.of(adult)
// Present minor → Optional.empty()
// Already empty → Optional.empty()

// Practical: validate and transform in a pipeline
Optional<String> validEmail = inputOpt
    .filter(s -> s.contains("@"))
    .filter(s -> s.length() <= 254)
    .map(String::toLowerCase);

// Avoid extracting just to filter:
// BAD:
if (userOpt.isPresent() && userOpt.get().isActive()) { ... }
// GOOD:
userOpt.filter(User::isActive).ifPresent(this::process);
Part 7

Side Effects: ifPresent, ifPresentOrElse

ifPresent (Java 8)

// Execute action only if value is present
userOpt.ifPresent(user -> auditLog.record("User accessed: " + user.id()));

// Equivalent imperative code:
if (user != null) {
    auditLog.record("User accessed: " + user.id());
}

ifPresentOrElse (Java 9+)

// Execute one of two branches — present or empty
userOpt.ifPresentOrElse(
    user -> response.setUser(user),          // present branch
    ()   -> response.setError("Not found")   // empty branch
);

// Compare to ternary with isPresent() — ifPresentOrElse is cleaner
// and avoids calling get()

Caution: ifPresent Is Not Return-Type-Aware

// This compiles but returns void — you cannot chain further
userOpt.ifPresent(user -> { /* ... */ });

// If you need a result, use map/orElse instead
String display = userOpt
    .map(user -> "Found: " + user.name())
    .orElse("Not found");
Part 8

or() and stream() (Java 9+)

or(Supplier<Optional<T>>)

or provides a fallback Optional when the primary is empty — enables chaining multiple potential sources.

// Try cache first, then DB, then default
Optional<User> user = cacheService.find(id)
    .or(() -> database.findById(id))
    .or(() -> Optional.of(User.anonymous()));

// This is cleaner than nested orElseGet/map chains

stream()

Optional.stream() converts an Optional<T> to a Stream<T> of zero or one elements — bridges Optional and Stream APIs.

// Filter out empty Optionals from a list of Optionals
List<Optional<User>> maybeUsers = fetchMaybeUsers();
List<User> presentUsers = maybeUsers.stream()
    .flatMap(Optional::stream)   // empty Optional → empty stream, present → one-element stream
    .collect(Collectors.toList());

// Stream pipeline that calls a method returning Optional
List<String> emails = userIds.stream()
    .map(userRepository::findById)     // returns Optional<User>
    .flatMap(Optional::stream)         // keeps only present results
    .map(User::email)
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
Part 9

Optional Chaining: Replacing Null Check Chains

The canonical motivating example for Optional is deeply nested null checks.

Before: Nested Null Checks

// Access order → customer → address → city
String city = null;
if (order != null) {
    Customer customer = order.getCustomer();
    if (customer != null) {
        Address address = customer.getAddress();
        if (address != null) {
            city = address.getCity();
        }
    }
}
String displayCity = city != null ? city : "Unknown";

After: Optional Chain

String displayCity = Optional.ofNullable(order)
    .map(Order::getCustomer)
    .map(Customer::getAddress)
    .map(Address::getCity)
    .orElse("Unknown");

The Optional chain expresses the same logic in one readable pipeline. Each map step either transforms the value or propagates Optional.empty() — null propagation is implicit and safe.

Rule of Thumb for Chains

Use flatMap when the method returns Optional<T>
Use map when the method returns T (possibly null)

// Mixed chain (some methods return Optional, some return T):
String postalCode = Optional.ofNullable(order)       // Order (possibly null)
    .flatMap(Order::getCustomer)                      // Optional<Customer>
    .map(Customer::getAddress)                        // Address (possibly null)
    .flatMap(Address::getPostalCode)                  // Optional<String>
    .orElse("UNKNOWN");
Part 10

The Critical Anti-Pattern: Optional for Fields and Parameters

This is the single most important rule about Optional, stated explicitly in the Java API documentation and by Brian Goetz (Java Language Architect):

> Optional was designed to provide a limited mechanism for library method return types where there is a clear need to represent "no result," and where using null for that is overwhelmingly likely to cause errors.

Anti-Pattern 1: Optional as a Field

// WRONG — Optional should never be a field
public class UserProfile {
    private Optional<String> nickname;  // BAD
    private Optional<Address> address;  // BAD

    // Problems:
    // 1. Optional is not Serializable — breaks JPA, Jackson, etc.
    // 2. Field can still be null (Optional<String> field itself is null)
    // 3. Memory overhead: extra object per field
    // 4. Confusing semantics: Optional.empty() vs null field
}

// CORRECT — use null fields + Optional in return type
public class UserProfile {
    private String nickname;     // null if absent
    private Address address;     // null if absent

    public Optional<String> getNickname() {
        return Optional.ofNullable(nickname);
    }
    public Optional<Address> getAddress() {
        return Optional.ofNullable(address);
    }
}

Anti-Pattern 2: Optional as a Method Parameter

// WRONG — Optional parameter forces caller to box their value
public void sendEmail(String to, Optional<String> subject) {  // BAD
    String subjectLine = subject.orElse("(no subject)");
    // ...
}

// Caller must wrap: sendEmail("x@y.com", Optional.of("Hello"));
// What if caller passes Optional.empty()? null? What's the contract?

// CORRECT — use overloading or @Nullable
public void sendEmail(String to, String subject) {
    // ...
}
public void sendEmail(String to) {
    sendEmail(to, "(no subject)");
}
// OR use @Nullable annotation and check internally
public void sendEmail(String to, @Nullable String subject) {
    String subjectLine = subject != null ? subject : "(no subject)";
}

Anti-Pattern 3: Optional in Collections

// WRONG — Optional in a collection element position
List<Optional<String>> names;       // BAD
Map<String, Optional<User>> cache;  // BAD

// A null value in a List is already representable as null at that index.
// Optional<T> in a collection adds zero value and doubles allocation.

// CORRECT — filter nulls out at the collection level
List<String> presentNames = names.stream()
    .filter(Objects::nonNull)
    .collect(Collectors.toList());

The Serialization Problem

Optional does not implement Serializable. This means:

  • JPA/Hibernate entities with Optional fields will fail to serialize.
  • Jackson (without special module) cannot deserialize JSON into Optional fields directly.
  • Java serialization (ObjectOutputStream) throws NotSerializableException.

If you use Optional in a class that is serialized (entity, DTO in RMI, cache value), you will encounter runtime errors. This is a deliberate design decision — Optional is a terminal value holder for method return types, not a domain model component.

Part 11

orElse vs orElseGet: Lazy Evaluation Deep Dive

This is one of the most commonly tested Optional interview topics because it represents a subtle performance trap.

// orElse: ALWAYS evaluates the argument
Optional<String> opt = Optional.of("hello");

// This method is ALWAYS called, even though opt has a value:
String result = opt.orElse(getDefault());   // getDefault() runs!

// orElseGet: LAZILY evaluates the supplier
String result2 = opt.orElseGet(() -> getDefault()); // getDefault() NOT called

When the Difference Matters

public class UserService {

    // BAD: creates the object even when userOpt is present
    public User getUser(Long id) {
        Optional<User> userOpt = cache.get(id);
        return userOpt.orElse(loadFromDatabase(id));   // DB call always runs!
    }

    // GOOD: only hits DB when cache is empty
    public User getUser(Long id) {
        Optional<User> userOpt = cache.get(id);
        return userOpt.orElseGet(() -> loadFromDatabase(id));
    }
}

Side-Effect Trap With orElse

int callCount = 0;

Optional<String> present = Optional.of("value");

// callCount becomes 1 even though value is present:
String r = present.orElse(sideEffectMethod());

// callCount stays 0 because supplier is not called:
String r2 = present.orElseGet(() -> sideEffectMethod());

Summary: orElse vs orElseGet

Feature orElse(T) orElseGet(Supplier<T>)
Argument evaluation Always (eager) Only when empty (lazy)
When to use Cheap constants, literals Expensive computation or I/O
Side effects Always triggered Only triggered when needed
Null default allowed Yes (result is null if opt empty) Must return non-null from supplier
Part 12

Optional in Serialization

Optional's non-serializable nature has specific implications across the Java ecosystem:

Jackson (JSON)

// Without module — Jackson cannot deserialize into Optional<String>
public class UserDto {
    private Optional<String> email;  // Problematic for Jackson
}

// With jackson-datatype-jdk8 module:
ObjectMapper mapper = new ObjectMapper()
    .registerModule(new Jdk8Module());  // enables Optional support

// Spring Boot auto-configures this — Optional works in Spring REST controllers
// @RequestBody UserDto dto where dto has Optional<String> fields — works in Spring Boot

Java Serialization

// Fails with NotSerializableException:
class Report implements Serializable {
    private Optional<String> comment;  // Optional is not Serializable!
}

// Fix option 1: transient + custom readObject/writeObject
class Report implements Serializable {
    private transient Optional<String> comment;
    private String commentValue;  // store raw value

    private void writeObject(ObjectOutputStream oos) throws IOException {
        commentValue = comment.orElse(null);
        oos.defaultWriteObject();
    }
    private void readObject(ObjectInputStream ois) throws Exception {
        ois.defaultReadObject();
        comment = Optional.ofNullable(commentValue);
    }
}

// Fix option 2: don't use Optional as field — use getter pattern

JPA / Hibernate

// WRONG — JPA cannot map Optional fields
@Entity
public class User {
    @Column
    private Optional<String> nickname;  // JPA will fail or ignore this
}

// CORRECT — Use Optional only in getter
@Entity
public class User {
    @Column
    private String nickname;

    public Optional<String> getNickname() {
        return Optional.ofNullable(nickname);
    }
}
Part 13

Primitive Optionals: OptionalInt, OptionalLong, OptionalDouble

To avoid boxing overhead, Java provides three primitive-specialised Optional variants:

OptionalInt    optInt    = OptionalInt.of(42);
OptionalLong   optLong   = OptionalLong.of(1_000_000L);
OptionalDouble optDouble = OptionalDouble.of(3.14);

OptionalInt empty = OptionalInt.empty();

// Getting values:
int val  = optInt.getAsInt();        // throws NoSuchElementException if empty
int safe = optInt.orElse(-1);
int lazy = optInt.orElseGet(() -> computeDefault());
optInt.ifPresent(v -> System.out.println(v));

// Important: primitive Optionals lack map, flatMap, filter!
// They only have: isPresent, isEmpty, getAs*, orElse, orElseGet, orElseThrow, ifPresent, stream

Comparison: Optional vs Primitive Optionals

Feature Optional<T> OptionalInt
Boxing overhead Yes (Integer, Long, etc.) None
map/flatMap/filter Yes No
Interop with Stream stream() → Stream<T> stream() → IntStream
Use case General objects Numeric computation results 
// Return from IntStream operations:
OptionalInt max = IntStream.of(3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9).max();
// max is OptionalInt, not Optional<Integer> — no boxing

// When to return OptionalInt from your own methods:
public OptionalInt findFirstPositiveIndex(int[] arr) {
    for (int i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) {
        if (arr[i] > 0) return OptionalInt.of(i);
    }
    return OptionalInt.empty();
}

Part 15

Common Pitfalls

Pitfall 1: Calling get() Without isPresent()

Optional<String> opt = findValue();
String v = opt.get();   // NoSuchElementException if empty — no better than NPE

// Fix: use orElse/orElseGet/orElseThrow/map instead

Pitfall 2: Using Optional.of() on a Possibly-Null Value

String maybeNull = legacyApi.getValue();
Optional<String> opt = Optional.of(maybeNull);   // NPE if maybeNull is null!
// Fix: use Optional.ofNullable(maybeNull)

Pitfall 3: isPresent() + get() Pattern

// Anti-pattern — verbose and imperative
if (userOpt.isPresent()) {
    doSomething(userOpt.get());
}
// Fix: userOpt.ifPresent(this::doSomething);

Pitfall 4: orElse With Side Effects

// Pitfall: updateDatabase() always called, even when opt is present
String name = nameOpt.orElse(updateDatabase("default"));
// Fix: orElseGet(() -> updateDatabase("default"))

Pitfall 5: Returning null From a Method That Declares Optional Return Type

// NEVER do this — callers get a null Optional reference, not Optional.empty()
public Optional<User> findUser(Long id) {
    User u = dao.find(id);
    if (u == null) return null;    // BAD: breaks Optional contract
    return Optional.of(u);
}
// Fix: return Optional.ofNullable(u) or Optional.empty()

Pitfall 6: Nested Optionals

// Optional<Optional<String>> — deeply wrong
Optional<Optional<String>> nested = Optional.of(Optional.of("value"));
// This can happen if you call map() with a function returning Optional<T>
// Fix: use flatMap() instead of map()
Optional<String> correct = outer.flatMap(inner -> inner);
Part 16

Performance Considerations

Optional<T> is an object wrapper — every Optional.of() allocates a new object on the heap. For performance-critical code (tight loops, high-frequency trading, low-latency paths), this has measurable overhead.

Allocation cost:
  Optional.of("value") → allocates 16 bytes (header) + 8 bytes (reference) = ~24 bytes
  For 1 million calls/second → 24 MB/s additional GC pressure

JIT optimisation:
  Modern JVMs (Graal JIT, C2) can sometimes escape-analyse Optional and eliminate
  the heap allocation entirely when Optional is consumed in the same stack frame.
  This is not guaranteed — profile before assuming JIT will save you.

Guidelines

Scenario Recommendation
Method return type — application layer Use Optional<T> freely
Method return type — numeric result Use OptionalInt/Long/Double
Inner loop, millions of calls/second Avoid Optional; use null + sentinel
Domain model field Never use Optional
Stream pipeline integration Use Optional.stream() for flatMap
Cache / Map value Use null or sentinel, not Optional
Part 17

Java Version Evolution

Version Feature
Java 8 Optional<T>, OptionalInt, OptionalLong, OptionalDouble: of, ofNullable, empty, isPresent, get, orElse, orElseGet, orElseThrow, map, flatMap, filter, ifPresent
Java 9 or(Supplier<Optional<T>>), ifPresentOrElse(Consumer, Runnable), stream()
Java 10 orElseThrow() no-arg overload (throws NoSuchElementException)
Java 11 isEmpty() — explicit check for empty state
Part 18

When to Use Optional: Decision Guide

Is this a METHOD RETURN TYPE?
├── YES → Does the method legitimately have "no result" as a valid outcome?
│         ├── YES → Use Optional<T>
│         └── NO  → Return T, throw exception for invalid states
└── NO (field, parameter, collection element)
      └── Do NOT use Optional
            ├── Field → use null + Optional getter
            ├── Parameter → use overloading or @Nullable
            └── Collection element → filter nulls at the collection level

Is the value a primitive?
└── Use OptionalInt / OptionalLong / OptionalDouble
    (avoids boxing, but loses map/flatMap/filter)

Is the code performance-critical (< 1ms latency requirement)?
└── Avoid Optional; profile first, use null+check pattern
Part 19

Production Pattern: Repository findById and Null-Safe Chains

The most prevalent real-world use of Optional in Java enterprise code is in Spring Data repositories and null-safe service layer transformations.

Repository Layer

// Spring Data JPA auto-generates:
public interface UserRepository extends JpaRepository<User, Long> {
    Optional<User> findById(Long id);               // built-in
    Optional<User> findByEmail(String email);       // derived query
    Optional<User> findByUsernameAndActiveTrue(String username);
}

Service Layer: Null-Safe Chains

@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class UserService {

    private final UserRepository userRepository;
    private final AddressRepository addressRepository;
    private final AuditService auditService;

    // Pattern 1: orElseThrow for mandatory resource
    public User getUser(Long id) {
        return userRepository.findById(id)
            .orElseThrow(() -> new UserNotFoundException("User not found: " + id));
    }

    // Pattern 2: map + orElse for optional data
    public String getUserCity(Long userId) {
        return userRepository.findById(userId)
            .map(User::getAddressId)
            .flatMap(addressRepository::findById)
            .map(Address::getCity)
            .orElse("City not available");
    }

    // Pattern 3: ifPresent for audit/side-effects
    public void updateEmail(Long userId, String newEmail) {
        userRepository.findById(userId)
            .ifPresentOrElse(
                user -> {
                    user.setEmail(newEmail);
                    userRepository.save(user);
                    auditService.logChange(userId, "email", newEmail);
                },
                () -> { throw new UserNotFoundException("User not found: " + userId); }
            );
    }

    // Pattern 4: or() for fallback sources
    public Optional<User> findUserWithFallback(Long id, String email) {
        return userRepository.findById(id)
            .or(() -> userRepository.findByEmail(email));
    }

    // Pattern 5: flatMap Optional chain into stream
    public List<String> getActiveUserEmails() {
        return userRepository.findAll().stream()
            .map(User::getEmail)                     // String, possibly null
            .flatMap(Optional::stream)               // filter nulls via Optional.stream()
            // Alternative: .filter(Objects::nonNull)
            .collect(Collectors.toList());
    }
}

DTO Projection with Optional

public UserProfileDto buildProfile(Long userId) {
    User user = userRepository.findById(userId)
        .orElseThrow(UserNotFoundException::new);

    return UserProfileDto.builder()
        .id(user.getId())
        .name(user.getName())
        .email(user.getEmail())
        .city(Optional.ofNullable(user.getAddress())
            .map(Address::getCity)
            .orElse("Unknown"))
        .premiumSince(Optional.ofNullable(user.getPremiumSince())
            .map(LocalDate::toString)
            .orElse("N/A"))
        .build();
}
Part 20

Spring Integration: Optional Return Types and REST 404 Handling

Spring MVC Controller: 404 via Optional

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/users")
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class UserController {

    private final UserService userService;

    // Pattern 1: orElseThrow with @ResponseStatus exception
    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public UserDto getUser(@PathVariable Long id) {
        return userService.findById(id)
            .map(this::toDto)
            .orElseThrow(() -> new ResponseStatusException(
                HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, "User not found: " + id));
    }

    // Pattern 2: map to ResponseEntity
    @GetMapping("/{id}/profile")
    public ResponseEntity<UserProfileDto> getUserProfile(@PathVariable Long id) {
        return userService.findById(id)
            .map(this::toProfileDto)
            .map(ResponseEntity::ok)
            .orElse(ResponseEntity.notFound().build());
    }

    // Pattern 3: orElseGet for conditional responses
    @GetMapping("/{id}/settings")
    public UserSettingsDto getSettings(@PathVariable Long id) {
        return userService.findById(id)
            .map(User::getSettings)
            .orElseGet(UserSettingsDto::defaults);
    }

    private UserDto toDto(User user) { /* ... */ return null; }
    private UserProfileDto toProfileDto(User user) { /* ... */ return null; }
}

Spring Data — Optional in Custom Queries

public interface ProductRepository extends JpaRepository<Product, Long> {

    // Derived query — returns Optional
    Optional<Product> findBySku(String sku);

    // JPQL — returning Optional
    @Query("SELECT p FROM Product p WHERE p.sku = :sku AND p.active = true")
    Optional<Product> findActiveProduct(@Param("sku") String sku);

    // Projection with Optional
    Optional<ProductNameOnly> findProjectedBySku(String sku);
}

// Service consuming Spring Data Optional:
@Service
public class ProductService {

    private final ProductRepository productRepository;

    public ProductDto getProductBySku(String sku) {
        return productRepository.findBySku(sku)
            .map(ProductMapper::toDto)
            .orElseThrow(() -> new ProductNotFoundException(sku));
    }

    public boolean isSkuAvailable(String sku) {
        return productRepository.findBySku(sku).isEmpty();
    }
}

@Autowired Optional Dependencies (Spring DI)

// Spring allows Optional injection for optional beans:
@Service
public class NotificationService {

    private final Optional<EmailService> emailService;   // injected if bean exists
    private final Optional<SmsService> smsService;       // injected if bean exists

    public NotificationService(Optional<EmailService> emailService,
                               Optional<SmsService> smsService) {
        this.emailService = emailService;
        this.smsService   = smsService;
    }

    public void notify(String message) {
        emailService.ifPresent(s -> s.send(message));
        smsService.ifPresent(s -> s.send(message));
    }
}
Part 21

Interview Deep Dive

Q1: What is the difference between orElse and orElseGet? Give a scenario where choosing the wrong one causes a bug.

Answer: orElse(T t) evaluates its argument eagerly — t is computed before the Optional's state is even checked. orElseGet(Supplier<T> s) is lazy — the supplier is only invoked if the Optional is empty. Bug scenario: configOpt.orElse(loadConfigFromDatabase()) — this executes the database call on every invocation even when the cache hit returns a present Optional, causing unnecessary I/O. The fix is configOpt.orElseGet(() -> loadConfigFromDatabase()).

Q2: Why should Optional not be used for domain model fields?

Answer: Three reasons. First, Optional is not Serializable — using it in a JPA entity, RMI object, or Java serialized class causes NotSerializableException. Second, Optional fields can themselves be null (the reference to the Optional object can be null, not just the Optional being empty) — you still need null checks. Third, it adds per-field heap allocation with no architectural benefit; the standard pattern is to use a nullable field with an Optional-returning accessor.

Q3: Why does Java have OptionalInt, OptionalLong, and OptionalDouble in addition to Optional<T>?

Answer: Primitive optionals avoid the boxing/unboxing overhead of Optional<Integer>, Optional<Long>, and Optional<Double>. When stream terminal operations like IntStream.max() return optional numeric results, they return OptionalInt to stay in the primitive domain. The trade-off is that OptionalInt lacks map, flatMap, and filter — it only provides isPresent, isEmpty, getAsInt, orElse, orElseGet, orElseThrow, ifPresent, and stream. Use primitive optionals for numeric computation; use Optional<T> when you need functional transformation methods.

Q4: Can you use Optional with Jackson JSON serialization?

Answer: By default, Jackson cannot deserialize JSON into Optional-typed fields. With the jackson-datatype-jdk8 module (registerModule(new Jdk8Module())), Jackson supports Optional in serialization/deserialization. Spring Boot 2.x+ auto-configures the Jdk8Module, so Optional in @RequestBody DTOs and @ResponseBody return types works out of the box. Serialization: Optional.of("x") serialises as "x"; Optional.empty() serialises as null (or omitted with @JsonInclude(NON_ABSENT)).

Q5: What does Optional.or() (Java 9+) do and how does it differ from orElseGet?

Answer: or(Supplier<Optional<T>>) returns this Optional if present, or the supplier's Optional<T> if empty. Unlike orElseGet, which returns a raw value T, or() returns another Optional<T> — enabling chained fallback sources while staying in the Optional context. Example: cacheOpt.or(() -> dbOpt).or(() -> Optional.of(defaultValue)) — each level tries the next source without unwrapping. orElseGet terminates the Optional chain and produces a value.

Q6: What is the Optional.stream() method useful for?

Answer: Optional.stream() (Java 9+) converts the Optional to a Stream<T> of zero elements (if empty) or one element (if present). Its primary use is in stream pipelines that call a method returning Optional<T> — you can use flatMap(Optional::stream) to filter-out empty Optionals and unwrap present ones in a single step. Before Java 9, this required filter(Optional::isPresent).map(Optional::get), which was verbose and called get() directly.

Part 22

Summary Table

Method Availability Behavior When Present Behavior When Empty
Optional.of(v) Java 8 Returns Optional containing v N/A (v null → NPE)
Optional.ofNullable(v) Java 8 Returns Optional containing v Returns Optional.empty()
Optional.empty() Java 8 N/A Returns empty Optional
isPresent() Java 8 true false
isEmpty() Java 11 false true
get() Java 8 Returns value Throws NoSuchElementException
orElse(T) Java 8 Returns value Returns default T (evaluated eagerly)
orElseGet(Supplier) Java 8 Returns value Invokes supplier (lazy)
orElseThrow(Supplier) Java 8 Returns value Throws supplied exception
orElseThrow() Java 10 Returns value Throws NoSuchElementException
map(Function) Java 8 Applies fn; wraps result Returns empty()
flatMap(Function→Optional) Java 8 Applies fn; returns its Optional Returns empty()
filter(Predicate) Java 8 Returns this if predicate true, else empty Returns empty()
ifPresent(Consumer) Java 8 Executes consumer No-op
ifPresentOrElse(Consumer, Runnable) Java 9 Executes consumer Executes runnable
or(Supplier<Optional>) Java 9 Returns this Returns supplier's Optional
stream() Java 9 Returns single-element Stream Returns empty Stream

When to Use vs Avoid

Use Optional Do NOT Use Optional
Method return type where absence is valid Class fields
Repository findBy* return types Method parameters
Service layer null-safe chains Collection elements
REST handler 404 pattern Primitives (use OptionalInt etc.)
Optional Spring DI injection Serializable classes (unless careful)
Replacing deeply nested null checks Performance-critical inner loops

Practice — Lesson 37

Easy

E1. Write a method Optional<String> findFirstLongWord(List<String> words) that returns the first word with length > 10, or empty if none.

public Optional<String> findFirstLongWord(List<String> words) {
    return words.stream()
        .filter(w -> w.length() > 10)
        .findFirst();
}

E2. Given Optional<String> rawInput, convert its value to uppercase if present, else return "DEFAULT". Do this without isPresent() or get().

String result = rawInput.map(String::toUpperCase).orElse("DEFAULT");

E3. Use ifPresentOrElse to print either "Found: <value>" or "Nothing found" depending on an Optional<Integer>.

opt.ifPresentOrElse(
    v -> System.out.println("Found: " + v),
    ()  -> System.out.println("Nothing found")
);

Medium

M1. Implement a null-safe property accessor chain. Given objects Order → Customer → Address → PostalCode (each getter may return null or be Optional), produce the postal code or "UNKNOWN" using Optional chaining.

// Assuming getters return nullable types:
String postalCode = Optional.ofNullable(order)
    .map(Order::getCustomer)
    .map(Customer::getAddress)
    .map(Address::getPostalCode)
    .orElse("UNKNOWN");

M2. Demonstrate the orElse vs orElseGet performance trap. Write a method that shows the lazy vs eager behavior with a side-effect counter.

AtomicInteger counter = new AtomicInteger(0);
Optional<String> present = Optional.of("value");

// orElse: counter incremented even though optional is present
present.orElse(compute(counter));           // counter = 1

// orElseGet: counter NOT incremented because optional is present
present.orElseGet(() -> compute(counter));  // counter still 1

static String compute(AtomicInteger c) {
    c.incrementAndGet();
    return "default";
}

M3. Use Optional.stream() with flatMap to extract all present email addresses from a List<Optional<String>> emails.

List<String> presentEmails = emails.stream()
    .flatMap(Optional::stream)
    .collect(Collectors.toList());

Advanced

A1. Chain three fallback sources using Optional.or():

  1. Try fetching user from L1 cache
  2. If absent, try L2 cache
  3. If absent, try database
  4. If absent, return a guest user
User user = l1Cache.get(id)
    .or(() -> l2Cache.get(id))
    .or(() -> userRepository.findById(id))
    .orElseGet(User::createGuest);

A2. Write a generic utility method <T, R> Optional<R> safeMap(T value, Function<T, R> mapper) that applies a mapper to a potentially-null value and wraps the result in Optional, handling NPE from the mapper.

public static <T, R> Optional<R> safeMap(T value, Function<T, R> mapper) {
    return Optional.ofNullable(value)
        .map(v -> {
            try { return mapper.apply(v); }
            catch (NullPointerException e) { return null; }
        });
}

Production

P1. In a Spring Boot REST controller, implement GET /api/products/{sku} that returns 200 OK with the product body if found, or 404 Not Found if not. Use Optional returned from the repository.

@GetMapping("/{sku}")
public ResponseEntity<ProductDto> getProduct(@PathVariable String sku) {
    return productRepository.findBySku(sku)
        .map(productMapper::toDto)
        .map(ResponseEntity::ok)
        .orElse(ResponseEntity.notFound().build());
}

P2. Implement a caching service pattern: check Redis cache first, then fall back to database, then fall back to computed default — all using Optional chaining with or().

public UserPreferences getPreferences(Long userId) {
    return redisCache.getPreferences(userId)          // Optional<UserPreferences>
        .or(() -> preferenceRepository.findByUserId(userId))
        .or(() -> Optional.of(UserPreferences.defaults(userId)))
        .get(); // safe: last or() always provides a value
}

Debugging

D1. Identify the bug:

Optional<String> opt = getFromService();
String value = opt.get();

Bug: get() throws NoSuchElementException if Optional is empty. Fix: Use opt.orElse("default") or opt.orElseThrow(() -> new ServiceException("Value not found")).

D2. Identify the bug:

public Optional<User> findUser(Long id) {
    User user = dao.find(id);
    if (user == null) return null;
    return Optional.of(user);
}

Bug: Returning null instead of Optional.empty() — callers will get a null reference, not an empty Optional, causing NPE when they call .isPresent() or .orElse(). Fix: return Optional.ofNullable(user).

D3. Identify the bug:

@Entity
public class Customer implements Serializable {
    @Column
    private Optional<String> middleName;  // nullable middle name
}

Bug: Optional is not Serializable — JPA and Java serialization will fail. Fix: Use private String middleName; with public Optional<String> getMiddleName() { return Optional.ofNullable(middleName); }.

Interview

I1. "What does Optional.of(null) do vs Optional.ofNullable(null)?"

Optional.of(null) throws NullPointerException immediately — it's designed for values you are certain are non-null. Optional.ofNullable(null) returns Optional.empty() — it safely wraps any value that might be null. Use of when you have a post-checked non-null value; use ofNullable when bridging legacy or external code that may return null.

I2. "Why is Optional not appropriate as a method parameter?"

Optional parameters force the caller to box their value in Optional.of(...) even when they have a concrete non-null value — it adds noise without benefit. The same result can be achieved with method overloading (one version without the parameter, one with) or @Nullable annotation. Additionally, a caller can still pass null as the Optional<T> parameter itself, which is even worse than the null parameter it was trying to avoid.

I3. "How do you handle Optional in Jackson/JSON serialization in a Spring Boot application?"

Spring Boot auto-registers the jackson-datatype-jdk8 module which teaches Jackson to handle Optional. Serialization: Optional.of("x") → "x" (the value, not {"value":"x"}); Optional.empty() → null (or omitted with @JsonInclude(Include.NON_ABSENT)). Deserialization: JSON "x" → Optional.of("x"); JSON null → Optional.empty(). The key annotation for controlling null/absent rendering in Optional fields is @JsonInclude(Include.NON_ABSENT).
