Part 1

Concept: Why a New Date/Time API?

Java had date and time support from its very first release in 1995. Two decades later, Java 8 introduced java.time (JSR-310) to replace it entirely. Understanding why the old API was replaced is essential context for every decision you will make with the new one.

The Legacy Failures

java.util.Date (1995)

Date was misnamed from birth. Despite its name, a Date object actually represents a point in time — an offset in milliseconds from the Unix epoch (January 1, 1970, 00:00:00 UTC). It knows nothing useful about calendar dates, months, or years. Its getters (getYear(), getMonth(), getDay()) were deprecated in Java 1.1 because they were fundamentally broken:

// Legacy Date - everything is wrong
Date d = new Date(2024, 1, 15);  // WRONG: year is offset from 1900, month is 0-indexed
// Actual date created: March 15, 3924 — not what you intended

Date now = new Date();
now.setTime(0);  // Mutated! now == epoch. Surprise to any caller holding a reference.

// Thread-safety: zero. Two threads formatting the same Date will corrupt output.

java.util.Calendar (1996)

Introduced to fix Date, it made things worse in practice:

// Calendar verbosity
Calendar cal = Calendar.getInstance();
cal.set(2024, Calendar.JANUARY, 15);  // still 0-indexed month!
cal.set(Calendar.HOUR_OF_DAY, 10);
cal.set(Calendar.MINUTE, 30);
cal.set(Calendar.SECOND, 0);

Date result = cal.getTime();  // converts back to Date — which is still mutable

// Adding one month
cal.add(Calendar.MONTH, 1);  // mutates cal in place — silent bug if shared

The problems were structural, not cosmetic:

Problem java.util.Date java.util.Calendar
Mutable Yes — setTime() Yes — set(), add()
Thread-safe No No
Month indexing 0-based (0 = Jan) 0-based (0 = Jan)
Year offset From 1900 None
Timezone handling Implicit, surprising Verbose, error-prone
Formatting SimpleDateFormat (not thread-safe!) Same SimpleDateFormat
DST awareness Poor Partial
Fluent API None None
Separation of concerns None (date + time + epoch in one) None

java.text.SimpleDateFormat

The formatter was perhaps the most dangerous piece: it stored parse state in instance fields, making it not thread-safe. A single SimpleDateFormat instance shared between threads (a very common pattern) produced silently garbled output.

JSR-310: The Redesign Principles

Joda-Time (2002) had already proven a better design was possible. JSR-310 (led by Stephen Colebourne, the Joda-Time author) brought those ideas into the JDK:

  1. Immutability — every type is immutable and final; operations return new instances
  2. Thread-safety — immutability implies thread-safety without synchronization
  3. Separation of concerns — distinct types for date-only, time-only, date+time, instant, duration, period
  4. Fluent API — method chaining reads like prose
  5. ISO-8601 by default — the international standard for date/time representation
  6. Timezone-explicit — timezone is a first-class concept, not an afterthought
  7. No magic constants — Month.JANUARY instead of 0, DayOfWeek.MONDAY instead of 2
Part 2

The `java.time` Type Hierarchy

The package ships with a rich type system where each type has a precise, non-overlapping responsibility.

╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║                    java.time TYPE HIERARCHY                                  ║
╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║                                                                              ║
║  HUMAN TIME (calendar-based)          MACHINE TIME (epoch-based)            ║
║  ─────────────────────────────        ───────────────────────────           ║
║                                                                              ║
║  LocalDate          ────────────────────────────────────────►               ║
║  (year-month-day)    2024-01-15                                             ║
║                                                                              ║
║  LocalTime          ────────────────────────────────────────►               ║
║  (hour-min-sec-nano) 10:30:00.000000000                                     ║
║                                                                              ║
║  LocalDateTime      ────────────────────────────────────────►               ║
║  (date + time)       2024-01-15T10:30:00        NO timezone                 ║
║                                                                              ║
║  OffsetDateTime     ────────────────────────────────────────►               ║
║  (date+time+offset)  2024-01-15T10:30:00+05:30  Fixed offset                ║
║                                                                              ║
║  ZonedDateTime      ────────────────────────────────────────►               ║
║  (date+time+zone)    2024-01-15T10:30:00+05:30[Asia/Kolkata]  Full DST      ║
║                                                                              ║
║  Instant            ────────────────────────────────────────►               ║
║  (epoch nanoseconds) 1705312200Z     ← always UTC, no calendar              ║
║                                                                              ║
╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║  AMOUNTS OF TIME                                                             ║
║  ─────────────                                                               ║
║  Period    → "2 years, 3 months, 5 days"   (date-based, calendar-aware)     ║
║  Duration  → "PT36H30M15.123456789S"       (time-based, nanosecond precise) ║
╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║  SUPPORTING TYPES                                                            ║
║  ────────────────                                                            ║
║  ZoneId        → "America/New_York", "Asia/Kolkata", "UTC"                  ║
║  ZoneOffset    → "+05:30", "-08:00", "Z"                                    ║
║  Month         → enum: JANUARY..DECEMBER                                    ║
║  DayOfWeek     → enum: MONDAY..SUNDAY                                       ║
║  MonthDay      → "--03-14" (recurring date without year)                    ║
║  YearMonth     → "2024-01" (month without day)                              ║
║  Clock         → injectable time source (for testing)                       ║
║  DateTimeFormatter → thread-safe formatting/parsing                         ║
╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝

The most important mental model: LocalDateTime is NOT an instant. It is a description of a wall-clock reading with no timezone attached. The same LocalDateTime value of 2024-03-10T02:30:00 does not even exist in America/New_York (it falls in the DST gap). Only ZonedDateTime and Instant represent unambiguous points in time.

Part 3

`LocalDate`: Calendar Dates Without Time

LocalDate represents a date in the ISO calendar: year, month, and day of month. It has no time, no timezone, no epoch milliseconds.

import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.time.Month;
import java.time.DayOfWeek;

// ── Creation ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
LocalDate today = LocalDate.now();                    // system clock, system TZ
LocalDate specific = LocalDate.of(2024, 1, 15);      // preferred: type-safe
LocalDate withEnum = LocalDate.of(2024, Month.JANUARY, 15);  // even clearer
LocalDate parsed = LocalDate.parse("2024-01-15");    // ISO-8601 default

// ── Reading fields ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
int year       = today.getYear();           // 2024
Month month    = today.getMonth();          // JANUARY
int monthNum   = today.getMonthValue();     // 1
int day        = today.getDayOfMonth();     // 15
DayOfWeek dow  = today.getDayOfWeek();      // MONDAY
int dayOfYear  = today.getDayOfYear();      // 15
boolean isLeap = today.isLeapYear();        // false (2024 is a leap year → true)

// ── Arithmetic (always returns new LocalDate) ──────────────────────────────
LocalDate nextWeek    = today.plusWeeks(1);
LocalDate nextMonth   = today.plusMonths(1);
LocalDate lastQuarter = today.minusMonths(3);
LocalDate lastDay     = today.withDayOfMonth(today.lengthOfMonth()); // last day

// ── Comparisons ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
LocalDate deadline = LocalDate.of(2024, 12, 31);
boolean overdue    = today.isAfter(deadline);
boolean inRange    = today.isAfter(LocalDate.of(2024, 1, 1))
                  && today.isBefore(deadline);

// ── Temporal adjusters ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import java.time.temporal.TemporalAdjusters;
LocalDate firstOfMonth  = today.with(TemporalAdjusters.firstDayOfMonth());
LocalDate lastOfMonth   = today.with(TemporalAdjusters.lastDayOfMonth());
LocalDate nextMonday    = today.with(TemporalAdjusters.next(DayOfWeek.MONDAY));
LocalDate firstMondayOfMonth = today.with(TemporalAdjusters.firstInMonth(DayOfWeek.MONDAY));

When to use LocalDate: Birthdates, contract dates, holidays, settlement dates, any date where time-of-day is irrelevant. Never use LocalDate when you need to represent "when something happened" — that requires an Instant.

Part 4

`LocalTime`: Time of Day Without a Date

LocalTime represents a time-of-day reading: hours, minutes, seconds, and nanoseconds. It has no date, no timezone.

import java.time.LocalTime;

// ── Creation ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
LocalTime now          = LocalTime.now();
LocalTime cutoff       = LocalTime.of(17, 30);              // 17:30:00
LocalTime precise      = LocalTime.of(10, 15, 30, 500_000); // nanoseconds
LocalTime midnight     = LocalTime.MIDNIGHT;                 // 00:00
LocalTime noon         = LocalTime.NOON;                     // 12:00
LocalTime parsed       = LocalTime.parse("17:30:00");

// ── Reading ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
int hour   = cutoff.getHour();          // 17
int minute = cutoff.getMinute();        // 30
int second = cutoff.getSecond();        // 0
int nano   = precise.getNano();         // 500000

// ── Arithmetic ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
LocalTime nextHour  = now.plusHours(1);
LocalTime earlier   = now.minusMinutes(45);

// ── Comparison ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
boolean afterCutoff = LocalTime.now().isAfter(LocalTime.of(17, 30));

// Banking example: check if order arrives before cut-off
LocalTime orderTime = LocalTime.of(14, 0);
LocalTime cutOff    = LocalTime.of(15, 30);
boolean sameDay     = orderTime.isBefore(cutOff);  // true → same-day settlement

Key point: LocalTime wraps around midnight. LocalTime.of(23, 59).plusMinutes(2) returns 00:01, not an exception. There is no concept of overflow into the next day — use Duration if you need to track that.

Part 5

`LocalDateTime`: Date and Time Without Timezone

LocalDateTime combines a LocalDate and a LocalTime in one object. It still carries no timezone information.

import java.time.LocalDateTime;

// ── Creation ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
LocalDateTime now       = LocalDateTime.now();
LocalDateTime dt        = LocalDateTime.of(2024, 1, 15, 10, 30, 0);
LocalDateTime fromParts = LocalDateTime.of(
    LocalDate.of(2024, 1, 15),
    LocalTime.of(10, 30)
);
LocalDateTime parsed    = LocalDateTime.parse("2024-01-15T10:30:00");

// ── Decomposition ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
LocalDate datePart = dt.toLocalDate();  // 2024-01-15
LocalTime timePart = dt.toLocalTime();  // 10:30

// ── Arithmetic ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
LocalDateTime nextWeek = dt.plusWeeks(1);
LocalDateTime later    = dt.plusHours(36).minusMinutes(15);

// ── Conversion to ZonedDateTime ────────────────────────────────────────────
import java.time.ZoneId;
ZonedDateTime zdt = dt.atZone(ZoneId.of("America/New_York"));
// Now it's a real point in time

// ── Common mistake ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
// WRONG: storing LocalDateTime as a database timestamp
// The value "2024-03-10T02:30:00" doesn't exist in New York (DST gap)
// Always use Instant or ZonedDateTime for timestamps

Use LocalDateTime for: Scheduled future events where the timezone is separately known and stored (e.g., "meeting at 2pm in the user's local time"), display values after converting from ZonedDateTime, or configuration file values.

Part 6

`Instant`: Machine Time (The Epoch Point)

Instant represents a single, unambiguous point on the global timeline — nanoseconds since the Unix epoch (1970-01-01T00:00:00Z). It is always UTC. It has no concept of years, months, or days.

import java.time.Instant;
import java.time.temporal.ChronoUnit;

// ── Creation ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Instant now    = Instant.now();                    // current moment, UTC
Instant epoch  = Instant.EPOCH;                    // 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z
Instant future = Instant.parse("2025-01-01T00:00:00Z");
Instant fromMs = Instant.ofEpochMilli(1705312200000L);
Instant fromSec = Instant.ofEpochSecond(1705312200L);
Instant fromSecNano = Instant.ofEpochSecond(1705312200L, 500_000_000L); // + 0.5s

// ── Reading ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
long epochSec  = now.getEpochSecond();
int  nanoAdj   = now.getNano();            // nanosecond-of-second
long epochMs   = now.toEpochMilli();       // legacy bridge

// ── Arithmetic ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Instant oneHourLater = now.plusSeconds(3600);
Instant tenMsLater   = now.plusMillis(10);
Instant truncated    = now.truncatedTo(ChronoUnit.SECONDS); // chop nanos

// ── Comparisons ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
boolean expired = Instant.now().isAfter(future);
long diffMs     = future.toEpochMilli() - now.toEpochMilli();

// ── Converting to/from ZonedDateTime ────────────────────────────────────────
ZonedDateTime inNewYork = now.atZone(ZoneId.of("America/New_York"));
ZonedDateTime inKolkata = now.atZone(ZoneId.of("Asia/Kolkata"));
// Both represent the same moment — only the display differs

// ── Bridge to legacy java.util.Date ───────────────────────────────────────
java.util.Date legacyDate = java.util.Date.from(now);
Instant back              = legacyDate.toInstant();

Golden rule: Store timestamps as Instant (or as UTC in the database). Display them by converting to ZonedDateTime in the user's timezone. Never store LocalDateTime as a timestamp — it loses timezone context permanently.

Part 7

`ZonedDateTime` and `OffsetDateTime`

ZoneId and ZoneOffset

import java.time.ZoneId;
import java.time.ZoneOffset;

// ZoneId: full timezone with DST rules
ZoneId utc       = ZoneId.of("UTC");
ZoneId newYork   = ZoneId.of("America/New_York");
ZoneId kolkata   = ZoneId.of("Asia/Kolkata");
ZoneId systemTz  = ZoneId.systemDefault();

// ZoneOffset: fixed numeric offset, no DST rules
ZoneOffset plus530 = ZoneOffset.of("+05:30");
ZoneOffset utcOff  = ZoneOffset.UTC;           // +00:00
ZoneOffset minus8  = ZoneOffset.ofHours(-8);

// List all available zone IDs
Set<String> allZones = ZoneId.getAvailableZoneIds();  // 600+

ZonedDateTime

ZonedDateTime is a LocalDateTime plus a ZoneId. It is the richest, most correct type for user-facing timestamp display.

import java.time.ZonedDateTime;

// ── Creation ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ZonedDateTime now     = ZonedDateTime.now(ZoneId.of("America/New_York"));
ZonedDateTime meeting = ZonedDateTime.of(
    LocalDateTime.of(2024, 3, 10, 9, 0),
    ZoneId.of("America/New_York")
);
ZonedDateTime parsed  = ZonedDateTime.parse("2024-01-15T10:30:00+05:30[Asia/Kolkata]");

// ── Timezone conversion ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ZonedDateTime inLondon  = meeting.withZoneSameInstant(ZoneId.of("Europe/London"));
ZonedDateTime inKolkata = meeting.withZoneSameInstant(ZoneId.of("Asia/Kolkata"));
// Same instant, different display — this is correct

// vs. changing the zone while keeping the local clock reading (RARE use case)
ZonedDateTime changedZone = meeting.withZoneSameLocal(ZoneId.of("Europe/London"));
// Different instant — the meeting moved in real time!

// ── DST awareness ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
// Adding 1 day across a DST transition — ZonedDateTime handles correctly
ZonedDateTime beforeDST  = ZonedDateTime.of(2024, 3, 9, 10, 0, 0, 0,
                               ZoneId.of("America/New_York"));
ZonedDateTime afterDST   = beforeDST.plusDays(1);
// beforeDST offset = -05:00, afterDST offset = -04:00 (clocks spring forward)

// ── Converting to Instant for storage ─────────────────────────────────────
Instant forStorage = meeting.toInstant();

OffsetDateTime

Use OffsetDateTime when you need a fixed offset (no DST rules) — common in APIs and JSON serialization:

import java.time.OffsetDateTime;

OffsetDateTime odt    = OffsetDateTime.now(ZoneOffset.UTC);
OffsetDateTime withOff = OffsetDateTime.of(2024, 1, 15, 10, 30, 0, 0, ZoneOffset.of("+05:30"));
String iso             = odt.toString();  // 2024-01-15T05:00:00Z

// JDBC / JPA: OffsetDateTime maps cleanly to TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE

ZonedDateTime vs OffsetDateTime: Use ZonedDateTime for user interfaces and scheduling (DST matters). Use OffsetDateTime for API contracts, JSON, and database columns that store timezone offset but don't need DST rules.

Part 8

`Duration` and `Period`: Amounts of Time

Duration — Time-Based Amount

Duration measures an amount of time in seconds and nanoseconds. It does not know about months or years — it is purely a number of seconds (and nanos).

import java.time.Duration;

// ── Creation ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Duration twoHours   = Duration.ofHours(2);
Duration tenMinutes = Duration.ofMinutes(10);
Duration precise    = Duration.ofSeconds(3, 500_000_000L); // 3.5 seconds
Duration parsed     = Duration.parse("PT2H30M");           // ISO-8601 duration

// ── Between two temporal objects ──────────────────────────────────────────
Instant start = Instant.now();
// ... some work ...
Instant end   = Instant.now();
Duration elapsed = Duration.between(start, end);

LocalTime t1 = LocalTime.of(9, 0);
LocalTime t2 = LocalTime.of(17, 30);
Duration workday = Duration.between(t1, t2);  // PT8H30M

// ── Reading ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
long totalSeconds = elapsed.getSeconds();
long totalMinutes = elapsed.toMinutes();     // total minutes (not the "minute" part)
long totalHours   = elapsed.toHours();
long partialNanos = elapsed.getNano();       // nano-of-second (0–999_999_999)
long totalNanos   = elapsed.toNanos();       // careful: can overflow for long durations

// ── Arithmetic ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Duration doubled   = twoHours.multipliedBy(2);
Duration halfHour  = twoHours.dividedBy(4);
Duration combined  = twoHours.plus(tenMinutes);

// ── Negative durations ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Duration negative  = Duration.ofHours(-1);
boolean isNeg      = negative.isNegative();  // true
Duration abs       = negative.abs();

Period — Date-Based Amount

Period measures an amount of time in years, months, and days. It respects calendar arithmetic.

import java.time.Period;

// ── Creation ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Period twoYears   = Period.ofYears(2);
Period sixMonths  = Period.ofMonths(6);
Period twoWeeks   = Period.ofWeeks(2);    // stored as 14 days
Period complex    = Period.of(1, 6, 15);  // 1 year, 6 months, 15 days
Period parsed     = Period.parse("P1Y6M15D");

// ── Between two dates ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
LocalDate birth    = LocalDate.of(1990, 6, 15);
LocalDate today    = LocalDate.now();
Period age         = Period.between(birth, today);
System.out.printf("Age: %d years, %d months, %d days%n",
    age.getYears(), age.getMonths(), age.getDays());

// ── Adding to a date ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
LocalDate renewalDate = LocalDate.of(2024, 1, 15).plus(Period.ofYears(1));
// 2025-01-15 — correctly handles leap years

// ── Duration vs Period: the crucial difference ─────────────────────────────
LocalDate start = LocalDate.of(2024, 1, 31);
LocalDate end   = start.plusMonths(1);   // 2024-02-29 (leap year)
Period p = Period.between(start, end);   // P1M (1 month) — calendar-aware
// Duration can't be used between LocalDates — it needs time components

The key difference in a table:

Aspect Duration Period
Represents Seconds + nanoseconds Years + months + days
Fixed? Yes — 1 hour = 3600 sec always No — 1 month varies (28–31 days)
Works with Instant, LocalTime, LocalDateTime LocalDate, LocalDateTime
DST-aware No Yes (via calendar)
Use for Timeouts, latencies, SLAs Ages, contract terms, billing cycles
Part 9

`DateTimeFormatter`: Thread-Safe Formatting and Parsing

SimpleDateFormat was not thread-safe. DateTimeFormatter is immutable and thread-safe — a single instance can be safely shared as a static final field.

import java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter;
import java.time.format.FormatStyle;
import java.util.Locale;

// ── Predefined formatters (ISO-8601) ───────────────────────────────────────
String isoDate     = LocalDate.now().format(DateTimeFormatter.ISO_LOCAL_DATE);
// "2024-01-15"
String isoDateTime = LocalDateTime.now().format(DateTimeFormatter.ISO_LOCAL_DATE_TIME);
// "2024-01-15T10:30:00"
String isoInstant  = Instant.now().toString();
// "2024-01-15T05:00:00Z" — Instant.toString() uses ISO_INSTANT

// ── Custom patterns ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DateTimeFormatter usDate   = DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("MM/dd/yyyy");
DateTimeFormatter euDate   = DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("dd.MM.yyyy");
DateTimeFormatter readable = DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("dd MMM yyyy, HH:mm");
DateTimeFormatter withZone = DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss z");

String formatted = LocalDate.of(2024, 1, 15).format(usDate);  // "01/15/2024"

// ── Locale-sensitive formatting ────────────────────────────────────────────
DateTimeFormatter localizedFr = DateTimeFormatter
    .ofLocalizedDate(FormatStyle.FULL)
    .withLocale(Locale.FRANCE);
String frDate = LocalDate.of(2024, 1, 15).format(localizedFr);
// "lundi 15 janvier 2024"

DateTimeFormatter localizedUs = DateTimeFormatter
    .ofLocalizedDateTime(FormatStyle.MEDIUM)
    .withLocale(Locale.US);

// ── Parsing ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DateTimeFormatter fmt = DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("MM/dd/yyyy");
LocalDate parsed = LocalDate.parse("01/15/2024", fmt);

// Parsing ZonedDateTime
DateTimeFormatter zdtFmt = DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss VV");
ZonedDateTime zdt = ZonedDateTime.parse("2024-01-15 10:30:00 America/New_York", zdtFmt);

// ── Safe static singleton pattern ─────────────────────────────────────────
// Formatter is immutable — safe as static final
public class DateUtils {
    public static final DateTimeFormatter ISO_DATE_TIME_MILLIS =
        DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ss.SSS");

    public static final DateTimeFormatter AUDIT_LOG_FORMAT =
        DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("yyyyMMdd_HHmmss_SSS");
}

// ── Pattern reference ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
// y  = year       M  = month (text if MM = 01, MMM = Jan, MMMM = January)
// d  = day        H  = hour-of-day (0-23)   h = hour-of-am/pm (1-12)
// m  = minute     s  = second               S  = fraction-of-second
// E  = day-of-week (E = Mon, EEEE = Monday)
// z  = timezone name   Z = zone offset (+0530)  VV = zone ID (Asia/Kolkata)
// '  = literal text delimiter
Part 10

Timezone Best Practices: Store UTC, Display Local

This is the single most important operational rule when working with date/time in production systems.

╔════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║               PRODUCTION TIMEZONE STRATEGY                                 ║
╠════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║                                                                            ║
║   USER INPUT                   STORAGE              DISPLAY                ║
║   ──────────                   ───────              ───────                ║
║                                                                            ║
║  "Jan 15, 2024"           →   Instant (UTC)    →  ZonedDateTime           ║
║  "10:30 AM IST"                epoch nanos          (user's TZ)           ║
║  ZoneId: Asia/Kolkata          2024-01-15           2024-01-15            ║
║                                T05:00:00Z           T10:30:00             ║
║                                                     +05:30[Asia/Kolkata]  ║
║                                                                            ║
║  ┌──────────────┐   atZone()    ┌──────────────┐                          ║
║  │  ZonedDateTime│  .toInstant()│    Instant    │  DB Column:             ║
║  │  (input TZ)  │ ───────────► │   (UTC only)  │  TIMESTAMP / BIGINT     ║
║  └──────────────┘              └──────────────┘                          ║
║                                       │                                   ║
║                                       │  .atZone(userTZ)                 ║
║                                       ▼                                   ║
║                                ┌──────────────┐                          ║
║                                │  ZonedDateTime│  → DateTimeFormatter    ║
║                                │  (display TZ) │  → String for UI        ║
║                                └──────────────┘                          ║
╚════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝

// Complete UTC store/retrieve/display pattern

public class EventService {

    // STORE: always convert to UTC Instant before persisting
    public void createEvent(LocalDateTime userInput, ZoneId userZone) {
        ZonedDateTime userZdt    = userInput.atZone(userZone);
        Instant       utcInstant = userZdt.toInstant();
        // Persist utcInstant.toEpochMilli() or utcInstant.toString() to DB
    }

    // DISPLAY: convert UTC Instant to user's timezone on retrieval
    public String displayEvent(long epochMillis, ZoneId userZone) {
        Instant       utcInstant = Instant.ofEpochMilli(epochMillis);
        ZonedDateTime userZdt    = utcInstant.atZone(userZone);
        return userZdt.format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("dd MMM yyyy, HH:mm z"));
    }
}

Why this matters:
- DST transitions: storing UTC means your stored value never changes when a timezone's offset changes
- Timezone database updates: the IANA timezone database changes periodically; UTC + ZoneId at read time means you always apply the current rules
- Multi-region: users in Tokyo and London see the same event at their correct local times

Part 11

`Clock`: Dependency Injection for Time (Testability)

Hard-coding Instant.now() or LocalDate.now() in production code makes tests brittle — they pass only if run at the right time. The Clock abstraction solves this.

import java.time.Clock;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.time.ZoneId;

// ── Built-in Clock implementations ────────────────────────────────────────
Clock systemClock   = Clock.systemUTC();                      // real time, UTC
Clock systemDefault = Clock.systemDefaultZone();              // real time, system TZ
Clock fixedClock    = Clock.fixed(
    Instant.parse("2024-01-15T10:00:00Z"),
    ZoneId.of("UTC")
);                                                            // always returns the same instant
Clock offsetClock   = Clock.offset(systemClock,
    java.time.Duration.ofHours(5));                          // shifted by 5 hours
Clock tickClock     = Clock.tick(systemClock,
    java.time.Duration.ofSeconds(1));                        // truncated to whole seconds

// ── Injecting Clock into a service ────────────────────────────────────────
public class SubscriptionService {
    private final Clock clock;  // injected — never hardcoded

    public SubscriptionService(Clock clock) {
        this.clock = clock;
    }

    public boolean isExpired(Instant expiryTime) {
        return Instant.now(clock).isAfter(expiryTime);
    }

    public LocalDate todayInUserZone(ZoneId userZone) {
        return LocalDate.now(clock.withZone(userZone));
    }
}

// ── In production Spring wiring ───────────────────────────────────────────
@Configuration
public class ClockConfig {
    @Bean
    public Clock clock() {
        return Clock.systemUTC();
    }
}

// ── In unit tests ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
@Test
void testExpiredSubscription() {
    Clock fixed = Clock.fixed(
        Instant.parse("2024-06-01T00:00:00Z"), ZoneId.of("UTC")
    );
    SubscriptionService svc = new SubscriptionService(fixed);
    Instant expiry = Instant.parse("2024-05-31T23:59:59Z");
    assertTrue(svc.isExpired(expiry));  // deterministic — no flakiness
}

Rule: Never call Instant.now(), LocalDate.now(), or LocalDateTime.now() directly in a service class. Always inject a Clock and call now(clock). This one practice eliminates an entire class of flaky tests.

Part 12

`TemporalAdjusters` and Custom Adjusters

TemporalAdjusters provides factory methods for the most common date adjustment patterns. You can also write your own.

import java.time.temporal.TemporalAdjusters;
import java.time.temporal.TemporalAdjuster;
import java.time.temporal.Temporal;

LocalDate date = LocalDate.of(2024, 1, 15);

// ── Built-in adjusters ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
LocalDate firstOfMonth  = date.with(TemporalAdjusters.firstDayOfMonth());   // 2024-01-01
LocalDate lastOfMonth   = date.with(TemporalAdjusters.lastDayOfMonth());    // 2024-01-31
LocalDate firstOfYear   = date.with(TemporalAdjusters.firstDayOfYear());    // 2024-01-01
LocalDate lastOfYear    = date.with(TemporalAdjusters.lastDayOfYear());     // 2024-12-31
LocalDate nextFriday    = date.with(TemporalAdjusters.next(DayOfWeek.FRIDAY));
LocalDate prevMonday    = date.with(TemporalAdjusters.previous(DayOfWeek.MONDAY));
LocalDate nextOrSameFri = date.with(TemporalAdjusters.nextOrSame(DayOfWeek.FRIDAY));
LocalDate thirdWednesday = date.with(TemporalAdjusters.dayOfWeekInMonth(3, DayOfWeek.WEDNESDAY));
LocalDate lastSunday    = date.with(TemporalAdjusters.lastInMonth(DayOfWeek.SUNDAY));

// ── Custom adjuster: next business day ────────────────────────────────────
public class NextBusinessDay implements TemporalAdjuster {

    private static final Set<DayOfWeek> WEEKEND = EnumSet.of(
        DayOfWeek.SATURDAY, DayOfWeek.SUNDAY
    );

    @Override
    public Temporal adjustInto(Temporal temporal) {
        LocalDate date = LocalDate.from(temporal);
        do {
            date = date.plusDays(1);
        } while (WEEKEND.contains(date.getDayOfWeek()));
        return temporal.with(date);
    }
}

// Usage:
LocalDate nextBizDay = LocalDate.of(2024, 1, 12)  // Friday
    .with(new NextBusinessDay());                   // 2024-01-15 (Monday)

// ── Lambda-style adjuster ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
TemporalAdjuster endOfQuarter = t -> {
    LocalDate d = LocalDate.from(t);
    int month = ((d.getMonthValue() - 1) / 3 + 1) * 3;  // 3, 6, 9, or 12
    return d.withMonth(month).with(TemporalAdjusters.lastDayOfMonth());
};
LocalDate q1End = LocalDate.of(2024, 2, 15).with(endOfQuarter); // 2024-03-31
Part 13

Banking and Financial Use Cases

The java.time API is the foundation of every serious financial application. These patterns appear directly in production banking code.

import java.time.*;
import java.time.temporal.*;

public class BankingDateCalculator {

    private static final ZoneId NY_ZONE = ZoneId.of("America/New_York");

    // ── Same-day ACH cut-off check ──────────────────────────────────────────
    // ACH same-day cut-off is typically 4:45 PM ET
    public boolean isEligibleForSameDayACH(Instant submissionTime) {
        ZonedDateTime eastern     = submissionTime.atZone(NY_ZONE);
        LocalTime     cutoff      = LocalTime.of(16, 45);
        DayOfWeek     day         = eastern.getDayOfWeek();
        boolean       isWeekend   = day == DayOfWeek.SATURDAY
                                 || day == DayOfWeek.SUNDAY;
        boolean       beforeCutoff = eastern.toLocalTime().isBefore(cutoff);
        return !isWeekend && beforeCutoff;
    }

    // ── Settlement date: T+2 business days ────────────────────────────────
    public LocalDate settlementDate(LocalDate tradeDate, int businessDaysToAdd) {
        LocalDate date = tradeDate;
        int added = 0;
        while (added < businessDaysToAdd) {
            date = date.plusDays(1);
            DayOfWeek dow = date.getDayOfWeek();
            if (dow != DayOfWeek.SATURDAY && dow != DayOfWeek.SUNDAY) {
                added++;
            }
        }
        return date;
    }

    // ── Loan maturity date: "1 year, 6 months from today" ─────────────────
    public LocalDate loanMaturityDate(LocalDate origination, Period term) {
        return origination.plus(term);
        // Period correctly handles month-end: Jan 31 + 1 month = Feb 28/29
    }

    // ── Interest accrual days (actual/365 or actual/actual) ───────────────
    public long daysAccrued(LocalDate from, LocalDate to) {
        return ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(from, to);  // always exact
    }

    // ── Statement period: first to last day of month ──────────────────────
    public record StatementPeriod(LocalDate start, LocalDate end) {}

    public StatementPeriod currentStatementPeriod() {
        LocalDate today = LocalDate.now();
        return new StatementPeriod(
            today.with(TemporalAdjusters.firstDayOfMonth()),
            today.with(TemporalAdjusters.lastDayOfMonth())
        );
    }

    // ── Check if date falls in a given range (inclusive) ──────────────────
    public boolean isInStatementPeriod(LocalDate date, StatementPeriod period) {
        return !date.isBefore(period.start()) && !date.isAfter(period.end());
    }

    // ── Convert legacy timestamp from DB (epoch millis) for display ────────
    public String formatTransactionTime(long epochMs, String userTimeZone) {
        return Instant.ofEpochMilli(epochMs)
            .atZone(ZoneId.of(userTimeZone))
            .format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("dd MMM yyyy HH:mm:ss z"));
    }
}
Part 14

Spring Boot Integration

JSON Serialization: @JsonFormat and Jackson

By default, Jackson serializes LocalDate as an array [2024,1,15]. Configure it to produce ISO strings:

// application.properties / application.yml
// spring.jackson.serialization.write-dates-as-timestamps=false
// spring.jackson.deserialization.adjust-dates-to-context-time-zone=false

// OR programmatic configuration
@Configuration
public class JacksonConfig {
    @Bean
    public ObjectMapper objectMapper() {
        return new ObjectMapper()
            .registerModule(new JavaTimeModule())
            .disable(SerializationFeature.WRITE_DATES_AS_TIMESTAMPS);
    }
}

// In your DTO
public class EventDto {

    @JsonFormat(shape = JsonFormat.Shape.STRING, pattern = "yyyy-MM-dd")
    private LocalDate eventDate;

    @JsonFormat(shape = JsonFormat.Shape.STRING, pattern = "yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ss",
                timezone = "UTC")
    private LocalDateTime scheduledAt;

    // For Instant — always serialize as ISO-8601 UTC string
    private Instant createdAt;   // renders as "2024-01-15T10:30:00Z"
}

JPA / Hibernate Mapping

import javax.persistence.*;
import java.time.*;

@Entity
@Table(name = "orders")
public class Order {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue
    private Long id;

    // Maps to DATE column — no time component
    @Column(name = "order_date")
    private LocalDate orderDate;

    // Maps to TIME column
    @Column(name = "requested_time")
    private LocalTime requestedTime;

    // Maps to TIMESTAMP column (no timezone) — CAUTION: timezone ambiguity
    @Column(name = "created_at_local")
    private LocalDateTime createdAtLocal;

    // Maps to TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE — PREFERRED for timestamps
    @Column(name = "created_at", columnDefinition = "TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE")
    private OffsetDateTime createdAt;

    // Store as epoch millis via @Column — maximum portability
    @Column(name = "event_ts_epoch")
    private Long eventTsEpoch;  // use Instant.toEpochMilli() / ofEpochMilli()

    @PrePersist
    protected void onCreate() {
        this.createdAt = OffsetDateTime.now(ZoneOffset.UTC);
    }
}

Hibernate 5+ / Spring Boot 2.5+: The hibernate-java8 types module is bundled — LocalDate, LocalDateTime, and OffsetDateTime map automatically without converters.

@DateTimeFormat for form binding (Spring MVC)

public class SearchForm {
    @DateTimeFormat(iso = DateTimeFormat.ISO.DATE)
    private LocalDate fromDate;  // binds "2024-01-15" from request param

    @DateTimeFormat(pattern = "MM/dd/yyyy")
    private LocalDate toDate;    // binds "01/15/2024"
}
Part 15

JDBC Mapping

JDBC 4.2 added native java.time support. Use PreparedStatement.setObject() / ResultSet.getObject() with the java.time types:

import java.sql.*;
import java.time.*;

public class JdbcDateTimeExample {

    // ── Writing ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    public void insertEvent(Connection conn, LocalDate date,
                            OffsetDateTime timestamp) throws SQLException {
        String sql = "INSERT INTO events (event_date, created_at) VALUES (?, ?)";
        try (PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement(sql)) {
            ps.setObject(1, date);       // JDBC 4.2 — LocalDate → DATE
            ps.setObject(2, timestamp);  // OffsetDateTime → TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE
            ps.executeUpdate();
        }
    }

    // ── Reading ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    public void readEvents(Connection conn) throws SQLException {
        String sql = "SELECT event_date, created_at FROM events";
        try (PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement(sql);
             ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery()) {
            while (rs.next()) {
                LocalDate      date  = rs.getObject("event_date", LocalDate.class);
                OffsetDateTime ts    = rs.getObject("created_at", OffsetDateTime.class);

                // Convert for display
                ZonedDateTime  local = ts.atZoneSameInstant(ZoneId.of("America/New_York"));
                System.out.println(date + " → " + local);
            }
        }
    }

    // ── Legacy driver fallback (pre-JDBC 4.2 drivers) ─────────────────────
    public void insertLegacy(PreparedStatement ps, LocalDate date) throws SQLException {
        ps.setDate(1, java.sql.Date.valueOf(date));  // LocalDate → java.sql.Date
    }

    public LocalDate readLegacy(ResultSet rs) throws SQLException {
        return rs.getDate("event_date").toLocalDate(); // java.sql.Date → LocalDate
    }
}

Column type mapping reference:

java.time type SQL standard type PostgreSQL MySQL
LocalDate DATE date date
LocalTime TIME time time
LocalDateTime TIMESTAMP timestamp datetime
OffsetDateTime TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE timestamptz N/A (use DATETIME + UTC)
Instant BIGINT (epoch ms) or TIMESTAMPTZ timestamptz BIGINT
Part 16

Converting Between Legacy and Modern Types

Production codebases invariably include legacy Date and Calendar code. Here is the complete conversion reference:

import java.util.Date;
import java.util.Calendar;
import java.sql.Timestamp;
import java.time.*;

// ── java.util.Date ↔ java.time ────────────────────────────────────────────
Date legacyDate   = new Date();
Instant instant   = legacyDate.toInstant();                  // Date → Instant
ZonedDateTime zdt = legacyDate.toInstant()
    .atZone(ZoneId.systemDefault());                          // Date → ZonedDateTime
LocalDateTime ldt = LocalDateTime.ofInstant(
    legacyDate.toInstant(), ZoneId.systemDefault());          // Date → LocalDateTime

Date fromInstant  = Date.from(Instant.now());                // Instant → Date
Date fromZdt      = Date.from(ZonedDateTime.now().toInstant()); // ZonedDateTime → Date

// ── java.sql.Timestamp ↔ java.time ────────────────────────────────────────
Timestamp sqlTs       = Timestamp.from(Instant.now());        // Instant → Timestamp
Instant fromTimestamp = sqlTs.toInstant();                    // Timestamp → Instant
LocalDateTime fromTs  = sqlTs.toLocalDateTime();              // Timestamp → LocalDateTime

// ── java.sql.Date ↔ LocalDate ──────────────────────────────────────────────
java.sql.Date sqlDate   = java.sql.Date.valueOf(LocalDate.now()); // LocalDate → sql.Date
LocalDate fromSqlDate   = sqlDate.toLocalDate();                   // sql.Date → LocalDate

// ── Calendar ↔ java.time ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
Calendar cal      = Calendar.getInstance();
Instant fromCal   = cal.toInstant();                          // Calendar → Instant
ZoneId calZone    = cal.getTimeZone().toZoneId();             // TimeZone → ZoneId
ZonedDateTime zdtFromCal = ZonedDateTime.ofInstant(
    cal.toInstant(), calZone);                                // Calendar → ZonedDateTime

// ── TimeZone ↔ ZoneId ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
java.util.TimeZone legacyTz = java.util.TimeZone.getTimeZone("America/New_York");
ZoneId zoneId               = legacyTz.toZoneId();
java.util.TimeZone backToLegacy = java.util.TimeZone.getTimeZone(zoneId);

Part 18

`ChronoUnit` and `ChronoField`

import java.time.temporal.ChronoUnit;
import java.time.temporal.ChronoField;

// ── ChronoUnit: units of time ─────────────────────────────────────────────
LocalDate today    = LocalDate.now();
LocalDate deadline = LocalDate.of(2024, 12, 31);

long daysUntil    = ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(today, deadline);
long weeksUntil   = ChronoUnit.WEEKS.between(today, deadline);
long monthsUntil  = ChronoUnit.MONTHS.between(today, deadline);
long yearsUntil   = ChronoUnit.YEARS.between(today, deadline);

// ChronoUnit also works with time types
LocalTime start = LocalTime.of(9, 0);
LocalTime end   = LocalTime.of(17, 30);
long hoursWorked  = ChronoUnit.HOURS.between(start, end);   // 8
long minutesTotal = ChronoUnit.MINUTES.between(start, end); // 510

// Adding via ChronoUnit
LocalDateTime plusTenDays = LocalDateTime.now().plus(10, ChronoUnit.DAYS);
LocalDateTime truncated   = LocalDateTime.now().truncatedTo(ChronoUnit.HOURS); // chop min/sec/nano

// ── ChronoField: reading/setting specific fields ───────────────────────────
LocalDate date = LocalDate.of(2024, 3, 15);

int dayOfYear   = date.get(ChronoField.DAY_OF_YEAR);     // 75
int dayOfMonth  = date.get(ChronoField.DAY_OF_MONTH);    // 15
int monthOfYear = date.get(ChronoField.MONTH_OF_YEAR);   // 3
int year        = date.get(ChronoField.YEAR);            // 2024

// Check if a field is supported before calling get()
boolean hasHour = date.isSupported(ChronoField.HOUR_OF_DAY); // false — LocalDate has no time
Part 19

`YearMonth`, `MonthDay`, and Other Supporting Types

import java.time.YearMonth;
import java.time.MonthDay;
import java.time.Year;

// ── YearMonth: credit card expiry, billing months ─────────────────────────
YearMonth cardExpiry     = YearMonth.of(2026, 12);
YearMonth currentMonth   = YearMonth.now();
boolean   isExpired      = cardExpiry.isBefore(currentMonth);
int       daysInMonth    = currentMonth.lengthOfMonth();   // 31, 28, 29, etc.
LocalDate firstOfMonth   = currentMonth.atDay(1);
LocalDate lastOfMonth    = currentMonth.atEndOfMonth();

// ── MonthDay: birthdays, annual recurring events ──────────────────────────
MonthDay birthday     = MonthDay.of(Month.JUNE, 15);
MonthDay today        = MonthDay.now();
boolean  isBirthday   = birthday.equals(today);

// Get birthday in the current year (handles Feb 29 in non-leap years)
LocalDate thisYearBirthday = birthday.atYear(Year.now().getValue());

// ── Year ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Year year2024 = Year.of(2024);
boolean isLeap  = year2024.isLeap();           // true
int length      = year2024.length();            // 366
LocalDate start = year2024.atDay(1);            // 2024-01-01
Part 20

Common Pitfalls and Anti-Patterns

Pitfall 1: Using LocalDateTime as a Timestamp

// WRONG: LocalDateTime stored in a column named "created_at"
LocalDateTime now = LocalDateTime.now(); // Which timezone? Nobody knows.

// RIGHT
Instant now = Instant.now(); // Unambiguous UTC point in time

Pitfall 2: Mixing SimpleDateFormat with java.time

// WRONG: using the old formatter with new types
SimpleDateFormat sdf = new SimpleDateFormat("yyyy-MM-dd"); // not thread-safe
sdf.format(localDate); // won't compile — LocalDate is not java.util.Date

// RIGHT
DateTimeFormatter dtf = DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("yyyy-MM-dd");
dtf.format(localDate); // thread-safe, works

Pitfall 3: DST-Unsafe Hour Arithmetic

// WRONG: adding 24 hours to "go to tomorrow"
ZonedDateTime today   = ZonedDateTime.now(ZoneId.of("America/New_York"));
ZonedDateTime tomorrow = today.plusHours(24); // Wrong on DST transition day!
// On spring-forward day, tomorrow is 25 hours later, not 24

// RIGHT: add calendar days
ZonedDateTime tomorrow = today.plusDays(1); // Correctly handles DST

Pitfall 4: Period.between Going Negative

LocalDate earlier = LocalDate.of(2024, 1, 15);
LocalDate later   = LocalDate.of(2024, 3, 10);
Period p = Period.between(later, earlier); // WRONG order
// p.getMonths() = -1, p.getDays() = -25 — confusing negative components
// RIGHT: always pass (earlier, later)
Period correct = Period.between(earlier, later); // P1M26D

Pitfall 5: Not Handling DateTimeParseException

// WRONG: no error handling on user input
LocalDate date = LocalDate.parse(userInput); // throws DateTimeParseException on bad input

// RIGHT
try {
    LocalDate date = LocalDate.parse(userInput, DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("MM/dd/yyyy"));
} catch (DateTimeParseException e) {
    throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid date format. Expected MM/dd/yyyy", e);
}

Pitfall 6: ZoneId.of() with Invalid ID

// WRONG: hardcoding offset strings that look like zone IDs
ZoneId bad = ZoneId.of("IST"); // Ambiguous! India Standard Time? Israel? Ireland?
// Also "EST" is not a valid IANA zone ID

// RIGHT: use IANA zone names
ZoneId india   = ZoneId.of("Asia/Kolkata");    // IST = UTC+5:30
ZoneId eastern = ZoneId.of("America/New_York"); // handles EST and EDT
ZoneId utc     = ZoneId.of("UTC");             // always unambiguous
Part 21

Interview: Key Comparisons

LocalDateTime vs ZonedDateTime vs Instant

This is the most common java.time interview question.

Aspect LocalDateTime ZonedDateTime Instant
Timezone None Full IANA zone + DST Always UTC
Unique point in time? No Yes Yes
Human readable? Yes (ambiguous) Yes (unambiguous) No (epoch nanos)
Store as timestamp? Never Possible (use .toInstant()) Yes — preferred
DST-aware? No Yes N/A
Use for Appointments in local time, UI display after conversion User-facing timestamps, scheduling Logging, DB storage, event ordering

Period vs Duration

Aspect Period Duration
Semantics Calendar-based Time-based
Fixed size? No — 1 month = 28–31 days Yes — 1 hour = 3600 seconds always
Works with LocalDate Instant, LocalTime, LocalDateTime
DST? Yes (via calendar rules) No
String form P1Y2M3D PT1H30M
Negative allowed? Yes Yes

ZonedDateTime vs OffsetDateTime

Aspect ZonedDateTime OffsetDateTime
Zone info Full IANA zone (DST rules) Fixed numeric offset only
DST transitions Handled automatically Not applicable
Serialization Includes zone ID [America/New_York] Only offset +05:30
Best for Scheduling, user display APIs, JSON, DB columns
JDBC Needs conversion Maps to TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE directly

Five Rapid-Fire Interview Questions

Q1: Can the same DateTimeFormatter be used from multiple threads?
A: Yes. DateTimeFormatter is immutable and thread-safe. SimpleDateFormat was not.

Q2: What does LocalDateTime.of(2024, 3, 10, 2, 30) return for New York time?
A: A LocalDateTime object — but that wall-clock time does not exist in America/New_York during DST spring-forward. Converting it with .atZone(ZoneId.of("America/New_York")) adjusts forward to 03:30.

Q3: What is the correct way to calculate someone's exact age in years?
A: Period.between(birthDate, LocalDate.now()).getYears() — never ChronoUnit.YEARS.between() would also work but Period gives you the complete breakdown.

Q4: You receive a long epoch millisecond from a database. How do you display it in the user's timezone?
A: Instant.ofEpochMilli(ms).atZone(ZoneId.of(userTz)).format(formatter)

Q5: Why should you inject Clock instead of calling Instant.now() directly?
A: To make code testable with deterministic time — Clock.fixed() in tests, Clock.systemUTC() in production.

What Phase 3 Gave You

Design Principle: Immutability as a Default
Lessons 32–38 collectively demonstrate that immutable, value-based objects eliminate an entire class of bugs: race conditions on shared state, unexpected mutation across call sites, and formatter thread-safety issues. The java.time package is the most consistent example of this principle in the JDK.

Functional Composition Chain
Every concept in Phase 3 composes with every other:

// All of Phase 3 in one pipeline
List<String> upcomingEventSummaries = events.stream()           // Lesson 35
    .filter(e -> e.getDate().isAfter(LocalDate.now()))           // Lesson 38
    .sorted(Comparator.comparing(Event::getDate))               // Lesson 28 (revisited)
    .map(e -> Optional.ofNullable(e.getTitle())                 // Lesson 37
        .map(String::toUpperCase)                               // Lesson 34
        .orElse("UNTITLED"))
    .collect(Collectors.toList());                              // Lesson 36

Production Mindset from Phase 3
- Streams: do not reuse, avoid shared mutable state in parallel pipelines
- Optionals: never get() without isPresent(); use map/orElse instead
- Date/Time: store Instant, display ZonedDateTime, inject Clock for testability

Part 1

Concept: What Is an Exception?

Every program encounters unexpected situations: a file is missing, a network drops, a value is null, or memory runs out. Java's exception mechanism is the formal, structured answer to the question: what should a program do when something goes wrong?

Before Java, error handling in C relied on return codes. You called a function, checked its return value, and decided whether it was an error code or real data. This approach had fatal flaws: developers forgot to check return codes, error codes were ambiguous, and error-handling code was tangled with business logic.

Java introduced a class-based, compile-time-enforced exception system. Exceptional conditions are objects, not magic numbers. They carry context (message, stack trace, cause), they flow up the call stack automatically, and the type system can enforce that certain errors are handled.

The architecture is built on a single inheritance hierarchy rooted at java.lang.Throwable. Everything you can throw or catch in Java is a subtype of Throwable. This design has a few key consequences:

  • You can catch Throwable and stop anything from escaping (rarely correct, but possible)
  • You can examine any thrown object uniformly (message, stack trace, cause)
  • The JVM itself throws things from this hierarchy (e.g., OutOfMemoryError)

Understanding the hierarchy is not just theoretical. In production systems, knowing exactly what type of problem you are dealing with determines whether you retry, log-and-continue, shut down, or page an on-call engineer.

The Complete Throwable Hierarchy

            └── java.lang.Exception                    (EXPECTED — application problems)
                    ├── java.lang.RuntimeException     (UNCHECKED — programming errors)

                    │       ├── IllegalStateException

                    ├── java.io.IOException            (CHECKED — external resource failures)
                    │       ├── FileNotFoundException
