                    ├── java.sql.SQLException          (CHECKED)
                    ├── java.lang.ReflectiveOperationException (CHECKED)
                    │       ├── ClassNotFoundException
                    │       ├── NoSuchMethodException
                    │       └── IllegalAccessException
                    ├── java.lang.CloneNotSupportedException (CHECKED)
                    └── java.lang.InterruptedException (CHECKED)

This tree is the foundation. Every decision about what to catch, what to declare, and what to rethrow maps to a node in this hierarchy.

Part 3

Throwable: The Root Class

java.lang.Throwable defines the universal contract for every throwable object:

public class Throwable implements Serializable {
    // The human-readable description of the problem
    private String detailMessage;

    // The exception that caused this one (exception chaining)
    private Throwable cause;

    // The captured stack trace at the time of construction
    private StackTraceElement[] stackTrace;

    // Suppressed exceptions (added by try-with-resources)
    private List<Throwable> suppressedExceptions;

    // Core API
    public String    getMessage()       { return detailMessage; }
    public String    getLocalizedMessage() { return getMessage(); }
    public Throwable getCause()         { return cause; }
    public void      printStackTrace()  { /* writes to stderr */ }
    public StackTraceElement[] getStackTrace() { return stackTrace.clone(); }

    // Exception chaining
    public synchronized Throwable initCause(Throwable cause) { ... }

    // Suppressed exceptions (Java 7+)
    public final synchronized void addSuppressed(Throwable exception) { ... }
    public final synchronized Throwable[] getSuppressed() { ... }

    // Performance escape hatch — skip expensive stack capture
    protected Throwable(String message, Throwable cause,
                        boolean enableSuppression,
                        boolean writableStackTrace) { ... }
}

The most expensive operation when constructing an exception is capturing the stack trace (fillInStackTrace()). Every stack frame at the time of new SomeException(...) is serialized into an array of StackTraceElement objects. For deep call stacks, this can be measurable overhead. The four-argument constructor allows you to skip this for hot-path, performance-sensitive exception types.

Part 4

Error: The "Do Not Catch" Branch

Error signals a serious problem that a reasonable application cannot and should not try to recover from. The JVM itself throws Error instances when it encounters conditions that compromise the integrity of the runtime environment.

OutOfMemoryError

// JVM throws this when the heap allocator fails
// There is no "handle it" — you may not be able to allocate the catch handler itself
try {
    byte[] large = new byte[Integer.MAX_VALUE];
} catch (OutOfMemoryError e) {
    // DANGEROUS: you are already in a low-memory state
    // Logging might allocate Strings. Even catching this is unreliable.
    // The correct response at the JVM level: -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError
    System.err.println("OOM — cannot recover");
}

In production, you should configure the JVM with -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError and -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError so the process exits cleanly and leaves a heap dump for post-mortem analysis instead of limping along in an unknown state.

StackOverflowError

// Caused by infinite recursion (or recursion too deep for the stack size)
public int factorial(int n) {
    return n * factorial(n - 1);  // no base case — infinite recursion
}
// Thread stack is finite. Default stack size is 512KB–1MB depending on JVM.
// -Xss to configure: -Xss4m for deep recursive algorithms

StackOverflowError is occasionally recoverable (the thread's stack is cleared when the error propagates), but catching it usually indicates a design flaw. Fix the recursion.

NoClassDefFoundError

// Class was present at compile time but missing at runtime
// Common cause: deployment packaging error (jar not included, wrong classpath)
// Different from ClassNotFoundException (which is a checked Exception thrown by Class.forName())
Error Thrown By Recovery
OutOfMemoryError JVM heap allocator No — restart process
StackOverflowError JVM stack allocator Rarely — fix recursion
NoClassDefFoundError Class loader No — fix classpath
AssertionError assert statement No — fix code
InternalError JVM internals No — JVM bug

Rule: Never catch (Error e). Never catch (Throwable t) unless you are a framework/container root handler that will immediately rethrow or shut down.

Part 5

Exception: The "Handle Me" Branch

Exception is the parent of all conditions that application code is expected to deal with. It splits into two fundamentally different sub-branches.

The Checked Branch (direct subclasses of Exception, excluding RuntimeException)

Checked exceptions represent external failures — problems that occur at the boundary between your code and the outside world. The compiler enforces that you either handle them or declare them:

// IOException is checked — compiler forces you to acknowledge it
public String readFile(String path) throws IOException {
    return Files.readString(Path.of(path));  // throws IOException
}

// Or handle it in-place
public String readFileSafe(String path) {
    try {
        return Files.readString(Path.of(path));
    } catch (IOException e) {
        log.error("Failed to read {}", path, e);
        return "";
    }
}

The Unchecked Branch (RuntimeException and subclasses)

Unchecked exceptions represent programming errors — bugs that should not occur if the code is written correctly:

// NullPointerException — null dereference
String s = null;
s.length();  // NPE at runtime, no compile-time warning

// IllegalArgumentException — wrong input to a method
public void setAge(int age) {
    if (age < 0 || age > 150) {
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("Age must be 0–150, got: " + age);
    }
    this.age = age;
}

// ClassCastException — invalid downcast
Object obj = "hello";
Integer i = (Integer) obj;  // ClassCastException at runtime
Part 6

Common Runtime Exceptions in Detail

NullPointerException (Java 14+ Helpful NPE)

// Before Java 14: "NullPointerException" — no context
// After Java 14 (JEP 358): precise message
account.getOwner().getAddress().getCity()
// Message: Cannot invoke "Address.getCity()" because the return value of
// "Owner.getAddress()" is null

// Defensive coding
String name = Optional.ofNullable(user)
    .map(User::getName)
    .orElse("Unknown");

// Objects.requireNonNull for API boundaries
public void process(Order order) {
    Objects.requireNonNull(order, "order must not be null");
    // ...
}

IllegalArgumentException vs IllegalStateException

// IllegalArgumentException: the ARGUMENT is invalid
public void transfer(BigDecimal amount) {
    if (amount.compareTo(BigDecimal.ZERO) <= 0) {
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("Transfer amount must be positive: " + amount);
    }
}

// IllegalStateException: the OBJECT STATE is wrong for this call
public void start() {
    if (running) {
        throw new IllegalStateException("Service is already running");
    }
    this.running = true;
}

ConcurrentModificationException

List<String> list = new ArrayList<>(List.of("a", "b", "c"));
for (String s : list) {
    if (s.equals("b")) {
        list.remove(s);  // ConcurrentModificationException — modifying while iterating
    }
}

// Fix: use Iterator.remove() or removeIf()
list.removeIf(s -> s.equals("b"));  // correct
Part 7

try-catch-finally

The fundamental exception handling construct:

public Account loadAccount(long id) {
    Connection conn = null;
    try {
        conn = dataSource.getConnection();
        PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement("SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE id = ?");
        ps.setLong(1, id);
        ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery();
        if (rs.next()) {
            return mapRow(rs);
        }
        throw new AccountNotFoundException("Account not found: " + id);
    } catch (SQLException e) {
        throw new DataAccessException("Failed to load account " + id, e);  // wrap
    } finally {
        // finally ALWAYS runs — even if catch re-throws, even if return in try
        if (conn != null) {
            try { conn.close(); } catch (SQLException ignored) {}
        }
    }
}

finally Execution Guarantees

// finally runs even when:
// 1. try completes normally
// 2. try throws and catch handles it
// 3. try throws and catch re-throws
// 4. try has a return statement

public int demo() {
    try {
        return 1;     // return value captured
    } finally {
        return 2;     // OVERWRITES return from try — returns 2
        // WARNING: returning from finally suppresses exceptions!
    }
}

// This is a common interview trap. Don't return from finally in production code.

finally Does NOT Run When

  • System.exit() is called
  • The JVM is killed (SIGKILL)
  • The JVM crashes (fatal native error)
Part 8

try-with-resources (Java 7+)

try-with-resources is the modern, correct way to handle resources that implement AutoCloseable. It eliminates the resource-leak bugs that plagued finally blocks.

// OLD WAY — verbose and leak-prone
BufferedReader br = null;
try {
    br = new BufferedReader(new FileReader("file.txt"));
    return br.readLine();
} finally {
    if (br != null) {
        try { br.close(); } catch (IOException e) { /* swallow or log */ }
    }
}

// NEW WAY — try-with-resources (Java 7+)
try (BufferedReader br = new BufferedReader(new FileReader("file.txt"))) {
    return br.readLine();
}  // br.close() is called automatically, even if readLine() throws

Multiple Resources — Closing Order

// Multiple resources are closed in REVERSE declaration order
try (
    Connection conn   = dataSource.getConnection();     // opened first, closed last
    PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement(sql);  // opened second, closed first
    ResultSet rs      = ps.executeQuery()               // opened third, closed first of all
) {
    return mapResults(rs);
}
// Closing order: rs → ps → conn

Custom AutoCloseable

public class DatabaseTransaction implements AutoCloseable {
    private final Connection connection;
    private boolean committed = false;

    public DatabaseTransaction(DataSource ds) throws SQLException {
        this.connection = ds.getConnection();
        this.connection.setAutoCommit(false);
    }

    public void commit() throws SQLException {
        connection.commit();
        committed = true;
    }

    @Override
    public void close() throws SQLException {
        try {
            if (!committed) {
                connection.rollback();  // auto-rollback if not committed
            }
        } finally {
            connection.close();
        }
    }
}

// Usage — automatically rolls back if exception occurs
try (DatabaseTransaction tx = new DatabaseTransaction(dataSource)) {
    accountDao.debit(fromId, amount);
    accountDao.credit(toId, amount);
    tx.commit();
}
Part 9

Multi-catch (Java 7+)

Before Java 7, catching two unrelated exception types required duplicated handlers or catching a common supertype (often too broad):

// PRE-JAVA 7 — duplication
try {
    riskyOperation();
} catch (IOException e) {
    log.error("IO error", e);
    throw new ServiceException(e);
} catch (SQLException e) {
    log.error("DB error", e);
    throw new ServiceException(e);   // identical body
}

// JAVA 7+ MULTI-CATCH — clean and precise
try {
    riskyOperation();
} catch (IOException | SQLException e) {
    // e is effectively final — cannot reassign
    log.error("Resource error", e);
    throw new ServiceException(e);
}

Multi-catch is syntactic sugar. The bytecode creates separate catch handlers that jump to the same handler block. The variable e is typed as the common supertype of the listed exceptions (in this case, both IOException and SQLException extend Exception), but you retain the actual runtime type for logging.

Part 10

Suppressed Exceptions

When try-with-resources closes a resource and the close() method itself throws, that secondary exception is suppressed to preserve the primary exception. Without this mechanism, resource-closing exceptions would shadow the original error.

public class BrokenResource implements AutoCloseable {
    @Override
    public void close() throws Exception {
        throw new Exception("close() failed");
    }
}

try (BrokenResource r = new BrokenResource()) {
    throw new RuntimeException("primary failure");
    // close() also throws — what happens?
}
// Result: RuntimeException("primary failure") is thrown
// Exception("close() failed") is SUPPRESSED — attached to the primary

Accessing Suppressed Exceptions

try {
    try (BrokenResource r = new BrokenResource()) {
        throw new RuntimeException("primary");
    }
} catch (RuntimeException e) {
    System.out.println("Primary: " + e.getMessage());
    for (Throwable suppressed : e.getSuppressed()) {
        System.out.println("Suppressed: " + suppressed.getMessage());
    }
}
// Output:
// Primary: primary
// Suppressed: close() failed

Manually Adding Suppressed Exceptions

RuntimeException primary = new RuntimeException("main error");
primary.addSuppressed(new IOException("cleanup failed"));
primary.addSuppressed(new SQLException("rollback failed"));
throw primary;
Part 11

Exception Chaining

Exception chaining (also called wrapping or cause chain) is the mechanism for translating low-level technical exceptions into higher-level domain exceptions without losing diagnostic information.

// Three-layer architecture: REST → Service → Repository
// Each layer wraps and re-throws with context

// Repository layer
public User findById(long id) {
    try {
        return jdbcTemplate.queryForObject(SQL, rowMapper, id);
    } catch (DataAccessException e) {
        throw new UserRepositoryException("Failed to find user " + id, e);
        //                                                               ^ cause preserved
    }
}

// Service layer
public UserDTO getUser(long id) {
    try {
        User user = userRepository.findById(id);
        return mapper.toDTO(user);
    } catch (UserRepositoryException e) {
        throw new UserServiceException("User lookup failed for id=" + id, e);
    }
}

// Traversing the cause chain
try {
    userService.getUser(42L);
} catch (UserServiceException e) {
    Throwable cause = e;
    while (cause != null) {
        System.out.println(cause.getClass().getSimpleName() + ": " + cause.getMessage());
        cause = cause.getCause();
    }
}
// UserServiceException: User lookup failed for id=42
// UserRepositoryException: Failed to find user 42
// DataAccessException: ...
// SQLException: ORA-00942: table or view does not exist

The full cause chain is printed automatically by printStackTrace() and by logging frameworks. Never discard the cause when wrapping.

Part 12

The Exception Table in Bytecode

When the JVM compiles exception handling, it does not implement it with special control-flow instructions. Instead, the compiler generates an exception table alongside the bytecode for each method.

// Source
public int divide(int a, int b) {
    try {
        return a / b;
    } catch (ArithmeticException e) {
        return -1;
    }
}

// javap -c output (simplified)
public int divide(int, int);
  Code:
    0: iload_1       // push a
    1: iload_2       // push b
    2: idiv          // a / b (may throw ArithmeticException)
    3: ireturn       // return result
    4: astore_3      // store exception in local var (catch handler)
    5: iconst_m1     // push -1
    6: ireturn       // return -1

  Exception table:
     from    to  target  type
        0     3       4  ArithmeticException

The exception table has four columns:
- from / to: the bytecode range that is "guarded" (exclusive)
- target: the bytecode offset of the catch handler
- type: the exception type to match (or any for finally)

When an exception is thrown, the JVM:
1. Walks the exception table for the current method
2. Finds a matching entry (type compatible, pc within from..to range)
3. Jumps to target
4. If no match, pops the current frame and checks the calling method's table
5. Repeats until a handler is found or the thread's stack is exhausted

This is table-driven dispatch — there is no overhead for the try block itself. Cost is only paid when an exception actually occurs.

Part 13

Stack Trace Construction

When new SomeException() is called, the JVM executes fillInStackTrace():

Thread stack at time of construction:
    Frame 6: com.example.OrderService.placeOrder(OrderService.java:87)
    Frame 5: com.example.PaymentService.charge(PaymentService.java:43)
    Frame 4: com.example.StripeGateway.execute(StripeGateway.java:120)
    Frame 3: java.net.http.HttpClient.send(HttpClient.java:...)
    Frame 2: java.lang.Thread.run(Thread.java:...)
    Frame 1: ...

Each frame becomes a StackTraceElement:

StackTraceElement ste = new StackTraceElement(
    "com.example.OrderService",   // declaringClass
    "placeOrder",                 // methodName
    "OrderService.java",          // fileName
    87                            // lineNumber
);

Reading a Stack Trace

java.lang.NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "String.length()" because "s" is null
    at com.example.StringUtils.process(StringUtils.java:42)   ← where it was thrown
    at com.example.OrderService.buildDescription(OrderService.java:118)
    at com.example.OrderService.placeOrder(OrderService.java:87)
    at com.example.OrderController.order(OrderController.java:55)
    at sun.reflect.NativeMethodAccessorImpl.invoke0(Native Method)
    ...

Read from top to bottom but focus on top non-framework frames first. The first line with your package name is where the exception originated.

Truncating Stack Traces for Performance

// If you throw an exception in a hot loop (e.g., validation),
// you can pre-create a sentinel exception with no stack trace
private static final ValidationException INVALID_AMOUNT =
    new ValidationException("Amount out of range") {
        @Override
        public synchronized Throwable fillInStackTrace() {
            return this;  // skip stack capture
        }
    };
Part 14

Exception Message Best Practices

Good exception messages are diagnostic gold. Poor messages waste hours of debugging time.

// BAD: no context
throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid value");

// GOOD: include the actual invalid value and constraints
throw new IllegalArgumentException(
    "Amount must be positive and ≤ 10,000, got: " + amount);

// GOOD: include IDs so you can correlate with logs
throw new OrderNotFoundException(
    "Order not found: orderId=" + orderId + ", customerId=" + customerId);

// BAD: exception type + message say the same thing
throw new NullPointerException("Null pointer");

// GOOD: explain what was null and where it came from
throw new NullPointerException(
    "shippingAddress must not be null for order " + order.getId());

The Diagnostic Checklist

Every exception message should contain:
1. What went wrong (concise noun phrase)
2. What value caused it (the actual invalid input)
3. What was expected (the valid range or constraint)
4. Identity (IDs, keys — to enable log correlation)

Part 15

Global Exception Handlers

For production systems, uncaught exceptions must be caught at the boundary and converted into appropriate responses.

Thread-Level: UncaughtExceptionHandler

// Set globally for all threads
Thread.setDefaultUncaughtExceptionHandler((thread, throwable) -> {
    log.error("Uncaught exception in thread {}", thread.getName(), throwable);
    metrics.increment("uncaught_exceptions");
    // Optionally: graceful shutdown for fatal errors
    if (throwable instanceof Error) {
        Runtime.getRuntime().halt(1);
    }
});

// Per thread or thread pool
ExecutorService executor = Executors.newCachedThreadPool(r -> {
    Thread t = new Thread(r);
    t.setUncaughtExceptionHandler((thread, ex) ->
        log.error("Worker thread {} died", thread.getName(), ex));
    return t;
});

Logging Stack Traces Correctly

// WRONG: toString() loses the stack trace
log.error("Error: " + exception.toString());   // only logs message

// WRONG: printing message separately
log.error("Error: " + exception.getMessage()); // stack trace gone

// CORRECT: pass exception as the last argument to SLF4J
log.error("Failed to process order {}", orderId, exception);
//                                                ^ SLF4J formats this as full stack trace
Part 16

Logging Patterns in Production

// Structured logging with MDC for request correlation
public class OrderService {
    public OrderResult processOrder(Order order) {
        MDC.put("orderId", order.getId().toString());
        MDC.put("customerId", order.getCustomerId().toString());
        try {
            return doProcess(order);
        } catch (PaymentException e) {
            // Expected failure — WARN level, no stack trace noise
            log.warn("Payment declined for order {}: {}", order.getId(), e.getMessage());
            return OrderResult.paymentDeclined(e.getMessage());
        } catch (Exception e) {
            // Unexpected failure — ERROR level with full stack trace
            log.error("Unexpected error processing order {}", order.getId(), e);
            throw new OrderProcessingException("Order processing failed", e);
        } finally {
            MDC.clear();
        }
    }
}
Log Level Use Case Stack Trace?
ERROR Unexpected failure, needs investigation Yes — always
WARN Expected failure, handled gracefully Rarely
INFO Normal operation milestones No
DEBUG Detailed flow for development Sometimes
Part 17

Spring @ExceptionHandler

In Spring MVC and Spring Boot, @ExceptionHandler maps specific exception types to response-handling methods within a single controller:

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/orders")
public class OrderController {

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public OrderDTO getOrder(@PathVariable Long id) {
        return orderService.getOrder(id);
        // orderService may throw OrderNotFoundException
    }

    // Handles OrderNotFoundException only within THIS controller
    @ExceptionHandler(OrderNotFoundException.class)
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND)
    public ErrorResponse handleNotFound(OrderNotFoundException e) {
        return new ErrorResponse("NOT_FOUND", e.getMessage());
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(ValidationException.class)
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST)
    public ErrorResponse handleValidation(ValidationException e) {
        return new ErrorResponse("VALIDATION_ERROR", e.getMessage());
    }
}
Part 18

Spring @ControllerAdvice

@ControllerAdvice is a global exception handler that applies across all controllers:

@RestControllerAdvice
public class GlobalExceptionHandler {

    @ExceptionHandler(EntityNotFoundException.class)
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND)
    public ErrorResponse handleNotFound(EntityNotFoundException e, HttpServletRequest req) {
        log.warn("Entity not found: {} at {}", e.getMessage(), req.getRequestURI());
        return ErrorResponse.of("NOT_FOUND", e.getMessage());
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(ConstraintViolationException.class)
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST)
    public ErrorResponse handleValidation(ConstraintViolationException e) {
        List<String> violations = e.getConstraintViolations()
            .stream()
            .map(cv -> cv.getPropertyPath() + ": " + cv.getMessage())
            .collect(toList());
        return ErrorResponse.of("VALIDATION_FAILED", violations);
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(AccessDeniedException.class)
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.FORBIDDEN)
    public ErrorResponse handleAccessDenied(AccessDeniedException e) {
        log.warn("Access denied: {}", e.getMessage());
        return ErrorResponse.of("ACCESS_DENIED", "Insufficient permissions");
        // Do NOT expose e.getMessage() — it may reveal resource names
    }

    // Catch-all for unexpected exceptions
    @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR)
    public ErrorResponse handleGeneral(Exception e, HttpServletRequest req) {
        String traceId = MDC.get("traceId");
        log.error("Unhandled exception on {} {}", req.getMethod(), req.getRequestURI(), e);
        return ErrorResponse.of("INTERNAL_ERROR",
            "An unexpected error occurred. Reference: " + traceId);
        // Never expose exception details to clients in production
    }
}

Exception Handler Resolution Order

1. @ExceptionHandler in the same @Controller (most specific)
2. @ExceptionHandler in @ControllerAdvice (global)
3. HandlerExceptionResolver chain (DefaultHandlerExceptionResolver, ResponseStatusExceptionResolver)
4. Container default error page (Tomcat's /error endpoint)
Part 19

Exception Handling Anti-Patterns

// ANTI-PATTERN 1: Swallowing exceptions silently
try {
    importantOperation();
} catch (Exception e) {
    // NOTHING HERE — exception disappears forever
}

// ANTI-PATTERN 2: Catching and immediately rethrowing without adding value
try {
    doSomething();
} catch (IOException e) {
    throw e;  // pointless — just let it propagate
}

// ANTI-PATTERN 3: Logging then rethrowing (double-logging)
try {
    doSomething();
} catch (IOException e) {
    log.error("IO error", e);   // logged here
    throw new ServiceException(e);  // logged again upstream
    // Stack trace will appear twice in logs
}
// FIX: Either log OR rethrow, not both (unless you are the final boundary)

// ANTI-PATTERN 4: Using exceptions for flow control
for (int i = 0; ; i++) {
    try {
        process(list.get(i));  // relies on IndexOutOfBoundsException to stop
    } catch (IndexOutOfBoundsException e) {
        break;  // exceptions are expensive — use list.size()
    }
}

// ANTI-PATTERN 5: Losing the cause
try {
    doSomething();
} catch (SQLException e) {
    throw new ServiceException("DB error");  // cause lost!
    // FIX:
    throw new ServiceException("DB error", e);  // cause preserved
}
Part 20

Performance Considerations

Exception construction is expensive primarily because of fillInStackTrace():

Benchmark: new RuntimeException() per second
  With stack capture (default):   ~500,000 ops/sec
  Without stack capture:         ~50,000,000 ops/sec  (100x faster)

Stack trace capture cost scales with stack depth:
  10 frames:   ~1 µs
  50 frames:   ~5 µs
  100 frames:  ~10 µs

Guidelines for performance-sensitive code:

  1. Never use exceptions for flow control — they are 100–1000x slower than conditional checks
  2. Pre-allocate sentinel exceptions for high-frequency validation failures (override fillInStackTrace)
  3. Profile first — most code throws exceptions rarely enough that performance is irrelevant
  4. Consider Result types (e.g., Either<Error, Value>) for high-frequency expected failures
// Performance-optimized sentinel exception
public class RateLimitExceededException extends RuntimeException {
    public static final RateLimitExceededException INSTANCE =
        new RateLimitExceededException();

    private RateLimitExceededException() {
        super("Rate limit exceeded", null, true, false);
        // enableSuppression=true, writableStackTrace=false
    }
}

// Usage: throw INSTANCE instead of new RateLimitExceededException()
if (rateLimiter.isExceeded(clientId)) {
    throw RateLimitExceededException.INSTANCE;
}
Part 21

Interview Questions

Q: What is the difference between Error and Exception?

Error represents serious JVM-level failures (OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError) that application code should not attempt to catch or recover from. Exception represents application-level problems that may be expected and handled. The practical rule: never catch Error; design your application to handle Exception appropriately.

Q: When does finally NOT execute?

finally does not execute when: System.exit() is called from within the try or catch block, the JVM is forcibly killed (SIGKILL), or the JVM crashes with a fatal native error. In all normal circumstances including thrown exceptions, returns from try, and caught exceptions — finally executes.

Q: What happens if both try and finally throw exceptions?

The exception from finally replaces the one from try, and the try exception is lost. This is why you should never throw from finally. try-with-resources solves this for close() calls by suppressing the secondary exception rather than replacing the primary.

Q: What are suppressed exceptions?

Introduced in Java 7 alongside try-with-resources. When a resource's close() method throws while the try block was already throwing, the close exception is attached as a "suppressed" exception to the primary exception via addSuppressed(). Access them via getSuppressed(). This ensures the original exception is preserved while the close failure is not silently discarded.

Q: What is the exception table in bytecode?

A metadata table attached to each method that maps bytecode ranges to catch handler offsets and exception types. The JVM consults this table at runtime when an exception is thrown. There is no overhead for try blocks that never throw — cost is only paid on exception occurrence.

Q: How does try-with-resources determine close order?

Resources are closed in reverse declaration order. If you declare Connection conn, then PreparedStatement ps, then ResultSet rs, they close in order: rs, ps, conn. This mirrors nested finally blocks.

Part 22

Summary Table

Concept Key Facts
Throwable Root of all exceptions/errors; carries message, cause, stack trace, suppressed list
Error JVM-level failures; never catch; configure JVM to exit on OOM
OutOfMemoryError Heap exhausted; use -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError in production
StackOverflowError Deep/infinite recursion; increase stack with -Xss only as last resort
NoClassDefFoundError Class missing at runtime; fix classpath/packaging
Exception Application-level problems; root of checked + unchecked branches
Checked Exception Compiler-enforced; must declare throws or catch; for external failures
RuntimeException Unchecked; no compile enforcement; for programming errors
NullPointerException Most common; Java 14+ gives precise helpful messages
try-catch-finally finally always runs except System.exit() / JVM crash
try-with-resources Java 7+; closes AutoCloseable in reverse order automatically
Multi-catch Java 7+; catch (A \| B e); e is effectively final
Suppressed exceptions Java 7+; secondary close() exceptions attached to primary
Exception chaining Pass cause to constructor; never lose the root cause
Exception table Bytecode structure; no overhead for non-throwing try blocks
fillInStackTrace Expensive; skip with 4-arg constructor for hot-path exceptions
@ExceptionHandler Spring; per-controller exception mapping
@ControllerAdvice Spring; global exception handler across all controllers
SLF4J logging Pass exception as last arg; never log + rethrow (double-log)
Anti-pattern: swallow Never empty catch blocks; at minimum log the exception
Anti-pattern: flow control Never use exceptions as if/else; 100–1000x slower

Practice — Lesson 39

Easy

  1. Write a method parseInt(String s) that catches NumberFormatException and returns Optional<Integer> instead of throwing.

  2. Create a class FileLoader that reads a file path from a constructor argument, uses try-with-resources with BufferedReader, and returns all lines as List<String>.

  3. Write a simple exception hierarchy: AppException → DatabaseException → ConnectionException. Demonstrate exception chaining by throwing a ConnectionException wrapping a SQLException.

  4. Identify all the anti-patterns in this code and fix them:

try {
    String result = processData(data);
    System.out.println(result);
} catch (Exception e) {
    throw e;
}

Medium

  1. Implement a RetryTemplate that executes a Callable<T>, catches IOException, and retries up to 3 times with exponential backoff (100ms, 200ms, 400ms). On final failure, rethrow wrapped in a RetryExhaustedException.

  2. Create a BrokenCloseable that throws from close(). Demonstrate that:
    - Without try-with-resources, the close exception replaces the primary exception
    - With try-with-resources, the close exception is suppressed and accessible via getSuppressed()

  3. Write a SafeExecutor that wraps Runnable submissions to an ExecutorService, installs an UncaughtExceptionHandler, and publishes exception metrics to a Counter interface.

  4. Implement MultiCloseable that holds a list of AutoCloseable resources, closes them all in reverse order in its own close() method, and collects all close exceptions as suppressed exceptions on the first one that fails.

Advanced

  1. Design a Result<T> monad for exception-free error propagation:
Result<Order> result = Result.of(() -> orderService.getOrder(id))
    .map(Order::validate)
    .flatMap(order -> paymentService.charge(order));
result.ifFailure(e -> log.error("Failed", e));

  1. Implement a custom exception hierarchy for a payment system with:

    • PaymentException (base, unchecked)
    • InsufficientFundsException (includes requiredAmount, availableAmount)
    • CardDeclinedException (includes declineCode, gateway)
    • FraudDetectedException (includes riskScore)

    Implement a @ControllerAdvice that maps each to appropriate HTTP status codes and structured error responses.

  2. Write a benchmark comparing:

    • Conditional check (if (x == null) return default)
    • Exception-based flow control (try { ... } catch (NPE))
    • Optional-based flow (Optional.ofNullable(x).orElse(default))

    Explain the JIT compilation implications for each approach.

Production

  1. Design a global exception handling strategy for a microservice with:

    • @ControllerAdvice with typed handlers for domain exceptions
    • Trace ID injection from MDC into all error responses
    • Different response detail levels for prod vs dev profiles
    • Metrics counting by exception type using Micrometer

  2. Your application logs show OutOfMemoryError: GC overhead limit exceeded in production. Walk through your diagnosis process:

    • JVM flags to add before next deployment
    • How to analyze the heap dump
    • Common causes and their fixes
    • Circuit breaker pattern to prevent memory exhaustion

Debugging

  1. A production service returns 500 errors intermittently. The only log entry is:
ERROR c.e.OrderController - Unhandled exception on POST /api/orders
java.lang.NullPointerException: null
    at com.example.OrderService.calculateShipping(OrderService.java:156)

- What information is missing from this log?
- What code changes would improve diagnosability?
- How would Java 14's helpful NPE messages change the output?
  1. You see this exception in logs:
java.lang.ClassCastException: class java.lang.String cannot be cast to class java.lang.Integer
    at com.example.cache.CacheService.get(CacheService.java:89)

- What are the likely causes?
- How would you fix the `CacheService` to prevent this?

Interview

  1. Explain the try-with-resources mechanism at the bytecode level. How does the compiler implement it? What bytecode pattern does it generate?

  2. When would you override fillInStackTrace() to return this? What are the trade-offs? Give a concrete production scenario where this optimization is justified.

  3. Your tech lead says "we should catch Throwable at the top level of our request handler to ensure no errors escape." Is this good advice? What are the risks? What is the correct approach?

  4. Describe three different ways a finally block can suppress an exception. Why is try-with-resources superior to manual finally for resource cleanup?

  5. Design an exception strategy for a batch processing job that processes 10,000 records. Should it fail fast on the first error or continue processing? How do you aggregate errors? How do you report partial success?

Part 1

Concept: The Great Exception Debate

Java's checked exception system is one of the most controversial design decisions in the language's history. When James Gosling's team designed Java in the early 1990s, checked exceptions were considered an innovation — a way to use the type system to guarantee that programs handled error conditions. Thirty years later, checked exceptions are widely considered one of Java's biggest mistakes.

Understanding this debate is not academic. As a Solution Architect, you will design APIs, define exception hierarchies, and establish team conventions. The checked vs unchecked decision affects how code reads, how APIs evolve, how lambdas compose, and how frameworks like Spring operate. A poor choice here propagates throws declarations through dozens of layers or creates chains of swallowed exceptions.

The fundamental question: Should the compiler force callers to handle an exception, or should that be the programmer's responsibility?

Java gives two answers:
- Checked exceptions: Yes — declare it in the signature, force callers to acknowledge it
- Unchecked exceptions: No — let it propagate freely; callers decide whether to handle

Every language that came after Java chose Option 2. Kotlin, Scala, C#, Python, Go, Rust — none have checked exceptions. This near-universal rejection is itself a strong signal.

Part 2

Checked Exceptions: The Compiler Contract

A checked exception is any Exception subclass that is not RuntimeException (or its subclasses). The compiler enforces two rules:

Rule 1: If a method throws a checked exception, it must declare it:
    public void readFile(String path) throws IOException { ... }

Rule 2: If you call a method that declares checked exceptions, you must EITHER:
    (a) catch them in a try-catch block, OR
    (b) declare them in your own throws clause

// OPTION A: Catch and handle
public String loadConfig(String path) {
    try {
        return Files.readString(Path.of(path));
    } catch (IOException e) {
        log.warn("Config not found at {}, using defaults", path);
        return DEFAULT_CONFIG;
    }
}

// OPTION B: Declare and propagate
public String loadConfig(String path) throws IOException {
    return Files.readString(Path.of(path));  // declare it — caller's problem now
}

The key insight: the compiler is checking that you have acknowledged the possibility of this failure. It does not check that you have handled it well — an empty catch block satisfies the compiler.

The JDK's Checked Exceptions

java.io.IOException
    ├── FileNotFoundException        — file does not exist
    ├── SocketException              — network socket error
    ├── SocketTimeoutException       — network timeout
    ├── EOFException                 — unexpected end of stream
    └── MalformedURLException        — invalid URL format

java.sql.SQLException               — database access error
    └── SQLIntegrityConstraintViolationException
    └── SQLTimeoutException
    └── SQLSyntaxErrorException

java.lang.ReflectiveOperationException
    ├── ClassNotFoundException       — Class.forName() target missing
    ├── NoSuchMethodException        — reflection method lookup failed
    ├── NoSuchFieldException         — reflection field lookup failed
    └── IllegalAccessException       — reflection access denied

java.lang.InterruptedException      — thread interrupted during wait/sleep
java.lang.CloneNotSupportedException — clone() on non-Cloneable
java.security.GeneralSecurityException
    └── NoSuchAlgorithmException
    └── InvalidKeyException
Part 3

Unchecked Exceptions: RuntimeException and Subclasses

Unchecked exceptions are RuntimeException and all its subclasses. The compiler imposes no requirements — you can throw them from any method without declaring them, and you can ignore them without catching them.

// No throws declaration needed
public void processOrder(Order order) {
    // These can all propagate without declaration
    Objects.requireNonNull(order, "order must not be null");  // throws NPE (unchecked)
    if (order.getItems().isEmpty()) {
        throw new IllegalStateException("Cannot process empty order");  // unchecked
    }
    // ...
}

The Rationale for RuntimeException Being Unchecked

The original design intent was:

  • Checked = conditions outside the program's control (file missing, network down, DB unavailable). The program must be prepared for these.
  • Unchecked = programming bugs. If you pass null where non-null is required, that is a code defect. The program should not be "handling" NullPointerException at every call site — it should be fixed.
Checked exceptions → "this might not work even if your code is correct"
Unchecked exceptions → "this means your code is wrong"

This reasoning is sound in theory. In practice, the line blurs considerably.

Part 4

The Checked Exception Problem (Joshua Bloch / Effective Java)

Joshua Bloch's Effective Java (Item 71) states: "Use checked exceptions for recoverable conditions and runtime exceptions for programming errors." But Bloch also warns that checked exceptions are overused in the Java ecosystem.

The core problems with checked exceptions at scale:

Problem 1: Viral Propagation

// Library declares:
public interface DataStore {
    User find(long id) throws IOException, SQLException;
}

// Your service layer must now declare:
public User getUser(long id) throws IOException, SQLException {
    return dataStore.find(id);
}

// Your controller must declare:
public ResponseEntity<UserDTO> getUser(@PathVariable Long id)
        throws IOException, SQLException {
    User user = userService.getUser(id);  // throws propagate up
    return ResponseEntity.ok(mapper.toDTO(user));
}
// Spring's dispatcher servlet cannot handle IOException/SQLException meaningfully
// You've polluted your entire API surface with low-level IO concerns

Problem 2: The Swallowing Trap

Because checked exceptions must be acknowledged, developers under pressure write the worst possible code:

// THE MOST DANGEROUS PATTERN IN ALL OF JAVA
try {
    return dataStore.find(id);
} catch (IOException | SQLException e) {
    // TODO: handle this later
    // (never handled, exception silently discarded)
}
return null;

The compiler is satisfied. The user sees a NullPointerException somewhere downstream with no diagnostic context. The original error is gone forever.

Problem 3: Interface Evolution

// Version 1.0 of your interface
public interface UserRepository {
    User findById(long id);  // simple, clean
}

// Version 2.0 — you need to add checked exception
public interface UserRepository {
    User findById(long id) throws DataAccessException;
    // BREAKS ALL EXISTING IMPLEMENTATIONS
}

Adding a checked exception to an interface is a binary-incompatible change. Every implementing class must be updated. This creates enormous friction in library evolution.

Problem 4: Lambdas Cannot Propagate Checked Exceptions

List<String> paths = List.of("a.txt", "b.txt", "c.txt");

// DOES NOT COMPILE
// Files.readString throws IOException (checked)
List<String> contents = paths.stream()
    .map(path -> Files.readString(Path.of(path)))  // compiler error!
    .collect(toList());

Function<T, R> does not declare throws Exception, so any lambda that calls a checked-exception method fails to compile. This is one of the most painful friction points in modern Java.

Part 5

The Decision Framework: When to Use Each

As an architect, apply this decision tree:

Is this a PROGRAMMING ERROR (violates a contract/precondition)?
    └── YES → Use RuntimeException (unchecked)
              Examples: NullPointerException, IllegalArgumentException,
                        IllegalStateException, IndexOutOfBoundsException

Is this an EXTERNAL SYSTEM FAILURE the caller genuinely can't prevent?
    └── YES → Consider checked IF the caller has a meaningful recovery path
              Examples: File truly might not exist (FileNotFoundException)
                        Network timeout in a retry-capable context
    └── NO → Use unchecked RuntimeException

Can the caller REALISTICALLY RECOVER from this exception?
    └── NO → Use unchecked (forcing the caller to declare it adds no value)
    └── YES → Checked might be appropriate (rare in typical business applications)

Is this exception crossing a LAYER BOUNDARY?
    └── YES → Use unchecked domain exceptions (don't leak IO/SQL across layers)
    └── NO → Either works, prefer unchecked for simplicity

Concrete Recommendations

Scenario Recommendation
Validation failure (business rule) Unchecked ValidationException
Entity not found Unchecked EntityNotFoundException
Unauthorized access Unchecked AccessDeniedException
DB connection failure Unchecked DataAccessException (wrap JDBC)
File I/O in batch job Checked might be appropriate
Config file missing at startup Unchecked (can't recover anyway)
Interruptible network call Preserve InterruptedException semantics
REST API error response Always unchecked + @ExceptionHandler
Public library API Prefer unchecked; let callers opt into handling
Part 6

Wrapping Checked in Unchecked

The most common pattern in modern Java: translate checked exceptions at the boundary where you interface with APIs that use them (JDBC, legacy IO, etc.), and propagate unchecked throughout your application.

// JDBC uses checked SQLException everywhere
// Wrap at the DAO layer boundary

public class UserRepository {

    public User findById(long id) {
        String sql = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?";
        try (Connection conn = dataSource.getConnection();
             PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement(sql)) {
            ps.setLong(1, id);
            try (ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery()) {
                if (rs.next()) {
                    return mapRow(rs);
                }
                throw new UserNotFoundException("User not found: " + id);
            }
        } catch (SQLException e) {
            // Translate to unchecked — callers don't need to know about SQL
            throw new DataAccessException("Failed to find user " + id, e);
        }
        // DataAccessException is unchecked — no throws declaration needed
    }
}

The Translation Pattern

External System (checked exceptions)
         │
         ▼
    DAO / Adapter Layer
         │   catches checked exceptions
         │   wraps in unchecked domain exceptions
         ▼
    Service Layer (unchecked exceptions only)
         │
         ▼
    Controller / API Layer
         │   @ExceptionHandler / @ControllerAdvice
         ▼
    HTTP Response (no exceptions escape)

This architecture means:
- Service layer code is clean — no throws declarations
- Domain exceptions are unchecked, self-documenting, and meaningful to callers
- The original cause is always preserved for logging

Part 7

Exception Translation in Practice

// Bad: leaking low-level exceptions through layers
public interface UserService {
    User getUser(long id) throws SQLException;  // service knows about SQL?
}

// Good: clean domain exception
public interface UserService {
    User getUser(long id);  // throws UserNotFoundException (unchecked) if not found
}

// Repository implementation translates
@Repository
public class JdbcUserRepository implements UserRepository {

    public User findById(long id) {
        try {
            return jdbcTemplate.queryForObject(SQL, rowMapper, id);
        } catch (EmptyResultDataAccessException e) {
            throw new UserNotFoundException("User not found: id=" + id, e);
        } catch (DataAccessException e) {
            throw new DatabaseException("Database error finding user " + id, e);
        }
    }
}

Preserving the Root Cause

// WRONG — cause discarded
throw new ServiceException("User not found");

// WRONG — creates new exception from scratch, original SQLState and error codes lost
throw new ServiceException("User not found: " + e.getMessage());

// CORRECT — cause chained
throw new ServiceException("User not found: id=" + id, e);
//                                                      ^ e is the cause

// The full chain is logged:
// ServiceException: User not found: id=42
//   Caused by: EmptyResultDataAccessException: Incorrect result size
//   Caused by: IncorrectResultSizeDataAccessException
Part 8

The SQLException Problem

SQLException is the canonical example of a poorly designed checked exception. It is a single class that represents every possible database error — connection failures, constraint violations, syntax errors, deadlocks, timeouts — differentiated only by an integer error code and a vendor-specific SQLState string.

// SQLException's terrible design
try {
    ps.executeUpdate();
} catch (SQLException e) {
    int errorCode = e.getErrorCode();      // vendor-specific integer
    String sqlState = e.getSQLState();     // 5-char standard code, but inconsistently set

    // To handle "unique constraint violation" you need vendor-specific magic:
    if ("23000".equals(sqlState)) {        // MySQL
        throw new DuplicateKeyException(...);
    } else if ("23505".equals(sqlState)) { // PostgreSQL
        throw new DuplicateKeyException(...);
    } else if (errorCode == 1) {           // Oracle ORA-00001
        throw new DuplicateKeyException(...);
    }
    // And you have to know your database vendor
}

This is exactly why Spring Data introduced DataAccessException — a rich unchecked hierarchy that translates vendor-specific error codes into meaningful, portable exception types:

org.springframework.dao.DataAccessException (unchecked)
    ├── DataIntegrityViolationException    — constraint violation
    │       └── DuplicateKeyException      — unique constraint
    ├── QueryTimeoutException              — query took too long
    ├── DeadlockLoserDataAccessException   — transaction deadlock
    ├── EmptyResultDataAccessException     — expected row not found
    ├── IncorrectResultSizeDataAccessException
    └── TransientDataAccessException       — retry-able failures
        └── TransientDataAccessResourceException

Spring's SQLErrorCodeSQLExceptionTranslator translates SQLException → the appropriate DataAccessException subclass automatically. This is the correct architectural pattern for working with checked exceptions from external libraries.

Part 9

Spring's Philosophy: Unchecked by Default

Spring Framework made a deliberate architectural choice: use unchecked exceptions throughout. James Gosling may have invented checked exceptions, but Rod Johnson (Spring creator) rejected them for framework code.

Spring's rationale (from the Spring documentation):

> "We feel that forcing API users to write exception handling code when they are not going to be able to recover from it creates messy code and bad practice. We therefore decided to use checked exceptions only where there is a realistic chance of recovery."

In practice, Spring uses:
- DataAccessException hierarchy (all unchecked) for data access
- BeansException hierarchy (all unchecked) for IoC container
- ApplicationContextException (unchecked) for context errors
- HttpMessageNotReadableException (unchecked) for HTTP errors

Part 10

@Transactional and Exception Rollback Behavior

This is one of the most important and frequently misunderstood aspects of Spring's exception handling:

@Service
public class PaymentService {

    @Transactional
    public void processPayment(Payment payment) throws CheckedPaymentException {
        debitAccount(payment.getFromAccount(), payment.getAmount());
        creditAccount(payment.getToAccount(), payment.getAmount());
        recordTransaction(payment);

        if (fraudDetector.isSuspicious(payment)) {
            throw new CheckedPaymentException("Fraud detected");
            // WARNING: @Transactional does NOT rollback for checked exceptions by default!
        }
    }
}

The Default Rollback Rules

@Transactional default behavior:
    ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │  Exception Type       │  Rollback?           │
    │─────────────────────────────────────────────│
    │  RuntimeException     │  YES — automatic     │
    │  Error                │  YES — automatic     │
    │  Checked Exception    │  NO — commits!       │
    └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

This is a critical gotcha. If your transactional method throws a checked exception, the transaction commits by default. Your data may be in an inconsistent state.

Fixing the Rollback Behavior

// Option 1: Make exception unchecked (PREFERRED)
@Transactional
public void processPayment(Payment payment) {
    // ...
    if (fraudDetector.isSuspicious(payment)) {
        throw new FraudDetectedException("Fraud detected");  // unchecked
        // → ROLLS BACK automatically
    }
}

// Option 2: Explicit rollback for specific checked exceptions
@Transactional(rollbackFor = CheckedPaymentException.class)
public void processPayment(Payment payment) throws CheckedPaymentException {
    // ...
    throw new CheckedPaymentException("Fraud detected");  // → ROLLS BACK
}

// Option 3: Rollback for all exceptions
@Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class)
public void processPayment(Payment payment) throws CheckedPaymentException {
    // ...
}

// Option 4: Prevent rollback for specific unchecked exceptions
@Transactional(noRollbackFor = OptimisticLockingFailureException.class)
public void processPayment(Payment payment) {
    // OptimisticLockingFailureException won't trigger rollback (you handle it)
}

Architect rule: Use unchecked exceptions in @Transactional methods. Using checked exceptions creates a hidden rollback-or-commit ambiguity that causes data corruption bugs.

Part 11

REST APIs: The Unchecked Standard

In REST API development, checked exceptions are almost universally rejected. The pattern is:

  1. Throw domain-specific unchecked exceptions from service/repository code
  2. Map exceptions to HTTP responses in @ControllerAdvice
  3. Never let exceptions propagate to the HTTP layer as-is
// Domain exceptions — all unchecked
public class ApiException extends RuntimeException {
    private final String code;
    private final HttpStatus status;

    public ApiException(String code, String message, HttpStatus status) {
        super(message);
        this.code = code;
        this.status = status;
    }
    public String getCode() { return code; }
    public HttpStatus getStatus() { return status; }
}

public class ResourceNotFoundException extends ApiException {
    public ResourceNotFoundException(String resourceType, Object id) {
        super("NOT_FOUND",
              resourceType + " not found: " + id,
              HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND);
    }
}

public class ValidationException extends ApiException {
    private final List<FieldError> fieldErrors;

    public ValidationException(List<FieldError> errors) {
        super("VALIDATION_FAILED",
              "Request validation failed",
              HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST);
        this.fieldErrors = errors;
    }
    public List<FieldError> getFieldErrors() { return fieldErrors; }
}

// Global exception handler
@RestControllerAdvice
public class GlobalExceptionHandler {

    @ExceptionHandler(ApiException.class)
    public ResponseEntity<ErrorResponse> handleApiException(
            ApiException e, HttpServletRequest req) {

        ErrorResponse body = ErrorResponse.builder()
            .code(e.getCode())
            .message(e.getMessage())
            .path(req.getRequestURI())
            .timestamp(Instant.now())
            .traceId(MDC.get("traceId"))
            .build();

        if (e.getStatus().is5xxServerError()) {
            log.error("API error [{}]: {}", e.getCode(), e.getMessage(), e);
        } else {
            log.warn("API error [{}]: {}", e.getCode(), e.getMessage());
        }

        return ResponseEntity.status(e.getStatus()).body(body);
    }
}

This pattern gives you:
- Clean service and repository code (no throws declarations)
- Consistent error response format
- Centralized logging strategy
- HTTP status codes in one place

Part 12

Checked Exceptions and Lambda Expressions

This is where checked exceptions cause the most friction in modern Java:

// Function<T, R> does not declare throws
@FunctionalInterface
public interface Function<T, R> {
    R apply(T t);  // NO checked exceptions
}

// Files.readString throws IOException (checked)
// This does NOT compile:
List<String> contents = paths.stream()
    .map(path -> Files.readString(Path.of(path)))  // COMPILE ERROR
    .collect(toList());

Solutions for Lambdas with Checked Exceptions

Solution 1: Inline try-catch (Verbose but Clear)

List<String> contents = paths.stream()
    .map(path -> {
        try {
            return Files.readString(Path.of(path));
        } catch (IOException e) {
            throw new UncheckedIOException(e);  // JDK wrapper
        }
    })
    .collect(toList());

Solution 2: Utility Wrapper Method

// Reusable wrapper that converts checked to unchecked
@FunctionalInterface
public interface ThrowingFunction<T, R> {
    R apply(T t) throws Exception;

    static <T, R> Function<T, R> wrap(ThrowingFunction<T, R> f) {
        return t -> {
            try {
                return f.apply(t);
            } catch (RuntimeException e) {
                throw e;
            } catch (Exception e) {
                throw new RuntimeException(e);
            }
        };
    }
}

// Usage — clean
List<String> contents = paths.stream()
    .map(ThrowingFunction.wrap(path -> Files.readString(Path.of(path))))
    .collect(toList());

Solution 3: Sneaky Throws (Advanced)

// Abuses Java's erasure to throw checked exceptions without declaring them
// Use with extreme caution — misleads callers
@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
public static <E extends Throwable> void sneakyThrow(Throwable e) throws E {
    throw (E) e;  // unchecked cast erased at runtime
}

// Lombok's @SneakyThrows does this automatically
@SneakyThrows(IOException.class)
public String readFile(String path) {
    return Files.readString(Path.of(path));  // IOException thrown without declaration
}

@SneakyThrows is controversial. It defeats the compiler's safety checks. Use only when you know the exception won't occur or when wrapping at a higher level is guaranteed.

Solution 4: UncheckedIOException (JDK 8+)

// java.io.UncheckedIOException wraps IOException
// Use this JDK-provided wrapper instead of RuntimeException for IO
try {
    return Files.readString(Path.of(path));
} catch (IOException e) {
    throw new UncheckedIOException(e);  // standard JDK wrapper
}
Part 13

Functional Interface Workarounds Summary

Problem: Stream/Function API uses non-throwing functional interfaces
Solutions (ordered by preference):

1. UncheckedIOException — use for IOException specifically
2. ThrowingFunction.wrap() — utility pattern for any checked exception
3. Collect-then-process — materialize the stream, then process with try-catch
4. @SneakyThrows — Lombok; use sparingly; misleads callers
5. Inline try-catch — verbose but always correct

// Pattern: process with error accumulation
record ProcessResult<T>(T value, Exception error) {
    static <T> ProcessResult<T> of(Callable<T> c) {
        try {
            return new ProcessResult<>(c.call(), null);
        } catch (Exception e) {
            return new ProcessResult<>(null, e);
        }
    }
    boolean isSuccess() { return error == null; }
}

List<ProcessResult<String>> results = paths.stream()
    .map(path -> ProcessResult.of(() -> Files.readString(Path.of(path))))
    .collect(toList());

long failures = results.stream().filter(r -> !r.isSuccess()).count();
Part 14

Checked Exceptions in Interface Design

The interface is where checked exceptions cause the most long-term pain:

// Version 1 — no checked exceptions
public interface OrderRepository {
    Optional<Order> findById(UUID id);
    void save(Order order);
    void delete(UUID id);
}

// Clean implementations:
@Repository
public class JpaOrderRepository implements OrderRepository {
    // Spring Data JPA wraps DataAccessException (unchecked) automatically
    @Override
    public Optional<Order> findById(UUID id) {
        return jpaRepo.findById(id);  // no checked exceptions!
    }
}

// Test doubles are trivial:
public class InMemoryOrderRepository implements OrderRepository {
    private final Map<UUID, Order> store = new HashMap<>();

    @Override
    public Optional<Order> findById(UUID id) {
        return Optional.ofNullable(store.get(id));  // no throws needed
    }
}

If you add throws SQLException to this interface, every implementation — including your InMemoryOrderRepository test double — must declare throws SQLException even though it can never throw one. This is noise that makes testing harder.

Rule: Never put checked exceptions in public interfaces unless the checked exception type is a genuine part of the contract that the interface always imposes (rare).

Part 15

Library Design Considerations

When designing a library (as opposed to an application), the calculus changes slightly:

Application code:
    → Always use unchecked exceptions
    → @ExceptionHandler handles everything at the boundary

Library code (used by many callers):
    → Consider checked for recoverable external failures
    → But: modern libraries (Guava, Reactor, Spring) prefer unchecked
    → The trend strongly favors unchecked in library design too

The "Meaningful Recovery" Test

Before making an exception checked, ask:

  1. Can a typical caller realistically recover? If the file is missing, can they use a default? If yes, checked might be appropriate. If the answer is "call an admin and fix the deployment," checked adds zero value.

  2. Will this force boilerplate catch blocks? If every caller will just catch (IOException e) { throw new RuntimeException(e); }, you've made their lives worse.

  3. Is this crossing a network/process boundary? REST clients, RPC calls, event-driven systems — these almost never benefit from checked exceptions.

  4. Does it appear in a functional interface? Any exception appearing in a Function, Consumer, Supplier, or Predicate must be unchecked.

Part 16

Error Codes vs Exceptions

Some teams use error codes (return values) instead of exceptions for expected failure conditions, borrowing Go's (value, error) pattern:

// Go-style error handling in Java
public record Result<T>(T value, String errorCode, String errorMessage) {

    public static <T> Result<T> success(T value) {
        return new Result<>(value, null, null);
    }

    public static <T> Result<T> failure(String code, String message) {
        return new Result<>(null, code, message);
    }

    public boolean isSuccess() { return errorCode == null; }
    public boolean isFailure() { return errorCode != null; }

    public T orElseThrow() {
        if (isFailure()) throw new BusinessException(errorCode, errorMessage);
        return value;
    }
}

// Usage
Result<User> result = userService.findUser(id);
if (result.isFailure()) {
    return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND)
        .body(ErrorResponse.of(result.errorCode(), result.errorMessage()));
}
User user = result.value();

Trade-offs:

Aspect Exceptions Error Codes
Stack trace Yes — invaluable for debugging No
Composability Poor (checked) / Good (unchecked) Good
Explicit at call site Yes (checked) / No (unchecked) Yes
Performance Stack capture overhead None
null risk No result.value() may be null
Java idiom Standard Unusual for Java
Nested calls Propagates automatically Must chain manually

For most Java applications, unchecked exceptions remain the right choice. Error codes are appropriate for domain validation results that the caller must inspect to make business decisions.

Part 17

Migration Strategies: Checked to Unchecked

When you inherit a codebase that over-uses checked exceptions, migrate systematically:

Step 1: Identify the source — which external APIs emit checked exceptions?
        (JDBC, legacy libraries, old internal APIs)

Step 2: Define your unchecked exception hierarchy
        AppException → DataException, BusinessException, InfrastructureException

Step 3: Add translation at the boundary (DAO/adapter layer)
        catch (CheckedException e) → throw new UncheckedException(msg, e)

Step 4: Remove throws declarations from service interfaces
        Start with the interface — implementations follow

Step 5: Remove try-catch blocks that only re-throw
        catch (IOException e) { throw new RuntimeException(e); }
        → delete the try-catch if there's now a translation layer below

Step 6: Update @Transactional methods — ensure rollback is on unchecked exceptions

Step 7: Add @ControllerAdvice to map unchecked exceptions to HTTP responses
Part 18

Reactive Streams and Exception Handling

In reactive programming (Project Reactor, RxJava), exceptions flow through the reactive pipeline differently:

// Reactor: exceptions are terminal signals
Mono<User> userMono = Mono.fromCallable(() -> userRepository.findById(id))
    .onErrorMap(DataAccessException.class,
                e -> new UserServiceException("DB failure", e))
    .onErrorReturn(UserNotFoundException.class, User.anonymous())
    .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5))
    .onErrorMap(TimeoutException.class,
                e -> new ServiceUnavailableException("User service timeout"));

// Reactor does not support checked exceptions in operators
// All lambdas passed to map(), flatMap(), filter() must not throw checked exceptions
// Use UncheckedIOException or ThrowingFunction.wrap() when needed

In reactive pipelines, the rule is even more absolute: checked exceptions cannot propagate through reactive operators. Design your reactive APIs with unchecked exceptions from the start.

Part 19

Kotlin Interoperability Considerations

Since many Java teams adopt Kotlin, understanding the interop is important:

// Kotlin has NO checked exceptions
// Calling Java's checked exception methods from Kotlin:

fun readFile(path: String): String {
    return Files.readString(Path.of(path))  // compiles! Kotlin ignores checked
}

// This can be a footgun: the IOException is not handled or declared
// Kotlin trusts the developer — the exception still propagates at runtime

// Best practice for Kotlin-Java interoperability:
// Design Java APIs with unchecked exceptions only
// Use @Throws annotation to document exceptions for Kotlin callers
@Throws(IOException::class)
fun readFileSafe(path: String): String = Files.readString(Path.of(path))
Part 20

Performance: Checked vs Unchecked

From a pure performance standpoint, there is no difference between checked and unchecked exceptions at runtime. Both:
- Capture a stack trace on construction (fillInStackTrace())
- Use the JVM exception table for dispatch
- Carry the same overhead

The performance difference is in how they are used:

Checked exceptions → tend to be caught immediately → shorter propagation path
Unchecked exceptions → may propagate many frames → potentially more stack unwinding

But: stack unwinding is O(depth), and depth is bounded by reasonable code
The dominant cost is always fillInStackTrace(), not unwinding

Optimization opportunities (checked vs unchecked identical):
1. Override fillInStackTrace() → return this; for sentinel exceptions
2. Use static pre-allocated exception instances for rate limiting / validation
3. Use Valhalla-era value types for Result<T> (future)
Part 21

Interview Questions

Q: Why does Java have checked exceptions and no other mainstream language adopted them?

Java's checked exceptions were inspired by Modula-3 and were intended to prevent the "ignoring error returns" problem from C. The compiler contract was: if a method declares it throws an exception, callers must acknowledge it. In theory, this prevents silent error swallowing. In practice, it led to viral throws declarations, swallowed exceptions with empty catch blocks, and painful interface evolution. Every language designed after Java (Kotlin, Scala, C#, Python, Go, Swift, Rust) either omitted checked exceptions entirely or provided alternative error-handling mechanisms (Result types, Option types, monadic error handling).

Q: What is the @Transactional rollback behavior for checked exceptions?

By default, @Transactional rolls back for RuntimeException and Error but does not roll back for checked exceptions. If your transactional method throws a checked exception, the transaction commits. To change this: use @Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class) or (preferred) make your exceptions unchecked. This is one of the most common sources of data corruption bugs in Spring applications.

Q: How do you handle checked exceptions in Java Streams?

Function<T, R> does not declare throws, so you cannot directly use methods that throw checked exceptions in stream lambdas. Options: (1) wrap in a try-catch and throw UncheckedIOException or RuntimeException, (2) create a ThrowingFunction utility that wraps to unchecked, (3) use Lombok's @SneakyThrows. The idiomatic approach is wrapping to unchecked at the point of use.

Q: Should you ever use checked exceptions in a new API?

Rarely. Consider checked exceptions only when: (1) the caller can realistically recover, (2) the exception type is an inherent, unavoidable part of the API contract (e.g., InterruptedException for blocking operations on threads), and (3) the exception will not appear in functional interface contexts. In practice, most modern Java code benefits from unchecked exceptions throughout with a single @ControllerAdvice or equivalent handler at the system boundary.

Q: What is the difference between ClassNotFoundException and NoClassDefFoundError?

ClassNotFoundException is a checked Exception thrown by Class.forName(), ClassLoader.loadClass(), and similar methods when the class cannot be found on the classpath at the time of the explicit load call. You can recover from it (try a different class loader, load from a different path, use a default).

NoClassDefFoundError is an Error thrown by the JVM when a class was present during compilation but is absent at runtime. It happens during class initialization, not explicit loading. You cannot recover from it — fix your classpath/packaging.

Part 22

Summary Table

Concept Key Facts
Checked exception Subclass of Exception but not RuntimeException; compiler-enforced
Unchecked exception RuntimeException or Error; no compiler enforcement
Compiler rule Checked: must catch or throws; unchecked: no requirement
Original intent Checked = external failures; unchecked = programming errors
Joshua Bloch's view Use checked for genuinely recoverable conditions only; most are overused
Viral propagation Checked exceptions pollute throws clauses through all layers
Swallowing trap Checked enforcement leads to empty catch blocks (worse than unchecked)
Interface evolution Adding checked to interface is binary-incompatible breaking change

Practice — Lesson 40

Easy

  1. Compile and explain the error:
List<Path> paths = List.of(Path.of("a.txt"), Path.of("b.txt"));
List<String> lines = paths.stream()
    .map(p -> Files.readString(p))
    .collect(Collectors.toList());

Fix it three different ways.

  1. Write a safeParseInt(String s) method that catches NumberFormatException and returns -1. Why is this a bad pattern? What would be better design?

  2. Demonstrate the Spring @Transactional rollback behavior:
    - Method throws a checked exception → transaction commits
    - Method throws an unchecked exception → transaction rolls back
    Write integration test scenarios for each.

  3. Convert this code to use unchecked exceptions with proper exception translation:

public String readConfig(String path) throws IOException {
    return Files.readString(Path.of(path));
}
public AppConfig loadConfig(String path) throws IOException {
    return ConfigParser.parse(readConfig(path));
}
public void start(String configPath) throws IOException {
    config = loadConfig(configPath);
}

Medium

  1. Implement a complete ThrowingFunction<T, R> utility:
@FunctionalInterface
interface ThrowingFunction<T, R> {
    R apply(T t) throws Exception;
    static <T, R> Function<T, R> wrap(ThrowingFunction<T, R> f) { ... }
    static <T, R> Function<T, Optional<R>> lift(ThrowingFunction<T, R> f) { ... }
    static <T, R> Function<T, R> withDefault(ThrowingFunction<T, R> f, R defaultValue) { ... }
}

  1. Design an exception hierarchy for an e-commerce platform:
    - EcommerceException (base, unchecked)
    - ProductException, OrderException, PaymentException, InventoryException
    - Each with appropriate subtypes and constructors
    - A @ControllerAdvice that maps each to HTTP status + structured error response

  2. Implement Result<T, E extends Exception> with:
    - map(), flatMap(), filter(), orElse(), orElseThrow()
    - fromCallable() factory that wraps checked exceptions
    - Demonstrate using it in a stream pipeline

  3. Write a JDBC DAO using raw java.sql.* (no Spring), implementing full exception translation from SQLException to domain exceptions. Handle at minimum: duplicate key, not found, connection failure, constraint violation.

Advanced

  1. Implement a RetryableOperation<T> that:
    - Executes a Callable<T> (which may throw checked exceptions)
    - Distinguishes retryable from non-retryable exceptions by type
    - Retries up to N times with configurable backoff
    - Collects all attempt exceptions as suppressed on final failure
    - Supports both checked and unchecked exception types

  2. Design a @Transactional-aware exception handler for a complex service that:
    - Uses @Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class)
    - Distinguishes between rollback-triggering exceptions and "expected" business exceptions (like InsufficientFundsException) that should not trigger rollback
    - Implements the TransactionAspectSupport.currentTransactionStatus().setRollbackOnly() pattern

  3. Benchmark the following exception patterns with JMH:
    - Regular try-catch with exception that is never thrown
    - Regular try-catch where exception is thrown at 1%, 10%, 100% rate
    - Exception with stack trace disabled (fillInStackTrace() returns this)
    - Exception with pre-allocated sentinel instance
    Report your findings and architectural implications.

Production

  1. Your team is migrating a 500,000-line legacy codebase from checked exceptions to unchecked. Design the migration strategy:
    - How do you identify all throws declaration sites?
    - What is the correct order of changes?
    - How do you ensure no exceptions are silently swallowed during migration?
    - How do you validate rollback behavior of @Transactional methods?
    - What CI checks prevent regression?

  2. A microservice handles 50,000 requests/second. The team notices 2–3% of requests throw ValidationException (expected, handled gracefully). Profile the exception handling overhead and propose optimizations that don't sacrifice stack trace availability for unexpected exceptions.

Debugging

  1. In production, you observe:
WARN: Payment processed successfully
ERROR: SQLException: connection reset by peer
ERROR: DataIntegrityViolationException: ...

The order looks correct in the database but the customer was charged twice. Explain the likely root cause related to exception handling and @Transactional rollback behavior.

  1. A Spring Boot service intermittently logs:
ERROR: Unexpected rollback: Transaction silently rolled back
       because it has been marked as rollback-only

What is RollbackOnlyException? When does Spring mark a transaction as rollback-only? What code patterns cause this?

Interview

  1. "Checked exceptions are a failed experiment." Argue both sides. What would you say to a senior engineer who insists on using checked exceptions throughout a new microservice?

  2. Walk through the exact rollback behavior of this code:

@Transactional
public void transfer(long fromId, long toId, BigDecimal amount) throws InsufficientFundsException {
    Account from = accountRepo.findById(fromId);
    Account to   = accountRepo.findById(toId);
    if (from.getBalance().compareTo(amount) < 0) {
        throw new InsufficientFundsException("Insufficient funds");
    }
    from.debit(amount);
    to.credit(amount);
}

Does the transaction commit or roll back when InsufficientFundsException is thrown? What if accountRepo.findById() throws DataAccessException? What changes would you make and why?

  1. How would you design exception handling for a Kafka consumer that processes messages from a payment topic? Consider: deserialization errors, business validation errors, transient downstream failures (DB timeout), and poison pill messages.

  2. Compare Java's checked exceptions with Rust's Result<T, E> type. What problems does each solve? What problems does each create? If you were designing a new JVM language today, what would you choose?

  3. A junior developer on your team suggests: "Let's just add throws Exception to every method signature. That way we satisfy the compiler and don't have to think about it." Explain everything wrong with this approach and what the correct architectural guidance should be.
