Part 1

Concept Overview

Custom exceptions are user-defined exception classes that extend Java's built-in exception hierarchy. They allow developers to model domain-specific error conditions with meaningful names, structured data, and precise semantics that generic exceptions like IllegalArgumentException or RuntimeException cannot express alone.

At the solution-architect level, custom exceptions are not just syntactic sugar — they form a critical layer of your application's contract. They communicate intent to callers, drive API design, and form the backbone of consistent error handling across microservices.

Why custom exceptions matter:

  • Expressiveness: PaymentFailedException communicates far more than RuntimeException("payment failed")
  • Contractual clarity: Checked custom exceptions force callers to handle known failure modes
  • Structured error data: Custom fields like error codes, correlation IDs, and HTTP status codes travel with the exception
  • Testability: Tests can assert on specific exception types rather than message strings
  • Observability: Monitoring tools can differentiate exception types automatically
Exception Hierarchy — Where Custom Exceptions Fit
===================================================

        Throwable
       /         \
   Error       Exception
               /        \
   IOException        RuntimeException
        |                    |
   FileNotFoundException  IllegalArgumentException
        |                    |
   [Checked Custom]   [Unchecked Custom]
   e.g. DataAccessEx  e.g. PaymentFailedEx
Part 2

Java Exception Class Hierarchy

Understanding the full hierarchy is prerequisite to designing custom exceptions correctly.

java.lang.Throwable
 ├── java.lang.Error                     (JVM-level, don't catch)
 │    ├── OutOfMemoryError
 │    ├── StackOverflowError
 │    └── AssertionError
 └── java.lang.Exception                 (application-level)
      ├── IOException                    (checked)
      ├── SQLException                   (checked)
      ├── ReflectiveOperationException   (checked)
      └── RuntimeException               (unchecked)
           ├── NullPointerException
           ├── IllegalArgumentException
           ├── IllegalStateException
           └── UnsupportedOperationException

Key design rule: Extend Exception for checked exceptions (callers must handle or declare), extend RuntimeException for unchecked exceptions (callers can choose to handle).

Part 3

Extending Exception vs RuntimeException

This is the foundational design decision for any custom exception.

Checked Custom Exception (extends Exception)

public class InsufficientFundsException extends Exception {
    public InsufficientFundsException(String message) {
        super(message);
    }
}

Callers must either catch or declare:

public void withdraw(BigDecimal amount) throws InsufficientFundsException {
    if (amount.compareTo(balance) > 0) {
        throw new InsufficientFundsException("Balance " + balance + " < " + amount);
    }
    balance = balance.subtract(amount);
}

Unchecked Custom Exception (extends RuntimeException)

public class PaymentFailedException extends RuntimeException {
    public PaymentFailedException(String message) {
        super(message);
    }
    public PaymentFailedException(String message, Throwable cause) {
        super(message, cause);
    }
}

Callers are not forced to handle it:

public void processPayment(Payment payment) {
    if (!gateway.authorize(payment)) {
        throw new PaymentFailedException("Gateway declined: " + payment.getId());
    }
}

Decision Matrix

Factor Use Checked (Exception) Use Unchecked (RuntimeException)
Caller can meaningfully recover? Yes No
Failure is expected/predictable? Yes No
Library/API boundary? Yes (forces awareness) Sometimes
Internal service layer? No Yes
Spring/framework code? Rarely Almost always
Microservice boundary errors? No Yes

Architect rule: In modern Java and Spring, most domain exceptions extend RuntimeException. Checked exceptions are appropriate for IO, database, and explicit recovery scenarios. Spring itself wraps all checked SQLExceptions into unchecked DataAccessException.

Part 4

Exception Naming Conventions

Java conventions for naming custom exceptions are enforced by tools like Checkstyle, SpotBugs, and SonarQube.

Rules:

  1. Always end with Exception: PaymentFailedException, not PaymentFailed
  2. Use noun phrases: OrderNotFoundException, not CannotFindOrder
  3. Be specific, not generic: InsufficientFundsException not MoneyException
  4. Domain prefix for disambiguation: UserAuthenticationException, UserAuthorizationException
  5. Avoid redundancy: PaymentPaymentException is wrong

Naming patterns by category:

Domain Exceptions:
  OrderNotFoundException
  ProductOutOfStockException
  CustomerAccountLockedException
  InsufficientFundsException
  PaymentDeclinedException

Validation Exceptions:
  InvalidEmailFormatException
  RequiredFieldMissingException
  ConstraintViolationException (standard)

Infrastructure Exceptions:
  DatabaseConnectionException
  ExternalServiceUnavailableException
  MessageBrokerException
  CacheException

Security Exceptions:
  UnauthorizedAccessException
  TokenExpiredException
  InvalidCredentialsException
Part 5

Constructor Patterns: Message, Cause, Message+Cause

A well-designed custom exception provides four standard constructors following the pattern established by RuntimeException itself.

public class OrderNotFoundException extends RuntimeException {

    // 1. No-arg (rarely used, but good for serialization)
    public OrderNotFoundException() {
        super();
    }

    // 2. Message only
    public OrderNotFoundException(String message) {
        super(message);
    }

    // 3. Cause only (wrapping another exception)
    public OrderNotFoundException(Throwable cause) {
        super(cause);
    }

    // 4. Message + Cause (most common for wrapping)
    public OrderNotFoundException(String message, Throwable cause) {
        super(message, cause);
    }
}

Why all four constructors?

The cause constructor enables exception chaining — the ability to preserve the original exception while wrapping it:

try {
    Order order = orderRepository.findById(orderId);
} catch (DataAccessException ex) {
    throw new OrderNotFoundException(
        "Order not found: " + orderId, ex  // original cause preserved
    );
}

This preserves the full stack trace in the suppressed exception chain, which is critical for debugging production issues.

Suppressed exceptions (Java 7+)

// try-with-resources automatically adds suppressed exceptions
try (Connection conn = ds.getConnection()) {
    // ...
} catch (SQLException ex) {
    OrderException oe = new OrderException("DB error");
    // Suppressed exceptions appear in stack traces
    oe.addSuppressed(ex);
    throw oe;
}
Part 6

Domain-Specific Exceptions: Real-World Examples

E-Commerce Domain

// Base domain exception (abstract or concrete)
public abstract class ECommerceException extends RuntimeException {
    private final String errorCode;

    protected ECommerceException(String message, String errorCode) {
        super(message);
        this.errorCode = errorCode;
    }

    protected ECommerceException(String message, String errorCode, Throwable cause) {
        super(message, cause);
        this.errorCode = errorCode;
    }

    public String getErrorCode() {
        return errorCode;
    }
}

// Specific domain exceptions
public class InsufficientFundsException extends ECommerceException {
    private final BigDecimal available;
    private final BigDecimal required;

    public InsufficientFundsException(BigDecimal available, BigDecimal required) {
        super(
            String.format("Insufficient funds: available=%.2f, required=%.2f", available, required),
            "PAYMENT_INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS"
        );
        this.available = available;
        this.required = required;
    }

    public BigDecimal getAvailable() { return available; }
    public BigDecimal getRequired() { return required; }
    public BigDecimal getShortfall() { return required.subtract(available); }
}

public class PaymentFailedException extends ECommerceException {
    private final String gatewayCode;

    public PaymentFailedException(String message, String gatewayCode) {
        super(message, "PAYMENT_GATEWAY_FAILED");
        this.gatewayCode = gatewayCode;
    }

    public PaymentFailedException(String message, String gatewayCode, Throwable cause) {
        super(message, "PAYMENT_GATEWAY_FAILED", cause);
        this.gatewayCode = gatewayCode;
    }

    public String getGatewayCode() { return gatewayCode; }
}

public class OrderNotFoundException extends ECommerceException {
    private final String orderId;

    public OrderNotFoundException(String orderId) {
        super("Order not found: " + orderId, "ORDER_NOT_FOUND");
        this.orderId = orderId;
    }

    public String getOrderId() { return orderId; }
}

Usage in service layer:

@Service
public class PaymentService {

    public PaymentResult processPayment(String orderId, BigDecimal amount) {
        Order order = orderRepository.findById(orderId)
            .orElseThrow(() -> new OrderNotFoundException(orderId));

        BigDecimal balance = accountService.getBalance(order.getCustomerId());
        if (balance.compareTo(amount) < 0) {
            throw new InsufficientFundsException(balance, amount);
        }

        try {
            GatewayResponse response = gateway.charge(order, amount);
            if (!response.isSuccess()) {
                throw new PaymentFailedException(
                    "Gateway declined payment for order: " + orderId,
                    response.getDeclineCode()
                );
            }
            return PaymentResult.success(response.getTransactionId());
        } catch (GatewayConnectionException ex) {
            throw new PaymentFailedException(
                "Gateway unreachable for order: " + orderId,
                "GATEWAY_UNAVAILABLE",
                ex
            );
        }
    }
}
Part 7

Error Codes in Exceptions

Error codes provide machine-readable identifiers for error conditions, enabling clients to react programmatically rather than parsing message strings.

Approach 1: String error code field

public class ApiException extends RuntimeException {
    private final String errorCode;
    private final int httpStatus;

    public ApiException(String message, String errorCode, int httpStatus) {
        super(message);
        this.errorCode = errorCode;
        this.httpStatus = httpStatus;
    }

    public String getErrorCode() { return errorCode; }
    public int getHttpStatus() { return httpStatus; }
}

Approach 2: Enum-based error codes (preferred for architects)

public enum ErrorCode {
    // Payment domain
    PAYMENT_INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS(4001, "Insufficient funds for transaction"),
    PAYMENT_GATEWAY_FAILED(4002, "Payment gateway returned failure"),
    PAYMENT_CARD_EXPIRED(4003, "Payment card is expired"),

    // Order domain
    ORDER_NOT_FOUND(4041, "Order does not exist"),
    ORDER_ALREADY_CANCELLED(4091, "Order has already been cancelled"),

    // Account domain
    ACCOUNT_LOCKED(4031, "Account is locked"),
    ACCOUNT_NOT_VERIFIED(4032, "Account email not verified");

    private final int code;
    private final String defaultMessage;

    ErrorCode(int code, String defaultMessage) {
        this.code = code;
        this.defaultMessage = defaultMessage;
    }

    public int getCode() { return code; }
    public String getDefaultMessage() { return defaultMessage; }
}

public class DomainException extends RuntimeException {
    private final ErrorCode errorCode;

    public DomainException(ErrorCode errorCode) {
        super(errorCode.getDefaultMessage());
        this.errorCode = errorCode;
    }

    public DomainException(ErrorCode errorCode, String detail) {
        super(detail);
        this.errorCode = errorCode;
    }

    public DomainException(ErrorCode errorCode, String detail, Throwable cause) {
        super(detail, cause);
        this.errorCode = errorCode;
    }

    public ErrorCode getErrorCode() { return errorCode; }
}

Error code vs separate field debate

Approach Pros Cons
String in exception Simple Typo-prone, no compile-time safety
Enum in exception Type-safe, discoverable Enum grows large in big systems
Separate error catalog Centralized, i18n-ready More indirection
HTTP status only Simple for REST Not granular enough

Architect recommendation: Use enum error codes within bounded contexts; expose them as string codes in API responses.

Part 8

Exception Hierarchy Design for Microservices

In a microservices architecture, exception hierarchy design is an architectural decision.

Exception Hierarchy for Order Service
======================================

RuntimeException
 └── OrderServiceException         (base for all order service errors)
      ├── OrderDomainException     (business rule violations)
      │    ├── OrderNotFoundException
      │    ├── OrderAlreadyCancelledException
      │    └── OrderItemOutOfStockException
      ├── OrderInfrastructureException  (infra failures)
      │    ├── OrderPersistenceException
      │    └── OrderEventPublishException
      └── OrderValidationException  (input validation)
           ├── InvalidOrderAmountException
           └── MissingShippingAddressException

Implementation:

// Base exception
public abstract class OrderServiceException extends RuntimeException {
    protected OrderServiceException(String message) { super(message); }
    protected OrderServiceException(String message, Throwable cause) {
        super(message, cause);
    }
}

// Category exceptions
public abstract class OrderDomainException extends OrderServiceException {
    protected OrderDomainException(String message) { super(message); }
}

public abstract class OrderInfrastructureException extends OrderServiceException {
    protected OrderInfrastructureException(String message, Throwable cause) {
        super(message, cause);
    }
}

// Leaf exceptions
public class OrderNotFoundException extends OrderDomainException {
    private final String orderId;
    public OrderNotFoundException(String orderId) {
        super("Order not found: " + orderId);
        this.orderId = orderId;
    }
    public String getOrderId() { return orderId; }
}

public class OrderPersistenceException extends OrderInfrastructureException {
    public OrderPersistenceException(String operation, Throwable cause) {
        super("Persistence failure during: " + operation, cause);
    }
}

Cross-service exception handling

Service A ──► Service B (REST)
              │
              └─► OrderNotFoundException
                      │
                      ▼
               @ControllerAdvice maps to
               HTTP 404 + ProblemDetail JSON

Service A receives 404 + JSON body,
translates to its own domain exception:
  ExternalOrderServiceException
Part 9

Checked vs Unchecked: Architect's Perspective

Decision Tree: Checked or Unchecked?
======================================

Is this exception expected/predictable?
  │
  ├── YES → Can caller meaningfully recover?
  │          │
  │          ├── YES → Consider CHECKED (Exception)
  │          │         e.g., FileNotFoundException → try alternate
  │          │
  │          └── NO → Use UNCHECKED (RuntimeException)
  │                   e.g., InvalidStateException
  │
  └── NO → Use UNCHECKED (RuntimeException)
           e.g., NullPointerException, programming error

Modern consensus (Google, Spring, Effective Java 3rd ed):
- Use unchecked exceptions by default in application code
- Use checked exceptions only at explicit integration boundaries where recovery is documented
- Never use checked exceptions inside Spring beans (Spring wraps them all)

Part 10

Exception Serialization

Custom exceptions passed over network boundaries (RMI, serialization) must be Serializable. Even if you don't use Java serialization, this is a good habit.

public class PaymentFailedException extends RuntimeException {

    // Required for Serializable
    private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;

    private final String gatewayCode;

    public PaymentFailedException(String message, String gatewayCode) {
        super(message);
        this.gatewayCode = gatewayCode;
    }

    public PaymentFailedException(String message, String gatewayCode, Throwable cause) {
        super(message, cause);
        this.gatewayCode = gatewayCode;
    }

    public String getGatewayCode() { return gatewayCode; }
}

Warning: Custom fields in exceptions must also be serializable. BigDecimal, String, primitives are fine. Non-serializable fields (e.g., service references) must be marked transient.

Part 11

Exception Chaining and Cause Preservation

Exception chaining is the practice of wrapping a low-level exception inside a higher-level domain exception.

// BAD: loses original cause
try {
    jdbcTemplate.queryForObject(sql, params, rowMapper);
} catch (DataAccessException ex) {
    throw new OrderNotFoundException(orderId); // cause lost!
}

// GOOD: preserves cause chain
try {
    jdbcTemplate.queryForObject(sql, params, rowMapper);
} catch (DataAccessException ex) {
    throw new OrderNotFoundException(orderId, ex); // cause preserved
}

Reading the cause chain:

try {
    orderService.findById("X");
} catch (OrderNotFoundException ex) {
    Throwable cause = ex.getCause(); // DataAccessException
    Throwable root = getRootCause(ex); // may be SocketTimeoutException

    log.error("Order lookup failed", ex); // logs full chain
}

// Utility to traverse cause chain
public static Throwable getRootCause(Throwable throwable) {
    Throwable cause = throwable.getCause();
    return (cause == null) ? throwable : getRootCause(cause);
}
Part 12

Spring: @ResponseStatus

@ResponseStatus is the simplest way to map a custom exception to an HTTP status code in Spring MVC/Boot.

import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.ResponseStatus;

@ResponseStatus(
    value = HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND,
    reason = "Order not found"
)
public class OrderNotFoundException extends RuntimeException {
    public OrderNotFoundException(String orderId) {
        super("Order not found: " + orderId);
    }
}

@ResponseStatus(
    value = HttpStatus.PAYMENT_REQUIRED,
    reason = "Insufficient funds"
)
public class InsufficientFundsException extends RuntimeException {
    // ...
}

@ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY)
public class OrderValidationException extends RuntimeException {
    // ...
}

When this exception escapes a @Controller or @RestController, Spring sets the HTTP status automatically.

Limitation: @ResponseStatus on exception classes only allows static status + reason. For dynamic error bodies, use @ControllerAdvice (see Lesson 42).

Part 13

ProblemDetail (RFC 7807) in Spring 6 / Spring Boot 3

RFC 7807 defines a standard JSON format for HTTP error responses. Spring 6 (Boot 3) introduces ProblemDetail as a first-class citizen.

Standard ProblemDetail JSON:

{
  "type": "https://api.example.com/errors/insufficient-funds",
  "title": "Insufficient Funds",
  "status": 402,
  "detail": "Account balance 50.00 is less than required 100.00",
  "instance": "/payments/tx-123",
  "errorCode": "PAYMENT_INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS",
  "availableBalance": 50.00,
  "requiredAmount": 100.00
}

Implementing with custom exception + ProblemDetail:

// Exception carries the data
public class InsufficientFundsException extends RuntimeException {
    private final BigDecimal available;
    private final BigDecimal required;

    public InsufficientFundsException(BigDecimal available, BigDecimal required) {
        super(String.format("Insufficient funds: %.2f < %.2f", available, required));
        this.available = available;
        this.required = required;
    }

    public BigDecimal getAvailable() { return available; }
    public BigDecimal getRequired() { return required; }
}

// ControllerAdvice maps exception to ProblemDetail
@RestControllerAdvice
public class PaymentExceptionHandler {

    @ExceptionHandler(InsufficientFundsException.class)
    public ProblemDetail handleInsufficientFunds(
            InsufficientFundsException ex,
            HttpServletRequest request) {

        ProblemDetail problem = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(
            HttpStatus.PAYMENT_REQUIRED,
            ex.getMessage()
        );
        problem.setTitle("Insufficient Funds");
        problem.setType(URI.create("https://api.example.com/errors/insufficient-funds"));
        problem.setInstance(URI.create(request.getRequestURI()));
        problem.setProperty("errorCode", "PAYMENT_INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS");
        problem.setProperty("availableBalance", ex.getAvailable());
        problem.setProperty("requiredAmount", ex.getRequired());
        return problem;
    }
}

Enabling ProblemDetail globally in Spring Boot 3:

# application.yml
spring:
  mvc:
    problemdetails:
      enabled: true

With this enabled, Spring automatically converts built-in exceptions like MethodArgumentNotValidException to ProblemDetail format.

Part 14

Custom Exceptions in Microservices: Transport Layer

When crossing service boundaries, exceptions must be serialized to a transport format (JSON, Protobuf) and deserialized on the receiving side.

Microservice Exception Flow
============================

Order Service              API Gateway / Client
      │                           │
      │  throws                   │
      │  OrderNotFoundException   │
      │         │                 │
      │  @ControllerAdvice        │
      │  maps to HTTP 404         │
      │  + ProblemDetail JSON ──► │
      │                           │  receives 404
      │                           │  parses JSON body
      │                           │  throws OrderServiceClientException
      │                           │  (local representation)

Client-side exception mapping:

// In client library / Feign client
@FeignClient(name = "order-service")
public interface OrderServiceClient {
    @GetMapping("/orders/{id}")
    OrderResponse getOrder(@PathVariable String id);
}

// Feign error decoder
@Component
public class OrderServiceErrorDecoder implements ErrorDecoder {

    @Override
    public Exception decode(String methodKey, Response response) {
        return switch (response.status()) {
            case 404 -> new OrderNotFoundException(extractOrderId(response));
            case 402 -> new InsufficientFundsException(extractFundsDetails(response));
            case 409 -> new OrderConflictException(extractDetail(response));
            default -> new OrderServiceClientException(
                "Unexpected error from order service: " + response.status()
            );
        };
    }
}
Part 15

Exception Translation Patterns

Exception translation means converting low-level technical exceptions into domain-meaningful exceptions.

@Repository
public class JpaOrderRepository implements OrderRepository {

    private final OrderJpaRepository jpa;

    @Override
    public Order findById(String id) {
        try {
            return jpa.findById(id)
                .map(this::toDomain)
                .orElseThrow(() -> new OrderNotFoundException(id));
        } catch (JpaSystemException | DataIntegrityViolationException ex) {
            throw new OrderPersistenceException("findById:" + id, ex);
        }
    }

    @Override
    public Order save(Order order) {
        try {
            OrderEntity entity = toEntity(order);
            return toDomain(jpa.save(entity));
        } catch (DataIntegrityViolationException ex) {
            if (isDuplicateKey(ex)) {
                throw new OrderAlreadyExistsException(order.getId(), ex);
            }
            throw new OrderPersistenceException("save", ex);
        }
    }
}

Translation rules:
1. Infrastructure exceptions (JDBC, JPA) → Domain infrastructure exceptions
2. External service HTTP errors → Client exception types
3. Validation framework exceptions → Domain validation exceptions
4. Never let NullPointerException escape — it indicates a programming bug

Part 16

API Design with Custom Exceptions

Custom exceptions define your API's error contract. Document them as thoroughly as success responses.

OpenAPI documentation with custom exceptions:

@Operation(
    summary = "Process payment",
    responses = {
        @ApiResponse(responseCode = "200", description = "Payment successful"),
        @ApiResponse(
            responseCode = "402",
            description = "Insufficient funds",
            content = @Content(schema = @Schema(implementation = ProblemDetail.class))
        ),
        @ApiResponse(
            responseCode = "404",
            description = "Order not found",
            content = @Content(schema = @Schema(implementation = ProblemDetail.class))
        ),
        @ApiResponse(
            responseCode = "422",
            description = "Payment validation failed"
        )
    }
)
@PostMapping("/payments")
public ResponseEntity<PaymentResult> processPayment(@RequestBody PaymentRequest request) {
    return ResponseEntity.ok(paymentService.process(request));
}
Part 17

Testing Custom Exceptions

Testing must verify both the exception type and its data payload.

@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class PaymentServiceTest {

    @Mock
    private OrderRepository orderRepository;

    @Mock
    private PaymentGateway gateway;

    @InjectMocks
    private PaymentService paymentService;

    @Test
    void shouldThrowOrderNotFoundWhenOrderMissing() {
        when(orderRepository.findById("INVALID")).thenReturn(Optional.empty());

        OrderNotFoundException ex = assertThrows(
            OrderNotFoundException.class,
            () -> paymentService.processPayment("INVALID", BigDecimal.TEN)
        );
        assertThat(ex.getOrderId()).isEqualTo("INVALID");
        assertThat(ex.getMessage()).contains("INVALID");
    }

    @Test
    void shouldThrowInsufficientFundsWithCorrectAmounts() {
        Order order = mockOrder("ORD-1", "CUST-1");
        when(orderRepository.findById("ORD-1")).thenReturn(Optional.of(order));
        when(accountService.getBalance("CUST-1")).thenReturn(new BigDecimal("50.00"));

        InsufficientFundsException ex = assertThrows(
            InsufficientFundsException.class,
            () -> paymentService.processPayment("ORD-1", new BigDecimal("100.00"))
        );

        assertThat(ex.getAvailable()).isEqualByComparingTo("50.00");
        assertThat(ex.getRequired()).isEqualByComparingTo("100.00");
        assertThat(ex.getShortfall()).isEqualByComparingTo("50.00");
    }

    @Test
    void shouldPreserveCauseWhenGatewayFails() {
        GatewayConnectionException gatewayEx = new GatewayConnectionException("timeout");
        when(gateway.charge(any(), any())).thenThrow(gatewayEx);

        PaymentFailedException ex = assertThrows(
            PaymentFailedException.class,
            () -> paymentService.processPayment("ORD-1", BigDecimal.TEN)
        );

        assertThat(ex.getCause()).isSameAs(gatewayEx);
        assertThat(ex.getGatewayCode()).isEqualTo("GATEWAY_UNAVAILABLE");
    }
}
Part 18

Anti-Patterns in Custom Exception Design

Anti-pattern 1: God exception

// BAD: One exception for everything
public class AppException extends RuntimeException {
    private int errorCode;
    private String field;
    private Object value;
    // ... 15 more fields
}

Anti-pattern 2: Exception wrapping without cause

// BAD: Cause chain destroyed
catch (DataAccessException ex) {
    throw new OrderNotFoundException("Order not found"); // ex lost!
}

Anti-pattern 3: Using exception message for programmatic logic

// BAD: Parsing message strings is fragile
catch (RuntimeException ex) {
    if (ex.getMessage().contains("not found")) { ... }
}

// GOOD: Use exception type or structured data
catch (OrderNotFoundException ex) {
    String orderId = ex.getOrderId();
}

Anti-pattern 4: Infinite exception hierarchy depth

// BAD: Too deep
BaseException
 └── ServiceException
      └── DomainException
           └── OrderException
                └── OrderItemException
                     └── OrderItemQuantityException  // nobody catches this specifically

Anti-pattern 5: Exceptions without context data

// BAD: No context
throw new PaymentFailedException("Payment failed");

// GOOD: Include relevant identifiers
throw new PaymentFailedException("Gateway declined payment", response.getDeclineCode(), orderId);
Part 19

Interview Question: When to Create a Custom Exception

Q: When should you create a custom exception instead of using a built-in one?

Answer framework:

  1. When the domain error has no built-in equivalent — InsufficientFundsException has no JDK equivalent.

  2. When you need structured data beyond a message string — OrderNotFoundException carrying orderId, customerId, timestamp.

  3. When you need type-specific catch blocks — Different HTTP status codes for different error types in @ControllerAdvice.

  4. When building a library/SDK — Published exceptions become part of your API contract.

  5. When the error code must be machine-readable — Clients react to ErrorCode.PAYMENT_CARD_EXPIRED differently from ErrorCode.PAYMENT_GATEWAY_FAILED.

When NOT to create a custom exception:

  • When IllegalArgumentException, IllegalStateException, or NullPointerException is perfectly clear
  • For internal utility methods where built-ins are standard
  • When the exception hierarchy would be so deep that nobody catches intermediate types
Part 20

Interview Question: Deep vs Shallow Exception Hierarchy

Q: Should you prefer a deep or shallow exception hierarchy?

Deep hierarchy:

OrderServiceException
 └── OrderDomainException
      └── OrderPaymentException
           └── OrderPaymentDeclinedException
                └── OrderPaymentCardExpiredException

Shallow hierarchy:

OrderServiceException
 ├── OrderNotFoundException
 ├── OrderPaymentFailedException
 └── OrderValidationException

Trade-offs:

Deep Shallow
Granularity High Lower
Catch flexibility Can catch at any level Catch all or specific
Maintenance Higher — more classes Lower — fewer classes
Clarity Can be confusing Easy to understand
Real-world use Rare catch at mid-levels Catches are typically leaf or base

Architect recommendation: Shallow-to-medium depth (2-3 levels max). Group by category (domain/infra/validation), not by detailed sub-types. Add leaf exception classes only when callers need to differentiate behavior.

Best Practice: 2-3 Level Hierarchy
====================================

[base]  OrderServiceException
          │
[category] ├── OrderDomainException
          │    ├── OrderNotFoundException       [leaf]
          │    └── OrderCancelledException      [leaf]
          │
          ├── OrderInfraException
          │    └── OrderPersistenceException    [leaf]
          │
          └── OrderValidationException          [leaf - or with children if needed]
Part 21

Quick Reference / Cheat Sheet

CUSTOM EXCEPTION CHEAT SHEET
==============================

CREATION:
  Checked     → extends Exception
  Unchecked   → extends RuntimeException (preferred in modern Java)

NAMING:
  ✓ OrderNotFoundException
  ✗ OrderNotFound, CannotFindOrder, OrderError

CONSTRUCTORS (provide all four):
  MyException()
  MyException(String message)
  MyException(Throwable cause)
  MyException(String message, Throwable cause)

ERROR CODES:
  → Use enum for type safety
  → Expose as String in API responses

HIERARCHY:
  → 2-3 levels max
  → Base → Category → Leaf

SPRING MAPPING:
  → @ResponseStatus on exception  (simple, static)
  → @ControllerAdvice (dynamic, ProblemDetail)
  → ProblemDetail (RFC 7807, Spring Boot 3)

TESTING:
  → assertThrows(MyException.class, () -> ...)
  → Assert exception fields, not just message

SERIALIZATION:
  → Add serialVersionUID
  → Keep custom fields Serializable
Part 22

Summary Table

Topic Key Rule Example
Checked vs Unchecked Prefer unchecked in modern apps extends RuntimeException
Naming Always *Exception suffix, noun phrases OrderNotFoundException
Constructors Provide 4 standard constructors message, cause, message+cause, no-arg
Error codes Use enum for type safety ErrorCode.PAYMENT_DECLINED
Context data Carry domain identifiers as fields orderId, customerId, amounts
Hierarchy depth 2-3 levels max Base → Category → Leaf
Cause preservation Always pass cause when wrapping new DomainEx(msg, originalCause)

Serialization Add serialVersionUID private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L
Testing Assert type AND payload fields assertThat(ex.getOrderId()).isEqualTo(...)

Practice

Exercise 1 — Design a Banking Exception Hierarchy

Design a custom exception hierarchy for a banking microservice with these requirements:
- Account not found (needs account ID)
- Insufficient funds (needs available vs required balance)
- Daily transfer limit exceeded (needs limit and attempted amount)
- Account frozen (needs freeze reason and date)
- External bank transfer failed (wraps a third-party SDK exception)

Provide: class diagram, all exception classes with fields and constructors, and a @ControllerAdvice that maps each to a ProblemDetail response.

Given a repository that throws JPA-level exceptions, implement an exception translation layer that:
- Converts EmptyResultDataAccessException → domain AccountNotFoundException
- Converts DataIntegrityViolationException with duplicate key → AccountAlreadyExistsException
- Wraps all other DataAccessException types → AccountPersistenceException
- Preserves original cause in all cases

Exercise 3 — ProblemDetail Integration

Implement a complete Spring Boot 3 error handling solution for an e-commerce API that:
- Returns RFC 7807 ProblemDetail for all custom exceptions
- Includes correlation ID (from MDC) in every error response
- Returns appropriate HTTP status codes per exception type
- Logs all infrastructure exceptions at ERROR level, domain exceptions at WARN level

Part 1

Concept Overview

Exception handling best practices separate professional-grade Java from code that technically compiles but fails in production. A single swallowed exception, an improper catch-all, or an uncorrelated log entry can cost hours of incident investigation. At the architect level, exception handling is a system-level concern — not a per-developer judgment call.

This lesson consolidates the accumulated wisdom of the Java ecosystem: from Josh Bloch's Effective Java to the Spring Framework's design philosophy, from distributed systems observability to Kafka dead-letter queue (DLQ) patterns.

What differentiates production-grade exception handling:

Junior Java Developer:
  try { ... } catch (Exception e) { e.printStackTrace(); }

Mid-level Developer:
  try { ... } catch (Exception e) { log.error("Error", e); }

Senior Developer:
  try { ... } catch (SpecificException e) {
      log.error("Payment failed [orderId={}]", orderId, e);
      throw new PaymentFailedException(orderId, e);
  }

Architect:
  - Exception strategy document defining handling per layer
  - Consistent ProblemDetail API contract
  - Correlation ID in every log and error response
  - DLQ strategy for async failures
  - Monitoring alerts on exception type + rate
  - Exception handling tested in integration tests
Part 2

Never Swallow Exceptions (Empty Catch)

The most dangerous exception handling practice is the empty catch block — silently discarding an exception.

The crime:

// WORST POSSIBLE CODE — never do this
try {
    processPayment(order);
} catch (Exception e) {
    // nothing here
}

// Slightly less bad but still terrible
try {
    sendEmail(user);
} catch (Exception e) {
    System.out.println("Email failed"); // message without context or stack trace
}

Why it's catastrophic:

  1. The failure is completely invisible — no logs, no metrics, no alerts
  2. The application continues in a potentially corrupt state
  3. Symptoms appear far from the root cause (data inconsistency hours later)
  4. Production debugging becomes archaeology

Acceptable alternatives:

// Option 1: Log + continue (when failure is truly non-critical)
try {
    auditLog.record(event);
} catch (AuditException e) {
    // Audit failure should not break the transaction
    log.warn("Audit logging failed for event [type={}, id={}]",
        event.getType(), event.getId(), e);
    // Optional: increment metrics counter
    metrics.increment("audit.failure");
}

// Option 2: Log + rethrow (when caller must know)
try {
    processPayment(order);
} catch (PaymentException e) {
    log.error("Payment failed [orderId={}, customerId={}]",
        order.getId(), order.getCustomerId(), e);
    throw e;
}

// Option 3: Log + wrap (translate to domain exception)
try {
    jdbcTemplate.update(sql, params);
} catch (DataAccessException e) {
    log.error("DB update failed [table=orders, orderId={}]", orderId, e);
    throw new OrderPersistenceException("Failed to persist order: " + orderId, e);
}

// Option 4: Comment when truly swallowing (rare, document why)
try {
    cache.evict(key);
} catch (CacheException e) {
    // Cache eviction failure is non-blocking; data will expire naturally.
    // Downstream reads will hit the DB instead.
    log.debug("Cache eviction failed for key [{}] — will expire normally", key, e);
}

Static analysis: Configure SonarQube, Checkstyle, or SpotBugs rules to flag empty catch blocks as build failures.

Part 3

Log and Rethrow vs Wrap

A common source of duplicate log entries in production is the log-and-rethrow pattern applied at multiple layers.

The duplicate log problem:

// Repository layer
try {
    return jpa.findById(id).orElseThrow();
} catch (Exception e) {
    log.error("DB error", e); // LOG #1
    throw e;
}

// Service layer
try {
    return repository.findOrder(id);
} catch (Exception e) {
    log.error("Service error", e); // LOG #2 — SAME EXCEPTION
    throw e;
}

// Controller layer
// @ControllerAdvice logs again — LOG #3

Result: 3 identical stack traces in production logs for a single failure. Noise that hides signal.

The rule: Log ONCE, at the appropriate boundary

Logging Responsibility by Layer
================================

Repository/DAO Layer:
  → Don't log; translate and throw domain exception
  → The domain exception carries context

Service Layer:
  → Don't log predictable domain exceptions (OrderNotFound is expected)
  → Do log unexpected infra exceptions before wrapping
  → One log entry per exception instance

Controller/@ControllerAdvice:
  → Log ALL unhandled exceptions here (the safety net)
  → Use log level by severity: WARN for expected, ERROR for unexpected

Cross-cutting:
  → @ControllerAdvice is the single logging point for HTTP layer
  → Kafka error handlers log once per failure

Correct pattern:

// Repository: translate only, no logging
@Repository
public class OrderRepositoryImpl implements OrderRepository {
    public Order findById(String id) {
        try {
            return jpa.findById(id)
                .map(this::toDomain)
                .orElseThrow(() -> new OrderNotFoundException(id));
        } catch (DataAccessException ex) {
            throw new OrderPersistenceException("findById:" + id, ex); // wrap, no log
        }
    }
}

// Service: no log for predictable domain errors
@Service
public class OrderService {
    public Order getOrder(String id) {
        return orderRepository.findById(id); // OrderNotFoundException propagates
    }
}

// ControllerAdvice: single logging point
@RestControllerAdvice
public class GlobalExceptionHandler {

    @ExceptionHandler(OrderNotFoundException.class)
    public ProblemDetail handleNotFound(OrderNotFoundException ex) {
        log.warn("Order not found [orderId={}]", ex.getOrderId()); // WARN, expected
        return ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, ex.getMessage());
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(OrderPersistenceException.class)
    public ProblemDetail handlePersistence(OrderPersistenceException ex) {
        log.error("Order persistence failure", ex); // ERROR, unexpected
        return ProblemDetail.forStatus(HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR);
    }
}
Part 4

Fail Fast

Fail fast means detecting and signaling errors as early as possible, at the point where the precondition is violated, not in some distant method downstream.

// BAD: Fail late — NullPointerException surfaces deep in processing
public void processOrder(Order order) {
    // 50 lines of code...
    String city = order.getShipping().getAddress().getCity(); // NPE here
}

// GOOD: Fail fast at entry point
public void processOrder(Order order) {
    Objects.requireNonNull(order, "order must not be null");
    Objects.requireNonNull(order.getShipping(), "order.shipping must not be null");
    if (order.getItems().isEmpty()) {
        throw new InvalidOrderException("Order must have at least one item");
    }
    // Now process with confidence
}

Guard clauses and validation:

import java.util.Objects;

public class PaymentService {

    public PaymentResult processPayment(String orderId, BigDecimal amount, String currency) {
        // Fail fast: validate inputs immediately
        Objects.requireNonNull(orderId, "orderId must not be null");
        Objects.requireNonNull(amount, "amount must not be null");
        Objects.requireNonNull(currency, "currency must not be null");

        if (orderId.isBlank()) {
            throw new InvalidPaymentRequestException("orderId must not be blank");
        }
        if (amount.compareTo(BigDecimal.ZERO) <= 0) {
            throw new InvalidPaymentRequestException(
                "amount must be positive, got: " + amount
            );
        }
        if (!SUPPORTED_CURRENCIES.contains(currency)) {
            throw new UnsupportedCurrencyException(currency, SUPPORTED_CURRENCIES);
        }

        // Main logic executes only with valid inputs
        return executePayment(orderId, amount, currency);
    }
}

Bean Validation (JSR-380) for fail fast at API boundary:

@RestController
public class PaymentController {

    @PostMapping("/payments")
    public ResponseEntity<PaymentResult> processPayment(
            @Valid @RequestBody PaymentRequest request) {  // @Valid triggers fail-fast
        return ResponseEntity.ok(paymentService.processPayment(request));
    }
}

public record PaymentRequest(
    @NotBlank(message = "orderId is required")
    String orderId,

    @NotNull @DecimalMin(value = "0.01", message = "amount must be positive")
    BigDecimal amount,

    @NotBlank @Size(min = 3, max = 3, message = "currency must be 3-letter ISO code")
    String currency
) {}
Part 5

Specific Catch Blocks

Catching broad exception types hides bugs and prevents precise handling.

The hierarchy problem:

// BAD: Catches everything — hides NPE, ClassCastException, programming errors
try {
    return processPayment(order);
} catch (Exception e) {
    log.error("Something went wrong", e);
    return PaymentResult.failure();
}

// BAD: Catches Throwable — never do this, includes Error
try {
    return processPayment(order);
} catch (Throwable t) {
    // ...
}

Specific catch blocks:

// GOOD: Specific and ordered from most-specific to least-specific
try {
    return gateway.charge(payment);
} catch (InsufficientFundsException ex) {
    // Known business condition — handle gracefully
    notifyCustomer(payment.getCustomerId(), ex);
    return PaymentResult.insufficientFunds(ex.getShortfall());
} catch (PaymentDeclinedException ex) {
    // Gateway declined — let customer retry
    return PaymentResult.declined(ex.getDeclineCode());
} catch (GatewayTimeoutException ex) {
    // Infrastructure issue — schedule retry
    retryScheduler.schedule(payment, Duration.ofMinutes(5));
    return PaymentResult.pending();
} catch (PaymentException ex) {
    // Any other payment exception — log and fail
    log.error("Unhandled payment exception [paymentId={}]", payment.getId(), ex);
    return PaymentResult.failure();
}

Multi-catch (Java 7+) for related exceptions:

// When two exceptions require identical handling
try {
    return orderRepository.findById(id);
} catch (OrderNotFoundException | OrderArchivedExceptionex ex) {
    return Optional.empty();
} catch (OrderPersistenceException ex) {
    throw new ServiceException("Data access failure", ex);
}

Rule: Order catch blocks from most-specific to most-general. The compiler enforces this for checked exceptions but not for unchecked ones.

Part 6

Don't Use Exceptions for Control Flow

Exceptions have significant performance overhead and semantic implications. Using them for normal flow control is an anti-pattern.

The anti-pattern:

// BAD: Using exception to check existence
try {
    User user = userService.findByEmail(email);
    return user;
} catch (UserNotFoundException ex) {
    return null; // exceptions as if/else
}

// BAD: Using NumberFormatException for input validation
public boolean isNumeric(String s) {
    try {
        Integer.parseInt(s);
        return true;
    } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
        return false; // exception as boolean return
    }
}

The correct approach:

// GOOD: Use Optional or explicit boolean check
Optional<User> user = userRepository.findByEmail(email);
user.ifPresent(this::sendWelcomeEmail);

// GOOD: Use regex or dedicated parser for validation
public boolean isNumeric(String s) {
    return s != null && s.matches("-?\\d+(\\.\\d+)?");
}

// GOOD: Use containsKey instead of catch
if (cache.containsKey(key)) {
    return cache.get(key);
}
return loadFromDatabase(key);

Why it matters — performance cost:

Exception object creation involves:
  1. Allocating the exception object
  2. Capturing the stack trace (most expensive — scans entire call stack)
  3. Filling in stack trace elements

Benchmark (approximate):
  Normal return:                ~1 ns
  Exception without stack:     ~20 ns
  Exception with stack trace:  ~1,000-5,000 ns (varies by stack depth)
  Exception 50-frame stack:    ~5,000-10,000 ns

For a 100 req/s endpoint using exceptions for "not found" (50% hit rate):
  50 exceptions/sec × 5,000 ns = 250 μs/sec overhead
  Cumulative over time: CPU pressure, GC pressure from short-lived objects

Stack trace suppression for performance (when appropriate):

// Custom exception that skips stack trace fill-in
// Only appropriate for known control-flow scenarios
public class CacheNotFoundException extends RuntimeException {

    public CacheNotFoundException(String key) {
        super("Cache miss: " + key, null, true, false); // writableStackTrace = false
    }
}
Part 7

Resource Management with try-with-resources

Java 7's try-with-resources (AutoCloseable) guarantees resource cleanup even when exceptions occur.

The problem with manual finally:

// BAD: Resource leak if getConnection() succeeds but close() throws
Connection conn = null;
try {
    conn = dataSource.getConnection();
    // process...
} catch (SQLException ex) {
    throw new DatabaseException(ex);
} finally {
    if (conn != null) {
        try {
            conn.close(); // What if this throws?
        } catch (SQLException ex) {
            // swallowed or logged — original exception may be lost
        }
    }
}

try-with-resources:

// GOOD: Guaranteed cleanup, suppressed exceptions preserved
try (Connection conn = dataSource.getConnection();
     PreparedStatement stmt = conn.prepareStatement(sql)) {

    stmt.setString(1, orderId);
    ResultSet rs = stmt.executeQuery();
    return mapResults(rs);

} catch (SQLException ex) {
    throw new OrderPersistenceException("Query failed", ex);
}
// conn and stmt closed automatically; close() exceptions become suppressed

Custom AutoCloseable resources:

public class DatabaseTransaction implements AutoCloseable {
    private final Connection conn;
    private boolean committed = false;

    public DatabaseTransaction(DataSource ds) throws SQLException {
        this.conn = ds.getConnection();
        this.conn.setAutoCommit(false);
    }

    public Connection getConnection() { return conn; }

    public void commit() throws SQLException {
        conn.commit();
        committed = true;
    }

    @Override
    public void close() throws SQLException {
        if (!committed) {
            try {
                conn.rollback(); // Rollback if not committed
            } finally {
                conn.close();
            }
        } else {
            conn.close();
        }
    }
}

// Usage
try (DatabaseTransaction tx = new DatabaseTransaction(dataSource)) {
    orderRepository.save(order, tx.getConnection());
    paymentRepository.save(payment, tx.getConnection());
    tx.commit();
} catch (SQLException ex) {
    // tx.close() rolls back automatically
    throw new TransactionFailedException("Order+payment save failed", ex);
}

try-with-resources with multiple resources and exception order:

// Both resources closed in reverse declaration order (stmt before conn)
// If both close() throw, first exception is primary, second is suppressed
try (Connection conn = ds.getConnection();
     Statement stmt = conn.createStatement()) {

    return stmt.executeQuery(sql);

} // stmt.close() first, then conn.close()
Part 8

Global Exception Handling in Microservices

Every microservice needs a consistent, centralized exception handling strategy.

Architecture diagram:

HTTP Request Flow — Exception Handling
========================================

HTTP Request
    │
    ▼
[Filter Chain]         SecurityException → 401/403
    │
    ▼
[DispatcherServlet]
    │
    ▼
[Controller]           ConstraintViolationException → 400
    │
    ▼
[Service]              OrderNotFoundException → 404
    │                  InsufficientFundsException → 402
    ▼
[Repository]           DataAccessException → 500

All unhandled exceptions ──► [@ControllerAdvice]
                               └── Logs, maps to ProblemDetail
                               └── Returns consistent JSON error body

Complete Spring Boot 3 global handler:

@RestControllerAdvice
@Slf4j
public class GlobalExceptionHandler {

    // Domain — client errors (4xx)
    @ExceptionHandler(OrderNotFoundException.class)
    public ProblemDetail handleOrderNotFound(
            OrderNotFoundException ex, HttpServletRequest req) {
        log.warn("Order not found [orderId={}, path={}]", ex.getOrderId(), req.getRequestURI());
        ProblemDetail pd = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, ex.getMessage());
        pd.setTitle("Order Not Found");
        pd.setInstance(URI.create(req.getRequestURI()));
        pd.setProperty("orderId", ex.getOrderId());
        pd.setProperty("correlationId", MDC.get("correlationId"));
        return pd;
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(InsufficientFundsException.class)
    public ProblemDetail handleInsufficientFunds(
            InsufficientFundsException ex, HttpServletRequest req) {
        log.warn("Insufficient funds [available={}, required={}]",
            ex.getAvailable(), ex.getRequired());
        ProblemDetail pd = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.PAYMENT_REQUIRED, ex.getMessage());
        pd.setTitle("Insufficient Funds");
        pd.setProperty("availableBalance", ex.getAvailable());
        pd.setProperty("requiredAmount", ex.getRequired());
        pd.setProperty("correlationId", MDC.get("correlationId"));
        return pd;
    }

    // Validation errors
    @ExceptionHandler(MethodArgumentNotValidException.class)
    public ProblemDetail handleValidation(MethodArgumentNotValidException ex) {
        Map<String, String> errors = ex.getBindingResult()
            .getFieldErrors()
            .stream()
            .collect(Collectors.toMap(
                FieldError::getField,
                fe -> Objects.requireNonNullElse(fe.getDefaultMessage(), "invalid")
            ));
        ProblemDetail pd = ProblemDetail.forStatus(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST);
        pd.setTitle("Validation Failed");
        pd.setDetail("Request validation failed");
        pd.setProperty("fieldErrors", errors);
        pd.setProperty("correlationId", MDC.get("correlationId"));
        return pd;
    }

    // Infrastructure errors — don't expose internals
    @ExceptionHandler(OrderPersistenceException.class)
    public ProblemDetail handlePersistence(OrderPersistenceException ex, HttpServletRequest req) {
        log.error("Persistence failure [path={}]", req.getRequestURI(), ex);
        ProblemDetail pd = ProblemDetail.forStatus(HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR);
        pd.setTitle("Internal Server Error");
        pd.setDetail("An internal error occurred. Please try again later.");
        pd.setProperty("correlationId", MDC.get("correlationId"));
        return pd;
    }

    // Safety net — catch all unexpected exceptions
    @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)
    public ProblemDetail handleUnexpected(Exception ex, HttpServletRequest req) {
        log.error("Unexpected exception [path={}]", req.getRequestURI(), ex);
        ProblemDetail pd = ProblemDetail.forStatus(HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR);
        pd.setTitle("Internal Server Error");
        pd.setDetail("An unexpected error occurred.");
        pd.setProperty("correlationId", MDC.get("correlationId"));
        return pd;
    }
}
Part 9

Monitoring: Sentry, Logging, Correlation IDs

Exception monitoring in production requires correlation, aggregation, and alerting.

Correlation ID implementation:

// Filter to inject correlationId into MDC at request boundary
@Component
@Order(Ordered.HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE)
public class CorrelationIdFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter {

    private static final String CORRELATION_ID_HEADER = "X-Correlation-ID";
    private static final String MDC_KEY = "correlationId";

    @Override
    protected void doFilterInternal(
            HttpServletRequest request,
            HttpServletResponse response,
            FilterChain chain) throws ServletException, IOException {

        String correlationId = Optional
            .ofNullable(request.getHeader(CORRELATION_ID_HEADER))
            .filter(h -> !h.isBlank())
            .orElse(UUID.randomUUID().toString());

        MDC.put(MDC_KEY, correlationId);
        response.setHeader(CORRELATION_ID_HEADER, correlationId);

        try {
            chain.doFilter(request, response);
        } finally {
            MDC.remove(MDC_KEY); // CRITICAL: always clean up MDC
        }
    }
}

Logback pattern with correlation ID:

<!-- logback-spring.xml -->
<pattern>%d{ISO8601} [%thread] [%X{correlationId}] %-5level %logger{36} - %msg%n</pattern>

Produces logs like:

2026-06-29T11:30:00Z [http-nio-8080-exec-1] [abc-123-def] ERROR c.e.PaymentService - Payment failed [orderId=ORD-456]

Sentry integration:

</dependency>

// Enrich Sentry events with domain context
@EventListener
public void onApplicationEvent(SentryBeforeSendCallbackEvent event) {
    // Sentry auto-captures uncaught exceptions
    // Add custom tags for better grouping
}

// Manual capture with context
try {
    processPayment(payment);
} catch (PaymentFailedException ex) {
    Sentry.withScope(scope -> {
        scope.setTag("orderId", payment.getOrderId());
        scope.setTag("customerId", payment.getCustomerId());
        scope.setExtra("gatewayCode", ex.getGatewayCode());
        Sentry.captureException(ex);
    });
    throw ex;
}

Exception metrics with Micrometer:

@Component
public class ExceptionMetrics {

    private final MeterRegistry registry;

    public ExceptionMetrics(MeterRegistry registry) {
        this.registry = registry;
    }

    public void recordException(Exception ex, String operation) {
        registry.counter("app.exceptions",
            "type", ex.getClass().getSimpleName(),
            "operation", operation
        ).increment();
    }
}

// Usage
try {
    return paymentService.processPayment(request);
} catch (PaymentFailedException ex) {
    exceptionMetrics.recordException(ex, "payment.process");
    throw ex;
}
Part 10

Architect: Exception Strategy Document

A mature engineering team needs a written exception handling strategy. This is a template for that document.

EXCEPTION HANDLING STRATEGY DOCUMENT
======================================
Service: Order Management Service
Version: 1.2
Owner: Platform Architecture Team

1. EXCEPTION TAXONOMY
   Domain Exceptions: business rules, client errors (4xx)
   Infrastructure Exceptions: DB, MQ, external services (503, 500)
   Validation Exceptions: input validation (400)
   Security Exceptions: auth/authz (401, 403)

2. LAYER RESPONSIBILITIES
   Controller:
     - @Valid on all inputs
     - No try/catch; let @ControllerAdvice handle
   Service:
     - Throw domain exceptions; don't log them
     - Catch infra exceptions, wrap with context, rethrow domain infra exception
   Repository:
     - Catch DataAccessException, translate to domain persistence exceptions
     - Never expose JPA/JDBC exceptions beyond repository boundary
   ControllerAdvice:
     - Single logging point for all HTTP exceptions
     - Map all exceptions to ProblemDetail (RFC 7807)
     - WARN for domain exceptions, ERROR for infra exceptions

3. HTTP STATUS CODE MAPPING
   OrderNotFoundException       → 404 Not Found
   InsufficientFundsException   → 402 Payment Required
   OrderValidationException     → 400 Bad Request
   OrderPersistenceException    → 500 Internal Server Error
   ExternalServiceException     → 503 Service Unavailable

4. LOGGING STANDARDS
   Format: structured JSON (logstash-logback-encoder)
   Fields: timestamp, level, correlationId, traceId, message, exception
   Levels: WARN for expected domain errors, ERROR for unexpected
   MDC: correlationId, traceId, userId, tenantId

5. MONITORING & ALERTING
   Tool: Sentry (errors), Datadog (metrics)
   Alert: >10 OrderPersistenceException/min → PagerDuty
   Alert: >5% payment failure rate → Slack #payments-alerts
   Dashboard: exception rate by type, p99 latency by exception

6. ASYNC EXCEPTION HANDLING
   Kafka: Dead Letter Topic (DLT) for all processing failures
   Retry: 3 attempts with exponential backoff (2s, 4s, 8s)
   DLT: manual review + reprocessing workflow
   Scheduler: retry after circuit breaker opens

7. PROHIBITED PATTERNS
   - Empty catch blocks (SonarQube rule: S108)
   - Log + rethrow at multiple layers (SonarQube rule: S2139)
   - catch Exception / catch Throwable in service/repo layers
   - Exceptions used for control flow
   - Stack traces in HTTP responses (production)
Part 11

Spring Boot: @ControllerAdvice

@ControllerAdvice is Spring's mechanism for centralizing exception handling across all controllers.

Anatomy:

// Applies to all @Controller and @RestController
@RestControllerAdvice
// OR scope it to a package or annotation:
// @RestControllerAdvice(basePackages = "com.example.api")
// @RestControllerAdvice(annotations = RestController.class)
public class ApiExceptionHandler {

    // Priority: most-specific exception class wins
    // If multiple handlers match, most-specific type takes precedence

    @ExceptionHandler(OrderNotFoundException.class)     // Specific type
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND)
    public ProblemDetail handleOrderNotFound(OrderNotFoundException ex) { ... }

    @ExceptionHandler(OrderDomainException.class)       // Category type
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY)
    public ProblemDetail handleDomainException(OrderDomainException ex) { ... }

    @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)                  // Safety net
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR)
    public ProblemDetail handleAll(Exception ex) { ... }
}

Exception handler precedence:

Exception Dispatch Order
=========================

1. @ExceptionHandler in the controller class itself (most specific)
2. @ExceptionHandler in @ControllerAdvice ordered by @Order annotation
   - Lower @Order value = higher priority
3. Default Spring handling (ResponseEntityExceptionHandler)

@Order(1)  → Custom security advice
@Order(2)  → Domain exception advice
@Order(3)  → Global safety net advice

Extending ResponseEntityExceptionHandler:

@RestControllerAdvice
public class ApiExceptionHandler extends ResponseEntityExceptionHandler {

    // Override default Spring MVC exception handling
    @Override
    protected ResponseEntity<Object> handleMethodArgumentNotValid(
            MethodArgumentNotValidException ex,
            HttpHeaders headers, HttpStatusCode status, WebRequest request) {

        ProblemDetail pd = ProblemDetail.forStatus(status);
        pd.setTitle("Validation Failed");
        pd.setProperty("fieldErrors", extractFieldErrors(ex));
        pd.setProperty("correlationId", MDC.get("correlationId"));
        return ResponseEntity.status(status)
            .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_PROBLEM_JSON)
            .body(pd);
    }

    private Map<String, String> extractFieldErrors(MethodArgumentNotValidException ex) {
        return ex.getBindingResult().getFieldErrors().stream()
            .collect(Collectors.toMap(
                FieldError::getField,
                fe -> Objects.requireNonNullElse(fe.getDefaultMessage(), "invalid"),
                (a, b) -> a // keep first on duplicate field
            ));
    }
}
Part 12

Spring Boot: ErrorController

ErrorController handles errors that bypass @ControllerAdvice — primarily errors from filters (security filters, rate limiting filters) and 404s from missing servlet mappings.

@Controller
@RequestMapping("${server.error.path:/error}")
public class CustomErrorController implements ErrorController {

    private final ErrorAttributes errorAttributes;
    private final HttpServletRequest request;

    public CustomErrorController(ErrorAttributes errorAttributes,
                                 HttpServletRequest request) {
        this.errorAttributes = errorAttributes;
        this.request = request;
    }

    @RequestMapping(produces = MediaType.APPLICATION_PROBLEM_JSON_VALUE)
    @ResponseBody
    public ProblemDetail handleError(WebRequest webRequest) {
        WebAttributeErrorAttributes attrs = errorAttributes
            .getErrorAttributes(webRequest, ErrorAttributeOptions.of(
                ErrorAttributeOptions.Include.MESSAGE,
                ErrorAttributeOptions.Include.EXCEPTION
            ));

        int status = (int) attrs.getOrDefault("status", 500);
        String message = (String) attrs.getOrDefault("message", "Unknown error");
        String path = (String) attrs.getOrDefault("path", "");

        ProblemDetail pd = ProblemDetail.forStatus(status);
        pd.setDetail(message);
        pd.setInstance(URI.create(path));
        pd.setProperty("correlationId", MDC.get("correlationId"));

        // Log filter-level errors
        if (status >= 500) {
            log.error("Unhandled error [status={}, path={}]: {}", status, path, message);
        }

        return pd;
    }
}

application.yml configuration:

server:
  error:
    include-message: never          # Don't expose internal messages in production
    include-exception: false        # Don't expose exception class names
    include-stacktrace: never       # Never expose stack traces
    include-binding-errors: always  # Include validation errors
    path: /error
Part 13

ProblemDetail in Spring Boot 3 (Full Implementation)

ProblemDetail (RFC 7807 / RFC 9457) is the standardized HTTP error response format.

Standard fields:

{
  "type": "https://docs.example.com/errors/order-not-found",
  "title": "Order Not Found",
  "status": 404,
  "detail": "No order with ID ORD-12345 exists in the system",
  "instance": "/orders/ORD-12345",
  "correlationId": "abc-123-def-456",
  "timestamp": "2026-06-29T11:30:00Z"
}

Full implementation with type URI registry:

// Error type URIs — keep centralized
public final class ProblemTypes {
    private static final String BASE = "https://api.example.com/errors/";

    public static final URI ORDER_NOT_FOUND = URI.create(BASE + "order-not-found");
    public static final URI INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS = URI.create(BASE + "insufficient-funds");
    public static final URI PAYMENT_FAILED = URI.create(BASE + "payment-failed");
    public static final URI VALIDATION_FAILED = URI.create(BASE + "validation-failed");
    public static final URI INTERNAL_ERROR = URI.create(BASE + "internal-error");

    private ProblemTypes() {}
}

// Builder helper for consistent ProblemDetail creation
public class ProblemDetailBuilder {

    public static ProblemDetail of(HttpStatus status, String title, String detail) {
        ProblemDetail pd = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(status, detail);
        pd.setTitle(title);
        pd.setProperty("correlationId", MDC.get("correlationId"));
        pd.setProperty("timestamp", Instant.now().toString());
        return pd;
    }

    public static ProblemDetail of(HttpStatus status, URI type, String title, String detail) {
        ProblemDetail pd = of(status, title, detail);
        pd.setType(type);
        return pd;
    }
}

// Usage in handler
@ExceptionHandler(InsufficientFundsException.class)
public ProblemDetail handleInsufficientFunds(InsufficientFundsException ex,
                                              HttpServletRequest req) {
    ProblemDetail pd = ProblemDetailBuilder.of(
        HttpStatus.PAYMENT_REQUIRED,
        ProblemTypes.INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS,
        "Insufficient Funds",
        ex.getMessage()
    );
    pd.setInstance(URI.create(req.getRequestURI()));
    pd.setProperty("availableBalance", ex.getAvailable());
    pd.setProperty("requiredAmount", ex.getRequired());
    return pd;
}
Part 14

Kafka: Error Handling

Kafka consumers require explicit error handling strategies because there is no HTTP request/response cycle to map exceptions to.

Kafka consumer error handling flow:

Kafka Consumer Error Handling
================================

Message arrives → Consumer.poll()
        │
        ▼
    process(message)
        │
   ┌────┴────┐
throws?      no
   │          │
   ▼          ▼
Retry?      Commit
   │        offset
   ├── YES → Retry 1, 2, 3...
   │              │
   │         Still fails?
   │              │
   └── NO ──►  Send to DLT
               (Dead Letter Topic)
               Commit original offset

Spring Kafka with DefaultErrorHandler:

@Configuration
@EnableKafka
public class KafkaConsumerConfig {

    @Bean
    public DefaultErrorHandler errorHandler(KafkaTemplate<String, Object> kafkaTemplate) {
        // Dead letter publishing recoverer
        DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer recoverer = new DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer(
            kafkaTemplate,
            // Route to {original-topic}.DLT
            (record, ex) -> new TopicPartition(record.topic() + ".DLT", record.partition())
        );

        // Exponential backoff: 2s, 4s, 8s (max 3 retries)
        ExponentialBackOffWithMaxRetries backoff = new ExponentialBackOffWithMaxRetries(3);
        backoff.setInitialInterval(2_000L);
        backoff.setMultiplier(2.0);
        backoff.setMaxInterval(8_000L);

        DefaultErrorHandler handler = new DefaultErrorHandler(recoverer, backoff);

        // Don't retry on these exceptions (send directly to DLT)
        handler.addNotRetryableExceptions(
            DeserializationException.class,    // message can never be deserialized
            InvalidOrderDataException.class    // domain validation — retry won't help
        );

        return handler;
    }
}

// Listener container factory wired with error handler
@Bean
public ConcurrentKafkaListenerContainerFactory<String, OrderEvent> orderEventFactory(
        ConsumerFactory<String, OrderEvent> cf,
        DefaultErrorHandler errorHandler) {
    ConcurrentKafkaListenerContainerFactory<String, OrderEvent> factory =
        new ConcurrentKafkaListenerContainerFactory<>();
    factory.setConsumerFactory(cf);
    factory.setCommonErrorHandler(errorHandler);
    return factory;
}

Consumer with error handling:

@Service
@Slf4j
public class OrderEventConsumer {

    @KafkaListener(
        topics = "order-events",
        containerFactory = "orderEventFactory"
    )
    public void handleOrderEvent(
            @Payload OrderEvent event,
            @Header(KafkaHeaders.RECEIVED_TOPIC) String topic,
            @Header(KafkaHeaders.OFFSET) long offset) {

        log.info("Processing order event [topic={}, offset={}, orderId={}]",
            topic, offset, event.getOrderId());

        try {
            orderEventProcessor.process(event);
        } catch (InvalidOrderDataException ex) {
            // Not retryable — log and let error handler send to DLT
            log.error("Invalid order event data [orderId={}] — sending to DLT",
                event.getOrderId(), ex);
            throw ex; // rethrow — error handler sends to DLT
        } catch (ExternalServiceException ex) {
            // Retryable — let error handler retry with backoff
            log.warn("External service failure for order [orderId={}] — will retry",
                event.getOrderId(), ex);
            throw ex;
        }
    }
}
Part 15

DLQ (Dead Letter Queue) Patterns

Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) is the safety net for messages that cannot be processed after all retries.

DLT message structure:

// Enrich DLT messages with failure metadata
@Component
public class DltMetadataEnricher implements ConsumerRecordRecoverer {

    private final KafkaTemplate<String, Object> kafkaTemplate;
    private final ObjectMapper objectMapper;

    @Override
    public void accept(ConsumerRecord<?, ?> record, Exception ex) {
        Map<String, Object> metadata = new HashMap<>();
        metadata.put("originalTopic", record.topic());
        metadata.put("originalPartition", record.partition());
        metadata.put("originalOffset", record.offset());
        metadata.put("failureReason", ex.getMessage());
        metadata.put("exceptionClass", ex.getClass().getName());
        metadata.put("failedAt", Instant.now().toString());
        metadata.put("retryCount", getRetryCount(record));

        ProducerRecord<String, Object> dltRecord = new ProducerRecord<>(
            record.topic() + ".DLT",
            record.partition(),
            (String) record.key(),
            record.value()
        );

        // Add metadata as headers
        metadata.forEach((k, v) ->
            dltRecord.headers().add(k, v.toString().getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8))
        );

        kafkaTemplate.send(dltRecord);
        log.error("Message sent to DLT [topic={}, key={}, reason={}]",
            record.topic(), record.key(), ex.getMessage(), ex);
    }
}

DLT reprocessing workflow:

@Service
@Slf4j
public class DltReprocessingService {

    private final KafkaTemplate<String, Object> kafkaTemplate;
    private final DltMessageRepository dltRepository;

    // Manual reprocessing endpoint for operations team
    public void reprocessMessage(String dltMessageId) {
        DltMessage message = dltRepository.findById(dltMessageId)
            .orElseThrow(() -> new DltMessageNotFoundException(dltMessageId));

        if (message.getStatus() != DltMessageStatus.PENDING) {
            throw new InvalidDltOperationException(
                "Cannot reprocess message in status: " + message.getStatus()
            );
        }

        // Send back to original topic
        kafkaTemplate.send(message.getOriginalTopic(), message.getKey(), message.getPayload());
        dltRepository.markAsReprocessed(dltMessageId);

        log.info("DLT message reprocessed [id={}, originalTopic={}]",
            dltMessageId, message.getOriginalTopic());
    }
}
Part 16

Exception Performance Cost

Understanding the performance implications of exceptions enables architects to make informed trade-off decisions.

JVM internals of exception creation:

new Exception() invocation:
  1. Object allocation on heap
  2. Throwable.<init>() called
  3. fillInStackTrace() called (native method)
     - Walks the entire JVM call stack
     - Captures StackTraceElement[] for each frame
     - This is the expensive step: O(stack depth)
  4. Object reference returned

Stack depth of 30 frames ≈ 3,000–5,000 ns
Stack depth of 100 frames ≈ 10,000–50,000 ns

Benchmarking exception overhead:

// JMH benchmark comparing exception vs return code
@BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime)
@OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)
public class ExceptionBenchmark {

    @Benchmark
    public Object normalReturn() {
        return findByIdWithOptional("key");
    }

    @Benchmark
    public Object exceptionReturn() {
        try {
            return findByIdWithException("key");
        } catch (NotFoundException ex) {
            return null;
        }
    }

    @Benchmark
    public Object exceptionNoStackTrace() {
        try {
            return findByIdNoStack("key");
        } catch (NotFoundException ex) {
            return null;
        }
    }
}

// Typical results:
// normalReturn:          ~2 ns
// exceptionReturn:    ~5,000 ns (with stack trace capture)
// exceptionNoStack:      ~50 ns (suppressed stack trace)

JVM optimization: -XX:OmitStackTraceInFastThrow

JVM flag: -XX:OmitStackTraceInFastThrow (default: enabled)

After throwing the same exception type ~10,000 times, the JIT compiler
will omit stack trace filling for that exception type.

Effect: Exception is faster, but stack traces disappear from logs.
Observation: Stack trace shows "null" or truncated in production.

To disable (get full stack traces always):
  -XX:-OmitStackTraceInFastThrow

Trade-off:
  - Disabled: full stack traces, higher CPU cost at exception hot spots
  - Enabled (default): empty stack traces at hot spots, lower CPU cost

Stack trace suppression pattern:

// For exceptions that will be thrown in high-throughput code paths
// and where stack trace is not useful (e.g., cache miss)
public class CacheMissException extends RuntimeException {
    // Disable stack trace filling — significant performance gain
    public CacheMissException(String key) {
        super("Cache miss: " + key,
              null,      // cause
              true,      // enableSuppression
              false);    // writableStackTrace = false
    }
}
Part 17

Multi-Catch and Re-throw

Java 7 multi-catch and the ability to rethrow without widening exception types are powerful features.

Multi-catch syntax:

// Before Java 7: code duplication
try {
    gateway.charge(payment);
} catch (PaymentDeclinedException ex) {
    log.warn("Payment declined", ex);
    notifyCustomer(ex);
} catch (PaymentTimeoutException ex) {
    log.warn("Payment timed out", ex);
    notifyCustomer(ex);
}

// Java 7+: multi-catch for identical handling
try {
    gateway.charge(payment);
} catch (PaymentDeclinedException | PaymentTimeoutException ex) {
    log.warn("Payment not completed [type={}]", ex.getClass().getSimpleName(), ex);
    notifyCustomer(ex);
}

// Note: multi-catch variable is effectively final
// Cannot reassign: ex = new PaymentDeclinedException(); // compile error

Precise rethrow (Java 7+):

// Before Java 7: compiler forced you to declare throws Exception
void processOrder() throws Exception { // had to be this broad

// Java 7+: compiler tracks actual thrown types
void processOrder() throws OrderNotFoundException, PaymentFailedException {
    try {
        doProcess();
    } catch (Exception ex) {
        // Compiler knows this can only throw OrderNotFoundException or PaymentFailedException
        throw ex; // precise rethrow — no widening
    }
}
Part 18

Exception Handling in Reactive Programming (WebFlux)

Reactive Mono/Flux pipelines require a different exception handling approach.

// Imperative style (Spring MVC)
public Order getOrder(String id) {
    try {
        return orderRepository.findById(id);
    } catch (OrderNotFoundException ex) {
        throw new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, ex.getMessage());
    }
}

// Reactive style (Spring WebFlux)
public Mono<Order> getOrder(String id) {
    return orderRepository.findById(id)               // returns Mono<Order>
        .switchIfEmpty(Mono.error(                    // handle empty
            new OrderNotFoundException(id)))
        .onErrorMap(DataAccessException.class,        // translate infra exceptions
            ex -> new OrderPersistenceException("findById:" + id, ex))
        .doOnError(OrderPersistenceException.class,   // log infra errors
            ex -> log.error("Persistence failure [id={}]", id, ex));
}

// Reactive global exception handler
@ControllerAdvice
public class ReactiveExceptionHandler {

    @ExceptionHandler(OrderNotFoundException.class)
    public Mono<ResponseEntity<ProblemDetail>> handleNotFound(OrderNotFoundException ex) {
        ProblemDetail pd = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, ex.getMessage());
        return Mono.just(ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND).body(pd));
    }
}
Part 19

Interview: catch Exception vs Specific Exceptions

Q: What are the problems with catch (Exception e) everywhere?

Answer:

  1. Masks programming bugs: NullPointerException, ClassCastException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException are programming errors — catching them with Exception means bugs silently hide in production.

  2. Prevents precise handling: You cannot react differently to InsufficientFundsException vs GatewayTimeoutException when both are caught as Exception.

  3. Forces lowest common denominator response: All errors become 500 Internal Server Error, even user errors that should be 400/402/404.

  4. Breaks exception escalation: Exceptions designed to propagate to a global handler (like @ControllerAdvice) are swallowed at the wrong layer.

  5. Hinders static analysis: Tools like SpotBugs, Checkstyle, and SonarQube cannot reason about exception flow when all are caught as Exception.

The rule: Catch only the exceptions you know how to handle. Let everything else propagate to the appropriate boundary handler.

// BAD
catch (Exception e) { return null; }

// ACCEPTABLE — documented safety net at the outermost boundary only
@ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)
public ProblemDetail handleAll(Exception ex) {
    log.error("Unhandled exception", ex);
    return ProblemDetail.forStatus(HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR);
}
Part 20

Interview: Exception Performance Cost

Q: Are exceptions expensive in Java? When does it matter?

Answer:

Yes, exceptions are expensive primarily because of fillInStackTrace() — the native JVM call that captures the entire call stack on exception creation.

Benchmark numbers:
- Normal method return: ~1–2 ns
- Exception creation (30-frame stack): ~3,000–5,000 ns
- Exception creation (100-frame stack): ~10,000–50,000 ns
- That's a 1,000–5,000x difference

When it matters:
- High-throughput paths (>10,000 req/s) where exceptions are frequent (e.g., "not found" is common)
- Loops that throw/catch exceptions per iteration
- Cache miss scenarios in hot code paths

When it doesn't matter:
- True exceptional conditions (payment failures, DB errors) — these are inherently rare
- Normal request processing where exceptions are the minority case
- Any code running < 1,000 times/sec

Mitigation strategies:
1. Don't use exceptions for control flow
2. Use writableStackTrace = false for high-frequency, low-information exceptions
3. Use Optional<T> or result types for "not found" scenarios
4. Monitor -XX:OmitStackTraceInFastThrow behavior in production

Key architect insight: The performance cost of exceptions is almost never the bottleneck in well-designed systems. Premature optimization by avoiding exceptions leads to unreadable code. Fix the design first (don't use exceptions for flow control), then optimize if profiling evidence demands it.
