Quick Reference / Cheat Sheet

EXCEPTION BEST PRACTICES CHEAT SHEET
=======================================

NEVER DO:
  ✗ Empty catch blocks
  ✗ catch (Exception e) or catch (Throwable t) in business logic
  ✗ Exceptions for control flow (use Optional, return codes)
  ✗ Log + rethrow at multiple layers (log once at boundary)
  ✗ Expose stack traces in HTTP responses (production)
  ✗ Swallow cause when wrapping: throw new Ex(msg) [missing cause]

ALWAYS DO:
  ✓ Fail fast: validate at method entry
  ✓ Specific catch blocks, most-specific first
  ✓ Preserve cause: throw new DomainEx(msg, originalCause)
  ✓ Log once at boundary (@ControllerAdvice / Kafka error handler)
  ✓ Include correlationId in all logs and error responses
  ✓ try-with-resources for all AutoCloseable resources
  ✓ Return ProblemDetail (RFC 7807) from REST APIs
  ✓ DLQ for Kafka processing failures

SPRING BOOT STACK:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  @Valid + @ControllerAdvice         │ HTTP layer
  │  ProblemDetail (RFC 7807)           │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  Domain exceptions (unchecked)      │ Service layer
  │  Exception translation in repos     │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  DefaultErrorHandler + DLT          │ Kafka layer
  │  ExponentialBackoff retries         │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────┤

  │  MDC correlationId in all logs      │
  └─────────────────────────────────────┘

PERFORMANCE:
  Exception with stack trace:  ~5,000 ns

  Rule: exceptions are for exceptional cases, not flow control

Part 1

Concept Overview

Multithreading is the ability of a program to execute multiple threads of control concurrently within a single process. It is one of the most powerful — and most dangerous — capabilities in the Java platform. Done correctly, it enables massive throughput gains, responsive UIs, and efficient resource utilisation. Done incorrectly, it produces race conditions, deadlocks, memory visibility failures, and heisenbugs that only reproduce under load at 3 AM on Black Friday.

Phase 5 of this handbook dedicates six lessons to building a complete mental model of Java concurrency — from the raw Thread class up to CompletableFuture, virtual threads, and the Java Memory Model. This first lesson establishes the indispensable foundation: what threads are, how they live and die, how to create them, and what the JVM does with them at the OS level.

Why this matters at the architect level:

Junior Developer:
  new Thread(() -> doWork()).start();
  // "It works on my machine"

Mid-level Developer:
  ExecutorService executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(10);
  executor.submit(() -> doWork());
  // Knows thread pools, doesn't understand sizing

Senior Developer:
  ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
      coreSize, maxSize, keepAlive, TimeUnit.SECONDS,
      new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(queueCapacity),
      new ThreadFactoryBuilder().setNameFormat("order-worker-%d").build(),
      new CallerRunsPolicy());
  // Sized based on CPU/IO profiling, named threads, rejection policy

Architect:
  - Thread model matches the workload type (CPU-bound vs IO-bound)
  - Virtual threads (Java 21) for IO-heavy services
  - Thread dumps readable in under 2 minutes during incidents
  - @Async properly bounded with custom executors
  - No unbounded queues anywhere in the system
  - Thread leak detection in production monitoring

By the end of this lesson, every thread state transition, lifecycle method, and architectural implication will be explicit and unambiguous.

Part 2

What is a Thread?

A thread is the smallest unit of execution scheduled by the operating system. A process is an isolated memory space (heap, code, data); threads within a process share the same heap but each have their own stack.

Process vs Thread Memory Layout

PROCESS MEMORY
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     HEAP (shared)                      │
│  Objects, static fields, class metadata (Metaspace)    │
├────────────┬────────────┬────────────┬─────────────────┤
│ Thread 1   │ Thread 2   │ Thread 3   │   Thread N      │
│  Stack     │  Stack     │  Stack     │   Stack         │
│  --------  │  --------  │  --------  │   --------      │
│  Frame 3   │  Frame 2   │  Frame 1   │   Frame 1       │
│  Frame 2   │  Frame 1   │            │                 │
│  Frame 1   │            │            │                 │
│            │            │            │                 │
│  PC Reg    │  PC Reg    │  PC Reg    │   PC Reg        │
│  (private) │  (private) │  (private) │   (private)     │
└────────────┴────────────┴────────────┴─────────────────┘

Per-thread private data:
- Stack — method call frames, local variables, partial results
- Program Counter (PC) — address of the next bytecode instruction to execute
- Native method stack — for JNI calls

Shared across all threads (heap):
- All object instances
- Static fields
- Class definitions (Metaspace)

This shared heap is the root cause of every concurrency problem. When multiple threads read and write the same object field simultaneously without coordination, data corruption follows.

Thread vs Task

These two terms are often conflated. At the architectural level, the distinction matters:

Concept Definition Managed by
Thread OS-scheduled unit of execution with its own stack JVM / OS kernel
Task (Runnable/Callable) A unit of work — a function to execute Application / Executor
Fiber / Virtual Thread Lightweight thread managed by JVM scheduler JVM (Java 21+)

Pre-Java 21: one Thread object = one OS thread. Java 21+ virtual threads decouple tasks from OS threads. This lesson focuses on the classical model first.

Part 3

Thread Lifecycle

A Java thread moves through a well-defined set of states defined in Thread.State. Understanding these states is mandatory for reading thread dumps during production incidents.

Thread State Machine (ASCII Diagram)

                        ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
                        │                                                     │
           new Thread() │                                                     │
           ┌────────────▼──────────┐                                         │
           │          NEW          │                                         │
           │   Thread created,     │                                         │
           │   not started yet     │                                         │
           └────────────┬──────────┘                                         │
                        │ thread.start()                                      │
           ┌────────────▼──────────┐    CPU time slice ends (yield/preempt)  │
           │       RUNNABLE        │◄────────────────────────────────────────┤
           │   Ready to run OR     │                                         │
           │   currently running   │                                         │
           └──┬─────┬──────┬───────┘                                         │
              │     │      │                                                  │
  wait()      │     │      │ sleep(ms) /           synchronized block        │
  notify()    │     │      │ join(ms) /            lock contention           │
  awaits...   │     │      │ parkNanos()                                     │
              │     │      │                                                  │
  ┌───────────▼──┐  │  ┌───▼──────────────┐   ┌──────────────────────────┐  │
  │   WAITING    │  │  │  TIMED_WAITING   │   │        BLOCKED           │  │
  │  Indefinite  │  │  │  Timed wait with │   │  Waiting to acquire      │  │
  │  wait until  │  │  │  timeout / sleep │   │  a monitor lock          │  │
  │  notified    │  │  │                  │   │  (synchronized block)    │  │
  └──────┬───────┘  │  └──────┬───────────┘   └──────────┬───────────────┘  │
         │          │         │                           │                  │
         │ notify() │  timeout│                           │ lock acquired    │
         │ /notify  │  expires│                           │                  │
         │  All()   │         │                           │                  │
         └──────────┼─────────┘                           │                  │
                    │                 returns to RUNNABLE  │                  │
                    └────────────────────────────────────►─┘                  │
                                                          │                  │
                                        run() returns ───►──────────────────►┤
                                        or throws                            │
                                                         ┌────────────────── ▼──┐
                                                         │      TERMINATED      │
                                                         │  run() completed or  │
                                                         │  threw an exception  │
                                                         └──────────────────────┘

State Descriptions

State Thread.State Enum Meaning
NEW Thread.State.NEW Thread object created, start() not called
RUNNABLE Thread.State.RUNNABLE Running on CPU or ready to run (waiting for CPU time slice)
BLOCKED Thread.State.BLOCKED Waiting to acquire a synchronized monitor lock
WAITING Thread.State.WAITING Indefinitely waiting: Object.wait(), Thread.join(), LockSupport.park()
TIMED_WAITING Thread.State.TIMED_WAITING Waiting with timeout: Thread.sleep(ms), Object.wait(ms), Thread.join(ms)
TERMINATED Thread.State.TERMINATED Execution completed; cannot be restarted

> Production Insight: In a thread dump, a large number of threads in BLOCKED state indicates lock contention. A large number in WAITING suggests a thread pool that is idle (normal) or a thread leak. A thread stuck in TIMED_WAITING on sleep() at the same stack frame across multiple dumps indicates a stuck worker.

Part 4

Creating Threads: `extends Thread`

The oldest way to create a thread is to subclass Thread and override run().

public class PrintThread extends Thread {

    private final String message;

    public PrintThread(String message) {
        super("print-thread-" + message); // name the thread
        this.message = message;
    }

    @Override
    public void run() {
        // This code executes in the new thread
        System.out.printf("[%s] %s%n",
            Thread.currentThread().getName(), message);
    }
}

// Usage
PrintThread t = new PrintThread("Hello");
t.start(); // DO NOT call t.run() directly — see Part 6

Why extends Thread is Discouraged

  1. Couples task logic with threading mechanism — the class cannot extend any other class
  2. Not reusable — once terminated, a Thread cannot be restarted
  3. Cannot be submitted to an Executor — requires wrapping
  4. Violates composition over inheritance

The only legitimate use case for extending Thread today is custom thread factories for thread pools, where you override thread properties but not run().

Part 5

Creating Threads: `implements Runnable` and `Callable`

Runnable — Fire and Forget

Runnable separates the task from the execution mechanism. It is the correct abstraction for tasks that do not return a result.

// Functional interface — one abstract method
@FunctionalInterface
public interface Runnable {
    void run(); // no return value, no checked exceptions
}

// Lambda form (Java 8+)
Runnable task = () -> System.out.println("Running in: "
    + Thread.currentThread().getName());

// Wrap in Thread (low-level, not recommended for production)
Thread t = new Thread(task, "my-worker");
t.start();

// Submit to Executor (correct approach)
ExecutorService executor = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor();
executor.submit(task);

Callable<V> — Tasks That Return a Value

Callable is the counterpart to Runnable when a result or checked exception is needed.

// Functional interface
@FunctionalInterface
public interface Callable<V> {
    V call() throws Exception; // returns V, can throw checked exceptions
}

Callable<Integer> computation = () -> {
    Thread.sleep(100); // simulate work
    return 42;
};

ExecutorService executor = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor();
Future<Integer> future = executor.submit(computation);

// Blocking get — retrieves result when available
Integer result = future.get(); // throws ExecutionException if call() threw
Integer resultWithTimeout = future.get(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); // with timeout

Future<V> — Handle on an Async Computation

Future<String> future = executor.submit(() -> fetchFromDatabase(id));

// Non-blocking check
if (future.isDone()) {
    String result = future.get(); // won't block
}

// Cancel a pending task
future.cancel(true); // true = interrupt if running

// Important: future.get() wraps exceptions in ExecutionException
try {
    String result = future.get();
} catch (ExecutionException e) {
    Throwable cause = e.getCause(); // the original exception from call()
    if (cause instanceof DatabaseException dbEx) {
        // handle
    }
} catch (InterruptedException e) {
    Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // ALWAYS restore interrupt status
}

Comparison: Thread Creation Mechanisms

Approach Returns value Checked exceptions Reusable as task Recommended
extends Thread No No No No (legacy)
implements Runnable No No Yes Yes (for void tasks)
implements Callable<V> Yes Yes Yes Yes (for valued tasks)
Lambda Runnable No No Yes Yes
Lambda Callable<V> Yes Yes Yes Yes
Part 6

`start()` vs `run()` — The Most Common Interview Question

This is the single most frequently asked Java threading interview question and a real source of production bugs for developers new to multithreading.

Thread t = new Thread(() -> {
    System.out.println("Thread name: " + Thread.currentThread().getName());
});

t.start(); // Prints: Thread name: Thread-0  (a NEW thread)
t.run();   // Prints: Thread name: main       (SAME thread — no new thread!)

Internals of start()

t.start()
    │
    ▼
Thread.start() [Java]
    │
    ▼
Thread.start0() [native JNI call]
    │
    ▼
JVM creates OS thread
    │
    ▼
OS thread calls Thread.run() [in new execution context]
    │
    ▼
Thread.run() calls target.run() (the Runnable)

run() called directly

When run() is called directly, no new thread is created. The run() method executes synchronously in the calling thread — the thread that called run(). This is functionally equivalent to a normal method call and provides zero concurrency.

// WRONG — runs synchronously in main thread, no concurrency
Thread t = new Thread(expensiveTask);
t.run();   // blocks main thread, no new thread created

// CORRECT — creates new OS thread, returns immediately
Thread t = new Thread(expensiveTask);
t.start(); // returns immediately, expensiveTask runs concurrently

> Rule: Never call run() directly on a Thread object. Use start(). Calling run() directly is a silent bug — no exception is thrown, and the behavior looks correct but is not concurrent.

Part 7

Thread Names and Thread Groups

Naming Threads

Thread names are critical for production debugging. Thread dumps identify threads by name — meaningless names like Thread-0 through Thread-247 make incident investigation painful.

// Default thread names: Thread-0, Thread-1, Thread-2 ...
Thread t1 = new Thread(task);

// Named thread
Thread t2 = new Thread(task, "payment-processor-1");

// Rename after creation
t2.setName("order-fulfillment-worker");

// Get current thread name
String name = Thread.currentThread().getName();

// Thread factory for executors (preferred in production)
ThreadFactory factory = r -> {
    Thread t = new Thread(r);
    t.setName("kafka-consumer-" + threadCounter.incrementAndGet());
    t.setDaemon(false);
    return t;
};

ExecutorService executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4, factory);

Thread Priorities

Java exposes thread priority via setPriority(int) with values 1–10 (MIN=1, NORM=5, MAX=10). In practice, this is almost entirely ignored by modern OS schedulers.

Thread t = new Thread(task);
t.setPriority(Thread.MAX_PRIORITY); // 10 — mostly ignored on Linux/macOS
t.setPriority(Thread.MIN_PRIORITY); // 1  — mostly ignored
t.setPriority(Thread.NORM_PRIORITY); // 5 — default

Why priorities don't matter:
- Linux (NPTL) maps Java threads to kernel threads via pthreads; user-space priority hints rarely affect kernel scheduling
- macOS uses Grand Central Dispatch with Quality of Service (QoS) levels, not numeric priorities
- Windows has some priority support but modern servers run Linux

> Architect Rule: Do not rely on thread priorities for correctness or performance. Design your system to work correctly at any scheduling order.

Part 8

Daemon vs User Threads

This distinction controls JVM shutdown behaviour and is a frequent source of production surprises.

User Threads (Non-daemon)

The JVM waits for all user threads to complete before exiting. The main thread is a user thread. Any thread started from main without setDaemon(true) is also a user thread by default.

Thread userThread = new Thread(() -> {
    try {
        Thread.sleep(10_000); // simulates long-running work
        System.out.println("User thread done");
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
    }
});
// userThread.isDaemon() == false by default
userThread.start();
// JVM will NOT exit until userThread completes, even if main() returns

Daemon Threads

Daemon threads are background service threads. The JVM exits when all user threads have finished, regardless of any daemon threads still running. Daemon threads are abruptly terminated on JVM shutdown — their finally blocks and shutdown hooks may not execute.

Thread daemonThread = new Thread(() -> {
    while (true) {
        // background task — e.g., metrics flush, cache eviction
        doBackgroundWork();
        try { Thread.sleep(1000); } catch (InterruptedException e) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
            break;
        }
    }
});
daemonThread.setDaemon(true); // MUST be set BEFORE start()
daemonThread.start();
// JVM will exit when main thread finishes, even if this is still looping

Daemon Thread Rules

DAEMON THREAD RULES
====================
1. setDaemon(true) MUST be called BEFORE start()
   Calling after start() throws IllegalThreadStateException

2. Child threads inherit daemon status from parent
   Thread spawned by daemon = daemon
   Thread spawned by user   = user

3. Daemon threads should NOT hold critical resources
   File handles, DB connections, locks — NOT SAFE in daemon threads
   The JVM can kill them without any cleanup

4. Use daemon threads for:
   ✓ Background metrics flush
   ✓ Cache eviction/TTL cleanup
   ✓ Log flushing (if logback/log4j manages its own cleanup separately)
   ✓ Heartbeat/health check threads

5. Do NOT use daemon threads for:
   ✗ Database writes that must complete
   ✗ Kafka producer flushes
   ✗ Transaction commit operations
   ✗ Any work that must not be abandoned mid-execution
Part 9

Thread Methods Reference

Thread.sleep(long millis)

Pauses the current thread for at least the specified time. Does not release any locks.

try {
    Thread.sleep(500); // sleep 500ms minimum
} catch (InterruptedException e) {
    Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // ALWAYS restore interrupt flag
    return; // or rethrow
}

thread.join()

Causes the calling thread to wait until the target thread terminates.

Thread worker = new Thread(expensiveTask);
worker.start();

// main thread blocks here until worker finishes
worker.join();
worker.join(5000); // wait at most 5 seconds

System.out.println("Worker finished, result is ready");

Thread.yield()

A hint to the scheduler that the current thread is willing to yield its time slice. Rarely used in practice; the scheduler may ignore it entirely.

thread.interrupt()

Sets the interrupted flag on the target thread. Does not stop the thread — it is a cooperative mechanism.

Thread t = new Thread(() -> {
    while (!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) {
        doWork();
    }
    System.out.println("Thread was interrupted, cleaning up");
});

t.start();
Thread.sleep(2000);
t.interrupt(); // requests the thread to stop

When a thread is blocking in sleep(), wait(), or join(), interrupt() causes those methods to throw InterruptedException, clearing the interrupted flag. The thread must either propagate the exception or call Thread.currentThread().interrupt() to restore the flag.

// The InterruptedException contract — ALWAYS do one of these:

// Option 1: Propagate (cleanest)
void doWork() throws InterruptedException {
    Thread.sleep(1000);
}

// Option 2: Restore + return (when can't propagate)
void doWork() {
    try {
        Thread.sleep(1000);
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // restore the flag
        return;                             // stop processing
    }
}

// Option 3: Wrap in RuntimeException (frameworks sometimes do this)
void doWork() {
    try {
        Thread.sleep(1000);
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        throw new TaskInterruptedException(e);
    }
}

// NEVER DO THIS — swallowing InterruptedException silently
void doWork() {
    try {
        Thread.sleep(1000);
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        // nothing — this is a bug
    }
}
Part 10

`ThreadLocal<T>`

ThreadLocal provides thread-scoped storage — each thread gets its own independent copy of the variable.

// Classic use: per-thread SimpleDateFormat (not thread-safe)
private static final ThreadLocal<SimpleDateFormat> dateFormat =
    ThreadLocal.withInitial(() -> new SimpleDateFormat("yyyy-MM-dd"));

public String formatDate(Date date) {
    return dateFormat.get().format(date); // each thread gets its own instance
}

ThreadLocal and Spring

Spring uses ThreadLocal extensively:
- SecurityContextHolder — stores the authenticated user per-request thread
- TransactionSynchronizationManager — stores the current transaction per thread
- RequestContextHolder — stores the current HTTP request per thread

// Spring Security under the hood (simplified)
public class SecurityContextHolder {
    private static final ThreadLocal<SecurityContext> contextHolder =
        new ThreadLocal<>();

    public static void setContext(SecurityContext context) {
        contextHolder.set(context);
    }

    public static SecurityContext getContext() {
        SecurityContext ctx = contextHolder.get();
        if (ctx == null) {
            ctx = new SecurityContextImpl();
            contextHolder.set(ctx);
        }
        return ctx;
    }
}

ThreadLocal Memory Leak Warning

THREADLOCAL MEMORY LEAK PATTERN
=================================
Thread pools reuse threads. If ThreadLocal.remove() is not called,
the value remains associated with the thread indefinitely.

ThreadPoolExecutor (10 threads, long-lived)
  Thread-0 → ThreadLocal: Connection(user=Alice)
  Thread-1 → ThreadLocal: Connection(user=Bob)
  ...

  If Alice's request sets ThreadLocal but doesn't remove() after,
  Thread-0's ThreadLocal retains Alice's connection for the
  lifetime of the thread pool — a memory/security leak.

FIX: Always call ThreadLocal.remove() in a finally block:

  try {
      threadLocal.set(value);
      doWork();
  } finally {
      threadLocal.remove(); // MANDATORY with thread pools
  }
Part 11

JVM Thread Model

One-to-One: Java Thread ↔ OS Thread (pre-Java 21)

APPLICATION CODE
    │
    │  new Thread(task).start()
    ▼
JVM Thread Object
    │
    │  Thread.start0() [native]
    ▼
POSIX pthread_create() [on Linux/macOS]
    │
    ▼
Kernel Thread (kernel scheduling unit)
    │
    ▼
CPU Core (runs ~1 kernel thread per core simultaneously)

Implications:
- Each Java thread consumes ~512KB–1MB of native stack memory (configurable with -Xss)
- Thread creation is expensive — involves a system call
- Context switching between OS threads has measurable overhead (~1–10 µs)
- At ~10,000 threads, memory pressure becomes severe
- This is why thread pools exist: reuse expensive OS threads

Thread Stack Size

# Default stack size varies by platform
# Linux x64: ~512KB per thread
# macOS: ~512KB per thread (main thread gets 8MB)

# JVM flag to reduce stack per thread (allows more threads)
java -Xss256k MyApp

# With 512KB stacks:
# 1GB heap available for stacks = ~2,048 concurrent threads
# With 256KB stacks: ~4,096 threads

# 10,000 threads × 512KB = 5GB just for thread stacks

Virtual Threads (Java 21) — Preview

TRADITIONAL (Platform) THREADS:
  Java Thread → OS Thread → CPU Core (1:1:1)
  Creating 10,000 threads = 10,000 OS threads = ~5GB stack memory

VIRTUAL THREADS (Java 21):
  Virtual Thread → Carrier (platform) Thread → CPU Core (M:N:P)
  Creating 10,000 virtual threads = perhaps 8 carrier threads
  Stack memory: minimal per virtual thread

  Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> handleRequest()); // Java 21

This lesson covers platform threads. Virtual threads are covered in Lesson 48.

Part 12

Executor Framework Preview

Creating raw Thread objects in production code is an anti-pattern. The java.util.concurrent.Executor framework, introduced in Java 5, provides thread pooling, task queuing, lifecycle management, and Future-based result retrieval.

RAW THREADS (anti-pattern in production):
  for (each request) {
      new Thread(requestHandler).start(); // unbounded thread creation
  }
  Problem: 10,000 concurrent requests = 10,000 OS threads = OOM

EXECUTOR FRAMEWORK (correct approach):
  ExecutorService executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(10);
  for (each request) {
      executor.submit(requestHandler); // pooled, bounded
  }
  Result: max 10 OS threads, tasks queue if all busy

Core Executor Implementations

Factory method Description When to use
newFixedThreadPool(n) Fixed number of threads, unbounded queue CPU-bound work with known concurrency
newCachedThreadPool() Grows unboundedly, idle threads expire in 60s Short-lived async tasks (dangerous in prod)
newSingleThreadExecutor() One thread, unbounded queue, serial execution Ordered task processing
newScheduledThreadPool(n) Fixed threads for scheduled/periodic tasks Cron-style background jobs
newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() One virtual thread per task (Java 21) IO-bound workloads

> Executor deep-dive: Lessons 46–47 cover ThreadPoolExecutor configuration, CompletableFuture, ForkJoinPool, and correct sizing formulas.

Part 13

`@Async` in Spring (Preview)

Spring's @Async annotation runs a method in a separate thread from the caller's thread, using a configurable TaskExecutor.

@Service
public class EmailService {

    @Async // runs in Spring's async thread pool
    public void sendWelcomeEmail(User user) {
        // This executes in a different thread
        emailClient.send(user.getEmail(), welcomeTemplate);
    }

    @Async
    public CompletableFuture<String> generateReport(ReportRequest request) {
        String report = reportGenerator.generate(request);
        return CompletableFuture.completedFuture(report);
    }
}

// Enable @Async on a @Configuration class
@EnableAsync
@Configuration
public class AsyncConfig {

    @Bean(name = "taskExecutor")
    public Executor taskExecutor() {
        ThreadPoolTaskExecutor executor = new ThreadPoolTaskExecutor();
        executor.setCorePoolSize(4);
        executor.setMaxPoolSize(16);
        executor.setQueueCapacity(100);
        executor.setThreadNamePrefix("async-email-");
        executor.setRejectedExecutionHandler(new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy());
        executor.initialize();
        return executor;
    }
}

Critical @Async caveat: @Async relies on Spring AOP proxy. If the method is called from within the same class (this.sendWelcomeEmail()), the proxy is bypassed and the call runs synchronously. This is a very common Spring concurrency bug.

> Full coverage: Lesson 47 covers @Async in depth, including @EnableAsync, custom executors, exception handling with AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler, and the proxy bypass pitfall.

Part 14

Thread-Safety Problem Introduction

Since threads share the heap, concurrent writes to the same field without synchronisation produce race conditions — outcomes that depend on the precise timing of thread scheduling.

public class Counter {
    private int count = 0; // shared mutable state

    public void increment() {
        count++; // NOT atomic — 3 bytecode operations:
                 // 1. GETFIELD count
                 // 2. IADD (add 1)
                 // 3. PUTFIELD count
    }

    public int getCount() {
        return count;
    }
}

// Two threads, each calling increment() 1000 times:
Counter counter = new Counter();
Thread t1 = new Thread(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) counter.increment(); });
Thread t2 = new Thread(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) counter.increment(); });
t1.start(); t2.start();
t1.join();  t2.join();

System.out.println(counter.getCount());
// Expected: 2000
// Actual:   1347 (or 1892, or 2000 — unpredictable)

Why the Count is Wrong

Thread 1                    Thread 2
--------                    --------
GETFIELD count  → reads 5
                            GETFIELD count  → reads 5
IADD (5+1=6)
PUTFIELD count = 6
                            IADD (5+1=6)   ← uses stale read of 5!
                            PUTFIELD count = 6

Result: count = 6 instead of 7
One increment was lost.

Solutions (covered in Lesson 44 — Synchronization and Lesson 45 — Java Memory Model):
- synchronized keyword
- java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger
- volatile keyword (for visibility only, not atomicity)
- ReentrantLock

Part 15

Uncaught Exception Handling

By default, uncaught exceptions in a thread print a stack trace to stderr and terminate that thread. The JVM continues running unless it was the last user thread.

// Set handler for a specific thread
Thread t = new Thread(riskyTask);
t.setUncaughtExceptionHandler((thread, ex) -> {
    log.error("Thread [{}] died with exception", thread.getName(), ex);
    metrics.incrementCounter("thread.uncaught.exception");
    alertingService.sendAlert("Thread death: " + thread.getName());
});

// Set default handler for all threads without a specific handler
Thread.setDefaultUncaughtExceptionHandler((thread, ex) -> {
    log.error("UNHANDLED exception in thread [{}]", thread.getName(), ex);
});

With thread pools, uncaught exceptions from Runnable tasks are silently discarded unless you set a handler or use Future.get() to observe the result:

ExecutorService executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4);

// Runnable — exception silently disappears!
executor.execute(() -> { throw new RuntimeException("silent death"); });

// Callable via submit — exception captured in Future
Future<?> f = executor.submit(() -> { throw new RuntimeException("captured"); });
try {
    f.get(); // ExecutionException thrown here with the original as cause
} catch (ExecutionException e) {
    log.error("Task failed", e.getCause());
}
Part 16

Thread Dump Analysis

Thread dumps are the primary tool for diagnosing production threading issues: deadlocks, thread leaks, high CPU by thread, stuck tasks.

HOW TO TAKE A THREAD DUMP:
  kill -3 <pid>                    → prints to stdout
  jstack <pid>                     → prints to stdout
  jcmd <pid> Thread.print          → preferred (safer, more info)
  VisualVM / JMC                   → GUI tools
  kill -3 in Kubernetes pod:
    kubectl exec -it <pod> -- jcmd 1 Thread.print

READING A THREAD DUMP ENTRY:
"payment-worker-3" #42 prio=5 os_prio=0 cpu=1234ms elapsed=300s
  tid=0x00007f... nid=0x3a runnable [0x00007f...]
  java.lang.Thread.State: RUNNABLE
    at com.example.PaymentService.processPayment(PaymentService.java:87)
    at com.example.PaymentWorker.run(PaymentWorker.java:45)
    ...

PARTS:
  "payment-worker-3"   → thread name (why naming matters!)
  #42                  → thread number
  prio=5               → Java priority
  os_prio=0            → OS priority
  cpu=1234ms           → CPU time consumed (high = hot thread)
  elapsed=300s         → wall time since thread started
  nid=0x3a             → native OS thread ID (hex)
  Thread.State: RUNNABLE → current state
  Stack trace          → where the thread is right now

Common Patterns in Thread Dumps

PATTERN: Thread pool properly sized and working
  30 threads named "http-nio-8080-exec-*"
  Mix of RUNNABLE (handling requests) and WAITING (idle, in pool)
  → Normal, healthy

PATTERN: Thread pool saturated
  All 200 "http-nio-8080-exec-*" threads in RUNNABLE
  Hundreds of pending connections in accept queue
  → Scale out, or find slow operations blocking threads

PATTERN: Deadlock
  Thread A: BLOCKED waiting for lock held by Thread B
  Thread B: BLOCKED waiting for lock held by Thread A
  jstack automatically detects and reports: "Found 1 deadlock"

PATTERN: Thread leak
  Count of threads grows over time in production
  → Missing executor.shutdown(), or Threads created outside pools
Part 17

Thread Safety Checklist

THREAD SAFETY CHECKLIST
========================

✓ IDENTIFY shared mutable state
  - Instance fields accessed from multiple threads
  - Static fields (shared across all instances)
  - Collections passed between threads
  - Mutable method arguments

✓ DECIDE on strategy per field:
  - Immutable? → thread-safe by design (String, Integer, record, etc.)
  - Confined to single thread? → no sync needed (stack variables, ThreadLocal)
  - Synchronized? → synchronized, Lock, or atomic
  - Volatile? → visibility only (not atomicity)

✓ DOCUMENT thread-safety in Javadoc
  @ThreadSafe   — safe for concurrent access
  @NotThreadSafe — NOT safe; caller is responsible
  @GuardedBy("lock") — field guarded by a specific lock

✓ PREFER immutability
  - final fields
  - Immutable value objects
  - Records (Java 16+)
  - Unmodifiable collections

✓ USE concurrent utilities (Lesson 45+)
  - AtomicInteger, AtomicReference, LongAdder
  - ConcurrentHashMap, CopyOnWriteArrayList
  - BlockingQueue, ConcurrentLinkedQueue
Part 18

Common Thread Pitfalls

Pitfall 1: Calling run() Instead of start()

// WRONG — no new thread; runs synchronously
new Thread(task).run();

// CORRECT — creates and starts new thread
new Thread(task).start();

Pitfall 2: Ignoring InterruptedException

// WRONG
try { Thread.sleep(1000); } catch (InterruptedException e) { /* ignore */ }

// CORRECT
try { Thread.sleep(1000); } catch (InterruptedException e) {
    Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
    return;
}

Pitfall 3: Creating Unbounded Threads

// WRONG — DDoS yourself
server.onRequest(request -> new Thread(() -> handle(request)).start());

// CORRECT — bounded pool
server.onRequest(request -> executor.submit(() -> handle(request)));

Pitfall 4: Daemon Thread with Critical Work

// WRONG — JVM may kill this before flush completes
Thread flushThread = new Thread(() -> database.flush());
flushThread.setDaemon(true); // JVM may exit before flush
flushThread.start();

// CORRECT — use user thread or shutdown hook
Runtime.getRuntime().addShutdownHook(new Thread(() -> database.flush()));

Pitfall 5: ThreadLocal Leak in Thread Pools

// WRONG — ThreadLocal value stays on pooled thread forever
threadLocal.set(user);
doWork();
// missing: threadLocal.remove()

// CORRECT
try {
    threadLocal.set(user);
    doWork();
} finally {
    threadLocal.remove();
}
Part 19

Production Best Practices

PRODUCTION THREADING RULES
============================

RULE 1: NEVER use new Thread() in production business logic
  Use ExecutorService, @Async, or reactive frameworks.
  Exception: custom ThreadFactory in pool configuration.

RULE 2: NAME every thread pool and thread
  "payment-processor-%d", "kafka-consumer-%d", "email-sender-%d"
  Thread dump debugging without names is archaeology.

RULE 3: SIZE pools based on workload type
  CPU-bound:  corePoolSize = Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() + 1
  IO-bound:   corePoolSize = (target_concurrency) / (1 - blocking_coefficient)
              (Little's Law: L = λW)
  Measure: don't guess. Use async-profiler in production.

RULE 4: BOUND your queues
  new LinkedBlockingQueue<>()   → unbounded, will OOM under load
  new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(500) → bounded, rejects when full (predictable)
  Use rejection policies: CallerRunsPolicy is usually safest.

RULE 5: ALWAYS shut down executors cleanly
  executor.shutdown();         // no new tasks
  executor.awaitTermination(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
  if (!executor.isTerminated()) executor.shutdownNow();

RULE 6: HANDLE uncaught exceptions in thread pools
  Use Future.get() to observe Callable exceptions
  Or decorate Runnable with try/catch logging

RULE 7: MONITOR thread pool metrics
  Active count, queue size, completed count, rejected count
  Alert on: queue size > 80% capacity, rejection count > 0

RULE 8: CLEAN UP ThreadLocals in every finally block
  Mandatory when using thread pools (threads are reused)

RULE 9: Document thread-safety contracts
  @ThreadSafe, @NotThreadSafe, @GuardedBy annotations on shared state

RULE 10: PREFER higher abstractions
  CompletableFuture > Future > Callable > Runnable > new Thread()
  Project Reactor / WebFlux for high-concurrency IO
  Virtual Threads (Java 21) for simple IO-bound blocking code
Part 20

Architecture Considerations

Thread Model Selection by Workload

WORKLOAD: CPU-BOUND (image processing, encryption, ML inference)
  Model:    Fixed thread pool, size ≈ CPU cores
  Reason:   More threads than cores causes context-switch overhead
  Pattern:  ForkJoinPool, parallel streams, ExecutorService.invokeAll()

WORKLOAD: IO-BOUND (database queries, HTTP calls, file reads)
  Classic:  Larger thread pool (threads block waiting for IO)
            Size formula: N_threads = N_cpus × (1 + W/C)
            W = wait time, C = compute time
  Modern:   Virtual threads (Java 21) — one virtual thread per IO op,
            carrier threads never block
  Pattern:  @Async, WebClient (reactive), virtual threads

WORKLOAD: MIXED (typical microservice: HTTP + DB + messaging)
  Separate thread pools per concern:
    http-pool:   handles incoming HTTP requests
    db-pool:     database operations
    kafka-pool:  Kafka consumer group threads
    email-pool:  async email sending
  Prevents "noisy neighbor" — slow Kafka from starving HTTP handlers

WORKLOAD: EVENT-DRIVEN (reactive, high-throughput)
  Model:    Event loop + non-blocking IO (Netty, Project Reactor)
  Threads:  N_cpus event loop threads handle millions of connections
  Pattern:  Spring WebFlux, Micronaut, Quarkus reactive
  Warning:  Never block in event loop threads

Thread Model in Spring Boot Microservices

SPRING BOOT (Servlet, blocking):
  Embedded Tomcat:
    http-nio-8080-exec-1..N (default max=200)
    Each request gets a thread for its full duration
    Thread blocked during DB query, HTTP call, etc.

  @Async pools (custom beans):
    async-email-1..16
    async-report-1..8
    kafka-consumer-1..3 (one per partition typically)

SPRING BOOT (WebFlux, reactive):
  reactor-http-nio-1..N (typically 2× CPU cores)
  Never blocked; single thread handles many requests via event loop
  Backpressure propagated via Flux/Mono pipeline
Part 21

Quick Reference / Cheat Sheet

THREAD FUNDAMENTALS CHEAT SHEET
=================================

STATES:          NEW → RUNNABLE → {BLOCKED/WAITING/TIMED_WAITING} → TERMINATED

CREATION (by preference):
  Best:    executor.submit(callable) / executor.execute(runnable)
  OK:      new Thread(runnable, "name").start()
  NEVER:   new Thread(runnable).run()  ← no concurrency!

KEY METHODS:
  thread.start()          → creates OS thread, calls run()
  thread.run()            → direct call, no new thread (bug!)
  Thread.sleep(ms)        → current thread pauses, keeps locks
  thread.join()           → caller waits for thread to finish
  thread.interrupt()      → sets interrupt flag (cooperative)
  Thread.currentThread()  → reference to current thread
  thread.isDaemon()       → true if daemon thread
  thread.getState()       → returns Thread.State enum

DAEMON vs USER:
  User:   JVM waits for completion. Default for all threads.
  Daemon: JVM exits without waiting. Set BEFORE start().

THREAD NAMING (production must-have):
  ThreadFactory factory = r -> {
      Thread t = new Thread(r, "pool-name-" + counter.incrementAndGet());
      t.setDaemon(false);
      return t;
  };

INTERRUPT HANDLING (always do one of these):
  catch (InterruptedException e) {
      Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // restore flag
      return;                             // or throw
  }

THREADLOCAL CLEANUP (mandatory with thread pools):
  try { tl.set(val); doWork(); } finally { tl.remove(); }

PRIORITY:   Mostly ignored on Linux/macOS. Don't rely on it.

EXECUTOR:   Use ExecutorService. Never new Thread() in business logic.

Interview

Q1: What is the difference between thread.start() and thread.run()? What happens if you call run() directly?

Q2: Explain the six Thread.State values. What transitions are possible, and what causes each transition? Give a real-world example for each state.
