Part 1

Concept Overview

Synchronisation is the mechanism by which threads coordinate access to shared mutable state. Without synchronisation, concurrent threads can interleave reads and writes in arbitrary ways, producing race conditions, stale reads, and data corruption that are nearly impossible to reproduce consistently.

Java provides two tiers of synchronisation:

  1. Intrinsic locks (built-in) — the synchronized keyword, available since Java 1.0
  2. Explicit locks — java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock and its variants, available since Java 5

This lesson covers the synchronized keyword exhaustively — including the wait()/notify() mechanism that rides on top of it. Understanding intrinsic locks is mandatory before any discussion of ReentrantLock, StampedLock, or lock-free algorithms.

What synchronisation solves:

WITHOUT SYNCHRONISATION:
  Thread A writes count = 5
  Thread B reads  count = 5      ← stale read from cache
  Thread A writes count = 6
  Thread B reads  count = 5      ← still stale!
  Thread A reads  count = 5      ← read its own write inconsistently

  Causes: CPU cache coherence, compiler reordering, JIT optimisation

WITH SYNCHRONISATION (synchronized):
  Thread A acquires lock, writes count = 5, releases lock
  Thread B acquires lock (waits if A holds it)
  Thread B reads count = 5      ← guaranteed fresh read
  Thread B writes count = 6, releases lock
  → Serial, correct, predictable

Architect's view of synchronisation cost:

Junior Developer:
  synchronized on everything — "safe but slow"

Mid-level Developer:
  synchronized on critical sections only

Senior Developer:
  Minimize lock scope, use atomic variables, prefer ConcurrentHashMap,
  understand lock contention metrics

Architect:
  - Lock granularity matches contention profile
  - Lock ordering documented to prevent deadlocks
  - synchronized singleton beans in Spring audited
  - Thread dumps read to identify BLOCKED threads under load
  - Benchmarked: lock-free vs synchronized vs ReentrantLock for hot paths
  - Deadlock detection in integration tests and production monitoring
Part 2

Race Conditions and the Need for Synchronisation

A race condition occurs when correctness depends on the relative timing or interleaving of operations in multiple threads. The result is non-deterministic — it may work correctly 99.9% of the time and fail catastrophically under load.

The Classic Race Condition

public class BankAccount {
    private double balance;

    public BankAccount(double initialBalance) {
        this.balance = initialBalance;
    }

    public void deposit(double amount) {
        balance = balance + amount; // READ → COMPUTE → WRITE (3 ops, not atomic)
    }

    public void withdraw(double amount) {
        balance = balance - amount;
    }

    public double getBalance() {
        return balance;
    }
}

// Concurrent deposits: two threads each deposit 100 into a 1000 account
BankAccount account = new BankAccount(1000.0);

Thread t1 = new Thread(() -> account.deposit(100.0));
Thread t2 = new Thread(() -> account.deposit(100.0));
t1.start(); t2.start();
t1.join();  t2.join();

// Expected: 1200.0
// Actual:   1100.0 (intermittently) — one deposit is lost

The Interleaving That Causes the Bug

Time  Thread 1                     Thread 2
----  --------                     --------
  1   READ balance → 1000
  2                                READ balance → 1000  ← reads stale!
  3   COMPUTE 1000 + 100 = 1100
  4   WRITE balance = 1100
  5                                COMPUTE 1000 + 100 = 1100 ← uses stale 1000
  6                                WRITE balance = 1100       ← overwrites t1's write

Result: balance = 1100 (one 100 deposit was lost)

What Synchronisation Guarantees

The synchronized keyword provides two guarantees:
1. Mutual exclusion — at most one thread executes the synchronised code at a time
2. Memory visibility — all writes made before releasing the lock are visible to the next thread that acquires it (happens-before relationship — covered in Lesson 45)

Part 3

`synchronized` on Instance Methods

Declaring a method synchronized means the thread must acquire the intrinsic lock of the object instance before entering the method. All other threads attempting to call any synchronised method on the same instance block until the lock is released.

public class BankAccount {
    private double balance;

    public BankAccount(double initialBalance) {
        this.balance = initialBalance;
    }

    // synchronized on 'this' — the BankAccount instance
    public synchronized void deposit(double amount) {
        balance = balance + amount; // now atomic with respect to other sync methods
    }

    public synchronized void withdraw(double amount) {
        if (amount > balance) throw new InsufficientFundsException(amount, balance);
        balance = balance - amount;
    }

    public synchronized double getBalance() {
        return balance; // also synchronized — ensures fresh read
    }
}

Lock Ownership: The Intrinsic Lock

Every Java object has exactly one intrinsic lock (also called a monitor lock). When a thread calls a synchronized instance method:

Thread enters synchronized method
    │
    ▼
Attempt to acquire 'this' object's intrinsic lock
    │
    ├── Lock is FREE → thread acquires lock, enters method, executes
    │
    └── Lock is HELD by another thread → current thread moves to BLOCKED state
        (waits until the lock holder releases it)

Thread exits synchronized method (normally OR via exception)
    │
    ▼
Lock is RELEASED → one BLOCKED thread wakes up and acquires the lock

Key Properties of synchronized Instance Methods

SCOPE:     Protects this specific object instance
           Two different BankAccount instances have two different locks
           account1.deposit() does NOT block account2.deposit()

REENTRANT: A thread that holds the lock can re-enter any synchronized
           method on the same object without deadlocking (see Part 7)

AUTOMATIC: Lock released on method exit (normal OR exception)
           No chance of forgetting to unlock (unlike ReentrantLock)

VISIBILITY: All writes before release are visible to next lock acquirer
Part 4

`synchronized` on Static Methods

Synchronising a static method uses the Class object's intrinsic lock — not the instance lock.

public class IdGenerator {
    private static long nextId = 0;

    // Acquires lock on IdGenerator.class — not on any instance
    public static synchronized long generateId() {
        return ++nextId;
    }
}

// These acquire DIFFERENT locks — no mutual exclusion between them:
IdGenerator gen = new IdGenerator();
gen.generateId();               // acquires IdGenerator.class lock
new IdGenerator().generateId(); // acquires same IdGenerator.class lock

// Instance method vs static method on same class:
// synchronized instance method → locks 'this'
// synchronized static method   → locks ClassName.class
// They do NOT block each other — different lock objects!

The Danger: Mixed Static and Instance Synchronisation

public class Counter {
    private static int count = 0;

    // Static method — locks Counter.class
    public static synchronized void increment() {
        count++;
    }

    // Instance method — locks 'this' — DIFFERENT LOCK!
    public synchronized int getCount() {
        return count; // NOT protected by the same lock as increment()!
    }
}

// BUG: Thread A calls Counter.increment() (holds Counter.class lock)
//      Thread B calls instance.getCount() (holds 'this' lock)
//      They run concurrently — count is not safely read!

Rule: If a static field is shared and mutated, protect all access with a static lock (either synchronized static methods or synchronized(ClassName.class) blocks).

Part 5

`synchronized` Blocks

synchronized methods lock the entire method. synchronized blocks allow fine-grained locking — only the critical section is locked, not the entire method body.

public class OrderService {
    private final Object orderLock = new Object(); // dedicated lock object
    private final Object inventoryLock = new Object();
    private int pendingOrders = 0;
    private int reservedInventory = 0;

    public void placeOrder(Order order) {
        // Validate order (no shared state, no sync needed)
        validate(order);

        // Only the critical section is synchronized
        synchronized (orderLock) {
            pendingOrders++;
        }

        // More work outside lock (better throughput)
        notifyWarehouse(order);

        synchronized (inventoryLock) {
            reservedInventory -= order.getQuantity();
        }
    }
}

Block vs Method: Scope Comparison

// COARSE-GRAINED — entire method locked
public synchronized void processOrder(Order order) {
    Order validated = validate(order);       // 10ms — no shared state, waste
    synchronized:                            // all of this is locked
    persistToDatabase(validated);            // 50ms — shared state, needed
    notifyWarehouse(validated);              // 20ms — no shared state, waste
    sendConfirmationEmail(validated.getUser()); // 30ms — no shared state, waste
    // Total lock held: 110ms — serialises all threads for 110ms each
}

// FINE-GRAINED — only critical section locked
public void processOrder(Order order) {
    Order validated = validate(order);       // 10ms — outside lock

    synchronized (dbLock) {
        persistToDatabase(validated);        // 50ms — lock held: 50ms only
    }

    notifyWarehouse(validated);              // 20ms — outside lock
    sendConfirmationEmail(validated.getUser()); // 30ms — outside lock
    // Total lock held: 50ms — 55% throughput improvement
}

Lock Object Selection

// Option 1: 'this' as lock object — same as synchronized method
synchronized (this) {
    balance += amount;
}

// Option 2: Dedicated private lock object — preferred
private final Object lock = new Object();
synchronized (lock) {
    balance += amount;
}

// Option 3: Class literal — for static state
synchronized (BankAccount.class) {
    totalAccounts++;
}

// NEVER: Synchronize on a publicly visible lock
public Object publicLock = new Object(); // external code can acquire this lock
synchronized (publicLock) { ... }       // → lock interference / deadlock risk

// NEVER: Synchronize on a String literal
synchronized ("lock") { ... }  // String literals are interned — shared!
                                // All code syncing on "lock" competes for same lock
Part 6

Intrinsic Lock (Monitor) Internals

The JVM implements every object's intrinsic lock as a monitor. The HotSpot JVM optimises monitors through three modes that adapt to contention level:

MONITOR STATES IN HOTSPOT JVM:
================================

1. BIASED LOCK (low contention — single thread)
   ● Object header stores thread ID
   ● Lock acquisition: compare-and-swap on header (< 1 clock cycle)
   ● Revocation cost: high if another thread arrives
   ● Java 15+: biased locking deprecated, Java 21: removed

2. LIGHTWEIGHT LOCK (low contention — rare second thread)
   ● Spin lock: competing thread spins in a busy loop briefly
   ● Avoids expensive OS context switch for short waits
   ● If spinning fails: escalates to heavyweight lock

3. HEAVYWEIGHT LOCK (high contention — multiple threads)
   ● OS mutex: blocked threads park (OS context switch)
   ● ~5,000–10,000 ns to acquire (vs ~2 ns uncontested)
   ● JVM associates a monitor object with the locked object

Object Header (mark word) — 64-bit in HotSpot:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Biased: thread_id | epoch | age | 1 | 01    │
  │ Thin:   ptr_to_lock_record         | 00    │
  │ Fat:    ptr_to_monitor             | 10    │
  │ GC:     forwarding_ptr             | 11    │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Monitor Structure

MONITOR (heavyweight lock)
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ owner: Thread reference (null if free)        │
│ entry count: 0 (how many times owner locked)  │
│                                               │
│ EntrySet:  [Thread-2, Thread-5, Thread-7]     │
│   Threads competing to acquire the lock       │
│   (BLOCKED state in thread dump)              │
│                                               │
│ WaitSet:   [Thread-3, Thread-8]               │
│   Threads that called wait()                  │
│   (WAITING state in thread dump)              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┘

When the owner releases the lock, one thread from the EntrySet wakes up and attempts to acquire. When notify() is called, one thread moves from WaitSet to EntrySet.

Part 7

Reentrant Locks

Java's intrinsic locks are reentrant: a thread that already holds a lock can re-acquire it without deadlocking. Each lock acquisition increments an internal entry count; each release decrements it. The lock is fully released when the count reaches zero.

public class ReentrantExample {
    public synchronized void outer() {
        System.out.println("outer — acquiring lock");
        inner(); // calls another synchronized method on 'this'
    }

    public synchronized void inner() {
        // If locks were NOT reentrant, this would deadlock:
        // outer() holds 'this' lock, then tries to acquire 'this' lock again
        System.out.println("inner — re-entering lock (count = 2)");
    }
}

// Entry count tracking:
// outer() called    → lock acquired, count = 1
// inner() called    → same thread re-acquires, count = 2
// inner() returns   → count decremented to 1
// outer() returns   → count decremented to 0, lock released

Reentrancy Enables Inheritance-Safe Synchronisation

public class Base {
    public synchronized void method() {
        System.out.println("Base.method()");
    }
}

public class Derived extends Base {
    @Override
    public synchronized void method() {
        super.method(); // re-acquires 'this' lock — safe because reentrant
        System.out.println("Derived.method()");
    }
}
Part 8

`wait()`, `notify()`, `notifyAll()`

wait() and notify() implement the monitor condition mechanism — threads can wait for a condition to become true, and other threads can signal when conditions change. This is the foundation of the Producer-Consumer pattern.

All three methods must be called from within a synchronized block or method (holding the lock on the object). Failing to do so throws IllegalMonitorStateException.

Producer-Consumer with wait() / notifyAll()

public class BoundedBuffer<T> {
    private final Queue<T> buffer = new LinkedList<>();
    private final int capacity;
    private final Object lock = new Object();

    public BoundedBuffer(int capacity) {
        this.capacity = capacity;
    }

    // PRODUCER: adds item; waits if buffer full
    public void put(T item) throws InterruptedException {
        synchronized (lock) {
            // ALWAYS use while loop, not if — see Part 9 (spurious wakeup)
            while (buffer.size() == capacity) {
                lock.wait(); // releases lock + waits; re-acquires on wake
            }
            buffer.add(item);
            lock.notifyAll(); // signal waiting consumers
        }
    }

    // CONSUMER: takes item; waits if buffer empty
    public T take() throws InterruptedException {
        synchronized (lock) {
            while (buffer.isEmpty()) {
                lock.wait(); // releases lock + waits; re-acquires on wake
            }
            T item = buffer.poll();
            lock.notifyAll(); // signal waiting producers
            return item;
        }
    }
}

wait() Mechanics — Step by Step

Thread calls object.wait() inside synchronized block:
    │
    ▼
1. Thread releases the intrinsic lock on 'object'
    │
    ▼
2. Thread moves to WaitSet (state: WAITING or TIMED_WAITING)
    │
    ▼
3. Another thread acquires the lock, modifies shared state
    │
    ▼
4. Other thread calls object.notify() or object.notifyAll()
    │
    ├─ notify():     one thread moved from WaitSet to EntrySet (BLOCKED)
    └─ notifyAll():  ALL threads moved from WaitSet to EntrySet (BLOCKED)
    │
    ▼
5. Notified thread(s) compete to acquire the lock
    │
    ▼
6. Winner acquires lock, returns from wait(), resumes after wait() call
    │
    ▼
7. Thread re-checks the condition (while loop!) before proceeding

notify() vs notifyAll() — When to Use Each

Method Behaviour Use when
notify() Wakes one arbitrary thread from WaitSet All waiting threads wait for the SAME condition AND one notification → one action (identical waiters)
notifyAll() Wakes ALL threads from WaitSet Waiting threads wait for DIFFERENT conditions, or when unsure — safer default

Why notifyAll() is usually safer:

// Scenario: 3 consumers waiting (buffer empty), 2 producers waiting (buffer full)
// Producer adds 1 item, calls notify() — only ONE thread wakes up
// If notify() happens to wake a PRODUCER (not a consumer), the producer
// sees buffer still full (it can't consume!), goes back to waiting.
// Result: all consumers still waiting, nothing consumed — potential livelock.

// With notifyAll(): ALL threads wake up, re-check condition, correct one acts.
// Performance cost: more wake-ups, but correctness is guaranteed.
Part 9

Spurious Wakeups

A spurious wakeup occurs when a thread returns from wait() without being notified, interrupted, or timed out. This is allowed by the Java specification (and POSIX threads) because implementing a guarantee against spurious wakeups is prohibitively expensive on some platforms.

// WRONG — using 'if' for condition check
synchronized (lock) {
    if (buffer.isEmpty()) {   // checked once
        lock.wait();          // might return spuriously!
    }
    T item = buffer.poll();   // called even if buffer is empty → NullPointerException
}

// CORRECT — using 'while' for condition check
synchronized (lock) {
    while (buffer.isEmpty()) { // re-checked every time wait() returns
        lock.wait();           // spurious wakeup handled: loops back to check
    }
    T item = buffer.poll();    // guaranteed: buffer is non-empty
}

The rule is absolute: the condition check in a wait() loop MUST always be a while loop, never an if. This handles both spurious wakeups and the case where multiple consumers wake up from notifyAll() but only one can consume.

WAIT() LOOP PATTERN (canonical):
==================================
synchronized (lock) {
    while (! condition) {   ← re-check condition on every wake
        lock.wait();        ← can be spurious, interrupted, or notified
    }
    // condition is now true — safe to proceed
    doWork();
    lock.notifyAll();       ← signal others if state changed
}
Part 10

`synchronized` vs `ReentrantLock` Preview

java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock, introduced in Java 5, provides the same mutual exclusion as synchronized but with additional capabilities.

import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock;

private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();

public void deposit(double amount) {
    lock.lock(); // acquire lock (blocks until available)
    try {
        balance += amount;
    } finally {
        lock.unlock(); // MUST be in finally — otherwise lock leaks on exception
    }
}

// ReentrantLock extras not available with synchronized:

// 1. Timed lock attempt — give up if can't acquire in time
if (lock.tryLock(100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) {
    try {
        balance += amount;
    } finally {
        lock.unlock();
    }
} else {
    // could not acquire lock — handle timeout
}

// 2. Interruptible lock acquisition
lock.lockInterruptibly(); // throws InterruptedException if interrupted while waiting

// 3. Fair lock — threads acquire in FIFO arrival order (prevents starvation)
ReentrantLock fairLock = new ReentrantLock(true);

// 4. Multiple conditions on same lock
Condition notFull  = lock.newCondition();
Condition notEmpty = lock.newCondition();
// notFull.await() / notFull.signal() — targeted condition signalling

Comparison Table

Feature synchronized ReentrantLock
Automatic release Yes (on exit/exception) No — must call unlock() in finally
Timed acquisition No Yes — tryLock(timeout)
Interruptible wait No Yes — lockInterruptibly()
Fairness option No (unfair only) Yes — new ReentrantLock(true)
Multiple conditions One (wait/notify) Multiple (Condition objects)
Lock query (debug) No Yes — getHoldCount(), getQueueLength()
Performance Comparable (JVM optimises well) Slightly higher raw throughput at high contention
Code simplicity Higher — no try/finally needed Lower — explicit lock/unlock required

> When to use ReentrantLock: timed acquisition (prevent indefinite blocking), multiple wait conditions (producer distinguishes full vs empty), fair scheduling to prevent starvation, or diagnostic query of lock state.
>
> Otherwise: prefer synchronized — simpler, less error-prone, JVM optimises aggressively.

Full coverage of ReentrantLock, ReadWriteLock, and StampedLock is in Lesson 46.

Part 11

Deadlock: The Four Conditions

A deadlock occurs when two or more threads are each waiting for a resource held by another, forming a cycle with no way to break it. The threads are stuck forever — they do not throw exceptions and do not time out (unless timed locks are used).

The Four Coffman Conditions

All four must hold simultaneously for deadlock to occur. Preventing any one prevents deadlock.

COFFMAN CONDITIONS FOR DEADLOCK:
==================================

1. MUTUAL EXCLUSION
   A resource can be held by at most one thread at a time.
   → synchronized blocks, locks, file handles, DB connections

2. HOLD AND WAIT
   A thread holds at least one resource while waiting for another.
   → Thread A holds Lock-1, waits for Lock-2
   → Thread B holds Lock-2, waits for Lock-1

3. NO PREEMPTION
   Resources cannot be forcibly taken from a thread.
   → Java intrinsic locks cannot be forcibly released
   → ReentrantLock.tryLock(timeout) enables preemption via timeout

4. CIRCULAR WAIT
   A circular chain: T1 waits for T2, T2 waits for T3, T3 waits for T1.
   → The cycle that makes the condition permanent

Deadlock Code Example

public class DeadlockDemo {
    private final Object lockA = new Object();
    private final Object lockB = new Object();

    public void methodOne() {
        synchronized (lockA) {          // Thread 1 acquires lockA
            System.out.println("Thread 1: holding lockA, waiting for lockB");
            try { Thread.sleep(100); } catch (InterruptedException e) {}
            synchronized (lockB) {      // Thread 1 waits for lockB (held by Thread 2)
                System.out.println("Thread 1: holding lockA and lockB");
            }
        }
    }

    public void methodTwo() {
        synchronized (lockB) {          // Thread 2 acquires lockB
            System.out.println("Thread 2: holding lockB, waiting for lockA");
            try { Thread.sleep(100); } catch (InterruptedException e) {}
            synchronized (lockA) {      // Thread 2 waits for lockA (held by Thread 1)
                System.out.println("Thread 2: holding lockA and lockB");
            }
        }
    }
}

DeadlockDemo demo = new DeadlockDemo();
Thread t1 = new Thread(demo::methodOne);
Thread t2 = new Thread(demo::methodTwo);
t1.start(); t2.start();
// Both threads hang forever — neither print statement executes
Part 12

Deadlock: ASCII Diagram

DEADLOCK STATE DIAGRAM
========================

Thread 1 (BLOCKED)              Thread 2 (BLOCKED)
┌─────────────────────┐         ┌─────────────────────┐
│                     │         │                     │
│  HOLDS lockA ───────┼────┐    │  HOLDS lockB ───────┼────┐
│                     │    │    │                     │    │
│  WAITING for lockB  │    │    │  WAITING for lockA  │    │
│         ▲           │    │    │          ▲          │    │
└─────────┼───────────┘    │    └──────────┼──────────┘    │
          │                │               │               │
          │                └───────────────┘               │
          │                    lockB held by Thread 2       │
          └────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
               lockA held by Thread 1

RESOURCE ALLOCATION GRAPH:
  Thread 1 ──(requests)──► lockB ──(held by)──► Thread 2
  Thread 2 ──(requests)──► lockA ──(held by)──► Thread 1
  Cycle detected → DEADLOCK

THREAD DUMP SIGNATURE:
  "thread-1" BLOCKED on <0xdeadbeef> (lockB) owned by "thread-2"
  "thread-2" BLOCKED on <0xcafebabe> (lockA) owned by "thread-1"
  jstack output: "Found 1 deadlock."

Three-Thread Deadlock

Thread 1 holds Lock-A, wants Lock-B
Thread 2 holds Lock-B, wants Lock-C
Thread 3 holds Lock-C, wants Lock-A

  T1 ──wants──► Lock-B ──held by──► T2
  T2 ──wants──► Lock-C ──held by──► T3
  T3 ──wants──► Lock-A ──held by──► T1

Cycle: T1 → T2 → T3 → T1 → DEADLOCK
Part 13

Deadlock Prevention Strategies

Strategy 1: Lock Ordering (Most Practical)

Always acquire multiple locks in the same global order across all code paths. If every thread acquires Lock-A before Lock-B, no circular wait can form.

public class AccountTransfer {
    private final Object lock = new Object();
    private double balance;
    private final int id;

    public AccountTransfer(int id, double balance) {
        this.id = id;
        this.balance = balance;
    }

    // WRONG: each call acquires locks in different order based on argument order
    public static void transfer_BROKEN(AccountTransfer from, AccountTransfer to, double amount) {
        synchronized (from) {       // Thread A: locks account-1, waits for account-2
            synchronized (to) {     // Thread B: locks account-2, waits for account-1 → DEADLOCK
                from.balance -= amount;
                to.balance += amount;
            }
        }
    }

    // CORRECT: always lock the lower-ID account first — consistent global order
    public static void transfer(AccountTransfer a, AccountTransfer b, double amount) {
        AccountTransfer first  = (a.id < b.id) ? a : b;
        AccountTransfer second = (a.id < b.id) ? b : a;

        synchronized (first) {       // always the lower-ID account
            synchronized (second) {  // always the higher-ID account
                if (a == first) {
                    a.balance -= amount;
                    b.balance += amount;
                } else {
                    b.balance -= amount;
                    a.balance += amount;
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

Strategy 2: Timed Lock Acquisition (with ReentrantLock)

If a thread cannot acquire all needed locks within a timeout, release what it has and retry.

private final ReentrantLock lock1 = new ReentrantLock();
private final ReentrantLock lock2 = new ReentrantLock();

public boolean transferWithTimeout(double amount) throws InterruptedException {
    while (true) {
        if (lock1.tryLock(50, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) {
            try {
                if (lock2.tryLock(50, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) {
                    try {
                        // Both locks acquired — do the work
                        doTransfer(amount);
                        return true;
                    } finally {
                        lock2.unlock();
                    }
                }
            } finally {
                lock1.unlock();
            }
        }
        // Failed to acquire both locks — back off and retry
        Thread.sleep(ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt(10, 50)); // jitter
    }
}

Strategy 3: Lock-Free Algorithms

For counters, accumulators, and simple CAS-based state, use java.util.concurrent.atomic.* classes which use compare-and-swap (CAS) CPU instructions — no locks, no deadlock possible.

// Lock-free counter using AtomicInteger
private final AtomicInteger count = new AtomicInteger(0);

public int increment() {
    return count.incrementAndGet(); // CAS instruction — no lock
}

// Lock-free reference update using AtomicReference
private final AtomicReference<State> state = new AtomicReference<>(State.INITIAL);

public boolean transition(State expected, State next) {
    return state.compareAndSet(expected, next); // atomic: read-compare-set
}

Strategy 4: Reduce Lock Scope and Nesting

Deadlock requires nested lock acquisition. Eliminating nesting eliminates deadlock from that code path.

// RISKY — nested locks
synchronized (lockA) {
    synchronized (lockB) { // nesting creates deadlock potential
        doWork();
    }
}

// SAFE — sequential (not nested) lock acquisition
String data;
synchronized (lockA) {
    data = readData(); // read while holding lockA
}                      // release lockA before acquiring lockB
synchronized (lockB) {
    writeData(data);   // write while holding lockB
}
Part 14

Deadlock Detection

JVM Built-in Detection

The JVM detects deadlocks involving monitor locks and reports them in thread dumps:

jstack <pid>
# Output contains:
# Found 1 deadlock.
# ...
# "thread-1":
#   waiting to lock monitor 0x00007f... (object 0x0..., a com.example.LockA),
#   which is held by "thread-2"
# "thread-2":
#   waiting to lock monitor 0x00007f... (object 0x0..., a com.example.LockB),
#   which is held by "thread-1"

Programmatic Detection

ThreadMXBean threadMXBean = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean();

// Detects deadlocks involving intrinsic monitors
long[] deadlockedThreads = threadMXBean.findMonitorDeadlockedThreads();

// Also detects ReentrantLock deadlocks
long[] allDeadlocked = threadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads();

if (allDeadlocked != null) {
    ThreadInfo[] info = threadMXBean.getThreadInfo(allDeadlocked, true, true);
    for (ThreadInfo ti : info) {
        log.error("DEADLOCK DETECTED: thread [{}] state [{}]",
            ti.getThreadName(), ti.getThreadState());
    }
    // Alert, dump state, consider graceful restart
}

Deadlock Detection in Tests

@Test
void shouldNotDeadlock() throws Exception {
    CountDownLatch startLatch = new CountDownLatch(1);
    CountDownLatch doneLatch = new CountDownLatch(2);
    AtomicBoolean completed = new AtomicBoolean(false);

    Thread t1 = new Thread(() -> {
        try {
            startLatch.await();
            accountService.transfer(account1, account2, 100.0);
            doneLatch.countDown();
        } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
    });
    Thread t2 = new Thread(() -> {
        try {
            startLatch.await();
            accountService.transfer(account2, account1, 50.0);
            doneLatch.countDown();
        } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
    });

    t1.start(); t2.start();
    startLatch.countDown(); // start both simultaneously

    boolean finished = doneLatch.await(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
    assertTrue(finished, "Transfer deadlocked — did not complete within 5 seconds");
}
Part 15

Livelock and Starvation

Two concurrency hazards related to but distinct from deadlock:

Livelock

Threads are active (not BLOCKED) but make no progress — each continuously responds to the other's actions.

LIVELOCK ANALOGY:
  Two people meet in a narrow corridor.
  Person A steps left, Person B steps right → still blocked.
  Person A steps right, Person B steps left → still blocked.
  Both moving, neither progressing.

LIVELOCK IN CODE:
  Thread 1: detects conflict → backs off → retries
  Thread 2: detects conflict → backs off → retries
  Both back off at exactly the same time repeatedly

SOLUTION: Add randomised backoff (jitter)
  Thread.sleep(ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt(10, 100));

Starvation

One thread is perpetually denied CPU time or lock access because other threads always preempt it.

STARVATION SCENARIO:
  Many high-priority threads (prio=10) and one low-priority thread (prio=1)
  High-priority threads always scheduled first
  Low-priority thread waits indefinitely

STARVATION WITH SYNCHRONIZED:
  Unfair lock: threads compete freely; same threads may win repeatedly
  A thread may wait arbitrarily long if others continuously acquire first

SOLUTION:
  ReentrantLock(true) — fair mode, FIFO ordering
  Rate limiting high-priority threads
  Ensure all threads eventually get scheduled
Part 16

`volatile` Keyword

volatile provides memory visibility without mutual exclusion. It guarantees that writes to a volatile variable are immediately visible to all threads, and prevents certain compiler/CPU reorderings.

public class StatusMonitor {
    // Without volatile: compiler/CPU may cache this in a register
    // Another thread's write may never be seen by this thread
    private volatile boolean running = true;

    public void stop() {
        running = false; // write is immediately flushed to main memory
    }

    public void monitor() {
        while (running) {        // read always from main memory, not cache
            checkSystemHealth();
        }
        System.out.println("Monitor stopped");
    }
}

volatile Guarantees and Non-Guarantees

volatile GUARANTEES:
  ✓ Visibility: writes visible to all threads immediately (no CPU cache staleness)
  ✓ Ordering: write happens-before subsequent reads (JMM guarantee)
  ✓ Atomicity: for single read/write of long and double (otherwise non-atomic on 32-bit JVM)
  ✓ Prevents certain reorderings (memory fence instruction)

volatile DOES NOT GUARANTEE:
  ✗ Atomicity for compound operations: count++ is still 3 ops (read, add, write)
  ✗ Mutual exclusion: two threads can still run concurrently
  ✗ Transactions: check-then-act is not atomic

CORRECT USE CASES:
  ✓ Single-writer, multiple-reader flags: volatile boolean shutdown = false
  ✓ Safely publishing an immutable object reference: volatile Config config
  ✓ Double-checked locking with volatile (see below)

WRONG USE CASES:
  ✗ Counter: volatile int count; count++; ← still a race condition!
  ✗ Conditional increment: if (count < max) count++; ← race between check and act

Double-Checked Locking with volatile

public class Singleton {
    // volatile ensures the object reference is fully visible before being assigned
    private static volatile Singleton instance;

    private Singleton() { }

    public static Singleton getInstance() {
        if (instance == null) {              // First check (no lock)
            synchronized (Singleton.class) {
                if (instance == null) {      // Second check (with lock)
                    instance = new Singleton(); // volatile ensures safe publication
                }
            }
        }
        return instance;
    }
}
// Without volatile on 'instance':
// JVM may partially construct the object and publish the reference before
// the constructor completes — another thread reads a broken object.
// volatile prevents this reordering.
Part 17

`synchronized` Singleton Beans in Spring: The Danger

Spring beans are singleton-scoped by default — one instance shared across all request threads. A synchronized method on a Spring bean becomes a global serialisation point in the application.

@Service
public class ReportService {
    private final ReportRepository repository;

    // DANGER: synchronized on a Spring singleton bean
    // Every request to generateReport() competes for ONE lock
    // 200 concurrent users → 199 threads BLOCKED at any moment
    public synchronized Report generateReport(ReportRequest request) {
        return repository.generate(request); // 500ms database query
    }
}

The Impact at Scale

THROUGHPUT CALCULATION:
  synchronized generateReport()  ← 500ms per call
  10 requests/second arriving
  With synchronized: only 2 req/s throughput (1000ms / 500ms = 2)
  Queued: 8 * 500ms = 4 seconds average wait time per request
  At 100 users: 99 threads BLOCKED, 1 running = terrible throughput

  Root cause: synchronization on a singleton bean serialises ALL access.

When to Actually Use synchronized on a Spring Bean

@Service
public class IdempotencyService {
    private final Set<String> processedIds = new HashSet<>(); // shared mutable state

    // synchronized protects shared mutable state (the Set)
    // This IS appropriate — the synchronisation protects actual state, not external IO
    public synchronized boolean markAndCheckProcessed(String idempotencyKey) {
        if (processedIds.contains(idempotencyKey)) {
            return false; // already processed
        }
        processedIds.add(idempotencyKey);
        return true; // first time — proceed
    }
}

// Better alternative: ConcurrentHashMap.putIfAbsent() — lock-free
private final Map<String, Boolean> processedIds = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

public boolean markAndCheckProcessed(String key) {
    return processedIds.putIfAbsent(key, Boolean.TRUE) == null;
}

Spring Singleton Concurrency Checklist

SPRING SINGLETON SAFETY AUDIT:
================================
For each @Service / @Component / @Repository:

✓ SAFE: No mutable instance fields (stateless service)
✓ SAFE: Only final fields (injected dependencies)
✓ SAFE: ThreadLocal state (per-request, not shared)
✓ SAFE: Immutable objects (records, Collections.unmodifiableX)

⚠ REVIEW: Mutable instance fields
  → Are they accessed from multiple threads?
  → Do they need synchronization?

✗ DANGER: Mutable fields without synchronization
✗ DANGER: synchronized method wrapping external IO (serializes requests)
✗ DANGER: Collections without concurrent variants (ArrayList, HashMap)
Part 18

Minimising `synchronized` Scope

The golden rule: hold locks for the shortest time possible. Every millisecond a lock is held is a millisecond all other threads wait.

Refactoring: From Method-Level to Block-Level

// BEFORE: entire method synchronized (slow)
@Service
public class OrderProcessor {
    private final Map<String, Integer> orderCounts = new HashMap<>();

    public synchronized ProcessedOrder process(Order order) {
        // Step 1: Validate (20ms, no shared state — doesn't need lock)
        validate(order);

        // Step 2: Enrich from external API (150ms, no shared state — doesn't need lock)
        OrderDetails details = enrichmentService.enrich(order);

        // Step 3: Update shared counter (1ms, NEEDS lock)
        orderCounts.merge(order.getType(), 1, Integer::sum);

        // Step 4: Persist (80ms, no shared state — doesn't need lock)
        return repository.save(details);
    }
    // Total lock held: 251ms
}

// AFTER: only critical section synchronized (fast)
@Service
public class OrderProcessor {
    private final Map<String, Integer> orderCounts = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); // better yet

    public ProcessedOrder process(Order order) {
        validate(order);                                        // 20ms — no lock
        OrderDetails details = enrichmentService.enrich(order); // 150ms — no lock

        // Only the actual shared-state update needs synchronisation
        orderCounts.merge(order.getType(), 1, Integer::sum);    // 1ms — ConcurrentHashMap: lock-free!

        return repository.save(details);                        // 80ms — no lock
    }
    // Total lock held: 0ms (ConcurrentHashMap handles its own locking internally)
}

Split Locks for Independent Data

// BEFORE: one lock for everything (unnecessary serialisation)
public class Statistics {
    private final Object lock = new Object();
    private int requestCount = 0;
    private int errorCount = 0;

    public synchronized void recordRequest() { requestCount++; }
    public synchronized void recordError()   { errorCount++;   }
    // recordRequest and recordError never interact — why share a lock?
}

// AFTER: separate locks for independent state
public class Statistics {
    private final AtomicInteger requestCount = new AtomicInteger();
    private final AtomicInteger errorCount   = new AtomicInteger();

    public void recordRequest() { requestCount.incrementAndGet(); }
    public void recordError()   { errorCount.incrementAndGet();   }
    // No contention between the two counters
}
Part 19

Lock Ordering Strategy

Documenting and enforcing lock ordering prevents deadlocks in complex systems. This is an architectural concern.

/**
 * LOCK ORDERING POLICY FOR OrderManagementService:
 *
 * When multiple locks must be held simultaneously, acquire in this order:
 *   1. customerLock  (lowest priority — acquired first)
 *   2. inventoryLock
 *   3. paymentLock   (highest priority — acquired last)
 *
 * NEVER acquire a lower-numbered lock while holding a higher-numbered lock.
 * Document any deviation from this policy with a detailed comment.
 */
public class OrderManagementService {
    @GuardedBy("customerLock")
    private final Object customerLock = new Object();
    @GuardedBy("inventoryLock")
    private final Object inventoryLock = new Object();
    @GuardedBy("paymentLock")
    private final Object paymentLock = new Object();

    public void placeOrder(Customer customer, List<Item> items, Payment payment) {
        // Acquire in documented order: customer → inventory → payment
        synchronized (customerLock) {
            synchronized (inventoryLock) {
                synchronized (paymentLock) {
                    customer.reserveCredit(payment.getAmount());
                    items.forEach(inventoryService::reserve);
                    payment.process();
                }
            }
        }
    }

    // COMPLIANT: acquiring subset of locks, in order
    public void updateInventory(List<Item> items) {
        synchronized (inventoryLock) { // no customerLock held — fine
            items.forEach(inventoryService::update);
        }
    }
}

Lock Ordering with System Identity Hash

For data-driven lock ordering (when you don't control lock creation):

private static void lockBoth(Object lockA, Object lockB, Runnable action) {
    // Use System.identityHashCode() for consistent ordering
    int hashA = System.identityHashCode(lockA);
    int hashB = System.identityHashCode(lockB);

    Object first  = (hashA <= hashB) ? lockA : lockB;
    Object second = (hashA <= hashB) ? lockB : lockA;

    synchronized (first) {
        synchronized (second) {
            action.run();
        }
    }
}
Part 20

Production Best Practices

SYNCHRONIZATION PRODUCTION RULES
===================================

RULE 1: MINIMIZE synchronized scope
  Lock only the critical section, not the entire method.
  IO operations (DB, HTTP, filesystem) should NEVER be inside a synchronized block
  unless the IO itself IS the shared resource being protected.

RULE 2: ESTABLISH and DOCUMENT lock ordering
  Before you write any code with multiple locks, define the ordering.
  Write it in a class-level Javadoc comment. Code review: enforce it.

RULE 3: PREFER concurrent utilities over synchronized
  ConcurrentHashMap > synchronized HashMap
  AtomicInteger > synchronized int counter
  CopyOnWriteArrayList > synchronized ArrayList (read-heavy lists)
  BlockingQueue > manual wait/notify producer-consumer
  These are better tested, documented, and often faster.

RULE 4: AUDIT synchronized singleton beans in Spring
  Every @Service with a synchronized method is a potential bottleneck.
  Strive for stateless services (no mutable instance fields).
  Use ConcurrentHashMap for caches, AtomicXxx for counters.

RULE 5: USE ReentrantLock when you need extras
  Timed tryLock, interruptible lock, multiple conditions, fair scheduling.
  ALWAYS unlock in a finally block — no exceptions.

RULE 6: NEVER hold locks across external IO
  While holding a lock, an external service call can block for seconds.
  All other threads wait for the entire duration.
  Extract the IO before or after the synchronized section.

RULE 7: MONITOR lock contention in production
  Expose thread pool metrics: active count, BLOCKED thread count
  Thread dump on high CPU or latency spikes
  async-profiler: lock profiling mode shows hot lock locations
  alert: BLOCKED thread count > N for > 30 seconds = incident

RULE 8: TEST for deadlocks
  Concurrency tests: use CountDownLatch to force concurrent entry
  Assert completion within timeout (e.g., 5 seconds)
  Use ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads() in integration tests

RULE 9: AVOID synchronized in constructors
  The 'this' reference may not be fully constructed yet
  Another thread calling a synchronized method on a partially-constructed
  object can observe inconsistent state
  → Use factory methods that complete construction before publication

RULE 10: DOCUMENT thread-safety guarantees on every shared class
  @ThreadSafe   — all public methods are safe for concurrent use
  @NotThreadSafe — external synchronization required
  @Immutable    — implicitly thread-safe (all fields final)
  @GuardedBy    — per-field/method annotation on the guard
Part 21

Quick Reference / Cheat Sheet

SYNCHRONIZATION CHEAT SHEET
==============================

SYNTAX:
  synchronized method:  public synchronized void method() { ... }
  synchronized block:   synchronized (lockObject) { ... }
  synchronized static:  public static synchronized void method() { ... }

LOCK OBJECTS:
  'this'         → instance method synchronized — locks the object
  ClassName.class → static method synchronized — locks the class
  private Object  → dedicated block lock (preferred)

INTRINSIC LOCK PROPERTIES:
  ✓ Reentrant: same thread can re-acquire without deadlock
  ✓ Automatic release: released on normal exit OR exception
  ✓ Memory visibility: writes before release visible after acquire
  ✗ Not interruptible (unlike ReentrantLock.lockInterruptibly())
  ✗ Not timed (unlike ReentrantLock.tryLock(timeout))

WAIT / NOTIFY CONTRACT:
  MUST be inside synchronized block on same object
  ALWAYS use while loop for condition check (not if):
    synchronized (lock) {
        while (!condition) { lock.wait(); }
        // condition is true
        lock.notifyAll();
    }
  notify()     → wakes ONE arbitrary thread from WaitSet
  notifyAll()  → wakes ALL threads from WaitSet (safer default)

DEADLOCK CONDITIONS (all 4 must hold):
  1. Mutual exclusion   2. Hold and wait
  3. No preemption      4. Circular wait
  PREVENT: lock ordering, timed tryLock, reduce nesting

volatile:
  ✓ Visibility of writes    ✗ Atomicity of compound ops
  Use for: flags, safe publication of immutable objects

PREFER OVER synchronized (when applicable):
  AtomicInteger/Long/Reference     → lock-free counters/references
  ConcurrentHashMap                → concurrent map
  BlockingQueue                    → producer-consumer
  ReentrantReadWriteLock           → many readers, few writers
  StampedLock                      → optimistic reads (Java 8+)

SPRING SINGLETON:
  ✗ synchronized method on @Service = global bottleneck
  ✓ Stateless services (no mutable fields)
  ✓ ConcurrentHashMap for shared caches

Lesson 44 Summary Table

Concept Key Rule Common Mistake
synchronized instance method Locks this; all threads share one lock per object instance Using on a Spring singleton creates a single global lock
synchronized static method Locks ClassName.class; different from instance lock Mixing static and instance synchronized — NOT mutually exclusive
synchronized block Fine-grained; lock only the critical section Holding lock during IO — unnecessary serialisation
Intrinsic lock (monitor) Every object has one; reentrant for the owning thread Forgetting reentrancy — calling synchronized method from synchronized method on same object is safe
wait() Releases lock + suspends; must be inside synchronized Not using while loop — fails on spurious wakeups
notify() vs notifyAll() notify() wakes one; notifyAll() wakes all Using notify() when threads wait on different conditions → some never wake
Spurious wakeups wait() may return without notification Using if instead of while for condition check
Deadlock 4 conditions: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait Acquiring locks in different orders in different code paths
Deadlock prevention Lock ordering, tryLock(timeout), reduce nesting No documented lock order → ad-hoc acquisition → deadlock risk grows
volatile Visibility only — NOT atomicity for compound ops Using volatile int for count++ — still a race condition
ReentrantLock Must unlock() in finally; enables timed/interruptible acquisition Forgetting to unlock in finally block → lock leaked forever
Starvation Unfair lock: same threads may win repeatedly Ignoring thread starvation — some tasks never complete
Lock scope Minimize: smaller scope = better throughput Whole-method lock when block lock suffices
@GuardedBy Document which lock protects which field Undocumented locks → incorrect concurrent modifications

Part 1

Concept Overview

The Java Memory Model (JMM) is a specification embedded in the Java Language Specification (JLS Chapter 17) and the Java Virtual Machine Specification that precisely defines when and how changes made by one thread become visible to other threads. It is the contract between the programmer, the compiler, the JVM, and the underlying hardware.

Without the JMM, writing correct multithreaded Java code would be impossible — you would have to understand every CPU architecture's cache coherence protocol, every JIT compiler's optimization strategy, and every OS thread scheduler. The JMM abstracts all of that into a single, portable set of rules.

Why the JMM exists: Modern hardware does not execute programs in the order written. CPUs reorder instructions to fill pipeline stalls. Compilers hoist reads, sink writes, eliminate dead stores. CPU caches introduce locally visible states not yet flushed to main memory. These optimizations are critical for performance. The JMM defines which reorderings are allowed so that compilers and CPUs can optimize freely, while giving programmers tools (synchronization, volatile, final) to impose ordering constraints where correctness demands it.

Core problems the JMM addresses:
1. Visibility — a write by Thread A may not be seen by Thread B
2. Ordering — Thread B may observe Thread A's writes in a different order than A performed them
3. Atomicity — compound operations (read-modify-write) may not execute without interleaving

Part 2

Main Memory vs. Thread Working Memory

The JMM defines an abstract memory model, not a map to physical hardware. Think of it as two layers:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     MAIN MEMORY                         │
│                                                         │
│   [x = 0]   [y = 0]   [flag = false]   [obj.field=0]  │
└──────────┬───────────────────────┬───────────────────────┘
           │   read/write          │   read/write
    ┌──────▼──────┐         ┌──────▼──────┐
    │  Thread A   │         │  Thread B   │
    │ Working Mem │         │ Working Mem │
    │             │         │             │
    │  x_copy=0   │         │  x_copy=??? │
    │  flag=false │         │  flag=???   │
    └─────────────┘         └─────────────┘
  • Main memory holds the master copy of all variables.
  • Each thread has its own working memory (conceptual — maps to CPU registers, L1/L2 caches, store buffers in practice).
  • A thread reads a variable by loading it from main memory into its working memory.
  • A thread writes a variable by updating its working memory copy; that write may or may not be flushed to main memory immediately.

This is why Thread B can read a stale value for a field that Thread A already updated: A's write is sitting in A's working memory / store buffer, not yet visible to B.

Part 3

The Visibility Problem in Detail

// Shared state (no synchronization)
boolean stopRequested = false;

// Thread A — background worker
new Thread(() -> {
    while (!stopRequested) {  // may loop FOREVER
        // do work
    }
    System.out.println("Thread A stopped");
}).start();

// Main Thread — controller
Thread.sleep(1000);
stopRequested = true;   // Thread A may NEVER see this!

What can go wrong without synchronization:

Timeline (no sync):

Main Thread:  writes stopRequested=true  → L1 cache of core 0
                                            NOT flushed to main memory

Thread A:     reads stopRequested        ← its own L1 cache on core 1
                                            (stale: false)
              loops forever

The JIT compiler can also hoist the read of stopRequested out of the loop entirely, effectively transforming it to:

// JIT-optimized version (legal without JMM guarantee!)
if (!stopRequested) {
    while (true) { /* infinite loop */ }
}

This is perfectly valid from the JMM's perspective unless you establish a happens-before relationship.

Part 4

The Ordering Problem

Consider two threads sharing two variables:

int x = 0;
boolean ready = false;

// Thread A
x = 42;
ready = true;

// Thread B
if (ready) {
    System.out.println(x);  // May print 0!
}

Without synchronization, Thread B observing ready == true does not guarantee it will see x == 42. The CPU or compiler may have reordered the stores in Thread A (writing ready = true before x = 42), or Thread B may load x from its stale cache.

Possible execution orderings visible to Thread B:

┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Thread A writes   │  Thread B reads    │  Output      │
├────────────────────┼────────────────────┼──────────────┤
│  x=42, ready=true  │  ready=true, x=42  │  42  ✓       │
│  ready=true, x=42  │  ready=true, x=0   │  0   ✗ BUG  │
│  x=42, ready=true  │  ready=false       │  (skips)     │
└────────────────────┴────────────────────┴──────────────┘
Part 5

The Atomicity Problem

long counter = 0L;

// Two threads calling increment concurrently
counter++;  // NOT atomic — read-modify-write

Even long reads/writes are not guaranteed atomic on 32-bit JVMs (two 32-bit operations). The ++ operation always expands to three bytecode instructions:

GETFIELD counter    // read
LADD / IADD         // add 1
PUTFIELD counter    // write

Between any two of these steps, another thread can interleave, causing lost updates:

Thread A: read(counter=0)
Thread B: read(counter=0)
Thread A: write(counter=1)
Thread B: write(counter=1)  ← lost A's update! Expected: 2, Got: 1
Part 6

Happens-Before: The Core JMM Rule

The JMM is formally specified using the happens-before (hb) relation. If action A happens-before action B, then:

  1. All effects of A (writes) are visible to B
  2. All actions of A appear to occur before B in program execution

Happens-before is NOT about physical time. It is about a formal ordering guarantee. If there is no happens-before edge between a write and a read, the read may legally see any value — even a value from the far past or a value that seems "impossible."

Formal definition (JLS 17.4.5):
    hb(A, B)  means:
        "If A happens-before B, then A is visible to and ordered before B"

hb is:
    - Reflexive:   hb(x, x)
    - Transitive:  hb(A,B) ∧ hb(B,C) → hb(A,C)   ← CRITICAL for chaining
    - Antisymmetric (no cycles in well-formed programs)
Part 7

The Six Happens-Before Rules

The JMM defines exactly six rules that create happens-before edges:

Rule 1: Program Order Rule

Within a single thread, every action happens-before every subsequent action in that thread.

Thread A:
  write x = 1   ─hb─▶  write y = 2   ─hb─▶  read z
  (all within same thread)

This does NOT mean they execute in that order on the CPU. It means from the perspective of that thread, the effects appear in order. The CPU can reorder freely as long as the single-thread view is consistent.

Rule 2: Monitor Lock Rule (synchronized)

An unlock of a monitor happens-before every subsequent lock of that same monitor.

synchronized(lock) {
    x = 42;
}   // ← unlock: hb edge created here

// ... later in another thread ...

synchronized(lock) {
    System.out.println(x);  // ← lock: guaranteed to see x=42
}

Thread A:                           Thread B:
  lock(monitor)                       ... (time passes) ...
  x = 42                              lock(monitor)  ←─── hb ─── Thread A's unlock
  unlock(monitor) ─── hb ──────────▶  read x  // sees 42

Rule 3: Volatile Variable Rule

A write to a volatile variable happens-before every subsequent read of that same volatile variable.

volatile boolean flag = false;
volatile int data = 0;

// Thread A
data = 42;        // (1)
flag = true;      // (2) volatile write

// Thread B
if (flag) {       // (3) volatile read ─── hb ──▶ sees (2)
    // Also sees (1) via transitivity!
    System.out.println(data);  // guaranteed 42
}

Rule 4: Thread Start Rule

A call to Thread.start() happens-before every action in the started thread.

x = 10;
thread.start();  // hb ──▶ everything inside thread's run()

The new thread is guaranteed to see x = 10.

Rule 5: Thread Termination Rule (join)

All actions in a thread happen-before another thread returns from Thread.join() on that thread.

thread.join();  // ← blocks until thread dies
// hb edge: everything thread did ──▶ code after join()
System.out.println(result);  // sees thread's writes

Rule 6: Object Construction Rule (final fields)

All writes to final fields in a constructor happen-before any thread reading those fields via a properly published reference.

class Immutable {
    final int x;
    Immutable() { x = 42; }  // write to final hb ──▶ any read of x
}
Part 8

Transitivity: The Power of Chained Happens-Before

Because hb is transitive, you can chain rules:

Thread A writes x=42           (program order)
Thread A writes volatile flag  (program order, hb from above)
Thread B reads volatile flag   (volatile rule: A's write hb B's read)
Thread B reads x               (transitivity: A's x=42 hb this read)

This is why a single volatile write/read can be used to publish an entire bundle of writes — all writes before the volatile write are visible to anyone who reads the volatile variable afterward.

Part 9

What the JMM Does NOT Guarantee

Understanding the absence of guarantees is as important as understanding the guarantees:

Scenario Guarantee?
Two threads writing/reading shared field with no sync None
Thread A writes field, Thread B reads it (no sync, no volatile) None — B may see stale value
Thread A writes x then y (no sync), Thread B reads y then x No ordering — B may see y new but x old
long or double field read/write Not guaranteed atomic (2 x 32-bit ops on 32-bit JVM)
Multiple volatile fields updated atomically Not guaranteed — each volatile op is individually ordered but not grouped
volatile int i; i++ Not atomic — still a read-modify-write race

Part 11

Double-Checked Locking: The Classic JMM Failure

Double-checked locking (DCL) is a pattern used to lazily initialize a singleton with minimal locking overhead. The naive version is broken without volatile:

Broken DCL (Pre-Java 5 / without volatile)

public class BrokenSingleton {
    private static BrokenSingleton instance;  // NOT volatile

    public static BrokenSingleton getInstance() {
        if (instance == null) {              // Check 1 (no lock)
            synchronized (BrokenSingleton.class) {
                if (instance == null) {      // Check 2 (with lock)
                    instance = new BrokenSingleton(); // PROBLEM HERE
                }
            }
        }
        return instance;
    }
}

Why it's broken: instance = new BrokenSingleton() compiles to three conceptual steps:

1. allocate memory for BrokenSingleton object
2. initialize the object (run constructor)
3. assign reference to instance variable

The JIT / CPU is allowed to reorder steps 2 and 3:

1. allocate memory
3. assign reference to instance  ← instance is now non-null but UNINITIALIZED!
2. initialize the object          ← runs after reference is visible

Thread B reads instance after step 3 but before step 2:
→ instance != null (passes first check)
→ returns a PARTIALLY CONSTRUCTED object
→ calling any method on it: undefined behavior / NPE / wrong values

Fixed DCL (Java 5+ with volatile)

public class SafeSingleton {
    private static volatile SafeSingleton instance; // volatile fixes it

    public static SafeSingleton getInstance() {
        if (instance == null) {
            synchronized (SafeSingleton.class) {
                if (instance == null) {
                    instance = new SafeSingleton();
                }
            }
        }
        return instance;
    }
}

The volatile write to instance creates a happens-before edge: all writes inside the constructor hb the volatile write to instance hb any thread's read of instance. No thread can see a partially constructed object.

Alternative: Initialization-on-Demand Holder (preferred)

public class HolderSingleton {
    private HolderSingleton() {}

    private static class Holder {
        static final HolderSingleton INSTANCE = new HolderSingleton();
    }

    public static HolderSingleton getInstance() {
        return Holder.INSTANCE;  // class loading is thread-safe by JVM spec
    }
}

This leverages the JVM class-loading guarantee: a class is initialized exactly once, and final field writes in static initializers are visible to all subsequent readers.

Part 12

JMM and the synchronized Block

synchronized provides both mutual exclusion and memory visibility. When a thread exits a synchronized block:

  1. All writes performed inside (and before) the block are flushed to main memory.
  2. When another thread enters a synchronized block on the same monitor, it sees all those writes (the unlock hb the lock).
class SafeCounter {
    private int count = 0;
    private final Object lock = new Object();

    public void increment() {
        synchronized (lock) {
            count++;  // read-modify-write under lock: safe
        }
    }

    public int get() {
        synchronized (lock) {
            return count;  // reading under lock: sees latest value
        }
    }
}

Critical point: Two synchronized blocks must use the same monitor to establish happens-before. Different monitors provide mutual exclusion to their respective critical sections but create no hb relationship between them.

Part 13

JMM and final Fields

Fields declared final receive special JMM treatment via the final field freeze guarantee:

class FinalExample {
    final int x;
    int y;  // NOT final

    FinalExample(int x, int y) {
        this.x = x;  // freeze of x happens at end of constructor
        this.y = y;  // no freeze
    }
}

// Publishing safely:
FinalExample ref = new FinalExample(42, 100);
sharedRef = ref;  // safe publication of final fields

Any thread that reads sharedRef is guaranteed to see x = 42, even without synchronization. The value of y is not guaranteed.

Warning: The freeze guarantee only applies if the reference does not "escape" the constructor:

FinalExample(int x) {
    sharedList.add(this);  // THIS ESCAPES — final freeze may not apply!
    this.x = x;
}
Part 14

Safe Publication Idioms

"Publishing" an object means making it accessible to other threads. Safe publication requires that all object state is visible when the reference is first read. Four safe publication mechanisms:

Mechanism How it works
static final field JVM class initialization is thread-safe; final fields freeze
volatile field volatile write hb any subsequent volatile read
synchronized block Unlock hb lock on same monitor
AtomicReference Uses volatile semantics internally
final field in constructor Freeze guarantee (see Part 13) 
// UNSAFE publication
class Holder {
    static Holder instance;  // not volatile, not final
}
// Thread B may see instance != null but with default-initialized fields

// SAFE publication
class Holder {
    static volatile Holder instance;
    // OR:
    static final Holder instance = new Holder();
}
Part 15

Memory Barriers (Under the Hood)

The JMM rules map to memory barriers (also called memory fences) inserted by the JIT compiler. These are hardware instructions that restrict the CPU's ability to reorder loads and stores.

Types of memory barriers:
┌─────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Barrier Type    │ Prevents                                         │
├─────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ LoadLoad        │ A load reordered before a prior load             │
│ LoadStore       │ A store reordered before a prior load            │
│ StoreLoad       │ A load reordered before a prior store  (costliest)│
│ StoreStore      │ A store reordered before a prior store           │
└─────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

A volatile write inserts a StoreStore barrier before it and a StoreLoad barrier after it. A volatile read inserts a LoadLoad + LoadStore barrier after it. synchronized unlock inserts a StoreLoad barrier. These barriers tell the CPU: "flush your store buffer" or "invalidate your load buffer."

Part 16

Common JMM Pitfalls in Practice

Pitfall 1: Assuming visibility without synchronization

// Thread pool task — worker reads shared config
class Task implements Runnable {
    private boolean active = true;  // NOT volatile

    public void cancel() { active = false; }  // called from another thread

    public void run() {
        while (active) { /* may loop forever */ }
    }
}

Fix: declare active as volatile boolean active = true;

Pitfall 2: Compound check-then-act without atomicity

// Thread-unsafe: check then act
if (map.get(key) == null) {
    map.put(key, computeValue());  // race: two threads may both insert
}

// Fix: use computeIfAbsent (atomic in ConcurrentHashMap)
map.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> computeValue());

Pitfall 3: Lazy initialization without safe publication

// Thread-unsafe lazy init
private ExpensiveObject cache;

public ExpensiveObject get() {
    if (cache == null) {
        cache = new ExpensiveObject();  // race + partial construction risk
    }
    return cache;
}

// Fix: volatile + DCL, or holder pattern (see Part 11)

Pitfall 4: Sharing mutable objects without synchronization

// Shared between threads — NOT safe without sync
class Config {
    public String host = "localhost";
    public int port = 8080;
}

Fix: use synchronized accessor methods, or make fields volatile, or use an immutable Config record with safe publication.

Part 17

JMM and the Java Happens-Before Visualization

│                                                                 │

│  ──────────────────           ──────────────────               │
│  write x=10                                                     │
│  write y=20                                                     │
│  lock(M)        ────hb────▶   lock(M) [same monitor]           │
│  write z=30                   read x   // sees 10              │
│  unlock(M) ─────hb────────▶   read y   // sees 20              │
│                               read z   // sees 30              │
│                               unlock(M)                        │

│                                                                 │

Part 18

Production Scenarios: Why JMM Matters

Scenario 1: Concurrent Cache Initialization

public class Cache {
    private volatile Map<String, Object> data;  // volatile for safe publication

    public Map<String, Object> getData() {
        if (data == null) {
            synchronized (this) {
                if (data == null) {
                    data = loadFromDatabase();  // expensive
                }
            }
        }
        return data;  // safe: volatile read sees fully constructed map
    }
}

Without volatile, Thread B may see data != null but observe a partially initialized Map (internal array not yet visible).

Scenario 2: Service Shutdown Flag

public class Worker implements Runnable {
    private volatile boolean running = true;  // must be volatile

    public void shutdown() {
        running = false;  // called from different thread
    }

    @Override
    public void run() {
        while (running) {
            processNextItem();
        }
        cleanup();
    }
}

The volatile keyword guarantees the worker sees running = false promptly. Without it, the JIT may cache the value in a register and the worker never terminates.

Scenario 3: State Machine with Visibility

public enum State { INIT, RUNNING, STOPPED }

public class Service {
    private volatile State state = State.INIT;  // visible across threads

    public void start() {
        state = State.RUNNING;
    }

    public boolean isRunning() {
        return state == State.RUNNING;
    }
}
Part 19

The JMM and happens-before in java.util.concurrent

The java.util.concurrent (j.u.c) package is built on JMM guarantees. The library's Javadoc specifies happens-before relationships for all its classes:

j.u.c Action Happens-before
lock.unlock() (ReentrantLock) subsequent lock.lock()
future.get() actions before future.complete()
CountDownLatch.countDown() return from await()
Semaphore.release() subsequent acquire()
Putting item in BlockingQueue taking that item from the queue
Completing a CompletableFuture callbacks/dependent stages

This is why you can safely pass data between threads via a BlockingQueue without any additional synchronization — the queue's internal synchronization creates the required hb edges.

Part 20

JMM Evolution: Java 9+ and VarHandle

Java 9 introduced VarHandle (java.lang.invoke.VarHandle), which exposes fine-grained memory ordering modes corresponding directly to hardware memory model primitives:

VarHandle COUNTER = MethodHandles.lookup()
    .findVarHandle(MyClass.class, "counter", int.class);

// Plain access — no ordering guarantee
COUNTER.set(this, 42);
int val = (int) COUNTER.get(this);

// Opaque — prevents tearing, prevents optimization (like volatile reads/writes)
COUNTER.setOpaque(this, 42);

// Release/Acquire — one-directional fence (cheaper than volatile)
COUNTER.setRelease(this, 42);  // like volatile write
int v = (int) COUNTER.getAcquire(this);  // like volatile read

// Volatile — full fence (most expensive, both directions)
COUNTER.setVolatile(this, 42);
int v2 = (int) COUNTER.getVolatile(this);

This maps to the C++ memory model ordering modes and allows Java code to use acquire-release semantics, which is cheaper than full volatile while still providing the essential visibility guarantee for producer-consumer patterns.

Part 21

Interview Questions and Answers

Q1: What is the Java Memory Model?

A: The JMM is a specification (JLS Chapter 17) that defines the rules governing when writes by one thread become visible to reads by another thread. It addresses visibility, ordering, and atomicity in multithreaded programs. The core abstraction is the happens-before relationship.

Q2: What does "happens-before" mean?

A: If action A happens-before action B, then all effects of A (writes to variables) are guaranteed to be visible to B, and A is ordered before B. It is a formal ordering relation — transitive, reflexive — not a statement about physical time. The JMM defines six rules that create hb edges: program order, monitor lock, volatile variable, thread start, thread join, and final field freeze.

Q3: Why is the naive double-checked locking broken?

A: Because object construction (new Singleton()) can be reordered by the JIT or CPU such that the reference is assigned before the constructor finishes. Another thread sees a non-null but partially initialized object. Adding volatile to the field prevents the reordering (via a StoreLoad barrier) and makes DCL safe.

Q4: What does synchronized guarantee beyond mutual exclusion?

A: synchronized provides memory visibility: all writes in the critical section (and before it) are flushed to main memory on unlock. The corresponding lock on the same monitor ensures the acquiring thread sees all those writes. This is the monitor lock happens-before rule.

Q5: Can two different synchronized blocks on different monitors create a happens-before?

A: No. The monitor lock rule only applies when the same monitor is used. Different monitors provide mutual exclusion within their respective critical sections but establish no ordering relationship between those sections.

Q6: What is safe publication?

A: Safe publication means making an object's reference available to other threads in a way that guarantees they see a fully initialized object. The mechanisms are: static final fields, volatile fields, objects shared via synchronized blocks, and final fields in constructors.

Part 22

Summary Table

Concept What It Means JMM Guarantee
Visibility One thread's write seen by another Only with hb relationship
Ordering Relative order of actions across threads Only with hb relationship
Atomicity Operation completes without interleaving Only with synchronized or Atomic*
Program Order Rule Actions in one thread ordered within that thread Always (per-thread illusion)
Monitor Lock Rule unlock hb subsequent lock (same monitor) YES — use for mutual exclusion + visibility
Volatile Rule volatile write hb subsequent volatile read YES — use for flags and safe publication
Thread Start Rule start() hb actions in new thread YES — writes before start visible in thread
Thread Join Rule actions in thread hb after join() YES — collect results after join
Final Field Rule constructor final writes hb any read via safe ref YES — immutable object safety
Transitivity hb(A,B) + hb(B,C) → hb(A,C) YES — chain hb across rules
DCL without volatile Broken — partial construction visible NO guarantee
DCL with volatile Safe — volatile write hb read YES — use this or holder pattern
safe publication volatile, synchronized, static final, final YES — use one of these

Practice Section

Exercise 1

Identify the bug and fix it:

class DataProcessor {
    private List<String> results = new ArrayList<>();
    private boolean done = false;

    public void process(List<String> input) {
        new Thread(() -> {
            for (String s : input) results.add(s.toUpperCase());
            done = true;
        }).start();
    }

    public List<String> getResults() {
        while (!done) { /* spin */ }
        return results;
    }
}

Hint: Two JMM problems — visibility of done and visibility/thread-safety of results.

Exercise 2

Given this code, which threads are guaranteed to see x = 42?

int x = 0;
volatile boolean v = false;

// Thread A
x = 42;
v = true;

// Thread B
if (v) System.out.println(x);  // (a)

// Thread C (no sync with A)
System.out.println(x);          // (b)

Answer: Thread B at (a) is guaranteed to see x = 42 if it reads v = true (volatile rule + transitivity). Thread C at (b) has no guarantee — it may see 0 or 42.

Exercise 3

Fix the broken DCL pattern using the initialization-on-demand holder idiom instead of volatile.

Exercise 4

Explain why this is safe:

class ImmutablePoint {
    final int x, y;
    ImmutablePoint(int x, int y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; }
}
static ImmutablePoint shared = new ImmutablePoint(3, 4);

Answer: shared is a static field initialized in the class initializer (thread-safe by JVM spec), and x, y are final (freeze guarantee). Any thread reading shared sees x=3, y=4.
