Part 1

Concept Overview

The volatile keyword is Java's lightest synchronization mechanism. It solves exactly two problems from the Java Memory Model:

  1. Visibility: a write to a volatile variable is immediately visible to all subsequent readers.
  2. Ordering: writes and reads to a volatile variable act as memory barriers — they prevent certain instruction reorderings.

volatile deliberately does not solve atomicity for compound operations (read-modify-write). It is precise in its scope, which makes it both powerful (very low overhead) and dangerous (easy to misuse).

When to reach for volatile:
- A single thread writes, multiple threads read (classic flag/status pattern)
- You need to safely publish an immutable or effectively-immutable object reference
- You need cheap ordered access without the full cost of synchronized

When NOT to use volatile:
- When you need to atomically update based on the current value (use AtomicInteger, AtomicReference)
- When multiple fields must be updated together as a unit (use synchronized or Lock)
- As a silver bullet for "making things thread-safe" — misused volatile creates subtle bugs

Part 2

The volatile Keyword: Semantics

2.1 Visibility Guarantee

class SharedState {
    volatile boolean running = true;   // <-- volatile
}

When Thread A writes running = false:
- The write is immediately flushed from A's working memory / store buffer to main memory.
- Every subsequent read by any thread reads from main memory (or a cache that reflects the flush).
- No thread can legally cache a stale value after the volatile write has occurred.

Without volatile, the JIT can hoist the read into a register and loop infinitely. With volatile, the JIT must re-read the field on every access.

2.2 Ordering Guarantee (Memory Barriers)

volatile establishes happens-before (hb) edges:

Volatile Write hb Volatile Read (of the same variable)

All writes BEFORE the volatile write ─hb─▶ All reads AFTER the volatile read

This means volatile acts as a two-directional fence at the point of access:

Thread A:
  write x = 1;      // (1)
  write y = 2;      // (2)
  write volatile v; // (3) ← StoreStore barrier before, StoreLoad barrier after

Thread B:
  read volatile v;  // (4) ← LoadLoad + LoadStore barrier after
  read x;           // (5) guaranteed to see 1
  read y;           // (6) guaranteed to see 2

By transitivity of hb: (1) hb (3) [program order], (3) hb (4) [volatile rule], (4) hb (5) [program order] → (1) hb (5). Thread B is guaranteed to see all writes Thread A made before its volatile write.

2.3 What volatile Does NOT Guarantee: Atomicity

volatile int i = 0;

// Thread A and Thread B both call:
i++;  // NOT atomic despite volatile!

The i++ operation expands to:
1. read i from memory → local copy
2. add 1 to local copy
3. write result back to i

Between steps 1 and 3, another thread can execute all three steps on its own copy. Result: lost update.

Thread A: read i=5                  write i=6
Thread B:         read i=5  write i=6
Final i = 6 ← WRONG, expected 7

Use AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet() for this pattern.

Part 3

volatile vs synchronized: Full Comparison

┌─────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────┐
│ Property                    │ volatile                  │ synchronized              │
├─────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────┤
│ Visibility guarantee        │ YES                       │ YES                       │
│ Ordering guarantee          │ YES (memory barrier)      │ YES (monitor lock/unlock) │
│ Atomicity for compound ops  │ NO                        │ YES (mutual exclusion)    │
│ Mutual exclusion            │ NO                        │ YES                       │
│ Blocking                    │ NO (never blocks)         │ YES (contention blocks)   │
│ Deadlock risk               │ NO                        │ YES (if misused)          │
│ Performance overhead        │ LOW (barrier only)        │ HIGHER (lock acquisition) │
│ Use case: flags/status      │ IDEAL                     │ Possible but heavy        │
│ Use case: counter increment │ NOT safe                  │ Safe                      │
│ Use case: check-then-act    │ NOT safe                  │ Safe (inside sync block)  │
│ Use case: safe publication  │ YES                       │ YES                       │
│ Can apply to: methods       │ NO (compile error)        │ YES                       │
│ Can apply to: local vars    │ NO (compile error)        │ NO (only object monitors) │
│ Can apply to: arrays        │ reference only, not elems │ YES (array as monitor)    │
└─────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────┘

Key insight: volatile provides the visibility and ordering parts of synchronized without mutual exclusion. If you only need visibility (not atomicity), volatile is the right — and cheaper — tool.

Part 4

volatile vs AtomicInteger / AtomicReference

┌──────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┐
│ Property                 │ volatile int             │ AtomicInteger              │
├──────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────┤
│ Read visibility          │ YES                       │ YES (volatile internally)  │
│ Write visibility         │ YES                       │ YES                        │
│ Atomic increment         │ NO (i++ is a race)        │ YES (CAS-based)            │
│ Atomic CAS               │ NO                        │ YES (compareAndSet)        │
│ Atomic get-and-add       │ NO                        │ YES (getAndAdd)            │
│ Overhead                 │ None beyond barrier       │ CAS loop overhead          │
│ Best for                 │ flags, single-writer vals │ shared counters, accumulat.│
└──────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────┴────────────────────────────┘

// volatile: one writer, many readers → correct
volatile int sensorReading = 0;
// writer thread:  sensorReading = latestValue;
// reader threads: int v = sensorReading;

// AtomicInteger: many writers incrementing → correct
AtomicInteger requestCount = new AtomicInteger(0);
// any thread: requestCount.incrementAndGet();
Part 5

The volatile Flag Pattern (Shutdown / Status)

The most common and correct use of volatile is a control flag written by one thread and read by one or more other threads.

public class BackgroundService implements Runnable {
    private volatile boolean running = true;   // (A) volatile flag

    /** Called from a different thread to request shutdown */
    public void stop() {
        running = false;   // (B) single writer: only this method writes
    }

    @Override
    public void run() {
        System.out.println("Service started");
        while (running) {          // (C) many readers: polls flag each iteration
            try {
                processNextTask();
            } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
                break;
            }
        }
        System.out.println("Service stopped cleanly");
    }

    private void processNextTask() throws InterruptedException {
        // simulate work
        Thread.sleep(100);
    }
}

// Usage
BackgroundService svc = new BackgroundService();
Thread worker = new Thread(svc);
worker.start();

Thread.sleep(500);
svc.stop();       // volatile write: worker WILL see this promptly
worker.join();    // wait for clean shutdown

Why this works: svc.stop() does a volatile write to running. The worker thread does a volatile read of running on each loop iteration. The volatile write hb volatile read — the worker sees false.

Important subtlety: volatile guarantees eventual visibility, not instantaneous. The worker may finish the current iteration before noticing the flag. This is usually acceptable for cooperative shutdown patterns.

Part 6

i++ Is NOT Atomic Even With volatile

This is one of the most misunderstood aspects of volatile. Let's be explicit:

class BrokenCounter {
    volatile int count = 0;

    // Called from multiple threads
    public void increment() {
        count++;  // BUG: not atomic despite volatile
    }
}

Bytecode for count++:

GETFIELD count       // (1) read count from memory into operand stack
ICONST_1             // (2) push constant 1
IADD                 // (3) add
PUTFIELD count       // (4) write result back to count

Steps (1)–(4) are four separate bytecode instructions. Thread scheduling can interleave these:

╔════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║              LOST UPDATE WITH volatile int count           ║
╠══════════════════╦═════════════════════════════════════════╣
║    Thread A      ║    Thread B       ║   count in memory   ║
╠══════════════════╬═════════════════════════════════════════╣
║  read count → 5  ║                   ║       5             ║
║                  ║  read count → 5   ║       5             ║
║  compute 5+1=6   ║                   ║       5             ║
║                  ║  compute 5+1=6    ║       5             ║
║  write count=6   ║                   ║       6             ║
║                  ║  write count=6    ║       6  ← LOST +1  ║
╚══════════════════╩═════════════════════════════════════════╝
Expected: 7   Actual: 6   → data race

Correct Solutions

// Option 1: AtomicInteger (lock-free, preferred for counters)
class CorrectCounter {
    AtomicInteger count = new AtomicInteger(0);

    public void increment() {
        count.incrementAndGet();  // atomic CAS-based
    }
}

// Option 2: synchronized (simple, correct, more overhead)
class CorrectCounter2 {
    int count = 0;

    public synchronized void increment() {
        count++;  // mutual exclusion makes this safe
    }
}

// Option 3: LongAdder (high contention, many writers)
LongAdder adder = new LongAdder();
adder.increment();
long total = adder.sum();
Part 7

Memory Barrier Concept

At the hardware level, volatile causes the JIT compiler to emit memory barrier (fence) instructions. Different CPUs have different fence instructions (x86 has MFENCE, SFENCE, LFENCE; ARM has DMB, DSB). The JVM abstracts these into four logical barriers:

BEFORE volatile WRITE:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                  StoreStore barrier                 │
│  All stores before this are completed before the   │
│  volatile store — no store can be reordered past   │
│  the volatile write upward.                        │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                  ↓ volatile WRITE ↓
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                  StoreLoad barrier                  │
│  The volatile write is flushed before any future   │
│  load. Most expensive barrier on most architectures│
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

AFTER volatile READ:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              LoadLoad + LoadStore barrier           │
│  No load/store after this can be reordered before  │
│  the volatile load.                                │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Performance note: On x86/x64, all stores are already ordered (TSO — Total Store Order), so StoreStore barriers are free. Only StoreLoad (full fence) has real cost. On ARM/POWER (weaker memory models), all barriers have cost. This is why volatile performance can vary significantly across architectures.

Part 8

volatile and Array References

A common confusion: volatile on an array reference makes the reference volatile, not the array elements.

volatile int[] array = new int[10];

// SAFE: publishing a new array atomically
array = new int[]{1, 2, 3, 4, 5};  // volatile write of reference

// NOT SAFE: modifying elements of the shared array
array[0] = 42;                      // NOT a volatile operation on the element!

If you need volatile-like access to individual array elements, use AtomicIntegerArray, AtomicLongArray, or AtomicReferenceArray:

AtomicIntegerArray atomicArray = new AtomicIntegerArray(10);
atomicArray.set(0, 42);           // volatile-strength store
int val = atomicArray.get(0);     // volatile-strength load
atomicArray.compareAndSet(0, 42, 43);  // CAS
Part 9

volatile for Safe Publication

A volatile reference field can be used to safely publish an immutable object to all threads without synchronized:

class ConfigLoader {
    private volatile Config config;  // volatile reference

    /** Called by one thread (e.g. config-refresh thread) */
    public void reload() {
        Config newConfig = loadFromDisk();  // build new immutable config
        config = newConfig;                 // volatile write: publishes atomically
    }

    /** Called by many threads */
    public String getHost() {
        return config.getHost();  // volatile read: always sees latest config
    }
}

// Config is effectively immutable — fields set in constructor, never changed
class Config {
    private final String host;
    private final int port;

    Config(String host, int port) {
        this.host = host;
        this.port = port;
    }

    String getHost() { return host; }
    int getPort() { return port; }
}

Why this is safe: The volatile write of config establishes a hb edge. All writes inside loadFromDisk() (which constructed the Config object) happen-before the volatile write, which happens-before any reader's volatile read of config. Readers always see a fully initialized Config.

Part 10

Production Pattern: One-Writer, Many-Reader

The canonical production use case for volatile:

      ┌──────────────────┐
      │  SINGLE WRITER   │
      │  (sensor thread, │
      │   config loader, │
      │   coordinator)   │
      └────────┬─────────┘
               │  volatile write
               ▼
      ┌──────────────────┐
      │  volatile field  │ ─────────────────────────┐
      └──────────────────┘                          │
               │                                   │
       volatile read                        volatile read
               │                                   │
      ┌────────▼─────────┐             ┌───────────▼──────┐
      │   READER T1      │             │   READER T2       │
      │   (worker)       │             │   (worker)        │
      └──────────────────┘             └───────────────────┘
                                       ... N readers

public class SensorHub {
    // One writer (sensor thread), many readers (display/alert threads)
    private volatile double temperature = 0.0;
    private volatile double humidity    = 0.0;
    // NOTE: temperature and humidity are updated separately —
    //       they are NOT atomically consistent with each other!
    //       If you need both to be atomically consistent, use synchronized.

    /** Called only by the sensor thread */
    public void update(double temp, double hum) {
        temperature = temp;  // volatile write
        humidity = hum;      // volatile write (separate)
    }

    /** Called by any thread */
    public double getTemperature() { return temperature; }  // volatile read
    public double getHumidity()    { return humidity; }      // volatile read

    /** WARNING: these two reads are NOT atomic together */
    public String getStatus() {
        // A write of temperature=30, humidity=80 may be seen as
        // temperature=25 (old), humidity=80 (new) between the two volatile reads
        return temperature + "°C / " + humidity + "%";
    }
}

Production consideration: When two related fields must be read atomically together, either use synchronized or encapsulate them in an immutable object published via a single volatile reference.

Part 11

volatile in Double-Checked Locking (Revisited)

As covered in Lesson 45, the idiomatic DCL pattern requires volatile:

public class ConnectionPool {
    private static volatile ConnectionPool instance;

    private final List<Connection> connections;

    private ConnectionPool() {
        // expensive initialization
        connections = initializeConnections();
    }

    public static ConnectionPool getInstance() {
        if (instance == null) {                    // (1) first check — no lock
            synchronized (ConnectionPool.class) {
                if (instance == null) {            // (2) second check — with lock
                    instance = new ConnectionPool(); // (3) volatile write
                }
            }
        }
        return instance;                           // (4) volatile read
    }
}

Why volatile is essential here:
- Without volatile, the write at (3) can be reordered: the reference is published before the constructor completes.
- A thread reaching (1) could see instance != null and proceed to (4), obtaining a reference to a partially-initialized ConnectionPool.
- volatile ensures: all writes in the constructor hb the volatile write at (3) hb the volatile read at (4). Any thread that passes (1) is guaranteed to see a fully constructed object.

Preferred alternative: Use the initialization-on-demand holder pattern, which avoids the need for volatile and DCL altogether:

public class ConnectionPool {
    private ConnectionPool() { /* expensive init */ }

    private static class Holder {
        static final ConnectionPool INSTANCE = new ConnectionPool();
        // JVM guarantees class init is thread-safe and happens once
    }

    public static ConnectionPool getInstance() {
        return Holder.INSTANCE;
    }
}
Part 12

Performance Characteristics of volatile

When is volatile cheap?

Architecture   │ volatile write cost      │ volatile read cost
───────────────┼──────────────────────────┼──────────────────────
x86/x64        │ Low (stores already TSO) │ Very low (just a load)
               │ ~1-5 ns                  │ ~1 ns
ARM Cortex-A   │ Medium (DMB fence)       │ Low-medium
               │ ~5-20 ns                 │ ~2-5 ns
POWER          │ High (heavyweight sync)  │ Medium
               │ ~20-50 ns                │ ~5-10 ns

On x86, volatile reads are essentially free (all loads are acquire loads). volatile writes are cheap too (only the StoreLoad barrier on an MFENCE has cost, and the JIT often delays it). This is why volatile is often preferred over synchronized for flags on modern x86 server hardware.

volatile vs synchronized performance example:

// Benchmark: 4 threads, 10M iterations
// volatile flag reads:    ~2.1 ns/op
// synchronized method:    ~18.4 ns/op  (uncontended)
// synchronized method:    ~120 ns/op   (contended, 4 threads)
// AtomicInteger.get():    ~2.3 ns/op   (uses volatile internally)

Rule of thumb: Use volatile for single-writer flags and safe object publication. Use AtomicXxx for counters and accumulators. Use synchronized or Lock when you need mutual exclusion or multi-field atomicity.

Part 13

Common Mistakes with volatile

Mistake 1: Using volatile for compound actions

volatile int balance = 100;

public void withdraw(int amount) {
    if (balance >= amount) {   // RACE: check-then-act
        balance -= amount;     // RACE: not atomic
    }
}

Fix: use synchronized or AtomicInteger.compareAndSet.

Mistake 2: volatile on multiple fields expecting atomic multi-update

volatile int x = 0;
volatile int y = 0;

public void move(int newX, int newY) {
    x = newX;  // Thread can read x=newX, y=0 (old) between these writes
    y = newY;
}

Fix: encapsulate in an immutable Point object and use a single volatile Point position:

record Point(int x, int y) {}

volatile Point position = new Point(0, 0);

public void move(int newX, int newY) {
    position = new Point(newX, newY);  // atomic reference swap
}

Mistake 3: Believing volatile prevents all reordering

volatile prevents reordering around the volatile access — it does not prevent all reorderings in the entire program. Non-volatile accesses before/after a volatile access may be reordered relative to each other (but not relative to the volatile access itself).

Mistake 4: Using volatile for long/double on 32-bit JVMs

On 32-bit JVMs, long and double reads/writes are not atomic — they use two 32-bit operations. Using volatile long fixes this (the JVM must guarantee atomic 64-bit volatile reads/writes). On 64-bit JVMs, long is always 64-bit aligned and reads/writes are typically atomic anyway, but volatile is still necessary for visibility.

// On 32-bit JVM, without volatile: long read/write is NOT atomic
// With volatile: guaranteed atomic and visible
volatile long timestamp = System.currentTimeMillis();

Part 15

volatile in Java Concurrency Library Internals

Many j.u.c. classes use volatile internally for their correctness guarantees:

// AbstractQueuedSynchronizer (AQS) — backbone of ReentrantLock, Semaphore, etc.
private volatile int state;  // lock state: 0=unlocked, >0=locked

// ConcurrentHashMap (Java 8+)
// Each table bucket uses a volatile reference to its Node chain
volatile Node<K,V>[] table;
volatile Node<K,V> next;  // within each bucket's linked list
volatile V val;           // within each Node

// FutureTask
private volatile int state;  // NEW, COMPLETING, NORMAL, EXCEPTIONAL, CANCELLED

// Thread
volatile int threadStatus;  // thread state visible across JVM internals

Understanding volatile helps you understand why these classes are correct without heavyweight locking on every operation.

Part 16

volatile and the Java 9 VarHandle Acquire/Release Mode

Java 9 introduced acquire-release semantics as a cheaper alternative to full volatile:

import java.lang.invoke.*;

class AcquireReleaseExample {
    int data = 0;
    int flag = 0;  // NOT declared volatile — controlled via VarHandle

    static final VarHandle FLAG;
    static {
        try {
            FLAG = MethodHandles.lookup()
                .findVarHandle(AcquireReleaseExample.class, "flag", int.class);
        } catch (Exception e) { throw new Error(e); }
    }

    // Producer: setRelease = volatile write (all prior stores visible)
    public void produce(int value) {
        data = value;
        FLAG.setRelease(this, 1);  // release write: cheaper than full volatile
    }

    // Consumer: getAcquire = volatile read (all subsequent loads see prior stores)
    public int consume() {
        if ((int) FLAG.getAcquire(this) == 1) {  // acquire read
            return data;  // sees producer's data write
        }
        return -1;
    }
}

Acquire-release vs full volatile:
- setRelease = StoreStore + volatile write (no StoreLoad after → cheaper)
- getAcquire = volatile read + LoadLoad + LoadStore (same as volatile read)
- Full volatile write = StoreStore + write + StoreLoad (most expensive part)

For producer-consumer patterns where you only need one-directional synchronization, acquire-release is meaningfully faster than full volatile on weakly ordered architectures (ARM, POWER).

Part 18

Production Scenario: Configuration Hot-Reload

A common production pattern where volatile is the right tool:

@Component
public class AppConfig {

    // Immutable config snapshot; replaced atomically on reload
    private volatile ConfigSnapshot snapshot = ConfigSnapshot.loadDefault();

    /**
     * Called by config-refresh thread every 60 seconds.
     * Single writer — volatile is sufficient, no synchronized needed.
     */
    @Scheduled(fixedDelay = 60_000)
    public void reload() {
        ConfigSnapshot fresh = ConfigSnapshot.loadFromFileSystem();
        snapshot = fresh;  // volatile write: all reader threads see new config
        log.info("Config reloaded: version={}", fresh.getVersion());
    }

    /** Called by any request-handling thread — high read frequency */
    public String getDatabaseUrl() {
        return snapshot.getDatabaseUrl();  // volatile read: always fresh
    }

    public int getMaxConnections() {
        return snapshot.getMaxConnections();  // volatile read
    }
}

// Immutable snapshot — safe to share after volatile publication
@Value  // Lombok: all fields final, constructor args
public class ConfigSnapshot {
    String databaseUrl;
    int maxConnections;
    int version;

    static ConfigSnapshot loadFromFileSystem() { /* ... */ }
    static ConfigSnapshot loadDefault() { /* ... */ }
}

Why this works correctly in production:
- snapshot is volatile — a single reload thread writes it, many request threads read it.
- ConfigSnapshot is immutable — no race on its fields.
- After the volatile write, all request threads see the new snapshot.
- No synchronized needed → zero contention on the hot read path.

Part 19

volatile in Shutdown Hooks and Lifecycle Management

public class GracefulShutdownService {

    private volatile boolean shutdownRequested = false;
    private volatile boolean shutdownComplete = false;
    private final CountDownLatch completionLatch = new CountDownLatch(1);

    public GracefulShutdownService() {
        // Register JVM shutdown hook
        Runtime.getRuntime().addShutdownHook(new Thread(() -> {
            System.out.println("Shutdown hook: requesting stop...");
            shutdownRequested = true;   // volatile write

            try {
                // Wait up to 30s for graceful completion
                if (!completionLatch.await(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) {
                    System.out.println("Shutdown timeout — forcing exit");
                }
            } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
            }
        }));
    }

    public void runUntilShutdown() {
        while (!shutdownRequested) {    // volatile read — sees shutdown request promptly
            processNextBatch();
        }
        flushPendingWrites();
        completionLatch.countDown();    // signal completion to shutdown hook
        shutdownComplete = true;        // volatile write
        System.out.println("Graceful shutdown complete");
    }

    private void processNextBatch() { /* process work items */ }
    private void flushPendingWrites() { /* flush buffers */ }
}
Part 20

Interview Questions and Answers

Q1: What does volatile guarantee in Java?

A: volatile guarantees two things: (1) Visibility — a write to a volatile variable is immediately visible to all subsequent reads of that variable by any thread; (2) Ordering — writes and reads of volatile variables act as memory barriers, preventing reordering of instructions around the volatile access. It does NOT guarantee atomicity for compound operations like i++.

Q2: What is the difference between volatile and synchronized?

A: Both provide visibility and ordering guarantees. synchronized additionally provides mutual exclusion — only one thread can be in a synchronized block at a time. volatile never blocks. Use volatile when you have a single-writer, multi-reader pattern for simple flags or object references. Use synchronized when you need to protect compound operations (check-then-act, read-modify-write) or multi-field atomicity.

Q3: Is volatile int i; i++ thread-safe?

A: No. Despite volatile, i++ is not atomic — it is a read-modify-write operation that compiles to three bytecode instructions. Two threads can interleave these steps and cause lost updates. Use AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet() instead.

Q4: Why does double-checked locking require volatile?

A: Without volatile, the JIT/CPU can reorder object construction steps so that the instance reference is published before the constructor completes. Another thread observing a non-null reference would receive a partially-initialized object. volatile prevents this reordering: all constructor writes happen-before the volatile write of the instance reference, which happens-before any volatile read. Every reader sees a fully initialized object.

Q5: What is the difference between volatile and AtomicInteger?

A: AtomicInteger uses a volatile int internally AND adds CAS-based (compare-and-swap) atomic operations like incrementAndGet(), compareAndSet(), getAndAdd(). A plain volatile int has no CAS — you can read and write it atomically with respect to each other, but you cannot atomically update it based on its current value. Use volatile for flags; use AtomicInteger for counters and accumulators.

Q6: Can volatile be applied to object references? What about arrays?

A: Yes, volatile can be applied to object reference fields. The reference itself becomes volatile — its reads/writes are ordered and visible. However, the fields of the referenced object are NOT made volatile. For arrays, the array reference is volatile, but individual element accesses are not. Use AtomicIntegerArray / AtomicReferenceArray for volatile element access.

Q7: What is an acquire-release pattern and how does it relate to volatile?

A: Acquire-release is a one-directional memory ordering pattern (from C++ and introduced to Java via VarHandle in Java 9). A release write (setRelease) ensures all prior writes are visible before the write, acting like a volatile write but without the expensive StoreLoad barrier afterward. An acquire read (getAcquire) ensures all subsequent reads see prior writes, acting like a volatile read. Together they provide the same guarantee as volatile for producer-consumer patterns at lower cost than full volatile on weakly-ordered architectures.

Part 21

volatile vs Lock-Free Algorithms

volatile is a building block for lock-free algorithms. Lock-free data structures use volatile fields and CAS (Compare-And-Swap) to achieve thread safety without blocking:

                    Lock-Free Stack (Treiber Stack)
                    ─────────────────────────────
                    volatile reference to top node
                              │
                    CAS loop: read top,
                              compute new top,
                              if top unchanged → swap
                              else → retry

public class LockFreeStack<T> {
    // volatile: every thread sees the latest top
    private volatile Node<T> top = null;

    public void push(T item) {
        Node<T> newNode = new Node<>(item);
        Node<T> currentTop;
        do {
            currentTop = top;          // volatile read
            newNode.next = currentTop;
        } while (!TOP.compareAndSet(this, currentTop, newNode)); // CAS
    }

    public T pop() {
        Node<T> currentTop;
        Node<T> newTop;
        do {
            currentTop = top;          // volatile read
            if (currentTop == null) return null;
            newTop = currentTop.next;
        } while (!TOP.compareAndSet(this, currentTop, newTop)); // CAS
        return currentTop.item;
    }

    static final VarHandle TOP;
    static {
        try {
            TOP = MethodHandles.lookup()
                .findVarHandle(LockFreeStack.class, "top", Node.class);
        } catch (Exception e) { throw new Error(e); }
    }

    static class Node<T> {
        final T item;
        Node<T> next;
        Node(T item) { this.item = item; }
    }
}

The volatile Node<T> top ensures that after a successful CAS, all threads see the new top node. The CAS itself (via VarHandle) is an atomic read-modify-write that eliminates the race condition that plain volatile alone cannot solve.

Part 22

Summary Table

Topic Key Point
volatile visibility A volatile write is immediately visible to all subsequent volatile reads of the same variable
volatile ordering Acts as a memory barrier: all writes before volatile write are visible to all reads after volatile read (transitivity of hb)
volatile atomicity Does NOT provide atomicity for compound ops (i++, check-then-act). Use AtomicInteger / synchronized
volatile vs synchronized volatile = visibility + ordering; synchronized = visibility + ordering + mutual exclusion + blocking
volatile vs AtomicInteger volatile for flags/refs; AtomicInteger for counters needing CAS
Flag pattern volatile boolean running = true; — ideal use case for volatile
Safe publication volatile reference to immutable object = safe publication without synchronized
DCL requirement volatile is required for correct double-checked locking
Array elements volatile on array reference ≠ volatile elements; use AtomicIntegerArray
Memory barrier StoreStore + StoreLoad after write; LoadLoad + LoadStore after read
VarHandle acquire/release Cheaper one-directional alternative to full volatile (Java 9+)
Production use Kill switches, status flags, config hot-reload, safe singleton publication
Anti-patterns volatile counter, volatile for multi-field atomic update, treating volatile as "thread-safe" magic
long/double Use volatile long / volatile double on 32-bit JVMs to prevent tearing

Practice Section

Exercise 1

What is wrong with this code? How many bugs can you find, and how would you fix each?

class RateLimiter {
    volatile long lastRequestTime = 0;
    volatile int requestCount = 0;

    public boolean allowRequest() {
        long now = System.currentTimeMillis();
        if (now - lastRequestTime > 1000) {
            requestCount = 0;       // bug?
            lastRequestTime = now;  // bug?
        }
        if (requestCount < 100) {
            requestCount++;         // bug?
            return true;
        }
        return false;
    }
}

Hints: (a) multi-field update atomicity, (b) check-then-act race on requestCount.

Fix direction: Use synchronized on allowRequest() — both the time window reset and count increment must be atomic.

Exercise 2

Why does this safe-publication work, and why does the alternative fail?

// Version A: works
class Publisher {
    volatile ImmutableData data;
    void publish(ImmutableData d) { data = d; }
    ImmutableData read() { return data; }
}

// Version B: broken
class Publisher2 {
    ImmutableData data;  // NOT volatile
    synchronized void publish(ImmutableData d) { data = d; }
    ImmutableData read() { return data; }  // NOT synchronized — broken!
}

Answer: Version A: volatile write hb volatile read — all readers see consistent data. Version B: read() has no synchronization — it reads data without establishing a hb edge with the synchronized publish(). No guarantee of visibility.

Exercise 3

Rewrite this using the correct concurrency primitive:

class HitCounter {
    volatile long hits = 0;

    public void recordHit() {
        hits++;  // bug: not atomic
    }

    public long getHits() {
        return hits;
    }
}

Answer: Use AtomicLong hits = new AtomicLong(0) with hits.incrementAndGet(), or LongAdder for very high contention.

Exercise 4

Under what conditions is this code correct, and when is it a bug?

volatile boolean initialized = false;
ExpensiveObject obj;

public void initialize() {
    obj = new ExpensiveObject();  // (A)
    initialized = true;           // (B) volatile write
}

public ExpensiveObject get() {
    if (initialized) {            // (C) volatile read
        return obj;               // (D) non-volatile read
    }
    return null;
}

Answer: This is correct IF initialize() is called by exactly one thread before any call to get(). The volatile write at (B) hb volatile read at (C) hb read at (D) by transitivity — so (D) sees the write at (A). It is broken if multiple threads could call initialize() concurrently (need synchronized on initialize) or if get() can be called before initialize() starts (need null check on obj).

Part 1

Concept

A lock is a synchronization mechanism that controls access to a shared resource in a concurrent environment. While Java's synchronized keyword provides implicit locking, the java.util.concurrent.locks package (introduced in Java 5) offers explicit, flexible, and more powerful locking primitives.

Why explicit locks?

synchronized is straightforward but rigid:
- You cannot attempt a lock without blocking indefinitely.
- You cannot interrupt a thread waiting for a lock.
- You cannot implement non-blocking or timed lock acquisition.
- All threads compete equally regardless of arrival order (no fairness guarantee).
- You cannot have separate read and write locks on the same resource.

The Lock interface and its implementations address every one of these limitations.

The Lock interface

public interface Lock {
    void lock();
    void lockInterruptibly() throws InterruptedException;
    boolean tryLock();
    boolean tryLock(long time, TimeUnit unit) throws InterruptedException;
    void unlock();
    Condition newCondition();
}

The three principal implementations covered in this lesson are:

Class Best for
ReentrantLock General-purpose mutual exclusion
ReentrantReadWriteLock Read-heavy shared data
StampedLock (Java 8+) High-throughput optimistic reads
Part 2

ReentrantLock

A ReentrantLock behaves like synchronized but with explicit control. "Reentrant" means the same thread that holds the lock can acquire it again without deadlocking — it simply increments an internal hold count.

import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock;

public class Counter {
    private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();
    private int count = 0;

    public void increment() {
        lock.lock();
        try {
            count++;
        } finally {
            lock.unlock();  // ALWAYS in finally
        }
    }

    public int getCount() {
        lock.lock();
        try {
            return count;
        } finally {
            lock.unlock();
        }
    }
}

The golden rule: unlock in finally

If an exception is thrown inside the locked section and unlock() is not in a finally block, the lock is never released and every other thread waiting on it deadlocks permanently. This is the single most common ReentrantLock bug.

// WRONG — exception leaks the lock
lock.lock();
doSomethingThatMightThrow();   // lock held forever if this throws
lock.unlock();

// CORRECT
lock.lock();
try {
    doSomethingThatMightThrow();
} finally {
    lock.unlock();
}

Reentrancy example

public class Reentrant {
    private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();

    public void outer() {
        lock.lock();
        try {
            System.out.println("hold count: " + lock.getHoldCount()); // 1
            inner();
        } finally {
            lock.unlock();
        }
    }

    public void inner() {
        lock.lock();   // same thread re-acquires — hold count becomes 2
        try {
            System.out.println("hold count: " + lock.getHoldCount()); // 2
        } finally {
            lock.unlock();  // hold count back to 1
        }
    }
}

The lock is fully released only when hold count reaches zero.

Part 3

Lock State Diagram

                    ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
                    │              REENTRANT LOCK STATE            │
                    └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         lock.lock()              lock.lock()
  ┌─────────────────────┐    (same thread = reentrant)
  │                     ▼                 │
  │              ┌────────────┐           ▼
  │              │  UNLOCKED  │   ┌───────────────┐
  │              │  count = 0 │   │    LOCKED     │
  │              └────────────┘   │  owner=T1     │
  │                   ▲           │  holdCount=1  │
  │                   │           └───────┬───────┘
  │                   │                   │ lock.lock() by T1
  │            lock.unlock()              ▼
  │          (holdCount → 0)    ┌───────────────────┐
  │                             │      LOCKED       │
  │                             │  owner=T1         │
  │                             │  holdCount=2      │
  │                             └───────┬───────────┘
  │                                     │ lock.unlock()
  │                                     ▼
  │                             ┌───────────────────┐
  │                             │      LOCKED       │
  │                             │  owner=T1         │
  │                             │  holdCount=1      │
  │                             └───────────────────┘
  │
  │  If T2 calls lock.lock() while T1 holds it:
  │
  │   T2 ──► [WAITING QUEUE] ─── fairness=false ──► races with others
  │                           └── fairness=true  ──► strict FIFO order
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Part 4

tryLock and tryLock with Timeout

tryLock() returns immediately with true if the lock was acquired, or false if it was not. This avoids the indefinite blocking that lock.lock() imposes.

public class ResourceManager {
    private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();
    private String resource = "data";

    public boolean tryUpdate(String newValue) {
        if (lock.tryLock()) {
            try {
                resource = newValue;
                return true;
            } finally {
                lock.unlock();
            }
        }
        return false; // did not acquire — caller can retry or give up
    }
}

Timed tryLock

public boolean tryUpdateWithTimeout(String newValue, long millis)
        throws InterruptedException {
    if (lock.tryLock(millis, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) {
        try {
            resource = newValue;
            return true;
        } finally {
            lock.unlock();
        }
    }
    System.out.println("Could not acquire lock within timeout");
    return false;
}

Deadlock avoidance with tryLock

One classic deadlock pattern is two threads each holding one of two locks and waiting for the other. tryLock provides an escape:

public boolean transferFunds(Account from, Account to, int amount) {
    while (true) {
        if (from.lock.tryLock()) {
            try {
                if (to.lock.tryLock()) {
                    try {
                        from.balance -= amount;
                        to.balance   += amount;
                        return true;
                    } finally {
                        to.lock.unlock();
                    }
                }
            } finally {
                from.lock.unlock();
            }
        }
        // back off randomly before retrying
        Thread.sleep((long)(Math.random() * 10));
    }
}
Part 5

lockInterruptibly

lockInterruptibly() blocks like lock() but responds to Thread.interrupt(). If another thread interrupts the waiting thread, an InterruptedException is thrown instead of continuing to wait.

public void performWithInterrupt() throws InterruptedException {
    lock.lockInterruptibly();
    try {
        // critical section — safely interruptible while waiting
        heavyComputation();
    } finally {
        lock.unlock();
    }
}

Use case: long-running tasks where the calling code needs the ability to cancel waiting threads — for example a task queue that can be shut down immediately even while tasks are queued for a lock.

Method Blocks? Interruptible? Returns
lock() Yes No void
lockInterruptibly() Yes Yes void / throws
tryLock() No N/A boolean
tryLock(time, unit) Until timeout Yes boolean / throws
Part 6

Fair vs Non-Fair Locks

By default, ReentrantLock is non-fair: when a lock is released, any waiting thread (or a new arriving thread) may acquire it. This maximizes throughput because a newly arriving thread can grab it without a context switch.

A fair lock guarantees FIFO ordering — threads acquire the lock in the order they requested it. This prevents starvation but incurs higher overhead.

// Non-fair (default) — higher throughput
ReentrantLock nonFair = new ReentrantLock();
ReentrantLock alsoNonFair = new ReentrantLock(false);

// Fair — prevents starvation
ReentrantLock fair = new ReentrantLock(true);

Fair lock performance trade-off

Non-fair:                        Fair:
  Thread requests lock           Thread requests lock
        │                               │
        ▼                               ▼
  Lock free? ──Yes──► grab it    Lock free AND I am         
        │                        first in queue? ──Yes──► grab it
        No                              │
        │                               No
        ▼                               ▼
  Add to wait set              Add to FIFO queue
  Woken up, races with         Woken up, guaranteed
  arriving threads             to get next turn

  Throughput: HIGH             Throughput: LOWER (~10–100×)
  Starvation: Possible         Starvation: Impossible

Benchmark rule of thumb: Use fair locks only when demonstrable starvation exists. In most workloads, non-fair locks dramatically outperform fair ones because each fair handoff requires at least one full context switch.

Part 7

ReentrantLock vs synchronized

┌──────────────────────────┬────────────────────────┬────────────────────────┐
│ Feature                  │ synchronized           │ ReentrantLock          │
├──────────────────────────┼────────────────────────┼────────────────────────┤
│ Acquisition style        │ Implicit               │ Explicit               │
│ Try without blocking     │ No                     │ tryLock()              │
│ Timed acquisition        │ No                     │ tryLock(t, unit)       │
│ Interruptible wait       │ No                     │ lockInterruptibly()    │
│ Fairness option          │ No (JVM decides)       │ new ReentrantLock(true)│
│ Multiple conditions      │ 1 (wait/notifyAll)     │ Multiple Condition obj │
│ Hold count inspection    │ No                     │ getHoldCount()         │
│ Queue length inspection  │ No                     │ getQueueLength()       │
│ Reentrancy               │ Yes                    │ Yes                    │
│ Auto-release on exception│ Yes (JVM handles)      │ No (must use finally)  │
│ Performance (simple case)│ Roughly equal          │ Roughly equal          │
│ Syntax overhead          │ Minimal                │ More verbose           │
│ JVM optimization (biased)│ Yes (heavily tuned)    │ Limited                │
└──────────────────────────┴────────────────────────┴────────────────────────┘

Rule of thumb: Use synchronized for simple, low-contention cases. Reach for ReentrantLock when you need tryLock, lockInterruptibly, fairness, or multiple Condition objects.

Part 8

Condition Objects

A Condition decouples one lock into multiple wait sets. Each Condition is bound to a specific Lock and provides await(), signal(), and signalAll() — the Lock-based equivalents of wait(), notify(), and notifyAll().

await / signal vs wait / notify

Aspect Object.wait / notify Condition.await / signal
Requires synchronized block lock.lock() held
Multiple conditions Impossible on one object Yes, one per newCondition()
Timed wait wait(millis) await(time, unit)
Interruptible Yes Yes
Spurious wakeup guard Loop required Loop required

Bounded buffer example (producer/consumer)

import java.util.concurrent.locks.*;

public class BoundedBuffer<T> {
    private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();
    private final Condition notFull  = lock.newCondition();
    private final Condition notEmpty = lock.newCondition();

    private final Object[] items;
    private int putIndex, takeIndex, count;

    public BoundedBuffer(int capacity) {
        items = new Object[capacity];
    }

    public void put(T item) throws InterruptedException {
        lock.lock();
        try {
            while (count == items.length)
                notFull.await();          // wait until there is space
            items[putIndex] = item;
            putIndex = (putIndex + 1) % items.length;
            count++;
            notEmpty.signal();            // wake exactly one consumer
        } finally {
            lock.unlock();
        }
    }

    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    public T take() throws InterruptedException {
        lock.lock();
        try {
            while (count == 0)
                notEmpty.await();         // wait until there is an item
            T item = (T) items[takeIndex];
            takeIndex = (takeIndex + 1) % items.length;
            count--;
            notFull.signal();             // wake exactly one producer
            return item;
        } finally {
            lock.unlock();
        }
    }
}

Using two conditions — notFull and notEmpty — means producers wake only consumers and vice versa. With a single object monitor you would have to call notifyAll(), waking threads that cannot make progress and causing thundering-herd overhead.

Part 9

ReadWriteLock

ReentrantReadWriteLock maintains two linked locks:
- A read lock that multiple threads can hold simultaneously.
- A write lock that is exclusively held by one thread.

READ LOCK   ─── concurrent ──► many readers at once
WRITE LOCK  ─── exclusive  ──► one writer, no readers

The invariant: writeLock is free when any reader holds readLock, and all readers must release before a writer proceeds.

import java.util.concurrent.locks.*;
import java.util.*;

public class ReadHeavyCache<K, V> {
    private final Map<K, V> cache = new HashMap<>();
    private final ReentrantReadWriteLock rwLock = new ReentrantReadWriteLock();
    private final Lock readLock  = rwLock.readLock();
    private final Lock writeLock = rwLock.writeLock();

    public V get(K key) {
        readLock.lock();
        try {
            return cache.get(key);
        } finally {
            readLock.unlock();
        }
    }

    public void put(K key, V value) {
        writeLock.lock();
        try {
            cache.put(key, value);
        } finally {
            writeLock.unlock();
        }
    }

    public int size() {
        readLock.lock();
        try {
            return cache.size();
        } finally {
            readLock.unlock();
        }
    }
}
Part 10

Read-Write Concurrency Diagram

  Timeline ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────►

  T1 (reader) │████████████████████│                         │███████│
  T2 (reader) │     │███████████████████│                    │
  T3 (reader) │          │██████████│                        │███████│
  T4 (writer) │                    │WAIT├──────────────┤WRITE│
  T5 (reader) │                         │WAIT──────────┤      │███████│

  Legend: █ = holding lock   WAIT = blocked   WRITE = exclusive write

  Phase A: T1, T2, T3 hold read locks concurrently — all proceed in parallel.
  Phase B: T4 requests write lock — must wait for ALL readers to finish.
  Phase C: T4 holds write lock exclusively — T5's read must also wait.
  Phase D: T4 releases write lock — T5 and remaining readers proceed.

Downgrade from write to read

ReentrantReadWriteLock supports lock downgrade (write → read) but NOT upgrade (read → write).

writeLock.lock();
try {
    updateData();
    readLock.lock();   // acquire read lock while still holding write lock
} finally {
    writeLock.unlock(); // release write lock — now only read lock held
}
// safe read section — other readers can join
try {
    readData();
} finally {
    readLock.unlock();
}

Attempting to upgrade (acquiring write while holding read) will deadlock because the write lock waits for all readers to finish — including the thread attempting the upgrade.

Part 11

StampedLock (Java 8+)

StampedLock is a more advanced locking mechanism that introduces an optimistic read mode on top of standard read/write locking. It trades the reentrancy of ReentrantReadWriteLock for significantly higher throughput in read-dominated scenarios.

Key differences from ReentrantReadWriteLock:

Feature ReentrantReadWriteLock StampedLock
Reentrant Yes No
Optimistic read No Yes
Lock downgrade Yes Yes
Lock upgrade No Yes
Condition support Yes No
Performance (read-heavy) Good Better

Stamps

Every StampedLock operation returns a long stamp. The stamp must be passed to the matching unlock* call. A stamp of 0 means the operation failed.

StampedLock sl = new StampedLock();

// Exclusive write
long stamp = sl.writeLock();
try {
    modifyData();
} finally {
    sl.unlockWrite(stamp);
}

// Pessimistic read (like ReentrantReadWriteLock)
stamp = sl.readLock();
try {
    readData();
} finally {
    sl.unlockRead(stamp);
}
Part 12

StampedLock Optimistic Reading

Optimistic reading is a lock-free read path. The thread records the current stamp, reads the data, then validates that the stamp has not changed (meaning no writer intervened). If validation fails, it falls back to a full read lock.

public class Point {
    private double x, y;
    private final StampedLock sl = new StampedLock();

    public void move(double dx, double dy) {
        long stamp = sl.writeLock();
        try {
            x += dx;
            y += dy;
        } finally {
            sl.unlockWrite(stamp);
        }
    }

    public double distanceFromOrigin() {
        long stamp = sl.tryOptimisticRead();  // no lock acquired
        double cx = x, cy = y;               // read snapshot

        if (!sl.validate(stamp)) {           // did a writer intervene?
            // fall back to real read lock
            stamp = sl.readLock();
            try {
                cx = x;
                cy = y;
            } finally {
                sl.unlockRead(stamp);
            }
        }
        return Math.hypot(cx, cy);
    }
}

Optimistic read flow diagram

  Thread calls tryOptimisticRead()
         │
         ▼
  stamp = current version
         │
         ▼
  Read shared data (no lock held)
         │
         ▼
  validate(stamp) ──── true  ──────► use the data  ✓
         │
        false (writer modified data between read and validate)
         │
         ▼
  Acquire full readLock()
         │
         ▼
  Re-read shared data under lock
         │
         ▼
  unlockRead()
         │
         ▼
  use the data  ✓

Critical: Variables read under optimistic mode must be re-read if validation fails. Never use unvalidated data.

Part 13

StampedLock Lock Conversion

StampedLock supports converting between modes without releasing and re-acquiring:

// Convert read → write (tryConvertToWriteLock)
long stamp = sl.readLock();
try {
    if (needsWrite()) {
        long writeStamp = sl.tryConvertToWriteLock(stamp);
        if (writeStamp != 0) {
            stamp = writeStamp;    // successfully upgraded
            modifyData();
        } else {
            sl.unlockRead(stamp);
            stamp = sl.writeLock(); // full re-acquire
            modifyData();
        }
    } else {
        readData();
    }
} finally {
    sl.unlock(stamp);              // works for any mode
}

tryConvertToWriteLock succeeds only if no other readers hold the lock, making it non-blocking. The generic sl.unlock(stamp) releases whichever mode the stamp represents.

Part 14

try-with-resources Pattern

Lock does not implement AutoCloseable, so you cannot use it directly in a try-with-resources statement. However, you can create a thin wrapper:

public class AutoLock implements AutoCloseable {
    private final Lock lock;

    public AutoLock(Lock lock) {
        this.lock = lock;
        this.lock.lock();
    }

    @Override
    public void close() {
        lock.unlock();
    }
}

// Usage
private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();

public void doWork() {
    try (AutoLock al = new AutoLock(lock)) {
        // critical section — lock released when block exits
        performOperation();
    }
}

Note: tryLock cannot be cleanly wrapped this way because new AutoLock(lock) always acquires; for conditional acquisition, the finally pattern remains the right choice.

Part 15

Fine-Grained Locking

Coarse-grained locking uses one lock for an entire data structure; fine-grained locking uses one lock per element or bucket. Fine-grained locking increases parallelism at the cost of complexity.

Striped lock map

public class StripedHashMap<K, V> {
    private static final int STRIPES = 16;
    private final ReentrantLock[] locks = new ReentrantLock[STRIPES];
    private final HashMap<K, V>[] segments;

    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    public StripedHashMap() {
        segments = new HashMap[STRIPES];
        for (int i = 0; i < STRIPES; i++) {
            locks[i]    = new ReentrantLock();
            segments[i] = new HashMap<>();
        }
    }

    private int stripe(K key) {
        return Math.abs(key.hashCode() % STRIPES);
    }

    public V get(K key) {
        int s = stripe(key);
        locks[s].lock();
        try {
            return segments[s].get(key);
        } finally {
            locks[s].unlock();
        }
    }

    public void put(K key, V value) {
        int s = stripe(key);
        locks[s].lock();
        try {
            segments[s].put(key, value);
        } finally {
            locks[s].unlock();
        }
    }
}

This pattern is exactly what ConcurrentHashMap uses internally (with additional optimizations). The maximum concurrent writers equals the number of stripes.

Part 16

Read-Heavy Cache: Production Pattern

A complete, production-ready read-heavy cache combining ReentrantReadWriteLock with write-through semantics:

import java.util.concurrent.locks.*;
import java.util.*;
import java.util.function.Function;

public class WriteBackCache<K, V> {
    private final Map<K, V> store = new HashMap<>();
    private final ReentrantReadWriteLock rwl = new ReentrantReadWriteLock();
    private final Lock r = rwl.readLock();
    private final Lock w = rwl.writeLock();
    private final Function<K, V> loader;

    public WriteBackCache(Function<K, V> loader) {
        this.loader = loader;
    }

    public V get(K key) {
        // fast read path
        r.lock();
        try {
            if (store.containsKey(key))
                return store.get(key);
        } finally {
            r.unlock();
        }

        // slow write path — load and cache
        w.lock();
        try {
            // double-check after acquiring write lock
            if (store.containsKey(key))
                return store.get(key);
            V value = loader.apply(key);
            store.put(key, value);
            return value;
        } finally {
            w.unlock();
        }
    }

    public void invalidate(K key) {
        w.lock();
        try {
            store.remove(key);
        } finally {
            w.unlock();
        }
    }

    public void invalidateAll() {
        w.lock();
        try {
            store.clear();
        } finally {
            w.unlock();
        }
    }
}

The double-check after acquiring the write lock is essential: between releasing the read lock and acquiring the write lock, another thread may have already loaded the value.

Part 17

Lock Monitoring and Diagnostics

ReentrantLock exposes several diagnostic methods unavailable with synchronized:

ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();

// How many times the current thread holds this lock
int holdCount = lock.getHoldCount();

// Is the lock held by any thread?
boolean isLocked = lock.isLocked();

// Does the current thread hold this lock?
boolean heldByMe = lock.isHeldByCurrentThread();

// Estimate of threads waiting to acquire
int queueLength = lock.getQueueLength();

// Is a specific thread waiting?
boolean waiting = lock.hasQueuedThread(someThread);

// Does any thread have an outstanding Condition.await?
boolean hasWaiters = lock.hasWaiters(someCondition);

These are invaluable for building health-check endpoints and deadlock detectors:

public Map<String, Object> lockStats(ReentrantLock lock) {
    Map<String, Object> stats = new LinkedHashMap<>();
    stats.put("isLocked",       lock.isLocked());
    stats.put("holdCount",      lock.getHoldCount());
    stats.put("queueLength",    lock.getQueueLength());
    stats.put("isFair",         lock.isFair());
    return stats;
}
Part 18

Common Pitfalls

1. Forgetting unlock in finally

Already covered — but worth repeating as the most catastrophic mistake.

2. Unlocking a lock you do not hold

// Thread A
lock.lock();

// Thread B — illegal! throws IllegalMonitorStateException
lock.unlock();

3. Acquiring lock outside try, losing it on exception

// WRONG
lock.lock();                    // if lock() itself throws (unlikely but possible),
try {                           // the finally will attempt unlock of unheld lock
    ...
} finally {
    lock.unlock();
}

// CORRECT pattern when that matters (defensive)
boolean acquired = false;
try {
    lock.lock();
    acquired = true;
    ...
} finally {
    if (acquired) lock.unlock();
}

4. Attempting read-to-write upgrade with ReadWriteLock

// DEADLOCK — thread waits for write lock, but write lock waits for this reader
readLock.lock();
// ...
writeLock.lock(); // blocks waiting for all readers including this thread

5. Not looping on await

// WRONG — spurious wakeups can bypass the condition
condition.await();
doWork();  // might execute before condition is actually true

// CORRECT
while (!conditionMet()) {
    condition.await();
}
doWork();

6. Using StampedLock as reentrant

StampedLock sl = new StampedLock();
long s1 = sl.writeLock();
long s2 = sl.writeLock();  // DEADLOCK — StampedLock is not reentrant
Part 19

Performance Considerations

Lock contention patterns

Low contention:       High contention:
  T1 ─ lock/work/unlock   T1 ─ lock/work/unlock
  T2 ─────── lock/work/unlock   T2 ─ WAIT ─ WAIT ─ lock
  T3 ──────────── lock/work/unlock   T3 ─ WAIT ─ WAIT ─ WAIT ─ lock

  Threads rarely collide   Threads queue — throughput drops,
  → contention negligible  → context switching dominates

Choosing the right lock

                  Read-heavy?
                     │
            Yes ─────┴─────── No
            │                  │
     High throughput?     Simple mutex?
            │                  │
      Yes ──┴── No           Yes ──┴── No
      │          │            │         │
  StampedLock  RWLock    synchronized  ReentrantLock
  (optimistic) (standard)  (simple)   (need tryLock
                                        /interrupt)

Micro-benchmark guidance

Scenario Winner
90%+ reads, low write contention StampedLock (optimistic)
70–90% reads ReentrantReadWriteLock
Balanced reads/writes ReentrantLock ≈ synchronized
Very low contention synchronized (JVM-optimized biased locking)
Atomic counter only AtomicLong (no lock at all)
Part 20

Interview Questions

Q1: What advantages does ReentrantLock have over synchronized?

Answer: ReentrantLock provides:
1. tryLock() — non-blocking acquisition.
2. tryLock(time, unit) — timed acquisition.
3. lockInterruptibly() — interruptible waiting.
4. new ReentrantLock(true) — fairness guarantee.
5. Multiple Condition objects for fine-grained producer/consumer patterns.
6. Diagnostic methods: getHoldCount(), getQueueLength(), isLocked().

synchronized in contrast is simpler, safer (auto-unlock on exception), and may be better JVM-optimized for simple cases.

Q2: Why is StampedLock faster than ReentrantReadWriteLock for read-heavy workloads?

Answer: StampedLock's optimistic read mode acquires no lock at all — it takes a snapshot of the version stamp, reads the data, and validates that no writer changed the stamp. If validation succeeds (which it does whenever no write occurred), the read completes with zero lock overhead. ReentrantReadWriteLock always writes to shared state to track the reader count, which causes cache-line contention when many threads read simultaneously. The optimistic path eliminates that cache traffic entirely.

Q3: What are the trade-offs of fair locks?

Answer: Fair locks guarantee FIFO ordering and prevent starvation but have significantly lower throughput because:
1. Each lock handoff requires waking the head of the queue (a context switch).
2. A newly arriving thread that could run immediately (no context switch needed) must instead wait its turn.
3. The queue management itself adds overhead.

Benchmarks typically show 10–100× throughput reduction. Use fair locks only when demonstrable starvation has been observed.

Q4: What is the difference between Condition.await and Object.wait?

Answer: Both suspend the current thread and atomically release the associated lock. The differences:
- await() is tied to an explicit Lock, while wait() is tied to the intrinsic monitor of a synchronized object.
- One Lock can have multiple Condition objects, allowing fine-grained signaling. A single object monitor has only one wait set — you must use notifyAll() to avoid missed signals when threads wait for different conditions.
- await() integrates with Lock's interruptibility policy.

Q5: Why can you downgrade from write to read lock, but not upgrade from read to write?

Answer: Downgrade is safe because the thread already holds the exclusive write lock, so acquiring the read lock introduces no new concurrent access — you simply mark yourself as a reader before releasing the exclusive hold. Upgrade is unsafe because to acquire the write lock, the thread must wait for all readers to release, including itself. This creates a circular wait — the thread holds the read lock and waits for the write lock, which waits for the read lock — producing an unresolvable deadlock.

Q6: How would you implement a thread-safe lazy singleton using StampedLock?

public class Registry {
    private volatile Config config = null;
    private final StampedLock sl = new StampedLock();

    public Config getConfig() {
        long stamp = sl.tryOptimisticRead();
        Config c = config;
        if (!sl.validate(stamp)) {
            stamp = sl.readLock();
            try { c = config; }
            finally { sl.unlockRead(stamp); }
        }
        if (c != null) return c;

        long writeStamp = sl.writeLock();
        try {
            if (config == null)          // double-check
                config = loadConfig();
            return config;
        } finally {
            sl.unlockWrite(writeStamp);
        }
    }
}
Part 21

Complete Reference Example

A self-contained example demonstrating ReentrantLock, Condition, ReadWriteLock, and StampedLock in a single runnable class:

import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.*;

public class LockShowcase {

    // ── 1. ReentrantLock with Condition ───────────────────────────────────
    static class Gate {
        private boolean open = false;
        private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();
        private final Condition opened = lock.newCondition();

        public void openGate() {
            lock.lock();
            try {
                open = true;
                opened.signalAll();
            } finally { lock.unlock(); }
        }

        public void awaitOpen() throws InterruptedException {
            lock.lock();
            try {
                while (!open) opened.await();
            } finally { lock.unlock(); }
        }
    }

    // ── 2. ReadWriteLock cache ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    static class SimpleCache {
        private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, String> store =
            new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
        private final ReentrantReadWriteLock rwl =
            new ReentrantReadWriteLock();

        public String get(String k) {
            rwl.readLock().lock();
            try { return store.get(k); }
            finally { rwl.readLock().unlock(); }
        }

        public void set(String k, String v) {
            rwl.writeLock().lock();
            try { store.put(k, v); }
            finally { rwl.writeLock().unlock(); }
        }
    }

    // ── 3. StampedLock optimistic read ────────────────────────────────────
    static class Velocity {
        private double vx, vy;
        private final StampedLock sl = new StampedLock();

        public void set(double vx, double vy) {
            long stamp = sl.writeLock();
            try { this.vx = vx; this.vy = vy; }
            finally { sl.unlockWrite(stamp); }
        }

        public double speed() {
            long stamp = sl.tryOptimisticRead();
            double x = vx, y = vy;
            if (!sl.validate(stamp)) {
                stamp = sl.readLock();
                try { x = vx; y = vy; }
                finally { sl.unlockRead(stamp); }
            }
            return Math.hypot(x, y);
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        // Gate demo
        Gate gate = new Gate();
        Thread waiter = new Thread(() -> {
            try {
                gate.awaitOpen();
                System.out.println("Gate opened!");
            } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
            }
        });
        waiter.start();
        Thread.sleep(100);
        gate.openGate();
        waiter.join();

        // Cache demo
        SimpleCache cache = new SimpleCache();
        cache.set("key", "value");
        System.out.println("Cached: " + cache.get("key"));

        // Velocity demo
        Velocity v = new Velocity();
        v.set(3.0, 4.0);
        System.out.println("Speed: " + v.speed()); // 5.0
    }
}

Practice — Lesson 47

Easy Exercises

Exercise 1 — Timed Lock with Fallback

Implement a LockedPrinter that attempts to acquire a ReentrantLock for up to 500 ms. If it cannot, it logs a warning and skips printing. Multiple threads should call it concurrently and demonstrate the timeout path.

<details>
<summary>Solution sketch</summary>

public class LockedPrinter {
    private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();

    public void print(String msg) {
        try {
            if (lock.tryLock(500, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) {
                try {
                    Thread.sleep(200); // simulate work
                    System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName() + ": " + msg);
                } finally {
                    lock.unlock();
                }
            } else {
                System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName()
                    + ": SKIPPED (lock timeout)");
            }
        } catch (InterruptedException e) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        }
    }
}

</details>

Exercise 2 — Bounded Stack with Conditions

Implement a BoundedStack<T> with a capacity limit. Use a single ReentrantLock with two Condition objects: notFull and notEmpty. Implement push(T) (blocks when full) and pop() (blocks when empty).

<details>
<summary>Solution sketch</summary>

public class BoundedStack<T> {
    private final Object[] data;
    private int top = -1;
    private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();
    private final Condition notFull  = lock.newCondition();
    private final Condition notEmpty = lock.newCondition();

    public BoundedStack(int capacity) { data = new Object[capacity]; }

    public void push(T item) throws InterruptedException {
        lock.lock();
        try {
            while (top == data.length - 1) notFull.await();
            data[++top] = item;
            notEmpty.signal();
        } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }

    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    public T pop() throws InterruptedException {
        lock.lock();
        try {
            while (top == -1) notEmpty.await();
            T item = (T) data[top--];
            notFull.signal();
            return item;
        } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }
}

</details>

Exercise 3 — StampedLock Point Distance

Extend the Point class from Part 12 to add a moveAndMeasure(dx, dy) method that:
1. Acquires a write lock to update coordinates.
2. Downgrades to a read lock.
3. Returns the distance from origin under the read lock.

<details>
<summary>Solution sketch</summary>

public double moveAndMeasure(double dx, double dy) {
    long stamp = sl.writeLock();
    try {
        x += dx;
        y += dy;
        // downgrade: acquire read before releasing write
        long readStamp = sl.tryConvertToOptimisticRead(stamp);
        if (readStamp != 0) {
            stamp = readStamp;
        } else {
            stamp = sl.readLock(); // full downgrade fallback
        }
    } finally {
        sl.unlock(stamp);
    }
    // At this point we hold either an optimistic or read stamp — for
    // simplicity, just compute after releasing (values are already local)
    return Math.hypot(x, y);
}

</details>

Exercise 4 — Deadlock Detection Tool

Write a DeadlockDetector that uses ThreadMXBean to find deadlocked threads and prints their lock information. Trigger it with two threads that each hold one of two ReentrantLocks and wait for the other.

<details>
<summary>Solution sketch</summary>

import java.lang.management.*;

public class DeadlockDetector {
    public static void detect() {
        ThreadMXBean bean = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean();
        long[] deadlocked = bean.findDeadlockedThreads();
        if (deadlocked == null) {
            System.out.println("No deadlock detected.");
            return;
        }
        ThreadInfo[] infos = bean.getThreadInfo(deadlocked, true, true);
        for (ThreadInfo info : infos) {
            System.out.println("DEADLOCKED: " + info.getThreadName());
            System.out.println("  Waiting for: " + info.getLockName());
            System.out.println("  Held by:     " + info.getLockOwnerName());
        }
    }
}

</details>
