Part 1

Concept

In concurrent programming, even a simple operation like counter++ is not thread-safe. It decomposes into three CPU instructions — read, modify, write — and another thread can interleave between any two of them, producing lost updates. The classical solution is to use synchronized or an explicit lock. But locking is expensive: it causes context switches, cache-line invalidations, and thread parking/unparking overhead.

The java.util.concurrent.atomic package (introduced in Java 5, JSR-166) provides a suite of classes that perform common read-modify-write operations atomically without locking, using CPU hardware primitives. These classes are the backbone of high-performance concurrent data structures and are used extensively inside the JDK itself — ConcurrentHashMap, ForkJoinPool, LongAdder, and many more depend on them.

The package at a glance

java.util.concurrent.atomic
│
├── Scalar atomics
│   ├── AtomicBoolean
│   ├── AtomicInteger
│   ├── AtomicLong
│   └── AtomicReference<V>
│
├── Array atomics
│   ├── AtomicIntegerArray
│   ├── AtomicLongArray
│   └── AtomicReferenceArray<E>
│
├── Field updaters (reflection-based, lower allocation)
│   ├── AtomicIntegerFieldUpdater<T>
│   ├── AtomicLongFieldUpdater<T>
│   └── AtomicReferenceFieldUpdater<T,V>
│
└── High-contention accumulators (Java 8+)
    ├── LongAdder
    ├── DoubleAdder
    ├── LongAccumulator
    └── DoubleAccumulator

All scalar atomics wrap a volatile field and delegate mutations to Unsafe.compareAndSwapXxx (Java 8) or VarHandle (Java 9+). You get both visibility (like volatile) and atomicity (like synchronized) at the cost of a single CPU instruction — LOCK CMPXCHG on x86.

Part 2

AtomicInteger

AtomicInteger is the workhorse of the package. It wraps a single int value and exposes every read-modify-write pattern you need.

import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

public class AtomicCounter {
    private final AtomicInteger value = new AtomicInteger(0);

    public void increment()            { value.incrementAndGet(); }
    public void decrement()            { value.decrementAndGet(); }
    public void add(int delta)         { value.addAndGet(delta); }
    public int  get()                  { return value.get(); }

    // Functional update — applies the function atomically (Java 8+)
    public int multiplyBy(int factor) {
        return value.updateAndGet(current -> current * factor);
    }

    // Accumulate — merges old value with provided value using a function
    public int addIfPositive(int delta) {
        return value.accumulateAndGet(delta,
            (current, d) -> current > 0 ? current + d : current);
    }
}

Complete AtomicInteger API

Method Returns Description
get() int Read the current value (volatile read)
set(v) void Write unconditionally (volatile write)
lazySet(v) void Eventually consistent write (ordered, not volatile)
getAndSet(v) int Atomically set and return old value
compareAndSet(expected, update) boolean CAS — write only if current == expected
compareAndExchange(expected, update) int Returns witness (Java 9+)
getAndIncrement() int Return old, then add 1
incrementAndGet() int Add 1, return new
getAndDecrement() int Return old, then subtract 1
decrementAndGet() int Subtract 1, return new
getAndAdd(delta) int Return old, then add delta
addAndGet(delta) int Add delta, return new
getAndUpdate(fn) int Return old, apply fn atomically
updateAndGet(fn) int Apply fn, return new
getAndAccumulate(v, fn) int Return old, merge with fn
accumulateAndGet(v, fn) int Merge with fn, return new

The lazySet method is a JMM-ordered store that is cheaper than a volatile write but does not guarantee immediate visibility to other threads. It is useful when writing to a field that will be observed by a subsequent volatile write or lock release.

Part 3

CAS (Compare-And-Swap) Operation

CAS is the single fundamental operation that makes all atomic classes work. It is a single, indivisible CPU instruction on modern hardware.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                  COMPARE-AND-SWAP (CAS) OPERATION               │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Inputs:  memory_address, expected_value, new_value
  Output:  boolean (or witness value in Java 9+)

  Atomic CPU instruction (LOCK CMPXCHG on x86):
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  if (*memory_address == expected_value) {        │
  │      *memory_address = new_value;                │
  │      return true;   ← SUCCESS                   │
  │  } else {                                        │
  │      return false;  ← FAILURE (retry needed)    │
  │  }                                               │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Java call:  atomicInteger.compareAndSet(expected, newValue)

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  Thread T1                          Thread T2
  ─────────────────                  ─────────────────
  reads value = 5
                                     reads value = 5
  CAS(5 → 6) ✓ succeeds
                                     CAS(5 → 6) ✗ fails!
                                       └─ memory holds 6, not 5
                                       └─ T2 retries: reads 6,
                                          CAS(6 → 7) ✓ succeeds

  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  CAS RETRY LOOP (the "spin" or "optimistic" pattern):

  int current;
  do {
      current = atomicInt.get();         // 1. read
  } while (!atomicInt.compareAndSet(     // 2. try to update
               current,                 //    expected = what we read
               current + delta));        //    new     = desired value
                                         // 3. if CAS fails, loop back

  This loop is guaranteed to make progress because:
  - If CAS fails, another thread succeeded → system-wide progress
  - If threads keep colliding, the JVM uses exponential backoff

CAS in Java source (simplified)

// java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger (conceptual)
public final int getAndIncrement() {
    for (;;) {
        int current = get();
        int next = current + 1;
        if (compareAndSet(current, next))
            return current;
        // CAS failed — another thread modified value — retry
    }
}
Part 4

AtomicLong

AtomicLong mirrors AtomicInteger but operates on long values. It is commonly used for sequence/ID generators and global counters.

import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong;

// Thread-safe ID generator
public class IdGenerator {
    private static final AtomicLong sequence = new AtomicLong(1_000_000L);

    public static long nextId() {
        return sequence.getAndIncrement();
    }
}

// Usage in parallel stream
long[] ids = LongStream.range(0, 10)
    .parallel()
    .map(i -> IdGenerator.nextId())
    .toArray();
// All 10 IDs are unique, even generated concurrently

On 32-bit JVMs, long operations are not atomic by default (they involve two 32-bit operations). AtomicLong guarantees atomicity even there. On 64-bit JVMs with a 64-bit JIT, the hardware already handles this, but AtomicLong still adds the CAS guarantee on top of volatile visibility.

Part 5

AtomicBoolean

AtomicBoolean is often used for one-shot flags — an action that must happen exactly once across multiple threads.

import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicBoolean;

public class OneTimeInitializer {
    private final AtomicBoolean initialized = new AtomicBoolean(false);

    public void initialize() {
        // Only the first thread to CAS from false → true proceeds
        if (initialized.compareAndSet(false, true)) {
            performExpensiveInit();
        }
        // All other threads: CAS returns false, skip initialization
    }

    private void performExpensiveInit() {
        System.out.println("Initializing by: " + Thread.currentThread().getName());
    }
}

This pattern is far simpler and more performant than double-checked locking with a volatile boolean + synchronized block.

Part 6

AtomicReference

AtomicReference<V> atomically swaps arbitrary object references. It is the generic building block for lock-free data structures.

import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicReference;

// Immutable snapshot + CAS-swap pattern
public class Configuration {
    record Config(String host, int port, int timeout) {}

    private final AtomicReference<Config> configRef =
        new AtomicReference<>(new Config("localhost", 8080, 30));

    // Thread-safe hot reload — no lock needed
    public void updateTimeout(int newTimeout) {
        Config current, updated;
        do {
            current = configRef.get();
            updated = new Config(current.host(), current.port(), newTimeout);
        } while (!configRef.compareAndSet(current, updated));
    }

    public Config get() { return configRef.get(); }
}

AtomicReference for lock-free stack

import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicReference;

public class LockFreeStack<T> {
    private record Node<T>(T value, Node<T> next) {}

    private final AtomicReference<Node<T>> top = new AtomicReference<>(null);

    public void push(T item) {
        Node<T> newNode, currentTop;
        do {
            currentTop = top.get();
            newNode = new Node<>(item, currentTop);
        } while (!top.compareAndSet(currentTop, newNode));
    }

    public T pop() {
        Node<T> currentTop, newTop;
        do {
            currentTop = top.get();
            if (currentTop == null) return null;
            newTop = currentTop.next();
        } while (!top.compareAndSet(currentTop, newTop));
        return currentTop.value();
    }
}
Part 7

AtomicIntegerArray and AtomicReferenceArray

These array variants allow individual elements to be updated atomically, unlike a plain volatile int[] which only makes the reference to the array volatile, not the individual elements.

import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicIntegerArray;

public class HitCounter {
    private final AtomicIntegerArray buckets;

    public HitCounter(int numBuckets) {
        this.buckets = new AtomicIntegerArray(numBuckets);
    }

    public void record(int bucketIndex) {
        buckets.incrementAndGet(bucketIndex);
    }

    public int getCount(int bucketIndex) {
        return buckets.get(bucketIndex);
    }

    public int total() {
        int sum = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < buckets.length(); i++) sum += buckets.get(i);
        return sum;
    }
}

import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicReferenceArray;

// Concurrent ring buffer of string slots
AtomicReferenceArray<String> ring = new AtomicReferenceArray<>(8);
// CAS into slot 3 only if currently null
ring.compareAndSet(3, null, "first-value");

Array atomics internally pad each element (Java 9+ via @Contended) to avoid false sharing — where two unrelated values share a CPU cache line and cause unnecessary cache invalidations.

Part 8

Field Updaters

Field updaters allow you to apply CAS operations on volatile fields of existing classes without wrapping them in an Atomic object. This is valuable when you have millions of instances and cannot afford the extra object allocation.

import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicIntegerFieldUpdater;

public class Node {
    // Must be volatile and NOT private (or in same package)
    volatile int state;

    private static final AtomicIntegerFieldUpdater<Node> STATE_UPDATER =
        AtomicIntegerFieldUpdater.newUpdater(Node.class, "state");

    public boolean transition(int from, int to) {
        return STATE_UPDATER.compareAndSet(this, from, to);
    }

    public int getState() {
        return STATE_UPDATER.get(this);
    }
}

When to use field updaters

  • You have objects (e.g., Node in a linked list) where each instance has an AtomicInteger purely for CAS — the updater avoids that extra object allocation.
  • Memory-sensitive data structures (low-latency trading, graph processing with millions of nodes).
  • Constraint: the field must be volatile, not final, and accessible from the updater's package.
Part 9

Core API Methods Deep Dive

set vs lazySet

AtomicInteger ai = new AtomicInteger(0);

// set() — full volatile write, immediately visible to all threads
ai.set(10);

// lazySet() — ordered store, eventually visible
// Cheaper than set() — avoids the StoreLoad memory fence
// Use when: updating a field that another volatile write will "flush" after
ai.lazySet(10);

lazySet maps to putOrderedInt (Java 8) / setRelease (Java 9+) on VarHandle. It guarantees that prior stores are ordered before this one, but does not insert the expensive StoreLoad barrier. Use it when you know a subsequent volatile write (e.g., a lock release or volatile flag) will make the value visible.

compareAndSet vs weakCompareAndSet

// compareAndSet — strong CAS: guaranteed to succeed if condition holds
boolean updated = ai.compareAndSet(5, 6);

// weakCompareAndSet (deprecated Java 9+, superseded by weakCompareAndSetPlain)
// May spuriously fail even when expected == current (on some architectures, e.g., ARM LL/SC)
// Only use inside a retry loop
boolean maybeUpdated = ai.weakCompareAndSetPlain(5, 6);

On x86 hardware, strong and weak CAS produce the same instruction. On ARM/PowerPC, weak CAS maps to STXR (store exclusive) which can fail spuriously, making it slightly cheaper in loops.

Part 10

CAS Loop Patterns

Pattern 1 — Conditional increment (only if positive)

public boolean incrementIfPositive(AtomicInteger counter) {
    int current;
    do {
        current = counter.get();
        if (current <= 0) return false;   // bail out condition
    } while (!counter.compareAndSet(current, current + 1));
    return true;
}

Pattern 2 — updateAndGet (Java 8+, cleaner)

// Java 8 updateAndGet is also a CAS loop internally
int result = counter.updateAndGet(v -> v > 0 ? v + 1 : v);

Pattern 3 — CAS-based max update

// Update to max of current and candidate — no lock needed
public void updateMax(AtomicLong max, long candidate) {
    long current;
    do {
        current = max.get();
        if (candidate <= current) return;  // candidate not larger
    } while (!max.compareAndSet(current, candidate));
}

CAS backoff under high contention

When dozens of threads spin on the same CAS, throughput degrades because failed attempts waste CPU cycles. Strategies:

// Exponential backoff
int backoff = 1;
while (!ai.compareAndSet(expected, newVal)) {
    expected = ai.get();
    newVal   = expected + delta;
    if (backoff < 1000) {
        Thread.onSpinWait();   // Java 9+ hint to CPU (PAUSE instruction on x86)
        backoff *= 2;
    } else {
        Thread.yield();
    }
}
Part 11

The ABA Problem

CAS checks only that the current value equals the expected value. It cannot detect if the value was changed from A → B → A in between the read and the CAS attempt.

Thread T1 reads value = "A"
                            Thread T2: A → B
                            Thread T2: B → A   (value is back to A)
Thread T1: CAS(A → C) succeeds!
           But the world changed — T1 may be working on stale assumptions

ABA matters in lock-free data structures

Consider a lock-free stack where T1 reads the top pointer (node A), T2 pops A, pushes B, pops B, re-uses node A's memory and pushes it back. T1's CAS on the top pointer succeeds, but its next pointer inside node A may now point to freed/reused memory.

Solution: AtomicStampedReference

import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicStampedReference;

AtomicStampedReference<String> ref =
    new AtomicStampedReference<>("A", 0);  // value, stamp (version)

int[] stampHolder = new int[1];
String current = ref.get(stampHolder);   // reads both value and stamp
int currentStamp = stampHolder[0];

// CAS only succeeds if BOTH value AND stamp match
boolean success = ref.compareAndSet(
    current, "C",           // expected value → new value
    currentStamp,           // expected stamp
    currentStamp + 1);      // new stamp

// Even if value cycles A→B→A, the stamp changes: 0→1→2
// A second attempt to CAS with stamp 0 will fail

The stamp is typically an integer version counter. AtomicMarkableReference uses a single boolean flag instead (sufficient for "is this node logically deleted?" patterns).

Part 12

LongAdder vs AtomicLong for High Contention

AtomicLong is a single volatile long that all threads CAS against. Under high thread counts, threads collide on the same memory cell, causing CPU cache ping-pong and wasted retries.

LongAdder (Java 8+) solves this with striping: it maintains an array of cells, each independently CAS-able, and distributes threads across cells using a thread-local probe hash. sum() aggregates all cells.

AtomicLong under 8-thread contention:
  T1 ─► [cell: 100] ◄─ T2   → all 8 threads collide on ONE cell
  T3 ─────────────────► CAS
  T4 ─────────────────► CAS   7 out of 8 attempts fail
  T5 ─────────────────► CAS
  T6 ─────────────────► CAS
  T7 ─────────────────► CAS
  T8 ─────────────────► CAS

LongAdder under 8-thread contention:
  T1 ─► [cell0: 12]   ← T5    each thread hits its own cell
  T2 ─► [cell1: 15]   ← T6
  T3 ─► [cell2: 18]   ← T7    near-zero contention
  T4 ─► [cell3: 21]   ← T8

  sum() = 12 + 15 + 18 + 21 + base = 66

import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder;

LongAdder requestCount = new LongAdder();

// In request handler (called concurrently by many threads):
requestCount.increment();
requestCount.add(payloadBytes);

// When you need the total (e.g., for metrics flush):
long total = requestCount.sum();       // non-atomic aggregate
long totalAndReset = requestCount.sumThenReset();  // useful for rate metrics

When to use which

Scenario Use
Single counter, low contention (< 4 threads) AtomicLong
Read result frequently (publish to other threads) AtomicLong
High-contention counter (metrics, stats) LongAdder
compareAndSet needed AtomicLong (LongAdder has no CAS)
Throughput is critical, exact value rarely needed LongAdder
Part 13

LongAccumulator

LongAccumulator generalizes LongAdder to arbitrary accumulation functions (not just addition):

import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAccumulator;

// Track maximum latency across all threads
LongAccumulator maxLatency = new LongAccumulator(Long::max, Long.MIN_VALUE);

// Each thread reports its measured latency
maxLatency.accumulate(measureLatency());

// Read the running maximum
long peak = maxLatency.get();
maxLatency.reset();

// Min temperature across sensor threads
LongAccumulator minTemp = new LongAccumulator(Long::min, Long.MAX_VALUE);

The function must be associative and commutative (order of application doesn't matter), because cells may be combined in any order. Addition, max, min, bitwise OR/AND all qualify. Subtraction does not.

Part 14

Lock-Free vs Lock-Based

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│          LOCK-FREE  vs  LOCK-BASED  COMPARISON                   │
├──────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Property         │ Lock-Free (CAS)       │ Lock-Based            │
├──────────────────┼───────────────────────┼───────────────────────┤
│ Thread blocking  │ Never blocks          │ Blocks on contention  │
│ Progress         │ System-wide           │ Only holder progresses│
│ Overhead         │ CPU spin on collision │ OS scheduler          │
│ Deadlock         │ Impossible            │ Possible              │
│ Priority invert  │ Impossible            │ Possible              │
│ Memory           │ No AQS queue          │ CLH/MCS queue nodes   │
│ Code complexity  │ Higher (ABA, backoff) │ Lower                 │
│ Best for         │ Short critical path   │ Long critical path    │
└──────────────────┴───────────────────────┴───────────────────────┘

Lock-free does not mean "fast in all cases." Under very high contention, CAS spinning can burn more CPU than a well-tuned ReentrantLock queue. Profile before choosing.

Obstruction-free, lock-free, wait-free

  • Obstruction-free: a thread makes progress if it runs alone (no other active threads interfere).
  • Lock-free: at least one thread makes progress globally, even with contention (CAS with retry).
  • Wait-free: every thread completes in a bounded number of steps (extremely hard to implement; rarely practical).

AtomicInteger operations are lock-free (CAS with unbounded retry). LongAdder operations are lock-free per cell.

Part 15

Production Patterns

Pattern 1 — Thread-safe request counter

@Component
public class MetricsCollector {
    private final AtomicLong requestCount = new AtomicLong(0);
    private final AtomicLong errorCount   = new AtomicLong(0);
    private final LongAdder  totalBytes   = new LongAdder();

    public void recordRequest(long bytes) {
        requestCount.incrementAndGet();
        totalBytes.add(bytes);
    }

    public void recordError() { errorCount.incrementAndGet(); }

    public Map<String, Long> snapshot() {
        return Map.of(
            "requests", requestCount.get(),
            "errors",   errorCount.get(),
            "bytes",    totalBytes.sum()
        );
    }
}

Pattern 2 — Lock-free sequence ID generator

public final class SequenceGenerator {
    private static final AtomicLong counter = new AtomicLong(
        System.currentTimeMillis() * 1_000_000  // epoch-based start
    );

    private SequenceGenerator() {}

    public static long next() { return counter.getAndIncrement(); }
}

Pattern 3 — Lazy singleton with AtomicReference

public class Registry {
    private static final AtomicReference<Registry> INSTANCE =
        new AtomicReference<>();

    public static Registry getInstance() {
        Registry inst = INSTANCE.get();
        if (inst != null) return inst;

        inst = new Registry();
        return INSTANCE.compareAndSet(null, inst)
            ? inst
            : INSTANCE.get();   // lost the CAS race, use winner's instance
    }
}

Pattern 4 — Circuit breaker state machine

public class CircuitBreaker {
    enum State { CLOSED, OPEN, HALF_OPEN }
    private final AtomicReference<State> state =
        new AtomicReference<>(State.CLOSED);
    private final AtomicInteger failureCount = new AtomicInteger(0);

    public void recordFailure() {
        if (failureCount.incrementAndGet() >= 5) {
            state.compareAndSet(State.CLOSED, State.OPEN);
        }
    }

    public boolean isCallPermitted() {
        return state.get() != State.OPEN;
    }

    public void reset() {
        failureCount.set(0);
        state.set(State.CLOSED);
    }
}
Part 16

Volatile vs Atomic

Both volatile and Atomic* provide visibility. But volatile provides no atomicity for compound operations.

volatile int v = 0;
// These two lines are NOT atomic together:
if (v == 0) v = 1;  // read-check-write: another thread can change v between read and write

AtomicInteger ai = new AtomicInteger(0);
ai.compareAndSet(0, 1);  // atomic: guaranteed — reads AND writes in a single instruction
Property volatile AtomicInteger
Visibility guarantee Yes Yes
Read atomicity Yes Yes
Write atomicity Yes Yes
Compound operation atomicity No Yes (CAS)
CAS support No Yes
Performance (no contention) Faster ~Same (wraps volatile)
Memory overhead 0 (field modifier) Object allocation

Rule: use volatile for a single flag that is only written by one thread and read by others. Use AtomicXxx whenever any read-modify-write pattern exists.

Part 17

Memory Ordering

AtomicInteger operations use VarHandle with these access modes (Java 9+):

VarHandle mode Fence Maps to
getPlain / setPlain None Unsafe getInt / putInt
getOpaque / setOpaque Compiler Intra-thread ordering only
getAcquire / setRelease LoadLoad / StoreStore lazySet / cheaper than volatile
getVolatile / setVolatile Full (StoreLoad) get() / set()
compareAndSet Full CAS with acquire-release semantics

AtomicInteger.get() is a volatile read; set() is a volatile write. Both impose full memory fences on x86. On ARM/POWER they map to LDAR/STLR (acquire/release load/store).

Part 18

Performance Considerations

Rough operation cost on modern x86 (nanoseconds, single socket):
  Plain read/write (non-volatile):  ~1 ns
  volatile read:                    ~3 ns
  volatile write:                   ~5 ns
  CAS (uncontended):                ~10 ns
  CAS (2 threads, same cache line): ~30-50 ns
  synchronized block (uncontended): ~15-20 ns  (JIT-biased lock)
  synchronized block (contended):   ~200-1000 ns (OS park/unpark)
  LongAdder.increment() (8 threads):~15 ns  (striped, low per-thread cost)
  AtomicLong.increment() (8 threads):~50-100 ns (CAS spin)

False sharing is a silent killer: two AtomicInteger fields that live on the same 64-byte cache line cause every CAS on one to invalidate the other's cache entry. The JDK's @Contended annotation (sun.misc) adds padding.

// Padded counter to avoid false sharing
@sun.misc.Contended
static final class PaddedAtomicLong extends AtomicLong {
    PaddedAtomicLong(long init) { super(init); }
}

LongAdder already applies @Contended to its Cell array — that's a large part of why it outperforms AtomicLong under contention.

Part 19

Common Pitfalls

Pitfall 1 — Ignoring CAS failures

// WRONG: discards the return value
atomicInt.compareAndSet(expected, newVal);

// CORRECT: check if the CAS succeeded
if (!atomicInt.compareAndSet(expected, newVal)) {
    // retry or handle failure
}

Pitfall 2 — Multiple CAS without coordination

// NOT atomic as a pair — another thread can change ai between the two calls
int v = ai.getAndIncrement();
ai.getAndDecrement();  // these are not a single atomic transaction

Pitfall 3 — AtomicReference with mutable objects

AtomicReference<List<String>> ref = new AtomicReference<>(new ArrayList<>());
// WRONG: mutating the list bypasses the CAS protection
ref.get().add("item");  // not thread-safe!

// CORRECT: copy-on-write pattern
List<String> oldList, newList;
do {
    oldList = ref.get();
    newList = new ArrayList<>(oldList);
    newList.add("item");
} while (!ref.compareAndSet(oldList, newList));

Pitfall 4 — LongAdder.sum() is not a consistent snapshot

sum() aggregates cells sequentially — it is not a single atomic read. Other threads may increment cells between aggregations. If you need an exact consistent snapshot, use AtomicLong.

Part 20

Interview Preparation

Q1: What is the difference between compareAndSet and compareAndExchange?

compareAndSet (Java original) returns a boolean. compareAndExchange (Java 9+, via VarHandle) returns the witness value — the actual current value at the time of the CAS. If the CAS failed, you get back the current value directly, avoiding a second get() call and reducing one memory fence in retry loops.

Q2: When would you use LongAdder instead of AtomicLong?

When many threads are incrementing a counter concurrently and the final sum is only read periodically (e.g., metrics flush every 10 seconds). LongAdder distributes the hot spot across multiple cells, reducing CAS contention by an order of magnitude. The tradeoff: sum() is more expensive and not a consistent snapshot.

Q3: What is the ABA problem and how does Java solve it?

ABA is when a CAS sees the expected value (A), but the value was secretly changed A→B→A between the read and the CAS. The CAS succeeds, but it should have noticed the intermediate change. Java solves this with AtomicStampedReference (version counter) or AtomicMarkableReference (boolean flag).

Q4: How does lazySet differ from set?

set performs a volatile write with a StoreLoad fence — all prior stores are flushed and visible to all threads immediately. lazySet (mapped to setRelease in Java 9+) only guarantees that prior stores are ordered before this store, but omits the expensive StoreLoad barrier. Other threads may not see the update immediately. Use lazySet to zero out an object reference in a queue (a prior lock release will flush it), saving ~10-30% on throughput-critical code.

Q5: Write a thread-safe counter that supports increment, decrement, and read-and-reset.

public class ResettableCounter {
    private final AtomicLong value = new AtomicLong(0);
    public void increment()          { value.incrementAndGet(); }
    public void decrement()          { value.decrementAndGet(); }
    public long readAndReset()       { return value.getAndSet(0); }
    public long get()                { return value.get(); }
}
Part 21

Quick Reference Cheat Sheet

CHOOSE THE RIGHT ATOMIC CLASS
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  Need to count / add integers?
    Low contention  → AtomicInteger / AtomicLong
    High contention → LongAdder

  Need to count with arbitrary function?
    → LongAccumulator (max, min, bit ops)

  Need CAS on an object reference?
    → AtomicReference<V>

  Need CAS on an array element?
    → AtomicIntegerArray / AtomicReferenceArray

  Need CAS on an existing class field (to avoid extra object alloc)?
    → AtomicIntegerFieldUpdater / AtomicReferenceFieldUpdater

  Need ABA protection?
    → AtomicStampedReference (version counter)
    → AtomicMarkableReference (boolean deletion mark)

COMMON METHOD PATTERNS
──────────────────────
  Read:           ai.get()
  Write:          ai.set(v)       // volatile
  Lazy write:     ai.lazySet(v)   // release semantics
  CAS:            ai.compareAndSet(expected, update)
  Post-increment: ai.getAndIncrement()   // returns OLD
  Pre-increment:  ai.incrementAndGet()   // returns NEW
  Functional:     ai.updateAndGet(v -> v * 2)
Part 22

Summary Table

Class Key Operation CAS Support High-Contention? Typical Use
AtomicBoolean compareAndSet Yes No One-shot flags, init guards
AtomicInteger compareAndSet, getAndIncrement Yes Moderate Counters, state machines
AtomicLong Same as AtomicInteger Yes Moderate ID generators, global counters
AtomicReference<V> compareAndSet on reference Yes No Config hot-swap, lock-free structures
AtomicIntegerArray Element-level CAS Yes No Per-bucket hit counts
AtomicReferenceArray<E> Element-level CAS on refs Yes No Concurrent arrays
AtomicIntegerFieldUpdater<T> CAS on existing volatile field Yes No Memory-saving in large graphs
LongAdder increment, add, sum No (no CAS API) Excellent Metrics, stats, throughput counters
LongAccumulator accumulate, custom fn No Excellent Max/min tracking across threads
AtomicStampedReference<V> compareAndSet with version Yes + stamp No ABA-safe lock-free structures
AtomicMarkableReference<V> compareAndSet with flag Yes + mark No Logical deletion in linked lists

Easy

E1. Create a class SafeCounter backed by AtomicInteger. Add methods: increment(), decrement(), addIfGreaterThanZero(int delta) (returns boolean), and reset(). Write a test that spawns 100 threads each calling increment() 1000 times and asserts final value is 100,000.

E2. Implement a UniqueIdGenerator using AtomicLong that starts from 1 and provides nextId(). Verify with 10 concurrent threads each generating 10,000 IDs that all 100,000 are unique (store in a ConcurrentHashMap).

E3. Use AtomicBoolean to implement a StartStopFlag where start() returns true only the first time it is called, and stop() resets the flag.

Medium

M1. Implement a lock-free BoundedCounter with a max value. increment() should return false (without incrementing) when the counter is already at max. Use a CAS retry loop.

public class BoundedCounter {
    private final AtomicInteger count;
    private final int max;
    // implement increment(), decrement(), get()
}

M2. Implement a thread-safe RateLimiter using AtomicLong that allows at most N requests per second. On each tryAcquire() call, check if the current second's slot still has capacity and atomically decrement it.

M3. Use AtomicIntegerArray to build a histogram with 10 buckets. Each thread reports a value in [0, 99]; the bucket index is value / 10. Verify totals after 1,000,000 concurrent observations.

Advanced

A2. Build an ABADemo that:

3. Fixes it with AtomicStampedReference.

Production

P1. Design a MetricsSink component:
- Uses LongAdder for request count, total latency, error count.
- Provides a snapshot() method that reads all values atomically-ish and resets them (use sumThenReset).
- Exposes metrics compatible with Micrometer/Prometheus.

P2. Implement a CircuitBreaker with states CLOSED, OPEN, HALF_OPEN using AtomicReference<State>. Include: configurable failure threshold, timeout after which it transitions to HALF_OPEN, and probe logic that transitions back to CLOSED on success.

Debugging

D1. The following code has a bug — find and fix it:

AtomicInteger tickets = new AtomicInteger(100);

public boolean buyTicket() {
    int current = tickets.get();
    if (current <= 0) return false;
    tickets.set(current - 1);   // BUG: not atomic with the check
    return true;
}

D2. A LongAdder-based rate counter shows wrong totals when read. Given the code below, identify why and provide a correct alternative:

LongAdder counter = new LongAdder();
// 10 threads each increment 1000 times
// Main thread reads: counter.sum() at arbitrary times
// Occasionally observes values lower than expected

Interview

I1. "Explain how AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet() works at the hardware level. What happens on x86 vs ARM?"

I2. "Your metrics service uses AtomicLong for a request counter and sees 15% CPU overhead under 200 rps. What change would you make and why?"

I3. "Compare synchronized, ReentrantLock, and AtomicInteger for implementing a simple counter. When would you choose each?"

I4. "You need to swap two AtomicReference values atomically (as a pair). Is this possible with the standard API? If not, how would you design it?"

Answer: Not directly — CAS only operates on one memory location. Solutions: wrap both in an immutable holder object and CAS the holder reference; or use StampedLock/synchronized to coordinate the two-reference update.

Part 1

Concept

Before Java 5, the only way to run code on a separate thread was to create a Thread object, assign a Runnable, and call start(). This raw model couples the what (the task) with the how (thread lifecycle management). Developers had to manually create threads, handle pooling, and manage shutdown — all error-prone and expensive.

The Executor Framework (JSR-166, Java 5) separates task submission from thread management. It provides a three-layer abstraction:

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   EXECUTOR FRAMEWORK LAYERS                      │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Layer 3 — Task abstraction                                      │
│    Runnable (no return)  |  Callable<V> (returns V, throws)      │
│                                                                  │
│  Layer 2 — Execution service                                     │
│    Executor ──► ExecutorService ──► ScheduledExecutorService     │
│                                                                  │
│  Layer 1 — Implementations                                       │
│    ThreadPoolExecutor  |  ForkJoinPool  |  ScheduledThreadPool   │
│                                                                  │
│  Layer 0 — Factory                                               │
│    Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n)                               │
│    Executors.newCachedThreadPool()          ← DANGER in prod     │
│    Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor()                           │
│    Executors.newScheduledThreadPool(n)                           │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The central idea: submit a task, get a result, let the framework manage threads. You decide the policy (pool size, queue type, rejection), the framework handles thread creation, reuse, and teardown.

Part 2

The Executor Interface

Executor is the root interface with a single method:

public interface Executor {
    void execute(Runnable command);
}

This simple interface allows the framework to be completely decoupled from task definitions. You can swap implementations without changing task code:

Executor e;

// Same task code — different execution strategies
e = Runnable::run;                           // same-thread (synchronous)
e = new Thread(command -> new Thread(command).start()); // always new thread
e = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4);         // pool of 4 threads
e = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(); // virtual thread per task (Java 21)

// Task code doesn't care which executor is used
e.execute(() -> System.out.println("Hello from " + Thread.currentThread().getName()));

Executor is fire-and-forget — no way to track when the task completes or get a return value. ExecutorService extends it with lifecycle and result-tracking.

Part 3

ExecutorService

ExecutorService adds task submission with results, batch execution, and lifecycle management:

public interface ExecutorService extends Executor {
    // Lifecycle
    void     shutdown();
    List<Runnable> shutdownNow();
    boolean  isShutdown();
    boolean  isTerminated();
    boolean  awaitTermination(long timeout, TimeUnit unit) throws InterruptedException;

    // Single task submission
    <T> Future<T> submit(Callable<T> task);
    <T> Future<T> submit(Runnable task, T result);
    Future<?>     submit(Runnable task);

    // Batch
    <T> List<Future<T>> invokeAll(Collection<? extends Callable<T>> tasks)
        throws InterruptedException;
    <T> List<Future<T>> invokeAll(Collection<? extends Callable<T>> tasks,
        long timeout, TimeUnit unit) throws InterruptedException;
    <T> T invokeAny(Collection<? extends Callable<T>> tasks)
        throws InterruptedException, ExecutionException;
    <T> T invokeAny(Collection<? extends Callable<T>> tasks,
        long timeout, TimeUnit unit) throws InterruptedException, ExecutionException, TimeoutException;
}

Basic usage

ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4);
try {
    Future<String> future = pool.submit(() -> fetchFromDatabase(id));
    // ... do other work ...
    String result = future.get(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS);  // blocks up to 5 s
    System.out.println(result);
} catch (TimeoutException e) {
    // task took too long
} catch (ExecutionException e) {
    // task threw an exception — unwrap it
    Throwable cause = e.getCause();
} finally {
    pool.shutdown();
}
Part 4

Executors Factory Methods

The Executors utility class provides four main factory methods:

newFixedThreadPool(int n)

ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors());
  • Creates exactly n threads. If all are busy, tasks queue in an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue.
  • Good for CPU-bound tasks where n ≈ availableProcessors.
  • Watch out: the queue is unbounded — OOM is possible if tasks are submitted faster than processed.

newCachedThreadPool()

ExecutorService pool = Executors.newCachedThreadPool();
  • Creates new threads on demand; reuses idle ones (kept alive for 60 seconds).
  • No queue — new thread created immediately if all are busy.
  • Never use in production for unbound workloads — can create thousands of threads and crash the JVM. Safe only for very short-lived tasks with known bounded concurrency.

newSingleThreadExecutor()

ExecutorService sequential = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor();
  • One thread, unbounded queue.
  • Guarantees tasks execute sequentially in submission order.
  • The single thread is replaced if it dies unexpectedly.
  • Useful for ordering events or writing to a shared resource.

newScheduledThreadPool(int n)

ScheduledExecutorService scheduler = Executors.newScheduledThreadPool(2);

// Run once after a delay
scheduler.schedule(() -> cleanup(), 10, TimeUnit.SECONDS);

// Run repeatedly with fixed delay between end-to-start
scheduler.scheduleWithFixedDelay(() -> poll(), 0, 5, TimeUnit.SECONDS);

// Run at fixed rate (start-to-start interval)
scheduler.scheduleAtFixedRate(() -> heartbeat(), 0, 1, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
Part 5

ThreadPoolExecutor Deep Dive

ThreadPoolExecutor is the implementation behind all Executors factory methods. Constructing it directly gives full control:

ThreadPoolExecutor executor = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
    4,                                    // corePoolSize
    16,                                   // maximumPoolSize
    60L, TimeUnit.SECONDS,               // keepAliveTime
    new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(1000),       // workQueue
    new CustomThreadFactory("worker"),    // threadFactory
    new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy() // rejectedExecutionHandler
);

The seven constructor parameters

Parameter Type Description
corePoolSize int Threads kept alive even when idle
maximumPoolSize int Hard ceiling on thread count
keepAliveTime long Idle time before a non-core thread dies
unit TimeUnit Unit for keepAliveTime
workQueue BlockingQueue<Runnable> Holds pending tasks
threadFactory ThreadFactory Creates new threads
handler RejectedExecutionHandler Called when pool is saturated
Part 6

ASCII: Thread Pool Task Flow Diagram

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                  ThreadPoolExecutor — TASK FLOW                      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  submit(task)
       │
       ▼
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Active threads < corePoolSize?                │
  │  YES → create new CORE thread, run task        │◄─── Even if idle
  │  NO  → go to queue check                       │     threads exist
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                       │ NO
                       ▼
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  workQueue.offer(task) succeeds?               │
  │  YES → task waits in queue                     │◄─── Core threads
  │  NO  → go to max check                         │     drain queue
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                       │ NO (queue full)
                       ▼
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Active threads < maximumPoolSize?             │
  │  YES → create NON-CORE thread, run task        │◄─── Temporary burst
  │  NO  → REJECTION                               │     thread
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                       │ REJECTED
                       ▼
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  RejectedExecutionHandler.          │
  │  rejectedExecution(task, executor)  │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────  │
  │  AbortPolicy      → throw RejEx     │
  │  CallerRunsPolicy → run in caller   │
  │  DiscardPolicy    → silently drop   │
  │  DiscardOldest    → drop head task  │
  └─────────────────────────────────────┘

  Thread lifecycle:
  CORE thread:  runs forever (unless allowCoreThreadTimeOut = true)
  NON-CORE thread: dies after keepAliveTime of idle time
Part 7

corePoolSize, maximumPoolSize and Queue Strategy

The relationship between queue type and pool growth is non-obvious and is one of the most commonly misunderstood parts of ThreadPoolExecutor:

Policy 1 — Fixed queue, no burst (Executors.newFixedThreadPool):
  corePoolSize = maximumPoolSize = N
  queue = LinkedBlockingQueue (unbounded)
  Non-core threads are NEVER created (max == core)
  Risk: queue grows without bound → OOM

Policy 2 — No queue, immediate burst (Executors.newCachedThreadPool):
  corePoolSize = 0
  maximumPoolSize = Integer.MAX_VALUE
  queue = SynchronousQueue (zero capacity — every offer needs a taker)
  New thread created for every task if none idle
  Risk: unbounded thread count → OutOfMemoryError

Policy 3 — Bounded queue + burst threads (RECOMMENDED for production):
  corePoolSize = N  (tuned for baseline load)
  maximumPoolSize = 2N or 3N  (tuned for burst)
  queue = ArrayBlockingQueue(capacity)  (bounded!)
  Risk: rejection when queue + burst threads exhausted — handle gracefully

Queue type trade-offs

Queue Capacity Behavior
LinkedBlockingQueue Unbounded (default) Tasks never rejected; burst threads never created
ArrayBlockingQueue(n) Bounded Tasks rejected after n; triggers burst threads
SynchronousQueue 0 Every task needs an immediate thread
PriorityBlockingQueue Unbounded, ordered Tasks run in priority order
DelayQueue Unbounded, timed Tasks become runnable after a delay
Part 8

RejectedExecutionHandler

When the pool is saturated (queue full AND at max threads), or the executor is shut down, the RejectedExecutionHandler is invoked:

public interface RejectedExecutionHandler {
    void rejectedExecution(Runnable r, ThreadPoolExecutor executor);
}

Built-in policies

// 1. AbortPolicy (DEFAULT) — throws RejectedExecutionException
new ThreadPoolExecutor.AbortPolicy()

// 2. CallerRunsPolicy — runs task in the SUBMITTING thread (natural back-pressure)
new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy()

// 3. DiscardPolicy — silently ignores the task
new ThreadPoolExecutor.DiscardPolicy()

// 4. DiscardOldestPolicy — discards the task at the HEAD of the queue, retries submit
new ThreadPoolExecutor.DiscardOldestPolicy()

Custom policy with metrics and alerting

public class AlertingRejectionHandler implements RejectedExecutionHandler {
    private final AtomicLong rejectionCount = new AtomicLong(0);
    private final String poolName;

    public AlertingRejectionHandler(String poolName) {
        this.poolName = poolName;
    }

    @Override
    public void rejectedExecution(Runnable r, ThreadPoolExecutor executor) {
        long count = rejectionCount.incrementAndGet();
        log.error("Task rejected from pool [{}]. Total rejections: {}. " +
                  "Pool: active={}, queue={}", poolName, count,
                  executor.getActiveCount(), executor.getQueue().size());
        if (count % 100 == 0) {
            alertService.fire("Thread pool " + poolName + " rejecting tasks");
        }
        // Optionally: CallerRuns fallback for critical tasks
        if (!executor.isShutdown()) {
            r.run();
        }
    }
}

Back-pressure with CallerRunsPolicy

CallerRunsPolicy is uniquely valuable: when the pool is saturated, the submitting thread executes the task itself. This:
1. Slows down the producer naturally (back-pressure).
2. Keeps all threads busy.
3. Prevents task loss.

It is the recommended default for server-side request handling where dropping work is unacceptable.

Part 9

Callable and Future

Runnable cannot return a value or throw checked exceptions. Callable<V> solves both:

@FunctionalInterface
public interface Callable<V> {
    V call() throws Exception;
}

Future<V> represents the pending result of an async computation:

import java.util.concurrent.*;

ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4);

// Submit a Callable — returns immediately
Future<Integer> future = pool.submit(() -> {
    int result = compute();  // long-running
    return result;
});

// Do other work while task runs...

try {
    // Blocks until result is ready (or timeout)
    Integer result = future.get(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
    System.out.println("Result: " + result);
} catch (TimeoutException e) {
    future.cancel(true);  // interrupt the task
    System.err.println("Task timed out");
} catch (ExecutionException e) {
    // Task threw an exception
    Throwable cause = e.getCause();
    log.error("Task failed", cause);
} catch (CancellationException e) {
    System.err.println("Task was cancelled");
} catch (InterruptedException e) {
    Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
    future.cancel(true);
}

pool.shutdown();

Future API

Method Description
get() Block indefinitely for result
get(timeout, unit) Block with timeout
isDone() True if completed (normally, exceptionally, or cancelled)
isCancelled() True if successfully cancelled
cancel(mayInterruptIfRunning) Attempt cancellation

Future has a key limitation: you cannot chain computations or attach callbacks. For that, use CompletableFuture (see Lesson 52).

Part 10

invokeAll and invokeAny

invokeAll — fan-out, collect all results

ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8);

List<Callable<String>> tasks = List.of(
    () -> fetchShard(0),
    () -> fetchShard(1),
    () -> fetchShard(2),
    () -> fetchShard(3)
);

// Submits all, blocks until ALL complete (or throw)
List<Future<String>> futures = pool.invokeAll(tasks);

List<String> results = new ArrayList<>();
for (Future<String> f : futures) {
    try {
        results.add(f.get());  // never blocks — task is already done
    } catch (ExecutionException e) {
        log.error("Shard failed", e.getCause());
    }
}

With timeout:

// All tasks must complete within 5 seconds, else remaining are cancelled
List<Future<String>> futures = pool.invokeAll(tasks, 5, TimeUnit.SECONDS);

invokeAny — fastest wins, cancel rest

// Submit multiple strategies — return result of whichever finishes first
// Remaining tasks are cancelled automatically
String result = pool.invokeAny(List.of(
    () -> queryPrimaryDB(),
    () -> queryReplicaDB(),
    () -> queryCacheFallback()
));

invokeAny is perfect for redundant request hedging (send a request to multiple nodes, use the first response) — a common pattern in high-availability systems.

Part 11

shutdown, shutdownNow, awaitTermination

Proper shutdown is critical. Leaked ExecutorService instances keep threads alive indefinitely, preventing JVM exit.

┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              ExecutorService LIFECYCLE STATES                   │
│                                                                │
│   RUNNING ──► SHUTDOWN ──► STOP ──► TIDYING ──► TERMINATED    │
│                                                                │
│   RUNNING:    accepts new tasks, processes queued tasks        │
│   SHUTDOWN:   no new tasks, finishes queued + running tasks    │
│   STOP:       no new tasks, tries to cancel running tasks      │
│   TIDYING:    all tasks terminated, running terminated() hook  │
│   TERMINATED: done                                             │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4);

// Submit tasks...

// Phase 1: stop accepting new tasks, let running/queued finish
pool.shutdown();

try {
    // Phase 2: wait for graceful completion
    if (!pool.awaitTermination(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) {
        // Phase 3: force-cancel running tasks
        pool.shutdownNow();
        // Phase 4: wait again for forced termination
        if (!pool.awaitTermination(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) {
            log.error("Pool did not terminate");
        }
    }
} catch (InterruptedException e) {
    pool.shutdownNow();
    Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
}

The difference

Method Behaviour
shutdown() Graceful — queued tasks run, no new tasks accepted
shutdownNow() Forceful — returns queued tasks as List<Runnable>, interrupts running threads
awaitTermination(t, u) Blocks calling thread until terminated or timeout

shutdownNow() sends Thread.interrupt() to running threads. Tasks must check Thread.interrupted() or use InterruptedException-throwing APIs to respond to interruption. A task that ignores interruptions will keep running until it finishes naturally.

Part 12

ThreadFactory

ThreadFactory controls how new threads are created — names, daemon status, priority, and exception handlers:

import java.util.concurrent.ThreadFactory;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

public class NamedThreadFactory implements ThreadFactory {
    private final String prefix;
    private final boolean daemon;
    private final AtomicInteger count = new AtomicInteger(1);

    public NamedThreadFactory(String prefix, boolean daemon) {
        this.prefix = prefix;
        this.daemon = daemon;
    }

    @Override
    public Thread newThread(Runnable r) {
        Thread t = new Thread(r, prefix + "-" + count.getAndIncrement());
        t.setDaemon(daemon);
        t.setPriority(Thread.NORM_PRIORITY);
        t.setUncaughtExceptionHandler((thread, ex) ->
            log.error("Uncaught exception in {}", thread.getName(), ex));
        return t;
    }
}

// Usage
ThreadPoolExecutor executor = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
    4, 16, 60, TimeUnit.SECONDS,
    new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(500),
    new NamedThreadFactory("payment-worker", false),
    new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy()
);

Named threads make stack traces and thread dumps immediately useful in production. Without custom names you see pool-1-thread-3 — useless in a system with ten pools.

Part 13

ScheduledExecutorService

ScheduledExecutorService scheduler = Executors.newScheduledThreadPool(2);

// One-shot delay
ScheduledFuture<?> onceTask = scheduler.schedule(
    () -> sendReminder(userId), 24, TimeUnit.HOURS);

// Periodic — scheduleAtFixedRate: fires every 'period' from start time
// If task overruns the period, next execution starts immediately (no pile-up)
ScheduledFuture<?> heartbeat = scheduler.scheduleAtFixedRate(
    () -> sendHeartbeat(), 0, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS);

// Periodic — scheduleWithFixedDelay: waits 'delay' AFTER previous completes
// Safer for tasks whose duration is variable
ScheduledFuture<?> poll = scheduler.scheduleWithFixedDelay(
    () -> pollExternalService(), 0, 5, TimeUnit.SECONDS);

// Cancel a scheduled task
heartbeat.cancel(false);  // false = don't interrupt if running

// Shutdown
scheduler.shutdown();

scheduleAtFixedRate vs scheduleWithFixedDelay

scheduleAtFixedRate (period = 10s, task takes 3s):
  T=0:  task starts, ends T=3
  T=10: task starts, ends T=13
  T=20: task starts, ends T=23  ← fires at 0, 10, 20, 30...

scheduleAtFixedRate (period = 10s, task takes 15s — OVERRUN):
  T=0:  task starts, ends T=15
  T=15: task starts immediately (overrun, no delay between runs)
  T=30: task starts immediately (no pile-up, runs serially)

scheduleWithFixedDelay (delay = 10s, task takes 15s):
  T=0:  task starts, ends T=15
  T=25: next starts (15 + 10 delay), ends T=40
  T=50: next starts (40 + 10 delay)  ← start times drift with task duration
Part 14

Production: Sizing Thread Pools

Sizing is the most important and most overlooked production concern. Wrong sizing causes either thread starvation or resource exhaustion.

CPU-bound tasks

Optimal pool size ≈ number of CPU cores

int cores = Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors();
int poolSize = cores;  // or cores + 1 to keep CPU busy during occasional I/O

Adding more threads than cores for CPU-bound work causes context-switching overhead without throughput gain.

I/O-bound tasks

Optimal pool size ≈ cores × (1 + wait_time / compute_time)

If a task spends 90% of its time waiting on I/O:
  wait_time / compute_time = 9
  poolSize = cores × (1 + 9) = 10 × cores

For 8-core machine: pool of ~80 threads for I/O-intensive work

Little's Law formulation

N = λ × W
  N = number of concurrent threads needed
  λ = arrival rate (requests per second)
  W = average time to complete one request (seconds)

If λ = 200 rps and W = 0.5 s:
  N = 200 × 0.5 = 100 threads

Monitoring a running pool

ThreadPoolExecutor tpe = (ThreadPoolExecutor) pool;

// At runtime — log or expose as metrics
int  active    = tpe.getActiveCount();
long completed = tpe.getCompletedTaskCount();
long queued    = tpe.getQueue().size();
int  poolSize  = tpe.getPoolSize();
int  largest   = tpe.getLargestPoolSize();

// Expose via Micrometer
Metrics.gauge("pool.active",    tpe, ThreadPoolExecutor::getActiveCount);
Metrics.gauge("pool.queued",    tpe, t -> t.getQueue().size());
Metrics.gauge("pool.completed", tpe, ThreadPoolExecutor::getCompletedTaskCount);
Part 15

Never Use `newCachedThreadPool` in Production

This is worth its own section because the mistake is pervasive.

// DANGER
ExecutorService pool = Executors.newCachedThreadPool();

newCachedThreadPool() is equivalent to:

new ThreadPoolExecutor(
    0,                    // corePoolSize — no permanent threads
    Integer.MAX_VALUE,    // maximumPoolSize — effectively unlimited!
    60L, TimeUnit.SECONDS,
    new SynchronousQueue<>()   // zero-capacity queue — every task needs a thread
);

What goes wrong

Under load, every task that cannot find an idle thread creates a new thread immediately. If your service receives 10,000 concurrent requests and each blocks on a database call for 2 seconds, the executor spins up 10,000 threads:

10,000 threads × ~512 KB stack = 5 GB stack space → OutOfMemoryError

The correct alternative

// Production-safe configuration
int cores = Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors();
ExecutorService pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
    cores * 2,            // corePoolSize — keeps these threads alive
    cores * 4,            // maximumPoolSize — bounded burst
    60, TimeUnit.SECONDS,
    new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(2000),       // BOUNDED queue — prevents OOM
    new NamedThreadFactory("api", false),
    new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy()  // back-pressure on caller
);

Rule: always use ThreadPoolExecutor directly in production. Never use newCachedThreadPool() or newFixedThreadPool() (unbounded queue) for anything handling external load.

Part 16

Spring `@Async` with ThreadPoolTaskExecutor

Spring's @Async annotation delegates method execution to a thread pool. The default executor (a SimpleAsyncTaskExecutor) creates a new thread per call — essentially newCachedThreadPool behavior.

Always define a custom ThreadPoolTaskExecutor.

@Configuration
@EnableAsync
public class AsyncConfig implements AsyncConfigurer {

    @Override
    public Executor getAsyncExecutor() {
        ThreadPoolTaskExecutor executor = new ThreadPoolTaskExecutor();
        executor.setCorePoolSize(8);
        executor.setMaxPoolSize(32);
        executor.setQueueCapacity(500);
        executor.setThreadNamePrefix("async-");
        executor.setRejectedExecutionHandler(
            new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy());
        executor.setWaitForTasksToCompleteOnShutdown(true);
        executor.setAwaitTerminationSeconds(30);
        executor.initialize();
        return executor;
    }

    @Override
    public AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler getAsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler() {
        return (ex, method, params) ->
            log.error("Async error in {}: {}", method.getName(), ex.getMessage(), ex);
    }
}

@Service
public class NotificationService {

    @Async  // runs on the configured executor
    public CompletableFuture<Void> sendEmailAsync(String to, String body) {
        emailClient.send(to, body);  // blocking I/O, off the request thread
        return CompletableFuture.completedFuture(null);
    }

    // Named executor — for a second pool dedicated to SMS
    @Async("smsExecutor")
    public void sendSmsAsync(String phone, String message) {
        smsClient.send(phone, message);
    }
}

Multiple named executors

@Bean("smsExecutor")
public Executor smsExecutor() {
    ThreadPoolTaskExecutor executor = new ThreadPoolTaskExecutor();
    executor.setCorePoolSize(4);
    executor.setMaxPoolSize(8);
    executor.setQueueCapacity(100);
    executor.setThreadNamePrefix("sms-");
    executor.initialize();
    return executor;
}
Part 17

ExecutorService with CompletableFuture

submit() returns a Future which has no composition API. CompletableFuture.supplyAsync() returns a CompletableFuture that can be chained:

ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8);

CompletableFuture<String> result = CompletableFuture
    .supplyAsync(() -> fetchUser(userId), pool)          // runs on pool
    .thenApplyAsync(user -> enrichWithProfile(user), pool) // also on pool
    .thenCombineAsync(
        CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> fetchPermissions(userId), pool),
        (user, perms) -> buildResponse(user, perms), pool)
    .exceptionally(ex -> {
        log.error("Pipeline failed", ex);
        return fallbackResponse();
    });

// Non-blocking — attach callback
result.thenAccept(response -> sendToClient(response));

By explicitly passing pool to each supplyAsync/thenApplyAsync, you avoid the global ForkJoinPool.commonPool() — important for I/O-bound work that shouldn't starve the common pool.

Part 18

Common Pitfalls

Pitfall 1 — Not shutting down the executor

// WRONG: executor is created but never shut down
ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4);
pool.submit(() -> doWork());
// method returns — pool threads keep JVM alive FOREVER

Always shutdown() in a finally or via try-with-resources (Java 19+):

// Java 19+ AutoCloseable
try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4)) {
    pool.submit(() -> doWork());
}  // pool.close() = shutdown() + awaitTermination(Long.MAX_VALUE)

Pitfall 2 — Calling future.get() from a pool thread

// DEADLOCK: all 4 pool threads are blocked in get(), waiting for tasks
// that are queued but can never run (all threads are blocked)
ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4);
for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) {
    pool.submit(() -> {
        Future<?> nested = pool.submit(() -> doInner());
        nested.get();  // DEADLOCK if pool is full
    });
}

Never call future.get() synchronously inside a pool thread on a task submitted to the same (or smaller) pool. Use CompletableFuture or a separate pool.

Pitfall 3 — Ignoring ExecutionException cause

try {
    result = future.get();
} catch (ExecutionException e) {
    throw e;  // WRONG: wraps the root cause — callers see ExecutionException, not NPE/SQLException
}

// CORRECT: unwrap
} catch (ExecutionException e) {
    Throwable cause = e.getCause();
    if (cause instanceof RuntimeException re) throw re;
    throw new RuntimeException("Task failed", cause);
}

Pitfall 4 — Mutable shared state in Callable

List<String> shared = new ArrayList<>();  // NOT thread-safe

List<Callable<Void>> tasks = new ArrayList<>();
for (String item : items) {
    tasks.add(() -> {
        shared.add(process(item));  // RACE CONDITION
        return null;
    });
}
pool.invokeAll(tasks);

Use ConcurrentLinkedQueue or collect via CompletableFuture chains instead.

Pitfall 5 — ThreadLocal leakage in pools

Pooled threads persist across tasks. ThreadLocal values set by one task are visible to the next task on the same thread:

// WRONG: ThreadLocal not cleaned up
static ThreadLocal<UserContext> context = new ThreadLocal<>();

pool.submit(() -> {
    context.set(new UserContext("alice"));
    doWork();
    // context.remove() MISSING — next task on this thread sees "alice"
});

Always call threadLocal.remove() in a finally block inside pooled tasks.

Part 19

Rejection Policy Decision Matrix

┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│            CHOOSING A REJECTION POLICY                         │
│                                                                │
│  Can you drop tasks?                                           │
│     YES → Is ordering important?                               │
│               YES → DiscardOldestPolicy (remove stale task)    │
│               NO  → DiscardPolicy (drop quietly)               │
│     NO  → Can the caller safely execute it?                    │
│               YES → CallerRunsPolicy (back-pressure)           │
│               NO  → AbortPolicy + catch + retry/alert          │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

CallerRunsPolicy is the most production-safe default because it:
- Slows the producer naturally (the caller blocks while running the task).
- Prevents OOM from unbounded queue growth.
- Keeps all cores busy.
- Never loses work silently.

Part 20

Interview Preparation

Q1: Describe the complete flow of task execution in ThreadPoolExecutor.

New task arrives → if activeThreads < corePoolSize, create a new core thread (even if idle threads exist). Otherwise, try workQueue.offer(task). If the queue is full and activeThreads < maxPoolSize, create a non-core thread. If still unable, invoke the RejectedExecutionHandler.

Q2: What are the four built-in rejection policies and when would you use each?

  • AbortPolicy (default): throw RejectedExecutionException. Use when failures must be explicit and callers handle them.
  • CallerRunsPolicy: run the task on the submitting thread. Best for preventing work loss with natural back-pressure.
  • DiscardPolicy: drop quietly. Use only for fire-and-forget telemetry where losing events is acceptable.
  • DiscardOldestPolicy: drop the oldest queued task and retry submission. Use when freshness matters more than completeness.

Q3: Why is Executors.newCachedThreadPool() dangerous in production?

It combines maximumPoolSize = Integer.MAX_VALUE with SynchronousQueue (zero capacity), so every task that arrives when no idle thread is available creates a new thread immediately. Under sudden load spikes, this can spawn thousands of threads, exhausting JVM heap with stack space and triggering OutOfMemoryError.

Q4: What happens when you call invokeAll vs invokeAny?

invokeAll blocks until all submitted tasks complete (or the timeout expires), returning a List<Future<T>> where each is already done. invokeAny blocks until any one task completes successfully, returning that result and cancelling all remaining tasks.

Q5: How do you properly tune a ThreadPoolExecutor for an I/O-bound workload?

Apply the formula: poolSize = cores × (1 + waitTime/computeTime). For a service making database calls averaging 100 ms with 10 ms compute time on an 8-core machine: 8 × (1 + 10) = 88 threads. Set a bounded ArrayBlockingQueue (e.g., capacity = poolSize × 10), use CallerRunsPolicy, and monitor queue.size() and activeCount with Micrometer to validate at runtime.

Q6: What is the difference between shutdown() and shutdownNow()?

shutdown() is graceful — it stops accepting new tasks but lets queued and running tasks complete. shutdownNow() is forceful — it returns queued tasks as a List<Runnable> and sends Thread.interrupt() to running threads. Tasks that don't respond to interruption keep running until they finish naturally.

Part 21

Quick Reference Cheat Sheet

CHOOSING THE RIGHT FACTORY METHOD
──────────────────────────────────
  Controlled parallelism, CPU-bound?   → newFixedThreadPool(n) — but set bounded queue manually
  Single-threaded, ordered?            → newSingleThreadExecutor()
  Scheduled/periodic?                  → newScheduledThreadPool(n)
  Production, I/O-bound?               → ThreadPoolExecutor directly (see Part 15)
  Virtual threads (Java 21+)?          → newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()
  NEVER in production:                 → newCachedThreadPool()

SUBMISSION METHODS
──────────────────
  Fire-and-forget:      execute(Runnable)
  With result:          submit(Callable<V>) → Future<V>
  All complete:         invokeAll(tasks)     → List<Future<V>>
  First complete:       invokeAny(tasks)     → V

SHUTDOWN PATTERN
────────────────
  pool.shutdown();
  if (!pool.awaitTermination(30, SECONDS)) {
      pool.shutdownNow();
      pool.awaitTermination(10, SECONDS);
  }

POOL SIZING FORMULA
───────────────────
  CPU-bound:  threads = availableProcessors + 1
  I/O-bound:  threads = availableProcessors × (1 + wait/compute)
  Mixed:      profile first, then tune

Practice — Lesson 49

Easy

E1. Create a ThreadPoolExecutor with corePoolSize=2, maxPoolSize=4, ArrayBlockingQueue(10), CallerRunsPolicy. Submit 20 tasks (each sleeps 100 ms). Log the active thread count and queue size every 500 ms.

E2. Write a TaskSubmitter that submits 5 Callable<Integer> tasks to a fixed-size pool, collects all Future<Integer> objects, and prints each result as it becomes available. Use Future.get(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS) for each.

E3. Implement a GracefulShutdown utility that wraps any ExecutorService and provides a shutdownAndAwait(long timeoutSeconds) method following the two-phase pattern from Part 11.

Medium

M1. Implement a BoundedExecutorService that wraps a ThreadPoolExecutor and adds a Semaphore to limit the number of tasks currently in-flight (queued + running) without relying on queue capacity alone:

public class BoundedExecutorService {
    private final ExecutorService pool;
    private final Semaphore semaphore;
    // implement submit(Callable<T>) that acquires semaphore, releases on completion
}

M2. Build a ParallelFetcher that fetches URLs in parallel using invokeAll with a 5-second total timeout. For each completed future, print the URL and content length. For cancelled/failed futures, print the error.

M3. Implement a PeriodicHealthChecker using ScheduledExecutorService that pings 3 services every 10 seconds. If any check fails 3 consecutive times, log a critical alert. Support stop() that shuts down the scheduler gracefully.

Advanced

A1. Implement a PriorityExecutor that wraps ThreadPoolExecutor with PriorityBlockingQueue. Define a PriorityTask<T> that implements Comparable<PriorityTask> and Callable<T>. Demonstrate that HIGH priority tasks run before LOW priority tasks even when the pool is busy.

A2. Implement a RetryingExecutorService decorator that wraps any ExecutorService. On task failure (caught ExecutionException), automatically re-submits the task up to N times with exponential backoff. Return a CompletableFuture<T> that completes when the task succeeds or exhausts retries.

A3. Build a thread pool benchmark comparing:
- Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8)
- ThreadPoolExecutor with ArrayBlockingQueue(1000) and CallerRunsPolicy
- Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() (Java 21)

Submit 100,000 I/O-simulated tasks (each sleeps 10 ms). Measure throughput and latency percentiles.

Production

P1. Design a production ThreadPoolTaskExecutor configuration for a Spring Boot REST service that:
- Has separate pools for HTTP handlers, database tasks, and email/async notifications.
- Each pool is properly named, bounded, and monitored via Micrometer gauges.
- Implements CallerRunsPolicy for all three pools.
- Exposes pool metrics via /actuator/metrics.

P2. Implement a WorkerPoolManager that:
- Creates a ThreadPoolExecutor with JMX monitoring enabled.
- Supports dynamic reconfiguration (setCorePoolSize, setMaximumPoolSize) at runtime via a REST endpoint.
- Alerts via a custom RejectedExecutionHandler when rejection rate exceeds 1% of submitted tasks.

Debugging

D1. The following code hangs indefinitely. Find the bug and fix it:

ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2);

Future<Integer> f1 = pool.submit(() -> {
    Future<Integer> inner = pool.submit(() -> 42);
    return inner.get();   // bug here
});

System.out.println(f1.get());

Hint: think about available threads.

D2. A scheduled task stops running after the first exception. Find why and fix it:

ScheduledExecutorService scheduler = Executors.newScheduledThreadPool(1);
scheduler.scheduleAtFixedRate(() -> {
    if (Math.random() < 0.3) throw new RuntimeException("transient error");
    doWork();
}, 0, 5, TimeUnit.SECONDS);

Hint: what does ScheduledExecutorService do when a periodic task throws?

Interview

I1. "Walk me through exactly what happens — step by step — when you call executor.submit(task) on a ThreadPoolExecutor with corePoolSize=4, maxPoolSize=8, and ArrayBlockingQueue(100)."

I2. "You are running a Spring Boot service under load and seeing RejectedExecutionException. What are the five knobs you can turn to fix this, in order of preference?"

Expected answer: increase corePoolSize → increase maxPoolSize → increase queue capacity → use CallerRunsPolicy → scale out horizontally.

I3. "Why is it a bad idea to call future.get() inside a pool thread on a task submitted to the same pool? What pattern would you use instead?"

I4. "You have a service that processes 500 requests/sec, each taking 200 ms of I/O wait and 10 ms of CPU on a 4-core server. How many threads do you configure in the pool?"

Answer: cores × (1 + 200/10) = 4 × 21 = 84 threads. Queue capacity = 84 × 10 = 840.
