Part 1

Concept

The Fork/Join framework is a specialised thread-pool architecture introduced in Java 7 that excels at divide-and-conquer, CPU-bound tasks. Its central insight is work stealing: idle threads do not wait — they steal tasks from the tail of busy threads' queues, keeping all cores saturated with useful work.

The framework lives in java.util.concurrent and is anchored by three classes:

Class Role
ForkJoinPool The pool itself; owns worker threads and their deques
RecursiveTask<V> A fork/join task that returns a value
RecursiveAction A fork/join task that returns void

The divide-and-conquer mental model

                    compute(1..8)
                   /             \
          compute(1..4)       compute(5..8)
          /        \           /        \
    compute(1..2) compute(3..4) compute(5..6) compute(7..8)
       /    \       /    \       /    \       /    \
     (1)   (2)   (3)   (4)   (5)   (6)   (7)   (8)

You recursively fork the problem in half until it is small enough to solve directly (the base case), then join the results back up the call tree.

Part 2

RecursiveTask

RecursiveTask<V> is the building block for computations that produce a result. You extend it and implement compute().

import java.util.concurrent.RecursiveTask;

public class SumTask extends RecursiveTask<Long> {
    private static final int THRESHOLD = 1_000;
    private final long[] data;
    private final int lo, hi;

    public SumTask(long[] data, int lo, int hi) {
        this.data = data;
        this.lo   = lo;
        this.hi   = hi;
    }

    @Override
    protected Long compute() {
        if (hi - lo <= THRESHOLD) {
            // Base case: sum the slice directly
            long sum = 0;
            for (int i = lo; i < hi; i++) sum += data[i];
            return sum;
        }
        int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;

        SumTask left  = new SumTask(data, lo, mid);
        SumTask right = new SumTask(data, mid, hi);

        left.fork();                    // schedule left asynchronously
        long rightResult = right.compute();  // compute right in this thread
        long leftResult  = left.join();      // wait for left

        return leftResult + rightResult;
    }
}

Usage:

long[] numbers = LongStream.rangeClosed(1, 10_000_000).toArray();
ForkJoinPool pool = new ForkJoinPool();
long total = pool.invoke(new SumTask(numbers, 0, numbers.length));
System.out.println("Sum: " + total); // 50000005000000

The fork-right, compute-left idiom

The pattern left.fork(); right.compute(); left.join() is deliberate:
- left.fork() pushes the left subtask onto this thread's deque.
- right.compute() runs on the current thread immediately — no scheduling overhead.
- left.join() retrieves the left result; if already done, it returns instantly; if not, the current thread may help by stealing work while waiting.

Part 3

RecursiveAction

RecursiveAction suits tasks with side effects and no return value — e.g. sorting, filling arrays, parallel I/O.

import java.util.concurrent.RecursiveAction;
import java.util.Arrays;

public class ParallelSortAction extends RecursiveAction {
    private static final int THRESHOLD = 4_096;
    private final int[] array;
    private final int lo, hi;

    public ParallelSortAction(int[] array, int lo, int hi) {
        this.array = array;
        this.lo = lo;
        this.hi = hi;
    }

    @Override
    protected void compute() {
        if (hi - lo <= THRESHOLD) {
            Arrays.sort(array, lo, hi);
            return;
        }
        int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
        ParallelSortAction left  = new ParallelSortAction(array, lo, mid);
        ParallelSortAction right = new ParallelSortAction(array, mid, hi);

        invokeAll(left, right);   // fork both, join both — convenience method
        // merge the two sorted halves
        merge(array, lo, mid, hi);
    }

    private void merge(int[] a, int lo, int mid, int hi) {
        int[] temp = Arrays.copyOfRange(a, lo, mid);
        int i = 0, j = mid, k = lo;
        while (i < temp.length && j < hi)
            a[k++] = (temp[i] <= a[j]) ? temp[i++] : a[j++];
        while (i < temp.length) a[k++] = temp[i++];
    }
}
Part 4

Work-Stealing Deque Architecture

Each worker thread in a ForkJoinPool owns a double-ended queue (deque). The work-stealing protocol is what distinguishes ForkJoinPool from a conventional ThreadPoolExecutor.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        ForkJoinPool                             │
│                                                                 │
│  Worker-0 deque          Worker-1 deque       Worker-2 deque   │
│  ┌──────────────┐        ┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────────┐ │
│  │ T8 T7 T6 T5  │        │   (empty)    │     │   T12 T11    │ │
│  └──────────────┘        └──────────────┘     └──────────────┘ │
│   ↑ PUSH/POP                 steal ←                steal ←    │
│   (owner operates            (Worker-1 steals T5)  (Worker-2   │
│    at the TOP)               from the BOTTOM)      steals T11) │
│                                                                 │
│  ┄ Owner pushes/pops from TOP (LIFO — hot cache locality)      │
│  ┄ Thieves steal from BOTTOM (FIFO — avoids contention at top) │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why LIFO for owner, FIFO for thieves?

  • LIFO for the owner means the most recently pushed (largest, newest) subtask is computed first — maximising cache reuse of the working set.
  • FIFO for thieves means they steal the oldest (largest, most coarse-grained) subtasks, which produces the most work per steal and minimises future steal events.
Part 5

ForkJoinPool Construction

// 1. Default: parallelism = Runtime.availableProcessors() - 1
ForkJoinPool pool = new ForkJoinPool();

// 2. Explicit parallelism level
ForkJoinPool pool = new ForkJoinPool(4);

// 3. Full constructor (Java 8+): custom thread factory, exception handler,
//    asyncMode flag (FIFO instead of LIFO for event-style tasks)
ForkJoinPool pool = new ForkJoinPool(
    Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors(),
    ForkJoinPool.defaultForkJoinWorkerThreadFactory,
    null,   // UncaughtExceptionHandler
    false   // asyncMode — false = LIFO (default for recursive tasks)
);

// 4. The common pool — shared JVM-wide instance
ForkJoinPool common = ForkJoinPool.commonPool();
int parallelism = ForkJoinPool.commonPool().getParallelism();

Parallelism ≠ thread count. A ForkJoinPool with parallelism P targets P active threads, but may create up to P + SPARE_CAPACITY threads to compensate for blocking.

Part 6

The Common Pool

ForkJoinPool.commonPool() is a single JVM-wide pool lazily initialised on first use. Its parallelism defaults to availableProcessors() - 1 (minimum 1) and can be overridden with the system property:

-Djava.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool.common.parallelism=8

Critical fact: parallelStream() and CompletableFuture (when no custom executor is provided) both use the common pool.

// Both of these submit to ForkJoinPool.commonPool()
list.parallelStream().map(this::heavyWork).collect(toList());
CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> heavyWork(x));

Production risk: if one component monopolises the common pool with blocking tasks, all other components that rely on it suffer latency spikes. Use a dedicated ForkJoinPool for long-running or I/O-bound work.

// Submitting parallelStream to a custom pool
ForkJoinPool customPool = new ForkJoinPool(8);
List<Result> results = customPool.submit(
    () -> list.parallelStream().map(this::heavyWork).collect(toList())
).get();
Part 7

invoke, submit, and execute

Method Blocks? Return Use when
pool.invoke(task) Yes Task result Synchronous call-and-wait
pool.submit(task) No ForkJoinTask<V> (Future) Async; retrieve result later
pool.execute(task) No void Fire-and-forget action
task.fork() No ForkJoinTask<V> Schedule from inside compute()
task.join() Yes Task result Retrieve result from inside compute()
ForkJoinTask.invokeAll(t1,t2) Yes void Fork both, join both 
ForkJoinPool pool = new ForkJoinPool(4);

// Synchronous
long sum = pool.invoke(new SumTask(data, 0, data.length));

// Asynchronous
ForkJoinTask<Long> future = pool.submit(new SumTask(data, 0, data.length));
// ... do other work ...
long sum = future.get(); // blocks until done
Part 8

Threshold Tuning

Choosing the right sequential threshold is the most important tuning decision. Too small a threshold creates enormous task-graph overhead; too large a threshold leaves cores underutilised.

┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              Threshold vs. Performance                     │
│                                                            │
│  Throughput                                                │
│     ▲                                                      │
│     │         ╭─────────────╮                             │
│     │       ╭─╯             ╰─╮                           │
│     │      ╱                   ╲                          │
│     │    ╱                       ╲                        │
│     │  ╱  too many tasks           too few tasks          │
│     │ ╱   (scheduling overhead)    (serial bottleneck)    │
│     └─────────────────────────────────► Threshold size    │
│                     ↑                                      │
│               sweet spot                                   │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Rules of thumb:
- For pure arithmetic: 1,000–10,000 elements per task.
- For heap-allocating work: 100–1,000 elements (GC pressure matters).
- Benchmark with JMH — the sweet spot is workload-specific.

Part 9

Managed Blocking

ForkJoinPool is designed for non-blocking CPU-bound tasks. When you must perform blocking I/O inside a fork/join task, wrap it with ManagedBlocker to signal the pool to compensate with a spare thread:

import java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool;
import java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool.ManagedBlocker;

public class BlockingDbTask extends RecursiveTask<String> {
    private final String query;

    public BlockingDbTask(String query) { this.query = query; }

    @Override
    protected String compute() {
        final String[] result = new String[1];

        try {
            ForkJoinPool.managedBlock(new ManagedBlocker() {
                volatile boolean done = false;

                @Override
                public boolean block() {
                    result[0] = expensiveDbCall(query); // blocks here
                    done = true;
                    return true;
                }

                @Override
                public boolean isReleasable() { return done; }
            });
        } catch (InterruptedException e) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        }
        return result[0];
    }

    private String expensiveDbCall(String q) {
        // simulate blocking DB call
        try { Thread.sleep(100); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
        return "result:" + q;
    }
}

Without ManagedBlocker, a blocking task parks its worker thread and the pool's parallelism drops by one, potentially starving other tasks.

Part 10

parallelStream() Under the Hood

Every parallelStream() operation is ultimately submitted to ForkJoinPool.commonPool() via a Spliterator-based divide-and-conquer pipeline.

// Conceptually equivalent fork/join task behind:
// list.parallelStream().map(fn).collect(toList())

class StreamTask<T, R> extends RecursiveTask<List<R>> {
    private final List<T> source;
    private final Function<T, R> fn;
    private final int lo, hi;

    @Override
    protected List<R> compute() {
        if (hi - lo <= THRESHOLD) {
            return source.subList(lo, hi).stream().map(fn).collect(toList());
        }
        int mid = (lo + hi) / 2;
        StreamTask<T,R> left  = new StreamTask<>(source, fn, lo, mid);
        StreamTask<T,R> right = new StreamTask<>(source, fn, mid, hi);
        left.fork();
        List<R> rightResult = right.compute();
        List<R> leftResult  = left.join();
        leftResult.addAll(rightResult);
        return leftResult;
    }
}

Key implication: The Spliterator of the source data structure controls how well the data can be split. ArrayList splits perfectly (index-based); LinkedList splits poorly (must traverse).

Part 11

ForkJoinPool vs ThreadPoolExecutor

This is the most important comparison for both production architecture and interviews.

Dimension ForkJoinPool ThreadPoolExecutor
Task model Recursive divide-and-conquer Independent Runnable/Callable tasks
Queue type Per-thread deque with work stealing Single shared queue (or array of queues)
Idle behaviour Steal from other threads Block on queue
Best for CPU-bound, tree-shaped problems I/O-bound, flat task graphs
Blocking tasks Use ManagedBlocker or avoid First-class; blocking is fine
Parallelism Targets P active threads Fixed core/max pool sizes
Task submission fork() from inside tasks execute() / submit() externally
Overhead Higher per-task (deque ops) Lower per-task
Used by parallelStream, CompletableFuture Spring @Async, Tomcat connectors

Decision rule:
- Tree-shaped, recursive, CPU-only → ForkJoinPool
- Flat independent tasks, I/O, external HTTP → ThreadPoolExecutor

Part 12

Monitoring and Diagnostics

ForkJoinPool pool = new ForkJoinPool(4);
// ... submit tasks ...

System.out.println("Parallelism:   " + pool.getParallelism());
System.out.println("Pool size:     " + pool.getPoolSize());
System.out.println("Active threads:" + pool.getActiveThreadCount());
System.out.println("Running threads:" + pool.getRunningThreadCount());
System.out.println("Queued tasks:  " + pool.getQueuedTaskCount());
System.out.println("Steal count:   " + pool.getStealCount());
System.out.println("Queue submissions:" + pool.getQueuedSubmissionCount());

getStealCount() is the single best indicator of work-stealing effectiveness. A high, growing steal count means the pool is staying busy by redistribution. A steal count of zero means one thread is doing all the work — check your threshold.

Part 13

Exception Handling

Exceptions thrown inside compute() are wrapped and re-thrown when join() or get() is called.

public class FailingTask extends RecursiveTask<Integer> {
    @Override
    protected Integer compute() {
        throw new RuntimeException("Something went wrong");
    }
}

ForkJoinPool pool = new ForkJoinPool();
ForkJoinTask<Integer> task = pool.submit(new FailingTask());

try {
    task.get();
} catch (ExecutionException e) {
    Throwable cause = e.getCause(); // the original RuntimeException
    System.err.println("Task failed: " + cause.getMessage());
} catch (InterruptedException e) {
    Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
}

// Or with join() — throws unchecked:
try {
    task.join();
} catch (RuntimeException e) {
    // cause is wrapped in RuntimeException
}

Partial failures in subtasks propagate upward: if any subtask throws, the parent's join() re-throws, unwinding the whole tree.

Part 14

CountedCompleter

CountedCompleter is an advanced ForkJoinTask subclass for pipeline-style tasks where a parent knows it has N children and should trigger completion logic when the last child finishes. It is the foundation for Java's parallel streams pipeline.

import java.util.concurrent.CountedCompleter;

public class MapReduceTask extends CountedCompleter<Void> {
    private final int[] data;
    private final int lo, hi;
    private final int[] results;

    public MapReduceTask(CountedCompleter<?> parent,
                         int[] data, int[] results, int lo, int hi) {
        super(parent);
        this.data = data; this.results = results;
        this.lo = lo; this.hi = hi;
    }

    @Override
    public void compute() {
        if (hi - lo <= 1_000) {
            for (int i = lo; i < hi; i++) results[i] = data[i] * 2;
            tryComplete(); // decrement parent's pending count
            return;
        }
        int mid = (lo + hi) / 2;
        setPendingCount(2);
        new MapReduceTask(this, data, results, mid, hi).fork();
        new MapReduceTask(this, data, results, lo, mid).compute();
    }

    @Override
    public void onCompletion(CountedCompleter<?> caller) {
        // called when all children complete — merge or finalize here
    }
}
Part 15

Production Pattern: Parallel File Tree Scan

A real-world use case: counting all .java files under a directory tree, splitting by subdirectory.

import java.io.File;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.RecursiveTask;

public class FileCountTask extends RecursiveTask<Integer> {
    private final File directory;

    public FileCountTask(File directory) {
        this.directory = directory;
    }

    @Override
    protected Integer compute() {
        File[] entries = directory.listFiles();
        if (entries == null) return 0;

        List<FileCountTask> subDirTasks = new ArrayList<>();
        int directCount = 0;

        for (File entry : entries) {
            if (entry.isDirectory()) {
                FileCountTask sub = new FileCountTask(entry);
                sub.fork();
                subDirTasks.add(sub);
            } else if (entry.getName().endsWith(".java")) {
                directCount++;
            }
        }

        int total = directCount;
        for (FileCountTask sub : subDirTasks) {
            total += sub.join();
        }
        return total;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ForkJoinPool pool = ForkJoinPool.commonPool();
        int count = pool.invoke(new FileCountTask(new File("/src")));
        System.out.println("Java files: " + count);
    }
}
Part 16

Production Pattern: Parallel Matrix Multiply

public class MatrixMultiplyTask extends RecursiveAction {
    private static final int THRESHOLD = 64;
    private final double[][] A, B, C;
    private final int row, col, size;

    public MatrixMultiplyTask(double[][] A, double[][] B, double[][] C,
                               int row, int col, int size) {
        this.A = A; this.B = B; this.C = C;
        this.row = row; this.col = col; this.size = size;
    }

    @Override
    protected void compute() {
        if (size <= THRESHOLD) {
            // Direct multiply for this block
            for (int i = row; i < row + size; i++)
                for (int j = col; j < col + size; j++)
                    for (int k = 0; k < A[0].length; k++)
                        C[i][j] += A[i][k] * B[k][j];
            return;
        }
        int half = size / 2;
        invokeAll(
            new MatrixMultiplyTask(A, B, C, row,        col,        half),
            new MatrixMultiplyTask(A, B, C, row,        col + half, half),
            new MatrixMultiplyTask(A, B, C, row + half, col,        half),
            new MatrixMultiplyTask(A, B, C, row + half, col + half, half)
        );
    }
}
Part 17

Shutdown and Lifecycle

ForkJoinPool pool = new ForkJoinPool(4);

// Initiate orderly shutdown — no new tasks accepted
pool.shutdown();

// Await termination
boolean done = pool.awaitTermination(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
if (!done) {
    // Force-cancel all running tasks
    pool.shutdownNow();
}

// Check state
System.out.println("Terminated: " + pool.isTerminated());
System.out.println("Shutdown:   " + pool.isShutdown());
System.out.println("Quiescent:  " + pool.isQuiescent()); // all tasks complete, no activity

Important: ForkJoinPool.commonPool() cannot be shut down — shutdown() and shutdownNow() are no-ops on it. The common pool lives for the entire JVM lifetime.

Part 18

Common Pitfalls

Pitfall 1 — Blocking without ManagedBlocker

// BAD: blocks a worker thread, starves the pool
protected Long compute() {
    Future<Long> f = httpClient.get(url);  // blocks
    return f.get();  // worker thread parked
}

// GOOD: compensate with ManagedBlocker
protected Long compute() {
    final Long[] result = {null};
    ForkJoinPool.managedBlock(new ManagedBlocker() {
        boolean done;
        public boolean block() { result[0] = httpClient.getSync(url); done = true; return true; }
        public boolean isReleasable() { return done; }
    });
    return result[0];
}

Pitfall 2 — Threshold too small

// BAD: creates millions of tasks for a 10M-element array
if (hi - lo <= 1) { ... }

// GOOD: granularity of ~1000-10000 elements
if (hi - lo <= 10_000) { ... }

Pitfall 3 — Calling join() before forking both subtasks

// BAD: sequential! left.join() blocks before right is ever forked
left.fork();
left.join();   // blocks here
right.fork();
right.join();

// GOOD: fork both, then join both
left.fork();
right.fork();
long r = right.join();
long l = left.join();

Pitfall 4 — Using the common pool for I/O

Tasks that block on network/disk in the common pool degrade parallelStream() performance globally. Always use a dedicated pool for I/O-bound fork/join work.

Part 19

Performance Considerations

┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│             ForkJoinPool Performance Profile                  │
│                                                               │
│  Scale-up (more cores)                                        │
│    ▲                                                          │
│    │  ●●●●●●●●●●●●●  ← ForkJoinPool (good scaling)           │
│    │  ●●●●●                                                   │
│    │  ●●●  ← ThreadPoolExecutor (contention on shared queue) │
│    │  ●●                                                      │
│    └──────────────────────────────► Cores                    │
│                                                               │
│  ForkJoinPool wins because:                                   │
│  1. No shared queue contention — each thread has its own     │
│  2. Work stealing keeps all cores busy                        │
│  3. Cache-affinity via LIFO owner-pop                         │
│                                                               │
│  ForkJoinPool loses when:                                     │
│  1. Task granularity is too fine (deque overhead > work)      │
│  2. Tasks block (threads park, parallelism drops)             │
│  3. Problem is inherently sequential (poor Amdahl fraction)   │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Amdahl's Law reminder: if 20% of your algorithm is serial, maximum speedup = 1 / 0.20 = 5×, regardless of core count.

Part 20

Interview Questions

Q1: What is work stealing and why does it improve throughput?

Work stealing ensures no thread idles while tasks remain queued. Each worker has its own deque; idle workers steal from the bottom of a random victim's deque. This minimises contention (owner operates at top, thief at bottom) and keeps all cores busy with the largest available units of work.

Q2: What is the difference between RecursiveTask and RecursiveAction?

RecursiveTask<V> returns a value from compute(); it extends ForkJoinTask<V>. RecursiveAction returns void; it extends ForkJoinTask<Void>. Use RecursiveTask for aggregation (sum, max, collect) and RecursiveAction for in-place mutations (sort, fill).

Q3: How does parallelStream() relate to ForkJoinPool?

parallelStream() submits spliterator-based recursive tasks to ForkJoinPool.commonPool(). The stream's data source provides a Spliterator that splits the input; each split becomes a subtask. The common pool's parallelism level (default: availableProcessors() - 1) determines the degree of parallelism.

Q4: How do you size the common pool?

Via JVM system property: -Djava.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool.common.parallelism=N. Set to availableProcessors() for I/O-tolerant workloads; keep the default (processors - 1) for pure CPU work to leave one core for OS/GC.

Q5: What happens if a RecursiveTask throws an exception?

The exception is stored internally. It is re-thrown (wrapped in a RuntimeException by join(), or in an ExecutionException by get()) when the caller retrieves the result. It propagates up the join chain, causing all ancestor tasks to fail as well.

Q6: When would you prefer ForkJoinPool over ThreadPoolExecutor?

When the workload is:
1. Recursive / tree-shaped (natural divide-and-conquer)
2. CPU-bound (no I/O blocking)
3. Data-parallel (same operation over large data set)
4. Variable granularity (tasks spawn child tasks dynamically)

Use ThreadPoolExecutor when tasks are independent, flat, I/O-bound, or when you need precise queue size, rejection policies, or thread lifecycle control.

Part 21

Complete Reference Example

import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.stream.LongStream;

/**
 * Demonstrates ForkJoinPool with:
 * - RecursiveTask for parallel sum
 * - Custom pool vs common pool
 * - Pool monitoring
 * - Exception propagation
 */
public class ForkJoinReference {

    // ---- RecursiveTask -----------------------------------------------
    static class ParallelSum extends RecursiveTask<Long> {
        private static final int THRESHOLD = 5_000;
        private final long[] data;
        private final int lo, hi;

        ParallelSum(long[] data, int lo, int hi) {
            this.data = data; this.lo = lo; this.hi = hi;
        }

        @Override
        protected Long compute() {
            if (hi - lo <= THRESHOLD) {
                long sum = 0;
                for (int i = lo; i < hi; i++) sum += data[i];
                return sum;
            }
            int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
            ParallelSum left  = new ParallelSum(data, lo, mid);
            ParallelSum right = new ParallelSum(data, mid, hi);
            left.fork();
            long r = right.compute();
            long l = left.join();
            return l + r;
        }
    }

    // ---- RecursiveAction (in-place array fill) -----------------------
    static class FillAction extends RecursiveAction {
        private static final int THRESHOLD = 10_000;
        private final int[] array;
        private final int lo, hi;
        private final int value;

        FillAction(int[] array, int lo, int hi, int value) {
            this.array = array; this.lo = lo; this.hi = hi; this.value = value;
        }

        @Override
        protected void compute() {
            if (hi - lo <= THRESHOLD) {
                java.util.Arrays.fill(array, lo, hi, value);
                return;
            }
            int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
            invokeAll(
                new FillAction(array, lo, mid, value),
                new FillAction(array, mid, hi, value)
            );
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        long[] numbers = LongStream.rangeClosed(1, 10_000_000).toArray();

        // --- Custom pool ---
        ForkJoinPool pool = new ForkJoinPool(
            Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors()
        );

        long sum = pool.invoke(new ParallelSum(numbers, 0, numbers.length));
        System.out.printf("Sum: %,d%n", sum); // 50,000,005,000,000

        // --- Monitor ---
        System.out.printf("Steals:  %d%n", pool.getStealCount());
        System.out.printf("Threads: %d%n", pool.getPoolSize());

        // --- Action ---
        int[] target = new int[1_000_000];
        pool.invoke(new FillAction(target, 0, target.length, 42));
        System.out.println("Filled[0]: " + target[0]); // 42

        // --- Common pool via parallelStream ---
        long streamSum = LongStream.rangeClosed(1, 10_000_000)
                                   .parallel()
                                   .sum();
        System.out.printf("Stream sum: %,d%n", streamSum);

        pool.shutdown();
        pool.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
    }
}

Practice — Lesson 50

Easy Exercises

Exercise 1 — Parallel Maximum

Implement a MaxTask extends RecursiveTask<Integer> that finds the maximum value in an int[]. Use a threshold of 10,000. Test with an array of 1,000,000 random integers.

<details>
<summary>Solution sketch</summary>

public class MaxTask extends RecursiveTask<Integer> {
    private static final int THRESHOLD = 10_000;
    private final int[] data;
    private final int lo, hi;

    public MaxTask(int[] data, int lo, int hi) {
        this.data = data; this.lo = lo; this.hi = hi;
    }

    @Override
    protected Integer compute() {
        if (hi - lo <= THRESHOLD) {
            int max = Integer.MIN_VALUE;
            for (int i = lo; i < hi; i++)
                if (data[i] > max) max = data[i];
            return max;
        }
        int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
        MaxTask left  = new MaxTask(data, lo, mid);
        MaxTask right = new MaxTask(data, mid, hi);
        left.fork();
        int r = right.compute();
        int l = left.join();
        return Math.max(l, r);
    }
}

</details>

Exercise 2 — Parallel Array Initialiser

Implement a FillRangeAction extends RecursiveAction that initialises a double[] so that array[i] = Math.sqrt(i) for all indices. Use a threshold of 5,000.

<details>
<summary>Solution sketch</summary>

public class FillRangeAction extends RecursiveAction {
    private static final int THRESHOLD = 5_000;
    private final double[] array;
    private final int lo, hi;

    public FillRangeAction(double[] array, int lo, int hi) {
        this.array = array; this.lo = lo; this.hi = hi;
    }

    @Override
    protected void compute() {
        if (hi - lo <= THRESHOLD) {
            for (int i = lo; i < hi; i++) array[i] = Math.sqrt(i);
            return;
        }
        int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
        invokeAll(
            new FillRangeAction(array, lo, mid),
            new FillRangeAction(array, mid, hi)
        );
    }
}

</details>

Exercise 3 — Pool Statistics Reporter

Create a PoolMonitor class that submits 20 SumTask instances to a ForkJoinPool(4) and, after all tasks complete, prints parallelism, poolSize, activeThreadCount, and stealCount.

<details>
<summary>Solution sketch</summary>

public class PoolMonitor {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        ForkJoinPool pool = new ForkJoinPool(4);
        long[] data = LongStream.rangeClosed(1, 1_000_000).toArray();
        List<ForkJoinTask<Long>> tasks = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++)
            tasks.add(pool.submit(new SumTask(data, 0, data.length)));
        for (ForkJoinTask<Long> t : tasks) t.get();

        System.out.println("Parallelism:    " + pool.getParallelism());
        System.out.println("Pool size:      " + pool.getPoolSize());
        System.out.println("Active threads: " + pool.getActiveThreadCount());
        System.out.println("Steal count:    " + pool.getStealCount());
        pool.shutdown();
    }
}

</details>

Exercise 4 — Custom Pool for parallelStream

Demonstrate the difference between submitting a parallelStream() computation to the common pool versus a custom ForkJoinPool(8). Print the thread names inside the stream's map to verify which pool's threads are used.

<details>
<summary>Solution sketch</summary>

ForkJoinPool custom = new ForkJoinPool(8);

// Common pool (thread names: ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-N)
List<String> common = IntStream.range(0, 20)
    .parallel()
    .mapToObj(i -> Thread.currentThread().getName())
    .collect(toList());

// Custom pool (thread names: ForkJoinPool-1-worker-N)
List<String> custom_ = custom.submit(() ->
    IntStream.range(0, 20)
        .parallel()
        .mapToObj(i -> Thread.currentThread().getName())
        .collect(toList())
).get();

System.out.println("Common pool threads: " + new HashSet<>(common));
System.out.println("Custom pool threads: " + new HashSet<>(custom_));

</details>

Part 1

Concept

CompletableFuture<T> (Java 8) is the premier mechanism for composable, non-blocking asynchronous programming in Java. It implements both Future<T> and CompletionStage<T>, combining the ability to hold a result with a rich pipeline of callback combinators.

The problem with Future<T>

Future<T>, introduced in Java 5, has three fundamental limitations:

  1. Blocking retrieval only — get() always blocks the calling thread.
  2. No composition — You cannot chain two Future results without blocking on the first.
  3. No manual completion — You cannot complete a Future programmatically from outside the computation.

CompletableFuture solves all three:

// Future — must block to get, cannot chain
Future<String> f = executor.submit(() -> fetchUser(id));
String user = f.get();             // BLOCKS
Future<String> f2 = executor.submit(() -> fetchOrders(user)); // sequential

// CompletableFuture — non-blocking chain
CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> fetchUser(id))
                 .thenCompose(user -> fetchOrdersAsync(user))
                 .thenAccept(orders -> render(orders));
// Returns immediately — callbacks run on background threads

The completion model

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              CompletableFuture State Machine                 │
│                                                              │
│     INCOMPLETE ──── normal result ──────► COMPLETED (value) │
│         │                                                    │
│         └───────── exceptional result ──► COMPLETED (ex)    │
│                                                              │
│  Once in a COMPLETED state it is immutable.                  │
│  All registered callbacks run exactly once.                  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Part 2

Creating CompletableFutures

import java.util.concurrent.*;

// 1. supplyAsync — produces a value; runs on ForkJoinPool.commonPool()
CompletableFuture<String> cf1 = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> fetchUser(42));

// 2. supplyAsync with custom executor
ExecutorService exec = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4);
CompletableFuture<String> cf2 = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> fetchUser(42), exec);

// 3. runAsync — no result (Runnable)
CompletableFuture<Void> cf3 = CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> sendEmail("x@y.com"));

// 4. Completed future — pre-completed with a known value
CompletableFuture<String> cf4 = CompletableFuture.completedFuture("cached-result");

// 5. Failed future — pre-completed exceptionally (Java 9+)
CompletableFuture<String> cf5 = CompletableFuture.failedFuture(new RuntimeException("error"));

// 6. Manual completion
CompletableFuture<String> promise = new CompletableFuture<>();
// Later, from any thread:
promise.complete("done");              // normal completion
promise.completeExceptionally(new RuntimeException("oops")); // exceptional
Part 3

Transformation: thenApply and thenApplyAsync

thenApply(Function<T,U>) transforms the result, analogous to Stream.map().

CompletableFuture<String> userId =
    CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> "42");

CompletableFuture<User> user =
    userId.thenApply(id -> userService.findById(id));

CompletableFuture<String> displayName =
    user.thenApply(u -> u.getFirstName() + " " + u.getLastName());

// Synchronous vs asynchronous variants:
// thenApply(fn)       — fn runs on the completing thread (or current thread if already done)
// thenApplyAsync(fn)  — fn runs on ForkJoinPool.commonPool()
// thenApplyAsync(fn, executor) — fn runs on the given executor

Thread continuation rule:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  thenApply(fn):                                             │
│    if CF already complete → fn runs on caller thread        │
│    if CF not yet complete → fn runs on completing thread    │
│                                                             │
│  thenApplyAsync(fn):                                        │
│    always submits fn to executor (commonPool by default)    │
│    predictable — recommended for CPU-intensive callbacks    │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Part 4

Side Effects: thenAccept and thenRun

CompletableFuture<Order> orderFuture = placeOrderAsync(cart);

// thenAccept: consume the value, return Void
CompletableFuture<Void> sentConfirmation =
    orderFuture.thenAccept(order -> emailService.sendConfirmation(order));

// thenRun: ignore the value, run an action
CompletableFuture<Void> metrics =
    orderFuture.thenRun(() -> metricsService.increment("orders.placed"));

// Async variants available: thenAcceptAsync, thenRunAsync
Method Input Output Use for
thenApply(fn) T U Transform result
thenAccept(fn) T Void Consume result (side effect)
thenRun(fn) — Void Run action after completion
Part 5

Chaining: thenCompose

thenCompose(Function<T, CompletableFuture<U>>) is flatMap for CompletableFuture. It chains two async operations, flattening the nested future.

// WITHOUT thenCompose — returns nested CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<Order>>
CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<Order>> bad =
    CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> getUser(id))
                     .thenApply(user -> placeOrderAsync(user.getCart()));

// WITH thenCompose — returns flat CompletableFuture<Order>
CompletableFuture<Order> good =
    CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> getUser(id))
                     .thenCompose(user -> placeOrderAsync(user.getCart()));

// Full async chain for microservice orchestration:
CompletableFuture<InvoiceDTO> invoice =
    inventoryService.checkStockAsync(productId)             // CF<StockStatus>
        .thenCompose(stock -> pricingService.getPriceAsync(stock))  // CF<Price>
        .thenCompose(price -> orderService.createOrderAsync(price)) // CF<Order>
        .thenCompose(order -> invoiceService.generateAsync(order));  // CF<InvoiceDTO>

thenApply vs thenCompose — the critical difference

thenApply:   T → U            (wraps result in new CF)
thenCompose: T → CF<U>        (flattens the result)

Use thenApply  when: the transformation is synchronous (no new CF created)
Use thenCompose when: the transformation itself returns a CompletableFuture
Part 6

Combining: thenCombine and thenAcceptBoth

thenCombine runs two independent futures in parallel and combines their results when both complete.

// Two independent async calls — run in parallel
CompletableFuture<UserProfile> profileFuture =
    CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> profileService.get(userId));

CompletableFuture<List<Order>> ordersFuture =
    CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> orderService.getOrders(userId));

// Combine: called with both results when both are done
CompletableFuture<DashboardDTO> dashboard =
    profileFuture.thenCombine(ordersFuture,
        (profile, orders) -> new DashboardDTO(profile, orders));

// thenAcceptBoth: combine and consume (no return value)
profileFuture.thenAcceptBoth(ordersFuture,
    (profile, orders) -> renderDashboard(profile, orders));
Part 7

CompletableFuture Chain Diagram

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     CompletableFuture Pipeline                               │
│                                                                              │
│                                                                              │
│  supplyAsync ──► thenApply ──► thenCompose ──► thenAccept                   │
│     (CF<A>)        (CF<B>)       (CF<C>)        (CF<Void>)                  │
│                                                                              │
│  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────              │
│                                                                              │
│  Parallel fan-out then fan-in:                                               │
│                                                                              │
│                 ┌─► supplyAsync(A) ─────────────┐                           │
│                 │                                ▼                           │
│  start ─────────┤                          thenCombine ──► thenApply        │
│                 │                                ▲                           │
│                 └─► supplyAsync(B) ─────────────┘                           │
│                                                                              │
│  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────              │
│                                                                              │
│  allOf fan-out:                                                              │
│                 ┌─► CF1                                                      │
│                 ├─► CF2   ──► allOf(CF1,CF2,CF3) ──► thenRun                │
│                 └─► CF3                                                      │
│                                                                              │
│  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────              │
│                                                                              │
│  Exception branch:                                                           │
│                                                                              │
│  CF ──► thenApply ──[throws]──► exceptionally ──► recovery value            │
│                │                                                             │
│                └─────────────► handle(v, ex) ──► always runs                │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Part 8

Exception Handling: exceptionally

exceptionally(Function<Throwable, T>) is the recovery mechanism — it is only invoked if the upstream stage completed exceptionally.

CompletableFuture<User> userFuture =
    CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> {
        if (Math.random() < 0.5) throw new RuntimeException("DB timeout");
        return userService.findById(42);
    })
    .exceptionally(ex -> {
        log.error("Failed to load user: {}", ex.getMessage());
        return User.anonymous();   // fallback value
    });

Key facts:
- If the upstream stage completes normally, exceptionally is skipped entirely.
- The function receives the actual exception (not wrapped in ExecutionException).
- The result type must match T — the same type as the upstream stage.

Part 9

Exception Handling: handle

handle(BiFunction<T, Throwable, U>) is always invoked — for both normal and exceptional completion. It combines thenApply and exceptionally into a single stage.

CompletableFuture<Response> response =
    CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> riskyApiCall())
        .handle((result, ex) -> {
            if (ex != null) {
                log.error("API call failed", ex);
                return Response.error(500, ex.getMessage());
            }
            return Response.ok(result);
        });
Part 10

Exception Handling: whenComplete

whenComplete(BiConsumer<T, Throwable>) is for observation — it runs for both outcomes but cannot change the result. The original result or exception passes through unchanged.

CompletableFuture<String> cf =
    CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> fetchData())
        .whenComplete((result, ex) -> {
            if (ex != null) metrics.incrementError("fetch.data");
            else metrics.incrementSuccess("fetch.data");
            // Cannot change the result here
        })
        .thenApply(String::toUpperCase); // receives original result
Method Invoked when Can change result Returns
exceptionally(fn) Exception only Yes (recovery) CF<T>
handle(fn) Always Yes CF<U>
whenComplete(fn) Always No CF<T> (pass-through)
Part 11

allOf: Wait for All

CompletableFuture.allOf(CF...) returns a CF<Void> that completes when all provided futures complete (normally or exceptionally).

CompletableFuture<String> cf1 = fetchFromServiceA();
CompletableFuture<String> cf2 = fetchFromServiceB();
CompletableFuture<String> cf3 = fetchFromServiceC();

CompletableFuture<Void> all = CompletableFuture.allOf(cf1, cf2, cf3);

// To collect results after all complete:
CompletableFuture<List<String>> allResults = all.thenApply(v ->
    Stream.of(cf1, cf2, cf3)
          .map(CompletableFuture::join)  // safe — all are done
          .collect(Collectors.toList())
);

allResults.thenAccept(results -> render(results));

Important: allOf completes with void; you must retrieve individual results from the original references. If any constituent future completes exceptionally, allOf itself completes exceptionally.

Part 12

anyOf: First to Complete

CompletableFuture.anyOf(CF...) returns a CF<Object> that completes as soon as any one of the provided futures completes.

// Query three replicas — use whichever responds first
CompletableFuture<String> replica1 = queryReplica("db-1");
CompletableFuture<String> replica2 = queryReplica("db-2");
CompletableFuture<String> replica3 = queryReplica("db-3");

CompletableFuture<Object> first = CompletableFuture.anyOf(replica1, replica2, replica3);

first.thenAccept(result -> renderPage((String) result));

Limitation: The return type is CF<Object> — you must cast the result. The other futures continue running; anyOf does not cancel them. For a cancel-on-first pattern, you need explicit cancellation:

first.whenComplete((r, ex) -> {
    if (ex == null) {
        replica1.cancel(true);
        replica2.cancel(true);
        replica3.cancel(true);
    }
});
Part 13

Custom Executor vs commonPool

By default, all *Async methods without an executor use ForkJoinPool.commonPool(). This is fine for CPU-bound tasks but problematic for I/O-bound work.

// BAD: Blocking HTTP calls on commonPool starve parallel streams
CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> httpClient.get(url)); // commonPool thread blocked

// GOOD: Dedicated executor for I/O
ExecutorService ioExecutor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(
    50,
    new ThreadFactoryBuilder().setNameFormat("cf-io-%d").build()
);

CompletableFuture<String> cf =
    CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> httpClient.get(url), ioExecutor);

Executor sizing guidelines

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│               Executor Sizing for CompletableFuture              │
│                                                                  │
│  CPU-bound tasks:                                                │
│    threads = availableProcessors()                               │
│    → Use commonPool (default) or ForkJoinPool                    │
│                                                                  │
│  I/O-bound tasks (HTTP, DB, files):                              │
│    threads ≈ availableProcessors × (1 + wait_time/cpu_time)     │
│    → For 95% I/O: cores × 20–50 threads                         │
│    → Consider virtual threads (Java 21): unlimited blocking      │
│                                                                  │
│  Mixed workloads:                                                │
│    → Separate executors per tier                                 │
│       ioExecutor: fixed/cached pool for I/O calls                │
│       cpuExecutor: ForkJoinPool for computation                  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Part 14

Timeout Patterns (Java 9+)

Java 9 added orTimeout and completeOnTimeout for deadline management.

// orTimeout: complete exceptionally with TimeoutException if not done in time
CompletableFuture<String> cf =
    CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> slowService.call())
        .orTimeout(500, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);

cf.exceptionally(ex -> {
    if (ex instanceof TimeoutException) return "timeout-fallback";
    throw new RuntimeException(ex);
});

// completeOnTimeout: complete normally with fallback value if not done in time
CompletableFuture<String> cf2 =
    CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> slowService.call())
        .completeOnTimeout("default-value", 500, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);

// Manual timeout (Java 8 compatible)
ScheduledExecutorService scheduler = Executors.newScheduledThreadPool(1);
CompletableFuture<String> manual = new CompletableFuture<>();
scheduler.schedule(
    () -> manual.completeExceptionally(new TimeoutException("deadline exceeded")),
    500, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS
);
CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> slowService.call())
    .whenComplete((r, ex) -> {
        if (ex == null) manual.complete(r);
        else manual.completeExceptionally(ex);
    });
Part 15

Production Pattern: Async Microservice Orchestration

A real-world service aggregation — enrich a user order response by calling three downstream services in parallel, with a timeout and fallback.

@Service
public class OrderDashboardService {

    private final UserServiceClient userClient;
    private final InventoryServiceClient inventoryClient;
    private final PricingServiceClient pricingClient;
    private final ExecutorService ioPool =
        Executors.newFixedThreadPool(20,
            r -> new Thread(r, "dashboard-io"));

    public CompletableFuture<DashboardDTO> buildDashboard(long orderId) {

        CompletableFuture<UserDTO> userFuture =
            CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(
                () -> userClient.getUser(orderId), ioPool)
            .orTimeout(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)
            .exceptionally(ex -> UserDTO.anonymous());

        CompletableFuture<List<StockItem>> stockFuture =
            CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(
                () -> inventoryClient.getStock(orderId), ioPool)
            .orTimeout(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)
            .exceptionally(ex -> Collections.emptyList());

        CompletableFuture<PriceDTO> priceFuture =
            CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(
                () -> pricingClient.getPrice(orderId), ioPool)
            .completeOnTimeout(PriceDTO.unknown(), 300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);

        return CompletableFuture.allOf(userFuture, stockFuture, priceFuture)
            .thenApply(v -> DashboardDTO.builder()
                .user(userFuture.join())
                .stock(stockFuture.join())
                .price(priceFuture.join())
                .build());
    }
}

This pattern:
1. Fires three HTTP calls in parallel on a dedicated I/O thread pool.
2. Each call has a 300 ms timeout with a graceful fallback.
3. allOf waits for all three, then assembles the result from already-completed futures.

Part 16

Spring @Async Returning CompletableFuture

Spring's @Async annotation can return CompletableFuture<T>, enabling the calling layer to compose async results without blocking.

// 1. Enable async in configuration
@Configuration
@EnableAsync
public class AsyncConfig implements AsyncConfigurer {

    @Bean(name = "asyncExecutor")
    public Executor asyncExecutor() {
        ThreadPoolTaskExecutor exec = new ThreadPoolTaskExecutor();
        exec.setCorePoolSize(5);
        exec.setMaxPoolSize(20);
        exec.setQueueCapacity(100);
        exec.setThreadNamePrefix("async-");
        exec.initialize();
        return exec;
    }
}

// 2. Service method
@Service
public class ReportService {

    @Async("asyncExecutor")
    public CompletableFuture<Report> generateReportAsync(Long reportId) {
        Report report = heavyReportGeneration(reportId); // runs in asyncExecutor
        return CompletableFuture.completedFuture(report);
    }
}

// 3. Controller — compose and return
@RestController
public class ReportController {

    @Autowired
    private ReportService reportService;

    @GetMapping("/reports/{id}")
    public CompletableFuture<ResponseEntity<Report>> getReport(@PathVariable Long id) {
        return reportService.generateReportAsync(id)
            .thenApply(report -> ResponseEntity.ok(report))
            .exceptionally(ex -> ResponseEntity.status(500).build());
    }
}

Spring MVC / WebFlux note: Returning CompletableFuture from a controller method enables Servlet 3.1 async dispatch — the HTTP thread is released immediately and the response is written when the future completes.

Part 17

Exception Propagation in Chains

Exception propagation in chains has nuances that trip up experienced developers.

CompletableFuture<String> chain =
    CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> {
        throw new RuntimeException("stage 1 failed");
    })
    .thenApply(s -> s.toUpperCase())     // SKIPPED — upstream failed
    .thenApply(s -> s + "!")             // SKIPPED — still failed
    .exceptionally(ex -> "recovered: " + ex.getMessage())  // catches here
    .thenApply(s -> "[" + s + "]");      // runs normally on recovered value

chain.thenAccept(System.out::println);
// Output: [recovered: stage 1 failed]

Catching exceptions in the middle of a chain

CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> riskyStep1())
    .exceptionally(ex -> fallbackForStep1(ex))  // local recovery
    .thenCompose(r1 -> riskyStep2(r1))
    .exceptionally(ex -> fallbackForStep2(ex))  // local recovery
    .thenAccept(r2 -> persist(r2));

Wrapping checked exceptions

// CompletableFuture lambdas don't allow checked exceptions
CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> {
    try {
        return Files.readString(Path.of("data.txt"));
    } catch (IOException e) {
        throw new CompletionException(e); // wrap in unchecked
    }
});
Part 18

Common Pitfalls

Pitfall 1 — Blocking inside async callbacks

// BAD: get() inside thenApplyAsync blocks a thread pool thread
CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> fetchUser(id))
    .thenApplyAsync(user -> {
        String orders = fetchOrdersAsync(user).get(); // BLOCKS pool thread!
        return new Dashboard(user, orders);
    });

// GOOD: use thenCompose
CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> fetchUser(id))
    .thenCompose(user -> fetchOrdersAsync(user)
        .thenApply(orders -> new Dashboard(user, orders)));

Pitfall 2 — Using thenApply when thenCompose is needed

// WRONG: wraps in nested future
CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<Order>> nested =
    getUser().thenApply(u -> createOrderAsync(u));  // double-wrapped

// CORRECT
CompletableFuture<Order> flat =
    getUser().thenCompose(u -> createOrderAsync(u)); // flat

Pitfall 3 — Forgetting to handle exceptions from allOf

// If any sub-future fails, allOf fails — but other sub-futures continue
CompletableFuture<Void> all = CompletableFuture.allOf(cf1, cf2, cf3);
all.join(); // throws CompletionException if any child failed — no partial results

// SAFE pattern: handle exceptions on each sub-future first
CompletableFuture<Void> safeAll = CompletableFuture.allOf(
    cf1.exceptionally(ex -> fallback1()),
    cf2.exceptionally(ex -> fallback2()),
    cf3.exceptionally(ex -> fallback3())
);

Pitfall 4 — Not specifying executor for I/O work

// BAD: blocks commonPool thread with HTTP call
CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> restTemplate.getForObject(url, String.class));

// GOOD: I/O on its own executor
CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(
    () -> restTemplate.getForObject(url, String.class),
    ioExecutor
);

Pitfall 5 — Ignoring completions / detached chains

// BAD: nobody holds a reference; exception is silently swallowed
CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> doWork())
    .thenAccept(r -> process(r)); // return value discarded

// GOOD: store reference or attach a terminal handler
CompletableFuture<Void> pipeline =
    CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> doWork())
        .thenAccept(r -> process(r))
        .exceptionally(ex -> { log.error("pipeline failed", ex); return null; });

Performance Considerations

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              CompletableFuture Performance Considerations            │
│                                                                      │
│  Thread model choice:                                                │
│                                                                      │
│  commonPool (ForkJoinPool):                                          │
│  ✓ Good for CPU-bound, short-lived transformations                   │
│  ✗ Bad for blocking I/O — starves parallel streams                   │
│                                                                      │
│  Fixed ThreadPool:                                                   │
│  ✓ Bounded; predictable latency under load                           │
│  ✓ Good for I/O-bound tasks with known concurrency ceiling           │
│  ✗ Threads are expensive; may need careful sizing                    │
│                                                                      │
│  Virtual Threads (Java 21):                                          │
│  ✓ Cheap blocking; no pool sizing needed for I/O                     │
│  ✓ Compatible with CompletableFuture via Executors.newVirtualThread  │
│  ✗ Pin on synchronized blocks — avoid native monitors in virtual threads│
│                                                                      │
│  Chaining overhead:                                                  │
│  Each stage allocates a Completion object (~40–80 bytes)             │
│  For millions of futures, consider batching or streaming alternatives│
│                                                                      │
│  thenApply vs thenApplyAsync:                                        │
│  thenApply: no thread switch if completed — lower latency but        │
│             risks callback thread monopolisation                      │
│  thenApplyAsync: always switches thread — higher latency but         │
│                  predictable, avoids thread starvation               │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Part 20

Interview Questions

Q1: What is the difference between thenApply and thenCompose?

thenApply(Function<T,U>) takes a synchronous function and wraps its result in a new CompletableFuture<U> — equivalent to map. thenCompose(Function<T, CompletableFuture<U>>) takes a function that itself returns a CompletableFuture and flattens the result — equivalent to flatMap. Use thenCompose when the transformation is asynchronous (returns its own CF); using thenApply in that case produces a doubly-nested CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<U>>.

Q2: How does exception propagation work in a CompletableFuture chain?

When a stage throws, subsequent thenApply/thenCompose/thenAccept stages are skipped and the exception passes down the chain until an exceptionally or handle stage catches it. exceptionally only fires on exception; handle fires on both normal and exceptional completion. whenComplete fires on both but cannot modify the result. If no stage handles the exception and you call get(), it is wrapped in ExecutionException; if you call join(), it is wrapped in CompletionException.

Q3: What is the difference between CompletableFuture.allOf and thenCombine?

thenCombine combines exactly two futures and produces a result. allOf waits for any number of futures but returns CF<Void> — you must retrieve individual results yourself. For n > 2 parallel operations, allOf + manual join() is the idiomatic pattern.

Q4: What executor does supplyAsync use by default and when should you override it?

It uses ForkJoinPool.commonPool(). Override with a custom executor when:
1. The task is I/O-bound (HTTP, DB) — blocking a commonPool thread degrades parallelStream() throughput globally.
2. You need thread naming, queue depth control, or rejection policies.
3. You need higher parallelism than availableProcessors() - 1.

Q5: How do you implement a timeout for a CompletableFuture?

In Java 9+: .orTimeout(500, MILLISECONDS) (complete exceptionally with TimeoutException) or .completeOnTimeout(fallback, 500, MILLISECONDS) (complete normally with fallback). In Java 8: use a ScheduledExecutorService to call completeExceptionally after a delay and combine with whenComplete to relay the result.

Q6: How does @Async in Spring interact with CompletableFuture?

When a @Async method returns CompletableFuture, Spring wraps the invocation: the actual method body runs in the async executor's thread. The returned CompletableFuture is a proxy through which Spring propagates the result or exception. The caller can compose further stages on this future without blocking the HTTP servlet thread, enabling Servlet 3.1 asynchronous request processing in MVC controllers.

Q7: What happens when you call join() vs get()?

Both block until the future completes. get() is declared to throw checked InterruptedException and ExecutionException; it is the Future<T> interface method. join() is a CompletableFuture-specific method that throws unchecked CompletionException on failure and does not declare InterruptedException. Inside async chains, always use join() (since you are already on a non-user thread and checked exceptions are inconvenient).

Part 21

Complete Reference Example

import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.stream.Stream;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;

/**
 * Demonstrates CompletableFuture:
 * - supplyAsync / runAsync
 * - thenApply, thenCompose, thenCombine
 * - exceptionally, handle, whenComplete
 * - allOf, anyOf
 * - orTimeout
 * - Custom executor
 */
public class CompletableFutureReference {

    private static final ExecutorService IO_POOL =
        Executors.newFixedThreadPool(10, r -> {
            Thread t = new Thread(r, "cf-io");
            t.setDaemon(true);
            return t;
        });

    // Simulated remote calls
    static String fetchUser(int id) {
        sleep(50); return "user-" + id;
    }
    static String fetchOrders(String user) {
        sleep(80); return "orders-for-" + user;
    }
    static String fetchRecommendations(String user) {
        sleep(120); return "recs-for-" + user;
    }
    static void sleep(long ms) {
        try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        }
    }

    // ---- 1. Basic supply and transform -----------------------------------
    static void basicChain() throws Exception {
        String result = CompletableFuture
            .supplyAsync(() -> fetchUser(42), IO_POOL)
            .thenApply(user -> user.toUpperCase())
            .thenApply(u -> "[" + u + "]")
            .get();
        System.out.println("basicChain: " + result);
    }

    // ---- 2. thenCompose for chained async calls --------------------------
    static void composedChain() throws Exception {
        String result = CompletableFuture
            .supplyAsync(() -> fetchUser(42), IO_POOL)
            .thenCompose(user ->
                CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> fetchOrders(user), IO_POOL))
            .get();
        System.out.println("composedChain: " + result);
    }

    // ---- 3. Parallel fan-out with thenCombine ----------------------------
    static void parallelCombine() throws Exception {
        CompletableFuture<String> ordersFuture =
            CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> fetchOrders("user-42"), IO_POOL);
        CompletableFuture<String> recsFuture =
            CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> fetchRecommendations("user-42"), IO_POOL);

        String combined = ordersFuture
            .thenCombine(recsFuture, (orders, recs) -> orders + " | " + recs)
            .get();
        System.out.println("parallelCombine: " + combined);
    }

    // ---- 4. allOf with result collection ---------------------------------
    static void allOfExample() throws Exception {
        List<CompletableFuture<String>> futures = List.of(
            CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> fetchUser(1), IO_POOL),
            CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> fetchUser(2), IO_POOL),
            CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> fetchUser(3), IO_POOL)
        );

        List<String> results = CompletableFuture
            .allOf(futures.toArray(new CompletableFuture[0]))
            .thenApply(v -> futures.stream()
                .map(CompletableFuture::join)
                .collect(Collectors.toList()))
            .get();
        System.out.println("allOf: " + results);
    }

    // ---- 5. Exception handling -------------------------------------------
    static void exceptionHandling() throws Exception {
        CompletableFuture<String> cf = CompletableFuture
            .supplyAsync(() -> {
                throw new RuntimeException("network error");
            })
            .exceptionally(ex -> "fallback: " + ex.getMessage())
            .thenApply(String::toUpperCase);

        System.out.println("exceptionally: " + cf.get());

        // handle — always runs
        CompletableFuture<String> cf2 = CompletableFuture
            .supplyAsync(() -> { throw new RuntimeException("oops"); })
            .handle((result, ex) ->
                ex != null ? "handled: " + ex.getMessage() : result);

        System.out.println("handle: " + cf2.get());
    }

    // ---- 6. Timeout (Java 9+) -------------------------------------------
    static void timeoutExample() throws Exception {
        CompletableFuture<String> cf = CompletableFuture
            .supplyAsync(() -> { sleep(2000); return "late result"; }, IO_POOL)
            .orTimeout(500, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)
            .exceptionally(ex -> ex instanceof TimeoutException
                ? "timed-out fallback" : "other error");

        System.out.println("timeout: " + cf.get());
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        basicChain();
        composedChain();
        parallelCombine();
        allOfExample();
        exceptionHandling();
        timeoutExample();
        IO_POOL.shutdown();
    }
}

Practice — Lesson 51

Easy Exercises

Exercise 1 — Sequential Async Chain

Build a chain that:
1. Fetches a user by ID asynchronously (simulate with Thread.sleep(50), return "user-123").
2. Fetches the user's profile (simulate with Thread.sleep(30), return "profile:user-123").
3. Converts the profile string to uppercase.
4. Prints the final result.

Use thenCompose between steps 1 and 2, thenApply for step 3, and thenAccept for step 4.

<details>
<summary>Solution sketch</summary>

CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> {
        sleep(50); return "user-123";
    })
    .thenCompose(user -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> {
        sleep(30); return "profile:" + user;
    }))
    .thenApply(String::toUpperCase)
    .thenAccept(System.out::println)
    .join();

</details>

Exercise 2 — Parallel Fan-Out with allOf

Query five "services" in parallel (simulate each with supplyAsync(() -> { sleep(random 50-200ms); return "result-N"; })). Use allOf to wait for all five and collect their results into a List<String>.

<details>
<summary>Solution sketch</summary>

List<CompletableFuture<String>> futures = IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 5)
    .mapToObj(i -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> {
        sleep(50 + (int)(Math.random() * 150));
        return "result-" + i;
    }))
    .collect(Collectors.toList());

List<String> results = CompletableFuture.allOf(futures.toArray(new CompletableFuture[0]))
    .thenApply(v -> futures.stream().map(CompletableFuture::join).collect(Collectors.toList()))
    .join();

System.out.println(results);

</details>

Exercise 3 — Exception Recovery

Create a CompletableFuture that randomly fails (50% chance) with RuntimeException("service unavailable"). Use exceptionally to return a fallback string "default-response". Verify both paths by running it multiple times.

<details>
<summary>Solution sketch</summary>

for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
    String result = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> {
        if (Math.random() < 0.5) throw new RuntimeException("service unavailable");
        return "live-response";
    })
    .exceptionally(ex -> "default-response")
    .join();
    System.out.println(result);
}

</details>

Exercise 4 — Timeout with Fallback

Implement a method fetchWithTimeout(long delayMs, long timeoutMs, String fallback) that:
1. Starts an async task that sleeps for delayMs then returns "real-result".
2. Applies completeOnTimeout(fallback, timeoutMs, MILLISECONDS).
3. Returns the result (either real or fallback).

Test with delayMs=200, timeoutMs=100 (triggers fallback) and delayMs=50, timeoutMs=200 (real result wins).

<details>
<summary>Solution sketch</summary>

static String fetchWithTimeout(long delayMs, long timeoutMs, String fallback) {
    return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> {
        sleep(delayMs);
        return "real-result";
    })
    .completeOnTimeout(fallback, timeoutMs, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)
    .join();
}

// Test:
System.out.println(fetchWithTimeout(200, 100, "fallback")); // fallback
System.out.println(fetchWithTimeout(50, 200, "fallback"));  // real-result

</details>
