Production Scenarios

Scenario 1 — Spring Boot Migration

Your team runs a Spring Boot 2.7 REST API on Java 17 using a newFixedThreadPool(200) configuration. Latency P99 is 800ms and the thread pool is often exhausted during peak traffic. Describe the migration plan to Java 21 virtual threads. Identify all risk areas and provide the configuration changes.

Expected answer outline:
- Upgrade to Java 21, Spring Boot 3.2
- Enable spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true
- Run load test with -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=short — identify pinned hotspots
- Inspect synchronized blocks in service layer touching DB or cache
- Replace synchronized methods with ReentrantLock where blocking occurs
- Verify HikariCP maximum-pool-size is tuned to actual DB connection limit (not 200)
- Re-run load test; compare P99 latency and RPS at saturation point

Scenario 2 — Memory Pressure Investigation

A virtual-thread-based service running 500,000 concurrent connections triggers GC pressure after 2 hours. Heap profiling shows millions of ThreadLocal map entries. Diagnose the root cause and fix it.

Root cause: a ThreadLocal<byte[]> buffer (4 KB each) cached per thread for serialization. With 500K virtual threads alive simultaneously: 500,000 × 4 KB = ~2 GB of ThreadLocal entries.

Fix: use a shared ArrayBlockingQueue<byte[]> buffer pool with a 1,000-entry cap; virtual thread borrows a buffer, uses it, returns it.

Debugging Exercises

Debug 1 — Silent Stall

The following service handles 10,000 concurrent requests but stalls at around 4 active requests. Identify the bug.

public class UserService {
    private final DataSource ds;

    // BUG: synchronized + blocking inside = PINNING
    public synchronized User loadUser(long id) throws SQLException {
        try (Connection c = ds.getConnection();  // blocks (Hikari wait)
             PreparedStatement ps = c.prepareStatement("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=?")) {
            ps.setLong(1, id);
            ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery();    // blocks (network)
            return mapRow(rs);
        }
    }
}

Diagnosis: The 4 carrier threads are all pinned by synchronized + blocking DB calls. No other virtual thread can run. Add -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=short to confirm. Fix: remove synchronized (it is providing false safety anyway — DataSource.getConnection() is already thread-safe).

Debug 2 — Unexpected OOM

A service using virtual threads runs fine in testing but crashes with OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space in production under load. Heap dump shows 10,000 Thread objects, each holding a javax.crypto.Cipher instance (32 KB each).

Root cause: ThreadLocal<Cipher> pattern — each of the 10,000 concurrent virtual threads initialized its own Cipher. Fix: use Cipher as a local variable (it is not thread-safe anyway and should not be reused across calls without re-initialization).

Interview Challenges

Challenge 1

"We have a Java service making 50 blocking HTTP calls per request, each taking ~20ms. We handle 500 requests/second. Our Tomcat thread pool is set to 200. What is the maximum theoretical throughput, and what would virtual threads change?"

Answer framework:
- Current: Little's Law — L = λW → 500 req/s × 1s average (50 × 20ms) = 10,000 concurrent threads needed. Pool of 200 → queue builds up → throughput limited to 200/1s = 200 RPS.
- With virtual threads: 10,000 virtual threads each blocking ~1s → 10,000 × (20ms CPU / 1s) = 20ms CPU per request. With 8 cores: 8000 ms/s ÷ 20ms = 400 RPS CPU-limited — network/DB is the bottleneck, not threads.
- Conclusion: virtual threads remove the thread-count bottleneck; true ceiling is I/O throughput.

Challenge 2

"Why does synchronized cause pinning but ReentrantLock does not?"

Answer: synchronized uses the JVM's intrinsic monitor (built into every object). When a virtual thread tries to enter a contested synchronized block, the JVM must interact with the OS-level monitor, which ties the virtual thread to its carrier. ReentrantLock is implemented using AbstractQueuedSynchronizer, which uses LockSupport.park() internally — and park() on a virtual thread calls continuation.yield(), cleanly unmounting the virtual thread from the carrier.

Challenge 3

"In a system with 4 CPU cores and 4 carrier threads, a virtual thread calls synchronized doWork() which takes 500ms (all blocking I/O inside). What happens to the other virtual threads?"

Answer: The calling virtual thread is pinned on its carrier for 500ms. The JVM detects pinning and may add a compensating carrier (up to maxPoolSize). If maxPoolSize is 4 and all 4 are pinned, new virtual threads are starved until a carrier frees. If maxPoolSize is 256, additional carriers are created on demand. This is why pinning degrades throughput — it forces carrier thread creation (expensive) or stalls virtual thread scheduling.

Key Takeaways

  • Virtual threads are not faster threads — they are cheaper threads that eliminate the OS-thread-count ceiling for I/O-bound workloads
  • One virtual thread per task is the correct model; never pool virtual threads (pooling defeats the purpose)
  • synchronized + blocking = pinning — the most common migration hazard; replace with ReentrantLock where blocking I/O occurs inside the lock
  • ThreadLocal at scale is dangerous — with millions of virtual threads, large ThreadLocal values cause memory pressure; prefer ScopedValue or per-call resource acquisition
  • Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() is the primary migration entry point for existing thread-pool code — it is a drop-in replacement
  • Add Semaphore back-pressure for bounded downstream resources (DB connections, rate-limited APIs) — virtual threads will saturate any resource without it
  • Structured concurrency (JEP 453 preview) makes virtual thread fan-out safe and leak-free by binding child task lifetimes to the parent scope
  • Reactive is not obsolete — keep WebFlux/R2DBC for backpressure pipelines; virtual threads target the simpler blocking-style use case
  • Phase 5 complete — you now hold the full Java concurrency stack, from JMM happens-before edges to Loom's user-space thread scheduler

Part 1

What Is Class Loading and Why It Matters

When you compile HelloWorld.java, the result is HelloWorld.class — a binary file containing JVM bytecode. That .class file sits inert on disk until the JVM decides it needs the class. Class loading is the process by which the JVM finds, reads, and prepares that binary into a live java.lang.Class object usable at runtime.

Understanding class loading is not academic. It explains:

  • Why adding a JAR to the wrong classpath location silently picks up the wrong version of a library
  • Why Spring Boot fat JARs work at all — and why they need a custom classloader
  • Why Tomcat can deploy 50 different web applications each with their own log4j version without conflict
  • Why ClassNotFoundException and NoClassDefFoundError are different errors with different root causes
  • Why dynamic languages, OSGi, and hot-reload frameworks (JRebel, Spring DevTools) are possible
High-Level View: From Source to Runtime Class
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  HelloWorld.java
        │
        ▼  javac
  HelloWorld.class   ← bytecode on disk (or inside a JAR)
        │
        ▼  ClassLoader.loadClass("HelloWorld")
  Class<HelloWorld>  ← live Class object in JVM heap / Metaspace
        │
        ▼  new HelloWorld()
  HelloWorld instance ← heap object
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Class loading is lazy by default: a class is loaded the first time it is referenced, not when the JVM starts. This is intentional — loading every class at startup would be prohibitively slow.

Part 2

The ClassLoader Hierarchy: Three Built-In Loaders

The JVM ships with three classloaders arranged in a strict parent-child hierarchy.

Bootstrap ClassLoader
        │
        ▼ (parent)
Platform ClassLoader (Java 9+) / Extension ClassLoader (Java 8)
        │
        ▼ (parent)
Application ClassLoader (a.k.a. System ClassLoader)
        │
        ▼ (parent)
  [Your custom ClassLoaders]

Bootstrap ClassLoader

  • Implemented in native C++, not in Java
  • Loads the JDK core: java.lang.*, java.util.*, java.io.* — everything in java.base module
  • Lives at $JAVA_HOME/lib/ (historically rt.jar, replaced by module system in Java 9)
  • ClassLoader.getParent() returns null for classes loaded by Bootstrap — it has no Java representation
  • Cannot be subclassed or replaced
// Bootstrap-loaded classes show null parent
System.out.println(String.class.getClassLoader());          // null (Bootstrap)
System.out.println(Object.class.getClassLoader());          // null (Bootstrap)

Platform ClassLoader (Java 9+) / Extension ClassLoader (Java 8)

  • Java 8: loads JARs from $JAVA_HOME/lib/ext/ — the extension mechanism
  • Java 9+: renamed to Platform ClassLoader; loads non-core JDK modules (java.sql, java.xml, etc.)
  • Parent is Bootstrap
  • Thread.currentThread().getContextClassLoader() is typically the Application ClassLoader, not this one

Application ClassLoader (System ClassLoader)

  • Loads classes from the application classpath (-classpath / -cp / CLASSPATH env var)
  • Default classloader for user-written code and third-party libraries
  • Retrieved via ClassLoader.getSystemClassLoader()
  • Parent is Platform ClassLoader
// Verify the hierarchy at runtime
ClassLoader app = ClassLoader.getSystemClassLoader();
System.out.println(app.getClass().getName());
// → jdk.internal.loader.ClassLoaders$AppClassLoader

System.out.println(app.getParent().getClass().getName());
// → jdk.internal.loader.ClassLoaders$PlatformClassLoader

System.out.println(app.getParent().getParent());
// → null (Bootstrap is not a Java object)
Part 3

The Three Phases: Loading, Linking, Initialization

Every class goes through exactly three phases before it is ready to use.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    Class Lifecycle                               │
│                                                                 │
│  LOADING          LINKING                       INITIALIZATION  │
│  ┌────────┐   ┌──────────────────────────┐   ┌───────────────┐ │
│  │ Find   │   │ Verify │ Prepare │ Resolve│   │ Run <clinit>  │ │
│  │ binary │→  │        │         │       │→  │ static inits  │ │
│  │ data   │   │ bytecode│ statics │ symrefs│  │ static fields │ │
│  └────────┘   └──────────────────────────┘   └───────────────┘ │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Phase 1 — Loading

The classloader locates the binary representation of the class (from disk, network, database, generated code, etc.) and creates a Class object in the Metaspace (method area). Key actions:

  1. Find the .class file or byte array
  2. Parse the binary format into a ClassFile structure
  3. Create a java.lang.Class instance representing it
  4. Store internal structures in Metaspace

The class is now defined but not ready.

Phase 2 — Linking

Linking has three sub-phases:

Verification: The JVM validates the bytecode is well-formed, type-safe, and won't corrupt the JVM. Checks include:
- Magic number 0xCAFEBABE is present
- Branch targets are valid
- Type assignments are legal
- Stack doesn't overflow or underflow
- No access-control violations

Preparation: The JVM allocates memory for static fields and sets them to default zero values — 0, false, null. The actual values from source code are NOT set yet.

class Config {
    static int MAX = 100;   // After preparation: MAX = 0 (not 100 yet!)
    static String NAME = "prod"; // After preparation: NAME = null
}

Resolution (may be deferred): Symbolic references in the constant pool (class names, method names, field names as strings) are resolved to direct memory references. Can be lazy — done when the reference is first used.

Phase 3 — Initialization

The JVM runs the class's <clinit> (class initializer) method — the synthetic method compiled from all static blocks and static field initializers, in textual order.

class Config {
    static int MAX = 100;           // sets MAX = 100
    static String NAME;
    static {
        NAME = System.getenv("APP_ENV") != null ? "prod" : "dev";
    }
    static final Logger LOG = Logger.getLogger(Config.class.getName());
}

Initialization is thread-safe: the JVM guarantees that <clinit> is executed exactly once, even if multiple threads race to use the class. This is the foundation of the Initialization-on-demand holder idiom (a safe, lazy singleton).

Part 4

The Delegation Model (Parent-First)

The most important behavioural rule in Java classloading is parent-first delegation:

> When a classloader is asked to load a class, it asks its parent first. Only if the parent cannot find the class does the child try to load it itself.

loadClass("com.example.Foo") on AppClassLoader:
    1. Check local cache (already loaded?)   → no
    2. Delegate to parent (PlatformClassLoader)
         2a. Delegate to parent (Bootstrap)
               - Not in java.base → return null
         2b. Not in platform modules → return null
    3. AppClassLoader searches classpath → found! Load it.
    4. Cache and return Class<Foo>

Why parent-first? Security and consistency

Without parent-first delegation, an attacker could put a malicious java/lang/String.class on the classpath and intercept all string operations. Parent-first ensures the trusted Bootstrap ClassLoader always wins for core classes.

Consistency: if String is loaded by Bootstrap for library code AND by Application ClassLoader for your code, you'd have TWO different Class objects for String. Casts between them would fail with ClassCastException. Parent-first prevents this.

// Proof: same Class object regardless of which classloader loads it
Class<?> c1 = Class.forName("java.lang.String");
Class<?> c2 = String.class;
System.out.println(c1 == c2);   // true — same Class object

The class identity equation

A class in the JVM is uniquely identified by the tuple: (fully qualified name, classloader). Two classes with the same name loaded by different classloaders are different classes — they cannot be cast to each other.

Part 5

Custom ClassLoaders

You extend ClassLoader to implement your own loading logic. Common use cases:

  • Load classes from a database, network, or encrypted JAR
  • Hot-reload: discard old class definitions and load updated ones
  • Plugin systems: isolate plugin code from application code
  • Bytecode transformation at load time (used by AOP frameworks, instrumentation agents)
public class ByteArrayClassLoader extends ClassLoader {

    private final Map<String, byte[]> classBytes;

    public ByteArrayClassLoader(Map<String, byte[]> classBytes, ClassLoader parent) {
        super(parent);
        this.classBytes = classBytes;
    }

    @Override
    protected Class<?> findClass(String name) throws ClassNotFoundException {
        byte[] bytes = classBytes.get(name);
        if (bytes == null) {
            throw new ClassNotFoundException("Class not found: " + name);
        }
        // defineClass validates the bytecode and creates the Class object
        return defineClass(name, bytes, 0, bytes.length);
    }
}

// Usage
Map<String, byte[]> classes = new HashMap<>();
classes.put("com.example.Plugin", readBytesFromDB("com.example.Plugin"));

ClassLoader loader = new ByteArrayClassLoader(classes, Thread.currentThread().getContextClassLoader());
Class<?> pluginClass = loader.loadClass("com.example.Plugin");
Object plugin = pluginClass.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance();

Key method contract

Method Purpose
loadClass(String name) Entry point — implements delegation logic
findClass(String name) Override this — your custom lookup
defineClass(...) Converts bytes → Class object; validates bytecode
findLoadedClass(String) Check if already loaded by this loader
getResourceAsStream(...) Load resources alongside classes

Rule: override findClass, not loadClass. Overriding loadClass breaks the delegation model unless you deliberately want child-first semantics (which Tomcat does for web-app isolation).

Part 6

Context ClassLoader: Solving the Inversion Problem

Parent-first delegation creates a visibility problem: Bootstrap-loaded code (like JDBC's DriverManager) needs to load application-level drivers (like com.mysql.jdbc.Driver), but Bootstrap cannot see the classpath.

The Thread Context ClassLoader was introduced to solve this:

// In DriverManager.getConnection() (simplified):
ClassLoader cl = Thread.currentThread().getContextClassLoader();
// Use cl to load the driver, bypassing parent-first for this specific lookup

// Framework code pattern: save, set, restore
ClassLoader original = Thread.currentThread().getContextClassLoader();
try {
    Thread.currentThread().setContextClassLoader(specificLoader);
    // ... code that relies on context classloader for service loading
} finally {
    Thread.currentThread().setContextClassLoader(original);
}

Java's ServiceLoader (for META-INF/services/ SPI files) and JNDI both use the context classloader internally.

Part 7

ClassNotFoundException vs NoClassDefFoundError

These two are not the same and are caused by different situations. Confusing them wastes hours in production debugging.

ClassNotFoundException

  • Checked exception (extends ReflectiveOperationException → Exception)
  • Thrown by Class.forName(...), ClassLoader.loadClass(...), ClassLoader.findSystemClass(...)
  • Meaning: the class binary cannot be found at load time
  • Cause: class is simply not on the classpath
try {
    Class.forName("com.mysql.jdbc.Driver");
} catch (ClassNotFoundException e) {
    // MySQL driver JAR is not on the classpath
}

Fix: add the missing JAR to the classpath.

NoClassDefFoundError

  • Error (extends LinkageError → Error)
  • Thrown when the JVM attempts to use a class that was present at compile time but is absent or failed at runtime
  • Silent — not a checked exception, often not caught

Three root causes:

1. Missing at runtime (most common):

Compiled against mysql-8.0.jar. Deployed without it.
JVM finds Class reference in bytecode → no binary → NoClassDefFoundError

2. Static initializer failure:

class Config {
    static {
        throw new RuntimeException("Init failed!");  // <clinit> throws
    }
}

// First access: ExceptionInInitializerError wraps the RuntimeException
Config c1 = new Config();  // ExceptionInInitializerError

// Every subsequent access: NoClassDefFoundError (class is now poisoned)
Config c2 = new Config();  // NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class Config

3. Class loaded by wrong classloader (common in web containers, OSGi).

Decision table

Symptom Exception Action
JAR not on classpath ClassNotFoundException Add JAR
JAR present but failed <clinit> ExceptionInInitializerError → then NoClassDefFoundError Fix static init code
Two versions of same JAR ClassCastException or NoSuchMethodError Remove duplicate JAR
Class loaded by wrong loader ClassCastException or NoClassDefFoundError Fix classloader hierarchy
Part 8

Metaspace: Where Class Metadata Lives

Before Java 8, class metadata was stored in PermGen (Permanent Generation) — a fixed-size heap region notorious for OutOfMemoryError: PermGen space when too many classes were loaded (common in Tomcat with hot deployment).

Java 8 replaced PermGen with Metaspace, which lives in native memory (outside the heap).

JVM Memory Layout (Java 8+):
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Java Heap (controlled by -Xmx)                                 │
│  ┌────────────┐  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Young Gen  │  │        Old Gen (Tenured)                   │ │
│  └────────────┘  └────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Metaspace (native memory — grows automatically by default)     │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
│  │  Class metadata, method bytecodes, constant pools,      │    │
│  │  runtime constant pool, field/method descriptors        │    │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Code Cache (JIT-compiled native code)                          │
│  Thread Stacks                                                  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Metaspace configuration

-XX:MetaspaceSize=256m        # initial commit size (triggers first GC when reached)
-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=512m     # hard limit (default: unlimited — will use all RAM!)
-XX:MinMetaspaceFreeRatio=40  # min % free after GC before expanding
-XX:MaxMetaspaceFreeRatio=70  # max % free before shrinking

Metaspace and class unloading

Classes are eligible for GC when their ClassLoader becomes unreachable. The GC collects the ClassLoader object, which releases all classes it defined, reclaiming Metaspace.

This is why:
- Application ClassLoader-loaded classes are never unloaded (the ClassLoader lives forever)
- Plugin systems and Tomcat web-app ClassLoaders CAN free Metaspace when an app is undeployed (if no leaks)

Part 9

ClassLoader Leaks: The Silent Memory Killer

A ClassLoader leak occurs when a ClassLoader (and all its classes) cannot be GC'd because something outside holds a strong reference to an object loaded by it.

ClassLoader (custom)
    └── defines class Foo
            └── Foo instance is stored in a JDK-level static cache
                    (e.g., java.beans.Introspector cache, JDBC DriverManager)
                            └── ClassLoader reference kept alive
                                    └── All classes defined by it stay in Metaspace
                                            └── Metaspace grows unboundedly → OOM

Common leak patterns

Pattern 1 — Static ThreadLocal:

// In a web app's servlet:
static ThreadLocal<MyObject> cache = new ThreadLocal<>();
// If the thread belongs to Tomcat's thread pool (Application ClassLoader level),
// and MyObject is defined by the web app's ClassLoader,
// undeploying the web app cannot free MyObject's ClassLoader.

Pattern 2 — JDBC Driver registration:

// mysql-connector.jar loaded by web app ClassLoader
// DriverManager (Bootstrap) holds a reference to the Driver instance
// → web app ClassLoader cannot be GC'd
// Fix: deregister on webapp shutdown:
Enumeration<Driver> drivers = DriverManager.getDrivers();
while (drivers.hasMoreElements()) {
    Driver d = drivers.nextElement();
    if (d.getClass().getClassLoader() == Thread.currentThread().getContextClassLoader()) {
        DriverManager.deregisterDriver(d);
    }
}

Pattern 3 — Shutdown hooks:

Runtime.getRuntime().addShutdownHook(new Thread(() -> cleanup()));
// The Thread references the Runnable, which may reference the webapp ClassLoader

Detection tools

# Monitor Metaspace in production
jstat -gc <pid> 5s

# Check class count
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_info

# Heap dump analysis (look for ClassLoader instances)
jmap -dump:format=b,file=heap.hprof <pid>
# Open in Eclipse MAT → "Leak Suspects" → look for ClassLoader objects
Part 10

Spring Boot Fat JAR: Nested ClassLoader Architecture

A Spring Boot fat JAR (executable JAR) packs your application and all dependencies into a single .jar file. The challenge: standard Java classloaders cannot load classes from JARs nested inside a JAR.

my-app.jar
├── BOOT-INF/
│   ├── classes/               ← your compiled classes
│   │   └── com/example/App.class
│   └── lib/                   ← all dependencies as JARs
│       ├── spring-core-6.x.jar
│       ├── jackson-2.x.jar
│       └── ...
├── META-INF/
│   └── MANIFEST.MF            ← Main-Class: org.springframework.boot.loader.JarLauncher
└── org/springframework/boot/loader/   ← the Boot launcher classes (flat, not nested)
    ├── JarLauncher.class
    ├── LaunchedURLClassLoader.class
    └── ...

How Spring Boot solves it

  1. MANIFEST.MF points to JarLauncher as the entry point
  2. JarLauncher creates a LaunchedURLClassLoader that understands the nested-JAR format
  3. LaunchedURLClassLoader can open a URL like jar:file:/app.jar!/BOOT-INF/lib/spring-core.jar!/
  4. This custom classloader uses child-first for BOOT-INF/classes but parent-first for JDK classes
Bootstrap ClassLoader
        │
Platform ClassLoader
        │
Application ClassLoader  ← loads JarLauncher itself
        │
LaunchedURLClassLoader   ← loads BOOT-INF/classes + BOOT-INF/lib/*.jar

Implications for architects

  • Reflection libraries must use Thread.currentThread().getContextClassLoader() — the LaunchedURLClassLoader is set as the context loader at startup
  • Native agents (JVM TI) see the LaunchedURLClassLoader not a standard AppClassLoader
  • -javaagent JARs are loaded by Bootstrap; they use Instrumentation.appendToSystemClassLoaderSearch() to add themselves to the correct loader
Part 11

Tomcat and Web Application ClassLoader Isolation

Tomcat deploys multiple web applications, each potentially using different versions of the same library. This is only possible because Tomcat uses isolated ClassLoaders per web application.

Bootstrap ClassLoader
        │
Platform ClassLoader
        │
System ClassLoader  ← Tomcat's core classes (catalina.jar, etc.)
      ┌───┴──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
      │                                                      │
WebApp ClassLoader (app1)          WebApp ClassLoader (app2)
  ├── WEB-INF/classes/               ├── WEB-INF/classes/
  └── WEB-INF/lib/                   └── WEB-INF/lib/
      ├── jackson-2.12.jar               ├── jackson-2.15.jar  (different version!)
      └── log4j-1.2.jar                  └── log4j-2.20.jar

Tomcat's WebApp ClassLoader uses child-first delegation (inverted): it searches WEB-INF/classes and WEB-INF/lib BEFORE delegating to the parent. This enables version isolation. The only exceptions are Java EE/Servlet API classes (which must come from the parent to ensure API compatibility).

Part 12

Dynamic Class Loading and Hot Reload

Hot reload means replacing a class definition at runtime without restarting the JVM.

Java agents (Instrumentation API)

// In a javaagent premain or agentmain:
Instrumentation inst = ...; // injected by JVM

// Redefine a class (must keep same schema — no new fields/methods)
ClassDefinition def = new ClassDefinition(MyService.class, newBytecode);
inst.redefineClasses(def);

// Retransform (for instrumentation with registered ClassFileTransformers)
inst.retransformClasses(MyService.class);

Limitations of redefineClasses:
- Cannot add/remove fields or methods
- Cannot change superclass or implemented interfaces
- Cannot change method signatures

Tools like JRebel work around this by generating proxy classes. Spring Boot DevTools instead restarts a restricted ClassLoader on change (simpler but not seamless).

Generating classes at runtime

Frameworks like Mockito, Hibernate, and Spring extensively generate proxy classes at runtime:

// Using java.lang.reflect.Proxy:
MyInterface proxy = (MyInterface) Proxy.newProxyInstance(
    MyInterface.class.getClassLoader(),
    new Class[]{MyInterface.class},
    (p, method, args) -> { /* intercept */ return null; }
);

Each proxy class is defined dynamically via defineClass into an anonymous classloader. As of Java 15+, anonymous classloaders are replaced by hidden classes (Lookup.defineHiddenClass) which have controlled visibility and lifecycle.

Part 13

Java 9 Module System and ClassLoaders

The JPMS (Java Platform Module System, introduced in Java 9) changed how core classloaders work.

Pre-Java 9:

Bootstrap: rt.jar
Extension: lib/ext/*.jar

Post-Java 9:

Bootstrap: java.base module (and a few others)
Platform:  java.sql, java.xml, java.logging, etc.
Application: module path + classpath

Named modules control visibility: a class in module A can only see a class in module B if module B exports the package to module A. This is enforced at the classloader level — even if the class is physically loadable, the JVM denies access.

module com.example.app {
    requires java.sql;              // may use java.sql classes
    requires com.example.library;   // may use exported packages
    // java.util.logging is part of java.logging module
    // requires it implicitly via java.base transitive
}

--add-opens and --add-exports flags bypass module boundaries — frequently needed for legacy frameworks that use deep reflection (Hibernate, Spring) against JDK internals.

Part 14

Class.forName() Deep Dive

Class.forName(String name) is the programmatic entry point for explicit class loading.

// Form 1: uses caller's classloader, initializes the class
Class<?> cls = Class.forName("com.example.MyClass");

// Form 2: full control
Class<?> cls = Class.forName(
    "com.example.MyClass",
    true,                            // initialize = run <clinit>?
    Thread.currentThread().getContextClassLoader()
);

// Form 3: initialize = false (only load and link, skip <clinit>)
Class<?> cls = Class.forName("com.example.MyClass", false, loader);

When to use initialize = false

Setting initialize = false is useful when you want to inspect class metadata (annotations, fields, methods) without triggering side effects of static initializers. Example: annotation processors, classpath scanners.

// Component scanner (simplified):
for (String className : classesOnClasspath) {
    try {
        Class<?> c = Class.forName(className, false, loader);
        if (c.isAnnotationPresent(Component.class)) {
            register(c);
        }
    } catch (ClassNotFoundException | NoClassDefFoundError e) {
        // skip
    }
}
Part 15

ClassLoader and Serialization

Serialization and classloading interact in non-obvious ways.

When you deserialize an object:

ObjectInputStream ois = new ObjectInputStream(inputStream);
MyClass obj = (MyClass) ois.readObject();

ObjectInputStream uses the context classloader (or a fallback chain) to find the MyClass definition. If the context classloader doesn't know about MyClass, deserialization throws ClassNotFoundException.

This is a common issue in:
- RMI (Remote Method Invocation) — the server receives serialized objects whose classes are on the client but not the server classpath
- Caching (Hazelcast, Infinispan) — distributed caches serialize/deserialize domain objects
- JMS messaging — message payloads are often serialized POJOs

Fix: always ensure the deserializing thread's context classloader can see the classes being deserialized.

Part 16

OSGi: The Most Sophisticated ClassLoader System

OSGi (Open Services Gateway initiative) is a dynamic module system where each bundle (a JAR with OSGi metadata) has its own ClassLoader, and visibility between bundles is controlled by Export-Package/Import-Package declarations in MANIFEST.MF.

MANIFEST.MF in bundle com.example.service:
  Bundle-SymbolicName: com.example.service
  Bundle-Version: 1.2.0
  Export-Package: com.example.service.api;version="1.2"
  Import-Package: org.slf4j;version="[1.7,2.0)"

OSGi achieves true versioned isolation: bundle A can use SLF4J 1.7 while bundle B uses SLF4J 2.0, even within the same JVM process.

Eclipse IDE, Apache Karaf, and Adobe Experience Manager are built on OSGi. The classloader complexity is why most modern projects avoid OSGi in favor of Spring Boot or the JPMS.

Part 17

Classloader in Microservices and Containers

In containerized microservices (Docker, Kubernetes), the JVM typically runs as a single application per container. This eliminates most classloader isolation concerns present in shared application servers (Tomcat, WebSphere). However:

GraalVM Native Image performs closed-world class loading at build time (ahead-of-time compilation). Dynamic class loading with Class.forName() or custom ClassLoaders requires reflection configuration (reflect-config.json) — otherwise the native image cannot include those classes.

// reflect-config.json for GraalVM:
[
  {
    "name": "com.example.MyClass",
    "allDeclaredConstructors": true,
    "allDeclaredMethods": true,
    "allDeclaredFields": true
  }
]

This matters for frameworks that rely on reflection and classloading: Hibernate, Jackson, Spring. All provide GraalVM hints via @RegisterReflectionForBinding, @ReflectiveAccess, or auto-generated hint files.

Part 18

Performance: Class Loading Overhead

Class loading is not free. In a large Spring Boot application, startup time can be dominated by class loading thousands of classes.

Startup class loading analysis (sample Spring Boot app):
  Total classes loaded:  12,847
  Class loading time:    ~1.2 seconds out of 3.5 seconds total startup
  Metaspace used:        ~128 MB

JVM flags for class loading analysis

# Log every class load/unload event
java -verbose:class -jar app.jar 2>&1 | grep "\[Loaded" | wc -l

# Print class loading statistics
java -XX:+PrintClassHistogramBeforeFullGC -jar app.jar

# Tiered class loading (default on Java 8+)
# Classes are loaded and then compiled progressively from interpreter → C1 → C2

AppCDS: Shared class archives

Application Class Data Sharing (AppCDS) reduces startup time by sharing read-only class metadata across JVM instances:

# Step 1: create class list
java -Xshare:off -XX:DumpLoadedClassList=classes.lst -jar app.jar
# (let app start, then stop)

# Step 2: create archive
java -Xshare:dump -XX:SharedClassListFile=classes.lst \
     -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app-cds.jsa -jar app.jar

# Step 3: use archive
java -Xshare:on -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app-cds.jsa -jar app.jar
# Result: 30-50% faster startup, reduced Metaspace
Part 19

Diagnosing ClassLoader Problems in Production

Step 1: Identify which ClassLoader loaded the class

Class<?> cls = obj.getClass();
System.out.println(cls.getName() + " loaded by: " + cls.getClassLoader());
// → com.example.Foo loaded by: jdk.internal.loader.ClassLoaders$AppClassLoader@5f4da5c3

Step 2: Find where on disk the class came from

URL resource = obj.getClass().getResource(
    "/" + obj.getClass().getName().replace('.', '/') + ".class"
);
System.out.println("Class file location: " + resource);
// → file:/Users/me/.m2/repository/com/example/library/1.0/library-1.0.jar!/com/example/Foo.class

Step 3: Metaspace monitoring

# Real-time Metaspace monitoring
jstat -gcmetacapacity <pid> 3s

# Output columns:
# MCMN: minimum Metaspace capacity committed
# MCMX: maximum Metaspace capacity
# MC:   current Metaspace capacity (committed)
# MU:   Metaspace utilization (used)
# CCSMN/CCSMX/CCSC/CCSU: compressed class space stats

Step 4: Classloader leak detection with heap analysis

jmap -dump:format=b,file=heap.hprof <pid>
# Open in Eclipse Memory Analyzer Tool (MAT)
# Query: SELECT * FROM java.lang.ClassLoader
# Look for custom ClassLoaders with large retained heap
Part 20

Sealed Classes, Records, and Classloading (Java 17+)

Sealed classes and records are normal Java classes from a classloading perspective — they follow all the same rules. However, the JVM enforces sealed class constraints at link time:

When class Shape is sealed with permits Circle, Rectangle, the JVM verifies during the verification phase (linking) that only Circle and Rectangle exist as direct subclasses. If a rogue .class file tries to subclass Shape, verification fails with a VerifyError.

Records compile to final classes with a synthetic <init> and explicit component accessor methods — the classloading lifecycle is identical to a regular final class.

Part 21

Interview Q&A and Architect Decision Matrix

Q1: What is the difference between ClassNotFoundException and NoClassDefFoundError?

Answer: ClassNotFoundException is a checked exception thrown when the JVM cannot find the class binary at the time Class.forName() or ClassLoader.loadClass() is called — the JAR is simply missing from the classpath. NoClassDefFoundError is an Error thrown when the class was present at compile time but is missing at runtime, or when the class's static initializer threw an exception (poisoning the class permanently). The first indicates a classpath configuration issue; the second often indicates a deployment or initialization failure.

Q2: Why does Tomcat use child-first classloading instead of parent-first?

Answer: Tomcat uses child-first for web application classloaders to achieve version isolation. Each web app gets its own ClassLoader that checks WEB-INF/classes and WEB-INF/lib before delegating to the parent. Without this, all web apps would be forced to share the same library versions from the parent, preventing deployment of apps with conflicting dependencies.

Q3: What is stored in Metaspace?

Answer: Metaspace stores class metadata: the internal Class object, bytecodes, the runtime constant pool, field and method descriptors, vtables (virtual dispatch tables), and JIT compilation data. It lives in native memory (not the Java heap), grows on demand, and is reclaimed when a ClassLoader becomes garbage-collectible.

Q4: How does Spring Boot load classes from nested JARs?

Answer: Spring Boot's JarLauncher creates a LaunchedURLClassLoader that understands the jar:file:!/BOOT-INF/lib/nested.jar!/ URL format. This custom classloader uses child-first delegation for BOOT-INF/classes and handles the nested JAR URL protocol that standard URLClassLoader cannot process.

Q5: How do you prevent ClassLoader leaks in a web application?

Answer: (1) Deregister JDBC drivers in ServletContextListener.contextDestroyed(). (2) Cancel all scheduled tasks and executor threads. (3) Remove custom classloader-referencing entries from JDK caches (Introspector, PropertyEditorManager). (4) Call ThreadLocal.remove() in servlet filters. (5) Remove shutdown hooks registered by your ClassLoader. Modern frameworks (Spring, Hibernate) handle most of these automatically, but custom integrations must be explicit.

Architect Decision Matrix: Classloading Strategy

Scenario Recommended Strategy
Single microservice, Docker Default Application ClassLoader; AppCDS for startup
Multiple apps, shared server Per-app ClassLoader (Tomcat model), child-first
Plugin system Custom ClassLoader per plugin, parent-first for API
Hot reload in dev ClassLoader-per-module reload; or Java agent retransform
GraalVM native image Closed-world; provide reflection config for dynamic loading
OSGi framework Bundle ClassLoader per bundle; Import/Export declarations
Part 22

Summary Table

Concept Key Detail
Bootstrap ClassLoader Native C++; loads java.base; parent = null
Platform ClassLoader Java 9+; loads JDK non-core modules; parent = Bootstrap
Application ClassLoader Loads classpath JARs; parent = Platform
Loading Phase Find binary → create Class object in Metaspace
Linking — Verify Validate bytecode structure and type safety
Linking — Prepare Allocate static fields with default zero values
Linking — Resolve Replace symbolic refs with direct references
Initialization Run <clinit>; thread-safe, exactly once
Delegation Model Parent-first; child loads only if parent cannot
Class Identity (name, classloader) tuple — two loaders = two classes
ClassNotFoundException Class binary not found at load time (checked)
NoClassDefFoundError Binary missing at runtime or <clinit> failed (Error)
Context ClassLoader Enables parent code to use child classloader (SPI, JNDI)
Metaspace Native memory; holds class metadata; auto-grows
ClassLoader Leak ClassLoader kept alive by static ref → Metaspace OOM
Spring Boot fat JAR LaunchedURLClassLoader reads nested JARs

AppCDS Shared class data archive; 30–50% faster startup
Custom ClassLoader Override findClass(), not loadClass()
Hidden Classes (Java 15+) Short-lived dynamic classes for frameworks/lambdas

Practice — Lesson 56

Easy Exercises

Exercise 1 — Explore the ClassLoader Hierarchy

Write a program that prints the classloader chain for String, java.sql.DriverManager, and your own class. Confirm Bootstrap shows as null.

public class ClassLoaderExplorer {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        printLoaderChain("java.lang.String");
        printLoaderChain("java.sql.DriverManager");
        printLoaderChain(ClassLoaderExplorer.class.getName());
    }

    static void printLoaderChain(String className) {
        try {
            Class<?> cls = Class.forName(className);
            System.out.println("\n=== " + className + " ===");
            ClassLoader loader = cls.getClassLoader();
            if (loader == null) {
                System.out.println("  Bootstrap (null)");
                return;
            }
            int level = 0;
            while (loader != null) {
                System.out.println("  " + "  ".repeat(level) + loader.getClass().getName());
                loader = loader.getParent();
                level++;
            }
            System.out.println("  " + "  ".repeat(level) + "Bootstrap (null)");
        } catch (ClassNotFoundException e) {
            System.err.println("Not found: " + className);
        }
    }
}

Exercise 2 — Locate the Physical Class File

For any class in your application, print the URL of the .class file on disk or inside a JAR.

public class ClassLocator {
    public static URL locate(Class<?> cls) {
        String path = "/" + cls.getName().replace('.', '/') + ".class";
        return cls.getResource(path);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(locate(String.class));
        System.out.println(locate(ClassLocator.class));
    }
}

Exercise 3 — Trigger and Catch ClassNotFoundException

Attempt to load a class that doesn't exist and handle ClassNotFoundException gracefully.

try {
    Class.forName("com.example.NonExistentClass");
} catch (ClassNotFoundException e) {
    System.out.println("Class not found: " + e.getMessage());
    System.out.println("Classloader used: " +
        Thread.currentThread().getContextClassLoader());
}

Medium Exercises

Exercise 4 — Custom ClassLoader from Byte Array

Implement a ByteArrayClassLoader that loads a class from a byte[] (simulating loading from a database or network).

public class ByteArrayClassLoader extends ClassLoader {

    public Class<?> loadFromBytes(String name, byte[] bytecode) {
        // First try parent delegation
        try {
            return getParent().loadClass(name);
        } catch (ClassNotFoundException e) {
            // Parent doesn't have it — define it ourselves
        }
        return defineClass(name, bytecode, 0, bytecode.length);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        // Read an existing .class file as bytes to test
        byte[] bytes = Files.readAllBytes(
            Path.of("target/classes/com/example/Greeter.class"));

        ByteArrayClassLoader loader = new ByteArrayClassLoader();
        Class<?> cls = loader.loadFromBytes("com.example.Greeter", bytes);

        Object instance = cls.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance();
        Method greet = cls.getMethod("greet", String.class);
        System.out.println(greet.invoke(instance, "World"));
    }
}

Exercise 5 — Demonstrate Class Identity Separation

Create two classloaders, each loading the same class. Show that the two Class objects are different and casting between them fails.

public class ClassIdentityDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        URL[] urls = {new File("target/classes").toURI().toURL()};

        URLClassLoader loader1 = new URLClassLoader(urls, null); // no parent!
        URLClassLoader loader2 = new URLClassLoader(urls, null);

        Class<?> cls1 = loader1.loadClass("com.example.Greeter");
        Class<?> cls2 = loader2.loadClass("com.example.Greeter");

        System.out.println("Same class? " + (cls1 == cls2));   // false!

        Object obj1 = cls1.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance();
        try {
            cls2.cast(obj1);  // ClassCastException!
        } catch (ClassCastException e) {
            System.out.println("Cast failed as expected: " + e.getMessage());
        }

        loader1.close();
        loader2.close();
    }
}

Exercise 6 — Reproduce NoClassDefFoundError from Failed Static Init

class PoisonedClass {
    static {
        if (true) throw new RuntimeException("Static init failed!");
    }
}

public class StaticInitDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
            try {
                new PoisonedClass();
            } catch (ExceptionInInitializerError e) {
                System.out.println("Attempt " + i + ": ExceptionInInitializerError");
            } catch (NoClassDefFoundError e) {
                System.out.println("Attempt " + i + ": NoClassDefFoundError — class is poisoned");
            }
        }
    }
}
// Output:
// Attempt 0: ExceptionInInitializerError
// Attempt 1: NoClassDefFoundError — class is poisoned
// Attempt 2: NoClassDefFoundError — class is poisoned

Advanced Exercises

Exercise 7 — Hot-Reload Simulator

Implement a classloader that watches a directory for .class file changes and reloads modified classes without restarting the JVM.

public class HotReloadClassLoader extends URLClassLoader {
    private final Map<String, Long> loadTimestamps = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final Path watchDir;

    public HotReloadClassLoader(Path watchDir, ClassLoader parent) throws MalformedURLException {
        super(new URL[]{watchDir.toUri().toURL()}, parent);
        this.watchDir = watchDir;
    }

    @Override
    public Class<?> loadClass(String name, boolean resolve) throws ClassNotFoundException {
        // Check if the .class file is newer than our cached version
        String path = name.replace('.', '/') + ".class";
        Path classFile = watchDir.resolve(path);

        if (Files.exists(classFile)) {
            long modified = classFile.toFile().lastModified();
            Long cached = loadTimestamps.get(name);

            if (cached != null && modified > cached) {
                // Class changed — we need a NEW ClassLoader (can't redefine in same loader)
                // For demo, skip re-creation; real impl would create a new loader instance
                System.out.println("[HOT-RELOAD] Detected change in: " + name);
            }

            if (cached == null) {
                // Load with child-first (bypass parent for app classes)
                try {
                    byte[] bytes = Files.readAllBytes(classFile);
                    Class<?> cls = defineClass(name, bytes, 0, bytes.length);
                    loadTimestamps.put(name, modified);
                    if (resolve) resolveClass(cls);
                    return cls;
                } catch (IOException e) {
                    // fall through to parent
                }
            }
        }
        return super.loadClass(name, resolve);
    }
}

Set up an AppCDS archive for a Spring Boot application. Measure cold startup time with and without the archive. Verify class count and Metaspace reduction.

Steps:
1. Start app with -Xshare:off -XX:DumpLoadedClassList=app-classes.lst
2. Dump archive: java -Xshare:dump -XX:SharedClassListFile=app-classes.lst -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa -jar app.jar
3. Run normally: time java -jar app.jar
4. Run with CDS: time java -Xshare:on -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa -jar app.jar
5. Compare startup time and -verbose:class class-load counts

Production Scenarios

Scenario 1 — Metaspace OOM in Tomcat

Your Tomcat server hosts 10 web applications. After 48 hours, the server logs OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace. jstat -gcmetacapacity shows Metaspace at 1.4 GB and growing after each app redeploy.

Diagnosis steps:
1. Take heap dump: jmap -dump:format=b,file=heap.hprof <pid>
2. Open in Eclipse MAT → OQL: SELECT * FROM java.lang.ClassLoader WHERE this.@retainedHeapSize > 10000000
3. Find WebAppClassLoader instances that should have been GC'd after undeploy
4. In retained set: identify the GC root keeping each ClassLoader alive (likely a static ThreadLocal or a Timer in one of the apps)

Expected findings:
- App #3 registered a ScheduledExecutorService as a static field but never shut it down on undeploy
- App #7 registered a JDBC driver but never called DriverManager.deregisterDriver()

Fix: Add ServletContextListener to each app that cleans up resources on contextDestroyed().

Scenario 2 — ClassCastException Despite Same Class Name

A ClassCastException: com.example.UserService cannot be cast to com.example.UserService appears in production. Same class name, but the cast fails.

Diagnosis: Two different ClassLoaders loaded UserService. This can happen when:
- A framework (e.g., Spring) has its own copy of a class in its own ClassLoader
- The class is on both WEB-INF/lib and the server's shared lib folder
- Two OSGi bundles each define the same class in their private space

Fix: Identify which ClassLoader is responsible for each instance:

log.error("Expected loader: {}, Actual loader: {}",
    UserService.class.getClassLoader(),
    obj.getClass().getClassLoader());

Remove the duplicate class from one of the classpath locations.

Debugging Exercises

Debug 1 — Missing JAR

The following stack trace appears at startup. What is the root cause and how do you fix it?

Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: org/slf4j/LoggerFactory
    at com.example.Application.<clinit>(Application.java:12)
Caused by: java.lang.ClassNotFoundException: org.slf4j.LoggerFactory
    at java.base/jdk.internal.loader.BuiltinClassLoader.loadClass(...)

Answer: The static final Logger LOG = LoggerFactory.getLogger(...) in Application's static initializer cannot find SLF4J. ClassNotFoundException (the cause) means slf4j-api.jar is not on the runtime classpath, even though it was present at compile time. Fix: add slf4j-api and an SLF4J binding (logback-classic or slf4j-simple) to the runtime classpath/dependencies.

Debug 2 — Metaspace Leak

jstat -gcmetacapacity shows Metaspace growing by ~20 MB per minute. The application uses a custom scripting engine that evaluates user-provided Groovy scripts at runtime. Identify the leak.

Answer: Each Groovy script evaluation creates a new GroovyClassLoader (or reuses one but generates a new class per script). If the classloaders are not closed and garbage collected, all generated class metadata accumulates in Metaspace. Fix:

// Wrong: create a new GroovyClassLoader per eval, never close it
GroovyClassLoader gcl = new GroovyClassLoader();
Script script = gcl.parseClass(scriptText).getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance();

// Right: use a shared, bounded script cache with GroovyShell + CompilerConfiguration
// or call gcl.close() when the script instance is done
try (GroovyClassLoader gcl = new GroovyClassLoader()) {
    return gcl.parseClass(scriptText).getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance();
}

Interview Challenges

Challenge 1

"A colleague says 'I can load the same class twice to get two independent instances with separate static state.' Is this possible, and how?"

Answer: Yes — but only if you load the class with two different ClassLoaders. The same ClassLoader caches classes by name (via findLoadedClass), so calling loadClass("Foo") twice on the same loader returns the same Class object. But two separate ClassLoader instances (with null parent, so no parent caching) will produce two distinct Class objects with independent static fields and independent <clinit> execution. This is exactly how Tomcat gives each web app independent static state for shared libraries.

Challenge 2

"You see this in the logs: NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class com.example.Config. What exactly happened, and how do you debug it?"

Answer: The class Config was successfully loaded (binary found) but its <clinit> method threw an exception. The very first access threw ExceptionInInitializerError, and now every subsequent access throws NoClassDefFoundError because the JVM marks the class as permanently uninitialized. Debug by searching logs for ExceptionInInitializerError (it appears earlier, possibly swallowed). Enable -verbose:class to confirm the class was loaded. Then review Config's static blocks and static field initializers for the failure point — common causes include reading a missing system property, parsing an invalid configuration file, or connecting to a resource not available at startup.

Challenge 3

"Describe the difference between URLClassLoader and SecureClassLoader. When would you use each?"

Answer: SecureClassLoader extends ClassLoader and adds the concept of code sources and protection domains — each defined class is tagged with where its bytecode came from (URL) and what permissions it has (via java.security.Policy). URLClassLoader extends SecureClassLoader and adds the ability to load classes from a list of URLs (files, directories, JARs). For most purposes you use URLClassLoader or its subclasses. You would work with SecureClassLoader directly only if you are implementing a custom security domain — for example, a sandbox that restricts the permissions of untrusted dynamically loaded plugins.

Key Takeaways

  • Three classloaders form the JVM default hierarchy: Bootstrap (C++, core JDK), Platform (non-core modules), Application (classpath)
  • Parent-first delegation ensures core classes (java.lang, java.util) are always loaded by Bootstrap, preventing substitution attacks and ClassCastException across loaders
  • Loading → Linking (Verify/Prepare/Resolve) → Initialization is the strict three-phase lifecycle; static fields are zero until Initialization; <clinit> runs exactly once
  • ClassNotFoundException = binary not found at load time; NoClassDefFoundError = binary missing at runtime OR <clinit> failed — these need different fixes
  • Metaspace replaced PermGen in Java 8; it lives in native memory and grows automatically — set -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize in production to prevent unbounded growth
  • ClassLoader leaks occur when objects loaded by a ClassLoader are referenced from GC roots outside it (statics, thread pools, JDBC drivers, shutdown hooks) — the ClassLoader and all its Metaspace is retained
  • Spring Boot fat JARs require a custom LaunchedURLClassLoader because standard classloaders cannot read JARs nested inside JARs
  • Tomcat/OSGi use child-first (inverted) delegation to achieve per-app version isolation
  • AppCDS archives shared class metadata across JVM instances, yielding 30–50% startup improvements
  • GraalVM native images perform closed-world class loading at build time — dynamic Class.forName() requires explicit reflection configuration
