Part 1

What Is Bytecode and Why It Exists

When the Java compiler (javac) compiles HelloWorld.java, it does not produce native machine code for your CPU. Instead it produces Java bytecode — an intermediate binary format designed to run on the Java Virtual Machine, not directly on hardware.

This is the origin of the Java promise: "Write Once, Run Anywhere."

Source Code → javac → Bytecode → JVM → Native Code
────────────────────────────────────────────────────
HelloWorld.java → HelloWorld.class → JVM interprets/JIT-compiles → x86/ARM/RISC-V

Bytecode is:
- Platform independent: the same .class file runs on Windows, Linux, macOS, ARM — any platform with a JVM
- Compact: bytecode instructions are 1–5 bytes long; much denser than source
- Verifiable: the JVM can cryptographically verify bytecode is well-formed before executing it
- Optimizable: the JIT compiler sees the bytecode and can apply aggressive platform-specific optimizations
- Not source code: bytecode is harder to read than Java but much easier to reverse-engineer than native binaries — this is why ProGuard/R8/Obfuscation tools exist

Other JVM languages (Kotlin, Scala, Groovy, Clojure) all compile to the same bytecode format. To the JVM, a Kotlin class and a Java class are indistinguishable at runtime.

Part 2

The .class File Format: Binary Layout

Every .class file follows a precise binary format defined in the JVM Specification. Understanding this structure is essential for tooling, instrumentation, and debugging.

ClassFile {
    u4             magic;               // 0xCAFEBABE
    u2             minor_version;       // e.g., 0
    u2             major_version;       // e.g., 65 (Java 21)
    u2             constant_pool_count;
    cp_info        constant_pool[constant_pool_count-1];
    u2             access_flags;        // ACC_PUBLIC, ACC_FINAL, etc.
    u2             this_class;          // index into constant pool
    u2             super_class;         // index into constant pool
    u2             interfaces_count;
    u2             interfaces[interfaces_count];
    u2             fields_count;
    field_info     fields[fields_count];
    u2             methods_count;
    method_info    methods[methods_count];
    u2             attributes_count;
    attribute_info attributes[attributes_count];
}

The magic number

Every .class file begins with 0xCAFEBABE. The JVM immediately rejects any file that doesn't start with this value. This is not arbitrary — it was chosen by James Gosling (Java's creator) as a playful identifier.

Class file version numbers

Java Version Major Version Minor Version
Java 8 52 0
Java 11 55 0
Java 17 61 0
Java 21 65 0
Java 24 68 0

If you compile with Java 21 (--release 21) and try to run on a Java 11 JVM, you get:

Error: LinkageError occurred while loading main class HelloWorld
    java.lang.UnsupportedClassVersionError: HelloWorld has been compiled by
    a more recent version of the Java Runtime (class file version 65.0),
    this version of the Java Runtime only recognizes class file versions up to 55.0
Part 3

The Constant Pool: The Class's Symbol Table

The constant pool is the most important structure in a .class file. It acts as the class's symbol table — a compact array of reusable constants that all other parts of the class file reference by index.

Constant Pool entries (types):
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#1   CONSTANT_Utf8          "HelloWorld"
#2   CONSTANT_Class         → #1          (class name reference)
#3   CONSTANT_Utf8          "java/lang/Object"
#4   CONSTANT_Class         → #3
#5   CONSTANT_Utf8          "main"
#6   CONSTANT_Utf8          "([Ljava/lang/String;)V"  (method descriptor)
#7   CONSTANT_NameAndType   → #5, #6      (method name + descriptor)
#8   CONSTANT_Utf8          "java/lang/System"
#9   CONSTANT_Class         → #8
#10  CONSTANT_Utf8          "out"
#11  CONSTANT_Utf8          "Ljava/io/PrintStream;"
#12  CONSTANT_NameAndType   → #10, #11    (field name + type)
#13  CONSTANT_Fieldref      → #9, #12     ("System.out" field)
#14  CONSTANT_Utf8          "Hello, World!"
#15  CONSTANT_String        → #14
...

Constant pool entry types

Tag Type Description
1 CONSTANT_Utf8 Modified UTF-8 string (class names, method names, descriptors)
3 CONSTANT_Integer 32-bit int constant
4 CONSTANT_Float 32-bit float constant
5 CONSTANT_Long 64-bit long constant
6 CONSTANT_Double 64-bit double constant
7 CONSTANT_Class Class or interface reference
8 CONSTANT_String java.lang.String literal
9 CONSTANT_Fieldref Field reference (class + name/type)
10 CONSTANT_Methodref Method reference (class + name/descriptor)
11 CONSTANT_InterfaceMethodref Interface method reference
12 CONSTANT_NameAndType Name + descriptor pair
15 CONSTANT_MethodHandle Lambdas, method references
16 CONSTANT_MethodType Lambda invocation type
17 CONSTANT_Dynamic Dynamic constant (JEP 309, Java 11)
18 CONSTANT_InvokeDynamic invokedynamic bootstrap info
19 CONSTANT_Module Module name (JPMS)
20 CONSTANT_Package Package name (JPMS)

Runtime Constant Pool

At class loading time, the constant pool in the .class file (a static structure) is transformed into the Runtime Constant Pool stored in Metaspace. Symbolic references (CONSTANT_Class, CONSTANT_Methodref, CONSTANT_Fieldref) are resolved to direct memory references (pointers to classes, method tables, field offsets) — either eagerly during resolution or lazily on first use.

Part 4

Type Descriptors and Method Signatures

Bytecode uses a compact notation for types. Understanding this notation is essential for reading javap output, writing bytecode directly (ASM), or debugging stack traces.

Field type descriptors

Descriptor Java Type
B byte
C char
D double
F float
I int
J long
S short
Z boolean
V void
Lfully/qualified/ClassName; Object reference
[descriptor Array of descriptor

Method descriptor examples

()V                              → void method()
(I)V                             → void method(int)
(Ljava/lang/String;)I            → int method(String)
([Ljava/lang/String;)V           → void main(String[])
(ILjava/lang/String;D)Z          → boolean method(int, String, double)
([[I)V                           → void method(int[][])

Method descriptors in bytecode carry no parameter names — names are optional and stored in the LocalVariableTable attribute (only if compiled with -g). This is why stack traces show parameter types but not names in older JVMs.

Part 5

The Stack-Based Execution Model

The JVM is a stack-based virtual machine. Unlike register-based machines (x86, ARM), the JVM has no general-purpose registers. Instead, each method execution uses two data structures:

Operand Stack

A LIFO stack for computation. Most instructions either push values onto it or pop values from it.

int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }

Operand stack evolution:
  []                  ← initial state
  [a]                 ← iload_1 (push local variable slot 1)
  [a, b]              ← iload_2 (push local variable slot 2)
  [a+b]               ← iadd (pop two ints, push their sum)
  []                  ← ireturn (pop result and return it to caller)

Local Variable Array

A fixed-size array (slots) holding method parameters and local variables. Slot 0 is this for instance methods.

int multiply(int x, int y) {
    int result = x * y;
    return result;
}

Local Variable Array:
  slot 0: this          (for instance method)
  slot 1: x (int)
  slot 2: y (int)
  slot 3: result (int)

long and double values occupy two consecutive slots.

Stack Frame

Each method call creates a stack frame on the JVM's call stack. The frame contains:
- The operand stack for the current method
- The local variable array
- A reference to the current method's runtime constant pool

Call Stack:
┌─────────────────────────────────┐
│ Frame: UserService.processOrder │  ← current method
│   local vars: [this, orderId]   │
│   operand stack: [order, userId]│
├─────────────────────────────────┤
│ Frame: OrderController.create   │
│   local vars: [this, request]   │
│   operand stack: []             │
├─────────────────────────────────┤
│ Frame: main                     │
│   local vars: [args]            │
│   operand stack: []             │
└─────────────────────────────────┘
Part 6

The javap Disassembler

javap is the JDK's built-in bytecode disassembler. It is an essential tool for understanding what the compiler actually generates.

# Disassemble with verbose output (shows constant pool, stack sizes, local var tables)
javap -verbose -p HelloWorld.class

# Show bytecode for all methods (including private)
javap -c -p HelloWorld.class

# Show line number table (source line → bytecode offset mapping)
javap -l HelloWorld.class

# Disassemble a class inside a JAR
javap -c -p -classpath app.jar com.example.HelloWorld

Sample javap output

// Source:
public class HelloWorld {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Hello, World!");
    }
}

// javap -verbose HelloWorld:
Classfile /path/HelloWorld.class
  Last modified: 2026-06-29; size 423 bytes
  SHA-256 checksum: abc123...
  Compiled from "HelloWorld.java"
public class HelloWorld
  minor version: 0
  major version: 65
  flags: (0x0021) ACC_PUBLIC, ACC_SUPER
  this_class: #21          // HelloWorld
  super_class: #2          // java/lang/Object
  interfaces: 0, fields: 0, methods: 2, attributes: 1

Constant pool:
   #1 = Methodref      #2.#3        // java/lang/Object."<init>":()V
   #2 = Class          #4           // java/lang/Object
   #3 = NameAndType    #5:#6        // "<init>":()V
   #4 = Utf8           java/lang/Object
   #5 = Utf8           <init>
   #6 = Utf8           ()V
   ...
  #21 = Class          #22          // HelloWorld
  #22 = Utf8           HelloWorld

public static void main(java.lang.String[]);
  descriptor: ([Ljava/lang/String;)V
  flags: (0x0009) ACC_PUBLIC, ACC_STATIC
  Code:
    stack=2, locals=1, args_size=1
       0: getstatic     #7     // Field java/lang/System.out:Ljava/io/PrintStream;
       3: ldc           #13    // String Hello, World!
       5: invokevirtual #15    // Method java/io/PrintStream.println:(Ljava/lang/String;)V
       8: return
    LineNumberTable:
      line 3: 0
      line 4: 8

Key fields in the Code attribute header:
- stack=2: operand stack depth needed (2 slots: one for System.out, one for the String)
- locals=1: one local variable slot (just args)
- args_size=1: one argument (String[] args)

Part 7

Core Opcode Categories

The JVM instruction set has ~200 opcodes organized into categories. Knowing the most important ones unlocks your ability to read any bytecode.

Load and Store Instructions

These move data between the local variable array and the operand stack.

iload_<n>   load int from local slot n          (n = 0,1,2,3)
lload_<n>   load long from local slot n
fload_<n>   load float from local slot n
dload_<n>   load double from local slot n
aload_<n>   load object reference from local slot n

istore_<n>  store int to local slot n
lstore_<n>  store long to local slot n
astore_<n>  store object reference to local slot n

iload       load int from slot (any index, follows with index byte)
aload       load reference from slot (any index)

// int x = 10; int y = x + 5;
bipush 10      // push byte constant 10 as int
istore_1       // store in slot 1 (x)
iload_1        // load x
iconst_5       // push constant 5
iadd           // pop 2 ints, push sum
istore_2       // store in slot 2 (y)

Constant Push Instructions

iconst_<n>   push int constant (n = -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
lconst_<n>   push long constant (n = 0, 1)
fconst_<n>   push float constant (n = 0, 1, 2)
dconst_<n>   push double constant (n = 0, 1)
aconst_null  push null reference
bipush       push byte as int (-128 to 127)
sipush       push short as int (-32768 to 32767)
ldc          load constant from constant pool (String, int, float, Class, MethodHandle)
ldc_w        load constant (wide index)
ldc2_w       load long/double constant (wide index)

Arithmetic Instructions

iadd, isub, imul, idiv, irem    int arithmetic
ladd, lsub, lmul, ldiv, lrem    long arithmetic
fadd, fsub, fmul, fdiv, frem    float arithmetic
dadd, dsub, dmul, ddiv, drem    double arithmetic
ineg, lneg, fneg, dneg          negate
iinc <index> <const>            increment local int variable by constant (for loops!)

Type Conversion Instructions

i2l, i2f, i2d, i2b, i2c, i2s    int → long/float/double/byte/char/short
l2i, l2f, l2d                    long → int/float/double
f2i, f2l, f2d                    float → int/long/double
d2i, d2l, d2f                    double → int/long/float
checkcast  <type>                cast reference (throws ClassCastException on failure)
instanceof <type>                test reference type (pushes 0 or 1)

Object and Array Instructions

new <class>             allocate object (without calling constructor)
invokespecial           call <init> constructor or super method
getfield  <field>       get instance field
putfield  <field>       set instance field
getstatic <field>       get static field
putstatic <field>       set static field
arraylength             get array length
newarray   <type>       create primitive array
anewarray  <class>      create reference array
multianewarray          create multi-dimensional array
Part 8

Method Invocation Opcodes

This is one of the most important opcode categories. There are five invocation opcodes, each for a different dispatch scenario.

invokevirtual

Used for instance method calls where the actual method depends on the runtime type of the object (polymorphism).

animal.speak();  // if Animal.speak() is overridden in Dog, calls Dog.speak() at runtime

aload_1         // push the 'animal' reference
invokevirtual  #5   // Animal.speak:()V  ← dispatched virtually at runtime

invokeinterface

Like invokevirtual but for interface method calls. Has slightly different dispatch mechanics (interface vtable vs object vtable).

List<String> list = new ArrayList<>();
list.add("hello");

aload_1
ldc            #3    // "hello"
invokeinterface #7, 2  // java/util/List.add:(Ljava/lang/Object;)Z

The extra argument 2 is the argument count (including the receiver), a historical artifact of the JVM spec.

invokespecial

Used for three specific cases:
1. Constructors (<init>)
2. private method calls (no virtual dispatch needed)
3. super.method() calls

super.processOrder(orderId);

aload_0         // push 'this'
iload_1         // push 'orderId'
invokespecial  #9   // BaseService.processOrder:(I)V

invokestatic

Used for static method calls. No object reference is passed as the first argument.

Math.max(a, b);

iload_1
iload_2
invokestatic  #11  // java/lang/Math.max:(II)I

invokedynamic

The most powerful and complex invocation opcode. Introduced in Java 7 for dynamic languages; used heavily since Java 8 for lambda expressions and string concatenation.

Runnable r = () -> System.out.println("Hello from lambda");

invokedynamic #1, 0   // #1 = BootstrapMethods[0]
                      // InvokeDynamic → java.lang.invoke.LambdaMetafactory.metafactory

On first call, invokedynamic calls a bootstrap method (LambdaMetafactory.metafactory) that generates an anonymous class implementing Runnable and links the call site to that class's run() method. On subsequent calls, the call site is already linked — overhead is minimal.

Part 9

Control Flow Instructions

if_icmpeq <offset>     branch if int top-of-stack == next
if_icmpne <offset>     branch if int !=
if_icmplt <offset>     branch if int <
if_icmpge <offset>     branch if int >=
if_icmpgt <offset>     branch if int >
if_icmple <offset>     branch if int <=
ifnull   <offset>      branch if reference == null
ifnonnull <offset>     branch if reference != null
ifeq, ifne, iflt, ifge, ifgt, ifle    branch on comparison to zero

goto     <offset>      unconditional branch
tableswitch            switch with continuous integer range (optimized)
lookupswitch           switch with sparse integers (binary-searched)

ireturn, lreturn, freturn, dreturn, areturn   return typed value
return                                          return void

How a for-loop compiles

for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
    sum += i;
}

iconst_0        // i = 0
istore_1        // store i
[loop_start: offset 3]
iload_1         // load i
bipush 10       // push 10
if_icmpge 20    // if i >= 10, jump to offset 20 (exit)
iload_2         // load sum
iload_1         // load i
iadd            // sum + i
istore_2        // store sum
iinc 1, 1       // i++ (increment local slot 1 by 1)
goto 3          // jump back to loop_start
[offset 20: exit]

The iinc instruction is a special optimization for loop counters — it modifies the local variable directly without going through the operand stack.

Part 10

Exception Handling in Bytecode

Java's try-catch-finally compiles to an exception table embedded in the method's Code attribute.

try {
    return doWork();
} catch (IOException e) {
    log.error("IO error", e);
    return -1;
} finally {
    cleanup();
}

Exception table:
 from    to    target    type
    0     8        12    java/io/IOException   // catch block
    0     8        24    any                   // finally (for normal path)
   12    16        24    any                   // finally (for catch block)

Each row means: if an exception of type is thrown at any bytecode offset in [from, to), jump to target. The any type means "match any Throwable" — this implements finally.

finally blocks are duplicated by the compiler: one copy appears for normal execution, one for each catch block. This is why finally cannot be optimized away and is guaranteed to run.

athrow instruction

Throwing an exception is a single bytecode instruction:

throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad input");

new           #5    // allocate IllegalArgumentException
dup                 // duplicate reference (one for constructor, one for throw)
ldc           #7    // "bad input"
invokespecial #9    // IllegalArgumentException.<init>:(Ljava/lang/String;)V
athrow              // pop and throw the exception
Part 11

String Concatenation Bytecode (Java 8 vs Java 9+)

String concatenation is a common operation with a fascinating bytecode evolution.

Java 8 and earlier: StringBuilder

String s = "Hello, " + name + "!";

Compiled in Java 8:

new           #3    // StringBuilder
dup
invokespecial #4    // StringBuilder.<init>
ldc           #5    // "Hello, "
invokevirtual #6    // StringBuilder.append:(Ljava/lang/String;)LStringBuilder;
aload_1             // name
invokevirtual #6    // StringBuilder.append:(Ljava/lang/String;)LStringBuilder;
ldc           #7    // "!"
invokevirtual #6    // StringBuilder.append:(Ljava/lang/String;)LStringBuilder;
invokevirtual #8    // StringBuilder.toString:()Ljava/lang/String;

Three method calls, object allocation, defensive copies.

Java 9+: invokedynamic + StringConcatFactory

String s = "Hello, " + name + "!";

Compiled in Java 9+:

aload_1                // push name
invokedynamic #1, 0    // StringConcatFactory.makeConcatWithConstants
                       // recipe = "Hello, \u0001!"  (\u0001 = placeholder for arg)

A single invokedynamic instruction. The StringConcatFactory bootstrap generates an optimized implementation at first call (potentially using VarHandle + byte[] manipulation, MethodHandle combinators, etc.). This is faster AND more compact than the Java 8 approach.

Part 12

Lambda Expressions in Bytecode

Lambdas are one of the most interesting bytecode-level features in modern Java.

List<String> names = List.of("Alice", "Bob", "Charlie");
names.stream()
     .filter(s -> s.startsWith("A"))
     .forEach(System.out::println);

The compiler generates two things:

1. A synthetic method in the enclosing class for the lambda body:

private static boolean lambda$main$0(java.lang.String);
  Code:
    aload_0
    ldc           #5    // "A"
    invokevirtual #6    // String.startsWith:(Ljava/lang/String;)Z
    ireturn

2. An invokedynamic call that links at runtime to a generated class implementing Predicate<String>:

invokedynamic #7, 0   // LambdaMetafactory.metafactory(...)
                      // → generates anonymous class:
                      //   class HelloWorld$$Lambda$1 implements Predicate<String> {
                      //     boolean test(String s) { return HelloWorld.lambda$main$0(s); }
                      //   }

The key insight: the anonymous Predicate class is generated at runtime, not compile time. This is why lambdas don't appear as .class files but as $$Lambda$ classes visible in profilers and heap dumps.

Capturing variables

Lambdas that capture local variables pass them as arguments to the generated class's constructor:

String prefix = "Hello";
Predicate<String> p = s -> s.startsWith(prefix);
// The generated class stores 'prefix' as a field, passed via constructor
Part 13

Generics and Type Erasure in Bytecode

Java generics exist only in source code. After compilation, all generic type parameters are erased:

// Source:
List<String> list = new ArrayList<>();
list.add("hello");
String s = list.get(0);

// Bytecode (types erased):
new java/util/ArrayList       // no <String>
invokespecial ArrayList.<init>:()V
astore_1

aload_1
ldc "hello"
invokeinterface List.add:(Ljava/lang/Object;)Z   // Object, not String
pop

aload_1
iconst_0
invokeinterface List.get:(I)Ljava/lang/Object;    // returns Object
checkcast java/lang/String                         // compiler inserts cast!
astore_2

The checkcast instruction is inserted by the compiler wherever a generic type is used in a non-Object context. This is why you get ClassCastException at the cast point, not at the add() site, when a heap pollution occurs.

Generic type information IS preserved in class metadata via Signature attributes — but this is used only by the compiler and reflection API, not by the JVM at execution time.

Part 14

The Code Attribute: Deep Dive

Every non-abstract, non-native method has a Code attribute containing:

Code {
    u2 attribute_name_index;     // "Code" in constant pool
    u4 attribute_length;
    u2 max_stack;                // maximum operand stack depth
    u2 max_locals;               // local variable array size
    u4 code_length;
    u1 code[code_length];        // the actual bytecode
    u2 exception_table_length;
    {   u2 start_pc;             // try block start
        u2 end_pc;               // try block end (exclusive)
        u2 handler_pc;           // catch block entry point
        u2 catch_type;           // exception type (0 = any, for finally)
    } exception_table[...];
    u2 attributes_count;
    attribute_info attributes[...];   // sub-attributes:
}

Key sub-attributes of Code

LineNumberTable: maps bytecode offsets to source line numbers. Used by the JVM to produce meaningful stack traces. Present only when compiled with debug info.

LineNumberTable:
  line 5: 0      // source line 5 → bytecode offset 0
  line 6: 4      // source line 6 → bytecode offset 4
  line 7: 8

LocalVariableTable: maps bytecode offset ranges to local variable names and types. Enables IDE debuggers to show named variables. Only present with -g flag.

LocalVariableTypeTable: for generics — stores the parameterized type signature of local variables (e.g., List<String> instead of just List).

StackMapTable: (Java 6+) pre-computed type state at each branch target and exception handler, enabling fast bytecode verification (the verifier no longer needs to do dataflow analysis).

Part 15

Bytecode Manipulation Libraries

Directly reading and modifying bytecode powers many foundational Java tools.

ASM

The lowest-level, fastest library. Used by the JVM itself (GroovyClassLoader, Kotlin compiler) and most other libraries.

// Use ASM to add a println to the start of every method
ClassWriter cw = new ClassWriter(ClassWriter.COMPUTE_FRAMES);
ClassReader cr = new ClassReader(originalBytecode);

cr.accept(new ClassVisitor(ASM9, cw) {
    @Override
    public MethodVisitor visitMethod(int access, String name, String desc,
                                     String signature, String[] exceptions) {
        MethodVisitor mv = super.visitMethod(access, name, desc, signature, exceptions);
        return new MethodVisitor(ASM9, mv) {
            @Override
            public void visitCode() {
                super.visitCode();
                // Inject: System.out.println("Entering " + name);
                mv.visitFieldInsn(GETSTATIC, "java/lang/System", "out", "Ljava/io/PrintStream;");
                mv.visitLdcInsn("Entering " + name);
                mv.visitMethodInsn(INVOKEVIRTUAL, "java/io/PrintStream",
                                   "println", "(Ljava/lang/String;)V", false);
            }
        };
    }
}, 0);

byte[] modifiedBytecode = cw.toByteArray();

Javassist

Higher-level — lets you write Java source code snippets that get compiled to bytecode:

ClassPool pool = ClassPool.getDefault();
CtClass cc = pool.get("com.example.UserService");
CtMethod method = cc.getDeclaredMethod("processOrder");

// Insert code before method body using Java syntax
method.insertBefore("System.out.println(\"Entering processOrder with: \" + $1);");
method.insertAfter("System.out.println(\"Exiting processOrder\");");

byte[] bytecode = cc.toBytecode();

ByteBuddy

The most modern library; used by Mockito, Hibernate, and Spring for proxy generation:

Class<?> dynamicType = new ByteBuddy()
    .subclass(Object.class)
    .method(ElementMatchers.named("toString"))
    .intercept(FixedValue.value("Hello from ByteBuddy!"))
    .make()
    .load(ClassLoader.getSystemClassLoader())
    .getLoaded();

System.out.println(dynamicType.newInstance().toString());
// → Hello from ByteBuddy!
Part 16

Practical javap Patterns for Production Debugging

javap is invaluable when debugging production issues where you suspect:
- Compiler optimizations changed behavior
- A library JAR version doesn't match what you expect
- You need to confirm whether a synchronized block was compiled correctly
- You're debugging a VerifyError or ClassFormatError

Pattern 1: Verify class version

# Quick check: what Java version compiled this class?
javap -verbose MyClass.class | grep "major version"
# major version: 55  →  Java 11

Pattern 2: Find all method calls in a method

javap -c -p com.example.UserService | grep "invoke"
# invokevirtual #23  // Method com/example/dao/UserDao.findById:(J)Ljava/util/Optional;
# invokestatic  #29  // Method org/slf4j/LoggerFactory.getLogger:(...)

Pattern 3: Confirm synchronized block structure

public void transfer(Account from, Account to, BigDecimal amount) {
    synchronized(from) {
        synchronized(to) {
            // transfer logic
        }
    }
}

javap -c AccountService.class
# You'll see: monitorenter / monitorexit pairs
# 0: aload_1
# 1: dup
# 2: astore_3         ← save monitor object for finally block
# 3: monitorenter
# ...
# 20: monitorexit     ← normal path
# ...
# 26: monitorexit     ← exception path (finally block)

Every monitorenter requires two monitorexit instructions (one for normal exit, one for exceptional exit) — the compiler generates the second in an implicit finally block.

Pattern 4: Understand switch optimization

switch (status) {
    case 0: return "OPEN";
    case 1: return "CLOSED";
    case 2: return "PENDING";
}

javap -c OrderService.class
# tableswitch { 0: ..., 1: ..., 2: ..., default: }
# Compiler chose tableswitch (continuous range: 0,1,2)

switch (status) {
    case 0: return "OPEN";
    case 100: return "CLOSED";
    case 9999: return "PENDING";
}

# lookupswitch { 0: ..., 100: ..., 9999: ..., default: }
# Sparse values → binary-searched lookupswitch is more efficient
Part 17

VerifyError and ClassFormatError

The JVM verifier rejects bytecode that would compromise runtime safety. Two common errors:

VerifyError

java.lang.VerifyError: Bad type on operand stack
    at java.base/java.lang.ClassLoader.defineClass1(ClassLoader.java)

Causes:
- Bytecode generated by a buggy ASM transformation (wrong operand type on stack)
- Manually crafted bytecode with wrong stack depth
- ClassWriter.COMPUTE_FRAMES not used when required (stack frames out of sync)
- Attempting to assign incompatible types to local variables

ClassFormatError

java.lang.ClassFormatError: Truncated class file

Causes:
- Corrupted .class file (disk error, incomplete write, truncated download)
- Binary that starts with 0xCAFEBABE but isn't a real class file
- Class file compiled for an unsupported future version

UnsupportedClassVersionError

java.lang.UnsupportedClassVersionError: HelloWorld has been compiled by 
a more recent version of the Java Runtime (class file version 65.0)

Always check java -version vs javac -version when this appears. The common cause is Docker images that include a newer JDK for compilation but an older JRE for running.

Part 18

JVM Bytecode and Performance

The bytecode is just the input to the JVM. The actual execution performance depends on what the JVM does with it.

Interpretation

When a class is first loaded, the JVM interprets the bytecode — an interpreter loop fetches each opcode and executes it. This is slow (10–100x slower than native code) but fast to start.

JIT Compilation (Tiered Compilation)

The HotSpot JVM uses tiered compilation with multiple levels:

Level 0: Interpreter
    ↓  (method called ≥ 2000 times OR loop iterated ≥ 10,000 times)
Level 1: C1 (client compiler) — quick, lightweight native code
    ↓  (continued "hot" usage)
Level 2–3: C1 with profiling data collection
    ↓  (method is truly hot — most CPU time)
Level 4: C2 (server compiler) — aggressive optimizations, peak performance

JIT-compiled code is stored in the Code Cache (native memory, separate from Metaspace).

What JIT can do with bytecode

  • Inlining: replace invokevirtual with the callee's code directly (eliminates call overhead)
  • Dead code elimination: remove code branches never taken
  • Loop unrolling: expand loop bodies to reduce branch overhead
  • Escape analysis: allocate objects on the stack instead of heap if they don't escape the method
  • Null check elimination: omit redundant null checks after the first
  • Intrinsics: replace known methods (Math.sqrt, System.arraycopy, String.equals) with hand-crafted CPU instructions

The bytecode is what JIT starts with; peak performance is driven by JIT quality, not bytecode quality.

Part 19

Bytecode and Java Agents

Java agents use the Instrumentation API to intercept class loading and transform bytecode before it is used. This is how APM tools (Datadog, New Relic, Dynatrace) add tracing without code changes.

// In a javaagent (loaded via -javaagent:agent.jar):
public class TracingAgent {
    public static void premain(String agentArgs, Instrumentation inst) {
        inst.addTransformer((loader, className, classBeingRedefined,
                             protectionDomain, classfileBuffer) -> {
            if (className.startsWith("com/example/")) {
                return addTracingBytecode(classfileBuffer);
            }
            return null; // null = no transformation
        });
    }

    private static byte[] addTracingBytecode(byte[] original) {
        ClassReader cr = new ClassReader(original);
        ClassWriter cw = new ClassWriter(cr, ClassWriter.COMPUTE_FRAMES);
        cr.accept(new TracingClassVisitor(cw), 0);
        return cw.toByteArray();
    }
}

The transformer receives the raw bytecode bytes before the JVM processes them. It can:
- Add method entry/exit tracing
- Inject performance counters
- Add null-check assertions
- Rewrite method bodies

This is also how coverage tools (JaCoCo), mutation testing (PIT), and security frameworks (RASP) work.

Part 20

Bytecode in Modern Java: Records, Sealed Classes, Text Blocks

Records (Java 16+)

A record compiles to a final class with synthetic accessor methods, equals, hashCode, and toString:

record Point(int x, int y) {}

// javap output:
public final class Point extends java.lang.Record {
  private final int x;
  private final int y;

  public Point(int, int);          // canonical constructor
  public int x();                  // accessor (not getX!)
  public int y();
  public boolean equals(Object);   // generated
  public int hashCode();           // generated
  public String toString();        // generated: "Point[x=1, y=2]"
}

Text Blocks (Java 15+)

String json = """
    {"name": "Alice", "age": 30}
    """;

Text blocks compile to a regular String constant in the constant pool. The compiler handles indentation stripping and line ending normalization at compile time — there is no runtime overhead.

Switch Expressions (Java 14+)

int result = switch (day) {
    case MONDAY, FRIDAY, SUNDAY -> 6;
    case TUESDAY                -> 7;
    default                     -> 8;
};

Switch expressions compile to tableswitch or lookupswitch just like switch statements. The arrow form is purely syntactic sugar — the bytecode uses the same structure, with the expression's value pushed onto the operand stack rather than stored via istore.

Part 21

Interview Q&A and Architect Decision Matrix

Q1: What is the difference between invokevirtual and invokeinterface?

Answer: Both perform virtual dispatch based on the runtime type of the receiver. invokevirtual is used when calling a method on a class reference — the JVM uses the class's vtable (virtual method table), indexed by a slot number known at compile time. invokeinterface is used when calling through an interface reference — the JVM cannot use a fixed vtable slot because the same interface may be implemented by unrelated classes at different vtable positions, so it performs a more expensive interface method table lookup. In practice, HotSpot optimizes invokeinterface with inline caches, minimizing the performance difference for monomorphic call sites.

Q2: Why does Java have both checkcast and instanceof opcodes?

Answer: checkcast performs a cast and throws ClassCastException if the check fails — it is used to implement explicit casts in source code (e.g., (String) obj). instanceof tests the type and pushes 1 (true) or 0 (false) onto the stack without throwing — it implements the instanceof operator. checkcast may throw an exception; instanceof never throws. The JVM uses these separately so the compiler can generate efficient code for the two distinct Java language semantics.

Q3: What is the StackMapTable attribute and why was it added?

Answer: Introduced in Java 6 (mandatory from Java 7+), the StackMapTable stores pre-computed type information at every branch target and exception handler entry point in a method. Before Java 6, the bytecode verifier had to perform a full dataflow analysis to determine what types were on the stack at each point — expensive for startup. With StackMapTable, verification is reduced to a single linear pass that checks the declared types against actual bytecode behavior. This significantly speeds up class loading and verification at the cost of slightly larger .class files.

Q4: How do lambda expressions avoid creating a .class file per lambda?

Answer: Pre-Java 8 anonymous inner classes created one .class file per instantiation site. Lambdas use invokedynamic + LambdaMetafactory: the bootstrap method generates an anonymous class implementing the functional interface at runtime, on first call. This class is a hidden class (Java 15+) not visible on the classpath. The benefit is deferred class creation (lazy), reduced JAR size (no lambda .class files), and potential for future JVM-level optimizations to the generated class.

Q5: A class compiled with Java 8 was recently migrated to Java 21. What bytecode changes can you expect without code changes?

Answer: (1) major_version changes from 52 to 65. (2) String concatenation changes from StringBuilder chains to a single invokedynamic (StringConcatFactory). (3) The StackMapTable attribute is now always generated. (4) If switch expressions or records are added (new Java features), corresponding synthetic methods and attributes appear. (5) Lambdas are unchanged in structure (still invokedynamic + LambdaMetafactory). (6) invokedynamic for string concat is the most visible difference in the bytecode.

Architect Decision Matrix: Bytecode Tooling

Task Tool Notes
Read and understand bytecode javap -c -verbose Ships with JDK, no dependencies
Instrument for APM/tracing ASM + Java Agent Lowest overhead; used by Datadog/New Relic
Generate proxy classes ByteBuddy Used by Mockito, Spring, Hibernate
Quick bytecode manipulation Javassist Java-source-level API, less control
Coverage instrumentation JaCoCo (uses ASM) Generates exec files for CI coverage
Obfuscation/optimization ProGuard / R8 Shrinks, renames, and optimizes bytecode
Decompile to source CFR / Fernflower Read library source or audit dependencies
Class version check javap -verbose or file cmd Verify class file compatibility
Part 22

Summary Table

Concept Key Detail
Bytecode Platform-independent binary format for the JVM; runs on any JVM
Magic Number 0xCAFEBABE — first 4 bytes of every .class file
Class File Version Java 21 → 65, Java 17 → 61, Java 11 → 55, Java 8 → 52
Constant Pool Symbol table of strings, classes, methods, fields; indexed by all bytecodes
Runtime Constant Pool Resolved constant pool stored in Metaspace; symbolic refs → direct refs
Type Descriptor I=int, J=long, Z=boolean, Lpackage/Class;=object, [=array
Method Descriptor (param-types)return-type, e.g., (Ljava/lang/String;I)V
Operand Stack LIFO computation stack per method invocation
Local Variable Array Slots for this, params, and local vars; long/double use 2 slots
Stack Frame Per-method call: operand stack + local vars + reference to constant pool
invokevirtual Virtual dispatch via vtable; class method calls
invokeinterface Virtual dispatch via interface table; interface method calls
invokespecial Non-virtual: constructors, private methods, super calls
invokestatic Static method calls; no receiver
invokedynamic Deferred linkage via bootstrap; used for lambdas and string concat
monitorenter/monitorexit Bytecode for synchronized blocks; always paired
Exception Table Maps [from, to) → handler PC for each exception type
checkcast Runtime type cast; throws ClassCastException on failure
instanceof Runtime type test; pushes 0 or 1; never throws
iinc Directly increment a local int variable; efficient loop counter
tableswitch Continuous-range switch; O(1) dispatch
lookupswitch Sparse-range switch; binary-searched
StackMapTable Pre-computed stack types at branches; enables fast linear verification
ASM Low-level bytecode generation/manipulation; used by most frameworks
ByteBuddy High-level dynamic class generation; used by Mockito, Hibernate

Practice — Lesson 57

Easy Exercises

Exercise 1 — Explore with javap

Compile the following class and run javap -c -verbose on it. Identify: the magic number, class file version, constant pool entry for the string "Hello", and the bytecode for the main method.

public class Greeter {
    private final String name;

    public Greeter(String name) {
        this.name = name;
    }

    public String greet() {
        return "Hello, " + name + "!";
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(new Greeter("World").greet());
    }
}

Expected findings:
- Magic: cafe babe
- Major version: 65 (Java 21) or 61 (Java 17)
- Constant pool: CONSTANT_String entry pointing to a CONSTANT_Utf8 for "Hello, " and "!"
- main: new, dup, ldc, invokespecial, invokevirtual (greet), invokevirtual (println), return

Exercise 2 — Read Type Descriptors

Without running any code, decode the following method descriptors into Java method signatures:

  1. (ILjava/lang/String;Z)Ljava/util/List;
  2. ([Ljava/lang/Object;II)V
  3. ()Ljava/util/concurrent/CompletableFuture;
  4. (Ljava/util/function/Predicate;)Ljava/util/stream/Stream;

Answers:
1. List method(int, String, boolean)
2. void method(Object[], int, int)
3. CompletableFuture method()
4. Stream method(Predicate)

Exercise 3 — Identify Opcode for Each Construct

Match each Java construct to its primary opcode:
- obj.toString() → invokevirtual
- new ArrayList<>() → new + invokespecial (for <init>)
- super.toString() → invokespecial
- Math.abs(x) → invokestatic
- list.add(item) (where list is List<String>) → invokeinterface
- () -> doWork() → invokedynamic

Medium Exercises

Exercise 4 — Trace Stack State

Manually trace the operand stack state at each step of the following bytecode sequence. Draw the stack after each instruction.

iconst_3       // ?
iconst_5       // ?
iadd           // ?
iconst_2       // ?
imul           // ?
istore_1       // ?

Answer:

iconst_3   → [3]
iconst_5   → [3, 5]
iadd       → [8]         (3+5)
iconst_2   → [8, 2]
imul       → [16]        (8*2)
istore_1   → []          (store 16 in slot 1)

Exercise 5 — javap a Lambda

Write a class that creates a Predicate<String> lambda. Compile it and use javap -p -c to find:
1. The synthetic private static method for the lambda body
2. The invokedynamic call site

import java.util.function.Predicate;

public class LambdaInspector {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String prefix = "Hello";
        Predicate<String> p = s -> s.startsWith(prefix);
        System.out.println(p.test("HelloWorld"));
    }
}

javap -p -c LambdaInspector.class

Look for:
- private static boolean lambda$main$0(java.lang.String, java.lang.String);
- In main: invokedynamic with LambdaMetafactory reference
- Captured variable (prefix) passed as argument to invokedynamic

Exercise 6 — String Concatenation Java 8 vs 21

Compile this class twice: once with --release 8 targeting Java 8 semantics and once normally for Java 21. Compare the bytecode of the concat method.

public class ConcatDemo {
    public static String concat(String first, String last) {
        return "Hello, " + first + " " + last + "!";
    }
}

# Java 8 style (if your JDK supports --release 8):
javac --release 8 ConcatDemo.java -d out8/
javap -c out8/ConcatDemo.class

# Java 21 style:
javac ConcatDemo.java -d out21/
javap -c out21/ConcatDemo.class

Expected difference: Java 8 output shows new java/lang/StringBuilder, multiple invokevirtual append calls, and a final invokevirtual toString. Java 21 output shows a single invokedynamic call referencing StringConcatFactory.makeConcatWithConstants.

Advanced Exercises

Exercise 7 — Write a Method Timing Agent Using ASM

Use ASM to write a Java agent that instruments every non-constructor method in a target package to log execution time.

public class TimingTransformer implements ClassFileTransformer {

    private final String targetPackage;

    public TimingTransformer(String targetPackage) {
        this.targetPackage = targetPackage.replace('.', '/');
    }

    @Override
    public byte[] transform(ClassLoader loader, String className, ...) {
        if (!className.startsWith(targetPackage)) return null;

        ClassReader cr = new ClassReader(classfileBuffer);
        ClassWriter cw = new ClassWriter(cr, ClassWriter.COMPUTE_FRAMES);
        cr.accept(new ClassVisitor(ASM9, cw) {
            @Override
            public MethodVisitor visitMethod(int access, String name, String desc,
                                             String signature, String[] exceptions) {
                MethodVisitor mv = super.visitMethod(access, name, desc, signature, exceptions);
                if (name.equals("<init>") || name.equals("<clinit>")) return mv;
                return new TimingMethodVisitor(ASM9, mv, className, name);
            }
        }, 0);
        return cw.toByteArray();
    }
}

class TimingMethodVisitor extends MethodVisitor {
    private final String className;
    private final String methodName;

    TimingMethodVisitor(int api, MethodVisitor mv, String className, String methodName) {
        super(api, mv);
        this.className = className;
        this.methodName = methodName;
    }

    @Override
    public void visitCode() {
        super.visitCode();
        // Inject: long _start = System.nanoTime();
        mv.visitMethodInsn(INVOKESTATIC, "java/lang/System", "nanoTime", "()J", false);
        mv.visitVarInsn(LSTORE, // find a free slot based on descriptor
            /* ... */ 10);
    }

    // Also intercept RETURN opcodes to inject: System.out.println(elapsed)
}

Exercise 8 — Bytecode Decompilation and Obfuscation Analysis

Download a third-party JAR (e.g., an old version of a library). Use javap or a decompiler (CFR: java -jar cfr.jar library.jar) to:
1. Find all methods that call Runtime.exec() — a security concern
2. Identify any obfuscated class names (single-character names)
3. Find classes compiled with Java 8 vs 11 vs 17

# Find all uses of Runtime.exec in a JAR
for class in $(jar tf suspicious.jar | grep '.class'); do
    classname="${class%.class}"
    javap -c -classpath suspicious.jar "$classname" 2>/dev/null \
        | grep -l "java/lang/Runtime.exec" && echo "$classname"
done

# Quick class version scan
javap -verbose -classpath suspicious.jar SomeClass | grep "major version"

Production Scenarios

Scenario 1 — VerifyError After Agent Instrumentation

After deploying a new version of your APM agent, production starts throwing:

java.lang.VerifyError: Bad type on operand stack
  Exception Details:
    Location: com/example/OrderService.processOrder(J)V @45: invokevirtual
    Reason: Type 'long' (current frame, stack[0]) is not assignable to 'com/example/OrderService'

Diagnosis: The ASM transformer forgot to use ClassWriter.COMPUTE_FRAMES when injecting code into a method that uses long parameters (which consume 2 stack slots). The generated StackMapTable is now incorrect, causing verification to fail.

Fix:

// Wrong:
ClassWriter cw = new ClassWriter(0);  // no frame computation

// Right:
ClassWriter cw = new ClassWriter(cr, ClassWriter.COMPUTE_FRAMES);
// or: ClassWriter.COMPUTE_MAXS to only recompute max_stack/max_locals

Prevention: Always use COMPUTE_FRAMES when your transformation adds new bytecodes, changes the control flow, or instruments methods with long/double parameters. The performance cost is minimal.

Scenario 2 — Unexpected ClassCastException in Deserialization

java.lang.ClassCastException: class com.example.UserEvent cannot be cast to class com.example.UserEvent
  (com.example.UserEvent is in unnamed module of loader 'app';
   com.example.UserEvent is in unnamed module of loader org.springframework.boot.devtools.restart.classloader.RestartClassLoader)

Diagnosis: Spring Boot DevTools is running in development. DevTools uses a restart classloader that reloads application classes on change. An old UserEvent instance (loaded by the restart classloader before a restart) is being compared with the new UserEvent class (loaded by the new restart classloader after the restart) — two different Class objects for the same name.

Fix (dev only): Restart cleanly instead of hot-reload, or configure DevTools to exclude the problematic class from restart: spring.devtools.restart.exclude=com/example/UserEvent.class.

Fix (production): DevTools should never run in production. Ensure spring.devtools.restart.enabled=false in production profile.

Debugging Exercises

Debug 1 — Identify the Opcode Bug

The following bytecode is supposed to compute (a + b) * c. It produces the wrong result. Find the bug.

iload_1    // a
iload_2    // b
iload_3    // c
iadd       // ?
imul       // ?
ireturn

Answer: The bug is in the order of loading. iload_3 (c) is pushed before iadd is called. The actual computation is: stack = [a, b, c], iadd pops b and c (not a and b!) → result is (b+c), then imul pushes the result of a * (b+c).

Correct bytecode:

iload_1    // a
iload_2    // b
iadd       // a+b
iload_3    // c
imul       // (a+b)*c
ireturn

Debug 2 — Find the Missing monitorenter

A class has synchronized keyword on a method but javap shows no monitorenter/monitorexit instructions. Why?

public synchronized void update(String value) {
    this.value = value;
}

Answer: Synchronized methods (as opposed to synchronized blocks) do NOT use monitorenter/monitorexit bytecodes. Instead, the ACC_SYNCHRONIZED flag is set in the method's access_flags. The JVM automatically acquires/releases the monitor on the receiver object (this) when it invokes or returns from a ACC_SYNCHRONIZED method — no explicit bytecode needed.

monitorenter/monitorexit only appear for synchronized blocks (synchronized(someObject) { ... }).

Interview Challenges

Challenge 1

"Can you write Java code that compiles successfully but fails at runtime with a VerifyError? Show an example."

Answer: You cannot produce a VerifyError from normal Java source code — javac ensures generated bytecode is always verifiable. VerifyError requires either (1) manually crafted bytecode (using ASM without COMPUTE_FRAMES), (2) a buggy bytecode transformer/agent, or (3) an extremely old classfile from a JVM bug. This is by design — javac is conservative and the verifier is the safety net against malicious or corrupt bytecode.

Challenge 2

"Why does Java's long type require two local variable slots in bytecode?"

Answer: The JVM local variable array uses 32-bit slots. long (64-bit) and double (64-bit) exceed 32 bits and therefore require two consecutive slots. This was a design decision made for the 32-bit CPUs of the early 1990s when Java was created — on a 32-bit architecture, 64-bit values naturally span two registers or stack words. The JVM spec reserves slot n and n+1 for a long/double at slot n, and slot n+1 cannot be independently accessed. This is also why lload_0 pushes 64 bits and the next available slot is lload_2 (not lload_1).

Challenge 3

"A senior engineer says: 'We can improve performance by writing our hot-path methods directly in bytecode using ASM, skipping the compiler's overhead.' Evaluate this claim."

Answer: The claim is almost always wrong for these reasons: (1) javac already generates near-optimal bytecode for straightforward Java code — the compiler's "overhead" is at compile time, not runtime. (2) The JIT compiler (C2) is what actually determines hot-path performance — it reads the bytecode and generates optimized native code. Hand-written bytecode that circumvents Java language constructs could actually prevent JIT optimizations (e.g., removing type information that escape analysis relies on). (3) The cost of writing, maintaining, and debugging hand-crafted ASM far exceeds any marginal gain. (4) The correct approach for hot paths is to write clear Java code, measure with JMH, and apply JVM flags or algorithmic improvements. Bytecode manipulation is appropriate for structural concerns (instrumentation, proxies) — not micro-optimizations.

Key Takeaways

  • Bytecode is platform-independent intermediate code — the JVM, not the OS, executes it; this enables "Write Once, Run Anywhere"
  • Every .class file begins with 0xCAFEBABE — the magic number the JVM uses to validate the file format before proceeding
  • The constant pool is the class's symbol table — all class names, method names, string literals, and numeric constants are stored here and referenced by index throughout the bytecode
  • The JVM is stack-based — computation happens by pushing and popping values on the operand stack; there are no general-purpose registers
  • Five invocation opcodes map to distinct dispatch semantics: invokevirtual (virtual class dispatch), invokeinterface (interface dispatch), invokespecial (constructors/private/super), invokestatic (static), invokedynamic (bootstrap-linked, used for lambdas and string concat)
  • javap -c -verbose is your primary tool for reading bytecode — know it well for debugging and interview situations
  • Lambdas compile to invokedynamic — the LambdaMetafactory bootstrap generates a hidden class at runtime; lambdas do NOT create .class files at compile time
  • String concatenation changed in Java 9 — from StringBuilder chains to a single invokedynamic backed by StringConcatFactory; this is faster and more compact
  • Generics are erased — the JVM sees Object at runtime; the compiler inserts checkcast instructions for type safety at usage sites
  • VerifyError means invalid bytecode — caused by buggy bytecode transformers (ASM without COMPUTE_FRAMES), never by valid Java source code
