Part 1

What Is the Execution Engine?

The execution engine is the heart of the JVM. Once the class loader subsystem has loaded, linked, and initialized a class, and once the bytecode verifier has certified that the bytecode is structurally sound, the execution engine is the component responsible for actually running the program.

At its core, the execution engine answers a single question: given a stream of bytecode instructions, what happens in the CPU? The answer involves several tightly interlocked subsystems:

  • The interpreter, which decodes and dispatches bytecodes one at a time
  • The JIT compiler (covered in Lesson 59), which translates hot bytecode paths into native machine code
  • The runtime data areas — specifically the Java stack, frames, operand stack, and local variable array
  • The native method interface (JNI), which bridges JVM-managed execution into native code
  • The garbage collector integration layer, which notifies GC of safepoints during execution
JVM Execution Pipeline (High Level):
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  .class bytecode                                                  │
│       │                                                           │
│       ▼                                                           │
│  ┌──────────────┐    ┌─────────────────┐    ┌──────────────────┐ │
│  │  Class Loader│───►│  Bytecode        │───►│ Execution Engine │ │
│  │  Subsystem   │    │  Verifier        │    │                  │ │
│  └──────────────┘    └─────────────────┘    │  ┌────────────┐  │ │
│                                              │  │Interpreter │  │ │
│                                              │  └─────┬──────┘  │ │
│                                              │        │ hot path │ │
│                                              │  ┌─────▼──────┐  │ │
│                                              │  │JIT Compiler│  │ │
│                                              │  └────────────┘  │ │
│                                              └──────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The execution engine is not a monolith — it is a mixed-mode system that dynamically decides, method by method and even loop iteration by loop iteration, whether to interpret or compile.

Part 2

Bytecode: The Language the Execution Engine Speaks

Java bytecode is a compact, stack-based instruction set. The JVM specification defines roughly 200 opcodes, each encoded as a single byte (hence "byte"code), optionally followed by operands.

Anatomy of a bytecode instruction

Bytecode stream example for: int x = a + b;
────────────────────────────────────────────────
Opcode   Mnemonic   Effect
0x15     iload_1    push local var 1 (a) onto operand stack
0x15     iload_2    push local var 2 (b) onto operand stack
0x60     iadd       pop two ints, push their sum
0x36     istore_3   pop top of stack, store into local var 3 (x)
────────────────────────────────────────────────

Each class file contains a Code attribute inside each method's method_info structure. This Code attribute packages:

Field Description
max_stack Maximum depth of the operand stack during execution
max_locals Number of local variable slots required
code[] The actual bytecode array
exception_table[] Maps bytecode ranges to exception handlers
attributes[] LineNumberTable, LocalVariableTable, StackMapTable

The StackMapTable attribute (introduced in Java 6 for split verifier) encodes the type state at each branch target, allowing the verifier to check type safety in a single linear pass instead of a fixpoint iteration.

Part 3

The Interpreter: Template-Based Dispatch

HotSpot's interpreter is not a simple switch statement. It is a template interpreter — a metaprogrammed machine-code generator that, at JVM startup, generates a native code snippet ("template") for each of the ~200 opcodes.

How template dispatch works

JVM startup:
  for each opcode in {iconst_0 .. lreturn}:
      generate native asm stub → store in dispatch_table[opcode]

Per-bytecode execution:
  fetch opcode byte from bytecode stream
  index into dispatch_table[opcode]
  jump (via indirect branch) to native stub
  stub executes, advances bytecode PC, jumps to next dispatch

This means the interpreter runs native machine code for each bytecode — there is no Java-level dispatch overhead, no switch, no virtual call. The dispatch table is a flat array of function pointers into a block of JIT-generated assembly.

Why a template interpreter instead of a C interpreter?

A classic C-based interpreter (switch(opcode) { case IADD: ... }) suffers from two problems:

  1. Branch misprediction at the central dispatch switch — the CPU cannot predict which case will be taken next
  2. Overhead from the C calling convention — stack frame setup/teardown per opcode

The template interpreter's generated stubs end with a computed jmp that jumps directly into the next stub with no return. This is called a threaded interpreter pattern and eliminates the central dispatch bottleneck.

Part 4

The Java Stack and Stack Frames

Every Java thread gets its own Java stack (the -Xss flag controls its size, default 512 KB to 1 MB). The stack holds stack frames, one per active method invocation.

Stack frame layout

Java Stack (grows downward, conceptually):
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Frame for main()                            │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  Local Variables [0..max_locals-1]    │  │
│  │  Operand Stack   [0..max_stack-1]     │  │
│  │  Frame Data      (return address,     │  │
│  │                   method reference,   │  │
│  │                   constant pool ref)  │  │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│  Frame for parseRequest()                    │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  Local Variables                       │  │
│  │  Operand Stack                         │  │
│  │  Frame Data                            │  │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│  Frame for parseInt()  ← top of stack        │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  Local Variables                       │  │
│  │  Operand Stack                         │  │
│  │  Frame Data                            │  │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────┘  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Local variable array

The local variable array is a zero-indexed array of slots, each holding a 32-bit value. long and double types occupy two consecutive slots. Slot 0 in an instance method is always this.

Example: void foo(int a, double b, String s)
  slot 0: this        (reference)
  slot 1: a           (int)
  slot 2: b           (double, low word)
  slot 3: b           (double, high word — conceptually slot 2-3)
  slot 4: s           (reference)
  slot 5+: local vars declared inside the method body

Frame data

The frame data section holds metadata needed to restore the caller's execution context when the current method returns:

  • Return address: the bytecode PC in the calling method to resume at
  • Pointer to the constant pool of the current method's class
  • Reference to the current method (for stack traces, reflection, etc.)
  • Saved registers (when transitioning to/from compiled code)
Part 5

The Operand Stack in Depth

The operand stack is the JVM's working register set. Unlike physical CPUs (which have named registers like rax, rbx), the JVM spec defines a stack of values that instructions push and pop.

Operand stack lifecycle example

// Source
int result = (a * b) + c;

// Bytecode
iload_1       // push a       → stack: [a]
iload_2       // push b       → stack: [a, b]
imul          // pop a,b → a*b → stack: [a*b]
iload_3       // push c       → stack: [a*b, c]
iadd          // pop a*b,c    → stack: [(a*b)+c]
istore 4      // pop, store   → stack: []

The max_stack field in the Code attribute tells the JVM the maximum depth this stack will ever reach (computed statically by javac). The JVM can allocate the operand stack as a fixed-size region within the frame.

Type safety on the operand stack

The bytecode verifier (Lesson 57) ensures that every instruction operates on values of the correct type. The iadd opcode is only valid when the top two stack entries are both int. There is no implicit coercion — ladd handles long, fadd handles float, dadd handles double. This strict type tagging is what allows the JVM to reason about type safety without runtime type checks on every arithmetic operation.

Part 6

Instruction Categories

The ~200 JVM opcodes fall into clean categories:

Category Example Opcodes Description
Load/Store iload, astore, lload_0 Move values between locals and operand stack
Arithmetic iadd, lmul, ddiv, ineg Integer, long, float, double arithmetic
Type Conversion i2l, d2f, l2i Widening and narrowing primitive conversions
Object Creation new, newarray, anewarray Allocate objects and arrays
Field Access getfield, putfield, getstatic Read/write instance and static fields
Method Invocation invokevirtual, invokespecial, invokestatic, invokeinterface, invokedynamic Call methods
Control Flow goto, ifeq, tableswitch, lookupswitch Branches and switches
Return ireturn, areturn, return Return from method
Stack Manipulation pop, dup, swap Manipulate operand stack directly
Monitor monitorenter, monitorexit Synchronized block entry/exit
Exception athrow Throw an exception

The invokedynamic opcode

Added in Java 7 to support dynamic languages (Groovy, JRuby) and later leveraged for lambda expressions in Java 8, invokedynamic defers method dispatch to a bootstrap method that produces a CallSite at first invocation. This CallSite contains a MethodHandle that becomes the actual dispatch target.

First execution of invokedynamic:
  JVM calls bootstrap method (e.g., LambdaMetafactory.metafactory)
  bootstrap returns a CallSite with a MethodHandle
  JVM links the call site → subsequent calls go directly to MethodHandle
Part 7

Method Invocation Opcodes Compared

Understanding the five invocation opcodes is essential for understanding dispatch performance:

invokevirtual

Used for non-private, non-static instance methods. The JVM looks up the method in the vtable (virtual method table) of the object's actual runtime type. Supports virtual dispatch — the correct override is called based on the runtime type of the receiver.

invokevirtual #5 <java/io/PrintStream.println>
  1. Pop receiver reference from operand stack
  2. Null-check receiver
  3. Load receiver's klass pointer
  4. Index into klass.vtable at offset stored in CP#5
  5. Jump to resolved method

invokeinterface

Similar to invokevirtual but used for interface method calls. The receiver could implement the interface at any position in its type hierarchy. HotSpot uses an itable (interface method table) per implementing class, searched by interface ID.

invokespecial

Used for constructors (<init>), private methods, and super.method() calls. Dispatch is static — the method is resolved at link time, no virtual dispatch.

invokestatic

Static method calls. No receiver, fully resolved at link time.

invokedynamic

As described above — deferred dispatch via bootstrap + CallSite.

Part 8

Mixed-Mode Execution

HotSpot does not use a pure interpreter or a pure JIT compiler. It uses mixed-mode execution: methods begin life interpreted, and the JVM monitors their execution frequency. Once a method crosses an invocation count threshold or a loop backedge crosses a loop iteration threshold, the method is queued for JIT compilation.

Mixed-Mode Execution Timeline:
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Method first called:  interpreted (slow but always correct)
  After ~2,000 calls:   C1 compiles (lightly optimized native)
  After ~10,000 calls:  C2 compiles (heavily optimized native)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
(Exact thresholds depend on -XX:CompileThreshold and tier settings)

This is the tiered compilation model — described in depth in Lesson 59. The key point here is that the execution engine must seamlessly handle a method being interpreted, then having its compiled version installed, all while other threads may be executing the same method.

How the switch from interpreted to compiled happens

  1. The JVM compilation broker queues the method for the C1 compiler
  2. The C1 compiler runs on a background compiler thread, producing native code
  3. The compiled code is installed into the code cache (a fixed-size memory region, default 240 MB)
  4. At the next method invocation, the interpreter checks whether compiled code exists for this method (via the method's _code pointer in its methodOop)
  5. If compiled code exists, the call is redirected there
Part 9

Safepoints and the Execution Engine

A safepoint is a point in the execution engine where the JVM can pause all threads in a consistent state. Safepoints are used for:

  • Stop-the-world GC phases
  • Deoptimization (reverting compiled frames to interpreted frames)
  • Thread dumps
  • Biased locking revocation

Where safepoints occur

The interpreter checks for safepoint requests at:
- Method returns
- Loop backedges (every iteration of a counted loop)

Compiled code generated by C1/C2 includes safepoint polls at:
- Method returns
- Loop backedges (for non-counted loops; counted loops may omit polls)

A safepoint poll is a load from a well-known memory page (SafepointSynchronize::_state). When the JVM wants to bring the world to a stop, it changes this page's protection to no-access. The next time a thread executes a safepoint poll, it takes a segfault, which HotSpot's signal handler intercepts to suspend the thread at a safe location.

Safepoint mechanism:
  Normal:   [thread reads polling page] → reads OK, continues
  Requested: JVM mprotects polling page → read triggers SIGSEGV
             signal handler: save register state, block thread
             GC/deopt runs
             JVM restores page → threads resume
Part 10

Exception Handling in the Execution Engine

When athrow is executed (or the JVM internally throws a NullPointerException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, etc.), the execution engine walks the exception table of the current method.

Exception table structure

Exception table for a try/catch/finally block:
┌───────┬─────┬─────────┬──────────────────────────────┐
│ Start │ End │ Handler │ Caught Type                   │
├───────┼─────┼─────────┼──────────────────────────────┤
│   0   │  12 │   15    │ java/io/IOException           │
│   0   │  12 │   28    │ java/lang/Exception           │
│   0   │  35 │   41    │ <any> (finally block)         │
└───────┴─────┴─────────┴──────────────────────────────┘

The JVM scans the exception table in order from top to bottom, looking for the first entry where:
1. The current bytecode PC falls in [start, end)
2. The thrown exception is an instance of the Caught Type (or Caught Type is <any>)

If no matching handler is found in the current method, the current frame is popped and the search continues in the calling method's exception table. This unwinding continues until a handler is found or the stack is exhausted (unhandled exception → thread termination).

Null pointer exceptions as hardware signals

HotSpot uses an operating-system trick to handle NullPointerException cheaply: rather than inserting explicit null checks before every field access, it maps the JVM heap such that address 0 is an unmapped page. A null dereference becomes a hardware segfault (SIGSEGV), which HotSpot's signal handler converts into a NullPointerException. This eliminates the cost of software null checks on the hot path.

Part 11

The Runtime Constant Pool

Each class has a runtime constant pool (RCP) — the in-memory counterpart of the class file's constant_pool[] array. The RCP holds:

  • Symbolic references that are resolved lazily as methods execute
  • Literal constants (String, int, long, float, double)
  • References to other classes, methods, and fields once resolved

Constant pool resolution

When bytecode first references an entry (e.g., invokevirtual #42), the entry at CP#42 may still be a symbolic reference — just strings naming the class, method name, and descriptor. Resolution replaces this with a direct pointer:

Before resolution:  CP#42 → {class="java/util/ArrayList", name="add", desc="(Ljava/lang/Object;)Z"}
After resolution:   CP#42 → direct methodOop* pointer in JVM heap

Resolution can trigger class loading (if the referenced class is not yet loaded), which in turn can trigger static initializers (<clinit>). This lazy resolution model means the full transitive closure of classes does not need to be loaded upfront.

Part 12

The `<clinit>` Method and Class Initialization

Every class may have a class initializer method, <clinit>, synthesized by javac from static { ... } blocks and static field initializers. The execution engine calls <clinit> exactly once per class, the first time the class is actively used (first instance creation, first static field access, or first static method call).

Initialization locking

The JVM must ensure <clinit> is called at most once, even in a multi-threaded environment. It achieves this via a per-class initialization lock:

Thread A and Thread B both first-use ClassX simultaneously:
  Thread A: acquires ClassX.init_lock, begins running <clinit>
  Thread B: tries to acquire ClassX.init_lock, blocks
  Thread A: <clinit> completes, sets state=INITIALIZED, releases lock
  Thread B: acquires lock, sees INITIALIZED, skips <clinit>, proceeds

This is the source of subtle deadlocks when two classes mutually reference each other in their static initializers.

Part 13

Stack Overflow: `StackOverflowError`

Each thread's Java stack has a fixed maximum size (-Xss). The execution engine allocates a new frame for each method call. If the stack grows beyond its limit (infinite recursion, very deep recursion), the JVM throws StackOverflowError.

HotSpot reserves a small yellow zone and red zone at the bottom of each thread's stack:

Thread Stack Layout:
┌──────────────────────────────────────┐ ← top (low address, stack grows down)
│  Active frames                        │
│  ...                                  │
│  ...                                  │
├──────────────────────────────────────┤ ← yellow zone start
│  Yellow zone (guard pages)            │  ← JVM throws StackOverflowError here
├──────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Red zone (reserved for JVM itself)   │  ← JVM uses to safely throw the Error
└──────────────────────────────────────┘ ← bottom (high address)

When a frame would encroach on the yellow zone, HotSpot's signal handler intercepts the page fault and throws StackOverflowError. Because the JVM needs some stack space to actually construct and throw this error, the red zone is kept as an emergency reserve.

Part 14

JNI: Java Native Interface

Java programs frequently need to call native code — operating system APIs, hardware drivers, high-performance C/C++ libraries (OpenSSL, SQLite, BLAS). The Java Native Interface (JNI) is the standard bridge.

Declaring a native method

public class NativeExample {
    static {
        System.loadLibrary("nativeexample");  // loads libnativeexample.so / .dll
    }

    public native int computeHash(byte[] data, int length);
}

The native keyword tells the compiler to emit no Code attribute for this method — the implementation lives in a C/C++ shared library.

JNI name mangling

The JVM locates the native function by a mangled name:

Java method: NativeExample.computeHash(byte[], int)
JNI function: Java_NativeExample_computeHash(JNIEnv*, jobject, jbyteArray, jint)

The JNIEnv pointer

Every JNI function receives a JNIEnv* as its first argument. This is a pointer to a table of function pointers (a vtable-like structure) that gives the native code access to JVM services:

JNIEXPORT jint JNICALL Java_NativeExample_computeHash(
    JNIEnv *env,    // JVM interface pointer
    jobject this,   // the Java 'this' reference
    jbyteArray data,
    jint length) {

    jbyte *buf = (*env)->GetByteArrayElements(env, data, NULL);
    jint result = my_hash_function(buf, length);
    (*env)->ReleaseByteArrayElements(env, data, buf, JNI_ABORT);
    return result;
}
Part 15

JNI Transition Cost

Crossing the JNI boundary is expensive relative to a plain Java call. The execution engine must:

  1. Save the current thread state: transition from _thread_in_Java to _thread_in_native
  2. Set up a native frame on the thread's stack (different layout from Java frames)
  3. Handle GC root registration: all jobject parameters must be wrapped in JNI handles so the GC can track them even though native code holds raw pointers
  4. On return, transition back to _thread_in_Java and potentially block at a safepoint if one was requested while the native method was running
  5. Check for pending exceptions the native code may have thrown via (*env)->Throw()
JNI Call Cost Breakdown (approximate):
  Java → native transition:   ~50–200 ns
  Plain virtual Java call:    ~1–5 ns (inline cache hit, interpreted)
  JIT-compiled virtual call:  ~0.5–2 ns

For this reason, JNI calls should be coarse-grained — do as much work as possible per JNI call rather than making many small calls.

Part 16

Critical JNI: `GetPrimitiveArrayCritical`

JNI provides a special set of "critical" functions that allow native code to access Java array/string data with reduced overhead:

jint *arr = (*env)->GetPrimitiveArrayCritical(env, javaArray, NULL);
// Process arr directly — may be a direct pointer into JVM heap
(*env)->ReleasePrimitiveArrayCritical(env, javaArray, arr, 0);

Between Get and Release, the JVM disables GC (or at least prevents the array from being moved). The native code may receive a direct pointer into the GC heap — zero copy. However, the window between Get and Release must be as short as possible, as GC is paused and other threads cannot allocate.

Part 17

JNI Local and Global References

JNI references come in three flavors, and mismanaging them causes either memory leaks or use-after-free crashes:

Reference Type Lifetime Creation Destruction
Local Current JNI call frame Automatic for params; NewLocalRef Freed on return; or DeleteLocalRef
Global Until explicitly deleted NewGlobalRef DeleteGlobalRef
Weak Global Until GC collects referent NewWeakGlobalRef DeleteWeakGlobalRef

A common bug: storing a jobject parameter in a global C variable. Since it is a local reference, it becomes invalid after the JNI call returns. The correct pattern is (*env)->NewGlobalRef(env, param) to promote it to a global reference that survives across calls.

Part 18

Interpreter and JNI: The Glue Layer

When the interpreter encounters a native method, it does not execute a bytecode stream — there is none. Instead, it calls the JNI stub that was generated for this method at link time. For a dynamically-linked JNI method:

Interpreter frame for native method:
  1. Build JNI argument frame (marshal Java args to C types)
  2. Switch thread state: _thread_in_Java → _thread_in_native
  3. Call native function pointer
  4. Switch thread state back: _thread_in_native → _thread_in_Java
  5. Check safepoint
  6. Check pending JNI exception → rethrow if set
  7. Unmarshal return value back to operand stack

HotSpot generates these stubs using its internal StubRoutines assembler framework, producing different stubs for methods with different signatures to minimize argument marshaling overhead.

Part 19

Synchronized Methods and `monitorenter`/`monitorexit`

The synchronized keyword compiles to monitorenter and monitorexit bytecodes (for synchronized blocks) or a flag in the method's access flags (for synchronized methods). The execution engine handles both.

Object monitor (mutex) implementation

Every Java object has a mark word in its object header (typically 64 bits). The mark word encodes:

Mark Word States:
  Unlocked:       [identity hash | age | 01]
  Biased locked:  [thread ID | epoch | age | 101]
  Thin locked:    [ptr to lock record on stack | 00]
  Inflated:       [ptr to ObjectMonitor | 10]
  GC marked:      [forwarding ptr | 11]

HotSpot uses biased locking (now disabled by default since Java 15) and thin locking (compare-and-swap on mark word) before escalating to a full ObjectMonitor (OS-level mutex). The execution engine handles these transitions transparently — the programmer just writes synchronized.

Part 20

The Execution Engine and the GC Collaboration

The execution engine and GC must cooperate because:

  • GC needs to find all live references — it must walk Java stack frames to discover object references held in local variables and on the operand stack
  • Moving GCs (G1, ZGC, Shenandoah) relocate objects — the execution engine must update references in frames

OopMaps: telling GC where references are

When a method is compiled, the JIT compiler generates OopMaps — tables that describe, at each safepoint, which stack slots and registers hold object references (oop = ordinary object pointer). The GC uses these maps to find and potentially update all references in compiled frames.

For interpreted frames, the execution engine always knows exactly which local variable slots hold references (from the method's LocalVariableTable and the JVM's internal type tracking), so OopMaps are only needed for compiled frames.

Part 21

Frame Popping and Deoptimization

When a compiled method must revert to interpreted execution — for example, because a rare branch was encountered that the JIT did not optimize for, or because a debugger wants to inspect frame state — the execution engine performs deoptimization.

Deoptimization steps:
  1. At a safepoint, compiled frame identified for deoptimization
  2. JVM "unpacks" compiled frame: reads register state and stack slots
  3. Constructs one or more interpreted frames that represent
     the same logical execution state
  4. Resumes execution in the interpreter from the equivalent bytecode PC

Deoptimization is covered in depth in Lesson 59. Here, the key point is that the execution engine maintains enough metadata in compiled code (OopMaps, debug info, scope data) to perform this rollback faithfully.

Part 22

Monitoring the Execution Engine

Several JVM flags and tools expose execution engine internals:

Key diagnostic flags

# Print which methods are being compiled
-XX:+PrintCompilation

# Disable JIT entirely (pure interpreted mode)
-Xint

# Mixed mode (default): interpreter + JIT
-Xmixed

# Force JIT compilation immediately (no warmup)
-Xcomp

# Print detailed compilation decisions
-XX:+PrintInlining
-XX:+PrintAssembly  # requires hsdis plugin

# Trace JNI calls
-verbose:jni

# Show safepoint statistics
-XX:+PrintSafepointStatistics  # (removed in newer JDKs, use -Xlog:safepoint)
-Xlog:safepoint=info

JVM Tool Interface (JVMTI)

JVMTI is the native API that profilers, debuggers, and coverage tools use to instrument execution:

JVMTI capabilities relevant to the execution engine:
  can_generate_method_entry_events     → callback on every method entry
  can_generate_frame_pop_events        → callback on every return
  can_access_local_variables           → read/write locals in any frame
  can_get_bytecodes                    → retrieve bytecode of live methods
  can_redefine_classes                 → replace class bytecode at runtime

Tools like JProfiler, async-profiler, and Java Flight Recorder all use JVMTI (or Linux perf/eBPF for async-profiler's CPU-sampling mode) to observe execution engine behavior without requiring explicit instrumentation of the application code.

Practice Section

Conceptual Questions

  1. Why does HotSpot use a template interpreter instead of a C switch-based interpreter? What specific performance problems does the template approach solve?

  2. Explain the difference between invokevirtual and invokeinterface dispatch. Why is invokeinterface historically slower?

  3. A method has max_stack=3 and max_locals=5. What does each field represent, and how is max_stack determined at compile time?

  4. Describe the full chain of events when Object.hashCode() is called on an object for the first time. Include constant pool resolution, vtable lookup, and the mark word interaction.

  5. Why does a JNI transition require saving thread state? What would go wrong if the GC ran while a thread was in native code without the state transition?

Hands-On Exercises

Exercise 1 — Bytecode Reading

Compile the following Java class and examine its bytecode with javap -c -verbose:

public class BytecodeExplorer {
    public int factorial(int n) {
        if (n <= 1) return 1;
        return n * factorial(n - 1);
    }
}

Identify: the operand stack depth at each step, how the recursive call is encoded, how the branch (if (n <= 1)) compiles, and the exception table (should be empty here).

Exercise 2 — JNI Hello World

Write a JNI program where Java calls a native C function that returns the current process ID. Steps:
1. Declare public native int getPid(); in Java
2. Generate the header with javac -h . NativeExample.java
3. Implement the C function using getpid()
4. Compile the shared library and run

Exercise 3 — Observing Mixed Mode

Run a microbenchmark (a simple loop summing integers) three times with different flags:
- -Xint (pure interpreted)
- -Xmixed (default)
- -Xcomp (force compile everything)

Use -XX:+PrintCompilation to observe when methods get compiled. Compare the elapsed times and explain the results.

Exercise 4 — Stack Overflow Depth

Write a recursive method with no base case and catch the StackOverflowError. Print the stack depth at which it occurs. Then repeat with -Xss256k, -Xss512k, and -Xss2m. Plot stack depth vs. -Xss size and explain the relationship.

Exercise 5 — Safepoint Latency

Use -Xlog:safepoint=info and run an application that does heavy object allocation. Observe the safepoint pause times in the log output. Identify which operations are triggering safepoints. Then compare behavior with G1 vs. ZGC and explain differences in safepoint frequency.

Key Terms Glossary

Term Definition
Template interpreter JVM interpreter that generates native code stubs for each bytecode opcode at startup
Operand stack LIFO stack within a stack frame where bytecode instructions push/pop working values
Local variable array Fixed-size slot array within a stack frame holding method parameters and local vars
Stack frame Per-method-invocation data structure on the Java stack holding locals, operand stack, and frame metadata
Mixed-mode execution JVM strategy of starting methods interpreted and JIT-compiling hot methods
OopMap Table in compiled code listing which stack slots/registers hold object references at safepoints
Safepoint A point in execution where all threads are in a consistent state for GC or deoptimization
JNI Java Native Interface — the API for calling native C/C++ code from Java and vice versa
JNI handle Wrapper around a jobject that the GC can track during native execution
Deoptimization Rolling back a compiled frame to interpreted frames when assumptions are violated
Runtime constant pool In-memory version of the class file constant pool with resolved direct pointers
<clinit> Class initializer method — called once per class on first active use

Part 1

Why JIT? The Case Against Pure Interpretation

The execution engine (Lesson 58) showed us that HotSpot starts every method in the interpreter. The interpreter is correct, safe, and always available — but it is 10× to 100× slower than optimized native code for CPU-bound work. The reason is structural: every bytecode dispatch involves an indirect branch, every value lives on a simulated stack (extra memory traffic), and there is no register allocation, no instruction scheduling, and no loop unrolling.

The Just-In-Time (JIT) compiler solves this by translating hot bytecode paths into native machine code at runtime, using the same kinds of optimizations a static C++ compiler applies — plus some that a static compiler cannot apply because they require runtime knowledge.

Performance spectrum:
  Pure interpreter (-Xint):   1× (baseline)
  C1-compiled code:           5–10× faster
  C2-compiled code:           20–100× faster
  GraalVM CE (Graal compiler): comparable to C2, sometimes better

Why not compile everything upfront?
  • Compilation takes time — slows startup
  • Most code runs rarely — waste to compile it
  • Runtime profiling enables better decisions than static analysis
Part 2

Tiered Compilation: The Five Levels

Since Java 7 (made default in Java 8), HotSpot uses tiered compilation — a pipeline of five execution levels, each with a different cost/quality tradeoff:

Tiered Compilation Levels:
┌───────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Level │ Description                                              │
├───────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  0    │ Interpreter — no compilation, full profiling             │
│  1    │ C1 — simple compilation, no profiling                    │
│  2    │ C1 — limited profiling (invocation + backedge counts)    │
│  3    │ C1 — full profiling (type profiles, branch profiles)     │
│  4    │ C2 — aggressive optimization using C1's profile data     │
└───────┴─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The typical hot method path

New method:   Level 0 (interpreted, collecting profile)
 ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
 invocation count > ~2000 OR backedge count > ~10000
 ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
 Level 3 (C1 with full profiling): fast native + collecting
 ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
 profile is mature (enough samples to trust)
 ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
 Level 4 (C2): aggressively optimized native code

Why C1 before C2?

C2 compilation is expensive — it can take tens of milliseconds for complex methods. Running in the interpreter for that entire warmup period would be slow. C1 provides a cheap intermediate layer: it compiles quickly (simple optimizations only) and installs instrumented native code that collects the profiling data C2 needs, all while executing much faster than the interpreter.

Part 3

The C1 Compiler

The C1 compiler (formerly "Client compiler") was designed for fast startup. It performs a relatively shallow optimization pipeline:

C1 compilation pipeline

Bytecode
  │
  ▼
HIR (High-Level IR) — platform-independent CFG of basic blocks
  │  • Value numbering
  │  • Constant folding
  │  • Null check elimination (simple cases)
  ▼
LIR (Low-Level IR) — closer to machine instructions
  │  • Linear scan register allocation
  │  • Instruction selection
  ▼
Native code + OopMaps + debug info + profile instrumentation

C1-compiled code contains profiling instrumentation at Level 3 — counters and type recording traps embedded in the native code that track:

  • How many times each call site is reached
  • What concrete types appear at virtual call sites (type profiles)
  • Which branches are taken most often

This data feeds directly into C2's optimization decisions.

Part 4

The C2 Compiler

The C2 compiler (formerly "Server compiler") is HotSpot's aggressive optimizer. It was written in C++ and implements a sea-of-nodes intermediate representation — a graph where nodes are operations and edges are data and control dependencies. This representation allows transformations that are difficult in CFG-based IRs.

C2 optimization pipeline (simplified)

C1-collected profile data
  │
  ▼
Parse bytecode → Ideal Graph (sea-of-nodes)
  │
  ├─► Inlining (using type profiles to devirtualize + inline)
  ├─► Escape analysis
  ├─► Loop transformations (unrolling, vectorization)
  ├─► Global value numbering
  ├─► Algebraic simplification
  ├─► Null check elimination
  ├─► Range check elimination
  │
  ▼
Machine-independent optimizations → schedule graph
  │
  ▼
Register allocation (graph-coloring)
  │
  ▼
Instruction selection + scheduling → native machine code

C2 can easily spend 50–500 ms compiling a complex method, running on a dedicated background compiler thread while the application continues using the C1 version.

Part 5

Method Inlining

Inlining is the single most impactful optimization in any JIT compiler. When a method is inlined, its body is copied directly into the caller — eliminating the call overhead and, more importantly, exposing the callee's code to the caller's optimizations.

Why inlining is transformative

// Before inlining
long sum = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) {
    sum += getValue(i);  // virtual call every iteration
}

// After inlining getValue()
long sum = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) {
    sum += arr[i] * multiplier;  // direct code — now loop-unrollable
}

Without inlining, the JIT cannot see what getValue() does — it cannot constant-fold, dead-code eliminate, or vectorize across the call boundary. With inlining, the entire loop body becomes visible.

Inlining decisions in C2

C2's inliner uses a cost model based on:

Factor Effect
Callee bytecode size Methods > ~325 bytes (-XX:MaxInlineSize) are not inlined by default
Call site frequency Rare calls are not worth inlining
Type profile Monomorphic call sites (one receiver type) are inlined; megamorphic (3+ types) are not
Recursion depth Recursive methods are inlined up to a configurable depth
Current inline budget Each compilation has a total inline depth limit (-XX:MaxInlineLevel, default 9)

Devirtualization: the key to inlining virtual calls

C2 uses type profiles from C1 to devirtualize virtual calls:

Type profile for call site: list.add(item)
  99.7% of calls: receiver is ArrayList
  0.3% of calls: receiver is LinkedList

C2 generates:
  if (list.getClass() == ArrayList.class) {
      // inlined ArrayList.add() body — fast path
  } else {
      // uncommon trap → deoptimize back to interpreter
  }

This speculative inlining is guarded by a type check. If the assumption is violated (the 0.3% case triggers the check), a deoptimization event fires and the method is re-compiled with the updated profile.

Part 6

On-Stack Replacement (OSR)

On-Stack Replacement (OSR) solves a specific problem: what if a method has a very long-running loop that is hot, but the method itself is only called once? Normal tiered compilation requires a method to be called many times before it qualifies for C2 compilation. A method called once would run in the interpreter forever.

How OSR works

Scenario: public void processAll() {
    for (int i = 0; i < 100_000_000; i++) {
        process(data[i]);  // very hot loop — millions of backedges
    }
}
// processAll() is only called ONCE, so invocation count stays at 1

OSR watches backedge counts — the number of times a loop's back edge is taken. When this exceeds a threshold (-XX:OnStackReplacePercentage, default ~14000 relative to compile threshold):

  1. The JVM requests OSR compilation of the method, starting from the loop header
  2. The JIT compiles only the portion of the method from the loop onward
  3. When compilation finishes, at the next loop backedge, the interpreter transfers control to the compiled loop mid-execution
  4. This transfer requires building a mapping from the interpreter's frame state (locals, operand stack) to the compiled code's register/stack layout
OSR transfer:
  Interpreter: i=5000000, executing loop body
         │
         │  (OSR code ready)
         ▼
  Compiled code: picks up execution at loop header
                 with i=5000000 in a register

After the OSR transition, the compiled version runs the remaining 95 million iterations at full speed.

Part 7

Escape Analysis

Escape analysis is a compile-time analysis that determines whether an object allocated inside a method can be observed from outside that method (i.e., whether it "escapes").

Three escape categories

NoEscape:    object is used only within the creating method
             → can be stack-allocated or scalar-replaced
ArgEscape:   object is passed to a method but does not escape globally
             → can be analyzed interprocedurally
GlobalEscape: object is stored in a field, returned, or put in a static
             → must be heap-allocated, cannot be optimized away

Stack allocation

If an object does not escape, HotSpot can allocate it on the stack rather than the heap. A stack-allocated object requires:

  • No GC scanning (GC never sees it)
  • No heap write barriers
  • Automatic deallocation when the frame is popped
// This iterator likely does not escape
for (Iterator<String> it = list.iterator(); it.hasNext(); ) {
    process(it.next());
}
// If escape analysis confirms: Iterator object → stack allocated, zero GC pressure

Scalar replacement

Even better than stack allocation: if an object does not escape and its fields are always accessed individually, the JIT can decompose the object into its primitive scalar fields stored in registers or stack slots. The object itself never materializes in memory.

Point p = new Point(x, y);  // Point does not escape
double dist = Math.sqrt(p.x * p.x + p.y * p.y);

// After scalar replacement:
double dist = Math.sqrt(x * x + y * y);  // Point object eliminated entirely

Synchronization elimination

If a synchronized object does not escape (i.e., no other thread can see it), all monitorenter/monitorexit operations on it are provably contention-free and can be eliminated by the JIT.

// Synchronized on a local — eliminated by escape analysis
synchronized (new Object()) {
    count++;
}
// Compiles to: count++  (no monitor operations)
Part 8

Deoptimization

JIT compilers make speculative assumptions based on profiling data. When reality violates an assumption, the JVM must undo the compiled code and fall back to interpreted execution. This process is called deoptimization.

Common deoptimization triggers

Trigger Description
Type assumption violation A virtual call site sees a new receiver type that was not profiled
Null check failure Code optimized assuming a value is never null encounters a null
Array bounds violation Bounds check eliminated by range analysis fails at runtime
Class loading A new class is loaded that invalidates inlining assumptions
Uncommon trap A branch predicted as never-taken is actually taken

Deoptimization mechanics

Deoptimization sequence:
  1. Compiled code reaches an uncommon trap (guard check fails)
  2. JVM calls deoptimization handler
  3. Current compiled frame is "unpacked":
     - Registers and stack slots are read using debug info / ScopeData
     - One or more interpreted frames are synthesized
  4. Execution resumes in the interpreter from the equivalent bytecode PC

  [Later: method may be recompiled with updated profile, more guards]

Deoptimization and code invalidation

Some deoptimizations invalidate the compiled code entirely (rather than just falling back from a single execution). This happens when, for example, a new class is loaded that is a subtype of a type the JIT assumed was a leaf class. In this case, HotSpot uses nmethod dependencies — a list of assumptions registered by each compiled method. When the assumption breaks (class loading event), all dependent compiled methods are marked for deoptimization and will be re-compiled on their next invocation.

Part 9

Loop Optimizations

Loops are where most CPU time is spent, so the JIT compiler applies aggressive loop transformations:

Loop unrolling

The JIT replicates the loop body N times per iteration, reducing branch overhead and enabling better instruction scheduling:

Original:  for (i=0; i<N; i++) { a[i] = b[i] * c; }

Unrolled (4×):
  for (i=0; i<N-3; i+=4) {
    a[i]   = b[i]   * c;
    a[i+1] = b[i+1] * c;
    a[i+2] = b[i+2] * c;
    a[i+3] = b[i+3] * c;
  }
  // + remainder loop for N % 4

C2 uses CountedLoop detection — recognizing that i increases by a constant each iteration with a known upper bound — to enable safe unrolling without overflow concerns.

Auto-vectorization (SIMD)

After unrolling, if multiple loop iterations perform the same operation on independent data, C2 (and especially GraalVM's compiler) can emit SIMD instructions (SSE2, AVX2, AVX-512):

Scalar:    vmovss xmm0, [b+i*4]
           vmulss xmm0, xmm0, xmm1  (c)
           vmovss [a+i*4], xmm0
           (×4 for unrolled loop)

AVX2:      vmovups ymm0, [b+i*4]  // load 8 floats at once
           vmulps  ymm0, ymm0, ymm1  // multiply 8 floats
           vmovups [a+i*4], ymm0   // store 8 floats

This gives 8× throughput for float operations with AVX2 (256-bit registers = 8 × 32-bit floats).

Range check elimination

For array accesses inside a counted loop where the JIT can prove the index is always within bounds, the per-iteration ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException check is hoisted out of the loop or eliminated entirely:

for (int i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) {
    sum += arr[i];  // bounds check hoisted out — proven safe by loop analysis
}
Part 10

Null Check Elimination and Redundant Check Removal

The JIT aggressively eliminates redundant safety checks that bytecode carries by specification:

String s = getKey();
int len = s.length();
char first = s.charAt(0);

Bytecode for each call includes an implicit null check. C2 realizes that after the first implicit null check on s (for length()), s is provably non-null for the remainder of the method's dominance region. All subsequent null checks on s are eliminated.

Similarly, after a checkcast or instanceof guard, the JIT propagates type information and eliminates redundant casts.

Part 11

Intrinsic Methods

Some methods are so performance-critical or hardware-specific that the JIT compiler does not translate their Java bytecode — instead, it recognizes them by name and emits hand-optimized native code directly:

JVM Intrinsics (selected):
  java.lang.System.arraycopy        → REP MOVSB / AVX memmove
  java.lang.String.equals           → SIMD string comparison
  java.lang.Math.sqrt               → VSQRTSD (single instruction)
  java.lang.Math.min/max            → CMOV / VMINSS
  java.util.Arrays.fill             → AVX vectorized fill
  sun.misc.Unsafe.compareAndSet*    → LOCK CMPXCHG
  java.security.MessageDigest       → SHA-NI hardware instructions
  java.lang.Integer.bitCount        → POPCNT instruction
  java.lang.Long.reverseBytes       → BSWAP instruction
  java.lang.String.indexOf          → SSE4.2 PCMPESTRI

Intrinsics bridge the gap between Java's portability and hardware-level performance. They are why Arrays.sort() can approach C sorting speeds and why ConcurrentHashMap's CAS operations have near-hardware latency.

Part 12

JIT Warmup: The Startup Problem

JIT warmup is the period between JVM start and when all hot code paths are fully compiled. During warmup:

  • Application latency is higher (C1/interpreter is slower)
  • CPU is shared between application threads and compiler threads
  • Throughput is lower until C2 compilation completes

Measuring warmup

Typical warmup profile for a microservice:
  t=0s:     JVM starts, all methods at Level 0 (interpreter)
  t=0.5s:   Hot paths hit C1 threshold → Level 3 compiled
  t=2s:     Profile matures → hot methods go to Level 4 (C2)
  t=5-30s:  All hot paths are C2-compiled → steady-state performance

Throughput curve:
  ▲
  │         ████████████████ (steady state — C2)
  │    ████ (C1 tier)
  │ ██ (interpreter)
  └────────────────────────► time

Strategies to reduce warmup time

1. AppCDS (Application Class Data Sharing)

Pre-share class metadata across JVM instances. Reduces class loading overhead.

# Create shared archive
java -Xshare:dump -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa -cp app.jar

# Use shared archive
java -Xshare:on -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa -jar app.jar

2. JVM profiling replay (experimental)

Collect profiles from a running instance and replay them in a fresh JVM to pre-warm the JIT.

3. Reducing compile thresholds

-XX:CompileThreshold=1000      # Start compiling sooner (default ~10000)
-XX:Tier4CompileThreshold=5000 # C2 threshold (default ~15000)

Trade-off: compiling earlier means less profile data, potentially worse C2 code quality.

Part 13

The Code Cache

JIT-compiled code lives in a fixed-size memory region called the code cache. When it is full, no more JIT compilation occurs and performance degrades.

Code Cache Segments (since Java 9):
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Non-profiled nmethods (C1 Level 1, C2 Level 4)          │
│  Profiled nmethods (C1 Level 2, 3)                        │
│  Non-nmethod code (stubs, interpreter, adapters)          │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Key flags

-XX:ReservedCodeCacheSize=256m    # Max code cache size (default 240m)
-XX:InitialCodeCacheSize=2m       # Starting size
-XX:+UseCodeCacheFlushing         # Allow flushing of old/unused compiled code
-XX:+PrintCodeCache               # Print code cache usage on exit

Code cache eviction

When the code cache fills, HotSpot can flush rarely-used compiled methods (nmethods) back to interpreted. This is tracked via a sweep mechanism that marks nmethods as "not entrant" (new calls go to interpreter) and then "zombie" (can be collected). The original bytecode is always preserved, so methods can be recompiled later.

Part 14

Compilation Threads and the Compiler Broker

JIT compilation is performed by background compiler threads managed by the CompilerBroker:

Compilation pipeline:
  Application thread calls method N times → threshold crossed
  CompilerBroker queues (method, level) compile task
  Background C1 thread picks task, compiles, installs nmethod
  Application thread: at next call, checks method._code != null
                       → jumps to compiled code

  [Later]: C2 thread picks C1-compiled method for upgrade

Number of compiler threads

-XX:CICompilerCount=4    # Total compiler threads (default: scales with CPU count)
# JVM splits these into: 1/3 C1 threads, 2/3 C2 threads (approximately)

For a 4-core machine with 4 compiler threads: ~1 C1, ~3 C2. Compilation happens concurrently with application execution — no pauses for compilation itself.

Compilation queue overflow

If the compile queue fills up (more methods wanting compilation than threads can handle), methods stay at their current level longer. This is a common cause of sustained high CPU during warmup: the application is doing real work AND compiling aggressively. -XX:+PrintCompilation shows the queue depth and compile decisions in real time.

Part 15

PrintCompilation Output Decoded

-XX:+PrintCompilation produces a line per compilation event:

  timestamp  compile_id  flags  tierlevel  class::method  (bytes)
    1234      127         !      3          java.util.HashMap::get (69 bytes)
    1235      128                4          com.example.Parser::parse (312 bytes)
    1236      129         %      4          com.example.Parser::parseLoop @ 45 (312 bytes)
    1237      127         made not entrant  java.util.HashMap::get
Flag Meaning
(no flag) Normal compilation
! Exception handler present
% OSR compilation (note the @ 45 = loop header bytecode offset)
s Synchronized method
b Compilation occurred in blocking mode
n Wrapper for native method
made not entrant Old compiled version invalidated (deoptimization)
made zombie Code cache entry can be reclaimed
Part 16

Profiling Data: What C1 Collects

The profile data that C1's Level 3 code collects is stored in MethodData objects attached to each method:

Invocation and backedge counters

Two counters per method track how often it is called and how many loop iterations it has executed. These drive the tiered compilation thresholds.

Type profiles at call sites

For every virtual/interface call site, C1 records the actual receiver types seen:

Call site: list.add(item)
  Receiver type histogram:
    ArrayList: 9,872 times
    LinkedList: 3 times
    (other): 0 times

C2 uses this to devirtualize and inline ArrayList.add() speculatively.

Branch profiles

For every conditional branch (ifeq, ifge, etc.), C1 records taken/not-taken counts. C2 uses this to decide which side to treat as the "fast path" (kept in the straight-line code) and which to push to an out-of-line "cold" region.

Trap counts (uncommon traps)

Each deoptimization point in C1-compiled code records how many times it was triggered. If a trap fires "too many" times (-XX:PerMethodTrapLimit, default 100), C2 will not speculatively eliminate that check — it treats the branch as genuinely possible.

Part 17

GraalVM: Next-Generation JIT

GraalVM is a high-performance JDK distribution from Oracle that ships a JIT compiler called the Graal compiler, written entirely in Java (a JIT compiler that can compile itself — the "metacircular" JIT).

Graal vs. C2 comparison

Aspect C2 Graal (in JVM)
Language C++ Java
IR Sea-of-nodes Sea-of-nodes (similar, cleaner API)
Partial Escape Analysis Limited Advanced (can sink allocation out of loops)
Vectorization Good Excellent (AutoVectorization improvements)
Speculative optimizations Yes Yes + more aggressive
Compilation time Moderate Slightly higher (Java overhead)

Using Graal as JIT in OpenJDK (JVMCI)

The JVM Compiler Interface (JVMCI) — introduced in Java 9 — allows replacing HotSpot's JIT with an alternative compiler:

java -XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions \
     -XX:+EnableJVMCI \
     -XX:+UseJVMCICompiler \
     -jar app.jar

This swaps C2 for the Graal compiler at Level 4. C1 still handles Levels 1-3.

Graal Native Image (AOT)

GraalVM also provides Native Image — an ahead-of-time (AOT) compiler that compiles a Java application to a self-contained native executable with no JVM at runtime:

native-image -jar app.jar --no-fallback app-native
./app-native  # runs without JVM, startup in ~10ms

Trade-offs of Native Image:
- Startup: milliseconds vs. seconds (no JVM, no JIT warmup)
- Peak throughput: often lower than JIT (no runtime profiling, no speculative inlining)
- Memory footprint: much lower (no JVM heap overhead)
- Dynamic features: reflection, proxies, class loading limited without configuration

Part 18

Graal Partial Escape Analysis

Graal's Partial Escape Analysis (PEA) is more powerful than C2's escape analysis. PEA can virtualize objects along some execution paths even if they escape along others:

Point p = new Point(x, y);
if (condition) {
    heap.store(p);   // p escapes here
    return;
}
// p does NOT escape here — only used locally
double dist = Math.sqrt(p.x * p.x + p.y * p.y);

C2 would heap-allocate p because it escapes on the condition branch. Graal's PEA virtualizes p on the non-escaping path and only materializes the heap allocation on the condition==true path. This eliminates allocation pressure on the common path.

Part 19

AOT Compilation in Standard JDK (JEP History)

Beyond GraalVM Native Image, the Java ecosystem has explored AOT compilation within the standard JDK:

JEP 295: Ahead-of-Time Compilation (Java 9, removed in Java 17)

Used jaotc to pre-compile classes to native code stored in a shared library. Loaded at JVM startup as pre-compiled code, reducing JIT warmup. Removed because GraalVM Native Image and CDS/AppCDS offered better alternatives.

JEP 483: Ahead-of-Time Class Loading & Linking (Java 24)

Pre-resolves and pre-links classes at build time, stored in an AOT cache. This is not full compilation but dramatically reduces class-loading and linking overhead at startup.

JEP 484: Class-File API + future JIT improvements (Java 24+)

The Class-File API gives the JVM (and tools) a standard API for reading/writing class files, enabling better toolchain integration for AOT and instrumentation.

Part 20

Benchmarking JIT: JMH and Avoiding Pitfalls

Measuring JIT-compiled performance correctly requires understanding JIT behavior. Naive benchmarks produce wildly misleading results.

Common JIT benchmarking pitfalls

1. Dead code elimination

// WRONG: JIT sees result is never used → eliminates the entire computation
long start = System.nanoTime();
for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
    compute(i);  // result discarded → JIT may eliminate this
}
long end = System.nanoTime();

Fix: Use JMH's Blackhole.consume() to prevent dead code elimination.

2. Constant folding across iterations

If all inputs to a computation are known at compile time, the JIT may compute the result once and return a constant.

Fix: Use @State objects with @Benchmark parameters that vary.

3. Warmup period included in measurement

The first N iterations are C1/interpreter. If you measure from iteration 1, you are measuring warmup, not steady-state performance.

Fix: Use JMH's @Warmup and @Measurement annotations.

JMH example

@BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime)
@OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)
@Warmup(iterations = 5, time = 1)
@Measurement(iterations = 10, time = 1)
@Fork(1)
@State(Scope.Benchmark)
public class HashMapBenchmark {

    private HashMap<Integer, String> map;

    @Setup
    public void setup() {
        map = new HashMap<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) map.put(i, "v" + i);
    }

    @Benchmark
    public String get(Blackhole bh) {
        return map.get(42);  // Blackhole is not needed here since we return
    }
}
Part 21

Observing JIT Decisions with Flags and Tools

Essential JIT diagnostic flags

# Print every method compiled + OSR events
-XX:+PrintCompilation

# Print inlining decisions (very verbose)
-XX:+PrintInlining

# Print compiled assembly (requires hsdis library)
-XX:+PrintAssembly
-XX:+PrintOptoAssembly    # C2 assembly only

# Print escape analysis decisions
-XX:+PrintEscapeAnalysis

# Disable specific optimizations for debugging
-XX:-DoEscapeAnalysis
-XX:-OptimizeStringConcat
-XX:-UseLoopPredicate

# Compile a specific method at a specific level
-XX:CompileCommand=compileonly,com/example/Foo.bar
-XX:CompileCommand=dontinline,com/example/Foo.baz

# Print code cache usage
-XX:+PrintCodeCache

# Unified logging (Java 9+) for JIT
-Xlog:jit*=debug:file=jit.log
-Xlog:compilation=info

JITWatch

JITWatch is a GUI tool that parses PrintCompilation and PrintInlining output and visualizes:

  • Which methods were compiled and at what level
  • Inlining trees — what was inlined into what
  • Reasons why methods were NOT inlined
  • Hot spot highlighting in Java source vs. bytecode vs. assembly
Part 22

JIT Compiler Summary and Mental Model

The complete JIT lifecycle

1. Method first invoked → Level 0 (interpreter + profiling counters)

2. Invocation count threshold crossed:
   → Queued for C1 compilation
   → Level 3 nmethod installed (C1 + full profiling)

3. Profile data matures (type profiles, branch profiles stable):
   → Queued for C2 compilation
   → C2 reads MethodData, aggressively inlines, applies EA, loop opts
   → Level 4 nmethod installed

4. If assumption violated (new type at call site, etc.):
   → Deoptimization: compiled frame rolled back to interpreter
   → Method re-profiled, eventually recompiled with updated profile

5. If code cache fills:
   → Old/cold nmethods evicted (made not entrant, then zombie)
   → Methods fall back to interpreter until recompiled

Key insight: JIT quality improves over time — a running application
gets faster as more of its hot paths are compiled at higher tiers.

When JIT helps most

  • Long-running processes (servers, batch jobs) — amortizes warmup cost
  • CPU-bound hot loops — SIMD, unrolling, register allocation
  • Polymorphic code with few actual types — devirtualization + inlining
  • Code with many allocations of short-lived objects — escape analysis eliminates allocations

When JIT helps least

  • Short-lived CLI tools — exits before warming up (→ use Native Image)
  • Truly megamorphic call sites (10+ types) — JIT gives up, stays as megamorphic dispatch
  • I/O-bound code — the bottleneck is network/disk, not CPU

Practice Section

Conceptual Questions

  1. Why does tiered compilation use Level 3 (C1 with full profiling) rather than going directly from the interpreter to C2? What would be wrong with interpreter → C2 directly?

  2. Explain OSR. In what scenario is OSR specifically necessary, and what is the technical challenge of performing the compiled/interpreter state transfer mid-loop?

  3. Describe how escape analysis enables synchronization elimination. Give an example where a developer might accidentally create a synchronized object that never contends, and explain how the JIT saves them from themselves.

  4. A virtual call site has been observed calling three different receiver types in profiling. Explain why C2 typically will NOT inline at this call site, and what -XX:MaxInlineLevel has to do with it.

  5. What is the difference between a deoptimization at an "uncommon trap" and a deoptimization triggered by a nmethod dependency violation? Which is more disruptive?

Hands-On Exercises

Exercise 1 — Observing Tiered Compilation

Write a method that computes the sum of an array of one million integers. Run it 50,000 times and add -XX:+PrintCompilation. Record:
- At what invocation count does C1 Level 3 appear?
- When does C2 Level 4 appear?
- Are there any OSR events (% flag)?

Compare the elapsed time of the first 100 invocations vs. invocations 10,000–10,100.

Exercise 2 — Inlining Depth

Create a call chain: A → B → C → D → E → F → G → H → I → J (10 levels deep), where each method does trivial arithmetic. Add -XX:+PrintInlining and observe how deep the inliner goes. Then set -XX:MaxInlineLevel=5 and observe the change. What performance difference do you see?

Exercise 3 — Escape Analysis Validation

Write a microbenchmark using JMH that compares:
- Creating a Point(x, y) object inside a tight loop and using its fields
- Computing x*x + y*y without creating an object

Run with -XX:+DoEscapeAnalysis (default) and -XX:-DoEscapeAnalysis. The results should converge with EA enabled (Point is scalar-replaced). Use -XX:+PrintEscapeAnalysis to confirm.

Exercise 4 — OSR Trigger

Write a single method called only once that contains a loop executing 50 million iterations. Add -XX:+PrintCompilation and observe the OSR event. Note the @N offset in the output — look up byte offset N in the bytecode with javap -c and confirm it is the loop's backedge.

Exercise 5 — GraalVM Native Image Comparison

Take a simple CPU-bound Java program (e.g., prime number sieve). Run it three ways:
1. Standard JDK with HotSpot JIT (measure after warmup)
2. GraalVM JDK with Graal JIT (-XX:+UseJVMCICompiler)
3. GraalVM Native Image (native-image)

Compare: startup time, peak throughput, and resident memory (/usr/bin/time -v on Linux or time on macOS).

Key Terms Glossary

Term Definition
Tiered compilation Five-level execution pipeline from interpreter to C2 with profiling at each stage
C1 compiler Fast, lightly-optimizing JIT compiler that also instruments code for profiling
C2 compiler Aggressive, slow JIT compiler using sea-of-nodes IR and full optimization suite
Sea of nodes IR where operations are graph nodes and edges encode data/control dependencies
OSR (On-Stack Replacement) Replacing an executing interpreted method with its compiled version mid-execution
Escape analysis Analysis determining whether an object reference leaves its creating method
Scalar replacement Decomposing a non-escaping object into its constituent primitive fields in registers/stack
Deoptimization Rolling back compiled execution to interpreted when a speculative assumption is violated
Uncommon trap Guard in compiled code that deoptimizes when a predicted-rare condition occurs
nmethod dependency Assumption registered by compiled code; violation triggers nmethod invalidation
Inlining Replacing a method call with the callee's body to expose cross-method optimizations
Devirtualization Resolving a virtual call to a concrete target using type profile, enabling inlining
Intrinsic Hand-optimized native code the JIT emits for specific well-known methods
JMH Java Microbenchmark Harness — official framework for correct JVM benchmarking
JVMCI JVM Compiler Interface — allows plugging in an alternative JIT compiler
Graal compiler Java-implemented JIT compiler; can replace C2 via JVMCI
Native Image GraalVM's AOT compiler producing native executables with no JVM runtime
Code cache Fixed-size memory region holding JIT-compiled nmethods
CompilerBroker JVM component that queues and dispatches JIT compilation tasks to background threads
MethodData Per-method object storing profiling data collected by C1 Level 2/3 code
