Part 1

Why Automatic Memory Management Exists

Manual memory management in C/C++ requires developers to call malloc/free (C) or new/delete (C++) explicitly. Every allocation must be paired with exactly one deallocation. The result:

  • Dangling pointers — freeing memory that is still referenced
  • Double-free bugs — deallocating the same memory twice, corrupting the heap
  • Memory leaks — forgetting to free, causing unbounded heap growth
  • Buffer overflows — writing past allocated boundaries

Java's solution: automatic garbage collection. The JVM tracks all allocated objects and reclaims memory for objects that are no longer reachable from the running program. The developer allocates objects with new; the JVM handles deallocation.

The contract: liveness vs reachability

The GC does not know whether an object is logically needed. It only knows whether it is reachable. An object is reachable if there exists any chain of references from a GC root to that object.

Reachability:
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  GC Root ──► ObjectA ──► ObjectB ──► ObjectC  ← REACHABLE   │
│                                                               │
│  ObjectD ──► ObjectE   (no path from any root) ← GARBAGE    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

If no GC root can reach an object — directly or through any chain of references — the object is eligible for collection.

Part 2

GC Roots: The Starting Points of Reachability

A GC root is an object reference that is always considered live regardless of any other analysis. The JVM treats the following as GC roots:

Categories of GC roots

GC Root Categories:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 1. Stack Local Variables                                         │
│    Every local variable and method parameter in every active     │
│    stack frame on every live thread                              │
│                                                                  │
│ 2. Static Fields                                                 │
│    All static fields of all loaded classes                       │
│    (static fields live as long as their class is loaded)         │
│                                                                  │
│ 3. JNI References                                                │
│    Java objects passed to or returned from native (JNI) code     │
│    — both local and global JNI references                        │
│                                                                  │
│ 4. Active Thread Objects                                         │
│    Every live java.lang.Thread object                            │
│    (and the objects each thread's stack frames reference)        │
│                                                                  │
│ 5. Synchronization Monitors                                      │
│    Objects used as locks in active synchronized blocks           │
│                                                                  │
│ 6. Class Loader References                                       │
│    Objects referenced by active ClassLoader instances            │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Practical implication

public class GCRootDemo {
    static Object staticRoot = new Object();   // GC root — static field

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Object stackRoot = new Object();       // GC root — local variable

        Object isolated = new Object();        // NOT a root
        Object chained  = isolated;            // NOT a root either

        isolated = null;   // both isolated and chained are now unreachable
        chained  = null;   // → eligible for GC

        // stackRoot is still live (local var in active frame)
        System.out.println(stackRoot);
    }
}

The importance of nulling references

// Common memory leak pattern — static collection holding objects forever
static List<byte[]> cache = new ArrayList<>();

void processRequest(byte[] data) {
    cache.add(data);          // data added to static field
    // ... process ...
    // Never removed → GC root chain exists forever → leak
}

// Fix: remove or use WeakReference (see Part 17)
Part 3

Object Allocation: Where New Objects Are Born

When you call new Object() in Java, the JVM allocates memory for that object in the heap. The heap is divided into regions; understanding where objects land is fundamental to understanding why GC is structured the way it is.

TLAB: Thread-Local Allocation Buffer

Every live thread has a TLAB — a private region of the heap pre-assigned to that thread for fast, lock-free allocation.

Object Allocation via TLAB:
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Thread-1 TLAB           Thread-2 TLAB         Thread-3 TLAB │
│ ┌──────────────┐        ┌──────────────┐       ┌───────────┐ │
│ │ObjA│ObjB│ObjC│ ←bump  │ObjD│ObjE│   │ ←bump │ObjF│      │ │
│ └──────────────┘        └──────────────┘       └───────────┘ │
│                                                               │
│ Bump pointer: allocation = pointer increment (no locking)     │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

TLAB allocation is essentially free — just incrementing a pointer. When the TLAB fills up, the JVM requests a new TLAB from the Eden space.

The Empirical Weakness of Objects

Decades of profiling Java applications produced the foundational insight of generational GC:

> Most objects die young.

More precisely: in most Java applications, 90–98% of objects become unreachable within milliseconds of allocation. A transient String, a loop variable, a DTO object assembled in a request handler — all are garbage before most GC cycles.

This observation is called the generational hypothesis and it drives the entire structure of the JVM heap.

Part 4

Generational Hypothesis and Heap Structure

Because most objects die young, it is inefficient to scan the entire heap every GC cycle. Instead, the JVM divides the heap into generations based on object age.

Classic generational heap layout

JVM Heap — Generational Layout (Serial/Parallel/G1 collectors):
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                          Java Heap                                   │
│                                                                      │
│  ┌─────────────────────────┐    ┌──────────────────────────────────┐│
│  │      Young Generation   │    │         Old Generation           ││
│  │                         │    │         (Tenured Space)          ││
│  │  ┌────────┐ ┌──┐  ┌──┐  │    │                                  ││
│  │  │  Eden  │ │S0│  │S1│  │    │  Long-lived objects               ││
│  │  │(alloc) │ │  │  │  │  │    │  Tenured after N minor GCs        ││
│  │  └────────┘ └──┘  └──┘  │    │                                  ││
│  │   ~80%     ~10% ~10%    │    │                                  ││
│  └─────────────────────────┘    └──────────────────────────────────┘│
│                                                                      │
│  Metaspace (off-heap): class metadata, interned strings, JIT code   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Components explained

Region Purpose GC Event
Eden All new objects allocated here (via TLAB) Cleared on Minor GC
Survivor 0 (S0) Objects that survived previous Minor GC Copied to S1 on next Minor GC
Survivor 1 (S1) Other survivor half Copied to S0 on next Minor GC
Old Generation Objects that survived MaxTenuringThreshold Minor GCs Cleared on Major/Full GC
Metaspace Class metadata (replaced PermGen in Java 8) Cleared on class unloading
Part 5

Minor GC: Collecting the Young Generation

A Minor GC (also called a Young GC) runs when Eden fills up. It is fast because it only processes the Young generation.

Minor GC algorithm (stop-the-world)

Minor GC Execution:
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. STOP THE WORLD
   All application threads paused

2. IDENTIFY LIVE OBJECTS IN EDEN + active Survivor
   Trace from GC roots into Young gen only
   (Old-to-Young references handled via card table — see Part 9)

3. COPY LIVE OBJECTS
   Live objects from Eden → S1  (or S0, whichever is "To" space)
   Live objects from S0   → S1  (if age < MaxTenuringThreshold)
   Live objects from S0   → Old (if age ≥ MaxTenuringThreshold)

4. INCREMENT OBJECT AGE
   Each surviving copy has its age counter incremented

5. CLEAR EDEN + old Survivor
   Eden and "From" survivor space are completely wiped

6. RESUME APPLICATION THREADS
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Object age and tenuring

// Conceptual view of object age counter (not directly accessible in Java)
// JVM stores age in the object header's mark word (4 bits → max age 15)

// Force tenuring threshold inspection:
// -XX:+PrintTenuringDistribution (Java 8–11)
// -Xlog:gc+age=trace (Java 9+)

// Default MaxTenuringThreshold = 15 (most collectors)
// -XX:MaxTenuringThreshold=8  ← tune for objects that live ~8 GC cycles

Why Minor GC is fast

Minor GC Efficiency:
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Young gen typically = 1/3 of heap (256 MB in a 768 MB heap) │
│  ~95% of Eden is garbage at GC time → almost nothing to copy │
│  Copying collector: cost ∝ live data, not allocated data      │
│  Typical Minor GC pause: 1–10 ms                             │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Part 6

The Mark-Sweep-Compact Algorithm

Major GC (also called Full GC) collects the Old generation and sometimes the entire heap. The classical algorithm is mark-sweep-compact, running in three phases.

Phase 1: Mark

Starting from all GC roots, the collector traverses all reachable objects and marks them as live.

Mark Phase:
GC Root ──► ObjA (MARKED) ──► ObjC (MARKED)
GC Root ──► ObjB (MARKED)
             ObjD (not marked — unreachable)
             ObjE (not marked — unreachable)

Marking requires a Stop-the-World (STW) pause — if the application mutates references during marking, the collector might miss a newly created live object or incorrectly keep a dead one.

Phase 2: Sweep

Walk the entire heap linearly. Any object NOT marked is considered garbage. The memory it occupied is added to a free list.

Sweep Phase (heap after marking):
┌─────┬─────┬─────┬─────┬─────┬─────┬─────┬─────┐
│ ObjA│DEAD │ ObjC│DEAD │DEAD │ ObjB│DEAD │DEAD │
│(L)  │     │(L)  │     │     │(L)  │     │     │
└─────┴─────┴─────┴─────┴─────┴─────┴─────┴─────┘
             ↑     ↑↑↑↑↑       ↑     ↑↑↑↑↑
             Gaps → heap fragmentation

Problem: Sweep leaves gaps between live objects (fragmentation). Subsequent allocations must find contiguous blocks large enough — allocation slows and may fail even when total free space exists.

Phase 3: Compact

Move all live objects together toward one end of the heap, eliminating gaps.

Compact Phase:
Before: [ObjA][    ][ObjC][    ][    ][ObjB][    ][    ]
After:  [ObjA][ObjC][ObjB][               free               ]

Compaction is expensive (O(heap size)) but gives back bump-pointer allocation speed.

Mark-Sweep-Compact cost profile

Phase Cost driver Pause type
Mark Proportional to live objects STW
Sweep Proportional to heap size STW (traditional) / Concurrent (G1)
Compact Proportional to live objects × relocation STW
Part 7

Stop-the-World (STW) Pauses

A Stop-the-World pause is the interval during which all application threads are suspended so the GC can safely inspect or modify the heap.

Why STW is necessary

Without STW — the tri-color problem:
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. GC marks ObjA as live (grey)
2. Application thread sets ObjA.ref = null; ObjB.ref = ObjC
3. GC finishes ObjA — ObjC was reachable only via ObjA
4. GC never sees ObjC from ObjB's perspective (ObjB not yet visited)
5. ObjC incorrectly collected → CRASH (use-after-free)
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

STW avoids this by freezing the reference graph during critical phases. Modern collectors minimize STW duration through concurrent phases but cannot eliminate it entirely.

Safepoints

The JVM cannot pause threads at arbitrary bytecode instructions. Threads are only paused at safepoints — well-defined execution points where the JVM has a consistent view of the thread's state.

Safepoint locations (compiled code):
- Method return points
- Loop back-edges (for long loops)
- JNI call return points
- Transition from native to Java code

-XX:+PrintSafepointStatistics    ← logs safepoint pause details
-Xlog:safepoint=info             ← Java 9+ equivalent

STW pause taxonomy

GC Event Typical STW Cause
Minor GC 1–20 ms Eden full
Major GC (CMS) 10–500 ms Old gen threshold reached
Full GC (Serial/Parallel) 100ms–10s Explicit, promotion failure, Metaspace
G1 GC Mixed 10–200 ms Old region collection
ZGC / Shenandoah 0.5–5 ms Root/remap pauses only
Part 8

Copying Collector: Young Gen's Secret Weapon

The Young generation does not use mark-sweep-compact — it uses a copying collector (also called semi-space or Cheney's algorithm).

How copying collection works

Copying Collection — Eden + S0 → S1:
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
"From" space (Eden + S0)         "To" space (S1)
┌────────────────────────┐       ┌───────────────────────────┐
│ObjA│ObjB│ObjC│ObjD│   │  →    │ObjA'│ObjC'│             │
│(L) │(D) │(L) │(D) │   │  →    │(age+1)(age+1)            │
└────────────────────────┘       └───────────────────────────┘
                                                  ↑
                                       bump pointer (fast alloc)
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
After copy: From space wiped in one memset → no sweep needed

Why copying beats mark-sweep for young objects

  • No fragmentation — "To" space is always contiguous
  • Cost proportional to live data (not all allocated data)
  • If 95% of Eden is garbage, 95% of the work is zero-cost (nothing to copy)
  • Allocation in "To" space is bump-pointer — same speed as TLAB

The 50% space overhead trade-off

Copying requires two survivor spaces, each half the size of the total survivor region. At any moment, one survivor is empty and one is active. This wastes 50% of survivor space — acceptable because survivors are small.

Part 9

Card Table and Remembered Sets

A key problem for generational GC: old objects can reference young objects. When running Minor GC, the collector only traces the young generation — but it must handle pointers from Old to Young.

The card table solution

The JVM divides the old generation heap into 512-byte cards. Whenever the application stores a reference into an old object, the JVM sets the corresponding card's entry to "dirty" — a write barrier records the mutation.

Card Table (Old Generation tracking):
┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Old Generation Heap                                          │
│  [card 0][card 1][card 2][card 3][card 4][card 5][card 6]... │
│     clean   DIRTY   clean   DIRTY   clean  clean   clean     │
│                                                               │
│  Card Table Array (1 byte per 512 bytes of heap):             │
│  [ 0 ][ 1 ][ 0 ][ 1 ][ 0 ][ 0 ][ 0 ]                        │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

During Minor GC, the collector scans only dirty cards to find Old-to-Young references. This avoids scanning the entire old generation.

Write barrier (pseudo-code)

// What the JVM inserts on every reference store:
// obj.field = newValue  →  compiled to:

store obj.field, newValue
card_table[obj_address >> 9] = DIRTY   // 512 = 2^9

Remembered sets in G1

G1GC uses a more precise structure called a Remembered Set (RSet) — each heap region maintains a set of cards in other regions that contain references into it. This allows G1 to collect individual regions in isolation.

Part 10

Promotion and Premature Tenuring

When objects survive enough Minor GCs (default threshold: 15), they are promoted (tenured) to the Old generation.

Normal promotion flow

Object Lifecycle (normal case):
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Allocation in Eden (age 0)
   │ Minor GC survives
   ▼
Survivor S0/S1 (age 1)
   │ Minor GC survives
   ▼
Survivor S0/S1 (age 2)
   │ ... survive 13 more GCs ...
   ▼
Old Generation (tenured at age 15)
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Premature tenuring (a GC antipattern)

If the Survivor spaces are too small to hold all live young objects, overflow objects are prematurely promoted to Old gen even if they would have died shortly. This crowds the Old gen with short-lived objects, triggering expensive Major GCs.

Premature Tenuring Diagnosis:
-Xlog:gc+age=debug          ← shows age distribution
-Xlog:gc*                   ← verbose GC logs

Symptoms:
  - Frequent Major GC despite low heap pressure
  - Old gen growing faster than expected
  - GC logs showing "To-space overflow" or "Evacuation Failure"

Tuning survivor spaces

# Ratio of Eden to each Survivor space (default = 8 → Eden is 8× each Survivor)
-XX:SurvivorRatio=6          # larger Survivors → less premature tenuring

# Dynamic survivor sizing (default on since Java 8)
-XX:+UseAdaptiveSizePolicy   # JVM adjusts Eden/Survivor sizes automatically

# Hard-fix tenuring threshold (use sparingly)
-XX:MaxTenuringThreshold=5   # tenure at age 5 instead of 15
Part 11

Major GC and Full GC

Major GC

A Major GC collects the Old generation. It is triggered when:

  1. Old generation space usage exceeds the configured occupancy threshold
  2. A Minor GC cannot find enough space to promote surviving young objects (promotion failure)
  3. Explicit System.gc() call (unless -XX:+DisableExplicitGC)

Major GC pauses are significantly longer than Minor GC because:
- Old generation is much larger
- Live data density is higher (objects survived many GCs)
- Mark-sweep-compact must scan/move more data

Full GC

A Full GC collects the entire heap: Young + Old + Metaspace. Triggers include:

Full GC Triggers (common):
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Explicit System.gc()
2. Old gen completely full (allocation failure after Major GC)
3. Metaspace exhausted (class loading storm)
4. JVM ergonomics decides heap needs complete cleanup
5. RMI-triggered (every hour by default — disable in production)
   → -XX:+DisableExplicitGC
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Diagnosing Full GC in logs

# Java 9+ unified GC logging
-Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,level,tags

# Example Full GC log entry:
[2026-06-29T12:03:45.123+0000][info][gc] GC(42) Pause Full (Ergonomics)
[2026-06-29T12:03:45.123+0000][info][gc,heap] GC(42) Eden: 512M->0M(512M)
[2026-06-29T12:03:45.123+0000][info][gc,heap] GC(42) Old: 1800M->980M(2048M)
[2026-06-29T12:03:47.891+0000][info][gc] GC(42) Pause Full 2768ms
#                                                              ^^^^^^ PROBLEM
Part 12

G1 Garbage Collector (Garbage-First)

G1GC (Garbage-First Garbage Collector) became the default JVM collector in Java 9. It is designed for large heaps (4 GB+) with predictable pause time goals.

G1 heap layout: region-based

G1 abandons the fixed Young/Old split and divides the heap into equal-sized regions (1–32 MB, power of 2, ~2048 regions total).

G1 Heap Layout (conceptual, 32 regions shown):
┌──┬──┬──┬──┬──┬──┬──┬──┐
│E │E │E │E │S │O │O │O │   E = Eden region
├──┼──┼──┼──┼──┼──┼──┼──┤   S = Survivor region
│O │O │F │F │E │E │E │H │   O = Old region
├──┼──┼──┼──┼──┼──┼──┼──┤   H = Humongous region (large objects)
│H │F │F │F │O │O │E │E │   F = Free (available)
├──┼──┼──┼──┼──┼──┼──┼──┤
│F │F │E │E │E │O │O │F │
└──┴──┴──┴──┴──┴──┴──┴──┘

Regions are dynamically assigned roles. G1 can collect any subset of regions in one GC cycle — this is the "Garbage-First" principle: prioritize the regions with the most garbage.

G1 GC phases

G1 Collection Cycle:
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Phase 1: Young-Only Phase
  ├─ Young Collection (STW)
  │    Copy Eden + Survivor regions → new Survivor regions
  │    Promote old-enough objects → Old regions
  │    Pause: 10–200 ms (configurable via MaxGCPauseMillis)
  │
  ├─ Concurrent Marking (background, no STW)
  │    Marks live objects in Old regions concurrently
  │    Uses SATB (Snapshot-At-The-Beginning) write barrier
  │
  └─ Remark (STW, short)
       Finalize marking; drain SATB buffers
       Pause: typically 5–50 ms

Phase 2: Space Reclamation (Mixed Collection)
  ├─ Mixed GC (STW)
  │    Collect Young regions + selected Old regions (highest garbage %)
  │    Selection: regions with most dead objects collected first
  │    Pause: similar to Young Collection
  │
  └─ Repeat mixed GCs until Old gen cleaned or heap occupancy low
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Key G1 tuning flags

# Target maximum GC pause time (default: 200ms)
-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=100

# G1 is default since Java 9 — no explicit flag needed
-XX:+UseG1GC

# Heap occupancy % that triggers concurrent marking (default: 45%)
-XX:InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent=35

# Region size (power of 2, 1–32 MB)
-XX:G1HeapRegionSize=8m

# Reserve for evacuation (default: 10% — reduce if Full GC frequent)
-XX:G1ReservePercent=10

# Tune mixed GC targets
-XX:G1MixedGCLiveThresholdPercent=65   # only collect regions with <65% live
-XX:G1HeapWastePercent=5               # stop mixed GC when waste < 5%

Humongous objects

Objects larger than 50% of a G1 region are classified as humongous and allocated in contiguous humongous regions. They bypass Eden entirely and are allocated directly in the Old generation.

// Humongous allocation — triggers region-spanning allocation
byte[] large = new byte[6 * 1024 * 1024];  // 6 MB in a 4 MB region → humongous

// Risk: humongous regions are only reclaimed during concurrent marking
// Many small humongous allocations → fragmentation → premature Full GC

// Mitigation: increase G1HeapRegionSize so fewer objects qualify
-XX:G1HeapRegionSize=16m  // objects < 8 MB are no longer humongous
Part 13

Concurrent Mark Sweep (CMS) — Legacy

CMS was the first concurrent low-pause collector in the JVM (Java 1.4.1). It was deprecated in Java 9 and removed in Java 14. Understanding CMS is valuable for legacy system maintenance and for understanding what G1 improved upon.

CMS phases

CMS Collection Phases:
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Initial Mark (STW, very short)
   Mark objects directly reachable from GC roots

2. Concurrent Mark (concurrent, application runs)
   Trace full reachability graph — most of the marking work
   Application threads continue running (mutations tracked)

3. Concurrent Preclean (concurrent)
   Process dirty cards from concurrent mark mutations

4. Remark (STW, short)
   Fix any changes made during concurrent mark
   Most significant STW pause in CMS

5. Concurrent Sweep (concurrent)
   Reclaim dead objects — does NOT compact (no STW for compaction)
   Leaves free list → fragmentation over time

6. Concurrent Reset (concurrent)
   Prepare data structures for next cycle
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

CMS limitations

  • No compaction — fragmentation builds up over time; may trigger Full GC with Serial compaction (long pause)
  • Concurrent mode failure — if Old gen fills up during concurrent mark, falls back to Serial Full GC
  • Floating garbage — objects that die during concurrent mark are not collected until the next cycle
  • CPU overhead — concurrent threads consume 25–50% of CPU during marking

CMS → G1 → ZGC is the evolutionary arc; modern applications should use G1 or ZGC.

Part 14

ZGC and Shenandoah: Sub-Millisecond Collectors

Java 15+ (ZGC GA) and Red Hat's Shenandoah (available via OpenJDK distributions) push pause times to sub-millisecond levels regardless of heap size.

ZGC design principles

ZGC Architecture:
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Region-based heap (Z pages: small/medium/large)
Colored pointers (load barriers in generated code)
Concurrent relocation — objects moved while application runs
NUMA-aware allocation

STW Pauses: only 3 (all very short, ~0.5–2 ms)
  1. Pause Mark Start     — establish GC roots
  2. Pause Mark End       — finalize marking
  3. Pause Relocate Start — establish relocation set

Everything else: concurrent (no application impact)
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Colored pointers (ZGC's key innovation)

ZGC stores metadata in unused bits of the 64-bit pointer itself (only works on 64-bit JVMs with heap < 16 TB).

64-bit ZGC pointer layout:
Bit 63    │ Bits 45-62 │ Bit 44 │ Bit 43 │ Bit 42 │ Bits 0-41
──────────┼────────────┼────────┼────────┼────────┼──────────────
Reserved  │  Unused    │Finaliz.│Remapped│ Marked │ Object addr
          │            │able    │        │ (0/1)  │

Choosing the right collector

GC Selection Decision Tree:
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Heap < 4 GB, throughput priority
  └─► Parallel GC (-XX:+UseParallelGC)

Heap 4–32 GB, balanced pause/throughput
  └─► G1GC (default since Java 9)

Heap > 32 GB OR pause < 10 ms required
  └─► ZGC (-XX:+UseZGC, Java 15+ GA)

Heap > 32 GB, OpenJDK, pause < 10 ms
  └─► Shenandoah (-XX:+UseShenandoahGC)

Containers / small heap / batch jobs
  └─► SerialGC (-XX:+UseSerialGC)
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

ZGC configuration

# Enable ZGC (Java 15+, GA)
-XX:+UseZGC

# Generational ZGC (Java 21+, recommended)
-XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational

# Soft max heap (ZGC tries to stay under this, but may exceed)
-XX:SoftMaxHeapSize=6g -Xmx8g

# Concurrent GC threads (default = CPU_count / 4)
-XX:ConcGCThreads=4
Part 15

Reference Types: Controlling Reachability

Java provides four reference strength levels that interact with GC reachability:

1. Strong Reference (default)

Object obj = new Object();  // Strong reference
// obj is eligible for GC only when no strong references exist

2. Soft Reference — evicted under memory pressure

import java.lang.ref.SoftReference;

SoftReference<byte[]> softRef = new SoftReference<>(new byte[1024 * 1024]);

byte[] data = softRef.get();  // null if GC collected it
if (data == null) {
    data = loadData();  // reload
    softRef = new SoftReference<>(data);
}

Use case: memory-sensitive caches. The JVM guarantees soft-referenced objects are cleared before OutOfMemoryError. Cleared in LRU order based on last access time (-XX:SoftRefLRUPolicyMSPerMB controls retention, default 1000ms/MB).

3. Weak Reference — collected at next GC

import java.lang.ref.WeakReference;

WeakReference<Object> weakRef = new WeakReference<>(new Object());
// Eligible for collection at the NEXT GC cycle (regardless of memory)

Object obj = weakRef.get();  // null after GC

Use case: canonical mappings, caches where stale entries should be promptly removed. WeakHashMap uses weak keys.

4. Phantom Reference — post-mortem finalization

import java.lang.ref.PhantomReference;
import java.lang.ref.ReferenceQueue;

ReferenceQueue<Object> queue = new ReferenceQueue<>();
PhantomReference<Object> phantomRef =
    new PhantomReference<>(new Object(), queue);

// phantomRef.get() always returns null — no access to referent
// Object is enqueued to queue AFTER finalization, before memory reclaim

Use case: off-heap memory cleanup, resource release after GC collects the wrapper object. Preferred over finalize() (which is deprecated and unreliable).

Reference reachability hierarchy

Reachability Levels (strongest to weakest):
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Strongly Reachable  → Never collected                        │
│ Softly Reachable    → Collected under memory pressure        │
│ Weakly Reachable    → Collected at next GC                   │
│ Phantom Reachable   → Finalized, enqueued, then reclaimed    │
│ Unreachable         → Immediately eligible                   │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Part 16

Finalization and the `finalize()` Deprecation

Object.finalize() was Java's original mechanism for resource cleanup before GC. It is deprecated since Java 9 and marked for removal — never use it in new code.

Why finalize() is broken

finalize() Problems:
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. No guaranteed execution time — may run seconds/minutes later
2. No guaranteed execution at all — JVM may exit before running
3. Objects can "resurrect" themselves by storing this in a static field
4. Finalizer thread is single-threaded → finalization backlog
5. Two GC cycles required to reclaim finalizable objects (delay)
6. Security vulnerability — attackers can exploit finalize() for
   partial initialization attacks
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Modern replacements

// WRONG — finalize() for resource cleanup
@Override
@Deprecated
protected void finalize() {
    connection.close();  // unreliable, may never run
}

// CORRECT — AutoCloseable / try-with-resources
public class ManagedResource implements AutoCloseable {
    private final Connection connection;

    @Override
    public void close() {
        connection.close();  // deterministic — called by try-with-resources
    }
}

try (ManagedResource r = new ManagedResource()) {
    r.use();
}  // close() called here, always

// CORRECT — Cleaner API (Java 9+, replacement for PhantomReference boilerplate)
import java.lang.ref.Cleaner;

public class NativeResource {
    private static final Cleaner CLEANER = Cleaner.create();
    private final Cleaner.Cleanable cleanable;
    private final long nativeHandle;

    public NativeResource(long handle) {
        this.nativeHandle = handle;
        this.cleanable = CLEANER.register(this, () -> freeNative(handle));
    }

    @Override
    public void close() {
        cleanable.clean();  // deterministic cleanup
    }

    private static native void freeNative(long handle);
}
Part 17

Memory Leaks in Managed Languages

Despite GC, Java applications can leak memory. All Java memory leaks share one root cause: a GC root holds a reference chain to objects that are logically dead but still reachable.

Common memory leak patterns

Pattern 1: Static collection accumulation

// LEAK — static list grows forever
static final List<Session> activeSessions = new ArrayList<>();

void onLogin(Session s) {
    activeSessions.add(s);         // added on login
    // BUG: never removed on logout → permanent strong reference chain
}

// FIX: remove on logout
void onLogout(Session s) {
    activeSessions.remove(s);
}

Pattern 2: Unclosed streams / resources (pre-Java 7)

// LEAK — InputStream holds file descriptor; GC eventually closes
// but "eventually" may be too late (file descriptor exhaustion)
InputStream is = new FileInputStream("data.txt");
// process...
// missing: is.close()

// FIX — try-with-resources
try (InputStream is = new FileInputStream("data.txt")) {
    // process
}

Pattern 3: Listener not deregistered

// LEAK — EventBus holds strong reference to listener
eventBus.register(this);         // registers listener
// ... widget lifecycle ends ...
// eventBus.unregister(this);    // missing → this object never GC'd

// FIX — symmetric register/unregister
eventBus.unregister(this);

// ALTERNATIVE — use WeakReference-based event bus

Pattern 4: Inner class capturing outer class

// LEAK — anonymous Runnable captures outer class instance
class MyActivity {
    void onCreate() {
        // Anonymous class holds implicit reference to MyActivity.this
        Runnable task = new Runnable() {
            @Override public void run() {
                // references MyActivity fields
            }
        };
        executor.submit(task);   // task survives MyActivity lifecycle
        // MyActivity can't be GC'd until task completes
    }
}

// FIX — use static nested class + WeakReference
static class SafeTask implements Runnable {
    private final WeakReference<MyActivity> actRef;
    SafeTask(MyActivity a) { this.actRef = new WeakReference<>(a); }

    @Override public void run() {
        MyActivity a = actRef.get();
        if (a != null) { /* use a */ }
    }
}

└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Production GC Tuning Guide

Heap sizing fundamentals

# Always set Xms = Xmx to prevent heap resize pauses
-Xms4g -Xmx4g

# Young gen sizing (G1 manages automatically; for Parallel GC)
-XX:NewRatio=2        # Old:Young = 2:1 → Young = 1/3 of heap
-XX:NewSize=1g        # explicit minimum young gen size
-XX:MaxNewSize=2g     # explicit maximum young gen size

# Container awareness (Java 8u191+, Java 10+)
-XX:+UseContainerSupport          # respect cgroup memory limits
-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0         # use 75% of container memory as Xmx

G1GC production configuration template

  -Xms8g -Xmx8g \
  -XX:+UseG1GC \
  -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=100 \
  -XX:InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent=35 \
  -XX:G1HeapRegionSize=8m \
  -XX:G1ReservePercent=15 \
  -XX:G1MixedGCLiveThresholdPercent=65 \
  -XX:G1HeapWastePercent=5 \

Common GC problems and fixes

Symptom Likely Cause Fix
Frequent Full GC Heap too small / promotion failure Increase -Xmx, check SurvivorRatio
Long Minor GC pauses Survivor overflow / too many live young objects Increase Eden (-XX:NewRatio)
Old gen growing steadily Memory leak Heap dump + leak analysis
High CPU from GC threads GC thrashing (heap too small) Increase heap; reduce allocation rate
OutOfMemoryError: GC overhead >98% time in GC, <2% progress Fundamental heap or leak issue
Humongous allocation warnings Large objects in G1 Increase G1HeapRegionSize
Promotion failure Survivor spaces too small Decrease SurvivorRatio or increase heap
Part 20

GC in Containers and Kubernetes

The container CPU/memory problem (pre-Java 10)

Before Java 8u191 / Java 10, the JVM read CPU and memory from the host machine — not the cgroup limits. A JVM in a 2-CPU, 2-GB container on a 32-CPU, 128-GB host would:

  • Create 32 GC threads (using all host CPUs)
  • Set default heap to ~32 GB (using host memory)
  • Immediately OOMKill the container

Container-aware JVM settings

# Java 11+ (preferred — automatic cgroup detection)
-XX:+UseContainerSupport    # enabled by default since Java 11

# Heap as percentage of container memory limit
-XX:InitialRAMPercentage=50.0   # Xms = 50% of container memory
-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0       # Xmx = 75% of container memory
-XX:MinRAMPercentage=25.0       # minimum heap for small containers

# CPU: GC threads scaled to container CPU limit automatically
# Override if needed:
-XX:ActiveProcessorCount=4

Kubernetes resource alignment

# Dockerfile / Kubernetes pod spec alignment
resources:
  requests:
    memory: "2Gi"
    cpu: "1"
  limits:
    memory: "2Gi"    # hard limit — OOMKill if exceeded
    cpu: "2"

# JVM flags for 2 GB container:
# -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 → Xmx ≈ 1.5 GB
# Remaining 512 MB for: Metaspace, code cache, thread stacks, off-heap

JVM memory footprint beyond the heap

Total JVM Memory = Heap + Non-Heap:
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Heap (Xmx)               ← tunable                          │
│ Metaspace                ← class metadata; tunable           │
│ Code Cache               ← JIT-compiled code; ~256 MB        │
│ Thread stacks            ← N threads × Xss (default 512 KB) │
│ Direct ByteBuffers       ← off-heap NIO buffers              │
│ GC data structures       ← card table, RSets (~1–3% heap)    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Rule of thumb: container memory = Xmx × 1.3 to 1.5
Part 21

Interview Q&A

Q1: Explain the difference between Minor GC, Major GC, and Full GC.

Answer:
- Minor GC collects only the Young generation (Eden + Survivor spaces). It is fast (1–20ms) and frequent.
- Major GC collects the Old generation. It is slower (10ms–seconds) and triggered by Old gen fill-up or promotion failure.
- Full GC collects the entire heap including Metaspace. It is the longest pause (100ms–10s+) and should be avoided in production. Triggered by explicit System.gc(), allocation failure after Major GC, or Metaspace exhaustion.

Q2: What are GC roots and why do they matter?

Answer: GC roots are the starting points for reachability analysis — objects that are always considered live. They include local variables in active stack frames, static fields of loaded classes, active thread objects, and JNI global references. If no path exists from any GC root to an object, that object is eligible for collection. Understanding GC roots explains why static collections cause memory leaks (static field = permanent GC root).

Q3: What is a Stop-the-World pause and why is it necessary?

Answer: An STW pause suspends all application threads while the GC performs critical work. It is necessary because the GC needs a consistent snapshot of the reference graph — if application threads mutate object references while the GC is traversing them, objects could be incorrectly classified as live or dead. Modern collectors minimize STW pauses by doing most work concurrently and only using STW for short phases like root scanning and remark.

Q4: How does G1 differ from Parallel GC?

Answer: Parallel GC uses a fixed generational layout (Young/Old) and collects entire generations in STW. G1 divides the heap into equal-sized regions and can collect any subset. G1 runs most work concurrently (not just Young GC), targets a user-defined pause goal (MaxGCPauseMillis), and prioritizes regions with the most garbage. G1 is better for large heaps (4 GB+) requiring predictable pauses; Parallel GC has higher throughput for batch workloads.

Q5: What is the generational hypothesis and how does it shape JVM GC design?

Answer: The generational hypothesis observes that most objects die young — typically 90–98% of allocated objects become unreachable within milliseconds. This means scanning the entire heap every GC cycle wastes effort on long-lived objects that survive anyway. By segregating objects into Young (frequently collected, cheap copying GC) and Old (infrequently collected, expensive mark-compact) generations, the JVM spends most GC CPU on the small, frequently garbage-heavy Young generation.

Q6: What is premature tenuring and how do you diagnose it?

Answer: Premature tenuring occurs when short-lived objects are promoted to Old gen before they die, because Survivor spaces are too small to hold all surviving young objects. This crowds Old gen with objects that would have died soon, triggering expensive Major GCs. Diagnosis: -Xlog:gc+age=debug shows the tenuring distribution — if many objects are promoted at age 1–2 instead of 15, Survivors are too small. Fix: decrease SurvivorRatio (larger Survivors) or enable -XX:+UseAdaptiveSizePolicy.

Q7: Architect's decision: when would you choose ZGC over G1GC?

Answer: Choose ZGC when:
1. Pause time SLO < 10 ms (ZGC achieves < 1–2 ms even on multi-terabyte heaps)
2. Heap size > 32 GB (G1 pauses scale with heap; ZGC does not)
3. Latency-sensitive workloads: real-time bidding, trading, gaming backends
4. Java 21+ is available (Generational ZGC offers better throughput than older ZGC)

Keep G1 when: heap is 4–32 GB, 100 ms pauses are acceptable, throughput is the primary metric, or running Java < 15.

Part 22

Phase 6 Context: GC in the JVM Internals Map

Garbage collection is the most user-visible aspect of JVM internals — it directly causes application pauses and determines memory limits. Understanding GC connects everything else in Phase 6:

Phase 6 — JVM Internals Knowledge Map (GC context):
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
CLASS LOADING (Lessons 56–58)
  └─ ClassLoader creates Class objects in Metaspace
  └─ Metaspace pressure → GC trigger (class unloading)

JVM STARTUP & BYTECODE (Lesson 59)
  └─ Bytecode execution allocates objects → Eden pressure
  └─ Object header layout (mark word) stores GC age, lock state

GARBAGE COLLECTION ← YOU ARE HERE (Lesson 60)
  └─ GC roots, generational heap, mark-sweep-compact
  └─ G1GC, ZGC, STW pauses, reference types, tuning

HEAP MEMORY DEEP DIVE (Lesson 61)
  └─ TLAB internals, object layout, compressed OOPs
  └─ Off-heap allocation (direct buffers, Unsafe)

JIT COMPILATION (Lessons 65–68)
  └─ JIT-compiled methods live in Code Cache (non-heap)
  └─ Escape analysis → stack allocation (bypasses GC)
  └─ Scalar replacement → object fields on stack

JVM TOOLING (Lessons 70–75)
  └─ JFR GC events, jstat, jmap, async-profiler
  └─ Heap dump analysis with Eclipse MAT / VisualVM
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

GC — key insights to carry forward

GC is not magic: it is a precise algorithm (mark, sweep, compact) operating on a reachability graph. Every object lifecycle decision — allocation in Eden, survival in Survivors, promotion to Old — is deterministic and measurable.

STW pauses are the enemy of latency: every architectural GC decision from CMS to G1 to ZGC is driven by reducing STW duration. The history of Java GC is the history of moving more and more work off the STW path.

Tuning starts with measurement: never change GC flags without GC logs. Enable -Xlog:gc* in all environments. The logs tell you whether you have Minor GC pressure, promotion failure, humongous allocations, or Full GC — each requiring a different fix.

Allocation rate is the root variable: the fastest way to improve GC is to reduce allocation. Object pooling, value types (Project Valhalla), and stack allocation via escape analysis all reduce Eden pressure before the GC has any work to do.

Practice — Lesson 60

Easy Exercises

Exercise 1 — GC Root Identification

For each code snippet, identify which objects are GC roots and which are eligible for collection:

public class GCRootExercise {
    static String staticStr = "alive";   // (a)

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String local = "also alive";     // (b)
        String temp  = new String("temporary"); // (c)
        temp = null;                     // after this line

        Object orphan = new Object();    // (d) - stored in local only
        orphan = new Object();           // first Object now?

        System.out.println(staticStr + local);
    }
}

Expected analysis:
- (a) staticStr — GC root (static field); never collected while class is loaded
- (b) local — GC root (local variable in active frame); lives until main() returns
- (c) first temp String — was eligible after temp = null; GC may collect it
- (d) first orphan Object — eligible for GC after orphan = new Object()

Exercise 2 — Reference Type Behavior

Write a program that demonstrates WeakReference collection:

import java.lang.ref.WeakReference;

public class WeakRefDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        Object strong = new Object();
        WeakReference<Object> weak = new WeakReference<>(strong);

        System.out.println("Before nulling: " + weak.get()); // not null

        strong = null;  // remove strong reference
        System.gc();    // suggest GC (not guaranteed, but usually runs in demo)

        Thread.sleep(100);  // give GC time
        System.out.println("After GC: " + weak.get()); // likely null

        // TODO: repeat with SoftReference — observe it survives unless heap is low

Exercise 3 — Identify the Memory Leak

Find the memory leak in this code and explain why it leaks:

public class EventManager {
    private static final List<Runnable> listeners = new ArrayList<>();

    public static void addListener(Runnable listener) {
        listeners.add(listener);
    }

    public void processEvent() {
        Runnable handler = () -> System.out.println("handling event in " + this);
        EventManager.addListener(handler);
        // ... process ...
    }
}

Answer: listeners is a static ArrayList. Every call to processEvent() adds a lambda that captures this (the EventManager instance). Since listeners is a static GC root, every lambda — and therefore every EventManager instance — is permanently reachable. Fix: remove listeners when no longer needed, or use WeakReference<Runnable>.

Medium Exercises

Exercise 4 — GC Log Analysis

Given the following GC log excerpt, answer the diagnostic questions:

[10.123s][info][gc] GC(5) Pause Young (Normal) 512M->480M(1024M) 25.3ms
[10.456s][info][gc] GC(6) Pause Young (Normal) 512M->495M(1024M) 28.1ms
[10.789s][info][gc] GC(7) Pause Young (Normal) 512M->510M(1024M) 30.2ms
[11.012s][info][gc] GC(8) Pause Young (Evacuation Failure) 512M->512M(1024M) 95.7ms
[11.018s][info][gc] GC(9) Pause Full (G1 Evacuation Pause) 512M->180M(1024M) 3240ms
  1. What is happening between GC(5) and GC(8)?
  2. What does "Evacuation Failure" mean?
  3. Why did a Full GC occur after GC(8)?
  4. What tunables would you adjust?

Expected answers:
1. Each Minor GC reclaims less — heap usage after GC is growing (480→495→510 MB). Objects are being promoted to Old faster than they die.
2. Evacuation Failure: G1 ran out of space to copy surviving Young objects (Old gen too full to accept promotions).
3. Evacuation Failure → G1 cannot continue incremental collection → falls back to Serial Full GC.
4. Increase -Xmx, decrease -XX:InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent (trigger concurrent marking earlier), investigate allocation rate.

Exercise 5 — Soft Cache Implementation

Implement a thread-safe SoftCache<K, V> using SoftReference that automatically evicts entries under memory pressure:

import java.lang.ref.SoftReference;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;

public class SoftCache<K, V> {
    private final ConcurrentHashMap<K, SoftReference<V>> cache =
        new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    public void put(K key, V value) {
        cache.put(key, new SoftReference<>(value));
    }

    public V get(K key) {
        SoftReference<V> ref = cache.get(key);
        if (ref == null) return null;

        V value = ref.get();
        if (value == null) {
            cache.remove(key, ref);  // clean up stale entry
            return null;
        }
        return value;
    }

    public int size() {
        // TODO: count entries where ref.get() is not null
        return (int) cache.values().stream()
            .filter(ref -> ref.get() != null)
            .count();
    }
}

Exercise 6 — G1 Region Sizing

Your application runs with -Xmx8g and reports frequent humongous allocations for a byte[5_000_000] (5 MB). What G1HeapRegionSize eliminates humongous allocation for this object, and how do you calculate it?

Answer:
- Humongous threshold = 50% of G1HeapRegionSize
- 5 MB object requires region size > 10 MB
- Valid G1 region sizes are powers of 2: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 MB
- Minimum valid size: 16 MB (50% = 8 MB > 5 MB object)
- Flag: -XX:G1HeapRegionSize=16m
- With 8 GB heap and 16 MB regions: 8192 MB / 16 MB = 512 regions (within G1's 2048 region maximum)

Advanced Exercises

Exercise 7 — Phantom Reference Cleaner

Implement a native resource wrapper using the Cleaner API that ensures off-heap memory is freed when the Java wrapper object is collected:

import java.lang.ref.Cleaner;

public class DirectMemory implements AutoCloseable {
    private static final Cleaner CLEANER = Cleaner.create();

    private final long address;    // off-heap memory address
    private final int  size;
    private final Cleaner.Cleanable cleanable;
    private volatile boolean closed = false;

    public DirectMemory(int size) {
        this.size    = size;
        this.address = allocate(size);   // native: malloc equivalent
        // Register cleanup — MUST use static inner class to avoid capturing 'this'
        this.cleanable = CLEANER.register(this, new CleanAction(address));
    }

    // Static inner class — no reference to outer DirectMemory instance
    private static class CleanAction implements Runnable {
        private final long address;
        CleanAction(long address) { this.address = address; }

        @Override
        public void run() {
            free(address);  // native: free equivalent
        }
    }

    @Override
    public void close() {
        if (!closed) {
            closed = true;
            cleanable.clean();   // deterministic cleanup
        }
    }

    // TODO: implement read/write methods at offset
    private static native long allocate(int size);
    private static native void free(long address);
}

Exercise 8 — GC Throughput Benchmark

Write a benchmark that measures how allocation rate affects Minor GC frequency:

import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong;

public class AllocationPressureBench {
    static final AtomicLong gcCount = new AtomicLong();

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        // Register GC notification listener (via MXBean)
        for (var gcBean : java.lang.management.ManagementFactory.getGarbageCollectorMXBeans()) {
            System.out.println("GC: " + gcBean.getName());
        }

        long start = System.currentTimeMillis();
        long iterations = 0;

        // Scenario A: short-lived objects (GC-friendly)
        while (System.currentTimeMillis() - start < 5000) {
            byte[] shortLived = new byte[1024];  // dies each loop
            iterations++;
        }
        System.out.println("Scenario A iterations: " + iterations);

        // Scenario B: objects that live across multiple loops
        // TODO: accumulate objects in a bounded ring buffer
        // Observe: different GC pressure despite same allocation rate
    }
}

Production Scenarios

Scenario 1 — High P99 Latency Spikes

A microservice serves 5,000 RPS with median latency 5 ms. P99 latency spikes to 800ms every ~90 seconds. GC logs show:

[90.015s][info][gc] GC(23) Pause Full (Ergonomics) 4096M->1200M(4096M) 780ms

Diagnose and provide the remediation plan.

Expected answer:
- Cause: Full GC triggered by ergonomics (heap 100% occupied). 780ms ≈ exactly the P99 spike.
- Root causes to investigate in order:
1. Heap too small — increase -Xmx. 4 GB Full GC suggests Old gen fills in 90s.
2. Concurrent marking not triggering early enough — lower InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent from 45% to 25–30%.
3. Check for humongous allocations: jcmd <pid> GC.heap_info or GC log gc,heap tag.
4. Heap dump at OOM to rule out memory leak: jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump.
- Immediate fix: -Xmx8g -XX:InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent=30
- Long-term: heap dump analysis in Eclipse MAT; check for accumulating Old gen objects.

Scenario 2 — Container OOMKilled

A Spring Boot service with -Xmx512m runs in a 1 GB Kubernetes container. It is OOMKilled after 30 minutes of traffic. Heap dump shows max heap usage 400 MB. Diagnose why.

Expected answer:
Total JVM memory = Heap (512 MB) + Metaspace (~100 MB) + Code Cache (~64 MB) + Thread stacks (200 threads × 512 KB = ~100 MB) + Direct ByteBuffers (NIO buffers) = ~900+ MB — exceeds 1 GB container limit.

Fixes:
- Increase container to 1.5 GB, or
- Reduce heap: -Xmx384m -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=50
- Cap thread count (Spring virtual threads)
- Limit Metaspace: -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=128m
- Monitor non-heap via JMX MemoryPoolMXBean

Debugging Exercises

Debug 1 — OutOfMemoryError Despite Ample Heap

Service throws OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space at 600 MB with -Xmx4g. GC logs show constant Full GC running every 500ms with no net reduction.

[0.500s] GC(1) Pause Full 600M->595M(4096M) 450ms
[1.000s] GC(2) Pause Full 600M->595M(4096M) 460ms
[1.500s] GC(3) Pause Full 600M->598M(4096M) 455ms

Diagnosis: GC runs continuously but barely reclaims anything — 99% of the heap is live. Either a genuine memory leak (static reference chain holding objects) or a data structure growing without bounds. The OOM is triggered by JVM ergonomics: more than 98% of time spent in GC with < 2% memory reclaimed → GC overhead limit exceeded.

Action: jmap -dump:live,format=b,file=dump.hprof <pid> → open in Eclipse MAT → "Leak Suspects" report → identify dominator objects holding large retained heap.

Debug 2 — GC Pause During Overnight Batch

A nightly batch processes 50M records. It completes normally for 47M records, then suddenly pauses for 45 seconds at 3 AM. No errors. GC logs unavailable.

Reconstruction approach:
1. Enable GC logs for next run: -Xlog:gc*:file=batch-gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags
2. Hypothesis: Old gen fills up at ~47M records (heap grows proportionally) → Full GC compaction
3. Verify: jstat -gcutil <pid> 5000 during run — watch Old gen O column approach 100%
4. Fix options: increase -Xmx, reduce heap retention (flush processed objects earlier), or switch to Parallel GC with larger Young gen for batch throughput

Interview Challenges

Challenge 1

"You have a 32 GB heap with G1GC. After running for 6 hours, the application experiences a 12-second Full GC. What are the three most likely causes and how do you investigate each?"

Answer framework:
1. Humongous allocation fragmentation — many humongous regions occupy contiguous space, forcing Full GC to compact. Check GC logs for Humongous regions count. Fix: increase G1HeapRegionSize.
2. Concurrent marking not keeping up — Old gen fills before marking cycle completes (concurrent mode failure). Check log for GC pause (G1 Humongous Allocation) or to-space exhausted. Fix: lower IHOP to start marking earlier.
3. Memory leak in Old gen — 6 hours of accumulation. Heap dump at hour 5 + Eclipse MAT dominator tree reveals the leaking class.

Challenge 2

"Explain what happens step by step when you call new byte[1024] in a virtual-thread-heavy Java 21 application under G1GC."

Answer:
1. JVM checks current virtual thread's TLAB for available space (bump pointer check)
2. If TLAB has space: bump pointer forward by ~1040 bytes (1024 + object header), object initialized — cost ≈ ~1 ns
3. If TLAB full: JVM requests new TLAB from Eden space (Minor GC may run if Eden full)
4. If Eden full: Minor GC triggers STW, copies surviving Eden+Survivor objects, ages them, promotes if age ≥ threshold
5. Object in Eden is traced from GC root only if reachable from active stack frame; if the virtual thread dies before Minor GC, the byte array is garbage
6. If byte array > 50% of G1 region size: humongous allocation path — directly to Old region, bypassing Eden

Challenge 3

"A senior engineer says: 'We should set -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch on our production JVM.' What does this do and when is it a good or bad idea?"

Answer: AlwaysPreTouch forces the JVM to touch (fault in) all heap pages at startup instead of lazily on first use. Effects:
- Good: startup is slower but first GC and allocation latencies are predictable — no page fault overhead during live traffic. Critical for latency-sensitive services where a cold heap can cause unpredictable first-request latency spikes.
- Bad: increases startup time and delays pod-ready state in Kubernetes. For services with rolling deploys where startup SLA < 10 seconds, this may violate readiness probe timeouts on a 16 GB heap.
- Verdict: good for stateful long-running services where startup time is not constrained; bad for short-lived batch jobs, serverless/FaaS, or fast-rolling Kubernetes deployments.

Key Takeaways

  • GC roots determine liveness — every memory leak is a GC root holding an unexpected reference chain; trace from roots to find the anchor
  • Generational hypothesis drives everything — most objects die young; Minor GC (copying) is cheap because it only processes what lives, not what dies
  • Mark-sweep-compact is the canonical algorithm — mark live objects from roots, sweep dead ones, compact survivors to eliminate fragmentation
  • STW pauses are proportional to live data, not heap size (for mark+compact phases) — the fewer live objects, the shorter the pause
  • G1GC is the correct default for heaps > 4 GB with latency requirements; tune MaxGCPauseMillis and IHOP before anything else
  • ZGC / Shenandoah are the choice when P99 pause SLO < 10 ms; sub-millisecond pauses at terabyte heap scale are achievable
  • Reference types are a GC contract — WeakReference for caches that should not prevent GC; SoftReference for caches that should survive unless heap is low; PhantomReference/Cleaner for resource cleanup
  • finalize() is dead — use AutoCloseable + try-with-resources or java.lang.ref.Cleaner for resource lifecycle management
  • GC logging is non-negotiable in production — -Xlog:gc* is near-zero overhead; you cannot diagnose GC problems without logs
  • Container-aware JVM — always use -XX:+UseContainerSupport (default Java 11+) and MaxRAMPercentage instead of hardcoded -Xmx in containerized environments

Part 1

What the Heap Is and Why It Exists

When a Java program calls new SomeObject(), the JVM must place that object somewhere. The heap is the dedicated runtime data area where all Java objects and arrays live for the duration of their lifetime. It is the largest and most managed memory region in the JVM.

The heap was designed around one central insight: objects have variable lifetimes and unknown sizes at compile time. Unlike stack frames — whose size is computable and whose lifetime is bounded by method scope — heap objects can outlive the method that created them, can be shared across threads, and can reference each other in arbitrary graphs. This demands a dedicated managed region with a runtime-driven allocator and a garbage collector.

Heap properties the JVM guarantees

Heap Memory Guarantees:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 1. Shared across all threads                                     │
│    Every thread reads and writes the same heap address space     │
│                                                                  │
│ 2. Garbage collected                                             │
│    Unreachable objects are automatically reclaimed               │
│                                                                  │
│ 3. Bounded by -Xms (initial) and -Xmx (maximum)                 │
│    JVM never grows beyond -Xmx; throws OOM if exhausted         │
│                                                                  │
│ 4. Subject to JVM memory model (JMM)                            │
│    Visibility of writes between threads is governed by JMM       │
│                                                                  │
│ 5. Inspectable                                                   │
│    Heap dumps, jmap, jstat, JFR all provide live heap analytics  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

What does not live on the heap: stack frames (per-thread), Metaspace (class metadata), Code Cache (JIT-compiled code), and direct ByteBuffer allocations (off-heap native memory). Understanding these boundaries is as important as understanding the heap itself.

Part 2

Heap Regions: Young and Old Generation

The JVM heap is divided into generations based on the generational hypothesis: most objects die young, and the few that survive tend to live a long time. This asymmetry allows the collector to apply cheap, fast algorithms to young objects and more thorough (but infrequent) algorithms to old objects.

Heap Layout — Generational Structure:
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                         JVM HEAP (-Xmx)                              │
│                                                                       │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────────────┐   │
│  │        YOUNG GENERATION         │  │      OLD GENERATION       │   │
│  │  (~25–33% of heap by default)   │  │  (~67–75% of heap)        │   │
│  │                                 │  │                           │   │
│  │  ┌──────────┐ ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐│  │  Long-lived objects:      │   │
│  │  │   Eden   │ │  S0  │ │  S1  ││  │  - Survived many Minor GC │   │
│  │  │  (80%)   │ │(10%) │ │(10%) ││  │  - Large objects          │   │
│  │  └──────────┘ └──────┘ └──────┘│  │  - Promoted by JVM        │   │
│  └─────────────────────────────────┘  └──────────────────────────┘   │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Young Generation

The Young Generation is where all new objects are born (with one exception: humongous objects). It is subdivided into three spaces:

  • Eden space — the primary allocation arena. New objects go here via TLAB (Part 4). Typically 80% of Young gen.
  • Survivor space S0 — one of two "from/to" spaces used during Minor GC copying.
  • Survivor space S1 — the other survivor space. At any point one is "from" and one is "to"; they alternate roles each Minor GC.

Old Generation (Tenured)

Objects that survive enough Minor GC cycles (configurable with -XX:MaxTenuringThreshold, default 15 for most collectors) are promoted to Old Gen. Old Gen also receives objects too large for Eden (large arrays, pre-sized collections). Old Gen is collected by Major GC or Full GC — less frequently, but with longer pauses.

Part 3

Eden Space: The Object Birthplace

Eden is where almost every object in a Java program begins its life. It is designed for extremely fast, lock-free allocation and near-zero-cost reclamation for short-lived objects.

Fast path allocation in Eden

Eden Allocation (bump-pointer):
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ TLAB-free region in Eden                                          │
│                                                                   │
│ Before: [ObjA][ObjB][ObjC][          free space          ]│      │
│                              ↑ allocation pointer                 │
│                                                                   │
│ new SomeObject() arrives:                                         │
│   1. Check: alloc_ptr + obj_size ≤ TLAB_end?  → yes              │
│   2. Write object header at alloc_ptr                             │
│   3. Zero-initialize object fields                                │
│   4. Bump alloc_ptr forward by obj_size                           │
│   5. Return previous alloc_ptr as object reference               │
│                                                                   │
│ After:  [ObjA][ObjB][ObjC][SomeObject][       free space  ]│     │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

This bump-pointer allocator is O(1) — just a comparison and an increment. It is orders of magnitude faster than malloc in C, which traverses free lists.

Eden collection

When Eden fills, a Minor GC (also called Young GC) fires. The collector traces live objects from GC roots into Eden, copies survivors to a Survivor space, then reclaims the entire Eden at once — a single pointer reset. Because most Eden objects are dead at collection time, the cost is proportional to survivors, not to the total Eden size.

Part 4

TLAB: Thread-Local Allocation Buffers

Multiple threads allocate objects concurrently. Without coordination, bumping the shared Eden allocation pointer would require atomic CAS operations on every allocation — catastrophic for performance. The solution is TLAB: Thread-Local Allocation Buffers.

How TLAB works

Each running thread owns a private chunk of Eden. Allocations within that thread bump a thread-local pointer — no synchronization needed at all.

TLAB Architecture:
┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                         Eden Space                                 │
│                                                                    │
│  Thread-1 TLAB         Thread-2 TLAB        Thread-3 TLAB        │
│  ┌─────────────┐       ┌─────────────┐      ┌─────────────┐      │
│  │ A │ B │ ░░░ │←bump  │ C │ ░░░░░░░ │←bump │ D │ E │ ░░░ │←bump │
│  └─────────────┘       └─────────────┘      └─────────────┘      │
│   start      end        start      end       start      end       │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
TLAB refill: when a TLAB is exhausted, the thread requests a new chunk
from Eden using a single CAS on the shared Eden pointer.

TLAB lifecycle

  1. JVM assigns a fresh TLAB chunk from Eden when a thread starts or when its previous TLAB is full.
  2. The thread allocates by bumping its private tlab_top pointer.
  3. When tlab_top + allocation_size > tlab_end, the thread retires the TLAB and requests a new one.
  4. During Minor GC, all active TLABs are parsed as part of Eden.

TLAB sizing flags

# View TLAB statistics per thread
java -XX:+PrintTLAB -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions ...

# Adjust TLAB refill waste threshold (default 64 B)
-XX:TLABWasteTargetPercent=1    # % of TLAB that can be wasted on refills

# Force minimum TLAB size
-XX:MinTLABSize=2k

If an object is too large to fit in any TLAB (e.g., a large array), it falls back to direct Eden allocation — a single CAS on the shared Eden pointer. If still too large for Eden (> ~50% of a G1 region), it becomes a humongous allocation and goes directly to Old Gen.

Part 5

Object Headers: What Every Heap Object Carries

Every object on the heap begins with one or two header words before its fields start. These headers carry metadata the JVM needs at runtime.

Header layout (64-bit HotSpot, non-compressed)

Object Header Layout (8-byte aligned):
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Word 0 — Mark Word (8 bytes)                                        │
│  ┌──────────────┬────────┬────────┬──────┬────────┬────────────────┐ │
│  │  HashCode    │ GC Age │  Lock  │ Bias │  Tag   │  (state bits)  │ │
│  │   (31 bits)  │(4 bits)│ State  │      │(2 bits)│                │ │
│  └──────────────┴────────┴────────┴──────┴────────┴────────────────┘ │
│                                                                       │
│  Word 1 — Klass Pointer (8 bytes, or 4 bytes with compressed oops)   │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │  Pointer to the Class object (in Metaspace) describing        │   │
│  │  the object's type, vtable, instance size, field layout       │   │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Total header: 16 bytes (without compressed oops) or 12 bytes (with)

Mark word states

The mark word encodes multiple states using the low tag bits:

Tag bits State Mark word content
01 Unlocked Identity hash + GC age
00 Lightweight lock Stack pointer to displaced mark word
10 Heavyweight lock Pointer to inflated monitor (OS mutex)
11 Marked by GC Forwarding pointer during compaction
01+bias Biased lock Thread ID + epoch (deprecated Java 15+)

GC age in the mark word

Bits 4–7 of the mark word store the tenuring age — how many Minor GC cycles the object has survived. When this age reaches MaxTenuringThreshold (default 15), the JVM promotes the object to Old Gen.

Practical impact: minimum object size

Even an object with no fields (new Object()) occupies 16 bytes (12 bytes header + 4 bytes padding to maintain 8-byte alignment). An Integer wrapping a single int occupies 16 bytes — 4× the size of a primitive int. This overhead drives optimization patterns like primitive arrays over boxed collections.

Part 6

Compressed Ordinary Object Pointers (Compressed Oops)

On a 64-bit JVM, every object reference is a 64-bit pointer. A heap of 1 million objects contains millions of such pointers — in object fields, arrays, and the GC's own data structures. This pointer width doubles memory consumption compared to a 32-bit JVM.

Compressed oops (-XX:+UseCompressedOops, default on for heaps ≤ 32 GB) encodes 64-bit heap addresses into 32-bit values by exploiting 8-byte alignment: since all objects are 8-byte aligned, the three low bits of any heap address are always zero. The JVM stores the address shifted right by 3 bits, fitting into 32 bits — effectively extending the addressable heap to 2^32 × 8 = 32 GB with 32-bit pointers.

Compressed Oops Encoding:
  Real address:   0x00000007_FF800000  (64-bit)
  Shift right 3:  0x00000000_FFF00000  (fits in 32 bits)
  Stored as:      0xFFF00000            (4 bytes in the object field)

  Decode:  stored_value << 3 + heap_base = real address

Impact: heap size cliff at 32 GB

Compressed Oops Memory Savings:
  Heap 4 GB   → 32-bit oops: saves ~20–30% heap (fewer pointer bytes)
  Heap 31 GB  → 32-bit oops still active
  Heap 32 GB  → compressed oops DISABLED → 64-bit oops
               → effective live data per GB drops ~20–30%

Rule: a 31 GB heap with compressed oops often outperforms
      a 33 GB heap without them — more objects fit per cache line.

Compressed class pointers

A companion optimization (-XX:+UseCompressedClassPointers) compresses the klass pointer in object headers from 8 bytes to 4 bytes. Both are enabled by default and should only be disabled when heap exceeds 32 GB.

Part 7

Heap Sizing: `-Xms` and `-Xmx`

The two most critical heap flags:

-Xms<size>   # Initial heap size (committed at startup)
-Xmx<size>   # Maximum heap size (JVM will never exceed this)

# Examples
-Xms512m -Xmx512m     # Fixed heap, no expansion (low-latency prod)
-Xms256m -Xmx4g       # Small start, grows to 4 GB under load
-Xmx8g                # Let JVM pick initial (usually 1/4 of Xmx)

What happens when heap grows

When the JVM needs more heap than currently committed, it calls the OS to commit additional pages (up to -Xmx). This involves a system call and page table updates — a cost that shows up as latency spikes in production when the heap is growing under load. Setting -Xms == -Xmx eliminates this by committing the full heap at startup.

Young gen sizing

-XX:NewRatio=2           # Old:Young ratio = 2:1 → Young gets 1/3 of heap
-XX:NewSize=512m         # Explicit Young gen initial size
-XX:MaxNewSize=2g        # Explicit Young gen maximum size
-Xmn1g                  # Shorthand: set both NewSize and MaxNewSize to 1g

For throughput-heavy workloads (batch processing, streaming), a larger Young gen reduces promotion pressure and lowers Old Gen fill rate. For services with many long-lived objects (caches, session stores), a larger Old Gen is appropriate.

Part 8

Survivor Spaces and Tenuring

The two Survivor spaces (S0 and S1) act as a staging area between Eden and Old Gen. This prevents prematurely promoting objects that are only slightly long-lived.

Minor GC — Survivor Space Rotation:
Before GC:
  Eden [A][B][C][D][E]   S0 [X][Y]   S1 [empty]   Old Gen [...]

After Minor GC:
  Eden [empty — reset]   S0 [empty]   S1 [A][X']   Old Gen [...][Y promoted]

  A — survived from Eden, age now 1, placed in S1
  X — survived from S0, age was N, placed in S1 with age N+1
  Y — age reached MaxTenuringThreshold → promoted to Old Gen
  B,C,D,E — unreachable → collected (no copy needed)

Next Minor GC roles swap: S1 becomes "from", S0 becomes "to"

Tenuring threshold and adaptive sizing

The JVM can dynamically adjust tenuring threshold with -XX:+UseAdaptiveSizePolicy (default on). It observes how many objects survive each Minor GC and adjusts the threshold to keep Survivor utilization near 50%. Use jstat -gcutil or -Xlog:gc* to monitor tenuring behavior.

Premature promotion (promotion failure)

If both Survivor spaces fill up, objects are force-promoted to Old Gen regardless of age. If Old Gen also lacks space, the JVM triggers a Full GC — the most expensive pause. Watch for "promotion failed" in GC logs as an early warning sign.

Part 9

Large Objects and Humongous Allocations

Objects whose size exceeds 50% of a G1GC region size (default region = 1–32 MB, configurable via -XX:G1HeapRegionSize) bypass Eden entirely and are allocated directly in humongous regions — contiguous Old Gen regions.

Humongous Allocation Path (G1GC):
  new byte[32 * 1024 * 1024]  →  G1HeapRegionSize = 32m
                                  32m ≥ 50% of 32m = 16m
                                  → HUMONGOUS ALLOCATION
                                  → directly to Old Gen region(s)
                                  → no TLAB, no Eden, no Minor GC

Humongous objects:
- Are never moved during Minor GC (they live in Old Gen from birth)
- Can only be collected during Major/Full GC or during concurrent marking
- Can cause fragmentation in the Old Gen region pool
- Show up in GC logs with Humongous regions: N entries

Tuning: if profiling reveals many humongous allocations (large byte arrays, caches, serialization buffers), either increase G1HeapRegionSize or pre-allocate pooled buffers to avoid repeated allocations.

Part 10

Heap Dumps: Capturing the Full Heap State

A heap dump is a point-in-time snapshot of every live object on the heap — their types, sizes, field values, and reference graph. It is the definitive diagnostic tool for memory leaks and OutOfMemoryError investigations.

Generating a heap dump

# Method 1: jmap (requires live JVM)
jmap -dump:live,format=b,file=heap.hprof <pid>
# live: only include reachable objects (smaller file, cleaner analysis)

# Method 2: jcmd (preferred — lower overhead)
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /path/to/heap.hprof

# Method 3: On OOM (automatic)
-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError
-XX:HeapDumpPath=/var/dumps/

# Method 4: Programmatic
java.lang.management.ManagementFactory
  .getPlatformMXBean(HotSpotDiagnosticMXBean.class)
  .dumpHeap("/path/heap.hprof", true);

Analyzing heap dumps

Eclipse MAT Workflow:
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 1. Open heap.hprof in Eclipse Memory Analyzer Tool (MAT)     │
│                                                              │
│ 2. Run "Leak Suspects Report"                                │
│    → Identifies the top dominator objects by retained heap   │
│                                                              │
│ 3. Check "Dominator Tree"                                    │
│    → Shows which object chains retain the most memory        │
│                                                              │
│ 4. Check "Histogram"                                         │
│    → Shows instance count + shallow/retained size per class  │
│                                                              │
│ 5. Use OQL (Object Query Language) for targeted queries:     │
│    SELECT * FROM java.util.HashMap WHERE size > 10000        │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Shallow vs retained heap

  • Shallow heap: memory consumed by the object itself (headers + fields), not including referenced objects.
  • Retained heap: total memory that would be freed if this object were collected — itself plus everything only reachable through it. A HashMap with 10,000 entries has small shallow heap but large retained heap.
Part 11

OutOfMemoryError: Causes and Variants

OutOfMemoryError (OOM) is the JVM's signal that a memory region is exhausted. Each variant points to a different memory area.

// 1. Heap space exhausted
java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space
// → Increase -Xmx, or fix memory leak

// 2. GC overhead limit exceeded
java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: GC overhead limit exceeded
// → JVM spent >98% of time in GC, reclaiming <2% each cycle
// → Indicates genuine leak; increase Xmx only buys time

// 3. Metaspace exhausted
java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace
// → ClassLoader leak (common in hot-deploy, OSGi, Tomcat)
// → Increase -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize or fix classloader leak

// 4. Direct buffer / off-heap memory
java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Direct buffer memory
// → NIO direct ByteBuffers exhausted; increase MaxDirectMemorySize

// 5. Unable to create native thread
java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: unable to create new native thread
// → OS process thread limit reached; reduce thread count or -Xss

OOM triage checklist

OOM Triage:
1. Check variant → routes to correct memory region
2. Enable -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError before OOM recurs
3. jstat -gcutil <pid> 2000 → watch Old gen % over time
4. If Old gen grows monotonically → memory leak
5. If Old gen stays stable → heap just undersized; increase Xmx
6. Heap dump → MAT Leak Suspects → find dominator chain
7. Check for static collections, listener registrations, caches
Part 12

Off-Heap Memory: Beyond `-Xmx`

The JVM uses memory outside the heap boundary. Not accounting for these regions causes container OOM kills even when heap metrics look fine.

Total JVM Memory Footprint:
┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Heap                    -Xmx (e.g., 4 GB)                │
│  Metaspace               -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize (e.g., 256m)│
│  Code Cache              -XX:ReservedCodeCacheSize (256m)  │
│  Thread Stacks           threads × -Xss (e.g., 200×512k)  │
│  Direct ByteBuffers      -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize           │
│  Unsafe/JNI native mem   Unaccounted (watch /proc/mem)     │
│  GC data structures      ~5–10% of heap (G1 remembered sets│
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Rule of thumb: container limit = Xmx × 1.5 at minimum

NIO Direct ByteBuffers

// Allocates OUTSIDE the heap (native memory)
ByteBuffer buf = ByteBuffer.allocateDirect(64 * 1024 * 1024);

// Check current direct buffer usage
java.lang.management.BufferPoolMXBean pool = 
    ManagementFactory.getPlatformMXBeans(BufferPoolMXBean.class)
        .stream().filter(b -> b.getName().equals("direct"))
        .findFirst().get();
System.out.println("Direct used: " + pool.getMemoryUsed());

jstat is the fastest way to observe live heap behavior without stopping the JVM.

# GC utilization: S0%, S1%, E(den)%, O(ld)%, M(etaspace)%
jstat -gcutil <pid> 2000
  S0     S1     E      O      M     CCS    YGC  YGCT  FGC  FGCT   GCT
  0.00  47.23  12.44  31.87  95.12  92.34   42  0.812   1  0.234  1.046

Part 14

Heap in Containers and Kubernetes

Container environments add two critical constraints: cgroup memory limits and CPU throttling on JVM ergonomics.

Container-aware heap sizing (Java 11+)

# Recommended for Kubernetes: use percentage of container limit
-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0      # Use 75% of container's memory limit
-XX:InitialRAMPercentage=50.0  # Start at 50%
-XX:MinRAMPercentage=25.0      # Floor for very small containers

# Verify JVM sees correct container limits
java -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+PrintContainerInfo -version

Why hard -Xmx fails in Kubernetes

# Kubernetes deployment snippet
resources:
  requests:
    memory: "1Gi"
  limits:
    memory: "1Gi"

If the app runs with -Xmx768m, the remaining 256 MB must cover Metaspace, Code Cache, thread stacks, and GC data structures. During load spikes, the total JVM footprint can exceed 1 GB, triggering OOMKill from the container runtime — with no Java-level OOM logged.

Best practices for containerized JVMs

# Production Kubernetes JVM flags (Java 17+)
-XX:+UseContainerSupport          # Default on; reads cgroup limits
-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0         # Leave headroom for non-heap
-XX:+UseG1GC                      # Predictable pauses
-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200          # Target pause
-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError
-XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps/          # Mount as emptyDir in K8s
-Xlog:gc*:file=/logs/gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags:filecount=5,filesize=20m
