Part 16

Production Heap Sizing Strategy

Heap sizing is not guesswork — it follows a measurement-driven process:

Heap Sizing Process:
Step 1: Measure live set size
  - Run realistic load, force Full GC, measure Old Gen after
  - Live set = memory consumed by long-lived objects
  - Baseline: live set × 3 = minimum -Xmx for comfortable headroom

Step 2: Measure allocation rate
  - jstat -gc 1000 | awk '{print $9}' | diff successive values
  - High allocation rate → larger Eden, consider -Xmn 25–33% of Xmx

Step 3: Set Young gen for Minor GC frequency target
  - Minor GC should occur no more than 1–2/s under normal load
  - If more frequent → Eden too small

Step 4: Validate pause targets
  - Enable GC logging, run 24h soak test
  - P99 GC pause should be < SLO
  - Adjust MaxGCPauseMillis, IHOP, or collector

Step 5: Add container headroom
  - Total JVM = Xmx + ~512 MB for non-heap (Metaspace, CC, stacks)
  - Container limit = total JVM × 1.2 for safety margin
Part 17

Memory Leaks: Common Patterns

A Java memory leak occurs when objects that are no longer logically needed remain reachable through a GC root. They never become garbage — the heap grows without bound.

// Pattern 1: Static collection accumulation
static final Map<String, byte[]> CACHE = new HashMap<>();
void processRequest(String key, byte[] data) {
    CACHE.put(key, data);  // never removed → unbounded growth
}
// Fix: use bounded cache (Caffeine, Guava), or eviction policy

// Pattern 2: Listener/callback registration without removal
button.addActionListener(new ActionListener() { /* holds references */ });
// Listeners hold outer class reference (anonymous inner class)
// Fix: removeActionListener in cleanup; use WeakReference-based listeners

// Pattern 3: ThreadLocal not cleaned up
static ThreadLocal<byte[]> BUFFER = new ThreadLocal<>();
void handle(HttpRequest req) {
    BUFFER.set(new byte[1024 * 1024]);  // sets per-thread
    process(req);
    // BUFFER.remove() missing → thread pool threads retain buffer forever
}
// Fix: always call BUFFER.remove() in finally block

// Pattern 4: ClassLoader leak (web containers)
// Class loaded by a custom ClassLoader keeps ClassLoader alive
// ClassLoader holds all loaded classes in Metaspace
// Fix: null references, weak-reference class caches
Part 18

Escape Analysis and Stack Allocation

The JIT compiler performs escape analysis to determine whether a heap-allocated object's references can escape the current method or thread. If an object does not escape, the JIT can:

  1. Stack-allocate it — place it in the stack frame, eliminating GC overhead entirely.
  2. Scalar replace it — decompose its fields into individual stack variables, eliminating object overhead.
// Candidate for escape analysis
void compute() {
    Point p = new Point(3, 4);   // does p escape this method?
    double dist = Math.sqrt(p.x * p.x + p.y * p.y);
    // p not returned, not stored in field, not passed elsewhere
    // → JIT can scalar-replace p into two int locals on stack
}

// Escaping object — cannot be stack-allocated
Point p;
void setGlobalPoint() {
    p = new Point(1, 2);  // p assigned to field → escapes
}

Verify escape analysis decisions with -XX:+PrintEscapeAnalysis -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions. JFR jdk.ObjectAllocationInNewTLAB events show allocations that could not be eliminated.

Part 19

Heap and the Java Memory Model

The JVM heap is shared across threads, making visibility and ordering critical. The Java Memory Model (JMM) defines when one thread's writes to heap objects become visible to other threads.

// Without synchronization: visibility not guaranteed
class Counter {
    int count = 0;  // heap field
    void increment() { count++; }  // read-modify-write, not atomic
    int get()        { return count; }
}
// Thread A writes count=1; Thread B may still read count=0
// (CPU cache, store buffer, compiler reordering)

// With volatile: visibility guaranteed, atomicity only for single writes
volatile int count = 0;

// With synchronized: both visibility and mutual exclusion
synchronized void increment() { count++; }

// With AtomicInteger: hardware-level CAS, no lock overhead
AtomicInteger count = new AtomicInteger(0);
count.incrementAndGet();

The heap itself does not enforce any ordering — that is the responsibility of volatile, synchronized, Lock, or Atomic* classes that establish happens-before relationships.

Part 21

Interview Q&A

Q: Why is setting -Xms equal to -Xmx a production best practice?
A: Eliminates heap expansion under load. When heap grows, the JVM commits new OS pages — a system call that can cause latency spikes. Fixed heap size commits all pages at startup (especially with -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch), giving completely predictable allocation behavior.

Q: What is the 32 GB compressed oops limit, and why does a 31 GB heap sometimes outperform a 33 GB heap?
A: Compressed oops encode 64-bit pointers into 32 bits for heaps ≤ 32 GB. This halves pointer size in object fields, meaning more objects fit per CPU cache line. At 33 GB, oops expand to 64 bits — each reference consumes twice the space. The cache efficiency loss can outweigh the extra 2 GB of heap, so total throughput drops.

Q: What is a TLAB and why is it critical for multi-threaded allocation performance?
A: A Thread-Local Allocation Buffer is a private chunk of Eden space assigned to each thread. Allocations within the TLAB are pure bump-pointer — no synchronization, no CAS, no locks. Without TLABs, every new in a multi-threaded application would contend on a shared atomic pointer, serializing allocation across all threads.

Q: Describe what happens when new byte[1_000_000_000] is called under G1GC with default settings.
A: 1 GB > 50% of default G1 region size → humongous allocation. The JVM searches for contiguous free regions in Old Gen sufficient to hold 1 GB. If available, the array is allocated directly there (bypassing Eden, TLAB). If unavailable, a Full GC fires to try to compact Old Gen. If still unavailable: OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space.

Q: A production service has -Xmx4g but is OOMKilled by Kubernetes at 3 GB container limit. How?
A: The container limit bounds total process memory, not just heap. A JVM with -Xmx4g reserves 4 GB for heap plus additional memory for Metaspace (~128–256 MB), Code Cache (~256 MB), thread stacks (threads × Xss), GC data structures, and native libraries. Total JVM footprint easily exceeds 4.5+ GB at 4g heap. Solution: set container limit to Xmx × 1.5, use -XX:MaxRAMPercentage instead of fixed -Xmx, or increase the limit.

Mark word Encodes GC age, lock state, identity hash GC age determines promotion; lock state drives lock optimization

Practice — Lesson 61

Easy Exercises

Exercise 1 — Eden vs Survivor

Consider the following program:

public class AllocationDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        for (int i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++) {
            String s = "value-" + i;   // (a)
        }
        String retained = "permanent";  // (b)
        System.out.println(retained);
    }
}

Questions:
1. Where does each String in the loop (a) live when first created?
2. After the loop completes, what happens to those strings during the next Minor GC?
3. Where does retained (b) live, and will it be collected?

Expected answers:
1. Each string created in the loop is allocated in Eden via TLAB. The string itself and its internal char[]/byte[] are both Eden objects.
2. At the next Minor GC, all loop strings are unreachable (local variable s is reassigned each iteration; the previous one loses its last reference). The entire Eden can be reset — cost is near zero because there are no survivors to copy.
3. retained is a local variable referencing a String object in Eden. Because it is still in scope and referenced from the stack frame (a GC root), it survives the Minor GC and is copied to a Survivor space. Over subsequent GCs, it could be promoted to Old Gen if it survives long enough.

Exercise 2 — Object Header Math

Calculate the minimum heap memory consumed by the following objects on a 64-bit JVM with compressed oops enabled:

Object empty = new Object();
Integer boxed = Integer.valueOf(42);
int[] arr = new int[10];

Expected answers:
- new Object(): 8 bytes (mark word) + 4 bytes (compressed klass ptr) = 12 bytes header, padded to 16 bytes (8-byte alignment).
- Integer.valueOf(42): 12 bytes header + 4 bytes (int value field) = 16 bytes.
- new int[10]: 12 bytes header + 4 bytes (array length field) + 40 bytes (10 × 4 bytes per int) = 56 bytes, padded to 56 bytes (already 8-byte aligned).

Exercise 3 — Flag Identification

Match each JVM flag to its purpose:

a) -Xmx4g
b) -XX:+UseCompressedOops
c) -XX:MaxTenuringThreshold=5
d) -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError
e) -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0

Expected answers:
- a → Sets maximum heap size to 4 GB
- b → Enables 32-bit compressed object pointers (saves memory for heaps ≤ 32 GB)
- c → Objects are promoted to Old Gen after surviving 5 Minor GCs (instead of default 15)
- d → Automatically writes a heap dump file when OOM occurs
- e → Sets max heap to 75% of the container's cgroup memory limit (preferred over -Xmx in K8s)

Medium Exercises

Exercise 4 — TLAB Mechanics

Trace through the TLAB allocation sequence for the following scenario:

  • Thread T1 has a TLAB starting at address 0x100, with 200 bytes remaining.
  • T1 calls new byte[180]. The byte array requires 192 bytes total (12-byte header + 180-byte body, padded to 192 bytes).
  • T1 then calls new Object(), which requires 16 bytes.

Questions:
1. Does the first allocation succeed in the current TLAB?
2. After the first allocation, how many bytes remain in T1's TLAB?
3. Does the second allocation succeed in the same TLAB?
4. What happens next for the new Object()?

Expected answers:
1. Yes — 192 bytes needed ≤ 200 bytes remaining. Bump pointer from 0x100 to 0x1C0 (192 bytes forward).
2. 200 − 192 = 8 bytes remaining.
3. No — new Object() requires 16 bytes but only 8 bytes remain. The current TLAB is retired (its remaining space is left as a fill object for GC parsing).
4. T1 requests a new TLAB from Eden (a single CAS on the shared Eden pointer). If Eden has space, a new TLAB is assigned and the Object is allocated at its start. If Eden is full, a Minor GC fires to reclaim Eden space and refill TLABs.

Exercise 5 — Heap Sizing Calculation

A service has the following measured characteristics:
- Live set size (Old Gen after Full GC): 1.2 GB
- Allocation rate: 200 MB/s
- GC pause SLO: P99 < 100ms
- Threads: 150 active
- Metaspace usage: 180 MB

Calculate:
1. Recommended -Xmx
2. Recommended Young gen size (-Xmn)
3. Required container memory limit

Expected answers:
1. Live set × 3 = 1.2 GB × 3 = 3.6 GB → round up to -Xmx4g. This gives Old Gen ample space to absorb promoted objects between Major GCs.
2. At 200 MB/s allocation rate, with target Minor GC every ~500ms: Young gen should absorb 200 × 0.5 = 100 MB per cycle. With 33% of heap as Young gen: 4 GB × 0.33 ≈ 1.3 GB → -Xmn1g (slightly conservative for headroom).
3. Container limit = Xmx + Metaspace + Code Cache + Thread stacks + buffer: 4 GB + 256 MB (max metaspace) + 256 MB (code cache) + 150 × 512 KB (~75 MB) + 128 MB safety = ≈4.8 GB → set container limit to 5.5 GB or 6 GB.

Exercise 6 — Compressed Oops Decision

Two teams propose:
- Team A: -Xmx31g (just under the 32 GB compressed oops threshold)
- Team B: -Xmx34g (beyond the threshold, 3 GB more heap)

Their application's live set is ~14 GB, with extremely pointer-dense data (many cross-linked objects, HashMap-heavy).

Which configuration would you choose and why?

Expected answer:
Choose Team A (-Xmx31g). With compressed oops, every object reference is 4 bytes instead of 8 bytes. In a pointer-dense application, this can reduce live data size by 20–30% — meaning more actual data fits per CPU cache line, reducing cache misses and improving throughput. At 14 GB live set, the 31 GB heap provides 17 GB of GC headroom — more than sufficient. Team B's extra 3 GB is likely consumed by the expanded pointer width, netting little additional useful capacity while degrading cache efficiency. The rule: always stay below 32 GB unless your live set provably requires more even with 32-bit oops.

Advanced Exercises

Exercise 7 — Escape Analysis Optimization

public class DistanceCalculator {
    record Point(double x, double y) {}

    public double distanceFromOrigin(double x, double y) {
        Point p = new Point(x, y);          // (1)
        return Math.sqrt(p.x() * p.x() + p.y() * p.y());
    }

    public Point getPoint(double x, double y) {
        return new Point(x, y);              // (2)
    }

    public void fillList(List<Point> list, double x, double y) {
        list.add(new Point(x, y));           // (3)
    }
}

For each allocation (1), (2), (3): will escape analysis eliminate the heap allocation? Justify your answer.

Expected answer:
1. (1) Stack-allocatable / scalar-replaced. Point p does not escape distanceFromOrigin — it is not returned, not stored in any field, not passed to another thread. The JIT can scalar-replace it: x and y become two double locals on the stack. No heap allocation occurs at steady state after JIT compilation.
2. (2) Cannot eliminate. The Point object is the return value — it escapes the method and is passed to the caller. The JIT cannot determine the caller's intent statically at this site. Heap allocation occurs.
3. (3) Cannot eliminate. The Point object is passed to list.add() which stores it inside the list — it escapes into an external data structure. Heap allocation occurs.

Exercise 8 — Humongous Allocation Diagnosis

A G1GC log contains:

[2.500s] GC(12) Pause Young (Normal) 512M->512M(1024M) 45ms
[2.501s] GC(12) Humongous regions: 16, Humongous waste: 24M
[3.000s] GC(13) Pause Young (Normal) 545M->544M(1024M) 47ms
[3.001s] GC(13) Humongous regions: 18, Humongous waste: 28M

Diagnose the problem and propose two independent solutions.

Expected answer:
- Diagnosis: Minor GC is not reducing heap usage — Old Gen stays at ~512 MB. The humongous region count grows each cycle (16 → 18), and each consumes G1 regions. These allocations bypass Eden, go directly to Old Gen at birth, and can only be freed during concurrent marking or Full GC. The waste values (24–28 MB) indicate fragmentation: humongous objects don't fill their reserved regions completely. Over time, Old Gen fills with uncollectable humongous objects, leading to Full GC.
- Solution 1: Increase G1HeapRegionSize. If humongous objects are, say, 500 KB, and region size is 1 MB, they consume 2 regions each. Increasing to 2 MB makes them exactly 1 region and makes them no longer humongous (< 50% of region size), returning to the normal Eden path.
- Solution 2: Profile the allocation sites (jfr, -XX:+PrintGCDetails, or async-profiler). Identify the code creating large arrays. Introduce an object pool (e.g., ArrayDeque<byte[]> protected by ReentrantLock) to reuse allocations rather than creating new large arrays every request.

Production Scenarios

Scenario 1 — Heap Undersizing in Production

A Java microservice runs with -Xmx2g in a Kubernetes pod with a 2.5 GB memory limit. After deploying a new feature, the pod is OOMKilled every 4–6 hours. Heap dump taken just before death shows Old Gen at 1.4 GB (70% of 2g). Metaspace is stable at 130 MB. The new feature added a server-side session cache backed by a ConcurrentHashMap.

Diagnose and fix:

The root cause is the session cache growing without eviction. The cache's entries are strongly reachable (stored in a static field or Spring bean), so GC never collects them. Over time the cache accumulates sessions from all users, growing Old Gen until a Full GC is insufficient to reclaim enough space.

Additionally, the container's 2.5 GB limit minus the 2 GB heap leaves only 500 MB for non-heap: Metaspace (130 MB used, could grow) + Code Cache (~200 MB for JIT-compiled Spring/Hibernate) + 50 threads × 512 KB stacks (~25 MB) ≈ 355 MB in use, leaving very little headroom. Any spike in class loading or JIT compilation can push total JVM memory past 2.5 GB.

Fixes:
1. Replace ConcurrentHashMap with a bounded, TTL-expiring cache (Caffeine: Caffeine.newBuilder().maximumSize(10000).expireAfterAccess(30, MINUTES).build()).
2. Increase container limit to 3.5 GB and switch to -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70.0.
3. Add -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256m to cap Metaspace and detect ClassLoader leaks early.

Scenario 2 — Compressed Oops Regression

After upgrading from a 28 GB JVM to a 36 GB JVM (adding 8 GB of heap for expected traffic growth), GC pause times increased and throughput decreased despite more available heap. The service is a graph database traversal engine with dense cross-object references.

Explain why this happened and how to address it.

Expected answer:
At 28 GB heap, compressed oops are active — all object references are 4 bytes. At 36 GB, compressed oops are disabled — references become 8 bytes. The graph database uses millions of cross-object pointers. With 8-byte pointers, the live data size in memory expands by ~25–30%:
- Fewer objects fit per CPU cache line → more cache misses per traversal
- GC must trace more pointer bytes → longer marking phases
- More memory bandwidth consumed per graph traversal

Solutions:
1. Downgrade to 31 GB heap — keep compressed oops, accept slightly smaller heap. The effective usable memory may be better due to cache efficiency.
2. If 36+ GB is truly necessary, enable Zero-based Compressed Oops diagnostics to confirm overhead: -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+PrintCompressedOopsMode.
3. Consider transitioning to a JVM with experimental 35-bit compressed oops support, or architect the data model to reduce cross-object pointer density (e.g., store indices instead of references, use primitive arrays).

Debugging Exercises

Debug 1 — Silent Heap Leak

A service runs for 8 hours, then becomes unresponsive. GC logs show Full GCs firing every 5 minutes, each reclaiming very little. jstat -gcutil output:

S0    S1    E    O     M     YGC  YGCT  FGC  FGCT
0.0  23.4  68.2  97.8  94.1   842  12.4   94  187.3

Diagnose the issue step by step.

Diagnosis:
- Old Gen at 97.8% — critically full. Full GC count (94) with 187 seconds spent in Full GC means the JVM is spending significant time in stop-the-world pauses.
- The leak is in Old Gen: objects are promoted (high Old gen %) and not being reclaimed by Full GC (old gen stays near 97% after each).
- Action 1: jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /dumps/leak.hprof — take heap dump while still running.
- Action 2: Open in Eclipse MAT → Leak Suspects → Dominator Tree → identify the top retained object chains.
- Action 3: Look for static fields holding collections that grow over time. Common culprits: static List, Map, event listener lists, Hibernate second-level cache, Spring request-scoped beans leaking into application scope.
- Action 4: Check GC.class_histogram for unexpected high instance counts of application classes — e.g., 8M instances of SessionData when you expected at most 1000 active sessions.

Debug 2 — OOM in Container Without High Heap Usage

A Spring Boot service with -Xmx1g is OOMKilled by Kubernetes despite heap metrics showing only 700 MB heap usage. Investigate.

Reconstruction:

  1. Heap at 700 MB (well under 1g) means heap is not the cause. Container limit was 1.2 GB.
  2. Check non-heap sources: ManagementFactory.getMemoryPoolMXBeans() — inspect Code Cache (Spring + Hibernate = heavy JIT = potentially 200 MB Code Cache).
  3. Check direct buffers: ManagementFactory.getPlatformMXBeans(BufferPoolMXBean.class) — Spring WebFlux / Netty uses direct ByteBuffers for I/O.
  4. Check thread count: jcmd <pid> Thread.print | wc -l — each thread has -Xss stack (default 512k). 200 threads = 100 MB. 500 threads = 250 MB.
  5. Total estimate: 1g heap + 200 MB Code Cache + 150 MB direct buffers + 200 threads × 512k = 200 MB threads ≈ 1.55 GB total JVM memory → exceeds 1.2 GB container limit.
  6. Fix: increase container to 1.8 GB, add -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=256m, -XX:ReservedCodeCacheSize=128m, reduce thread pool size, or use virtual threads.

Interview Challenges

Challenge 1

"Walk me through exactly what the JVM does, step by step, when a Java program calls new HashMap<>()."

Answer:
1. JVM checks whether Thread T's TLAB has space for the HashMap object (~48 bytes: 12 header + 4 loadFactor + 4 size + 4 modCount + 4 threshold + 8 table ref + 8 entrySet ref + 4 padding ≈ 48 bytes).
2. If TLAB has space: bump T's tlab_top pointer by 48 bytes; zero-initialize all fields; write klass pointer to Metaspace's HashMap class object; return the address. Cost: ~1 ns.
3. If TLAB full: retire current TLAB (JVM writes a fill object over the wasted bytes so GC can parse TLAB boundaries), request new TLAB via CAS on Eden's shared allocation pointer.
4. If Eden full: Minor GC fires (STW); live objects in Eden + current "from" Survivor are copied to "to" Survivor; survivors aged; objects at max threshold promoted to Old Gen; Eden reset.
5. The HashMap constructor sets loadFactor = 0.75, leaves table array null (deferred until first put).
6. When the first put fires, HashMap.resize() allocates a Node[] array (default 16 elements × 8 bytes per ref = 128+ bytes for the array) — a separate Eden allocation.

Challenge 2

"You receive a heap dump from a production JVM. How do you determine within 5 minutes whether the OOM is caused by a memory leak or an undersized heap?"

Answer:
1. Open in Eclipse MAT: File → Open Heap Dump.
2. Check Heap Composition Overview: if retained heap is dominated by application data types (e.g., UserSession, OrderData) with counts far exceeding expected maximums → leak.
3. Check Dominator Tree: if a single object or chain retains > 50% of the heap — classic leak signature. If many small independent objects fill the heap proportionally → may just be undersized.
4. Check Object count trends (need multiple dumps or JFR): if counts grow linearly over time without stabilization → definitive leak.
5. Check GC log (if available): if Old Gen is at 100% after Full GC → live set exceeds capacity. If Old Gen drops significantly after Full GC → heap is undersized for peak load, not leaking.
6. Five-minute verdict: Leak Suspects report in MAT gives a direct answer in ~2 minutes. "Problem Suspect 1: X instances of Y hold Z MB retained" — if Y is your application class, it's a leak. If Y is a JDK class (e.g., byte[] from legitimate data processing), it may be a sizing problem.

Challenge 3

"A tech lead proposes: 'We should always use -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch and -Xms equal to -Xmx in production.' Do you agree? When would you disagree?"

Answer:
Agree for: long-running, latency-sensitive services (web APIs, trading systems, real-time processing) where:
- Stable, predictable latency is critical from the first request
- Heap expansion under load would cause OS page fault latency spikes
- Services run for hours/days, amortizing startup cost
- Container memory reservation is predictable (fixed allocation)

Disagree for:
- Kubernetes with aggressive bin-packing: Fixed heap commitment wastes memory on lightly loaded pods. Pods competing for memory on the same node all commit full heap, even if most are idle. Use MaxRAMPercentage with dynamic sizing instead.
- Short-lived batch jobs or CLI tools: startup time matters; committing 4 GB of heap pages at startup (especially with AlwaysPreTouch) for a 30-second job is wasteful.
- Serverless / function-as-a-service: cold start time is a billable SLO. Pre-touching a 2 GB heap during cold start costs hundreds of milliseconds.
- Development environments: wastes memory on developer machines.

Verdict: it is a best practice for specific contexts, not a universal rule. Evaluate against the service's startup SLA, container strategy, and operational memory budget.

Part 1

What the Stack Is and Why Java Needs It

Every running thread in the JVM has exactly one Java Virtual Machine Stack — a private, ordered data structure that tracks the execution state of that thread. The stack is not shared between threads; it exists solely to support method invocation and return.

The stack solves a fundamental problem in program execution: how does a method know where to return when it finishes? The answer is: the caller's state is pushed onto the stack before the call, and popped off when the callee returns. The stack is the mechanism that makes recursive and nested method calls work correctly without methods overwriting each other's local state.

Stack vs Heap — the fundamental distinction

Stack vs Heap — Memory Comparison:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                         STACK                                        │
│  Per-thread    Automatically managed (LIFO)   Fixed-size per thread  │
│  Stores:  method frames, local variables, operand stack              │
│  Lifetime: exactly as long as the method call                        │
│  Speed: O(1) — just a stack pointer decrement                        │
│  Failure: StackOverflowError (too deep)                              │
│                                                                       │
│                         HEAP                                          │
│  Shared        GC-managed                     Grows dynamically       │
│  Stores:  all Java objects and arrays                                 │
│  Lifetime: until no GC root can reach the object                     │
│  Speed: TLAB bump pointer (fast) but GC overhead on collection       │
│  Failure: OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space (too large / leak)       │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

What lives on the stack (and what does not)

On the stack: primitive local variables (int, long, double, etc.), object references as local variables (the reference itself — not the object it points to), method parameters, return addresses, and the operand stack used by bytecode execution.

Off the stack and on the heap: every actual Java object (new X()), arrays, and the this pointer's object. A local variable like String s = "hello" stores the reference s on the stack, but the String object itself resides on the heap.

Part 2

Stack Frames: The Unit of the JVM Stack

Every method invocation creates exactly one stack frame that is pushed onto the calling thread's stack. When the method returns, its frame is popped. At any point in time, the topmost frame is the one currently executing.

Anatomy of a stack frame

JVM Stack Frame Structure:
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                          Stack Frame                                  │
│                                                                       │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  Local Variable Array                                          │  │
│  │  [this (for instance methods)] [param1] [param2] [local1] ... │  │
│  │  Index 0       Index 1         Index 2   Index 3              │  │
│  │  Each slot is 4 bytes; long/double occupy 2 consecutive slots  │  │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                                                                       │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  Operand Stack                                                  │  │
│  │  Working area for bytecode instructions                         │  │
│  │  push/pop semantics; size determined at compile time            │  │
│  │  Example: iload_1 + iload_2 + iadd + istore_3                  │  │
│  │           push a   push b    pop,add  store result              │  │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                                                                       │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  Frame Data                                                     │  │
│  │  - Return address (bytecode PC of caller's next instruction)   │  │
│  │  - Reference to the runtime constant pool of current class     │  │
│  │  - Exception dispatch table reference                          │  │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Frame lifecycle with a concrete example

public class FrameDemo {
    public static int multiply(int a, int b) {  // (2) new frame pushed
        int result = a * b;                      // local vars: a=3, b=4, result=12
        return result;                           // (3) frame popped, result returned
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {     // (1) frame pushed at startup
        int x = multiply(3, 4);                  // calls (2)
        System.out.println(x);                   // (4) x=12 in main's locals
    }
}

Stack state during multiply execution:

Thread stack (top = current frame):
┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
│ multiply frame: a=3, b=4, result=12 │ ← top (executing)
├─────────────────────────────────────┤
│ main frame:     args=ref, x=?       │ ← waiting for multiply to return
└─────────────────────────────────────┘

After return result;, the multiply frame is discarded. Execution resumes in main's frame at the instruction after the invokestatic multiply call, with x now holding 12.

Part 3

Local Variable Array: What Frames Store

The local variable array is an indexed array of 4-byte slots at the base of each stack frame. The compiler determines its size at compile time (stored in the class file's Code attribute as max_locals).

Slot assignment rules

Local Variable Array — Slot Assignments:
For instance methods:
  Slot 0: this (reference to the current object)
  Slot 1: first parameter
  Slot 2: second parameter
  ...
  Slot N: first local variable declared in method body

For static methods:
  Slot 0: first parameter (no 'this')
  ...

Special rule: long and double occupy 2 consecutive slots
  (they are 64-bit values; each slot is 32 bits)

public class SlotDemo {
    //       slot0: this
    //       slot1: x (int, 1 slot)
    //       slot2-3: d (double, 2 slots)
    //       slot4: s (String reference, 1 slot)
    public void method(int x, double d, String s) {
        int local = x + 1;  // slot5: local (int, 1 slot)
        // max_locals = 6
    }
}

Slot reuse by the compiler

After a local variable's scope ends, the compiler may reuse its slot for a subsequent variable:

void compute() {
    {
        int temp = 42;   // slot 1
    }
    // temp is out of scope; slot 1 is available
    int result = 10;     // slot 1 (reused)
}

This is a JVM optimization — slots are reused where scopes do not overlap, keeping frame size minimal.

Part 4

Operand Stack: Where Bytecode Computation Happens

The operand stack is the working area within each frame where bytecode instructions push and pop values to perform computations. It is a stack-within-a-stack.

Bytecode execution trace

int add(int a, int b) {
    return a + b;
}

Compiled bytecode:

iload_1          // push local var slot 1 (a=3) onto operand stack
iload_2          // push local var slot 2 (b=4) onto operand stack
iadd             // pop 3 and 4, push result 7
ireturn          // pop 7, return it to caller

Operand stack states:

Before iload_1:  []
After iload_1:   [3]
After iload_2:   [3, 4]
After iadd:      [7]
After ireturn:   []  (frame popped)

The maximum depth of the operand stack is fixed at compile time (max_stack in the Code attribute). The JVM verifier ensures no bytecode can underflow or overflow this bounded stack.

Part 5

Stack Size Configuration: `-Xss`

Each thread's stack has a configurable maximum size set by -Xss (stack size). This is the single most important tuning knob for stack memory.

-Xss<size>       # Set the maximum stack size per thread

# Common values:
-Xss512k         # 512 KB per thread (default on most 64-bit JVMs)
-Xss256k         # Aggressive reduction for thread-heavy apps
-Xss1m           # Increase for deep recursion or large local arrays
-Xss2m           # For highly recursive algorithms

Default stack sizes by platform

Platform Default -Xss
Linux 64-bit 512 KB
macOS 64-bit 512 KB (main thread: 8 MB)
Windows 64-bit 320 KB or 256 KB
Java 21 virtual threads 1 KB (initial, grows dynamically)

Memory impact of -Xss

With 500 platform threads:

Total thread stack memory:
  500 threads × 512 KB = 256 MB  (default)
  500 threads × 256 KB = 128 MB  (reduced Xss)
  500 threads × 1 MB   = 500 MB  (increased Xss)

This memory is OUTSIDE the heap (-Xmx does not cover it).
Include it in container memory limit calculations.

Sizing strategy

  • Start with default (512 KB). Only change if you observe StackOverflowError (increase) or need to run thousands of threads (decrease).
  • For recursive algorithms: measure maximum recursion depth, estimate frame size per call, calculate needed stack: depth × frame_size_bytes ≈ required Xss.
  • For virtual threads (Java 21+): -Xss does not apply. Virtual thread stacks start at ~1 KB and grow dynamically up to a configured limit; they are heap-allocated.
Part 6

StackOverflowError: Causes and Diagnosis

StackOverflowError (SOE) is thrown when a thread's stack exceeds its -Xss limit — there is no room to push another frame.

Common causes

// Cause 1: Infinite recursion (most common)
public int factorial(int n) {
    return n * factorial(n - 1);  // Missing base case: n == 0
}
// After ~5000–10000 frames (depending on Xss), throws StackOverflowError

// Cause 2: Deep but legitimate recursion with large frames
public long processTree(TreeNode node) {
    if (node == null) return 0;
    byte[] buffer = new byte[4096];  // 4 KB local array in each frame
    // With 512 KB stack: only ~128 recursive calls before overflow
    return processTree(node.left) + processTree(node.right);
}

// Cause 3: Mutual recursion
void a() { b(); }
void b() { a(); }  // infinite mutual recursion

// Cause 4: toString() / equals() / hashCode() cycle
class Node {
    Node next;
    public String toString() {
        return "Node(" + next.toString() + ")";  // infinite if circular
    }
}

Reading a StackOverflowError stack trace

Exception in thread "main" java.lang.StackOverflowError
    at com.app.TreeProcessor.processTree(TreeProcessor.java:23)
    at com.app.TreeProcessor.processTree(TreeProcessor.java:26)
    at com.app.TreeProcessor.processTree(TreeProcessor.java:26)
    at com.app.TreeProcessor.processTree(TreeProcessor.java:26)
    ... (hundreds more identical lines)

The repeated method name confirms recursion. The line number difference between lines (23 vs 26) reveals where the recursive call occurs and where the computation is — helping identify the missing base case.

Fixing StackOverflowError

// Fix 1: Add base case to recursion
public int factorial(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) return 1;  // base case
    return n * factorial(n - 1);
}

// Fix 2: Convert deep recursion to iteration with explicit stack
public long processTree(TreeNode root) {
    Deque<TreeNode> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
    stack.push(root);
    long sum = 0;
    while (!stack.isEmpty()) {
        TreeNode node = stack.pop();
        if (node == null) continue;
        sum += node.value;
        stack.push(node.left);
        stack.push(node.right);
    }
    return sum;
}

// Fix 3: Increase stack size (last resort; hides the real problem)
java -Xss2m MyApp
Part 7

Stack Frames and the JIT Compiler

The interpretation of stack frames described in Parts 2–4 is the interpreted execution model. Once the JIT compiler optimizes a method, the physical stack layout changes significantly.

JIT frame transformations

Interpreted Frame (HotSpot Interpreter):
  - Precisely matches JVM spec: local var array + operand stack + frame data
  - Heap references tracked exactly for GC

JIT-Compiled Frame:
  - CPU registers replace many local variables and operand stack slots
  - Stack layout is method-specific (no standard format)
  - JIT generates "OopMaps" — metadata maps telling GC where heap
    references are at any safe point
  - Frame is much smaller (no interpreter overhead)
  - Methods may be inlined — several logical stack frames collapse
    into one physical stack frame

Inlining and its effect on stack depth

// Three logical methods:
void a() { b(); }
void b() { c(); }
void c() { /* compute */ }

// JIT may inline all three into a single compiled frame:
// Physical stack: just one frame for the inlined a+b+c
// Logical stack (for stack traces): JIT preserves virtual frame info
// via "inline tree" metadata for correct stack trace generation

This is why JIT-compiled methods show up correctly in Thread.currentThread().getStackTrace() even though they may share a physical stack frame.

Part 8

Native Stack vs Java Stack

Each Java thread has two stacks: the Java stack (JVM-managed, described above) and the native stack (OS-managed).

Thread Memory Layout:
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    Platform Thread                            │
│                                                              │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │              Java Stack (-Xss)                          │ │
│  │  Java method frames (interpreter + JIT frames)          │ │
│  │  Grows downward from initial stack pointer              │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                              │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │              Native Stack (OS default)                  │ │
│  │  JVM internal frames (GC, classloading, JIT)            │ │
│  │  JNI calls to native C/C++ code                         │ │
│  │  VM runtime code (safepoints, exception handling)       │ │
│  │  OS thread creation overhead                            │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The native stack is sized by the OS (typically 8 MB on Linux for the main thread, 2 MB for subsequent threads). It is separate from -Xss, which controls only the Java stack portion.

JNI and stack interaction

When Java calls a native method via JNI, the call transitions from the Java stack to the native stack. Native code can push arbitrary frames; stack overflows in native code produce a native crash (SIGSEGV) rather than a Java StackOverflowError.

// JNI call: transitions to native stack
public native int compute(int x);  // implemented in C via JNI

// After calling compute():
// Java stack top: frame for the calling Java method
// Native stack: frames for compute() C function + any it calls
Part 9

Virtual Thread Stacks (Java 21+)

Java 21's Project Loom introduces virtual threads (Thread.ofVirtual()), which have fundamentally different stack management.

Platform thread vs virtual thread stacks

Platform Thread Stack:           Virtual Thread Stack:
  Fixed size at creation           Heap-allocated, grows dynamically
  OS native thread = 1:1          Mounted on carrier thread when running
  -Xss controls size               Starts at ~1 KB, grows as needed
  Lives on OS stack                Lives on heap as Object[]
  Cannot be GC'd while running     Can be unmounted/parked, GC'd when idle
  OS context switch on park        Cheap continuation-swap on park

How virtual thread stack works

Virtual Thread Lifecycle:
1. Created: tiny stack object (~1 KB) allocated on heap
2. Scheduled: mounted onto a carrier (platform) thread
3. Running: frames pushed onto heap-based continuation stack
4. Blocking (e.g., I/O): UNMOUNTED from carrier thread
   - Stack state saved as heap object (continuation)
   - Carrier thread freed to run another virtual thread
5. Unblocking: mounted onto any available carrier thread
   - Stack state restored from heap continuation
6. Terminated: stack heap-allocated objects become GC-eligible

Key: 100,000 virtual threads = 100,000 tiny heap objects
     vs 100,000 platform threads = ~50 GB of committed native stack memory

Configuration for virtual thread stacks

# Virtual threads inherit most settings from the JVM
# No -Xss equivalent — stacks grow dynamically from heap

# Limit carrier thread pool size (carrier threads are platform threads)
-Djdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism=8   # default: CPU count
-Djdk.virtualThreadScheduler.maxPoolSize=256

# Monitor virtual thread stacks
jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json /tmp/threads.json
Part 10

Thread Dumps: Reading Stack State

A thread dump captures the stack state of every thread in the JVM at a single point in time. It is the primary tool for diagnosing deadlocks, thread starvation, and high CPU usage.

Generating a thread dump

# Method 1: kill signal (Linux/macOS)
kill -3 <pid>       # Sends SIGQUIT; JVM prints thread dump to stdout/stderr

# Method 2: jstack (most reliable)
jstack <pid> > threads.txt
jstack -l <pid>     # Long format: includes lock info and ownable synchronizers

# Method 3: jcmd (preferred)
jcmd <pid> Thread.print > threads.txt
jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json /tmp/threads.json  # Java 21+

# Method 4: VisualVM / JDK Mission Control (GUI)
# Programmatic:
ThreadMXBean bean = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean();
ThreadInfo[] infos = bean.dumpAllThreads(true, true);

Anatomy of a thread dump entry

"http-nio-8080-exec-1" #42 daemon prio=5 os_prio=0 cpu=1234ms elapsed=3600s
   java.lang.Thread.State: BLOCKED (on object monitor)
    at com.app.OrderService.processOrder(OrderService.java:87)
    - waiting to lock <0x0000000741234abc> (a java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock)
    at com.app.RequestHandler.handle(RequestHandler.java:45)
    at org.apache.tomcat.util.net.NioEndpoint$SocketProcessor.doRun(NioEndpoint.java:1741)
    at ...

   Locked ownable synchronizers:
    - <0x0000000741235def> (a java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock)

Reading each field:
- "http-nio-8080-exec-1" — thread name (set by Thread.setName())
- #42 — JVM-internal thread ID
- daemon — whether this is a daemon thread
- prio=5 — Java thread priority
- cpu=1234ms — total CPU time this thread has consumed
- java.lang.Thread.State: BLOCKED — current thread state (see Part 11)
- waiting to lock <0x...> — address of the monitor this thread is waiting for
- Locked ownable synchronizers — locks currently held by this thread

Part 11

Thread States: What the Stack Tells You

Every thread's state in a thread dump reveals what it is doing at that moment.

Thread States and Their Meaning:
┌──────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ State            │ What it means                                 │
├──────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ RUNNABLE         │ Executing Java code or waiting for CPU        │
│                  │ May be: in pure computation, doing I/O (OS),  │
│                  │ or waiting on OS but JVM thinks it's running  │
├──────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ BLOCKED          │ Waiting for a synchronized monitor lock       │
│                  │ Another thread holds the lock                 │
│                  │ Classic sign: multiple threads BLOCKED on     │
│                  │ same lock → contention or deadlock            │
├──────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ WAITING          │ Indefinitely waiting for notification         │
│                  │ Caused by: Object.wait(), LockSupport.park(), │
│                  │ Thread.join() with no timeout                 │
├──────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ TIMED_WAITING    │ Waiting with a timeout                        │
│                  │ Thread.sleep(), Object.wait(timeout),         │
│                  │ LockSupport.parkNanos()                       │
├──────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ NEW              │ Created but not yet started                   │
├──────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ TERMINATED       │ Execution completed                           │
└──────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Thread dump pattern recognition

Pattern 1 — Deadlock:
  Thread A: BLOCKED waiting for lock X, holding lock Y
  Thread B: BLOCKED waiting for lock Y, holding lock X
  → jstack marks: "Found one Java-level deadlock"

Pattern 2 — Thread Pool Starvation:
  All executor threads: BLOCKED on same database connection pool lock
  → Connection pool exhausted; add more connections or reduce thread count

Pattern 3 — Lock Contention:
  20 threads all BLOCKED on same ReentrantLock address
  → Hot lock; consider lock striping, ConcurrentHashMap, or lock-free design

Pattern 4 — CPU Spike:
  1-2 threads RUNNABLE at same method in a tight loop (e.g., HashMap.get)
  → Infinite loop, tight retry loop, or hash collision causing O(n) traversal

Pattern 5 — Healthy Thread Pool:
  N threads WAITING at pool.take() or LockSupport.park
  N threads RUNNABLE at business logic
  → Normal: threads waiting for work are idle correctly
Part 12

Deadlock Detection via Thread Dump

Deadlocks are automatically detected by jstack and reported at the end of the thread dump.

Found one Java-level deadlock:
=============================
"Thread-B":
  waiting to lock monitor 0x0000000741234abc (object 0x000000076b1b4cd0, a java.lang.String),
  which is held by "Thread-A"

"Thread-A":
  waiting to lock monitor 0x0000000741235def (object 0x000000076b1b4de0, a java.lang.String),
  which is held by "Thread-B"

Java stack information for the threads listed above:
===================================================
"Thread-B":
    at DeadlockDemo.methodB(DeadlockDemo.java:28)
    - waiting to lock <0x000000076b1b4cd0> (a java.lang.String)
    - locked <0x000000076b1b4de0> (a java.lang.String)
    at DeadlockDemo.run(DeadlockDemo.java:15)

"Thread-A":
    at DeadlockDemo.methodA(DeadlockDemo.java:18)
    - waiting to lock <0x000000076b1b4de0> (a java.lang.String)
    - locked <0x000000076b1b4cd0> (a java.lang.String)
    at DeadlockDemo.run(DeadlockDemo.java:10)

Prevention strategies

// Strategy 1: Consistent lock ordering
// Always acquire locks in the same order across all threads
void transfer(Account from, Account to, int amount) {
    Account first  = from.id < to.id ? from : to;   // consistent order
    Account second = from.id < to.id ? to : from;
    synchronized (first)  {
        synchronized (second) {
            from.balance -= amount;
            to.balance   += amount;
        }
    }
}

// Strategy 2: tryLock with timeout (ReentrantLock)
boolean result = lock1.tryLock(100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
if (result) {
    try {
        if (lock2.tryLock(100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) {
            try { /* work */ } finally { lock2.unlock(); }
        }
    } finally { lock1.unlock(); }
}

// Strategy 3: Use higher-level concurrency utilities
// ConcurrentHashMap, atomic operations, actor model
// avoid explicit locking entirely
Part 13

Stack Depth Limits and Recursion Patterns

The maximum recursion depth before StackOverflowError depends on:
1. -Xss value
2. Frame size of each recursive call
3. JVM overhead per frame

Estimating safe recursion depth

Estimation formula:
  safe_depth ≈ (Xss_bytes × 0.9) / avg_frame_bytes

  Frame size for a simple int recursion:
    Local var array:   ~16–32 bytes (return addr, frame ptr, 1-2 locals)
    Operand stack:     ~8–16 bytes
    Frame metadata:    ~32 bytes
    Safety margin overhead: ~64 bytes
  ≈ 120–160 bytes per simple recursive frame

  With -Xss512k:
    safe_depth ≈ (512 × 1024 × 0.9) / 150 ≈ 3072 levels

  With local byte[] buffer in each frame:
    Frame size ≈ 4096 (buffer) + 150 (overhead) ≈ 4246 bytes
    safe_depth ≈ (512 × 1024 × 0.9) / 4246 ≈ 108 levels (!!)

Trampoline pattern for deep recursion in Java

// Problem: mutual recursion causes SOE for large inputs
boolean isEven(int n) { return n == 0 || isOdd(n - 1); }
boolean isOdd(int n)  { return n != 0 && isEven(n - 1); }
// isEven(100_000) → StackOverflowError

// Solution: Trampoline — convert recursive call to a returned thunk
@FunctionalInterface interface Thunk { Object get(); }

Object trampolineIsEven(int n) {
    if (n == 0) return Boolean.TRUE;
    return (Thunk) () -> trampolineIsOdd(n - 1);
}
Object trampolineIsOdd(int n) {
    if (n == 0) return Boolean.FALSE;
    return (Thunk) () -> trampolineIsEven(n - 1);
}

// Driver: iterates thunks without growing the stack
boolean trampoline(int n) {
    Object result = trampolineIsEven(n);
    while (result instanceof Thunk t) result = t.get();
    return (Boolean) result;
}
// trampoline(100_000) → works; only 2 stack frames at a time
Part 14

Stack and Garbage Collection Interaction

Stack frames are GC roots. Every object reference stored in any local variable in any stack frame on any live thread is a GC root — the GC considers these objects live and will not collect them.

Safepoints and stack scanning

The GC cannot scan stack frames at arbitrary points in time — it needs a safepoint: a position in the bytecode stream where the JVM knows exactly which stack slots contain object references (from the JIT's OopMaps).

GC Pause Initiation via Safepoints:
1. JVM signals all threads to reach safepoint
2. Threads reach safepoints at: method calls, loop back edges, JNI returns
3. JVM waits for all threads to report in (time-to-safepoint = TTSP)
4. GC runs with all threads stopped (STW)
5. GC scans each thread's stack frames using OopMaps
6. References in stack frames = GC roots; trace from these
7. JVM releases threads; they resume from their safepoints

Null-ing references to help GC

void processLargeData() {
    byte[] bigBuffer = new byte[100 * 1024 * 1024];  // 100 MB
    process(bigBuffer);
    bigBuffer = null;    // explicit null: reference removed from local var slot
    // From this point, GC can collect bigBuffer if no other reference exists
    doOtherWork();       // GC may run here and collect the 100 MB
}

// Without null:
// bigBuffer remains in local var slot until method returns
// GC root chain persists for the entire method duration
// If doOtherWork() causes a GC, bigBuffer is held live unnecessarily
Part 15

Stack Memory in Practice: Thread Count and Memory Budget

In production systems with many threads, stack memory is a significant contributor to total JVM footprint.

Platform thread memory budget

Platform Thread Memory Breakdown:
  Java stack:          -Xss (default 512 KB)
  Native stack:        OS default (~256 KB–2 MB depending on OS/JVM)
  Thread object:       ~few KB on heap (java.lang.Thread object)
  OS kernel structures: ~8–16 KB per thread in kernel space
  Total per thread:    ~1–3 MB minimum

Example: 500 platform threads
  Java stacks:   500 × 512 KB = 256 MB
  Native stacks: 500 × 512 KB ≈ 256 MB (rough estimate)
  Total: ~512 MB just for thread stacks — OUTSIDE the heap

Virtual threads change the equation

Virtual Thread Memory Budget (Java 21):
  Unmounted virtual thread: ~2–4 KB on heap (continuation object)
  Mounted virtual thread: carrier thread stack + heap continuation

  100,000 virtual threads (mostly parked on I/O):
    Heap: 100,000 × 4 KB ≈ 400 MB  (continuations on heap)
    vs platform threads: 100,000 × 1 MB = 100 GB (!!)

Right-sizing thread pools and stack sizes

# For thread-heavy applications with simple stack patterns:
-Xss256k    # Reduce from 512 KB → saves 128 MB for 1000 threads

# Verify 256 KB is sufficient:
# 1. Run load test with -Xss256k
# 2. Monitor for StackOverflowError
# 3. Thread dump: check max frame depth at peak load

# For Java 21 virtual-thread applications:
# Remove explicit thread pools for I/O-bound work
# Use VirtualThread executor; no -Xss tuning needed
ExecutorService exec = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor();

ThreadMXBean tmx = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean();

// Detect deadlocks programmatically
long[] deadlocked = tmx.findDeadlockedThreads();
if (deadlocked != null) {
    ThreadInfo[] infos = tmx.getThreadInfo(deadlocked, true, true);
    for (ThreadInfo info : infos) {

}

Part 17

Stack Traces in Production: Cost and Best Practices

Creating a Throwable (or any Exception) captures the current stack trace. This is expensive — the JVM must walk the entire call stack and record frame information for each level.

Stack trace capture cost

// Expensive: captures full stack trace
new Exception("debug").printStackTrace();
throw new RuntimeException("something failed");

// For exceptions thrown in hot paths, this can dominate CPU:
// 10,000 exceptions/second × 50-frame stack = 500,000 frame captures/sec

// Mitigation 1: Override fillInStackTrace to skip capture
class NoStackException extends RuntimeException {
    @Override
    public synchronized Throwable fillInStackTrace() {
        return this;  // No-op: stack trace never captured
    }
}

// Mitigation 2: Pre-create exception instances (reuse in non-exceptional paths)
private static final NoStackException RATE_LIMIT_EX =
    new NoStackException("Rate limited");

// Mitigation 3: JVM flag to disable stack trace capture on hot exceptions
-XX:-OmitStackTraceInFastThrow  // Default: JVM DOES omit after N throws
                                 // → you may see exceptions with empty traces
                                 // → add this flag to restore full traces in prod

Reading stack traces for root cause analysis

Exception chain reading order:
java.lang.RuntimeException: Order processing failed   ← outer exception
    at com.app.OrderService.process(OrderService.java:45)   ← where wrapped
    at com.app.RequestHandler.handle(RequestHandler.java:23)
    at ...
Caused by: java.sql.SQLException: Connection timed out  ← root cause
    at com.mysql.jdbc.MysqlIO.send(MysqlIO.java:3671)
    at ...
Caused by: java.net.SocketTimeoutException: Read timed out ← deepest cause
    at java.net.SocketInputStream.socketRead0(Native Method)
    at ...

Reading strategy:
1. Start with the LAST "Caused by" — that is the original failure
2. Work upward through the chain to find the application code responsible
3. The first application class in the deepest "Caused by" is the root cause location
Part 18

Stack and JVM Safepoints Deep Dive

Safepoint latency (TTSP — time-to-safepoint) is a critical JVM performance metric often overlooked in favor of GC pause time. The total STW pause = TTSP + GC work time.

What delays safepoint

// Problem 1: Long-running bytecode in a tight loop (no safepoint opportunities)
for (int i = 0; i < Integer.MAX_VALUE; i++) {
    sum += array[i];  // JIT may place safepoint at loop back edge
    // But with -XX:+UseCountedLoopSafepoints (default Java 11+): fine
}

// Problem 2: JNI call in progress
// Native code is not subject to JVM safepoint mechanism
// JVM marks the thread as "at native" and proceeds without it
// → Long JNI calls do NOT delay GC safepoint

// Problem 3: JIT optimization removed safepoint poll
// Aggressive JIT inlining can create long stretches without a poll
// Diagnosable with: -XX:+SafepointTimeout -XX:SafepointTimeoutDelay=1000

Diagnosing safepoint issues

# Log safepoint events
-Xlog:safepoint*:file=safepoints.log:time,uptime,level,tags

# Key output lines to watch:
# "vmop[Revoke bias] ..." → biased lock revocation safepoint
# "Vmop[G1CollectForAllocation]" → GC-triggered safepoint
# "Total: 45ms  Spin: 38ms" → 38ms of TTSP (threads slow to reach safepoint)

# Identify threads delaying safepoint:
# -XX:+PrintSafepointStatistics -XX:PrintSafepointStatisticsCount=1
Part 19

Production Stack Sizing Guide

Stack Sizing Decision Tree:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 1. What is your concurrency model?                                   │
│    ├─ Virtual threads (Java 21+) → no -Xss tuning needed            │
│    └─ Platform threads → continue below                              │
│                                                                      │
│ 2. Do you see StackOverflowError in production or staging?          │
│    ├─ Yes → increase -Xss (512k → 1m → 2m); find and fix recursion  │
│    └─ No  → default 512k is likely fine                             │
│                                                                      │
│ 3. How many platform threads does your application use?             │
│    ├─ < 200 threads → default 512k; total: ~100 MB stack memory     │
│    ├─ 200-1000 threads → consider 256k; profile first               │
│    └─ > 1000 threads → migrate to virtual threads                   │
│                                                                      │
│ 4. Does your application use deep recursive algorithms?             │
│    ├─ Yes → test maximum depth + increase Xss if needed             │
│    │        OR convert recursion to iteration                        │
│    └─ No  → default is fine                                         │
│                                                                      │
│ 5. Container sizing:                                                 │
│    Add (thread_count × Xss) to memory budget OUTSIDE of -Xmx       │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Production JVM flags for stack and threads

# Core stack/thread settings
-Xss512k                          # Default; adjust only with justification

# Thread creation diagnostics (when OOM: unable to create native thread)
-XX:+PrintVMOptions                # Confirm Xss value in use

# Enable JVMTI thread monitoring (for APMs like Datadog, NewRelic)
# These agents inspect thread stacks via JVMTI without thread dumps

# Java 21 virtual threads
-Djdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism=$(nproc)  # Match CPU count

# Stack trace completeness (disable JVM's "fast throw" optimization)
-XX:-OmitStackTraceInFastThrow     # Restore full traces for NPE/ArrayIOOB

# Safepoint logging (use only when diagnosing latency anomalies)
-Xlog:safepoint*:file=/logs/safepoint.log:time,uptime,level,tags:filecount=3,filesize=10m

Thread Dump Analysis Workflow

Thread Dump Analysis Workflow for Production Incidents:
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ STEP 1: Capture multiple thread dumps (3, spaced 10s apart)         │
│   jstack <pid> > td1.txt; sleep 10; jstack <pid> > td2.txt        │
│   → Threads stuck across multiple dumps = genuine problem          │
│                                                                     │
│ STEP 2: Count threads by state                                      │
│   grep "Thread.State" td1.txt | sort | uniq -c                     │
│   → Many BLOCKED → lock contention or deadlock                     │
│   → Many WAITING → starvation or connection pool exhaustion        │
│   → High RUNNABLE with same method → CPU spike / tight loop        │
│                                                                     │
│ STEP 3: Check for JVM-reported deadlocks                           │
│   grep -A 30 "deadlock" td1.txt                                    │
│   → JVM reports deadlock cycles automatically                      │
│                                                                     │
│ STEP 4: Find the most common stack patterns                        │
│   → Group threads by their top frame                               │
│   → Same top frame for many threads = bottleneck                   │
│                                                                     │
│ STEP 5: Correlate with CPU / metrics                               │
│   → RUNNABLE at business logic + high CPU = hot code path          │
│   → RUNNABLE at wait / native = I/O bound with wrong state report  │
│   → All idle threads WAITING = load dropped / pool starvation      │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Part 21

Interview Q&A

Q: What is the difference between StackOverflowError and OutOfMemoryError: unable to create new native thread?
A: StackOverflowError means one thread's stack exceeded its -Xss limit — typically due to infinite recursion. The thread is out of stack space for new frames. OutOfMemoryError: unable to create new native thread means the JVM tried to create a new thread (allocate new OS thread + stack memory) but the OS refused — either because the process hit its thread count limit (ulimit -u) or because there isn't enough virtual memory for another thread stack. The fix for SOE is to reduce recursion depth or increase -Xss. The fix for thread-creation OOM is to reduce thread count (use virtual threads, smaller pools) or increase OS limits.

Q: Where does an object reference live vs where does the object it references live?
A: The reference (a 4- or 8-byte pointer value) lives wherever the variable is declared — if it's a local variable, it lives in the local variable array of the current stack frame (on the thread stack). If it's a field of an object, it lives inside that object's layout on the heap. The object itself always lives on the heap — the new keyword always allocates on the heap (except when the JIT's escape analysis stack-allocates or scalar-replaces it).

Q: Why can't Java platform threads be cheaply scaled to 100,000 concurrent connections?
A: Each platform thread is backed by an OS thread with a dedicated native stack (1–2 MB). 100,000 threads × 1 MB native stack = 100 GB of committed stack memory. OS context switching between 100,000 threads is also expensive: the CPU scheduler must time-slice all threads, producing significant overhead. Virtual threads (Java 21+) solve this by unmounting from their carrier thread when blocking on I/O, freeing the carrier for other work. 100,000 virtual threads mostly parked on I/O cost ~400 MB of heap, not 100 GB.

Q: A thread is RUNNABLE in a thread dump but the CPU spike is caused by a tight loop with no blocking. How do you find which line of code is responsible?
A: Take multiple thread dumps and find threads consistently RUNNABLE at the same method and line number — the repeated frame is the hot loop. For precision, use async-profiler (-d 30 -e cpu): it samples stack traces at CPU interrupts without requiring JVM safepoints, giving accurate CPU attribution per method. jstat -gcutil can rule out GC as the cause. jcmd <pid> Compiler.queue shows JIT compilation queue — a method being repeatedly deoptimized can also spike CPU.

Q: How does the JVM scan stack frames during GC without stopping in the middle of a method?
A: The JVM uses safepoints — predefined positions in compiled code (method returns, loop back edges, JNI boundaries) where the JVM guarantees all object references are in known, inspectable locations. The JIT compiler generates OopMaps — metadata tables mapping each stack position at each safepoint to the type of value stored there (heap reference vs primitive). When GC needs to run, it signals all threads to pause at their next safepoint. Once at a safepoint, each thread's stack can be safely scanned using its OopMaps to locate all heap references, which become GC roots.

Part 22

Summary Table

Concept Key Detail Production Relevance
JVM Stack Per-thread, private, LIFO; stores frames for active methods Not shared; each thread has its own stack sized by -Xss
Stack frame Local variable array + operand stack + frame data; pushed per method call Understanding frames is key to reading stack traces and thread dumps
Local variable array Indexed slots (4 bytes each); slot 0 = this for instance methods; long/double use 2 slots Slot assignment determined at compile time by javac
Operand stack Working stack for bytecode instructions (push/pop); bounded by max_stack Only relevant when reading bytecode; JIT replaces with registers
-Xss Maximum stack size per thread; default 512 KB on 64-bit Linux Include threads × Xss in container memory budget
StackOverflowError Thread's stack exceeds -Xss; most often infinite recursion Fix recursion; convert to iteration as last resort to raise -Xss
Native stack OS-managed; separate from Java stack; used by JVM internals and JNI Cannot be controlled by -Xss; long JNI calls don't delay GC
Virtual thread stacks Heap-allocated continuations; start ~1 KB, grow dynamically Replaces platform thread pools for I/O-bound concurrency
Thread dump Point-in-time snapshot of all thread stacks; primary diagnostic tool Take 3 dumps 10s apart; threads stuck across dumps = real issue
Thread states RUNNABLE / BLOCKED / WAITING / TIMED_WAITING Many BLOCKED → contention; many WAITING → starvation
Deadlock Detected automatically by jstack; threads circularly blocked Prevent with consistent lock ordering or tryLock with timeout
Safepoints Positions where JVM can safely inspect all thread stacks TTSP is part of total GC pause; long JNI or tight loops delay safepoints
Stack as GC root All local variables in all active frames are GC roots Null out large local references after use to help GC
OopMaps JIT-generated metadata: at each safepoint, which slots hold heap refs Required for GC correctness in JIT-compiled frames
Stack trace cost Exception creation = full stack walk; expensive in hot paths Use fillInStackTrace() override for perf-sensitive exceptions
