Part 1

Introduction and Motivation

Garbage collection is perhaps the most consequential engineering decision embedded in a JVM application's runtime configuration. It operates invisibly most of the time, but when it surfaces — in the form of latency spikes, throughput degradation, or stop-the-world pauses — it can dominate everything else. A microservice that achieves 99.9% of requests under 20ms will spectacularly violate that SLA the moment the GC pauses for 800ms.

Understanding GC algorithms is not academic. The choice between G1 and ZGC determines whether your application can guarantee sub-10ms pause times. The difference between mark-sweep and mark-compact determines whether your heap fragments over time. The distinction between throughput-oriented and latency-oriented collectors determines which metrics you optimize.

This lesson provides a comprehensive treatment of every major GC algorithm available in production JVMs: the fundamental collection strategies (mark-sweep, mark-compact, copying), the generational hypothesis and why it drives JVM design, and a deep-dive into each major collector (Serial, Parallel, CMS, G1, ZGC, Shenandoah). You will leave with a clear mental model for selecting and tuning the right collector for any production scenario.

Part 2

Fundamental GC Problem: Object Reachability

Before examining specific algorithms, establish the core problem: the JVM must determine which objects are live (reachable from program roots) and which are garbage (unreachable and safe to reclaim).

2.1 The Reachability Graph

At any moment, the JVM maintains a directed graph where nodes are objects and edges are references. An object is live if and only if a path exists from a GC root to that object.

GC roots include:
- Local variables on all thread stacks
- Static fields of loaded classes
- JNI references held by native code
- Active thread objects
- Objects referenced from Metaspace (class-level statics)
- Finalization references and references from the finalizer thread
- JVM internals (class loaders, interned strings, etc.)

Everything unreachable from these roots is garbage, regardless of how many objects reference it in cycles. This is the key advantage of tracing GC over reference counting: it correctly handles cycles.

2.2 The GC Trade-off Triangle

All GC algorithms must balance three competing goals:

         Throughput
        /          \
       /            \
  Latency ———— Footprint (Memory)

No collector excels at all three simultaneously:
- Maximizing throughput means spending CPU on application work, accepting occasional long pauses
- Minimizing latency means doing GC work concurrently with the application, spending CPU on GC overhead
- Minimizing footprint means collecting aggressively, which increases CPU and potentially latency

Understanding this triangle is the foundation of all GC selection decisions.

Part 3

Core Collection Strategies

All GC algorithms are built from three fundamental strategies. Modern collectors combine them.

3.1 Mark-Sweep

Phase 1 — Mark: Starting from GC roots, traverse the entire object graph, marking each reachable object.

Phase 2 — Sweep: Scan the entire heap linearly. Any unmarked object is garbage; reclaim its space into a free list.

Characteristics:
- Does not move objects → no pointer updates required
- Heap becomes fragmented over time → free list allocations are slower than pointer-bump allocations
- Cannot satisfy large allocations even when total free space is sufficient (fragmentation)
- Mark phase cost is proportional to live data size; sweep phase cost is proportional to heap size

When used: CMS's old generation collection. The original basis for most GC research.

Before sweep:
[ A | dead | B | dead | dead | C | dead | D ]

After sweep (free list):
[ A | FREE | B |    FREE     | C | FREE | D ]
         ↑_____________________↑________↑  <- fragmented free blocks

3.2 Mark-Compact

Phase 1 — Mark: Same as mark-sweep.

Phase 2 — Compact: Move all live objects to one end of the heap, maintaining their relative order. Update all references to point to new locations.

Characteristics:
- Eliminates fragmentation entirely
- Enables fast pointer-bump allocation (allocation = increment one pointer)
- Moving objects requires updating all references → expensive for large heaps
- Two passes needed: one to compute new locations, one to move objects and update references
- All application threads must stop while objects are being moved (references must be consistent)

When used: Full GC in HotSpot heap (Serial, Parallel old-gen GC), G1's evacuation, CMS concurrent mode failure fallback.

Before compact:
[ A | dead | B | dead | dead | C | dead | D ]

After compact:
[ A | B | C | D |         FREE SPACE         ]
                 ↑________________________________ pointer-bump allocates here

3.3 Copying (Semi-Space)

Split the heap into two equal halves: from-space and to-space. During GC:

  1. Traverse live objects in from-space
  2. Copy each live object to to-space
  3. Update all references to point to to-space copies
  4. Flip the role of from/to spaces

Characteristics:
- Automatically compacts (all live objects are consecutively packed in to-space)
- Fast allocation (pointer-bump in to-space)
- Only half of heap is usable at any time — 50% overhead
- Cost proportional to live data size, not heap size (great for short-lived objects, bad for long-lived)
- Dead objects are simply abandoned in from-space; no per-object processing needed

When used: Young generation (Eden, survivor spaces in all generational collectors). Shenandoah's new-to-old region copy, G1's evacuation of regions.

from-space:        to-space (initially empty):
[ A | dead | B | dead | C ]  |  [              ]

After copy:
[ old A | dead | old B | dead | old C ]  |  [ A | B | C |      ]
   ↑ forwarding pointers point here →          ↑ pointer-bump here

3.4 Why Copying Wins for Young Generation

Young generation objects are almost all short-lived (the weak generational hypothesis). If 95% of objects die before the first collection, the copying collector processes only 5% of the region (the survivors) and evacuates them. The remaining 95% is simply abandoned. Cost is proportional to survivors, not allocated objects.

Part 4

Why Java Provides This

The generational design of all major JVM collectors rests on a foundational observation:

> Most objects die young. Objects that survive the first collection are likely to survive for a long time.

This bimodal survival distribution allows the JVM to apply different strategies to different age cohorts:

  • Young generation (Eden + Survivors): Small, collected frequently with copying GC. Cost is low because most objects are dead by collection time.
  • Old generation (Tenured/Old): Large, collected infrequently with mark-based algorithms. Objects here are long-lived and rarely become garbage.

4.1 Object Promotion

Each object has an age counter (incremented each time it survives a young GC without being promoted). When an object's age exceeds TenuringThreshold (default: 15), it is promoted to old generation.

Objects are also promoted immediately if:
- Survivor space is full (survivor overflow → premature promotion)
- Object is larger than survivor space capacity
- -XX:PretenureSizeThreshold is exceeded (large objects go directly to old gen)

Premature promotion is a frequent performance problem: young-gen collection fills up survivors, overflows to old gen, which fills up and triggers expensive full GC.

4.2 The Card Table and Remembered Sets

Generational GC creates a challenge: an old-generation object might hold a reference to a young-generation object. When collecting the young generation, the collector must consider these old-to-young references as additional roots.

Solution: Remembered Set — a data structure that tracks which old-generation regions contain references into young generation.

The classic implementation is the Card Table: divide the heap into 512-byte cards. When a reference is written to an object in old gen, the JVM's write barrier marks that card as "dirty." During young GC, dirty cards are scanned to find old-to-young references.

Write barriers add a small overhead to every reference assignment (~1–3 ns per write), a constant cost paid throughout application execution to enable generational GC.

Part 5

Internal Working

Flags: -XX:+UseSerialGC
Default on: Single-CPU machines, client-class machines (detection heuristic based on CPU count and RAM)

5.1 Architecture

Serial GC is the simplest JVM collector. It uses:
- Young generation: Single-threaded mark-copy (stop-the-world)
- Old generation: Single-threaded mark-compact (stop-the-world)

Every collection pauses all application threads and performs GC on a single thread. There is no concurrency, no parallelism, no background work.

5.2 When To Use Serial GC

Despite its simplicity, Serial GC is the right choice in specific scenarios:

  • Containerized microservices with very small heaps (< 256 MB): With small heaps, pause times are short (< 10ms) even with single-threaded collection. Parallel collectors add overhead for thread coordination that outweighs their benefit.
  • Batch jobs: If a batch process runs for 5 minutes and total GC pause time is 1 second, serial GC is fine. The overhead of parallel GC thread management is wasted.
  • Memory-constrained environments: Serial GC has the lowest memory overhead of any JVM collector.

5.3 Performance Profile

  • Young GC pause: proportional to survivor count + Eden copy work
  • Full GC pause: proportional to heap size (must scan entire old gen)
  • Throughput: Highest of all collectors when heap is small (no coordination overhead)
  • Latency: Acceptable for small heaps; unacceptable for large heaps (full GC on 4 GB heap = multi-second pause)
Part 6

Parallel Collector (Throughput GC)

Flags: -XX:+UseParallelGC
Default on: Server-class machines in Java 8 and earlier

6.1 Architecture

Parallel GC uses multiple threads to perform both young and old generation collections. The number of GC threads defaults to min(N, 8) + (N-8) * 5/8 where N is the number of CPU cores. Override with -XX:ParallelGCThreads=<n>.

  • Young generation: Parallel mark-copy (stop-the-world, multiple threads)
  • Old generation: Parallel mark-compact (stop-the-world, multiple threads)

All GC still stops the world — parallelism reduces pause duration but does not eliminate pauses.

6.2 Adaptive Sizing Policy

Parallel GC introduced adaptive heap sizing: the JVM automatically adjusts Eden size, survivor ratios, and old generation size to meet throughput and pause time goals:

-XX:GCTimeRatio=<N>       # Target: GC uses at most 1/(1+N) of total time
                           # Default 99 = target < 1% GC overhead
-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=<ms> # Target maximum pause time (best effort, not guaranteed)

When you set MaxGCPauseMillis, the JVM shrinks generation sizes to reduce pause duration, accepting lower throughput. When you set GCTimeRatio, it expands generations to amortize GC cost over more allocation, accepting longer pauses.

6.3 Performance Profile

  • Throughput: Best among all major collectors for pure compute tasks
  • Pause times: Predictable but potentially long for large heaps (seconds for multi-GB heaps)
  • Overhead: Low — no concurrent marking threads, no write barrier overhead beyond card table
  • Best for: Batch processing, offline analytics, scientific computing where total runtime matters more than individual pause times

6.4 Parallel GC Example Flags

-XX:+UseParallelGC
-XX:ParallelGCThreads=8
-XX:GCTimeRatio=19        # Allow up to 5% GC overhead
-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=500  # Target pauses under 500ms (guidance, not guarantee)
-Xms4g -Xmx4g            # Fixed heap to avoid sizing overhead
Part 7

CMS Collector (Concurrent Mark-Sweep)

Flags: -XX:+UseConcMarkSweepGC
Deprecated in Java 9, removed in Java 14

CMS was the first major attempt at low-latency GC in HotSpot. It achieved short old-generation collection pauses by doing most marking work concurrently with running application threads. Understanding CMS is essential because G1 and ZGC inherit and improve upon its design principles.

7.1 CMS Architecture

Young generation: Same parallel copying as Parallel GC (ParNew collector).

Old generation: CMS — mostly concurrent, with two stop-the-world phases:

  1. Initial Mark (STW): Mark objects directly reachable from GC roots. Short pause.
  2. Concurrent Mark: Trace the object graph concurrently with the application. Application continues running, creating "floating garbage" (newly dead objects that CMS won't collect this cycle).
  3. Concurrent Preclean: Attempt to reduce work remaining for remark phase.
  4. Remark (STW): Re-scan objects modified since concurrent mark. Must stop the world to get a consistent snapshot. The most variable and potentially longest pause in CMS.
  5. Concurrent Sweep: Reclaim dead objects concurrently. Does not compact.
  6. Concurrent Reset: Reset data structures for next cycle.

7.2 The Floating Garbage Problem

During concurrent mark, the application continues modifying the object graph. Objects that die after being marked as live will not be collected in this cycle — they become floating garbage, reclaimed in the next cycle. CMS must account for this by leaving headroom in old gen.

7.3 Concurrent Mode Failure

CMS's worst failure mode: if old generation fills up before CMS can complete a concurrent collection cycle, CMS falls back to a stop-the-world full GC using serial mark-compact. This is exactly the long pause CMS was designed to avoid, and it's significantly longer than a Parallel GC full GC because:

  1. CMS doesn't compact in normal operation, so the heap is fragmented
  2. Fragmentation means even with free space, large allocations may fail
  3. The serial fallback compacts the entire heap in one massive STW pause

This is called Concurrent Mode Failure (CMF) and is the primary operational hazard of CMS. The trigger is when old generation occupancy at the start of a CMS cycle exceeds -XX:CMSInitiatingOccupancyFraction (default ~70%). If allocation rate is high, old gen fills up before the cycle completes.

7.4 CMS Fragmentation

CMS uses mark-sweep (not mark-compact) for old generation. Over time, the old generation becomes fragmented: many small free blocks interspersed with live objects. This causes:
- Slower allocation (free list scan instead of pointer bump)
- Eventual allocation failure for large objects even when total free space is sufficient
- Ultimately triggers a full GC with compaction

7.5 Why CMS Was Deprecated

  • Fragmentation leading to concurrent mode failures
  • Complex, difficult-to-tune behavior
  • No real improvement path without fundamental redesign
  • G1 provides better latency with compaction
Part 8

G1 Collector (Garbage-First)

Flags: -XX:+UseG1GC
Default on: Java 9+ on server-class machines

G1 is the most important collector to understand for modern Java production work. It represents a fundamental rethink of JVM heap layout and collection strategy.

8.1 G1 Heap Architecture: Region-Based Layout

G1 divides the heap into equal-sized regions (default 1–32 MB, calculated to create ~2048 regions). Regions are not permanently designated as young or old — they are assigned roles dynamically:

  • Eden regions: New allocations go here
  • Survivor regions: Objects surviving young GC evacuate here
  • Old regions: Promoted or long-surviving objects
  • Humongous regions: Objects larger than 50% of region size get dedicated regions
Heap: 8 GB, Region size: 4 MB → 2048 regions

[E][E][E][S][O][O][H][H][E][E][S][O][O][E]...
 ↑  ↑  ↑  ↑  ↑  ↑  ↑  ↑
 Eden   Surv Old  Huge  More Eden

This layout enables incremental collection: G1 can choose which regions to collect in each cycle rather than collecting the entire old generation at once.

8.2 The Garbage-First Principle

G1's name comes from its collection priority: it prefers to collect regions with the most garbage first. When a collection cycle completes, G1 builds a remembered set for each old region tracking which regions reference it, enabling it to calculate the "collection value" (garbage reclaimed per unit pause time) for each region.

During the mixed collection phase, G1 selects the N most valuable old-generation regions (alongside all young regions) to collect in a single pause, targeting the configured pause goal.

8.3 G1 Collection Phases

Young-Only Phase:

  1. Young GC (STW evacuation pause): Collect all Eden and Survivor regions. Evacuate survivors to new Survivor regions; promote old-enough objects to Old regions. This is purely stop-the-world but targets the MaxGCPauseMillis goal.

  2. Concurrent Marking (overlapping with young GCs):
    - Initial Mark (piggybacks on a young GC STW pause)
    - Concurrent Root Region Scanning
    - Concurrent Mark: Traces live objects concurrently
    - Remark (STW, but shorter than CMS remark)
    - Cleanup (STW, very short): Identifies completely empty regions for immediate reclamation

Mixed Phase:

  1. Mixed GC (STW evacuation): Collects all young regions PLUS selected old-generation regions (those with most garbage). Mixed GCs continue until old-generation occupancy drops below -XX:G1HeapWastePercent.

8.4 G1 Key Flags

-XX:+UseG1GC
-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200      # Pause time goal (default 200ms)
-XX:G1HeapRegionSize=<size>   # Override region size (1m-32m, power of 2)
-XX:G1NewSizePercent=5        # Min young generation size as % of heap (default 5)
-XX:G1MaxNewSizePercent=60    # Max young generation size as % of heap (default 60)
-XX:G1MixedGCLiveThresholdPercent=85  # Exclude regions with >85% live data from mixed GC
-XX:G1HeapWastePercent=5      # Stop mixed GCs when waste < 5% of heap
-XX:G1MixedGCCountTarget=8    # Target 8 mixed GCs per concurrent cycle
-XX:ConcGCThreads=4           # Concurrent marking thread count
-XX:InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent=45  # Start concurrent cycle at 45% heap occupancy

8.5 G1 Performance Characteristics

  • Throughput: 5–15% lower than Parallel GC (concurrent marking overhead, write barriers for remembered sets)
  • Latency: Predictable pauses targeting MaxGCPauseMillis (200ms default, achievable to 50ms)
  • Footprint: Higher than Parallel/Serial due to per-region remembered sets (~20–30% metadata overhead)
  • Best for: Server applications requiring predictable latency without ultra-low pause requirements

8.6 G1 Evacuation Failure

G1's failure mode: if survivor regions fill during evacuation (no region available to evacuate to), G1 falls back to in-place mark-compact, similar to CMS's concurrent mode failure. Triggered by:
- Sudden allocation spike
- Heap too full (not enough free regions for evacuation)
- Humongous allocation pressure

Symptom: GC log shows [GC (G1 Evacuation Pause) ... to-space exhausted]

Prevention: Keep old-gen occupancy well below InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent; increase heap if evacuation failures are frequent.

Part 9

Performance Analysis

Flags: -XX:+UseZGC
Stable since: Java 15 (experimental in Java 11)
Generational ZGC available: Java 21+ (strongly recommended)

ZGC is designed with a single non-negotiable goal: sub-millisecond GC pauses regardless of heap size. A JVM with a 1 TB heap should have the same pause duration as one with a 1 GB heap.

9.1 ZGC Architecture: Load Barriers and Colored Pointers

ZGC achieves concurrent object relocation through two novel mechanisms:

Colored Pointers: In ZGC, every 64-bit object reference uses some bits to store GC metadata:

64-bit reference:
[ 0000 | Finalizable | Remapped | Marked1 | Marked0 | 42-bit address ]

These metadata bits allow ZGC to track the state of each reference without a side table. When a thread loads a reference, it can immediately determine whether that reference needs updating.

Load Barriers: Every time the application reads a reference from the heap (an object field load), ZGC inserts a small code fragment — the load barrier — that checks the reference's metadata bits and fixes up the reference if needed.

// Application code:
Object obj = array[i];

// What JIT generates with ZGC:
Object tmp = array[i];
if (tmp.metadata_bits != expected_state) {
    tmp = ZGC_slow_path(tmp);  // Fix the reference
}
Object obj = tmp;

Load barriers are the most impactful overhead of ZGC — every heap reference read goes through the barrier. Modern CPUs predict the fast path (no fixup needed) and execute it in ~1 extra cycle, making average overhead ~5–10%.

9.2 ZGC Collection Phases

ZGC performs almost all work concurrently:

  1. Pause Mark Start (STW, ~1ms): Scan GC roots; mark them with Mark0/Mark1 bits.
  2. Concurrent Mark: Trace the entire object graph concurrently; load barrier redirects unvisited references.
  3. Pause Mark End (STW, ~1ms): Synchronization point; process reference queues.
  4. Concurrent Prepare for Relocation: Select relocation sets (regions to compact).
  5. Pause Relocate Start (STW, ~1ms): Scan roots again for relocation.
  6. Concurrent Relocate: Move live objects concurrently. Load barriers detect moved objects and forward references.
  7. Concurrent Remap: Update all references to relocated objects (can be deferred to next mark cycle).

Three stop-the-world pauses, each targeting < 1ms. The 1ms target is nearly independent of heap size because pauses only scan GC roots (proportional to thread count, not heap size).

9.3 Generational ZGC (Java 21+)

The original ZGC (Java 11–20) was non-generational: it treated the entire heap uniformly. This meant every collection scanned the entire heap, with throughput overhead proportional to total heap size.

Java 21 introduced Generational ZGC (-XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational). It adds:
- Separate young generation (minor) and old generation (major) cycles
- Young objects are collected much more frequently (like traditional generational GC)
- The weak generational hypothesis reduces overall collection work significantly

Result: Generational ZGC typically delivers 10–30% higher throughput than non-generational ZGC while maintaining the same < 1ms pause goal. For new deployments on Java 21+, always use Generational ZGC.

9.4 ZGC Performance Profile

  • Throughput: 5–20% lower than Parallel GC; comparable to G1 (Generational ZGC narrows the gap)
  • Latency: < 1ms pauses regardless of heap size. The headline capability.
  • Heap size: Scales to multi-terabyte heaps. The larger the heap, the more compelling ZGC becomes relative to G1.
  • Best for: Latency-sensitive applications: financial trading systems, gaming servers, ad bidding engines, real-time recommendation systems

9.5 ZGC Flags

-XX:+UseZGC
-XX:+ZGenerational           # Java 21+: enable generational mode (recommended)
-Xms<size> -Xmx<size>        # Set heap bounds (ZGC works best with static heap sizing)
-XX:ConcGCThreads=<n>        # Concurrent GC thread count (default: CPU-count-based)
-XX:ZCollectionInterval=<s>  # Force a collection every N seconds (for predictable behavior)
-XX:ZUncommitDelay=300       # Return uncommitted memory to OS after 300s idle
-Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log        # GC logging
Part 10

Time Complexity

Flags: -XX:+UseShenandoahGC
Available in: OpenJDK (all editions); absent from Oracle JDK
Stable since: Java 15

Shenandoah was developed by Red Hat and has a design goal similar to ZGC: sub-10ms pauses. Its approach to concurrent relocation differs from ZGC's.

10.1 Shenandoah Architecture: Brooks Pointers

Instead of colored pointers in references (ZGC's approach), Shenandoah uses Brooks pointers (forwarding pointers): every object has an extra word prepended to it that contains the object's canonical address.

Object memory layout with Shenandoah:
[ Forwarding Pointer | Header | Field 1 | Field 2 | ... ]
         ↑
         During relocation: points to new location
         Otherwise: points to self (identity)

When Shenandoah relocates an object, it updates the forwarding pointer to the new location. All accesses go through the forwarding pointer. This adds a one-word memory overhead per object but allows read and write barriers to be simpler than ZGC's colored pointer approach.

10.2 Shenandoah Collection Phases

  1. Initial Mark (STW, short): Mark GC roots.
  2. Concurrent Mark: Trace the heap concurrently.
  3. Final Mark (STW, short): Drain remaining mark queues.
  4. Concurrent Cleanup: Reclaim empty regions immediately.
  5. Concurrent Evacuation: Copy live objects from selected regions to free regions. This is concurrent with the application.
  6. Init Update References (STW, very short): Ensure all threads see the current state.
  7. Concurrent Update References: Walk the heap updating all references from old to new locations.
  8. Final Update References (STW, short): Update GC roots.
  9. Concurrent Cleanup: Reclaim old regions.

10.3 Shenandoah vs ZGC

Aspect Shenandoah ZGC
Pointer metadata Brooks forwarding pointers Colored pointer bits
Object overhead 1 extra word per object No per-object overhead
Barrier type Read + write barriers Load barrier only
Pause target < 10ms < 1ms
Heap support Up to ~1 TB Designed for very large heaps
Generational Shenandoah 2.0 (experimental) Java 21 generational mode
Oracle JDK Not included Included
Best for Red Hat/OpenJDK users needing low latency Ultra-low latency, large heaps

10.4 Shenandoah Modes

Shenandoah offers three heuristic modes:

  • Adaptive (default): Dynamically adjusts collection frequency based on heap occupancy and allocation rate
  • Compact: Aggressive collection; low footprint but higher CPU overhead
  • Aggressive: Continuous concurrent cycles; for extremely latency-sensitive workloads at the cost of high CPU usage
-XX:ShenandoahGCHeuristics=adaptive    # Default
-XX:ShenandoahGCHeuristics=compact     # Lower memory, higher CPU
-XX:ShenandoahGCHeuristics=aggressive  # Minimum latency at all costs
Part 11

Throughput vs Latency: The Core Trade-off

Understanding the GC trade-off qualitatively is insufficient for production decisions. You need quantitative intuition.

11.1 Throughput Definition

GC throughput = fraction of time spent on application work:

Throughput = (Total time - GC pause time) / Total time

Example:
- Application runs 60 seconds
- Total GC pause time: 3 seconds (1 Young + 1 Mixed/Full)
- Throughput = (60 - 3) / 60 = 95%

High-throughput collectors (Parallel GC) minimize total GC time by doing all work in batch STW pauses, amortizing GC overhead over larger allocations.

11.2 Latency Definition

In GC context, latency = maximum (or 99th percentile) pause duration experienced by any application thread.

A collector with 99% throughput but 2-second full GC pauses is unacceptable for an API that requires 99.9th percentile response time < 100ms. Latency and throughput are not directly correlated.

11.3 Pause Time Breakdown by Collector

For a 4 GB heap with 60% live data and moderate allocation rate:

Collector Young GC Pause Old/Mixed GC Pause Full GC Pause Throughput
Serial 50–200ms N/A 5–15s ~99%
Parallel 20–80ms N/A 1–8s ~99.5%
CMS 20–50ms (ParNew) ~50ms (remark) 5–20s (CMF) ~97%
G1 (default 200ms target) 20–150ms 50–200ms 1–5s (evac fail) ~96%
ZGC < 1ms < 1ms < 1ms ~92–95%
Shenandoah 2–10ms 2–10ms 2–10ms ~90–95%

Note: Full GC is a failure mode for CMS and G1 (should be rare with proper tuning).

Part 12

Collector Selection Matrix

Use this framework to select a collector for any given workload.

12.1 Decision Tree

Start here:
│
├─ Is the heap < 512 MB?
│   └─ YES → Serial GC (minimal overhead, pauses short for small heaps)
│
├─ Is your workload batch/offline (run-to-completion, total time matters)?
│   └─ YES → Parallel GC (maximum throughput)
│
├─ Are you on Java 21+?
│   └─ YES → Generational ZGC for latency, G1 for balanced, Parallel for throughput
│
├─ Do you require < 1ms pauses?
│   └─ YES → ZGC (Java 15+), Generational ZGC (Java 21+)
│
├─ Do you require < 10ms pauses with good throughput?
│   └─ YES → G1 with MaxGCPauseMillis=50-100ms, or Shenandoah
│
├─ Is your heap > 16 GB?
│   └─ YES → G1 or ZGC (Parallel GC pauses become multi-second)
│
└─ Default: G1 (best all-around, default since Java 9)

12.2 Workload Profiles and Recommended Collectors

Workload Recommended Collector Key Flags
Batch ETL, data processing Parallel GC -XX:GCTimeRatio=19
REST API (< 100ms SLA) G1 -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=50
REST API (< 10ms SLA) ZGC (Java 21) -XX:+ZGenerational
Financial trading (< 1ms) ZGC -XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational
Large JVM (> 32 GB heap) ZGC or G1 Depends on latency req.
Containerized microservice G1 or ZGC With MaxMetaspaceSize set
Application server (Tomcat) G1 Default is fine
Memory-constrained IoT/edge Serial Minimal overhead
Interactive desktop app G1 or ZGC Short pauses prevent UI jank

12.3 Anti-Patterns

Anti-pattern 1: Using CMS in new projects
CMS is removed in Java 14. Any new development should use G1 or ZGC.

Anti-pattern 2: Using Parallel GC for latency-sensitive services
Parallel GC's full GC pauses can be multi-second on large heaps. A 2-second full GC will violate every sub-100ms SLA.

Anti-pattern 3: Setting MaxGCPauseMillis too aggressively with G1
Setting -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=10 with G1 forces it to use tiny young generation sizes, causing extremely frequent young GCs and reducing throughput dramatically without achieving ZGC-level latency.

Anti-pattern 4: Not setting MaxMetaspaceSize with any collector
Metaspace leaks manifest as process OOM with all collectors. Always set this.

Anti-pattern 5: Mixing collector flags from different collectors
Some flags only apply to specific collectors. Mixing -XX:+UseConcMarkSweepGC with G1 flags or ZGC flags has no effect or causes errors.

Part 13

Safepoints: The Hidden Latency Factor

All JVM garbage collectors (even ZGC) require application threads to pause at safepoints — consistent states where all thread stacks and CPU registers can be examined by the GC.

13.1 What Is a Safepoint?

A safepoint is a point in a thread's execution where the thread's JVM state is fully known and can be inspected/modified. The JVM periodically inserts safepoint polls into compiled code:
- Back edges of loops (JIT-emitted polls)
- Method calls
- Thread state transitions (JNI entry/exit)

When the JVM needs all threads at safepoints (for STW GC), it sets a global flag. Each thread checks this flag at the next safepoint poll and suspends. The GC begins when all threads have reached safepoints.

13.2 Time-to-Safepoint

If a thread is executing compiled code with a tight loop that runs for 50ms between safepoint polls, the entire JVM stops for the GC only after that thread hits its next safepoint. This creates time-to-safepoint (TTSP) latency — the delay between the JVM requesting a pause and all threads being paused.

In the worst case, a buggy tight loop without safepoint polls can delay GC indefinitely, causing memory exhaustion.

Force safepoint polls in long-running loops with -XX:+UseCountedLoopSafepoints (Java 16+) or by adding explicit safepoint operations.

13.3 Safepoint and GC Pause Measurement

The "GC pause" reported in GC logs includes TTSP. A 5ms GC pause might consist of:
- 3ms waiting for all threads to reach safepoints
- 2ms of actual GC work

For precise latency tuning, -Xlog:safepoint reveals TTSP separately from GC work time.

Part 14

Write Barriers in Detail

Every generational and concurrent collector uses write barriers — code injected at every reference assignment. The barrier's cost is paid by the application, not GC threads.

14.1 Post-Write Barrier (Generational)

// Application code:
object.field = ref;

// With G1 write barrier:
object.field = ref;
if (ref != null && in_old_gen(object) && in_young_gen(ref)) {
    mark_card_dirty(object);  // Log this cross-generational reference
}

G1's write barrier uses a two-phase approach (pre-write SATB barrier + post-write card mark) to support both generational and concurrent marking.

14.2 SATB Barrier (Snapshot-At-The-Beginning)

G1 and Shenandoah use SATB barriers for concurrent marking correctness. When the application overwrites a reference during concurrent marking, the old reference value is logged to ensure it gets scanned:

// Object graph before concurrent mark:
A → B → C

// Application code during concurrent marking:
A.ref = D;  // Overwrites reference to B

// Without SATB: B might not be marked (marking follows A's current refs)
// With SATB: Old value (B) is logged; marker scans B even though A no longer points to it

SATB barriers add cost to reference writes. This is part of why ZGC and G1 have lower throughput than Parallel GC.

Part 15

Microservice Usage

Every production JVM should log GC activity. Understanding the log format is essential for diagnosing GC problems.

15.1 Enabling Unified GC Logging (Java 9+)

-Xlog:gc*:file=/var/log/app/gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags:filecount=10,filesize=50m

This rotates GC logs into 10 files of 50 MB each, preserving history for post-incident analysis.

15.2 Reading G1 GC Logs

[0.540s][info][gc] GC(3) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 256M->45M(512M) 12.345ms
         ↑         ↑     ↑                    ↑                      ↑    ↑     ↑     ↑
         time      GC#   pause type           reason                 before->after (heap) duration

Key patterns to watch:
- Pause Young (Normal): Routine young GC — should be below MaxGCPauseMillis
- Pause Young (Concurrent Start): Young GC that initiates concurrent marking
- Pause Remark: Concurrent marking remark phase
- Pause Cleanup: Short cleanup after concurrent marking
- Pause Mixed: Mixed GC collecting young + old regions
- Pause Full (Allocation Failure): Emergency full GC — investigate if frequent

15.3 Key Metrics from GC Logs

Metric How to Measure Alert When
Young GC pause Duration of Pause Young events > MaxGCPauseMillis
Full GC frequency Count of Pause Full events > 1 per hour
Full GC pause Duration of Pause Full events > 1s
Heap utilization After-GC heap size / max heap > 85% consistently
GC overhead Sum(pause durations) / total uptime > 5%
Promotion rate Old gen growth between young GCs Rapidly growing
Part 16

Allocation Rate and GC Interaction

The single biggest driver of GC frequency is allocation rate — how fast the application creates new objects.

16.1 Measuring Allocation Rate

# Using JVM flags:
-Xlog:gc+heap=debug   # Logs heap size before/after each GC

# Allocation rate ≈ (heap before GC - heap after GC) / time between GCs

# Using JFR:
jcmd <pid> JFR.start duration=60s filename=app.jfr
jfr print --events jdk.ObjectAllocationInNewTLAB app.jfr

16.2 Thread-Local Allocation Buffers (TLABs)

Each thread gets a private chunk of Eden called a TLAB (Thread-Local Allocation Buffer). Object allocation in a TLAB is a simple pointer increment with no synchronization. When a TLAB is exhausted, the thread requests a new one from the global Eden space (requires synchronization).

TLABs are why Java object allocation is extremely fast (comparable to C++ stack allocation in the common case) but becomes expensive when TLABs are exhausted frequently (indicating very high allocation rate).

16.3 Allocation Pressure and GC Tuning

High allocation rate → frequent young GC → high promotion rate → frequent old GC → high full GC risk.

The correct fix for allocation-driven GC pressure is usually:
1. Reduce allocation rate (profile with JFR, reduce object creation in hot paths)
2. Increase young generation size (reduces GC frequency, increases pause per GC)
3. Optimize TLAB sizing (-XX:TLABSize)

Object pooling, value types (Java project Valhalla), and off-heap storage can eliminate allocation pressure in extreme cases.

Part 17

JFR and GC Introspection

Java Flight Recorder provides the most detailed GC introspection available without application modification.

# Record for 2 minutes
jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=gc-analysis duration=120s filename=/tmp/gc.jfr settings=profile

# Analyze with JFR CLI
jfr print --events jdk.GCHeapSummary,jdk.GarbageCollection,jdk.GCPauseL90 /tmp/gc.jfr

JFR events of interest:
- jdk.GarbageCollection: Every GC event with duration, cause, and type
- jdk.GCHeapSummary: Heap state before and after each GC
- jdk.YoungGarbageCollection / jdk.OldGarbageCollection: Generation-specific events
- jdk.ObjectAllocationInNewTLAB: High-rate allocation events (sampled)
- jdk.ObjectAllocationOutsideTLAB: Large-object allocations (non-sampled)
- jdk.PromoteObjectInNewPLAB: Object promotion events

JDK Mission Control (JMC) provides a GUI for JFR analysis with automated GC analysis reports.

Part 18

The Epsilon Collector (No-Op GC)

Flags: -XX:+UseEpsilonGC
Purpose: Testing and benchmarking only

Epsilon GC is a "no-op" collector: it allocates memory but never collects. When the heap is full, the JVM terminates with OOM.

Use cases:
- Performance testing: Eliminate GC noise from benchmarks to measure pure allocation performance
- Ultra-short-lived applications: A lambda function that completes in 100ms and uses 50 MB will never need GC
- Testing OOM handling: Deliberately trigger OOM to test application error handling

Never use Epsilon GC for production workloads unless the application guarantees it will finish before the heap fills.

Part 19

Future: Value Types and GC

Java's Project Valhalla introduces value types — objects without object identity that the JVM can store inline (no heap allocation). When value types are fully available, many small "data carrier" objects (coordinates, money amounts, pairs) can be stored on the stack or inlined in arrays, eliminating GC pressure entirely for those use cases.

Java 23+ preview features include preliminary value type support. This is the most significant future change to GC behavior in Java's history.

Part 20

GC Algorithm Internals: Tri-Color Marking

All concurrent collectors use the tri-color marking abstraction to reason about concurrent marking correctness.

Objects are classified into three colors:
- White: Not yet visited by the marker — either live (not reached yet) or garbage
- Gray: Reachable, but some references not yet scanned
- Black: Reachable, all references scanned

Invariant: No black object may directly reference a white object (would miss the white object as live).

The application, running concurrently, can violate this invariant by:
1. Storing a reference from a black object to a white object, AND
2. Destroying all paths from gray objects to that white object

Both conditions must hold simultaneously for a live object to be incorrectly collected. Collectors prevent this via:
- SATB (Snapshot-At-The-Beginning): Log old reference value before overwrite (G1, Shenandoah). Preserves condition 2.
- Incremental Update: Log new reference value after store (CMS). Prevents condition 1.
- Load barriers: Redirect reads through the marker's check (ZGC). Prevents reads of stale references.

Part 21

Performance Benchmarking GC

Properly benchmarking GC behavior requires careful methodology.

21.1 JMH for GC Benchmarks

@BenchmarkMode(Mode.Throughput)
@Warmup(iterations = 5, time = 1)
@Measurement(iterations = 10, time = 2)
@Fork(value = 1, jvmArgs = {"-Xmx1g", "-XX:+UseG1GC", "-Xlog:gc"})
@State(Scope.Thread)
public class GCBenchmark {

    @Benchmark
    public Object allocateSmall() {
        return new byte[256];  // Small allocation
    }

    @Benchmark
    public Object allocateLarge() {
        return new byte[1024 * 1024];  // 1MB humongous allocation
    }
}

21.2 Eliminating Confounders

  • Always run benchmarks with JIT warm-up (JMH handles this)
  • Use fixed heap sizes (-Xms == -Xmx) to eliminate heap resizing effects
  • Measure with GC logging enabled to correlate throughput drops with GC events
  • Run multiple JVM restarts and report variance

21.3 GC Benchmarking Tooling

  • SPECjvm2008: Industry standard; includes GC-heavy workloads
  • Dacapo benchmark suite: Real-application-derived benchmarks including Eclipse, H2, Tomcat
  • JITWatch: Visualizes JIT compilation and GC interactions from JFR recordings
Part 22

Summary and Key Takeaways

Garbage collection algorithms represent decades of research and engineering trade-offs. The practical knowledge to carry into production:

Fundamental Strategies: Mark-sweep (fragmentation), mark-compact (moves objects, eliminates fragmentation), copying (fast allocation, best for short-lived objects). Modern collectors combine all three.

Generational Hypothesis: Most objects die young. All major collectors exploit this to focus collection effort where it has the most impact.

Collector Profiles:
- Serial: Single-threaded, simplest, lowest overhead, only for small heaps or batch
- Parallel: Multi-threaded STW, highest throughput, for compute-bound workloads
- CMS: Deprecated. Concurrent old-gen, fragmentation problems. Use G1 instead.
- G1: Region-based, predictable pauses (targeting 200ms by default), balanced all-around choice
- ZGC: Sub-millisecond pauses at any heap size, Generational ZGC (Java 21) for better throughput
- Shenandoah: Sub-10ms pauses, Red Hat distribution, Brooks pointer forwarding

Selection Rule of Thumb: Parallel for batch, G1 for services (SLA > 50ms), ZGC for latency-critical services (SLA < 10ms).

Safepoints: Hidden latency source. TTSP can add milliseconds to nominally short GC pauses.

Allocation rate is primary: The biggest lever for GC performance is reducing allocation rate, not tuning collector flags.

Practice — Lesson 64

Easy Exercises

Conceptual Questions

  1. Explain why mark-compact requires all application threads to stop while mark-sweep does not. What property of compaction makes concurrent execution impossible without additional mechanisms?

  2. A G1 GC log shows frequent Pause Full (Allocation Failure) events. List three distinct root causes that could produce this symptom and describe how you would distinguish between them using available JVM tooling.

  3. ZGC achieves < 1ms pauses on a 1 TB heap. Explain how this is possible given that marking 1 TB of live data takes minutes. What specifically happens during the stop-the-world phases?

  4. Describe the Floating Garbage problem in CMS. Does G1's concurrent marking have the same problem? Does ZGC? Explain the mechanism each uses.

  5. An engineer proposes solving high GC overhead by switching from G1 to Parallel GC. Under what specific conditions would this be correct advice, and under what conditions would it be harmful?

  6. Explain the tri-color marking invariant. Give a concrete scenario (object graph + application mutation) where violating this invariant would cause a live object to be incorrectly collected.

Hands-On Exercises

Exercise 1: Collector Comparison
Write a Java application that allocates 10M short-lived objects per second (use JMH) and measures throughput and 99th-percentile latency. Run with Parallel GC, G1, and ZGC. Plot the trade-off and identify the crossover point where ZGC's throughput disadvantage is outweighed by its latency advantage.

Exercise 2: GC Log Analysis
Start a Spring Boot application with -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,uptime. Drive 1000 concurrent requests for 2 minutes. Parse the GC log to extract: average young GC pause, maximum pause, GC frequency, and total GC overhead percentage.

Exercise 3: Humongous Allocation Investigation
Write code that repeatedly allocates 512KB byte arrays with a 2GB G1 heap (G1 will classify these as humongous with default region sizes). Enable -Xlog:gc+humongous=debug. Observe the impact on GC behavior. Then adjust -XX:G1HeapRegionSize=2m so the allocation is no longer humongous and compare GC behavior.

Exercise 4: Allocation Rate Measurement
Use JFR to record ObjectAllocationInNewTLAB events in a running application for 60 seconds. Calculate the total allocation rate in MB/s. Compare this to the young GC frequency and verify that (allocation rate × time between GCs) ≈ Eden size.

Exercise 5: Safepoint Latency
Write a benchmark that has a tight long-running loop without natural safepoint polls. Measure TTSP by enabling -Xlog:safepoint. Then add a safepoint poll (Thread.sleep(0) or a volatile read) and observe TTSP reduction.
