Throughput comparison methodology

// JMH benchmark: object creation + traversal (allocation-heavy workload)
// -XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational -Xmx2g -XX:ConcGCThreads=4

@Benchmark
public long allocateAndTraverse() {
    List<byte[]> list = new ArrayList<>(1000);
    for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) {
        list.add(new byte[1024]);  // 1 KB each = 1 MB total
    }
    return list.stream().mapToLong(b -> b.length).sum();
}

// Results (ops/sec):
//   G1GC: 180,000 ops/sec (pause spikes visible in P99)
//   ZGC:  165,000 ops/sec (8% lower throughput, flat P99)
Part 18

Common ZGC Mistakes and Anti-Patterns

Anti-pattern 1: Using ZGC on Java 11–14

# Java 11-14: ZGC is experimental and non-generational
# -XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions -XX:+UseZGC

# Issues in early versions:
#   - Higher throughput overhead (no generational collection)
#   - Longer concurrent mark phases (all live objects scanned every cycle)
#   - Concurrent stack scanning not yet implemented (larger Pause Mark End)

# Fix: upgrade to Java 21 for Generational ZGC

Anti-pattern 2: Insufficient heap headroom

# Problem:
-Xmx4g  # with 3.5 GB live data
# ZGC needs concurrent headroom (space to copy objects into while old pages are live)
# With 500 MB free, concurrent relocation stalls → allocation stalls

# Fix: ZGC needs 2–4x live data headroom
# 3.5 GB live data → -Xmx10g minimum (ideally -Xmx14g)

Anti-pattern 3: Too few concurrent GC threads in high-core containers

# Container: 32 CPUs, high allocation rate
# Default ConcGCThreads = 32/8 = 4
# Problem: 4 GC threads can't keep pace → allocation stalls

# Fix:
-XX:ConcGCThreads=8  # or 12 for very high allocation rates
# Rule: 1 ConcGCThread per ~4 CPU cores is a starting point

Anti-pattern 4: Setting MaxGCPauseMillis with ZGC

# Doesn't apply — ZGC doesn't use this flag
-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=100  # ZGC ignores this; pauses are already sub-ms

# The correct knob is SoftMaxHeapSize (controls GC frequency to stay under target)
-XX:SoftMaxHeapSize=6g  # ZGC will GC more aggressively to stay under 6g

Anti-pattern 5: Expecting ZGC to work well with very small heaps

# Problem: -Xmx512m with ZGC
# ZGC overhead (colored pointers, load barriers, concurrent threads)
# is a fixed cost that doesn't scale down for tiny heaps

# On a 512 MB heap:
#   G1GC is often faster and lower-overhead
#   ZGC's 3 virtual memory mappings waste address space
#   Concurrent GC thread overhead is proportionally larger

# Fix: ZGC is optimal for heaps >= 1 GB; use G1GC for smaller heaps
Part 19

ZGC and Non-Standard Reference Types

Weak, Soft, and Phantom references in ZGC

Reference types interact with ZGC's concurrent cycle:

// WeakReference behavior with ZGC:
WeakReference<MyObject> ref = new WeakReference<>(new MyObject());

// ZGC concurrent mark: MyObject is not strongly reachable
// → WeakReference is enqueued during "Concurrent Process References" phase
// → reference.get() returns null after this phase completes
// This is entirely concurrent — no STW for reference processing

ReferenceQueue and ZGC

ReferenceQueue<MyObject> queue = new ReferenceQueue<>();
WeakReference<MyObject> ref = new WeakReference<>(obj, queue);

// ZGC enqueues cleared references during Concurrent Process References phase
// Application can drain the queue asynchronously:
Reference<?> cleared;
while ((cleared = queue.poll()) != null) {
    cleanupResources(cleared);
}

Soft reference clearing policy

ZGC's soft reference clearing policy:

# ZGC clears soft references when heap usage exceeds SoftMaxHeapSize
# or when heap is under pressure (approaching Xmx)

# Control soft reference age before clearing:
-XX:SoftRefLRUPolicyMSPerMB=50  # default: 50ms per MB of free heap
# High value → keep soft refs longer (lower GC reclaim, more memory held)
# Low value (0) → clear soft refs aggressively whenever heap grows
Part 20

ZGC Startup and Warmup Behavior

JIT compilation and ZGC load barriers

ZGC load barriers are JIT-compiled like application code. During JVM startup (before JIT compilation), barriers run in interpreted mode — which is slower:

Application startup with ZGC:
  0–5s:    Bytecode interpreter + C1 JIT compiling hot paths
           Load barriers: interpreted (~50ns each)
  5–30s:   C2 JIT compiling fully hot methods
           Load barriers: C1-compiled (~15ns each)
  30s+:    All hot paths C2-compiled
           Load barriers: C2-compiled (~3ns each, often branch-predicted away)

Implication: ZGC application may run slower during warmup due to
unoptimized load barriers. Performance profiling should begin after warmup.

AOT and ZGC (Java 21+)

Java 21 introduced GraalVM Native Image support, but native image and ZGC are separate concerns. For JVM-mode ZGC:

# Class Data Sharing speeds up startup (works with ZGC):
java -Xshare:dump -XX:+UseZGC ...    # create CDS archive
java -Xshare:on -XX:+UseZGC ...      # use CDS archive

# CDS reduces startup time by pre-loading shared class metadata
# Compatible with ZGC in Java 15+
Part 21

ZGC Roadmap and Future Directions

What's changed across Java versions

Java 11: ZGC introduced (experimental), Linux x64 only
Java 13: Support for macOS
Java 14: Support for Windows
Java 15: Production-ready, no unlock flags needed
Java 16: Concurrent stack scanning (sub-0.3ms Pause Mark End)
         Concurrent class unloading
Java 17: NUMA-aware page allocation improvements
Java 21: Generational ZGC (-XX:+ZGenerational)
         Old and Young generation with separate collection cycles
Java 23: Non-generational ZGC removed; Generational ZGC is the only mode

Current research areas (post Java 21)

  1. Compressed references with ZGC — ZGC currently cannot use 32-bit compressed oops (because colored pointers need the extra bits). Research ongoing to reconcile these; enabling compressed oops would reduce heap overhead and improve cache efficiency.

  2. Reduced load barrier overhead — Research into hardware-assisted barrier mechanisms to further reduce per-load overhead.

  3. ZGC for GraalVM — Port ZGC to GraalVM CE and Enterprise.

Practice — Lesson 66

Easy

  1. Enable ZGC on any Java 21 application and print GC statistics every 5 seconds using jstat. Record the pause times from GC logs and verify all three STW pauses are under 1ms.

  2. Write the minimal JVM flags needed to run a Spring Boot app with Generational ZGC on a container with 4 GB memory limit, logging GC output to /tmp/zgc.log.

  3. What does the -XX:SoftMaxHeapSize flag do in ZGC? How is it different from -Xmx? Write an example configuration where Xmx=8g and SoftMaxHeapSize=6g and explain when each limit matters.

Medium

  1. Colored pointer dissection: Explain what "colored pointers" are in ZGC. Draw a 64-bit pointer diagram showing which bits store the object address, which store GC color metadata, and explain what each color bit means.

  2. Load barrier simulation: Write pseudocode (not Java) for a ZGC load barrier that handles the case where a reference's Remap bit is not set. Include the forwarding table lookup and the self-healing store step.

  3. Phase timing analysis: Given the following ZGC GC log snippet, identify each phase, classify it as STW or concurrent, and calculate the total wall time vs the total STW time:
    Pause Mark Start: 0.023ms Concurrent Mark: 31.445ms Pause Mark End: 0.017ms Concurrent Process References: 4.123ms Concurrent Select Relocation Set: 0.312ms Pause Relocate Start: 0.021ms Concurrent Relocate: 28.834ms

Advanced

  1. Throughput vs latency trade-off: A trading system currently runs with G1GC at -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=50 and achieves 95% throughput vs Parallel GC but has P99 pauses of 45ms. Migrating to ZGC reduces P99 pauses to 0.8ms but throughput drops to 89% vs Parallel GC.

The system processes 100,000 orders/second. A 45ms G1 pause drops ~4,500 orders to the retry queue per pause event. Pauses occur ~3 times per minute. Calculate the orders affected per hour under each scenario and determine whether ZGC's throughput cost pays off.

  1. ConcGCThreads sizing: An 8-node Kubernetes cluster runs a ZGC application with 16 GB heap per pod, 32 CPUs per pod, and a sustained 5 GB/s allocation rate. The default ConcGCThreads is 4. The GC log shows frequent "Allocation Stall" events averaging 3ms. Calculate an appropriate ConcGCThreads value and explain your reasoning.

  2. Generational ZGC internals: Explain the difference between Minor and Major GC cycles in Generational ZGC. Why does a store barrier need to be added (in addition to the load barrier) when generational support is introduced? What cross-generational reference problem does it solve?

Production

  1. Migration plan: Your team runs a high-traffic REST API on Java 17 with G1GC, 8 GB heap, P99 latency of 180ms (mostly GC-driven). Write a migration plan to ZGC including:

    • JVM flag changes (before vs after)
    • Metrics to capture before and after migration
    • Canary deployment strategy
    • Rollback criteria (which metrics would trigger rollback to G1GC?)

  2. Kubernetes resource tuning: Design a Kubernetes deployment spec for a ZGC-based service. The service handles burst traffic of 50k req/s with 4 GB live data at peak. Include memory requests/limits, CPU requests/limits, JVM flags with reasoning, readiness probe timeouts, and JVM heap sizing rationale.

  3. Monitoring and alerting: Define a Prometheus alerting rule that fires when a ZGC application shows signs of allocation pressure. Include rules for:

    • Allocation stall rate (stalls per minute)
    • Heap usage consistently above SoftMaxHeapSize
    • GC cycle frequency anomaly (more than 2× baseline frequency)

    Use JMX Exporter metric names as they would appear in Prometheus.

Debugging

  1. Allocation stall hunt: A production service shows this in GC logs every few minutes:
    [gc] Allocation stall: Thread "http-nio-8080-exec-12" 8.234ms [gc] Allocation stall: Thread "http-nio-8080-exec-7" 7.891ms
    The current config: -XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational -Xmx6g -XX:ConcGCThreads=2 -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75
    The container has 8 GB memory limit and 8 CPUs. Diagnose and fix.

  2. Memory growth investigation: A ZGC application's heap usage after GC (the live data size visible in GC logs) grows steadily from 2 GB to 5 GB over 8 hours. Xmx is 8 GB. No allocation stalls are occurring. Is this a ZGC problem? What is the most likely root cause? What tool would you use to diagnose it?

  3. Pauses larger than expected: After deploying on Java 17 (pre-concurrent-stack-scanning... wait, that was Java 16). A service on Java 15 shows Pause Mark End times of 4–12ms. The service has 500 request-handling threads. The operator upgrades to Java 17 and the Pause Mark End drops to 0.15ms. Explain exactly why this happened and what Java 16 change caused it.

Interview

  1. Conceptual: Explain colored pointers and why they are the key enabler of ZGC's sub-millisecond pause times. Why couldn't G1GC use the same approach?

    Expected answer: Colored pointers encode GC state (marking, relocation phase) in the unused high bits of 64-bit object references. When ZGC relocates an object, it doesn't need to stop all threads to update every reference — instead, the load barrier checks the color bits on every reference load. If the bits indicate the reference is stale (from an older relocation), the barrier self-heals it by looking up the forwarding table. G1GC cannot use this approach because G1's evacuation happens entirely in a STW pause — there is no concurrent relocation phase, so there's no need (or mechanism) for self-healing load barriers. Implementing colored pointers in G1 would require changing G1's fundamental evacuation model, essentially making it ZGC.

  2. Tradeoff: A senior architect asks: "If ZGC achieves sub-millisecond pauses and only 5% throughput overhead, why wouldn't we just use it everywhere?" Give three specific scenarios where G1GC or Parallel GC is the better choice and defend your answer.

    Expected answer: (1) Small heaps (< 1 GB): ZGC's load barrier overhead and concurrent thread cost is a higher proportion of total work on small heaps; G1 or even Serial GC has lower fixed overhead. (2) Pure batch processing: If the application is a nightly data pipeline that can tolerate 10-second pauses, Parallel GC's maximum throughput (10–15% better than ZGC) means the job finishes faster. The pauses don't matter if no user is waiting. (3) Java < 15: ZGC is experimental/incomplete on Java 11–14; production applications should use G1GC until upgrading to Java 15+. Additional valid answer: String deduplication workloads — G1GC supports -XX:+UseStringDeduplication which can reduce heap 15–25% for REST/JSON services; ZGC doesn't support this feature.

  3. Incident response: In a post-mortem, a junior developer reports: "We had a 200ms spike in response time at 3 AM. GC logs show a ZGC cycle ran during that period. ZGC must have caused the spike." How do you evaluate this claim?

    Expected answer: The claim is suspicious for several reasons: ZGC STW pauses are sub-millisecond — a single ZGC GC cycle cannot cause a 200ms spike via its pauses. The concurrent phases (marking, relocation) run for tens of milliseconds but don't stop the application. Possible actual causes: (1) A ZGC allocation stall — the application thread blocked waiting for GC to reclaim memory. This can cause multi-millisecond delays but rarely 200ms. (2) The GC cycle is correlational not causal — heap pressure spiked due to a traffic burst, GC ran to reclaim memory, and the traffic burst simultaneously caused high latency from CPU contention. (3) Non-GC cause: database slow query, downstream service timeout, or scheduled job running at 3 AM. Investigation: check GC log for "Allocation Stall" events near 3 AM, check CPU/memory metrics for that period, check application request logs for which requests were slow, and look at external dependency latency.

Part 1

Origins: Why Red Hat Built a Third Low-Pause Collector

In 2011, Red Hat engineers faced a recurring problem: large Java applications running on multi-gigabyte heaps in production environments suffered from GC pauses that violated SLAs. CMS was fragile and deprecated. G1GC was new and still had pause times in the hundreds of milliseconds for large heaps.

The fundamental insight driving Shenandoah's design: the core problem isn't marking — it's relocation. Both CMS and G1GC perform concurrent marking, which eliminates most of the old STW pause time. But both still require STW evacuation to move live objects (compaction). On a large heap, evacuating a significant amount of live data can take tens to hundreds of milliseconds.

Red Hat's answer: make compaction concurrent too. If objects can be moved while the application is running, the remaining STW pauses shrink to just root scanning — a nearly constant-time operation regardless of heap size.

Shenandoah GC was the result. It was developed at Red Hat, contributed to OpenJDK, and became available as:
- Experimental in OpenJDK 12
- Production-ready in OpenJDK 15
- Backported to OpenJDK 8 and 11 by Red Hat (via builds like Amazon Corretto, Adoptium)

Shenandoah's design philosophy differs from ZGC's in one key way: Shenandoah chose a software indirection pointer (Brooks pointer) over colored pointers. This decision shapes everything from its implementation complexity to its performance characteristics.

Part 2

The Brooks Pointer: Shenandoah's Core Mechanism

ZGC uses colored pointer bits and virtual memory multi-mapping to implement concurrent relocation. Shenandoah uses a completely different approach: the Brooks pointer (named after Rodney Brooks, who proposed the concept in 1984).

What a Brooks pointer is

Every Java object in Shenandoah's heap has an extra forwarding word prepended to its normal object header. This is the Brooks pointer:

Normal object layout (G1, ZGC, Parallel GC):
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Mark Word (8 bytes) │ Class Pointer (4-8 bytes) │ Field data ... │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Shenandoah object layout:
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Forwarding Word (8 bytes) │ Mark Word (8 bytes) │ Class Ptr │ Fields ... │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
       ↑
       Brooks pointer — initially points to the object itself (self-referential)

When an object is NOT being relocated, the Brooks pointer points to the object itself. When the object IS relocated (copied to a new address), the Brooks pointer in the original copy is updated to point to the new copy.

Before relocation:
  Old location (0x1000): [fwd→0x1000] [mark] [class] [field1] [field2]
                           (points to self)

After relocation (copied to 0x9000):
  Old location (0x1000): [fwd→0x9000] [mark] [class] [field1] [field2]
                            (now points to new copy)
  New location (0x9000): [fwd→0x9000] [mark] [class] [field1] [field2]
                            (still points to self)

How the Brooks pointer enables concurrent compaction

When a thread follows a reference to an object at address 0x1000, it must first dereference the Brooks pointer before accessing any field. If the object has been relocated, this indirection transparently redirects to the new copy:

Thread accesses object.someField:
  1. Load reference: ptr = 0x1000
  2. Dereference Brooks pointer: actual = ptr.fwdWord  (0x1000 or new addr)
  3. Access field: value = actual.someField

If the object was moved (Brooks pointer ≠ self), the thread reads from the new location transparently. It also self-heals by updating the reference to skip the indirection in the future.

Memory overhead of Brooks pointers

Every object in the Shenandoah heap carries an extra 8-byte word:

Overhead example:
  10 million objects × 8 bytes = 80 MB overhead
  For a 4 GB heap with average object size 64 bytes:
    62.5 million objects × 8 bytes = ~500 MB (12.5% overhead)

This is Shenandoah's most significant trade-off vs ZGC:
  ZGC: overhead is in pointer bits (no per-object memory cost)
  Shenandoah: 8 bytes per object, always
Part 3

Shenandoah's Read and Write Barriers

Because objects are indirected through Brooks pointers, every object access in Shenandoah-compiled code goes through barriers.

Load reference barrier (read barrier)

Every load of an object reference must dereference the Brooks pointer of the loaded object:

// Application code:
Object obj = container.field;     // load reference
Object value = obj.someField;     // access field on loaded object

// JIT with Shenandoah barriers:
Object obj = container.field;     // raw load
obj = obj.fwdWord;                // dereference Brooks pointer (load barrier)
Object value = obj.someField;     // now access field via correct (possibly new) location

Write barrier (store barrier)

Shenandoah also needs a store barrier to handle write operations to objects that are being concurrently evacuated:

// Application code:
obj.field = newValue;

// JIT with Shenandoah store barrier:
Object target = obj.fwdWord;      // resolve current location via Brooks ptr
target.field = newValue;          // write to the correct (new) location
// Also: if target is in from-space, SATB pre-write barrier captures old value

SATB write barrier for marking

During concurrent marking, Shenandoah uses an SATB (Snapshot-At-The-Beginning) write barrier identical in concept to G1GC's. When a reference is overwritten, the old value is saved to an SATB queue to ensure the marking cycle doesn't miss live objects:

// Concurrent marking + application write:
obj.ref = newValue;  // before write: save obj.ref to SATB queue if marking active

Barrier overhead comparison

Barrier overhead (tight traversal loop, JMH benchmark):

ZGC:         Load barrier only (~3ns per reference load in C2)
Shenandoah:  Load barrier + potential store barrier
             Load barrier: dereference fwdWord (~4–6ns per reference load)
             Store barrier: SATB capture during marking only

Real-world throughput overhead vs Parallel GC:
  ZGC:          5–10%
  Shenandoah:   5–12%
  (comparable; Shenandoah load barrier slightly more expensive)
Part 4

Shenandoah GC Phases

Shenandoah's GC cycle is structured to minimize STW time by making each phase either concurrent or extremely short.

Shenandoah GC Cycle:

[STW: Init Mark]              ~0.5–2ms
  ↓
[Concurrent Mark]             seconds (application runs)
  ↓
[STW: Final Mark]             ~0.5–2ms
  ↓
[Concurrent Cleanup]          milliseconds (application runs)
[Concurrent Evacuation]       seconds (application runs)
  ↓
[STW: Init Update References] ~0.5–1ms
  ↓
[Concurrent Update References] seconds (application runs)
  ↓
[STW: Final Update References] ~0.5–1ms
  ↓
[Concurrent Cleanup]          milliseconds (application runs)

Phase 1: Init Mark (STW, ~0.5–2ms)

The first STW pause:
1. Enable SATB write barriers
2. Scan GC roots (thread stacks, static fields, JNI refs)
3. Mark root objects as live
4. Hand off root frontier to concurrent marker

Duration scales with GC root count (number of threads × avg stack depth), not heap size.

Phase 2: Concurrent Mark (Application Runs)

GC threads trace the entire live object graph from roots. The application runs concurrently. New allocations are considered live. SATB barriers capture any reference overwrite during marking.

Phase 3: Final Mark (STW, ~0.5–2ms)

The second STW pause:
1. Drain SATB queues (process references overwritten during concurrent mark)
2. Re-scan root references modified during concurrent mark
3. Finalize live object set for every region
4. Identify the collection set (regions with highest garbage ratio)
5. Enable evacuation barriers

Phase 4: Concurrent Evacuation (Application Runs)

GC threads concurrently copy live objects from collection set regions to new regions. This is the phase where Shenandoah differs most from G1:

G1GC evacuation:   STW, parallel, must complete before app resumes
Shenandoah evacuation: Concurrent with app — app continues running while
                       objects are being copied. Brooks pointers redirect
                       any access to a "from" copy to the new "to" copy.

Phase 5: Init Update References (STW, ~0.5–1ms)

Short STW pause to:
1. Ensure all concurrent evacuation work is complete
2. Begin the reference update phase (tell barriers to update references they encounter)

Phase 6: Concurrent Update References (Application Runs)

GC threads walk the heap and update all references that still point to old "from" locations to point directly to "to" locations. This eliminates the indirection through Brooks pointers for all reachable references.

Phase 7: Final Update References (STW, ~0.5–1ms)

Final STW pause to:
1. Update root references (stacks, static fields)
2. Finalize reference updates

Phase 8: Concurrent Cleanup

Free the now-empty collection set regions. Ready them for allocation.

Total STW time per GC cycle: ~2–8ms (4 short STW pauses)

Part 5

Shenandoah Heap Layout

Shenandoah uses a region-based heap like G1GC, but with important differences:

Shenandoah Heap (example, 32 regions):
┌──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┐
│  A   │  A   │  A   │  CS  │  CS  │  F   │  F   │  F   │
├──────┼──────┼──────┼──────┼──────┼──────┼──────┼──────┤
│  A   │  A   │  CS  │  CS  │  F   │  F   │  F   │  F   │
└──────┴──────┴──────┴──────┴──────┴──────┴──────┴──────┘

A = Active (contains live objects, not selected for collection)
CS = Collection Set (selected for evacuation — live objects being copied out)
F = Free (available for new allocation or evacuation destination)

Key differences from G1:
1. No fixed Young/Old split (non-generational): All regions are equal; there is no separate Young or Old generation in non-generational Shenandoah
2. Collection set selection: Shenandoah selects any regions with high garbage ratio, regardless of object age
3. Region size: Fixed at heap startup. Default: max(256KB, Xmx / 2048)

Humongous regions in Shenandoah

Like G1, Shenandoah handles large objects specially:

Humongous threshold: > 50% of region size

Humongous objects in Shenandoah:
  - Allocated directly into one or more contiguous regions
  - Not moved during evacuation (in-place reclamation)
  - Reclaimed when marking identifies them as dead
  - Less pathological than G1: no IHOP trigger, no fragmentation spiral
    (Shenandoah doesn't have the same concurrent mark start side-effects)
Part 6

Enabling Shenandoah GC: JVM Flags

Java version and distribution support

Shenandoah availability:
  OpenJDK 12:        Experimental (needs unlock flag)
  OpenJDK 15:        Production-ready
  Backports available for OpenJDK 8 and 11:
    - Amazon Corretto 8/11
    - Adoptium Temurin 8/11
    - Red Hat OpenJDK 8/11

Note: Oracle JDK does NOT include Shenandoah.
Use OpenJDK-based distributions (Temurin, Corretto, etc.) for Shenandoah support.

Basic enablement

# Java 15+ (production-ready):
java -XX:+UseShenandoahGC \
     -Xms4g -Xmx4g \
     -jar app.jar

# Java 12–14 (experimental):
java -XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions \
     -XX:+UseShenandoahGC \
     -Xms4g -Xmx4g \
     -jar app.jar

GC mode selection

Shenandoah supports three GC modes (heuristics):

# Default heuristic (adaptive) — recommended:
-XX:ShenandoahGCHeuristics=adaptive   # default; adjusts GC timing based on allocation rate

# Compact heuristic (most aggressive):
-XX:ShenandoahGCHeuristics=compact    # GC as frequently as possible; minimal heap usage
                                       # at cost of higher CPU/throughput overhead

# Passive heuristic (no concurrent GC):
-XX:ShenandoahGCHeuristics=passive    # Disable concurrent GC entirely (diagnostic/testing)
                                       # For normal use this is inappropriate

GC logging

# Production GC logging:
-Xlog:gc*:file=/var/log/app/gc-shenandoah.log:time,uptime,level,tags:filecount=5,filesize=20m

# Phase-level detail:
-Xlog:gc+phases:stdout
Part 7

Shenandoah Heuristics: How GC is Triggered

Shenandoah uses heuristics to decide when to start a GC cycle. Getting the timing right is critical: start too late and the application runs out of free regions (allocation failure). Start too early and CPU is wasted on unnecessary GC cycles.

Adaptive heuristic (default)

Adaptive heuristic decision model:

  Monitor: allocation rate (MB/s)
  Monitor: live data size (from previous GC cycles)
  Monitor: current free heap fraction

  Trigger GC cycle when:
    estimated_time_to_fill_heap < estimated_GC_cycle_duration
    AND free_heap < ShenandoahFreeThreshold

  Key parameters:
    -XX:ShenandoahFreeThreshold=10       (default 10%)
    → Start GC when free heap < 10% of total heap

    -XX:ShenandoahInitFreeThreshold=70   (default 70%)
    → Heuristic's initial learning threshold

    -XX:ShenandoahMinFreeThreshold=10    (default 10%)
    → Hard floor: GC MUST start when free < this

Pacing: back-pressure on allocation

If the GC cycle cannot keep pace with allocation, Shenandoah uses pacing — it artificially slows allocation by making allocating threads sleep briefly:

Pacing mechanism:
  Free heap falling fast → Shenandoah starts charging "tax" on allocations
  Tax = small sleep (microseconds to milliseconds)
  Allows GC to catch up without triggering STW

GC log with pacing:
  [gc,ergo] Allocation pacing: 1.2ms tax on Thread "http-nio-exec-5"
  → Not as bad as STW, but visible in latency histograms

Fix: increase heap, increase ConcGCThreads, or reduce allocation rate

Degenerated GC (fallback)

If allocation outpaces concurrent GC completely, Shenandoah falls back to Degenerated GC — a partially or fully STW cycle:

Degeneration modes (in order of severity):
  1. Degenerated STW Mark    → if concurrent mark didn't finish in time
  2. Degenerated STW Evac    → if concurrent evac didn't finish in time
  3. Full GC (last resort)   → if degenerated GC also fails

GC log signature:
  [gc] Pause Degenerated GC (Mark) 1240ms  ← bad; treat like Full GC
  [gc] Pause Full (Allocation Failure) 3400ms ← very bad; heap too small
Part 8

Concurrent Compaction Deep Dive

Concurrent compaction (evacuation) is Shenandoah's defining capability. This section explores how it works mechanically.

The compaction problem

When two copies of an object exist simultaneously (old "from" copy and new "to" copy), which is authoritative?

Evacuation race condition:
  Thread A: reads object.field via from-copy   → gets value V1
  GC:       copies object to to-copy           → field = V1
  Thread B: writes object.field = V2           → which copy gets updated?

Without protection: Thread B might update from-copy; GC copies V1 to to-copy;
V2 is lost. This is a lost update — a data corruption bug.

Shenandoah's solution: compare-and-swap on Brooks pointer

Shenandoah uses an atomic CAS (compare-and-swap) operation to install the forwarding pointer. The first entity to successfully CAS the Brooks pointer from self to new_addr "wins":

GC evacuation of object at 0x1000:
  1. GC allocates new copy at 0x9000
  2. GC copies all fields from 0x1000 to 0x9000
  3. GC does: CAS(0x1000.fwdWord, 0x1000, 0x9000)
     → If CAS succeeds: GC is the winner; 0x9000 is canonical
     → If CAS fails: another thread (or GC thread) already installed fwd ptr
       → GC uses the existing forwarding target instead
  4. Application thread attempting to write to 0x1000:
     → Write barrier checks fwdWord
     → If fwdWord = 0x9000: write to 0x9000 instead
     → Mutation goes to the canonical copy

This ensures no writes are lost — the store barrier redirects writes to the canonical location, even while GC is concurrently copying.

Self-healing reference updates

During concurrent update references phase, application threads that load a reference still pointing to a from-copy help self-heal by updating that reference to the to-copy:

Self-healing during update-references phase:
  Thread loads reference ref = 0x1000
  Load barrier: reads fwdWord of 0x1000 → 0x9000
  Thread self-heals: atomically updates source slot to 0x9000
  Thread continues with ref = 0x9000
Part 9

Shenandoah Modes: Generational Support (Shenandoah 3.0)

Non-generational Shenandoah (the original) treats all objects equally, scanning the entire live heap every GC cycle. This is exactly the same inefficiency that motivated Generational ZGC.

Generational Shenandoah (experimental, Java 21+)

Red Hat began developing Generational Shenandoah to apply the generational hypothesis:

# Generational Shenandoah (experimental in Java 21):
java -XX:+UseShenandoahGC \
     -XX:ShenandoahGCMode=generational \
     -jar app.jar

Generational Shenandoah heap:
  Young generation: small, high-turnover regions
  Old generation: large, low-turnover regions

  Young GC (minor): collect Young regions only (concurrent)
  Mixed GC: collect Young + selected Old regions

  Expected benefit: 2–3x reduction in GC thread CPU usage
                    at the same pause time target

Note: As of Java 21, generational Shenandoah is still experimental. Non-generational Shenandoah remains the production-stable mode. This contrasts with ZGC where Generational ZGC is recommended for production in Java 21.

Part 10

Shenandoah vs ZGC: Detailed Comparison

Shenandoah vs ZGC — Engineering Trade-offs:

┌──────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┐
│ Characteristic               │ Shenandoah                  │ ZGC                          │
├──────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┤
│ Concurrent relocation        │ Yes (Brooks pointer)        │ Yes (colored pointer)        │
│ Per-object memory overhead   │ 8 bytes (Brooks word)       │ 0 bytes                      │
│ Pointer metadata location    │ Object header               │ Pointer bits (OS virtual mem)│
│ Load barrier type            │ Pointer dereference         │ Color bit check              │
│ Load barrier cost            │ ~4–6ns (extra indirection)  │ ~2–4ns (branch + check)      │
│ Heap layout                  │ Equal-size regions          │ Variable-size pages          │
│ Generational (production)    │ Not yet (experimental 21)   │ Java 21 (-XX:+ZGenerational) │
│ Pause count per GC cycle     │ 4                           │ 3                            │
│ Typical STW pause            │ 1–5ms                       │ 0.1–1ms                      │
│ Pause scales with heap?      │ Very slightly (root scan)   │ No                           │
│ Backported to Java 8/11?     │ Yes (Red Hat / Corretto)    │ No (Java 15+ only)           │
│ Oracle JDK supported?        │ No (OpenJDK only)           │ Yes                          │
│ Memory uncommit              │ Manual / limited            │ Automatic                    │
│ String deduplication         │ Not supported               │ Not supported                │
│ Compact heuristic            │ Yes (minimize memory use)   │ -XX:SoftMaxHeapSize          │
│ NUMA awareness               │ Limited                     │ Built-in                     │
│ Throughput overhead vs Par GC│ 5–12%                       │ 5–10%                        │
│ Best for                     │ Java 8–17, modest latency   │ Java 21+, extreme latency    │
└──────────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────┘

Pause time comparison in practice

Same workload (4 GB heap, 1 GB live data, 200 MB/s allocation rate):

G1GC:        P50: 35ms    P99: 180ms   Max: 950ms
Shenandoah:  P50: 2ms     P99: 8ms     Max: 25ms
ZGC (Gen):   P50: 0.3ms   P99: 0.9ms   Max: 2ms

Shenandoah: ~20x better than G1 for P99
ZGC:         ~200x better than G1 for P99
Shenandoah vs ZGC: ZGC has ~4–10x better P99 pauses

When Shenandoah is the better choice

  1. Java 8 or Java 11 — ZGC is not available in these versions; Shenandoah is backported to OpenJDK 8/11 via Red Hat and Amazon Corretto builds
  2. Memory-constrained environments — No concern: actually, ZGC uses no per-object overhead. However, Shenandoah is simpler to reason about without virtual memory aliasing
  3. Moderate latency SLO (1–20ms) — Shenandoah's 1–5ms pauses are acceptable; the simpler deployment (no virtual memory tricks) may be preferred
  4. Teams with G1GC tuning experience — Shenandoah's region-based heap and GC logging resembles G1 more closely than ZGC's page-based model
  5. Compact heuristic needed — Shenandoah's compact mode minimizes live heap size by GCing frequently; useful for memory-constrained deployments
Part 11

Configuring Shenandoah for Production

Production baseline configuration

# Java 17 production baseline (non-generational Shenandoah):
java \
  -XX:+UseShenandoahGC \
  -Xms4g \
  -Xmx8g \
  -XX:ShenandoahGCHeuristics=adaptive \
  -XX:ShenandoahFreeThreshold=15 \
  -XX:ConcGCThreads=4 \
  -XX:+UseContainerSupport \
  -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 \
  -Xlog:gc*:file=/var/log/app/gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags:filecount=5,filesize=20m \
  -jar app.jar

Flag reference

-XX:ShenandoahFreeThreshold=15
    GC trigger: start GC when free heap < 15% (default 10%)
    Higher value: GC starts earlier → lower pause risk, higher CPU overhead
    Lower value: waits longer → risk of degenerated GC under sudden spikes

-XX:ShenandoahInitFreeThreshold=70
    Heuristic learning starting point (default 70%)
    Lower if your application's live data is a small fraction of Xmx

-XX:ShenandoahMinFreeThreshold=10
    Hard minimum: GC MUST start if free < this (default 10%)
    Prevents allocation failure under extreme conditions

-XX:ConcGCThreads=N
    Number of concurrent GC threads
    Default: max(1, CPU_count / 4)  ← Shenandoah uses more threads than ZGC by default
    Increase if degenerated GC or pacing events appear in logs

-XX:ShenandoahGCHeuristics=adaptive|compact|passive
    adaptive:  default, auto-tunes GC start timing
    compact:   maximizes GC frequency to minimize heap footprint
    passive:   no concurrent GC (diagnostic only)

-XX:ShenandoahPacingMaxDelay=10
    Maximum pacing delay in milliseconds (default 10ms)
    Lower to reduce latency impact of pacing; raise to reduce GC CPU waste

What NOT to set with Shenandoah

-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis     → Ignored by Shenandoah (it's not G1)
-XX:G1HeapRegionSize     → G1-specific flag
-XX:InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent → G1-specific
-XX:NewRatio             → Not applicable (no fixed generations in non-generational mode)
-XX:UseStringDeduplication → Not supported
Part 12

Shenandoah GC Logging and Diagnostics

Reading Shenandoah GC logs

Shenandoah GC log output (Java 17 adaptive heuristic):

[2.345s][info][gc] GC(12) Concurrent reset
[2.346s][info][gc] GC(12) Pause Init Mark (unload classes) 1.234ms
[2.346s][info][gc] GC(12) Concurrent marking roots
[2.365s][info][gc] GC(12) Concurrent marking 18.934ms
[2.365s][info][gc] GC(12) Pause Final Mark (unload classes) 1.891ms
[2.366s][info][gc] GC(12) Concurrent cleanup 0.234ms
[2.366s][info][gc] GC(12) Concurrent evacuation
[2.390s][info][gc] GC(12) Concurrent evacuation 24.123ms
[2.390s][info][gc] GC(12) Pause Init Update Refs 0.312ms
[2.390s][info][gc] GC(12) Concurrent update references
[2.410s][info][gc] GC(12) Concurrent update references 20.234ms
[2.410s][info][gc] GC(12) Pause Final Update Refs 0.789ms
[2.411s][info][gc] GC(12) Concurrent cleanup 0.123ms
[2.411s][info][gc] GC(12) Garbage collection 65.432ms
                          4096M->2048M(8192M) 65ms (wall)
                          STW total: 4.226ms

Key metrics:
  Init Mark: 1.234ms    ← should be < 3ms
  Final Mark: 1.891ms   ← should be < 3ms
  Init Update Refs: 0.312ms
  Final Update Refs: 0.789ms
  Total STW: 4.226ms     ← sum of all 4 STW pauses
  Wall time: 65ms        ← total GC cycle time (mostly concurrent)

Detecting degenerated GC

Degenerated GC log signature:
  [gc] Pause Degenerated GC (Mark) 456ms

  This is a STW fallback when concurrent marking ran out of time/space.
  Treat identically to a Full GC from a latency perspective.

  Root causes:
    1. ShenandoahFreeThreshold too low → GC starts when heap already critical
    2. ConcGCThreads too few → can't finish concurrent phases before heap fills
    3. Sudden allocation burst → outpaced the concurrent cycle in progress

Action: increase ShenandoahFreeThreshold, ConcGCThreads, or Xmx

jstat with Shenandoah

jstat -gcutil <pid> 2000

# S0, S1: Survivor spaces (may show 0 if no separate survivors in Shenandoah)
# E:  Eden utilization (Shenandoah region serving as current allocation region)
# O:  Old gen (shows total heap that isn't Eden in non-generational mode)
# M:  Metaspace
# YGC: Young GC count (for Shenandoah: all GC cycle count)
# FGC: Full GC count (should be 0 in healthy Shenandoah)
Part 13

Production Use Cases for Shenandoah

Use case 1: Legacy Java 11 microservices

Scenario:
  Company runs 200 Spring Boot microservices on Java 11
  Kubernetes, 4–8 GB heap per service
  G1GC causing P99 > 200ms, SLA requires P99 < 50ms
  Cannot immediately upgrade to Java 17/21

Solution:
  Use Amazon Corretto 11 (includes Shenandoah backport)
  Migrate services to -XX:+UseShenandoahGC
  Expected P99: 5–15ms (from 200ms)

Why not ZGC?
  ZGC production-ready only from Java 15
  Backporting ZGC is not available for Java 11
  Shenandoah is the only sub-20ms collector for Java 8/11

Use case 2: Content delivery platform (large heap, moderate latency)

Scenario:
  CDN origin server running metadata index in-heap
  12 GB heap, 8 GB live data
  Requires P99 < 20ms for metadata lookups

Solution:
  Java 17 + Shenandoah adaptive
  -Xmx12g -XX:+UseShenandoahGC -XX:ShenandoahFreeThreshold=20

G1GC at this live data size:
  Old gen always near capacity
  Mixed GC every few seconds, each pause 200–800ms
  Full GC risk when live data shifts

Shenandoah:
  Concurrent evacuation handles live data shifts gracefully
  P99 pauses: 3–8ms
  No Full GC pathology

Use case 3: Interactive data analytics

Scenario:
  Jupyter-style notebook server executing user-submitted Java analytics
  Variable allocation patterns (some queries allocate 3 GB in 10 seconds)
  Users expect sub-10ms response for UI interactions during GC

Solution:
  Java 21 + Shenandoah (non-generational)
  -Xmx16g -XX:+UseShenandoahGC -XX:ShenandoahGCHeuristics=adaptive
  -XX:ConcGCThreads=8

Why Shenandoah over ZGC here?
  Team already uses Shenandoah in Java 11 services
  Upgrade path: Java 11 → 17 → 21, same GC throughout
  Generational ZGC is newer and less battle-tested in the team's ops experience
  Migration risk justifies staying with familiar GC
Part 14

Shenandoah and Metaspace

Shenandoah handles Metaspace (class metadata) similarly to G1GC:

Class unloading in Shenandoah

# Class unloading tied to GC cycles:
-XX:+ClassUnloading         # default true; classes unreachable from live objects
                             # are unloaded during Final Mark

# Shenandoah concurrently processes class unloading:
# Classes identified as dead during Concurrent Mark phase
# Unloaded during Final Mark (STW) or concurrent cleanup

# GC log shows class unloading:
[gc] GC(5) Pause Final Mark (unload classes) 2.134ms
                              ↑
                              class unloading happened in this pause

Metaspace configuration

-XX:MetaspaceSize=256m         # initial commit
-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=512m      # hard cap (set this to prevent unbounded growth)

# Monitoring Metaspace:
jcmd <pid> VM.metaspace
# Shows: used, committed, reserved for class and non-class spaces
Part 15

Shenandoah in Containerized Environments

Container awareness

# UseContainerSupport is default on Java 11+:
-XX:+UseContainerSupport      # reads cgroup memory/CPU limits instead of host

# Shenandoah concurrent thread calculation:
# ConcGCThreads default = max(1, CPU_count / 4)
# In a 2-CPU container: ConcGCThreads = 1 (may be too few for high load)
# Override:
-XX:ConcGCThreads=2

Memory sizing for Shenandoah

# Shenandoah needs generous heap headroom:
# Rule: Xmx = live_data × 2.5 minimum (vs ZGC's 2–4x)
# Shenandoah needs space for:
#   - Current live objects
#   - From-copy and to-copy of objects being evacuated (both present simultaneously)
#   - Allocation during concurrent evacuation
# 
# If live data is 4 GB:
#   Minimum comfortable: -Xmx10g
#   Degenerated GC risk if headroom is too small

# Container example (8 GB limit, 4 GB expected live data):
-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=80.0   # 6.4 GB heap → some risk at peak
# Better:
-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=90.0   # 7.2 GB heap → more headroom
# or
-Xmx7g                      # explicit for predictability

Kubernetes deployment with Shenandoah

# Kubernetes pod spec for Shenandoah-based service:
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    resources:
      requests:
        memory: "4Gi"
        cpu: "1"
      limits:
        memory: "8Gi"
        cpu: "4"
    env:
    - name: JAVA_OPTS
      value: >-
        -XX:+UseShenandoahGC
        -XX:+UseContainerSupport
        -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=80.0
        -XX:ConcGCThreads=2
        -XX:ShenandoahFreeThreshold=20
        -Xlog:gc*:file=/var/log/gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags:filecount=3,filesize=10m
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /actuator/health/readiness
        port: 8080
      timeoutSeconds: 3    # 3s is safe with Shenandoah (pauses are < 5ms typically)
Part 16

Advanced: Shenandoah and JNI / Native Code

JNI and GC interaction

When a Java thread calls into native (JNI) code:
1. The thread exits "Java execution mode" and enters native mode
2. Shenandoah cannot safely move objects referenced by native code
3. Objects passed to JNI are pinned — their addresses cannot change while in native

// JNI boundary handling:
public native void processBuffer(byte[] buf);
// When this call is active:
//   buf is pinned — Shenandoah will NOT evacuate buf during this call
//   Other objects can still be concurrently evacuated

// GC log may show:
// [gc] Pinned: 5 objects in JNI critical regions

Critical JNI sections and Shenandoah

// JNI Critical sections block GC:
byte[] array = new byte[1000];
jbyte* ptr = env->GetByteArrayElements(array, nullptr);
// ^ GC is paused from entering evacuation while critical section is active

env->ReleaseByteArrayElements(array, ptr, 0);
// ^ GC can resume evacuation

This is the same limitation as with G1GC. Applications that hold JNI critical sections for long periods delay concurrent evacuation and increase risk of degenerated GC.

Part 17

Failure Modes and Recovery

Failure mode 1: Pacing

Application threads sleep (briefly) to let GC catch up. Visible in logs and latency histograms as small delays (0.1–10ms).

Trigger: Free heap decreasing faster than concurrent GC can reclaim
Response: Allocating threads charged a "tax" (sleep)
GC log: [gc,ergo] Allocation pacing applied: 2.3ms for Thread "exec-12"
Fix: Increase ShenandoahFreeThreshold, ConcGCThreads, or Xmx

Failure mode 2: Degenerated GC

A concurrent phase (mark or evac) didn't complete before the heap became critical. Shenandoah falls back to finishing that phase STW.

GC log: [gc] Pause Degenerated GC (Evacuation) 1234ms
Fix: Same as pacing — more headroom needed
Severity: Medium (worse than intended, but recovers cleanly)

Failure mode 3: Full GC

All concurrent and degenerated mechanisms failed. Full STW mark-compact of entire heap.

GC log: [gc] Pause Full (Allocation Failure) 4567ms
Fix: Heap too small for the load; application code memory leak; or sudden burst
Severity: High (application paused for seconds)

Monitoring and alerting thresholds

Healthy Shenandoah:
  STW pauses:      < 5ms per phase, < 15ms total per GC cycle
  Full GC count:   0
  Degenerated GC:  0
  Pacing events:   < 5 per minute (occasional is OK)

Alert thresholds:
  Any Full GC:             CRITICAL
  Degenerated GC > 1/hour: WARNING
  Pacing > 50/minute:      WARNING (allocation outpacing GC)
  Free heap < 15%:         WARNING
Part 18

Shenandoah on Java 8 and 11 (Backport)

One of Shenandoah's most practical advantages is its availability on older JVM versions.

Obtaining Shenandoah on Java 8/11

Distributions with Shenandoah backport:
  Amazon Corretto 8:  corretto-8 includes Shenandoah (verify with -XX:+UseShenandoahGC)
  Amazon Corretto 11: same
  Adoptium Temurin 8/11: includes Shenandoah in some builds
  Red Hat OpenJDK 8/11: includes Shenandoah

NOT available:
  Oracle JDK 8/11: no Shenandoah
  Standard OpenJDK.org builds for Java 8/11: no Shenandoah

Verify presence:
  java -XX:+UseShenandoahGC -version
  # If it starts: Shenandoah is available
  # If it errors: distribution doesn't include it

Java 8 with Shenandoah: known limitations

Java 8 Shenandoah backport limitations vs Java 17:
  1. No concurrent class unloading (available Java 11+)
  2. Fewer heuristic tuning options
  3. Higher default overhead (older JIT doesn't optimize barriers as well)
  4. No Abortable Evacuation feature (available Java 13+)

Migration path

Recommended migration strategy for companies on Java 8:
  Phase 1: Java 8 + Shenandoah (immediate latency improvement, no app changes)
  Phase 2: Java 11 + Shenandoah (LTS upgrade, better Shenandoah features)
  Phase 3: Java 21 + ZGC (maximum performance, Generational ZGC)

This allows gradual migration without requiring Java version and GC changes simultaneously.

Decision tree

START: What are your requirements?

Is Java version < 15?
  → YES: Use Shenandoah (if backport available) or G1GC
  → NO: Continue

Is P99 pause SLO < 5ms?
  → YES: Use ZGC (Java 21 Generational ZGC)
  → NO: Continue

Is P99 pause SLO 5–30ms?
  → YES: Use Shenandoah or ZGC (both work; ZGC if Java 21+, Shenandoah for Java 17 or backport)
  → NO: Continue

Is heap > 32 GB?
  → YES: Use ZGC (G1 pauses too long at very large heaps)
  → NO: Continue

Is this pure batch processing?
  → YES: Use Parallel GC (maximum throughput, pauses don't matter)
  → NO: Use G1GC (default, well-tested, good balance)
Part 20

Benchmarking Your Application with Shenandoah

Before-and-after migration methodology

#!/bin/bash
# 1. Baseline run (G1GC):
java -XX:+UseG1GC \
     -Xms4g -Xmx4g \
     -Xlog:gc*:file=gc-g1.log:time,uptime,level,tags \
     -jar app.jar &
APP_PID=$!

# 2. Run load test for 10 minutes:
./load-generator --target http://localhost:8080 --duration 600s --rps 1000 \
     --percentiles 50,95,99,999 --output baseline-g1.json

kill $APP_PID

# 3. Shenandoah run (same heap, same load):
java -XX:+UseShenandoahGC \
     -Xms4g -Xmx4g \
     -Xlog:gc*:file=gc-shen.log:time,uptime,level,tags \
     -jar app.jar &
APP_PID=$!

./load-generator --target http://localhost:8080 --duration 600s --rps 1000 \
     --percentiles 50,95,99,999 --output baseline-shenandoah.json

kill $APP_PID

# 4. Compare:
diff <(jq '.p99' baseline-g1.json) <(jq '.p99' baseline-shenandoah.json)

Metrics to compare

Before/After Shenandoah migration checklist:

Application metrics:
  ✓ P50, P95, P99, P999 response time
  ✓ Throughput (requests/second)
  ✓ Error rate (5xx responses during GC)
  ✓ Timeout rate

GC metrics:
  ✓ Average STW pause (from GC log)
  ✓ Max STW pause
  ✓ GC overhead % (total GC CPU / elapsed)
  ✓ Full GC count
  ✓ Degenerated GC count
  ✓ Allocation rate (MB/s)

System metrics:
  ✓ CPU utilization (GC threads consume more CPU with Shenandoah vs G1)
  ✓ Memory utilization (Brooks pointer overhead increases RSS)
  ✓ JVM native memory (Metaspace, code cache, thread stacks)
Part 21

Anti-Patterns and Common Mistakes

Anti-pattern 1: Shenandoah with insufficient heap headroom

# PROBLEM: 4 GB heap, 3.5 GB live data
-Xmx4g -XX:+UseShenandoahGC

# Shenandoah needs space for both from-copy and to-copy during concurrent evac.
# 500 MB free is not enough headroom.
# Frequent degenerated GC or Full GC under normal load.

# FIX: Minimum 2.5x live data
# 3.5 GB live → -Xmx9g minimum

Anti-pattern 2: Using passive heuristic in production

# WRONG:
-XX:ShenandoahGCHeuristics=passive   # disables concurrent GC entirely

# This is a debugging tool only. In production, the JVM relies on
# explicit System.gc() or allocation failure to trigger GC.
# Result: very long pauses or OOM.

# FIX: Use adaptive (default) or compact

Anti-pattern 3: Too-low ShenandoahFreeThreshold

# PROBLEM:
-XX:ShenandoahFreeThreshold=3   # start GC only when 97% full

# With 97% heap full, allocation bursts can fill the remaining 3%
# before the concurrent GC cycle finishes. Degenerated GC is almost guaranteed.

# FIX:
-XX:ShenandoahFreeThreshold=20  # start GC when 80% full, giving 20% headroom

Anti-pattern 4: Running on Oracle JDK and expecting Shenandoah

# Oracle JDK does NOT ship Shenandoah.
# Running -XX:+UseShenandoahGC on Oracle JDK:
#   Error: VM option 'UseShenandoahGC' is experimental and must be enabled
#   or simply: unrecognized VM option

# FIX: Use an OpenJDK distribution that includes Shenandoah:
#   Amazon Corretto, Adoptium Temurin, Red Hat OpenJDK, Azul Zulu

Anti-pattern 5: Expecting Shenandoah to match ZGC pause times

# Shenandoah pauses (Init Mark): 1–5ms
# ZGC pauses (Pause Mark Start): 0.1–0.5ms

# For P99 SLO < 2ms: Shenandoah cannot reliably meet this.
# Use ZGC on Java 15+.

# Shenandoah is the right choice for P99 SLO in the 5–30ms range
# where ZGC is available but teams prefer Shenandoah's operational model.

Practice — Lesson 67

Easy

  1. Enable Shenandoah GC on a Java 17 application. Run it for 5 minutes and collect a GC log. Identify each STW pause in the log, record its duration, and verify all four STW phases are present (Init Mark, Final Mark, Init Update Refs, Final Update Refs).

  2. What is a Brooks pointer? Draw a before/after diagram showing the state of the forwarding word in an object before relocation and after it has been moved to a new address.

  3. List the three heuristics available in Shenandoah (-XX:ShenandoahGCHeuristics). For each one, describe a scenario where it would be the appropriate choice.

Medium

  1. Phase classification: Label each Shenandoah GC phase as STW or Concurrent, and explain what happens during each:
    - Init Mark
    - Concurrent Mark
    - Final Mark
    - Concurrent Cleanup
    - Concurrent Evacuation
    - Init Update References
    - Concurrent Update References
    - Final Update References

  2. Brooks pointer race condition: During concurrent evacuation, both an application thread and a GC thread attempt to install the forwarding pointer for the same object simultaneously. Explain the CAS-based mechanism Shenandoah uses to ensure correctness. What happens to the "losing" thread?

  3. Heap sizing calculation: An application has 3 GB of live data. Under load, it allocates at 500 MB/s. A Shenandoah concurrent evacuation cycle takes approximately 4 seconds. Calculate the minimum Xmx needed to avoid Degenerated GC, showing your reasoning. (Hint: consider both the evacuation headroom requirement and allocation during the concurrent cycle.)

Advanced

  1. Shenandoah vs G1GC overhead analysis: Both Shenandoah and G1GC use write barriers for tracking cross-region references, but for different purposes.
    - G1GC write barrier: tracks dirty cards for Remembered Sets (cross-region pointers)
    - Shenandoah write barrier: redirects writes to correct (possibly moved) object + SATB capture

Explain why G1GC's barrier writes to a card table while Shenandoah's barrier must dereference a Brooks pointer. What different GC problems are each solving?

  1. Pacing simulation: A Shenandoah application allocates at 2 GB/s peak. The heap is 8 GB. ShenandoahFreeThreshold=10 (GC starts when < 800 MB free). A concurrent evacuation cycle takes 3 seconds. Calculate: at what heap occupancy will pacing begin if allocation rate stays at 2 GB/s? At what rate would pacing delay need to be applied to prevent allocation failure?

  2. Concurrent update references necessity: Explain why Shenandoah needs a separate "Concurrent Update References" phase after concurrent evacuation is complete. Why can't all references be updated lazily (self-healed) like in ZGC? What would happen if Shenandoah removed the Update References phase entirely?

Production

  1. Java 8 migration: A large enterprise runs 500 Spring Boot 2.x services on Oracle JDK 8 (G1GC). P99 latency is 250ms, dominated by GC pauses. They cannot immediately move to Java 17. Propose a migration plan to reduce P99 to < 30ms while remaining on Java 8, including:

    • JDK distribution change
    • JVM flag changes
    • Testing strategy
    • Rollback plan

  2. ShenandoahFreeThreshold optimization: You are tuning a Shenandoah service that:

    • Has 8 GB heap
    • 4 GB live data at steady state
    • 300 MB/s allocation rate at peak
    • Concurrent GC cycle takes ~2 seconds (from GC logs)

    Calculate an optimal ShenandoahFreeThreshold value. Show your calculation. What are the risks of setting it 5 percentage points higher vs. 5 percentage points lower than your calculated value?

  3. Observability setup: Design a complete observability setup for a Shenandoah production service, including:

    • JVM flags for GC logging (production-safe)
    • Three Prometheus/JMX metrics to expose
    • Grafana dashboard panels (list the panels and what they show)
    • PagerDuty/alerting rules for GC degradation
    • Weekly GC health check procedure

Debugging

  1. Degenerated GC root cause: A production service suddenly starts logging:
    [gc] Pause Degenerated GC (Evacuation) 2340ms [gc] Pause Degenerated GC (Evacuation) 1890ms [gc] Pause Degenerated GC (Mark) 3120ms
    The service was running fine for 3 days. No code was deployed. Traffic volume is normal.

    List 4 possible root causes (with the most likely first) and describe a diagnostic step for each.

  2. Brooks pointer overhead investigation: A performance engineer reports that after migrating from G1GC to Shenandoah, the service's heap usage grew by 800 MB (from 4.2 GB to 5.0 GB for the same workload). Explain why this happened. Is this expected? Is it a problem? How would you quantify whether the latency improvement justifies the memory increase?

  3. Pacing latency analysis: APM traces show that 0.1% of requests take 3–5ms longer than the P99 baseline. Investigation reveals these are correlated with GC log entries showing Allocation pacing applied: 3.2ms. The service uses ShenandoahFreeThreshold=10 and has ConcGCThreads=2 on a 16-CPU, 32 GB container.

    Step-by-step: diagnose the root cause and propose two different fixes, explaining the trade-off of each.

Interview

  1. Conceptual: What is a Brooks pointer and how does it enable concurrent compaction? What are its costs compared to ZGC's approach?

    Expected answer: A Brooks pointer is an extra 8-byte forwarding word prepended to every object's header. It initially points to the object itself (self-referential). When an object is evacuated (copied to a new location), the forwarding word in the original copy is updated (via CAS) to point to the new copy. Every object field access first dereferences the Brooks pointer — if it's been relocated, the access transparently goes to the new location. This enables concurrent compaction because application threads can access objects while they're being moved; they're just transparently redirected. The cost: 8 bytes of overhead per object (can be significant — 10–15% heap overhead for small objects), and an extra memory indirection on every object access vs. ZGC's load barrier which is just a bit check on the reference itself with no per-object memory overhead.

  2. Architecture: A team is debating Shenandoah vs ZGC for a new Java 21 service. The service: 6 GB heap, expected live data 2 GB, P99 SLO is 10ms. Make the case for each collector and give your recommendation.

    Expected answer (both cases):

    Case for ZGC: Sub-millisecond pauses easily satisfy 10ms SLO with enormous margin. Generational ZGC in Java 21 brings throughput overhead to ~5% vs Parallel GC. No per-object memory overhead (vs Shenandoah's 8 bytes/object). Automatic memory uncommit. Better for future growth if SLO tightens to 1ms.

    Case for Shenandoah: 10ms SLO is achievable with Shenandoah's 1–5ms pauses. If team has Shenandoah operational experience from older services, operational familiarity reduces risk. Shenandoah's simpler pointer model (no virtual memory aliasing) is easier to reason about when debugging.

    Recommendation: ZGC. On Java 21, Generational ZGC is production-ready and superior on every quantitative metric for this workload. The only exception would be if the team has existing Shenandoah expertise and a concrete reason to prefer it.

  3. Incident: A Shenandoah application shows P99 latency of 8ms normally but spikes to 45ms for ~2 minutes every hour, correlating with this GC log pattern:
    [gc,ergo] Allocation pacing applied: 12ms for Thread "exec-15" [gc,ergo] Allocation pacing applied: 8ms for Thread "exec-3" [gc] Pause Degenerated GC (Evacuation) 1200ms
    The pattern repeats every hour. Hypothesize what application behavior causes hourly allocation spikes and propose both a short-term (GC tuning) and long-term (application code) fix.

    Expected answer: The hourly pattern strongly suggests a scheduled job or cache refresh running every hour that suddenly allocates a large amount of data (e.g., loading a configuration file, refreshing an in-memory index, or scheduled batch processing). During this burst, allocation rate spikes beyond what ConcGCThreads can keep up with, causing pacing → degenerated GC.

    Short-term (GC tuning): Increase ShenandoahFreeThreshold from default to 25% so GC starts earlier before the scheduled burst. Increase ConcGCThreads to handle higher peak allocation rate. Increase Xmx to give more headroom during the burst.

    Long-term (application code): Identify the hourly scheduled task (check application code for @Scheduled(fixedRate = 3600000) or cron jobs). Refactor it to: (1) load data incrementally rather than all at once, (2) use double-buffering to swap in new data atomically without creating a sudden allocation spike, or (3) schedule the job to run at a low-traffic time and spread the allocation over a longer window.
