Part 1

Why JVM Tuning Matters

The JVM ships with default settings designed to work acceptably across a wide range of workloads. Those defaults are not optimized for your application. A Java microservice running with out-of-box settings on a 4-CPU, 8 GB container will routinely mis-size its heap, choose the wrong GC collector, under-provision metaspace, and fail to report accurate CPU availability to ergonomics — all before you write a single line of application code.

JVM tuning is the practice of systematically adjusting the runtime's behavior to match your workload's real characteristics. Done well, it can:
- Reduce GC pause time from hundreds of milliseconds to single digits
- Prevent OutOfMemoryError from metaspace exhaustion
- Halve memory footprint without changing application code
- Eliminate false OOMKiller kills in Kubernetes pods
- Cut p99 latency spikes caused by stop-the-world collection

Done badly, it turns a stable application into an unpredictable one. The goal of this lesson is to give you a principled, evidence-based methodology — not a cargo-cult list of flags to copy-paste.

The tuning hierarchy:
1. Profile first — never tune blind
2. Understand what each flag does mechanically
3. Change one variable at a time
4. Measure against a stable baseline
5. Test in an environment that resembles production

Every decision in this lesson follows this order.

Part 2

JVM Flag Categories and Diagnostic Switches

The JVM has thousands of flags. They fall into three stability tiers:

Tier Prefix Description Support guarantee
Standard - (e.g. -Xmx) Documented, stable across releases Stable
Non-standard -X (e.g. -Xss) Implementation-specific, may change Best-effort
Unstable -XX: Diagnostic/experimental, no guarantees None

The -XX: flags are further divided:
- -XX:+FlagName — enable a boolean flag
- -XX:-FlagName — disable a boolean flag
- -XX:FlagName=value — set a key-value flag

Diagnostic flags you should know immediately:

# Print all JVM flags with their current effective values
java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version

# Print all flags that differ from their defaults
java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep -E ":="

# Print flags set via command line (not defaults or ergonomics)
java -XX:+PrintCommandLineFlags -version

# At runtime, via jcmd
jcmd <pid> VM.flags
jcmd <pid> VM.command_line
jcmd <pid> VM.system_properties

Finding the right flag:

# Search for heap-related flags
java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep -i heap

# Get all GC-related flags
java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep -i "gc"

Always verify your flags are actually being applied with PrintFlagsFinal. A misspelled flag silently ignored by the JVM is a common tuning mistake.

Part 3

Heap Sizing: -Xms, -Xmx, and the Cost of Growth

The heap is divided into Young generation (Eden + Survivor spaces) and Old generation. -Xms sets the initial heap size and -Xmx sets the maximum.

-Xms512m    # Initial heap: 512 MB
-Xmx2g      # Maximum heap: 2 GB

Why set -Xms equal to -Xmx in production:

When the heap starts small and grows, the JVM requests more memory from the OS, which involves system calls and page faults. During growth, the GC also works harder to keep up with the expanding live set. Setting both equal eliminates heap resizing entirely — the JVM claims all memory at startup and never releases it.

# Stable production setting: fixed heap size
-Xms2g -Xmx2g

The downside: pods/containers with co-located processes cannot benefit from idle Java processes releasing memory. For batch jobs or development, allowing shrinkage is fine.

Heap sizing rules of thumb:

  • Never allocate more than 70–75% of available physical memory to the heap
  • Leave room for: metaspace, thread stacks, code cache, off-heap buffers, OS overhead
  • For G1GC with large heaps: leave at least 20% for GC overhead
  • Monitor gc.live_data_size over time — the minimum heap is 1.5× to 3× your steady-state live set

Calculating steady-state live set:

# Trigger a full GC and read old-gen usage afterward
jcmd <pid> GC.run
jstat -gc <pid> 1000 5
# S0C S1C S0U S1U EC EU OC OU MC MU ...
# OC = Old capacity, OU = Old used → this is your live set
Part 4

Young Generation Tuning

The Young generation is where most objects are allocated. Short-lived objects die in Eden; survivors are promoted through Survivor spaces to Old gen.

Key Young generation flags:

-XX:NewSize=512m           # Initial young gen size
-XX:MaxNewSize=1g          # Maximum young gen size
-XX:NewRatio=2             # Old:Young ratio (default 2 → young = 1/3 of heap)
-XX:SurvivorRatio=8        # Eden:Survivor ratio (default 8 → each survivor = 1/10 of young)
-XX:MaxTenuringThreshold=15 # Max GC cycles before promotion to Old

For G1GC specifically:

With G1GC, do not set -XX:NewSize or -XX:MaxNewSize. G1 manages region assignment dynamically. The correct levers are:

-XX:G1NewSizePercent=5      # Minimum young gen as % of heap (default 5)
-XX:G1MaxNewSizePercent=60  # Maximum young gen as % of heap (default 60)

Signs the Young generation is too small:
- Frequent minor GC pauses (several per second)
- High allocation rate in profiler
- Objects being promoted too early (premature tenuring)

Signs the Young generation is too large:
- Minor GC pause times growing (more memory to scan)
- Old generation filling slowly with truly short-lived objects that survived just because Survivor space was too small

Survivor tuning:

-XX:+PrintTenuringDistribution  # (use with GC logging) shows age distribution

If most objects promote at age 1 or 2, increase MaxTenuringThreshold. If objects linger in survivor but never promote, decrease it.

Part 5

GC Collector Selection and Core Flags

Choosing the right collector is the single most impactful tuning decision.

Collector Best for Java version Pause type
Serial GC Single-CPU, tiny heaps All Full STW
Parallel GC Batch/throughput, multi-CPU All Full STW
G1GC General purpose, >4 GB 9+ (default) Bounded STW
ZGC Ultra-low latency 15+ (production) Sub-ms
Shenandoah Low latency 12+ (OpenJDK) Concurrent

Selecting a collector:

-XX:+UseSerialGC
-XX:+UseParallelGC
-XX:+UseG1GC
-XX:+UseZGC
-XX:+UseShenandoahGC

G1GC core tuning flags:

# Pause time target — the most important G1 flag
-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200   # Target: keep pauses under 200ms (default 200)

# Region size (1–32 MB, power of 2; default auto-calculated)
-XX:G1HeapRegionSize=4m

# Concurrent GC threads
-XX:ConcGCThreads=4

# Parallel GC threads (default: number of CPUs, capped at 8 for >8 CPUs)
-XX:ParallelGCThreads=8

# Initiate concurrent mark early enough to avoid evacuation failure
-XX:InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent=45  # default 45

# Reserve heap for GC overhead
-XX:G1ReservePercent=10  # default 10

ZGC core tuning flags (Java 15+):

-XX:+UseZGC
-XX:ZCollectionInterval=5      # Force GC every 5 seconds (avoids lazy collection)
-XX:ZUncommitDelay=300         # Uncommit unused memory after 5 min
-XX:+ZGenerational             # Enable generational ZGC (Java 21+, highly recommended)
-XX:SoftMaxHeapSize=3g         # Soft ceiling (ZGC stays below this unless forced)
Part 6

GC Logging Configuration

GC logs are the primary diagnostic tool for tuning. Always enable them in production.

Java 9+ unified logging (all modern releases):

-Xlog:gc*:file=/var/log/app/gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags:filecount=5,filesize=20m

Breaking this down:
- gc* — all GC-related log tags
- file=/var/log/app/gc.log — write to file (not stdout)
- time,uptime,level,tags — decorators for each line
- filecount=5,filesize=20m — rolling log: 5 files × 20 MB = 100 MB max

Fine-grained GC logging options:

# Just GC summary lines (low volume)
-Xlog:gc:file=gc.log:time,uptime

# GC + heap details
-Xlog:gc+heap:file=gc.log:time,uptime

# GC + phases (see individual G1 phases)
-Xlog:gc+phases:file=gc.log:time,uptime

# Everything (verbose, use for short diagnosis sessions)
-Xlog:gc*=debug:file=gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags

Analyzing GC logs:

Use GCEasy or GCViewer to parse and visualize GC log files. Key metrics to review:
- Pause time distribution (p50/p95/p99/max)
- Allocation rate (MB/s)
- Promotion rate (MB/s into Old gen)
- Heap occupancy before/after each collection
- Frequency of Full GC (should be rare or zero in steady state)

Part 7

Metaspace Tuning

Metaspace stores class metadata (class definitions, method bytecode references, constant pools). It lives in native memory outside the heap.

Key metaspace flags:

# No hard limit by default — can grow unboundedly if not set
-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256m

# Initial metaspace commit (pre-commit to avoid resize overhead)
-XX:MetaspaceSize=128m

# Per-classloader chunk size (reduce fragmentation for many classloaders)
-XX:MetaspaceExpansionSize=32m

# Compressed class space (for class pointer encoding, 64-bit only)
-XX:CompressedClassSpaceSize=128m

When to tune metaspace:

  • Application dynamically generates classes (Groovy, CGLIB, reflection-heavy frameworks like Spring)
  • java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace errors in production
  • GC logs show frequent metadata GC threshold adjustments

Diagnosing metaspace usage:

# Current metaspace usage via jstat
jstat -gcmetacapacity <pid>

# Detailed class loading
jcmd <pid> VM.class_hierarchy | wc -l

# Number of loaded classes
jcmd <pid> VM.classloader_stats

Spring Boot / reflection-heavy apps:

Frameworks using CGLIB proxies (Spring AOP, Hibernate lazy loading) generate synthetic classes at runtime. A typical Spring Boot app with JPA loads 10,000–15,000 classes. Set metaspace to at least 256 MB; monitor with -verbose:class to count peak class loading.

Part 8

Thread Stack Tuning

Each thread has its own stack in native memory. Default stack size is platform-dependent (typically 512 KB on 64-bit Linux, 1 MB on macOS).

-Xss256k    # Set thread stack size to 256 KB

Why reduce stack size:

Each thread costs Xss bytes of native memory. An application with 1000 threads and default 512 KB stacks uses 512 MB of native memory just for stacks. Reducing to 256 KB saves 256 MB.

When stack size matters:

  • Deeply recursive algorithms (increase stack size to prevent StackOverflowError)
  • High thread count microservices (reduce to save native memory)
  • Virtual threads (Java 21+) — carry frames on heap, stack size is irrelevant for virtual threads

Safe minimum:

256 KB works for most applications. Test for StackOverflowError under load before reducing below the default.

# Check current thread memory via native tooling
jcmd <pid> Thread.print | grep "java.lang.Thread.State" | wc -l
Part 9

JVM Ergonomics: Automatic Sizing

JVM ergonomics is the mechanism by which the JVM automatically selects GC algorithm, heap size, and thread counts based on detected hardware at startup.

What ergonomics configures automatically:

Resource Ergonomics logic
GC collector Defaults to G1GC on machines with ≥2 CPUs and ≥1792 MB memory
Initial heap (-Xms) 1/64 of physical memory
Max heap (-Xmx) 1/4 of physical memory
GC threads Based on available CPUs
JIT compilation threads Based on available CPUs

Viewing ergonomics decisions:

java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep -E "MaxHeapSize|InitialHeapSize|UseG1GC|ParallelGCThreads"

Why ergonomics fail in containers:

Before Java 8u191 and Java 10, the JVM read hardware limits from the host OS, not the container's cgroup limits. A container limited to 2 CPUs on a 32-CPU host would see 32 CPUs. A container with a 512 MB memory limit on a 128 GB host would set -Xmx to 32 GB and immediately OOM.

This was the single most common cause of Java container OOM failures between 2015 and 2020.

Part 10

Container Awareness Flags

Modern JVMs (Java 8u191+, Java 10+) support container-aware ergonomics. These flags tell the JVM to read limits from the container's cgroup instead of the host OS.

Core container flags:

# Enable container-aware resource detection (default ON since Java 10)
-XX:+UseContainerSupport

# Set heap as % of container memory limit (replaces -Xmx for containers)
-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0

# Set initial heap as % of container memory
-XX:InitialRAMPercentage=50.0

# Minimum heap as % of container memory
-XX:MinRAMPercentage=25.0

# Explicit RAM limit (overrides container detection)
-XX:MaxRAM=2g

Verifying container detection:

# Should show container memory limit, not host memory
java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep MaxHeapSize
java -XshowSettings:all -version 2>&1 | grep "heap"

Recommended container heap formula:

container_memory_limit × MaxRAMPercentage / 100 = heap size

For a 4 GB container:
- MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 → 3 GB heap
- Remaining 1 GB: metaspace (~256 MB) + code cache (~256 MB) + thread stacks + GC overhead + OS

Important: Never use -Xmx and -XX:MaxRAMPercentage together. MaxRAMPercentage is ignored if -Xmx is explicitly set.

Part 11

Kubernetes JVM Configuration

In Kubernetes, JVM resource configuration must align with Pod resource requests and limits.

Pod spec and JVM alignment:

resources:
  requests:
    memory: "2Gi"
    cpu: "1"
  limits:
    memory: "2Gi"
    cpu: "2"

# JVM flags for the above pod
JAVA_OPTS="-XX:+UseContainerSupport \
           -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 \
           -XX:InitialRAMPercentage=50.0 \
           -XX:+UseG1GC \
           -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200 \
           -Xss256k"

CPU limits and GC threads:

The JVM uses Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() to size GC thread pools. In Kubernetes, CPU limits are enforced via CFS bandwidth throttling — the JVM may still see the host's CPU count while being throttled to 1 CPU.

# Explicitly set GC thread counts for CPU-limited containers
-XX:ParallelGCThreads=2     # Match CPU limit
-XX:ConcGCThreads=1         # Half of ParallelGCThreads

Java 19+ Active Processors override:

# Cap the JVM's view of available CPUs
-XX:ActiveProcessorCount=2

JVM for Kubernetes liveness/readiness probes:

Startup probes must account for JIT warm-up time. The JVM's JIT compiler optimizes code over the first 30–90 seconds. Liveness probe initialDelaySeconds should be ≥60s for JVM applications.

Part 12

Memory Beyond the Heap: Native Memory Tracking

Many Java developers account only for heap memory. In production, the JVM uses significant native (off-heap) memory:

Memory region Typical size Controlled by
Heap 1–32 GB -Xmx
Metaspace 64–512 MB -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize
Code Cache 64–256 MB -XX:ReservedCodeCacheSize
Thread stacks n × Xss -Xss × thread count
GC data structures 5–15% of heap Implicit
Direct ByteBuffers Unlimited by default -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize
JNI native allocations Application-dependent —

Enabling Native Memory Tracking:

# Enable NMT (adds ~5% overhead)
-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary
# or: detail (more granular, more overhead)
-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=detail

# At runtime
jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary
jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory detail
jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory baseline
# ... after some time ...
jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary.diff

Code cache tuning:

-XX:ReservedCodeCacheSize=256m     # Default 240 MB in Java 11+
-XX:InitialCodeCacheSize=2m
-XX:+UseCodeCacheFlushing          # Allow eviction of old compilations (default ON)

If code cache fills up, the JIT compiler stops compiling and performance degrades catastrophically. Monitor with:

jstat -compiler <pid>
# Check "Failed" column — should be 0
Part 13

JIT Compiler Tuning

The JIT (Just-in-Time) compiler is tiered: interpreted → C1 (client compiler) → C2 (server compiler).

Tiered compilation flags:

# Tiered compilation (default ON since Java 8)
-XX:+TieredCompilation

# Force interpreted-only mode (testing/debugging, catastrophic performance)
-Xint

# Skip C1, compile directly to C2 (legacy server mode)
-XX:-TieredCompilation -server

# Compilation threshold for C1 (default 2000 invocations)
-XX:Tier3InvocationThreshold=2000

# Compilation threshold for C2 (default 15000 invocations)
-XX:CompileThreshold=10000

JIT diagnostic tools:

# Print methods being compiled
-XX:+PrintCompilation

# Print inlining decisions
-XX:+PrintInlining

# Disable specific optimization (debugging deoptimization issues)
-XX:DisableIntrinsic=_currentTimeMillis

Ahead-of-Time compilation (AppCDS):

Application Class Data Sharing pre-computes class metadata and shares it across JVM processes. Critical for containers with frequent restarts.

# Step 1: generate class list during training run
java -Xshare:off -XX:DumpLoadedClassList=app.classlist -jar app.jar

# Step 2: create shared archive
java -Xshare:dump -XX:SharedClassListFile=app.classlist \
     -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa -jar app.jar

# Step 3: use archive in production
java -Xshare:on -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa -jar app.jar

This reduces startup time by 30–50% and lowers memory footprint for multiple co-located JVM processes sharing the same archive.

Part 14

Diagnostic and Monitoring Flags

GC overhead limit:

# Throw OOM if >98% of time is spent in GC collecting <2% of heap
-XX:+UseGCOverheadLimit  # default ON
# Adjust thresholds
-XX:GCTimeLimit=90       # % time in GC before OOM
-XX:GCHeapFreeLimit=5    # % heap freed before OOM

Heap dump on OOM (essential in production):

-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError
-XX:HeapDumpPath=/var/dumps/heap-$(date +%s).hprof

JVM crash logs:

# Custom error file path
-XX:ErrorFile=/var/log/app/hs_err_pid%p.log

Verbose class loading:

-verbose:class            # Print every class loaded and unloaded
-XX:+TraceClassLoading
-XX:+TraceClassUnloading

Safe-point and pause analysis:

# Show application threads stopped for safe-point operations (not just GC)
-XX:+PrintSafepointStatistics
-XX:PrintSafepointStatisticsCount=1

This is important because many non-GC operations (code deoptimization, class redefinition, biased lock revocation) also cause stop-the-world pauses that don't appear in GC logs.

Part 15

Tuning Methodology: A Systematic Approach

Tuning JVMs without methodology wastes time and often makes things worse. Follow this process:

Step 1: Establish a baseline

Before changing anything:

# Capture current heap and GC configuration
jcmd <pid> VM.flags > baseline_flags.txt
jstat -gcutil <pid> 1000 60 > baseline_gc.txt

Define your success metric: "p99 GC pause < 50ms" or "heap footprint < 1.5 GB" or "zero Full GC events per hour".

Step 2: Profile, don't guess

Use JFR (Java Flight Recorder) to record a representative traffic window:

# Start recording
jcmd <pid> JFR.start duration=60s filename=/tmp/recording.jfr settings=profile

# Analyze with JDK Mission Control
jmc

Key JFR views:
- GC → pause times, cause, collection counts
- Memory → allocation rate, promotion rate, live set
- Threads → thread count, lock contention
- Method Profiling → CPU hotspots

Step 3: Change one flag at a time

Never change five flags simultaneously. You cannot attribute the observed effect to any individual change.

Step 4: Load test under realistic conditions

GC behavior is load-dependent. A flag that eliminates Full GC at 10 req/s may cause evacuation failure at 1000 req/s.

Step 5: Verify in staging before production

Part 16

Throughput vs Latency Trade-offs

Every GC tuning decision is a point on the throughput/latency/footprint triangle. You can optimize for two; the third will suffer.

Maximize throughput (batch jobs, data pipelines):

-XX:+UseParallelGC
-XX:GCTimeRatio=19          # 95% app time, 5% GC time (default)
-XX:AdaptiveSizePolicyWeight=90
-Xms8g -Xmx8g

Parallel GC runs all GC phases stop-the-world but uses all CPUs maximally for GC work. Perfect for map-reduce style jobs where latency is irrelevant and throughput is everything.

Minimize latency (real-time APIs, user-facing services):

-XX:+UseZGC
-XX:+ZGenerational          # Java 21+
-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=10     # ZGC targets sub-ms but respects this as hint
-Xms4g -Xmx4g
-XX:ZCollectionInterval=1

ZGC achieves pauses under 1 ms for most workloads by doing all mark/relocate work concurrently.

Balance (most web services):

-XX:+UseG1GC
-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200
-XX:G1HeapRegionSize=8m
-Xms4g -Xmx4g

G1GC with a 200ms pause target works for most HTTP APIs where p99 < 500ms is acceptable.

Part 17

Handling GC Pressure: Common Scenarios

Scenario 1: Frequent Full GC (Heap exhaustion)

Symptoms: Full GC (Heap Dump Initiated) or Full GC (Ergonomics) in logs.

# Diagnosis: watch live data growing per collection
jstat -gcutil <pid> 1000 | awk '{print $8}'  # OU = old gen used %

# Fix options:
# 1. Increase heap (if memory available)
-Xmx6g

# 2. Find memory leak (next lesson)
# 3. Increase IHOP to start concurrent mark earlier
-XX:InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent=35

Scenario 2: Evacuation failure (G1GC)

Symptoms: (to-space exhausted) or (promotion failed) in GC logs.

# Fix: increase heap, increase reserve, tune IHOP
-XX:G1ReservePercent=15
-XX:InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent=40

Scenario 3: Humongous object allocation in G1GC

Objects larger than 50% of a G1 region are "humongous" and bypass Young gen entirely, allocated directly into Old gen contiguous regions.

# Symptom: frequent Young GC triggered by humongous allocation
# Fix: increase region size so objects are no longer humongous
-XX:G1HeapRegionSize=16m   # or 32m for very large objects

Scenario 4: Code cache full

Symptoms: CodeCache is full. Compiler has been disabled. in logs.

-XX:ReservedCodeCacheSize=512m
Part 18

Production Monitoring: JVM Metrics to Track

Essential JVM metrics for production monitoring (Micrometer / Prometheus):

Metric Alert threshold Meaning
jvm_memory_used_bytes{area="heap"} >85% of max Heap pressure
jvm_gc_pause_seconds_max >500ms Pause SLO breach
jvm_gc_live_data_size_bytes Growing over days Potential memory leak
jvm_memory_used_bytes{area="nonheap"} >80% of max Metaspace pressure
jvm_threads_live Unexpected growth Thread leak
jvm_classes_loaded Unexpected growth Classloader leak

JMX-based monitoring:

# Enable JMX remotely (use with authentication in production)
-Dcom.sun.management.jmxremote
-Dcom.sun.management.jmxremote.port=9999
-Dcom.sun.management.jmxremote.authenticate=true
-Dcom.sun.management.jmxremote.ssl=true

# Connect with JConsole or VisualVM
jconsole <host>:9999

Java Flight Recorder continuous recording (production-safe):

# Enable always-on JFR with low overhead (< 1%)
-XX:StartFlightRecording=delay=30s,duration=0s,name=continuous,\
  filename=/var/jfr/continuous.jfr,maxsize=200m,maxage=6h,\
  settings=default,dumponexit=true,path-to-gc-roots=false

This gives you a rolling 6-hour window of JVM behavior, available immediately when an incident occurs.

Part 19

Production JVM Tuning Checklist

Use this checklist before deploying any Java application to production:

Heap configuration:
- [ ] -Xms equals -Xmx (prevents heap resizing)
- [ ] Heap is 60–75% of container/machine memory limit
- [ ] Or: MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 if using container-aware sizing
- [ ] Heap size validated against actual live data set size from staging load test

GC configuration:
- [ ] Explicit GC collector chosen (don't rely on ergonomics default)
- [ ] GC logging enabled and writing to persistent storage
- [ ] GC pause time target set (MaxGCPauseMillis)
- [ ] No System.gc() calls in application code (or -XX:+DisableExplicitGC)

Metaspace:
- [ ] MaxMetaspaceSize set to prevent unbounded native growth
- [ ] Value validated against actual class count from staging

Diagnostics:
- [ ] -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError enabled
- [ ] HeapDumpPath writable and has sufficient disk space
- [ ] Error file path set (-XX:ErrorFile)
- [ ] JFR continuous recording enabled

Container:
- [ ] -XX:+UseContainerSupport verified (should be default ON)
- [ ] ActiveProcessorCount set if CPU limits apply
- [ ] ParallelGCThreads and ConcGCThreads explicitly set for CPU-limited containers

Performance:
- [ ] AppCDS archive generated for containerized deployments
- [ ] Startup time measured; adjust liveness probe delays accordingly

Part 20

Spring Boot JVM Options

Spring Boot applications have specific characteristics: annotation processing, CGLIB proxies, embedded Tomcat/Netty, and significant startup class loading.

Recommended production Spring Boot JVM flags:

JAVA_OPTS="\
  -server \
  -XX:+UseContainerSupport \
  -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 \
  -XX:InitialRAMPercentage=50.0 \
  -XX:+UseG1GC \
  -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200 \
  -XX:G1HeapRegionSize=8m \
  -XX:+G1UseAdaptiveIHOP \
  -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256m \
  -Xss256k \
  -XX:ReservedCodeCacheSize=256m \
  -XX:+TieredCompilation \
  -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError \
  -XX:HeapDumpPath=/tmp/heap.hprof \
  -XX:ErrorFile=/tmp/jvm_crash_%p.log \
  -Xlog:gc*:file=/var/log/app/gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags:filecount=5,filesize=20m \
  -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8 \
  -Djava.security.egd=file:/dev/./urandom"

Spring Boot startup optimization:

# Lazy initialization (Spring Boot 2.2+) — reduces startup time ~30%
spring.main.lazy-initialization=true

# Spring AOT (Spring Boot 3+) + GraalVM native image for sub-100ms startup
# (different from JVM tuning — replaces JIT with AOT compilation)

For Spring Boot with virtual threads (Java 21 + Spring Boot 3.2+):

spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true

# JVM: virtual threads are lightweight; reduce platform thread pool sizes
server.tomcat.threads.max=50   # Much lower than default 200

Actuator JVM metrics endpoint:

management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,info,metrics,prometheus
  metrics:
    export:
      prometheus:
        enabled: true

Access /actuator/metrics/jvm.gc.pause and /actuator/metrics/jvm.memory.used for live JVM data.

Part 21

Common JVM Tuning Mistakes

Mistake 1: Setting -Xmx too large in containers

# WRONG: JVM thinks it has 64 GB; container has 4 GB
java -Xmx64g -jar app.jar

# RIGHT
java -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 -jar app.jar

Mistake 2: Using -XX:+UseConcMarkSweepGC on Java 14+

CMS was removed in Java 14. Specifying it causes the JVM to print a warning and fall back to serial GC — catastrophic performance.

Mistake 3: Disabling explicit GC without understanding implications

# -XX:+DisableExplicitGC prevents System.gc() from working
# This breaks off-heap buffer reclamation in NIO / direct ByteBuffers
# Use -XX:+ExplicitGCInvokesConcurrent instead (keeps G1 concurrent)
-XX:+ExplicitGCInvokesConcurrent

Mistake 4: Setting GC pause target too aggressively

# 5ms target with G1GC on a 16 GB heap — G1 physically cannot achieve this
# Result: G1 constantly tries, collects tiny sets, heap fills faster than it can reclaim
-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=5   # Too low for G1GC; use ZGC instead

Mistake 5: Ignoring non-heap memory

The sum of heap + metaspace + code cache + thread stacks + direct buffers must fit in container memory. Many OOMKiller kills are not heap OOM — they're the container's cgroup memory limit being exceeded by native memory.

Mistake 6: Tuning in isolation without load testing

JVM GC behavior is highly load-dependent. A flag combination that looks perfect at 10% load can cause evacuation failures at peak traffic.

Part 22

Advanced Flags: Biased Locking, NUMA, and Large Pages

Biased locking (Java 8–14, removed Java 21):

# Disabled by default in Java 15+ due to poor real-world performance
-XX:-UseBiasedLocking   # Disable explicitly if on Java 8–14 with contended locks

NUMA-aware heap allocation (multi-socket servers):

-XX:+UseNUMA   # Enable NUMA-aware allocation (requires NUMA hardware + OS support)
# Allocates Eden regions on the NUMA node closest to the allocating thread

Effective on large multi-socket servers; negligible or harmful on single-socket machines or VMs.

Large pages (HugeTLB):

-XX:+UseLargePages           # Enable large page mapping for heap
-XX:+UseTransparentHugePages # Use kernel THP (Linux-specific)
-XX:LargePageSizeInBytes=2m  # Usually 2 MB

Large pages reduce TLB pressure on large heaps. Requires OS configuration (/proc/sys/vm/nr_hugepages). Can improve throughput 5–15% on heap-intensive workloads.

GraalVM JIT (Java 21+ with Graal JIT):

# Enable experimental Graal JIT (replaces C2 for advanced optimizations)
-XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions -XX:+UseJVMCICompiler

Practice

Exercise 1 — Baseline and Flag Audit

  1. Start a Spring Boot application with default flags.
  2. Run jcmd <pid> VM.flags and compare initial heap (InitialHeapSize) with max heap (MaxHeapSize) — note the ergonomics-calculated values.
  3. Run java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep -E "UseG1GC|UseParallelGC|UseZGC" to confirm which collector was selected by ergonomics.
  4. Add -XX:+PrintCommandLineFlags to the startup command and verify your explicit flags appear.

Exercise 2 — Container Heap Sizing

  1. Run a Spring Boot container with docker run -m 512m.
  2. Without container flags: observe the heap set to 1/4 of host memory (wrong).
  3. Add -XX:+UseContainerSupport -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0.
  4. Verify heap is now ~384 MB via jcmd <pid> VM.flags | grep MaxHeapSize.

Exercise 3 — GC Log Analysis

  1. Run a load test against a Spring Boot app with G1GC and GC logging enabled.
  2. Download the GC log and upload to gceasy.io.
  3. Record: p99 pause time, allocation rate (MB/s), whether any Full GC events occurred.
  4. Adjust MaxGCPauseMillis up or down by 50% and re-run. Observe the effect on throughput.

Exercise 4 — Native Memory Tracking

  1. Start an app with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary.
  2. Run jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory baseline.
  3. Send traffic for 5 minutes.
  4. Run jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary.diff.
  5. Identify which memory category grew the most.

Exercise 5 — Production Checklist Review

Take an existing production deployment's JAVA_OPTS. Run through the 20-item production checklist from Part 19. Identify any missing items and add them. Measure startup time before and after adding AppCDS.

Part 1

What Is a Java Memory Leak?

In a garbage-collected language like Java, a "memory leak" is technically a reachability leak: objects that are no longer needed by the application but remain reachable through a reference chain that the developer forgot to clean up. Because the GC cannot collect reachable objects, they accumulate over time until the heap fills and the JVM throws OutOfMemoryError.

This is different from a C/C++ memory leak, where memory is freed with no remaining reference. In Java, the objects exist and are accessible — the program simply forgot to stop holding them.

The classic definition:

> A Java memory leak occurs when objects accumulate in the heap faster than they can be GC'd, either because live references are never released or because the live set grows unboundedly.

Three root causes:

  1. Explicit retention: code intentionally holds references (in a cache, list, map) but never removes entries
  2. Implicit retention: framework or platform code holds references on behalf of the application (listener registries, thread-local variables, classloader-retained static fields)
  3. Classloader leaks: classes stay loaded (and their statics) because a classloader remains reachable

Memory leak vs. memory pressure:

A memory pressure situation is temporary: the heap is large because the application is under high load, but objects are collected between bursts. If you restart and the heap grows at the same rate regardless of traffic, you likely have a memory pressure issue, not a leak. A leak is characterized by monotonically increasing heap occupancy over time, with the live set growing after each Full GC.

Part 2

Recognizing Memory Leak Symptoms

In GC logs:

# Healthy: Old gen oscillates; Old gen after Full GC is stable
[GC pause (G1 Evacuation Pause) ... 4G->3.8G(8G)]
[Full GC (Ergonomics) ... 7.9G->3.1G(8G)]  ← periodic, live set stable

# Leaking: Old gen minimum after Full GC grows each time
[Full GC (Ergonomics) ... 7G->3.1G(8G)]   # after restart
[Full GC (Ergonomics) ... 7G->3.4G(8G)]   # 1 hour later
[Full GC (Ergonomics) ... 7G->3.8G(8G)]   # 2 hours later  ← live set growing
[Full GC (Ergonomics) ... 7G->4.5G(8G)]   # 6 hours later

The key signal is the post-Full-GC live data size trending upward over time.

In metrics dashboards:
- jvm_gc_live_data_size_bytes (Micrometer) grows monotonically over days
- jvm_memory_used_bytes{area="heap"} never drops below previous cycle's minimum
- Full GC frequency increasing over hours/days without increasing traffic

In application behavior:
- Gradually degrading response times
- Increasing GC pause duration and frequency
- Eventual OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space
- Pods restarting with OOMKilled in Kubernetes

Part 3

Heap Dump Generation: Overview

A heap dump is a snapshot of all objects in the JVM heap at a point in time, written to a binary .hprof file. It contains:
- Every object instance and its class
- Every field value of every object
- The complete reference graph (who holds what)
- Object sizes (shallow and retained)

A heap dump is the definitive tool for memory leak analysis. Everything else (jstat, thread dumps, metrics) gives you indicators — only the heap dump shows you which objects are leaking and why.

Heap dump timing strategy:

  • Capture when Old generation is at a high-water mark (just before a Full GC, or right after an OOM)
  • Avoid capturing during heavy transient load — you'll see large temporary data structures
  • For long-running leaks: capture two dumps 1 hour apart, compare the delta
Part 4

jmap: Heap Dump Acquisition

jmap is the primary command-line tool for acquiring heap dumps from a running JVM.

Basic heap dump:

# Write full heap dump (all live objects) to file
jmap -dump:live,format=b,file=/tmp/heap.hprof <pid>

# Without 'live': includes unreachable objects (larger file, rarely needed)
jmap -dump:format=b,file=/tmp/heap.hprof <pid>

The live option triggers a Full GC before dumping, ensuring you capture only the retained live set — exactly what you need for leak analysis.

Heap histogram (no dump required):

# Print object count and size, sorted by size
jmap -histo:live <pid> | head -50

# Output format:
# num    #instances  #bytes  class name
#   1:       142851  45234256  [B        ← byte arrays (often leak indicator)
#   2:        89234  28938576  [C        ← char arrays
#   3:        12345   1234560  java.lang.String
#   4:         8901    712080  com.example.UserSession  ← suspicious count?

This is fast (seconds) and safe for production — use it as a first triage step before committing to a full heap dump.

Heap summary:

jmap -heap <pid>
# Shows: GC algorithm, heap configuration, heap usage by region

jcmd alternative (preferred for modern JVMs):

jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump filename=/tmp/heap.hprof
jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram -all

jcmd is preferred in production over jmap for newer JVMs because it uses the JVM's attach API safely.

Part 5

Automatic Heap Dump on OOM

Always configure this in production — by the time an OOM crashes the process, you have a chance to capture what happened:

-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError
-XX:HeapDumpPath=/var/dumps/

# Or with PID in filename
-XX:HeapDumpPath=/var/dumps/heap_%p_%t.hprof

In Kubernetes: The dump directory must be a persistent volume, not the container overlay FS (which may be destroyed when the pod restarts). Mount a PVC or use a shared NFS path:

volumeMounts:
  - name: heap-dumps
    mountPath: /var/dumps
volumes:
  - name: heap-dumps
    persistentVolumeClaim:
      claimName: heap-dump-pvc

OOM signal for alerting:

Configure your log aggregator to alert on:

java.lang.OutOfMemoryError
Heap dump file created
Part 6

Eclipse Memory Analyzer Tool (MAT): Setup

Eclipse MAT is the industry-standard tool for heap dump analysis. It handles dumps from kilobytes to dozens of gigabytes efficiently.

Installation:

  1. Download the standalone MAT from https://eclipse.dev/mat/downloads.php
  2. MAT is separate from the Eclipse IDE — download the standalone "MemoryAnalyzer" package
  3. For large heap dumps (>4 GB), increase MAT's own heap in MemoryAnalyzer.ini:
-Xmx12g
-XX:+UseG1GC

Opening a heap dump:

File → Open Heap Dump → select heap.hprof

MAT parses the dump and builds index files alongside the .hprof. This is a one-time operation per dump — subsequent opens are fast.

MAT overview screen:

After parsing, the overview shows:
- Total heap size captured
- Total object count
- System properties at capture time
- Links to key analysis views

Part 7

Leak Suspects Report

The Leak Suspects Report is MAT's automated analysis that identifies the most likely memory leak candidates.

Reports → Leak Suspects

MAT performs an automated dominator tree analysis and identifies objects that:
- Retain an unusually large portion of the heap
- Are not expected to retain that much memory

Reading the report:

Problem Suspect 1
=================
One instance of "org.springframework.context.support.GenericApplicationContext"
loaded by "sun.misc.Launcher$AppClassLoader @ 0xc1234567"
occupies 1,847,223,456 (72.4%) bytes.

The memory is accumulated in one instance of
"java.util.HashMap$Entry[]", loaded by "<system class loader>"
which occupies 1,844,890,112 (72.3%) bytes.

Keywords: HashMap, UserSessionCache, GenericApplicationContext

This tells you: a HashMap inside the Spring ApplicationContext is retaining 72% of the heap. The path from ApplicationContext → HashMap tells you which bean and which field.

Important: Leak Suspects are hypotheses, not conclusions. Always verify by examining the dominator tree and reference paths manually.

Part 8

Dominator Tree Analysis

The dominator tree is the most powerful view in MAT. It shows every object in the heap, sorted by retained heap — the amount of memory that would be freed if that object and everything it references were collected.

Window → Heap Dump Details → Dominator Tree

Key columns:
- Shallow Heap: memory occupied by the object itself (not its references)
- Retained Heap: memory freed if this object were GC'd (itself + everything it exclusively references)
- % of total: retained heap as percentage of total heap

Identifying a leak in the dominator tree:

Class Name                          Shallow    Retained    %
com.example.cache.SessionCache      48 B       1.2 GB      74%
  └─ HashMap$Entry[]                64 B       1.1 GB      68%
       └─ [80,000 entries]
            └─ UserSession          192 B       ...
                 └─ byte[] (data)   2.3 MB      ...

This shows SessionCache retains 1.2 GB because it holds 80,000 UserSession objects that were never evicted.

Grouping objects by class:

Window → Heap Dump Details → Histogram

Sort by "Retained Heap" column. Any class with an unexpectedly high count or size is a candidate.

Part 9

Leak Pattern: Static Collection Leaks

The most common Java memory leak pattern: a static field holds a Map, List, or Set that grows without bound because entries are added but never removed.

Example:

public class RequestTracker {
    // LEAK: static map grows forever; sessions added but never removed
    private static final Map<String, RequestContext> activeRequests
        = new HashMap<>();

    public static void trackRequest(String id, RequestContext ctx) {
        activeRequests.put(id, ctx);   // added here
    }
    // no removeRequest() method, or it's never called
}

Why this is insidious:

  • The map is reachable via the static field (which is a GC root via the classloader)
  • Every RequestContext it holds is also reachable
  • Everything referenced by RequestContext is also reachable
  • The GC has no choice — it cannot collect any of it

Recognizing in MAT:

In the dominator tree, you'll see a HashMap or HashMap$Entry[] with a very high retained heap, dominated by a class that has a static field. To find the path:

MAT → Right-click on object → Path to GC Roots → exclude weak/soft references

The path will show: static field RequestTracker.activeRequests → HashMap → ...

Fix:

// Option 1: Use a cache with expiration
private static final Cache<String, RequestContext> activeRequests =
    Caffeine.newBuilder().expireAfterAccess(30, TimeUnit.MINUTES).build();

// Option 2: Use a bounded map
private static final Map<String, RequestContext> activeRequests =
    Collections.synchronizedMap(new LinkedHashMap<>() {
        @Override
        protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry eldest) {
            return size() > 10_000;
        }
    });

// Option 3: Clean up explicitly
public static void endRequest(String id) {
    activeRequests.remove(id);
}
Part 10

Leak Pattern: Event Listener Leaks

Listener/observer leaks occur when objects register themselves as listeners on a long-lived event source but forget to deregister.

Example:

public class MetricsCollector {
    private final ApplicationEventPublisher publisher;

    public MetricsCollector(ApplicationEventPublisher publisher) {
        this.publisher = publisher;
        // LEAK: registers 'this' as listener, never unregisters
        ((ApplicationEventMulticaster) publisher).addApplicationListener(this::onEvent);
    }

    private void onEvent(ApplicationEvent event) { ... }
    // No destroy() / cleanup() / @PreDestroy method
}

How the leak works:

ApplicationEventMulticaster (singleton, application lifetime)
  └─ listeners list
       └─ MetricsCollector instance (lambda reference)
            └─ everything MetricsCollector references

Each time a MetricsCollector is created (e.g., per-request in a prototype bean), a new reference is added to the multicaster's listener list. None are ever removed.

Recognizing in MAT:

High count of a class that implements a listener interface. The path to GC roots leads through a singleton event source's listener collection.

Common leak scenarios:
- Spring ApplicationListener beans created as prototypes
- Swing ActionListener registered on a button from a dialog that was closed
- JMX NotificationListener never removed
- MessageListener added to JMS connection but connection never closed

Fix:

@Component
public class MetricsCollector implements ApplicationListener<ApplicationEvent>,
                                         DisposableBean {
    private final ApplicationEventMulticaster multicaster;

    public MetricsCollector(ApplicationEventMulticaster multicaster) {
        this.multicaster = multicaster;
        multicaster.addApplicationListener(this);
    }

    @Override
    public void destroy() {
        multicaster.removeApplicationListener(this);  // cleanup
    }
}
Part 11

Leak Pattern: ThreadLocal Leaks

ThreadLocal variables are stored in the thread's ThreadLocalMap. They are GC'd when the thread terminates. In thread pool environments (Tomcat, virtual threads pre-21), threads are never terminated — they live for the application's lifetime. Any ThreadLocal value set but not removed persists indefinitely.

Example:

public class SecurityContext {
    private static final ThreadLocal<User> currentUser = new ThreadLocal<>();

    public static void setUser(User user) {
        currentUser.set(user);  // set on entry to request handler
    }

    public static User getUser() {
        return currentUser.get();
    }

    // LEAK: no remove() call after request completes
    // Thread returns to pool with User still in ThreadLocalMap
}

The leak mechanism:

Thread (from Tomcat thread pool, lives forever)
  └─ ThreadLocalMap
       └─ Entry[ThreadLocal<User> → User instance]
            └─ User.session (HttpSession)
                 └─ User.cart (ShoppingCart with product data)
                      └─ ...

The User cannot be GC'd because the thread is alive and holds a strong reference to it via ThreadLocalMap. In Tomcat's 200-thread pool, 200 User objects are permanently retained — one per thread, replaced on each request but the old one retained until the thread processes the next request.

Recognizing in MAT:

Large number of instances of a class associated with HTTP request context (User, Session, RequestContext), pointed to from ThreadLocal$ThreadLocalMap$Entry objects.

Fix:

// Always use try-finally or servlet filter cleanup
public class UserContextFilter implements Filter {
    @Override
    public void doFilter(ServletRequest req, ServletResponse res, FilterChain chain)
            throws IOException, ServletException {
        try {
            SecurityContext.setUser(extractUser(req));
            chain.doFilter(req, res);
        } finally {
            SecurityContext.clear();  // CRITICAL: always remove
        }
    }
}

InheritableThreadLocal creates additional risk: values are copied to child threads at creation time. In ForkJoinPool (used by parallelStream()), this copies context into pool threads, which then retain it.

Part 12

Leak Pattern: Classloader Leaks

Classloader leaks are the most severe leak pattern in Java because they prevent entire class sets from being collected. Common in application servers, hot-deploy frameworks, and plugin architectures.

How classloader leaks work:

Every class holds a reference to its classloader. If anything outside the classloader holds a reference to any class (or instance of a class) loaded by that classloader, the entire classloader — and every class it loaded — cannot be collected.

Static field in JDK class (long-lived)
  └─ instance of com.example.plugin.MyListener (loaded by PluginClassLoader)
       └─ PluginClassLoader (classloader for the plugin)
            └─ [every class loaded by this classloader]
                 └─ static fields of those classes → more objects

Common triggers:

  1. JDBC driver registration: java.sql.DriverManager holds a static registry of drivers. If a plugin registers a JDBC driver and then undeploys without deregistering it, the driver (and its classloader) leaks.
// In plugin's shutdown, deregister:
Enumeration<Driver> drivers = DriverManager.getDrivers();
while (drivers.hasMoreElements()) {
    Driver driver = drivers.nextElement();
    if (driver.getClass().getClassLoader() == Thread.currentThread().getContextClassLoader()) {
        DriverManager.deregisterDriver(driver);
    }
}

  1. java.util.logging: LogManager holds references to Logger instances. Loggers registered by plugin code retain the plugin's classloader.

  2. RMI references: java.rmi.server.UnicastRemoteObject stubs registered in JVM-global registries.

  3. Static fields in plugin classes: if a plugin class has a static Map<String, Object> populated at runtime, the map keeps the classloader alive because: plugin instance → classloader → all plugin classes → static fields → map contents.

Recognizing in MAT:

Reports → Leak Suspects

Look for ClassLoader instances with high retained heap. Follow the reference path to identify what's holding the classloader alive.

Window → Heap Dump Details → List Objects → class: java.lang.ClassLoader

Sort by retained heap. Any classloader retaining significant memory after a hot-deploy cycle is a leak candidate.

Part 13

Leak Pattern: Inner Class and Closure Leaks

Non-static inner classes and anonymous classes (lambdas that capture this) hold an implicit reference to their enclosing instance.

Example:

public class DataService {
    private final byte[] cache = new byte[10 * 1024 * 1024];  // 10 MB

    public Runnable createTask() {
        // LEAK: this anonymous Runnable holds an implicit reference to DataService
        return new Runnable() {
            @Override
            public void run() {
                // even if this method never uses 'cache', the reference exists
                System.out.println("task running");
            }
        };
    }
}

// Usage
scheduler.schedule(dataService.createTask(), 1, TimeUnit.HOURS);
// If dataService is no longer needed but the task is scheduled,
// the entire DataService (including 10 MB cache) is kept alive for 1 hour

Lambda captures and closures:

public class ReportGenerator {
    private final LargeDataSet data;  // 500 MB

    public void scheduleReport() {
        // Lambda captures 'this' implicitly via 'data' field access
        executor.submit(() -> processData(this.data));
        // Until the executor task runs, 'this' (and 500 MB data) is retained
    }
}

Fix:

public void scheduleReport() {
    LargeDataSet snapshot = this.data;  // copy reference, not 'this'
    executor.submit(() -> processData(snapshot));
    // Only 'snapshot' is captured — 'this' and all other fields can be GC'd
}
Part 14

Leak Pattern: Cache Without Eviction

Caches are intentional memory consumers — the risk is implementing them without size bounds or TTL.

Unbounded cache:

public class QueryCache {
    // LEAK: grows without bound; never evicted
    private final Map<String, QueryResult> cache = new HashMap<>();

    public QueryResult execute(String sql) {
        return cache.computeIfAbsent(sql, this::runQuery);
    }
}

Soft and weak references:

Java provides SoftReference and WeakReference for cache-friendly retention:

// WeakReference: GC'd eagerly when no strong reference exists
private final Map<Key, WeakReference<Value>> weakCache = new WeakHashMap<>();

// SoftReference: GC'd only when heap is under pressure
private final Map<Key, SoftReference<Value>> softCache = new HashMap<>();

WeakHashMap automatically removes entries when the key is GC'd. Useful for keying on objects with external lifecycle control.

Production cache libraries (preferred over manual implementation):

// Caffeine (recommended for modern Java)
Cache<String, QueryResult> cache = Caffeine.newBuilder()
    .maximumSize(10_000)
    .expireAfterWrite(10, TimeUnit.MINUTES)
    .expireAfterAccess(5, TimeUnit.MINUTES)
    .softValues()             // evict values under memory pressure
    .recordStats()            // enable hit rate monitoring
    .build();

Monitor cache hit rates and memory usage. A cache with a hit rate below 50% may be storing data that's never reused — pure memory waste.

Part 15

VisualVM: Interactive Heap Analysis

VisualVM is a GUI profiler bundled with the JDK (and available standalone) for interactive heap analysis of running JVMs.

Connecting to a running JVM:

jvisualvm   # Launch (older JDKs)
# or download standalone from https://visualvm.github.io/

VisualVM discovers local JVMs automatically via the process list. For remote JVMs, enable JMX:

-Dcom.sun.management.jmxremote.port=9999
-Dcom.sun.management.jmxremote.authenticate=false  # dev only
-Dcom.sun.management.jmxremote.ssl=false           # dev only

Heap and live object monitoring:

The Monitor tab shows:
- Heap used vs. heap max (live chart)
- Metaspace usage
- GC activity timeline
- Thread count

Click Perform GC to force a collection and observe whether heap drops back to baseline (if not, suspect a leak).

Heap Dump in VisualVM:

Right-click on the process → Heap Dump

VisualVM opens the dump in its built-in analyzer. The Classes tab shows instances by count/size. The Instances view shows individual objects and their field values.

Memory sampling (no heap dump needed):

Profiler tab → Memory → Start

Shows live object count and size per class, sampled every few seconds. Useful for confirming a growing class count without the overhead of a full heap dump.

Part 16

JVM Flags for Memory Analysis

Heap dump on OOM (covered in Part 5, expanded here):

-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError
-XX:HeapDumpPath=/var/dumps/
-XX:OnOutOfMemoryError="kill -9 %p"  # terminate after dump (prevents zombie pod)

GC ergonomics for easier leak detection:

# Print class histogram after each Full GC
-XX:+PrintClassHistogramAfterFullGC

# More verbose GC details
-Xlog:gc+heap*:file=gc-heap.log:time,uptime

Triggering heap histogram without a dump:

# Via jcmd (safe, recommended)
jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram | head -30

# Sorted by instance count (good for finding runaway object creation)
jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram | sort -rn -k2 | head -20

Continuous heap monitoring with jstat:

# Print GC stats every second, 60 times
jstat -gcutil <pid> 1000 60

# Column meanings:
# S0  S1  E    O    M   CCS  YGC  YGCT  FGC  FGCT  GCT
# 0   0   45   72   93  89   143  3.2   2    0.9   4.1
# S0/S1: Survivor % used
# E: Eden % used
# O: Old % used  ← watch this grow in a leak
# FGC: Full GC count  ← should be low/stable
Part 17

Heap Histogram as a First Response Tool

When you suspect a leak but can't afford a full heap dump during business hours, the heap histogram is your best friend. It's generated in milliseconds and has minimal impact.

Getting a histogram:

# Most common approach: via jmap
jmap -histo:live <pid> | head -30

# Via jcmd (equivalent, preferred)
jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram -all

Reading the histogram:

 num     #instances         #bytes  class name
 ---     ----------         ------  ----------
   1:       8432156      1349144960  [B                          ← byte[]
   2:       7231893       578551440  [C                          ← char[]
   3:       5893421       471473680  java.lang.String
   4:        512893       123094320  com.example.UserSession     ← suspicious
   5:        512893        98474256  com.example.SessionData
   6:        512893        16412576  com.example.UserPreferences

The 512,893 UserSession objects, each also pointing to a SessionData and UserPreferences, is clearly anomalous if you're not serving 500,000 concurrent users.

Comparing histograms over time:

# Capture baseline
jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram > hist_1.txt

# Wait 30 minutes
sleep 1800

# Capture second histogram
jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram > hist_2.txt

# Diff — look for classes growing in instance count
diff hist_1.txt hist_2.txt | grep ">" | sort -rn -k3 | head -20

Any class growing at a rate disproportionate to traffic is a leak candidate.

Part 18

Production Incident Workflow

When a production JVM is leaking memory and an OutOfMemoryError is imminent, follow this systematic workflow:

Phase 1: Triage (0–5 minutes)

# 1. Confirm it's a heap issue (vs metaspace or native)
jstat -gcutil <pid> 1000 5
# O% (Old gen) consistently >90%? → heap leak

# 2. Quick histogram to identify top leaking classes
jmap -histo:live <pid> | head -30

# 3. Check if heap is still growing or plateaued
watch -n 5 "jstat -gc <pid> | awk '{print \$8}'"  # OC (Old capacity used)

Phase 2: Diagnosis (5–20 minutes)

# 4. Generate full heap dump (may take 30s–5min depending on heap size)
# IMPORTANT: this pauses the JVM while writing — warn the team
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump filename=/var/dumps/heap_$(date +%s).hprof

# 5. Check dump file size (should be close to retained heap size)
ls -lh /var/dumps/heap_*.hprof

Phase 3: Stabilization (parallel with diagnosis)

# 6. If system is degraded, restart in controlled fashion
# For Kubernetes: cordon the node, delete the pod, let it reschedule
kubectl cordon <node>
kubectl delete pod <pod> -n <namespace>

# 7. If more time is needed: force GC to buy time
jcmd <pid> GC.run

Phase 4: Analysis (20 minutes – 2 hours)

  1. Copy heap dump to analysis workstation (avoid analyzing on production host)
  2. Open in MAT
  3. Run Leak Suspects report
  4. Examine dominator tree for largest retained sets
  5. For each suspect: path to GC roots, identify which code holds the reference
  6. Cross-reference with recent deployments and code changes

Phase 5: Fix and Verify

# After deploying fix:
# Monitor live set growth rate for 24 hours
# Compare post-Full-GC Old gen level to pre-fix baseline
jstat -gcutil <new_pid> 60000 60   # every minute for 1 hour
Part 19

OutOfMemoryError Types and Root Causes

Not all OOMs are heap leaks. Diagnosing the OOM message is critical to choosing the right tool.

OOM Message Root cause Fix
Java heap space Heap leak or undersized heap MAT analysis, increase -Xmx
GC overhead limit exceeded Heap pressure, not necessarily a leak Increase heap, fix allocation rate
Metaspace Too many classes loaded (classloader leak) MAT classloader analysis, set MaxMetaspaceSize
unable to create new native thread Too many threads, OS thread limit Reduce thread count, increase OS limits
Direct buffer memory NIO direct ByteBuffer not released Fix direct buffer lifecycle, set MaxDirectMemorySize
Compressed class space Too many class definitions Increase CompressedClassSpaceSize
request size bytes for reason. Out of swap space? Native heap OOM Use NMT to investigate native memory

Distinguishing heap OOM from native OOM:

A heap OOM throws java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space and can be caught. A native memory OOM is a SIGSEGV that crashes the JVM entirely, writing an hs_err_pid.log file.

# Parse hs_err log to understand crash reason
head -100 hs_err_pid<N>.log
# Look for: "Native memory allocation ... failed to allocate"
Part 20

Framework-Specific Leak Patterns

Spring context leaks:

// LEAK: creating ApplicationContext without closing it
ApplicationContext ctx = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(Config.class);
// used and forgotten — all Spring beans retained until JVM exit
// Fix:
try (ConfigurableApplicationContext ctx =
        new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(Config.class)) {
    ctx.getBean(MyService.class).run();
}  // automatically closes, destroys beans, clears caches

Hibernate/JPA session leaks:

// LEAK: EntityManager not closed
EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager();
// ...forgot em.close()
// Hibernate's first-level cache (per-session identity map) retains all loaded entities

Spring @Cacheable with unlimited size:

@Cacheable("products")
public Product getProduct(String id) { ... }

Without configuration, Spring's ConcurrentMapCacheManager (default) stores all values indefinitely. In production, always configure a bounded cache:

@Bean
public CacheManager cacheManager() {
    return new CaffeineCacheManager("products") {{
        setCaffeine(Caffeine.newBuilder()
            .maximumSize(10_000)
            .expireAfterWrite(1, TimeUnit.HOURS));
    }};
}
Part 21

Automated Leak Detection

Java Flight Recorder with heap analysis:

# Record with heap statistics enabled
jcmd <pid> JFR.start duration=300s filename=/tmp/leak_check.jfr \
  settings=profile name=leak_check
# Then in JDK Mission Control: Memory tab → Object Statistics → watch trends

Heap leak detection in tests (unit/integration):

Use the jqwik or Plumbr libraries, or a simple manual approach:

@Test
public void testNoCacheLeak() throws Exception {
    long before = Runtime.getRuntime().totalMemory() - Runtime.getRuntime().freeMemory();

    for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) {
        service.processRequest("key-" + i);
    }

    System.gc();
    Thread.sleep(100);
    System.gc();

    long after = Runtime.getRuntime().totalMemory() - Runtime.getRuntime().freeMemory();
    long growthMB = (after - before) / (1024 * 1024);

    assertTrue("Heap grew by " + growthMB + " MB, possible leak", growthMB < 10);
}

This is not a rigorous test (GC is non-deterministic) but catches gross leaks in CI.

Micrometer / Prometheus alerting for leaks:

# Alert rule: live data set growing > 5% per hour for 3 consecutive hours
- alert: JavaHeapLeak
  expr: |
    increase(jvm_gc_live_data_size_bytes[1h]) /
    jvm_gc_live_data_size_bytes offset 1h > 0.05
  for: 3h
  labels:
    severity: warning
  annotations:
    summary: "Possible Java heap leak in {{ $labels.instance }}"
Part 22

Prevention and Best Practices

Code review checklist for memory safety:

  • [ ] All caches have a maximum size or TTL
  • [ ] All event listeners have a corresponding deregister path
  • [ ] All ThreadLocal variables have remove() called in a finally block
  • [ ] Non-static inner classes and anonymous Runnables in long-lived contexts are static or use field references, not this captures
  • [ ] EntityManager and ApplicationContext are closed in try-with-resources
  • [ ] JDBC drivers registered by plugins are deregistered on shutdown
  • [ ] Collections used as accumulator (add-only) have documented size bounds

Architectural patterns that prevent leaks:

  1. Prefer value objects over mutable stateful sessions: short-lived, fully contained objects are collected immediately
  2. Use WeakReference for caches where the key's lifecycle controls value retention
  3. Use message queues instead of in-memory collections for cross-thread work queues
  4. Use bounded queues (ArrayBlockingQueue) instead of unbounded ones (LinkedList) for producer-consumer patterns
  5. Expose cache statistics and alert on size growth

Static analysis tools:

  • SpotBugs with fb-contrib plugin: detects some leak patterns statically
  • IntelliJ IDEA: warns about non-static inner classes capturing enclosing references
  • SonarQube rules: java:S2165 (ThreadLocal not removed), java:S1948 (serialization leak), java:S5164 (ThreadLocal not cleaned up)

Coding disciplines:

// Prefer try-with-resources for all closeable resources
try (InputStream is = Files.newInputStream(path);
     BufferedReader reader = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(is))) {
    return reader.lines().collect(Collectors.joining("\n"));
}  // all resources closed automatically, even on exception

// Always remove ThreadLocals in finally blocks
threadLocal.set(value);
try {
    doWork();
} finally {
    threadLocal.remove();  // non-negotiable
}

// Use Caffeine for all application-level caches
Cache<K, V> cache = Caffeine.newBuilder()
    .maximumSize(capacity)
    .expireAfterAccess(ttl, unit)
    .weakValues()       // allow GC under pressure
    .recordStats()      // monitor in production
    .build();

Practice

Exercise 1 — Heap Histogram Triage

  1. Write a simple Java class with a static HashMap that accumulates entries in a loop (never removing any).
  2. Run it and after 10 seconds, capture jmap -histo:live <pid> | head -20.
  3. Identify the suspect class by its instance count.
  4. Capture two histograms 30 seconds apart and compare the growth.

Exercise 2 — MAT: Dominator Tree and Leak Suspects

  1. Write a program that registers 10,000 listeners on an EventBus but never deregisters them.
  2. Let it run for 30 seconds, then force a Full GC and capture a heap dump.
  3. Open the dump in MAT, run the Leak Suspects report.
  4. Navigate the dominator tree to find the EventBus listener list.
  5. Use "Path to GC Roots" to confirm the reference chain from the leak to a GC root.

Exercise 3 — ThreadLocal Leak Simulation

  1. Create a servlet filter that sets a ThreadLocal with a large object (1 MB byte array) on each request but never calls remove().
  2. Send 1,000 requests to the application.
  3. Capture jmap -histo:live — count the number of byte arrays.
  4. Fix the filter to call remove() in a finally block and repeat the test.
  5. Compare histograms before and after the fix.

Exercise 4 — JFR Heap Trend Analysis

  1. Enable JFR continuous recording on a Spring Boot application.
  2. Run a load test for 5 minutes.
  3. Open the recording in JDK Mission Control.
  4. Navigate to Memory → Heap Usage and look for a monotonic trend in live set size after each GC.
  5. Navigate to Memory → Object Statistics and identify the top-growing classes by instance delta.

Exercise 5 — Production Incident Simulation

  1. Deploy a Spring Boot application with an intentional @Cacheable without bounds.
  2. Send traffic that populates the cache with unique keys.
  3. Simulate the incident response: capture histogram, identify suspect class, generate heap dump, analyze in MAT.
  4. Fix the cache configuration (add maximumSize) and verify the live set stops growing.
  5. Write an alert rule (as YAML) that would have caught this leak 2 hours before OOM.
