Part 1

Why Profiling Is Not Optional

Performance optimization without profiling is guesswork. The human intuition about where time is spent is wrong more than 80% of the time — this is the core finding of decades of systems performance research. You optimize the wrong method, measure nothing, and ship a slower binary with more complexity.

The Three Profiling Lies:

  1. "The loop looks slow — let me optimize it." → The loop runs 100ns. The serialization call inside it runs 40ms. You saved 0.02%.
  2. "Adding a cache will fix it." → The hot path never calls the database. The bottleneck is object allocation in the mapper. You added complexity with zero benefit.
  3. "It's the network." → Thread contention during lock acquisition adds 200ms of wall-clock latency before the first byte goes over the wire. The network takes 5ms.

The profiling contract:

Observe → Measure → Hypothesis → Isolate → Change → Verify

Every step must be backed by data. The profiling tools in this lesson — JFR, async-profiler, jcmd — give you the data. Without them, you are not doing performance engineering; you are doing performance folklore.

The two axes of JVM profiling:

Axis Questions Answered
CPU (on-CPU time) Which methods burn CPU cycles? What is the hot path?
Allocation (off-CPU) Which methods allocate the most objects? Which sites trigger GC?

A service that is slow because it allocates 2 GB/s has a CPU profile that looks normal. A service bottlenecked by lock contention has low CPU usage but terrible throughput. You need both axes to diagnose production performance problems.

Part 2

The JVM Profiling Stack

The JVM provides multiple layers at which profiling can occur, from JVM-internal events to user-space instrumentation.

JVM Profiling Stack (bottom to top):
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
OS LAYER
  perf / dtrace / eBPF       ← kernel-level, sees C frames
  CPU hardware counters       ← cache misses, branch mispredicts
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
JVM LAYER
  JVMTI (JVM Tool Interface)  ← async profiling, used by async-profiler
  JFR (Java Flight Recorder)  ← built into JVM, near-zero overhead
  JMX (Java Management Ext.)  ← metrics beans, runtime info
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
FRAMEWORK LAYER
  Micrometer                  ← vendor-neutral metrics instrumentation
  OpenTelemetry               ← traces, metrics, logs (OTLP protocol)
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
OBSERVABILITY BACKENDS
  Datadog / Dynatrace / APM   ← continuous profiling, trace correlation
  Prometheus + Grafana        ← self-hosted metrics and dashboards
  JDK Mission Control (JMC)   ← local JFR analysis IDE
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Tool selection by scenario:

Scenario Tool
CPU hotspot in development async-profiler or VisualVM
Allocation hotspot in development async-profiler (--alloc), JFR
Production profiling (low-overhead) JFR continuous recording
Production profiling (async-safe) async-profiler (attach mode)
Runtime metrics and alerting Micrometer + Prometheus
Distributed trace + profiling APM (Datadog, Dynatrace, etc.)
Lock contention diagnosis async-profiler (--lock) or JFR
Part 3

Java Flight Recorder (JFR): Architecture and Design

JFR (Java Flight Recorder) is the production-grade profiling solution built into the JDK. It has been open-sourced and included in OpenJDK since Java 11 (previously Oracle JDK commercial feature).

Design goals:
- Near-zero overhead: < 1–2% CPU overhead at default settings
- Always-on capable: can run continuously in production without performance impact
- Comprehensive: captures CPU, allocation, I/O, GC, locking, compilation, class loading, exceptions, and custom application events
- Binary format: .jfr files are compact, fast-to-write ring buffers
- Safe in production: data is written to per-thread buffers and flushed — no stop-the-world required

JFR internal architecture:

Thread 1 ──► [Thread-local buffer 256 KB] ──┐
Thread 2 ──► [Thread-local buffer 256 KB] ──┤──► [Global buffer] ──► .jfr file
Thread N ──► [Thread-local buffer 256 KB] ──┘
                                                ▲
                                            periodic flush
                                          (default: 1 second)

Each JVM thread writes JFR events to its own thread-local buffer. When the buffer fills or the flush interval fires, the data is moved to a global buffer and written to the .jfr file. This design avoids lock contention between threads.

JFR event model:

Every piece of data captured by JFR is a jdk.jfr.Event subclass:

// Built-in JVM events (examples):
// jdk.CPUSample           — sampled CPU stack trace (default: 20Hz)
// jdk.ObjectAllocationInNewTLAB — allocation exceeding TLAB
// jdk.GCHeapSummary       — heap state before/after each GC
// jdk.JavaMonitorEnter    — lock acquisition event
// jdk.SocketRead          — network I/O read event

// Custom application event:
import jdk.jfr.*;

@Label("Database Query")
@Description("Records each database query with its duration")
@Category({"Application", "Database"})
@StackTrace(true)
public class DatabaseQueryEvent extends Event {
    @Label("SQL")       String sql;
    @Label("Rows")      int rowCount;
    @Label("Database")  String database;
}

// Usage:
DatabaseQueryEvent event = new DatabaseQueryEvent();
event.begin();
try {
    ResultSet rs = stmt.executeQuery(sql);
    event.rowCount = countRows(rs);
    event.sql = sql;
    event.database = dbName;
} finally {
    event.commit(); // JFR records this event only if duration > threshold
}
Part 4

Starting and Stopping JFR Recordings

JFR can be started several ways: JVM flags at startup, jcmd at runtime, or programmatic API.

Method 1: JVM startup flags

# Continuous recording with 1-hour rotation, max 100 MB file size:
java -XX:StartFlightRecording=name=continuous,\
       maxsize=100m,\
       maxage=1h,\
       settings=profile,\
       filename=/tmp/app.jfr \
     -jar app.jar

# Settings profiles:
# default  — ~1% overhead, suitable for always-on
# profile  — ~2% overhead, more detail (method sampling at 20Hz vs default 10Hz)

Method 2: jcmd at runtime (attach to running JVM)

# Start a timed 60-second recording:
jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=diag settings=profile duration=60s filename=/tmp/diag.jfr

# Start an open-ended recording:
jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=longrun settings=default

# Check recording status:
jcmd <pid> JFR.check

# Dump what has been recorded so far (without stopping):
jcmd <pid> JFR.dump name=longrun filename=/tmp/snapshot.jfr

# Stop and save:
jcmd <pid> JFR.stop name=longrun filename=/tmp/final.jfr

Method 3: Programmatic API (Java 9+)

import jdk.jfr.Recording;
import jdk.jfr.consumer.*;

// Start a recording programmatically:
Recording recording = new Recording();
recording.setName("in-process");
recording.setMaxAge(Duration.ofMinutes(10));
recording.setMaxSize(50 * 1024 * 1024); // 50 MB
recording.enable("jdk.CPUSample").withPeriod(Duration.ofMillis(50));
recording.enable("jdk.ObjectAllocationInNewTLAB");
recording.start();

// Later: dump and analyze in-process:
Path path = Files.createTempFile("rec-", ".jfr");
recording.dump(path);
recording.stop();

// Stream events from the file:
try (RecordingFile rf = new RecordingFile(path)) {
    while (rf.hasMoreEvents()) {
        RecordedEvent e = rf.readEvent();
        System.out.println(e.getEventType().getName() + " @ " + e.getStartTime());
    }
}
Part 5

JFR Settings and Event Configuration

JFR settings files (.jfc) control which events are recorded and at what threshold. The default.jfc and profile.jfc files live inside $JAVA_HOME/lib/jfr/.

Viewing and customizing settings:

# List available configuration files:
jfr configure --list

# Print the default settings file:
cat $JAVA_HOME/lib/jfr/default.jfc

# Create a custom settings file:
jfr configure \
  --add jdk.CPUSample#period=10ms \
  --add jdk.ObjectAllocationInNewTLAB#enabled=true \
  --add jdk.JavaMonitorEnter#threshold=1ms \
  --output custom.jfc

Key events and their tuning:

Event Default Profile What It Captures
jdk.CPUSample 10ms 10ms CPU stack traces
jdk.ObjectAllocationInNewTLAB enabled enabled Large TLAB allocations
jdk.ObjectAllocationOutsideTLAB enabled enabled All outside-TLAB allocations
jdk.JavaMonitorEnter 10ms threshold 10ms threshold Lock acquisition waits
jdk.JavaMonitorWait 10ms threshold 10ms threshold Object.wait() durations
jdk.SocketRead 10ms threshold 10ms threshold Blocking socket reads
jdk.FileRead / FileWrite 10ms threshold 10ms threshold File I/O
jdk.Compilation disabled enabled JIT compilation events
jdk.GCHeapSummary every GC every GC Heap occupancy stats
jdk.ExceptionStatistics period=1s period=1s Exception throw rate

Reducing overhead for high-frequency allocation profiling:

<!-- In custom.jfc: capture only allocations above 512 bytes -->
<event name="jdk.ObjectAllocationInNewTLAB">
  <setting name="enabled">true</setting>
  <setting name="stackTrace">true</setting>
  <setting name="minSize">512</setting>
</event>
Part 6

Analyzing JFR Files with JDK Mission Control (JMC)

JDK Mission Control (JMC) is the GUI tool for analyzing .jfr files. It ships separately from the JDK but is free and open source.

Key JMC views:

JMC Navigation:
├── General
│   ├── Overview          — timeline of all event categories
│   ├── Threads           — per-thread state over time (running/waiting/blocked)
│   └── Exceptions        — thrown exceptions with stack traces
├── Memory
│   ├── GC                — GC pause timeline, promotion rates
│   ├── Heap              — heap occupancy over time
│   └── Allocations       — allocation hotspots by class and stack
├── Code
│   ├── Hot Methods       — CPU time by method (sampled stack traces)
│   ├── Call Tree         — flame graph as a tree
│   └── Compilations      — JIT compilation activity
└── I/O
    ├── File I/O          — file read/write operations
    └── Socket I/O        — network read/write with remote addresses

Command-line JFR analysis with jfr print:

# Print all events (verbose):
jfr print /tmp/diag.jfr

# Filter to specific event types:
jfr print --events jdk.CPUSample /tmp/diag.jfr

# Print allocation events sorted by size:
jfr print --events jdk.ObjectAllocationInNewTLAB \
          --json /tmp/diag.jfr | jq '.events | sort_by(.fields.allocationSize) | reverse | .[0:10]'

# Print GC summary:
jfr print --events jdk.GCHeapSummary /tmp/diag.jfr

# Print thread stall events (lock contention):
jfr print --events jdk.JavaMonitorEnter /tmp/diag.jfr

Programmatic streaming analysis (Java 14+ JFR Event Streaming):

// Stream JFR events from a running JVM in real time:
try (var rs = new RecordingStream()) {
    rs.enable("jdk.CPUSample").withPeriod(Duration.ofMillis(100));
    rs.enable("jdk.ObjectAllocationInNewTLAB");

    rs.onEvent("jdk.CPUSample", event -> {
        RecordedStackTrace stack = event.getStackTrace();
        if (stack != null) {
            String topFrame = stack.getFrames().get(0).getMethod().getType().getName()
                + "." + stack.getFrames().get(0).getMethod().getName();
            System.out.println("CPU: " + topFrame);
        }
    });

    rs.onEvent("jdk.ObjectAllocationInNewTLAB", event -> {
        System.out.printf("Alloc: %s %d bytes%n",
            event.getClass("objectClass").getName(),
            event.getLong("allocationSize"));
    });

    rs.startAsync();
    Thread.sleep(30_000);
}
Part 7

async-profiler: Architecture and Advantages

async-profiler is a low-overhead sampling profiler for Java that solves the safepoint bias problem that affects most JVM-based profilers.

The safepoint bias problem:

Traditional JVM profilers (including VisualVM's sampler) can only collect stack traces at JVM safepoints. Safepoints occur at predictable locations in bytecode — typically at method returns and loop back-edges. This means:

  1. Methods that run long stretches without reaching a safepoint are invisible to the profiler
  2. The profiler systematically over-reports time in methods that loop and under-reports native code
  3. Long-running native methods (JNI calls, system calls) appear to consume zero CPU

async-profiler solution:

async-profiler uses AsyncGetCallTrace — a JVMTI extension that can collect stack traces at any point, not just safepoints. It sends SIGPROF to the JVM process, which interrupts any thread at the current instruction and captures a true async stack trace. This gives accurate CPU time measurement regardless of safepoint placement.

Additional capabilities:

Mode Flag What It Profiles
CPU (default) On-CPU stack traces via AsyncGetCallTrace + perf_events
Allocation --alloc Object allocation sites via JVMTI allocation callbacks
Wall-clock --wall All threads including sleeping/blocked (I/O wait analysis)
Lock --lock Java monitor contention hotspots
Cache miss --event cache-misses L1/L2/L3 cache miss distribution
Page faults --event page-faults Virtual memory paging activity

Installing and running async-profiler:

# Download and extract (Linux/macOS):
curl -L https://github.com/async-profiler/async-profiler/releases/latest/download/async-profiler-*.tar.gz | tar xz

# CPU profiling — attach to running process for 30s:
./bin/asprof -d 30 -f cpu.html <pid>
# Opens a flame graph HTML in your browser

# Allocation profiling — 512-byte sampling interval:
./bin/asprof -e alloc -i 512k -d 30 -f alloc.html <pid>

# Wall-clock profiling (all threads including blocked):
./bin/asprof -e wall -d 30 -f wall.html <pid>

# Lock contention profiling:
./bin/asprof -e lock -d 30 -f lock.html <pid>

# JFR-compatible output (can be opened in JMC):
./bin/asprof -d 60 -o jfr -f profile.jfr <pid>

Using the Java API for programmatic control:

# Start profiling from within the JVM (via agent):
java -agentpath:/path/to/libasyncProfiler.so=start,event=cpu,file=cpu.html \
     -jar app.jar

# Start/stop via API calls from application code:
java -agentpath:/path/to/libasyncProfiler.so=listen \
     -jar app.jar
# Then call API via socket from another process
Part 8

Flame Graphs: Reading and Interpretation

A flame graph is a visualization of sampled stack traces. Each frame on the call stack is a rectangle; width represents the proportion of samples in which that frame appeared.

Anatomy of a flame graph:

                        ┌───────────────────────────────────────────┐
                        │         processOrder() [WIDE = HOT]       │
           ┌────────────┼───────────────────┐  ┌────────────────────┤
           │  validateCart()  │  applyTax()  │  │   chargePayment()  │
    ┌──────┤  [narrow]        │  [narrow]    │  │    [very wide]     │
    │JSON  │                  │              │  ├──────────┬─────────┤
    │parse │                  │              │  │  callAPI │ waitLock│
    └──────┘                  └──────────────┘  └──────────┴─────────┘
    ^bottom = root frames (main, thread start)
    ^top = leaf frames (where CPU is actually spent)

Reading rules:
- Width = % of CPU time (or samples) the frame appears on the call stack
- Height = call depth
- Wide tops = the actual hot methods (CPU is being consumed here)
- Wide bottoms, narrow tops = method is called frequently but delegates quickly — the real work is in children
- Color = in async-profiler output, green = Java, orange = native/JVM internals, red = C++ kernel code

Flame graph navigation:

In async-profiler HTML output:
- Click any frame to zoom in — the selected frame fills the view and its children's proportions become visible
- Right-click → "Reset zoom" to return to full view
- Search box (top-right) highlights all frames matching a pattern

Reversed flame graphs (icicle graphs):

async-profiler also supports --reverse which flips the graph so hot leaf frames appear at the bottom and callers grow upward. Useful for identifying which callers drive a specific hot method.

Differential flame graphs:

When comparing a before/after profile, generate a differential flame graph where widths represent the change in time rather than absolute time. Blue = improved, red = regressed.

# Generate two profiles:
./bin/asprof -d 30 -f before.jfr <pid>
# (apply your change)
./bin/asprof -d 30 -f after.jfr <pid>

# Create differential flame graph using JFR Diff tool or FlameScope
Part 9

CPU Profiling Deep Dive

CPU profiling answers: which methods consume the most processor time?

Sampling vs instrumentation:

Approach How It Works Overhead Accuracy
Sampling Interrupt threads periodically, record stack Low (1–5%) Statistical — accurate for hot paths
Instrumentation Insert bytecode at every method entry/exit High (50–300%) Exact — but overhead changes behavior

Always prefer sampling for production and near-production environments. Use instrumentation only in isolated dev tests for very specific micro-benchmarks.

Interpreting CPU profiles for common problems:

Problem 1: Serialization is the hot path

Symptom: Jackson/Gson frames are wide in the CPU flame graph
Root cause: Returning large domain objects as JSON
Fix: Use DTOs/projections; avoid serializing lazy-loaded collections

Problem 2: Reflection overhead

Symptom: java.lang.reflect.Method.invoke appears wide
Root cause: Framework calling methods via reflection in a hot path
Fix: Use method handles (MethodHandle) or annotation processors to
     generate direct calls at compile time

Problem 3: String operations

Symptom: String.format, StringBuilder.append in hot path
Root cause: Log statements that execute even at INFO level when DEBUG is off
Fix: Use parameterized logging (logger.debug("val={}", val))
     or guard with logger.isDebugEnabled()

Practical CPU profiling workflow:

# 1. Reproduce the load (benchmark, load test, real traffic)
# 2. Attach async-profiler and capture 30 seconds of CPU data:
./bin/asprof -d 30 -f /tmp/cpu-$(date +%s).html $(pgrep -f app.jar)

# 3. Open the HTML file and identify the widest top-level frames
# 4. Click into the hottest frame — check its callers (is this called unexpectedly?)
# 5. Correlate with code — is this logic avoidable? Can it be cached?

# For server-side Java, also consider capturing separate profiles per endpoint:
# Add -e wall to see time waiting in I/O or lock contention alongside CPU
Part 10

Allocation Profiling Deep Dive

Allocation profiling answers: which code paths create the most objects and drive GC?

Why allocation matters:

Modern GCs are fast, but they are not free. Every object allocation:
1. Consumes a TLAB (Thread-Local Allocation Buffer) slot
2. Increases the rate at which Eden fills
3. Increases GC frequency and pause count
4. Creates pressure on CPU caches (allocating large objects evicts cache lines)

A service generating 2 GB/s of allocation rate will run GC nearly continuously, burning 10–20% of CPU on collection overhead regardless of how well the GC is tuned. The solution is to reduce allocation, not to tune the GC.

async-profiler allocation profiling:

# Allocation profiling — sample every 512 KB allocated:
./bin/asprof -e alloc -i 512k -d 30 -f alloc.html <pid>

# Higher resolution (sample every 64 KB — more overhead):
./bin/asprof -e alloc -i 64k -d 30 -f alloc-fine.html <pid>

The resulting flame graph shows allocation stack traces — the code paths that called new. Wide frames at the top are the classes being allocated; the stack below shows what called into those constructors.

Common allocation anti-patterns:

Pattern 1: Autoboxing in hot loops

// BAD: autoboxes every loop iteration → 1M Integer objects
long sum = 0;
for (Integer i : integerList) {  // unboxes to primitive
    sum += i;                     // re-boxes to Long... wait, this is fine
}

// ACTUALLY BAD pattern:
Map<String, Long> counts = new HashMap<>();
for (String key : keys) {
    counts.merge(key, 1L, Long::sum);  // 1L autoboxes to Long each call
}

// FIX: use a primitive map library (Eclipse Collections, Koloboke)
// or accumulate in a primitive array

Pattern 2: String concatenation in loops

// BAD: creates a new StringBuilder and String on every iteration
String result = "";
for (String part : parts) {
    result += part + ", ";  // O(n²) allocations
}

// GOOD: reuse one StringBuilder
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
for (String part : parts) {
    sb.append(part).append(", ");
}
String result = sb.toString();

Pattern 3: Unnecessary defensive copies

// BAD: copies a potentially huge list on every read
public List<Order> getOrders() {
    return new ArrayList<>(this.orders);  // defensive copy always
}

// BETTER: return unmodifiable view (no copy)
public List<Order> getOrders() {
    return Collections.unmodifiableList(this.orders);
}
Part 11

jcmd: The Swiss Army Knife

jcmd is the JDK's built-in diagnostic command tool. It can attach to any running JVM process and issue commands without requiring the process to be started with any special flags.

Listing available commands:

# List all running JVM processes:
jcmd

# List all available commands for a specific PID:
jcmd <pid> help

# Get help for a specific command:
jcmd <pid> help VM.flags

Key jcmd commands for performance work:

# ── JFR (Java Flight Recorder) ──────────────────────────────────
jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=prof settings=profile duration=30s filename=/tmp/p.jfr
jcmd <pid> JFR.stop name=prof
jcmd <pid> JFR.check
jcmd <pid> JFR.dump name=prof filename=/tmp/snap.jfr

# ── JVM diagnostics ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# Print all JVM flags (including defaults):
jcmd <pid> VM.flags

# Print JVM system properties:
jcmd <pid> VM.system_properties

# Print JVM uptime:
jcmd <pid> VM.uptime

# Print JVM command line:
jcmd <pid> VM.command_line

# ── Thread diagnostics ──────────────────────────────────────────
# Thread dump (like kill -3 but goes to stdout):
jcmd <pid> Thread.print

# Thread dump in JSON format (Java 17+):
jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json /tmp/threads.json

# ── Memory ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Histogram of live objects by class:
jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram

# Force GC (use with extreme caution in production):
jcmd <pid> GC.run

# Print heap info:
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_info

# Heap dump (binary hprof format):
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /tmp/heap.hprof

# ── Compiler diagnostics ────────────────────────────────────────
# Print CodeCache statistics:
jcmd <pid> Compiler.codecache

# Print codecache usage per compilation unit:
jcmd <pid> Compiler.queue

# ── Native memory (if -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary is set) ──
jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary
jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory baseline
# (make changes)
jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary.diff
Part 12

Production-Safe Profiling Principles

Profiling in production requires a different discipline than development profiling. The goal is to get actionable data with minimal disruption to live traffic.

Safety rules for production profiling:

  1. Use JFR default settings first — settings=default has < 1% overhead; switch to profile only for 30–60 second diagnostic windows
  2. Time-bound all recordings — always set duration= on JFR.start; never leave an open-ended high-overhead recording running
  3. Use disk-safe paths — write .jfr files to /tmp or a mounted PVC with adequate free space; a full disk is worse than the original problem
  4. One recording at a time — concurrent JFR recordings multiply overhead; stop existing recordings before starting diagnostic ones
  5. Do not force GC — jcmd <pid> GC.run in production causes a full STW pause; never do this on live traffic
  6. Test attach behavior first — verify jcmd and async-profiler attach work in your staging environment before using in production; some container hardening blocks JVMTI attach

Continuous profiling pattern (recommended for production):

# Start at JVM launch with disk-rotating ring buffer:
java -XX:StartFlightRecording=\
       name=continuous,\
       settings=default,\
       maxsize=200m,\
       maxage=2h,\
       disk=true,\
       filename=/var/log/jfr/continuous.jfr \
     -jar app.jar

With this configuration, the JVM maintains a 2-hour rolling window of profiling data. When an incident occurs, dump the recording immediately:

jcmd <pid> JFR.dump name=continuous filename=/tmp/incident-$(date +%s).jfr

You now have the full 2 hours of pre-incident data to analyze — no need to reproduce the incident.

Container/Kubernetes considerations:

# In Kubernetes, mount a PVC for JFR output and enable profiling:
containers:
  - name: app
    env:
      - name: JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
        value: >-
          -XX:StartFlightRecording=name=continuous,settings=default,
          maxsize=200m,maxage=2h,disk=true,filename=/jfr/continuous.jfr
    volumeMounts:
      - name: jfr-data
        mountPath: /jfr
Part 13

Micrometer: Application-Level Metrics

Micrometer is the de facto standard for application-level metrics in Java. It provides a vendor-neutral API that exports to Prometheus, Datadog, CloudWatch, InfluxDB, and 20+ other backends.

Core abstractions:

Type Use Case Example
Counter Monotonically increasing count requests served, errors thrown
Gauge Point-in-time value queue depth, active sessions
Timer Duration + count HTTP request latency, DB query time
DistributionSummary Distribution of values request size, response size
LongTaskTimer Duration of long-running tasks batch job, scheduled task

Adding Micrometer to a Spring Boot application:

<!-- pom.xml: -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.micrometer</groupId>
    <artifactId>micrometer-registry-prometheus</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId>
</dependency>

# application.yml:
management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: prometheus, health, info
  metrics:
    export:
      prometheus:
        enabled: true

Instrumenting application code:

@Service
public class OrderService {

    private final MeterRegistry registry;
    private final Timer orderProcessingTimer;
    private final Counter orderErrorCounter;
    private final AtomicInteger activeOrders;

    public OrderService(MeterRegistry registry) {
        this.registry = registry;

        this.orderProcessingTimer = Timer.builder("order.processing.duration")
            .description("Time to fully process an order")
            .tag("region", "us-east-1")
            .publishPercentiles(0.5, 0.95, 0.99)
            .publishPercentileHistogram()
            .register(registry);

        this.orderErrorCounter = Counter.builder("order.errors.total")
            .description("Total order processing errors")
            .tag("type", "payment")
            .register(registry);

        this.activeOrders = registry.gauge(
            "order.active.count",
            new AtomicInteger(0));
    }

    public Order processOrder(OrderRequest request) {
        activeOrders.incrementAndGet();
        return orderProcessingTimer.record(() -> {
            try {
                return doProcessOrder(request);
            } catch (PaymentException e) {
                orderErrorCounter.increment();
                throw e;
            } finally {
                activeOrders.decrementAndGet();
            }
        });
    }
}

Prometheus scraping and Grafana alerting:

# Prometheus scrape config:
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: 'java-app'
    metrics_path: '/actuator/prometheus'
    static_configs:
      - targets: ['app-host:8080']

# Grafana alert for high P99 latency:
# order_processing_duration_seconds{quantile="0.99"} > 0.5
Part 14

APM Tools: Datadog, Dynatrace, and OpenTelemetry

Application Performance Monitoring (APM) tools combine distributed tracing, continuous profiling, and metrics into a single observability platform.

APM vs traditional profiling:

Capability JFR / async-profiler APM (Datadog/Dynatrace)
Overhead < 2% 2–5%
Setup Manual per-JVM Agent-based auto-instrument
Distributed tracing No Yes (trace per request)
Continuous profiling Yes (JFR) Yes (always-on)
Correlation: trace → flame graph No Yes (in Datadog Continuous Profiler)
Historical retention Local file Cloud backend (weeks/months)

Datadog Java agent:

# Attach Datadog agent at startup:
java -javaagent:/opt/dd-java-agent.jar \
     -Ddd.service=order-service \
     -Ddd.env=production \
     -Ddd.version=2.1.0 \
     -Ddd.profiling.enabled=true \
     -Ddd.logs.injection=true \
     -jar app.jar

The Datadog agent auto-instruments Spring Boot, JDBC, HTTP clients, Kafka, and Redis — capturing span traces for each operation with timing, error rates, and resource attribution, all correlated to the continuous profiler flame graph.

OpenTelemetry (vendor-neutral tracing):

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.opentelemetry.instrumentation</groupId>
    <artifactId>opentelemetry-spring-boot-starter</artifactId>
</dependency>

@RestController
public class OrderController {

    private final Tracer tracer;

    public OrderController(OpenTelemetry openTelemetry) {
        this.tracer = openTelemetry.getTracer("order-service");
    }

    @PostMapping("/orders")
    public ResponseEntity<Order> createOrder(@RequestBody OrderRequest req) {
        Span span = tracer.spanBuilder("createOrder")
            .setAttribute("order.customer_id", req.getCustomerId())
            .startSpan();
        try (Scope scope = span.makeCurrent()) {
            Order order = orderService.process(req);
            span.setAttribute("order.id", order.getId());
            return ResponseEntity.ok(order);
        } catch (Exception e) {
            span.recordException(e);
            span.setStatus(StatusCode.ERROR);
            throw e;
        } finally {
            span.end();
        }
    }
}
Part 15

Lock Contention Profiling

Lock contention is one of the most insidious performance problems: CPU utilization looks low, throughput is terrible, and thread dumps show most threads in BLOCKED or WAITING state.

Detecting contention with thread dumps:

# Take three thread dumps 3 seconds apart:
for i in 1 2 3; do
    jcmd <pid> Thread.print >> /tmp/tdump.txt
    sleep 3
done

# Look for:
# - Many threads in state BLOCKED
# - Multiple threads waiting on the same monitor address
# - "waiting to lock <0x00000000c2a3b450>"

Detecting contention with JFR:

# Start a recording with low lock threshold (1ms):
jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=lock settings=profile duration=30s \
     filename=/tmp/lock.jfr

# In JMC: navigate to Code → Lock Instances
# Shows: monitor address, class, average wait time, contending threads

Detecting contention with async-profiler:

# Lock profiling mode:
./bin/asprof -e lock -d 30 -f lock.html <pid>
# The flame graph shows the stack traces that ACQUIRED locks (holders)
# Wide frames = locks held for long time = source of contention

Common lock contention patterns and fixes:

// ANTI-PATTERN: Wide synchronized scope
public synchronized OrderResult processOrder(Order order) {
    validateOrder(order);       // no shared state needed
    chargePayment(order);       // external API call — SLOW!
    updateInventory(order);     // DB write — held lock during network I/O
    return buildResult(order);
}

// FIX: Minimize lock scope — only lock shared state writes
public OrderResult processOrder(Order order) {
    validateOrder(order);           // no lock needed
    PaymentResult payment = chargePayment(order);   // no lock needed
    synchronized (inventoryLock) {
        updateInventory(order);     // only the actual shared state mutation
    }
    return buildResult(order, payment);
}
Part 16

Wall-Clock Profiling and I/O Analysis

CPU profiling shows where processor time is spent. Wall-clock profiling shows where elapsed time is spent — including blocked threads, sleeping threads, and threads waiting on I/O or locks.

When to use wall-clock profiling:

  • Service latency is high but CPU usage is low
  • Thread dumps show many threads in TIMED_WAITING or WAITING
  • You suspect the bottleneck is network I/O, database latency, or thread sleep

async-profiler wall-clock mode:

# Wall-clock profiling — samples ALL threads including blocked/sleeping:
./bin/asprof -e wall -t -d 30 -f wall.html <pid>
# -t : separate per-thread flame graphs in the output

Reading wall-clock vs CPU flame graphs:

CPU flame graph:     Shows only threads on-CPU. I/O wait is invisible.
Wall-clock graph:    Shows ALL threads. Blocked threads appear wide if
                     they spend most elapsed time blocked.

Example: DB query method
  CPU:   narrow (CPU time is microseconds — just sending the bytes)
  Wall:  WIDE   (elapsed time is 20ms — waiting for DB response)

JFR I/O event analysis:

# Print all socket read events longer than 10ms:
jfr print --events jdk.SocketRead /tmp/diag.jfr | \
  grep -A5 "duration > 10ms"

# Print file read events:
jfr print --events jdk.FileRead /tmp/diag.jfr

Identifying slow downstream dependencies:

The JFR jdk.SocketRead and jdk.SocketWrite events capture the remote address. This immediately tells you whether the latency is in your own service, the database, an upstream API, or a message broker.

Part 17

Benchmarking with JMH

Profiling identifies the hot path. Benchmarking validates that a proposed fix actually improves performance. JMH (Java Microbenchmark Harness) is the standard tool for writing reliable Java microbenchmarks.

Why raw timing loops are wrong:

// THIS IS NOT A VALID BENCHMARK:
long start = System.nanoTime();
for (int i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++) {
    result = expensiveMethod(i);
}
long elapsed = System.nanoTime() - start;
System.out.println(elapsed / 1_000_000 + " ns/op");

Problems: JIT warmup is not accounted for, dead code elimination removes result, JVM startup state affects measurements, no statistical analysis.

JMH setup:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.openjdk.jmh</groupId>
    <artifactId>jmh-core</artifactId>
    <version>1.37</version>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.openjdk.jmh</groupId>
    <artifactId>jmh-generator-annprocess</artifactId>
    <version>1.37</version>
    <scope>provided</scope>
</dependency>

A proper JMH benchmark:

@BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime)
@OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)
@State(Scope.Benchmark)
@Fork(value = 2, jvmArgs = {"-Xms512m", "-Xmx512m"})
@Warmup(iterations = 5, time = 1)
@Measurement(iterations = 10, time = 1)
public class StringBenchmark {

    @Param({"10", "100", "1000"})
    int size;

    private List<String> data;

    @Setup
    public void setup() {
        data = IntStream.range(0, size)
            .mapToObj(i -> "item-" + i)
            .collect(Collectors.toList());
    }

    @Benchmark
    public String concatenationPlus(Blackhole bh) {
        String result = "";
        for (String s : data) result += s;
        return result;
    }

    @Benchmark
    public String stringJoin(Blackhole bh) {
        return String.join("", data);
    }

    @Benchmark
    public String stringBuilder() {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        for (String s : data) sb.append(s);
        return sb.toString();
    }
}

# Build and run:
mvn package -q
java -jar target/benchmarks.jar -rf json -rff results.json

Connecting JMH with async-profiler:

# Profile the benchmark execution to see allocation profile:
java -jar target/benchmarks.jar StringBenchmark.concatenationPlus \
     -prof async:libPath=/path/to/libasyncProfiler.so\;event=alloc\;output=flamegraph\;dir=/tmp/jmh-prof
Part 18

Profiling GC Pressure

High GC pressure is a performance problem that appears in profiling as: high CPU usage in GC threads, short intervals between GC pauses, and high allocation rates in JFR.

Identifying GC pressure with JFR:

# Open the JFR file in JMC:
# Memory → Heap → look for:
# - Allocation Rate (bytes/sec) — healthy: < 1 GB/s, problematic: > 2 GB/s
# - GC Pause Frequency — healthy: < 10/sec, problematic: > 50/sec
# - Heap occupancy growth — healthy: stable sawtooth, problematic: rising baseline

# From the command line, extract GC summary:
jfr print --events jdk.GCHeapSummary,jdk.YoungGarbageCollection,jdk.OldGarbageCollection \
    /tmp/diag.jfr | head -100

Profiling allocation rate with jcmd:

# Print live allocation rate using GC class histogram delta:
jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram > /tmp/h1.txt
sleep 10
jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram > /tmp/h2.txt
diff /tmp/h1.txt /tmp/h2.txt
# Classes with increasing instance counts are being allocated and surviving GC

The allocation rate → GC frequency formula:

GC Frequency ≈ Eden Size / Allocation Rate

Eden Size (G1GC) = Young Gen size × (1 - survivor ratio)
                 = ~200 MB (default 25% of 1 GB heap)

At 1 GB/s allocation rate:
GC Frequency = 200 MB / 1000 MB/s = 0.2s = 5 Young GC/sec

At 200 MB/s allocation rate:
GC Frequency = 200 MB / 200 MB/s = 1s = 1 Young GC/sec

Reducing allocation by 5× reduces GC frequency by 5×. This is why allocation profiling has more leverage than GC tuning for allocation-heavy applications.

Part 19

Profiling in Containerized Environments

JVM profiling in Docker/Kubernetes requires additional configuration because container isolation affects JVMTI signal delivery and file system access.

Container-specific issues:

Issue Cause Fix
jcmd cannot connect Non-root UID mismatch Run jcmd as the same UID as the JVM process
async-profiler fails to attach ptrace capability missing Add SYS_PTRACE capability to pod spec
/proc/self/maps unreadable Security policy Use --fdtransfer mode in async-profiler
Signal delivery fails Container signal masking Use JVMTI callback mode instead of SIGPROF

Kubernetes pod spec for profiling:

securityContext:
  capabilities:
    add:
      - SYS_PTRACE     # required for async-profiler attach
containers:
  - name: app
    # Mount async-profiler as a sidecar volume or init container
    volumeMounts:
      - name: profiler
        mountPath: /profiler
      - name: jfr-output
        mountPath: /jfr
initContainers:
  - name: profiler-setup
    image: ghcr.io/async-profiler/async-profiler:latest
    command: ["cp", "-r", "/async-profiler/.", "/profiler/"]
    volumeMounts:
      - name: profiler
        mountPath: /profiler

Remote JFR trigger via exec:

# Trigger JFR dump from outside the pod:
kubectl exec <pod> -- jcmd 1 JFR.start name=diag settings=profile \
  duration=30s filename=/jfr/diag.jfr

# Wait for completion, then copy the file:
kubectl cp <pod>:/jfr/diag.jfr ./diag.jfr

# Analyze locally in JMC:
jmc -open diag.jfr
Part 20

Interview Questions and Answers

Q1: What is the difference between CPU profiling and allocation profiling? When would you use each?

A: CPU profiling captures stack traces of threads actively using CPU cycles — it identifies methods that burn processor time. Allocation profiling captures stack traces at object creation sites — it identifies which code paths drive GC pressure by creating the most objects.

Use CPU profiling when: response latency is high and CPU utilization is also high, suggesting computation-bound bottlenecks (loops, parsing, serialization).

Use allocation profiling when: GC overhead is high (visible in JVM metrics or GC logs), heap memory is consumed faster than expected, or you need to reduce memory footprint to allow more live objects without increasing heap size.

Q2: What is safepoint bias and how does async-profiler avoid it?

A: Traditional JVM-based profilers can only collect stack traces at JVM safepoints — specific locations where the JVM can pause all threads consistently (method returns, loop back-edges). Methods with long-running sections between safepoints (tight inner loops, JNI calls) appear in fewer samples than they should, making the profiler report misleadingly low time for them.

async-profiler uses the AsyncGetCallTrace JVMTI function combined with POSIX SIGPROF signals to interrupt threads at any instruction, not just safepoints. This gives an accurate statistical sample of where CPU time is actually spent.

Q3: Explain how JFR achieves near-zero overhead.

A: JFR uses three mechanisms to minimize overhead:
1. Thread-local buffers: each thread writes events to its own in-memory buffer (default 256 KB) without synchronization; no lock contention between threads
2. Binary format: events are serialized to a compact binary format directly — no text formatting, no allocation of strings during event recording
3. Threshold filtering: most events (I/O, locks) are only recorded if they exceed a configurable threshold (default 10ms), eliminating the vast majority of fast operations from the event stream

The combination keeps normal-settings overhead below 1% for most applications.

Q4: You observe 15% CPU time in GC on a production service. What is your diagnostic approach?

A:
1. Start a JFR recording for 60 seconds: jcmd <pid> JFR.start settings=profile duration=60s filename=/tmp/gc.jfr
2. In JMC, open Memory → Allocations. Identify the top 3 allocating classes and their stack traces.
3. Check allocation rate: if > 1 GB/s, the problem is excessive allocation, not GC tuning.
4. Run async-profiler in allocation mode to get a flame graph of allocation sites.
5. Identify the dominant allocation pattern (autoboxing, string concatenation, unnecessary copies, etc.)
6. Reduce allocation at the hot sites — verify with JMH benchmark.
7. Re-profile to confirm allocation rate has dropped; GC overhead should follow.

Q5: What Micrometer metrics would you instrument in a typical REST service for performance monitoring?

A: Essential metrics for a production REST service:
- http.server.requests (Timer with uri, method, status tags) — automatic with Spring Boot Actuator
- DB query duration: db.query.duration (Timer with query_type, table tags)
- External HTTP client calls: http.client.requests (Timer with target_host, method tags)
- Cache hit/miss ratio: cache.gets counter with result=hit/miss tag
- Executor queue size: executor.queue.size gauge (for thread pool saturation monitoring)
- JVM GC overhead: jvm.gc.pause (auto-collected by Micrometer JVM metrics binder)
- Heap usage: jvm.memory.used{area=heap} gauge

Q6: A service has high P99 latency but normal P50. The CPU profile looks clean. What do you investigate next?

A: High P99 with normal P50 and clean CPU profile indicates the bottleneck is not computation — it is contention or waiting:

  1. Lock contention: Run async-profiler in lock mode (-e lock). Thread dump shows BLOCKED threads.
  2. Thread pool exhaustion: Check executor.queue.size metric or jcmd <pid> Thread.print — if all threads are busy, new requests queue, inflating P99.
  3. GC pauses: Even 50ms STW pauses appear as P99 spikes. Check JFR GC events or GC logs.
  4. Downstream latency outliers: A DB query that normally takes 2ms occasionally takes 400ms (slow query, lock timeout). Wall-clock profiling (-e wall) will show blocked threads in the DB driver.
  5. JIT deoptimization: Rare deoptimization events cause sudden slowdowns. Check JFR Compiler events.
Part 21

Profiling Workflow: End-to-End Playbook

Step 1: Establish a baseline

# Capture JFR recording during normal load:
jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=baseline settings=default duration=120s \
     filename=/tmp/baseline.jfr

# Record key metrics:
# - CPU utilization (%)
# - Allocation rate (MB/s from JFR or GC logs)
# - GC overhead (% from JFR)
# - P50/P95/P99 latency (from Micrometer / APM)
# - Throughput (req/s)

Step 2: Identify the dominant bottleneck

Decision tree:
Is CPU > 80%?
  YES → CPU profiling (async-profiler CPU mode or JFR hot methods)
  NO →
    Is GC overhead > 10%?
      YES → Allocation profiling (async-profiler alloc mode or JFR allocations)
      NO →
        Is P99 >> P50?
          YES → Wall-clock profiling + lock profiling + thread dump analysis
          NO →
            Is throughput low but latency OK?
              YES → Thread pool saturation check + connection pool analysis

Step 3: Generate and read the flame graph

# CPU flame graph:
./bin/asprof -d 30 -f /tmp/cpu.html <pid>
# Look for: wide frames at the top of stacks = compute hot spots

# Allocation flame graph:
./bin/asprof -e alloc -i 512k -d 30 -f /tmp/alloc.html <pid>
# Look for: wide frames = dominant allocation classes and their callers

Step 4: Validate the fix with JMH + re-profiling

# Before fix:
java -jar benchmarks.jar OriginalMethod -rf json -rff before.json

# Apply fix, rebuild, then:
java -jar benchmarks.jar OptimizedMethod -rf json -rff after.json

# Compare:
jq '.[] | {benchmark: .benchmark, score: .primaryMetric.score}' before.json after.json

# Re-profile in staging to confirm the flame graph changed:
./bin/asprof -d 30 -f /tmp/cpu-after.html <pid>

Step 5: Monitor in production

# After deploying the fix, watch Micrometer metrics:
# - allocation_rate should drop
# - gc_overhead should drop
# - P99 latency should improve

# Keep JFR continuous recording active for post-deploy verification
Part 22

Phase 6 Completion: JVM Internals Summary (Lessons 56–70)

Phase 6 at a glance

Phase 6 is the deepest dive into what makes Java work — the JVM itself. You started at the very beginning of program execution and ended at the tools you use to observe and optimize it in production. Every lesson in this phase builds on the previous one.

Key insights from Phase 6

The JVM is a complete runtime system. Class loading (Lesson 56) to bytecode execution (Lesson 58) to JIT compilation (Lesson 59) to memory management (Lessons 60–65) to observability (Lesson 70) forms a complete stack. Understanding each layer makes you a dramatically more effective Java engineer — you can reason from first principles about performance problems instead of guessing.

JIT compilation is your invisible co-developer. The C2 compiler inlines methods, eliminates dead code, and vectorizes loops — but only for hot paths. Understanding tiered compilation (Lesson 59) explains why benchmarks need warmup, why startup performance differs from steady-state, and why artificially small benchmarks are misleading.

GC is a system, not a button. The GC lessons (60–65) established that garbage collectors are engineering systems with tradeoffs: G1GC for bounded latency at large heaps, ZGC for sub-millisecond pauses, Serial for embedded/single-core. No collector is universally best. Choosing the right GC and configuring it correctly requires understanding its internals.

Profiling closes the loop. Every optimization insight from this phase — JIT deoptimization, excessive allocation, lock contention, GC pressure — is detectable only through profiling tools. JFR, async-profiler, and jcmd (Lesson 70) are not advanced features; they are the required finishing tools for production Java engineering.

Practice — Lesson 70

Easy Exercises

Exercise 1 — First JFR Recording

Start any Java application (even a simple one that loops) and capture a 30-second JFR recording using jcmd. Open the resulting .jfr file with jfr print and identify three different event types in the output.

# Start the application, get its PID:
jcmd

# Start a 30-second recording:
jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=first settings=default duration=30s filename=/tmp/first.jfr

# After 30 seconds, verify the file was created:
ls -lh /tmp/first.jfr

# Print a sample of events:
jfr print --events jdk.CPUSample /tmp/first.jfr | head -40
jfr print --events jdk.GCHeapSummary /tmp/first.jfr | head -40

Exercise 2 — jcmd Exploration

Use jcmd to answer the following questions about a running JVM:
1. What GC is in use? (VM.flags — look for +UseG1GC etc.)
2. What is the current heap size? (GC.heap_info)
3. How many threads are running? (Thread.print — count the entries)
4. What is the top object by instance count? (GC.class_histogram | head -20)

Medium Exercises

Exercise 4 — Allocation Profiling with async-profiler

Write a Java program that has a clear allocation hotspot — for example, a method that repeatedly converts int[] to List<Integer> via autoboxing in a loop. Run async-profiler in allocation mode for 30 seconds and verify the hotspot appears as a wide frame at the top of the allocation flame graph.

public class AllocationHotspot {
    public static long processData(int[] data) {
        // This creates Integer objects (autoboxing) on every call:
        List<Integer> boxed = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i : data) boxed.add(i);         // autoboxes each int
        return boxed.stream().mapToLong(Integer::longValue).sum();
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        int[] data = IntStream.range(0, 10_000).toArray();
        while (true) {
            processData(data);   // run continuously so async-profiler can sample
        }
    }
}

# In another terminal, attach async-profiler:
./bin/asprof -e alloc -i 512k -d 30 -f /tmp/alloc.html $(pgrep -f AllocationHotspot)

Advanced Exercises

Exercise 7 — End-to-End Profiling Playbook

Build a small Spring Boot application with an intentional performance problem (suggestions: a sorting endpoint that re-creates a large array on every request; a statistics endpoint that iterates a CopyOnWriteArrayList of 100K entries; or a logging endpoint that calls String.format 10K times in a loop).

Perform the full profiling workflow:
1. Establish a baseline with JFR (capture allocation rate and CPU %%)
2. Use async-profiler CPU mode to locate the hot method
3. Use async-profiler allocation mode to identify the allocation source
4. Write a JMH benchmark that isolates the hot method
5. Fix the problem and re-benchmark
6. Verify with JFR that allocation rate dropped

Production Scenarios

Scenario 1 — P99 Spike Investigation

Your order processing service has stable P50=12ms but P99=850ms. CPU utilization is 40% on 8 cores. GC log shows no Full GC and Young GC pauses of ~15ms occurring 3 times per second. Thread pool has 200 threads; metrics show average queue depth of 180. Diagnose and fix.

Expected analysis:
- Queue depth of 180 on a 200-thread pool means the pool is nearly saturated. New requests wait in queue before processing even begins.
- Queuing adds latency at the tail (P99) without affecting median (P50) because median requests enter an empty queue.
- Root cause: thread pool is too small for the request rate, or a subset of requests is slow and blocking threads.
- Diagnostic steps: wall-clock profiling to find slow-request stack traces; check DB connection pool usage; look for lock contention on slow requests.
- Fix options: (1) increase thread pool size; (2) find and fix slow requests blocking threads; (3) migrate to virtual threads to eliminate the pool size ceiling.

Scenario 2 — Memory Growth After Deployment

After a new deployment, the JVM heap grows from 512 MB to 1.8 GB over 4 hours and eventually triggers an OOM. GC class histogram shows 45 million String objects occupying 900 MB. No single code path was changed that would obviously cause this. Diagnose.

Root cause investigation approach:
1. Take a heap dump: jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /tmp/oom.hprof
2. Open in Eclipse MAT → Dominator Tree → identify what holds all the String objects
3. Look for: a cache with no eviction policy, a list appended to without trimming, a global map keyed by request parameters, log output captured to a String buffer
4. Take a JFR recording and look at jdk.ObjectAllocationInNewTLAB for the String class — the stack trace will show exactly which code path allocates them
5. Common root cause: Map<String, ...> used as a cache with request path + parameters as keys — unbounded growth as the set of unique URLs grows

Debugging Exercises

Debug 1 — The Invisible CPU Spike

The following method appears to consume 0% CPU in VisualVM's sampler but the service's overall CPU usage is 80% and all threads are in this method. Explain why and how to properly profile it.

public long computeChecksum(byte[] data) {
    long checksum = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < data.length; i++) {  // tight inner loop
        checksum ^= (data[i] & 0xFFL) * PRIME_TABLE[i % PRIME_TABLE.length];
    }
    return checksum;
}

Diagnosis: VisualVM's sampler suffers from safepoint bias. This tight loop over a primitive array runs with no safepoints — the loop body never reaches a back-edge safepoint check because the JIT optimized it. The sampler cannot interrupt the thread and sees zero samples in this method.

Fix: Use async-profiler which uses SIGPROF + AsyncGetCallTrace — it will interrupt the thread at any instruction and correctly attribute CPU time to computeChecksum. Alternatively, add -XX:+PrintSafepointStatistics to confirm safepoint delays.

Debug 2 — Allocation Rate Mystery

JFR reports an allocation rate of 3 GB/s. The application processes 500 requests/second. That implies 6 MB of objects allocated per request — but the request payload is 2 KB and the response is 5 KB. Where are the 6 MB coming from?

Diagnosis approach:
1. Run async-profiler allocation profiling: -e alloc -i 64k
2. Look for unexpectedly wide frames in the allocation flame graph
3. Common hidden allocation sources:
- JSON deserializer creating intermediate JsonNode tree: a 2 KB JSON creates ~200 intermediate objects
- Log statements calling toString() on domain objects even when log level is disabled
- ArrayList.toArray() defensive copy in every response mapper
- Exception creation capturing a stack trace on every request (even handled exceptions): each new Exception() allocates ~4 KB of stack trace objects

Interview Challenges

Challenge 1

"We have a Java service with P99 of 800ms. CPU is 30%, memory is stable, GC overhead is 2%. What is causing the latency?"

Answer framework: With low CPU, stable memory, and low GC overhead, the bottleneck is waiting — not computation or GC. Investigate: (1) thread pool saturation (check queue depth metric); (2) downstream dependency latency (check socket read events in JFR or spans in APM); (3) lock contention (async-profiler lock mode); (4) thread context switching at scale (wall-clock profiling). The P99 implies infrequent events — check for periodic GC pauses, periodic lock flushes, or time-based cache invalidations that affect only the slowest requests.

Challenge 2

"Describe how you would safely profile a production JVM that is currently under load and cannot be restarted."

Answer: Use tools that attach to a running JVM without restart:
1. JFR (already running or started via jcmd): jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=diag settings=default duration=60s filename=/tmp/p.jfr — < 1% overhead, safe for production
2. async-profiler: attach via asprof -d 30 -f /tmp/cpu.html <pid> — uses JVMTI attach; < 3% overhead; run only for 30–60 second windows
3. Thread dump: jcmd <pid> Thread.print — instantaneous, zero ongoing overhead
4. jcmd diagnostics: VM.flags, GC.heap_info, GC.class_histogram — all safe for running production JVMs

Avoid: GC.run (forces Full GC), GC.heap_dump during peak traffic (pauses JVM to copy heap), settings=profile for continuous recording.

Challenge 3

"What is the difference between JFR and Micrometer, and when would you use each?"

Answer: They operate at different layers and serve complementary purposes.

JFR is a JVM-level diagnostic recorder that captures events from inside the JVM itself — method execution stack traces, GC events, lock acquisitions, I/O operations, JIT compilation events. It is used for post-hoc incident investigation and profiling — you dump a recording after an incident and analyze what happened inside the JVM.

Micrometer is an application-level metrics instrumentation library that captures business and operational metrics that you define — request latency, error rates, queue depth, business KPIs. It is used for continuous monitoring, alerting, and dashboards — it feeds data to Prometheus, Grafana, or an APM tool on an ongoing basis.

Use JFR to answer why the JVM behaved a certain way. Use Micrometer to answer when your service is behaving poorly so you know to go investigate with JFR.

Key Takeaways

  • Profile before you optimize — the bottleneck is almost never where you think it is; profiling data ends the guessing and delivers the 80/20 opportunity immediately
  • JFR is always-on capable — settings=default with maxage=2h maxsize=200m costs less than 1% overhead and gives you 2 hours of pre-incident data; enable it in production from day one
  • async-profiler fixes safepoint bias — traditional JVM samplers systematically miss tight loops and native methods; async-profiler's AsyncGetCallTrace + SIGPROF gives accurate, unbiased CPU time attribution
  • Flame graphs are scannable at a glance — wide frames at the top of the flame graph are where time is actually spent; learn to read them before you need them in a production incident
  • Allocation is usually the real problem — services with "GC overhead too high" almost always have an allocation problem, not a GC configuration problem; reduce allocation rate first, then tune GC
  • Wall-clock profiling exposes I/O and lock waits — when CPU is low but latency is high, switch from CPU to wall-clock mode; blocked threads become visible as wide frames
  • jcmd is always available — no flags needed at startup; attach to any JVM process for thread dumps, heap histograms, JFR control, and runtime flag inspection
  • Micrometer is non-optional for production — instrument request latency, error rates, and queue depth from day one; add JVM GC and memory binders; export to Prometheus
  • JMH for validation — every performance claim must be validated with a proper JMH benchmark; System.nanoTime loops are not benchmarks; JIT warmup and dead code elimination invalidate naïve measurements
  • Phase 6 complete — you now hold the full JVM internals stack, from class loading and bytecode through JIT compilation, memory management, GC algorithms, and production observability
