Part 1

Networking Fundamentals: The Java Perspective

Every modern Java application touches the network. Whether it is a Spring Boot REST API receiving HTTP requests, a Kafka consumer reading from a broker, a microservice calling a downstream dependency, or a database connection pool maintaining persistent TCP connections — networking is unavoidable infrastructure.

The two fundamental transport protocols:

TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)
  ├─ Connection-oriented: three-way handshake before data flows
  ├─ Reliable: data arrives in order, retransmitted if lost
  ├─ Flow control: sender rate adapted to receiver capacity
  ├─ Use cases: HTTP, HTTPS, JDBC, Redis, Kafka, SMTP, FTP
  └─ Java class: java.net.Socket / java.net.ServerSocket

UDP (User Datagram Protocol)
  ├─ Connectionless: no handshake, fire-and-forget
  ├─ Unreliable: packets may arrive out of order or not at all
  ├─ No flow control: sender can overwhelm receiver
  ├─ Lower overhead: no connection state per client
  ├─ Use cases: DNS, VoIP, live streaming, game state updates, metrics (StatsD)
  └─ Java class: java.net.DatagramSocket / java.net.DatagramPacket

The OSI model and where Java operates:

OSI Layers and Java's Position:
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
Layer 7 — Application   ← HTTP, SMTP, FTP, Kafka protocol
                           Java: HttpURLConnection, HttpClient, OkHttp
Layer 6 — Presentation  ← TLS/SSL encryption, data encoding
                           Java: javax.net.ssl.SSLSocket, SSLEngine
Layer 5 — Session       ← Session management (part of TLS)
Layer 4 — Transport     ← TCP, UDP
                           Java: Socket, ServerSocket, DatagramSocket
Layer 3 — Network       ← IP addressing, routing
                           Java: InetAddress
Layer 2 — Data Link     ← Ethernet frames (OS/hardware)
Layer 1 — Physical      ← Cables, WiFi signals (hardware)
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
Java code operates at Layers 4–7. The OS handles Layers 1–3.

The socket abstraction:

A socket is an endpoint for network communication identified by an IP address and a port number. The OS manages the actual file descriptors; Java wraps them in Socket, ServerSocket, and DatagramSocket objects. Every network connection in any Java program — HTTP request, JDBC connection, Kafka message — ultimately uses a socket.

Part 2

InetAddress: Working with IP Addresses

java.net.InetAddress represents an IP address (IPv4 or IPv6) and provides DNS resolution.

import java.net.*;

// DNS resolution — looks up hostname → IP:
InetAddress google = InetAddress.getByName("www.google.com");
System.out.println(google.getHostAddress());    // e.g., "142.250.80.36"
System.out.println(google.getHostName());        // "www.google.com"
System.out.println(google.getCanonicalHostName()); // fully qualified hostname

// All IP addresses for a hostname (round-robin DNS):
InetAddress[] all = InetAddress.getAllByName("www.google.com");
for (InetAddress addr : all) {
    System.out.println(addr.getHostAddress());
}

// Reverse lookup — IP → hostname:
InetAddress byIP = InetAddress.getByAddress(new byte[]{8, 8, 8, 8}); // 8.8.8.8
System.out.println(byIP.getCanonicalHostName()); // "dns.google"

// Local machine information:
InetAddress localhost = InetAddress.getLocalHost();
System.out.println(localhost.getHostName());    // machine name
System.out.println(localhost.getHostAddress()); // local IP

// Loopback address (always works, no DNS):
InetAddress loopback = InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress();
System.out.println(loopback.getHostAddress()); // "127.0.0.1" or "::1"

// Reachability check (uses ICMP ping or TCP port 7 echo):
boolean reachable = google.isReachable(3000); // 3 second timeout

IPv4 vs IPv6 in Java:

// Java automatically handles both IPv4 and IPv6:
InetAddress ipv4 = InetAddress.getByName("192.168.1.1");    // Inet4Address
InetAddress ipv6 = InetAddress.getByName("2001:db8::1");    // Inet6Address

System.out.println(ipv4 instanceof Inet4Address); // true
System.out.println(ipv6 instanceof Inet6Address); // true

// Force IPv4 (useful for legacy systems):
// java -Djava.net.preferIPv4Stack=true -jar app.jar

// Prefer IPv6 for new connections when both are available:
// java -Djava.net.preferIPv6Addresses=true -jar app.jar

DNS caching in the JVM:

The JVM caches DNS results in a security manager-controlled cache. By default, successful lookups are cached for 30 seconds (or indefinitely if a security manager is installed). This can cause problems in containerized environments where service IPs change:

# In jre/lib/security/java.security:
networkaddress.cache.ttl=30          # success cache TTL (seconds)
networkaddress.cache.negative.ttl=10 # failure cache TTL (seconds)

# Or set programmatically:
Security.setProperty("networkaddress.cache.ttl", "5");
Part 3

TCP Sockets: Socket and ServerSocket

java.net.Socket represents one end of a TCP connection; java.net.ServerSocket listens for incoming connection requests.

Server-side: ServerSocket

import java.net.*;
import java.io.*;

public class EchoServer {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        // Bind to port 8080 on all interfaces:
        // backlog=50: OS queues up to 50 pending connections before refusing new ones
        try (ServerSocket serverSocket = new ServerSocket(8080, 50)) {
            System.out.println("Server listening on port " + serverSocket.getLocalPort());

            while (true) {
                // Blocks until a client connects:
                Socket clientSocket = serverSocket.accept();
                System.out.println("Client connected: " + clientSocket.getRemoteSocketAddress());

                // Handle in a thread (blocking I/O requires one thread per connection):
                new Thread(() -> handleClient(clientSocket)).start();
            }
        }
    }

    private static void handleClient(Socket socket) {
        try (socket;
             BufferedReader in = new BufferedReader(
                 new InputStreamReader(socket.getInputStream()));
             PrintWriter out = new PrintWriter(socket.getOutputStream(), true)) {

            String line;
            while ((line = in.readLine()) != null) {
                System.out.println("Received: " + line);
                out.println("Echo: " + line); // autoFlush=true on PrintWriter
            }
        } catch (IOException e) {
            System.err.println("Client handler error: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}

Client-side: Socket

public class EchoClient {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        // Connect to server at localhost:8080, timeout 5 seconds:
        try (Socket socket = new Socket()) {
            socket.connect(new InetSocketAddress("localhost", 8080), 5000);

            // Configure socket options:
            socket.setSoTimeout(10_000);    // read timeout: 10 seconds
            socket.setTcpNoDelay(true);     // disable Nagle's algorithm (low latency)
            socket.setKeepAlive(true);      // OS sends TCP keepalive probes

            PrintWriter out = new PrintWriter(socket.getOutputStream(), true);
            BufferedReader in = new BufferedReader(
                new InputStreamReader(socket.getInputStream()));

            out.println("Hello, server!");
            String response = in.readLine();
            System.out.println("Server said: " + response);

            out.println("How are you?");
            System.out.println("Server said: " + in.readLine());
        }
    }
}

Important Socket options:

Option Method Purpose
Connect timeout socket.connect(addr, millis) Fail fast if server is unreachable
Read timeout socket.setSoTimeout(millis) Throw SocketTimeoutException if read blocks too long
TCP_NODELAY socket.setTcpNoDelay(true) Disable Nagle's algorithm — reduces latency for small packets
SO_KEEPALIVE socket.setKeepAlive(true) OS probes connection to detect dead peers
SO_LINGER socket.setSoLinger(true, 0) close() sends RST immediately instead of FIN
Receive/Send buffer socket.setReceiveBufferSize(n) Tune OS socket buffer for throughput
Part 4

Building a TCP Protocol: Request/Response Pattern

Real protocols on top of TCP send structured messages. The naive line-by-line approach breaks for binary data. A robust framing approach uses a length prefix.

Length-prefixed protocol:

// Protocol: [4 bytes: message length][N bytes: message body]
// Both sides agree on this framing.

public class MessageFramer {

    // Write a framed message:
    public static void writeMessage(OutputStream out, byte[] message) throws IOException {
        DataOutputStream dos = new DataOutputStream(out);
        dos.writeInt(message.length);  // 4-byte big-endian length
        dos.write(message);
        dos.flush();
    }

    // Read a complete framed message (blocks until full message arrives):
    public static byte[] readMessage(InputStream in) throws IOException {
        DataInputStream dis = new DataInputStream(in);
        int length = dis.readInt();               // blocks until 4 bytes available
        if (length < 0 || length > 64 * 1024 * 1024) {
            throw new IOException("Invalid message length: " + length);
        }
        byte[] body = new byte[length];
        dis.readFully(body);                       // blocks until all length bytes arrive
        return body;
    }
}

// Server using framed protocol:
public class FramedServer {
    private static void handleClient(Socket socket) throws IOException {
        try (socket) {
            while (true) {
                byte[] request = MessageFramer.readMessage(socket.getInputStream());
                String requestText = new String(request, StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
                System.out.println("Request: " + requestText);

                // Process and respond:
                String responseText = "Processed: " + requestText.toUpperCase();
                MessageFramer.writeMessage(socket.getOutputStream(),
                    responseText.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
            }
        }
    }
}

Why readFully is essential:

TCP is a stream protocol — there is no guarantee that a read() call returns all requested bytes at once. A 100-byte message might arrive as 47 bytes + 53 bytes in two separate read() calls. DataInputStream.readFully() loops internally until all requested bytes are received, which is the correct way to read a known-length message from a TCP stream.

Part 5

UDP: DatagramSocket and DatagramPacket

UDP is connectionless. Each packet is independent — no stream, no ordering, no retry.

UDP server:

public class UdpEchoServer {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        try (DatagramSocket socket = new DatagramSocket(9000)) {
            System.out.println("UDP server listening on port 9000");

            byte[] buffer = new byte[1024];
            DatagramPacket packet = new DatagramPacket(buffer, buffer.length);

            while (true) {
                socket.receive(packet);  // blocks until a datagram arrives

                String message = new String(packet.getData(), 0,
                    packet.getLength(), StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
                System.out.println("Received from " + packet.getSocketAddress() + ": " + message);

                // Echo back to sender:
                byte[] response = ("Echo: " + message).getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
                DatagramPacket reply = new DatagramPacket(
                    response, response.length,
                    packet.getAddress(), packet.getPort());
                socket.send(reply);

                // Reset buffer for next packet:
                packet.setLength(buffer.length);
            }
        }
    }
}

UDP client:

public class UdpClient {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException, SocketTimeoutException {
        try (DatagramSocket socket = new DatagramSocket()) {
            socket.setSoTimeout(3000); // 3-second receive timeout

            InetAddress serverAddr = InetAddress.getByName("localhost");
            int serverPort = 9000;

            // Send:
            String message = "Hello UDP!";
            byte[] data = message.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
            DatagramPacket packet = new DatagramPacket(data, data.length, serverAddr, serverPort);
            socket.send(packet);

            // Receive response (may timeout if server doesn't reply):
            byte[] responseBuffer = new byte[1024];
            DatagramPacket response = new DatagramPacket(responseBuffer, responseBuffer.length);
            try {
                socket.receive(response);
                System.out.println("Response: " + new String(
                    response.getData(), 0, response.getLength(), StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
            } catch (SocketTimeoutException e) {
                System.err.println("No response within 3 seconds — packet may have been lost");
            }
        }
    }
}

UDP multicast (one sender, multiple receivers):

// Join a multicast group (224.0.0.0 – 239.255.255.255 are multicast addresses):
MulticastSocket mcastSocket = new MulticastSocket(5000);
InetAddress group = InetAddress.getByName("224.0.0.1");
mcastSocket.joinGroup(group);

// Receive multicast messages:
byte[] buf = new byte[1024];
DatagramPacket packet = new DatagramPacket(buf, buf.length);
mcastSocket.receive(packet);

// Leave the group:
mcastSocket.leaveGroup(group);
mcastSocket.close();
Part 6

URL and URI: Working with Addresses

java.net.URL represents a Uniform Resource Locator and provides simple HTTP/HTTPS connectivity. java.net.URI represents any Uniform Resource Identifier and is used for parsing and manipulation.

URL parsing and components:

URL url = new URL("https://api.example.com:8443/v1/orders?status=pending&limit=50#section2");

System.out.println(url.getProtocol());  // "https"
System.out.println(url.getHost());      // "api.example.com"
System.out.println(url.getPort());      // 8443
System.out.println(url.getPath());      // "/v1/orders"
System.out.println(url.getQuery());     // "status=pending&limit=50"
System.out.println(url.getRef());       // "section2"

// Open a stream directly (simple GET request, no configuration options):
try (InputStream stream = url.openStream()) {
    String body = new String(stream.readAllBytes(), StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
    System.out.println(body);
}

URI vs URL:

// URI — handles any scheme, can be relative, supports encoding:
URI uri = new URI("https", "api.example.com", "/v1/orders", "status=pending", null);
System.out.println(uri.toString()); // correctly percent-encoded

// URI to URL (only works for absolute URIs with known schemes):
URL fromUri = uri.toURL();

// Building URIs safely (avoids injection):
URI safe = new URI("https", "api.example.com", "/search",
    "q=hello world&lang=en",  // URI encodes the space automatically
    null);
System.out.println(safe); // https://api.example.com/search?q=hello%20world&lang=en
Part 7

HttpURLConnection: The Built-in HTTP Client (Legacy)

HttpURLConnection is the original Java HTTP client — available since Java 1.1. It is verbose and has significant usability problems, but you will encounter it in legacy codebases. Understanding it helps you appreciate the modern alternatives.

GET request with HttpURLConnection:

public class LegacyHttpClient {

    public static String get(String urlString) throws IOException {
        URL url = new URL(urlString);
        HttpURLConnection conn = (HttpURLConnection) url.openConnection();

        conn.setRequestMethod("GET");
        conn.setRequestProperty("Accept", "application/json");
        conn.setRequestProperty("Authorization", "Bearer " + getToken());
        conn.setConnectTimeout(5_000);  // connection timeout: 5 seconds
        conn.setReadTimeout(30_000);    // read timeout: 30 seconds
        conn.setInstanceFollowRedirects(true);

        int statusCode = conn.getResponseCode();
        System.out.println("Status: " + statusCode + " " + conn.getResponseMessage());

        // Must read from error stream on 4xx/5xx, not input stream:
        InputStream responseStream = (statusCode >= 400)
            ? conn.getErrorStream()
            : conn.getInputStream();

        try (responseStream) {
            return new String(responseStream.readAllBytes(), StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
        } finally {
            conn.disconnect();
        }
    }

    public static String post(String urlString, String body) throws IOException {
        URL url = new URL(urlString);
        HttpURLConnection conn = (HttpURLConnection) url.openConnection();

        conn.setRequestMethod("POST");
        conn.setRequestProperty("Content-Type", "application/json");
        conn.setRequestProperty("Accept", "application/json");
        conn.setDoOutput(true);  // MUST call this before writing to output stream
        conn.setConnectTimeout(5_000);
        conn.setReadTimeout(30_000);

        // Write request body:
        try (OutputStream os = conn.getOutputStream()) {
            os.write(body.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
        }

        int statusCode = conn.getResponseCode();
        InputStream responseStream = (statusCode >= 400)
            ? conn.getErrorStream()
            : conn.getInputStream();

        try (responseStream) {
            return new String(responseStream.readAllBytes(), StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
        } finally {
            conn.disconnect();
        }
    }
}

Why HttpURLConnection is considered legacy:

Problem Description
Verbose boilerplate 20+ lines for a simple GET
No HTTP/2 support HTTP/1.1 only
No async support Blocking I/O only
Error stream confusion Different stream for 4xx/5xx
Redirect handling Manual for HTTPS→HTTP
No connection pooling Creates a new connection per request (unless using a proxy)

Modern replacement: java.net.http.HttpClient (Java 11+) — see Part 8.

Part 8

Java 11 HttpClient: The Modern HTTP API

Java 11 introduced java.net.http.HttpClient — a modern, fluent, HTTP/2-capable, asynchronous HTTP client.

Building the HttpClient:

import java.net.http.*;
import java.net.http.HttpResponse.*;

// Create a shared, reusable HttpClient (expensive to create — make it a singleton):
HttpClient client = HttpClient.newBuilder()
    .version(HttpClient.Version.HTTP_2)          // prefer HTTP/2, fall back to HTTP/1.1
    .followRedirects(HttpClient.Redirect.NORMAL) // follow redirects (not HTTPS→HTTP)
    .connectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5))
    .executor(Executors.newFixedThreadPool(10))  // custom thread pool for async ops
    .build();

Synchronous GET request:

HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder()
    .uri(URI.create("https://api.example.com/v1/orders"))
    .header("Accept", "application/json")
    .header("Authorization", "Bearer " + token)
    .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(30))
    .GET()
    .build();

HttpResponse<String> response = client.send(request, BodyHandlers.ofString());

System.out.println("Status: " + response.statusCode());
System.out.println("Body: " + response.body());
System.out.println("Content-Type: " + response.headers().firstValue("Content-Type").orElse("none"));

Synchronous POST with JSON body:

String orderJson = """
    {
      "customerId": 42,
      "productId": "WIDGET-001",
      "quantity": 3
    }
    """;

HttpRequest postRequest = HttpRequest.newBuilder()
    .uri(URI.create("https://api.example.com/v1/orders"))
    .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
    .header("Accept", "application/json")
    .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(30))
    .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(orderJson))
    .build();

HttpResponse<String> postResponse = client.send(postRequest, BodyHandlers.ofString());

if (postResponse.statusCode() == 201) {
    System.out.println("Order created: " + postResponse.body());
} else {
    System.err.println("Error " + postResponse.statusCode() + ": " + postResponse.body());
}

Asynchronous requests:

// sendAsync returns CompletableFuture — non-blocking:
CompletableFuture<HttpResponse<String>> futureResponse = client.sendAsync(
    request, BodyHandlers.ofString());

// Chain processing asynchronously:
futureResponse
    .thenApply(HttpResponse::body)
    .thenApply(body -> parseOrders(body))
    .thenAccept(orders -> processOrders(orders))
    .exceptionally(ex -> {
        log.error("HTTP request failed", ex);
        return null;
    });

// Or block when you need the result:
HttpResponse<String> result = futureResponse.get(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS);

Parallel requests with CompletableFuture:

// Fan-out: call multiple endpoints concurrently:
List<String> endpoints = List.of(
    "https://api.example.com/v1/inventory",
    "https://api.example.com/v1/pricing",
    "https://api.example.com/v1/promotions"
);

List<CompletableFuture<HttpResponse<String>>> futures = endpoints.stream()
    .map(url -> client.sendAsync(
        HttpRequest.newBuilder().uri(URI.create(url)).GET().build(),
        BodyHandlers.ofString()))
    .toList();

// Wait for all to complete:
CompletableFuture.allOf(futures.toArray(new CompletableFuture[0])).join();

// Collect results:
List<String> results = futures.stream()
    .map(f -> f.join().body())
    .toList();
Part 9

SSL/TLS: Secure Connections

All production network communication must be encrypted. Java's TLS support is built into the standard library via javax.net.ssl.

HTTPS with HttpClient (automatic TLS):

// HttpClient handles TLS transparently for https:// URIs:
HttpClient secureClient = HttpClient.newBuilder()
    .version(HttpClient.Version.HTTP_2)
    .build();

// The TLS handshake happens automatically:
HttpResponse<String> response = secureClient.send(
    HttpRequest.newBuilder()
        .uri(URI.create("https://api.example.com/v1/data"))
        .build(),
    BodyHandlers.ofString());

Custom TLS configuration (mutual TLS, custom certificate authorities):

// Load a custom trust store (contains trusted CA certificates):
KeyStore trustStore = KeyStore.getInstance("JKS");
try (InputStream ts = new FileInputStream("truststore.jks")) {
    trustStore.load(ts, "truststore-password".toCharArray());
}

TrustManagerFactory tmf = TrustManagerFactory.getInstance(
    TrustManagerFactory.getDefaultAlgorithm());
tmf.init(trustStore);

// Load a client key store (for mutual TLS — client certificate authentication):
KeyStore keyStore = KeyStore.getInstance("PKCS12");
try (InputStream ks = new FileInputStream("client-cert.p12")) {
    keyStore.load(ks, "key-password".toCharArray());
}

KeyManagerFactory kmf = KeyManagerFactory.getInstance(
    KeyManagerFactory.getDefaultAlgorithm());
kmf.init(keyStore, "key-password".toCharArray());

// Build an SSLContext:
SSLContext sslContext = SSLContext.getInstance("TLS");
sslContext.init(kmf.getKeyManagers(), tmf.getTrustManagers(), new SecureRandom());

// Use in HttpClient:
HttpClient mTlsClient = HttpClient.newBuilder()
    .sslContext(sslContext)
    .build();

TLS socket directly:

SSLSocketFactory factory = (SSLSocketFactory) SSLSocketFactory.getDefault();
try (SSLSocket sslSocket = (SSLSocket) factory.createSocket("api.example.com", 443)) {
    sslSocket.setEnabledProtocols(new String[]{"TLSv1.3", "TLSv1.2"});
    sslSocket.startHandshake();

    SSLSession session = sslSocket.getSession();
    System.out.println("Protocol: " + session.getProtocol());
    System.out.println("Cipher: " + session.getCipherSuite());
    System.out.println("Server cert: " + session.getPeerPrincipal());

    // Communicate over the encrypted socket...
}
Part 10

TCP Connection Pooling

Creating a new TCP connection for every request is expensive: the three-way handshake adds ~1 RTT of latency; TLS adds another 1–2 RTTs. Connection pooling reuses established connections.

Why connection pooling matters:

Without pooling (per-request connection):
  Request 1: [TCP handshake 30ms] [TLS 60ms] [HTTP 20ms] = 110ms total
  Request 2: [TCP handshake 30ms] [TLS 60ms] [HTTP 20ms] = 110ms total

With pooling (reuse connection):
  Request 1: [TCP handshake 30ms] [TLS 60ms] [HTTP 20ms] = 110ms total
  Request 2: [HTTP 20ms] = 20ms total  ← 5.5× faster
  Request N: [HTTP 20ms] = 20ms total

Java 11 HttpClient connection pooling:

The HttpClient manages connection pools internally. HTTP/2 multiplexes multiple requests over a single connection. HTTP/1.1 maintains a pool of keep-alive connections.

// This single HttpClient instance manages the connection pool:
// Share it application-wide as a singleton/bean
HttpClient client = HttpClient.newBuilder()
    .version(HttpClient.Version.HTTP_2)  // HTTP/2 = one connection handles all concurrent requests
    .connectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(10))
    .build();
// No explicit pool configuration needed — HttpClient handles it internally

OkHttp connection pooling (widely used library):

// OkHttp gives explicit pool configuration:
ConnectionPool pool = new ConnectionPool(
    20,               // maxIdleConnections: keep up to 20 idle connections
    5, TimeUnit.MINUTES  // keepAliveDuration: discard idle connections after 5 min
);

OkHttpClient okClient = new OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .connectionPool(pool)
    .connectTimeout(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
    .readTimeout(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
    .writeTimeout(15, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
    .retryOnConnectionFailure(true)
    .build();

// Make a request:
Request request = new Request.Builder()
    .url("https://api.example.com/v1/orders")
    .header("Authorization", "Bearer " + token)
    .build();

try (Response response = okClient.newCall(request).execute()) {
    System.out.println(response.code());
    System.out.println(response.body().string());
}

JDBC connection pooling (HikariCP — the JVM standard):

// Database connections ARE TCP connections:
HikariConfig config = new HikariConfig();
config.setJdbcUrl("jdbc:postgresql://db-host:5432/mydb");
config.setUsername("app_user");
config.setPassword("secret");
config.setMaximumPoolSize(20);           // max concurrent DB connections
config.setMinimumIdle(5);               // keep 5 connections warm
config.setConnectionTimeout(30_000);    // wait max 30s for a connection from pool
config.setIdleTimeout(600_000);         // close idle connections after 10 min
config.setMaxLifetime(1_800_000);       // recycle connections after 30 min
config.setConnectionTestQuery("SELECT 1"); // validate connections before use

HikariDataSource dataSource = new HikariDataSource(config);
// Spring Boot autoconfigures HikariCP by default when spring-boot-starter-jdbc is present
Part 11

REST Client Basics: OkHttp and Apache HttpClient

Before Spring RestTemplate/WebClient (covered in Part 13), understanding the raw HTTP client libraries is essential for non-Spring contexts and for configuring the underlying clients used by framework abstractions.

OkHttp — the modern standard HTTP client library:

// OkHttp wraps Java's HttpClient with a more ergonomic API and middleware:
OkHttpClient client = new OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .connectTimeout(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
    .readTimeout(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
    .addInterceptor(new LoggingInterceptor())  // add request/response logging
    .addInterceptor(new RetryInterceptor(3))   // retry on connection failures
    .build();

// GET with query parameters:
HttpUrl url = HttpUrl.parse("https://api.example.com/v1/orders").newBuilder()
    .addQueryParameter("status", "pending")
    .addQueryParameter("limit", "50")
    .build();

Request request = new Request.Builder()
    .url(url)
    .header("Authorization", "Bearer " + token)
    .build();

// Synchronous:
try (Response response = client.newCall(request).execute()) {
    if (!response.isSuccessful()) throw new IOException("HTTP " + response.code());
    String body = response.body().string();
    List<Order> orders = mapper.readValue(body, new TypeReference<List<Order>>(){});
}

// Asynchronous:
client.newCall(request).enqueue(new Callback() {
    @Override
    public void onFailure(Call call, IOException e) {
        log.error("Request failed", e);
    }
    @Override
    public void onResponse(Call call, Response response) throws IOException {
        try (response) {
            log.info("Got response: {}", response.code());
        }
    }
});

OkHttp interceptors — cross-cutting concerns:

// Logging interceptor:
public class LoggingInterceptor implements Interceptor {
    @Override
    public Response intercept(Chain chain) throws IOException {
        Request request = chain.request();
        long start = System.currentTimeMillis();

        log.info("→ {} {}", request.method(), request.url());
        Response response = chain.proceed(request);
        long elapsed = System.currentTimeMillis() - start;
        log.info("← {} {} ({}ms)", response.code(), request.url(), elapsed);

        return response;
    }
}

// Authentication interceptor — adds token to every request:
public class AuthInterceptor implements Interceptor {
    private final TokenProvider tokenProvider;

    @Override
    public Response intercept(Chain chain) throws IOException {
        Request authenticated = chain.request().newBuilder()
            .header("Authorization", "Bearer " + tokenProvider.getToken())
            .build();
        return chain.proceed(authenticated);
    }
}
Part 12

HTTP Error Handling and Retry Patterns

Production HTTP clients must handle failures gracefully. Transient failures (network blip, upstream restart) should be retried; permanent failures (4xx, invalid data) should not.

Retry logic with exponential backoff:

public class ResilientHttpClient {
    private final HttpClient httpClient;
    private static final int MAX_RETRIES = 3;
    private static final long BASE_DELAY_MS = 100;

    public String getWithRetry(String url) throws Exception {
        int attempt = 0;
        Exception lastException = null;

        while (attempt < MAX_RETRIES) {
            try {
                HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder()
                    .uri(URI.create(url))
                    .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(10))
                    .GET()
                    .build();

                HttpResponse<String> response = httpClient.send(
                    request, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString());

                // Retry on 5xx (server errors — potentially transient):
                if (response.statusCode() >= 500) {
                    throw new IOException("Server error: " + response.statusCode());
                }
                // Don't retry on 4xx (client errors — permanent):
                if (response.statusCode() >= 400) {
                    throw new IllegalStateException("Client error: " + response.statusCode()
                        + " " + response.body());
                }

                return response.body();

            } catch (IOException e) {
                lastException = e;
                attempt++;
                if (attempt < MAX_RETRIES) {
                    // Exponential backoff with jitter:
                    long delay = BASE_DELAY_MS * (1L << attempt)
                        + ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextLong(50);
                    log.warn("Request failed (attempt {}), retrying in {}ms: {}", attempt, delay, e.getMessage());
                    Thread.sleep(delay);
                }
            }
        }
        throw new RuntimeException("Request failed after " + MAX_RETRIES + " attempts", lastException);
    }
}

HTTP status code categories:

1xx — Informational: 100 Continue, 101 Switching Protocols
2xx — Success: 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content
3xx — Redirect: 301 Moved Permanently, 302 Found, 304 Not Modified
4xx — Client Error: 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden,
                    404 Not Found, 409 Conflict, 422 Unprocessable Entity,
                    429 Too Many Requests (rate limited)
5xx — Server Error: 500 Internal Server Error, 502 Bad Gateway,
                    503 Service Unavailable, 504 Gateway Timeout

Retry strategy:
  RETRY:   5xx, connection timeout, read timeout, network error
  NO RETRY: 4xx (the request is wrong, retrying won't help)
  RETRY with new token: 401 (token expired — refresh and retry once)

Circuit breaker pattern (Resilience4j):

CircuitBreakerConfig cbConfig = CircuitBreakerConfig.custom()
    .failureRateThreshold(50)           // open circuit if 50% of calls fail
    .waitDurationInOpenState(Duration.ofSeconds(30)) // stay open 30s
    .slidingWindowSize(10)              // evaluate over last 10 calls
    .permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState(3)
    .build();

CircuitBreaker cb = CircuitBreaker.of("order-service", cbConfig);

// Wrap HTTP call with circuit breaker:
Supplier<String> decoratedCall = CircuitBreaker.decorateSupplier(cb,
    () -> httpClient.getWithRetry("https://order-service/v1/orders"));

try {
    String result = decoratedCall.get();
} catch (CallNotPermittedException e) {
    // Circuit is open — return cached data or fallback:
    return getOrdersFromCache();
}
Part 13

Spring RestTemplate and WebClient (Preview)

Spring Framework provides two HTTP client abstractions over the underlying library: the blocking RestTemplate and the reactive WebClient. This is a preview — full reactive programming is covered in a later lesson.

RestTemplate (Spring 5 and earlier — synchronous, blocking):

// RestTemplate is thread-safe — create once and reuse:
@Bean
public RestTemplate restTemplate(RestTemplateBuilder builder) {
    return builder
        .connectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5))
        .readTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(30))
        .additionalInterceptors(new LoggingClientHttpRequestInterceptor())
        .build();
}

// Usage:
@Service
public class OrderServiceClient {
    private final RestTemplate restTemplate;
    private final String baseUrl = "https://order-service";

    // GET — returns a POJO directly (Jackson deserialization automatic):
    public Order getOrder(Long id) {
        return restTemplate.getForObject(baseUrl + "/v1/orders/{id}", Order.class, id);
    }

    // GET with ResponseEntity (access headers + status code):
    public ResponseEntity<Order> getOrderWithMeta(Long id) {
        return restTemplate.getForEntity(baseUrl + "/v1/orders/{id}", Order.class, id);
    }

    // POST:
    public Order createOrder(CreateOrderRequest req) {
        return restTemplate.postForObject(baseUrl + "/v1/orders", req, Order.class);
    }

    // GET list (TypeReference required for generics):
    public List<Order> getAllOrders() {
        return restTemplate.exchange(
            baseUrl + "/v1/orders",
            HttpMethod.GET,
            null,
            new ParameterizedTypeReference<List<Order>>(){}
        ).getBody();
    }

    // Error handling:
    public Optional<Order> getOrderSafe(Long id) {
        try {
            return Optional.ofNullable(getOrder(id));
        } catch (HttpClientErrorException.NotFound e) {
            return Optional.empty();
        } catch (HttpServerErrorException e) {
            throw new ServiceUnavailableException("Order service error", e);
        }
    }
}

WebClient (Spring WebFlux — non-blocking, reactive):

// WebClient — the modern Spring HTTP client:
@Bean
public WebClient webClient(WebClient.Builder builder) {
    return builder
        .baseUrl("https://order-service")
        .defaultHeader(HttpHeaders.ACCEPT, MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE)
        .codecs(c -> c.defaultCodecs().maxInMemorySize(1 * 1024 * 1024)) // 1 MB
        .build();
}

// Usage — reactive (Mono/Flux):
public Mono<Order> getOrder(Long id) {
    return webClient.get()
        .uri("/v1/orders/{id}", id)
        .retrieve()
        .onStatus(HttpStatus::is4xxClientError, response ->
            Mono.error(new OrderNotFoundException(id)))
        .onStatus(HttpStatus::is5xxServerError, response ->
            Mono.error(new ServiceException("Order service error")))
        .bodyToMono(Order.class)
        .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5))
        .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(100)));
}

// Blocking usage (when you're not in a reactive pipeline):
public Order getOrderBlocking(Long id) {
    return getOrder(id).block(Duration.ofSeconds(10));
}

RestTemplate vs WebClient:

Aspect RestTemplate WebClient
Threading model Blocking (one thread per request) Non-blocking (event loop)
Throughput Limited by thread pool Very high (handles thousands of concurrent requests)
API style Imperative, familiar Reactive (Mono/Flux)
Spring status Maintenance mode (no new features) Recommended for all new code
Use when Simple scripts, legacy Spring MVC Any new Spring application
Part 14

Timeouts: The Most Critical HTTP Configuration

Missing timeouts are the single most common production networking failure mode. A service with no timeouts will hang indefinitely waiting for a downstream call that will never return.

The three timeout types:

1. Connection Timeout
   What: time to establish the TCP connection
   Missing: thread blocks "forever" if server is unreachable
   Typical value: 1–10 seconds

2. Read Timeout (Socket Timeout)
   What: max time between two consecutive data packets after connection established
   Missing: thread blocks indefinitely if server stalls mid-response
   Typical value: 5–60 seconds depending on the operation

3. Write Timeout
   What: max time to write the request body
   Missing: thread blocks if network is very slow or server stops reading
   Typical value: 5–30 seconds

The cascade failure scenario:

Scenario (no timeouts configured):
1. Service A has 200 threads in its thread pool
2. Downstream Service B becomes slow (responds in 120 seconds)
3. Each request to A that calls B occupies a thread for 120 seconds
4. Within minutes, all 200 threads are stuck waiting on B
5. Service A becomes completely unresponsive — it cannot serve ANY requests
6. Services calling A now also hang... cascade failure spreads

With 10-second read timeout:
1. Each request to B times out after 10 seconds
2. Thread is released back to the pool
3. Service A remains responsive with a SocketTimeoutException error response
4. Cascade failure is prevented

// Java 11 HttpClient:
HttpClient.newBuilder()
    .connectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5))
    .build();
HttpRequest.newBuilder()
    .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(30))  // overall request timeout
    ...

// OkHttp:

    .connectTimeout(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
    .readTimeout(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
    .writeTimeout(15, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
    .callTimeout(60, TimeUnit.SECONDS)  // total call timeout
    ...

    .connectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5))
    .readTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(30))
    ...

// Spring WebClient:

    .uri(...)
    .retrieve()
    .bodyToMono(String.class)

    ...

// Spring application.yml (global defaults):
spring:
  mvc:
    async:
      request-timeout: 30000  # milliseconds
Part 15

Network I/O and Virtual Threads (Java 21)

Java 21's virtual threads fundamentally change the economics of blocking network I/O. The "one thread per connection" model that was expensive with platform threads becomes cheap with virtual threads.

Why blocking I/O was a problem with platform threads:

Platform thread = OS thread = ~1 MB stack memory
100K concurrent connections = 100K platform threads = 100 GB RAM (impossible)

Traditional workaround: NIO (non-blocking I/O) with event loops (Netty)
  → Extremely complex programming model
  → Callback hell or reactor chains
  → Hard to debug, test, and profile

With virtual threads (Java 21):
Virtual thread = JVM fiber = ~1 KB stack memory
100K concurrent connections = 100K virtual threads = ~100 MB RAM (trivial)
  → No callback hell — write blocking I/O code normally
  → JVM transparently parks the virtual thread when it blocks
  → Scales like non-blocking I/O, reads like sequential code

Virtual threads with socket I/O:

// Blocking socket server that scales to 100K concurrent connections:
try (ServerSocket serverSocket = new ServerSocket(8080)) {
    // Use a virtual thread executor:
    ExecutorService executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor();

    while (true) {
        Socket clientSocket = serverSocket.accept();
        // Each connection gets its own virtual thread — no thread pool sizing needed:
        executor.submit(() -> handleClient(clientSocket));
        // handleClient can block freely — it's a virtual thread
    }
}

Virtual threads with HttpClient:

// The Java 11 HttpClient uses virtual threads internally when available:
HttpClient client = HttpClient.newBuilder()
    .executor(Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor())
    .build();

// This now scales to thousands of concurrent requests with blocking API:
List<HttpRequest> requests = buildRequests(10_000);
List<CompletableFuture<HttpResponse<String>>> futures = requests.stream()
    .map(req -> client.sendAsync(req, BodyHandlers.ofString()))
    .toList();

Spring Boot 3.2 with virtual threads:

# application.yml:
spring:
  threads:
    virtual:
      enabled: true  # All Spring MVC request-handling threads become virtual

With this setting, each HTTP request to a Spring Boot application runs on a virtual thread. Blocking database calls, HTTP client calls, and file I/O all park the virtual thread while waiting — no thread pool exhaustion, no reactive programming required.

DNS, Proxies, and Network Configuration

Production Java applications often run behind proxies or in environments with specific DNS requirements.

HTTP proxy configuration:

// System proxy settings (read from JVM system properties):
// java -Dhttp.proxyHost=proxy.company.com -Dhttp.proxyPort=8080
//      -Dhttps.proxyHost=proxy.company.com -Dhttps.proxyPort=8443

// Programmatic proxy for a single HttpClient:
ProxySelector proxy = ProxySelector.of(
    new InetSocketAddress("proxy.company.com", 8080));

HttpClient client = HttpClient.newBuilder()
    .proxy(proxy)
    .build();

// No proxy for specific hosts:
ProxySelector selector = ProxySelector.of(
    new InetSocketAddress("proxy.company.com", 8080));

HttpClient clientWithBypass = HttpClient.newBuilder()
    .proxy(new ProxySelector() {
        @Override
        public List<Proxy> select(URI uri) {
            if (uri.getHost().endsWith(".internal.company.com")) {
                return List.of(Proxy.NO_PROXY);
            }
            return selector.select(uri);
        }
        @Override
        public void connectFailed(URI uri, SocketAddress sa, IOException e) {}
    })
    .build();

Network interface binding:

// Bind a ServerSocket to a specific IP (e.g., listen only on internal interface):

ServerSocket server = new ServerSocket(8080, 50, bindAddress);
// Only accepts connections on the 10.0.0.1 interface
// Requests arriving on 0.0.0.0 or other interfaces are ignored

// Bind a client socket to a specific local interface:
Socket socket = new Socket();
socket.bind(new InetSocketAddress("10.0.0.1", 0)); // 0 = OS picks the port
socket.connect(new InetSocketAddress("remote-server", 9000));

Network Troubleshooting with Java Tools

Diagnosing connection problems:

// Connectivity check — can we reach the host?
public static boolean isReachable(String host, int port, int timeoutMs) {
    try (Socket socket = new Socket()) {
        socket.connect(new InetSocketAddress(host, port), timeoutMs);
        return true;  // connection established
    } catch (IOException e) {
        return false; // connection refused, timeout, or network error
    }
}

// Extended diagnostic:
public static void diagnose(String host, int port) {
    System.out.println("=== Network Diagnostic ===");

    // Step 1: DNS resolution
    try {
        InetAddress addr = InetAddress.getByName(host);
        System.out.println("DNS: " + host + " → " + addr.getHostAddress());
    } catch (UnknownHostException e) {
        System.err.println("DNS FAILED: " + e.getMessage());
        return;
    }

    // Step 2: TCP connection
    long start = System.currentTimeMillis();
    try (Socket socket = new Socket()) {
        socket.connect(new InetSocketAddress(host, port), 5000);
        long elapsed = System.currentTimeMillis() - start;
        System.out.println("TCP connect to " + host + ":" + port + " ← " + elapsed + "ms");
    } catch (IOException e) {
        System.err.println("TCP FAILED: " + e.getMessage());
    }
}

@Configuration
public class HttpClientConfig {

    public HttpClient httpClient() {

            .version(HttpClient.Version.HTTP_2)
            .followRedirects(HttpClient.Redirect.NORMAL)

            .addNetworkInterceptor(new GzipRequestInterceptor())

Part 20

Interview Questions and Answers

Q1: What is the difference between TCP and UDP? When would you use each in Java?

A: TCP is connection-oriented and reliable: it establishes a connection via three-way handshake, guarantees ordered delivery, and retransmits lost packets. UDP is connectionless: packets are sent independently with no delivery guarantee or ordering. Use TCP for most application protocols (HTTP, JDBC, Kafka, Redis) where reliability and ordering are required. Use UDP for applications that tolerate packet loss and prioritize low latency: DNS lookups, VoIP, live video streaming, real-time game state, and metrics aggregation (StatsD). In Java: TCP uses Socket/ServerSocket; UDP uses DatagramSocket/DatagramPacket.

Q2: What happens if you don't set timeouts on HTTP connections?

A: Without timeouts, any failure mode that prevents the server from responding will cause the client thread to block indefinitely. For connection timeout: if the server is unreachable (wrong IP, firewall blocking, server crashed), the OS TCP SYN packet will wait until the OS's own timeout (which can be minutes). For read timeout: if the server accepts the connection but stops sending data mid-response (slow query, garbage collection pause, server crash), the client thread waits forever. In a multi-threaded server, this causes thread pool exhaustion: all threads eventually become stuck waiting on slow downstream calls, and the service becomes completely unresponsive — a cascade failure.

Q3: Explain the three-way TCP handshake and what happens during Socket connection.

A: When new Socket("host", port) is called, the OS initiates the TCP three-way handshake:
1. SYN — client sends a SYN packet to the server with a random sequence number
2. SYN-ACK — server receives SYN, responds with SYN-ACK (acknowledges client's sequence, sends its own)
3. ACK — client sends ACK, connection is established

After step 3, the connection is in ESTABLISHED state and data can flow. The Socket constructor returns after the handshake completes. If the server is not listening on that port, it returns RST immediately, causing ConnectException. If the server is unreachable, the handshake times out based on the connectTimeout argument.

Q4: How does connection pooling work and why is it important?

A: Connection pooling maintains a set of pre-established connections to a target host. Instead of creating a new TCP connection (with its associated handshake and, for HTTPS, TLS overhead) for every request, the pool reuses existing connections. A request acquires a connection from the pool, uses it, and returns it when done. For database connections (HikariCP), this saves 30–100ms of connection setup per query. For HTTP clients (OkHttp), HTTP/2 takes this further: multiple requests are multiplexed over a single connection. Without connection pooling, high-throughput services spend more time establishing connections than doing actual work. HikariCP for JDBC and Java 11 HttpClient with HTTP/2 for REST are the production standards.

Q5: What is the difference between RestTemplate and WebClient?

A: Both are Spring abstractions for making HTTP calls. RestTemplate is synchronous and blocking — each call occupies a thread until the response arrives. It is in maintenance mode (no new features) but is simple and familiar. WebClient is non-blocking and reactive — it returns Mono<T> or Flux<T> that are executed on an event loop; a single thread can handle thousands of concurrent calls. WebClient is recommended for all new Spring code. However, with Java 21 virtual threads and spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true, RestTemplate's blocking model becomes much less of a concern, as virtual threads park cheaply while waiting for I/O.

Q6: How do you handle transient HTTP failures and implement retry logic?

A: Retry logic should be conditional. Retry on: connection timeouts, read timeouts, 503 Service Unavailable, 502 Bad Gateway, 504 Gateway Timeout, and IOException. Do NOT retry on: 4xx client errors (400, 404, 422 — the request is wrong, retrying won't help), 401/403 (authentication/authorization failures — retrying without fixing credentials is pointless). Implement exponential backoff with jitter: wait BASE * 2^attempt + random(0, BASE) milliseconds between attempts. For production systems, use Resilience4j's CircuitBreaker to stop retrying when the downstream service is consistently failing — open the circuit, return a fallback, and try again after a cool-down period. Without a circuit breaker, retry loops can amplify load on an already-struggling downstream service.

Part 21

Networking in Microservices: Service Discovery and Load Balancing

In a microservice architecture, services do not call each other by IP address. IPs are ephemeral — containers are restarted, scaled, and replaced. Service discovery provides the current addresses.

Client-side load balancing with Spring Cloud LoadBalancer:

// With Spring Cloud Kubernetes or Eureka, use service names not IPs:
@Bean
@LoadBalanced  // intercepts calls and resolves service name to actual IP
public RestTemplate restTemplate() {
    return new RestTemplate();
}

// Now call by service name — LoadBalancer resolves the current instances:
@Service
public class OrderClient {
    private final RestTemplate restTemplate;

    public Order getOrder(Long id) {
        // "order-service" is resolved to one of the current instance IPs:
        return restTemplate.getForObject(
            "http://order-service/v1/orders/{id}", Order.class, id);
    }
}

Service mesh networking (Istio, Linkerd):

In a service mesh, the network layer adds:
  ├─ Mutual TLS (mTLS) between all services automatically
  ├─ Retries and circuit breaking at the infrastructure level
  ├─ Distributed tracing headers injected (Zipkin/Jaeger)
  ├─ Traffic splitting for canary deployments
  └─ Rate limiting and authorization policies

Your Java code calls services normally (no special library needed)
The sidecar proxy (Envoy) handles all the above transparently

Health check endpoints for load balancer integration:

// Spring Boot Actuator provides /actuator/health automatically:
// Load balancers check this endpoint before routing traffic:

@Component
public class DatabaseHealthIndicator implements HealthIndicator {
    private final DataSource dataSource;

    @Override
    public Health health() {
        try (Connection conn = dataSource.getConnection();
             Statement stmt = conn.createStatement()) {
            stmt.execute("SELECT 1");
            return Health.up()
                .withDetail("database", "Reachable")
                .build();
        } catch (SQLException e) {
            return Health.down(e)
                .withDetail("database", "Unreachable")
                .build();
        }
    }
}
// If this returns DOWN, the load balancer stops routing traffic to this instance

Practice — Lesson 72

Easy Exercises

Exercise 1 — DNS Resolution Tool

Write a command-line utility that takes a hostname argument and prints:
1. All resolved IP addresses
2. Whether each is IPv4 or IPv6
3. The time taken for DNS resolution

public class DnsLookup {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        String host = args[0];
        long start = System.nanoTime();
        InetAddress[] addresses = InetAddress.getAllByName(host);
        long elapsed = (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000;

        System.out.printf("DNS lookup for %s (%dms):%n", host, elapsed);
        for (InetAddress addr : addresses) {
            System.out.printf("  %s  [%s]%n",
                addr.getHostAddress(),
                addr instanceof Inet6Address ? "IPv6" : "IPv4");
        }
    }
}

Production Scenarios

Scenario 1 — Cascade Failure from Missing Read Timeout

Your user-facing API service calls an inventory service. During a deployment of the inventory service, it gets stuck in a GC pause and stops responding for 90 seconds. Within 2 minutes, your API service becomes completely unresponsive — no requests are served, health checks fail, and Kubernetes begins restarting the pod.

Analysis:
- Root cause: no read timeout was set on the HTTP client used to call the inventory service.
- Symptom chain: inventory service pauses → API service threads block on HTTP read → all 50 threads exhausted → API service health check also blocks → pod restarted.
- Fix: add readTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(10)) to the HTTP client. Now, when inventory service is slow, the call fails with HttpTimeoutException after 10 seconds instead of blocking indefinitely. The API service returns 503 to the caller, but remains responsive for other requests.
- Monitoring: instrument with Micrometer — add alert for http.client.requests with outcome=TIMEOUT rising above threshold.

Scenario 2 — Service-to-Service mTLS Configuration

You are migrating internal service communication to mutual TLS. Service A must present a client certificate to Service B, and Service B must present a server certificate that Service A trusts. Both certificates are signed by an internal CA.

Implementation steps:
1. Generate a PKCS12 keystore for Service A's client cert and private key
2. Generate a JKS trust store containing the internal CA certificate
3. Configure Service A's HttpClient with a custom SSLContext (see Part 9)
4. Configure Service B's ServerSocket with an SSLServerSocket requiring client auth:

SSLServerSocketFactory ssf = sslContext.getServerSocketFactory();
SSLServerSocket server = (SSLServerSocket) ssf.createServerSocket(8443);
server.setNeedClientAuth(true);  // require client certificate
  1. Verify the mTLS handshake by logging session.getPeerPrincipal() on both sides.

Debugging Exercises

Debug 1 — Thread Pool Exhaustion

The following service has 20 worker threads and processes 50 requests per second. After 10 minutes in production, all requests start timing out. CPU is at 5%, memory is stable.

@Service
public class AggregationService {
    private final RestTemplate restTemplate;  // no timeout configured

    public AggregateResult aggregate(Long id) {
        // Calls 3 downstream services:
        Inventory inv = restTemplate.getForObject("http://inventory-svc/items/" + id, Inventory.class);
        Pricing pricing = restTemplate.getForObject("http://pricing-svc/prices/" + id, Pricing.class);
        Reviews reviews = restTemplate.getForObject("http://reviews-svc/reviews/" + id, Reviews.class);
        return new AggregateResult(inv, pricing, reviews);
    }
}

Diagnosis: restTemplate has no timeout. If any of the three downstream services is slow or unresponsive, the calling thread blocks indefinitely. With 50 req/s and no timeout, one slow downstream service (say, reviews-svc) causes 20 threads to become occupied in about 400ms. Fix: add timeouts to restTemplate, call all three services concurrently (not sequentially), and add circuit breakers for each downstream service.

Debug 2 — SSL Handshake Failure

javax.net.ssl.SSLHandshakeException: PKIX path building failed:
  sun.security.provider.certpath.SunCertPathBuilderException:
  unable to find valid certification path to requested target

Diagnosis and fix: The server's SSL certificate chain is not trusted by the JVM's default trust store ($JAVA_HOME/lib/security/cacerts). This happens for: self-signed certificates, certificates signed by an internal/private CA, or expired certificates. Fix options: (1) add the CA certificate to the JVM trust store: keytool -import -alias internal-ca -file ca.crt -keystore $JAVA_HOME/lib/security/cacerts; (2) create a custom trust store and configure it in the SSLContext (see Part 9); (3) if the server certificate is expired, renew it — never disable validation as a workaround.

Interview Challenges

Challenge 1

"Design a production-grade HTTP client wrapper class that your entire backend team should use for all outbound HTTP calls. What features does it include and why?"

Answer framework: (1) Singleton/Bean — HttpClient is expensive to create, maintains connection pools; one instance application-wide. (2) Timeouts always set — connection, read, write timeouts; no defaults should be zero or infinite. (3) Retry with backoff — 3 retries on transient errors (5xx, network errors), exponential backoff with jitter; NO retry on 4xx. (4) Circuit breaker — wraps each logical downstream service in a Resilience4j circuit breaker; prevents cascade failures. (5) Micrometer instrumentation — records latency, status codes, timeouts per endpoint; feeds Prometheus alerts. (6) Logging interceptor — logs request/response at DEBUG with timing; logs errors at WARN. (7) TLS configuration — no cert validation disabling; supports custom trust stores. (8) Virtual thread executor (Java 21) — eliminates thread pool sizing concerns.

Challenge 2

"Walk me through exactly what happens at the network level when a Spring Boot service makes an HTTPS REST call to another service."

Answer: The sequence:
1. DNS: the hostname is resolved via InetAddress.getByName() — checks JVM DNS cache, then OS resolver, then DNS server. Result: IP address.
2. TCP handshake: client sends SYN, server responds SYN-ACK, client sends ACK. Three packets, ~1 RTT. Socket constructor returns after this.
3. TLS handshake: client sends ClientHello (supported cipher suites, TLS version). Server responds ServerHello + Certificate. Client validates the certificate (checks CA chain, expiry, hostname). Both sides derive symmetric session keys. ~1–2 RTTs. Additional RTT if HTTP/2 ALPN negotiation.
4. HTTP request: serialized (Jackson ObjectMapper → bytes), sent over the TLS-encrypted TCP stream.
5. Server processes: receives bytes, JVM decrypts via TLS, Spring dispatcher servlet handles the request, business logic runs, response serialized.
6. HTTP response: bytes sent back over the same TLS TCP connection.
7. Connection returned to pool: HttpClient puts the connection back in the pool for reuse.

Key Takeaways

  • Sockets are the foundation — every Java network operation (HTTP, JDBC, Kafka, Redis) ultimately uses a Socket or DatagramSocket; understanding their options (timeout, keepalive, nodelay) explains framework behavior
  • Timeouts are not optional — missing timeouts cause cascade failures; configure connection, read, and write timeouts on every HTTP client
  • TCP is a stream protocol — never assume one read() returns a complete message; always use readFully() or framing protocols for reliable message boundaries
  • HttpURLConnection is legacy — use java.net.http.HttpClient (Java 11+) or OkHttp for new code; they support HTTP/2, async, and have clean APIs
  • Connection pooling multiplies performance — reusing established TCP+TLS connections saves 30–100ms per request; HikariCP for JDBC, HttpClient's built-in pool for HTTP
  • Retry only transient failures — retry 5xx and network errors with exponential backoff; never retry 4xx; add a circuit breaker to prevent retry storms
  • Virtual threads (Java 21) change the I/O model — one virtual thread per connection is now affordable; blocking I/O code scales like non-blocking without the reactive complexity
  • TLS is mandatory in production — configure timeouts even on TLS handshake; never disable certificate validation; add internal CA certificates to the JVM trust store
  • Monitor HTTP client metrics — instrument request latency, error rate, and timeout rate with Micrometer; alert on P99 latency and error rate increases
  • Microservice networking is serialization + HTTP + discovery — Lessons 71 and 72 together cover the complete data exchange stack between services

End of Lesson 72 — Next: Lesson 73: NIO
