Part 1

The Problem with Classic Java I/O

Java's original I/O API (java.io) was introduced in Java 1.0. It is built around streams — InputStream and OutputStream for bytes, Reader and Writer for characters. Every stream operation is blocking: when you call read(), the calling thread sleeps until data arrives. When you call write(), the calling thread sleeps until the kernel accepts the bytes.

This model is intuitive for simple programs, but it creates a fundamental scalability wall. A server that needs to handle 10,000 simultaneous connections using the blocking model must maintain 10,000 threads. Threads are expensive:

  • The JVM default thread stack is 512 KB to 1 MB.
  • Context-switching between thousands of OS threads causes significant CPU overhead.
  • Thread scheduling becomes a bottleneck well before the actual I/O work does.

The C10K problem — how to handle 10,000 concurrent connections efficiently — drove the design of operating system features like epoll (Linux), kqueue (macOS/BSD), and IOCP (Windows). Java NIO, introduced in Java 1.4 (JSR-51), was designed to expose these OS primitives in a portable API. The result is a system where a small number of threads can multiplex I/O across thousands of channels.

Understanding NIO is not just academic. It underpins Netty, Vert.x, reactive Spring WebFlux, Tomcat's NIO connector, and virtually every high-throughput Java server in production.

Part 2

The NIO Mental Model

NIO flips the classic stream model in three key ways:

  1. Channels instead of streams. A Channel is a bidirectional conduit to an I/O resource (a file, socket, pipe). Unlike a stream, a channel can be both readable and writable.

  2. Buffers instead of byte arrays. Data does not flow directly between your code and the channel. It flows through a Buffer — a fixed-capacity, position-tracked block of memory.

  3. Selectors for multiplexing. A Selector monitors multiple channels and notifies your code when one or more become ready for I/O. A single thread running a selector loop can serve thousands of channels.

These three components work together. You create a channel. You allocate a buffer. You register the channel with a selector. You ask the selector which channels are ready. You read from or write to ready channels via the buffer.

Part 3

The Buffer Abstraction

java.nio.Buffer is the abstract base class. The concrete subclasses you use most are:

  • ByteBuffer — raw bytes (by far the most common)
  • CharBuffer, IntBuffer, LongBuffer, FloatBuffer, DoubleBuffer — typed views
  • ShortBuffer

Every Buffer has four key state variables:

Property Meaning
capacity Total number of elements the buffer can hold. Fixed at creation.
limit The first element that should not be read or written.
position The index of the next element to be read or written.
mark An optional saved position for reset().

The invariant is always: 0 ≤ mark ≤ position ≤ limit ≤ capacity.

ByteBuffer buf = ByteBuffer.allocate(1024);
// capacity=1024, limit=1024, position=0
Part 4

ByteBuffer flip() and clear() in Depth

This is the single most common source of NIO bugs for developers new to the API. The confusion stems from the fact that a buffer plays two roles: it is both the destination of a channel read and the source for a channel write. The flip() and clear() methods switch between these modes.

Writing into the buffer (reading from a channel):

channel.read(buf);
// position advances to however many bytes were read
// limit stays at capacity

Preparing to drain the buffer (writing to a channel or processing bytes):

buf.flip();
// limit = position (marks the end of valid data)
// position = 0 (reset to start)

Now you iterate from position to limit, consuming the data you just read.

Resetting for the next read:

buf.clear();
// position = 0
// limit = capacity
// (data is NOT erased — it is just "forgotten")

compact() is an alternative to clear() for the case where you have partially consumed the buffer:

buf.compact();
// unread bytes are shifted to position 0
// position = number of remaining bytes
// limit = capacity

The idiom for a copy loop:

ByteBuffer buf = ByteBuffer.allocate(4096);
while (sourceChannel.read(buf) != -1) {
    buf.flip();
    while (buf.hasRemaining()) {
        sinkChannel.write(buf);
    }
    buf.clear();
}
Part 5

Direct vs. Heap Buffers

ByteBuffer has two allocation strategies:

ByteBuffer heap   = ByteBuffer.allocate(4096);     // on JVM heap
ByteBuffer direct = ByteBuffer.allocateDirect(4096); // off-heap, native memory

Heap buffers live in the Java heap. They are subject to GC. Before the JVM passes a heap buffer to the OS for I/O, it must copy it to a temporary native buffer, because the GC may move the heap object during the I/O operation.

Direct buffers live outside the Java heap in native memory allocated via malloc (or mmap). The OS can perform DMA directly from this memory without copying. This eliminates a memory copy on every I/O operation.

Tradeoffs:

Factor Heap Buffer Direct Buffer
Allocation speed Fast Slow
I/O throughput Lower (extra copy) Higher (zero-copy capable)
GC pressure Higher None (outside heap)
Memory leak risk None (GC managed) High if not managed
Best for Short-lived, small Long-lived, large I/O

Production NIO servers pool direct buffers (Netty's PooledByteBufAllocator does exactly this) to amortize the allocation cost while avoiding the extra copy.

Part 6

Channels Overview

The java.nio.channels package provides channel types for every kind of I/O resource:

Channel Class Purpose
FileChannel File I/O. Not selectable, always blocking.
SocketChannel TCP client socket.
ServerSocketChannel TCP server socket — accepts incoming connections.
DatagramChannel UDP sockets.
Pipe.SourceChannel Reading end of an in-process pipe.
Pipe.SinkChannel Writing end of an in-process pipe.

All network channels implement SelectableChannel, which means they can be registered with a Selector. FileChannel does not implement SelectableChannel; file I/O in Java NIO is still synchronous (though it benefits from buffers and transferTo).

Opening channels:

SocketChannel       sc  = SocketChannel.open();
ServerSocketChannel ssc = ServerSocketChannel.open();
DatagramChannel     dc  = DatagramChannel.open();
FileChannel         fc  = FileChannel.open(path, StandardOpenOption.READ);
Part 7

Non-Blocking Mode

By default, SocketChannel and ServerSocketChannel operate in blocking mode — just like classic java.io sockets. To use them with a Selector, you must switch to non-blocking mode:

SocketChannel sc = SocketChannel.open();
sc.configureBlocking(false);
sc.connect(new InetSocketAddress("example.com", 80));

In non-blocking mode:
- connect() returns immediately (possibly before the connection is established).
- read() returns 0 if no data is available (instead of blocking).
- write() may write fewer bytes than requested (instead of blocking until all bytes are written).
- accept() on a ServerSocketChannel returns null if no connection is waiting.

Your code must handle all of these partial / zero results correctly.

Part 8

The Selector

A Selector is a multiplexer. You register channels with it, annotating each registration with the set of operations you are interested in. You then call select(), which blocks until at least one of the registered channels becomes ready. select() returns the number of channels that became ready; you retrieve the ready set and process each.

Interest set operations (defined as constants on SelectionKey):

Constant Value Meaning
OP_READ 1 Channel has data to read.
OP_WRITE 4 Channel can accept writes without blocking.
OP_CONNECT 8 Non-blocking connect has completed.
OP_ACCEPT 16 ServerSocketChannel has an incoming conn. 
Selector selector = Selector.open();

ServerSocketChannel ssc = ServerSocketChannel.open();
ssc.bind(new InetSocketAddress(8080));
ssc.configureBlocking(false);
ssc.register(selector, SelectionKey.OP_ACCEPT);

while (true) {
    selector.select(); // blocks until at least one event
    Set<SelectionKey> keys = selector.selectedKeys();
    Iterator<SelectionKey> it = keys.iterator();
    while (it.hasNext()) {
        SelectionKey key = it.next();
        it.remove(); // MUST remove manually

        if (key.isAcceptable()) handleAccept(key);
        else if (key.isReadable()) handleRead(key);
        else if (key.isWritable()) handleWrite(key);
    }
}

The it.remove() call is mandatory. The Selector does not remove keys from the selected set automatically; if you forget, you will process the same event infinitely.

Part 9

A Complete Non-Blocking Echo Server

import java.io.IOException;
import java.net.*;
import java.nio.*;
import java.nio.channels.*;
import java.util.*;

public class NioEchoServer {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        Selector selector = Selector.open();

        ServerSocketChannel server = ServerSocketChannel.open();
        server.bind(new InetSocketAddress(9090));
        server.configureBlocking(false);
        server.register(selector, SelectionKey.OP_ACCEPT);

        System.out.println("Echo server listening on port 9090");

        while (true) {
            selector.select();
            Iterator<SelectionKey> it = selector.selectedKeys().iterator();

            while (it.hasNext()) {
                SelectionKey key = it.next();
                it.remove();

                if (!key.isValid()) continue;

                if (key.isAcceptable()) {
                    SocketChannel client = server.accept();
                    client.configureBlocking(false);
                    client.register(selector, SelectionKey.OP_READ);
                    System.out.println("Accepted: " + client.getRemoteAddress());

                } else if (key.isReadable()) {
                    SocketChannel client = (SocketChannel) key.channel();
                    ByteBuffer buf = ByteBuffer.allocate(256);
                    int bytesRead = client.read(buf);

                    if (bytesRead == -1) {
                        key.cancel();
                        client.close();
                    } else {
                        buf.flip();
                        // Echo back
                        client.write(buf);
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

This single-threaded server correctly handles any number of simultaneous clients without allocating a thread per connection.

Part 10

SelectionKey Attachment

Each SelectionKey can carry an attachment — an arbitrary object associated with the channel registration. This is the standard way to store per-connection state (buffers, session objects, HTTP parsers):

ByteBuffer clientBuffer = ByteBuffer.allocate(4096);
channel.register(selector, SelectionKey.OP_READ, clientBuffer);

// later, in the handler:
ByteBuffer buf = (ByteBuffer) key.attachment();

In real servers, the attachment is typically a connection handler object or a state machine instance, not a raw buffer.

Part 11

FileChannel and transferTo

FileChannel is NIO's file I/O channel. While it is not non-blocking (it is always synchronous), it offers two features that classic streams do not:

Memory-mapped files:

FileChannel fc = FileChannel.open(path, StandardOpenOption.READ);
MappedByteBuffer mbb = fc.map(FileChannel.MapMode.READ_ONLY, 0, fc.size());
// mbb now acts as a ByteBuffer backed directly by the file's pages
byte b = mbb.get(42); // OS page-faults in the data on demand

Memory mapping is ideal for large read-heavy files (logs, indexes) that need random access. The OS handles caching and eviction automatically.

Zero-copy transfer:

FileChannel source = FileChannel.open(srcPath, StandardOpenOption.READ);
FileChannel dest   = FileChannel.open(dstPath, StandardOpenOption.WRITE,
                                      StandardOpenOption.CREATE);
source.transferTo(0, source.size(), dest);

transferTo() delegates to the OS sendfile() system call where available. Data moves from the kernel's file buffer cache directly to the destination without being copied into user space at all. This is the same mechanism used by Nginx for serving static files.

Part 12

NIO.2: AsynchronousChannel

Java 7 introduced NIO.2 (java.nio.channels.AsynchronousChannel), which provides truly asynchronous I/O backed by OS completion ports / io_uring equivalents:

AsynchronousFileChannel afc = AsynchronousFileChannel.open(path,
    StandardOpenOption.READ);

ByteBuffer buf = ByteBuffer.allocate(1024);
afc.read(buf, 0, buf, new CompletionHandler<Integer, ByteBuffer>() {
    @Override
    public void completed(Integer bytesRead, ByteBuffer attachment) {
        attachment.flip();
        // process bytes
    }
    @Override
    public void failed(Throwable exc, ByteBuffer attachment) {
        exc.printStackTrace();
    }
});

AsynchronousServerSocketChannel and AsynchronousSocketChannel provide the same pattern for network I/O. The callback model can be replaced with Future<Integer> for simpler cases.

NIO.2 async channels are less commonly used directly than Selector-based NIO, partly because the callback hell is hard to manage and partly because frameworks like Netty and virtual threads (Java 21) provide better abstractions.

Part 13

NIO vs. Classic I/O: When to Use Each

The choice is not always NIO. Classic I/O is simpler and often fast enough:

Scenario Recommendation
< 100 concurrent connections Classic I/O or virtual threads
File processing in batch jobs Classic I/O or Files API
Large file transfer with zero-copy FileChannel.transferTo()
High-concurrency network servers (no vthreads) NIO with Selector
Building a network framework NIO (or Netty on top)
Java 21+ with virtual threads available Virtual threads + classic I/O
Streaming media / gaming servers NIO + direct ByteBuffers

The key insight: NIO is valuable when the number of connections is large relative to the number of threads you can afford. Virtual threads (Project Loom, Java 21) partially eliminate this tension by making blocking I/O cheap again, but NIO's zero-copy and memory-mapping capabilities remain uniquely valuable.

Part 14

Scatter/Gather I/O

NIO supports vectored I/O — reading into or writing from multiple buffers in a single system call. This maps directly to the POSIX readv/writev syscalls.

ByteBuffer header = ByteBuffer.allocate(128);
ByteBuffer body   = ByteBuffer.allocate(4096);
ByteBuffer[] buffers = { header, body };

// Scatter read: fills header first, then body
long bytesRead = channel.read(buffers);

// Gather write: drains header first, then body
header.flip();
body.flip();
long bytesWritten = channel.write(buffers);

This is particularly useful for network protocols with fixed headers: you parse the header without copying it into the body buffer, and the OS handles the rest.

Part 15

Pipe

Pipe creates a unidirectional, in-process channel pair. It is useful for passing data between threads without shared memory:

Pipe pipe = Pipe.open();
Pipe.SinkChannel   sink   = pipe.sink();
Pipe.SourceChannel source = pipe.source();

// Thread A writes:
sink.write(ByteBuffer.wrap("hello".getBytes()));

// Thread B reads:
ByteBuffer buf = ByteBuffer.allocate(64);
source.read(buf);
buf.flip();
System.out.println(StandardCharsets.UTF_8.decode(buf));

SourceChannel is selectable, so you can register it with a Selector and wake up a selector loop from another thread.

Part 16

CharBuffer and Charset Encoding

Network protocols transmit bytes, but application logic works with strings. NIO's Charset, CharsetEncoder, and CharsetDecoder bridge this gap efficiently:

Charset utf8       = StandardCharsets.UTF_8;
CharsetDecoder dec = utf8.newDecoder();
CharsetEncoder enc = utf8.newEncoder();

// Decode bytes to chars
ByteBuffer bytes = ByteBuffer.wrap("héllo".getBytes(utf8));
CharBuffer chars = dec.decode(bytes);

// Encode chars to bytes
ByteBuffer out = enc.encode(CharBuffer.wrap("wörld"));

Unlike new String(bytes, charset), the Charset APIs can work incrementally on partial buffers — essential for a streaming protocol parser where a multi-byte character may arrive split across two read() calls.

Part 17

Common NIO Pitfalls

1. Forgetting to remove from the selected key set.
selector.selectedKeys() is not cleared between select() calls. Always call it.remove().

2. Not checking key.isValid().
A key becomes invalid when you cancel it or close the channel. Always guard with key.isValid().

3. Writing a partial buffer.
channel.write(buf) may not write all bytes. Loop:

while (buf.hasRemaining()) channel.write(buf);

Or register for OP_WRITE and continue in the write handler.

4. Leaking direct buffers.
Direct ByteBuffers are not collected by normal GC. They rely on Cleaner/phantom references. Leak enough of them and you get OutOfMemoryError: Direct buffer memory. Pool them.

5. Blocking inside the selector loop.
Any blocking call inside the selector loop stalls all other channels. Offload heavy processing to a worker thread pool.

6. flip() / clear() confusion.
Forgetting to flip() before a write results in writing 0 bytes. Forgetting to clear() before a read results in overwriting buffered data.

Part 18

Netty: NIO at Industrial Scale

Raw NIO is powerful but verbose. Netty is the de facto standard framework for building high-performance network servers in Java. It is used by Cassandra, Elasticsearch, gRPC-Java, Dubbo, and countless others.

Netty's core concepts map onto raw NIO:

Raw NIO Concept Netty Abstraction
ByteBuffer ByteBuf (pooled, ref-counted)
SocketChannel Channel
Selector loop EventLoop
Thread pool EventLoopGroup
Per-connection state ChannelHandler / pipeline

A minimal Netty echo server:

EventLoopGroup boss   = new NioEventLoopGroup(1);
EventLoopGroup worker = new NioEventLoopGroup();

new ServerBootstrap()
    .group(boss, worker)
    .channel(NioServerSocketChannel.class)
    .childHandler(new ChannelInitializer<SocketChannel>() {
        @Override
        protected void initChannel(SocketChannel ch) {
            ch.pipeline().addLast(new EchoHandler());
        }
    })
    .bind(8080).sync()
    .channel().closeFuture().sync();

Netty handles all the flip()/clear() logic, partial writes, key management, and direct buffer pooling for you.

Part 19

Virtual Threads and NIO (Java 21+)

Project Loom, GA in Java 21, introduces virtual threads — lightweight threads managed by the JVM, not the OS. When a virtual thread performs a blocking I/O operation, the JVM internally parks it and unmounts it from the OS thread, freeing the carrier thread to run other virtual threads.

This means the classic blocking I/O model scales to millions of concurrent connections when using virtual threads, closing the gap with NIO's non-blocking model for many use cases:

try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) {
        executor.submit(() -> {
            // Classic blocking I/O — scales fine with virtual threads
            try (var socket = new Socket("example.com", 80)) {
                socket.getOutputStream().write("GET / HTTP/1.0\r\n\r\n".getBytes());
                socket.getInputStream().readAllBytes();
            }
        });
    }
}

However, NIO's FileChannel.transferTo() and memory-mapped files remain valuable even with virtual threads, because their advantage is zero-copy, not concurrency.

Part 20

Production Patterns: Buffer Pooling

Allocating and collecting millions of ByteBuffers per second is a GC burden. Production servers pool them:

public class ByteBufferPool {
    private final ArrayDeque<ByteBuffer> pool = new ArrayDeque<>();
    private final int bufferSize;

    public ByteBufferPool(int bufferSize) {
        this.bufferSize = bufferSize;
    }

    public synchronized ByteBuffer acquire() {
        ByteBuffer buf = pool.poll();
        if (buf == null) buf = ByteBuffer.allocateDirect(bufferSize);
        buf.clear();
        return buf;
    }

    public synchronized void release(ByteBuffer buf) {
        pool.push(buf);
    }
}

Netty's PooledByteBufAllocator is a far more sophisticated implementation using thread-local caches, size classes, and slab allocation to minimize contention and fragmentation.

Part 21

Production Patterns: Reactor and Proactor

The architectural pattern behind Selector-based NIO is the Reactor pattern:

  1. A Selector (the reactor) demultiplexes I/O events.
  2. Event handlers are invoked synchronously in the reactor thread.
  3. Long-running handlers delegate to a worker pool.

A single-threaded reactor is appropriate for CPU-bound protocols. For I/O-bound workloads with many cores, a multi-reactor architecture (one reactor per CPU core) is better — exactly what Netty's NioEventLoopGroup implements.

The Proactor pattern (NIO.2's AsynchronousChannel) inverts control: the OS calls your handler when an operation completes, rather than you polling the OS for readiness. The benefit is that you do not need to manage the read/write calls; the downside is a more complex callback model.

Part 22

Benchmarking and Observability

Measuring NIO performance requires looking beyond throughput (requests/sec) to:

  • Latency percentiles (p99, p999) — tail latency is dominated by selector delays and GC pauses.
  • Direct buffer usage — monitor with -verbose:gc and JFR DirectBufferStatistics event or java.nio.BufferPool MXBean:
    java List<BufferPoolMXBean> pools = ManagementFactory.getPlatformMXBeans(BufferPoolMXBean.class); pools.forEach(p -> System.out.printf("%s: %d buffers, %d bytes%n", p.getName(), p.getCount(), p.getMemoryUsed()));
  • Selector key count — selector.keys().size() tells you how many connections are registered.
  • Thread utilization — a well-tuned NIO server's selector threads should be near 100% CPU during load, not blocked in I/O.

Use JFR (jcmd <pid> JFR.start) and async-profiler to find selector hot spots. Look for time spent in sun.nio.ch.EPollArrayWrapper.epollWait — that is idle time (good) vs. time in your handler code (the thing to optimize).

Practice

Exercise 1 — Buffer Mechanics
Write a method copyFile(Path src, Path dst) using only FileChannel and a ByteBuffer.allocateDirect(8192). Ensure the buffer is correctly flip()-ed and clear()-ed for each iteration.

Exercise 2 — Non-Blocking Echo Server
Extend the echo server from Part 9 to handle partial writes correctly. Store any unwritten bytes in the SelectionKey attachment and register for OP_WRITE when the buffer is not fully drained. Deregister OP_WRITE once the buffer is empty.

Exercise 3 — Buffer Pool
Implement a DirectByteBufferPool with acquire() and release() methods. Verify with a load test that direct buffer memory usage plateaus rather than growing.

Exercise 4 — Scatter/Gather HTTP
Write a minimal HTTP/1.0 response sender using scatter/gather I/O: one ByteBuffer for the status line and headers, a second for the body. Confirm with wireshark or tcpdump that both buffers are sent in a single syscall.

Exercise 5 — Netty vs. Raw NIO
Implement the same simple protocol (length-prefixed messages) in both raw NIO and Netty. Compare lines of code, handling of partial reads, and benchmark throughput using wrk or hey.

Key Takeaways:
- NIO's three pillars — Channels, Buffers, Selectors — give you OS-level I/O multiplexing from Java.
- flip() before reading from a buffer; clear() before writing into it. Getting this wrong is the single most common NIO bug.
- Direct ByteBuffers avoid a copy on every I/O operation; pool them to avoid native memory leaks.
- The Selector + SelectionKey pattern is the foundation of every major Java networking framework.
- Virtual threads (Java 21) reduce the motivation for raw NIO in new code, but zero-copy (transferTo, memory mapping) and frameworks built on NIO remain ubiquitous.

Part 1

Why the Files API Replaced File

Java's original java.io.File class has been available since Java 1.0. It works, but its design predates modern expectations:

  • delete() returns a boolean instead of throwing an exception when it fails. You easily miss errors.
  • list() returns null (not an empty array) if the path is not a directory or if an I/O error occurs.
  • No support for symbolic links, file metadata, POSIX permissions, or atomic moves.
  • No event-based directory watching.
  • Poor interoperability with streams and NIO channels.

Java 7 (JSR-203, "NIO.2") introduced the java.nio.file package with a completely redesigned API built around three central types: Path, Files, and FileSystem. This API is expressive, composable, and exception-first — every error is a IOException that you must handle, not a silent boolean failure.

Understanding the Files API thoroughly pays dividends in every Java application that touches the filesystem: configuration loading, log rotation, data pipelines, build tools, test fixtures, and microservice deployments.

Part 2

Path: The Immutable Filesystem Pointer

Path is the successor to java.io.File. It represents a sequence of names that form a path in a particular filesystem. It is immutable — operations on it return new Path objects.

Path p1 = Path.of("/home/user/docs/report.pdf");   // Java 11+
Path p2 = Paths.get("/home/user/docs/report.pdf"); // Java 7+, same result

Path relative = Path.of("config/app.yaml");
Path absolute = relative.toAbsolutePath(); // resolves against process cwd

Key Path methods:

Method Returns
getFileName() Last component: Path("report.pdf")
getParent() Parent path, or null
getRoot() Root component: / on Unix, C:\ on Windows
getNameCount() Number of name elements
getName(int index) The name element at the given index
subpath(int begin, int end) A sub-path
resolve(Path other) Concatenate paths
resolveSibling(Path other) Replace filename with sibling
relativize(Path other) Compute a relative path between two paths
normalize() Remove . and .. elements
toRealPath() Resolve symlinks, canonicalize
toFile() Convert back to legacy java.io.File
Part 3

Path Resolution and Relativization

resolve() and relativize() are the two most important Path composition methods.

Path base   = Path.of("/var/app");
Path config = base.resolve("config/db.yaml");
// => /var/app/config/db.yaml

Path absolute = Path.of("/var/app/config/db.yaml");
Path rel = base.relativize(absolute);
// => config/db.yaml

// resolve + relativize are inverse operations:
assert base.resolve(rel).normalize().equals(absolute);

resolve() with an absolute argument replaces the base entirely:

Path p = Path.of("/var/app").resolve(Path.of("/etc/hosts"));
// => /etc/hosts  (absolute argument wins)

This is important for security: never use untrusted input in resolve() without first checking the resolved path is still under the expected root:

Path safeRoot = Path.of("/var/uploads").toRealPath();
Path resolved = safeRoot.resolve(userInput).toRealPath();
if (!resolved.startsWith(safeRoot)) {
    throw new SecurityException("Path traversal detected: " + userInput);
}
Part 4

The Files Utility Class

java.nio.file.Files is a static utility class (similar to java.util.Collections) that provides essentially every file operation you need. It operates on Path objects and throws IOException on failure.

Reading files:

// Entire file as a string (small files only)
String content = Files.readString(path, StandardCharsets.UTF_8);

// Entire file as a byte array
byte[] bytes = Files.readAllBytes(path);

// All lines as a List<String>
List<String> lines = Files.readAllLines(path, StandardCharsets.UTF_8);

// Streaming lines (lazy, good for large files)
try (Stream<String> lines = Files.lines(path, StandardCharsets.UTF_8)) {
    lines.filter(l -> l.startsWith("ERROR")).forEach(System.out::println);
}

Writing files:

// Overwrite with a string
Files.writeString(path, "hello world\n", StandardCharsets.UTF_8);

// Append to a file
Files.writeString(path, "more data\n",
    StandardCharsets.UTF_8,
    StandardOpenOption.APPEND,
    StandardOpenOption.CREATE);

// Write bytes
Files.write(path, byteArray);

// Write all lines
Files.write(path, List.of("line1", "line2"), StandardCharsets.UTF_8);

Existence and metadata:

boolean exists = Files.exists(path);
boolean isDir  = Files.isDirectory(path);
boolean isFile = Files.isRegularFile(path);
boolean isLink = Files.isSymbolicLink(path);
long    size   = Files.size(path);
FileTime lastModified = Files.getLastModifiedTime(path);
Part 5

Creating, Copying, Moving, and Deleting

// Create directories (including parents)
Files.createDirectories(Path.of("/var/app/logs/2026"));

// Create a single directory (parent must exist)
Files.createDirectory(Path.of("/var/app/logs"));

// Create a file (fails if it already exists)
Files.createFile(path);

// Copy (fails if destination exists by default)
Files.copy(src, dst);
Files.copy(src, dst, StandardCopyOption.REPLACE_EXISTING);
Files.copy(src, dst, StandardCopyOption.COPY_ATTRIBUTES);

// Move (atomic on same filesystem, falls back to copy+delete otherwise)
Files.move(src, dst);
Files.move(src, dst, StandardCopyOption.ATOMIC_MOVE);

// Delete (throws NoSuchFileException if absent)
Files.delete(path);

// Delete if exists (returns boolean, no exception if absent)
Files.deleteIfExists(path);

StandardCopyOption.ATOMIC_MOVE is critical for safe file replacement. Writing to a temp file and atomically moving it over the target ensures readers never see a half-written file:

Path target = Path.of("/var/app/config.json");
Path temp   = Files.createTempFile(target.getParent(), ".tmp-config-", ".json");
try {
    Files.writeString(temp, newConfig);
    Files.move(temp, target, StandardCopyOption.ATOMIC_MOVE,
                             StandardCopyOption.REPLACE_EXISTING);
} catch (IOException e) {
    Files.deleteIfExists(temp);
    throw e;
}
Part 6

Temporary Files and Directories

// Temp file in the system temp directory
Path tmp = Files.createTempFile("prefix-", ".suffix");

// Temp file in a specific directory
Path tmp2 = Files.createTempFile(Path.of("/var/tmp"), "app-", ".dat");

// Temp directory
Path tmpDir = Files.createTempDirectory("app-work-");

Always clean up temp files. The idiomatic pattern with try-finally:

Path tmp = Files.createTempFile("report-", ".csv");
try {
    // use tmp
    generateReport(tmp);
    Files.copy(tmp, destination, StandardCopyOption.REPLACE_EXISTING);
} finally {
    Files.deleteIfExists(tmp);
}

In tests, JUnit 5's @TempDir annotation injects and auto-cleans a temp directory.

Part 7

try-with-resources and AutoCloseable Streams

Files.lines(), Files.list(), Files.walk(), and Files.find() all return Stream<T>. These streams are backed by open file handles and must be closed when you are done. The idiomatic form is try-with-resources:

try (Stream<Path> entries = Files.list(directory)) {
    entries.filter(Files::isRegularFile)
           .map(Path::getFileName)
           .forEach(System.out::println);
}

try (Stream<String> lines = Files.lines(logFile)) {
    long errorCount = lines.filter(l -> l.contains("ERROR")).count();
    System.out.println("Errors: " + errorCount);
}

Forgetting the try-with-resources leaks a file descriptor. Under load, this causes Too many open files (EMFILE) errors. This is one of the most common subtle bugs in Java file processing code.

Part 8

Walking Directory Trees with Files.walk

Files.walk() performs a depth-first traversal of a directory tree, returning a Stream<Path>. It follows symbolic links only if you explicitly pass FileVisitOption.FOLLOW_LINKS.

// List all .java files recursively
try (Stream<Path> paths = Files.walk(srcRoot)) {
    paths.filter(p -> p.toString().endsWith(".java"))
         .forEach(System.out::println);
}

// Delete a directory tree
try (Stream<Path> paths = Files.walk(dirToDelete)) {
    paths.sorted(Comparator.reverseOrder()) // delete deepest first
         .forEach(p -> {
             try { Files.delete(p); }
             catch (IOException e) { throw new UncheckedIOException(e); }
         });
}

// Limit depth
try (Stream<Path> paths = Files.walk(root, 2)) {
    paths.forEach(System.out::println);
}

For complex traversal logic with pre/post-visit callbacks and fine-grained error handling, use Files.walkFileTree() with a FileVisitor<Path> implementation.

Part 9

Files.find: Filtered Walking

Files.find() combines walking with filtering in one method, which is slightly more efficient than walk().filter() because the predicate is evaluated before the path is added to the stream:

try (Stream<Path> found = Files.find(root, Integer.MAX_VALUE,
        (path, attrs) -> attrs.isRegularFile()
                      && attrs.size() > 1_000_000
                      && path.toString().endsWith(".log"))) {
    found.forEach(p -> System.out.println(p + " (" + attrs.size() + " bytes)"));
}

The BiPredicate<Path, BasicFileAttributes> receives both the path and its pre-fetched attributes — no extra stat syscall needed.

Part 10

File Attributes

Files provides access to standard and platform-specific file attributes:

// Basic attributes (all platforms)
BasicFileAttributes attrs = Files.readAttributes(path, BasicFileAttributes.class);
System.out.println(attrs.creationTime());
System.out.println(attrs.lastModifiedTime());
System.out.println(attrs.size());
System.out.println(attrs.isDirectory());

// POSIX attributes (Unix only)
PosixFileAttributes posix = Files.readAttributes(path, PosixFileAttributes.class);
System.out.println(posix.owner().getName());
System.out.println(PosixFilePermissions.toString(posix.permissions()));

// Set permissions
Set<PosixFilePermission> perms = PosixFilePermissions.fromString("rwxr-x---");
Files.setPosixFilePermissions(path, perms);

// File owner
UserPrincipal owner = Files.getOwner(path);
Files.setOwner(path, FileSystems.getDefault()
                                .getUserPrincipalLookupService()
                                .lookupPrincipalByName("appuser"));
Part 11

Symbolic Links

// Create a symlink
Files.createSymbolicLink(link, target);

// Read what a symlink points to (one hop only)
Path target = Files.readSymbolicLink(link);

// Resolve the full real path (follows all symlinks)
Path real = link.toRealPath(); // throws if any component doesn't exist
Path realNoFollow = link.toRealPath(LinkOption.NOFOLLOW_LINKS);

// Check for symlink without following
boolean isLink = Files.isSymbolicLink(path);

Most Files methods follow symlinks by default. Pass LinkOption.NOFOLLOW_LINKS to operate on the link itself rather than its target.

Part 12

The WatchService API

WatchService provides event-driven filesystem monitoring — the Java equivalent of inotify (Linux), FSEvents (macOS), or ReadDirectoryChangesW (Windows).

WatchService watcher = FileSystems.getDefault().newWatchService();

Path dir = Path.of("/var/app/config");
dir.register(watcher,
    StandardWatchEventKinds.ENTRY_CREATE,
    StandardWatchEventKinds.ENTRY_MODIFY,
    StandardWatchEventKinds.ENTRY_DELETE);

// Poll loop (typically on a dedicated daemon thread)
while (true) {
    WatchKey key;
    try {
        key = watcher.take(); // blocks until an event
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        break;
    }

    for (WatchEvent<?> event : key.pollEvents()) {
        WatchEvent.Kind<?> kind = event.kind();

        if (kind == StandardWatchEventKinds.OVERFLOW) continue;

        @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
        WatchEvent<Path> pathEvent = (WatchEvent<Path>) event;
        Path changed = dir.resolve(pathEvent.context());

        System.out.println(kind.name() + ": " + changed);
    }

    boolean valid = key.reset(); // MUST reset to receive further events
    if (!valid) break;           // directory was deleted
}

Critical: call key.reset() after processing events. Without it, the key is in a consumed state and no further events will be delivered for that directory.

Part 13

WatchService in Production: Config Reloading

A common production pattern is hot-reloading application configuration without a restart:

public class ConfigWatcher implements Runnable, Closeable {
    private final WatchService watcher;
    private final Path configDir;
    private final AtomicReference<AppConfig> config;
    private volatile boolean running = true;

    public ConfigWatcher(Path configDir, AtomicReference<AppConfig> config) throws IOException {
        this.watcher   = FileSystems.getDefault().newWatchService();
        this.configDir = configDir;
        this.config    = config;
        configDir.register(watcher,
            StandardWatchEventKinds.ENTRY_MODIFY,
            StandardWatchEventKinds.ENTRY_CREATE);
    }

    @Override
    public void run() {
        while (running) {
            WatchKey key;
            try {
                key = watcher.poll(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
                if (key == null) continue;
            } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
                break;
            }

            for (WatchEvent<?> event : key.pollEvents()) {
                Path changed = configDir.resolve(
                    ((WatchEvent<Path>) event).context());
                if (changed.getFileName().toString().equals("app.yaml")) {
                    reloadConfig(changed);
                }
            }
            key.reset();
        }
    }

    private void reloadConfig(Path file) {
        try {
            AppConfig newConfig = AppConfig.load(file);
            config.set(newConfig);
            System.out.println("Config reloaded from " + file);
        } catch (IOException e) {
            System.err.println("Failed to reload config: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }

    @Override
    public void close() throws IOException {
        running = false;
        watcher.close();
    }
}

This pattern is used by frameworks like Spring Boot (DevTools), Quarkus (live reload), and numerous logging systems.

Part 14

FileSystems and Custom Providers

FileSystems.getDefault() returns the platform filesystem. But NIO's FileSystem abstraction supports custom providers — alternative filesystems accessed through the same Path / Files API:

ZIP/JAR filesystem (built in):

URI jarUri = URI.create("jar:file:/path/to/archive.jar");
try (FileSystem jar = FileSystems.newFileSystem(jarUri, Map.of())) {
    Path entry = jar.getPath("/META-INF/MANIFEST.MF");
    String manifest = Files.readString(entry);
    System.out.println(manifest);
}

// Creating a new ZIP:
try (FileSystem zip = FileSystems.newFileSystem(
        URI.create("jar:file:/tmp/out.zip"),
        Map.of("create", "true"))) {
    Files.writeString(zip.getPath("/hello.txt"), "Hello from ZIP");
}

Third-party FileSystemProvider implementations exist for S3, HDFS, SSH (SFTP), and in-memory filesystems (useful for testing). Code written against Path + Files works with any of them without modification.

Part 15

BufferedReader/Writer via Files

Files integrates cleanly with classic character-based I/O when you need line-by-line processing with full stream control:

// Buffered reading
try (BufferedReader reader = Files.newBufferedReader(path, StandardCharsets.UTF_8)) {
    String line;
    while ((line = reader.readLine()) != null) {
        process(line);
    }
}

// Buffered writing
try (BufferedWriter writer = Files.newBufferedWriter(path,
        StandardCharsets.UTF_8,
        StandardOpenOption.CREATE,
        StandardOpenOption.TRUNCATE_EXISTING)) {
    for (String record : records) {
        writer.write(record);
        writer.newLine();
    }
}

Files.newBufferedReader and Files.newBufferedWriter are preferred over manually wrapping an InputStreamReader around Files.newInputStream because they apply the charset correctly and use an appropriate buffer size.

Part 16

Probing Content Type and MIME Detection

String mimeType = Files.probeContentType(path);
// => "text/plain", "application/pdf", "image/png", etc.
// Returns null if the type cannot be determined

The implementation is OS-dependent (relies on file extension databases or magic bytes). For production use, prefer a library like Apache Tika which performs content detection by reading file signatures:

// Apache Tika
Tika tika = new Tika();
String detected = tika.detect(path.toFile());
Part 17

Stream-to-Path and Path-to-Stream Integration

Files integrates directly with InputStream / OutputStream:

// Copy an InputStream into a file
try (InputStream is = url.openStream()) {
    Files.copy(is, destination, StandardCopyOption.REPLACE_EXISTING);
}

// Copy a file into an OutputStream
try (OutputStream os = response.getOutputStream()) {
    Files.copy(source, os);
}

// Open as InputStream/OutputStream
try (InputStream is = Files.newInputStream(path)) { ... }
try (OutputStream os = Files.newOutputStream(path, StandardOpenOption.APPEND)) { ... }

These integrate naturally with HTTP clients, message queues, and any API that works with streams.

Part 18

Production File Processing Patterns

Pattern 1: Large CSV processing with Files.lines

try (Stream<String> lines = Files.lines(csvPath, StandardCharsets.UTF_8)) {
    lines.skip(1) // skip header
         .parallel()
         .map(line -> line.split(","))
         .filter(cols -> cols.length >= 5)
         .map(cols -> new Record(cols[0], cols[1], cols[4]))
         .forEach(this::persist);
}

Pattern 2: Atomic file replacement (safe config update)

public static void writeAtomic(Path target, String content) throws IOException {
    Path tmp = Files.createTempFile(target.getParent(), ".tmp-", ".atomic");
    try {
        Files.writeString(tmp, content, StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
        Files.move(tmp, target,
            StandardCopyOption.ATOMIC_MOVE,
            StandardCopyOption.REPLACE_EXISTING);
    } catch (IOException e) {
        Files.deleteIfExists(tmp);
        throw e;
    }
}

Pattern 3: Directory size calculation

public static long directorySize(Path dir) throws IOException {
    try (Stream<Path> paths = Files.walk(dir)) {
        return paths.filter(Files::isRegularFile)
                    .mapToLong(p -> {
                        try { return Files.size(p); }
                        catch (IOException e) { return 0L; }
                    })
                    .sum();
    }
}
Part 19

Spring Resource Abstraction

Spring's org.springframework.core.io.Resource interface is an abstraction over any addressable resource — classpath entries, filesystem paths, URLs, or in-memory bytes. It bridges the Spring ecosystem with Java's native file API.

// Inject via @Value
@Value("classpath:templates/email.html")
private Resource emailTemplate;

// Inject via constructor
public ReportService(ResourceLoader loader) {
    Resource r = loader.getResource("file:/var/app/reports/config.json");
    // or "classpath:config.json"
    // or "https://config-server/app.json"
}

Key Resource methods:

resource.exists();
resource.isReadable();
resource.contentLength();
resource.lastModified();
resource.getInputStream();           // InputStream
resource.getFile();                  // java.io.File (filesystem only)
resource.getURL();                   // java.net.URL
resource.toURI();                    // java.net.URI
resource.getFilename();              // last path component

Converting a Spring Resource to an NIO Path:

Path path = resource.getFile().toPath(); // for filesystem resources
// or:
Path path = Path.of(resource.getURI()); // more portable

ResourcePatternResolver (implemented by ApplicationContext) supports Ant-style wildcards:

Resource[] configs = resolver.getResources("classpath*:config/**/*.yaml");

This is used internally by Spring Boot's @ConfigurationProperties scanning and component scanning.

Part 20

Testing with In-Memory FileSystems

The jimfs library (Google) provides an in-memory FileSystem that is fully NIO-compatible. It makes file-system-dependent code trivially testable without touching disk:

// pom.xml: com.google.jimfs:jimfs:1.3.0
FileSystem fs = Jimfs.newFileSystem(Configuration.unix());
Path root = fs.getPath("/");

// Use exactly like the real filesystem:
Path config = root.resolve("app/config.yaml");
Files.createDirectories(config.getParent());
Files.writeString(config, "port: 8080\n");

// Test your code:
ConfigLoader loader = new ConfigLoader(config);
AppConfig cfg = loader.load();
assertEquals(8080, cfg.getPort());

fs.close(); // cleans up automatically

Because your code only sees Path and Files, it works with Jimfs without any changes. Inject the FileSystem (or the root Path) rather than hardcoding real paths.

Part 21

Common Mistakes and Pitfalls

1. Not closing streams from Files.walk / Files.lines.
These hold open file descriptors. Always use try-with-resources.

2. Using Files.readAllBytes for huge files.
Reads the entire file into a byte array. For a 10 GB log file this OOMs instantly. Use Files.lines() or Files.newBufferedReader().

3. Non-atomic writes.
Writing directly to the target file means readers may see partial content. Use the temp-file-then-atomic-move pattern.

4. Ignoring the return value of WatchKey.reset().
If reset() returns false, the directory was deleted. Not checking this leads to an infinite loop on an invalid key.

5. Path traversal vulnerabilities.
Never resolve user-supplied paths without checking the result is under the expected root. Use toRealPath() and startsWith() as shown in Part 3.

6. Forgetting that Files.delete throws on missing file.
Use deleteIfExists() when absence is acceptable.

7. Assuming ATOMIC_MOVE works across filesystems.
ATOMIC_MOVE only works within the same filesystem (same device). Across devices (e.g., temp dir on /tmp which is tmpfs, target on /var which is ext4), the JVM falls back to copy+delete, which is not atomic.

Part 22

Performance Considerations and Benchmarking

Reading strategy comparison:

Method Use Case Notes
Files.readAllBytes() Small files (< 10 MB) Simple but loads fully into memory
Files.lines() Line-oriented, large files Lazy; close the stream
Files.newBufferedReader() Character-level processing Good default for text
FileChannel + ByteBuffer Binary, performance-critical Full NIO control
MappedByteBuffer Random-access, read-heavy OS caching; careful with large files

WatchService latency:
On Linux, WatchService is backed by inotify, which is near-instantaneous. On macOS, the JDK's default implementation polls every 10 seconds (a known JDK limitation). Use the macOS FSEvents-based provider for sub-second latency on macOS.

Parallel directory traversal:

try (Stream<Path> paths = Files.walk(root)) {
    long count = paths.parallel()
                      .filter(Files::isRegularFile)
                      .count();
}

parallel() on Files.walk() uses the ForkJoinPool. It is beneficial for compute-heavy predicates but adds overhead for simple I/O-bound operations. Benchmark before enabling.

Practice

Exercise 1 — Safe Config Writer
Implement a ConfigStore class with save(String content) and load(): String methods backed by the filesystem. save() must use atomic replacement so readers never see a partial write.

Exercise 2 — Directory Sync
Write a method sync(Path src, Path dst) that:
- Copies files present in src but not in dst.
- Overwrites files in dst that differ from src (compare by last-modified time and size).
- Deletes files in dst not present in src.
Use Files.walk() and atomic move/copy.

Exercise 3 — WatchService Daemon
Build a LogWatcher that monitors a directory for new .log files, reads each new file line by line as it is appended (using Files.lines() or RandomAccessFile), and prints lines containing the word ERROR.

Exercise 4 — ZIP Packaging
Use the built-in ZIP FileSystem provider to create a ZIP archive of a directory tree. Each entry in the ZIP should preserve the relative path from the source root.

Exercise 5 — Jimfs Unit Test
Refactor an existing class that takes hardcoded filesystem paths so it accepts an injected Path root. Write a JUnit 5 test using Jimfs that exercises the class entirely in-memory without touching the disk.

Key Takeaways:
- Path is immutable and composable; Files is the static utility that does the actual work.
- Always use try-with-resources with streams returned by Files.walk(), Files.lines(), and Files.list() — they hold open file descriptors.
- Atomic moves (StandardCopyOption.ATOMIC_MOVE) prevent readers from seeing partial writes; write to a temp file first.
- WatchService gives you filesystem event notifications backed by OS primitives (inotify, FSEvents); always call key.reset().
- Spring's Resource abstraction wraps Path + Files for classpath, HTTP, and filesystem resources uniformly.
- Inject Path roots and use Jimfs for deterministic, disk-free unit tests.
