Part 1

Why Cryptography Belongs in Every Java Developer's Toolkit

Cryptography is not an exotic speciality reserved for security researchers. Every Java application that stores user data, transmits information across a network, or needs to verify the integrity of a file is already using cryptography — whether the developer is aware of it or not. The question is not whether to use cryptography, but whether you are using it correctly.

The cost of using cryptography incorrectly is asymmetric. A subtle error — using an unauthenticated cipher mode, storing passwords with a fast hash, or generating an IV from a predictable source — can make an application completely insecure while appearing secure. Unlike a logic bug that surfaces as an exception, a cryptographic vulnerability is invisible under normal operation. It only manifests when an adversary actively exploits it.

The three goals of cryptography:

Confidentiality  → Only intended recipients can read the data
                   (AES-GCM encryption, RSA/ECDH key exchange)

Integrity        → Data has not been altered in transit or at rest
                   (HMAC-SHA256, AES-GCM authentication tag, digital signatures)

Authenticity     → Data came from who it claims to come from
                   (Digital signatures, HMAC with shared secret, certificates)

A note on building versus using: you should almost never implement a cryptographic primitive from scratch. You should use well-audited implementations from the JCA/JCE, Bouncy Castle, or established libraries. This lesson focuses on using the JDK's cryptography APIs correctly — not on the mathematics underlying them.

Part 2

The Java Cryptography Architecture (JCA/JCE)

The Java Cryptography Architecture (JCA) is the framework that defines the APIs and provider model for cryptographic operations in the JDK. The Java Cryptography Extension (JCE) extends JCA with additional algorithms — symmetric ciphers, key agreement, and message authentication codes — that were historically subject to US export restrictions.

The provider model:

Application Code
      │
      ▼
JCA API (javax.crypto.*, java.security.*)
      │
      ▼
Provider Selection (algorithm name → provider lookup)
      │
   ┌──┴────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │                                               │
SunJCE Provider       BouncyCastle Provider     PKCS#11 Provider
(built-in JDK)        (third-party, HSM bridge) (hardware tokens)
AES, RSA, SHA-256      AES-SIV, Argon2           FIPS-certified ops

Obtaining an algorithm instance:

// The factory method pattern — JCA uses algorithm strings, not concrete classes
MessageDigest sha256 = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256");
Cipher aesCbc = Cipher.getInstance("AES/CBC/PKCS5Padding");
Cipher aesGcm = Cipher.getInstance("AES/GCM/NoPadding");  // preferred
KeyGenerator aesKeyGen = KeyGenerator.getInstance("AES");
KeyPairGenerator rsaKeyGen = KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("RSA");
Mac hmacSha256 = Mac.getInstance("HmacSHA256");
Signature rsaSha256 = Signature.getInstance("SHA256withRSA");

Key classes in the JCA:

java.security
├── MessageDigest       — hashing (SHA-256, SHA-3)
├── Signature           — digital signatures (RSA, ECDSA)
├── KeyPairGenerator    — generate asymmetric key pairs
├── KeyFactory          — convert key material to/from Key objects
├── KeyStore            — persistent storage of keys and certificates
├── SecureRandom        — cryptographically secure random numbers
└── Provider            — registers algorithm implementations

javax.crypto
├── Cipher              — symmetric/asymmetric encryption (AES, RSA)
├── Mac                 — message authentication codes (HMAC)
├── KeyGenerator        — generate symmetric keys
├── SecretKeyFactory    — derive keys from passwords (PBKDF2)
├── KeyAgreement        — key exchange protocols (ECDH, DH)
└── SecretKey / SecretKeySpec — symmetric key representations
Part 3

Hashing with MessageDigest

A cryptographic hash function maps an arbitrary-length input to a fixed-length digest. A secure hash function is:
- Preimage resistant: Given a digest, it is computationally infeasible to find any input that produces it
- Second-preimage resistant: Given an input and its digest, it is computationally infeasible to find a different input with the same digest
- Collision resistant: It is computationally infeasible to find any two inputs with the same digest

Current algorithm recommendations:

Algorithm Output Size Status Use Case
SHA-256 256 bits Recommended File integrity, HMAC, certificates
SHA-384 384 bits Recommended High-security contexts
SHA-512 512 bits Recommended Long-term integrity, digital signatures
SHA3-256 256 bits Recommended When SHA-2 family is prohibited
MD5 128 bits Broken Do not use for security
SHA-1 160 bits Deprecated Do not use for security

Computing a hash:

import java.security.MessageDigest;
import java.security.NoSuchAlgorithmException;
import java.util.HexFormat;

public class HashingExample {

    public static byte[] sha256(byte[] data) throws NoSuchAlgorithmException {
        MessageDigest digest = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256");
        return digest.digest(data);
    }

    public static String sha256Hex(String input) throws NoSuchAlgorithmException {
        MessageDigest digest = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256");
        byte[] hashBytes = digest.digest(input.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
        return HexFormat.of().formatHex(hashBytes);
    }

    // Streaming hash for large files
    public static String sha256File(Path filePath) throws Exception {
        MessageDigest digest = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256");
        try (InputStream is = Files.newInputStream(filePath)) {
            byte[] buffer = new byte[8192];
            int bytesRead;
            while ((bytesRead = is.read(buffer)) != -1) {
                digest.update(buffer, 0, bytesRead);
            }
        }
        return HexFormat.of().formatHex(digest.digest());
    }

    // Constant-time comparison — critical for preventing timing attacks
    public static boolean verifyHash(byte[] computed, byte[] expected) {
        return MessageDigest.isEqual(computed, expected);
        // Do NOT use Arrays.equals() or String.equals() — they short-circuit on first mismatch
        // This creates a timing side-channel revealing how many bytes match
    }
}

Why timing attacks matter:

A naive computed.equals(expected) check returns false as soon as the first different byte is found. An attacker who can measure response times can submit many candidates and use the timing difference to learn how close their guess is. MessageDigest.isEqual() always compares all bytes in constant time, eliminating this channel.

Part 4

HMAC: Keyed Message Authentication

A plain hash provides integrity — it proves the data has not changed — but not authenticity. Anyone can compute SHA-256 of any data. An HMAC (Hash-based Message Authentication Code) adds a secret key, so only parties who know the key can produce or verify the MAC.

HMAC-SHA256(key, message) = SHA256((key ⊕ opad) || SHA256((key ⊕ ipad) || message))

Typical use cases: Webhook signature verification, API request signing, CSRF tokens, stateless session cookies.

import javax.crypto.Mac;
import javax.crypto.spec.SecretKeySpec;
import java.util.HexFormat;

public class HmacExample {

    public static String computeHmac(byte[] key, byte[] message) throws Exception {
        Mac mac = Mac.getInstance("HmacSHA256");
        SecretKeySpec keySpec = new SecretKeySpec(key, "HmacSHA256");
        mac.init(keySpec);
        byte[] hmacBytes = mac.doFinal(message);
        return HexFormat.of().formatHex(hmacBytes);
    }

    // Webhook signature verification (e.g., GitHub/Stripe style)
    public static boolean verifyWebhookSignature(
            byte[] signingKey, byte[] payload, String receivedSignature) throws Exception {
        String computed = computeHmac(signingKey, payload);
        // Constant-time comparison prevents timing oracle
        return MessageDigest.isEqual(
            computed.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8),
            receivedSignature.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8)
        );
    }
}

Key generation for HMAC:

// Generate a 256-bit HMAC key
KeyGenerator keyGen = KeyGenerator.getInstance("HmacSHA256");
keyGen.init(256);
SecretKey hmacKey = keyGen.generateKey();
byte[] rawKey = hmacKey.getEncoded(); // store this securely
Part 5

Symmetric Encryption: AES

AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) is the standard symmetric cipher. It takes a 128, 192, or 256-bit key and encrypts 128-bit blocks. The key question is which mode of operation to use.

Mode comparison:

Mode Authenticated IV Required Parallelizable Recommendation
ECB No No Yes Never use — identical blocks produce identical ciphertext
CBC No Yes Decrypt only Acceptable but error-prone; requires separate MAC
CTR No Yes Yes Use with HMAC; do not reuse IV+key pair
GCM Yes Yes Yes Preferred — provides both encryption and authentication
CCM Yes Yes No Use in constrained environments (IoT)

AES-GCM (the right choice):

import javax.crypto.*;
import javax.crypto.spec.*;
import java.security.*;

public class AesGcmExample {

    private static final int KEY_SIZE = 256;       // bits
    private static final int GCM_IV_LENGTH = 12;   // bytes — 96-bit IV is NIST-recommended for GCM
    private static final int GCM_TAG_LENGTH = 128; // bits — 128-bit authentication tag

    // Generate a new AES key
    public static SecretKey generateKey() throws NoSuchAlgorithmException {
        KeyGenerator keyGen = KeyGenerator.getInstance("AES");
        keyGen.init(KEY_SIZE, new SecureRandom());
        return keyGen.generateKey();
    }

    // Encrypt — returns IV prepended to ciphertext
    public static byte[] encrypt(SecretKey key, byte[] plaintext) throws Exception {
        byte[] iv = new byte[GCM_IV_LENGTH];
        new SecureRandom().nextBytes(iv); // unique random IV per encryption — CRITICAL

        Cipher cipher = Cipher.getInstance("AES/GCM/NoPadding");
        GCMParameterSpec parameterSpec = new GCMParameterSpec(GCM_TAG_LENGTH, iv);
        cipher.init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, key, parameterSpec);

        byte[] ciphertext = cipher.doFinal(plaintext);

        // Prepend IV to ciphertext — IV is not secret, only unique
        byte[] ivAndCiphertext = new byte[iv.length + ciphertext.length];
        System.arraycopy(iv, 0, ivAndCiphertext, 0, iv.length);
        System.arraycopy(ciphertext, 0, ivAndCiphertext, iv.length, ciphertext.length);
        return ivAndCiphertext;
    }

    // Decrypt — expects IV prepended to ciphertext
    public static byte[] decrypt(SecretKey key, byte[] ivAndCiphertext) throws Exception {
        byte[] iv = Arrays.copyOfRange(ivAndCiphertext, 0, GCM_IV_LENGTH);
        byte[] ciphertext = Arrays.copyOfRange(ivAndCiphertext, GCM_IV_LENGTH, ivAndCiphertext.length);

        Cipher cipher = Cipher.getInstance("AES/GCM/NoPadding");
        GCMParameterSpec parameterSpec = new GCMParameterSpec(GCM_TAG_LENGTH, iv);
        cipher.init(Cipher.DECRYPT_MODE, key, parameterSpec);

        // AES-GCM automatically verifies the authentication tag during decryption
        // If tampered, throws AEADBadTagException — do NOT catch and continue
        return cipher.doFinal(ciphertext);
    }
}

The IV (Initialization Vector) rule: Never reuse the same IV with the same key. Each encryption must use a fresh random IV. With AES-GCM specifically, IV reuse is catastrophic — it allows the attacker to XOR two ciphertexts to recover the plaintext XOR difference, completely defeating confidentiality.

Additional Associated Data (AAD): GCM supports AAD — plaintext data that is authenticated but not encrypted. Use it to bind ciphertext to context (e.g., the database row ID, the recipient's user ID). If the ciphertext is moved to a different row, decryption fails.

cipher.updateAAD(contextBytes); // call before doFinal()
Part 6

Asymmetric Encryption: RSA

RSA is the most widely used asymmetric cipher. It uses a key pair: a public key for encryption (or signature verification) and a private key for decryption (or signing).

RSA key generation:

KeyPairGenerator keyPairGen = KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("RSA");
keyPairGen.initialize(4096, new SecureRandom()); // 4096-bit for long-lived keys; 2048 is minimum
KeyPair keyPair = keyPairGen.generateKeyPair();

PublicKey publicKey = keyPair.getPublic();
PrivateKey privateKey = keyPair.getPrivate();

// Serialize to bytes for storage
byte[] publicKeyBytes = publicKey.getEncoded();   // DER/X.509 format
byte[] privateKeyBytes = privateKey.getEncoded(); // DER/PKCS#8 format

// Restore a key from bytes
KeyFactory keyFactory = KeyFactory.getInstance("RSA");
PublicKey restoredPublicKey = keyFactory.generatePublic(new X509EncodedKeySpec(publicKeyBytes));
PrivateKey restoredPrivateKey = keyFactory.generatePrivate(new PKCS8EncodedKeySpec(privateKeyBytes));

RSA encryption with OAEP (correct padding):

// OAEP (Optimal Asymmetric Encryption Padding) is the correct padding for RSA encryption.
// PKCS1Padding (v1.5) is vulnerable to Bleichenbacher's attack — do not use for new code.
Cipher rsaCipher = Cipher.getInstance("RSA/ECB/OAEPWithSHA-256AndMGF1Padding");

// Encrypt with public key (sender)
rsaCipher.init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, publicKey);
byte[] encryptedKey = rsaCipher.doFinal(aesKeyBytes); // RSA encrypts the AES key

// Decrypt with private key (recipient)
rsaCipher.init(Cipher.DECRYPT_MODE, privateKey);
byte[] decryptedKey = rsaCipher.doFinal(encryptedKey);

Hybrid encryption pattern (correct approach for large data):

RSA can only encrypt data smaller than the key size minus padding overhead (~190 bytes for a 2048-bit key with OAEP). For real data, use a hybrid scheme:

1. Generate a random AES-256 key (session key)
2. Encrypt the actual data with AES-GCM using the session key
3. Encrypt the session key with RSA-OAEP using the recipient's public key
4. Transmit: RSA-encrypted session key + AES-encrypted data

This is exactly how TLS, PGP, and CMS work internally.

Part 7

Password Hashing: The Right Way

Passwords must never be stored as plaintext, reversibly encrypted, or hashed with a general-purpose hash (MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256). General-purpose hashes are designed to be fast — which is the opposite of what you want for password storage. An attacker with your database can compute billions of SHA-256 hashes per second on commodity GPUs.

The right approach: Use a purposefully slow, salted, adaptive password hashing algorithm.

BCrypt:

import org.springframework.security.crypto.bcrypt.BCryptPasswordEncoder;

// Cost factor 12 ≈ 200–400ms on modern hardware.
// Increase as hardware improves. Never go below 10.
BCryptPasswordEncoder encoder = new BCryptPasswordEncoder(12);

// Hash a password (salt is generated internally and embedded in the hash)
String hash = encoder.encode("userPassword123!");
// Output: $2a$12$N9qo8uLOickgx2ZMRZoMyeIjZAgcfl7p92ldGxad68LJZdL17lhWy
//          ↑ version ↑ cost ↑ 22-char salt ↑ 31-char hash

// Verify a password
boolean matches = encoder.matches("userPassword123!", hash); // true
boolean wrong   = encoder.matches("wrongPassword",   hash); // false

// Spring Security DelegatingPasswordEncoder — supports multiple algorithms in one app
PasswordEncoder delegating = PasswordEncoderFactories.createDelegatingPasswordEncoder();
// Prefixes hash with {bcrypt} — enables algorithm migration without requiring password resets

Argon2 (OWASP's top recommendation, 2023+):

// Argon2 is harder to attack with ASICs/GPUs than BCrypt due to memory hardness
// Requires Bouncy Castle or Spring Security 5.8+
import org.springframework.security.crypto.argon2.Argon2PasswordEncoder;

// Parameters: saltLength=16, hashLength=32, parallelism=1, memory=65536 KB, iterations=3
Argon2PasswordEncoder argon2 = new Argon2PasswordEncoder(16, 32, 1, 65536, 3);
String hash = argon2.encode("userPassword123!");
boolean matches = argon2.matches("userPassword123!", hash);

PBKDF2 (JDK-native, FIPS-compliant):

import javax.crypto.SecretKeyFactory;
import javax.crypto.spec.PBEKeySpec;

public static byte[] pbkdf2(char[] password, byte[] salt, int iterations, int keyLength)
        throws Exception {
    PBEKeySpec spec = new PBEKeySpec(password, salt, iterations, keyLength);
    try {
        SecretKeyFactory factory = SecretKeyFactory.getInstance("PBKDF2WithHmacSHA256");
        return factory.generateSecret(spec).getEncoded();
    } finally {
        spec.clearPassword(); // zero the password from memory
    }
}

// Generate a salt (new salt per password)
byte[] salt = new byte[16];
new SecureRandom().nextBytes(salt);
byte[] hash = pbkdf2(password, salt, 310_000, 256); // OWASP recommends 310,000 iterations for PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256

Why MD5 and SHA-1 are disqualified for passwords:

  • No salt embedded by default → identical passwords produce identical hashes → rainbow tables
  • Extremely fast → 10+ billion MD5 hashes/second on a single GPU → brute force is trivial
  • MD5 has demonstrated collisions (though collision resistance is a separate property from preimage resistance, the algorithm is structurally compromised)
Part 8

SecureRandom: Cryptographically Secure Randomness

java.util.Random uses a linear congruential generator — a simple mathematical formula. Given any output, the next output is entirely predictable. It is suitable for simulations, games, and test data generation. It must never be used for security-sensitive values.

java.security.SecureRandom uses an OS-backed entropy source (e.g., /dev/urandom on Linux, CryptGenRandom on Windows). Its output is computationally indistinguishable from a true random sequence.

import java.security.SecureRandom;
import java.util.Base64;

public class SecureRandomExample {

    private static final SecureRandom SECURE_RANDOM = new SecureRandom();
    // SecureRandom instances are thread-safe; sharing one instance is fine

    // Generate a URL-safe random token (e.g., for password reset, session ID, API key)
    public static String generateToken(int byteLength) {
        byte[] bytes = new byte[byteLength];
        SECURE_RANDOM.nextBytes(bytes);
        return Base64.getUrlEncoder().withoutPadding().encodeToString(bytes);
    }

    // 32 bytes → 43 characters of Base64url — 256 bits of entropy
    public static String generateSessionId() {
        return generateToken(32);
    }

    // Generate a random integer in a range without bias
    public static int randomInt(int bound) {
        return SECURE_RANDOM.nextInt(bound);
    }

    // SecureRandom algorithm selection
    public static SecureRandom getStrongRandom() throws NoSuchAlgorithmException {
        // SecureRandom.getInstanceStrong() uses the strongest available algorithm
        // On Linux: NativePRNGBlocking (may block if entropy pool is exhausted)
        // For most applications, the default new SecureRandom() is sufficient and non-blocking
        return SecureRandom.getInstanceStrong();
    }
}

Common pitfall — seeding SecureRandom:

// WRONG: seeding with a predictable value defeats the purpose
SecureRandom bad = new SecureRandom(new byte[]{1, 2, 3, 4});

// RIGHT: let the OS seed it
SecureRandom good = new SecureRandom(); // seeded from OS entropy automatically
Part 9

Digital Signatures

A digital signature proves both authenticity (the message was produced by the holder of the private key) and integrity (the message has not been modified). The private key signs; the public key verifies.

import java.security.*;
import java.security.spec.*;
import java.util.Base64;

public class DigitalSignatureExample {

    // Sign data with a private key
    public static byte[] sign(PrivateKey privateKey, byte[] data) throws Exception {
        Signature signer = Signature.getInstance("SHA256withRSA");
        // For ECDSA (more efficient): "SHA256withECDSA"
        // For RSA-PSS (better padding): "SHA256withRSA/PSS"
        signer.initSign(privateKey, new SecureRandom());
        signer.update(data);
        return signer.sign();
    }

    // Verify a signature with a public key
    public static boolean verify(PublicKey publicKey, byte[] data, byte[] signature)
            throws Exception {
        Signature verifier = Signature.getInstance("SHA256withRSA");
        verifier.initVerify(publicKey);
        verifier.update(data);
        return verifier.verify(signature);
    }

    // Sign large data streams (e.g., a file)
    public static byte[] signFile(PrivateKey privateKey, Path filePath) throws Exception {
        Signature signer = Signature.getInstance("SHA256withRSA");
        signer.initSign(privateKey);

        try (InputStream is = Files.newInputStream(filePath)) {
            byte[] buffer = new byte[8192];
            int bytesRead;
            while ((bytesRead = is.read(buffer)) != -1) {
                signer.update(buffer, 0, bytesRead);
            }
        }
        return signer.sign();
    }
}

ECDSA vs RSA signatures:

RSA (SHA256withRSA) ECDSA (SHA256withECDSA)
Key size for 128-bit security 3072 bits 256 bits (P-256 curve)
Signature size ~384 bytes ~72 bytes
Signing speed Slower Faster
Verification speed Faster Slower
Usage Legacy, FIPS Modern, TLS 1.3, JWT ES256
Part 10

KeyStore: Managing Keys and Certificates

A KeyStore is a JDK-managed container for cryptographic keys and X.509 certificates. It abstracts the storage mechanism — the same API works whether keys are stored in a file, an HSM, or OS keychain.

import java.security.*;
import java.security.cert.Certificate;
import java.io.*;

public class KeyStoreExample {

    // Create a new PKCS12 keystore and store a key pair
    public static void createAndStore(KeyPair keyPair, X509Certificate cert,
                                      String alias, char[] password, Path outputPath)
            throws Exception {
        KeyStore keyStore = KeyStore.getInstance("PKCS12"); // PKCS12 is the modern standard
        keyStore.load(null, password); // initialize empty keystore

        // Store private key with its certificate chain
        keyStore.setKeyEntry(alias, keyPair.getPrivate(), password,
            new Certificate[]{cert});

        try (OutputStream os = Files.newOutputStream(outputPath)) {
            keyStore.store(os, password);
        }
    }

    // Load a keystore and retrieve a private key
    public static PrivateKey loadPrivateKey(Path keystorePath, char[] storePassword,
                                             String alias, char[] keyPassword) throws Exception {
        KeyStore keyStore = KeyStore.getInstance("PKCS12");
        try (InputStream is = Files.newInputStream(keystorePath)) {
            keyStore.load(is, storePassword);
        }
        return (PrivateKey) keyStore.getKey(alias, keyPassword);
    }

    // Store a symmetric AES key in a keystore (PKCS12 does not support symmetric keys;
    // use JCEKS format for symmetric keys in a file-backed keystore)
    public static void storeSecretKey(SecretKey aesKey, String alias,
                                       char[] password, Path outputPath) throws Exception {
        KeyStore keyStore = KeyStore.getInstance("JCEKS");
        keyStore.load(null, password);
        KeyStore.SecretKeyEntry entry = new KeyStore.SecretKeyEntry(aesKey);
        KeyStore.ProtectionParameter protection = new KeyStore.PasswordProtection(password);
        keyStore.setEntry(alias, entry, protection);
        try (OutputStream os = Files.newOutputStream(outputPath)) {
            keyStore.store(os, password);
        }
    }
}

KeyStore types:

Type Extension Notes
PKCS12 .p12, .pfx Standard; interoperable with OpenSSL, browsers; stores asymmetric keys + certs
JKS .jks Java-proprietary; deprecated — migrate to PKCS12
JCEKS .jceks Java-proprietary; supports symmetric key storage
PKCS11 (HSM) Hardware Security Module; keys never leave hardware
Part 11

Key Derivation: PBKDF2 and HKDF

When you need to derive cryptographic keys from a password or a shared secret, use a Key Derivation Function (KDF).

PBKDF2 — deriving an encryption key from a password:

public class KeyDerivation {

    // Derive an AES-256 key from a user password + salt
    public static SecretKey deriveAesKey(char[] password, byte[] salt) throws Exception {
        PBEKeySpec spec = new PBEKeySpec(
            password,
            salt,
            310_000,   // iterations — OWASP 2023 minimum for PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256
            256        // desired key size in bits
        );
        try {
            SecretKeyFactory factory = SecretKeyFactory.getInstance("PBKDF2WithHmacSHA256");
            byte[] keyBytes = factory.generateSecret(spec).getEncoded();
            return new SecretKeySpec(keyBytes, "AES");
        } finally {
            spec.clearPassword();
        }
    }

    // HKDF (RFC 5869) — expand a high-entropy secret into multiple keys
    // Use when you already have a strong shared secret (e.g., from ECDH key agreement)
    // Bouncy Castle provides HKDF; the JDK does not have a direct HKDF API
    public static byte[] hkdfExpand(byte[] inputKeyMaterial, byte[] salt, byte[] info,
                                     int outputLength) throws Exception {
        // Pseudo-code pattern using HmacSHA256:
        // Extract: pseudoRandomKey = HMAC-SHA256(salt, ikm)
        Mac mac = Mac.getInstance("HmacSHA256");
        mac.init(new SecretKeySpec(salt, "HmacSHA256"));
        byte[] prk = mac.doFinal(inputKeyMaterial);

        // Expand: okm = T(1) || T(2) || ... where T(i) = HMAC(prk, T(i-1) || info || i)
        byte[] okm = new byte[outputLength];
        byte[] t = new byte[0];
        int offset = 0;
        int blockNum = 1;
        while (offset < outputLength) {
            mac.init(new SecretKeySpec(prk, "HmacSHA256"));
            mac.update(t);
            mac.update(info);
            mac.update((byte) blockNum++);
            t = mac.doFinal();
            int toCopy = Math.min(t.length, outputLength - offset);
            System.arraycopy(t, 0, okm, offset, toCopy);
            offset += toCopy;
        }
        return okm;
    }
}
Part 12

Key Exchange: ECDH

ECDH (Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman) allows two parties to establish a shared secret over an insecure channel without transmitting the secret itself. This is how TLS 1.3 establishes its session keys.

import javax.crypto.KeyAgreement;
import java.security.*;
import java.security.spec.*;

public class EcdhExample {

    // Each party generates their own EC key pair on the same curve
    public static KeyPair generateEcKeyPair() throws Exception {
        KeyPairGenerator kpg = KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC");
        kpg.initialize(new ECGenParameterSpec("secp256r1")); // P-256 curve
        return kpg.generateKeyPair();
    }

    // Each party computes the shared secret using their private key + the other's public key
    public static byte[] computeSharedSecret(PrivateKey myPrivateKey, PublicKey theirPublicKey)
            throws Exception {
        KeyAgreement ecdh = KeyAgreement.getInstance("ECDH");
        ecdh.init(myPrivateKey);
        ecdh.doPhase(theirPublicKey, true);
        byte[] sharedSecret = ecdh.generateSecret();

        // Do NOT use the shared secret directly as an AES key.
        // The raw ECDH output has non-uniform distribution.
        // Derive a symmetric key using HKDF or PBKDF2.
        return sharedSecret; // pass through HKDF before use
    }
}
Part 13

Spring Security Crypto Module

Spring Security provides a high-level cryptography module (spring-security-crypto) that wraps JCA with sensible defaults and eliminates most of the IV/salt management boilerplate.

import org.springframework.security.crypto.encrypt.*;

public class SpringCryptoExample {

    // AES-256/CBC with PKCS5 padding and random salt (text encryption)
    // Key derivation: PBKDF2 with 1024 iterations from the provided password
    TextEncryptor encryptor = Encryptors.text("strongPassword", "deadbeef01234567");
    // "deadbeef01234567" = 16-char hex salt (8 bytes) — must be stored alongside the encrypted data

    String encrypted = encryptor.encrypt("sensitive data");
    String decrypted = encryptor.decrypt(encrypted);

    // AES-256/GCM for byte array encryption (Spring Security 5.3+)
    BytesEncryptor gcmEncryptor = Encryptors.stronger("password", "saltHex");
    byte[] encryptedBytes = gcmEncryptor.encrypt("data".getBytes());
    byte[] decryptedBytes = gcmEncryptor.decrypt(encryptedBytes);

    // Password encoding (high-level — just use this in Spring apps)
    PasswordEncoder encoder = new BCryptPasswordEncoder(12);
    String hash = encoder.encode("userPassword");
    boolean valid = encoder.matches("userPassword", hash);
}

Spring Vault integration — keys stored in HashiCorp Vault:

// application.yml
// spring:
//   cloud:
//     vault:
//       uri: https://vault.internal:8200
//       authentication: KUBERNETES
//       transit:
//         enabled: true
//         key-name: myapp-encryption-key

@Service
public class VaultEncryptionService {

    @Autowired
    private VaultTemplate vaultTemplate;

    public String encrypt(String plaintext) {
        VaultTransitContext context = VaultTransitContext.builder().build();
        return vaultTemplate.opsForTransit().encrypt("myapp-encryption-key",
            plaintext.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8), context);
        // Returns "vault:v1:..." — Vault holds the key, your app never sees raw key material
    }

    public String decrypt(String ciphertext) {
        VaultTransitContext context = VaultTransitContext.builder().build();
        byte[] plaintext = vaultTemplate.opsForTransit().decrypt("myapp-encryption-key",
            ciphertext, context);
        return new String(plaintext, StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
    }
}
Part 14

Envelope Encryption Pattern

Envelope encryption is the industry standard pattern for encrypting application data at scale. It separates key management (handled by a Key Management Service) from data encryption (handled locally).

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Envelope Encryption Flow                                        │
│                                                                  │
│  Data Encryption Key (DEK)         Key Encryption Key (KEK)     │
│  ─────────────────────────         ─────────────────────────    │
│  • Random AES-256 key              • Stored in KMS (AWS KMS,    │
│  • Generated fresh per record        GCP Cloud KMS, Vault)      │
│  • Encrypts the actual data        • Never leaves the KMS        │
│  • Encrypted by KEK and stored     • Used to encrypt/decrypt     │
│    alongside the data                DEKs only                   │
│                                                                  │
│  Write path:                                                     │
│  1. Request DEK from KMS → KMS returns {plaintext DEK,          │
│                                          ciphertext DEK}         │
│  2. Encrypt data with plaintext DEK (AES-GCM)                   │
│  3. Store: {ciphertext DEK, IV, ciphertext data}                │
│  4. Zero the plaintext DEK from memory                          │
│                                                                  │
│  Read path:                                                      │
│  1. Read: {ciphertext DEK, IV, ciphertext data}                 │
│  2. Send ciphertext DEK to KMS → KMS returns plaintext DEK     │
│  3. Decrypt data with plaintext DEK                             │
│  4. Zero the plaintext DEK from memory                          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

// AWS KMS envelope encryption example
@Service
public class EnvelopeEncryptionService {

    @Autowired
    private KmsClient kmsClient;

    private final String kmsKeyId = System.getenv("KMS_KEY_ARN");

    public EncryptedRecord encrypt(byte[] plaintext) {
        // Request a data key from KMS
        GenerateDataKeyRequest dataKeyRequest = GenerateDataKeyRequest.builder()
            .keyId(kmsKeyId)
            .keySpec(DataKeySpec.AES_256)
            .build();
        GenerateDataKeyResponse dataKeyResponse = kmsClient.generateDataKey(dataKeyRequest);

        byte[] plaintextDek = dataKeyResponse.plaintext().asByteArray();
        byte[] encryptedDek = dataKeyResponse.ciphertextBlob().asByteArray();

        try {
            // Encrypt the data locally with the plaintext DEK
            SecretKey dek = new SecretKeySpec(plaintextDek, "AES");
            byte[] encryptedData = AesGcmExample.encrypt(dek, plaintext);
            return new EncryptedRecord(encryptedDek, encryptedData);
        } finally {
            Arrays.fill(plaintextDek, (byte) 0); // zero the DEK from memory immediately
        }
    }
}
Part 15

X.509 Certificates and Certificate Chains

An X.509 certificate binds a public key to an identity, signed by a Certificate Authority (CA). Java's CertificateFactory and KeyStore APIs handle certificate parsing and storage.

import java.security.cert.*;
import java.io.*;

public class CertificateExample {

    // Parse a PEM certificate
    public static X509Certificate parsePem(String pemContent) throws Exception {
        byte[] der = Base64.getDecoder().decode(
            pemContent
                .replace("-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----", "")
                .replace("-----END CERTIFICATE-----", "")
                .replaceAll("\\s", "")
        );
        CertificateFactory cf = CertificateFactory.getInstance("X.509");
        return (X509Certificate) cf.generateCertificate(new ByteArrayInputStream(der));
    }

    // Validate a certificate chain against a trust anchor
    public static void validateChain(List<X509Certificate> chain, KeyStore trustStore)
            throws Exception {
        CertPathBuilder builder = CertPathBuilder.getInstance("PKIX");

        X509CertSelector selector = new X509CertSelector();
        selector.setCertificate(chain.get(0)); // the end-entity certificate

        PKIXBuilderParameters params = new PKIXBuilderParameters(trustStore, selector);
        params.setRevocationEnabled(true); // check CRL/OCSP
        params.addCertStore(CertStore.getInstance("Collection",
            new CollectionCertStoreParameters(chain)));

        CertPathBuilderResult result = builder.build(params);
        // Throws CertPathBuilderException if chain is invalid
    }

    // Extract information from a certificate
    public static void inspectCertificate(X509Certificate cert) throws Exception {
        System.out.println("Subject:    " + cert.getSubjectX500Principal().getName());
        System.out.println("Issuer:     " + cert.getIssuerX500Principal().getName());
        System.out.println("Valid from: " + cert.getNotBefore());
        System.out.println("Valid to:   " + cert.getNotAfter());
        System.out.println("Serial:     " + cert.getSerialNumber().toString(16));
        System.out.println("Algorithm:  " + cert.getSigAlgName());

        // Check if expired
        try {
            cert.checkValidity(); // throws CertificateExpiredException or CertificateNotYetValidException
            System.out.println("Status:     Valid");
        } catch (CertificateExpiredException e) {
            System.out.println("Status:     EXPIRED");
        }
    }
}
Part 16

Authenticated Encryption in Practice

Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD) combines confidentiality and integrity in a single operation. AES-GCM is the canonical AEAD cipher in the JDK. The authentication tag (16 bytes appended to the ciphertext) is a MAC over the ciphertext and any AAD.

Practical storage format for encrypted records:

┌─────────┬──────┬─────────────┬───────────┐
│  12 bytes│      │ variable    │  16 bytes │
│  GCM IV  │ AAD  │ ciphertext  │ auth tag  │
│ (random) │      │             │ (GCM)     │
└─────────┴──────┴─────────────┴───────────┘

public class AeadRecord {

    private static final int IV_BYTES = 12;
    private static final int TAG_BITS = 128;

    public static byte[] seal(SecretKey key, byte[] plaintext, byte[] aad) throws Exception {
        byte[] iv = new byte[IV_BYTES];
        new SecureRandom().nextBytes(iv);

        Cipher cipher = Cipher.getInstance("AES/GCM/NoPadding");
        cipher.init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, key, new GCMParameterSpec(TAG_BITS, iv));
        if (aad != null) cipher.updateAAD(aad);
        byte[] ciphertext = cipher.doFinal(plaintext); // includes 16-byte auth tag

        ByteBuffer buf = ByteBuffer.allocate(IV_BYTES + ciphertext.length);
        buf.put(iv);
        buf.put(ciphertext);
        return buf.array();
    }

    public static byte[] open(SecretKey key, byte[] sealedData, byte[] aad) throws Exception {
        ByteBuffer buf = ByteBuffer.wrap(sealedData);
        byte[] iv = new byte[IV_BYTES];
        buf.get(iv);
        byte[] ciphertext = new byte[buf.remaining()];
        buf.get(ciphertext);

        Cipher cipher = Cipher.getInstance("AES/GCM/NoPadding");
        cipher.init(Cipher.DECRYPT_MODE, key, new GCMParameterSpec(TAG_BITS, iv));
        if (aad != null) cipher.updateAAD(aad);
        return cipher.doFinal(ciphertext); // throws AEADBadTagException if tampered
    }
}
Part 17

Common Cryptographic Pitfalls

Pitfall 1 — Reusing IV with the same key (GCM)

// CATASTROPHIC: encrypting two messages with the same key and IV
Cipher cipher = Cipher.getInstance("AES/GCM/NoPadding");
byte[] fixedIv = "1234567890ab".getBytes(); // never do this
cipher.init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, key, new GCMParameterSpec(128, fixedIv));
byte[] ct1 = cipher.doFinal(plaintext1);
cipher.init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, key, new GCMParameterSpec(128, fixedIv)); // SAME IV
byte[] ct2 = cipher.doFinal(plaintext2);
// ct1 XOR ct2 = plaintext1 XOR plaintext2 — both messages are compromised

// FIX: generate a fresh random IV for every encryption (see Part 5)

Pitfall 2 — ECB mode

// ECB encrypts each 16-byte block independently — identical plaintext blocks → identical ciphertext blocks
// The classic demonstration: encrypt a bitmap image — the ECB-encrypted image still shows the outline
Cipher ecb = Cipher.getInstance("AES/ECB/PKCS5Padding"); // never use for real data
// Use AES/GCM/NoPadding

Pitfall 3 — String-based keys

// WRONG: using a string as an AES key directly (likely not 128/192/256 bits, not cryptographic)
SecretKey bad = new SecretKeySpec("mypassword12345".getBytes(), "AES");

// RIGHT: derive a key from a password with PBKDF2 (if input is a password)
// or generate a random key (if no password)
SecretKey good = KeyGenerator.getInstance("AES").generateKey();

Pitfall 4 — Non-constant-time comparison

// WRONG: exits early on mismatch — leaks information via timing
if (Arrays.equals(computedMac, receivedMac)) { ... }

// RIGHT: always compares all bytes
if (MessageDigest.isEqual(computedMac, receivedMac)) { ... }

Pitfall 5 — Rolling your own crypto

Never implement AES, RSA, SHA, or any other cryptographic primitive from scratch, no matter how straightforward the algorithm description looks. Subtle errors in constant-time operations, modular arithmetic, or padding are invisible to functional tests and catastrophic in production.

Part 18

Cryptography in Microservices

Service-to-service encryption:

In a microservices architecture, internal traffic should be encrypted with mTLS (mutual TLS). Each service has its own certificate, issued by an internal CA. The service mesh (Istio, Linkerd) handles certificate rotation and mTLS transparently.

# Istio PeerAuthentication — require mTLS for all services in namespace
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: default
  namespace: production
spec:
  mtls:
    mode: STRICT  # reject plaintext connections

At-rest encryption with Spring Boot and JPA:

// JPA AttributeConverter for transparent field-level encryption
@Converter
public class EncryptedStringConverter implements AttributeConverter<String, String> {

    @Autowired
    private AeadRecord aeadRecord;

    @Autowired
    private SecretKey dataEncryptionKey;

    @Override
    public String convertToDatabaseColumn(String plaintext) {
        if (plaintext == null) return null;
        try {
            byte[] encrypted = AeadRecord.seal(dataEncryptionKey,
                plaintext.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8), null);
            return Base64.getEncoder().encodeToString(encrypted);
        } catch (Exception e) {
            throw new RuntimeException("Encryption failed", e);
        }
    }

    @Override
    public String convertToEntityAttribute(String ciphertext) {
        if (ciphertext == null) return null;
        try {
            byte[] decrypted = AeadRecord.open(dataEncryptionKey,
                Base64.getDecoder().decode(ciphertext), null);
            return new String(decrypted, StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
        } catch (Exception e) {
            throw new RuntimeException("Decryption failed", e);
        }
    }
}

// Use in entity:
@Entity
public class UserProfile {
    @Convert(converter = EncryptedStringConverter.class)
    private String socialSecurityNumber; // transparently encrypted in DB
}
Part 19

FIPS 140-2 Compliance

FIPS 140-2 is the US government standard for cryptographic module validation. Applications deployed to government systems or highly regulated industries (banking, healthcare, defence) may require FIPS compliance.

Enabling FIPS mode in the JDK:

# Java 11+ — use the SunPKCS11 provider in FIPS mode
# This requires an OS-level FIPS-validated PKCS11 module (e.g., NSS with FIPS enabled)
java -Dcom.sun.jndi.ldap.object.trustURLCodebase=false \
     -Djava.security.properties=/etc/java/fips.security \
     -jar app.jar

# fips.security — restricts to FIPS-approved algorithms
security.provider.1=SunPKCS11 /etc/pki/nss-fips.cfg
jdk.tls.disabledAlgorithms=SSLv3, TLSv1, TLSv1.1, RC4, DES, MD5withRSA, ...

FIPS-approved algorithms (symmetric):

  • AES (128, 192, 256 bit): Approved
  • 3DES (TDEA): Approved for legacy; being phased out
  • DES: Not approved
  • RC4, RC2, Blowfish: Not approved

FIPS-approved algorithms (hash/MAC):

  • SHA-1, SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512, SHA-3 family: Approved
  • MD5: Not approved for general use (only in TLS 1.2 legacy compatibility mode)
Part 20

Cryptographic Agility

Cryptographic agility is the ability to swap cryptographic algorithms without changing application code. As algorithms age and new vulnerabilities are discovered (or quantum computers mature), you need to migrate keys and ciphertexts.

// Algorithm identifier stored alongside every encrypted value
public record EncryptedValue(
    String algorithm,   // "AES256GCM_v1", "AES256GCM_v2_with_AAD"
    int keyVersion,     // supports key rotation — which version of the key was used
    byte[] ciphertext   // the encrypted data (IV prepended)
) {
    public static EncryptedValue of(String algo, int keyVer, byte[] ct) {
        return new EncryptedValue(algo, keyVer, ct);
    }
}

@Service
public class AgileEncryptionService {

    // Key versioning: current key + previous keys for decryption
    private final Map<Integer, SecretKey> keyVersions;
    private final int currentKeyVersion;

    public EncryptedValue encrypt(byte[] plaintext) throws Exception {
        SecretKey currentKey = keyVersions.get(currentKeyVersion);
        byte[] ciphertext = AeadRecord.seal(currentKey, plaintext, null);
        return EncryptedValue.of("AES256GCM_v1", currentKeyVersion, ciphertext);
    }

    public byte[] decrypt(EncryptedValue ev) throws Exception {
        SecretKey key = keyVersions.get(ev.keyVersion());
        if (key == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown key version: " + ev.keyVersion());
        return AeadRecord.open(key, ev.ciphertext(), null);
    }

    // Re-encrypt with the current key — call during maintenance windows to retire old keys
    public EncryptedValue reencrypt(EncryptedValue old) throws Exception {
        byte[] plaintext = decrypt(old);
        return encrypt(plaintext);
    }
}
Part 21

Cryptography Checklist for Production

Before deploying any feature that uses cryptography, verify each item:

Algorithm choices:
- [ ] AES-256-GCM (not ECB, not raw CBC without MAC) for symmetric encryption
- [ ] RSA-4096 with OAEP or ECDSA P-256/P-384 for asymmetric operations
- [ ] SHA-256 or SHA-3-256 for hashing (not MD5, not SHA-1)
- [ ] BCrypt(12), Argon2id, or PBKDF2(310k iter) for password hashing
- [ ] SecureRandom for all token/key/IV generation

Key management:
- [ ] Keys stored in KeyStore, HSM, or a KMS — not in source code or plain configuration files
- [ ] IV/nonce is unique per encryption (random, from SecureRandom)
- [ ] Salt is unique per password hash (random, stored alongside the hash)
- [ ] Key rotation policy defined and implemented

Code safety:
- [ ] Constant-time comparison for MAC and hash comparison (MessageDigest.isEqual)
- [ ] char[] used for passwords; zeroed after use
- [ ] Sensitive byte arrays zeroed after use (Arrays.fill(buf, (byte) 0))
- [ ] No cryptographic operations in catch blocks that silently discard failures
- [ ] AEADBadTagException from GCM decryption is treated as an integrity violation, not retried

Testing:
- [ ] Unit tests verify that ciphertexts cannot be decrypted with wrong keys
- [ ] Tests verify that tampered ciphertexts throw on decryption
- [ ] NIST test vectors validated for each algorithm in use

Summary Table

Practice — Lesson 76

Easy

1. Write a method that computes the SHA-256 hash of a UTF-8 string and returns it as a lowercase hex string. Verify your result against the known hash of the empty string: e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855.

2. Generate a 256-bit AES key using KeyGenerator, encrypt the string "Hello, Cryptography!" with AES/GCM/NoPadding, then decrypt it and assert that the decrypted value equals the original.

3. Using BCryptPasswordEncoder with cost factor 12, hash the password "test1234" and verify that matches("test1234", hash) returns true and matches("wrong", hash) returns false.

Medium

4. Implement a SecureTokenService with two methods: generateToken() that returns a 256-bit (32-byte) URL-safe Base64 token using SecureRandom, and constantTimeEquals(String a, String b) that compares two tokens in constant time.

5. Implement HMAC-SHA256 webhook signature verification. Given a signingKey byte array, a payload byte array, and a signature string in the format "sha256=<hex>", return true if the signature is valid.

6. Write a PasswordMigrationService that, given a plaintext password and a stored hash string, detects whether the stored hash is a legacy MD5 hash (by checking if it is exactly 32 hex characters) or a BCrypt hash (by checking the $2a$ prefix), verifies the password against the appropriate algorithm, and on success calls an upgradeCallback that stores the BCrypt re-hash.

Advanced

7. Implement a FileEncryptor that encrypts an arbitrary file using AES-256-GCM with envelope encryption: generate a random DEK per file, encrypt the DEK with an RSA-4096 public key using OAEP padding, and write a binary output file containing: a 4-byte big-endian integer for the encrypted DEK length, the encrypted DEK, and the AES-GCM ciphertext (IV prepended). Implement the corresponding FileDecryptor.

8. Implement CryptoAgileStorage with a Map<Integer, SecretKey> of versioned keys and a currentVersion int. Implement encrypt(byte[] plaintext) returning a record SealedData(int keyVersion, byte[] ciphertext), and decrypt(SealedData) that dispatches to the correct key version. Implement reencrypt(SealedData old) to migrate from an old key version to the current one. Write a unit test that encrypts with version 1, adds version 2 as current, and shows that both old (v1) and new (v2) data decrypt correctly.

Production

9. Design and implement a FieldEncryptionConverter for JPA that encrypts/decrypts a String column using AES-256-GCM. The key is injected from the environment (FIELD_ENC_KEY_HEX). Write a Spring integration test that persists an entity with an encrypted field, queries the raw database value and confirms it is not plaintext, then reads the entity through JPA and confirms the decrypted value matches the original.

10. Implement a Spring Boot @RestController endpoint POST /api/tokens/sign that accepts a SignRequest { String subject, Map<String, Object> claims, int expirySeconds }, signs a JWT using RS256 with a private key loaded from a PKCS12 file at ${JWT_KEYSTORE_PATH}, and returns the compact JWT. Implement GET /api/tokens/verify?token=... that verifies the JWT using the corresponding public key and returns the extracted claims. Keys must be loaded once at startup, not per-request.

Debugging

11. A colleague's AES encryption code throws javax.crypto.AEADBadTagException: Tag mismatch on decryption of data that was encrypted moments ago. They are storing IV + ciphertext as a Base64 string in a database VARCHAR column. What are the three most likely root causes, and how do you diagnose each?

> Root causes to consider: (a) Base64 encoding/decoding mismatch (standard vs URL-safe, with vs without padding); (b) the IV extraction on decrypt is reading the wrong byte range because the length calculation is off; (c) AAD was passed during encryption but not during decryption (or vice versa).

12. An application uses PBKDF2 for password hashing with 1000 iterations and stores the hash in a database. Penetration testers report they cracked 40% of hashes from a leaked database dump in 4 hours using commodity hardware. What is the remediation plan, and how do you migrate existing users without forcing immediate password resets?

Interview

Q: Explain the difference between encryption, hashing, and signing. Give a concrete Java API for each.

A: Encryption is a reversible transformation that converts plaintext to ciphertext using a key; the original plaintext can be recovered by the holder of the corresponding decryption key. Java API: javax.crypto.Cipher with AES/GCM/NoPadding. Use case: storing sensitive data that must be retrievable (credit card numbers, PII).

Hashing is an irreversible one-way function that produces a fixed-length digest from arbitrary input. Java API: java.security.MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256"). Use case: file integrity verification, password storage (with a slow hash like BCrypt — not raw SHA-256), Merkle tree construction.

Signing uses a private key to produce a value that proves the data's origin and integrity; anyone with the corresponding public key can verify the signature. Java API: java.security.Signature.getInstance("SHA256withRSA"). Use case: JWT signing, software release signing, code signing, document signing.

Q: Why is AES-ECB mode never appropriate for encrypting real data?

A: ECB (Electronic Codebook) mode encrypts each 16-byte block independently with the same key. The consequence is that identical plaintext blocks always produce identical ciphertext blocks. For structured data (database records with repeated headers, images, compressible text), an attacker can observe patterns in the ciphertext without decrypting it — they can tell whether two records have the same value in a particular field, which blocks are repeated, and roughly what structure the plaintext has. The canonical demonstration is encrypting a bitmap image with ECB mode — the encrypted image still clearly shows the penguin shape.

AES-GCM (or CBC with a proper MAC) randomises the ciphertext using an IV, so identical plaintexts produce different ciphertexts for each encryption.

Q: What is the difference between password hashing (BCrypt/Argon2) and general-purpose hashing (SHA-256)?

A: General-purpose cryptographic hash functions are designed to be fast — SHA-256 processes gigabytes per second. This is desirable for file integrity checks and digital signatures. For password storage, speed is the adversary's advantage. An attacker with a stolen password database can compute billions of SHA-256 guesses per second on commodity hardware, cracking short or common passwords in seconds.

BCrypt and Argon2 are intentionally slow and work-factor adjustable. BCrypt at cost 12 takes ~200ms per hash. Argon2id is additionally memory-hard, requiring hundreds of megabytes of RAM per guess — which defeats GPU and ASIC attacks that gain speed from processing many guesses in parallel.

Both also embed a random salt to prevent pre-computation attacks (rainbow tables): every hash of the same password is different.

Q: A developer argues that storing an AES key in an environment variable is "good enough" for production. How do you respond?

A: Environment variables are a meaningful improvement over storing keys in source code or plain configuration files, but they have important weaknesses that a dedicated Key Management Service addresses:

  1. No rotation without restart: Rotating an environment-variable key requires redeploying the application, a maintenance window, and re-encrypting all data encrypted with the old key.
  2. No audit trail: You cannot tell which process read the key, when, or how many times.
  3. Visible in process memory dumps and /proc: On Linux, cat /proc/<pid>/environ exposes all environment variables of a running process to any user with the appropriate privileges.
  4. No HSM-backed protection: An environment variable key is just bytes in RAM. An HSM or cloud KMS key never leaves the hardware; all crypto operations happen inside the KMS.
  5. No access control: Any code in the process has access to all environment variables.

For production, a KMS (AWS KMS, GCP Cloud KMS, HashiCorp Vault) provides: audited access, key rotation without service restart, access control per service, HSM-backed key protection, and envelope encryption that limits the blast radius of a key compromise.

Q: What is the significance of constant-time comparison in cryptographic code?

A: A timing side-channel attack exploits the fact that a non-constant-time comparison (like Arrays.equals or String.equals) returns false as soon as the first mismatched byte is found. An attacker who can measure the time difference between a request that matches the first byte vs. one that matches no bytes can determine, one byte at a time, the correct MAC or secret value. Over thousands of requests, they can reconstruct the correct value entirely — without knowing the key.

MessageDigest.isEqual() and equivalent constant-time comparison functions always iterate over all bytes regardless of where the first mismatch occurs, ensuring the comparison time is independent of the input values. This eliminates the timing oracle.

In practice, this matters most for HMAC verification, session token comparison, and CSRF token validation. For password verification, BCrypt's checkpw is already constant-time by design.

Key Takeaways

  • Use AES-256-GCM for symmetric encryption — it provides both confidentiality and integrity in one operation; always generate a fresh random 12-byte IV per encryption; never reuse IV+key pairs
  • BCrypt or Argon2id for passwords, never SHA-256 — fast hashes are not password hashes; cost factor 12 for BCrypt; Argon2id is the OWASP 2023 top recommendation for new systems
  • SecureRandom everywhere randomness matters — java.util.Random is predictable; session IDs, API keys, IVs, salts, and nonces must all come from SecureRandom
  • Constant-time comparison is not optional — use MessageDigest.isEqual() for all MAC and hash comparisons; timing side-channels can reconstruct secrets one byte at a time
  • Keys belong in a KeyStore or KMS — raw key bytes in source code or properties files fail audits and cannot be rotated; PKCS12 for file-backed keystores; cloud KMS for production
  • Hybrid encryption for large data — RSA encrypts small session keys (DEK); AES-GCM encrypts the data; this is the pattern used by TLS, PGP, and every proper encryption system
  • Cryptographic agility from day one — store an algorithm identifier and key version alongside every encrypted value; you will need to migrate algorithms as they age
  • The JCA provider model is your safety net — use Cipher.getInstance("AES/GCM/NoPadding"), not a hand-rolled cipher; provider selection, initialization, and padding are handled correctly by the JDK implementations
