Part 1

Why Design Patterns Still Matter

Design patterns are not abstract academic concepts — they are compressed, named solutions to recurring design problems. When you tell a colleague "this uses the Strategy pattern," you communicate an entire structural decision in two words: there is a family of interchangeable algorithms, they share a common interface, and callers are decoupled from the specific implementation. Without the pattern vocabulary, you need a paragraph.

The GoF (Gang of Four) book — Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software (1994) — catalogued 23 patterns in three categories. Java's standard library and Spring Framework implement most of these patterns internally. You interact with them daily without necessarily naming them.

The three pattern categories:

Creational Patterns      → How objects are created
                           (hide creation complexity, control instantiation)
                           Singleton, Factory Method, Abstract Factory,
                           Builder, Prototype

Structural Patterns      → How objects are composed
                           (combine objects/classes into larger structures)
                           Adapter, Bridge, Composite, Decorator,
                           Facade, Flyweight, Proxy

Behavioral Patterns      → How objects communicate
                           (algorithms and responsibility distribution)
                           Strategy, Observer, Template Method, Command,
                           Iterator, State, Chain of Responsibility,
                           Visitor, Mediator, Memento, Interpreter

Modern relevance: Modern Java (records, sealed classes, lambdas, switch expressions) provides more concise idioms for some classical patterns. A Strategy pattern that once required an interface and several concrete classes can often be expressed as a lambda. Understanding the pattern behind the idiom — not just the idiom — lets you reason about the design, not just write the code.

Part 2

Singleton Pattern

Intent: Ensure a class has exactly one instance and provide a global access point to it.

Real-world need: A shared configuration registry, a connection pool, a logging facade, or a hardware device driver that must not be initialized more than once.

The evolution of Singleton in Java:

// Version 1: Lazy initialization — not thread-safe
public class Registry {
    private static Registry instance;
    private Registry() {}
    public static Registry getInstance() {
        if (instance == null) {
            instance = new Registry(); // race condition: two threads may both enter here
        }
        return instance;
    }
}

// Version 2: Synchronized — thread-safe but slow (synchronizes on every access)
public static synchronized Registry getInstance() {
    if (instance == null) instance = new Registry();
    return instance;
}

// Version 3: Double-checked locking — fast and thread-safe (Java 5+ with volatile)
public class Registry {
    private static volatile Registry instance;
    private Registry() {}
    public static Registry getInstance() {
        if (instance == null) {
            synchronized (Registry.class) {
                if (instance == null) {
                    instance = new Registry(); // volatile ensures write is visible before reference publication
                }
            }
        }
        return instance;
    }
}

// Version 4: Initialization-on-demand holder — best practice (lazy, thread-safe, no synchronization overhead)
public class Registry {
    private Registry() {}
    private static final class Holder {
        private static final Registry INSTANCE = new Registry();
        // Class loading of Holder is lazy and guaranteed to happen exactly once by the JVM
    }
    public static Registry getInstance() {
        return Holder.INSTANCE;
    }
}

// Version 5: Enum Singleton — serialization-safe, reflection-safe (Effective Java, Item 3)
public enum Config {
    INSTANCE;
    private final Map<String, String> properties = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    public String get(String key) { return properties.get(key); }
    public void set(String key, String value) { properties.put(key, value); }
}

Singleton in Spring: In Spring, every @Bean in a Spring ApplicationContext is a singleton by default (scope singleton). You almost never need to implement the Singleton pattern yourself in a Spring application — the container manages it. The pattern is most relevant for non-Spring utility classes or for understanding how the container works.

Singleton pitfalls:
- Hidden global state — Singletons create implicit coupling between all callers
- Difficult to mock in tests — use dependency injection; inject the singleton as an interface
- Concurrency hazards — mutable singleton state must be thread-safe (use ConcurrentHashMap, AtomicReference, or synchronized blocks)

Part 3

Factory Method and Abstract Factory

Factory Method: Defines an interface for creating an object but lets subclasses decide which class to instantiate. The method that creates is declared in an abstract class or interface and overridden in subclasses.

// The product interface
public interface MessageParser {
    Message parse(byte[] data);
}

// Concrete implementations
public class JsonMessageParser implements MessageParser {
    @Override
    public Message parse(byte[] data) {
        return objectMapper.readValue(data, Message.class);
    }
}

public class ProtobufMessageParser implements MessageParser {
    @Override
    public Message parse(byte[] data) {
        return MessageProto.parseFrom(data);
    }
}

// The factory — caller decides which parser to use without knowing the concrete class
public class MessageParserFactory {
    public static MessageParser create(String contentType) {
        return switch (contentType) {
            case "application/json"     -> new JsonMessageParser();
            case "application/protobuf" -> new ProtobufMessageParser();
            case "application/avro"     -> new AvroMessageParser();
            default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unsupported content type: " + contentType);
        };
    }
}

// Extension: registry-based factory (open for extension without modification)
public class MessageParserRegistry {
    private final Map<String, Supplier<MessageParser>> registry = new HashMap<>();

    public void register(String contentType, Supplier<MessageParser> factory) {
        registry.put(contentType, factory);
    }

    public MessageParser create(String contentType) {
        Supplier<MessageParser> supplier = registry.get(contentType);
        if (supplier == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown: " + contentType);
        return supplier.get();
    }
}

Abstract Factory: Creates families of related objects. Instead of a factory that creates one product, an Abstract Factory creates a set of related products that must be used together.

// GUI toolkit abstract factory — creates consistent UI components
public interface UIFactory {
    Button createButton();
    TextField createTextField();
    Dialog createDialog();
}

public class MaterialUIFactory implements UIFactory {
    @Override public Button createButton() { return new MaterialButton(); }
    @Override public TextField createTextField() { return new MaterialTextField(); }
    @Override public Dialog createDialog() { return new MaterialDialog(); }
}

public class CupertinoUIFactory implements UIFactory {
    @Override public Button createButton() { return new CupertinoButton(); }
    @Override public TextField createTextField() { return new CupertinoTextField(); }
    @Override public Dialog createDialog() { return new CupertinoDialog(); }
}

// Caller only depends on the abstract factory — switching themes requires one line
UIFactory factory = isApple ? new CupertinoUIFactory() : new MaterialUIFactory();
Button btn = factory.createButton();

JDK examples of Factory Method: DocumentBuilderFactory.newInstance(), SSLContext.getInstance("TLS"), Calendar.getInstance(), NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance().

Part 4

Builder Pattern

Intent: Separate the construction of a complex object from its representation, allowing the same construction process to create different representations.

Problem it solves: A constructor with 10 parameters is unmaintainable. Some parameters are optional, some are mutually exclusive, and some have complex validation dependencies.

// The classic anti-pattern: telescoping constructor
public Order(String productId, int quantity, String customerId, String shippingAddress,
             String billingAddress, String couponCode, boolean giftWrap, String giftMessage,
             PaymentMethod paymentMethod, ShippingSpeed speed) { ... }

// The Builder pattern solution
public final class Order {
    // All fields are final — Order is immutable once built
    private final String productId;
    private final int quantity;
    private final String customerId;
    private final String shippingAddress;
    private final String billingAddress;
    private final String couponCode;         // optional
    private final boolean giftWrap;          // optional, default false
    private final String giftMessage;        // optional
    private final PaymentMethod paymentMethod;
    private final ShippingSpeed speed;

    private Order(Builder builder) {
        this.productId      = Objects.requireNonNull(builder.productId, "productId required");
        this.quantity       = builder.quantity;
        this.customerId     = Objects.requireNonNull(builder.customerId, "customerId required");
        this.shippingAddress = Objects.requireNonNull(builder.shippingAddress, "shippingAddress required");
        this.billingAddress  = builder.billingAddress != null ? builder.billingAddress : builder.shippingAddress;
        this.couponCode     = builder.couponCode;
        this.giftWrap       = builder.giftWrap;
        this.giftMessage    = builder.giftMessage;
        this.paymentMethod  = Objects.requireNonNull(builder.paymentMethod, "paymentMethod required");
        this.speed          = builder.speed != null ? builder.speed : ShippingSpeed.STANDARD;

        if (quantity <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Quantity must be positive");
        if (giftMessage != null && !giftWrap) throw new IllegalStateException("giftMessage requires giftWrap=true");
    }

    public static Builder builder() { return new Builder(); }

    // Getters (omitted for brevity)

    public static class Builder {
        private String productId;
        private int quantity = 1;
        private String customerId;
        private String shippingAddress;
        private String billingAddress;
        private String couponCode;
        private boolean giftWrap = false;
        private String giftMessage;
        private PaymentMethod paymentMethod;
        private ShippingSpeed speed;

        public Builder productId(String productId) { this.productId = productId; return this; }
        public Builder quantity(int quantity) { this.quantity = quantity; return this; }
        public Builder customerId(String customerId) { this.customerId = customerId; return this; }
        public Builder shippingAddress(String addr) { this.shippingAddress = addr; return this; }
        public Builder billingAddress(String addr) { this.billingAddress = addr; return this; }
        public Builder couponCode(String code) { this.couponCode = code; return this; }
        public Builder giftWrap(boolean giftWrap) { this.giftWrap = giftWrap; return this; }
        public Builder giftMessage(String msg) { this.giftMessage = msg; this.giftWrap = true; return this; }
        public Builder paymentMethod(PaymentMethod method) { this.paymentMethod = method; return this; }
        public Builder shippingSpeed(ShippingSpeed speed) { this.speed = speed; return this; }

        public Order build() { return new Order(this); }
    }
}

// Usage — reads like documentation
Order order = Order.builder()
    .productId("SKU-12345")
    .quantity(2)
    .customerId("CUST-789")
    .shippingAddress("123 Main St, Springfield, IL 62701")
    .paymentMethod(PaymentMethod.CREDIT_CARD)
    .giftMessage("Happy Birthday!")  // implicitly sets giftWrap=true
    .shippingSpeed(ShippingSpeed.OVERNIGHT)
    .build();

Lombok @Builder: Lombok's @Builder annotation generates the Builder class at compile time, eliminating the boilerplate while keeping the pattern.

Java records and builders: Records provide compact immutable data holders but have a single canonical constructor. For records with many optional fields, a Builder class alongside the record is still the right approach.

Part 5

Adapter Pattern

Intent: Convert the interface of a class into another interface that clients expect. Adapter lets classes work together that could not otherwise because of incompatible interfaces.

// Legacy payment processor — interface you cannot change
public class LegacyPaymentProcessor {
    public boolean processPayment(String cardNumber, String expiry, double amount) {
        // legacy SOAP call
        return true;
    }
}

// Modern payment interface that your application uses
public interface PaymentGateway {
    PaymentResult charge(PaymentRequest request);
}

// The Adapter wraps the legacy class and adapts its interface
public class LegacyPaymentAdapter implements PaymentGateway {

    private final LegacyPaymentProcessor legacy;

    public LegacyPaymentAdapter(LegacyPaymentProcessor legacy) {
        this.legacy = legacy;
    }

    @Override
    public PaymentResult charge(PaymentRequest request) {
        boolean success = legacy.processPayment(
            request.cardNumber(),
            request.expiry().format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("MM/yy")),
            request.amountCents() / 100.0
        );
        return success
            ? PaymentResult.success(UUID.randomUUID().toString())
            : PaymentResult.failure("Payment declined by legacy processor");
    }
}

Object Adapter vs Class Adapter:

  • Object Adapter (above): wraps an instance of the adaptee; can adapt subclasses too; preferred in Java
  • Class Adapter: uses multiple inheritance (not possible in Java for classes; can use interfaces for limited scenarios)

JDK examples: Arrays.asList() (adapts array to List), Collections.enumeration() (adapts Collection to Enumeration), InputStreamReader (adapts InputStream to Reader), OutputStreamWriter (adapts OutputStream to Writer).

Part 6

Decorator Pattern

Intent: Attach additional responsibilities to an object dynamically. Decorators provide a flexible alternative to subclassing for extending functionality.

The key insight: Both the decorator and the component implement the same interface. The decorator holds a reference to a component and delegates to it, adding behaviour before or after the delegation.

// Component interface
public interface DataProcessor {
    String process(String data);
}

// Concrete component
public class BaseDataProcessor implements DataProcessor {
    @Override
    public String process(String data) {
        return data.trim();
    }
}

// Abstract decorator — holds component reference, delegates by default
public abstract class DataProcessorDecorator implements DataProcessor {
    protected final DataProcessor delegate;
    public DataProcessorDecorator(DataProcessor delegate) { this.delegate = delegate; }
    @Override
    public String process(String data) { return delegate.process(data); }
}

// Concrete decorators — each adds one responsibility
public class EncryptingDecorator extends DataProcessorDecorator {
    private final SecretKey key;
    public EncryptingDecorator(DataProcessor delegate, SecretKey key) {
        super(delegate);
        this.key = key;
    }
    @Override
    public String process(String data) {
        String processed = delegate.process(data);
        return encrypt(processed, key); // add encryption after base processing
    }
}

public class LoggingDecorator extends DataProcessorDecorator {
    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(LoggingDecorator.class);
    public LoggingDecorator(DataProcessor delegate) { super(delegate); }
    @Override
    public String process(String data) {
        log.debug("Processing {} bytes", data.length());
        String result = delegate.process(data);
        log.debug("Processing complete, output {} bytes", result.length());
        return result;
    }
}

public class CompressionDecorator extends DataProcessorDecorator {
    public CompressionDecorator(DataProcessor delegate) { super(delegate); }
    @Override
    public String process(String data) {
        return Base64.getEncoder().encodeToString(
            compress(delegate.process(data).getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8))
        );
    }
}

// Compose decorators at runtime — order matters!
DataProcessor pipeline = new LoggingDecorator(
    new CompressionDecorator(
        new EncryptingDecorator(
            new BaseDataProcessor(), encKey)));

String result = pipeline.process(rawData);
// Execution order: logging → compression → encryption → base

JDK examples: BufferedInputStream(new FileInputStream(...)) is a classic decorator — it wraps any InputStream and adds buffering. Collections.synchronizedList(list) decorates any List with synchronization. Collections.unmodifiableMap(map) decorates with immutability.

Decorator vs Inheritance: Subclassing is static (the combination is fixed at compile time). Decorators are dynamic — you can choose at runtime which combination of behaviours to apply. With N orthogonal behaviours, subclassing requires 2^N subclasses; decorating requires N decorator classes.

Part 7

Proxy Pattern

Intent: Provide a surrogate or placeholder for another object to control access to it.

Types of proxy:

  • Virtual Proxy: Delays expensive initialization until the object is actually needed (lazy initialization)
  • Protection Proxy: Controls access based on permissions (authorization)
  • Remote Proxy: Represents an object in a different address space (RMI, gRPC stub)
  • Caching Proxy: Caches results of expensive operations (Spring @Cacheable)
  • Logging Proxy: Records all calls for audit purposes
// Protection Proxy — controls access based on the caller's role
public interface DocumentRepository {
    Document findById(Long id);
    void save(Document document);
    void delete(Long id);
}

public class JpaDocumentRepository implements DocumentRepository {
    @Override public Document findById(Long id) { return entityManager.find(Document.class, id); }
    @Override public void save(Document document) { entityManager.persist(document); }
    @Override public void delete(Long id) { entityManager.remove(findById(id)); }
}

public class SecurityProxyDocumentRepository implements DocumentRepository {

    private final DocumentRepository delegate;
    private final AuthorizationService authService;

    public SecurityProxyDocumentRepository(DocumentRepository delegate,
                                            AuthorizationService authService) {
        this.delegate = delegate;
        this.authService = authService;
    }

    @Override
    public Document findById(Long id) {
        authService.checkPermission(Action.READ, "Document:" + id);
        Document doc = delegate.findById(id);
        authService.checkOwnership(doc); // post-access check
        return doc;
    }

    @Override
    public void save(Document document) {
        authService.checkPermission(Action.WRITE, "Document");
        delegate.save(document);
    }

    @Override
    public void delete(Long id) {
        authService.checkPermission(Action.DELETE, "Document:" + id);
        delegate.delete(id);
    }
}

Dynamic Proxy with Java reflection:

// java.lang.reflect.Proxy — creates a proxy at runtime for any interface
public class LoggingProxyFactory {

    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    public static <T> T createLoggingProxy(T target, Class<T> iface) {
        return (T) Proxy.newProxyInstance(
            iface.getClassLoader(),
            new Class<?>[]{iface},
            (proxy, method, args) -> {
                long start = System.nanoTime();
                try {
                    Object result = method.invoke(target, args);
                    long elapsed = TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS.toMillis(System.nanoTime() - start);
                    log.info("[{}] {}ms", method.getName(), elapsed);
                    return result;
                } catch (InvocationTargetException e) {
                    log.error("[{}] failed: {}", method.getName(), e.getCause().getMessage());
                    throw e.getCause();
                }
            }
        );
    }
}

DocumentRepository proxied = LoggingProxyFactory.createLoggingProxy(
    new JpaDocumentRepository(), DocumentRepository.class);
// Every method call is now logged with execution time

Spring AOP is built on the Proxy pattern: @Transactional, @Cacheable, @Async, and @PreAuthorize all work by wrapping the target bean with a proxy that intercepts method calls and applies cross-cutting logic. Understanding the Proxy pattern explains why @Transactional doesn't work on self-invoked method calls — the call bypasses the proxy.

Part 8

Strategy Pattern

Intent: Define a family of algorithms, encapsulate each one, and make them interchangeable. Strategy lets the algorithm vary independently from the clients that use it.

Before and after:

// BEFORE: algorithm embedded in the service — hard to test, hard to extend
public class PricingService {
    public BigDecimal calculatePrice(Order order, String customerType) {
        if (customerType.equals("PREMIUM")) {
            return order.basePrice().multiply(BigDecimal.valueOf(0.8));
        } else if (customerType.equals("BULK")) {
            return order.quantity() > 10
                ? order.basePrice().multiply(BigDecimal.valueOf(0.85))
                : order.basePrice();
        } else {
            return order.basePrice();
        }
    }
}

// AFTER: Strategy pattern — each algorithm is a separate, testable unit
@FunctionalInterface
public interface PricingStrategy {
    BigDecimal calculatePrice(Order order);
}

// Strategies as lambda-friendly implementations
public class PricingStrategies {
    public static final PricingStrategy STANDARD = order -> order.basePrice();

    public static final PricingStrategy PREMIUM = order ->
        order.basePrice().multiply(BigDecimal.valueOf(0.80));

    public static final PricingStrategy BULK = order ->
        order.quantity() > 10
            ? order.basePrice().multiply(BigDecimal.valueOf(0.85))
            : order.basePrice();

    public static final PricingStrategy SEASONAL_SALE = order ->
        order.basePrice().multiply(BigDecimal.valueOf(0.70));
}

// Registry of strategies
public class PricingService {
    private final Map<String, PricingStrategy> strategies = new HashMap<>();

    public PricingService() {
        strategies.put("STANDARD", PricingStrategies.STANDARD);
        strategies.put("PREMIUM",  PricingStrategies.PREMIUM);
        strategies.put("BULK",     PricingStrategies.BULK);
    }

    public void registerStrategy(String name, PricingStrategy strategy) {
        strategies.put(name, strategy); // open for extension without modification
    }

    public BigDecimal calculatePrice(Order order, String customerType) {
        PricingStrategy strategy = strategies.getOrDefault(customerType, PricingStrategies.STANDARD);
        return strategy.calculatePrice(order);
    }
}

Java lambdas and Strategy: When the Strategy interface is @FunctionalInterface, the entire pattern collapses to a lambda assignment. Comparator<T> is the canonical example — it is a Strategy for comparison, and every lambda passed to List.sort() is a Strategy instance.

JDK examples: Comparator (sorting strategy), Executor (task execution strategy), Predicate (filtering strategy), Function (transformation strategy).

Part 9

Observer Pattern

Intent: Define a one-to-many dependency between objects so that when one object changes state, all its dependents are notified and updated automatically.

The modern Java approach uses the event model rather than implementing Observer manually:

// Event class
public record OrderPlacedEvent(
    String orderId,
    String customerId,
    BigDecimal amount,
    Instant timestamp
) {}

// Subject / Event source
@Service
public class OrderService {

    private final ApplicationEventPublisher eventPublisher;

    public OrderService(ApplicationEventPublisher eventPublisher) {
        this.eventPublisher = eventPublisher;
    }

    public Order placeOrder(PlaceOrderRequest request) {
        Order order = createOrder(request);
        orderRepository.save(order);

        // Publish event — does not know who is listening or how many listeners exist
        eventPublisher.publishEvent(new OrderPlacedEvent(
            order.id(), order.customerId(), order.totalAmount(), Instant.now()));

        return order;
    }
}

// Observers — completely decoupled from the subject
@Component
public class EmailNotificationObserver {
    @EventListener
    public void onOrderPlaced(OrderPlacedEvent event) {
        emailService.sendOrderConfirmation(event.customerId(), event.orderId());
    }
}

@Component
public class InventoryObserver {
    @EventListener
    public void onOrderPlaced(OrderPlacedEvent event) {
        inventoryService.reserveItems(event.orderId());
    }
}

@Component
public class AnalyticsObserver {
    @EventListener
    @Async  // runs in a separate thread — doesn't slow down the main transaction
    public void onOrderPlaced(OrderPlacedEvent event) {
        analyticsService.trackPurchase(event.customerId(), event.amount());
    }
}

JDK Observable / Observer (deprecated Java 9): java.util.Observer and java.util.Observable were the JDK's Observer implementation — they are deprecated because Observable is a class (preventing alternative inheritance), and the design is not well-suited to modern concurrent applications. Use Spring events, Guava EventBus, or Reactive Streams (Flow API, Project Reactor) instead.

Reactive Observer with Project Reactor:

// Flux<T> is a cold or hot stream that multiple subscribers (observers) can subscribe to
Flux<OrderEvent> orderEvents = orderEventSource.asFlux()
    .filter(e -> e.amount().compareTo(BigDecimal.valueOf(1000)) > 0) // high-value orders
    .publish()                // multicast — all subscribers see every event
    .autoConnect(1);          // start publishing when first subscriber connects

// Each subscriber is an observer
orderEvents.subscribe(event -> emailHighValueAlert(event));
orderEvents.subscribe(event -> flagForFraudReview(event));
Part 10

Template Method Pattern

Intent: Define the skeleton of an algorithm in an operation, deferring some steps to subclasses. Template Method lets subclasses redefine certain steps of an algorithm without changing the algorithm's structure.

// Abstract class defines the template (the algorithm skeleton)
public abstract class DataImporter {

    // The template method — final to prevent subclasses from breaking the algorithm
    public final ImportResult importData(InputStream source) {
        ImportContext context = new ImportContext();
        try {
            byte[] rawData = readRaw(source);                  // step 1: subclass hook
            byte[] validatedData = validate(rawData, context); // step 2: subclass hook
            List<Record> records = parse(validatedData);       // step 3: subclass hook
            List<Record> transformed = transform(records);     // step 4: subclass hook
            persist(transformed, context);                     // step 5: default implementation
            return ImportResult.success(context);
        } catch (ValidationException e) {
            return ImportResult.failure(e.getMessage(), context);
        } finally {
            cleanup(context);                                  // step 6: always runs
        }
    }

    // Abstract hooks — subclasses must implement these
    protected abstract byte[] readRaw(InputStream source) throws IOException;
    protected abstract byte[] validate(byte[] data, ImportContext context) throws ValidationException;
    protected abstract List<Record> parse(byte[] data) throws ParseException;
    protected abstract List<Record> transform(List<Record> records);

    // Default implementation — subclasses may override
    protected void persist(List<Record> records, ImportContext context) {
        recordRepository.saveAll(records);
        context.setRecordsImported(records.size());
    }

    // Hook with empty default — subclasses opt in to override
    protected void cleanup(ImportContext context) {}
}

// Concrete subclass 1 — CSV import
public class CsvDataImporter extends DataImporter {
    @Override
    protected byte[] readRaw(InputStream source) throws IOException {
        return source.readAllBytes(); // CSV is text — read everything
    }
    @Override
    protected byte[] validate(byte[] data, ImportContext ctx) throws ValidationException {
        String content = new String(data, StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
        if (!content.startsWith("id,name,email")) throw new ValidationException("Missing CSV header");
        ctx.setFormat("CSV");
        return data;
    }
    @Override
    protected List<Record> parse(byte[] data) {
        return CsvParser.parse(new String(data, StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
    }
    @Override
    protected List<Record> transform(List<Record> records) {
        return records.stream()
            .map(r -> r.withEmail(r.email().toLowerCase()))
            .toList();
    }
}

// Concrete subclass 2 — JSON import (different steps, same algorithm structure)
public class JsonDataImporter extends DataImporter {
    @Override protected byte[] readRaw(InputStream source) throws IOException { return source.readAllBytes(); }
    @Override
    protected byte[] validate(byte[] data, ImportContext ctx) throws ValidationException {
        jsonSchemaValidator.validate(data); // throws if schema invalid
        ctx.setFormat("JSON");
        return data;
    }
    @Override protected List<Record> parse(byte[] data) { return objectMapper.readValue(data, LIST_TYPE); }
    @Override
    protected List<Record> transform(List<Record> records) {
        return records.stream().filter(r -> r.active()).toList();
    }
}

Template Method vs Strategy:
- Template Method uses inheritance — the algorithm structure is fixed in the parent; subclasses customise steps
- Strategy uses composition — the algorithm is encapsulated in a separate object that can be swapped at runtime
- Prefer Strategy when the algorithm needs to vary at runtime; use Template Method when the structure is fixed and only specific steps vary

Part 11

Command Pattern

Intent: Encapsulate a request as an object, thereby allowing parameterization, queueing, logging, and undo operations.

// Command interface
public interface Command {
    void execute();
    void undo();
}

// Receiver — performs the actual work
@Service
public class DocumentService {
    public void save(Document document) { /* persist */ }
    public void delete(Long documentId) { /* delete */ }
    public void restore(Document document) { /* restore */ }
}

// Concrete commands
public class SaveDocumentCommand implements Command {
    private final DocumentService service;
    private final Document document;
    private Long savedId;

    public SaveDocumentCommand(DocumentService service, Document document) {
        this.service = service;
        this.document = document;
    }

    @Override
    public void execute() {
        service.save(document);
        savedId = document.getId(); // capture for undo
    }

    @Override
    public void undo() {
        if (savedId != null) service.delete(savedId);
    }
}

// Invoker — manages command history and undo stack
public class CommandInvoker {
    private final Deque<Command> history = new ArrayDeque<>();
    private final Deque<Command> redoStack = new ArrayDeque<>();

    public void execute(Command command) {
        command.execute();
        history.push(command);
        redoStack.clear();
    }

    public void undo() {
        if (history.isEmpty()) throw new IllegalStateException("Nothing to undo");
        Command command = history.pop();
        command.undo();
        redoStack.push(command);
    }

    public void redo() {
        if (redoStack.isEmpty()) throw new IllegalStateException("Nothing to redo");
        Command command = redoStack.pop();
        command.execute();
        history.push(command);
    }
}

Command in Spring Batch: Spring Batch's Step abstraction is essentially the Command pattern — each step encapsulates a unit of work that can be retried, skipped, and monitored independently.

Part 12

Chain of Responsibility Pattern

Intent: Pass a request along a chain of handlers. Each handler decides either to handle the request or to pass it to the next handler in the chain.

// Handler interface
public abstract class RequestHandler {
    protected RequestHandler next;

    public RequestHandler setNext(RequestHandler next) {
        this.next = next;
        return next; // return next for fluent chaining
    }

    public abstract Optional<Response> handle(Request request);

    protected Optional<Response> passToNext(Request request) {
        if (next != null) return next.handle(request);
        return Optional.empty(); // end of chain — no handler could process the request
    }
}

// Concrete handlers
public class AuthenticationHandler extends RequestHandler {
    @Override
    public Optional<Response> handle(Request request) {
        if (!request.hasValidToken()) {
            return Optional.of(Response.unauthorized("Missing or invalid token"));
        }
        return passToNext(request);
    }
}

public class RateLimitHandler extends RequestHandler {
    private final RateLimiter rateLimiter;

    @Override
    public Optional<Response> handle(Request request) {
        if (!rateLimiter.tryAcquire(request.clientId())) {
            return Optional.of(Response.tooManyRequests("Rate limit exceeded"));
        }
        return passToNext(request);
    }
}

public class InputValidationHandler extends RequestHandler {
    @Override
    public Optional<Response> handle(Request request) {
        List<String> errors = validator.validate(request.body());
        if (!errors.isEmpty()) {
            return Optional.of(Response.badRequest("Validation errors: " + errors));
        }
        return passToNext(request);
    }
}

public class BusinessLogicHandler extends RequestHandler {
    @Override
    public Optional<Response> handle(Request request) {
        return Optional.of(orderService.processOrder(request.body()));
    }
}

// Build the chain
RequestHandler chain = new AuthenticationHandler();
chain.setNext(new RateLimitHandler(rateLimiter))
     .setNext(new InputValidationHandler(validator))
     .setNext(new BusinessLogicHandler(orderService));

// Process a request through the chain
Optional<Response> response = chain.handle(incomingRequest);

Spring Security's filter chain is the Chain of Responsibility pattern applied to HTTP requests. Each Filter in the chain handles one concern (authentication, CSRF, session management) and calls filterChain.doFilter() to pass control to the next filter.

Part 13

State Pattern

Intent: Allow an object to alter its behaviour when its internal state changes. The object will appear to change its class.

// Order state transitions:
// PENDING → CONFIRMED → SHIPPED → DELIVERED
//         → CANCELLED (from PENDING or CONFIRMED)
//         → REFUND_REQUESTED (from DELIVERED)

public interface OrderState {
    void confirm(Order order);
    void ship(Order order);
    void deliver(Order order);
    void cancel(Order order);
    String getStatus();
}

public class PendingState implements OrderState {
    @Override
    public void confirm(Order order) {
        order.setState(new ConfirmedState());
        order.notifyCustomer("Order confirmed");
    }
    @Override public void ship(Order order) { throw new IllegalStateException("Cannot ship unconfirmed order"); }
    @Override public void deliver(Order order) { throw new IllegalStateException("Cannot deliver unshipped order"); }
    @Override
    public void cancel(Order order) {
        order.setState(new CancelledState());
        order.refundPayment();
    }
    @Override public String getStatus() { return "PENDING"; }
}

public class ConfirmedState implements OrderState {
    @Override public void confirm(Order order) { throw new IllegalStateException("Already confirmed"); }
    @Override
    public void ship(Order order) {
        order.setState(new ShippedState());
        order.sendTrackingNotification();
    }
    @Override public void deliver(Order order) { throw new IllegalStateException("Not yet shipped"); }
    @Override
    public void cancel(Order order) {
        order.setState(new CancelledState());
        order.refundPayment();
        order.restoreInventory();
    }
    @Override public String getStatus() { return "CONFIRMED"; }
}

// The context — Order delegates all state-dependent behaviour to the current state
public class Order {
    private OrderState state = new PendingState();
    // ... other fields

    public void confirm() { state.confirm(this); }
    public void ship()    { state.ship(this); }
    public void deliver() { state.deliver(this); }
    public void cancel()  { state.cancel(this); }
    public String getStatus() { return state.getStatus(); }
    void setState(OrderState newState) { this.state = newState; }
}
Part 14

Spring Framework Pattern Implementations

Spring is a living design pattern catalogue. Understanding which pattern each Spring feature implements clarifies both the feature's behaviour and its limitations.

Spring Feature Pattern Why
ApplicationContext bean management Singleton Every @Bean is a managed singleton by default
@Autowired / ApplicationContext.getBean() Service Locator / Dependency Injection Decouples component creation from use
@Transactional Proxy (AOP) Wraps beans with transaction management proxy
@Cacheable Proxy + Decorator Wraps methods with caching logic
ApplicationEventPublisher / @EventListener Observer Decoupled pub/sub within the application
HandlerInterceptor / Filter chain Chain of Responsibility Ordered chain of request handlers
RestTemplate / WebClient builder Builder Fluent API for constructing configured HTTP clients
FactoryBean<T> Factory Method Creates complex beans with custom instantiation logic
BeanFactoryPostProcessor Template Method Customise bean factory before beans are instantiated
JdbcTemplate Template Method Handles connection, error mapping; caller provides the SQL and row mapper
@Async Proxy Wraps method call to run in a TaskExecutor
@ConditionalOnProperty Strategy Selects which beans to create based on configuration

JdbcTemplate as Template Method:

// JdbcTemplate eliminates all JDBC boilerplate using Template Method
// You provide only the varying parts: the SQL query and the RowMapper
List<Order> orders = jdbcTemplate.query(
    "SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = ?",
    (rs, rowNum) -> new Order(
        rs.getLong("id"),
        rs.getString("customer_id"),
        rs.getBigDecimal("total_amount"),
        rs.getTimestamp("created_at").toInstant()
    ),
    customerId
);
// JdbcTemplate handles: connection acquisition, PreparedStatement creation,
// parameter binding, execution, result set iteration, exception translation, cleanup
Part 15

Microservices Patterns

Design patterns extend beyond class-level OOP into system-level architecture. Microservices introduce a new category of patterns for distributed systems.

Circuit Breaker (Resilience4j):

// Prevent cascade failures: stop calling a failing downstream service
@Bean
public CircuitBreaker paymentCircuitBreaker(CircuitBreakerRegistry registry) {
    CircuitBreakerConfig config = CircuitBreakerConfig.custom()
        .failureRateThreshold(50)              // open if 50% of calls fail
        .waitDurationInOpenState(Duration.ofSeconds(60)) // wait before trying again
        .slidingWindowSize(20)                 // evaluate over last 20 calls
        .permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState(3)
        .build();
    return registry.circuitBreaker("payment", config);
}

@Service
public class OrderService {
    private final CircuitBreaker circuitBreaker;
    private final PaymentClient paymentClient;

    public PaymentResult processPayment(PaymentRequest request) {
        return circuitBreaker.executeSupplier(() -> paymentClient.charge(request));
        // If circuit is OPEN, throws CallNotPermittedException immediately
        // Use fallback pattern to handle gracefully
    }
}

Saga Pattern — distributed transaction management:

// Choreography-based Saga: each service publishes events, others react
// Order Service → publishes OrderCreated
// Payment Service → listens, charges card, publishes PaymentCompleted or PaymentFailed
// Inventory Service → listens to PaymentCompleted, reserves stock, publishes StockReserved
// Shipping Service → listens to StockReserved, creates shipment

// Each step has a compensating transaction if a later step fails:
// PaymentFailed → OrderService cancels the order (compensating)
// StockUnavailable → PaymentService refunds the charge (compensating)

@Component
public class PaymentSagaParticipant {

    @EventListener
    public void onOrderCreated(OrderCreatedEvent event) {
        try {
            PaymentResult result = chargeCard(event.orderId(), event.amount());
            eventPublisher.publishEvent(new PaymentCompletedEvent(event.orderId(), result.transactionId()));
        } catch (PaymentException e) {
            eventPublisher.publishEvent(new PaymentFailedEvent(event.orderId(), e.getMessage()));
        }
    }
}

Outbox Pattern — guaranteed event delivery:

// Problem: writing to DB and publishing to message broker are two separate operations.
// If the broker call fails after the DB commit, the event is lost.
// Solution: write the event to an "outbox" table in the SAME transaction as the domain data.
// A separate poller reads the outbox and publishes to the broker.

@Transactional
public Order placeOrder(PlaceOrderRequest request) {
    Order order = createOrder(request);
    orderRepository.save(order);

    // In the same transaction — atomically saved
    outboxRepository.save(new OutboxEvent(
        UUID.randomUUID().toString(),
        "OrderPlaced",
        objectMapper.writeValueAsString(new OrderPlacedEvent(order))
    ));

    return order;
    // No direct broker publish here — the outbox poller handles delivery with at-least-once guarantee
}
Part 16

Composite Pattern

Intent: Compose objects into tree structures to represent part-whole hierarchies. Composite lets clients treat individual objects and compositions of objects uniformly.

public interface FileSystemNode {
    String getName();
    long getSize();
    void print(String indent);
}

// Leaf node
public record FileNode(String name, long size) implements FileSystemNode {
    @Override public long getSize() { return size; }
    @Override public void print(String indent) { System.out.println(indent + name + " (" + size + " bytes)"); }
}

// Composite node
public class DirectoryNode implements FileSystemNode {
    private final String name;
    private final List<FileSystemNode> children = new ArrayList<>();

    public DirectoryNode(String name) { this.name = name; }
    public void add(FileSystemNode node) { children.add(node); }
    public void remove(FileSystemNode node) { children.remove(node); }

    @Override public String getName() { return name; }
    @Override public long getSize() { return children.stream().mapToLong(FileSystemNode::getSize).sum(); }

    @Override
    public void print(String indent) {
        System.out.println(indent + name + "/");
        children.forEach(child -> child.print(indent + "  "));
    }
}

// Usage — client code treats files and directories the same way
DirectoryNode root = new DirectoryNode("project");
DirectoryNode src = new DirectoryNode("src");
src.add(new FileNode("Main.java", 4096));
src.add(new FileNode("Config.java", 2048));
root.add(src);
root.add(new FileNode("pom.xml", 8192));

System.out.println("Total: " + root.getSize() + " bytes");
root.print("");
Part 17

Flyweight Pattern

Intent: Use sharing to support large numbers of fine-grained objects efficiently. The flyweight stores shared (intrinsic) state; extrinsic state is passed by the caller.

// Problem: a text editor that creates a Character object for every character on screen
// A large document has millions of characters — one object per character is too expensive

// Flyweight: shared character data (intrinsic state — immutable, shared)
public record CharacterStyle(String fontName, int fontSize, Color color) {
    // CharacterStyle instances are shared — many characters can reference the same style
}

// Factory maintains the pool
public class CharacterStyleFactory {
    private final Map<CharacterStyle, CharacterStyle> pool = new HashMap<>();

    public CharacterStyle getStyle(String font, int size, Color color) {
        CharacterStyle key = new CharacterStyle(font, size, color);
        return pool.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> k); // return existing or add new
    }

    public int poolSize() { return pool.size(); }
}

// Character in the document: stores only the char + position (extrinsic state)
// The style (intrinsic) is shared
public record DocumentCharacter(char value, int position, CharacterStyle style) {}

// Result: 1 million characters with the same style → 1 million DocumentCharacter objects
// (cheap: char + int + reference = ~16 bytes each)
// but only 1 CharacterStyle object (instead of 1 million)

JDK examples: String.intern() (String pool), Integer.valueOf() for values -128 to 127 (Integer cache), Boolean.TRUE/Boolean.FALSE.

Part 18

Facade Pattern

Intent: Provide a unified interface to a set of interfaces in a subsystem. Facade defines a higher-level interface that makes the subsystem easier to use.

// Complex subsystem: video processing involves codec, transcoder, thumbnail generator, metadata extractor
public class VideoFacade {

    private final CodecFactory codecFactory;
    private final Transcoder transcoder;
    private final ThumbnailGenerator thumbnailGenerator;
    private final MetadataExtractor metadataExtractor;
    private final StorageService storageService;

    // The facade simplifies a complex multi-step process into one method call
    public ProcessedVideo processUpload(InputStream videoStream, String filename) {
        // Step 1: detect codec
        Codec codec = codecFactory.detectCodec(videoStream);

        // Step 2: transcode to standard formats
        TranscodedVideo hd = transcoder.transcode(videoStream, codec, Resolution.HD_1080P);
        TranscodedVideo mobile = transcoder.transcode(videoStream, codec, Resolution.MOBILE_480P);

        // Step 3: generate thumbnails
        Thumbnail thumbnail = thumbnailGenerator.generateAtTimecode(videoStream, Duration.ofSeconds(5));

        // Step 4: extract metadata
        VideoMetadata metadata = metadataExtractor.extract(videoStream);

        // Step 5: store everything
        String hdUrl = storageService.store(hd.data(), filename + "_hd.mp4");
        String mobileUrl = storageService.store(mobile.data(), filename + "_mobile.mp4");
        String thumbUrl = storageService.store(thumbnail.data(), filename + "_thumb.jpg");

        return new ProcessedVideo(hdUrl, mobileUrl, thumbUrl, metadata);
    }
}
Part 19

Patterns in Practice: Choosing the Right Pattern

Choosing a pattern is about identifying the specific problem, not fitting the code to a pattern name. The diagnostic questions:

Is the creation of objects complex or needs to be controlled?
    → Singleton, Factory Method, Abstract Factory, Builder, Prototype

Do you need to extend an object's behaviour without subclassing?
    → Decorator

Do you need to control access to an object?
    → Proxy

Does the interface of an existing class not match what clients expect?
    → Adapter

Do you need to simplify a complex subsystem?
    → Facade

Do you have multiple interchangeable algorithms?
    → Strategy

Does an algorithm have a fixed structure but variable steps?
    → Template Method

Do you have one-to-many notification requirements?
    → Observer

Do you need to undo/redo or queue operations?
    → Command

Does an object's behaviour change based on its state?
    → State

Do you have a request that multiple handlers might process?
    → Chain of Responsibility

Anti-pattern: pattern worship. Applying a pattern where it adds complexity without solving a real problem is an anti-pattern in itself. A simple if/else or switch is often the right answer. Reach for patterns when the problem they solve is actually present — not to demonstrate that you know them.

Part 20

Modern Java Idioms and Pattern Simplification

Modern Java features provide more concise alternatives to classical pattern boilerplate.

Strategy → Lambda:

// Classic Strategy: interface + multiple classes
// Modern: @FunctionalInterface + lambda
Comparator<Order> byAmount = Comparator.comparing(Order::totalAmount).reversed();
orders.sort(byAmount);

Command → Lambda / Method Reference:

// Classic Command: interface + concrete class per operation
// Modern: Runnable / Supplier / lambda
Deque<Runnable> commandQueue = new ArrayDeque<>();
commandQueue.offer(() -> emailService.sendConfirmation(order));
commandQueue.offer(() -> inventoryService.reserve(order));
commandQueue.forEach(Runnable::run);

Observer → Reactive Streams:

// Classic Observer: explicit register/notify machinery
// Modern: Project Reactor Flux, Java Flow API
Flux.fromIterable(orders)
    .filter(o -> o.totalAmount().compareTo(threshold) > 0)
    .flatMap(o -> notificationService.notify(o))
    .subscribe();

Builder → Records (for simple cases):

// For simple immutable data with few fields, use a record
// For complex construction with validation, use a Builder alongside the record
public record Point(double x, double y) {
    public static Point of(double x, double y) { return new Point(x, y); }
}

Sealed classes for State and Visitor:

// Sealed hierarchy for payment states — exhaustive switch ensures all states handled
public sealed interface PaymentState
    permits PendingPayment, AuthorisedPayment, CapturedPayment, RefundedPayment {}

public record PendingPayment(String paymentIntentId) implements PaymentState {}
public record AuthorisedPayment(String paymentIntentId, BigDecimal authorisedAmount) implements PaymentState {}

// Exhaustive switch — compiler error if a state is not handled
String status = switch (paymentState) {
    case PendingPayment p -> "PENDING";
    case AuthorisedPayment a -> "AUTHORISED: " + a.authorisedAmount();
    case CapturedPayment c -> "CAPTURED";
    case RefundedPayment r -> "REFUNDED";
};
Part 21

Testing Design Patterns

Patterns affect testability. Well-applied patterns make components easier to test in isolation.

Testing Strategy pattern:

@Test
void bulkDiscountAppliesWhenQuantityExceedsTen() {
    PricingStrategy bulkStrategy = PricingStrategies.BULK;
    Order highQuantity = Order.builder().quantity(15).basePrice(BigDecimal.valueOf(100)).build();
    Order lowQuantity  = Order.builder().quantity(5).basePrice(BigDecimal.valueOf(100)).build();

    assertThat(bulkStrategy.calculatePrice(highQuantity)).isEqualTo(new BigDecimal("85.00"));
    assertThat(bulkStrategy.calculatePrice(lowQuantity)).isEqualTo(new BigDecimal("100.00"));
}

Testing Observer with Spring events:

@SpringBootTest
class OrderServiceEventTest {

    @Autowired private OrderService orderService;
    @Autowired private ApplicationEventPublisher publisher;
    @SpyBean private EmailNotificationObserver emailObserver;

    @Test
    void placingOrderPublishesOrderPlacedEvent() {
        orderService.placeOrder(testRequest());
        verify(emailObserver, times(1)).onOrderPlaced(any(OrderPlacedEvent.class));
    }
}

Testing Proxy/AOP — @Transactional:

// Test that transactional behaviour works correctly
@SpringBootTest
@Transactional  // rolls back after each test
class OrderRepositoryTransactionalTest {

    @Test
    void failedOrderDoesNotPersist() {
        assertThrows(ConstraintViolationException.class,
            () -> orderService.placeOrder(invalidRequest()));
        assertThat(orderRepository.count()).isEqualTo(0); // rolled back
    }
}

Mocking with the Proxy pattern:

Mockito creates dynamic proxies of interfaces and classes. When you call mock(OrderService.class), Mockito uses Proxy.newProxyInstance (or byte-buddy for concrete classes) to create an instance that intercepts every method call and records it.

Practice — Lesson 77

Easy

1. Implement a thread-safe Singleton configuration registry using the Initialization-on-Demand Holder pattern. The registry should hold a Map<String, String> of properties and expose get(String key) and set(String key, String value) methods.

2. Implement a NotificationFactory using the Factory Method pattern that creates a Notification for channels "EMAIL", "SMS", and "PUSH". Each notification type implements a send(String recipient, String message) method. Use a switch expression.

3. Write a HttpRequest Builder class with fields url (required), method (required), headers (optional, Map<String, String>), body (optional, String), and timeoutMs (optional, default 5000). Validate that url is not blank and method is one of GET/POST/PUT/DELETE in build().

Medium

4. Implement the Decorator pattern for a Logger interface with a log(Level level, String message) method. Write three decorators: TimestampDecorator (prepends ISO-8601 timestamp), CorrelationIdDecorator (prepends the current MDC.get("correlationId") if present), and SamplingDecorator (only logs 1/n messages, using SecureRandom). Compose them and write a unit test that verifies the composition.

5. Implement the Strategy pattern for a SortService that sorts a List<String> using different strategies: LEXICOGRAPHIC (natural order), REVERSE_LEXICOGRAPHIC, CASE_INSENSITIVE, and BY_LENGTH. Strategies should be registered in a map by name. Write a unit test covering all four strategies.

6. Implement the Chain of Responsibility for an HTTP request validator. Write three handlers: ContentTypeHandler (rejects if Content-Type is not application/json), BodySizeHandler (rejects if body > 1 MB), and SchemaValidationHandler (validates against a JSON schema using a provided JsonSchemaValidator). Build and invoke the chain, asserting that each handler correctly short-circuits the chain on failure.

Advanced

7. Implement the full Observer pattern using Spring ApplicationEventPublisher. Create an OrderService that publishes an OrderCreatedEvent when placeOrder() is called. Write three listeners: InventoryListener (updates stock), EmailListener (sends confirmation), and AuditListener (records to an audit log). Write a Spring integration test that verifies all three listeners fire exactly once per order placement.

8. Implement the State pattern for an ATM machine with states: IDLE, CARD_INSERTED, PIN_VERIFIED, TRANSACTION_IN_PROGRESS. Implement transitions: insertCard(), verifyPin(int pin), selectTransaction(TransactionType type), complete(), cancel(). Each invalid transition should throw an IllegalStateException with a descriptive message. Write a test that walks through a complete successful ATM session and verifies that calling verifyPin() from IDLE state throws.

Production

9. Design and implement an envelope-encryption service using the Decorator pattern. Your EncryptingRepository decorator should wrap any Repository<String, byte[]> and transparently encrypt all values before storing and decrypt after reading. Use AES-256-GCM. The key should be loaded from System.getenv("ENCRYPTION_KEY_HEX"). Write an integration test that: stores a value via the encrypting repository, reads the raw stored bytes directly from the underlying repository and asserts they are not equal to the original, then reads through the decorator and asserts the decrypted value matches.

10. Implement a Circuit Breaker proxy using java.lang.reflect.Proxy that wraps any service interface. The proxy should track a rolling count of failures in the last 10 calls, open the circuit if ≥5 fail, and re-enter HALF_OPEN state after a configurable wait duration. In HALF_OPEN, allow one test call; if it succeeds, close the circuit; if it fails, re-open. Write a unit test that drives the circuit through all three states.

Debugging

11. A @Transactional service method calls a private helper method in the same class. The helper method throws an exception, but the transaction is not rolled back. Explain the root cause in terms of the Proxy pattern, and give two fixes.

> Root cause: Spring's @Transactional works via a Proxy. When serviceA() calls helperMethod() on the same object, the call is a direct Java method invocation, not a proxy invocation — the AOP interceptor never fires and no transaction management occurs. Fix 1: Extract the helper to a separate @Service bean and inject it. Fix 2: Inject the bean itself via @Autowired and call self.helperMethod() (not recommended for readability).

12. A team uses the Singleton pattern for a ConnectionPool singleton. In production, the application occasionally hangs. Thread dumps show many threads blocked on ConnectionPool.getConnection(). Diagnose the three most likely causes related to the singleton's concurrency design, and describe how to fix each.

Interview

Q: Explain the Open/Closed Principle and show how the Strategy and Decorator patterns implement it.

A: The Open/Closed Principle states that a software entity should be open for extension but closed for modification. You should be able to add new behaviour without changing existing, tested code.

The Strategy pattern implements OCP for algorithms: when a new pricing strategy is needed, you add a new class implementing PricingStrategy — you do not modify PricingService. The registry-based Strategy goes further: new strategies are registered at runtime without even recompiling the service.

The Decorator pattern implements OCP for object behaviour: when a new cross-cutting concern must be added to a DataProcessor (e.g., auditing), you write a new AuditingDecorator that wraps the existing chain — you do not modify BaseDataProcessor, EncryptingDecorator, or any other existing class. The new decorator slots in without touching existing code.

Both patterns achieve this by programming to interfaces, not implementations. The key decision is whether the extension point is about switching algorithms (Strategy) or stacking capabilities (Decorator).

Q: Why doesn't @Transactional work on self-invoked methods, and what is the fix?

A: Spring @Transactional works by creating a proxy around the bean. When an external caller invokes orderService.placeOrder(), the call goes through the proxy, which starts a transaction, then delegates to the real orderService. If placeOrder() internally calls this.helperMethod() — where helperMethod() is also @Transactional — the call bypasses the proxy entirely. this refers to the real object, not the proxy. The proxy never intercepts the call, and no new transaction is started.

The fix is to extract helperMethod() to a separate Spring bean, inject that bean, and call injectedBean.helperMethod(). The call now goes through the proxy for that bean. Alternatively, inject the current bean itself via @Autowired ApplicationContext ctx and call ctx.getBean(OrderService.class).helperMethod() — this forces the call through the proxy — but this is generally considered an anti-pattern.

Q: What is the difference between Proxy, Decorator, and Adapter? When would you choose each?

A: All three wrap an object and delegate to it, but they serve different purposes:

Adapter changes the interface. You have an object with interface A; the client needs interface B. The Adapter implements B and delegates to the A object. The purpose is compatibility — bridging incompatible interfaces, typically at integration boundaries between systems.

Decorator keeps the same interface and adds behaviour. Both the decorator and the original implement the same interface. The purpose is augmentation — adding logging, caching, encryption, or retry logic without modifying the original. Multiple decorators can be stacked.

Proxy keeps the same interface and controls access. Like a Decorator, it implements the same interface. But the purpose is access control, lazy initialization, or transparent remote invocation — not behaviour augmentation. A caching proxy is on the border (adds behaviour + same interface), which is why Spring's @Cacheable is described as both Proxy (the implementation mechanism) and Decorator (the conceptual effect).

Choose Adapter when interfaces are incompatible. Choose Decorator when you want to add stackable behaviours at runtime. Choose Proxy when you want to control access, delay initialization, or intercept calls transparently.

Q: You need to implement a distributed rate limiter for a microservice API. Which patterns would you use, and why?

A: A distributed rate limiter involves several design concerns, each addressed by a pattern:

Proxy pattern: The rate limiter wraps the service interface. Callers interact with the proxy; the proxy checks the rate limit before delegating to the actual service. If the limit is exceeded, the proxy throws an exception without invoking the service at all.

Strategy pattern: The rate limiting algorithm (token bucket, leaky bucket, fixed window, sliding window) is a Strategy. The proxy holds a RateLimitStrategy and delegates the counting decision to it. Switching algorithms requires changing the injected strategy, not the proxy.

Chain of Responsibility: In a Spring application, the rate limiter is a HandlerInterceptor or Filter in the chain. It runs before the controller. If the rate limit is exceeded, it short-circuits the chain and returns 429 Too Many Requests without reaching the handler.

Observer / Event pattern: Rate limit violations are published as events. Downstream observers (alerting system, audit log, adaptive firewall) react independently. The rate limiter itself does not need to know about alerting or logging.

Flyweight pattern: Per-client rate limit counters (stored in Redis) use the client identifier as the key. The counter objects are lightweight value objects shared across requests by key — the Flyweight approach prevents creating per-request counter objects.

Q: When is the Singleton pattern an anti-pattern?

A: The Singleton pattern becomes an anti-pattern when:

  1. It holds mutable global state: Singletons that can be mutated by any caller create hidden coupling. Test A might mutate the singleton's state, causing Test B to fail non-deterministically depending on test execution order. The fix is to make singletons immutable or to scope state to the relevant operation.

  2. It makes testing difficult: If PaymentService directly calls Config.INSTANCE.get("payment.api.key") rather than receiving the config object through dependency injection, you cannot substitute a test config without modifying the Singleton — which breaks test isolation. The fix is dependency injection: inject the singleton as an interface.

  3. It violates Single Responsibility: A Singleton that acts as a god object — holding unrelated state, performing IO, managing connections — is a design smell. The Singleton scope should be separate from the object's responsibilities.

  4. It is used as a workaround for poor dependency management: In a well-structured Spring application, dependency injection eliminates most legitimate uses of hand-rolled Singletons. If you find yourself reaching for the Singleton pattern, ask whether the Spring container should be managing the lifecycle instead.

Key Takeaways

  • Patterns are vocabulary, not rules — naming a pattern communicates design intent to teammates in two words; applying patterns blindly without a clear problem to solve adds complexity
  • Strategy enables Open/Closed — use it whenever you have a family of interchangeable algorithms that you expect to extend; each algorithm is a separate, independently testable unit
  • Decorator stacks behaviours — both the decorator and the component implement the same interface; this is the correct pattern for cross-cutting concerns like logging, caching, and retry logic
  • Spring is a pattern catalogue — @Transactional is Proxy, @EventListener is Observer, JdbcTemplate is Template Method; understanding the underlying patterns explains Spring's behaviour and its limitations (e.g., self-invocation bypasses the proxy)
  • Proxy is why @Transactional has gotchas — when a method calls another method on the same bean (this.method()), the proxy is bypassed; always extract transactional sub-methods to a separate bean
  • Builder for complex construction — more than 4 optional constructor parameters is a signal to reach for Builder; validate invariants in build(), not in setters
  • Modern Java simplifies patterns — lambdas collapse Strategy to a function assignment; sealed classes + switch replace State pattern state hierarchies; records replace many Builder targets
  • Microservices patterns are patterns too — Circuit Breaker (Proxy + State), Outbox (Command + durability), Saga (Chain of Responsibility across services); the GoF vocabulary scales to the distributed level
