@snippet produces properly syntax-highlighted, IDE-linked code samples in Javadoc, replacing <pre>{@code ...}</pre>.

Java 19–20: Continuation of preview features:

Java 19 and 20 were primarily consolidation releases, re-previewing:
- Virtual threads (preview 1 and 2) → standardized in Java 21
- Structured concurrency (incubator → preview) → preview in Java 21
- Scoped values (incubator → preview) → preview in Java 21
- Record patterns (preview 1 and 2) → standardized in Java 21

Part 19

Record Patterns (Java 21)

Record patterns extend pattern matching to deconstruct record components inline, enabling deep nested matching.

Basic record pattern:

record Point(int x, int y) {}

Object obj = new Point(3, 4);

// Before record patterns
if (obj instanceof Point p) {
    System.out.println("x=" + p.x() + ", y=" + p.y());
}

// With record patterns: destructure inline
if (obj instanceof Point(int x, int y)) {
    System.out.println("x=" + x + ", y=" + y);  // x and y are in scope
}

Nested record patterns:

record Line(Point start, Point end) {}
record Point(int x, int y) {}

Object obj = new Line(new Point(0, 0), new Point(3, 4));

// Deep destructuring
if (obj instanceof Line(Point(int x1, int y1), Point(int x2, int y2))) {
    double length = Math.sqrt(Math.pow(x2 - x1, 2) + Math.pow(y2 - y1, 2));
    System.out.println("Length: " + length);
}

Record patterns in switch:

static String describe(Object obj) {
    return switch (obj) {
        case Point(int x, int y) when x == 0 && y == 0 -> "origin";
        case Point(int x, int y) when x == 0           -> "y-axis at " + y;
        case Point(int x, int y) when y == 0           -> "x-axis at " + x;
        case Point(int x, int y)                       -> "(" + x + ", " + y + ")";
        case Line(Point(var x1, var y1), Point(var x2, var y2)) ->
            "line from (" + x1 + "," + y1 + ") to (" + x2 + "," + y2 + ")";
        default -> "unknown shape";
    };
}
Part 20

Migrating to Modern Java

Upgrading from Java 8 or 11 to 21 is a common enterprise task. Here is a systematic approach.

Migration checklist:

Phase 1: Assessment
□ Run jdeps on the application to identify internal API usage
□ Check third-party library compatibility with Java 21
□ Identify uses of SecurityManager (removed in Java 17)
□ Identify uses of sun.misc.* or com.sun.* packages

Phase 2: Compile and Fix
□ Update build tool (Maven 3.9+, Gradle 8+)
□ Update Spring to 3.x (requires Java 17+)
□ Update Hibernate to 6.x
□ Update Mockito to 5.x, Byte Buddy to 1.14+
□ Add --add-opens flags for remaining reflection needs
□ Fix deprecated API calls

Phase 3: Test and Validate
□ Run full test suite on Java 21
□ Run performance benchmarks — baseline vs Java 21
□ Run security scan for deserialization vulnerabilities

Phase 4: Adopt New Features
□ Replace anonymous classes with records where applicable
□ Replace abstract classes + subtypes with sealed + records
□ Enable virtual threads in Spring Boot 3.2+
□ Replace ThreadLocal with ScopedValue where appropriate

Running jdeps:

# Find internal API usage
jdeps --jdk-internals --multi-release 21 app.jar

# Output example:
# app.jar -> JDK removed internal API
#   com.example.Util → sun.misc.BASE64Encoder (JDK internal)
#   Replace with java.util.Base64.getEncoder()

Part 22

Modern Java in Production: Practical Decision Guide

Which LTS should you target?

Java 11 → Only if constrained by a legacy framework that cannot upgrade.
          (Spring Boot 2.x EOL. Migrate to Spring Boot 3.x / Java 17+.)

Java 17 → Minimum recommended for new projects (LTS until 2029).
          Sealed classes, records, text blocks, pattern instanceof.

Java 21 → Best choice for new projects (LTS until 2031).
          Virtual threads, pattern switch, record patterns, sequenced collections.

Language feature adoption roadmap:

Start immediately:
  var             → reduces boilerplate without loss of clarity
  text blocks     → eliminate escape hell in SQL/JSON/HTML strings
  List.of/Map.of  → concise, safe immutable collections

Adopt for new code:
  records         → replace value-carrying POJOs and DTOs
  switch expressions → replace verbose if-else chains and statement switches
  instanceof patterns → eliminate redundant casts

Adopt with intent:
  sealed classes  → design domain models that make illegal states impossible
  pattern switch  → replace visitor pattern and manual type dispatch
  record patterns → deeply destructure nested data in pattern matching

Evaluate carefully:
  virtual threads → adopt via Spring Boot flag; verify no pinned synchronized blocks
  JPMS            → adopt if building a published library or standalone tool
  structured concurrency/scoped values → still preview; evaluate in Java 23+

Modern Java code style example — everything together:

// A payment processor using Java 21 idioms
public sealed interface PaymentResult
    permits PaymentResult.Success, PaymentResult.Declined, PaymentResult.Error {}

public record Success(String txId, Instant at, BigDecimal amount)
    implements PaymentResult {}
public record Declined(String reason)
    implements PaymentResult {}
public record Error(String code, Exception cause)
    implements PaymentResult {}

@Service
public class PaymentService {
    private static final ScopedValue<TraceContext> TRACE = ScopedValue.newInstance();

    public PaymentResult process(PaymentRequest request) {
        var amount = request.amount();
        var gateway = resolveGateway(request.method());

        try (var scope = new StructuredTaskScope.ShutdownOnFailure()) {
            var validation = scope.fork(() -> validate(request));
            var riskScore  = scope.fork(() -> riskEngine.score(request));

            scope.join().throwIfFailed();

            if (riskScore.get() > 0.8) {
                return new Declined("High risk score: " + riskScore.get());
            }

            return gateway.charge(amount);

        } catch (Exception e) {
            return new Error("PROCESSING_FAILED", e);
        }
    }

    private String formatResult(PaymentResult result) {
        return switch (result) {
            case Success(var txId, var at, var amt) ->
                "Paid %.2f at %s (tx: %s)".formatted(amt, at, txId);
            case Declined(var reason) ->
                "Declined: " + reason;
            case Error(var code, var cause) ->
                "Error %s: %s".formatted(code, cause.getMessage());
        };
    }
}

This single class demonstrates: sealed types, records with components, record pattern destructuring in switch, structured concurrency, scoped values, var, text blocks (in the format string style), and switch expressions — all features standardized or previewed in Java 9–21.

Practice

Exercise 1 — Records migration: Take any POJO class in your codebase (or create one) that has only fields, constructor, getters, equals/hashCode, and toString. Convert it to a record. Add a compact constructor for validation. Run your tests to verify equivalence.

Exercise 2 — Sealed type domain model: Model a bank account transaction as a sealed interface with three record subtypes: Deposit(BigDecimal amount, Instant at), Withdrawal(BigDecimal amount, Instant at, String recipient), and Fee(BigDecimal amount, String description). Write a method that uses a switch expression to compute a running balance from a List<Transaction>.

Exercise 3 — Virtual threads load test: Create a Spring Boot 3.2+ application with a single endpoint that calls an external API (mock with a local delay using Thread.sleep(100)). Run 1000 concurrent requests with and without spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true. Measure and compare p99 latency and thread count.

Exercise 4 — Switch expression refactoring: Find a switch statement in any project that uses break and fall-through. Refactor it into a switch expression. Verify the compiler enforces exhaustiveness.

Exercise 5 — HttpClient async pipeline: Using the Java 11 HttpClient, fetch five URLs in parallel using sendAsync. Handle errors gracefully (return an empty string on failure). Collect all results and print them. Measure the elapsed time vs. sequential fetching.

Exercise 6 — Feature timeline quiz: Without looking at the table, write down (a) when var was introduced, (b) when records became standard, (c) when virtual threads became standard, (d) what Java 9 added to collections, (e) which Java version standardized text blocks. Then check against Part 21.

Exercise 7 — Pattern matching refactoring: Find any code in a project that uses a chain of if (x instanceof Foo) ... else if (x instanceof Bar) ... else if (x instanceof Baz). Convert it to a switch expression with type patterns. If the types are from your own codebase, consider whether making the common supertype sealed would improve safety.

Part 1

Why Best Practices Are Architecture Decisions

Best practices are not style preferences. They are constraints that prevent entire categories of failures. When a team adopts a practice — always use Optional for nullable returns, always close resources with try-with-resources, always prefer immutable value objects — they are making a decision that affects every line of code written for the lifetime of the codebase. Undisciplined code accumulates technical debt geometrically: each shortcut makes the next shortcut cheaper and the next correct decision harder.

The Java ecosystem has evolved through eight major platform versions in the last six years (Java 11 through Java 21 LTS). Each version has deprecated old patterns and introduced better replacements. A Java professional in 2024 who still writes null checks instead of Optional, raw types instead of generics, Thread directly instead of ExecutorService, or java.util.Date instead of java.time is not writing Java — they are writing 2004 Java in a 2024 runtime. The JVM can run it. The team will pay for it.

The three dimensions of Java best practices:

Code Quality
  ├─ Naming — communicates intent without a comment
  ├─ Structure — methods < 20 lines, classes < 500 lines
  ├─ Immutability — reduces state-related bugs
  └─ Null discipline — eliminates NullPointerException as a class

Robustness
  ├─ Exception handling — specific, meaningful, recoverable
  ├─ Logging — observable, structured, not a security risk
  ├─ Testing — high coverage of critical paths, not line count
  └─ Resource management — no leaks, no half-open handles

Architecture
  ├─ API design — stable contracts, backward-compatible evolution
  ├─ Dependency management — minimal, explicit, auditable
  ├─ Configuration — externalized, validated, never hardcoded
  └─ Governance — ADRs, code review standards, LTS strategy

Why these choices compound over time:

A codebase that enforces immutability from day one is trivially thread-safe for most operations. A codebase that uses structured logging from day one has production observability without retrofitting. A codebase that writes unit tests as part of development — not after — has a living specification of intent. The cost of each good practice is one decision at the beginning of a project. The cost of retrofitting a bad practice at scale is measured in weeks of engineering time.

The solution architect's responsibility:

Individual developers write best practices in their own methods. Architects codify them as standards — in AGENTS.md, in Checkstyle configurations, in code review checklists, in ADRs that explain why a decision was made. This lesson synthesizes the practices from all 79 preceding lessons into a single reference that serves both the individual contributor and the technical lead.

Part 2

Java Naming Conventions

Naming is the first API a reader encounters. A well-named method, class, or variable eliminates the need for a comment explaining what it does. Poor naming forces every reader to reverse-engineer intent from implementation — a cost paid on every read, forever.

Class naming:

// Classes are nouns — they represent things
OrderProcessor        // ✓ noun, describes the thing
UserRepository        // ✓ noun, describes the thing
InvoiceValidator      // ✓ noun, describes the thing
ProcessOrders         // ✗ verb — this is a method name, not a class name
DoValidation          // ✗ verb — wrong abstraction level

// Concrete classes: plain nouns
class OrderProcessor { ... }

// Abstract classes: abstract noun or adjective prefix
abstract class AbstractRepository { ... }
abstract class BaseEntity { ... }

// Interfaces: adjective (capability) or noun (contract)
interface Serializable { ... }   // capability — what the object CAN do
interface OrderRepository { ... } // contract — what the object IS
interface Comparable<T> { ... }  // capability — use -able suffix for capabilities

// Avoid "I" prefix (IOrderRepository) — it is a .NET convention, not Java
// Avoid "Impl" suffix only — OrderRepositoryImpl is acceptable, but prefer descriptive names:
class JdbcOrderRepository implements OrderRepository { ... }    // ✓ describes implementation
class CachedOrderRepository implements OrderRepository { ... }  // ✓ describes behavior
class OrderRepositoryImpl implements OrderRepository { ... }    // acceptable but uninformative

Method naming:

// Methods are verbs or verb phrases
calculateTax()          // ✓ verb phrase, describes action
findByEmail()           // ✓ describes intent (Spring Data convention)
isActive()              // ✓ boolean — "is" prefix for boolean state
hasPermission()         // ✓ boolean — "has" prefix for boolean containment
getUser()               // ✓ accessor
setName()               // ✓ mutator (use sparingly — prefer immutable builders)

// Boolean method names must read as yes/no questions
user.isActive()         // "Is the user active?" — yes or no
order.hasItems()        // "Does the order have items?" — yes or no
service.canProcess()    // "Can the service process?" — yes or no

// Factory methods
Order.of(...)           // Static factory — short form for simple construction
Order.create(...)       // Static factory — verb form
Order.fromJson(...)     // Static factory — describes input transformation
Order.empty()           // Static factory — describes the result

// Avoid misleading names
void process(Order o)   // ✗ what does "process" mean? too vague
void submitForFulfillment(Order o)  // ✓ specific, unambiguous

Variable and constant naming:

// Variables: camelCase, descriptive nouns
int itemCount;                    // ✓ count of what? items
List<Order> pendingOrders;        // ✓ what kind of orders? pending
Duration connectionTimeout;       // ✓ timeout for what? connection

// Loop variables: short names are acceptable for trivial loops only
for (int i = 0; i < items.size(); i++) { ... }      // acceptable
for (Order order : orders) { ... }                   // ✓ preferred for-each

// Avoid single-letter variables outside math/algorithms
int x;  // ✗ unless it genuinely represents a coordinate

// Constants: SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE
static final int MAX_RETRY_ATTEMPTS = 3;
static final Duration DEFAULT_TIMEOUT = Duration.ofSeconds(30);
static final String CORRELATION_ID_HEADER = "X-Correlation-ID";

// Enum constants: SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE
enum OrderStatus {
    PENDING, PROCESSING, SHIPPED, DELIVERED, CANCELLED
}

Package naming:

// Lowercase, reverse domain, functional grouping
com.company.product.domain.order     // domain model
com.company.product.application      // use cases / services
com.company.product.infrastructure   // adapters, repositories
com.company.product.api              // controllers, DTOs
com.company.product.config           // Spring configuration classes

// Avoid:
com.company.product.util             // ✗ catch-all — every utility ends up here
com.company.product.common           // ✗ catch-all — loses meaning immediately
com.company.product.helpers          // ✗ same as util
Part 3

Code Organization and Package Structure

How code is organized in packages reflects the mental model used to reason about the system. A package structure that mirrors the domain makes navigation intuitive. A package structure organized by technical layer (controllers, services, repositories) makes navigating a feature requires jumping between packages.

Layered architecture (traditional Spring Boot):

com.company.app
  ├─ controller/         ← HTTP layer: @RestController, @RequestMapping
  ├─ service/            ← Business logic: @Service, @Transactional
  ├─ repository/         ← Data access: @Repository, JPA/JDBC
  ├─ model/              ← Domain objects: entities, value objects
  ├─ dto/                ← Data Transfer Objects: request/response shapes
  ├─ config/             ← @Configuration classes
  └─ exception/          ← Custom exceptions, @ControllerAdvice

Domain-driven package structure (recommended for larger codebases):

com.company.app
  ├─ order/
  │   ├─ Order.java               ← aggregate root
  │   ├─ OrderItem.java           ← entity
  │   ├─ OrderStatus.java         ← enum
  │   ├─ OrderRepository.java     ← interface (domain port)
  │   ├─ OrderService.java        ← domain service
  │   ├─ OrderController.java     ← web adapter
  │   └─ JdbcOrderRepository.java ← infrastructure adapter
  ├─ customer/
  │   ├─ Customer.java
  │   └─ ...
  └─ shared/
      ├─ Money.java               ← shared value object
      └─ AuditFields.java         ← shared embedded entity

Class size limits — the practical guidelines:

Method:         ≤ 20 lines of logic (not counting comments/blank lines)
                ≤ 3 levels of nesting (if inside for inside try = 3)
                ≤ 4 parameters (use builder or parameter object above this)

Class:          ≤ 500 lines total
                ≤ 10 methods per class (Single Responsibility)
                ≤ 5 constructor parameters (use @Builder above this)

File:           1 public class per file (mandatory)
                Package-private helper classes: allowed but prefer separate files

The Humble Object pattern for testability:

// Hard to test: business logic mixed with I/O
@Service
public class InvoiceService {
    public void generateInvoice(Long orderId) {
        Order order = db.findById(orderId);           // I/O
        BigDecimal tax = order.getTotal().multiply(TAX_RATE);  // business logic
        Invoice invoice = new Invoice(order, tax);
        s3.upload(invoice.toPdf());                   // I/O
        emailSender.send(order.getCustomer().getEmail(), invoice); // I/O
    }
}

// Better: extracted core logic is pure and testable
@Service
public class InvoiceService {

    public Invoice buildInvoice(Order order) {
        // Pure function — no I/O, trivially testable
        BigDecimal tax = order.getTotal().multiply(TAX_RATE);
        return new Invoice(order, tax);
    }

    public void generateAndSend(Long orderId) {
        Order order = orderRepository.findById(orderId).orElseThrow();
        Invoice invoice = buildInvoice(order);      // pure, testable
        invoiceStorage.store(invoice);              // I/O boundary
        notificationService.sendInvoice(invoice);   // I/O boundary
    }
}
Part 4

Immutability: Design for Correctness

An immutable object has only one possible state: the state it was initialized with. It cannot be corrupted by concurrent modification. It can be shared freely without defensive copying. It can be cached without fear of staleness. It requires no synchronization. Immutability is the single most effective tool for eliminating an entire class of concurrency bugs.

Making a class immutable — the checklist:

// The five rules of immutability:
// 1. Declare the class final (prevent subclasses from adding mutable state)
// 2. All fields must be private and final
// 3. No setter methods
// 4. Defensively copy mutable inputs in the constructor
// 5. Defensively copy mutable fields in getters

public final class Money {
    private final BigDecimal amount;
    private final Currency currency;

    public Money(BigDecimal amount, Currency currency) {
        // Defensive input validation
        Objects.requireNonNull(amount, "amount must not be null");
        Objects.requireNonNull(currency, "currency must not be null");
        if (amount.compareTo(BigDecimal.ZERO) < 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount must not be negative");
        }
        this.amount = amount;
        this.currency = currency;
    }

    public Money add(Money other) {
        if (!this.currency.equals(other.currency)) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Cannot add different currencies");
        }
        return new Money(this.amount.add(other.amount), this.currency); // new instance, not mutation
    }

    public BigDecimal getAmount() { return amount; }     // BigDecimal is already immutable
    public Currency getCurrency() { return currency; }  // Currency is immutable

    // equals, hashCode, toString — always implement for value objects
    @Override
    public boolean equals(Object o) {
        if (this == o) return true;
        if (!(o instanceof Money m)) return false;
        return amount.compareTo(m.amount) == 0 && currency.equals(m.currency);
    }

    @Override
    public int hashCode() { return Objects.hash(amount, currency); }

    @Override
    public String toString() { return amount + " " + currency.getCurrencyCode(); }
}

Java Records — the immutable value object shorthand (Java 16+):

// A record is implicitly: final class, all-args constructor, getters, equals, hashCode, toString
public record Money(BigDecimal amount, Currency currency) {

    // Compact constructor for validation
    public Money {
        Objects.requireNonNull(amount, "amount must not be null");
        Objects.requireNonNull(currency, "currency must not be null");
        if (amount.compareTo(BigDecimal.ZERO) < 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount must not be negative");
        }
    }

    public Money add(Money other) {
        if (!this.currency.equals(other.currency)) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Cannot add different currencies");
        }
        return new Money(this.amount.add(other.amount), this.currency);
    }
}

// Usage:
Money price = new Money(new BigDecimal("19.99"), Currency.getInstance("USD"));
Money tax = new Money(new BigDecimal("2.00"), Currency.getInstance("USD"));
Money total = price.add(tax);     // new record instance — price and tax unchanged

Defensive copying for mutable fields:

public final class DateRange {
    private final LocalDate start;
    private final LocalDate end;
    private final List<LocalDate> holidays;

    public DateRange(LocalDate start, LocalDate end, List<LocalDate> holidays) {
        this.start = Objects.requireNonNull(start);
        this.end = Objects.requireNonNull(end);
        if (end.isBefore(start)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("end must not be before start");
        // Defensive copy — caller might mutate their list after construction
        this.holidays = List.copyOf(holidays);   // unmodifiable + copy
    }

    public List<LocalDate> getHolidays() {
        return holidays;   // already unmodifiable via List.copyOf — safe to return directly
    }
}

When mutability is justified:

Not everything should be immutable. Builder objects accumulate state by definition. Entity objects with identity (JPA @Entity) have mutable state that represents lifecycle. StringBuilder is mutable because it is explicitly a temporary accumulator. The rule is: prefer immutability for value objects and data transfer objects; accept controlled mutability for entities and builders.

Part 5

Null Safety: Avoiding the Billion-Dollar Mistake

Tony Hoare, who introduced the null reference in ALGOL W in 1965, called it "my billion-dollar mistake." Java 8's Optional does not eliminate null from the language — it provides a type-safe way to represent the absence of a value in method signatures, making the possibility of absence explicit and compiler-enforceable.

The Optional contract — when to use and when not to:

// USE Optional as a method return type when absence is a valid, expected outcome
public Optional<User> findByEmail(String email) {
    return userRepository.findByEmail(email);  // returns Optional from Spring Data
}

// DO NOT use Optional:
// - as a field type (use null + @Nullable annotation instead)
// - as a method parameter (use @Nullable or overloads instead)
// - in collections (use an empty collection instead of Optional<List<T>>)

// ✗ Wrong: Optional as parameter
void sendEmail(Optional<User> user) { ... }   // forces caller to wrap

// ✓ Correct: nullable parameter with contract annotation
void sendEmail(@Nullable User user) { ... }   // clear, direct

The complete Optional API — use the right method:

Optional<User> optUser = userService.findByEmail(email);

// DO NOT chain .get() after .isPresent() — defeats the purpose
if (optUser.isPresent()) {
    User u = optUser.get();  // ✗ verbose, no better than null check
}

// USE orElse — provide a default value (always evaluated)
User user = optUser.orElse(User.anonymous());

// USE orElseGet — provide a default supplier (evaluated lazily — preferred when default is expensive)
User user = optUser.orElseGet(() -> createDefaultUser(email));

// USE orElseThrow — mandatory value, throw if absent
User user = optUser.orElseThrow(() -> new UserNotFoundException(email));

// USE map — transform the value if present
String displayName = optUser.map(User::getDisplayName).orElse("Guest");

// USE flatMap — chain Optional-returning operations
Optional<Address> address = optUser
    .flatMap(u -> addressService.findPrimary(u.getId()));

// USE ifPresent — side effect if present
optUser.ifPresent(u -> auditLog.record(u.getId(), "LOGIN"));

// USE ifPresentOrElse — handle both present and absent cases (Java 9+)
optUser.ifPresentOrElse(
    u -> auditLog.record(u.getId(), "LOGIN"),
    () -> log.warn("Login attempt for unknown email: {}", email)
);

// USE filter — narrow down inside the Optional chain
Optional<User> activeUser = optUser.filter(User::isActive);

Null handling at system boundaries:

// External inputs (HTTP, database, config) may be null — validate at entry points
public UserDto createUser(CreateUserRequest request) {
    // Validate all nullable fields at the API boundary
    if (request.getEmail() == null || request.getEmail().isBlank()) {
        throw new ValidationException("email is required");
    }
    if (request.getName() == null || request.getName().isBlank()) {
        throw new ValidationException("name is required");
    }
    // Inside the validated domain, null is now unexpected — use requireNonNull
    return userMapper.toDto(userService.create(
        Objects.requireNonNull(request.getEmail()).toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT),
        Objects.requireNonNull(request.getName()).trim()
    ));
}

// Use @NonNull / @Nullable annotations to communicate contract
public void process(@NonNull Order order, @Nullable String correlationId) {
    Objects.requireNonNull(order, "order must not be null");  // runtime guard
    // correlationId may be null — handle it
    String traceId = correlationId != null ? correlationId : UUID.randomUUID().toString();
}
Part 6

Exception Handling Best Practices

Exceptions communicate failure modes. How you throw, catch, wrap, and propagate exceptions defines how observable and recoverable your application's failures are. Poor exception handling is the primary cause of "silent failures" — bugs where something went wrong, nothing was logged, and the system silently continued in an invalid state.

The exception handling hierarchy — what to use when:

/*
 * RuntimeException (unchecked)          — caller is not required to handle
 *   ├─ IllegalArgumentException         — invalid method argument (caller bug)
 *   ├─ IllegalStateException            — invalid object state (caller bug)
 *   ├─ NullPointerException             — null where object expected (caller bug)
 *   ├─ UnsupportedOperationException    — operation not supported by this impl
 *   └─ Your domain exceptions           — OrderNotFoundException, InsufficientFundsException
 *
 * Exception (checked)                   — caller MUST handle or declare
 *   ├─ IOException                      — I/O failures (recoverable by design)
 *   ├─ SQLException                     — database failures
 *   └─ InterruptedException             — thread interrupted
 *
 * Error (never catch)                   — JVM-level, not recoverable
 *   ├─ OutOfMemoryError                 — heap exhausted
 *   └─ StackOverflowError               — infinite recursion
 */

Custom domain exceptions — the correct structure:

// Domain exception hierarchy — allows callers to catch specific or broad
public class ApplicationException extends RuntimeException {
    public ApplicationException(String message) { super(message); }
    public ApplicationException(String message, Throwable cause) { super(message, cause); }
}

// Entity not found — common enough to be its own type
public class EntityNotFoundException extends ApplicationException {
    private final Class<?> entityType;
    private final Object id;

    public EntityNotFoundException(Class<?> entityType, Object id) {
        super(entityType.getSimpleName() + " not found with id: " + id);
        this.entityType = entityType;
        this.id = id;
    }

    public Class<?> getEntityType() { return entityType; }
    public Object getId() { return id; }
}

// Business rule violation — represents domain logic failures
public class BusinessRuleException extends ApplicationException {
    private final String ruleCode;

    public BusinessRuleException(String ruleCode, String message) {
        super(message);
        this.ruleCode = ruleCode;
    }

    public String getRuleCode() { return ruleCode; }
}

// Usage:
throw new EntityNotFoundException(Order.class, orderId);
throw new BusinessRuleException("INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS",
    "Account balance " + balance + " is less than required " + required);

Exception handling anti-patterns to avoid:

// ✗ SWALLOWING — silent failure
try {
    sendNotification(user);
} catch (Exception e) {
    // empty catch block — the failure disappears
}

// ✓ At minimum, log the exception
try {
    sendNotification(user);
} catch (NotificationException e) {
    log.error("Failed to send notification to user {}: {}", user.getId(), e.getMessage(), e);
    // decide: rethrow, return result with error, or continue depending on business requirement
}

// ✗ CATCHING TOO BROADLY — masks bugs
try {
    processOrder(order);
} catch (Exception e) {
    log.error("Something went wrong", e);
    return false;
}

// ✓ Catch specific exceptions — different failures have different handling
try {
    processOrder(order);
} catch (InsufficientFundsException e) {
    return ProcessingResult.failed("INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS", e.getMessage());
} catch (InventoryException e) {
    return ProcessingResult.failed("INVENTORY_UNAVAILABLE", e.getMessage());
}
// Let unexpected exceptions propagate — don't mask bugs

// ✗ LOSING CAUSE — breaks stack trace chain
try {
    return mapper.readValue(json, Order.class);
} catch (JsonProcessingException e) {
    throw new OrderParsingException("Failed to parse order");  // original cause lost
}

// ✓ Always wrap with cause
throw new OrderParsingException("Failed to parse order JSON", e);

Exception handling in Spring Boot — the global handler:

@RestControllerAdvice
public class GlobalExceptionHandler {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(GlobalExceptionHandler.class);

    @ExceptionHandler(EntityNotFoundException.class)
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND)
    public ErrorResponse handleNotFound(EntityNotFoundException ex) {
        return new ErrorResponse("NOT_FOUND", ex.getMessage());
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(BusinessRuleException.class)
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY)
    public ErrorResponse handleBusinessRule(BusinessRuleException ex) {
        return new ErrorResponse(ex.getRuleCode(), ex.getMessage());
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(MethodArgumentNotValidException.class)
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST)
    public ErrorResponse handleValidation(MethodArgumentNotValidException ex) {
        String message = ex.getBindingResult().getFieldErrors().stream()
            .map(fe -> fe.getField() + ": " + fe.getDefaultMessage())
            .collect(Collectors.joining(", "));
        return new ErrorResponse("VALIDATION_FAILED", message);
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR)
    public ErrorResponse handleUnexpected(Exception ex, HttpServletRequest request) {
        log.error("Unhandled exception for {} {}", request.getMethod(), request.getRequestURI(), ex);
        return new ErrorResponse("INTERNAL_ERROR", "An unexpected error occurred");
    }
}
Part 7

Effective Logging

Logging is the primary observability mechanism for production systems. When a bug occurs at 2 AM on a Sunday, the logs are what you have. Logs that are too sparse leave you guessing. Logs that are too verbose obscure the signal in noise. Logs that contain sensitive data are a security liability. Structured logging at the right level with the right context is the difference between a 10-minute investigation and a 3-hour one.

Log levels — use them correctly:

TRACE — Fine-grained diagnostic: method entry/exit, loop iterations, SQL params
        Use: development debugging only. Never enable in production unless investigating.

DEBUG — Diagnostic for developers: object states, branch decisions, timing
        Use: investigating specific issues in production (enable per-class, short-lived).

INFO  — Notable events in normal operation: startup, shutdown, config loaded, key business milestones
        Use: always enabled; every log line should have value to an operator.

WARN  — Something unexpected that the system handled: retry attempted, fallback used, degraded mode
        Use: should trigger investigation but not necessarily a page.

ERROR — Something failed that the system could NOT handle: exception uncaught, data corruption, circuit open
        Use: every ERROR should trigger a monitoring alert.

Structured logging with SLF4J and Logback:

import org.slf4j.Logger;
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;

@Service
public class OrderService {

    // Always private, static, final — one logger per class
    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(OrderService.class);

    public Order submit(SubmitOrderCommand command) {
        log.info("Submitting order: customerId={}, itemCount={}, total={}",
            command.getCustomerId(), command.getItems().size(), command.getTotal());

        Order order;
        try {
            order = orderRepository.save(buildOrder(command));
        } catch (DataAccessException e) {
            log.error("Failed to persist order for customerId={}: {}",
                command.getCustomerId(), e.getMessage(), e);
            throw new OrderPersistenceException("Order could not be saved", e);
        }

        log.info("Order submitted successfully: orderId={}, customerId={}",
            order.getId(), command.getCustomerId());
        return order;
    }
}

Mapped Diagnostic Context (MDC) — add correlation to every log line:

// In a servlet filter or Spring interceptor — add context before the request runs:
@Component
public class CorrelationIdFilter implements Filter {

    @Override
    public void doFilter(ServletRequest req, ServletResponse res, FilterChain chain)
            throws IOException, ServletException {
        HttpServletRequest request = (HttpServletRequest) req;
        String correlationId = request.getHeader("X-Correlation-ID");
        if (correlationId == null) correlationId = UUID.randomUUID().toString();

        MDC.put("correlationId", correlationId);
        MDC.put("userId", extractUserId(request));  // from JWT, session, etc.
        ((HttpServletResponse) res).setHeader("X-Correlation-ID", correlationId);

        try {
            chain.doFilter(req, res);
        } finally {
            MDC.clear();  // CRITICAL: clear MDC after request — thread pool reuse
        }
    }
}

// logback.xml pattern that includes MDC:
// %d{yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss} %-5level [%X{correlationId}] [%X{userId}] %logger{36} - %msg%n
// Every log line now carries correlation and user context — trivial to trace a request

What NOT to log:

// ✗ NEVER log sensitive data
log.info("User authenticated: email={}, password={}", email, password);     // PII + secret
log.debug("Processing payment: cardNumber={}, cvv={}", card, cvv);          // PCI violation
log.info("Token generated: jwt={}", jwtToken);                              // secret

// ✓ Log identifiers and outcomes, not the sensitive data
log.info("User authenticated: userId={}", user.getId());
log.info("Payment processed: orderId={}, last4={}", orderId, card.getLast4());
log.info("Token issued: userId={}, expiresAt={}", userId, expiresAt);

// ✗ NEVER log inside tight loops — log at loop boundaries
for (Item item : items) {
    log.debug("Processing item {}", item.getId());   // 10,000 items → 10,000 log lines
    process(item);
}

// ✓ Log before/after with summary
log.debug("Processing {} items for orderId={}", items.size(), orderId);
items.forEach(this::process);
log.debug("Completed processing {} items for orderId={}", items.size(), orderId);
Part 8

Clean Code Principles in Java

Clean code reads like well-written prose — the intent is clear from the code itself. Robert Martin's principles, applied specifically to Java, produce code that is readable at first glance and maintainable at scale.

Method extraction and the Single Level of Abstraction:

// ✗ Mixed abstraction levels — high-level intent buried in low-level details
public void checkout(Cart cart, PaymentInfo payment) {
    BigDecimal subtotal = cart.getItems().stream()
        .map(i -> i.getPrice().multiply(new BigDecimal(i.getQuantity())))
        .reduce(BigDecimal.ZERO, BigDecimal::add);
    BigDecimal tax = subtotal.multiply(new BigDecimal("0.08"));
    BigDecimal total = subtotal.add(tax);

    if (payment.getType() == PaymentType.CREDIT_CARD) {
        String authCode = paymentGateway.authorize(payment.getCardToken(), total);
        if (authCode == null) throw new PaymentDeclinedException();
        paymentRepository.save(new Payment(authCode, total, CREDIT_CARD));
    } else if (payment.getType() == PaymentType.PAYPAL) {
        // ... more low-level detail
    }
    orderRepository.save(new Order(cart, total, PENDING));
}

// ✓ Single level of abstraction — each method does ONE thing at ONE level
public void checkout(Cart cart, PaymentInfo payment) {
    Money total = calculateOrderTotal(cart);
    authorize(payment, total);
    placeOrder(cart, total);
}

private Money calculateOrderTotal(Cart cart) {
    Money subtotal = cart.getItems().stream()
        .map(Item::lineTotal)
        .reduce(Money.ZERO_USD, Money::add);
    return subtotal.add(calculateTax(subtotal));
}

private void authorize(PaymentInfo payment, Money total) {
    Payment result = paymentService.authorize(payment, total);
    if (!result.isApproved()) throw new PaymentDeclinedException(result.getDeclineReason());
    paymentRepository.save(result);
}

private void placeOrder(Cart cart, Money total) {
    orderRepository.save(Order.from(cart, total, OrderStatus.PENDING));
}

The boy scout rule — leave code cleaner than you found it:

Every time you touch a file — to fix a bug, add a feature, or review a change — you leave it slightly better. Rename an unclear variable. Extract a repeated expression. Remove a comment that narrates code instead of explaining intent. Delete dead code. These micro-improvements, applied consistently, prevent the slow accumulation of technical debt.

Comments — the right ones:

// ✗ Narrating comments — the code says this already
// Increment the counter
count++;

// ✗ Outdated comment — was true once, no longer accurate
// Returns null if user not found
public Optional<User> findById(Long id) { ... }

// ✓ Explaining WHY, not WHAT — the code says what, only a comment can say why
// BCrypt cost 12 provides ~250ms hash time, making brute-force attacks impractical
// while keeping login latency acceptable for interactive users (Java 21, Ryzen 9 6900HX)
private static final int BCRYPT_COST = 12;

// ✓ Documenting non-obvious constraint
// Thread-unsafe: called only during initialization under the startup lock
private void loadConfig() { ... }

// ✓ TODO with ticket reference — not a permanent TODO
// TODO(JIRA-4521): Replace with async call when notification-service supports webhooks
notificationService.send(notification);
Part 9

SOLID Principles Applied to Java

SOLID is not academic theory — it is a set of constraints that make code easier to change. Every principle has a direct Java translation.

S — Single Responsibility Principle:

// ✗ Violates SRP: OrderService knows about payment, inventory, notification, and persistence
@Service
public class OrderService {
    public void placeOrder(Order order) {
        paymentGateway.charge(order.getPayment());   // payment concern
        inventory.reserve(order.getItems());          // inventory concern
        emailSender.sendConfirmation(order);          // notification concern
        orderRepository.save(order);                  // persistence concern
    }
}

// ✓ Delegates to specialized services — each service has one reason to change
@Service
public class OrderService {
    public void placeOrder(Order order) {
        paymentService.processPayment(order);         // payment service owns payment
        inventoryService.reserve(order);              // inventory service owns stock
        orderRepository.save(order);                  // persistence
        eventPublisher.publish(new OrderPlacedEvent(order)); // notification via event
    }
}

O — Open/Closed Principle:

// ✓ Open for extension, closed for modification — strategy pattern
public interface DiscountStrategy {
    Money apply(Order order);
}

public class PercentageDiscount implements DiscountStrategy {
    private final BigDecimal rate;
    public Money apply(Order order) {
        return order.getTotal().multiply(rate);
    }
}

public class LoyaltyDiscount implements DiscountStrategy {
    public Money apply(Order order) {
        int points = loyaltyService.getPoints(order.getCustomerId());
        return Money.of(points / 100);   // 1 cent per 100 points
    }
}

// Adding a new discount type requires a new class — OrderProcessor never changes
public class OrderProcessor {
    private final DiscountStrategy discount;
    public Money finalPrice(Order order) {
        return order.getTotal().subtract(discount.apply(order));
    }
}

L — Liskov Substitution Principle:

// ✗ Violates LSP: ReadOnlyList extends ArrayList but throws on mutation
// Callers who expect ArrayList.add() to work will get UnsupportedOperationException
public class ReadOnlyList<E> extends ArrayList<E> {
    @Override
    public boolean add(E e) { throw new UnsupportedOperationException(); }
}

// ✓ Use the correct interface — communicate capability through types
// List.copyOf() returns an unmodifiable list; use List<E> as the type, not ArrayList<E>
List<String> items = List.copyOf(originalItems);  // clients receive List<String>, no mutation expected

I — Interface Segregation Principle:

// ✗ Fat interface — forces implementors to implement methods they don't need
public interface Repository<T> {
    T save(T entity);
    T findById(Long id);
    List<T> findAll();
    void delete(T entity);
    long count();
    void bulkInsert(List<T> entities);   // only batch importers need this
    void vacuum();                        // only administrators call this
}

// ✓ Segregated interfaces — implementors implement what they use
public interface ReadRepository<T> {
    Optional<T> findById(Long id);
    List<T> findAll();
}

public interface WriteRepository<T> {
    T save(T entity);
    void delete(T entity);
}

public interface BatchRepository<T> extends WriteRepository<T> {
    void bulkInsert(List<T> entities);
}

D — Dependency Inversion Principle:

// ✗ High-level module depends on low-level module — tight coupling
public class OrderService {
    private final MySQLOrderRepository repository = new MySQLOrderRepository();  // concrete
}

// ✓ Both depend on abstraction — decoupled, testable
public class OrderService {
    private final OrderRepository repository;  // interface

    public OrderService(OrderRepository repository) {  // injected
        this.repository = Objects.requireNonNull(repository);
    }
}
// In tests: inject MockOrderRepository
// In production: inject JdbcOrderRepository (Spring autowires it)
Part 10

Effective Use of Modern Java Features

Java 14–21 introduced sealed classes, records, pattern matching, text blocks, and sequenced collections. Using them correctly reduces boilerplate and makes intent explicit.

Sealed classes for modeling closed hierarchies (Java 17+):

// A Shape is ONLY a Circle, Rectangle, or Triangle — no other subtypes allowed
public sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Rectangle, Triangle {
    double area();
}

public record Circle(double radius) implements Shape {
    public double area() { return Math.PI * radius * radius; }
}

public record Rectangle(double width, double height) implements Shape {
    public double area() { return width * height; }
}

public record Triangle(double base, double height) implements Shape {
    public double area() { return 0.5 * base * height; }
}

// Pattern matching with switch — exhaustiveness is compiler-checked
public String describe(Shape shape) {
    return switch (shape) {
        case Circle c -> "Circle with radius " + c.radius() + ", area " + c.area();
        case Rectangle r -> "Rectangle " + r.width() + "x" + r.height();
        case Triangle t -> "Triangle base=" + t.base() + " height=" + t.height();
        // No default needed — compiler knows Shape is exhaustively covered
    };
}

Text blocks for readable multi-line strings (Java 15+):

// ✗ String concatenation — hard to read, easy to break
String sql = "SELECT u.id, u.email, u.created_at\n" +
             "FROM users u\n" +
             "JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id\n" +
             "WHERE o.status = ?" +
             "  AND u.created_at > ?";

// ✓ Text block — reads exactly like the SQL it represents
String sql = """
        SELECT u.id, u.email, u.created_at
        FROM users u
        JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id
        WHERE o.status = ?
          AND u.created_at > ?
        """;

Pattern matching for instanceof (Java 16+):

// ✗ Traditional — verbose cast
if (event instanceof OrderPlacedEvent) {
    OrderPlacedEvent placed = (OrderPlacedEvent) event;
    processPlacedOrder(placed.getOrder());
}

// ✓ Pattern matching — eliminates the redundant cast
if (event instanceof OrderPlacedEvent placed) {
    processPlacedOrder(placed.getOrder());
}

// Combined with switch — replace complex if-else chains
public void handle(DomainEvent event) {
    switch (event) {
        case OrderPlacedEvent e -> processPlacement(e.getOrder());
        case OrderCancelledEvent e -> processCancellation(e.getOrderId(), e.getReason());
        case OrderShippedEvent e -> notifyCustomer(e.getOrder(), e.getTrackingId());
        default -> log.debug("Unhandled event type: {}", event.getClass().getSimpleName());
    }
}
Part 11

Collections Best Practices

Choose the right collection:

Collection choice decision tree:
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
Need ordering?
  YES → insertion order?  → ArrayList (random access) or LinkedList (frequent insert/delete at ends)
         sort order?      → TreeSet / TreeMap
         no preference    → ArrayList (default choice)
  NO  → unique elements?  → HashSet (O(1)) or LinkedHashSet (+ insertion order)
         key-value pairs? → HashMap (O(1)) or LinkedHashMap (+ insertion order)
                            TreeMap (sorted by key, O(log n))
  Concurrency?
    read-heavy           → CopyOnWriteArrayList / CopyOnWriteArraySet
    read-write balanced  → ConcurrentHashMap
    producer-consumer    → ArrayBlockingQueue / LinkedBlockingQueue

Immutable collections (Java 9+):

// List.of — unmodifiable, null-hostile, value-based equals
List<String> roles = List.of("ADMIN", "USER", "VIEWER");

// Map.of — unmodifiable, null-hostile, no duplicate keys
Map<String, Integer> scores = Map.of("Alice", 95, "Bob", 87, "Carol", 92);

// Map.copyOf — defensive copy of a mutable map
Map<String, String> config = Map.copyOf(mutableConfig);

// Set.of — unmodifiable, null-hostile, no duplicate elements
Set<String> allowed = Set.of("GET", "POST", "PUT", "DELETE");

// List.copyOf — unmodifiable copy of existing collection
List<Order> snapshot = List.copyOf(mutableOrderList);

Stream best practices:

// Prefer method references over lambdas when the lambda just calls a method
orders.stream()
    .filter(Order::isPending)           // ✓ method reference
    .map(Order::getCustomerId)          // ✓ method reference
    .distinct()
    .collect(Collectors.toUnmodifiableList());

// Use Collectors.groupingBy for group-by operations — avoid manual Map building
Map<OrderStatus, List<Order>> byStatus = orders.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Order::getStatus));

// Use Collectors.toMap carefully — handle duplicate keys explicitly
Map<Long, Order> byId = orders.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.toMap(
        Order::getId,
        Function.identity(),
        (existing, duplicate) -> { throw new IllegalStateException("Duplicate order id"); }
    ));

// Avoid modifying external state inside streams — use collect(), not forEach()
// ✗ Side effect inside stream:
List<Order> result = new ArrayList<>();
orders.stream().filter(Order::isPending).forEach(result::add);  // mutable accumulation

// ✓ Collect:
List<Order> result = orders.stream()
    .filter(Order::isPending)
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
Part 12

Concurrency Best Practices

Prefer high-level concurrency utilities over raw threads:

// ✗ Raw Thread — no lifecycle management, no error handling, uncontrolled resource usage
Thread t = new Thread(() -> processOrder(order));
t.start();

// ✓ ExecutorService — controlled pool, lifecycle, Future for results
ExecutorService executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor();  // Java 21
Future<ProcessingResult> future = executor.submit(() -> processOrder(order));

// ✓ CompletableFuture — async pipeline with composition
CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> orderService.fetchOrder(orderId))
    .thenApply(inventoryService::checkAvailability)
    .thenApply(paymentService::chargePayment)
    .thenAccept(result -> notificationService.sendConfirmation(result))
    .exceptionally(ex -> {
        log.error("Order processing failed for {}", orderId, ex);
        return null;
    });

Synchronization — use the right primitive:

// Prefer AtomicLong/AtomicInteger for counters — no synchronization overhead
AtomicLong requestCount = new AtomicLong(0);
requestCount.incrementAndGet();

// Prefer ConcurrentHashMap over synchronized HashMap
ConcurrentHashMap<String, Session> sessions = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
sessions.put(sessionId, session);

// Use ReentrantLock when you need tryLock or interruptible locking
ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();
if (lock.tryLock(100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) {
    try {
        // critical section
    } finally {
        lock.unlock();  // always unlock in finally
    }
}

// Virtual threads (Java 21) — one per task, no pool sizing
try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    List<Future<Result>> futures = IntStream.range(0, 1000)
        .mapToObj(i -> executor.submit(() -> callExternalService(i)))
        .collect(Collectors.toList());
}
Part 13

API Design Best Practices

An API is a contract. Breaking it breaks every caller. Designing APIs for stability, clarity, and evolvability requires forethought.

Design for the caller, not the implementor:

// ✓ Method signatures tell the caller exactly what to provide and what to expect
public interface OrderService {
    // Command — creates side effect, returns result
    Order submit(SubmitOrderCommand command);

    // Query — no side effect, returns value
    Optional<Order> findById(OrderId id);

    // Collection query — never return null for collections
    List<Order> findByCustomerId(CustomerId customerId);  // empty list if none

    // Paginated query — pagination metadata in response
    Page<Order> findAll(Pageable pageable);
}

// ✓ Use strong types, not primitives
// ✗ void transfer(Long fromId, Long toId, double amount)  — which id is which? what currency?
void transfer(AccountId from, AccountId to, Money amount);  // ✓ impossible to confuse arguments

Builder pattern for complex construction:

// When a constructor has more than 3-4 parameters, use a builder
Order order = Order.builder()
    .customerId(customerId)
    .items(items)
    .shippingAddress(address)
    .paymentMethod(paymentMethod)
    .requestedDeliveryDate(LocalDate.now().plusDays(3))
    .notes("Please leave at door if absent")
    .build();  // validates invariants in build()

API versioning for HTTP endpoints:

// URL versioning — explicit, cache-friendly, widely supported
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/v1/orders")
public class OrderControllerV1 { ... }

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/v2/orders")
public class OrderControllerV2 { ... }

// Deprecate old versions — annotate and document timeline
@Deprecated(since = "2.0", forRemoval = true)
@RequestMapping("/api/v1/orders")
Part 14

The Testing Pyramid

The testing pyramid describes the composition of a healthy test suite. More fast, isolated unit tests form the base. Fewer, slower integration tests form the middle. Minimal end-to-end tests sit at the top.

The three layers:

                ┌───────────────┐
                │  E2E Tests    │  5–10%
                │  (Selenium,   │  Full system, slowest, most fragile
                │   REST API)   │  Test user journeys, not every code path
                ├───────────────┤
                │ Integration   │ 20–30%
                │  Tests        │ Real DB (Testcontainers), Spring context
                │  (@DataJpa,   │ Test interaction between layers
                │  @WebMvcTest) │
                ├───────────────┤
                │  Unit Tests   │ 60–70%
                │  (JUnit 5,    │ Fast (<1ms), isolated, mock dependencies
                │  Mockito)     │ Test each class in isolation
                └───────────────┘

Unit testing with JUnit 5 and Mockito — best practices:

@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class OrderServiceTest {

    @Mock
    private OrderRepository orderRepository;

    @Mock
    private PaymentService paymentService;

    @InjectMocks
    private OrderService orderService;

    @Test
    @DisplayName("submit() should persist order and charge payment when items are valid")
    void submitOrder_validCommand_persistsAndCharges() {
        // Arrange — explicit setup, no magic
        SubmitOrderCommand command = buildValidCommand();
        Order expectedOrder = buildOrder(command);
        when(orderRepository.save(any(Order.class))).thenReturn(expectedOrder);
        when(paymentService.charge(any(), any())).thenReturn(PaymentResult.approved("AUTH_001"));

        // Act — single operation
        Order result = orderService.submit(command);

        // Assert — verify output and interactions
        assertThat(result.getId()).isNotNull();
        assertThat(result.getStatus()).isEqualTo(OrderStatus.PENDING);
        verify(orderRepository).save(any(Order.class));
        verify(paymentService).charge(eq(command.getPaymentMethod()), any(Money.class));
    }

    @Test
    @DisplayName("submit() should throw PaymentDeclinedException when payment is declined")
    void submitOrder_declinedPayment_throwsException() {
        SubmitOrderCommand command = buildValidCommand();
        when(paymentService.charge(any(), any())).thenReturn(PaymentResult.declined("INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS"));

        assertThatThrownBy(() -> orderService.submit(command))
            .isInstanceOf(PaymentDeclinedException.class)
            .hasMessageContaining("INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS");

        verify(orderRepository, never()).save(any());  // no order persisted on declined payment
    }
}

Integration testing with Testcontainers:

@SpringBootTest
@Testcontainers
@ActiveProfiles("test")
class OrderRepositoryIntegrationTest {

    @Container
    static PostgreSQLContainer<?> postgres = new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16-alpine")
        .withDatabaseName("testdb")
        .withUsername("test")
        .withPassword("test");

    @DynamicPropertySource
    static void configureProperties(DynamicPropertyRegistry registry) {
        registry.add("spring.datasource.url", postgres::getJdbcUrl);
        registry.add("spring.datasource.username", postgres::getUsername);
        registry.add("spring.datasource.password", postgres::getPassword);
    }

    @Autowired
    private OrderRepository orderRepository;

    @Test
    void findByCustomerId_returnsOnlyCustomerOrders() {
        // Uses a real PostgreSQL database — tests actual SQL, not H2 behavior
        Order order1 = orderRepository.save(buildOrder(CUSTOMER_A));
        Order order2 = orderRepository.save(buildOrder(CUSTOMER_A));
        Order order3 = orderRepository.save(buildOrder(CUSTOMER_B));

        List<Order> customerAOrders = orderRepository.findByCustomerId(CUSTOMER_A);

        assertThat(customerAOrders).hasSize(2)
            .extracting(Order::getId)
            .containsExactlyInAnyOrder(order1.getId(), order2.getId());
    }
}
Part 15

Dependency Injection and Configuration

Constructor injection over field injection:

// ✗ Field injection — hides dependencies, makes testing harder
@Service
public class OrderService {
    @Autowired
    private OrderRepository orderRepository;   // hidden dependency

    @Autowired
    private PaymentService paymentService;     // hidden dependency
}

// ✓ Constructor injection — dependencies are explicit, final, and easily mocked
@Service
public class OrderService {
    private final OrderRepository orderRepository;
    private final PaymentService paymentService;

    public OrderService(OrderRepository orderRepository, PaymentService paymentService) {
        this.orderRepository = Objects.requireNonNull(orderRepository);
        this.paymentService = Objects.requireNonNull(paymentService);
    }
}
// In tests: new OrderService(mockRepository, mockPaymentService) — no Spring context needed

Externalized configuration with validation:

@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "app.payment")
@Validated
public class PaymentProperties {

    @NotBlank
    private String gatewayUrl;

    @Min(1) @Max(10)
    private int maxRetries = 3;

    @NotNull
    @DurationMin(millis = 100)
    private Duration timeout = Duration.ofSeconds(10);

    // getters and setters (or use @ConstructorBinding with records in Spring Boot 3)
}

// application.yml — externalized, environment-specific
// app:
//   payment:
//     gateway-url: https://payment.internal.company.com
//     max-retries: 3
//     timeout: 10s
Part 16

Production Readiness Checklist

A Spring Boot service is not production-ready when it runs. It is production-ready when it is observable, operable, and resilient under failure conditions.

Observability:

# application.yml — expose metrics, health, and info
management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health, metrics, info, prometheus
  endpoint:
    health:
      show-details: when_authorized
  metrics:
    export:
      prometheus:
        enabled: true

// Instrument business operations with Micrometer
@Service
public class OrderService {
    private final Counter ordersSubmitted;
    private final Counter ordersDeclined;
    private final Timer orderSubmissionTimer;

    public OrderService(MeterRegistry meterRegistry, ...) {
        this.ordersSubmitted = Counter.builder("orders.submitted")
            .description("Total orders submitted successfully")
            .register(meterRegistry);
        this.ordersDeclined = Counter.builder("orders.declined")
            .description("Total orders declined at payment")
            .register(meterRegistry);
        this.orderSubmissionTimer = Timer.builder("orders.submission.duration")
            .description("Time to process order submission")
            .register(meterRegistry);
    }

    public Order submit(SubmitOrderCommand command) {
        return orderSubmissionTimer.record(() -> {
            try {
                Order order = doSubmit(command);
                ordersSubmitted.increment();
                return order;
            } catch (PaymentDeclinedException e) {
                ordersDeclined.increment();
                throw e;
            }
        });
    }
}

Resilience with Resilience4j:

@Service
public class ExternalInventoryService {

    private final CircuitBreaker circuitBreaker;
    private final Retry retry;

    public ExternalInventoryService(CircuitBreakerRegistry circuitBreakerRegistry,
                                     RetryRegistry retryRegistry) {
        this.circuitBreaker = circuitBreakerRegistry.circuitBreaker("inventory-service");
        this.retry = retryRegistry.retry("inventory-service");
    }

    public InventoryStatus checkAvailability(ProductId productId) {
        // Retry 3 times with backoff, then open circuit after 50% failures
        Supplier<InventoryStatus> decorated = CircuitBreaker.decorateSupplier(
            circuitBreaker,
            Retry.decorateSupplier(retry, () -> inventoryClient.getStatus(productId))
        );

        return Try.ofSupplier(decorated)
            .recover(CallNotPermittedException.class, e -> InventoryStatus.UNKNOWN_CIRCUIT_OPEN)
            .recover(Exception.class, e -> InventoryStatus.UNKNOWN_DOWNSTREAM_ERROR)
            .get();
    }
}
Part 17

Performance Best Practices

String operations:

// ✗ String concatenation in a loop — creates O(n) intermediate objects
String result = "";
for (String part : parts) {
    result += part + ", ";   // each iteration creates a new String
}

// ✓ StringBuilder — amortized O(1) append
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
for (String part : parts) {
    sb.append(part).append(", ");
}
String result = sb.toString();

// ✓ String.join — even cleaner for joining a collection
String result = String.join(", ", parts);

// ✓ Collectors.joining in streams
String result = parts.stream().collect(Collectors.joining(", "));

Object allocation and reuse:

// ✗ Creating expensive objects repeatedly
public List<Order> filterOrders(List<Order> orders) {
    Pattern pattern = Pattern.compile("^ORD-\\d{8}$");  // compiled on every call
    return orders.stream()
        .filter(o -> pattern.matcher(o.getId()).matches())
        .collect(Collectors.toList());
}

// ✓ Compile once, reuse everywhere
private static final Pattern ORDER_ID_PATTERN = Pattern.compile("^ORD-\\d{8}$");

public List<Order> filterOrders(List<Order> orders) {
    return orders.stream()
        .filter(o -> ORDER_ID_PATTERN.matcher(o.getId()).matches())
        .collect(Collectors.toList());
}

JVM startup with GraalVM native image (for CLI and serverless):

Standard JVM startup: 300–800ms for a Spring Boot application
GraalVM native image: 10–50ms startup, lower memory footprint

When to use native:
  ✓ CLI tools — user-facing latency matters
  ✓ Serverless / AWS Lambda — cold start latency matters
  ✓ High-density deployments — memory savings at scale matter

When NOT to use native:
  ✗ Applications using heavy reflection (dynamic proxies, Groovy scripting)
  ✗ Teams without native image build infrastructure
  ✗ Long-running services where startup time is irrelevant
Part 18

Security Best Practices Checklist

This checklist synthesizes Lesson 75 (Security) into actionable items for every service:

Authentication and Authorization
  ☐ JWT validation: signature, expiry, issuer, audience — all verified
  ☐ Passwords hashed with BCrypt (cost ≥ 12) or Argon2 — never MD5/SHA-1
  ☐ Spring Security configured: CSRF for web, stateless for APIs
  ☐ @PreAuthorize on every service method that changes state
  ☐ Principle of least privilege: each service account has minimum DB permissions

Input Validation
  ☐ All HTTP inputs validated with @Valid + @NotNull, @Size, @Pattern
  ☐ SQL: PreparedStatement or named parameters only — no string concatenation
  ☐ HTML output: encoding applied — no raw user data in templates
  ☐ File uploads: filename sanitized, MIME type validated, size limited

Secrets Management
  ☐ No secrets in source code, git history, or application.properties in VCS
  ☐ Secrets loaded from environment variables or secrets manager at runtime
  ☐ Database credentials rotated quarterly; rotation supported by connection pool

Transport Security
  ☐ TLS 1.2 minimum, TLS 1.3 preferred
  ☐ No certificate validation disabled (no trustAllCerts in production)
  ☐ Internal service communication: mTLS or service mesh

Dependencies
  ☐ OWASP Dependency Check or Snyk in CI — fail on HIGH CVEs
  ☐ Direct dependencies pinned to specific versions in pom.xml / build.gradle
  ☐ Java native deserialization: ObjectInputFilter allowlist in place
Part 19

Code Review Checklist

A code review checklist ensures that quality standards are applied consistently across every pull request, not just when a reviewer happens to notice an issue.

Correctness
  ☐ Does the code do what the PR description says?
  ☐ Are all edge cases handled? (null inputs, empty collections, max values)
  ☐ Are exceptions handled specifically (not caught as Exception)?
  ☐ Are all resources closed? (connections, streams, file handles)
  ☐ Is every public method covered by a meaningful unit test?

Design
  ☐ Does the class have a single clear responsibility?
  ☐ Are methods ≤ 20 lines? Classes ≤ 500 lines?
  ☐ Is there unnecessary duplication that should be extracted?
  ☐ Are abstractions at the right level? (no mixing high-level and low-level)
  ☐ Are dependencies injected (not instantiated with new)?

Safety
  ☐ Are Optional, not null, used for nullable return types?
  ☐ Are collections returned as unmodifiable copies where appropriate?
  ☐ Are fields final where they should be?
  ☐ Is shared mutable state protected by appropriate synchronization?

Observability
  ☐ Are errors logged at ERROR level with the exception object?
  ☐ Are key business events logged at INFO level?
  ☐ Is no sensitive data (passwords, tokens, PII) in log statements?
  ☐ Are new business metrics instrumented with Micrometer?

Performance
  ☐ Are N+1 query problems introduced? (JPA: use JOIN FETCH or @BatchSize)
  ☐ Are expensive objects created inside loops instead of once?
  ☐ Are database queries paginated for potentially large result sets?

Security
  ☐ Is user input validated before use?
  ☐ Is SQL parameterized (no string concatenation into queries)?
  ☐ Are new endpoints protected with appropriate authorization?
  ☐ Are new dependencies free of known CVEs (OWASP check green)?
Part 20

Architectural Governance and Architecture Decision Records

Architecture evolves. Every significant technical decision — a new framework, a database choice, a communication pattern, a security mechanism — should be recorded with its context, options considered, and rationale. Without records, the same decision is re-made by each new team member, often differently.

Architecture Decision Records (ADR) — the lightweight format:

# ADR-0042: Use PostgreSQL as the primary persistence store

## Status
Accepted — 2024-03-15

## Context
The orders service requires ACID transactions for multi-item order operations,
full-text search for order history, and JSON storage for flexible order metadata.
Three options were evaluated.

## Options Considered

| Option      | ACID | Full-Text | JSON | Operational complexity |
|-------------|------|-----------|------|------------------------|
| PostgreSQL  | ✓    | ✓         | ✓    | Low (managed RDS)      |
| MongoDB     | ✓*   | ✓         | ✓    | Medium                 |
| MySQL       | ✓    | Limited   | ✓    | Low (managed RDS)      |

*MongoDB multi-document transactions added in 4.0 but have higher operational complexity.

## Decision
Use PostgreSQL 16 on Amazon RDS. PostgreSQL provides ACID guarantees, native JSONB
for flexible metadata, pg_trgm for full-text search, and is well-supported by the
team's existing operational runbooks.

## Consequences
- Spring Data JPA + Hibernate for ORM layer
- Flyway for schema migrations
- pgBouncer for connection pooling in high-concurrency deployments
- Team must be trained on PostgreSQL-specific features (CTEs, window functions, JSONB)

Governance mechanisms:

Code-level governance:
  ├─ Checkstyle or Spotless: enforce naming, import order, line length
  ├─ ArchUnit: enforce package dependencies (domain must not import from infrastructure)
  ├─ PMD / SpotBugs: enforce common quality rules (no System.out, no empty catch)
  └─ OWASP Dependency Check: block dependencies with HIGH CVEs

Process governance:
  ├─ Required code review: no direct push to main
  ├─ CI gates: tests pass, coverage ≥ threshold, security check green
  ├─ ADR required for: new frameworks, new datastores, breaking API changes
  └─ RFC process for: cross-team API changes, architectural changes

ArchUnit example — enforce hexagonal architecture:

@AnalyzeClasses(packages = "com.company.app")
public class ArchitectureTest {

    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule domainMustNotDependOnInfrastructure =
        noClasses()
            .that().resideInAPackage("..domain..")
            .should().dependOnClassesThat()
            .resideInAPackage("..infrastructure..");

    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule servicesMustNotDependOnControllers =
        noClasses()
            .that().resideInAPackage("..service..")
            .should().dependOnClassesThat()
            .resideInAPackage("..controller..");
}
Part 21

Java LTS Strategy and Upgrade Planning

The Java release train:

Java Release Cadence (since Java 9):
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
Feature releases: every 6 months (March and September)
  └─ Short-term support: Oracle supports for 6 months
  └─ Example: Java 20 (March 2023), Java 22 (March 2024)

LTS releases: every 2 years (every 4 feature releases)
  └─ Long-term support: Oracle/vendors support for 8+ years
  └─ Example: Java 11 (2018), Java 17 (2021), Java 21 (2023), Java 25 (2025)

Current LTS versions (as of 2024):
  Java 11 — Extended support until 2026 (Oracle), 2027+ (Azul, Amazon Corretto)
  Java 17 — Extended support until 2029 (Oracle)
  Java 21 — Extended support until 2031 (Oracle)
  Java 25 — LTS, expected September 2025
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Upgrade strategy for production systems:

Phase 1 — Preparation (3–4 weeks before target LTS)
  ├─ Audit dependencies: identify libraries that do not yet support target version
  ├─ Run jdeprscan: identify use of deprecated APIs removed in target version
  ├─ Run migration tool (e.g., OpenRewrite): automate safe mechanical changes
  └─ Update build tooling: Maven/Gradle, plugins, Docker base image

Phase 2 — Development (feature branch, CI on target version)
  ├─ Enable preview features in build if evaluating upcoming LTS features
  ├─ Fix compiler warnings: unchecked casts, deprecated API usage
  ├─ Run full test suite against new JVM
  └─ Profile startup and heap behavior: new GC defaults may need tuning

Phase 3 — Staging validation (2 weeks)
  ├─ Run staging load tests: new JIT and GC may change performance profile
  ├─ Validate observability: JVM metrics, GC logs, flight recorder
  └─ Confirm no serialization compatibility issues across rolling deploy

Phase 4 — Canary deployment
  ├─ Deploy to 5% of pods; monitor GC pause times, error rates, latency p99
  ├─ Gradually increase percentage over 48–72 hours
  └─ Keep rollback plan ready: keep old image tagged, not deleted

Key features by LTS version — what you gain:

Java 11 (LTS — baseline for most teams)
  ├─ var for local type inference
  ├─ HttpClient (java.net.http) — replaces HttpURLConnection
  ├─ String methods: isBlank(), strip(), lines(), repeat()
  └─ Running single-file Java programs: java HelloWorld.java

Java 17 (LTS — current recommended minimum)
  ├─ Sealed classes and interfaces (Pattern Matching preparation)
  ├─ Records (immutable value objects)
  ├─ Text blocks (multiline strings)
  ├─ Pattern matching for instanceof
  └─ Strong encapsulation of JDK internals (--add-opens no longer default)

Java 21 (LTS — current latest LTS)
  ├─ Virtual threads (Project Loom) — one per task at near-zero cost
  ├─ Structured concurrency (preview → standard in 21)
  ├─ Sequenced Collections — SequencedList, SequencedMap, SequencedSet
  ├─ Pattern matching for switch (standard in 21)
  └─ Record patterns in switch expressions

Summary Table

Phase 7 Completion: Advanced Java (Lessons 71–80)

Phase 7 brings together the capabilities that define a Java professional from a Java developer. The ten lessons in this phase cover the complete lifecycle of production Java: how data crosses service boundaries, how the operating system exposes file and network resources, how security is layered from the JVM through the application, how performance is understood and tuned, and how a professional codebase is maintained over time.

Lesson Topic Core Capability Gained
71 Serialization Java native serialization, Externalizable, JSON/Protobuf/Avro formats, deserialization security filters
72 Networking TCP/UDP sockets, HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 with java.net.http.HttpClient, SSL/TLS configuration, connection pooling
73 NIO Non-blocking I/O with Selector, Channels, Buffers; NIO.2 path API; AsynchronousFileChannel
74 Files API java.nio.file: Path, Files, WatchService; file locking; memory-mapped files
75 Security Authentication vs authorization, Spring Security, SQL injection prevention, OWASP Top 10, JCA/JCE
76 Cryptography Basics MessageDigest, HMAC, symmetric encryption (AES-GCM), asymmetric (RSA), key management
77 Reactive Programming Project Reactor: Mono/Flux, backpressure, WebFlux, reactive database access with R2DBC
78 Microservices Patterns Service discovery, API gateway, circuit breaker, saga pattern, event sourcing, CQRS
79 Cloud-Native Java Containers, Kubernetes health probes, GraalVM native image, Spring Cloud, Micrometer tracing
80 Java Best Practices Naming, immutability, null safety, exceptions, logging, testing pyramid, SOLID, governance, LTS strategy

Phase 7 Architectural Takeaway: Advanced Java is not about knowing more API surface area — it is about understanding the production lifecycle of a distributed system and applying principled design to each layer. A developer who has mastered Phase 7 can architect a greenfield service, reason about its failure modes, tune its JVM configuration, secure its attack surface, and plan its evolution over multiple LTS versions.

Full Handbook Completion: All 80 Lessons Across 7 Phases

This handbook was designed around a single thesis: the path from Java syntax to production-grade system design is continuous, not a series of disconnected topics. Each phase builds on the previous; each lesson extends the mental model developed in the lessons before it.

Phase Lessons Theme Capability Milestone
Phase 1: Java Fundamentals 1–10 Syntax, OOP, types Write correct, compiling Java in any IDE
Phase 2: Core Java Concepts 11–20 Access, enums, generics, reflection, modules Understand the type system and platform model
Phase 3: Collections & Functional 21–38 Collections, streams, lambdas, Optional, Date/Time Write idiomatic modern Java (Java 8–17 style)
Phase 4: Exception Handling 39–42 Exception hierarchy, checked/unchecked, custom exceptions Design robust error contracts in any API
Phase 5: Concurrency 43–55 Threads, locks, atomics, CompletableFuture, virtual threads Write correct, scalable concurrent programs
Phase 6: JVM Internals 56–70 Class loading, bytecode, JIT, GC algorithms, G1/ZGC/Shenandoah, tuning, profiling Diagnose and tune any JVM application
Phase 7: Advanced Java 71–80 Serialization, networking, NIO, security, cryptography, reactive, microservices, cloud, best practices Architect, secure, and operate production-grade distributed systems

The 80-lesson arc in one paragraph:

You began with a Java file that printed "Hello, World" and ended with the skills to design a microservice that serializes domain events to Avro, communicates over mTLS-secured HTTP/2 with virtual threads, stores data in PostgreSQL with Flyway-managed schema migrations, exposes Prometheus metrics, deploys as a GraalVM native image on Kubernetes, and passes a security audit. The JVM is not a runtime detail — it is the foundation that makes all of this reliable, observable, and tunable. The practices in this lesson are the thread that connects all 79 lessons into a coherent professional discipline.

Solution Architect Readiness Checklist

A Solution Architect is responsible for technical decisions that affect teams, systems, and business outcomes over multi-year timescales. The following checklist maps the handbook's 80 lessons to the competencies required at the architect level.

System Design and Architecture

- [ ] Can choose the right data store for each access pattern: OLTP, read-heavy, event streams, caches (Lesson 78)

JVM and Runtime

Concurrency and Scalability

Security

Team and Process
