Recommended Next Steps for the Learner

Completing this handbook establishes the foundation. Production mastery is built on top of it through deliberate practice, system exposure, and contribution. The following roadmap is sequenced from most immediately actionable to most transformative.

Immediate (Next 30 days)
- Build a complete end-to-end project applying all Phase 7 patterns: Spring Boot 3 + virtual threads + Testcontainers + Flyway + Micrometer + Resilience4j + Docker Compose. Commit it to a public repository as a portfolio artifact.
- Set up a local JVM profiling workflow: run JFR on a Spring Boot application under load (k6 or Gatling), analyze in JDK Mission Control, tune GC settings and measure the delta.
- Take the Oracle Java SE 21 Developer Professional exam if certification is a career goal. The handbook covers every objective.

Short-term (Next 90 days)
- Read Effective Java (3rd Edition, Joshua Bloch). The handbook teaches the Java platform; Bloch teaches you how to think about Java API design. Items 17 (minimize mutability), 18 (favor composition), and 78–84 (concurrency) reinforce and deepen what you have learned here.
- Contribute to an open-source Java project on GitHub. Reading production code at the quality level of Spring Framework, Netty, or Guava exposes patterns and idioms that no tutorial covers. A merged pull request teaches you the review culture of senior engineers.
- Study the Spring Framework source code for one component you use daily (e.g., DispatcherServlet, TransactionInterceptor, or AbstractBeanFactory). Understanding the internals of your primary framework eliminates an entire category of debugging ambiguity.

Medium-term (Next 6–12 months)
- Pursue cloud architect certification: AWS Solutions Architect Professional or Google Cloud Professional Architect. These exams force you to reason about distributed systems at the infrastructure level — complementing the JVM-level depth this handbook provides.
- Adopt a production incident as a learning opportunity: participate in an on-call rotation, write a post-mortem for a real failure, and instrument a monitoring gap you discover. Nothing builds observability discipline faster than being paged at 3 AM.
- Study Designing Data-Intensive Applications (Martin Kleppmann). It covers consistency, replication, and distributed transactions with rigor that the microservices patterns lesson introduced but did not fully explore.

Long-term (12+ months)
- Architect a non-trivial greenfield system from requirements to production: own the ADRs, the CI/CD pipeline, the observability stack, and the first on-call rotation. This is the inflection point where knowledge becomes judgment.
- Explore adjacent JVM languages: Kotlin for Spring Boot services (superior null safety and DSL capability), Scala for stream processing (Apache Spark, Akka), or Clojure for functional-first system design. Knowing multiple JVM languages deepens your understanding of the platform's constraints and capabilities.
- Consider contributing to the Java ecosystem: a JEP discussion, a JDK bug report, or a library contribution. The JDK is open source; engaging with its development process connects you to the engineers who shape the platform you build on.

The Handbook in One Sentence

Java mastery is the disciplined application of platform knowledge, design principles, and operational experience — and this handbook is where that journey begins.

Practice — Lesson 80

Problem 1 — Immutable Value Object

Design a fully immutable Price record that wraps an int amount in cents and a String currency code. Requirements:
- Validate that amount is ≥ 0 and currencyCode is exactly 3 uppercase letters
- Provide add(Price other), multiply(int factor), and toDisplay() (e.g., "$19.99" for 1999 USD)
- Ensure equals() and hashCode() work correctly for use as a Map key

public record Price(int amountInCents, String currencyCode) {

    private static final Pattern CURRENCY_CODE = Pattern.compile("[A-Z]{3}");

    public Price {
        if (amountInCents < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount must be non-negative");
        Objects.requireNonNull(currencyCode, "currencyCode must not be null");
        if (!CURRENCY_CODE.matcher(currencyCode).matches())
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("currencyCode must be 3 uppercase letters, got: " + currencyCode);
    }

    public Price add(Price other) {
        if (!this.currencyCode.equals(other.currencyCode))
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Cannot add " + currencyCode + " and " + other.currencyCode);
        return new Price(this.amountInCents + other.amountInCents, this.currencyCode);
    }

    public Price multiply(int factor) {
        if (factor < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("factor must be non-negative");
        return new Price(this.amountInCents * factor, this.currencyCode);
    }

    public String toDisplay() {
        BigDecimal value = BigDecimal.valueOf(amountInCents, 2);
        String symbol = switch (currencyCode) {
            case "USD" -> "$";
            case "EUR" -> "€";
            case "GBP" -> "£";
            default -> currencyCode + " ";
        };
        return symbol + value.toPlainString();
    }
}

Problem 2 — Exception Hierarchy

Build a domain exception hierarchy for a lending service with:
- LendingException (base, unchecked)
- LoanNotFoundException(Long loanId) — extends LendingException
- LoanLimitExceededException(int limit, int requested) — extends LendingException
- RepaymentScheduleException(Long loanId, String reason) — extends LendingException

Add a Spring @RestControllerAdvice that maps each to the correct HTTP status (404, 422, 409) with a structured ErrorResponse body.

public class LendingException extends RuntimeException {
    public LendingException(String message) { super(message); }
    public LendingException(String message, Throwable cause) { super(message, cause); }
}

public class LoanNotFoundException extends LendingException {
    private final Long loanId;
    public LoanNotFoundException(Long loanId) {
        super("Loan not found: " + loanId);
        this.loanId = loanId;
    }
    public Long getLoanId() { return loanId; }
}

public class LoanLimitExceededException extends LendingException {
    private final int limit;
    private final int requested;
    public LoanLimitExceededException(int limit, int requested) {
        super("Loan limit " + limit + " exceeded by request for " + requested);
        this.limit = limit;
        this.requested = requested;
    }
    public int getLimit() { return limit; }
    public int getRequested() { return requested; }
}

public class RepaymentScheduleException extends LendingException {
    private final Long loanId;
    public RepaymentScheduleException(Long loanId, String reason) {
        super("Repayment schedule conflict for loan " + loanId + ": " + reason);
        this.loanId = loanId;
    }
    public Long getLoanId() { return loanId; }
}

@RestControllerAdvice
public class LendingExceptionHandler {

    @ExceptionHandler(LoanNotFoundException.class)
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND)
    public ErrorResponse handleNotFound(LoanNotFoundException ex) {
        return new ErrorResponse("LOAN_NOT_FOUND", ex.getMessage());
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(LoanLimitExceededException.class)
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY)
    public ErrorResponse handleLimitExceeded(LoanLimitExceededException ex) {
        return new ErrorResponse("LOAN_LIMIT_EXCEEDED",
            "Requested " + ex.getRequested() + " exceeds limit of " + ex.getLimit());
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(RepaymentScheduleException.class)
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.CONFLICT)
    public ErrorResponse handleSchedule(RepaymentScheduleException ex) {
        return new ErrorResponse("REPAYMENT_SCHEDULE_CONFLICT", ex.getMessage());
    }
}

Problem 3 — Code Review Simulation

Review the following UserService class and identify all violations of the best practices covered in this lesson. Provide a corrected version.

// Original — has multiple issues
public class UserService {

    UserRepository repo = new UserRepository();

    public User getUser(Long id) {
        try {
            return repo.findById(id);
        } catch (Exception e) {
            System.out.println("Error: " + e);
            return null;
        }
    }

    public boolean login(String email, String password) {
        User u = repo.findByEmail(email);
        if (u != null) {
            if (u.getPassword().equals(password)) {
                System.out.println("User " + email + " logged in with password " + password);
                return true;
            }
        }
        return false;
    }
}

// Corrected
@Service
public class UserService {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(UserService.class);

    private final UserRepository userRepository;

    public UserService(UserRepository userRepository) {
        this.userRepository = Objects.requireNonNull(userRepository);
    }

    public Optional<User> findById(Long id) {
        return userRepository.findById(id);    // returns Optional — absence is explicit
    }

    public boolean login(String email, String rawPassword) {
        Objects.requireNonNull(email, "email must not be null");
        Objects.requireNonNull(rawPassword, "password must not be null");

        Optional<User> user = userRepository.findByEmail(email);
        if (user.isEmpty()) {
            log.warn("Login attempt for unknown email: {}", email);   // no PII leakage beyond email
            return false;
        }

        boolean authenticated = passwordEncoder.matches(rawPassword, user.get().getPasswordHash());
        if (authenticated) {
            log.info("User authenticated successfully: userId={}", user.get().getId());
        } else {
            log.warn("Failed authentication attempt for userId={}", user.get().getId());
        }
        return authenticated;
        // Changes made:
        // 1. Field injection → constructor injection (testable, explicit)
        // 2. Broad Exception catch → removed; let repository exceptions propagate (or handle specifically)
        // 3. Returning null → returning Optional (caller handles absence explicitly)
        // 4. System.out.println → SLF4J logger
        // 5. Plain-text password comparison → BCrypt hash comparison
        // 6. Logging plaintext password → logging only userId (no sensitive data in logs)
    }
}

Advanced Exercises

Exercise 4 — ArchUnit Enforcement

Write three ArchUnit rules for a hexagonal architecture Spring Boot project:
1. No class in the domain package may import from infrastructure or web
2. All @Service classes must be in the application or service package
3. No class may use System.out.println or System.err.println

@AnalyzeClasses(packages = "com.company.app")
public class HexagonalArchitectureTest {

    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule domainIsolation =
        noClasses()
            .that().resideInAPackage("..domain..")
            .should().dependOnClassesThat()
            .resideInAnyPackage("..infrastructure..", "..web..", "..controller..");

    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule servicesInCorrectPackage =
        classes()
            .that().areAnnotatedWith(Service.class)
            .should().resideInAnyPackage("..application..", "..service..");

    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule noSysout =
        noClasses()
            .should().callMethod(System.class, "println", Object.class)
            .orShould().callMethod(PrintStream.class, "println", Object.class)
            .because("Use SLF4J logger instead of System.out");
}

Exercise 5 — Testing Pyramid Implementation

Implement the full testing pyramid for an AccountService.transfer(from, to, amount) method:

  1. Unit test: mock the repository, verify transfer logic, assert InsufficientFundsException on low balance
  2. Integration test: use Testcontainers PostgreSQL, verify the database state after a successful transfer
  3. API test: use @SpringBootTest + MockMvc, POST to /api/v1/transfers, verify HTTP 200 and response body

Production Scenarios

Scenario 1 — Technical Debt Remediation Plan

Your team has inherited a 5-year-old Spring Boot 2 / Java 11 monolith. Initial assessment reveals:
- Field injection throughout (@Autowired on fields, not constructors)
- null returns instead of Optional in service methods
- catch (Exception e) with empty bodies in 23 places
- No structured logging — System.out.println in 47 classes
- Zero test coverage on 40% of the service layer
- Java 11 — two LTS versions behind (Java 17, 21 available)

Remediation strategy:

Priority 1 — Safety (Sprint 1–2, blocks production incidents)
  ├─ Replace all empty catch blocks: add logging at minimum
  ├─ Replace System.out.println with SLF4J — automated by OpenRewrite recipe
  └─ Add MDC correlation filter — instant observability improvement

Priority 2 — Reliability (Sprint 3–4, reduces bug rate)
  ├─ Add unit tests for all service methods that touch money or authorization
  ├─ Replace null returns with Optional in the most-called service methods
  └─ Add @Validated + @NotNull to all HTTP request DTOs

Priority 3 — Maintainability (Sprint 5–8, enables future development)
  ├─ Migrate field injection to constructor injection class by class
  ├─ Upgrade to Java 17 (LTS) — run on both 11 and 17 in CI first
  └─ Add ArchUnit tests to prevent regression

Priority 4 — Modernization (Quarter 2, strategic)
  ├─ Extract top 3 most-changed service boundaries into separate services
  ├─ Upgrade to Spring Boot 3 / Java 21 — virtual threads, records, sealed classes
  └─ Implement Micrometer metrics and Grafana dashboard for the core flows

Scenario 2 — Code Review Gate Failure

A PR introducing a new PaymentProcessor is blocked by your CI quality gate. The gate reports:

[CHECKSTYLE] PaymentProcessor.java:47: Method 'processRefund' has 6 parameters (max 4)
[CHECKSTYLE] PaymentProcessor.java:89: Method length is 34 lines (max 20)
[SPOTBUGS] PaymentProcessor.java:112: NP_NULL_ON_SOME_PATH — potential null dereference
[OWASP-DC] spring-security-oauth2-autoconfigure:2.2.5 has CVE-2023-XXXXX (HIGH)

Resolution checklist:

  1. Replace the 6-parameter processRefund method with a RefundCommand record — eliminates the parameter count violation and improves readability
  2. Extract the 34-line method into 3 private methods each under 15 lines following single-level-of-abstraction
  3. Change the null dereference path to use Optional — compiler now forces the null case to be handled
  4. Update spring-security-oauth2-autoconfigure to the patched version — block the PR until the dependency is clean; security CVEs are never merged

Debugging Exercises

Debug 1 — Thread Safety Violation

The following singleton service is used in a multi-threaded Spring Boot application and occasionally returns incorrect pricing:

@Service
public class PricingService {
    private BigDecimal lastCalculatedPrice;   // shared mutable field — race condition

    public BigDecimal getPrice(ProductId productId) {
        BigDecimal basePrice = pricingRepository.getBasePrice(productId);
        lastCalculatedPrice = basePrice.multiply(taxRate);  // non-atomic write + read
        applyDiscount();
        return lastCalculatedPrice;   // may return another thread's result
    }

    private void applyDiscount() {
        if (lastCalculatedPrice.compareTo(THRESHOLD) > 0) {
            lastCalculatedPrice = lastCalculatedPrice.multiply(DISCOUNT_RATE);
        }
    }
}

Diagnosis: lastCalculatedPrice is shared mutable state modified by every concurrent request. Thread A writes the price, Thread B overwrites it before Thread A reads it back from applyDiscount().

Fix: eliminate the shared mutable field — pass price as a local variable parameter:

@Service
public class PricingService {

    public BigDecimal getPrice(ProductId productId) {
        BigDecimal basePrice = pricingRepository.getBasePrice(productId);
        BigDecimal taxedPrice = basePrice.multiply(taxRate);
        return applyDiscount(taxedPrice);   // no shared state — thread-safe by design
    }

    private BigDecimal applyDiscount(BigDecimal price) {
        return price.compareTo(THRESHOLD) > 0
            ? price.multiply(DISCOUNT_RATE)
            : price;
    }
}

Debug 2 — Resource Leak Under Load

The application works correctly for low traffic but begins throwing Too many open files OS errors after 10 minutes of production load:

public String readConfig(String path) throws IOException {
    BufferedReader reader = new BufferedReader(new FileReader(path));
    StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
    String line;
    while ((line = reader.readLine()) != null) {
        sb.append(line).append("\n");
    }
    // reader.close() never called if an exception occurs mid-read
    reader.close();
    return sb.toString();
}

Diagnosis: If readLine() throws an IOException, reader.close() is skipped. Each leaked FileReader holds an OS file descriptor. Under sustained load, the OS limit is reached.

Fix: use try-with-resources — close() is guaranteed even on exception:

public String readConfig(String path) throws IOException {
    try (BufferedReader reader = new BufferedReader(new FileReader(path))) {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        String line;
        while ((line = reader.readLine()) != null) {
            sb.append(line).append("\n");
        }
        return sb.toString();
    }   // reader.close() called automatically here — no leak possible
    // Modern alternative: Files.readString(Path.of(path)) for whole-file reads
}

Interview Challenges

Challenge 1

"A junior developer on your team says: 'I avoid using Optional because it just adds boilerplate — I can just check for null.' How do you respond?"

Answer framework: Acknowledge the concern — Optional does add method calls. But the key point is not convenience; it is contractual clarity. When a method returns Optional<User>, the signature explicitly communicates that the caller MUST handle the absent case. A @Nullable User annotation communicates the same intent but relies on the caller reading the annotation and acting on it — there is no compiler enforcement. With Optional, if you call .map(), .orElse(), or .orElseThrow(), you have handled the absent case structurally. You cannot accidentally call methods on a missing value. The billion-dollar mistake (Tony Hoare's term) was not null itself — it was creating a type system that cannot distinguish between "always has a value" and "may not have a value." Optional restores that distinction in return type signatures.

Challenge 2

"Walk me through how you would onboard a new engineer onto a complex Java microservices codebase. What are the first five things you make sure they understand?"

Answer:
1. The domain model — not the code, the business domain. Every naming decision, every exception, every service boundary makes sense only if you understand what an Order, a Customer, a Payment, and a Shipment mean to the business. Start with the domain glossary, not the code.
2. The architecture decision record (ADR) index — why the team chose Kafka over RabbitMQ, why PostgreSQL over MongoDB, why JWT over session cookies. The ADRs contain the reasoning that the code cannot.
3. The CI/CD pipeline — how a change moves from PR to production. What the quality gates are. What the deployment unit is. How to roll back. An engineer who cannot ship safely is not yet autonomous.
4. The observability stack — how to read a Grafana dashboard, how to trace a request in Jaeger, how to query Loki for logs. An engineer who cannot observe production cannot debug production.
5. The on-call runbook for one service they own — what the common alerts mean, what the remediation steps are, where the runbook lives. Owning one service end-to-end — from code to incident response — builds more understanding in one month than reading documentation for six months.

Key Takeaways

  • Naming is the first API — a well-named method, class, or variable eliminates the need for a comment; invest in naming at the time of writing, not as a refactoring task
  • Immutability eliminates concurrency bugs by design — prefer final fields, immutable collections (List.of()), and records for value objects; accept mutability only where entity lifecycle requires it
  • Optional is a return type contract, not a null wrapper — use it to communicate that absence is a valid, expected outcome; use .orElseGet(), .map(), and .orElseThrow() — never .get() after .isPresent()
  • Exception specificity is observability — catch the most specific exception you can handle; always wrap with cause when rethrowing; never swallow exceptions silently
  • Logs are your production debugger — use SLF4J with MDC correlation; log at the right level; never log passwords, tokens, or PII; test your log output as part of code review
  • The testing pyramid is a cost-quality trade-off — 60–70% fast unit tests, 20–30% integration tests, 5–10% E2E; a test that takes 200ms is 200x more expensive to run than one that takes 1ms
  • SOLID principles reduce change cost — SRP reduces surprise; OCP reduces risk; LSP prevents contract violations; ISP reduces coupling; DIP enables testability
  • Code review checklist = quality floor — checklists make quality decisions consistent and reviewable; what is not in the checklist is optional, what is in it is not
  • ADRs are organizational memory — the decision is easy to find in the code; the reason for the decision is lost without an ADR; write ADRs for any choice that would cause pain if reversed
  • LTS strategy is a business decision — running Java 11 in 2025 carries security risk, misses virtual threads, and limits your library choices; plan LTS upgrades as engineering investments, not interruptions
